Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammāsambuddhassa

Homage to the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.

Khuddakanikāye

Khuddaka Nikāya

Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā

Jātaka Commentary

(Paṭhamo bhāgo)

(First Part)

Ganthārambhakathā

Introduction to the Text

Jātikoṭisahassehi[P 1.0001][M 1.0001][V 1.0001], pamāṇarahitaṃ hitaṃ;

Lokassa lokanāthena, kataṃ yena mahesinā.

By that Great Sage, the Lord of the World, immeasurable benefit for the world was accomplished throughout thousands of crores of births.

Tassa pāde namassitvā, katvā dhammassa cañjaliṃ;

Saṅghañca patimānetvā, sabbasammānabhājanaṃ.

Having paid homage to his feet, having made a reverential salutation to the Dhamma, and having honored the Saṅgha, the recipient of all honor;

Namassanādino [V 1.0002] assa, puññassa ratanattaye;

Pavattassānubhāvena, chetvā sabbe upaddave.

Through the power of this merit arisen from paying homage and so forth to the Triple Gem, having cut off all misfortunes;

Taṃ taṃ kāraṇamāgamma, desitāni jutīmatā;

Apaṇṇakādīni purā, jātakāni mahesinā.

The Jātakas, beginning with the Apaṇṇaka, were taught of old by the radiant Great Sage for various reasons;

Yāni yesu ciraṃ satthā, lokanittharaṇatthiko;

Anante bodhisambhāre, paripācesi nāyako.

In which the Teacher, the Leader, intent on liberating the world, for a long time ripened the immeasurable requisites of enlightenment;

Tāni sabbāni ekajjhaṃ, āropentehi saṅgahaṃ;

Jātakaṃ nāma saṅgītaṃ, dhammasaṅgāhakehi yaṃ.

That which was chanted as the Jātaka by the compilers of the Dhamma, who brought all those together into a single collection;

Buddhavaṃsassa etassa, icchantena ciraṭṭhitiṃ;

Yācito abhigantvāna, therena atthadassinā.

I was requested, having been approached by the elder who discerned the benefit, who desired the long persistence of this lineage of the Buddha;

Asaṃsaṭṭhavihāre[M 1.0002], sadā suddhavihārinā;

Tatheva buddhamittena, santacittena viññunā.

By him who, dwelling in seclusion, was ever pure in conduct; and likewise by Buddhamitta, serene of mind and discerning;

Mahiṃsāsakavaṃsamhi, sambhūtena nayaññunā;

Buddhadevena ca tathā, bhikkhunā suddhabuddhinā.

By him born in the Mahiṃsāsaka lineage, who knew the right method; and likewise by Buddhadeva, a bhikkhu of pure intellect.

Mahāpurisacariyānaṃ, ānubhāvaṃ acintiyaṃ;

Tassa vijjotayantassa, jātakassatthavaṇṇanaṃ.

An exposition of the meaning of that Jātaka, which illuminates the inconceivable power of the conduct of the Great Beings.

Mahāvihāravāsīnaṃ, vācanāmagganissitaṃ;

Bhāsissaṃ bhāsato taṃ me, sādhu gaṇhantu sādhavoti.

Relying on the path of recitation of the residents of the Mahāvihāra, I will speak. As I speak, may the virtuous accept my speech well.

Nidānakathā

The Story of the Origins

Sā [V 1.0003][P 1.0002] panāyaṃ jātakassa atthavaṇṇanā dūrenidānaṃ, avidūrenidānaṃ, santikenidānanti imāni tīṇi nidānāni dassetvā vaṇṇiyamānā ye naṃ suṇanti, tehi samudāgamato paṭṭhāya viññātattā yasmā suṭṭhu viññātā nāma hoti, tasmā taṃ tāni nidānāni dassetvā vaṇṇayissāma.

Now this exposition of the meaning of the Jātaka, being expounded after showing these three origins—the Distant Origin, the Intermediate Origin, and the Proximate Origin—is indeed thoroughly understood, because it has been apprehended by those who listen to it from its very inception onwards. Therefore, we shall expound it after showing those origins.

Tattha ādito tāva tesaṃ nidānānaṃ paricchedo veditabbo. Dīpaṅkarapādamūlasmiñhi katābhinīhārassa mahāsattassa yāva vessantarattabhāvā cavitvā tusitapure nibbatti, tāva pavatto kathāmaggo dūrenidānaṃ nāma. Tusitabhavanato pana cavitvā yāva bodhimaṇḍe sabbaññutappatti, tāva pavatto kathāmaggo avidūrenidānaṃ nāma. Santikenidānaṃ pana tesu tesu ṭhānesu viharato tasmiṃ tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne labbhatīti.

Herein, first of all, the distinction of those origins should be understood. From the time the Great Being made his resolution at the feet of Dīpaṅkara until his passing away from the existence as Vessantara and rebirth in the Tusita realm, the course of the narrative is called the Distant Origin. Then, from his passing away from the Tusita abode until his attainment of omniscience at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, the course of the narrative is called the Intermediate Origin. As for the Proximate Origin, it is obtained in each of those very places where he dwelt.

1. Dūrenidānakathā

1. The Story of the Distant Origin

Tatridaṃ dūrenidānaṃ nāma – ito kira kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake amaravatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi. Tattha sumedho nāma brāhmaṇo paṭivasati ubhato sujāto mātito [M 1.0003] ca pitito ca saṃsuddhagahaṇiko yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā akkhitto anupakuṭṭho jātivādena abhirūpo dassanīyo pāsādiko paramāya vaṇṇapokkharatāya samannāgato. So aññaṃ kammaṃ akatvā brāhmaṇasippameva uggaṇhi. Tassa daharakāleyeva mātāpitaro kālamakaṃsu. Athassa rāsivaḍḍhako amacco āyapotthakaṃ āharitvā suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādibharite gabbhe vivaritvā “ettakaṃ te, kumāra, mātu santakaṃ, ettakaṃ pitu santakaṃ, ettakaṃ ayyakapayyakāna”nti yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā dhanaṃ ācikkhitvā “etaṃ paṭipajjāhī”ti āha. Sumedhapaṇḍito cintesi – “imaṃ dhanaṃ saṃharitvā mayhaṃ pitupitāmahādayo paralokaṃ gacchantā ekaṃ kahāpaṇampi gahetvā na gatā, mayā pana gahetvā gamanakāraṇaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So rañño ārocetvā nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā mahājanassa dānaṃ datvā tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Imassa panatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne sumedhakathā kathetabbā[V 1.0004]. Sā panesā kiñcāpi buddhavaṃse nirantaraṃ āgatāyeva, gāthāsambandhena pana āgatattā na suṭṭhu pākaṭā. Tasmā taṃ antarantarā gāthāya sambandhadīpakehi vacanehi saddhiṃ kathessāma.

This is what is called the Distant Origin. It is said that, more than four incalculable periods and one hundred thousand aeons ago, there was a city named Amaravatī. There lived a brahmin named Sumedha, well-born on both his mother’s and father’s side, of pure lineage up to the seventh generation, unblemished and unreproached by reason of birth, handsome, comely, and pleasing to behold, endowed with the highest beauty of complexion. Without engaging in any other work, he mastered only the brahminical arts. While he was still young, his parents passed away. Then his treasurer brought the account books and, opening the treasure chambers filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and other valuables, declared: “Young master, this much is your mother’s property, this much your father’s, and this much belongs to your ancestors up to the seventh generation.” He then instructed, “Take charge of this.” The wise Sumedha reflected: “Having accumulated this wealth, my father, grandfather, and other ancestors departed for the next world without taking even a single coin with them. I, however, must find a way to take it with me when I go.” So, having informed the king, he had a drum beaten throughout the city, gave his great wealth in alms to the populace, and went forth into the life of an ascetic. To clarify this matter, the story of Sumedha should be told here. Although this account is indeed found continuously in the Buddhavaṃsa, because it is presented in verse, it is not entirely clear. Therefore, we will narrate it, interspersing it with prose that illuminates the connection between the verses.

Sumedhakathā

The Story of Sumedha

Kappasatasahassādhikānañhi catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake dasahi saddehi avivittaṃ “amaravatī”ti ca “amara”nti ca laddhanāmaṃ nagaraṃ ahosi, yaṃ sandhāya buddhavaṃse vuttaṃ –

Indeed, more than four incalculable and one hundred thousand aeons ago, there was a city named 'Amaravatī' and also 'Amarā,' which was ever-resounding with ten sounds, concerning which it is stated in the Buddhavaṃsa:

“Kappe [P 1.0003] ca satasahasse, caturo ca asaṅkhiye;

Amaraṃ nāma nagaraṃ, dassaneyyaṃ manoramaṃ;

Dasahi saddehi avivittaṃ, annapānasamāyuta”nti.

After one hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable aeons, there was a city named Amara, lovely to behold and delightful, ever-resounding with ten sounds, and endowed with food and drink.

Tattha dasahi saddehi avivittanti hatthisaddena, assasaddena, rathasaddena, bherisaddena, mudiṅgasaddena, vīṇāsaddena, sammasaddena, tāḷasaddena, saṅkhasaddena “asnātha, pivatha, khādathā”ti dasamena saddenāti imehi dasahi saddehi avivittaṃ ahosi. Tesaṃ pana saddānaṃ ekadesameva gahetvā –

Herein, 'ever-resounding with ten sounds' means it was uninterrupted by the sound of elephants, the sound of horses, the sound of chariots, the sound of kettle drums, the sound of long drums, the sound of lutes, the sound of cymbals, the sound of clapping, the sound of conch shells, and the tenth sound, “Eat! Drink! Chew!” Thus, it was ever-resounding with these ten sounds. But taking only a part of those sounds—

“Hatthisaddaṃ [M 1.0004] assasaddaṃ, bherisaṅkharathāni ca;

Khādatha pivatha ceva, annapānena ghosita”nti. –

The sound of elephants, the sound of horses, drums, conch shells, and chariots; “Eat!” and “Drink!”, and resounding with food and drink.

Buddhavaṃse imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā –

Having spoken this verse in the Buddhavaṃsa—

“Nagaraṃ sabbaṅgasampannaṃ, sabbakammamupāgataṃ;

Sattaratanasampannaṃ, nānājanasamākulaṃ;

Samiddhaṃ devanagaraṃva, āvāsaṃ puññakamminaṃ.

A city complete in all its parts, a center of all kinds of crafts, endowed with the seven treasures, and crowded with various people; prosperous like a city of the gods, a dwelling place for those of meritorious deeds.

“Nagare amaravatiyā, sumedho nāma brāhmaṇo;

Anekakoṭisannicayo, pahūtadhanadhaññavā.

In the city of Amarāvatī, there was a brahmin named Sumedha, who had an accumulation of many crores of wealth and possessed abundant riches and grain.

“Ajjhāyako [V 1.0005] mantadharo, tiṇṇaṃ vedāna pāragū;

Lakkhaṇe itihāse ca, sadhamme pāramiṃ gato”ti. – vuttaṃ;

A reciter and bearer of mantras, a master of the three Vedas; he had attained perfection in the science of signs and in legends, and in his own doctrine.” – so it was said.

Athekadivasaṃ so sumedhapaṇḍito uparipāsādavaratale rahogato hutvā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisinno cintesi – “punabbhave, paṇḍita, paṭisandhiggahaṇaṃ nāma dukkhaṃ, tathā nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne sarīrabhedanaṃ, ahañca jātidhammo jarādhammo byādhidhammo maraṇadhammo, evaṃbhūtena mayā ajātiṃ ajaraṃ abyādhiṃ adukkhaṃ sukhaṃ sītalaṃ amatamahānibbānaṃ pariyesituṃ vaṭṭati, avassaṃ bhavato muccitvā nibbānagāminā ekena maggena bhavitabba”nti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then one day, the wise Sumedha, secluded on the upper terrace of his excellent palace, sat cross-legged and reflected: “The taking of rebirth in a future existence is indeed suffering, as is the dissolution of the body in each and every place of rebirth. I am subject to birth, aging, sickness, and death. Being thus, it is fitting for me to seek the unborn, ageless, sickness-free, sorrowless, blissful, cool, deathless, great Nibbāna. Surely, having been liberated from existence, there must be one path leading to Nibbāna.” Thus it was said—

“Rahogato nisīditvā, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā;

Dukkho punabbhavo nāma, sarīrassa ca bhedanaṃ.

Secluded and sitting, thus I thought at that time: ‘Rebirth, indeed, is suffering, and the breaking up of the body.’

“Jātidhammo jarādhammo, byādhidhammo sahaṃ tadā;

Ajaraṃ amataṃ khemaṃ, pariyesissāmi nibbutiṃ.

Being then subject to birth, aging, and sickness, I will seek Nibbāna, the unaging, deathless, and secure state of peace.

“Yaṃnūnimaṃ pūtikāyaṃ, nānākuṇapapūritaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gaccheyyaṃ, anapekkho anatthiko.

What if I were to discard this foul body, filled with various corpses, and depart without longing or attachment?

“Atthi [P 1.0004] hehiti so maggo, na so sakkā na hetuye;

Pariyesissāmi taṃ maggaṃ, bhavato parimuttiyā”ti.

That path exists, it surely will be; it is not possible for it not to be. I will seek that path for the sake of complete liberation from becoming.

Tato [M 1.0005] uttaripi evaṃ cintesi – yathā hi loke dukkhassa paṭipakkhabhūtaṃ sukhaṃ nāma atthi, evaṃ bhave sati tappaṭipakkhena vibhavenāpi bhavitabbaṃ. Yathā ca uṇhe sati tassa vūpasamabhūtaṃ sītampi atthi, evaṃ rāgādīnaṃ aggīnaṃ vūpasamena nibbānenāpi bhavitabbaṃ. Yathā ca pāpassa lāmakassa dhammassa paṭipakkhabhūto kalyāṇo anavajjadhammopi atthiyeva, evameva pāpikāya jātiyā sati sabbajātikkhepanato ajātisaṅkhātena nibbānenāpi bhavitabbamevāti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then he further reflected thus: Just as in the world there exists happiness, the opposite of suffering, so too, when there is becoming, its opposite, non-becoming, must also exist. And just as when there is heat, there is also coolness, which is its appeasement, so too, with the appeasement of the fires of lust and so forth, Nibbāna must also exist. And just as there exists good and blameless Dhamma, the opposite of evil and base Dhamma, so too, when there is miserable birth, there must also exist, through the casting off of all births, Nibbāna, designated as the unborn. Thus it was said—

“Yathāpi [V 1.0006] dukkhe vijjante, sukhaṃ nāmapi vijjati;

Evaṃ bhave vijjamāne, vibhavopi icchitabbako.

Just as where suffering exists, happiness is also found; so too, where becoming exists, non-becoming is to be sought.

“Yathāpi uṇhe vijjante, aparaṃ vijjati sītalaṃ;

Evaṃ tividhaggi vijjante, nibbānaṃ icchitabbakaṃ.

Just as where heat exists, its opposite, coolness, is found; so too, where the triple fires exist, Nibbāna is to be desired.

“Yathāpi pāpe vijjante, kalyāṇamapi vijjati;

Evameva jāti vijjante, ajātipicchitabbaka”nti.

Just as where evil exists, the good is also found; just so, where birth exists, the unborn is to be sought.

Aparampi cintesi – yathā nāma gūtharāsimhi nimuggena purisena dūrato pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchannaṃ mahātaḷākaṃ disvā “katarena nu kho maggena ettha gantabba”nti taṃ taḷākaṃ gavesituṃ yuttaṃ. Yaṃ tassa agavesanaṃ, na so taḷākassa doso. Evameva kilesamaladhovane amatamahānibbānataḷāke vijjante tassa agavesanaṃ na amatanibbānamahātaḷākassa doso. Yathā ca corehi samparivārito puriso palāyanamagge vijjamānepi sace na palāyati, na so maggassa doso, purisasseva doso. Evameva kilesehi parivāretvā gahitassa purisassa vijjamāneyeva nibbānagāmimhi sive magge maggassa agavesanaṃ nāma na maggassa doso, puggalasseva doso. Yathā ca byādhipīḷito puriso vijjamāne byādhitikicchake vejje sace taṃ vejjaṃ gavesitvā byādhiṃ na tikicchāpeti, na so vejjassa doso, purisasseva doso. Evameva yo kilesabyādhipīḷito puriso kilesavūpasamamaggakovidaṃ vijjamānameva ācariyaṃ na gavesati, tasseva doso, na kilesavināsakassa ācariyassāti. Tena vuttaṃ –

He further reflected: Just as it is fitting for a man submerged in a heap of filth, seeing from afar a great lake covered with five-colored lotuses, to seek that lake, thinking, “By which path should one go to reach it?” If he does not seek it, that is not the fault of the lake. In the same way, when the great lake of deathless Nibbāna exists for washing away the stains of defilements, not seeking it is not the fault of the great lake of deathless Nibbāna. And just as when a man surrounded by thieves does not flee even though an escape route exists, that is not the fault of the path—it is the man’s own fault. Similarly, for a man seized and surrounded by defilements, when the peaceful path leading to Nibbāna exists, not seeking that path is not the fault of the path—it is the individual’s own fault. And just as when a man afflicted by illness does not seek out a doctor skilled in treating diseases, even though such a doctor exists, and thus fails to have his illness treated, that is not the doctor’s fault—it is the man’s own fault. In the same way, for a man tormented by the disease of defilements who does not seek out a teacher skilled in the path that pacifies defilements, even though such a teacher exists, the fault lies with him, not with the teacher who destroys defilements. Therefore, it is said—

“Yathā gūthagato puriso, taḷākaṃ disvāna pūritaṃ;

Na gavesati taṃ taḷākaṃ, na doso taḷākassa so.

Just as a man in filth, seeing a full lake, does not seek that lake, that is not the fault of the lake.

“Evaṃ [M 1.0006] kilesamaladhove, vijjante amatantaḷe;

Na gavesati taṃ taḷākaṃ, na doso amatantaḷe.

Similarly, when the deathless lake for washing away the stain of defilements exists, if one does not seek that lake, that is not the fault of the deathless lake.

“Yathā [P 1.0005] arīhi pariruddho, vijjante gamanampathe;

Na palāyati so puriso, na doso añjasassa so.

Just as a man surrounded by enemies, though a path of escape exists, does not flee, that is not the fault of the path.

“Evaṃ [V 1.0007] kilesapariruddho, vijjamāne sive pathe;

Na gavesati taṃ maggaṃ, na doso sivamañjase.

Similarly, surrounded by defilements, when the peaceful path exists, if one does not seek that path, that is not the fault of the peaceful path.

“Yathāpi byādhito puriso, vijjamāne tikicchake;

Na tikicchāpeti taṃ byādhiṃ, na doso so tikicchake.

Just as a man afflicted by illness, when a physician is available, does not have that illness treated, that is not the fault of the physician.

“Evaṃ kilesabyādhīhi, dukkhito paripīḷito;

Na gavesati taṃ ācariyaṃ, na doso so vināyake”ti.

Similarly, one who is suffering and tormented by the diseases of defilements, if he does not seek that teacher, that is not the fault of the guide.

Aparampi cintesi – yathā maṇḍanajātiko puriso kaṇṭhe āsattaṃ kuṇapaṃ chaḍḍetvā sukhī gacchati, evaṃ mayāpi imaṃ pūtikāyaṃ chaḍḍetvā anapekkhena nibbānanagaraṃ pavisitabbaṃ. Yathā ca naranāriyo ukkārabhūmiyaṃ uccārapassāvaṃ katvā na taṃ ucchaṅgena vā ādāya dasantena vā veṭhetvā gacchanti, jigucchamānā pana anapekkhāva chaḍḍetvā gacchanti, evaṃ mayāpi imaṃ pūtikāyaṃ anapekkhena chaḍḍetvā amataṃ nibbānanagaraṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭati. Yathā ca nāvikā nāma jajjaraṃ nāvaṃ anapekkhā chaḍḍetvā gacchanti, evaṃ ahampi imaṃ navahi vaṇamukhehi paggharantaṃ kāyaṃ chaḍḍetvā anapekkho nibbānapuraṃ pavisissāmi. Yathā ca puriso nānāratanāni ādāya corehi saddhiṃ maggaṃ gacchanto attano ratananāsabhayena te chaḍḍetvā khemaṃ maggaṃ gaṇhāti, evaṃ ayampi karajakāyo ratanavilopakacorasadiso. Sacāhaṃ ettha taṇhaṃ karissāmi, ariyamaggakusaladhammaratanaṃ me nassissati. Tasmā mayā imaṃ corasadisaṃ kāyaṃ chaḍḍetvā nibbānanagaraṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭatīti. Tena vuttaṃ –

He further reflected: Just as a man fond of ornaments, having removed a rotting corpse tied to his neck, goes away happy, so too should I, having discarded this foul body without attachment, enter the city of Nibbāna. And just as men and women, having relieved themselves on a refuse heap, do not carry it away in their lap or wrapped in the hem of their garment, but, disgusted, discard it without attachment and go away, so too is it fitting for me, having discarded this foul body without attachment, to enter the deathless city of Nibbāna. And just as sailors abandon a dilapidated boat without attachment and go away, so too shall I, having abandoned this body that oozes from nine wound-like openings, enter the city of Nibbāna without attachment. And just as a man carrying various jewels, traveling a road with thieves, abandons them out of fear for the loss of his jewels and takes a safe path, so too is this karma-born body like a thief that plunders jewels. If I generate craving for it, the jewel of the noble path and wholesome states will be lost to me. Therefore, it is fitting for me to discard this thief-like body and enter the city of Nibbāna. Thus it is said—

“Yathāpi kuṇapaṃ puriso, kaṇṭhe baddhaṃ jigucchiya;

Mocayitvāna gaccheyya, sukhī serī sayaṃvasī.

Just as a person, disgusted by a corpse tied to the neck, would cast it off and go, happy, free, and his own master.

“Tathevimaṃ [M 1.0007] pūtikāyaṃ, nānākuṇapasañcayaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gaccheyyaṃ, anapekkho anatthiko.

Just so, this foul body, a heap of various corpses, having cast it aside, I would depart, without longing, without need.

“Yathā uccāraṭṭhānamhi, karīsaṃ naranāriyo;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gacchanti, anapekkhā anatthikā.

Just as men and women at a place of excrement, having discarded feces, go away, unconcerned, without need.

“Evamevāhaṃ [V 1.0008] imaṃ kāyaṃ, nānākuṇapapūritaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gacchissaṃ, vaccaṃ katvā yathā kuṭiṃ.

Just so, this body, filled with various corpses, having cast it aside, I will go, as one leaves a privy after discharging excrement.

“Yathāpi jajjaraṃ nāvaṃ, paluggaṃ udagāhiniṃ;

Sāmī chaḍḍetvā gacchanti, anapekkhā anatthikā.

Just as a worn-out boat, dilapidated and taking on water, the owners abandon and go, unconcerned and without need.

“Evamevāhaṃ [P 1.0006] imaṃ kāyaṃ, navacchiddaṃ dhuvassavaṃ;

Chaḍḍayitvāna gacchissaṃ, jiṇṇanāvaṃva sāmikā.

Even so, having discarded this body with its nine openings, constantly oozing, I shall depart, as owners abandon an old boat.

“Yathāpi puriso corehi, gacchanto bhaṇḍamādiya;

Bhaṇḍacchedabhayaṃ disvā, chaḍḍayitvāna gacchati.

Just as a man, traveling with thieves while carrying goods, seeing the danger of losing his goods, abandons them and goes on.

“Evameva ayaṃ kāyo, mahācorasamo viya;

Pahāyimaṃ gamissāmi, kusalacchedanābhayā”ti.

Even so, this body is like a great robber. I shall abandon it and go, for fear of the destruction of wholesome qualities.

Evaṃ sumedhapaṇḍito nānāvidhāhi upamāhi imaṃ nekkhammūpasaṃhitaṃ atthaṃ cintetvā sakanivesane aparimitaṃ bhogakkhandhaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayena kapaṇaddhikādīnaṃ vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ datvā vatthukāme ca kilesakāme ca pahāya amaranagarato nikkhamitvā ekakova himavante dhammikaṃ nāma pabbataṃ nissāya assamaṃ katvā tattha paṇṇasālañca caṅkamañca māpetvā pañcahi nīvaraṇadosehi vivajjitaṃ “evaṃ samāhite citte”tiādinā nayena vuttehi aṭṭhahi kāraṇaguṇehi samupetaṃ abhiññāsaṅkhātaṃ balaṃ āharituṃ tasmiṃ assamapade navadosasamannāgataṃ sāṭakaṃ pajahitvā dvādasaguṇasamannāgataṃ vākacīraṃ nivāsetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbaji. Evaṃ pabbajito aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ taṃ paṇṇasālaṃ pahāya dasaguṇasamannāgataṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upagantvā sabbaṃ dhaññavikatiṃ pahāya pavattaphalabhojano hutvā nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkamanavaseneva padhānaṃ padahanto sattāhabbhantareyeva aṭṭhannaṃ samāpattīnaṃ pañcannañca abhiññānaṃ lābhī ahosi. Evaṃ taṃ yathāpatthitaṃ abhiññābalaṃ pāpuṇi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Thus, the wise Sumedha, having reflected on this meaning connected with renunciation through various similes, distributed the immeasurable mass of wealth in his own dwelling, as previously described, to the poor, travelers, and the like, and gave a great gift. Having abandoned both sensual objects and defiling desires, he departed from the city of Amaravatī. Alone, in the Himalayas, relying on a mountain named Dhammika, he built a hermitage there and constructed a leaf-hut and a walking path. In that hermitage, he discarded the robe endowed with nine faults and donned the bark garment endowed with twelve virtues, embracing the ascetic life of a sage, in order to obtain the power known as higher knowledge, which is free from the five faults of the hindrances and endowed with the eight causal qualities as stated in the passage beginning 'Thus, with a composed mind...' Having thus gone forth, he abandoned that leaf-hut, which was fraught with eight faults, and took up residence at the foot of a tree, endowed with ten virtues. Giving up all foods made from grain, he became one who lived on fallen fruits. By striving diligently through sitting, standing, and walking, within seven days he attained the eight meditative attainments and the five higher knowledges. Thus, he achieved the power of higher knowledge as he had aspired. Therefore, it is said:

“Evāhaṃ [M 1.0008] cintayitvāna, nekakoṭisataṃ dhanaṃ;

Nāthānāthānaṃ datvāna, himavantamupāgamiṃ.

Having thus reflected, I gave away wealth amounting to many hundreds of crores to those with and without protectors, and then I went to the Himalayas.

“Himavantassāvidūre[V 1.0009], dhammiko nāma pabbato;

Assamo sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā.

Not far from the Himalayas, there is a mountain named Dhammika. My hermitage was well-made, my leaf-hut skillfully constructed.

“Caṅkamaṃ tattha māpesiṃ, pañcadosavivajjitaṃ;

Aṭṭhaguṇasamupetaṃ, abhiññābalamāhariṃ.

I had a walking path constructed there, free from five faults; endowed with eight qualities, I brought forth the power of higher knowledge.

“Sāṭakaṃ pajahiṃ tattha, navadosamupāgataṃ;

Vākacīraṃ nivāsesiṃ, dvādasaguṇamupāgataṃ.

I abandoned the robe there, which was endowed with nine faults; I donned the bark garment, which was endowed with twelve virtues.

“Aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ, pajahiṃ paṇṇasālakaṃ;

Upāgamiṃ rukkhamūlaṃ, guṇe dasahupāgataṃ.

I abandoned the leaf-hut, teeming with eight faults; I approached the foot of a tree, endowed with ten virtues.

“Vāpitaṃ ropitaṃ dhaññaṃ, pajahiṃ niravasesato;

Anekaguṇasampannaṃ, pavattaphalamādiyiṃ.

I completely abandoned sown and planted grain; endowed with many qualities, I partook of fallen fruit.

“Tatthappadhānaṃ [P 1.0007] padahiṃ, nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame;

Abbhantaramhi sattāhe, abhiññābalapāpuṇi”nti.

There I strove with exertion, in sitting, standing, and walking; within seven days I attained the power of higher knowledge.

Tattha “assamo sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā”ti imāya pāḷiyā sumedhapaṇḍitena assamapaṇṇasālācaṅkamā sahatthā māpitā viya vuttā. Ayaṃ panettha attho – mahāsattaṃ “himavantaṃ ajjhogāhetvā ajja dhammikaṃ pabbataṃ pavisissāmī”ti nikkhantaṃ disvā sakko devānamindo vissakammadevaputtaṃ āmantesi – “tāta, ayaṃ sumedhapaṇḍito pabbajissāmīti nikkhanto, etassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ māpehī”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā ramaṇīyaṃ assamaṃ, suguttaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ, manoramaṃ caṅkamañca māpesi. Bhagavā pana tadā attano puññānubhāvena nipphannaṃ taṃ assamapadaṃ sandhāya sāriputta, tasmiṃ dhammikapabbate –

Here, by this Pāli passage—‘My hermitage was well-made, my leaf-hut skillfully constructed’—it is said as if the wise Sumedha had constructed the hermitage, leaf-hut, and walking path with his own hands. Herein this is the meaning: seeing the Great Being setting out with the thought, 'Having plunged into the Himalayas, today I will enter Mount Dhammika,' Sakka, the lord of the gods, addressed the divine son Vissakamma: 'Dear one, this wise Sumedha has set forth intending to go forth. Prepare a dwelling place for him.' Accepting his command, he constructed a delightful hermitage, a well-protected leaf-hut, and a charming walking path. The Blessed One, however, then, referring to that hermitage produced by the power of his own merit, said, 'Sāriputta, on that Mount Dhammika—'

“Assamo sukato mayhaṃ, paṇṇasālā sumāpitā;

Caṅkamaṃ tattha māpesiṃ, pañcadosavivajjita”nti. –

‘My hermitage was well-made, my leaf-hut skillfully constructed. There I had a walking path made, free from the five faults.’

Āha[V 1.0010]. Tattha sukato mayhanti sukato mayā. Paṇṇasālā sumāpitāti paṇṇacchadanasālāpi me sumāpitā ahosi.

He said. Therein, 'my well-made [hermitage]' means 'well-made by me.' 'A leaf-hut skillfully constructed' means 'my leaf-covered hut was also skillfully constructed by me.'

Pañcadosavivajjitanti [M 1.0009] pañcime caṅkamadosā nāma – thaddhavisamatā, antorukkhatā, gahanacchannatā, atisambādhatā, ativisālatāti. Thaddhavisamabhūmibhāgasmiñhi caṅkame caṅkamantassa pādā rujjanti, phoṭā uṭṭhahanti, cittaṃ ekaggaṃ na labhati, kammaṭṭhānaṃ vipajjati. Mudusamatale pana phāsuvihāraṃ āgamma kammaṭṭhānaṃ sampajjati. Tasmā thaddhavisamabhūmibhāgatā eko dosoti veditabbo. Caṅkamassa anto vā majjhe vā koṭiyaṃ vā rukkhe sati pamādamāgamma caṅkamantassa nalāṭaṃ vā sīsaṃ vā paṭihaññatīti antorukkhatā dutiyo doso. Tiṇalatādigahanacchanne caṅkame caṅkamanto andhakāravelāyaṃ uragādike pāṇe akkamitvā vā māreti, tehi vā daṭṭho dukkhaṃ āpajjatīti gahanacchannatā tatiyo doso. Atisambādhe caṅkame vitthārato ratanike vā aḍḍharatanike vā caṅkamantassa paricchede pakkhalitvā nakhāpi aṅguliyopi bhijjantīti atisambādhatā catuttho doso. Ativisāle caṅkame caṅkamantassa cittaṃ vidhāvati, ekaggataṃ na labhatīti ativisālatā pañcamo doso. Puthulato pana diyaḍḍharatanaṃ dvīsu passesu ratanamattaanucaṅkamaṃ dīghato saṭṭhihatthaṃ mudutalaṃ samavippakiṇṇavālukaṃ caṅkamaṃ vaṭṭati cetiyagirimhi dīpappasādakamahindattherassa caṅkamanaṃ viya, tādisaṃ taṃ ahosi. Tenāha “caṅkamaṃ tattha māpesiṃ, pañcadosavivajjita”nti.

“Free from the five faults” means that these are the five faults of a walking path: hardness and unevenness, trees within, being overgrown with thickets, excessive narrowness, and excessive spaciousness. For when walking on a hard and uneven surface, one's feet are injured, blisters arise, the mind cannot attain one-pointedness, and the object of meditation is lost. But on a soft and level ground, one dwells comfortably, and the object of meditation is accomplished. Therefore, hardness and unevenness should be understood as the first fault. If there are trees within, in the middle, or at the end of the walking path, the walker, through heedlessness, may strike his forehead or head against them; thus, trees within is the second fault. When walking on a path overgrown with grass, creepers, and thickets, the walker may, in the darkness, step on and kill creatures such as snakes, or being bitten by them, he comes to suffering; thus, being overgrown with thickets is the third fault. On an excessively narrow path, one cubit or half a cubit in width, the walker, stumbling at the boundary, may break his nails and toes; thus, excessive narrowness is the fourth fault. On an excessively spacious path, the walker’s mind scatters and cannot achieve one-pointedness; thus, excessive spaciousness is the fifth fault. A suitable walking path should be one and a half cubits in width, with a border of one cubit on each side; sixty cubits in length, with a soft surface and evenly spread sand—like the walking path of the Elder Mahinda, who brought light to the island, on Cetiyagiri. Such was that path. Therefore it is said: ‘I had a walking path made there, free from the five faults.’

Aṭṭhaguṇasamupetanti aṭṭhahi samaṇasukhehi upetaṃ. Aṭṭhimāni samaṇasukhāni nāma – dhanadhaññapariggahābhāvo, anavajjapiṇḍapātapariyesanabhāvo, nibbutapiṇḍapātabhuñjanabhāvo, raṭṭhaṃ pīḷetvā dhanasāraṃ vā sīsakahāpaṇādīni vā gaṇhantesu rājakulesu raṭṭhapīḷanakilesābhāvo, upakaraṇesu nicchandarāgabhāvo, coravilope nibbhayabhāvo, rājarājamahāmattehi asaṃsaṭṭhabhāvo, catūsu disāsu appaṭihatabhāvoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ [P 1.0008] hoti – yathā tasmiṃ assame vasantena sakkā honti imāni aṭṭha samaṇasukhāni vindituṃ, evaṃ aṭṭhaguṇasamupetaṃ taṃ assamaṃ māpesinti.

“Endowed with eight qualities” means endowed with eight monastic satisfactions. These eight monastic satisfactions are: the absence of possessing wealth and grain, the blameless seeking of alms-food, the peaceful partaking of alms-food, the absence of the defilement from oppressing the country when rulers seize wealth, valuables, or lead coins and so on by force, a lack of craving for requisites, fearlessness of thieves, non-association with kings and their great ministers, and being unimpeded in the four directions. This is to say: that hermitage was made endowed with these eight qualities, so that one dwelling in that hermitage could obtain these eight monastic satisfactions.

Abhiññābalamāharinti pacchā tasmiṃ assame vasanto kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā abhiññānaṃ samāpattīnañca uppādanatthāya aniccato dukkhato vipassanaṃ ārabhitvā thāmappattaṃ vipassanābalaṃ āhariṃ. Yathā tasmiṃ vasanto taṃ balaṃ [M 1.0010] āharituṃ sakkomi, evaṃ taṃ assamaṃ tassa abhiññatthāya vipassanābalassa anucchavikaṃ katvā māpesinti attho.

“I developed the power of higher knowledge” means that later, dwelling in that hermitage, after preparing the kasiṇa, to generate the higher knowledges and attainments, I commenced insight meditation on impermanence and suffering, and I developed the strength of insight that had reached its full capacity. Just as I was able to develop that strength while dwelling there, so that hermitage was built, made suitable for that higher knowledge and strength of insight. This is the meaning.

Sāṭakaṃ [V 1.0011] pajahiṃ tattha, navadosamupāgatanti etthāyaṃ anupubbikathā – tadā kira kuṭileṇacaṅkamādipaṭimaṇḍitaṃ pupphūpagaphalūpagarukkhasañchannaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ madhurasalilāsayaṃ apagatavāḷamigabhiṃsanakasakuṇaṃ pavivekakkhamaṃ assamaṃ māpetvā alaṅkatacaṅkamassa ubhosu antesu ālambanaphalakaṃ saṃvidhāya nisīdanatthāya caṅkamavemajjhe samatalaṃ muggavaṇṇasilaṃ māpetvā antopaṇṇasālāyaṃ jaṭāmaṇḍalavākacīratidaṇḍakuṇḍikādike tāpasaparikkhāre, maṇḍape pānīyaghaṭapānīyasaṅkhapānīyasarāvāni, aggisālāyaṃ aṅgārakapalladāruādīnīti evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ pabbajitānaṃ upakārāya saṃvattati, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ māpetvā paṇṇasālāya bhittiyaṃ “ye keci pabbajitukāmā ime parikkhāre gahetvā pabbajantū”ti akkharāni chinditvā devalokameva gate vissakammadevaputte sumedhapaṇḍito himavantapabbatapāde girikandarānusārena attano nivāsānurūpaṃ phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ olokento nadīnivattane vissakammanimmitaṃ sakkadattiyaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ assamaṃ disvā caṅkamanakoṭiṃ gantvā padavalañjaṃ apassanto “dhuvaṃ pabbajitā dhuragāme bhikkhaṃ pariyesitvā kilantarūpā āgantvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā nisinnā bhavissantī”ti cintetvā thokaṃ āgametvā “ativiya cirāyanti, jānissāmī”ti paṇṇāsālākuṭidvāraṃ vivaritvā anto pavisitvā ito cito ca olokento mahābhittiyaṃ akkharāni vācetvā “mayhaṃ kappiyaparikkhārā ete, ime gahetvā pabbajissāmī”ti attano nivatthapārutaṃ sāṭakayugaṃ pajahi. Tenāha “sāṭakaṃ pajahiṃ tatthā”ti. Evaṃ paviṭṭho ahaṃ, sāriputta, tassaṃ paṇṇasālāyaṃ sāṭakaṃ pajahiṃ.

“There I discarded the garment, which had come to be with nine faults.” Herein is the sequential account: At that time, a hermitage had been constructed, adorned with huts, caves, walking paths, and the like; covered with flowering and fruit-bearing trees; delightful, with reservoirs of sweet water; and free from fearsome beasts and birds, suitable for seclusion. A support plank had been prepared at both ends of the walking path, and in the middle of the path, a level stone slab the color of mung beans was made for sitting. Within the leaf-hut were the ascetic requisites: a coil of matted hair, bark garments, a triple staff, a water pot, and the like. In the pavilion were water pots, water conches, and water bowls; in the fire hall, charcoal, firewood, and so forth. Thus, whatever was conducive to the welfare of those who have gone forth, all that was prepared. On the wall of the leaf-hut, letters were inscribed: ‘Whoever wishes to go forth, taking these requisites, may go forth.’ When Vissakamma the devaputta had departed for the deva realm, the wise Sumedha, while searching at the foot of the Himalayas and along mountain caves for a suitable and comfortable dwelling, saw the delightful hermitage, created by Vissakamma and bestowed by Sakka, at a bend in the river. Reaching the end of the walking path and seeing no footprints, he thought: ‘Surely, the renunciants, weary from seeking alms in a remote village, have returned and are sitting inside the leaf-hut.’ After waiting a short while, he thought: ‘They are taking too long; I must ascertain.’ Opening the door of the leaf-hut, he entered and looked around. Reading the letters on the main wall, he declared: ‘These are suitable requisites for me; taking these, I shall go forth.’ Then he discarded his own pair of garments. Therefore, it is said: ‘There I discarded the garment.’ Thus having entered, O Sāriputta, into that leaf-hut, I discarded the garment.

Navadosamupāgatanti sāṭakaṃ pajahanto nava dose disvā pajahinti dīpeti. Tāpasapabbajjaṃ pabbajitānañhi sāṭakasmiṃ nava dosā upaṭṭhahanti. Tesu tassa mahagghabhāvo eko doso, parapaṭibaddhatāya uppajjanabhāvo eko, paribhogena lahuṃ kilissanabhāvo eko. Kiliṭṭho hi dhovitabbo ca rajitabbo ca hoti. Paribhogena jīraṇabhāvo eko. Jiṇṇassa hi tunnaṃ vā aggaḷadānaṃ vā kātabbaṃ hoti[M 1.0011]. Puna pariyesanāya durabhisambhavabhāvo eko, tāpasapabbajjāya asāruppabhāvo eko, paccatthikānaṃ sādhāraṇabhāvo eko. Yathā hi naṃ paccatthikā na gaṇhanti, evaṃ gopetabbo hoti. Paribhuñjantassa vibhūsanaṭṭhānabhāvo eko, gahetvā vicarantassa khandhabhāramahicchabhāvo ekoti.

“Which had come to be with nine faults” means that this explains that he abandons the garment upon seeing nine faults. For those who have gone forth into asceticism, nine faults are present in regard to a garment. Among these, its high price is one fault; its arising being dependent on others is one; its quickly becoming soiled through use is one, for when soiled, it must be washed and dyed. Its wearing out through use is one, for when worn out, it must be patched or reinforced. The difficulty of obtaining another is one; its unsuitability for the ascetic life is one; its being coveted by adversaries is one, for it must be guarded lest they take it. Its being a basis for adornment for the one who uses it is one; and its being a great burden for the shoulder and a cause of great desire for one carrying it while wandering is one.

Vākacīraṃ nivāsesinti tadāhaṃ, sāriputta, ime nava dose disvā sāṭakaṃ pahāya vākacīraṃ nivāsesiṃ, muñjatiṇaṃ [P 1.0009] hīraṃ hīraṃ katvā ganthetvā katavākacīraṃ nivāsanapārupanatthāya ādiyinti attho.

“Wearing bark garments”—this means that I, Sāriputta, having seen these nine faults, abandoned the garment and wore bark garments. The meaning is that I took up for wearing and draping a bark garment made by shredding muñja grass into strips and weaving them together.

Dvādasaguṇamupāgatanti [V 1.0012] dvādasahi ānisaṃsehi samannāgataṃ. Vākacīrasmiñhi dvādasa ānisaṃsā – appagghaṃ sundaraṃ kappiyanti ayaṃ tāva eko ānisaṃso, sahatthā kātuṃ sakkāti ayaṃ dutiyo, paribhogena saṇikaṃ kilissati, dhoviyamānepi papañco natthīti ayaṃ tatiyo, paribhogena jiṇṇepi sibbitabbābhāvo catuttho, puna pariyesantassa sukhena karaṇabhāvo pañcamo, tāpasapabbajjāya sāruppabhāvo chaṭṭho, paccatthikānaṃ nirupabhogabhāvo sattamo, paribhuñjantassa vibhūsanaṭṭhānābhāvo aṭṭhamo, dhāraṇe sallahukabhāvo navamo, cīvarapaccaye appicchabhāvo dasamo, vākuppattiyā dhammikaanavajjabhāvo ekādasamo, vākacīre naṭṭhepi anapekkhabhāvo dvādasamoti.

“Endowed with twelve virtues” means endowed with twelve benefits. For bark garments, there are twelve benefits: first, they are inexpensive, beautiful, and suitable; second, they can be made by one’s own hand; third, they soil slowly through use, and when washed, there is no complication; fourth, even when worn out through use, there is no need to sew them; fifth, they are easy to make when one seeks another; sixth, they are suitable for the ascetic life; seventh, they are of no use to adversaries; eighth, they are not a basis for adornment for one who uses them; ninth, they are light to carry; tenth, they cause little desire regarding the requisite of robes; eleventh, their acquisition is lawful and blameless; twelfth, even if the bark garment is lost, one is unconcerned.

Aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ, pajahiṃ paṇṇasālakanti. Kathaṃ pajahi? So kira varasāṭakayugaṃ omuñcitvā cīvaravaṃse laggitaṃ anojapupphadāmasadisaṃ rattaṃ vākacīraṃ gahetvā nivāsetvā, tassūpari aparaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ vākacīraṃ paridahitvā, punnāgapupphasantharasadisaṃ sakhuraṃ ajinacammaṃ ekaṃsaṃ katvā jaṭāmaṇḍalaṃ paṭimuñcitvā cūḷāya saddhiṃ niccalabhāvakaraṇatthaṃ sārasūciṃ pavesetvā muttajālasadisāya sikkāya pavāḷavaṇṇaṃ kuṇḍikaṃ odahitvā tīsu ṭhānesu vaṅkakājaṃ ādāya ekissā kājakoṭiyā kuṇḍikaṃ, ekissā aṅkusapacchitidaṇḍakādīni olaggetvā khāribhāraṃ aṃse katvā, dakkhiṇena hatthena kattaradaṇḍaṃ gahetvā paṇṇasālato nikkhamitvā saṭṭhihatthe mahācaṅkame aparāparaṃ caṅkamanto attano vesaṃ oloketvā – “mayhaṃ manoratho matthakaṃ patto, sobhati vata me pabbajjā, buddhapaccekabuddhādīhi sabbehi dhīrapurisehi vaṇṇitā thomitā [M 1.0012] ayaṃ pabbajjā nāma, pahīnaṃ me gihibandhanaṃ, nikkhantosmi nekkhammaṃ, laddhā me uttamapabbajjā, karissāmi samaṇadhammaṃ, labhissāmi maggaphalasukha”nti ussāhajāto khārikājaṃ otāretvā caṅkamavemajjhe muggavaṇṇasilāpaṭṭe suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya nisinno divasabhāgaṃ vītināmetvā sāyanhasamayaṃ paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā, bidalamañcakapasse kaṭṭhattharikāya nipanno sarīraṃ utuṃ gāhāpetvā, balavapaccūse pabujjhitvā attano āgamanaṃ āvajjesi “ahaṃ gharāvāse ādīnavaṃ disvā amitabhogaṃ anantayasaṃ pahāya araññaṃ pavisitvā nekkhammagavesako hutvā pabbajito, ito dāni paṭṭhāya pamādacāraṃ carituṃ na vaṭṭati.

“Overcome by eight faults, I abandoned the leaf hut.” How did he abandon it? It is said that he took off a fine pair of robes, hung them on a clothes rack, and put on a red bark garment resembling a garland of Anojā flowers. Over that, he draped another bark garment of golden hue. He placed over one shoulder an antelope skin with its hoofs, which resembled a spread of Punnāga flowers, secured his coiled matted hair, and inserted a needle made of heartwood into his topknot to keep it steady. He placed a coral-colored water pot in a carrying net that resembled a net of pearls. Taking a crooked carrying pole, he hung the water pot from one end of the pole, and a goad, a small basket, a staff, and other items from the other. Then, placing the carrying pole on his shoulder, he took a cutter-staff in his right hand and left the leaf hut. Walking back and forth along a sixty-cubit-long cloister, he observed his own appearance and thought: ‘My heart’s desire has been fulfilled. Truly, my renunciation is splendid! This renunciation is praised and esteemed by the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and all wise persons. I have abandoned the bondage of household life, gone forth into homelessness, and attained the highest renunciation. I will practice the ascetic’s duty and attain the bliss of the path and its fruits.’ Filled with enthusiasm, he set down his carrying pole and sat in the middle of the cloister on a mug-bean-colored stone slab, like a golden statue, spending the day there. In the evening, he entered the leaf hut and lay down on a wooden mat beside the split-bamboo bed, allowing his body to adjust to the climate. Waking up at early dawn, he reflected on his arrival: ‘Having seen the drawbacks of household life, I left behind immeasurable wealth and endless fame to enter the wilderness as a seeker of renunciation and went forth. Now, from this point onward, it is not fitting to live carelessly.’

Pavivekañhi pahāya vicarantaṃ micchāvitakkamakkhikā khādanti, idāni mayā vivekamanubrūhetuṃ vaṭṭati. Ahañhi gharāvāsaṃ palibodhato disvā nikkhanto, ayañca manāpā paṇṇasālā, beluvapakkavaṇṇaparibhaṇḍakatā bhūmi, rajatavaṇṇā setabhittiyo, kapotapādavaṇṇaṃ paṇṇacchadanaṃ[V 1.0013], vicittattharaṇavaṇṇo bidalamañcako, nivāsaphāsukaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, na etto atirekatarā viya me gehasampadā paññāyatī”ti paṇṇasālāya dose vicinanto aṭṭha dose passi.

For one wandering after abandoning seclusion, the gnats of wrong thought bite. Now it is fitting for me to cultivate seclusion. Having seen the household life as an obstruction, I went forth. And this lovely leaf hut—the ground is adorned with the color of ripe beluva fruit, the walls are silver-white, the thatched roof is the color of a pigeon's foot, the split-bamboo couch has the hue of a colorful spread, the dwelling is comfortable—no greater household splendor than this is apparent to me. Examining the faults of the leaf hut, he saw eight faults.

Paṇṇasālāparibhogasmiñhi aṭṭha ādīnavā – mahāsamārambhena dabbasambhāre samodhānetvā karaṇapariyesanabhāvo eko ādīnavo, tiṇapaṇṇamattikāsu patitāsu tāsaṃ [P 1.0010] punappunaṃ ṭhapetabbatāya nibandhajagganabhāvo dutiyo, senāsanaṃ nāma mahallakassa pāpuṇāti, avelāya vuṭṭhāpiyamānassa cittekaggatā na hotīti uṭṭhāpaniyabhāvo tatiyo, sītuṇhapaṭighātena kāyassa sukhumālakaraṇabhāvo catuttho, gehaṃ paviṭṭhena yaṃkiñci pāpaṃ sakkā kātunti garahāpaṭicchādanabhāvo pañcamo, “mayha”nti pariggahakaraṇabhāvo chaṭṭho, gehassa atthibhāvo nāma sadutiyakavāsoti sattamo, ūkāmaṅgulagharagoḷikādīnaṃ sādhāraṇatāya bahusādhāraṇabhāvo aṭṭhamo. Iti ime aṭṭha ādīnave disvā mahāsatto paṇṇasālaṃ pajati. Tenāha “aṭṭhadosasamākiṇṇaṃ, pajahiṃ paṇṇasālaka”nti.

In using a leaf hut, there are eight dangers: The first danger is the great undertaking of gathering materials and supplies, and the effort of its construction. The second is the need for constant upkeep, as fallen grass, leaves, and clay must be repeatedly replaced. The third is the liability of being disturbed; when roused at an unsuitable time, one's concentration is lost. The fourth is that by protecting the body from cold and heat, it makes it delicate. The fifth is the concealment of blame, as any wrongdoing can be committed within a house. The sixth is the act of appropriation that arises from thinking, 'This is mine.' The seventh is that having a house means living with a companion. The eighth is that it is shared with many, being common to lice, insects, house geckos, and so forth. Seeing these eight dangers, the great being abandoned the leaf hut. Hence it is said: 'I abandoned the leaf hut, fraught with eight faults.'

Upāgamiṃ rukkhamūlaṃ, guṇe dasahupāgatanti channaṃ paṭikkhipitvā dasahi guṇehi upetaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upagatosmīti vadati. Tatrime dasa guṇā – appasamārambhatā eko guṇo, upagamanamattakameva hi tattha hoti; apaṭijagganatā [M 1.0013] dutiyo, tañhi sammaṭṭhampi asammaṭṭhampi paribhogaphāsukaṃ hotiyeva. Anuṭṭhāpariyabhāvo tatiyo, garahaṃ nappaṭicchādeti; tattha hi pāpaṃ karonto lajjatīti garahāya appaṭicchannabhāvo catuttho; abbhokāsavāso viya kāyaṃ na santhambhetīti kāyassa asanthambhanabhāvo pañcamo; pariggahakaraṇābhāvo chaṭṭho; gehālayapaṭikkhepo sattamo; bahusādhāraṇagehe viya “paṭijaggissāmi naṃ, nikkhamathā”ti nīharaṇakābhāvo aṭṭhamo; vasantassa sappītikabhāvo navamo; rukkhamūlasenāsanassa gatagataṭṭhāne sulabhatāya anapekkhabhāvo dasamoti ime dasa guṇe disvā rukkhamūlaṃ upāgatosmīti vadati.

I approached the foot of a tree, endowed with ten virtues—having rejected the six, he says, 'I have gone to the foot of a tree, endowed with ten virtues.' Herein, these are the ten virtues: The first virtue is that it requires little effort, for only the going there is needed. The second is that it requires no upkeep, for whether swept or unswept, it is comfortable for use. The third is not being liable to be disturbed. The fourth is the non-concealment of blame, for one feels shame to do evil there. The fifth is that it does not make the body stiff, as a dwelling in the open air might. The sixth is the absence of appropriation. The seventh is the rejection of attachment to a house. The eighth is that there is no need for eviction, as there might be in a shared house, saying, 'I will look after it, you must leave.' The ninth is the joy of one who dwells there. The tenth is the lack of concern, due to the ease of finding a dwelling at the foot of a tree in any place one goes. Seeing these ten virtues, he says, 'I have gone to the foot of a tree.'

Imāni ettakāni kāraṇāni sallakkhetvā mahāsatto punadivase bhikkhāya gāmaṃ pāvisi. Athassa sampattagāme manussā mahantena ussāhena bhikkhaṃ adaṃsu. So bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā assamaṃ āgamma nisīditvā cintesi “nāhaṃ āhāraṃ na labhāmīti pabbajito, siniddhāhāro nāmesa mānamadapurisamade vaḍḍheti, āhāramūlakassa ca dukkhassa anto natthi. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ vāpitaropitadhaññanibbattaṃ āhāraṃ pajahitvā pavattaphalabhojano bhaveyya”nti. So tato [V 1.0014] ṭṭhāya tathā katvā ghaṭento vāyamanto sattāhabbhantareyeva aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca abhiññāyo ca nibbattesi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Considering these many reasons, the Great Being entered the village for alms the next day. Then the people in the village, with great enthusiasm, gave him alms. Having finished his meal, he returned to the hermitage, sat down, and reflected: "I did not go forth because I could not obtain food; indeed, rich food only increases pride, intoxication, and vanity in a person, and there is no end to the suffering rooted in food. Why don't I give up food produced from sown and planted grain, and live on fallen fruit?" From that moment, he practiced accordingly, striving and exerting himself, and within seven days, he attained the eight meditative attainments and the five higher knowledges. Therefore, it is said:

“Vāpitaṃ ropitaṃ dhaññaṃ, pajahiṃ niravasesato;

Anekaguṇasampannaṃ, pavattaphalamādiyiṃ.

"The sown and planted grain I completely abandoned; Endowed with many virtues, I obtained the fallen fruit.

“Tatthappadhānaṃ padahiṃ, nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame;

Abbhantaramhi sattāhe, abhiññābalapāpuṇi”nti.

"There I strove with exertion, in sitting, standing, and walking. Within seven days, I attained the power of the higher knowledges."

Evaṃ abhiññābalaṃ patvā sumedhatāpase samāpattisukhena vītināmente dīpaṅkaro nāma satthā loke udapādi. Tassa paṭisandhijātisambodhidhammacakkappavattanesu sakalāpi dasasahassī lokadhātu saṃkampi [P 1.0011] sampakampi sampavedhi, mahāviravaṃ viravi, dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni pāturahesuṃ. Sumedhatāpaso samāpattisukhena vītināmento neva taṃ saddamassosi, na tāni nimittāni addasa. Tena vuttaṃ –

Having thus attained the power of the higher knowledges, while the ascetic Sumedha was passing his time in the bliss of meditative attainment, a Teacher named Dīpaṅkara arose in the world. At his conception, birth, awakening, and the setting in motion of the Wheel of Dhamma, the entire ten-thousand world-system shook, quaked, and trembled. A great roar resounded, and the thirty-two premonitory signs appeared. The ascetic Sumedha, passing his time in the bliss of meditative attainment, neither heard that sound nor saw those signs. Therefore, it is said:

“Evaṃ [M 1.0014] me siddhippattassa, vasībhūtassa sāsane;

Dīpaṅkaro nāma jino, uppajji lokanāyako.

"Thus for me, who had attained success and gained mastery in the Dispensation, the Victor named Dīpaṅkara, the Leader of the world, arose.

“Uppajjante ca jāyante, bujjhante dhammadesane;

Caturo nimitte nāddasaṃ, jhānaratisamappito”ti.

"At his arising and birth, at his awakening and teaching of the Dhamma, I did not see the four signs, being devoted to the delight of jhāna."

Tasmiṃ kāle dīpaṅkaradasabalo catūhi khīṇāsavasatasahassehi parivuto anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno rammaṃ nāma nagaraṃ patvā sudassanamahāvihāre paṭivasati. Rammanagaravāsino “dīpaṅkaro kira samaṇissaro paramātisambodhiṃ patvā pavattavaradhammacakko anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno rammanagaraṃ patvā sudassanamahāvihāre paṭivasatī”ti sutvā sappinavanītādīni ceva bhesajjāni vatthacchādanāni ca gāhāpetvā gandhamālādihatthā yena buddho, yena dhammo, yena saṅgho, tanninnā tappoṇā tappabbhārā hutvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā ekamantaṃ nisinnā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā svātanāya nimantetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkamiṃsu.

At that time, Dīpaṅkara of the Ten Powers, surrounded by four hundred thousand destroyers of the cankers, was wandering on tour in due course. He arrived at the city of Ramma and stayed at the Sudassana Great Monastery. The citizens of Ramma heard: "It is said that Dīpaṅkara, the lord of ascetics, having attained supreme full awakening and set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma, is wandering on tour in due course. He has arrived at the city of Ramma and is staying at the Sudassana Great Monastery." Hearing this, they had ghee, fresh butter, and other medicines, as well as cloth for robes, procured. With perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in hand, having become inclined, devoted, and slanted towards the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha, they approached the Teacher, paid homage, honored him with perfumes and garlands, and sat to one side. After listening to the Dhamma discourse, they invited him for the following day. Then, rising from their seats, they departed.

Te punadivase mahādānaṃ sajjetvā nagaraṃ alaṅkaritvā dasabalassa āgamanamaggaṃ alaṅkarontā [V 1.0015] udakabhinnaṭṭhānesu paṃsuṃ pakkhipitvā samaṃ bhūmitalaṃ katvā rajatapaṭṭavaṇṇaṃ vālukaṃ ākiranti, lājāni ceva pupphāni ca vikiranti, nānāvirāgehi vatthehi dhajapaṭāke ussāpenti, kadaliyo ceva puṇṇaghaṭapantiyo ca patiṭṭhāpenti. Tasmiṃ kāle sumedhatāpaso attano assamapadā uggantvā tesaṃ manussānaṃ uparibhāgena ākāsena gacchanto te haṭṭhatuṭṭhe manusse disvā “kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti ākāsato oruyha ekamantaṃ ṭhito manusse pucchi – “ambho kassa tumhe imaṃ maggaṃ alaṅkarothā”ti? Tena vuttaṃ –

On the following day, having prepared a great offering and adorned the city, they beautified the path for the arrival of the Ten-Powered One. Where the ground was broken by water, they filled it with earth, made the surface level, and strewed sand the color of silver cloth. They also scattered parched grain and flowers, hoisted banners and flags of diverse hues, and set up banana plants and rows of full pots. At that time, the ascetic Sumedha, emerging from his hermitage, was going through the air above those people. Seeing the people joyful and delighted, he descended from the sky and, standing to one side, asked the people, 'Friends, for whom are you adorning this road?' Thus it was said:

“Paccantadesavisaye, nimantetvā tathāgataṃ;

Tassa āgamanaṃ maggaṃ, sodhenti tuṭṭhamānasā.

In a frontier region, having invited the Tathāgata, with joyful minds they clear the path for his arrival.

“Ahaṃ tena samayena, nikkhamitvā sakassamā;

Dhunanto vākacīrāni, gacchāmi ambare tadā.

At that time, having left my own hermitage, shaking my bark garments, I was going through the air then.

“Vedajātaṃ janaṃ disvā, tuṭṭhahaṭṭhaṃ pamoditaṃ;

Orohitvāna gaganā, manusse pucchi tāvade.

Seeing the people filled with rapture, joyful and delighted, descending from the sky, I immediately asked the people.

“‘Tuṭṭhahaṭṭho [P 1.0012][M 1.0015] pamudito, vedajāto mahājano;

Kassa sodhīyati maggo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyana’”nti.

‘The great multitude is joyful, delighted, filled with rapture; for whom is this path being cleared, this straight and direct way?’

Manussā āhaṃsu “bhante sumedha, na tvaṃ jānāsi, dīpaṅkaradasabalo sammāsambodhiṃ patvā pavattitavaradhammacakko cārikaṃ caramāno amhākaṃ nagaraṃ patvā sudassanamahāvihāre paṭivasati. Mayaṃ taṃ bhagavantaṃ nimantayimhā, tassetaṃ buddhassa bhagavato āgamanamaggaṃ alaṅkaromā”ti. Sumedhatāpaso cintesi – “buddhoti kho ghosamattakampi loke dullabhaṃ, pageva buddhuppādo, mayāpi imehi manussehi saddhiṃ dasabalassa maggaṃ alaṅkarituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So te manusse āha – “sace bho tumhe etaṃ maggaṃ buddhassa alaṅkarotha, mayhampi ekaṃ okāsaṃ detha, ahampi tumhehi saddhiṃ maggaṃ alaṅkarissāmī”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā “sumedhatāpaso iddhimā”ti jānantā udakabhinnokāsaṃ sallakkhetvā “tvaṃ imaṃ ṭhānaṃ alaṅkarohī”ti adaṃsu. Sumedho buddhārammaṇaṃ pītiṃ gahetvā cintesi “ahaṃ imaṃ okāsaṃ iddhiyā alaṅkarituṃ sakkomi, evaṃ alaṅkato pana mama manaṃ na paritosessati, ajja mayā kāyaveyyāvaccaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti paṃsuṃ āharitvā tasmiṃ padese pakkhipi.

The people said, "Venerable Sumedha, do you not know? The Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara, having attained Perfect Self-Enlightenment and set in motion the supreme Wheel of Dhamma, is wandering on tour and has arrived at our city. He is dwelling in the Sudassana Great Monastery. We have invited that Blessed One, and we are decorating this path for the arrival of the Buddha, the Blessed One." The ascetic Sumedha thought, "Even the mere sound of 'Buddha' is rare in the world, how much more so the arising of a Buddha! It is fitting for me too to decorate the path for the Ten-Powered One along with these people." He then said to those people, "If you, sirs, are decorating this path for the Buddha, grant me a space as well. I too shall decorate the path with you." They agreed, saying, "Good," and knowing that the ascetic Sumedha possessed psychic powers, they pointed out a water-logged area and said, "You may decorate this spot." Sumedha, having taken up joy with the Buddha as its object, thought, "I am able to decorate this space by psychic power, but if it is decorated thus, my mind will not be satisfied. Today, I must perform bodily service." He then brought earth and placed it in that spot.

Tassa [V 1.0016] tasmiṃ padese analaṅkateyeva dīpaṅkaro dasabalo mahānubhāvānaṃ chaḷabhiññānaṃ khīṇāsavānaṃ catūhi satasahassehi parivuto devatāsu dibbagandhamālādīhi pūjayantīsu dibbasaṅgītesu pavattantesu manussesu mānusakagandhehi ceva mālādīhi ca pūjayantesu anantāya buddhalīḷāya manosilātale vijambhamāno sīho viya taṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajji. Sumedhatāpaso akkhīni ummīletvā alaṅkatamaggena āgacchantassa dasabalassa dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ asītiyā anubyañjanehi anurañjitaṃ byāmappabhāya samparivāritaṃ maṇivaṇṇagaganatale nānappakārā vijjulatā viya āveḷāveḷabhūtā ceva yugalayugalabhūtā ca chabbaṇṇaghanabuddharasmiyo vissajjentaṃ rūpaggappattaṃ attabhāvaṃ oloketvā “ajja mayā dasabalassa jīvitapariccāgaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, mā bhagavā kalalaṃ akkami, maṇiphalakasetuṃ pana akkamanto viya saddhiṃ catūhi khīṇāsavasatasahassehi mama piṭṭhiṃ maddamāno gacchatu, taṃ me [M 1.0016] bhavissati dīgharattaṃ hitāya sukhāyā”ti kese mocetvā ajinacammajaṭāmaṇḍalavākacīrāni [P 1.0013] kāḷavaṇṇe kalale pattharitvā maṇiphalakasetu viya kalalapiṭṭhe nipajji. Tena vuttaṃ –

While that spot was still unadorned, the Ten-Powered One, Dīpaṅkara, surrounded by four hundred thousand Arahants of great might, endowed with the six higher knowledges, while deities were honoring him with divine fragrances, garlands, and so forth, and divine music was playing, and humans were honoring him with human fragrances, garlands, and so forth, displaying boundless Buddha-grace, strode forth like a lion stretching himself on a red arsenic slab, entering upon the adorned and prepared path. The ascetic Sumedha, opening his eyes, beheld the Ten-Powered One approaching along the adorned path, his body adorned with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and embellished with the eighty minor characteristics, surrounded by a fathom-wide aura, emitting dense six-colored Buddha-rays that were like various lightning streaks, entwined and paired, in a sky of jewel-hue, his physical form having reached the peak of beauty. Reflecting, "Today it is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for the Ten-Powered One. May the Blessed One not step into the mire, but rather, as if stepping on a bridge of gemstones, may he, along with the four hundred thousand Arahants, tread upon my back. That will be for my long-term welfare and happiness," he loosened his hair, spread out his deer-skin, his matted locks, and his bark garments on the dark-colored mire, and lay down like a bridge of gemstones upon the muddy ground. Thus it is said:

“Te me puṭṭhā viyākaṃsu, ‘buddho loke anuttaro;

Dīpaṅkaro nāma jino, uppajji lokanāyako;

Tassa sodhīyati maggo, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ’.

When questioned by me, they replied: ‘A Buddha, unsurpassed in the world, a Victor named Dīpaṅkara, the world's leader, has arisen. For him this path is being cleared, this straight and direct way.’

“Buddhoti mama sutvāna, pīti uppajji tāvade;

Buddho buddhoti kathayanto, somanassaṃ pavedayiṃ.

Having heard ‘Buddha,’ joy instantly arose in me; uttering ‘Buddha, Buddha,’ I manifested my gladness.

“Tattha ṭhatvā vicintesiṃ, tuṭṭho saṃviggamānaso;

‘Idha bījāni ropissaṃ, khaṇo eva mā upaccagā’.

Standing there, I reflected, joyful and with a mind stirred by spiritual urgency: ‘Here I shall sow the seeds; let not this moment pass me by.’

“Yadi buddhassa sodhetha, ekokāsaṃ dadātha me;

Ahampi sodhayissāmi, añjasaṃ vaṭumāyanaṃ.

‘If you are clearing the way for the Buddha, grant me a single spot; I too shall clear the path, the straight and direct way.’

“Adaṃsu te mamokāsaṃ, sodhetuṃ añjasaṃ tadā;

Buddho buddhoti cintento, maggaṃ sodhemahaṃ tadā.

They gave me a spot to clear the straight path then; thinking ‘Buddha, Buddha,’ I cleared the path then.

“Aniṭṭhite [V 1.0017] mamokāse, dīpaṅkaro mahāmuni;

Catūhi satasahassehi, chaḷabhiññehi tādihi;

Khīṇāsavehi vimalehi, paṭipajji añjasaṃ jino.

While my spot was not yet finished, the great sage Dīpaṅkara, the Victor, proceeded along the straight path with four hundred thousand such steadfast ones, who had destroyed the cankers, were stainless, and possessed the six higher knowledges.

“Paccuggamanā vattanti, vajjanti bheriyo bahū;

Āmoditā naramarū, sādhukāraṃ pavattayuṃ.

Welcoming ceremonies took place, many drums were beaten; men and gods rejoiced, and uttered shouts of approval.

“Devā manusse passanti, manussāpi ca devatā;

Ubhopi te pañjalikā, anuyanti tathāgataṃ.

Gods saw humans, and humans also saw the gods; both, with palms joined in reverence, followed the Tathāgata.

“Devā dibbehi turiyehi, manussā mānusehi ca;

Ubhopi te vajjayantā, anuyanti tathāgataṃ.

Gods with divine musical instruments, and humans with human ones; both, playing music, followed the Tathāgata.

“Dibbaṃ mandāravaṃ pupphaṃ, padumaṃ pārichattakaṃ;

Disodisaṃ okiranti, ākāsanabhagatā marū.

Divine Mandārava flowers, lotuses, and Pāricchattaka flowers, the gods abiding in the sky scattered in all directions.

“Campakaṃ [M 1.0017] salalaṃ nīpaṃ, nāgapunnāgaketakaṃ;

Disodisaṃ ukkhipanti, bhūmitalagatā narā.

Men on the ground tossed up Campaka, Salala, Nīpa, Nāgapunnāga, and Ketaka flowers in all directions.

“Kese muñcitvāhaṃ tattha, vākacīrañca cammakaṃ;

Kalale pattharitvāna, avakujjo nipajjahaṃ.

Having loosened my hair there, and my bark garment and hide, I spread them on the mire and lay face down.

“Akkamitvāna maṃ buddho, saha sissehi gacchatu;

Mā naṃ kalale akkamittho, hitāya me bhavissatī”ti.

Let the Buddha step over me and go forth with his disciples; may he not step into the mire, for that will be for my welfare.

So kalalapiṭṭhe nipannakova puna akkhīni ummīletvā dīpaṅkaradasabalassa buddhasiriṃ sampassamāno evaṃ cintesi – “sacāhaṃ iccheyyaṃ, sabbakilese jhāpetvā saṅghanavako hutvā rammanagaraṃ paviseyyaṃ. Aññātakavesena [P 1.0014] pana me kilese jhāpetvā nibbānappattiyā kiccaṃ natthi. Yaṃnūnāhaṃ dīpaṅkaradasabalo viya paramābhisambodhiṃ patvā dhammanāvaṃ āropetvā mahājanaṃ saṃsārasāgarā [V 1.0018] uttāretvā pacchā parinibbāyeyyaṃ, idaṃ mayhaṃ patirūpa”nti. Tato aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā buddhabhāvāya abhinīhāraṃ katvā nipajji. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, lying on the mire, he opened his eyes again and beheld the Buddha-splendor of the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara, and thought thus: "If I wished, I could burn up all defilements and, becoming a newly ordained monk, enter the delightful city. But I have no need to burn up my defilements and attain Nibbāna in an unknown guise. What if I, like the Ten-Powered Dīpaṅkara, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment, were to board the ship of the Dhamma, ferry the great multitude across the ocean of saṃsāra, and afterwards attain final Nibbāna? This would be fitting for me." Having thus reflected, he brought together the eight qualities, made the aspiration for Buddhahood, and then lay down. Therefore, it is said:

“Pathaviyaṃ nipannassa, evaṃ me āsi cetaso;

‘Icchamāno ahaṃ ajja, kilese jhāpaye mama.

As I lay on the ground, this thought arose in my mind: 'If I wished, today I could burn away my defilements.

‘Kiṃ me aññātavesena, dhammaṃ sacchikatenidha;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, buddho hessaṃ sadevake.

'What use is it to me to realize the Dhamma here in an unknown guise? Having attained omniscience, I shall become a Buddha in the world with its devas.

‘Kiṃ me ekena tiṇṇena, purisena thāmadassinā;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, santāressaṃ sadevake.

'What use is it to me, a man of steadfast strength, to cross over alone? Having attained omniscience, I shall ferry across the world with its devas.

‘Iminā me adhikārena, katena purisuttame;

Sabbaññutaṃ pāpuṇitvā, tāremi janataṃ bahuṃ.

'By this act of service of mine, performed for the Supreme Man, having attained omniscience, I shall ferry many people across.

‘Saṃsārasotaṃ chinditvā, viddhaṃsetvā tayo bhave;

Dhammanāvaṃ samāruyha, santāressaṃ sadevake’”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.54-58);

'Having cut off the stream of saṃsāra, having shattered the three realms of existence, having boarded the ship of the Dhamma, I shall ferry across the world with its devas.'

Yasmā pana buddhattaṃ patthentassa –

For one aspiring to Buddhahood—

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59);

Human existence, perfection of sex, the cause, seeing the Teacher; renunciation, perfection of qualities, dedication, and aspiration; when these eight qualities are combined, the aspiration is fulfilled.

Manussattabhāvasmiṃyeva [M 1.0018] hi ṭhatvā buddhattaṃ patthentassa patthanā samijjhati, na nāgassa vā supaṇṇassa vā devatāya vā patthanā samijjhati. Manussattabhāvepi purisaliṅge ṭhitasseva patthanā samijjhati, na itthiyā vā paṇḍakanapuṃsakaubhatobyañjanakānaṃ vā patthanā samijjhati. Purisassāpi tasmiṃ attabhāve arahattappattiyā hetusampannasseva patthanā samijjhati, no itarassa. Hetusampannassāpi jīvamānakabuddhasseva santike patthentassa patthanā samijjhati, parinibbute buddhe cetiyasantike vā bodhimūle vā patthentassa na samijjhati. Buddhānaṃ santike patthentassāpi [V 1.0019] pabbajjāliṅge ṭhitasseva samijjhati, no gihiliṅge ṭhitassa. Pabbajitassāpi pañcābhiññassa aṭṭhasamāpattilābhinoyeva samijjhati, na imāya guṇasampattiyā virahitassa. Guṇasampannenāpi yena attano jīvitaṃ buddhānaṃ pariccattaṃ hoti, tassa iminā adhikārena adhikārasampannasseva samijjhati, na itarassa. Adhikārasampannassāpi yassa buddhakārakadhammānaṃ atthāya mahanto chando ca ussāho ca vāyāmo ca pariyeṭṭhi ca, tasseva samijjhati, na itarassa.

For it is indeed only when one is established in the human state that the aspiration of one aspiring to Buddhahood succeeds; the aspiration of a Nāga, a Supaṇṇa, or a deity does not succeed. Even in the human state, the aspiration succeeds only for one established in the male sex; the aspiration of a female, a paṇḍaka, a napuṃsaka, or one with both sexual characteristics does not succeed. And even for a male, the aspiration succeeds only for one endowed with the causes for attaining arahantship in that very existence, not for another. Even for one endowed with the causes, the aspiration succeeds only when aspiring in the presence of a living Buddha; it does not succeed when aspiring before a shrine or at the foot of the Bodhi tree after the Buddha’s parinibbāna. And even for one aspiring in the presence of Buddhas, it succeeds only for one established in the state of a renunciate, not for one established in the state of a householder. Even for a renunciate, it succeeds only for one who possesses the five higher knowledges and has attained the eight meditative attainments, not for one lacking this perfection of qualities. And even for one endowed with these qualities, it succeeds only for one who has dedicated his life to the Buddhas, thus being endowed with this dedication, not for another. And even for one endowed with this dedication, it succeeds only for one who has great aspiration, energy, effort, and searching for the sake of the qualities that make a Buddha, not for another.

Tatridaṃ chandamahantatāya opammaṃ – sace hi evamassa “yo sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ ekodakībhūtaṃ attano bāhubalena uttaritvā pāraṃ gantuṃ samattho[P 1.0015], so buddhattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Yo vā pana sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ veḷugumbasañchannaṃ byūhitvā madditvā padasā gacchanto pāraṃ gantuṃ samattho, so buddhattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Yo vā pana sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ sattiyo ākoṭetvā nirantaraṃ sattiphalasamākiṇṇaṃ padasā akkamamāno pāraṃ gantuṃ samattho, so buddhattaṃ pāpuṇāti. Yo vā pana sakalacakkavāḷagabbhaṃ vītaccitaṅgārabharitaṃ pādehi maddamāno pāraṃ gantuṃ samattho, so buddhattaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti. Yo etesu ekampi attano dukkaraṃ na maññati, “ahaṃ etampi taritvā vā gantvā vā pāraṃ gahessāmī”ti evaṃ mahantena chandena ca ussāhena ca vāyāmena ca pariyeṭṭhiyā ca samannāgato hoti, tassa patthanā samijjhati, na itarassa. Sumedhatāpaso pana ime aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā buddhabhāvāya abhinīhāraṃ katvā nipajji.

Here is a simile for the greatness of this aspiration: Suppose it were said, 'Whoever is able, by the strength of his own arms, to cross the entire world-system, become a single mass of water, and reach the far shore—he attains Buddhahood. Or, whoever is able to push aside and crush the entire world-system, covered with bamboo thickets, and, proceeding on foot, reach the far shore—he attains Buddhahood. Or, whoever is able to tread on foot across the entire world-system, continuously strewn with spear-blades hammered into it, and reach the far shore—he attains Buddhahood. Or, whoever is able to crush with his feet the entire world-system, filled with smokeless embers, and reach the far shore—he attains Buddhahood.' He for whom not even one of these tasks is considered difficult, who is endowed with such great aspiration, energy, effort, and searching as to think, 'I will cross or traverse even this and reach the far shore'—his aspiration succeeds, not another's. The ascetic Sumedha, having brought together these eight qualities, made his aspiration for Buddhahood and lay down.

Dīpaṅkaropi [M 1.0019] bhagavā āgantvā sumedhatāpasassa sīsabhāge ṭhatvā maṇisīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭento viya pañcavaṇṇappasādasampannāni akkhīni ummīletvā kalalapiṭṭhe nipannaṃ sumedhatāpasaṃ disvā “ayaṃ tāpaso buddhattāya abhinīhāraṃ katvā nipanno, ijjhissati nu kho imassa patthanā, udāhu no”ti anāgataṃsañāṇaṃ pesetvā upadhārento “ito kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni atikkamitvā gotamo nāma buddho bhavissatī”ti ñatvā ṭhitakova parisamajjhe byākāsi – “passatha no tumhe imaṃ uggatapaṃ tāpasaṃ kalalapiṭṭhe nipanna”nti? “Evaṃ, bhante”ti. “Ayaṃ buddhattāya abhinīhāraṃ katvā nipanno, samijjhissati imassa patthanā, ito kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake gotamo nāma buddho bhavissati. Tasmiṃ panassa attabhāve kapilavatthu nāma nagaraṃ nivāso bhavissati, māyā nāma devī mātā, suddhodano nāma rājā pitā, aggasāvako upatisso nāma thero, dutiyasāvako kolito nāma, buddhupaṭṭhāko ānando nāma, aggasāvikā khemā nāma [V 1.0020] therī, dutiyasāvikā uppalavaṇṇā nāma therī bhavissati, paripakkañāṇo mahābhinikkhamanaṃ katvā mahāpadhānaṃ padahitvā nigrodhamūle pāyāsaṃ paṭiggahetvā nerañjarāya tīre paribhuñjitvā bodhimaṇḍaṃ āruyha assattharukkhamūle abhisambujjhissatī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ –

The Blessed One Dīpaṅkara also arrived and stood at the head of the ascetic Sumedha. As if opening a jeweled lion-cage, he opened his eyes, radiant with the five colors, and saw the ascetic Sumedha lying on the muddy ground. He thought, "This ascetic has made a resolution for Buddhahood and lies here. Will his aspiration succeed, or not?" Sending forth his knowledge of the future and reflecting, he knew: "After passing beyond four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise." Standing in the midst of the assembly, he then declared: "Do you see this ascetic of severe austerities lying on the muddy ground?" "Yes, Lord," they replied. "This ascetic has made a resolution for Buddhahood and lies here. His aspiration will succeed. At the end of four incalculable periods and a hundred thousand eons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. In that existence, his dwelling place will be the city of Kapilavatthu. His mother will be Queen Māyā, his father King Suddhodana. His chief disciple will be the elder named Upatissa, his second disciple Kolita. His attendant will be Ānanda. His chief female disciple will be the elder nun Khemā, his second female disciple the elder nun Uppalavaṇṇā. Having ripened his wisdom, he will undertake the great renunciation, strive with great effort, accept milk-rice at the foot of a banyan tree, consume it on the bank of the Nerañjarā River, ascend the seat of enlightenment, and attain supreme awakening at the foot of the Assattha tree." Thus it was said:

“Dīpaṅkaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Ussīsake maṃ ṭhatvāna, idaṃ vacanamabravi.

Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the Receiver of Offerings, standing at my head, spoke this word:

‘Passatha imaṃ tāpasaṃ, jaṭilaṃ uggatāpanaṃ;

Aparimeyye ito kappe, buddho loke bhavissati.

“Behold this ascetic, with matted hair, practicing fierce austerities; in immeasurable eons from now, he will become a Buddha in the world.”

‘Ahu [P 1.0016] kapilavhayā rammā, nikkhamitvā tathāgato;

Padhānaṃ padahitvāna, katvā dukkarakārikaṃ.

“From the delightful city named Kapila the Tathāgata will go forth; having striven in the struggle, he will perform the difficult practice.”

‘Ajapālarukkhamūle, nisīditvā tathāgato;

Tattha pāyāsaṃ paggayha, nerañjaramupehiti.

“Having sat down at the foot of the Ajapāla tree, the Tathāgata will there accept the milk-rice and proceed to the Nerañjarā.”

‘Nerañjarāya tīramhi, pāyāsaṃ ada so jino;

Paṭiyattavaramaggena, bodhimūlamūpehiti.

“On the bank of the Nerañjarā, that Victor will eat the milk-rice; by the excellent prepared path, he will approach the foot of the Bodhi tree.”

‘Tato [M 1.0020] padakkhiṇaṃ katvā, bodhimaṇḍaṃ anuttaro;

Assattharukkhamūlamhi, bujjhissati mahāyaso.

“Then, having circumambulated the Bodhimaṇḍa, the unsurpassed one, the greatly renowned one, will awaken at the foot of the Assattha tree.”

‘Imassa janikā mātā, māyā nāma bhavissati;

Pitā suddhodano nāma, ayaṃ hessati gotamo.

“His birth-giving mother will be named Māyā. His father will be named Suddhodana, and this one will be Gotama.”

‘Anāsavā vītarāgā, santacittā samāhitā;

Kolito upatisso ca, aggā hessanti sāvakā;

Ānando nāmupaṭṭhāko, upaṭṭhissati taṃ jinaṃ.

“Taintless, free from passion, with tranquil minds, well-concentrated, Kolita and Upatissa shall be the foremost disciples; the attendant named Ānanda will attend upon that Victor.”

‘Khemā [V 1.0021] uppalavaṇṇā ca, aggā hessanti sāvikā;

Anāsavā vītarāgā, santacittā samāhitā;

Bodhi tassa bhagavato, assatthoti pavuccatī’”ti.

“Khemā and Uppalavaṇṇā shall be the foremost female disciples, taintless, free from passion, with tranquil minds, well-concentrated; the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is said to be the Assattha.”

Sumedhatāpaso “mayhaṃ kira patthanā samijjhissatī”ti somanassappatto ahosi. Mahājano dīpaṅkaradasabalassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sumedhatāpaso kira buddhabījaṃ buddhaṅkuro”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭho ahosi. Evañcassa ahosi “yathā nāma puriso nadiṃ taranto ujukena titthena uttarituṃ asakkonto heṭṭhātitthena uttarati, evameva mayampi dīpaṅkaradasabalassa sāsane maggaphalaṃ alabhamānā anāgate yadā tvaṃ buddho bhavissasi, tadā tava sammukhā maggaphalaṃ sacchikātuṃ samatthā bhaveyyāmā”ti patthanaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Dīpaṅkaradasabalopi bodhisattaṃ pasaṃsitvā aṭṭhahi pupphamuṭṭhīhi pūjetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi, tepi catusatasahassasaṅkhā khīṇāsavā bodhisattaṃ gandhehi ca mālehi ca pūjetvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu. Devamanussā pana tatheva pūjetvā vanditvā pakkantā.

The ascetic Sumedha, thinking, "Indeed, my aspiration will succeed," became filled with joy. The great multitude, upon hearing the words of Dīpaṅkara, the one with Ten Powers, were delighted and thrilled, saying, "Indeed, the ascetic Sumedha is a Buddha-seed, a Buddha-sprout." And it occurred to them: "Just as a man crossing a river, unable to cross by the direct ford, crosses by a lower ford, in the same way, we too, not attaining the path and its fruits in the dispensation of Dīpaṅkara, the one with Ten Powers, will make this aspiration: 'When you become a Buddha in the future, may we be able to realize the path and its fruits in your presence.'" Thus they made their aspiration. Dīpaṅkara, the one with Ten Powers, having praised the Bodhisatta, honored him with eight handfuls of flowers, circumambulated him, and departed. Those four hundred thousand taintless ones also honored the Bodhisatta with perfumes and garlands, circumambulated him, and departed. The gods and humans, having likewise honored and paid homage, then departed.

Bodhisatto sabbesaṃ paṭikkantakāle sayanā vuṭṭhāya “pāramiyo vicinissāmī”ti puppharāsimatthake pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdi. Evaṃ nisinne bodhisatte sakaladasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā sannipatitvā sādhukāraṃ datvā “ayya sumedhatāpasa, porāṇakabodhisattānaṃ pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ‘pāramiyo vicinissāmā’ti nisinnakāle yāni pubbanimittāni nāma paññāyanti, tāni sabbānipi ajja pātubhūtāni, nissaṃsayena [M 1.0021] tvaṃ buddho bhavissasi[P 1.0017], mayampetaṃ jānāma ‘yassetāni nimittāni paññāyanti, ekantena so buddho hoti’, tvaṃ attano vīriyaṃ daḷhaṃ katvā paggaṇhā”ti bodhisattaṃ nānappakārāhi thutīhi abhitthuniṃsu. Tena vuttaṃ –

When everyone had departed, the Bodhisatta rose from where he lay, thinking, “I shall investigate the perfections,” and sat cross-legged upon the heap of flowers. As the Bodhisatta sat thus, all the deities of the ten-thousandfold world system assembled, gave a cry of 'Sādhu!', and said: “Venerable Sumedha, ascetic, the portents that are known to appear when the Bodhisattas of old sat cross-legged thinking, ‘We shall investigate the perfections,’ have all manifested today. Without a doubt, you will become a Buddha. We too know this: ‘For whomever these signs appear, he certainly becomes a Buddha.’ Make your own effort firm and persevere!” Thus they extolled the Bodhisatta with various kinds of praise. Therefore, it is said—

“Idaṃ sutvāna vacanaṃ, asamassa mahesino;

Āmoditā naramarū, buddhabījaṃ kira ayaṃ.

“Having heard this word of the unequalled Great Sage, humans and gods rejoiced, thinking, 'Surely this is a Buddha-seed!'”

‘Ukkuṭṭhisaddā vattanti, apphoṭenti hasanti ca;

Katañjalī namassanti, dasasahassī sadevakā.

“Cries of acclamation arose, they clapped their hands and laughed; with joined palms, the ten-thousandfold world system with its gods paid homage.”

‘Yadimassa [V 1.0022] lokanāthassa, virajjhissāma sāsanaṃ;

Anāgatamhi addhāne, hessāma sammukhā imaṃ.

“If we should miss the dispensation of this Lord of the World, in a future time we shall be in his presence.”

‘Yathā manussā nadiṃ tarantā, paṭibhitthaṃ virajjhiya;

Heṭṭhātitthe gahetvāna, uttaranti mahānadiṃ.

‘Just as people crossing a river, having missed the direct ford, take hold of a lower ford and cross the great river.’

‘Evameva mayaṃ sabbe, yadi muñcāmimaṃ jinaṃ;

Anāgatamhi addhāne, hessāma sammukhā imaṃ’.

‘Even so, all of us, if we should miss this Victor, in a future time we shall be in his presence.’

‘Dīpaṅkaro lokavidū, āhutīnaṃ paṭiggaho;

Mama kammaṃ pakittetvā, dakkhiṇaṃ pādamuddhari.

“Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World, the Receiver of Offerings, having proclaimed my deed, raised his right foot.”

‘Ye tatthāsuṃ jinaputtā, sabbe padakkhiṇamakaṃsu maṃ;

Narā nāgā ca gandhabbā, abhivādetvāna pakkamuṃ.

‘All the Conqueror's sons who were there circumambulated me; men, nāgas, and gandhabbas too, having paid homage, departed.

‘Dassanaṃ me atikkante, sasaṅghe lokanāyake;

Haṭṭhatuṭṭhena cittena, āsanā vuṭṭhahiṃ tadā.

‘When the leader of the world, together with the Sangha, had passed from my sight, with a glad and delighted mind, I then rose from my seat.

‘Sukhena sukhito homi, pāmojjena pamodito;

Pītiyā ca abhissanno, pallaṅkaṃ ābhujiṃ tadā.

‘I became happy with happiness, joyful with gladness; pervaded by rapture, I then folded my legs into the cross-legged posture.

‘Pallaṅkena nisīditvā, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā;

‘Vasībhūto ahaṃ jhāne, abhiññāsu pāramiṃ gato.

‘Having sat cross-legged, I then reflected thus: “I have become a master of jhāna, I have gone to perfection in the higher knowledges.

‘Sahassiyamhi lokamhi, isayo natthi me samā;

Asamo iddhidhammesu, alabhiṃ īdisaṃ sukhaṃ’.

‘In this thousandfold world, there is no sage equal to me; unmatched in the qualities of psychic power, I have obtained such happiness’.

‘Pallaṅkābhujane [M 1.0022] mayhaṃ, dasasahassādhivāsino;

Mahānādaṃ pavattesuṃ, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Upon my folding of the cross-legged posture, the inhabitants of the ten-thousandfold world-system uttered a great cry: “Surely, you will become a Buddha!

‘Yā [V 1.0023] pubbe bodhisattānaṃ, pallaṅkavaramābhuje;

Nimittāni padissanti, tāni ajja padissare.

‘The signs that formerly appeared when Bodhisattas assumed the excellent cross-legged seat, those signs appear today.

‘Sītaṃ byapagataṃ hoti, uṇhañca upasammati;

Tāni ajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘The cold has departed, and the heat has subsided; these signs appear today, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Dasasahassī lokadhātū, nissaddā honti nirākulā;
