Tāni ajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘The ten-thousandfold world-system becomes silent and untroubled; these signs appear today, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Mahāvātā [P 1.0018] na vāyanti, na sandanti savantiyo;

Tāni ajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Great winds do not blow, and rivers do not flow; these signs appear today, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Thalajā dakajā pupphā, sabbe pupphanti tāvade;

Tepajja pupphitā sabbe, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Flowers born on land and in water all bloom at that time; today they are all in bloom, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Latā vā yadi vā rukkhā, phalabhārā honti tāvade;

Tepajja phalitā sabbe, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Creepers and trees become laden with fruit at that time; today they all bear fruit, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Ākāsaṭṭhā ca bhūmaṭṭhā, ratanā jotanti tāvade;

Tepajja ratanā jotanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Jewels in the sky and on the earth shine at that time; today those jewels are shining, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Mānusakā ca dibbā ca, turiyā vajjanti tāvade;

Tepajjubho abhiravanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Human and divine musical instruments play at that time; today they both resound, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Vicittapupphā gaganā, abhivassanti tāvade;

Tepi ajja pavassanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Various flowers rain down from the sky at that time; today they also rain down, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Mahāsamuddo ābhujati, dasasahassī pakampati;

Tepajjubho abhiravanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘The great ocean roars, the ten-thousandfold world-system quakes; today both resound, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Nirayepi [V 1.0024] dasasahasse, aggī nibbanti tāvade;

Tepajja nibbutā aggī, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘In the hells of the ten-thousandfold world-system, fires are extinguished at that time; today those fires are extinguished, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Vimalo hoti sūriyo, sabbā dissanti tārakā;

Tepi ajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘The sun becomes spotless, all the stars are seen; these also appear today, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Anovaṭṭhena [M 1.0023] udakaṃ, mahiyā ubbhijji tāvade;

Tampajjubbhijjate mahiyā, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Water, not from rain, springs forth from the earth at that time; that also springs forth from the earth today, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Tārāgaṇā virocanti, nakkhattā gaganamaṇḍale;

Visākhā candimāyuttā, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘The hosts of stars shine brightly, the constellations in the celestial sphere; Visākhā is conjoined with the moon, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Bilāsayā darīsayā, nikkhamanti sakāsayā;

Tepajja āsayā chuddhā, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Those dwelling in holes and caves emerge from their own abodes; today their abodes are abandoned, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Na hoti arati sattānaṃ, santuṭṭhā honti tāvade;

Tepajja sabbe santuṭṭhā, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘There is no discontent among beings, they become content at that time; today all are content, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Rogā tadūpasammanti, jighacchā ca vinassati;

Tānipajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Diseases then subside, and hunger is destroyed; these signs appear today, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Rāgo tadā tanu hoti, doso moho vinassati;

Tepajja vigatā sabbe, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Lust then grows thin, hatred and delusion are destroyed; today they are all gone, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Bhayaṃ tadā na bhavati, ajjapetaṃ padissati;

Tena liṅgena jānāma, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Fear does not exist then, and today this is seen; by this sign we know, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Rajo nuddhaṃsati uddhaṃ, ajjapetaṃ padissati;

Tena liṅgena jānāma, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Dust is not scattered upwards, and today this is seen; by this sign we know, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Aniṭṭhagandho [V 1.0025] pakkamati, diṭṭhagandho pavāyati;

Sopajja vāyati gandho, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Unpleasant odors depart, and pleasant fragrances pervade; that fragrance also wafts today, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Sabbe [P 1.0019] devā padissanti, ṭhapayitvā arūpino;

Tepajja sabbe dissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘All devas appear, except for the formless ones; today they are all seen, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Yāvatā nirayā nāma, sabbe dissanti tāvade;

Tepajja sabbe dissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘However many hells there are by name, all are seen at that time; today they are all seen, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Kuṭṭā kavāṭā selā ca, na hontāvaraṇā tadā;

Ākāsabhūtā tepajja, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Walls, doors, and rocks are not then an obstruction; today they have become like space, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Cutī ca upapatti ca, khaṇe tasmiṃ na vijjati;

Tānipajja padissanti, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasi.

‘Passing away and rebirth do not occur in that moment; these signs appear today, surely you will become a Buddha.

‘Daḷhaṃ [M 1.0024] paggaṇha vīriyaṃ, mā nivatta abhikkama;

Mayampetaṃ vijānāma, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavissasī’”ti.

‘Firmly exert your energy, do not turn back, go forward! We also know this, surely you will become a Buddha.’”

Bodhisatto dīpaṅkaradasabalassa ca dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatānañca vacanaṃ sutvā bhiyyoso mattāya sañjātussāho hutvā cintesi “buddhā nāma amoghavacanā, natthi buddhānaṃ kathāya aññathattaṃ. Yathā hi ākāse khittaleḍḍussa patanaṃ dhuvaṃ, jātassa maraṇaṃ dhuvaṃ, aruṇe uggate sūriyassuṭṭhānaṃ, āsayā nikkhantasīhassa sīhanādanadanaṃ, garugabbhāya itthiyā bhāramoropanaṃ avassaṃbhāvī, evameva buddhānaṃ vacanaṃ nāma dhuvaṃ amoghaṃ, addhā ahaṃ buddho bhavissāmī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Hearing the words of Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, and of the deities of the ten-thousandfold world-sphere, the Bodhisatta, filled with even greater enthusiasm, reflected thus: “Indeed, Buddhas speak words that are never in vain; there is no deviation in the speech of the Buddhas. Just as the fall of a clod of earth thrown into the sky is certain, as death is certain for one who is born, as the sun must rise when dawn appears, as a lion emerging from its lair must roar its lion's roar, as a woman heavy with child must surely lay down her burden—so too is the word of the Buddhas certain and unfailing. Surely, I shall become a Buddha.” Thus it is said:

“Buddhassa vacanaṃ sutvā, dasasahassīna cūbhayaṃ;

Tuṭṭhahaṭṭho pamodito, evaṃ cintesahaṃ tadā.

“Having heard the word of the Buddha and of those of the ten-thousandfold world-system, delighted, joyful, and elated, thus I thought at that time.

“Advejjhavacanā buddhā, amoghavacanā jinā;

Vitathaṃ natthi buddhānaṃ, dhuvaṃ buddho bhavāmahaṃ.

“The Buddhas speak words that are certain, the Conquerors' words are never in vain; there is no falsehood in the Buddhas, surely I shall become a Buddha.

“Yathā [V 1.0026] khittaṃ nabhe leḍḍu, dhuvaṃ patati bhūmiyaṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

“Just as a clod thrown into the sky surely falls to the ground, so too is the word of the foremost Buddhas certain and eternal.

“Yathāpi sabbasattānaṃ, maraṇaṃ dhuvasassataṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

“Just as for all beings death is certain and eternal, so too is the word of the foremost Buddhas certain and eternal.

“Yathā rattikkhaye patte, sūriyuggamanaṃ dhuvaṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

“Just as, when the night has ended, the rising of the sun is certain, so too is the word of the foremost Buddhas certain and eternal.

“Yathā nikkhantasayanassa, sīhassa nadanaṃ dhuvaṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassataṃ.

Just as the roar of a lion is certain when it leaves its lair, so too is the word of the supreme Buddhas, certain and eternal.

“Yathā āpannasattānaṃ, bhāramoropanaṃ dhuvaṃ;

Tatheva buddhaseṭṭhānaṃ, vacanaṃ dhuvasassata”nti.

Just as for afflicted beings, the setting down of the burden is certain, so too is the word of the supreme Buddhas, certain and everlasting.

So “dhuvāhaṃ buddho bhavissāmī”ti evaṃ katasanniṭṭhāno buddhakārake dhamme upadhāretuṃ “kahaṃ nu kho buddhakārakadhammā, kiṃ [P 1.0020] uddhaṃ, udāhu adho, disāsu, vidisāsū”ti anukkamena sakalaṃ dhammadhātuṃ vicinanto porāṇakabodhisattehi āsevitanisevitaṃ paṭhamaṃ dānapāramiṃ disvā evaṃ attānaṃ ovadi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya paṭhamaṃ dānapāramiṃ pūreyyāsi. Yathā hi nikkujjito udakakumbho nissesaṃ katvā udakaṃ [M 1.0025] vamatiyeva, na paccāharati, evameva dhanaṃ vā yasaṃ vā puttaṃ vā dāraṃ vā aṅgapaccaṅgaṃ vā anoloketvā sampattayācakānaṃ sabbaṃ icchiticchitaṃ nissesaṃ katvā dadamāno bodhirukkhamūle nisīditvā buddho bhavissasī”ti paṭhamaṃ dānapāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

'Surely, I will become a Buddha.' Having made this firm resolution, he sought to ascertain the qualities that make a Buddha, thinking, 'Where are the qualities that make a Buddha? Above, or below, in the cardinal directions, or the intermediate directions?' Gradually examining the entire realm of the Dhamma, he first saw the perfection of giving, practiced and cultivated by ancient Bodhisattas. He then admonished himself thus: 'Wise Sumedha, from now on, you must first fulfill the perfection of giving. Just as an overturned water pot pours out all its water completely, not taking any back, so too, without regard for wealth, fame, son, wife, or even your major and minor limbs, you must give everything desired to those who ask, holding nothing back. Seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, you will become a Buddha.' Thus, he firmly resolved upon the first perfection of giving. Therefore, it was said:

“Handa buddhakare dhamme, vicināmi ito cito;

Uddhaṃ adho dasa disā, yāvatā dhammadhātuyā.

Come, let me investigate the Buddha-making qualities, searching here and there; upwards, downwards, and in the ten directions, as far as the realm of the Dhamma extends.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, anuciṇṇaṃ mahāpathaṃ.

Searching, then I saw the first perfection of giving, a great path frequented by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ [V 1.0027] tvaṃ paṭhamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Dānapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This you must first firmly undertake: go to the perfection of giving, if you wish to attain enlightenment.

“Yathāpi kumbho sampuṇṇo, yassa kassaci adhokato;

Vamatevudakaṃ nissesaṃ, na tattha parirakkhati.

Just as a pot filled to the brim, overturned by anyone at all, empties out all its water completely, and nothing is retained there.

“Tatheva yācake disvā, hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime;

Dadāhi dānaṃ nissesaṃ, kumbho viya adhokato”ti.

So too, upon seeing beggars—lowly, superior, or middling—give a gift without reservation, like an overturned pot.

Athassa “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato dutiyaṃ sīlapāramiṃ disvā etadahosi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya sīlapāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Yathā hi camarīmigo nāma jīvitampi anoloketvā attano vālameva rakkhati, evaṃ tvampi ito paṭṭhāya jīvitampi anoloketvā sīlameva rakkhanto buddho bhavissasī”ti dutiyaṃ sīlapāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, considering further, 'There must not be only these qualities for making one a Buddha,' he saw the second perfection of virtue and thought: 'Wise Sumedha, from now on you should fulfill the perfection of virtue as well. For just as the yak, not caring for its life, guards its own tail, so too, from now on, without regard for your life, you must guard your virtue and thus become a Buddha.' Thus, he firmly resolved upon the second perfection of virtue. Therefore, it is said:

“Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Not only these are the Buddha-qualities; I shall seek out other qualities too, which conduce to awakening.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, dutiyaṃ sīlapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Searching, then I saw the second perfection of virtue, cultivated and frequented by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ tvaṃ dutiyaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Sīlapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This second one you must first firmly undertake: go to the perfection of virtue, if you wish to attain awakening.

“Yathāpi camarī vālaṃ, kismiñci paṭilaggitaṃ;

Upeti maraṇaṃ tattha, na vikopeti vāladhiṃ.

Just as a yak, when its tail is caught on something, meets death there rather than damaging its tail.

“Tatheva [P 1.0021] catūsu[M 1.0026], bhūmīsu, sīlāni paripūraya;

Parirakkha sabbadā sīlaṃ, camarī viya vāladhi”nti.

Just so, in the four planes, fulfill the virtues; always guard your virtue, like a yak its tail.

Athassa [V 1.0028] “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato tatiyaṃ nekkhammapāramiṃ disvā etadahosi “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya nekkhammapāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Yathā hi ciraṃ bandhanāgāre vasamāno puriso na tattha sinehaṃ karoti, atha kho ukkaṇṭhitoyeva avasitukāmo hoti, evameva tvampi sabbabhave bandhanāgārasadise katvā sabbabhavehi ukkaṇṭhito muccitukāmo hutvā nekkhammābhimukhova hohi, evaṃ buddho bhavissasī”ti tatiyaṃ nekkhammapāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, considering further, 'There must not be only these qualities for making one a Buddha,' he saw the third perfection of renunciation, and thought: 'Wise Sumedha, from now on you should also fulfill the perfection of renunciation. Just as a man living long in a prison does not develop affection for it, but rather longs to be free, so too should you regard all existences as like a prison and, longing to be freed from all existences, be intent on renunciation—thus will you become a Buddha.' Thus, he firmly resolved upon the third perfection of renunciation. Therefore, it is said:

“Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Not only these are the Buddha-qualities; I shall seek out other qualities too, which conduce to awakening.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, tatiyaṃ nekkhammapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Searching, then I saw the third perfection of renunciation, cultivated and frequented by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ tvaṃ tatiyaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Nekkhammapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This third one you must first firmly undertake: go to the perfection of renunciation, if you wish to attain awakening.

“Yathā andughare puriso, ciravuttho dukhaṭṭito;

Na tattha rāgaṃ janeti, muttimeva gavesati.

Just as a man in a prison house, long confined and suffering, does not conceive affection for it, but only seeks release.

“Tatheva tvaṃ sabbabhave, passa andughare viya;

Nekkhammābhimukho hohi, bhavato parimuttiyā”ti.

So too should you see all existences as a prison house; be intent on renunciation for complete liberation from existence.

Athassa “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato catutthaṃ paññāpāramiṃ disvā etadahosi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya paññāpāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Hīnamajjhimukkaṭṭhesu kañci avajjetvā sabbepi paṇḍite upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ puccheyyāsi. Yathā hi piṇḍacāriko bhikkhu hīnādikesu kulesu kiñci avajjetvā paṭipāṭiyā piṇḍāya caranto khippaṃ yāpanaṃ labhati, evaṃ tvampi sabbapaṇḍite upasaṅkamitvā pañhaṃ pucchanto buddho bhavissasī”ti catutthaṃ paññāpāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, considering further, 'There must not be only these qualities for making one a Buddha,' he saw the fourth perfection of wisdom and thought: 'Wise Sumedha, from now on you should fulfill the perfection of wisdom as well. Without omitting anyone, whether inferior, middling, or superior, you should approach all the wise and ask questions. Just as a monk on alms-round, without omitting any families, whether lowly or high, going for alms in due order, quickly obtains his sustenance, so too, by approaching all the wise and asking questions, you will become a Buddha.' Thus, he firmly resolved upon the fourth perfection of wisdom. Therefore, it is said:

“Na [V 1.0029][M 1.0027] hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Not only these are the Buddha-qualities; I shall seek out other qualities too, which conduce to awakening.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, catutthaṃ paññāpāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Searching, then I saw the fourth perfection of wisdom, cultivated and frequented by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ tvaṃ catutthaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Paññāpāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

This fourth one you must first firmly undertake: go to the perfection of wisdom, if you wish to attain awakening.

“Yathāpi [P 1.0022] bhikkhu bhikkhanto, hīnamukkaṭṭhamajjhime;

Kulāni na vivajjento, evaṃ labhati yāpanaṃ.

Just as a monk on alms round, not omitting families whether lowly, high, or middling, thus obtains his sustenance.

“Tatheva tvaṃ sabbakālaṃ, paripucchanto budhaṃ janaṃ;

Paññāpāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti.

Just so you, always questioning the wise, having gone to the perfection of wisdom, will attain perfect awakening.

Athassa “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato pañcamaṃ vīriyapāramiṃ disvā etadahosi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya vīriyapāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Yathā hi sīho migarājā sabbairiyāpathesu daḷhavīriyo hoti, evaṃ tvampi sabbabhavesu sabbairiyāpathesu daḷhavīriyo anolīnavīriyo samāno buddho bhavissasī”ti pañcamaṃ vīriyapāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, considering further, "One should not be content with just these qualities that make a Buddha," he saw the fifth perfection of energy and thought: "Wise Sumedha, from now on you should fulfill the perfection of energy as well. Just as the lion, the king of beasts, is firm in energy in all postures, so too, you, being firm in energy and unflagging in energy in all existences and all postures, will become a Buddha." Thus, having made the fifth perfection of energy firm, he made his resolution. Therefore, it was said:

“Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Not only these are the Buddha-qualities; I shall seek out other qualities too, which are conducive to awakening.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, pañcamaṃ vīriyapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Searching, I then saw the fifth perfection of energy, cultivated and frequented by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ tvaṃ pañcamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Vīriyapāramitaṃ gaccha, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

First, take up this fifth one, having made it firm; go to the perfection of energy, if you wish to attain awakening.

“Yathāpi [V 1.0030] sīho migarājā, nisajjaṭṭhānacaṅkame;

Alīnavīriyo hoti, paggahitamano sadā.

Just as the lion, the king of beasts, in sitting, standing, and walking, is unflagging in energy, with an exerted mind always.

“Tatheva tvaṃ sabbabhave, paggaṇha vīriyaṃ daḷhaṃ;

Vīriyapāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti.

Just so, in every existence, take up firm energy; having gone to the perfection of energy, you will attain perfect awakening.

Athassa “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato chaṭṭhaṃ khantipāramiṃ disvā etadahosi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito [M 1.0028] paṭṭhāya khantipāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Sammānanepi avamānanepi khamova bhaveyyāsi. Yathā hi pathaviyaṃ nāma sucimpi pakkhipanti asucimpi, na tena pathavī sinehaṃ, na paṭighaṃ karoti, khamati sahati adhivāsetiyeva, evaṃ tvampi sammānanāvamānanakkhamova samāno buddho bhavissasī”ti chaṭṭhaṃ khantipāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, considering further, "One should not be content with just these qualities that make a Buddha," he saw the sixth perfection of patience and thought: "Wise Sumedha, from now on you should fulfill the perfection of patience as well. Whether honored or dishonored, you should be patient. Just as the earth, indeed, when they cast clean and unclean things upon it, does not for that reason feel affection or aversion, but just endures, bears, and tolerates it—so too, you, being patient with honor and dishonor, will become a Buddha." Thus, having made the sixth perfection of patience firm, he made his resolution. Therefore, it was said:

“Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Not only these are the Buddha-qualities; I shall seek out other qualities too, which are conducive to awakening.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, chaṭṭhamaṃ khantipāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Searching, I then saw the sixth perfection of patience, cultivated and frequented by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ tvaṃ chaṭṭhamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Tattha advejjhamānaso, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

First, take up this sixth one, having made it firm; there, with an unwavering mind, you will attain perfect awakening.

“Yathāpi [P 1.0023] pathavī nāma, sucimpi asucimpi ca;

Sabbaṃ sahati nikkhepaṃ, na karoti paṭighaṃ tayā.

Just as the earth, indeed, endures everything cast upon it, both clean and unclean, and does not react with aversion thereto.

“Tatheva tvampi sabbesaṃ, sammānāvamānakkhamo;

Khantipāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti.

Just so, you too, patient with the honor and dishonor from all, having gone to the perfection of patience, will attain perfect awakening.

Athassa “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato sattamaṃ saccapāramiṃ disvā etadahosi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya saccapāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Asaniyā [V 1.0031] matthake patamānāyapi dhanādīnaṃ atthāya chandādivasena sampajānamusāvādaṃ nāma mākāsi. Yathā hi osadhitārakā nāma sabbautūsu attano gamanavīthiṃ jahitvā aññāya vīthiyā na gacchati, sakavīthiyāva gacchati, evameva tvampi saccaṃ pahāya musāvādaṃ nāma akarontoyeva buddho bhavissasī”ti sattamaṃ saccapāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, considering further, "One should not be content with just these qualities that make a Buddha," he saw the seventh perfection of truth and thought: "Wise Sumedha, from now on you should fulfill the perfection of truth as well. Even if a thunderbolt were to fall on your head, you should never knowingly speak a falsehood for the sake of wealth and so forth, or because of desire and so on. Just as the Osadhi star, indeed, in all seasons, never abandons its own course to take another; it goes only on its own course. Even so, you, by not abandoning truth and not speaking falsehood, will become a Buddha." Thus, having made the seventh perfection of truth firm, he made his resolution. Therefore, it was said:

“Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Not only these are the Buddha-qualities; I shall seek out other qualities too, which are conducive to awakening.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, sattamaṃ saccapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Searching, I then saw the seventh perfection of truth, cultivated and frequented by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ [M 1.0029] tvaṃ sattamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Tattha advejjhavacano, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

First, take up this seventh one, having made it firm; there, with unwavering speech, you will attain perfect awakening.

“Yathāpi osadhī nāma, tulābhūtā sadevake;

Samaye utuvasse vā, na vokkamati vīthito.

Just as the Osadhi star, a standard for the world with its gods, does not deviate from its path in any season or time of year.

“Tatheva tvampi saccesu, mā vokkamasi vīthito;

Saccapāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti.

Just so, you too, in the truths, do not deviate from the path; having gone to the perfection of truth, you will attain perfect awakening.

Athassa “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato aṭṭhamaṃ adhiṭṭhānapāramiṃ disvā etadahosi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya adhiṭṭhānapāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Yaṃ adhiṭṭhāsi, tasmiṃ adhiṭṭhāne niccalo bhaveyyāsi. Yathā hi pabbato nāma sabbadisāsu vātehi pahaṭopi na kampati na calati, attano ṭhāneyeva tiṭṭhati, evameva tvampi attano adhiṭṭhāne niccalo hontova buddho bhavissasī”ti aṭṭhamaṃ adhiṭṭhānapāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, considering further, "One should not be content with just these qualities that make a Buddha," he saw the eighth perfection of determination and thought: "Wise Sumedha, from now on you should fulfill the perfection of determination as well. In whatever you determine, you should be unshakable in that determination. Just as a mountain, indeed, though struck by winds from all directions, does not tremble or shake, but remains in its own place, even so, you, being unshakable in your determination, will become a Buddha." Thus, having made the eighth perfection of determination firm, he made his resolution. Therefore, it was said:

“Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

Not only these are the Buddha-qualities; I shall seek out other qualities too, which are conducive to awakening.

“Vicinanto [V 1.0032][P 1.0024] tadādakkhiṃ, aṭṭhamaṃ adhiṭṭhānapāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

Searching, I then saw the eighth perfection of determination, cultivated and frequented by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ tvaṃ aṭṭhamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Tattha tvaṃ acalo hutvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

First, take up this eighth one, having made it firm; there, being unwavering, you shall attain perfect awakening.

“Yathāpi pabbato selo, acalo suppatiṭṭhito;

Na kampati bhusavātehi, sakaṭṭhāneva tiṭṭhati.

Just as a rocky mountain, unmoving and well-established, does not tremble in strong winds, but remains in its own place.

“Tatheva tvampi adhiṭṭhāne, sabbadā acalo bhava;

Adhiṭṭhānapāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti.

Just so, you too, in your determination, always be unwavering; having gone to the perfection of determination, you will attain perfect awakening.

Athassa “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato navamaṃ mettāpāramiṃ disvā etadahosi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya navamaṃ mettāpāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Ahitesupi hitesupi ekacitto bhaveyyāsi. Yathā hi udakaṃ nāma pāpajanassāpi kalyāṇajanassāpi sītibhāvaṃ ekasadisaṃ katvā pharati, evameva tvampi sabbasattesu [M 1.0030] mettacittena ekacittova honto buddho bhavissasī”ti navamaṃ mettāpāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, reflecting further, "One should not rest content with just these qualities conducive to Buddhahood," he saw the ninth perfection, loving-kindness, and it occurred to him: "Wise Sumedha, from now on you shall fulfill the ninth perfection of loving-kindness as well. You shall be of one mind towards both those who are hostile and those who are friendly. Just as water spreads its coolness equally to both the wicked and the virtuous, even so shall you, with a mind of loving-kindness toward all beings, remaining of one mind, become a Buddha." Having made firm the ninth perfection of loving-kindness, he resolved. Therefore, it is said:

“Na hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

"These are not the only qualities of a Buddha; I shall seek out other qualities too, which are conducive to awakening.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, navamaṃ mettāpāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

"Searching, I saw the ninth perfection, loving-kindness, cultivated and practiced by the great sages of old.

“Imaṃ tvaṃ navamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Mettāya asamo hohi, yadi bodhiṃ pattumicchasi.

"First, firmly undertake this ninth one; be unequalled in loving-kindness, if you wish to attain awakening.

“Yathāpi udakaṃ nāma, kalyāṇe pāpake jane;

Samaṃ pharati sītena, pavāheti rajomalaṃ.

"Just as water, indeed, on both good and bad people, equally spreads its coolness and carries away dirt and grime.

“Tatheva [V 1.0033] tvampi ahitahite, samaṃ mettāya bhāvaya;

Mettāpāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti.

"So too shall you cultivate loving-kindness equally towards those who are hostile and those who are friendly; having reached the perfection of loving-kindness, you will attain perfect enlightenment."

Athassa “na ettakeheva buddhakārakadhammehi bhavitabba”nti uttaripi upadhārayato dasamaṃ upekkhāpāramiṃ disvā etadahosi – “sumedhapaṇḍita, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya upekkhāpāramimpi pūreyyāsi. Sukhepi dukkhepi majjhattova bhaveyyāsi. Yathā hi pathavī nāma sucimpi asucimpi pakkhippamānā majjhattāva hoti, evameva tvampi sukhadukkhesu majjhattova honto buddho bhavissasī”ti dasamaṃ upekkhāpāramiṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, considering further, "One should not be content with just these qualities conducive to Buddhahood," he saw the tenth perfection, equanimity, and it occurred to him: "Wise Sumedha, from now on you shall fulfill the perfection of equanimity as well. You shall remain neutral in both pleasure and pain. Just as the earth remains neutral when pure or impure things are thrown upon it, even so shall you, remaining neutral in pleasure and pain, become a Buddha." Having made firm the tenth perfection, equanimity, he resolved. Therefore, it is said:

“Na [P 1.0025] hete ettakāyeva, buddhadhammā bhavissare;

Aññepi vicinissāmi, ye dhammā bodhipācanā.

"These are not the only qualities of a Buddha; I shall seek out other qualities too, which are conducive to awakening.

“Vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, dasamaṃ upekkhāpāramiṃ;

Pubbakehi mahesīhi, āsevitanisevitaṃ.

"Searching, I saw the tenth perfection, equanimity, cultivated and practiced by the great sages of the past.

“Imaṃ tvaṃ dasamaṃ tāva, daḷhaṃ katvā samādiya;

Tulābhūto daḷho hutvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasi.

"First, firmly undertake this tenth one; being steadfast like a balance, you will attain perfect enlightenment.

“Yathāpi pathavī nāma, nikkhittaṃ asuciṃ suciṃ;

Upekkhati ubhopete, kopānunayavajjitā.

"Just as the earth, indeed, regards with equanimity both the pure and the impure deposited on it, devoid of aversion and attraction.

“Tatheva tvampi sukhadukkhe, tulābhūto sadā bhava;

Upekkhāpāramitaṃ gantvā, sambodhiṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti.

"So too shall you always be balanced regarding pleasure and pain; having reached the perfection of equanimity, you will attain perfect enlightenment."

Tato [M 1.0031] cintesi – “imasmiṃ loke bodhisattehi pūretabbā bodhiparipācanā buddhakārakadhammā ettakāyeva, dasa pāramiyo ṭhapetvā aññe natthi, imāpi dasa pāramiyo uddhaṃ ākāsepi natthi, heṭṭhā pathaviyampi, puratthimādīsu disāsupi natthi, mayhameva pana hadayamaṃsabbhantare patiṭṭhitā”ti. Evaṃ tāsaṃ hadaye patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ disvā sabbāpi tā daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāya punappunaṃ sammasanto anulomapaṭilomaṃ sammasati, pariyante gahetvā ādiṃ pāpeti, ādimhi gahetvā pariyante ṭhapeti, majjhe gahetvā ubhato osāpeti, ubhato koṭīsu [V 1.0034] hetvā majjhe osāpeti. Bāhirakabhaṇḍapariccāgo dānapāramī nāma, aṅgapariccāgo dānaupapāramī nāma, jīvitapariccāgo dānaparamatthapāramī nāmāti dasa pāramiyo dasa upapāramiyo dasa paramatthapāramiyo yantatelaṃ vinivaṭṭento viya mahāmeruṃ matthaṃ katvā cakkavāḷamahāsamuddaṃ āluḷento viya ca sammasi. Tassevaṃ dasa pāramiyo sammasantassa dhammatejena catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalā ayaṃ mahāpathavī hatthinā akkantanaḷakalāpo viya, pīḷiyamānaṃ ucchuyantaṃ viya ca mahāviravaṃ viravamānā saṅkampi sampakampi sampavedhi, kulālacakkaṃ viya telayantacakkaṃ viya ca paribbhami. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then he reflected: "In this world, the qualities conducive to the ripening of enlightenment and to Buddhahood, to be fulfilled by bodhisattas, are only these—there are none other than the ten perfections. These ten perfections exist neither in the sky above nor in the earth below, nor in the eastern and other directions. They are established within my own heart and flesh." Seeing them thus established in his heart, he made a firm resolve and repeatedly contemplated them, examining them forwards and backwards. Taking the end, he reached the beginning; taking the beginning, he set it at the end. Taking the middle, he extended it to both sides; taking both extremities, he extended them to the middle. The relinquishment of external possessions is called the perfection of giving (dānapāramī). The relinquishment of limbs is called the sub-perfection of giving (dānaupapāramī). The relinquishment of life is called the ultimate perfection of giving (dānaparamatthapāramī). Thus, the ten perfections, the ten sub-perfections, and the ten ultimate perfections—like one extracting oil by press, like one churning the great ocean of the cosmos with Mount Meru as the churning stick—he thoroughly contemplated. As he thus contemplated the ten perfections, the power of his Dhamma caused this great earth, two hundred and forty thousand leagues thick, to tremble, shake, and quake violently, like a clump of reeds trampled by an elephant, like sugarcane being pressed in a mill, roaring with a great roar, spinning like a potter’s wheel or an oil press. Therefore, it is said:

“Ettakāyeva te loke, ye dhammā bodhipācanā;

Tatuddhaṃ natthi aññatra, daḷhaṃ tattha patiṭṭhaha.

"These are the only qualities in the world that conduce to the ripening of enlightenment; beyond these there is nothing else, so stand firm in them.

“Ime dhamme sammasato, sabhāvasarasalakkhaṇe;

Dhammatejena vasudhā, dasasahassī pakampatha.

"While contemplating these qualities, with their intrinsic nature, essence, and characteristics, by the power of the Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world system trembled.

“Calatī ravatī pathavī, ucchuyantaṃva pīḷitaṃ;

Telayante yathā cakkaṃ, evaṃ kampati medanī”ti.

"The earth trembles and roars, as if pressed in a sugarcane mill; like a wheel in an oil press, so the ground shakes."

Mahāpathaviyā [P 1.0026] kampamānāya rammanagaravāsino saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontā yugantavātabbhāhatā mahāsālā viya mucchitamucchitāva papatiṃsu, ghaṭādīni [M 1.0032] kulālabhājanāni pavaṭṭantāni aññamaññaṃ paharantāni cuṇṇavicuṇṇāni ahesuṃ. Mahājano bhītatasito satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ nu kho bhagavā nāgāvaṭṭo ayaṃ bhūtayakkhadevatāsu aññatarāvaṭṭoti na hi mayaṃ etaṃ jānāma, apica kho sabbopi ayaṃ mahājano upadduto, kiṃ nu kho imassa lokassa pāpakaṃ bhavissati, udāhu kalyāṇaṃ, kathetha no etaṃ kāraṇa”nti āha. Atha satthā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “tumhe mā bhāyatha mā cintayittha, natthi vo itonidānaṃ bhayaṃ. Yo so mayā ajja sumedhapaṇḍito ‘anāgate gotamo nāma buddho bhavissatī’ti byākato, so dasa pāramiyo sammasati, tassa dasa pāramiyo sammasantassa viloḷentassa dhammatejena sakaladasasahassilokadhātu ekappahārena kampati, ceva, ravati cā”ti āha. Tena vuttaṃ –

When the great earth trembled, the inhabitants of the city of Ramma, unable to stand firm, fell down senseless again and again like great sāla trees struck by a storm at the end of an aeon. Pots and other vessels made by potters rolled about, striking each other, and were shattered into tiny pieces. The terrified and agitated people approached the Teacher and said, "What is this, Blessed One? Is this a convulsion of a nāga, or a convulsion of some spirit, yakkha, or deity? We do not know. But indeed, all these people are distressed. Will this bring evil or good to the world? Please tell us the reason." Then the Teacher, hearing their words, said, "Do not fear or worry. There is no danger for you arising from this. The wise Sumedha, whom I declared today, saying, 'In the future, he will become the Buddha named Gotama,' is contemplating the ten perfections. As he contemplates and churns the ten perfections, by the power of his Dhamma the entire ten-thousandfold world-system trembles and resounds at once." Thus it was said:

“Yāvatā parisā āsi, buddhassa parivesane;

Pavedhamānā sā tattha, mucchitā sesi bhūmiyaṃ.

The entire assembly that was in the Buddha's presence trembled there and lay senseless upon the ground.

“Ghaṭānekasahassāni[V 1.0035], kumbhīnañca satā bahū;

Sañcuṇṇamathitā tattha, aññamaññaṃ paghaṭṭitā.

Many thousands of pots and many hundreds of jars were shattered and crushed there, striking against one another.

“Ubbiggā tasitā bhītā, bhantā byadhitamānasā;

Mahājanā samāgamma, dīpaṅkaramupāgamuṃ.

Agitated, terrified, frightened, bewildered, and with afflicted minds, the great multitude gathered and approached Dīpaṅkara.

‘Kiṃ bhavissati lokassa, kalyāṇamatha pāpakaṃ;

Sabbo upadduto loko, taṃ vinodehi cakkhuma’.

‘What will befall the world—good or evil? The whole world is afflicted. Dispel this, O Visionary One.’

“Tesaṃ tadā saññāpesi, dīpaṅkaro mahāmuni;

Vissatthā hotha mā bhātha, imasmiṃ pathavikampane.

Then the great sage Dīpaṅkara reassured them: ‘Be at ease, do not fear this earthquake.’

“Yamahaṃ ajja byākāsiṃ, buddho loke bhavissati;

Eso sammasati dhammaṃ, pubbakaṃ jinasevitaṃ.

‘The one whom I predicted today will become a Buddha in the world is contemplating the Dhamma practiced by former Conquerors.’

“Tassa sammasato dhammaṃ, buddhabhūmiṃ asesato;

Tenāyaṃ kampitā pathavī, dasasahassī sadevake”ti.

‘As he contemplates the Dhamma, the state of Buddhahood in its entirety, this ten-thousandfold world with its deities trembles on that account.’

Mahājano tathāgatassa vacanaṃ sutvā haṭṭhatuṭṭho mālāgandhavilepanaṃ ādāya rammanagarā nikkhamitvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā mālādīhi pūjetvā [M 1.0033] vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā rammanagarameva pāvisi. Bodhisattopi dasa pāramiyo sammasitvā vīriyaṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāya nisinnāsanā vuṭṭhāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Hearing the Tathāgata's words, the great multitude, delighted and joyful, taking garlands, perfumes, and unguents, left the city of Ramma, approached the Bodhisatta, honored him with garlands and the like, paid homage, circumambulated him, and re-entered the city of Ramma. The Bodhisatta, having reflected on the ten perfections, strengthened his energy, made a firm determination, and rose from his seat. Thus it was said:

“Buddhassa [P 1.0027] vacanaṃ sutvā, mano nibbāyi tāvade;

Sabbe maṃ upasaṅkamma, punāpi abhivandisuṃ.

“Hearing the Buddha's words, their minds were immediately calmed; all approached me and paid homage to me once more.”

“Samādiyitvā buddhaguṇaṃ, daḷhaṃ katvāna mānasaṃ;

Dīpaṅkaraṃ namassitvā, āsanā vuṭṭhahiṃ tadā”ti.

“Having resolved upon the qualities of a Buddha and made my mind firm, I paid homage to Dīpaṅkara and then rose from my seat.”

Atha bodhisattaṃ āsanā vuṭṭhahantaṃ sakaladasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā sannipatitvā dibbehi mālāgandhehi [V 1.0036] pūjetvā vanditvā “ayya sumedhatāpasa, tayā ajja dīpaṅkaradasabalassa pādamūle mahatī patthanā patthitā, sā te anantarāyena samijjhatu, mā te bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vā ahosi, sarīre appamattakopi rogo mā uppajji, khippaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā sammāsambodhiṃ paṭivijjha. Yathā pupphūpagaphalūpagā rukkhā samaye pupphanti ceva phalanti ca, tatheva tvampi samayaṃ anatikkamitvā khippaṃ sambodhimuttamaṃ phusassū”tiādīni thutimaṅgalāni payirudāhaṃsu, evaṃ payirudāhitvā attano attano devaṭṭhānameva agamaṃsu. Bodhisattopi devatāhi abhitthuto “ahaṃ dasa pāramiyo pūretvā kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ catunnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake buddho bhavissāmī”ti vīriyaṃ daḷhaṃ katvā adhiṭṭhāya nabhaṃ abbhuggantvā himavantameva agamāsi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then, as the Bodhisatta rose from his seat, all the deities from the ten-thousandfold world-system gathered. They honored him with divine garlands and perfumes, paid homage, and said: "Venerable ascetic Sumedha, today you have made a great aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, the Possessor of the Ten Powers. May it be fulfilled for you without hindrance. May you have no fear or trembling. May no illness, however slight, arise in your body. Quickly fulfill the perfections and realize supreme enlightenment. Just as flowering and fruit-bearing trees bloom and bear fruit in due season, so too may you, without exceeding the right time, swiftly attain the highest enlightenment." Having thus uttered auspicious praises, they each returned to their own divine abodes. The Bodhisatta, praised by the deities, strengthened his energy and made a firm determination, saying: "Having fulfilled the ten perfections, I shall become a Buddha at the end of four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more." Strengthening his determination, he soared into the sky and went to the Himalayas. Thus it was said:

“Dibbaṃ mānusakaṃ pupphaṃ, devā mānusakā ubho;

Samokiranti pupphehi, vuṭṭhahantassa āsanā.

“Both gods and humans shower divine and human flowers upon him as he rises from his seat.”

“Vedayanti ca te sotthiṃ, devā mānusakā ubho;

Mahantaṃ patthitaṃ tuyhaṃ, taṃ labhassu yathicchitaṃ.

“Both gods and humans wish you well: ‘Your aspiration is great; may you attain it just as you wish.’”

“Sabbītiyo vivajjantu, soko rogo vinassatu;

Mā te bhavantvantarāyā, phusa khippaṃ bodhimuttamaṃ.

“May all misfortunes be averted, may sorrow and disease be destroyed; may no obstacles befall you, may you quickly attain supreme enlightenment.”

“Yathāpi samaye patte, pupphanti pupphino dumā;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, buddhañāṇena pupphassu.

“Just as when the season arrives, flowering trees bloom; just so, O great hero, may you blossom with the Buddha's wisdom.”

“Yathā [M 1.0034] ye keci sambuddhā, pūrayuṃ dasa pāramī;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, pūraya dasa pāramī.

“Just as all Buddhas whatsoever fulfilled the ten perfections, so too, O great hero, fulfill the ten perfections.”

“Yathā ye keci sambuddhā, bodhimaṇḍamhi bujjhare;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, bujjhassu jinabodhiyaṃ.

“Just as all Buddhas whatsoever awakened at the seat of enlightenment, in the same way, O great hero, may you awaken to the enlightenment of a Victor.”

“Yathā ye keci sambuddhā, dhammacakkaṃ pavattayuṃ;

Tatheva tvaṃ mahāvīra, dhammacakkaṃ pavattaya.

“Just as all Buddhas whatsoever turned the Wheel of Dhamma, so too, O great hero, turn the Wheel of Dhamma.”

“Puṇṇamāye [V 1.0037] yathā cando, parisuddho virocati;

Tatheva tvaṃ puṇṇamano, viroca dasasahassiyaṃ.

“Just as the full moon shines, perfectly pure, so too, with a fulfilled mind, may you shine in the ten-thousandfold world-system.”

“Rāhumutto [P 1.0028] yathā sūriyo, tāpena atirocati;

Tatheva lokā muccitvā, viroca siriyā tuvaṃ.

“Just as the sun, freed from Rāhu, shines forth exceedingly with its heat, so too, freed from the world, may you shine with glory.”

“Yathā yā kāci nadiyo, osaranti mahodadhiṃ;

Evaṃ sadevakā lokā, osarantu tavantike.

“Just as all rivers whatsoever flow down to the great ocean, so may the worlds with their gods flow down to your presence.”

“Tehi thutappasattho so, dasa dhamme samādiya;

Te dhamme paripūrento, pavanaṃ pāvisī tadā”ti.

“Praised and extolled by them, he resolved upon the ten qualities; fulfilling those qualities, he then entered the forest.”

Sumedhakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Story of Sumedha is concluded.

Rammanagaravāsinopi kho nagaraṃ pavisitvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā mahājanaṃ saraṇādīsu patiṭṭhāpetvā rammanagaramhā nikkhamitvā tato uddhampi yāvatāyukaṃ tiṭṭhanto sabbaṃ buddhakiccaṃ katvā anukkamena anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ buddhavaṃse vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Vuttañhi tattha –

The residents of Ramma City also, having entered the city, offered a great alms-giving to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. The Teacher, having taught them the Dhamma and established the great multitude in the refuges and so on, then departed from Ramma City. From there onwards, abiding for as long as his life lasted, having completed all the duties of a Buddha, he gradually attained final Nibbāna without residue. Whatever should be said about this, all should be understood in the manner stated in the Buddhavaṃsa. For it is said there:

“Tadā te bhojayitvāna, sasaṅghaṃ lokanāyakaṃ;

Upagacchuṃ saraṇaṃ tassa, dīpaṅkarassa satthuno.

Then, having fed the World Leader together with the Sangha, they went for refuge to that Teacher, Dīpaṅkara.

“Saraṇāgamane kañci, niveseti tathāgato;

Kañci pañcasu sīlesu, sīle dasavidhe paraṃ.

The Tathāgata establishes some in the going for refuge, some in the five precepts, and others in the ten precepts.

“Kassaci [M 1.0035] deti sāmaññaṃ, caturo phalamuttame;

Kassaci asame dhamme, deti so paṭisambhidā.

To some, he gives the ascetic life and the four supreme fruits; to others, he gives the unequalled Dhamma and the analytical knowledges.

“Kassaci [V 1.0038] varasamāpattiyo, aṭṭha deti narāsabho;

Tisso kassaci vijjāyo, chaḷabhiññā pavecchati.

To some, the Bull of Men gives the eight supreme attainments; to some, the three knowledges; and he bestows the six supernormal knowledges.

“Tena yogena janakāyaṃ, ovadati mahāmuni;

Tena vitthārikaṃ āsi, lokanāthassa sāsanaṃ.

By that method, the Great Sage instructed the populace; thus, the Teaching of the World-Protector became widespread.

“Mahāhanusabhakkhandho, dīpaṅkarasanāmako;

Bahū jane tārayati, parimoceti duggatiṃ.

The one named Dīpaṅkara, with a great jaw and bull-like shoulders, carries many people across, freeing them from states of woe.

“Bodhaneyyaṃ janaṃ disvā, satasahassepi yojane;

Khaṇena upagantvāna, bodheti taṃ mahāmuni.

Seeing a person ready for enlightenment, even from a hundred thousand yojanas away, the Great Sage would approach in an instant and enlighten them.

“Paṭhamābhisamaye buddho, koṭisatamabodhayi;

Dutiyābhisamaye nātho, navutikoṭimabodhayi.

At the first penetration, the Buddha awakened a hundred koṭis; at the second penetration, the Protector awakened ninety koṭis.

“Yadā ca devabhavanamhi, buddho dhammamadesayi;

Navutikoṭisahassānaṃ, tatiyābhisamayo ahu.

And when the Buddha taught the Dhamma in the deva-realm, a third penetration occurred for ninety thousand koṭis.

“Sannipātā [P 1.0029] tayo āsuṃ, dīpaṅkarassa satthuno;

Koṭisatasahassānaṃ, paṭhamo āsi samāgamo.

There were three assemblies for the Teacher Dīpaṅkara: the first gathering was of a hundred thousand koṭis.

“Puna nāradakūṭamhi, pavivekagate jine;

Khīṇāsavā vītamalā, samiṃsu satakoṭiyo.

Again, when the Conqueror dwelt in solitude at Nāradakūṭa, a hundred koṭis of those with taints destroyed and free from stain assembled.

“Yamhi kāle mahāvīro, sudassanasiluccaye;

Navutikoṭisahassehi, pavāresi mahāmuni.

At the time when the Great Hero was on the beautiful Sudassana peak, the Great Sage held the Pavāraṇā with ninety thousand koṭis.

“Ahaṃ tena samayena, jaṭilo uggatāpano;

Antalikkhamhi caraṇo, pañcābhiññāsu pāragū.

At that time, I was a matted-hair ascetic of fierce austerity, wandering in the sky, skilled in the five supernormal knowledges.

“Dasavīsasahassānaṃ[V 1.0039], dhammābhisamayo ahu;

Ekadvinnaṃ abhisamayā, gaṇanāto asaṅkhiyā.

For ten thousand and for twenty thousand, there was a penetration of the Dhamma; the penetrations of one or two were beyond reckoning.

“Vitthārikaṃ bāhujaññaṃ, iddhaṃ phītaṃ ahu tadā;

Dīpaṅkarassa bhagavato, sāsanaṃ suvisodhitaṃ.

Then the Dispensation of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara was extensive, populous, prosperous and thriving, and very well purified.

“Cattāri [M 1.0036] satasahassāni, chaḷabhiññā mahiddhikā;

Dīpaṅkaraṃ lokaviduṃ, parivārenti sabbadā.

Four hundred thousand with the six supernormal knowledges and great psychic power always attended upon Dīpaṅkara, the Knower of the World.

“Ye keci tena samayena, jahanti mānusaṃ bhavaṃ;

Apattamānasā sekkhā, garahitā bhavanti te.

Whoever at that time abandoned the human state as trainees who had not attained their aim, they were censured.

“Supupphitaṃ pāvacanaṃ, arahantehi tādihi;

Khīṇāsavehi vimalehi, upasobhati sadevake.

The Teaching, well-flowered, adorned by such Arahants—those whose taints are destroyed, the stainless ones—shines forth in the world with its devas.

“Nagaraṃ rammavatī nāma, sudevo nāma khattiyo;

Sumedhā nāma janikā, dīpaṅkarassa satthuno.

The city was named Rammavatī, the khattiya was named Sudeva; Sumedhā was the mother of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.

“Sumaṅgalo ca tisso ca, ahesuṃ aggasāvakā;

Sāgato nāmupaṭṭhāko, dīpaṅkarassa satthuno.

Sumaṅgala and Tissa were the chief disciples; Sāgata was the attendant of the Teacher Dīpaṅkara.

“Nandā ceva sunandā ca, ahesuṃ aggasāvikā;

Bodhi tassa bhagavato, pipphalīti pavuccati.

Nandā and Sunandā were the chief female disciples; the Bodhi tree of that Blessed One is called Pipphalī.

“Asītihatthamubbedho, dīpaṅkaro mahāmuni;

Sobhati dīparukkhova, sālarājāva phullito.

Eighty cubits in height was Dīpaṅkara, the Great Sage; he shone like a lamp-tree, like a blossoming Sāla king-tree.

“Satasahassavassāni, āyu tassa mahesino;

Tāvatā tiṭṭhamāno so, tāresi janataṃ bahuṃ.

The lifespan of that great sage was one hundred thousand years. Remaining for that long, he helped many people across.

“Jotayitvāna [V 1.0040] saddhammaṃ, santāretvā mahājanaṃ;

Jalitvā aggikhandhova, nibbuto so sasāvako.

Having illuminated the true Dhamma, and ferried the multitude across, blazing like a mass of fire, he was extinguished along with his disciples.

“Sā ca iddhi so ca yaso, tāni ca pādesu cakkaratanāni;

Sabbaṃ tamantarahitaṃ, nanu rittā sabbasaṅkhārā”ti.

That psychic power and that glory, and those jewel-wheels on his feet—all that has disappeared. Surely all conditioned things are empty!

Dīpaṅkarassa [P 1.0030] pana bhagavato aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā koṇḍañño nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassaṃ, dutiye koṭisahassaṃ, tatiye navutikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto vijitāvī nāma cakkavattī hutvā koṭisatasahassasaṅkhassa buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adāsi. Satthā bodhisattaṃ “buddho bhavissasī”ti byākaritvā dhammaṃ desesi. So satthu dhammakathaṃ sutvā rajjaṃ niyyādetvā pabbaji. So tīṇi [M 1.0037] piṭakāni uggahetvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo pañca abhiññāyo ca uppādetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke nibbatti. Koṇḍaññassa buddhassa pana rammavatī nāma nagaraṃ, sunando nāma khattiyo pitā, sujātā nāma devī mātā, bhaddo ca subhaddo ca dve aggasāvakā, anuruddho nāmupaṭṭhāko, tissā ca upatissā ca dve aggasāvikā, sālakalyāṇī bodhi, aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ, vassasatasahassaṃ āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi.

Now, after the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, when one incalculable aeon had passed, a Teacher named Koṇḍañña arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples: in the first assembly, one hundred thousand koṭis; in the second, one thousand koṭis; and in the third, ninety koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, as the wheel-turning monarch named Vijitāvī, gave a great offering to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, headed by the Buddha, numbering one hundred thousand koṭis. The Teacher declared of the Bodhisatta: 'You will become a Buddha,' and then taught the Dhamma. Having heard the Teacher's Dhamma talk, he relinquished his kingdom and went forth. Having mastered the three Piṭakas, and having generated the eight attainments and the five supernormal powers, he was reborn in the Brahma world without losing his jhānas. Now, for the Buddha Koṇḍañña, the city was named Rammavatī, the khattiya Sunanda was his father, the queen Sujātā was his mother, Bhadda and Subhadda were his two chief disciples, Anuruddha was his attendant, Tissā and Upatissā were his two chief female disciples, the Sālakalyāṇī was his Bodhi tree, his body was eighty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

“Dīpaṅkarassa aparena, koṇḍañño nāma nāyako;

Anantatejo amitayaso, appameyyo durāsado”ti.

After Dīpaṅkara, there was the leader named Koṇḍañña, of endless energy and boundless fame, immeasurable, hard to assail.

Tassa aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā ekasmiṃyeva kappe caturo buddhā nibbattiṃsu maṅgalo, sumano, revato, sobhitoti. Maṅgalassa bhagavato tayo sannipātā ahesuṃ. Tesu paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassaṃ bhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye koṭisahassaṃ, tatiye navutikoṭiyo. Vemātikabhātā kirassa ānandakumāro nāma navutikoṭisaṅkhāya parisāya saddhiṃ dhammassavanatthāya satthu santikaṃ agamāsi. Satthā tassa anupubbiṃ kathaṃ kathesi, so saddhiṃ parisāya saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Satthā tesaṃ kulaputtānaṃ pubbacaritaṃ olokento iddhimayapattacīvarassa upanissayaṃ disvā dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā “etha, bhikkhavo”ti āha. Sabbe taṅkhaṇaññeva iddhimayapattacīvaradharā saṭṭhivassamahātherā viya ākappasampannā hutvā satthāraṃ vanditvā parivārayiṃsu. Ayamassa tatiyo sāvakasannipāto ahosi.

After that, when one incalculable eon had passed, four Buddhas arose in the same eon: Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, and Sobhita. For the Blessed One Maṅgala, there were three assemblies. In the first assembly, there were one trillion bhikkhus; in the second, ten billion; and in the third, nine hundred million. It is said that his step-brother, named Ānandakumāra, went to the Teacher’s presence with an assembly of nine hundred million to hear the Dhamma. The Teacher taught him a progressive discourse, and he, along with the assembly, attained arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. As the Teacher observed the past conduct of these sons of good families, he saw the supportive condition for robes and alms bowls produced by psychic power. Extending his right hand, he said: 'Come, bhikkhus!' Instantly, all of them, possessing robes and alms bowls produced by psychic power and appearing like senior bhikkhus of sixty years, paid homage to the Teacher and surrounded him. This was his third assembly of disciples.

Yathā [V 1.0041] pana aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ samantā asītihatthappamāṇāyeva sarīrappabhā ahosi, na evaṃ tassa tassa pana bhagavato sarīrappabhā niccakālaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi. Rukkhapathavipabbatasamuddādayo antamaso ukkhalikādīni upādāya suvaṇṇapaṭṭapariyonaddhā viya ahesuṃ. Āyuppamāṇaṃ panassa navutivassasahassāni ahosi. Ettakaṃ kālaṃ candimasūriyādayo attano pabhāya virocituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, rattindivaparicchedo na paññāyittha. Divā sūriyālokena viya sattā niccaṃ [P 1.0031][M 1.0038] buddhālokeneva vicariṃsu, sāyaṃ pupphitakusumānaṃ, pāto ravanakasakuṇādīnañca vasena loko rattindivaparicchedaṃ sallakkhesi.

Whereas the bodily radiance of other Buddhas extended only eighty cubits around, it was not so with that Blessed One; his bodily radiance constantly pervaded the ten-thousandfold world system. Trees, earth, mountains, oceans, and even down to pots and the like, appeared as if enveloped in golden plates. His lifespan was ninety thousand years. For that entire time, the sun, moon, and other luminaries could not shine with their own light, and the distinction between night and day was not discernible. Beings moved about constantly in the Buddha’s light, just as they would in sunlight. Only in the evening, by the blooming of flowers, and in the morning, by the cries of birds, did the world perceive the division of night and day.

Kiṃ pana aññesaṃ buddhānaṃ ayamānubhāvo natthīti? No natthi. Tepi hi ākaṅkhamānā dasasahassiṃ vā lokadhātuṃ tato vā bhiyyo ābhāya phareyyuṃ. Maṅgalassa pana bhagavato pubbapatthanāvasena aññesaṃ byāmappabhā viya sarīrappabhā niccakālameva dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi. So kira bodhisattacariyakāle vessantarasadise attabhāve ṭhito saputtadāro vaṅkapabbatasadise pabbate vasi. Atheko kharadāṭhiko nāma yakkho mahāpurisassa dānajjhāsayataṃ sutvā brāhmaṇavaṇṇena upasaṅkamitvā mahāsattaṃ dve dārake yāci. Mahāsatto “dadāmi brāhmaṇassa puttake”ti haṭṭhapahaṭṭho udakapariyantaṃ pathaviṃ kampento dvepi dārake adāsi. Yakkho caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ālambanaphalakaṃ nissāya ṭhatvā passantasseva mahāsattassa mūlakalāpe viya dve dārake khādi. Mahāpurisassa yakkhaṃ oloketvā mukhe vivaṭamatte aggijālaṃ viya lohitadhāraṃ uggiramānaṃ tassa mukhaṃ disvāpi kesaggamattampi domanassaṃ na uppajji. “Sudinnaṃ vata me dāna”nti cintayato panassa sarīre mahantaṃ pītisomanassa udapādi. So “imassa me nissandena anāgate imināva nīhārena rasmiyo nikkhamantū”ti patthanaṃ akāsi. Tassa taṃ patthanaṃ nissāya buddhabhūtassa sarīrato rasmiyo nikkhamitvā ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ phariṃsu.

Do other Buddhas, then, not possess this power? It is not so. For they too, if they wished, could illuminate the ten-thousandfold world system or even more with their radiance. However, due to the Blessed One Maṅgala’s previous aspiration, his bodily radiance, unlike the span-radiance of other Buddhas, constantly pervaded the ten-thousandfold world system. It is said that during his Bodhisatta practice, in a life similar to that of Vessantara, he lived on a mountain resembling Vaṅka Peak, together with his wife and children. Then a yakkha named Kharadāṭhika, hearing of the Great Being’s inclination for generosity, approached him in the guise of a brahmin and asked the Great Being for his two children. The Great Being, overjoyed, said: 'I give the children to the brahmin,' and as he gave them away, the earth shook up to the ocean’s edge. The yakkha, leaning against a board at the end of the walking path, devoured the two children right before the Great Being’s eyes, as if they were bundles of roots. When the Great Being saw the yakkha, with his mouth wide open, spewing a stream of blood like a flame, not even a hair’s breadth of sorrow arose in him. Instead, reflecting: 'My gift has been well given,' immense joy and delight arose in his body. He then made this aspiration: 'May rays of light emanate from my body in the future as a result of this giving, with this same outflow.' It was because of this aspiration that, when he became a Buddha, rays of light issued from his body and pervaded that extent.

Aparampissa pubbacaritaṃ atthi. So kira bodhisattakāle ekassa buddhassa cetiyaṃ disvā “imassa buddhassa mayā jīvitaṃ pariccajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti daṇḍadīpikāveṭhananiyāmena sakalasarīraṃ veṭhāpetvā ratanamattamakuḷaṃ satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ sappissa pūrāpetvā tattha sahassavaṭṭiyo jālāpetvā taṃ sīsenādāya sakalasarīraṃ jālāpetvā cetiyaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto sakalarattiṃ vītināmesi. Evaṃ yāva aruṇuggamanā vāyamantassāpissa lomakūpamattampi usumaṃ na gaṇhi. Padumagabbhaṃ paviṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Dhammo hi nāmesa attānaṃ rakkhantaṃ rakkhati. Tenāha bhagavā –

Moreover, there is another past story about him. It is said that during his Bodhisatta period, upon seeing a stupa of a Buddha, he thought: 'It is fitting for me to sacrifice my life for this Buddha.' Following the method of wrapping with torch wicks, he wrapped his entire body. He filled a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand with ghee, lit a thousand wicks in it, placed it on his head, and set his whole body ablaze. While circumambulating the stupa, he passed the entire night in this way. Even as he exerted himself until the rising of the dawn, not even a pore of his body grew warm. It was as if he had entered the interior of a lotus. For the Dhamma, indeed, protects one who protects oneself. Thus the Blessed One said:

“Dhammo [V 1.0042][M 1.0039] have rakkhati dhammacāriṃ, dhammo suciṇṇo sukhamāvahāti;

Esānisaṃso dhamme suciṇṇe, na duggatiṃ gacchati dhammacārī”ti. (theragā. 303; jā. 1.10.102; 1.15.385);

The Dhamma, indeed, protects the Dhamma-farer; The Dhamma, well practiced, brings happiness; This is the benefit of the Dhamma well practiced; The Dhamma-farer does not go to a bad destination.

Imassāpi [P 1.0032] kammassa nissandena tassa bhagavato sarīrobhāso dasasahassilokadhātuṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi.

By the residual effect of this deed, the radiance of that Blessed One's body spread throughout the ten-thousandfold world system and remained pervading it.

Tadā amhākaṃ bodhisatto suruci nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā “satthāraṃ nimantessāmī”ti upasaṅkamitvā madhuradhammakathaṃ sutvā “sve mayhaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhatha, bhante”ti āha. Brāhmaṇa, kittakehi te bhikkhūhi atthoti? “Kittakā pana vo, bhante, parivārabhikkhū”ti āha. Tadā pana satthu paṭhamasannipātoyeva hoti, tasmā “koṭisatasahassa”nti āha. Bhante, sabbehipi saddhiṃ mayhaṃ gehe bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathāti. Satthā adhivāsesi. Brāhmaṇo svātanāya nimantetvā gehaṃ gacchanto cintesi – “ahaṃ ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ yāgubhattavatthādīni dātuṃ sakkomi, nisīdanaṭṭhānaṃ pana kathaṃ bhavissatī”ti.

At that time, our Bodhisatta, having become a brahmin named Suruci, thought: 'I will invite the Teacher.' He approached, listened to the sweet Dhamma talk, and said: 'Venerable sir, please accept my alms offering tomorrow.' 'Brahmin, how many bhikkhus do you need?' 'But how many bhikkhus are in your retinue, Venerable sir?' he asked. At that time, it was the Teacher's very first assembly, so he said: 'One trillion.' 'Venerable sir, please accept alms at my home together with all of them.' The Teacher consented. The brahmin, having invited them for the next day, thought as he was going home: 'I am capable of giving rice gruel, food, robes, and so on to so many bhikkhus, but how will there be seating arrangements for them?'

Tassa sā cintā caturāsītiyojanasahassamatthake ṭhitassa devarañño paṇḍukambalasilāsanassa uṇhabhāvaṃ janesi. Sakko “ko nu kho maṃ imamhā ṭhānā cāvetukāmo”ti dibbacakkhunā olokento mahāpurisaṃ disvā “suruci nāma brāhmaṇo buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā nisīdanaṭṭhānatthāya cintesi, mayāpi tattha gantvā puññakoṭṭhāsaṃ gahetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vaḍḍhakivaṇṇaṃ nimminitvā vāsipharasuhattho mahāpurisassa purato pāturahosi. So “atthi nu kho kassaci bhatiyā kattabba”nti āha. Mahāpuriso taṃ disvā “kiṃ kammaṃ karissasī”ti āha. “Mama ajānanasippaṃ nāma natthi, gehaṃ vā maṇḍapaṃ vā yo yaṃ kāreti, tassa taṃ kātuṃ jānāmī”ti. “Tena hi mayhaṃ kammaṃ atthī”ti. “Kiṃ ayyā”ti? “Svātanāya me koṭisatasahassabhikkhū nimantitā, tesaṃ nisīdanamaṇḍapaṃ karissasī”ti. “Ahaṃ nāma kareyyaṃ, sace mama bhatiṃ dātuṃ sakkhissathā”ti. “Sakkhissāmi tātā”ti. “Sādhu karissāmī”ti gantvā ekaṃ padesaṃ olokesi, dvādasaterasayojanappamāṇo padeso kasiṇamaṇḍalaṃ [M 1.0040] viya samatalo ahosi. So “ettake ṭhāne sattaratanamayo maṇḍapo uṭṭhahatū”ti cintetvā olokesi. Tāvadeva pathaviṃ bhinditvā maṇḍapo uṭṭhahi. Tassa sovaṇṇamayesu thambhesu rajatamayā ghaṭakā ahesuṃ, rajatamayesu sovaṇṇamayā, maṇitthambhesu pavāḷamayā, pavāḷatthambhesu maṇimayā, sattaratanamayesu sattaratanamayāva ghaṭakā ahesuṃ[V 1.0043]. Tato “maṇḍapassa antarantarena kiṅkiṇikajālaṃ olambatū”ti olokesi, saha olokaneneva kiṅkiṇikajālaṃ olambi, yassa mandavāteritassa pañcaṅgikasseva tūriyassa madhurasaddo niggacchati, dibbasaṅgītivattanakālo viya hoti. “Antarantarā gandhadāmamālādāmāni olambantū”ti cintesi, dāmāni olambiṃsu. “Koṭisatasahassasaṅkhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [P 1.0033] āsanāni ca ādhārakāni ca pathaviṃ bhinditvā uṭṭhahantū”ti cintesi, tāvadeva uṭṭhahiṃsu. “Koṇe koṇe ekekā udakacāṭiyo uṭṭhahantū”ti cintesi, udakacāṭiyo uṭṭhahiṃsu.

The thought of that brahmin caused the Paṇḍukambala stone seat of Sakka, the king of devas, which was situated eighty-four thousand yojanas high, to become warm. Sakka, wondering, “Who now wishes to remove me from this position?” looked with his divine eye and saw the Great Being. “A brahmin named Suruci has invited the community of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head and is thinking of a place for them to sit. It is fitting for me to go there and take a share of merit,” he thought. Creating the form of a carpenter, he appeared before the Great Being with an axe and adze in his hand. He asked, “Is there any work to be done for hire?” The Great Being, seeing him, asked, “What work can you do?” “There is no craft unknown to me. Whatever house or pavilion one wishes to have built, I know how to make it.” “Then I have work for you.” “What is it, sir?” “For tomorrow, I have invited a hundred thousand koṭi bhikkhus. Will you build a seating pavilion for them?” “I could do it, if you are able to provide my wages.” “I can, dear one.” “Good, I will do it.” He went and surveyed a spot. An area twelve or thirteen yojanas in extent was as level as a kasiṇa disc. He thought, “Let a pavilion made of the seven precious gems arise in this space,” and looked. Instantly, the earth split open, and the pavilion arose. Its golden pillars had silver capitals, silver pillars had golden capitals, jeweled pillars had coral capitals, coral pillars had jeweled capitals, and pillars made of the seven gems had capitals of the seven gems. Then he looked, thinking, “Let a net of tinkling bells hang between the pillars.” As soon as he looked, the net of bells hung there. When a gentle breeze stirred them, they produced a sweet sound like a five-part orchestra, as if it were the time for divine music. He thought, “Let garlands of fragrant flowers hang at intervals,” and the garlands hung. “Let seats and supports for a hundred thousand koṭi bhikkhus rise from the earth,” he thought, and instantly they arose. “Let a water pot rise at each corner,” he thought, and the water pots arose.

Ettakaṃ māpetvā brāhmaṇassa santikaṃ gantvā “ehi ayya, tava maṇḍapaṃ oloketvā mayhaṃ bhatiṃ dehī”ti āha. Mahāpuriso gantvā maṇḍapaṃ olokesi, olokentassevassa sakalasarīraṃ pañcavaṇṇāya pītiyā nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ ahosi. Athassa maṇḍapaṃ olokayato etadahosi – “nāyaṃ maṇḍapo manussabhūtena kato, mayhaṃ pana ajjhāsayaṃ mayhaṃ guṇaṃ āgamma addhā sakkabhavanaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi, tato sakkena devaraññā ayaṃ maṇḍapo kārito bhavissatī”ti. “Na kho pana me yuttaṃ evarūpe maṇḍape ekadivasaṃyeva dānaṃ dātuṃ, sattāhaṃ dassāmī”ti cintesi. Bāhirakadānañhi kittakampi samānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ tuṭṭhiṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti, alaṅkatasīsaṃ pana chinditvā añjitaakkhīni uppāṭetvā hadayamaṃsaṃ vā ubbaṭṭetvā dinnakāle bodhisattānaṃ cāgaṃ nissāya tuṭṭhi nāma hoti. Amhākampi hi bodhisattassa sivijātake devasikaṃ pañca kahāpaṇasatasahassāni vissajjetvā catūsu dvāresu nagaramajjhe ca dānaṃ dentassa taṃ dānaṃ cāgatuṭṭhiṃ uppādetuṃ nāsakkhi. Yadā panassa brāhmaṇavaṇṇena āgantvā sakko devarājā akkhīni yāci, tadā tāni uppāṭetvā dadamānasseva hāso uppajji, kesaggamattampi cittassa aññathattaṃ nāhosi. Evaṃ dānaṃ nissāya bodhisattānaṃ titti nāma natthi. Tasmā sopi mahāpuriso [M 1.0041] “sattāhaṃ mayā koṭisatasahassasaṅkhānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā tasmiṃ maṇḍape buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nisīdāpetvā sattāhaṃ gavapānaṃ nāma dānaṃ adāsi. Gavapānanti mahante mahante kolambe khīrassa pūretvā uddhanesu āropetvā ghanapākapakke khīre thoke taṇḍule pakkhipitvā pakkamadhusakkarācuṇṇasappīhi abhisaṅkhataṃ bhojanaṃ vuccati. Manussāyeva pana parivisituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, devāpi ekantarikā hutvā parivisiṃsu. Dvādasaterasayojanappamāṇaṃ ṭhānampi bhikkhū gaṇhituṃ nappahosiyeva. Te pana bhikkhū attano attano ānubhāvena nisīdiṃsu. Pariyosānadivase sabbabhikkhūnaṃ pattāni dhovāpetvā bhesajjatthāya sappinavanītamadhuphāṇitādīni pūretvā ticīvarehi saddhiṃ adāsi, saṅghanavakabhikkhunā laddhacīvarasāṭakā satasahassagghanakā ahesuṃ.

Having had that much built, he went to the brahmin and said, “Come, sir, look at your pavilion and give me my wages.” The Great Being went and looked at the pavilion. As he looked, his entire body was pervaded with uninterrupted joy of five colors. Then, as he surveyed the pavilion, this thought occurred to him: “This pavilion was not made by a human being. Surely, on account of my aspiration and my virtue, Sakka's abode must have become hot, and so Sakka, the king of devas, must have had this pavilion built.” “It is not fitting for me to give alms in such a pavilion for just one day. I will give for seven days,” he thought. For external gifts, no matter how great, cannot bring satisfaction to the Bodhisattas. But when one cuts off one’s adorned head, plucks out one’s anointed eyes, or tears out one’s heart-flesh to give—at the time of such giving, joy based on generosity arises in the Bodhisattas. Indeed, even when our Bodhisatta, in the Sivi Jātaka, gave away five hundred thousand kahāpaṇas daily and distributed alms at the four city gates and in the city center, that giving could not produce the joy of generosity. But when Sakka, the king of devas, came in the guise of a brahmin and asked for his eyes, then as he was plucking them out and giving them, laughter arose in him, and his mind did not alter even a hair’s breadth. Thus, for the Bodhisattas, there is no satisfaction based on ordinary giving. Therefore, that Great Being thought, “It is fitting for me to give alms to a hundred thousand koṭi bhikkhus for seven days.” So, having seated the community of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head in that pavilion, he gave the alms called Gavapāna for seven days. Gavapāna refers to a meal prepared by filling very large pots with milk, placing them on hearths, and when the milk is cooked to a thick consistency, adding a little rice, and preparing it with molasses, sugar, flour, and ghee. Humans alone were unable to serve, so the devas also took turns serving. Even the space measuring twelve or thirteen yojanas was not sufficient for the bhikkhus to occupy. But those bhikkhus sat according to their own respective powers. On the final day, after having the bowls of all the bhikkhus washed, he filled them with medicinal items such as ghee, fresh butter, honey, and molasses, and gave them along with the three robes. The robes and cloths received by a new bhikkhu of the Sangha were worth a hundred thousand.

Satthā [V 1.0044] anumodanaṃ karonto “ayaṃ puriso evarūpaṃ mahādānaṃ adāsi, ko nu kho bhavissatī”ti upadhārento “anāgate kappasatasahassādhikānaṃ dvinnaṃ asaṅkhyeyyānaṃ matthake gotamo nāma buddho bhavissatī”ti disvā mahāpurisaṃ āmantetvā “tvaṃ ettakaṃ [P 1.0034] nāma kālaṃ atikkamitvā gotamo nāma buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Mahāpuriso byākaraṇaṃ sutvā “ahaṃ kira buddho bhavissāmi, ko me gharāvāsena attho, pabbajissāmī”ti cintetvā tathārūpaṃ sampattiṃ kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya pahāya satthu santike pabbajitvā buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā āyupariyosāne brahmaloke nibbatti.

The Teacher, rejoicing, considered, “This man has given such a great gift; who might he become?” Then, foreseeing, “In the future, after two incalculable periods and a hundred thousand eons, a Buddha named Gotama will arise,” he addressed the Great Being and declared, “After such a long time, you will become a Buddha named Gotama.” Hearing the prediction, the Great Being thought, “I will indeed become a Buddha; what use is household life to me? I shall go forth.” Thus, abandoning such wealth as if it were a lump of spittle, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher, learned the Buddha's word, developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and at the end of his life was reborn in the Brahma world.

Maṅgalassa pana bhagavato nagaraṃ uttaraṃ nāma ahosi, pitāpi uttaro nāma khattiyo, mātāpi uttarā nāma devī, sudevo ca dhammaseno ca dve aggasāvakā, pālito nāmupaṭṭhāko, sīvalī ca asokā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkho bodhi, aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi. Navutivassasahassāni ṭhatvā parinibbute pana tasmiṃ bhagavati ekappahāreneva dasa cakkavāḷasahassāni ekandhakārāni ahesuṃ. Sabbacakkavāḷesu manussānaṃ mahantaṃ ārodanaparidevanaṃ ahosi.

For the Blessed One Maṅgala, the city was named Uttara, his father was the khattiya Uttara, his mother the queen Uttarā, his two chief disciples were Sudeva and Dhammasena, his attendant was named Pālita, his two chief female disciples were Sīvalī and Asokā, his Bodhi tree was a nāga tree, and his body was eighty-eight cubits tall. He lived for ninety thousand years and, upon his Parinibbāna, in one instant, ten thousand world-systems were plunged into darkness. Throughout all the world-systems, there was great lamentation and wailing among the people.

“Koṇḍaññassa [M 1.0042] aparena, maṅgalo nāma nāyako;

Tamaṃ loke nihantvāna, dhammokkamabhidhārayī”ti.

“After Koṇḍañña, there was the leader named Maṅgala; having dispelled the darkness in the world, he held high the torch of the Dhamma.”

Evaṃ dasasahassilokadhātuṃ andhakāraṃ katvā parinibbutassa tassa bhagavato aparabhāge sumano nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye kañcanapabbatamhi navutikoṭisahassāni, tatiye asītikoṭisahassāni. Tadā mahāsatto atulo nāma nāgarājā ahosi mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo. So “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā ñātisaṅghaparivuto nāgabhavanā nikkhamitvā koṭisatasahassabhikkhuparivārassa tassa bhagavato dibbatūriyehi upahāraṃ kāretvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā paccekaṃ dussayugāni datvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāsi. Sopi naṃ satthā “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato nagaraṃ khemaṃ nāma ahosi, sudatto nāma rājā pitā, sirimā nāma mātā, saraṇo ca bhāvitatto ca dve aggasāvakā, udeno nāmupaṭṭhāko, soṇā ca upasoṇā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkho bodhi, navutihatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ, navutiyeva vassasahassāni āyuppamāṇaṃ ahosi.

Thus that Blessed One attained Parinibbāna, plunging the ten-thousandfold world-system into darkness. In a later period, a Teacher named Sumana arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were a hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, on Mount Kañcana, ninety thousand koṭis; and in the third, eighty thousand koṭis. At that time, the Great Being was a nāga king named Atula, of great power and might. Hearing that “a Buddha has arisen,” he left his nāga palace surrounded by his relatives. He arranged offerings with divine musical instruments for that Blessed One, who was attended by a hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus, held a great almsgiving, presented pairs of cloths to each one, and was established in the Refuges. That Teacher also prophesied to him, “In the future, you will become a Buddha.” That Blessed One’s city was named Khema, his father was King Sudatta, and his mother was Sirimā. Sāraṇa and Bhāvitatto were his two chief disciples, Udena was his attendant, and Soṇā and Upasoṇā were his two chief female disciples. The Nāga tree was his Bodhi tree. His body was ninety cubits tall, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

“Maṅgalassa [V 1.0045] aparena, sumano nāma nāyako;

Sabbadhammehi asamo, sabbasattānamuttamo”ti.

“After Maṅgala, there was a leader named Sumana, unequaled in all things, the supreme among all beings.”

Tassa [P 1.0035] aparabhāge revato nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte gaṇanā natthi, dutiye koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, tathā tatiye. Tadā bodhisatto atidevo nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ ṭhapetvā tassa satthuno kilesappahāne vaṇṇaṃ vatvā uttarāsaṅgena pūjaṃ akāsi. Sopi naṃ “buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa pana bhagavato nagaraṃ dhaññavatī nāma ahosi, pitā vipulo nāma khattiyo, mātāpi vipulā nāma devī, varuṇo ca brahmadevo ca dve aggasāvakā, sambhavo nāmupaṭṭhāko, bhaddā ca subhaddā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkhova bodhi, sarīraṃ asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, āyu saṭṭhi vassasahassānīti.

Subsequently, a Teacher named Revata arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, the number was uncountable; in the second, there were a hundred thousand koṭis of monks, and likewise in the third. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a brahmin named Atideva, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, was established in the Refuges. Placing his joined hands on his head, he praised that Teacher for the abandonment of defilements and made an offering with his upper robe. That Teacher also declared concerning him, “You will become a Buddha.” The city of that Blessed One was named Dhaññavatī, his father was the khattiya Vipula, and his mother was Queen Vipulā. Varuṇa and Brahmadeva were the two chief disciples, Sambhava was the attendant, Bhaddā and Subhaddā were the two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was a nāga tree, his body was eighty cubits tall, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.

“Sumanassa [M 1.0043] aparena, revato nāma nāyako;

Anūpamo asadiso, atulo uttamo jino”ti.

“After Sumana, there was the leader named Revata, incomparable, unequalled, peerless, the supreme Victor.”

Tassa aparabhāge sobhito nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto ajito nāma brāhmaṇo hutvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adāsi. Sopi naṃ “buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa pana bhagavato sudhammaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, pitāpi sudhammo nāma rājā, mātāpi sudhammā nāma devī, asamo ca sunetto ca dve aggasāvakā, anomo nāmupaṭṭhāko, nakulā ca sujātā ca dve aggasāvikā, nāgarukkhova bodhi, aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi, navuti vassasahassāni āyuppamāṇanti.

Subsequently, a Teacher named Sobhita arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were a hundred koṭis of monks; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a brahmin named Ajita, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, was established in the Refuges and gave a great alms to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. That Teacher also declared concerning him, “You will become a Buddha.” The city of that Blessed One was named Sudhamma. His father was King Sudhamma, and his mother was Queen Sudhammā. Asama and Sunetta were the two chief disciples, Anoma was the attendant, Nakulā and Sujātā were the two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was a nāga tree, his body was fifty-eight cubits tall, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

“Revatassa aparena, sobhito nāma nāyako;

Samāhito santacitto, asamo appaṭipuggalo”ti.

“After Revata, there was the leader named Sobhita, composed, with a peaceful mind, unequalled, without a counterpart.”

Tassa aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā ekasmiṃyeva kappe tayo buddhā nibbattiṃsu anomadassī padumo nāradoti. Anomadassissa bhagavato tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte bhikkhū aṭṭhasatasahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye satta, tatiye cha. Tadā bodhisatto [V 1.0046] eko yakkhasenāpati ahosi mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo anekakoṭisatasahassānaṃ [P 1.0036] yakkhānaṃ adhipati. So “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā āgantvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ adāsi. Satthāpi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Anomadassissa pana bhagavato candavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, yasavā nāma rājā pitā, yasodharā nāma mātā, nisabho ca anomo ca dve aggasāvakā, varuṇo nāmupaṭṭhāko, sundarī ca sumanā ca dve aggasāvikā, ajjunarukkho bodhi, aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

Subsequently, after passing through one incalculable aeon, three Buddhas arose in a single aeon: Anomadassī, Paduma, and Nārada. The Blessed One Anomadassī had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were eight hundred thousand monks; in the second, seven hundred thousand; and in the third, six hundred thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a yakkha commander, possessing great power and might, the lord of many hundreds of thousands of koṭis of yakkhas. Hearing that ‘a Buddha had arisen,’ he came and offered a great almsgiving to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. The Teacher then declared concerning him, “In the future, you will become a Buddha.” The city of the Blessed One Anomadassī was named Candavatī, his father was King Yasavā, and his mother was Queen Yasodharā. Nisabha and Anoma were the two chief disciples, Varuṇa was the attendant, Sundarī and Sumanā were the two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was an ajjuna tree, his body was fifty-eight cubits tall, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

“Sobhitassa aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Anomadassī amitayaso, tejassī duratikkamo”ti.

“After Sobhita, there was the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, Anomadassī, of immeasurable glory, radiant, hard to overcome.”

Tassa [M 1.0044] aparabhāge padumo nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo bhāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye tīṇi satasahassāni, tatiye agāmake araññe mahāvanasaṇḍavāsīnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dve satasahassāni. Tadā tathāgate tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe vasante bodhisatto sīho hutvā satthāraṃ nirodhasamāpattiṃ samāpannaṃ disvā pasannacitto vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pītisomanassajāto tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ naditvā sattāhaṃ buddhārammaṇapītiṃ avijahitvā pītisukheneva gocarāya apakkamitvā jīvitapariccāgaṃ katvā payirupāsamāno aṭṭhāsi.
