Satthā sattāhaccayena nirodhā vuṭṭhito sīhaṃ oloketvā “bhikkhusaṅghepi cittaṃ pasādetvā saṅghaṃ vandissatīti bhikkhusaṅgho āgacchatū”ti cintesi. Bhikkhū tāvadeva āgamiṃsu. Sīho saṅghe cittaṃ pasādesi. Satthā tassa manaṃ oloketvā “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Padumassa pana bhagavato campakaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, asamo nāma rājā pitā, asamā nāma devī mātā, sālo ca upasālo ca dve aggasāvakā, varuṇo nāmupaṭṭhāko, rāmā ca surāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, soṇarukkho nāma bodhi, aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ sarīraṃ ahosi, āyu vassasatasahassanti.

Subsequently, a Teacher named Paduma arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were a hundred thousand koṭis of monks; in the second, three hundred thousand; and in the third, two hundred thousand monks dwelling in the great forest wilderness, in the uninhabited forest. At that time, while the Tathāgata was dwelling in that forest grove, the Bodhisatta, having become a lion, saw the Teacher absorbed in the attainment of cessation. Filled with faith, he paid homage, circumambulated him, and, filled with joy and gladness, roared his lion’s roar three times. For seven days, he did not relinquish the joy inspired by the Buddha; with that same blissful happiness, without departing for pasture, he made a sacrifice of his life and stood attending upon him. After seven days, the Teacher emerged from cessation and, seeing the lion, thought, ‘He will also be inspired with faith in the Sangha and will pay homage to the Sangha. Let the Sangha come.’ The monks arrived immediately. The lion was inspired with faith in the Sangha. The Teacher, discerning his mind, declared concerning him, ‘In the future, you will become a Buddha.’ The city of the Blessed One Paduma was named Campaka, his father was King Asama, and his mother was Queen Asamā. Sāla and Upasāla were the two chief disciples, Varuṇa was the attendant, Rāmā and Surāmā were the two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was a soṇa tree, his body was fifty-eight cubits tall, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

“Anomadassissa aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Padumo nāma nāmena, asamo appaṭipuggalo”ti.

“After Anomadassī, there was the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, Paduma by name, unequalled, without a counterpart.”

Tassa aparabhāge nārado nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye [P 1.0037] navutikoṭisahassāni, tatiye asītikoṭisahassāni[V 1.0047]. Tadā bodhisatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcasu abhiññāsu aṭṭhasu ca samāpattīsu ciṇṇavasī hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā lohitacandanena pūjaṃ akāsi. Sopi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato dhaññavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, sudevo nāma khattiyo pitā, anomā nāma mātā, saddasālo ca jitamitto ca dve aggasāvakā, vāseṭṭho nāmupaṭṭhāko[M 1.0045], uttarā ca phaggunī ca dve aggasāvikā, mahāsoṇarukkho nāma bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, navutivassasahassāni āyūti.

Subsequently, a Teacher named Nārada arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were a hundred thousand koṭis of monks; in the second, ninety thousand koṭis; and in the third, eighty thousand koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having gone forth into the ascetic life, having mastered the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments, offered a great almsgiving to the community of monks headed by the Buddha and made an offering with red sandalwood. He then declared concerning him, “In the future, you will become a Buddha.” The city of that Blessed One was named Dhaññavatī, his father was King Sudeva, and his mother was Queen Anomā. Bhaddasāla and Jitamitta were the two chief disciples, Vāseṭṭha was the attendant, Uttarā and Phaggunī were the two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was a mahāsoṇa tree, his body was eighty-eight cubits tall, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

“Padumassa aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Nārado nāma nāmena, asamo appaṭipuggalo”ti.

“After Paduma, there was the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, Nārada by name, unequalled, without a counterpart.”

Nāradabuddhassa aparabhāge ekaṃ asaṅkhyeyyaṃ atikkamitvā ito satasahassakappamatthake ekasmiṃ kappe ekova padumuttarabuddho nāma udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhame koṭisatasahassabhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye vebhārapabbate navutikoṭisahassāni, tatiye asītikoṭisahassāni. Tadā bodhisatto jaṭilo nāma mahāraṭṭhiyo hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sacīvaraṃ dānaṃ adāsi. Sopi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Padumuttarassa pana bhagavato kāle titthiyā nāma nāhesuṃ. Sabbe devamanussā buddhameva saraṇaṃ agamaṃsu. Tassa nagaraṃ haṃsavatī nāma ahosi, pitā ānando nāma khattiyo, mātā sujātā nāma devī, devalo ca sujāto ca dve aggasāvakā, sumano nāmupaṭṭhāko, amitā ca asamā ca dve aggasāvikā, salalarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, sarīrappabhā samantato dvādasa yojanāni gaṇhi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

Subsequently, after the Buddha Nārada, having passed one incalculable aeon, one hundred thousand aeons ago, in one aeon, there arose a single Buddha named Padumuttara. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first, there were a hundred thousand koṭis of monks; in the second, on Mount Vebhāra, ninety thousand koṭis; and in the third, eighty thousand koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a great provincial governor named Jaṭila, gave a gift including robes to the community of monks with the Buddha at its head. He then declared concerning him, “In the future, you will become a Buddha.” During the time of the Blessed One Padumuttara, there were no sectarians. All gods and humans went for refuge to the Buddha alone. His city was named Haṃsavatī, his father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Queen Sujātā. Devala and Sujāta were the two chief disciples, Sumana was the attendant, Amitā and Asamā were the two chief female disciples. His Bodhi tree was a salala tree, his body was fifty-eight cubits tall, the radiance of his body extended twelve yojanas all around, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

“Nāradassa aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Padumuttaro nāma jino, akkhobho sāgarūpamo”ti.

“After Nārada, there was the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, Padumuttara by name, the Victor, unshaken like the ocean.”

Tassa aparabhāge sattati kappasahassāni atikkamitvā sumedho sujāto cāti ekasmiṃ kappe dve buddhā nibbattiṃsu. Sumedhassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ, paṭhamasannipāte sudassananagare koṭisatakhīṇāsavā ahesuṃ, dutiye pana navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto uttaro nāma māṇavo hutvā nidahitvā ṭhapitaṃyeva asītikoṭidhanaṃ [V 1.0048][P 1.0038] vissajjetvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā dhammaṃ sutvā saraṇesu patiṭṭhāya [M 1.0046] nikkhamitvā pabbaji. Sopi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Sumedhassa bhagavato sudassanaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, sudatto nāma rājā pitā, mātāpi sudattā nāma, saraṇo ca sabbakāmo ca dve aggasāvakā, sāgaro nāmupaṭṭhāko, rāmā ca surāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, mahānīparukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhāsītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, āyu navuti vassasahassānīti.

After him, having passed seventy thousand aeons, in one aeon two Buddhas arose: Sumedha and Sujāta. Sumedha also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, in the city of Sudassana, there were a hundred koṭis of arahants; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a young brahmin named Uttara, having disbursed eighty koṭis of wealth that had been set aside, gave a great offering to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. Hearing the Dhamma, he established himself in the refuges, went forth from the household life, and became an ascetic. He too prophesied to him, "In the future, you will become a Buddha." The city of that Blessed One Sumedha was named Sudassana, his father was King Sudatta, his mother was also named Sudattā, his two chief disciples were Saraṇa and Sabbakāma, his attendant was named Sāgara, his two chief female disciples were Rāmā and Surāmā, his Bodhi tree was the great Nīpa tree, his body was eighty-eight cubits tall, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

“Padumuttarassa aparena, sumedho nāma nāyako;

Durāsado uggatejo, sabbalokuttamo munī”ti.

After Padumuttara, there was the leader named Sumedha; hard to approach, of fierce energy, the supreme sage in all the world.

Tassa aparabhāge sujāto nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte saṭṭhi bhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye paññāsaṃ, tatiye cattālīsaṃ. Tadā bodhisatto cakkavattirājā hutvā “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa saddhiṃ sattahi ratanehi catumahādīparajjaṃ datvā satthu santike pabbaji. Sakalaraṭṭhavāsino raṭṭhuppādaṃ gahetvā ārāmikakiccaṃ sādhentā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa niccaṃ mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Sopi naṃ satthā “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato nagaraṃ sumaṅgalaṃ nāma ahosi, uggato nāma rājā pitā, pabhāvatī nāma mātā, sudassano ca sudevo ca dve aggasāvakā, nārado nāmupaṭṭhāko, nāgā ca nāgasamālā ca dve aggasāvikā, mahāveḷurukkho bodhi. So kira mandacchiddo ghanakkhandho upari niggatāhi mahāsākhāhi morapiñchakalāpo viya virocittha. Tassa bhagavato sarīraṃ paṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, āyu navuti vassasahassānīti.

After him, a Teacher named Sujāta arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were sixty hundred-thousand bhikkhus; in the second, fifty; and in the third, forty. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a wheel-turning monarch, heard that "a Buddha has arisen," approached him, listened to the Dhamma, and gave the rule over the four great continents, along with the seven treasures, to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. He then went forth in the presence of the Teacher. The inhabitants of the entire country, taking the produce of the kingdom and fulfilling the duties of monastery attendants, constantly gave a great offering to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha. He too prophesied to him, "In the future, you will become a Buddha." The city of that Blessed One was named Sumaṅgala, his father was King Uggata, his mother was Pabhāvatī, his two chief disciples were Sudassana and Sudeva, his attendant was named Nārada, his two chief female disciples were Nāgā and Nāgasamālā, and his Bodhi tree was the great bamboo tree. It is said that it had few openings and a thick trunk, and its great branches, spreading out above, shone like a peacock's tail-plume. The Blessed One's body was fifty cubits tall, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

“Tattheva maṇḍakappamhi, sujāto nāma nāyako;

Sīhahanusabhakkhandho, appameyyo durāsado”ti.

In that same Maṇḍa aeon, there was the leader named Sujāta; with a lion's jaw and a bull's shoulders, immeasurable, hard to approach.

Tassa aparabhāge ito aṭṭhārasakappasatamatthake ekasmiṃ kappe piyadassī, atthadassī, dhammadassīti tayo buddhā nibbattiṃsu. Piyadassissāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhame koṭisatasahassā bhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto kassapo nāma māṇavo tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāraṃ gato hutvā [M 1.0047] satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā koṭisatasahassadhanapariccāgena saṅghārāmaṃ [P 1.0039] kāretvā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ [V 1.0049] satthā “aṭṭhārasakappasataccayena buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato anomaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, pitā sudinno nāma rājā, mātā candā nāma devī, pālito ca sabbadassī ca dve aggasāvakā, sobhito nāmupaṭṭhāko, sujātā ca dhammadinnā ca dve aggasāvikā, kakudharukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, navuti vassasahassāni āyūti.

After him, eighteen hundred aeons ago, in one aeon three Buddhas arose: Piyadassī, Atthadassī, and Dhammadassī. Piyadassī also had three assemblies of disciples. In the first, there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a young brahmin named Kassapa who had mastered the three Vedas, having heard the Teacher’s teaching and having caused a monastery to be built by donating one hundred thousand koṭis of wealth, established himself in the refuges and the precepts. Then the Teacher prophesied to him, "After eighteen hundred aeons, you will become a Buddha." The city of that Blessed One was named Anoma, his father was King Sudinna, his mother was Queen Candā. Pālita and Sabbadassī were his two chief disciples, Sobhita was his attendant, Sujātā and Dhammadinnā were his two chief female disciples, the Kakudha tree was his Bodhi tree, his body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

“Sujātassa aparena, sayambhū lokanāyako;

Durāsado asamasamo, piyadassī mahāyaso”ti.

After Sujāta, there was the self-existent leader of the world, Piyadassī of great renown; unassailable, without equal.

Tassa aparabhāge atthadassī nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhame aṭṭhanavuti bhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye aṭṭhāsītisatasahassāni, tathā tatiye. Tadā bodhisatto susīmo nāma mahiddhiko tāpaso hutvā devalokato mandāravapupphacchattaṃ āharitvā satthāraṃ pūjesi, sopi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato sobhitaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, sāgaro nāma rājā pitā, sudassanā nāma mātā, santo ca upasanto ca dve aggasāvakā, abhayo nāmupaṭṭhāko, dhammā ca sudhammā ca dve aggasāvikā, campakarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, sarīrappabhā samantato sabbakālaṃ yojanamattaṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi, āyu vassasatasahassanti.

After him, a Teacher named Atthadassī arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first, there were ninety-eight hundred-thousand bhikkhus; in the second, eighty-eight hundred-thousand; and likewise in the third. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a powerful ascetic named Susīma, having brought a parasol of mandārava flowers from the deva world, honored the Teacher. He too prophesied to him, "In the future, you will become a Buddha." The city of that Blessed One was named Sobhita. His father was King Sāgara, and his mother was Sudassanā. His two chief disciples were Santo and Upasanto. His attendant was named Abhaya. His two chief female disciples were Dhammā and Sudhammā. His Bodhi tree was a campaka tree. His body was eighty cubits tall, and the radiance from his body constantly spread for a league in all directions. His lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

“Tattheva maṇḍakappamhi, atthadassī narāsabho;

Mahātamaṃ nihantvāna, patto sambodhimuttama”nti.

In that same Maṇḍa aeon, there was Atthadassī, a bull among men; having dispelled the great darkness, he attained supreme enlightenment.

Tassa aparabhāge dhammadassī nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhame koṭisataṃ bhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye sattatikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto sakko devarājā hutvā dibbagandhapupphehi ca dibbatūriyehi ca pūjaṃ akāsi, sopi naṃ “anāgate buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato saraṇaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, pitā saraṇo nāma rājā, mātā sunandā nāma, padumo ca phussadevo ca dve aggasāvakā, sunetto nāmupaṭṭhāko[M 1.0048], khemā ca sabbanāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, rattaṅkurarukkho bodhi, “bimbijālo”tipi vuccati, sarīraṃ panassa asītihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

After him, a Teacher named Dhammadassī arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first, there were one hundred koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, seventy koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta was Sakka, king of the devas, and made an offering with divine perfumes and flowers, and with celestial music. He too prophesied to him, 'In the future, you will become a Buddha.' The city of that Blessed One was named Saraṇa, his father was King Saraṇa, and his mother was named Sunandā. His two chief disciples were Paduma and Phussadeva, his attendant was named Sunetta, and his two chief female disciples were Khemā and Sabbanāmā. His Bodhi tree was the Rattaṅkura tree, also called 'Bimbijāla.' His body was eighty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

“Tattheva [V 1.0050] maṇḍakappamhi, dhammadassī mahāyaso;

Tamandhakāraṃ vidhamitvā, atirocati sadevake”ti.

In that very Maṇḍa aeon, Dhammadassī of great renown, having dispelled that darkness, outshines the world with its devas.

Tassa [P 1.0040] aparabhāge ito catunavutikappamatthake ekasmiṃ kappe ekova siddhattho nāma buddho udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte koṭisatasahassaṃ bhikkhū ahesuṃ, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto uggatejo abhiññābalasampanno maṅgalo nāma tāpaso hutvā mahājambuphalaṃ āharitvā tathāgatassa adāsi. Satthā taṃ phalaṃ paribhuñjitvā “catunavutikappamatthake buddho bhavissasī”ti bodhisattaṃ byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato nagaraṃ vebhāraṃ nāma ahosi, pitā jayaseno nāma rājā, mātā suphassā nāma, sambalo ca sumitto ca dve aggasāvakā, revato nāmupaṭṭhāko, sīvalī ca surāmā ca dve aggasāvikā, kaṇikārarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ saṭṭhihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

After him, ninety-four aeons ago from the present, in one aeon a single Buddha named Siddhattha arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred thousand koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic named Maṅgala, of fierce energy and endowed with supernormal powers; having brought a large jambu fruit, he offered it to the Tathāgata. The Teacher, having consumed that fruit, prophesied to the Bodhisatta, 'Ninety-four aeons hence, you will become a Buddha.' The city of that Blessed One was named Vebhāra, his father was King Jayasena, and his mother was named Suphassā. His two chief disciples were Sambala and Sumitta, his attendant was named Revata, and his two chief female disciples were Sīvalī and Surāmā. His Bodhi tree was the Kaṇikāra tree, his body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

“Dhammadassissa aparena, siddhattho nāma nāyako;

Nihanitvā tamaṃ sabbaṃ, sūriyo abbhuggato yathā”ti.

After Dhammadassī, the leader named Siddhattha, having struck down all darkness, was like the sun risen forth.

Tassa aparabhāge ito dvānavutikappamatthake tisso phussoti ekasmiṃ kappe dve buddhā nibbattiṃsu. Tissassa bhagavato tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte bhikkhūnaṃ koṭisataṃ ahosi, dutiye navutikoṭiyo, tatiye asītikoṭiyo. Tadā bodhisatto mahābhogo mahāyaso sujāto nāma khattiyo hutvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā mahiddhikabhāvaṃ patvā “buddho uppanno”ti sutvā dibbamandāravapadumapāricchattakapupphāni ādāya catuparisamajjhe gacchantaṃ tathāgataṃ pūjesi, ākāse pupphavitānaṃ akāsi. Sopi naṃ satthā “ito dvānavutikappe buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato khemaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, pitā janasandho nāma khattiyo, mātā padumā nāma[M 1.0049], brahmadevo ca udayo ca dve aggasāvakā, samaṅgo nāmupaṭṭhāko, phussā ca sudattā ca dve aggasāvikā, asanarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ saṭṭhihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vassasatasahassaṃ āyūti.

In a later period, ninety-two aeons ago from the present, in one aeon two Buddhas, Tissa and Phussa, arose. The Blessed One Tissa had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were one hundred koṭis of bhikkhus; in the second, ninety koṭis; and in the third, eighty koṭis. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a wealthy and illustrious khattiya named Sujāta. Having renounced the world to become an ascetic and attained great psychic powers, he heard that 'a Buddha has arisen.' Taking divine mandārava, paduma, and pāricchattaka flowers, he honored the Tathāgata as he was proceeding into the midst of the fourfold assembly, creating a canopy of flowers in the sky. That Teacher also prophesied to him, 'Ninety-two aeons hence, you will become a Buddha.' The city of that Blessed One was named Khema. His father was the khattiya Janasandha, and his mother was named Padumā. His two chief disciples were Brahmadeva and Udaya, his attendant was named Samaṅga, and his two chief female disciples were Phussā and Sudattā. His Bodhi tree was the asana tree. His body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was one hundred thousand years.

“Siddhatthassa aparena, asamo appaṭipuggalo;

Anantasīlo amitayaso, tisso lokagganāyako”ti.

After Siddhattha, the matchless, the incomparable one, of endless virtue and immeasurable fame, was Tissa, the world's foremost leader.

Tassa [V 1.0051] aparabhāge phusso nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte saṭṭhi bhikkhusatasahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye paṇṇāsa, tatiye dvattiṃsa. Tadā bodhisatto vijitāvī nāma khattiyo hutvā mahārajjaṃ pahāya satthu santike pabbajitvā tīṇi piṭakāni [P 1.0041] uggahetvā mahājanassa dhammakathaṃ kathesi, sīlapāramiñca pūresi. Sopi naṃ “buddho bhavissasī”ti tatheva byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato kāsī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, jayaseno nāma rājā pitā, sirimā nāma mātā, surakkhito ca dhammaseno ca dve aggasāvakā, sabhiyo nāmupaṭṭhāko, cālā ca upacālā ca dve aggasāvikā, āmalakarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ aṭṭhapaṇṇāsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, navuti vassasahassāni āyūti.

In a later period, a Teacher named Phussa arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were six million bhikkhus; in the second, five million; and in the third, three million two hundred thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a khattiya named Vijitāvī. Having renounced his great kingdom, he went forth under the Teacher. Having mastered the three Piṭakas, he preached the Dhamma to the great populace and fulfilled the perfection of virtue. That Teacher also prophesied to him, saying, 'You will become a Buddha.' The Blessed One's city was named Kāsī, his father was King Jayasena, and his mother was Sirimā. His two chief disciples were Surakkhita and Dhammasena, his attendant was named Sabhiya, and his two chief female disciples were Cālā and Upacālā. His Bodhi tree was the Āmalaka tree. His body was fifty-eight cubits in height, and his lifespan was ninety thousand years.

“Tattheva maṇḍakappamhi, ahu satthā anuttaro;

Anūpamo asamasamo, phusso lokagganāyako”ti.

In that very Maṇḍa aeon, there was the Teacher, the unsurpassed one, incomparable, without an equal: Phussa, the world's foremost leader.

Tassa aparabhāge ito ekanavutikappe vipassī nāma bhagavā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte aṭṭhasaṭṭhi bhikkhusatasahassaṃ ahosi, dutiye ekasatasahassaṃ, tatiye asītisahassāni. Tadā bodhisatto mahiddhiko mahānubhāvo atulo nāma nāgarājā hutvā sattaratanakhacitaṃ sovaṇṇamayaṃ mahāpīṭhaṃ bhagavato adāsi. Sopi naṃ “ito ekanavutikappe buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato bandhumatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, bandhumā nāma rājā pitā, bandhumatī nāma mātā, khaṇḍo ca tisso ca dve aggasāvakā, asoko nāmupaṭṭhāko, candā ca candamittā ca dve aggasāvikā, pāṭalirukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ asītihatthubbedhaṃ [M 1.0050] ahosi, sarīrappabhā sadā satta yojanāni pharitvā aṭṭhāsi, asīti vassasahassāni āyūti.

In a later period, ninety-one aeons ago from the present, the Blessed One named Vipassī arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were six million eight hundred thousand bhikkhus; in the second, one hundred thousand; and in the third, eighty thousand. At that time the Bodhisatta was a nāga king named Atula, of great psychic power and might, who presented the Blessed One with a great golden throne adorned with the seven kinds of jewels. He also prophesied to him, saying, 'Ninety-one aeons hence, you will become a Buddha.' The Blessed One's city was named Bandhumatī, his father was King Bandhumā, and his mother was Bandhumatī. His two chief disciples were Khaṇḍa and Tissa, his attendant was named Asoka, and his two chief female disciples were Candā and Candamittā. His Bodhi tree was the Pāṭali tree. His body was eighty cubits in height, the radiance of his body always extended for seven leagues, and his lifespan was eighty thousand years.

“Phussassa ca aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Vipassī nāma nāmena, loke uppajji cakkhumā”ti.

And after Phussa, the Fully Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, Vipassī by name, the Seeing One, arose in the world.

Tassa aparabhāge ito ekatiṃsakappe sikhī ca vessabhū cāti dve buddhā ahesuṃ. Sikhissāpi bhagavato tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte bhikkhusatasahassaṃ ahosi, dutiye asītisahassāni, tatiye sattattisahassāni. Tadā bodhisatto arindamo nāma rājā hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sacīvaraṃ mahādānaṃ pavattetvā sattaratanapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ hatthiratanaṃ datvā hatthippamāṇaṃ katvā kappiyabhaṇḍaṃ adāsi. Sopi naṃ “ito [V 1.0052] katiṃsakappe buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato aruṇavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, aruṇo nāma khattiyo pitā, pabhāvatī nāma mātā, abhibhū ca sambhavo ca dve aggasāvakā, khemaṅkaro nāmupaṭṭhāko, sakhilā ca padumā ca dve aggasāvikā, puṇḍarīkarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ [P 1.0042] sattatihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, sarīrappabhā yojanattayaṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi, sattati vassasahassāni āyūti.

In a later period, thirty-one aeons ago, two Buddhas named Sikhī and Vessabhū appeared. For the Blessed One Sikhī, there were three assemblies of disciples. The first assembly consisted of one hundred thousand monks, the second of eighty thousand, and the third of seventy-seven thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta was a king named Arindama. He offered a great gift of robes to the Sangha of monks headed by the Buddha, presented an elephant adorned with the seven treasures, and provided suitable requisites equal in amount to the value of the elephant. The Buddha then predicted to him, "In thirty-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha." That Blessed One's city was named Aruṇavatī, his father was the nobleman Aruṇa, and his mother was Pabhāvatī. His two chief disciples were Abhibhū and Sambhava, his attendant was Khemaṅkara, and his two chief female disciples were Sakhilā and Padumā. His Bodhi tree was the puṇḍarīka tree, his body was seventy cubits tall, the radiance of his body extended for three yojanas, and his lifespan was seventy thousand years.

“Vipassissa aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Sikhivhayo nāma jino, asamo appaṭipuggalo”ti.

"After Vipassī, the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, was the Conqueror named Sikhī, unequalled, without a peer."

Tassa aparabhāge vessabhū nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi tayo sāvakasannipātā ahesuṃ. Paṭhamasannipāte asīti bhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ, dutiye sattati, tatiye saṭṭhi. Tadā bodhisatto sudassano nāma rājā hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sacīvaraṃ mahādānaṃ datvā tassa santike pabbajitvā ācāraguṇasampanno buddharatane cittīkārapītibahulo ahosi. Sopi naṃ bhagavā “ito ekatiṃsakappe buddho bhavissasī”ti byākāsi. Tassa pana bhagavato anomaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, suppatīto nāma rājā pitā, yasavatī nāma mātā[M 1.0051], soṇo ca uttaro ca dve aggasāvakā, upasanto nāmupaṭṭhāko, dāmā ca samālā ca dve aggasāvikā, sālarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ saṭṭhihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, saṭṭhi vassasahassāni āyūti.

In a later period, the Teacher named Vessabhū arose. He too had three assemblies of disciples. In the first assembly, there were eighty thousand bhikkhus; in the second, seventy thousand; and in the third, sixty thousand. At that time, the Bodhisatta, a king named Sudassana, after offering a great gift of robes to the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, went forth in his presence. Endowed with virtuous conduct, he was filled with joy and reverence for the Buddha-jewel. The Blessed One then predicted of him, "In thirty-one aeons from now, you will become a Buddha." For that Blessed One, the city was named Anoma; his father, King Suppatīta; and his mother, Yasavatī. His two chief disciples were Soṇa and Uttara; his attendant, Upasanta; and his two chief female disciples, Dāmā and Samālā. His Bodhi tree was the Sāla tree, his body was sixty cubits in height, and his lifespan was sixty thousand years.

“Tattheva maṇḍakappamhi, asamo appaṭipuggalo;

Vessabhū nāma nāmena, loke uppajji so jino”ti.

"In that very Maṇḍa aeon, unequalled and peerless, that Conqueror, Vessabhū by name, arose in the world."

Tassa aparabhāge imasmiṃ kappe cattāro buddhā nibbattā kakusandho, koṇāgamano, kassapo, amhākaṃ bhagavāti. Kakusandhassa bhagavato ekova sāvakasannipāto, tattha cattālīsa bhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ. Tadā bodhisatto khemo nāma rājā hutvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa sapattacīvaraṃ mahādānañceva añjanādibhesajjāni ca datvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbaji. Sopi naṃ satthā byākāsi. Kakusandhassa pana bhagavato khemaṃ nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, aggidatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā, visākhā nāma brāhmaṇī mātā, vidhuro ca sañjīvo ca dve aggasāvakā, buddhijo nāmupaṭṭhāko, sāmā ca campakā ca dve aggasāvikā[V 1.0053], mahāsirīsarukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ cattālīsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, cattālīsa vassasahassāni āyūti.

In a later period, in this very aeon, four Buddhas have arisen: Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, Kassapa, and our Blessed One. For the Blessed One Kakusandha, there was only one assembly of disciples, at which there were forty thousand bhikkhus. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a king named Khema, gave a great gift of bowls and robes to the community of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, as well as medicines such as collyrium, and after hearing the Teacher's discourse, he went forth. That Teacher also made a prediction concerning him. For the Blessed One Kakusandha, the city was named Khema, his father was the brahmin Aggidatta, his mother was the brahmin woman Visākhā, Vidhura and Sañjīva were the two chief disciples, Buddhija was the attendant, Sāmā and Campakā were the two chief female disciples, the great Sirīsa tree was the Bodhi tree, his body was forty cubits in height, and his lifespan was forty thousand years.

“Vessabhussa aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Kakusandho nāma nāmena, appameyyo durāsado”ti.

"After Vessabhū, the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, Kakusandha by name, immeasurable, difficult to approach."

Tassa [P 1.0043] aparabhāge koṇāgamano nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi eko sāvakasannipāto, tattha tiṃsa bhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ. Tadā bodhisatto pabbato nāma rājā hutvā amaccagaṇaparivuto satthu santikaṃ gantvā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā paṭṭuṇṇacīnapaṭṭakoseyyakambaladukūlāni ceva suvaṇṇapādukañca datvā satthu santike pabbaji. Sopi naṃ byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato sobhavatī nāma nagaraṃ ahosi, yaññadatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā, uttarā nāma brāhmaṇī mātā, bhiyyaso ca uttaro ca dve aggasāvakā, sotthijo nāmupaṭṭhāko, samuddā ca uttarā ca dve aggasāvikā, udumbararukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ tiṃsahatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, tiṃsa vassasahassāni āyūti.

In a later period, a Teacher named Koṇāgamana arose. For him too, there was one assembly of disciples, in which thirty thousand bhikkhus were present. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a king named Pabbata, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, went to the Teacher, heard the Dhamma discourse, invited the Bhikkhu Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, and held a great offering. He gave cloths of wool, Chinese silk, silk, woolen blankets, and fine linen, as well as golden sandals, and then went forth in the Teacher’s presence. He too, made a prediction concerning him. The city of that Blessed One was named Sobhavatī. His father was the brahmin Yaññadatta, his mother the brahmin woman Uttarā. His two chief disciples were Bhiyyasa and Uttara, his attendant Sotthija. His two chief female disciples were Samuddā and Uttarā. His Bodhi tree was the Udumbara tree. His body was thirty cubits in height, and his lifespan was thirty thousand years.

“Kakusandhassa [M 1.0052] aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Koṇāgamano nāma jino, lokajeṭṭho narāsabho”ti.

"After Kakusandha, the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds; Koṇāgamana by name, the Conqueror, foremost in the world, a bull among men."

Tassa aparabhāge kassapo nāma satthā udapādi. Tassāpi eko sāvakasannipāto, tattha vīsati bhikkhusahassāni ahesuṃ. Tadā bodhisatto jotipālo nāma māṇavo hutvā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū bhūmiyañca antalikkhe ca pākaṭo ghaṭīkārassa kumbhakārassa mitto ahosi. So tena saddhiṃ satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammakathaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā āraddhavīriyo tīṇi piṭakāni uggahetvā vattāvattasampattiyā buddhassa sāsanaṃ sobhesi. Sopi naṃ byākāsi. Tassa bhagavato jātanagaraṃ bārāṇasī nāma ahosi, brahmadatto nāma brāhmaṇo pitā, dhanavatī nāma brāhmaṇī mātā, tisso ca bhāradvājo ca dve aggasāvakā, sabbamitto nāmupaṭṭhāko, anuḷā ca uruveḷā ca dve aggasāvikā, nigrodharukkho bodhi, sarīraṃ vīsatihatthubbedhaṃ ahosi, vīsati vassasahassāni āyūti.

In a later period, a Teacher named Kassapa arose. For him too, there was one assembly of disciples, in which twenty thousand bhikkhus were present. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having become a young brahmin named Jotipāla, was a master of the three Vedas and renowned both on earth and in the sky. He was a friend of Ghaṭīkāra the potter. Together with him, he approached the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma talk, and then went forth. With aroused energy, he mastered the three Piṭakas and adorned the Buddha’s dispensation through his accomplishment in the major and minor duties. He too, made a prediction concerning him. The birth city of that Blessed One was named Bārāṇasī. His father was the brahmin Brahmadatta, his mother the brahmin woman Dhanavatī. His two chief disciples were Tissa and Bhāradvāja, his attendant Sabbamitta. His two chief female disciples were Anuḷā and Uruveḷā. His Bodhi tree was the Banyan tree, his body was twenty cubits in height, and his lifespan was twenty thousand years.

“Koṇāgamanassa aparena, sambuddho dvipaduttamo;

Kassapo nāma gottena, dhammarājā pabhaṅkaro”ti.

After Koṇāgamana, the Perfectly Enlightened One, supreme among bipeds, was Kassapa by name and clan, the Radiant King of the Dhamma.

Yasmiṃ [V 1.0054] pana kappe dīpaṅkaro dasabalo udapādi, tasmiṃ aññepi tayo buddhā ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ santikā bodhisattassa byākaraṇaṃ natthi, tasmā [P 1.0044] te idha na dassitā. Aṭṭhakathāyaṃ pana tamhā kappā paṭṭhāya sabbepi buddhe dassetuṃ idaṃ vuttaṃ –

In the aeon in which Dīpaṅkara, the Ten-Powered One, arose, there were also three other Buddhas. No prediction was made to the Bodhisatta in their presence; therefore, they are not presented here. However, in the commentary, this was stated in order to present all the Buddhas starting from that aeon—

“Taṇhaṅkaro medhaṅkaro, athopi saraṇaṅkaro;

Dīpaṅkaro ca sambuddho, koṇḍañño dvipaduttamo.

Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and also Saraṇaṅkara; Dīpaṅkara, the Perfectly Enlightened One, and Koṇḍañña, supreme among bipeds.

“Maṅgalo ca sumano ca, revato sobhito muni;

Anomadassī padumo, nārado padumuttaro.

Maṅgala and Sumana, Revata and Sobhita the sage; Anomadassī, Paduma, Nārada, and Padumuttara.

“Sumedho ca sujāto ca, piyadassī mahāyaso;

Atthadassī dhammadassī, siddhattho lokanāyako.

Sumedha and Sujāta, Piyadassī of great fame; Atthadassī and Dhammadassī, Siddhattha, the leader of the world.

“Tisso phusso ca sambuddho, vipassī sikhi vessabhū;

Kakusandho koṇāgamano, kassapo cāti nāyako.

Tissa and Phussa, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones; Vipassī, Sikhī, Vessabhū; Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa, the leaders.

“Ete [M 1.0053] ahesuṃ sambuddhā, vītarāgā samāhitā;

Sataraṃsīva uppannā, mahātamavinodanā;

Jalitvā aggikhandhāva, nibbutā te sasāvakā”ti.

These were the Perfectly Enlightened Ones, free from passion, composed; having arisen like the sun, dispelling great darkness; having blazed like a mass of fire, they and their disciples were extinguished.

Tattha amhākaṃ bodhisatto dīpaṅkarādīnaṃ catuvīsatiyā buddhānaṃ santike adhikāraṃ karonto kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni āgato. Kassapassa pana bhagavato orabhāge ṭhapetvā imaṃ sammāsambuddhaṃ añño buddho nāma natthi. Iti dīpaṅkarādīnaṃ catuvīsatiyā buddhānaṃ santike laddhabyākaraṇo pana bodhisatto yenena –

There, our Bodhisatta, while performing his duties in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, came through four incalculable ages and a hundred thousand eons. However, apart from this Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, there was no other Buddha in the period after the Blessed One Kassapa. Thus, the Bodhisatta, having received his prediction in the presence of the twenty-four Buddhas beginning with Dīpaṅkara, then—

“Manussattaṃ liṅgasampatti, hetu satthāradassanaṃ;

Pabbajjā guṇasampatti, adhikāro ca chandatā;

Aṭṭhadhammasamodhānā, abhinīhāro samijjhatī”ti. (bu. vaṃ. 2.59) –

Human existence, perfection of gender, the cause, seeing the Teacher; going forth, the perfection of qualities, a meritorious act, and strong desire; when these eight conditions are in harmony, the aspiration succeeds.

Ime aṭṭha dhamme samodhānetvā dīpaṅkarapādamūle katābhinīhārena “handa buddhakare dhamme, vicināmi ito [V 1.0055] cito”ti ussāhaṃ katvā “vicinanto tadādakkhiṃ, paṭhamaṃ dānapārami”nti dānapāramitādayo buddhakārakadhammā diṭṭhā, te pūrentoyeva yāva vessantarattabhāvā āgami. Āgacchanto ca ye te katābhinīhārānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ ānisaṃsā saṃvaṇṇitā –

Having combined these eight qualities, and having made his aspiration at the feet of Dīpaṅkara, he made the effort, thinking, 'Come now, let me seek out the qualities that make a Buddha from here and there.' While seeking, he first saw the perfection of giving. Thus, the qualities that make a Buddha, beginning with the perfection of giving, were seen, and he came to be fulfilling them up to the state of Vessantara. And as he came, those benefits described for the Bodhisattas who have made such an aspiration accrued to him—

“Evaṃ sabbaṅgasampannā, bodhiyā niyatā narā;

Saṃsaraṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ, kappakoṭisatehipi.

Thus, endowed with all factors, these persons, destined for Awakening, wander through the long course of saṃsāra, even for hundreds of koṭis of aeons.

“Avīcimhi nuppajjanti, tathā lokantaresu ca;

Nijjhāmataṇhā khuppipāsā, na honti kālakañjakā.

They are not reborn in Avīci, nor in the Lokāntarika hells; they do not become those burnt by craving or afflicted by hunger and thirst, nor are they Kālakañjakas.

“Na honti khuddakā pāṇā, uppajjantāpi duggatiṃ;

Jāyamānā [P 1.0045] manussesu, jaccandhā na bhavanti te.

They do not become small creatures, even when reborn in a woeful state; when born among humans, they are not blind from birth.

“Sotavekallatā natthi, na bhavanti mūgapakkhikā;

Itthibhāvaṃ na gacchanti, ubhatobyañjanapaṇḍakā.

There is no deafness, nor are they mute or crippled; they do not attain the state of womanhood, nor are they hermaphrodites or eunuchs.

“Na bhavanti pariyāpannā, bodhiyā niyatā narā;

Muttā ānantarikehi, sabbattha suddhagocarā.

These persons, destined for Awakening, are not bound; freed from the deeds of immediate retribution, they roam everywhere with pure range.

“Micchādiṭṭhiṃ [M 1.0054] na sevanti, kammakiriyadassanā;

Vasamānāpi saggesu, asaññaṃ nūpapajjare.

They do not resort to wrong view, having insight into action and its result; even though they dwell in heavens, they are not reborn in the realm of non-perception.

“Suddhāvāsesu devesu, hetu nāma na vijjati;

Nekkhammaninnā sappurisā, visaṃyuttā bhavābhave;

Caranti lokatthacariyāyo, pūrenti sabbapāramī”ti.

No cause for their rebirth is found among the gods of the Pure Abodes; these good persons, inclined to renunciation, detached from one state of existence or another, wander, practicing for the world's benefit, fulfilling all perfections.

Te ānisaṃse adhigantvāva āgato. Pāramiyo pūrentassa cassa akittibrāhmaṇakāle saṅkhabrāhmaṇakāle dhanañcayarājakāle mahāsudassanakāle mahāgovindakāle nimimahārājakāle candakumārakāle visayhaseṭṭhikāle sivirājakāle vessantarakāleti dānapāramitāya pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa sasapaṇḍitajātake –

Having attained these benefits, he came. For him, while fulfilling the perfections, there is no measure to the states of existence in which the perfection of generosity was fulfilled, such as in the time of the brahmin Akitti, the brahmin Saṅkha, King Dhanañjaya, the great King Sudassana, the great Govinda, the great King Nimi, Prince Canda, the merchant Visayha, King Sivi, and Prince Vessantara. However, in the Sasapaṇḍita Jātaka, it is definitively stated—

“Bhikkhāya [V 1.0056] upagataṃ disvā, sakattānaṃ pariccajiṃ;

Dānena me samo natthi, esā me dānapāramī”ti. (cariyā. 1.tassudānaṃ) –

Seeing one who had come for alms, I relinquished my own self; there is no one equal to me in generosity, this is my perfection of giving.

Evaṃ attapariccāgaṃ karontassa dānapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Tathā sīlavarājakāle campeyyanāgarājakāle bhūridattanāgarājakāle chaddantanāgarājakāle jayaddisarājaputtakāle alīnasattukumārakāleti sīlapāramitāya pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa saṅkhapālajātake –

Thus, for one making such self-sacrifice, the perfection of giving became the ultimate perfection. Likewise, there is no measure to the states of existence in which the perfection of virtue was fulfilled, such as in the time of King Sīlavarāja, Campeyya the Nāga King, Bhūridatta the Nāga King, Chaddanta the Nāga King, Prince Jayaddisa, and Prince Alīnasattu. However, in the Saṅkhapāla Jātaka, it is definitively stated—

“Sūlehi vijjhiyantopi, koṭṭiyantopi sattihi;

Bhojaputte na kuppāmi, esā me sīlapāramī”ti. (cariyā. 2.91) –

Though pierced with stakes or hacked with spears, I am not angry with the sons of Bhoja; this is my perfection of virtue.

Evaṃ attapariccāgaṃ karontassa sīlapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Tathā somanassakumārakāle, hatthipālakumārakāle, ayogharapaṇḍitakāleti mahārajjaṃ pahāya nekkhammapāramitāya pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa cūḷasutasomajātake –

Similarly, there is no measure to the states of existence in which the perfection of renunciation was fulfilled by abandoning great kingdoms, such as in the time of Prince Somanassa, Prince Hatthipāla, and Ayogharapaṇḍita. However, in the Cūḷasutasoma Jātaka, it is definitively stated—

“Mahārajjaṃ [P 1.0046] hatthagataṃ, kheḷapiṇḍaṃva chaḍḍayiṃ;

Cajato na hoti laggaṃ, esā me nekkhammapāramī”ti. –

I cast away great kingship, though it was in my hand, like a lump of spittle; for one who renounces, there is no attachment—this is my perfection of renunciation.

Evaṃ [M 1.0055] nissaṅgatāya rajjaṃ chaḍḍetvā nikkhamantassa nekkhammapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Tathā vidhurapaṇḍitakāle, mahāgovindapaṇḍitakāle, kuddālapaṇḍitakāle, arakapaṇḍitakāle, bodhiparibbājakakāle, mahosadhapaṇḍitakāleti, paññāpāramitāya pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa sattubhastajātake senakapaṇḍitakāle –

Thus, for one who renounced the kingdom and went forth with such detachment, the perfection of renunciation became the ultimate perfection. Likewise, there is no measure to the states of existence in which the perfection of wisdom was fulfilled, such as in the time of Vidhura the Wise, Mahāgovinda the Wise, Kuddāla the Wise, Araka the Wise, Bodhi the Wanderer, and Mahosadha the Wise. However, in the Sattubhasta Jātaka, in the time of Senaka the Wise, it is definitively stated—

“Paññāya vicinantohaṃ, brāhmaṇaṃ mocayiṃ dukhā;

Paññāya me samo natthi, esā me paññāpāramī”ti. –

By wisdom I investigated and freed the brahmin from suffering; none is equal to me in wisdom; this is my perfection of wisdom.

Antobhastagataṃ sappaṃ dassentassa paññāpāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Tathā vīriyapāramitādīnampi pūritattabhāvānaṃ parimāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Ekantena panassa mahājanakajātake –

The perfection of wisdom, when it reveals the snake hidden in the inner garment, is called the ultimate perfection. Likewise, there is no limit to the fulfillment of the perfections of energy and the others. But concerning him, in the Mahājanaka Jātaka –

“Atīradassī [V 1.0057] jalamajjhe, hatā sabbeva mānusā;

Cittassa aññathā natthi, esā me vīriyapāramī”ti. –

"Though seeing no shore in the midst of the water, and all men had perished, there was no change in my mind—this is my perfection of energy."

Evaṃ mahāsamuddaṃ tarantassa pavattā vīriyapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Khantivādijātake –

Thus, the perfection of energy, which arose while he was crossing the great ocean, is called the ultimate perfection. In the Khantivādī Jātaka –

“Acetanaṃva koṭṭente, tiṇhena pharasunā mamaṃ;

Kāsirāje na kuppāmi, esā me khantipāramī”ti. –

"Even if they were to chop me like a lifeless thing with a sharp axe, I would not be angry with the king of Kāsī—this is my perfection of patience."

Evaṃ acetanabhāvena viya mahādukkhaṃ adhivāsentassa khantipāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Mahāsutasomajātake –

Thus, the perfection of patience, when he endured great suffering as if without consciousness, is called the ultimate perfection. In the Mahāsutasoma Jātaka –

“Saccavācaṃ anurakkhanto, cajitvā mama jīvitaṃ;

Mocesiṃ ekasataṃ khattiye, esā me saccapāramī”ti. –

"Protecting truthful speech, relinquishing my own life, I released a hundred nobles—this is my perfection of truth."

Evaṃ jīvitaṃ cajitvā saccamanurakkhantassa saccapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Mūgapakkhajātake –

Thus, the perfection of truth, when he relinquished life while protecting the truth, is called the ultimate perfection. In the Mūgapakkha Jātaka –

“Mātā pitā na me dessā, napi me dessaṃ mahāyasaṃ;

Sabbaññutaṃ piyaṃ mayhaṃ, tasmā vatamadhiṭṭhahi”nti. (cariyā. 3.6 thokaṃ visadisaṃ) –

"Neither mother nor father are hateful to me, nor is great fame hateful to me. Omniscience is dear to me; therefore, I undertook the vow."

Evaṃ [P 1.0047] jīvitampi cajitvā vataṃ adhiṭṭhahantassa adhiṭṭhānapāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Ekarājajātake –

Thus, the perfection of resolution, when he undertook the vow even having given up life, is called the ultimate perfection. In the Ekarāja Jātaka –

“Na [M 1.0056] maṃ koci uttasati, napihaṃ bhāyāmi kassaci;

Mettābalenupatthaddho, ramāmi pavane tadā”ti. (cariyā. 3.113) –

"No one intimidates me, nor do I fear anyone; supported by the power of loving-kindness, I rejoice in the forest then."

Evaṃ jīvitampi anoloketvā mettāyantassa mettāpāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Lomahaṃsajātake –

Thus, the perfection of loving-kindness, when he practiced loving-kindness without even regarding his own life, is called the ultimate perfection. In the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka –

“Susāne [V 1.0058] seyyaṃ kappemi, chavaṭṭhikaṃ upadhāyahaṃ;

Gāmaṇḍalā upāgantvā, rūpaṃ dassentinappaka”nti. (cariyā. 3.119) –

"I make my bed in the charnel ground, using a corpse's bone as my pillow; village youths come, showing me various forms."

Evaṃ gāmadārakesu niṭṭhubhanādīhi ceva mālāgandhūpahārādīhi ca sukhadukkhaṃ uppādentesupi upekkhaṃ anativattantassa upekkhāpāramitā paramatthapāramī nāma jātā. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthārato panesa attho cariyāpiṭakato gahetabbo. Evaṃ pāramiyo pūretvā vessantarattabhāve ṭhito –

Thus, the perfection of equanimity, when he did not transgress equanimity even when village children caused pleasure and pain by spitting and by offering garlands, perfumes, and other gifts, is called the ultimate perfection. This is the summary here; the detailed meaning should be taken from the Cariyāpiṭaka. Having thus fulfilled the perfections, while in the state of Vessantara –

“Acetanāyaṃ pathavī, aviññāya sukhaṃ dukhaṃ;

Sāpi dānabalā mayhaṃ, sattakkhattuṃ pakampathā”ti. (cariyā. 1.124) –

"This earth, being inanimate, unaware of pleasure or pain, even it shook seven times by the power of my giving."

Evaṃ mahāpathavikampanādīni mahāpuññāni katvā āyupariyosāne tato cuto tusitabhavane nibbatti. Iti dīpaṅkarapādamūlato paṭṭhāya yāva ayaṃ tusitapure nibbatti, ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ dūrenidānaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

Having thus performed great meritorious deeds such as causing the great earth to quake, at the end of his life-span, he passed away from there and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Thus, from the time at the feet of Dīpaṅkara up to this rebirth in the Tusita city, this much should be known as the Distant Account.

Dūrenidānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Distant Origin is concluded.

2. Avidūrenidānakathā

2. The Account of the Not-Far-Distant Origin

Tusitapure vasanteyeva pana bodhisatte buddhakolāhalaṃ nāma udapādi. Lokasmiñhi tīṇi kolāhalāni uppajjanti – kappakolāhalaṃ, buddhakolāhalaṃ, cakkavattikolāhalanti. Tattha “vassasatasahassassa accayena kappuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissatī”ti lokabyūhā nāma kāmāvacaradevā muttasirā vikiṇṇakesā rudamukhā assūni hatthehi puñchamānā rattavatthanivatthā ativiya virūpavesadhārino hutvā manussapathe vicarantā evaṃ ārocenti “mārisā [M 1.0057] ito vassasatasahassassa accayena kappuṭṭhānaṃ bhavissati, ayaṃ loko vinassissati, mahāsamuddopi sussissati[P 1.0048], ayañca mahāpathavī sineru ca pabbatarājā uḍḍayhissanti vinassissanti, yāva brahmalokā lokavināso bhavissati, mettaṃ mārisā bhāvetha, karuṇaṃ, muditaṃ, upekkhaṃ mārisā bhāvetha, mātaraṃ upaṭṭhahatha, pitaraṃ upaṭṭhahatha, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyino hothā”ti. Idaṃ kappakolāhalaṃ nāma. Vassasahassassa accayena pana sabbaññubuddho loke uppajjissatīti lokapāladevatā “ito [V 1.0059] mārisā vassasahassassa accayena buddho loke uppajjissatī”ti ugghosentā āhiṇḍanti. Idaṃ buddhakolāhalaṃ nāma. Vassasatassa accayena cakkavattī rājā uppajjissatīti devatā “ito mārisā vassasatassa accayena cakkavattī rājā loke uppajjissatī”ti ugghosentiyo āhiṇḍanti. Idaṃ cakkavattikolāhalaṃ nāma. Imāni tīṇi kolāhalāni mahantāni honti.

While the Bodhisatta was dwelling in the Tusita city, an event called the “Buddha Uproar” arose. In the world, indeed, three uproars arise: the Aeon Uproar, the Buddha Uproar, and the Wheel-turning Monarch Uproar. Therein, the deities of the sensual realm called Lokabyūhā, with loosened hair, disheveled hair, weeping faces, wiping away tears with their hands, dressed in red clothes, wearing exceedingly disfigured attire, wandering in the path of humans, announce thus: “Friends, after the passing of one hundred thousand years from now, there will be the dissolution of the aeon. This world will be destroyed. Even the great ocean will dry up, and this great earth and Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, will be burned up and destroyed. The destruction of the world will extend up to the Brahma realm. Friends, cultivate loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity. Attend to your mother, attend to your father, be respectful to the elders in your family.” This is called the Aeon Uproar. But after the passing of a thousand years, an All-Knowing Buddha will arise in the world; the world-guardian deities wander about, proclaiming: “Friends, after the passing of a thousand years from now, a Buddha will arise in the world!” This is called the Buddha Uproar. After the passing of a hundred years, a Wheel-turning Monarch will arise; the deities wander about, proclaiming: “Friends, after the passing of a hundred years from now, a Wheel-turning Monarch will arise in the world!” This is called the Wheel-turning Monarch Uproar. These three uproars are great.

Tesu buddhakolāhalasaddaṃ sutvā sakaladasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā ekato sannipatitvā “asuko nāma satto buddho bhavissatī”ti ñatvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā āyācanti. Āyācamānā ca pubbanimittesu uppannesu āyācanti. Tadā pana sabbāpi devatā ekekacakkavāḷe catumahārājasakkasuyāmasantusitasunimmitavasavattimahābrahmehi saddhiṃ ekacakkavāḷe sannipatitvā tusitabhavane bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “mārisā tumhehi dasa pāramiyo pūrentehi na sakkasampattiṃ, na mārasampattiṃ, na brahmasampattiṃ, na cakkavattisampattiṃ patthentehi pūritā, lokanittharaṇatthāya pana sabbaññutaṃ patthentehi pūritā, so vo idāni kālo mārisā buddhattāya samayo, mārisā buddhattāya samayo”ti yāciṃsu.

Hearing the sound of the Buddha Uproar, all the deities from the ten-thousand world-systems gathered together and, knowing that “such and such a being will become a Buddha,” approached and entreated him. And they entreat him when the preliminary signs have appeared. At that time, all the deities from every world-system, together with the Four Great Kings, Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Vasavatti, and the Great Brahma, assembled in one world-system. They went to the presence of the Bodhisatta in the Tusita heaven and entreated him, saying: “Good sir, you have fulfilled the ten perfections not desiring the state of Sakka, nor the state of Māra, nor the state of Brahma, nor the state of a wheel-turning monarch, but desiring omniscience for the sake of delivering the world. Good sir, now is your time, the right time for Buddhahood; good sir, the right time for Buddhahood.”

Atha mahāsatto devatānaṃ paṭiññaṃ adatvāva kāladīpadesakulajanettiāyuparicchedavasena pañcamahāvilokanaṃ nāma vilokesi. Tattha “kālo nu kho, akālo nu kho”ti paṭhamaṃ kālaṃ vilokesi. Tattha vassasatasahassato uddhaṃ vaḍḍhitaāyukālo kālo nāma na hoti. Kasmā? Tadā hi sattānaṃ jātijarāmaraṇāni na paññāyanti. Buddhānañca dhammadesanā tilakkhaṇamuttā nāma natthi. Tesaṃ “aniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ, anattā”ti kathentānaṃ “kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathentī”ti neva sotabbaṃ na saddhātabbaṃ [M 1.0058] maññanti, tato abhisamayo na hoti, tasmiṃ asati aniyyānikaṃ sāsanaṃ hoti. Tasmā so akālo. Vassasatato ūnaāyukālopi kālo na hoti. Kasmā? Tadā sattā ussannakilesā honti, ussannakilesānañca dinno ovādo ovādaṭṭhāne na tiṭṭhati, udake daṇḍarāji viya khippaṃ vigacchati[P 1.0049]. Tasmā sopi akālo. Vassasatasahassato pana paṭṭhāya heṭṭhā, vassasatato paṭṭhāya uddhaṃ āyukālo kālo nāma. Tadā ca vassasatakālo. Atha mahāsatto “nibbattitabbakālo”ti kālaṃ passi.

Then, without giving his pledge to the deities, the Great Being made what is called the five great investigations, concerning the time, the continent, the country, the family, and the mother's lifespan. Therein, he first investigated the time: “Is it the right time or not?” In this regard, a time when the lifespan extends beyond a hundred thousand years is not the right time. Why? Because at such a time, the birth, aging, and death of beings are not apparent. And the teaching of the Buddhas is never apart from the three characteristics. When they are told, “Impermanent, suffering, non-self,” they think, “What is this they are saying?” and do not consider it worth listening to or believing. Consequently, there is no realization, and without that, the teaching does not lead to liberation. Therefore, that is not the right time. A time when the lifespan is less than a hundred years is also not the right time. Why? Because at such a time, beings are overcome by defilements, and advice given to those overcome by defilements does not take hold; it quickly vanishes, like a line drawn on water. Therefore, that too is not the right time. However, a time when the lifespan is from a hundred thousand years downwards, and from a hundred years upwards, is called the right time. And at that time, the lifespan was a hundred years. Then the Great Being saw: “It is the time to be born.”

Tato dīpaṃ vilokento saparivāre cattāro dīpe oloketvā “tīsu dīpesu buddhā na nibbattanti, jambudīpeyeva nibbattantī”ti dīpaṃ passi.

Then, investigating the continent, he surveyed the four continents with their surrounding islands and saw: “Buddhas do not arise in the three other continents; they arise only in Jambudīpa.”

Tato [V 1.0060] “jambudīpo nāma mahā dasayojanasahassaparimāṇo, katarasmiṃ nu kho padese buddhā nibbattantī”ti okāsaṃ vilokento majjhimadesaṃ passi. Majjhimadeso nāma – “puratthimāya disāya gajaṅgalaṃ nāma nigamo, tassa aparena mahāsālo, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Pubbadakkhiṇāya disāya sallavatī nāma nadī, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Dakkhiṇāya disāya setakaṇṇikaṃ nāma nigamo, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Pacchimāya disāya thūṇaṃ nāma brāhmaṇagāmo, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe. Uttarāya disāya usīraddhajo nāma pabbato, tato paraṃ paccantimā janapadā, orato majjhe”ti evaṃ vinaye (mahāva. 259) vutto padeso. So āyāmato tīṇi yojanasatāni, vitthārato aḍḍhateyyāni, parikkhepato nava yojanasatānīti etasmiṃ padese buddhā, paccekabuddhā, aggasāvakā, asīti mahāsāvakā, cakkavattirājā aññe ca mahesakkhā khattiyabrāhmaṇagahapatimahāsālā uppajjanti. Idañcettha kapilavatthu nāma nagaraṃ, tattha mayā nibbattitabbanti niṭṭhaṃ agamāsi.

Then, investigating the region, thinking, 'Jambudīpa is vast, ten thousand yojanas in extent. In what place do Buddhas arise?' he saw the Middle Country. The Middle Country is the region described in the Vinaya thus: 'In the eastern direction is the market town named Gajaṅgala; beyond that is Mahāsāla; beyond that are the border regions; within this is the middle. In the southeastern direction is the river named Sallavatī; beyond that are the border regions; within this is the middle. In the southern direction is the market town named Setakaṇṇika; beyond that are the border regions; within this is the middle. In the western direction is the brahmin village named Thūṇa; beyond that are the border regions; within this is the middle. In the northern direction is the mountain named Usīraddhaja; beyond that are the border regions; within this is the middle.' This region is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty in breadth, and nine hundred in circumference. In this region Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, chief disciples, the eighty great disciples, wheel-turning monarchs, and other powerful khattiyas, brahmins, and wealthy householders arise. 'And in this place is the city named Kapilavatthu; there I must be born.' Thus he came to a decision.

Tato kulaṃ vilokento “buddhā nāma vessakule vā suddakule vā na nibbattanti, lokasammate pana khattiyakule vā brāhmaṇakulevāti dvīsuyeva kulesu nibbattanti. Idāni ca khattiyakulaṃ lokasammataṃ[M 1.0059], tattha nibbattissāmi. Suddhodano nāma rājā me pitā bhavissatī”ti kulaṃ passi.

Then, investigating the family, he thought: 'Buddhas are not born into the Vessa or Sudda castes, but are born only into one of two castes esteemed by the world: the Khattiya or the Brāhmaṇa. Now, the Khattiya caste is esteemed by the world; therein I shall be born. King Suddhodana will be my father.' Thus he determined the family.

Tato mātaraṃ vilokento “buddhamātā nāma lolā surādhuttā na hoti, kappasatasahassaṃ pana pūritapāramī jātito paṭṭhāya akhaṇḍapañcasīlāyeva hoti. Ayañca mahāmāyā nāma devī edisī, ayaṃ me mātā bhavissati, kittakaṃ panassā āyūti dasannaṃ māsānaṃ upari satta divasānī”ti passi.

Then, investigating the mother, he thought: 'The mother of a Buddha is not fickle or addicted to intoxicants. For a hundred thousand eons she has fulfilled the perfections, and from birth she has observed the five precepts unbroken. This Queen Mahāmāyā is such a one; she will be my mother. But what is her lifespan?' He saw, 'Ten months and seven days more.'

Iti imaṃ pañcamahāvilokanaṃ viloketvā “kālo me mārisā buddhabhāvāyā”ti devatānaṃ saṅgahaṃ karonto paṭiññaṃ datvā “gacchatha, tumhe”ti tā devatā uyyojetvā tusitadevatāhi parivuto tusitapure nandanavanaṃ pāvisi. Sabbadevalokesu hi nandanavanaṃ atthiyeva. Tattha naṃ devatā “ito cuto sugatiṃ gaccha, ito cuto sugatiṃ gacchā”ti pubbe katakusalakammokāsaṃ sārayamānā [P 1.0050] vicaranti. So evaṃ devatāhi kusalaṃ sārayamānāhi parivuto tattha vicaranto cavitvā mahāmāyāya deviyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi.

Thus, having made these five great investigations, showing favor to the deities and giving his promise, he said, “Sirs, it is time for me to become a Buddha.” Then, dismissing those deities by saying, “You may go,” he, surrounded by the Tusita deities, entered the Nandana Grove in the Tusita city. For in all deva worlds there is a Nandana Grove. There, the deities wander about, reminding him of his past meritorious deeds, saying, “Departing from here, go to a good destination! Departing from here, go to a good destination!” And so, surrounded by deities reminding him of his wholesome deeds, while wandering there he passed away and took conception in the womb of Queen Mahāmāyā.

Tassa [V 1.0061] āvibhāvatthaṃ ayamanupubbikathā – tadā kira kapilavatthunagare āsāḷhinakkhattaṃ saṅghuṭṭhaṃ ahosi, mahājano nakkhattaṃ kīḷati. Mahāmāyāpi devī pure puṇṇamāya sattamadivasato paṭṭhāya vigatasurāpānaṃ mālāgandhavibhūtisampannaṃ nakkhattakīḷaṃ anubhavamānā sattame divase pātova uṭṭhāya gandhodakena nhāyitvā cattāri satasahassāni vissajjetvā mahādānaṃ datvā sabbālaṅkāravibhūsitā varabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā uposathaṅgāni adhiṭṭhāya alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā sirisayane nipannā niddaṃ okkamamānā imaṃ supinaṃ addasa – ‘cattāro kira naṃ mahārājāno sayaneneva saddhiṃ ukkhipitvā himavantaṃ netvā saṭṭhiyojanike manosilātale sattayojanikassa mahāsālarukkhassa heṭṭhā ṭhapetvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhaṃsu. Atha nesaṃ deviyo āgantvā deviṃ anotattadahaṃ netvā manussamalaharaṇatthaṃ nhāpetvā dibbavatthaṃ nivāsāpetvā gandhehi vilimpāpetvā dibbapupphāni piḷandhāpetvā tato avidūre eko rajatapabbato atthi, tassa anto kanakavimānaṃ atthi[M 1.0060], tattha pācīnasīsakaṃ dibbasayanaṃ paññāpetvā nipajjāpesuṃ. Atha bodhisatto setavaravāraṇo hutvā tato avidūre eko suvaṇṇapabbato atthi, tattha vicaritvā tato oruyha rajatapabbataṃ abhiruhitvā uttaradisato āgamma rajatadāmavaṇṇāya soṇḍāya setapadumaṃ gahetvā koñcanādaṃ naditvā kanakavimānaṃ pavisitvā mātusayanaṃ tikkhattuṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā dakkhiṇapassaṃ phāletvā kucchiṃ paviṭṭhasadiso ahosī’ti. Evaṃ uttarāsāḷhanakkhattena paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi.

To reveal the meaning of this, here is the sequential account: At that time, it is said, in the city of Kapilavatthu, the Āsāḷhī festival was proclaimed. The great populace was enjoying the festival. Queen Mahāmāyā, from the seventh day before the full moon, had been observing the festival free from intoxicants, endowed with garlands, perfumes, and ornaments. On the seventh day, she rose early, bathed in scented water, gave away four hundred thousand in a great donation, adorned herself with all ornaments, partook of excellent food, undertook the Uposatha precepts, entered her adorned and prepared royal chamber, lay down on the royal couch, and as she was falling asleep, she saw this dream: 'Four great kings, it is said, lifted her up along with the couch and took her to the Himalayas. They placed her on a sixty-yojana-wide slab of red arsenic beneath a great sal tree seven yojanas high and stood to one side. Then, their queens came and took the queen to Lake Anotatta, bathed her to remove human stains, had her dressed in divine garments, anointed her with perfumes, and adorned her with divine flowers. Not far from there was a silver mountain, and within it stood a golden palace. There, they prepared a divine couch with its head facing east and had her lie down. Then, the Bodhisatta, having become a splendid white elephant, after roaming on a nearby golden mountain, descended from it, ascended the silver mountain, and coming from the north, with a trunk the color of a silver chain, took a white lotus, trumpeted, entered the golden palace, circumambulated his mother’s couch three times, and appearing to split her right side, he seemed to enter her womb.' Thus, he took conception under the Uttarāsāḷha constellation.

Punadivase pabuddhā devī taṃ supinaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā catusaṭṭhimatte brāhmaṇapāmokkhe pakkosāpetvā gomayaharitūpalittāya lājādīhi katamaṅgalasakkārāya bhūmiyā mahārahāni āsanāni paññāpetvā tattha nisinnānaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ sappimadhusakkharābhisaṅkhatassa varapāyāsassa suvaṇṇarajatapātiyo pūretvā suvaṇṇarajatapātīhiyeva paṭikujjitvā adāsi, aññehi ca ahatavatthakapilagāvidānādīhi te santappesi. Atha nesaṃ sabbakāmehi santappitānaṃ supinaṃ ārocāpetvā “kiṃ bhavissatī”ti pucchi. Brāhmaṇā āhaṃsu “mā cintayi, mahārāja, deviyā te kucchimhi gabbho patiṭṭhito, so ca [P 1.0051] kho purisagabbho, na itthigabbho, putto te bhavissati. So sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasissati, rājā bhavissati cakkavattī; sace agārā nikkhamma pabbajissati, buddho bhavissati loke vivaṭṭacchado”ti.

The next day, the awakened queen reported the dream to the king. The king had sixty-four eminent brahmins summoned. On ground smeared with fresh cow dung and green clay, where auspicious offerings of parched rice and so forth had been made, he had valuable seats prepared. To the brahmins seated there, he gave golden and silver bowls filled with the finest milk-rice prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, covered with golden and silver bowls. He also satisfied them with other gifts such as new clothes and tawny cows. Then, after they had been satisfied with all desirable things, he had the dream recounted and asked, 'What will come of this?' The brahmins said, 'Do not worry, great king. A conception has been established in your queen’s womb—and it is a male conception, not a female one. You will have a son. If he lives the household life, he will become a wheel-turning king; but if he goes forth from home into homelessness, he will become a Buddha in the world, one who has rolled back the veil.'

Bodhisattassa pana mātukucchimhi paṭisandhiggahaṇakkhaṇe ekappahāreneva sakaladasasahassī lokadhātu saṅkampi sampakampi sampavedhi. Bāttiṃsapubbanimittāni pāturahesuṃ – dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu appamāṇo obhāso phari. Tassa taṃ siriṃ daṭṭhukāmā viya andhā cakkhūni [V 1.0062] paṭilabhiṃsu, badhirā saddaṃ suṇiṃsu, mūgā samālapiṃsu, khujjā ujugattā ahesuṃ, paṅgulā padasā gamanaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu, bandhanagatā sabbasattā andubandhanādīhi mucciṃsu, sabbanarakesu aggi nibbāyi, pettivisaye khuppipāsā vūpasami, tiracchānānaṃ bhayaṃ nāhosi, sabbasattānaṃ rogo vūpasami, sabbasattā piyaṃvadā ahesuṃ, madhurenākārena assā hasiṃsu, vāraṇā gajjiṃsu, sabbatūriyāni sakasakaninnādaṃ muñciṃsu, aghaṭṭitāniyeva manussānaṃ hatthūpagādīni ābharaṇāni viraviṃsu, sabbadisā vippasannā ahesuṃ[M 1.0061], sattānaṃ sukhaṃ uppādayamāno mudusītalavāto vāyi, akālamegho vassi, pathavitopi udakaṃ ubbhijjitvā vissandi, pakkhino ākāsagamanaṃ vijahiṃsu, nadiyo asandamānā aṭṭhaṃsu, mahāsamudde madhuraṃ udakaṃ ahosi, sabbatthakameva pañcavaṇṇehi padumehi sañchannatalo ahosi, thalajajalajādīni sabbapupphāni pupphiṃsu, rukkhānaṃ khandhesu khandhapadumāni, sākhāsu sākhāpadumāni, latāsu latāpadumāni pupphiṃsu, thale silātalāni bhinditvā uparūpari satta satta hutvā daṇḍapadumāni nāma nikkhamiṃsu, ākāse olambakapadumāni nāma nibbattiṃsu, samantato pupphavassā vassiṃsu, ākāse dibbatūriyāni vajjiṃsu, sakaladasasahassilokadhātu vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhamālāguḷo viya, uppīḷetvā baddhamālākalāpo viya, alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ mālāsanaṃ viya ca ekamālāmālinī vipphurantavāḷabījanī pupphadhūmagandhaparivāsitā paramasobhaggappattā ahosi.

At the very moment the Bodhisatta took conception in his mother’s womb, the entire ten-thousandfold world system shook, quaked, and trembled. Thirty-two portents appeared. An immeasurable radiance spread throughout the ten thousand world-spheres. As if desiring to see his glory, the blind regained their sight, the deaf heard sound, the mute spoke, the hunchbacked became straight-bodied, the lame regained the ability to walk on their own feet, and all beings in bondage were freed from their fetters and bonds. In all the hells, the fires were extinguished. In the realm of the departed, hunger and thirst subsided. Animals had no fear. The sickness of all beings subsided. All beings became kind-spoken. Horses neighed sweetly, elephants trumpeted, and all musical instruments sounded of their own accord. Ornaments worn on people's hands and so forth jingled without being struck. All directions became clear. A gentle, cool breeze blew, bringing happiness to beings. An unseasonal cloud rained. Water welled up from the earth and flowed forth. Birds ceased their flight in the sky. Rivers stood still, not flowing. The water in the great ocean became sweet. The entire surface of the earth was covered with five-colored lotuses. All flowers—whether land-born or water-born—bloomed. On the trunks of trees, trunk-lotuses blossomed; on their branches, branch-lotuses; and on vines, vine-lotuses. On land, breaking through stone slabs, stem-lotuses emerged, seven upon seven. In the sky, hanging-lotuses appeared. Showers of flowers rained down all around. In the sky, divine instruments played. The entire ten-thousandfold world system—like a ball of garlands sent rolling, like a tightly bound bouquet, and like a decorated and prepared flower-seat—became adorned with a single garland, radiant with waving whisks, perfumed with flowers, incense, and scents, and attained supreme glory.

Evaṃ gahitapaṭisandhikassa bodhisattassa paṭisandhito paṭṭhāya bodhisattassa ceva bodhisattamātuyā ca upaddavanivāraṇatthaṃ khaggahatthā cattāro devaputtā ārakkhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Bodhisattamātu pana purisesu rāgacittaṃ nuppajji, lābhaggayasaggappattā ca ahosi sukhinī akilantakāyā. Bodhisattañca antokucchigataṃ [P 1.0052] vippasanne maṇiratane āvutapaṇḍusuttaṃ viya passati. Yasmā ca bodhisattena vasitakucchi nāma cetiyagabbhasadisā hoti, na sakkā aññena sattena āvasituṃ vā paribhuñjituṃ vā, tasmā bodhisattamātā sattāhajāte bodhisatte kālaṃ katvā tusitapure nibbattati. Yathā ca aññā itthiyo dasa māse apatvāpi atikkamitvāpi nisinnāpi nipannāpi vijāyanti, na evaṃ bodhisattamātā. Sā pana bodhisattaṃ dasa māse kucchinā pariharitvā ṭhitāva vijāyati. Ayaṃ bodhisattamātudhammatā.

From the moment the Bodhisatta was conceived, four divine beings, sword in hand, took up guard to protect both the Bodhisatta and his mother from harm. The Bodhisatta’s mother felt no lustful thoughts toward men, and she was happy, free from weariness, having attained the highest gain and renown. And she saw the Bodhisatta inside her womb as if he were a clear jewel wrapped in a pale yellow thread. Because the womb where the Bodhisatta had dwelt is like a shrine chamber, no other being could dwell there or make use of it. Thus, seven days after the Bodhisatta's birth, his mother passed away and was reborn in the Tusita heaven. Unlike other women, who give birth before or after ten months, or while sitting or lying down, the Bodhisatta’s mother carried him in her womb for ten full months and gave birth while standing. This is the nature of the Bodhisatta’s mother.

Mahāmāyāpi devī pattena telaṃ viya dasa māse kucchinā bodhisattaṃ pariharitvā paripuṇṇagabbhā ñātigharaṃ gantukāmā suddhodanamahārājassa ārocesi – “icchāmahaṃ, deva, kulasantakaṃ devadahanagaraṃ gantu”nti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā kapilavatthuto yāva devadahanagarā maggaṃ samaṃ kāretvā kadalipuṇṇaghaṭadhajapaṭākādīhi alaṅkārāpetvā devi suvaṇṇasivikāya [V 1.0063] nisīdāpetvā amaccasahassena ukkhipāpetvā mahantena [M 1.0062] parivārena pesesi. Dvinnaṃ pana nagarānaṃ antare ubhayanagaravāsīnampi lumbinīvanaṃ nāma maṅgalasālavanaṃ atthi, tasmiṃ samaye mūlato paṭṭhāya yāva aggasākhā sabbaṃ ekapāliphullaṃ ahosi, sākhantarehi ceva pupphantarehi ca pañcavaṇṇā bhamaragaṇā nānappakārā ca sakuṇasaṅghā madhurassarena vikūjantā vicaranti. Sakalaṃ lumbinīvanaṃ cittalatāvanasadisaṃ, mahānubhāvassa rañño susajjitaṃ āpānamaṇḍalaṃ viya ahosi. Deviyā taṃ disvā sālavanakīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmatācittaṃ udapādi. Amaccā deviṃ gahetvā sālavanaṃ pavisiṃsu. Sā maṅgalasālamūlaṃ gantvā sālasākhaṃ gaṇhitukāmā ahosi, sālasākhā suseditavettaggaṃ viya onamitvā deviyā hatthapathaṃ upagañchi. Sā hatthaṃ pasāretvā sākhaṃ aggahesi. Tāvadeva cassā kammajavātā caliṃsu. Athassā sāṇiṃ parikkhipitvā mahājano paṭikkami. Sālasākhaṃ gahetvā tiṭṭhamānāya evassā gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. Taṅkhaṇaṃyeva cattāro visuddhacittā mahābrahmāno suvaṇṇajālaṃ ādāya sampattā tena suvaṇṇajālena bodhisattaṃ sampaṭicchitvā mātu purato ṭhapetvā “attamanā, devi, hohi, mahesakkho te putto uppanno”ti āhaṃsu.

Queen Mahāmāyā, having carried the Bodhisatta in her womb for ten months as carefully as oil in a bowl, and being full with child, wished to go to her family home. She informed King Suddhodana, saying, "Your Majesty, I wish to go to Devadaha, the city of my clan." The king consented, saying, "Very well," and had the road from Kapilavatthu to Devadaha leveled. He had it adorned with banana trees, full water pots, banners, and flags, then seated the queen in a golden palanquin. Having it lifted by a thousand ministers, he sent her off with a great retinue. Between the two cities, there was an auspicious sal grove called Lumbinīvana, belonging to the inhabitants of both cities. At that time, from its roots to its topmost branches, the entire grove was a mass of blossoms. Among the branches and flowers, swarms of five-colored bees and flocks of various kinds of birds flitted about, singing sweetly. The entire Lumbinīvana was like the Cittalatā Grove, like the well-adorned pleasure pavilion of a mighty king. Seeing this, a desire arose in the queen to enjoy the delights of the sal grove. The ministers led the queen into the sal grove. She went to the foot of an auspicious sal tree and wished to take hold of a branch. The sal branch, like the tip of a well-steamed reed, bent down and came within reach of the queen's hand. She stretched out her hand and grasped the branch. At that very moment, her labor pains began. The people then surrounded her with a screen and withdrew. As she stood there holding the sal branch, the birth took place. At that instant, four great Brahmās with purified minds arrived with a golden net. Receiving the Bodhisatta in that golden net, they placed him before his mother and said, "Rejoice, O queen, a son of great power has been born to you."

Yathā pana aññe sattā mātukucchito nikkhamantā paṭikūlena asucinā makkhitā nikkhamanti, na evaṃ bodhisatto. So pana [P 1.0053] dhammāsanato otaranto dhammakathiko viya, nisseṇito otaranto puriso viya, ca dve ca hatthe dve ca pāde pasāretvā ṭhitakova mātukucchisambhavena kenaci asucinā amakkhito suddho visado kāsikavatthe nikkhittamaṇiratanaṃ viya jotayanto mātukucchito nikkhami. Evaṃ santepi bodhisattassa ca bodhisattamātuyā ca sakkāratthaṃ ākāsato dve udakadhārā nikkhamitvā bodhisattassa ca mātuyā ca sarīre utuṃ gāhāpesuṃ.

Whereas other beings, when they emerge from their mother’s womb, are smeared with repulsive, impure matter, it was not so with the Bodhisatta. Like a Dhamma teacher descending from the Dhamma seat, or a man descending a staircase, he emerged from his mother’s womb with his two hands and two feet fully extended, unstained by any impurity from the womb, pure, clear, and shining like a jewel placed on a cloth of Kāsi silk. Nevertheless, to honor both the Bodhisatta and his mother, two streams of water came forth from the sky and provided a comfortable temperature for the bodies of the Bodhisatta and his mother.

Atha naṃ suvaṇṇajālena paṭiggahetvā ṭhitānaṃ brahmānaṃ hatthato cattāro mahārājāno maṅgalasammatāya sukhasamphassāya ajinappaveṇiyā gaṇhiṃsu, tesaṃ hatthato manussā dukūlacumbaṭakena. Manussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāya puratthimadisaṃ olokesi, anekāni cakkavāḷasahassāni ekaṅgaṇāni ahesuṃ. Tattha devamanussā gandhamālādīhi [M 1.0063] pūjayamānā “mahāpurisa, idha tumhehi sadiso añño natthi, kutettha uttaritaro”ti āhaṃsu. Evaṃ catasso disā, catasso anudisā, heṭṭhā, uparīti dasa disā anuviloketvā attanā sadisaṃ kañci adisvā “ayaṃ uttarādisā”ti sattapadavītihārena agamāsi, mahābrahmunā setacchattaṃ dhāriyamāno, suyāmena vāḷabījaniṃ, aññāhi ca devatāhi sesarājakakudhabhaṇḍahatthāhi [V 1.0064] anugammamāno. Tato sattamapade ṭhito “aggohamasmiṃ lokassā”tiādikaṃ āsabhiṃ vācaṃ nicchārento sīhanādaṃ nadi.

Then, from the hands of the Brahmās who stood having received him in a golden net, the Four Great Kings took him on a rug of antelope hide, considered auspicious and pleasant to the touch. From their hands, humans received him with a cushion of fine cloth. Released from the hands of humans, he stood firmly on the earth and looked towards the eastern direction, and many thousands of world-systems appeared as a single open space. There, gods and humans, honoring him with perfumes and garlands, said, 'Great Being, there is none like you here—how could there be any superior?' Thus he surveyed the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, below, and above—the ten directions in all. Seeing no one equal to himself, he took seven strides to the north, the supreme direction. As he advanced, Mahābrahmā held a white parasol, Suyāma a yak-tail whisk, and other deities followed, bearing the remaining royal regalia. Then, standing at the seventh step, he roared a lion's roar, uttering the bull-like speech: 'I am the foremost in the world!' and so forth.

Bodhisatto hi tīsu attabhāvesu mātukucchito nikkhantamattova vācaṃ nicchāresi mahosadhattabhāve, vessantarattabhāve, imasmiṃ attabhāveti. Mahosadhattabhāve kirassa mātukucchito nikkhantamattasseva sakko devarājā āgantvā candanasāraṃ hatthe ṭhapetvā gato, so taṃ muṭṭhiyaṃ katvāva nikkhanto. Atha naṃ mātā “tāta, kiṃ gahetvā āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Osadhaṃ, ammā”ti. Iti osadhaṃ gahetvā āgatattā “osadhadārako”tvevassa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ osadhaṃ gahetvā cāṭiyaṃ pakkhipiṃsu, āgatāgatānaṃ andhabadhirādīnaṃ tadeva sabbarogavūpasamāya bhesajjaṃ ahosi. Tato “mahantaṃ idaṃ osadhaṃ, mahantaṃ idaṃ osadha”nti uppannavacanaṃ upādāya “mahosadho”tvevassa nāmaṃ jātaṃ. Vessantarattabhāve pana mātukucchito nikkhanto dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā “atthi nu kho, amma, kiñci gehasmiṃ, dānaṃ dassāmī”ti vadanto nikkhami. Athassa mātā “sadhane kule nibbattosi, tātā”ti puttassa hatthaṃ attano [P 1.0054] hatthatale katvā sahassatthavikaṃ ṭhapesi. Imasmiṃ pana attabhāve imaṃ sīhanādaṃ nadīti evaṃ bodhisatto tīsu attabhāvesu mātukucchito nikkhantamattova vācaṃ nicchāresi. Yathā ca paṭisandhiggahaṇakkhaṇe, jātakkhaṇepissa dvattiṃsa pubbanimittāni pāturahesuṃ. Yasmiṃ pana samaye amhākaṃ bodhisatto lumbinīvane jāto, tasmiṃyeva samaye rāhulamātā devī, ānandatthero, channo amacco, kāḷudāyī amacco, kaṇḍako assarājā, mahābodhirukkho, catasso nidhikumbhiyo [M 1.0064] ca jātā. Tattha ekā gāvutappamāṇā, ekā aḍḍhayojanappamāṇā, ekā tigāvutappamāṇā, ekā yojanappamāṇā ahosīti. Ime satta sahajātā nāma.

For the Bodhisatta, in three existences, as soon as he emerged from his mother's womb, he uttered words: in the existence as Mahosadha, in the existence as Vessantara, and in this present existence. In the existence as Mahosadha, it is said that as soon as he emerged from his mother's womb, Sakka, king of the devas, came and placed sandalwood essence in his hand and then departed. He emerged with it clenched in his fist. Then his mother asked him, “Dear son, what have you come holding?” “Medicine, mother.” Because he had come holding medicine, they gave him the name “Osadhadāraka.” They placed that medicine in a jar, and for the blind, deaf, and others who came, it became the remedy for the pacification of all diseases. Then, on account of the saying that arose, “This medicine is great, this medicine is great,” his name became “Mahosadha.” In the existence as Vessantara, emerging from his mother's womb, he stretched out his right hand and emerged saying, “Mother, is there anything in the house? I wish to give a gift.” Then his mother said, “You are born into a wealthy family, dear son,” and placing her son’s hand in her own palm, she put a purse of a thousand coins in it. In this present existence, he uttered this lion’s roar. Thus, in three existences, the Bodhisatta uttered words as soon as he emerged from his mother's womb. And just as at the moment of his conception, so too at the moment of his birth, the thirty-two portents appeared. At the very moment our Bodhisatta was born in the Lumbinī Grove, at that same moment the lady Rāhulamātā, the elder Ānanda, the minister Channa, the minister Kāḷudāyī, Kaṇḍaka the king of horses, the great Bodhi tree, and four treasure jars were also born. Of these jars, one was a gāvuta in size, one was half a yojana, one was three gāvutas, and one was a yojana. These are called the seven co-nascent ones.

Ubhayanagaravāsino bodhisattaṃ gahetvā kapilavatthunagarameva agamaṃsu.
