Taṃ divasaṃyeva ca “kapilavatthunagare suddhodanamahārājassa putto jāto, ayaṃ kumāro bodhitale nisīditvā buddho bhavissatī”ti tāvatiṃsabhavane haṭṭhatuṭṭhā devasaṅghā celukkhepādīni pavattentā kīḷiṃsu. Tasmiṃ samaye suddhodanamahārājassa kulūpako aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī kāḷadevīlo nāma tāpaso bhattakiccaṃ katvā divāvihāratthāya tāvatiṃsabhavanaṃ gantvā tattha divāvihāraṃ nisinno tā devatā kīḷamānā disvā “kiṃkāraṇā tumhe evaṃ tuṭṭhamānasā kīḷatha, mayhampetaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathethā”ti pucchi. Devatā āhaṃsu “mārisa, suddhodanarañño putto jāto, so bodhitale nisīditvā buddho hutvā dhammacakkaṃ pavattessati, tassa anantaṃ buddhalīḷaṃ daṭṭhuṃ dhammañca sotuṃ lacchāmāti iminā kāraṇena tuṭṭhāmhā”ti. Tāpaso tāsaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā khippaṃ devalokato oruyha rājanivesanaṃ [V 1.0065] pavisitvā paññattāsane nisinno “putto kira te, mahārāja, jāto, passissāmi na”nti āha. Rājā alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ kumāraṃ āharāpetvā tāpasaṃ vandāpetuṃ abhihari, bodhisattassa pādā parivattitvā tāpasassa jaṭāsu patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Bodhisattassa hi tenattabhāvena vanditabbayuttako nāma añño natthi. Sace hi ajānantā bodhisattassa sīsaṃ tāpasassa pādamūle ṭhapeyyuṃ, sattadhā tassa muddhā phaleyya. Tāpaso “na me attānaṃ nāsetuṃ yutta”nti uṭṭhāyāsanā bodhisattassa añjaliṃ paggahesi. Rājā taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā attano puttaṃ vandi.

The inhabitants of both cities took the Bodhisatta and went to the city of Kapilavatthu. On that very day, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, the joyous and delighted assembly of gods played and celebrated, tossing their robes and the like, exclaiming, “In the city of Kapilavatthu, a son has been born to the great king Suddhodana; this prince, seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, will become a Buddha.” At that time, a sage named Kāḷadevila, a family attendant of the great king Suddhodana who had attained the eight meditative attainments, having finished his meal, went to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven for his midday rest. Seated there in his midday rest, he saw those gods playing and asked, “For what reason are you playing with such delighted minds? Tell me this reason also.” The gods said, “Sir, a son has been born to King Suddhodana. Seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, he will become a Buddha and set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma. We shall get to see his boundless Buddha-grace and hear the Dhamma; for this reason we are delighted.” Hearing their words, the sage quickly descended from the world of the devas, entered the king’s residence, and, seated on the prepared seat, said, “Great king, I hear a son has been born to you. I wish to see him.” The king had the adorned and prepared prince brought forth to have him pay homage to the sage. The Bodhisatta’s feet turned around and rested on the sage’s matted locks. For in that existence, there was no one else fit to be venerated by the Bodhisatta. Indeed, if anyone, not knowing, were to place the Bodhisatta’s head at the sage’s feet, the sage's head would split into seven pieces. The sage, thinking, “It is not right for me to destroy myself,” rose from his seat and paid homage to the Bodhisatta with raised hands. The king, seeing this marvel, bowed to his own son.

Tāpaso atīte cattālīsa kappe, anāgate cattālīsāti asīti kappe anussarati. Bodhisattassa lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā “bhavissati nu kho buddho, udāhu no”ti āvajjetvā upadhārento “nissaṃsayaṃ buddho bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “acchariyapuriso aya”nti sitaṃ [P 1.0055] akāsi. Tato “ahaṃ imaṃ buddhabhūtaṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhissāmi nu kho, no”ti upadhārento “na labhissāmi, antarāyeva kālaṃ katvā buddhasatenapi [M 1.0065] buddhasahassenapi gantvā bodhetuṃ asakkuṇeyye arūpabhave nibbattissāmī”ti disvā “evarūpaṃ nāma acchariyapurisaṃ buddhabhūtaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhissāmi, mahatī vata me jāni bhavissatī”ti parodi.

The sage could recollect forty aeons into the past and forty aeons into the future—eighty aeons in total. Observing the perfection of the Bodhisatta’s marks, he considered, “Will he become a Buddha, or not?” and, upon discerning, “Without a doubt, he will become a Buddha,” he smiled, thinking, “This is a marvelous person.” Then, pondering, “Will I get to see him as a Buddha, or not?” he realized, “I will not. I will die before then and be reborn in the formless realm, where one cannot be awakened even by a hundred or a thousand Buddhas.” Seeing this, he wept, lamenting, “Alas, I will not get to see such a marvelous person who has become a Buddha. Great indeed will be my loss!”

Manussā disvā “amhākaṃ ayyo idāneva hasitvā puna parodi. Kiṃ nu kho, bhante, amhākaṃ ayyaputtassa koci antarāyo bhavissatī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Natthetassa antarāyo, nissaṃsayena buddho bhavissatī”ti. Atha “kasmā paroditthā”ti? “Evarūpaṃ purisaṃ buddhabhūtaṃ daṭṭhuṃ na labhissāmi, ‘mahatī vata me jāni bhavissatī’ti attānaṃ anusocanto rodāmī”ti āha. Tato so “kiṃ nu kho me ñātakesu koci etaṃ buddhabhūtaṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhissati, na labhissatī”ti upadhārento attano bhāgineyyaṃ nāḷakadārakaṃ addasa. So bhaginiyā gehaṃ gantvā “kahaṃ te putto nāḷako”ti? “Atthi gehe, ayyā”ti. “Pakkosāhi na”nti pakkosāpetvā attano santikaṃ āgataṃ kumāraṃ āha – “tāta, suddhodanamahārājassa kule putto jāto, buddhaṅkuro esa, pañcatiṃsa vassāni atikkamitvā buddho bhavissati, tvaṃ etaṃ daṭṭhuṃ labhissasi, ajjeva pabbajāhī”ti. Sattāsītikoṭidhane kule nibbattadārakopi “na maṃ mātulo anatthe niyojessatī”ti cintetvā tāvadeva antarāpaṇato kāsāyāni ceva mattikāpattañca āharāpetvā kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyāni vatthāni acchādetvā “yo loke uttamapuggalo, taṃ uddissa mayhaṃ pabbajjā”ti bodhisattābhimukhaṃ añjaliṃ paggayha pañcapatiṭṭhitena vanditvā pattaṃ thavikāya pakkhipitvā aṃsakūṭe laggetvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā samaṇadhammaṃ [V 1.0066] akāsi. So paramābhisambodhiṃ pattaṃ tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā nāḷakapaṭipadaṃ kathāpetvā puna himavantaṃ pavisitvā arahattaṃ patvā ukkaṭṭhapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno satteva māse āyuṃ pāletvā ekaṃ suvaṇṇapabbataṃ nissāya ṭhitakova anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi.

Seeing him, the people asked, "Our lord just now laughed and then wept again. What, venerable sir, could be the danger to our lord's son?" "There is no danger to him. Without a doubt, he will become a Buddha," he replied. Then they asked, "Why did you weep?" He replied, "I will not live to see such a man become a Buddha. 'Great indeed will be my loss,' I lamented, weeping for myself." Then he thought, "Will any of my relatives see him as a Buddha, or not?" Reflecting thus, he saw his nephew, the boy Nāḷaka. Going to his sister's house, he asked, "Where is your son Nāḷaka?" "He is in the house, lord," she replied. "Call him here." When the boy was summoned and came to him, he said, "Dear one, a son has been born in the family of King Suddhodana. He is a Buddha-to-be. After thirty-five years, he will become a Buddha. You will see him. Go forth today." Though born into a family with eighty-seven crores of wealth, the boy thought, "My uncle would not urge me to what is unprofitable." Immediately, he had ochre robes and an earthen bowl brought from the marketplace. Shaving off his hair and beard, he donned the ochre robes. With hands raised in reverence towards the Bodhisatta, he paid homage with the fivefold prostration, saying, "My going forth is for the sake of the supreme person in the world." Placing the bowl in a bag, he hung it on his shoulder and entered the Himalayas, where he practiced the recluse's duties. He approached the Tathāgata, who had attained supreme enlightenment, had him preach the discourse on the Nāḷaka Practice, and then re-entered the Himalayas. There, he attained arahantship. Following the supreme practice, he maintained his life for only seven months, then, while standing near a golden mountain, he attained final Nibbāna with no residue remaining.

Bodhisattampi kho pañcame divase sīsaṃ nhāpetvā “nāmaggahaṇaṃ gaṇhissāmā”ti rājabhavanaṃ catujjātikagandhehi vilimpitvā lājāpañcamakāni pupphāni vikiritvā asambhinnapāyāsaṃ pacāpetvā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāraṅgate aṭṭhasatabrāhmaṇe nimantetvā rājabhavane nisīdāpetvā subhojanaṃ [M 1.0066] bhojetvā mahāsakkāraṃ [P 1.0056] katvā “kiṃ nu kho bhavissatī”ti lakkhaṇāni pariggahāpesuṃ. Tesu –

On the fifth day, having had the Bodhisatta's head washed and intending, "We will perform the name-taking ceremony," they had the royal palace anointed with the four kinds of fragrances, scattered flowers with parched rice as the fifth, and had excellent milk-rice prepared. They invited one hundred and eight Brahmins who were masters of the three Vedas, seated them in the royal palace, served them with excellent food, and paid them great honor. Then they had them examine the marks, asking, "What, indeed, will he become?" Among them—

“Rāmo dhajo lakkhaṇo cāpi mantī, koṇḍañño ca bhojo suyāmo sudatto;

Ete tadā aṭṭha ahesuṃ brāhmaṇā, chaḷaṅgavā mantaṃ viyākariṃsū”ti. –

"Rāma, Dhaja, Lakkhaṇa, and also Mantī, Koṇḍañña, Bhoja, Suyāma, and Sudatta; These were the eight brahmins at that time, versed in the six branches of knowledge, who expounded the sacred texts."

Ime aṭṭheva brāhmaṇā lakkhaṇapariggāhakā ahesuṃ. Paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase supinopi eteheva pariggahito. Tesu satta janā dve aṅguliyo ukkhipitvā dvedhā byākariṃsu – “imehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgato agāraṃ ajjhāvasamāno rājā hoti cakkavattī, pabbajamāno buddho”ti, sabbaṃ cakkavattirañño sirivibhavaṃ ācikkhiṃsu. Tesaṃ pana sabbadaharo gottato koṇḍañño nāma māṇavo bodhisattassa varalakkhaṇanipphattiṃ oloketvā – “imassa agāramajjhe ṭhānakāraṇaṃ natthi, ekantenesa vivaṭṭacchado buddho bhavissatī”ti ekameva aṅguliṃ ukkhipitvā ekaṃsabyākaraṇaṃ byākāsi. Ayañhi katādhikāro pacchimabhavikasatto paññāya itare satta jane abhibhavitvā “imehi lakkhaṇehi samannāgatassa agāramajjhe ṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, asaṃsayaṃ buddho bhavissatī”ti ekameva gatiṃ addasa, tasmā ekaṃ aṅguliṃ ukkhipitvā evaṃ byākāsi. Athassa nāmaṃ gaṇhantā sabbalokassa atthasiddhikarattā “siddhattho”ti nāmamakaṃsu.

These eight brahmins were the interpreters of the marks. The dream on the day of conception was also interpreted by these very ones. Among them, seven raised two fingers and made a twofold prediction: "One endowed with these marks, if he lives the household life, will become a wheel-turning monarch; if he goes forth, he will become a Buddha." And they described in full all the glory and power of a wheel-turning monarch. However, the youngest among them, a young brahmin named Koṇḍañña by clan, having examined the perfection of the Bodhisatta’s excellent marks, raised only one finger and made a one-pointed prediction: "For this one, there is no reason to remain in the household life; without a doubt, he will become a Buddha with the covering removed." For he, being one who had made his aspiration and a being in his final existence, surpassed the other seven men in wisdom and saw only one destiny: "One endowed with these marks has no place in the household life; undoubtedly, he will become a Buddha." Therefore, he raised one finger and spoke thus. Then, when they gave him a name, because he would accomplish the welfare of the whole world, they gave him the name "Siddhattha."

Atha te brāhmaṇā attano gharāni gantvā putte āmantayiṃsu – “tātā, amhe mahallakā, suddhodanamahārājassa puttaṃ sabbaññutaṃ pattaṃ mayaṃ sambhaveyyāma vā no vā, tumhe tasmiṃ kumāre sabbaññutaṃ patte tassa sāsane pabbajeyyāthā”ti. Te sattapi janā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gatā, koṇḍaññamāṇavova arogo ahosi. So mahāsatte vuḍḍhimanvāya mahābhinikkhamanaṃ [V 1.0067] abhinikkhamitvā anukkamena uruvelaṃ gantvā “ramaṇīyo, vata ayaṃ bhūmibhāgo, alaṃ vatidaṃ kulaputtassa [M 1.0067] padhānatthikassa padhānāyā”ti cittaṃ uppādetvā tattha vāsaṃ upagate “mahāpuriso pabbajito”ti sutvā tesaṃ brāhmaṇānaṃ putte upasaṅkamitvā evamāha “siddhatthakumāro kira pabbajito, so nissaṃsayaṃ buddho bhavissati. Sace tumhākaṃ pitaro arogā assu, ajja nikkhamitvā pabbajeyyuṃ. Sace tumhepi iccheyyātha, etha, ahaṃ taṃ purisaṃ anupabbajissāmī”ti. Te sabbe ekacchandā bhavituṃ nāsakkhiṃsu[P 1.0057], tayo janā na pabbajiṃsu. Koṇḍaññabrāhmaṇaṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā itare cattāro pabbajiṃsu. Te pañcapi janā pañcavaggiyattherā nāma jātā.

Then those brahmins, having returned to their homes, addressed their sons: "Dear ones, we are old. We may or may not live to see the son of King Suddhodana attain omniscience, but when that prince attains omniscience, you should go forth in his teaching." Those seven men lived for the remainder of their lifespans and passed on according to their karma; only the young man Koṇḍañña remained healthy. When the Great Being, in the course of his development, went forth in the great renunciation and, proceeding in stages, reached Uruvelā, he gave rise to the thought, "Indeed, this region is delightful! It is truly suitable for a clansman intent on striving to strive!" and took up residence there. Hearing that "the Great Man has gone forth," Koṇḍañña approached the sons of those brahmins and said: "It is said that Prince Siddhattha has gone forth. Without a doubt, he will become a Buddha. If your fathers were healthy, they would go forth today. If you also wish it, come, I will go forth in his footsteps." They were not all of one mind, and three did not go forth. With the brahmin Koṇḍañña as their eldest, the other four went forth. These five became known as the Elders of the Group of Five.

Tadā pana rājā “kiṃ disvā mayhaṃ putto pabbajissatī”ti pucchi. “Cattāri pubbanimittānī”ti. “Katarañca katarañcā”ti? “Jarājiṇṇaṃ, byādhitaṃ, kālakataṃ, pabbajita”nti. Rājā “ito paṭṭhāya evarūpānaṃ mama puttassa santikaṃ upasaṅkamituṃ mā adattha, mayhaṃ puttassa buddhabhāvena kammaṃ natthi, ahaṃ mama puttaṃ dvisahassadīpaparivārānaṃ catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ issariyādhipaccaṃ rajjaṃ kārentaṃ chattiṃsayojanaparimaṇḍalāya parisāya parivutaṃ gaganatale vicaramānaṃ passitukāmo”ti. Evañca pana vatvā imesaṃ catuppakārānaṃ nimittānaṃ kumārassa cakkhupathe āgamananivāraṇatthaṃ catūsu disāsu gāvute gāvute ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Taṃ divasaṃ pana maṅgalaṭṭhāne sannipatitesu asītiyā ñātikulasahassesu ekeko ekamekaṃ puttaṃ paṭijāni – “ayaṃ buddho vā hotu rājā vā, mayaṃ ekamekaṃ puttaṃ dassāma. Sacepi buddho bhavissati, khattiyasamaṇeheva purakkhataparivārito vicarissati. Sacepi rājā bhavissati, khattiyakumāreheva purakkhataparivārito vicarissatī”ti. Rājāpi bodhisattassa uttamarūpasampannā vigatasabbadosā dhātiyo paccupaṭṭhāpesi. Bodhisatto anantena parivārena mahantena sirisobhaggena vaḍḍhati.

Then the king asked, "Having seen what, will my son renounce?" "The four omens," they replied. "Which ones?" "An old person, a sick person, a dead person, and a renunciant." The king declared, "From now on, do not allow such people to approach my son. My son has no need of Buddhahood. I wish to see my son exercising sovereignty and dominion over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand islands, ruling a kingdom, surrounded by an assembly thirty-six yojanas in circumference, moving through the sky." Having said this, to prevent these four omens from coming within the prince's sight, he stationed guards at every gāvuta in all four directions. On that day, eighty thousand families of kinsmen gathered at the auspicious place, each pledged a son—"Let this one become either a Buddha or a king. We will each offer a son. If he becomes a Buddha, he will wander attended by khattiya ascetics. If he becomes a king, he will wander attended by khattiya princes." The king also appointed nurses of supreme beauty, free from all faults, to attend upon the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta grew up with an immense retinue, flourishing with great glory and splendor.

Athekadivasaṃ rañño vappamaṅgalaṃ nāma ahosi. Taṃ divasaṃ sakalanagaraṃ devavimānaṃ viya alaṅkaronti. Sabbe dāsakammakarādayo ahatavatthanivatthā gandhamālādipaṭimaṇḍitā rājakule sannipatanti. Rañño kammante naṅgalasahassaṃ yojīyati. Tasmiṃ pana divase ekenūnaaṭṭhasatanaṅgalāni saddhiṃ balibaddarasmiyottehi rajataparikkhatāni honti, rañño ālambananaṅgalaṃ [M 1.0068] pana rattasuvaṇṇaparikkhataṃ hoti. Balibaddānaṃ siṅgarasmipatodāpi suvaṇṇaparikkhatāva honti. Rājā mahatā parivārena nikkhanto puttaṃ gahetvā agamāsi. Kammantaṭṭhāne eko jamburukkho bahalapalāso sandacchāyo ahosi. Tassa heṭṭhā kumārassa sayanaṃ [V 1.0068] paññapāpetvā upari suvaṇṇatārakakhacitaṃ vitānaṃ bandhāpetvā sāṇipākārena parikkhipāpetvā ārakkhaṃ ṭhapāpetvā rājā sabbālaṅkāraṃ alaṅkaritvā amaccagaṇaparivuto naṅgalakaraṇaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Tattha rājā suvaṇṇanaṅgalaṃ gaṇhāti, amaccā ekenūnaṭṭhasatarajatanaṅgalāni, kassakā sesanaṅgalāni. Te tāni gahetvā ito cito ca kasanti. Rājā pana orato vā pāraṃ gacchati, pārato vā oraṃ āgacchati. Etasmiṃ ṭhāne mahāsampatti [P 1.0058] ahosi. Bodhisattaṃ parivāretvā nisinnā dhātiyo “rañño sampattiṃ passissāmā”ti antosāṇito bahi nikkhantā. Bodhisatto ito cito ca olokento kañci adisvā vegena uṭṭhāya pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ānāpāne pariggahetvā paṭhamajjhānaṃ nibbattesi. Dhātiyo khajjabhojjantare vicaramānā thokaṃ cirāyiṃsu. Sesarukkhānaṃ chāyā nivattā, tassa pana rukkhassa parimaṇḍalā hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Dhātiyo “ayyaputto ekato”ti vegena sāṇiṃ ukkhipitvā anto pavisamānā bodhisattaṃ sayane pallaṅkena nisinnaṃ tañca pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā gantvā rañño ārocesuṃ – “deva, kumāro evaṃ nisinno, aññesaṃ rukkhānaṃ chāyā nivattā, jamburukkhassa pana parimaṇḍalā ṭhitā”ti. Rājā vegenāgantvā pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā – “idaṃ te, tāta, dutiyaṃ vandana”nti puttaṃ vandi.

Then one day, the king had a plowing festival called Vappamaṅgala. On that day, the entire city was adorned like a celestial palace. All the servants, laborers, and so forth, dressed in fresh clothes and adorned with perfumes and garlands, gathered at the royal palace. For the king’s plowing ceremony, a thousand plows were yoked. On that day, one hundred and seven plows, along with their yokes and reins, were adorned with silver, while the king’s ceremonial plow was adorned with red gold. The horns, reins, and goads of the oxen were also adorned with gold. The king, accompanied by a large retinue, went forth taking the Bodhisatta. At the plowing site, there was a rose-apple tree with dense foliage and cool shade. Beneath it, a bed was prepared for the Bodhisatta, and above, a canopy studded with golden stars was hung. A screen of cloth was set up around it, and guards were stationed. After adorning himself with all his regalia, the king, surrounded by his ministers, went to the plowing area. There, the king took the golden plow, the ministers took the one hundred and seven silver plows, and the farmers took the remaining plows. Holding them, they plowed here and there. The king plowed from one side to the other, and from the other side back to this side. At that place, there was great splendor. The nurses who sat around the Bodhisatta, thinking, "We will see the king’s prosperity," went outside the screen. The Bodhisatta, looking around and seeing no one, quickly rose, sat cross-legged, took up mindfulness of breathing, and attained the first jhāna. The nurses, wandering about among snacks and food, delayed a little. The shadows of the other trees shifted, but the shadow of that tree remained perfectly round and still. The nurses, thinking, "The young lord is alone," quickly lifted the screen and entered. Seeing the Bodhisatta seated cross-legged on the bed and witnessing this marvel, they went and reported to the king: "Your Majesty, the Bodhisatta is sitting like this. The shadows of the other trees have moved, but the shadow of the rose-apple tree remains perfectly round." The king hurriedly came, saw the marvel, and said, "This, dear son, is my second homage to you," and paid homage to his son.

Atha anukkamena bodhisatto soḷasavassuddesiko jāto. Rājā bodhisattassa tiṇṇaṃ utūnaṃ anucchavike tayo pāsāde kāresi – ekaṃ navabhūmakaṃ, ekaṃ sattabhūmakaṃ, ekaṃ pañcabhūmakaṃ, cattālīsasahassā ca nāṭakitthiyo upaṭṭhāpesi. Bodhisatto devo viya accharāsaṅghaparivuto, alaṅkatanāṭakaparivuto, nippurisehi tūriyehi paricāriyamāno mahāsampattiṃ anubhavanto utuvārena tesu pāsādesu viharati. Rāhulamātā panassa devī aggamahesī ahosi.

Then gradually the Bodhisatta reached the age of sixteen. The king had three palaces built for the Bodhisatta suitable for the three seasons—one with nine stories, one with seven stories, and one with five stories—and appointed forty thousand dancing girls to attend him. The Bodhisatta, surrounded by throngs of nymphs as if he were a deva, attended by adorned dancers, served by music played exclusively by women, enjoying great prosperity, dwelt in those palaces according to the seasons. And Rāhula's mother became his chief queen.

Tassevaṃ [M 1.0069] mahāsampattiṃ anubhavantassa ekadivasaṃ ñātisaṅghassa abbhantare ayaṃ kathā udapādi – “siddhattho kīḷāpasutova vicarati, kiñci sippaṃ na sikkhati, saṅgāme paccupaṭṭhite kiṃ karissatī”ti. Rājā bodhisattaṃ pakkosāpetvā – “tāta, tava ñātakā ‘siddhattho kiñci sippaṃ asikkhitvā kīḷāpasutova vicaratī’ti vadanti, ettha kiṃ pattakāle maññasī”ti. Deva, mama sippaṃ sikkhanakiccaṃ natthi, nagare mama sippadassanatthaṃ bheriṃ carāpetha “ito sattame divase ñātakānaṃ sippaṃ dassessāmī”ti. Rājā tathā akāsi. Bodhisatto akkhaṇavedhivālavedhidhanuggahe sannipātāpetvā mahājanassa majjhe aññehi dhanuggahehi asādhāraṇaṃ [V 1.0069] ñātakānaṃ dvādasavidhaṃ sippaṃ dassesi. Taṃ sarabhaṅgajātake āgatanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Tadāssa ñātisaṅgho nikkaṅkho ahosi.

While he was enjoying such great prosperity, one day this discussion arose among his kinsmen: "Siddhattha wanders about absorbed in play and learns no skill; what will he do if a battle arises?" The king had the Bodhisatta summoned and said, "Dear one, your kinsmen say, 'Siddhattha wanders about absorbed in play, having learned no skill'; what do you think is the proper course at this time?" "Sire, there is no need for me to learn a skill. Have a drum beaten throughout the city to announce: 'On the seventh day from now, I will display my skill to my kinsmen.'" The king did so. The Bodhisatta had archers who could hit a hair and shoot without missing assembled, and in the midst of a great crowd, he displayed to his kinsmen the twelve kinds of skill, which were unmatched by other archers. This should be understood in the manner related in the Sarabhaṅga Jātaka. Then his assembly of kinsmen was free from doubt.

Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto uyyānabhūmiṃ gantukāmo sārathiṃ āmantetvā “rathaṃ yojehī”ti āha. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā mahārahaṃ uttamarathaṃ sabbālaṅkārena alaṅkaritvā kumudapattavaṇṇe cattāro [P 1.0059] maṅgalasindhave yojetvā bodhisattassa paṭivedesi. Bodhisatto devavimānasadisaṃ rathaṃ abhiruhitvā uyyānābhimukho agamāsi. Devatā “siddhatthakumārassa abhisambujjhanakālo āsanno, pubbanimittaṃ dassessāmā”ti ekaṃ devaputtaṃ jarājajjaraṃ khaṇḍadantaṃ palitakesaṃ vaṅkaṃ obhaggasarīraṃ daṇḍahatthaṃ pavedhamānaṃ katvā dassesuṃ. Taṃ bodhisatto ceva sārathi ca passanti. Tato bodhisatto sārathiṃ – “samma, ko nāmesa puriso, kesāpissa na yathā aññesa”nti mahāpadāne āgatanayena pucchitvā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “dhīratthu vata bho jāti, yatra hi nāma jātassa jarā paññāyissatī”ti saṃviggahadayo tatova paṭinivattitvā pāsādameva abhiruhi. Rājā “kiṃ kāraṇā mama putto khippaṃ paṭinivattī”ti pucchi. “Jiṇṇakaṃ purisaṃ disvā devā”ti. “Jiṇṇakaṃ disvā pabbajissatīti āhaṃsu, kasmā maṃ nāsetha, sīghaṃ puttassa nāṭakāni sajjetha, sampattiṃ anubhavanto pabbajjāya satiṃ na karissatī”ti vatvā ārakkhaṃ vaḍḍhetvā sabbadisāsu aḍḍhayojane aḍḍhayojane ṭhapesi.

Then one day, the Bodhisatta, wishing to go to the pleasure grounds, summoned his charioteer and said, "Harness the chariot." Replying, "Very well," the charioteer prepared a magnificent, excellent chariot adorned with all ornaments, yoked four auspicious Sindhava horses the color of white water lily petals, and informed the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta mounted the chariot, which resembled a celestial mansion, and set out toward the pleasure grounds. The deities thought, "The time for Prince Siddhattha's full enlightenment is near; we will show him a premonitory sign." They created and showed the form of a deva who was old and decrepit, with broken teeth, gray hair, a bent and broken-down body, holding a staff and trembling. Both the Bodhisatta and the charioteer saw him. Then the Bodhisatta asked the charioteer, "Friend, who is this man? His hair is not like that of others." He inquired in the manner related in the Mahāpadāna, and upon hearing the answer, exclaimed, "Shame on this thing called birth, where old age becomes manifest for one who is born!" With a heart deeply stirred, he turned back from there and ascended his palace. The king asked, "For what reason has my son returned so quickly?" "He saw an old man, Your Majesty." "They said he would renounce upon seeing an old man—why do you destroy me? Quickly, prepare entertainments for my son. While experiencing prosperity, he will not set his mind on renunciation." Saying this, he increased the guard and stationed them every half-yojana in all directions.

Punekadivasaṃ [M 1.0070] bodhisatto tatheva uyyānaṃ gacchanto devatāhi nimmitaṃ byādhitaṃ purisaṃ disvā purimanayeneva pucchitvā saṃviggahadayo nivattitvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Rājāpi pucchitvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva saṃvidahitvā puna vaḍḍhetvā samantā tigāvutappamāṇe padese ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Aparaṃ ekadivasaṃ bodhisatto tatheva uyyānaṃ gacchanto devatāhi nimmitaṃ kālakataṃ disvā purimanayeneva pucchitvā saṃviggahadayo puna nivattitvā pāsādaṃ abhiruhi. Rājāpi pucchitvā heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva saṃvidahitvā puna vaḍḍhetvā samantā yojanappamāṇe padese ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Aparaṃ pana ekadivasaṃ uyyānaṃ gacchanto tatheva devatāhi nimmitaṃ sunivatthaṃ supārutaṃ pabbajitaṃ disvā “ko nāmeso sammā”ti sārathiṃ pucchi. Sārathi kiñcāpi buddhuppādassa abhāvā pabbajitaṃ vā pabbajitaguṇe vā na jānāti, devatānubhāvena pana “pabbajito nāmāyaṃ devā”ti vatvā pabbajjāya guṇe vaṇṇesi. Bodhisatto pabbajjāya ruciṃ uppādetvā taṃ divasaṃ uyyānaṃ agamāsi. Dīghabhāṇakā panāhu “cattāri nimittāni ekadivaseneva disvā agamāsī”ti.

On another day, the Bodhisatta, while going to the pleasure grounds as before, saw a sick man created by the devas. After questioning in the same manner as before, with a stirred heart he returned and ascended the palace. The king also, having inquired and made arrangements in the manner described above, again increased the guard and stationed it in the surrounding area of three gāvutas. On a subsequent day, the Bodhisatta, while going to the pleasure grounds as before, saw a dead man created by the devas. After questioning in the same manner as before, with a stirred heart he again returned and ascended the palace. The king also, having inquired and made arrangements in the manner described above, again increased the guard and stationed it in the surrounding area of one yojana. Then on another day, while going to the pleasure grounds as before, he saw a well-dressed and well-robed renunciant created by the devas and asked the charioteer, "Friend, who is this?" Although the charioteer, due to the non-arising of a Buddha, knew neither of a renunciant nor of the virtues of a renunciant, by the power of the devas he replied, "This is a renunciant, sire," and praised the virtues of renunciation. The Bodhisatta, having developed a liking for renunciation, went to the pleasure grounds that day. The reciters of the Long Discourses, however, say, "Having seen the four signs in a single day, he went."

So [V 1.0070] tattha divasabhāgaṃ kīḷitvā maṅgalapokkharaṇiyaṃ nhāyitvā atthaṅgate sūriye maṅgalasilāpaṭṭe nisīdi attānaṃ alaṅkārāpetukāmo. Athassa paricārakapurisā nānāvaṇṇāni dussāni nānappakārā ābharaṇavikatiyo mālāgandhavilepanāni ca ādāya samantā parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakkassa nisinnāsanaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi[P 1.0060]. So “ko nu kho maṃ imamhā ṭhānā cāvetukāmo”ti upadhārento bodhisattassa alaṅkāretukāmataṃ ñatvā vissakammaṃ āmantesi “samma vissakamma, siddhatthakumāro ajja aḍḍharattasamaye mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamissati, ayamassa pacchimo alaṅkāro, uyyānaṃ gantvā mahāpurisaṃ dibbālaṅkārehi alaṅkarohī”ti. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā devatānubhāvena taṅkhaṇaṃyeva upasaṅkamitvā tasseva kappakasadiso hutvā kappakassa hatthato veṭhanadussaṃ gahetvā bodhisattassa sīsaṃ veṭhesi. Bodhisatto hatthasamphasseneva “nāyaṃ manusso, devaputto eso”ti aññāsi. Veṭhanena veṭhitamatte sīse moḷiyaṃ maṇiratanākārena dussasahassaṃ abbhuggañchi. Puna veṭhentassa dussasahassanti dasakkhattuṃ veṭhentassa dasa dussasahassāni abbhuggacchiṃsu[M 1.0071]. “Sīsaṃ khuddakaṃ, dussāni bahūni, kathaṃ abbhuggatānī”ti na cintetabbaṃ. Tesu hi sabbamahantaṃ āmalakapupphappamāṇaṃ, avasesāni kusumbakapupphappamāṇāni ahesuṃ. Bodhisattassa sīsaṃ kiñjakkhagavacchitaṃ viya kuyyakapupphaṃ ahosi.

Having played during the day, he bathed in the auspicious lotus pond and, as the sun set, sat on the auspicious stone slab, wishing to adorn himself. Then his attendant men brought various colored cloths, ornaments of different kinds, garlands, perfumes, and unguents, surrounding him on all sides and stood by. At that moment, Sakka’s throne became warm. Realizing, "Who wishes to dislodge me from this seat?" and discerning the Bodhisatta’s desire to adorn himself, he addressed Vissakamma: "Dear Vissakamma, Prince Siddhattha will go forth on the Great Renunciation at midnight. This is his final adornment. Go to the park and adorn the great man with divine ornaments." Saying, "Very well," he agreed and, by the power of the devas, approached instantly, appearing in the guise of a barber. Taking the turban cloth from the barber’s hand, he wrapped it around the Bodhisatta’s head. The Bodhisatta knew by the touch of his hand, "This is no human, but a son of devas." As soon as the cloth was wrapped around his head, a thousand cloths rose up in the form of a jeweled topknot. As he wrapped it again, a thousand cloths rose; when he wrapped it ten times, ten thousand cloths rose. One should not think, "The head is small, the cloths are many—how did they rise?" For among them, the largest was the size of an emblic myrobalan flower, while the rest were like safflower blossoms. The Bodhisatta’s head appeared like a kuyyaka flower covered with pollen.

Athassa sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitassa sabbatālāvacaresu sakāni sakāni paṭibhānāni dassayantesu, brāhmaṇesu “jayanandā”tiādivacanehi, sūtamāgadhādīsu nānappakārehi maṅgalavacanatthutighosehi sambhāventesu sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ rathavaraṃ abhiruhi. Tasmiṃ samaye “rāhulamātā puttaṃ vijātā”ti sutvā suddhodanamahārājā “puttassa me tuṭṭhiṃ nivedethā”ti sāsanaṃ pahiṇi. Bodhisatto taṃ sutvā “rāhu jāto, bandhanaṃ jāta”nti āha. Rājā “kiṃ me putto avacā”ti pucchitvā taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “ito paṭṭhāya me nattā rāhulakumāroyeva nāma hotū”ti āha.

Then, fully adorned with all ornaments, as those skilled in various arts displayed their respective talents, with brahmins uttering auspicious words like "Victory and joy!", and bards and minstrels offering various auspicious praises and songs of eulogy, he mounted the excellent chariot, adorned with all ornaments. At that time, King Suddhodana, having heard "Rāhula's mother has given birth to a son," sent a message: "Announce my joy to my son." Hearing this, the Bodhisatta said, "A rāhu has been born, a fetter has arisen." The king asked, "What did my son say?" and upon hearing that statement, declared, "From now on, let my grandson be named Prince Rāhula."

Bodhisattopi kho rathavaraṃ āruyha mahantena yasena atimanoramena sirisobhaggena nagaraṃ pāvisi. Tasmiṃ samaye kisāgotamī nāma khattiyakaññā uparipāsādavaratalagatā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ kurumānassa bodhisattassa rūpasiriṃ disvā pītisomanassajātā idaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

The Bodhisatta, mounting the excellent chariot, entered the city with great glory and exceedingly delightful splendor and beauty. At that time, a noble maiden named Kisāgotamī, standing on the upper level of the palace, saw the Bodhisatta’s splendor of form as he circumambulated the city. Filled with joy and gladness, she uttered this exclamation:

“Nibbutā [V 1.0071] nūna sā mātā, nibbuto nūna so pitā;

Nibbutā nūna sā nārī, yassāyaṃ īdiso patī”ti.

"Surely at rest is that mother, surely at rest is that father; Surely at rest is that woman, whose husband is such as this!"

Bodhisatto [P 1.0061] taṃ sutvā cintesi “ayaṃ evamāha ‘evarūpaṃ attabhāvaṃ passantiyā mātu hadayaṃ nibbāyati, pitu hadayaṃ nibbāyati, pajāpatiyā hadayaṃ nibbāyatī’ti! Kismiṃ nu kho nibbute hadayaṃ nibbutaṃ nāma hotī”ti? Athassa kilesesu virattamānasassa etadahosi – “rāgaggimhi nibbute nibbutaṃ nāma hoti, dosaggimhi nibbute nibbutaṃ nāma hoti, mohaggimhi nibbute nibbutaṃ nāma hoti, mānadiṭṭhiādīsu sabbakilesadarathesu nibbutesu nibbutaṃ nāma hoti. Ayaṃ me sussavanaṃ sāvesi, ahañhi nibbānaṃ gavesanto carāmi, ajjeva mayā gharāvāsaṃ chaḍḍetvā nikkhamma pabbajitvā [M 1.0072] nibbānaṃ gavesituṃ vaṭṭati, ayaṃ imissā ācariyabhāgo hotū”ti kaṇṭhato omuñcitvā kisāgotamiyā satasahassagghanakaṃ muttāhāraṃ pesesi. Sā “siddhatthakumāro mayi paṭibaddhacitto hutvā paṇṇākāraṃ pesesī”ti somanassajātā ahosi.

Hearing this, the Bodhisatta reflected: "She says, ‘Upon seeing such a being, the mother’s heart is cooled, the father’s heart is cooled, the wife’s heart is cooled!’ But in what being cooled is the heart said to be cooled?" Then, as his mind became dispassionate towards defilements, this occurred to him: "When the fire of lust is extinguished, it is called cooled; when the fire of hatred is extinguished, it is called cooled; when the fire of delusion is extinguished, it is called cooled; when all the agitations of defilements such as conceit, wrong views, and so forth, are extinguished, it is called cooled. This woman has proclaimed a good message to me. For I am seeking Nibbāna. Today, I must abandon household life, go forth, and seek Nibbāna. Let this be her teacher’s fee." So saying, he removed from his neck a pearl necklace worth a hundred thousand and sent it to Kisāgotamī. She, thinking, "Prince Siddhattha, his heart is attached to me, has sent me a present," was filled with joy.

Bodhisattopi mahantena sirisobhaggena attano pāsādaṃ abhiruhitvā sirisayane nipajji. Tāvadeva ca naṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā naccagītādīsu susikkhitā devakaññā viya rūpasobhaggappattā itthiyo nānātūriyāni gahetvā samparivārayitvā abhiramāpentiyo naccagītavāditāni payojayiṃsu. Bodhisatto kilesesu virattacittatāya naccādīsu anabhirato muhuttaṃ niddaṃ okkami. Tāpi itthiyo “yassatthāya mayaṃ naccādīni payojema, so niddaṃ upagato, idāni kimatthaṃ kilamāmā”ti gahitaggahitāni tūriyāni ajjhottharitvā nipajjiṃsu, gandhatelappadīpā jhāyanti. Bodhisatto pabujjhitvā sayanapiṭṭhe pallaṅkena nisinno addasa tā itthiyo tūriyabhaṇḍāni avattharitvā niddāyantiyo – ekaccā paggharitakheḷā, lālākilinnagattā, ekaccā dante khādantiyo, ekaccā kākacchantiyo, ekaccā vippalapantiyo, ekaccā vivaṭamukhā, ekaccā apagatavatthā, pākaṭabībhacchasambādhaṭṭhānā. So tāsaṃ taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā bhiyyosomattāya kāmesu virattacitto ahosi. Tassa alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ sakkabhavanasadisampi taṃ mahātalaṃ apaviddhanānākuṇapabharitaṃ āmakasusānaṃ viya upaṭṭhāsi, tayo bhavā ādittagehasadisā khāyiṃsu – “upaddutaṃ vata bho, upassaṭṭhaṃ vata bho”ti udānaṃ pavattesi, ativiya pabbajjāya cittaṃ nami.

The Bodhisatta, with great splendor and beauty, ascended his palace and lay down on his magnificent bed. At that very moment, women adorned with all ornaments, well-trained in dance, song, and so forth, having attained beauty like that of celestial maidens, surrounded him, holding various musical instruments, and entertained him with dance, song, and music. The Bodhisatta, his mind dispassionate towards defilements, found no delight in the dancing and so forth, and for a moment, fell asleep. Then those women thought, "He for whose sake we perform these dances and so forth has fallen asleep; why should we now weary ourselves?" So they cast aside the instruments they had taken up and lay down, while the perfumed oil lamps burned. The Bodhisatta awoke and, sitting cross-legged on his bed, saw those women sleeping with their musical instruments cast aside—some were drooling, their bodies moist with saliva; some were grinding their teeth; some were snoring; some were muttering; some had their mouths agape; some had their garments fallen away, revealing their private parts in a disgusting and offensive state. Seeing this disfigured state of theirs, he became even more dispassionate towards sensual pleasures. To him, that great hall, though adorned and prepared like Sakka's palace, appeared like a charnel ground filled with various discarded corpses; the three realms of existence seemed like a burning house. "Oh, how distressed! Oh, how afflicted!" he uttered, and his mind inclined intensely toward renunciation.

So “ajjeva mayā mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sayanā uṭṭhāya dvārasamīpaṃ [V 1.0072] gantvā “ko etthā”ti āha. Ummāre [P 1.0062] sīsaṃ katvā nipanno channo “ahaṃ ayyaputta channo”ti āha. “Ahaṃ ajja mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitukāmo, ekaṃ me assaṃ kappehī”ti āha. So “sādhu devā”ti assabhaṇḍikaṃ gahetvā assasālaṃ gantvā gandhatelapadīpesu jalantesu sumanapaṭṭavitānassa heṭṭhā ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge ṭhitaṃ kaṇḍakaṃ assarājānaṃ disvā “ajja mayā imameva kappetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kaṇḍakaṃ kappesi. So kappiyamānova aññāsi “ayaṃ kappanā atigāḷhā[M 1.0073], aññesu divasesu uyyānakīḷādigamane kappanā viya na hoti, mayhaṃ ayyaputto ajja mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhamitukāmo bhavissatī”ti. Tato tuṭṭhamānaso mahāhasitaṃ hasi. So saddo sakalanagaraṃ pattharitvā gaccheyya, devatā pana taṃ saddaṃ nirumbhitvā na kassaci sotuṃ adaṃsu.

Thinking, "Today it is right for me to go forth in the Great Renunciation," he rose from his bed, went to the door, and said, "Who is there?" Channa, who was lying with his head on the threshold, replied, "It is I, young master, Channa." "I wish to go forth in the Great Renunciation today," he said. "Prepare a horse for me." Channa replied, "Very well, sire," and taking the horse's trappings, he went to the stable. There, with perfumed oil lamps burning, beneath a canopy of jasmine flowers, on a delightful spot of ground, stood Kanthaka, the king of horses. Seeing him, Channa thought, "Today it is right for me to prepare this very horse." So he saddled Kanthaka. As he was being saddled, Kanthaka knew, "This saddling is exceedingly tight; it is not like the saddling on other days for going to sport in the park and so forth. My young master must wish to go forth in the Great Renunciation today." Then, with a joyful heart, he let out a great neigh. That sound would have spread throughout the entire city, but the devas suppressed the sound and did not let anyone hear it.

Bodhisattopi kho channaṃ pesetvāva “puttaṃ tāva passissāmī”ti cintetvā nisinnapallaṅkato uṭṭhāya rāhulamātāya vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā gabbhadvāraṃ vivari. Tasmiṃ khaṇe antogabbhe gandhatelapadīpo jhāyati, rāhulamātā sumanamallikādīnaṃ pupphānaṃ ambaṇamattena abhippakiṇṇasayane puttassa matthake hatthaṃ ṭhapetvā niddāyati. Bodhisatto ummāre pādaṃ ṭhapetvā ṭhitakova oloketvā “sacāhaṃ deviyā hatthaṃ apanetvā mama puttaṃ gaṇhissāmi, devī pabujjhissati, evaṃ me gamanantarāyo bhavissati, buddho hutvāva āgantvā puttaṃ passissāmī”ti pāsādatalato otari. Yaṃ pana jātakaṭṭhakathāyaṃ “tadā sattāhajāto rāhulakumāro hotī”ti vuttaṃ, taṃ sesaṭṭhakathāsu natthi, tasmā idameva gahetabbaṃ.

Having sent Channa, the Bodhisatta thought, "First, I will see my son." Rising from his seat, he went to the dwelling of Rāhula's mother and opened the chamber door. At that moment, a lamp of fragrant oil was burning inside the chamber. Rāhula's mother was asleep on a bed strewn with an ambaṇa's measure of flowers such as jasmine and mallikā, with her hand placed on her son's head. The Bodhisatta, placing his foot on the threshold, stood and looked. He thought, "If I move the queen's hand to take my son, the queen will awaken. Thus, there will be an obstacle to my departure. Only after becoming a Buddha will I come back and see my son." Then he descended from the palace terrace. However, what is stated in the Jātaka commentary, "At that time, Prince Rāhula was seven days old," is not found in the other commentaries; therefore, this version alone should be accepted.

Evaṃ bodhisatto pāsādatalā otaritvā assasamīpaṃ gantvā evamāha – “tāta kaṇḍaka, tvaṃ ajja ekarattiṃ maṃ tāraya, ahaṃ taṃ nissāya buddho hutvā sadevakaṃ lokaṃ tāressāmī”ti. Tato ullaṅghitvā kaṇḍakassa piṭṭhiṃ abhiruhi. Kaṇḍako gīvato paṭṭhāya āyāmena aṭṭhārasahattho hoti tadanucchavikena ubbedhena samannāgato thāmajavasampanno sabbaseto dhotasaṅkhasadiso. So sace haseyya vā padasaddaṃ vā kareyya, saddo sakalanagaraṃ avatthareyya. Tasmā devatā attano ānubhāvena tassa yathā na koci suṇāti, evaṃ hasitasaddaṃ sannirumbhitvā akkamanaakkamanapadavāre hatthatalāni upanāmesuṃ. Bodhisatto assavarassa piṭṭhivemajjhagato channaṃ assassa [P 1.0063] vāladhiṃ gāhāpetvā aḍḍharattasamaye mahādvārasamīpaṃ patto. Tadā pana rājā “evaṃ bodhisatto yāya kāyaci velāya nagaradvāraṃ vivaritvā nikkhamituṃ na sakkhissatī”ti dvīsu dvārakavāṭesu ekekaṃ purisasahassena vivaritabbaṃ kārāpesi. Bodhisatto thāmabalasampanno, hatthigaṇanāya koṭisahassahatthīnaṃ balaṃ dhāreti, purisagaṇanāya dasakoṭisahassapurisānaṃ[M 1.0074][V 1.0073]. So cintesi “sace dvāraṃ na vivarīyati, ajja kaṇḍakassa piṭṭhe nisinnova vāladhiṃ gahetvā ṭhitena channena saddhiṃyeva kaṇḍakaṃ ūrūhi nippīḷetvā aṭṭhārasahatthubbedhaṃ pākāraṃ uppatitvā atikkamissāmī”ti. Channopi cintesi “sace dvāraṃ na vivarīyati, ahaṃ ayyaputtaṃ khandhe nisīdāpetvā kaṇḍakaṃ dakkhiṇena hatthena kucchiyaṃ parikkhipanto upakacchantare katvā pākāraṃ uppatitvā atikkamissāmī”ti. Kaṇḍakopi cintesi “sace dvāraṃ na vivarīyati, ahaṃ attano sāmikaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ yathānisinnameva channena vāladhiṃ gahetvā ṭhitena saddhiṃyeva ukkhipitvā pākāraṃ uppatitvā atikkamissāmī”ti. Sace dvāraṃ na avāpurīyittha, yathācintitameva tesu tīsu janesu aññataro sampādeyya. Dvāre adhivatthā devatā pana dvāraṃ vivari.

Thus, the Bodhisatta descended from the palace terrace, approached his horse, and said: 'Dear Kaṇḍaka, carry me across for this one night. Relying on you, I shall become a Buddha and liberate the world with its gods.' Then, leaping up, he mounted Kaṇḍaka's back. Kaṇḍaka was eighteen cubits in length from his neck, with a corresponding height, endowed with strength and speed, all white like a polished conch shell. If he were to neigh or make a hoof sound, the noise would fill the entire city. Therefore, the deities, by their power, suppressed his neighing so that no one would hear, and at each step, they placed their hands beneath his hooves. The Bodhisatta, seated in the middle of the excellent horse's back, had Channa hold the horse's tail, and at midnight, reached the great gate. Now, the king, thinking, 'The Bodhisatta will not be able to open the city gate and depart at any time,' had caused each of the two gate leaves to be made such that it required a thousand men to open it. The Bodhisatta was endowed with great strength, possessing the strength of ten billion elephants and, by count of men, one hundred billion men. He thought, 'If the gate is not opened, today, while seated on Kaṇḍaka's back with Channa holding the tail, I will press Kaṇḍaka with my thighs and leap over the eighteen-cubit-high city wall to cross it.' Channa also thought, 'If the gate is not opened, I will seat the noble son on my shoulders, tuck Kaṇḍaka under my arm, and leap over the city wall to cross it.' Kaṇḍaka too thought, 'If the gate is not opened, I will carry my master on my back just as he is seated, together with Channa holding the tail, and leap over the city wall to cross it.' Had the gate not been opened, any one of these three would have accomplished what they intended. But the deity dwelling at the gate opened it.

Tasmiṃyeva khaṇe māro “bodhisattaṃ nivattessāmī”ti āgantvā ākāse ṭhito āha – “mārisa, mā nikkhama, ito te sattame divase cakkaratanaṃ pātubhavissati, dvisahassaparittadīpaparivārānaṃ catunnaṃ mahādīpānaṃ rajjaṃ kāressasi, nivatta mārisā”ti. “Kosi tva”nti? “Ahaṃ vasavattī”ti. “Māra, jānāmahaṃ mayhaṃ cakkaratanassa pātubhāvaṃ, anatthikohaṃ rajjena, dasasahassilokadhātuṃ unnādetvā buddho bhavissāmī”ti āha. Māro “ito dāni te paṭṭhāya kāmavitakkaṃ vā byāpādavitakkaṃ vā vihiṃsāvitakkaṃ vā cintitakāle jānissāmī”ti otārāpekkho chāyā viya anapagacchanto anubandhi.

At that very moment, Māra, thinking, 'I will turn the Bodhisatta back,' approached and stood in the air, saying, 'Good sir, do not go forth! On the seventh day from now, the Wheel-Treasure will appear to you. You will rule as king over the four great continents surrounded by two thousand attendant islands. Turn back, good sir!' 'Who are you?' 'I am Vasavattī.' 'Māra, I know about the appearance of my Wheel-Treasure. I have no need for kingship. Having caused the ten-thousandfold world-system to resound, I will become a Buddha,' he said. Māra, looking for an opportunity, thought, 'From now on, whenever he considers a thought of sensual desire, ill-will, or harm, I will know it.' Like a shadow that does not depart, he followed him.

Bodhisattopi hatthagataṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ kheḷapiṇḍaṃ viya anapekkho chaḍḍetvā mahantena sakkārena nagarā nikkhami āsāḷhipuṇṇamāya uttarāsāḷhanakkhatte vattamāne. Nikkhamitvā ca puna nagaraṃ oloketukāmo jāto. Evañca panassa citte uppannamatteyeva “mahāpurisa, na tayā nivattitvā olokanakammaṃ kata”nti vadamānā viya mahāpathavī kulālacakkaṃ viya bhijjitvā parivatti. Bodhisatto nagarābhimukho ṭhatvā nagaraṃ oloketvā tasmiṃ pathavippadese kaṇḍakanivattanacetiyaṭṭhānaṃ dassetvā gantabbamaggābhimukhaṃ kaṇḍakaṃ katvā [P 1.0064] pāyāsi mahantena sakkārena uḷārena sirisobhaggena. Tadā kirassa devatā purato saṭṭhi ukkāsahassāni dhārayiṃsu, pacchato saṭṭhi, dakkhiṇapassato saṭṭhi, vāmapassato [M 1.0075] saṭṭhi, aparā devatā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ aparimāṇā ukkā dhārayiṃsu, aparā devatā ca nāgasupaṇṇādayo ca dibbehi gandhehi mālāhi cuṇṇehi dhūmehi pūjayamānā gacchanti. Pāricchattakapupphehi ceva mandāravapupphehi ca ghanameghavuṭṭhikāle dhārāhi viya nabhaṃ nirantaraṃ ahosi, dibbāni saṃgītāni pavattiṃsu[V 1.0074], samantato aṭṭhasaṭṭhi tūriyasatasahassāni pavajjiṃsu, samuddakucchiyaṃ meghatthanitakālo viya yugandharakucchiyaṃ sāgaranigghosakālo viya vattati.

The Bodhisatta, regarding the wheel-turning monarch's kingship that had come into his hands like a lump of spittle, discarded it without concern and left the city with great honor. It was the full moon day of Āsāḷhī, while the constellation of Uttarāsāḷha was in ascendancy. After leaving, he felt the desire to look back at the city. Just as this thought arose in his mind, as if saying, 'Great man, you should not turn back to look,' the great earth turned like a potter’s wheel. The Bodhisatta stood facing the city, looked at it, and indicated the place where the Kaṇḍaka Turning Shrine would later be established. Then, turning the horse Kaṇḍaka toward the path he must take, he set out with great honor and immense glory and splendor. At that time, it is said, sixty thousand deities carried torches before him, sixty thousand behind him, sixty thousand to the right, and sixty thousand to the left. Other deities held countless torches around the circumference of the world. Still other deities, along with divine nāgas and garuḍas, honored him with divine perfumes, garlands, powders, and incense as he went. The sky was filled without gaps, like a downpour from a dense cloud, with flowers from the Pāricchattaka and Mandārava trees. Divine music played, and all around, sixty-eight hundred thousand musical instruments sounded. It was like the thunder of clouds in the ocean’s depths or the roar of the sea in the belly of Mount Yugandhara.

Iminā sirisobhaggena gacchanto bodhisatto ekaratteneva tīṇi rajjāni atikkamma tiṃsayojanamatthake anomānadītīraṃ pāpuṇi. “Kiṃ pana asso tato paraṃ gantuṃ na sakkotī”ti? “No, na sakko”ti. So hi ekaṃ cakkavāḷagabbhaṃ nābhiyā ṭhitacakkassa nemivaṭṭiṃ maddanto viya antantena caritvā purepātarāsameva āgantvā attano sampāditaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjituṃ samattho. Tadā pana devanāgasupaṇṇādīhi ākāse ṭhatvā ossaṭṭhehi gandhamālādīhi yāva ūruppadesā sañchannaṃ sarīraṃ ākaḍḍhitvā gandhamālājaṭaṃ chindantassa atippapañco ahosi, tasmā tiṃsayojanamattameva agamāsi. Atha bodhisatto nadītīre ṭhatvā channaṃ pucchi – “kinnāmā ayaṃ nadī”ti? “Anomā nāma, devā”ti. “Amhākampi pabbajjā anomā bhavissatī”ti paṇhiyā ghaṭṭento assassa saññaṃ adāsi. Asso uppatitvā aṭṭhūsabhavitthārāya nadiyā pārimatīre aṭṭhāsi.

With this glorious splendor, the Bodhisatta traveled and in a single night crossed three kingdoms, reaching the bank of the Anomā River at a distance of thirty yojanas. "But could the horse go any further?" "No, he could not." For that horse, having traversed an entire world-system from end to end as if pressing the rim of a wheel placed on its hub, was capable of returning by early morning to eat the food prepared for him. But at that time, gods, nāgas, and supaṇṇas stood in the sky, showering him with perfumes and garlands, so that his body was covered up to his thighs. As he cut through this tangle of perfumes and garlands, there was an excessive delay; therefore, he only went thirty yojanas. Then the Bodhisatta, standing on the riverbank, asked Channa, "What is the name of this river?" "It is called Anomā, lord." "Then our renunciation shall also be Anomā (noble)," he said, striking the horse with his heel as a signal. The horse leapt and stood on the far shore of the river, which was eight usabhas in width.

Bodhisatto assapiṭṭhito oruyha rajatapaṭṭasadise vālukāpuline ṭhatvā channaṃ āmantesi – “samma, channa, tvaṃ mayhaṃ ābharaṇāni ceva kaṇḍakañca ādāya gaccha, ahaṃ pabbajissāmī”ti. “Ahampi, deva, pabbajissāmī”ti. Bodhisatto “na labbhā tayā pabbajituṃ, gaccha tva”nti tikkhattuṃ paṭibāhitvā ābharaṇāni ceva kaṇḍakañca paṭicchāpetvā cintesi “ime mayhaṃ kesā samaṇasāruppā na hontī”ti. Añño bodhisattassa kese chindituṃ yuttarūpo natthi, tato “sayameva khaggena chindissāmī”ti dakkhiṇena hatthena asiṃ gaṇhitvā vāmahatthena moḷiyā [M 1.0076] saddhiṃ cūḷaṃ gahetvā chindi, kesā dvaṅgulamattā hutvā dakkhiṇato āvattamānā sīsaṃ allīyiṃsu. Tesaṃ yāvajīvaṃ tadeva pamāṇaṃ ahosi, massu ca tadanurūpaṃ, puna kesamassuohāraṇakiccaṃ nāma nāhosi. Bodhisatto [P 1.0065] saha moḷiyā cuḷaṃ gahetvā “sacāhaṃ buddho bhavissāmi, ākāse tiṭṭhatu, no ce, bhūmiyaṃ patatū”ti antalikkhe khipi. Taṃ cūḷāmaṇiveṭhanaṃ yojanappamāṇaṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Sakko devarājā dibbacakkhunā oloketvā yojaniyaratanacaṅkoṭakena sampaṭicchitvā tāvatiṃsabhavane cūḷāmaṇicetiyaṃ nāma patiṭṭhāpesi.

The Bodhisatta dismounted from the horse and stood on the sandbank, which was like a silver sheet. He addressed Channa, "Friend Channa, take my ornaments and Kaṇḍaka and go; I shall go forth." "I too, lord, shall go forth." The Bodhisatta refused him three times, saying, "It is not for you to go forth. Go." After entrusting the ornaments and Kaṇḍaka to him, he thought, "This hair of mine is not suitable for an ascetic." As there was no one else fit to cut the Bodhisatta’s hair, he thought, "I shall cut it myself with my sword." Taking the sword in his right hand and grasping his topknot together with the diadem with his left, he cut it off. His hair, becoming two finger-widths long, curled to the right and clung to his head. For the rest of his life it remained that length, and his beard was of a corresponding length; there was never again any need to cut his hair or shave. The Bodhisatta, holding the topknot with the diadem, tossed it into the air, saying, "If I am to become a Buddha, let it remain in the sky; if not, let it fall to the ground." That jeweled topknot traveled a distance of a yojana and remained in the sky. Sakka, king of the gods, observing this with his divine eye, received it in a jeweled casket a yojana in size, and established in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven the Cūḷāmaṇi Cetiya.

“Chetvāna moḷiṃ varagandhavāsitaṃ, vehāyasaṃ ukkhipi aggapuggalo;

Sahassanetto sirasā paṭiggahi, suvaṇṇacaṅkoṭavarena vāsavo”ti.

Cutting off his topknot, scented with the finest fragrance, the foremost individual cast it into the sky. The thousand-eyed one, Vāsava, received it on his head with a superior golden casket.

Puna [V 1.0075] bodhisatto cintesi “imāni kāsikavatthāni mayhaṃ na samaṇasāruppānī”ti. Athassa kassapabuddhakāle purāṇasahāyako ghaṭīkāramahābrahmā ekaṃ buddhantaraṃ jaraṃ apattena mittabhāvena cintesi – “ajja me sahāyako mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto, samaṇaparikkhāramassa gahetvā gacchissāmī”ti.

Again, the Bodhisatta thought, "These Kasi cloths are not suitable for me as an ascetic." Then, his old friend from the time of Kassapa Buddha, the great Brahmā Ghaṭīkāra, whose friendship had not grown old over a Buddha-interval, thought: "Today my friend has undertaken the great renunciation; I will go, taking the requisites of an ascetic for him."

“Ticīvarañca patto ca, vāsī sūci ca bandhanaṃ;

Parissāvanena aṭṭhete, yuttayogassa bhikkhuno”ti. –

The three robes, the bowl, the razor, the needle, the belt, and with the water strainer—these eight are for the monk engaged in the practice.

Ime aṭṭha samaṇaparikkhāre āharitvā adāsi. Bodhisatto arahaddhajaṃ nivāsetvā uttamapabbajjāvesaṃ gaṇhitvā “channa, mama vacanena mātāpitūnaṃ ārogyaṃ vadehī”ti vatvā uyyojesi. Channo bodhisattaṃ vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Kaṇḍako pana channena saddhiṃ mantayamānassa bodhisattassa vacanaṃ suṇanto ṭhatvā “natthi dāni mayhaṃ puna sāmino dassana”nti cakkhupathaṃ vijahanto sokaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto hadayena phalitena kālaṃ katvā tāvatiṃsabhavane kaṇḍako nāma devaputto hutvā nibbatti. Channassa paṭhamaṃ ekova soko [M 1.0077] ahosi, kaṇḍakassa pana kālakiriyāya dutiyena sokena pīḷito rodanto paridevanto nagaraṃ agamāsi.

Bringing these eight requisites of an ascetic, he gave them. The Bodhisatta, having put on the banner of the Arahants and taken up the supreme appearance of one who has gone forth, said to Channa, "Channa, in my name, convey my respects to my mother and father," and then dismissed him. Channa paid homage to the Bodhisatta, circumambulated him, and departed. But Kaṇḍaka, who had been standing and listening to the Bodhisatta's words as he conversed with Channa, thought, "Now I shall not see my master again." As the Bodhisatta passed from his sight, Kaṇḍaka was unable to endure his grief; his heart shattered, and he died, to be reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven as the deva Kaṇḍaka. At first, Channa had only one sorrow, but now afflicted by a second sorrow at Kaṇḍaka’s death, he went to the city, weeping and lamenting.

Bodhisattopi pabbajitvā tasmiṃyeva padese anupiyaṃ nāma ambavanaṃ atthi, tattha sattāhaṃ pabbajjāsukhena vītināmetvā ekadivaseneva [P 1.0066] tiṃsayojanamaggaṃ padasā gantvā rājagahaṃ pāvisi. Pavisitvā sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya cari. Sakalanagaraṃ bodhisattassa rūpadassanena dhanapālakena paviṭṭharājagahaṃ viya asurindena paviṭṭhadevanagaraṃ viya ca saṅkhobhaṃ agamāsi. Rājapurisā gantvā “deva, evarūpo nāma satto nagare piṇḍāya carati, ‘devo vā manusso vā nāgo vā supaṇṇo vā ko nāmeso’ti na jānāmā”ti ārocesuṃ. Rājā pāsādatale ṭhatvā mahāpurisaṃ disvā acchariyabbhutajāto purise āṇāpesi – “gacchatha bhaṇe, vīmaṃsatha, sace amanusso bhavissati, nagarā nikkhamitvā antaradhāyissati, sace devatā bhavissati, ākāsena gacchissati, sace nāgo bhavissati, pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā gamissati, sace manusso bhavissati, yathāladdhaṃ bhikkhaṃ paribhuñjissatī”ti.

Having gone forth, the Bodhisatta spent seven days enjoying the bliss of renunciation in a mango grove named Anupiya in that same region. Then, in a single day, he walked a thirty-yojana path on foot and entered Rājagaha. Upon entering, he went for alms from house to house in sequence. The entire city was stirred by the sight of the Bodhisatta’s form, as if Rājagaha had been entered by the elephant Dhanapālaka, or the city of the gods had been entered by the chief of the asuras. The king’s men went and reported to the king: "Sire, a being of such appearance is walking for alms in the city. We do not know whether he is a deva, a human, a nāga, or a supaṇṇa." The king, standing on the palace terrace, saw the Great Being and, filled with wonder and astonishment, ordered his men: "Go, sirs, and investigate. If he is a non-human being, he will leave the city and disappear. If he is a deity, he will depart through the sky. If he is a nāga, he will sink into the earth and go. If he is a human, he will consume the alms he has received."

Mahāpurisopi kho missakabhattaṃ saṃharitvā “alaṃ me ettakaṃ yāpanāyā”ti ñatvā paviṭṭhadvāreneva nagarā nikkhamitvā paṇḍavapabbatacchāyāya puratthābhimukho nisīditvā āhāraṃ paribhuñjituṃ [V 1.0076] āraddho. Athassa antāni parivattitvā mukhena nikkhamanākārappattāni viya ahesuṃ. Tato tena attabhāvena evarūpassa āhārassa cakkhunāpi adiṭṭhapubbatāya tena paṭikūlāhārena aṭṭiyamāno evaṃ attanāva attānaṃ ovadi “siddhattha, tvaṃ sulabhannapāne kule tivassikagandhasālibhojanaṃ nānaggarasehi bhuñjanaṭṭhāne nibbattitvāpi ekaṃ paṃsukūlikaṃ disvā ‘kadā nu kho ahampi evarūpo hutvā piṇḍāya caritvā bhuñjissāmi, bhavissati nu kho me so kālo’ti cintetvā nikkhanto, idāni kiṃ nāmetaṃ karosī”ti. Evaṃ attanāva attānaṃ ovaditvā nibbikāro hutvā āhāraṃ paribhuñji.

The Great Being, having gathered a mixed meal and knowing, 'This is enough for my sustenance,' left the city through the same gate he had entered. He sat facing east in the shade of the Pandava mountain and began to eat the food. Then his intestines turned over, appearing as if they were about to come out of his mouth. At that moment, because in this life he had never before seen such food with his own eyes, he felt repulsed by that unappetizing meal and admonished himself thus: 'Siddhattha, though you were born into a family where food and drink were easily available, in a place where you ate three-year-old fragrant rice with various excellent flavors, you once saw a rag-robed ascetic and thought, "When will I too become like that, wandering for alms and eating? Will that time ever come for me?"—and so you went forth. Now, what is this you are doing?' Having thus admonished himself, he became unperturbed and consumed the food.

Rājapurisā taṃ pavattiṃ disvā gantvā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā dūtavacanaṃ sutvā vegena nagarā nikkhamitvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā iriyāpathasmiṃyeva pasīditvā bodhisattassa sabbaṃ issariyaṃ niyyādesi[M 1.0078]. Bodhisatto “mayhaṃ, mahārāja, vatthukāmehi vā kilesakāmehi vā attho natthi, ahaṃ paramābhisambodhiṃ patthayanto nikkhanto”ti āha. Rājā anekappakāraṃ yācantopi tassa cittaṃ alabhitvā “addhā tvaṃ buddho bhavissasi, buddhabhūtena pana te paṭhamaṃ mama vijitaṃ āgantabba”nti paṭiññaṃ gaṇhi. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana “pabbajjaṃ kittayissāmi, yathā pabbaji cakkhumā”ti imaṃ pabbajjāsuttaṃ (su. ni. 407 ādayo) saddhiṃ aṭṭhakathāya oloketvā veditabbo.

The royal attendants, having seen this occurrence, went and reported it to the king. Hearing the messenger's words, the king swiftly left the city and, approaching the Bodhisatta, was delighted merely by his deportment and offered all his sovereignty to him. The Bodhisatta said, 'Great king, I have no need for material pleasures or defiled desires; I have gone forth seeking supreme enlightenment.' Though the king pleaded in many ways, he could not obtain his compliance, and the king extracted a promise, saying, 'Surely, you will become a Buddha, but when you have become a Buddha, you must first come to my kingdom.' This is the summary here; for the detailed account, one should refer to the Pabbajjā Sutta (Sutta Nipāta 407 ff.) along with its commentary, which begins, 'I shall praise the going forth, how the one with vision went forth.'

Bodhisattopi rañño paṭiññaṃ datvā anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno āḷārañca kālāmaṃ udakañca rāmaputtaṃ upasaṅkamitvā samāpattiyo nibbattetvā “nāyaṃ maggo bodhāyā”ti tampi [P 1.0067] samāpattibhāvanaṃ analaṅkaritvā sadevakassa lokassa attano thāmavīriyasandassanatthaṃ mahāpadhānaṃ padahitukāmo uruvelaṃ gantvā “ramaṇīyo vatāyaṃ bhūmibhāgo”ti tattheva vāsaṃ upagantvā mahāpadhānaṃ padahi. Tepi kho koṇḍaññappamukhā pañca pabbajitā gāmanigamarājadhānīsu bhikkhāya carantā tattha bodhisattaṃ sampāpuṇiṃsu. Atha naṃ chabbassāni mahāpadhānaṃ padahantaṃ “idāni buddho bhavissati, idāni buddho bhavissatī”ti pariveṇasammajjanādikāya vattapaṭipattiyā upaṭṭhahamānā santikāvacarāvassa ahesuṃ. Bodhisattopi kho “koṭippattaṃ dukkarakāriyaṃ karissāmī”ti ekatilataṇḍulādīhipi vītināmesi, sabbasopi āhārūpacchedaṃ akāsi, devatāpi lomakūpehi ojaṃ upasaṃharamānā paṭikkhipi.

The Bodhisatta, having given his promise to the king, journeyed on by stages. Approaching Āḷāra Kālāma and Uddaka Rāmaputta and attaining their meditative states, he concluded, 'This is not the path to enlightenment.' Not being content with that development of meditative attainments, and desiring to undertake the great exertion to demonstrate his own strength and energy to the world with its gods, he went to Uruvelā. Thinking, 'Indeed, this region is delightful,' he took up residence there and undertook the great exertion. Then the five ascetics led by Koṇḍañña, while wandering for alms in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, came upon the Bodhisatta there. As he engaged in the great exertion for six years, they attended to him, thinking, 'Now he will become a Buddha, now he will become a Buddha,' performing duties such as sweeping his dwelling place, and they remained in his vicinity. The Bodhisatta, resolving, 'I will perform the utmost ascetic practice,' sustained himself on as little as a single sesame seed or grain of rice, and eventually ceased all intake of food. He even refused the nutritive essence that deities offered to introduce through his pores.

Athassa tāya nirāhāratāya paramakasimānappattakāyassa suvaṇṇavaṇṇo kāyo kāḷavaṇṇo ahosi. Bāttiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni paṭicchannāni ahesuṃ. Appekadā appāṇakaṃ jhānaṃ jhāyanto [V 1.0077] mahāvedanāhi abhitunno visaññībhūto caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ patati. Atha naṃ ekaccā devatā “kālakato samaṇo gotamo”ti vadanti, ekaccā “vihāroveso arahata”nti āhaṃsu. Tattha yāsaṃ “kālakato”ti ahosi, tā gantvā suddhodanamahārājassa ārocesuṃ “tumhākaṃ putto kālakato”ti. Mama putto buddho hutvā kālakato, ahutvāti? Buddho bhavituṃ nāsakkhi, padhānabhūmiyaṃyeva patitvā [M 1.0079] kālakatoti. Idaṃ sutvā rājā “nāhaṃ saddahāmi, mama puttassa bodhiṃ appatvā kālakiriyā nāma natthī”ti paṭikkhipi. Kasmā pana rājā na saddahatīti? Kāḷadevīlatāpasassa vandāpanadivase jamburukkhamūle ca pāṭihāriyānaṃ diṭṭhattā.

Due to that lack of food, his body, which had reached the utmost emaciation, turned from a golden hue to a dark color. The thirty-two marks of a great man became obscured. Sometimes, while absorbed in the breathless meditation, overwhelmed by severe pains, he would collapse unconscious at the end of the walking path. Then, some deities would say, 'The ascetic Gotama has died,' while others would declare, 'This is the state of an Arahant.' Those among them who thought he had died went and informed King Suddhodana, saying, 'Your son has died.' The king asked, 'Has my son died after becoming a Buddha, or without becoming one?' They replied, 'He could not become a Buddha; he died having fallen right there on the ground of striving.' Hearing this, the king rejected it, saying, 'I do not believe it. For my son, there is no such thing as dying without attaining enlightenment.' And why did the king not believe? Because of the miracles he had witnessed, both on the day he had the ascetic Kāḷadevala pay homage and at the foot of the Jambu tree.

Puna bodhisatte saññaṃ paṭilabhitvā uṭṭhite tā devatā gantvā “arogo te mahārāja putto”ti ārocenti. Rājā “jānāmahaṃ puttassa amaraṇabhāva”nti vadati. Mahāsattassa chabbassāni dukkarakāriyaṃ karontassa ākāse gaṇṭhikaraṇakālo viya ahosi. So “ayaṃ dukkarakārikā nāma bodhāya maggo na hotī”ti oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhāretuṃ gāmanigamesu piṇḍāya caritvā āhāraṃ āhari, athassa bāttiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇāni pākatikāni ahesuṃ, kāyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ahosi. Pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū “ayaṃ chabbassāni dukkarakārikaṃ karontopi sabbaññutaṃ paṭivijjhituṃ nāsakkhi, idāni gāmādīsu [P 1.0068] piṇḍāya caritvā oḷārikaṃ āhāraṃ āhariyamāno kiṃ sakkhissati, bāhuliko esa padhānavibbhanto, sīsaṃ nhāyitukāmassa ussāvabindutakkanaṃ viya amhākaṃ etassa santikā visesatakkanaṃ, kiṃ no iminā”ti mahāpurisaṃ pahāya attano attano pattacīvaraṃ gahetvā aṭṭhārasayojanamaggaṃ gantvā isipatanaṃ pavisiṃsu.

When the Bodhisatta regained consciousness and arose, those deities went and announced, 'Great king, your son is well.' The king said, 'I know that my son will not die.' For the Great Being, performing austere practices for six years was like trying to tie a knot in the sky. He thought, 'This practice of austerities is not the path to enlightenment.' Then, in order to take substantial food, he went for alms in villages and market towns and gathered food. Thereupon, his thirty-two marks of a great man reappeared, and his body regained its golden hue. The monks of the group of five thought, 'Even after performing severe austerities for six years, he could not penetrate omniscience. Now that he is wandering for alms in villages and taking substantial food, what can he achieve? He has become indulgent, he has strayed from the striving. For us, to expect any special attainment from him is like someone wanting to wash their head expecting help from a drop of dew. What use is he to us?' Abandoning the Great Being, they took their bowls and robes and, traveling a distance of eighteen yojanas, entered Isipatana.

Tena kho pana samayena uruvelāyaṃ senānigame senānikuṭumbikassa gehe nibbattā sujātā nāma dārikā vayappattā ekasmiṃ nigrodharukkhe patthanaṃ akāsi “sace samajātikaṃ kulagharaṃ gantvā paṭhamagabbhe puttaṃ labhissāmi, anusaṃvaccharaṃ te satasahassapariccāgena balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti. Tassā sā patthanā samijjhi. Sā mahāsattassa dukkarakārikaṃ karontassa chaṭṭhe vasse paripuṇṇe visākhapuṇṇamāyaṃ balikammaṃ kātukāmā hutvā puretaraṃ dhenusahassaṃ laṭṭhimadhukavane carāpetvā tāsaṃ khīraṃ pañca dhenusatāni pāyetvā tāsaṃ khīraṃ aḍḍhatiyānīti evaṃ yāva soḷasannaṃ dhenūnaṃ khīraṃ aṭṭha dhenuyo pivanti, tāva khīrassa bahalatañca madhuratañca ojavantatañca patthayamānā khīraparivattanaṃ nāma akāsi. Sā visākhapuṇṇamadivase “pātova balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti rattiyā paccūsasamayaṃ paccuṭṭhāya tā aṭṭha dhenuyo duhāpesi. Vacchakā [V 1.0078][M 1.0080] dhenūnaṃ thanamūlaṃ nāgamiṃsu, thanamūle pana navabhājane upanītamatte attano dhammatāya khīradhārā pavattiṃsu. Taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā sujātā sahattheneva khīraṃ gahetvā navabhājane pakkhipitvā sahattheneva aggiṃ katvā pacituṃ ārabhi.

At that time, in the village of Senānigama near Uruvelā, a girl named Sujātā was born in the household of the householder Senāni. When she came of age, she made a vow at a certain banyan tree: "If I marry into a family of equal status and bear a son in my first pregnancy, I will make an offering worth a hundred thousand each year." Her wish was fulfilled. In the sixth year of the Great Being’s ascetic practice, on the full moon day of Visākha, she wished to make her offering. Earlier, she had a thousand cows graze in the laṭṭhimadhuka forest. From their milk, she fed five hundred cows; then from their milk, two hundred and fifty; and so on, until the milk of sixteen cows was fed to eight cows. Desiring the milk to be thick, sweet, and nourishing, she performed what is called the "milk transformation." On the full moon day of Visākha, thinking, "I will make the offering early in the morning," she rose at dawn and had those eight cows milked. The calves did not approach the cows’ udders, but as soon as new vessels were brought near the udders, streams of milk flowed spontaneously by their own nature. Seeing this marvel, Sujātā herself took the milk, poured it into a new vessel, kindled a fire herself, and began to cook it.

Tasmiṃ pāyāse paccamāne mahantamahantā bubbuḷā uṭṭhahitvā dakkhiṇāvattā hutvā sañcaranti, ekaphusitampi bahi na patati, uddhanato appamattakopi dhūmo na uṭṭhahati. Tasmiṃ samaye cattāro lokapālā āgantvā uddhane ārakkhaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, mahābrahmā chattaṃ dhāresi, sakko alātāni samānento aggiṃ jālesi. Devatā dvisahassadīpaparivāresu catūsu mahādīpesu devānañca manussānañca upakappanaojaṃ attano devānubhāvena daṇḍakabaddhaṃ madhupaṭalaṃ pīḷetvā madhuṃ gaṇhamānā viya saṃharitvā tattha pakkhipiṃsu. Aññesu hi kālesu devatā kabaḷe kabaḷe ojaṃ pakkhipanti, sambodhidivase ca pana parinibbānadivase ca ukkhaliyaṃyeva pakkhipanti. Sujātā ekadivaseyeva [P 1.0069] tattha attano pākaṭāni anekāni acchariyāni disvā puṇṇaṃ dāsiṃ āmantesi “amma puṇṇe, ajja amhākaṃ devatā ativiya pasannā, mayā ettake kāle evarūpaṃ acchariyaṃ nāma na diṭṭhapubbaṃ, vegena gantvā devaṭṭhānaṃ paṭijaggāhī”ti. Sā “sādhu, ayye”ti tassā vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā turitaturitā rukkhamūlaṃ agamāsi.

While that milk-rice was cooking, very large bubbles arose and moved clockwise, not a single drop spilled out, and not even a tiny wisp of smoke rose from the hearth. At that time, the Four Guardians of the World arrived and stood guard over the hearth, Mahābrahmā held a parasol, and Sakka, arranging the firebrands, kindled the fire. The deities, in the four great continents surrounded by two thousand smaller islands, gathered by their divine power the nutritive essence for the benefit of gods and humans—as if squeezing honey from a honeycomb bound with reeds—and placed it therein. At other times, deities add nutritive essence morsel by morsel, but on the day of enlightenment and the day of final nirvana, they pour it directly into the cooking pot. Sujātā, seeing many wonders manifest there in a single day, addressed her maid Puṇṇā: "Dear Puṇṇā, today our deity is exceedingly pleased. In all this time, I have never before seen such a wonder. Go quickly and tend to the deity's shrine." She replied, "Very well, mistress," and accepting her words, hurried to the foot of the tree.

Bodhisattopi kho tasmiṃ rattibhāge pañca mahāsupine disvā pariggaṇhanto “nissaṃsayenāhaṃ ajja buddho bhavissāmī”ti katasanniṭṭhāno tassā rattiyā accayena katasarīrapaṭijaggano bhikkhācārakālaṃ āgamayamāno pātova āgantvā tasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisīdi attano pabhāya sakalarukkhaṃ obhāsayamāno. Atha kho sā puṇṇā āgantvā addasa bodhisattaṃ rukkhamūle pācīnalokadhātuṃ olokayamānaṃ nisinnaṃ, sarīrato cassa nikkhantāhi pabhāhi sakalarukkhaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ. Disvā tassā etadahosi – “ajja amhākaṃ devatā rukkhato oruyha sahattheneva balikammaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ nisinnā maññe”ti ubbegappattā hutvā vegenāgantvā sujātāya etamatthaṃ ārocesi.

Meanwhile, the Bodhisatta, having seen five great dreams during that portion of the night and reflecting on them, became resolute: "Without a doubt, today I shall become a Buddha." At the end of that night, having attended to his bodily needs and awaiting the time for the alms-round, he arrived at the foot of that tree at dawn and sat there, illuminating the entire tree with his radiance. Then Puṇṇā, arriving, saw the Bodhisatta seated at the foot of the tree, gazing toward the eastern world-sphere, while from his body emanated rays that turned the whole tree golden in color. Seeing this, it occurred to her: "Today, our deity must have descended from the tree and is seated here to accept the offering with his own hand!" Overcome with excitement, she hurried back and reported the matter to Sujātā.

Sujātā [M 1.0081] tassā vacanaṃ sutvā tuṭṭhamānasā hutvā “ajja dāni paṭṭhāya mama jeṭṭhadhītuṭṭhāne tiṭṭhāhī”ti dhītu anucchavikaṃ sabbālaṅkāraṃ adāsi. Yasmā pana buddhabhāvaṃ pāpuṇanadivase satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, tasmā sā “suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ pāyāsaṃ pakkhipissāmī”ti cittaṃ uppādetvā satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ nīharāpetvā tattha pāyāsaṃ [V 1.0079] pakkhipitukāmā pakkabhājanaṃ āvajjesi. ‘Sabbo pāyāso padumapattā udakaṃ viya vinivattitvā pātiyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi, ekapātipūramattova ahosi’. Sā taṃ pātiṃ aññāya suvaṇṇapātiyā paṭikujjitvā odātavatthena veṭhetvā sabbālaṅkārehi attabhāvaṃ alaṅkaritvā taṃ pātiṃ attano sīse ṭhapetvā mahantena ānubhāvena nigrodharukkhamūlaṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ oloketvā balavasomanassajātā “rukkhadevatā”ti saññāya diṭṭhaṭṭhānato paṭṭhāya onatonatā gantvā sīsato pātiṃ otāretvā vivaritvā suvaṇṇabhiṅkārena gandhapupphavāsitaṃ udakaṃ gahetvā bodhisattaṃ upagantvā aṭṭhāsi. Ghaṭīkāramahābrahmunā dinno mattikāpatto ettakaṃ addhānaṃ bodhisattaṃ avijahitvā tasmiṃ khaṇe adassanaṃ gato, bodhisatto pattaṃ apassanto dakkhiṇahatthaṃ pasāretvā udakaṃ sampaṭicchi. Sujātā saheva pātiyā pāyāsaṃ mahāpurisassa hatthe ṭhapesi, mahāpuriso sujātaṃ olokesi. Sā ākāraṃ sallakkhetvā “ayya, mayā tumhākaṃ pariccattaṃ, gaṇhitvā yathāruciṃ gacchathā”ti vanditvā “yathā mayhaṃ manoratho nipphanno[P 1.0070], evaṃ tumhākampi nipphajjatū”ti vatvā satasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇapātiyā purāṇapaṇṇe viya anapekkhā hutvā pakkāmi.

Hearing her words, Sujātā, delighted in mind, said, 'From today onwards, you shall hold the place of my eldest daughter.' Then she gave her all the ornaments befitting a daughter. Since on the day he would attain Buddhahood, it was fitting for him to receive a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, she thought, 'I will put the milk-rice in a golden bowl,' and had a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand brought out. Intending to put the milk-rice in it, she tilted the cooking vessel. All the milk-rice, like water from a lotus leaf, rolled off and settled in the bowl, filling it completely. She then covered that bowl with another golden bowl, wrapped it in a white cloth, adorned herself with all her ornaments, placed the bowl on her head, and with great majesty went to the foot of the banyan tree. Seeing the Bodhisatta, she was filled with overwhelming joy. Mistaking him for a tree deity, from the very spot where she saw him, she went forward, bowing repeatedly. She took the bowl from her head, uncovered it, and taking water scented with perfumes and flowers in a golden ewer, she approached the Bodhisatta and stood there. The earthenware bowl given by Ghaṭīkāra the Great Brahmā, which had not left the Bodhisatta for so long, disappeared at that very moment. Not seeing the bowl, the Bodhisatta stretched out his right hand and received the water. Sujātā placed the milk-rice, along with the bowl, into the Great Being’s hand. The Great Being looked at Sujātā. Observing his demeanor, she paid homage and said, 'Venerable sir, I have given this to you; take it and go as you please.' Then she added, 'Just as my wish has been fulfilled, may yours also be fulfilled.' Without any attachment to the golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, as if it were an old leaf, she departed.

Bodhisattopi kho nisinnaṭṭhānā uṭṭhāya rukkhaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pātiṃ ādāya nerañjarāya tīraṃ gantvā anekesaṃ bodhisattasahassānaṃ abhisambujjhanadivase otaritvā nhānaṭṭhānaṃ suppatiṭṭhitatitthaṃ nāma atthi, tassa tīre pātiṃ ṭhapetvā otaritvā nhatvā anekabuddhasatasahassānaṃ nivāsanaṃ arahaddhajaṃ nivāsetvā puratthābhimukho nisīditvā ekaṭṭhitālapakkappamāṇe ekūnapaññāsa piṇḍe katvā sabbaṃ appodakaṃ madhupāyāsaṃ paribhuñji. So eva hissa buddhabhūtassa sattasattāhaṃ bodhimaṇḍe vasantassa ekūnapaññāsa divasāni āhāro ahosi. Ettakaṃ kālaṃ [M 1.0082] neva añño āhāro atthi, na nhānaṃ, na mukhadhovanaṃ, na sarīravaḷañjo, jhānasukhena maggasukhena phalasukhena ca vītināmesi. Taṃ pana pāyāsaṃ paribhuñjitvā suvaṇṇapātiṃ gahetvā “sacāhaṃ, ajja buddho bhavituṃ sakkhissāmi, ayaṃ pāti paṭisotaṃ gacchatu, no ce sakkhissāmi, anusotaṃ gacchatū”ti vatvā nadīsote pakkhipi. Sā sotaṃ chindamānā nadīmajjhaṃ gantvā majjhamajjhaṭṭhāneneva javasampanno asso viya asītihatthamattaṭṭhānaṃ paṭisotaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ āvaṭṭe nimujjitvā kāḷanāgarājabhavanaṃ gantvā tiṇṇaṃ buddhānaṃ paribhogapātiyo “kili kilī”ti ravaṃ kārayamānā paharitvāva tāsaṃ sabbaheṭṭhimā hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Kāḷo nāgarājā taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “hiyyo eko buddho nibbatto, puna ajja eko nibbatto”ti vatvā anekehi padasatehi thutiyo vadamāno uṭṭhāsi. Tassa kira [V 1.0080] mahāpathaviyā ekayojanatigāvutappamāṇaṃ nabhaṃ pūretvā ārohanakālo “ajja vā hiyyo vā”ti sadiso ahosi.

The Bodhisatta, rising from his seat, circumambulated the tree, took the bowl, and went to the bank of the Nerañjarā River. There is a well-established bathing place named Suppatiṭṭhita, where many thousands of Bodhisattas had descended to bathe on the day of their supreme enlightenment. Placing the bowl on the bank, he descended and bathed. After bathing, he donned the banner of an Arahant, the garment worn by many hundreds of thousands of Buddhas. Facing east, he sat down and consumed forty-nine lumps of the thick, honeyed milk-rice, each the size of a single palmyra fruit. This very meal was his only nourishment for the forty-nine days that he, having become a Buddha, dwelt at the seat of Awakening for seven weeks. During this time, he had no other food, no bathing, no washing of the face, nor any bodily ablutions; he passed the time with the bliss of absorption, the bliss of the path, and the bliss of its fruit. After eating the milk-rice, he took the golden bowl and declared, 'If today I am to become a Buddha, may this bowl go upstream. If not, may it go downstream.' With these words, he cast the bowl into the river's current. Cutting through the current, it went to the middle of the river and, like a swift horse, sped upstream for eighty cubits before sinking in a whirlpool and reaching the abode of the Nāga king Kāḷa. There, it struck the bowls used by the three previous Buddhas, making a 'kili-kili' sound, and came to rest beneath them all. Hearing the sound, the Nāga king Kāḷa exclaimed, 'Yesterday a Buddha arose, and today another has arisen!' and rose up, uttering praises in many hundreds of verses. Indeed, his time of ascent, filling the sky for a distance of one yojana and three gāvutas, was like the span from yesterday to today.

Bodhisattopi nadītīramhi supupphitasālavane divāvihāraṃ katvā sāyanhasamaye pupphānaṃ vaṇṭato muccanakāle devatāhi alaṅkatena aṭṭhūsabhavitthārena maggena sīho viya vijambhamāno bodhirukkhābhimukho pāyāsi. Nāgayakkhasupaṇṇādayo dibbehi gandhapupphādīhi pūjayiṃsu, dibbasaṅgītādīni pavattayiṃsu, dasasahassī lokadhātu ekagandhā ekamālā ekasādhukārā ahosi. Tasmiṃ samaye sotthiyo nāma tiṇahārako tiṇaṃ ādāya paṭipathe āgacchanto mahāpurisassa ākāraṃ ñatvā aṭṭha tiṇamuṭṭhiyo adāsi. Bodhisatto tiṇaṃ gahetvā bodhimaṇḍaṃ [P 1.0071] āruyha dakkhiṇadisābhāge uttarābhimukho aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe dakkhiṇacakkavāḷaṃ osīditvā heṭṭhā avīcisampattaṃ viya ahosi, uttaracakkavāḷaṃ ullaṅghitvā upari bhavaggappattaṃ viya ahosi. Bodhisatto “idaṃ sambodhiṃ pāpuṇanaṭṭhānaṃ na bhavissati maññe”ti padakkhiṇaṃ karonto pacchimadisābhāgaṃ gantvā puratthābhimukho aṭṭhāsi, tato pacchimacakkavāḷaṃ osīditvā heṭṭhā avīcisampattaṃ viya ahosi, puratthimacakkavāḷaṃ ullaṅghitvā upari bhavaggappattaṃ viya ahosi. Ṭhitaṭṭhitaṭṭhāne kirassa nemivaṭṭipariyante akkante nābhiyā patiṭṭhitamahāsakaṭacakkaṃ viya [M 1.0083] mahāpathavī onatunnatā ahosi. Bodhisatto “idampi sambodhiṃ pāpuṇanaṭṭhānaṃ na bhavissati maññe”ti padakkhiṇaṃ karonto uttaradisābhāgaṃ gantvā dakkhiṇābhimukho aṭṭhāsi, tato uttaracakkavāḷaṃ osīditvā heṭṭhā avīcisampattaṃ viya ahosi, dakkhiṇacakkavāḷaṃ ullaṅghitvā upari bhavaggappattaṃ viya ahosi. Bodhisatto “idampi sambodhiṃ pāpuṇanaṭṭhānaṃ na bhavissati maññe”ti padakkhiṇaṃ karonto puratthimadisābhāgaṃ gantvā pacchimābhimukho aṭṭhāsi. Puratthimadisābhāge pana sabbabuddhānaṃ pallaṅkaṭṭhānaṃ, taṃ neva chambhati, na kampati. Mahāsatto “idaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitaṃ acalaṭṭhānaṃ kilesapañjaraviddhaṃsanaṭṭhāna”nti ñatvā tāni tiṇāni agge gahetvā cālesi, tāvadeva cuddasahattho pallaṅko ahosi. Tānipi kho tiṇāni tathārūpena saṇṭhānena saṇṭhahiṃsu, yathārūpaṃ sukusalopi cittakāro vā potthakāro vā ālikhitumpi samattho natthi. Bodhisatto bodhikkhandhaṃ piṭṭhito katvā puratthābhimukho daḷhamānaso hutvā –

The Bodhisatta, having spent the day in a beautifully flowering sāla grove on the riverbank, set out towards the Bodhi tree in the evening, at the time when flowers are released from their stalks. He moved with the majestic stride of a lion along a path eight usabhas in width, adorned by deities. Nāgas, yakkhas, supaṇṇas, and others honored him with divine perfumes and flowers, and celestial music was played.
