The ten-thousandfold world system became of one fragrance, one garland, and one shout of approval. At that time, a grass-carrier named Sotthiya, carrying grass, came along the path and, recognizing the Great Being’s noble appearance, gave him eight handfuls of grass. The Bodhisatta took the grass, ascended to the terrace of the Bodhi tree, and stood in the southern quarter, facing north. At that moment, the southern world-system seemed to sink down, as if reaching Avīci below, while the northern world-system seemed to rise up, as if reaching the summit of existence above. The Bodhisatta thought, “I believe this will not be the place for attaining perfect enlightenment,” and, circumambulating, he went to the western quarter and stood facing east. Then the western world-system seemed to sink down, as if reaching Avīci below, while the eastern world-system seemed to rise up, as if reaching the summit of existence above. It is said that in whatever place he stood, the great earth rose and fell, like a great cartwheel resting on its hub that tilts when its rim is trodden upon. The Bodhisatta thought, “I believe this too will not be the place for attaining perfect enlightenment,” and, circumambulating, he went to the northern quarter and stood facing south. Then the northern world-system seemed to sink down, as if reaching Avīci below, while the southern world-system seemed to rise up, as if reaching the summit of existence above. The Bodhisatta thought, “I believe this too will not be the place for attaining perfect enlightenment,” and, circumambulating, he went to the eastern quarter and stood facing west. The eastern quarter, however, is the place of the throne of all Buddhas; it neither sinks nor shakes. The Great Being, knowing, “This is the unabandoned, unmoving place of all Buddhas, the place for shattering the cage of defilements,” took that grass by the tips and shook it. At that very moment, a fourteen-cubit throne appeared. And that grass settled in such a formation that not even a most skilled painter or illustrator would be able to draw it. The Bodhisatta, with the trunk of the Bodhi tree at his back, faced east and, becoming firm-minded, resolved:

“Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatu;

Upasussatu nissesaṃ, sarīre maṃsalohitaṃ”.

“Let only skin, sinews, and bone remain; let all the flesh and blood in my body dry up.”

Na [V 1.0081] tvevāhaṃ sammāsambodhiṃ appatvā imaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bhindissāmīti asanisatasannipātenapi abhejjarūpaṃ aparājitapallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdi.

“Indeed, I will not break this cross-legged posture until I have attained perfect enlightenment.” Thus, he sat, folding his legs into the unconquered posture, unbreakable even by the impact of a hundred thunderbolts.

Tasmiṃ samaye māro devaputto “siddhatthakumāro mayhaṃ vasaṃ atikkamitukāmo, na dānissa atikkamituṃ dassāmī”ti mārabalassa santikaṃ gantvā etamatthaṃ ārocetvā māraghosanaṃ nāma ghosāpetvā mārabalaṃ ādāya nikkhami. Sā mārasenā mārassa purato dvādasayojanā hoti, dakkhiṇato ca vāmato ca dvādasayojanā, pacchato yāva cakkavāḷapariyantaṃ katvā ṭhitā, uddhaṃ navayojanubbedhā, yassā unnadantiyā unnādasaddo yojanasahassato [P 1.0072] paṭṭhāya pathaviundriyanasaddo viya suyyati. Atha māro devaputto diyaḍḍhayojanasatikaṃ girimekhalaṃ nāma hatthiṃ abhiruhitvā bāhusahassaṃ māpetvā nānāvudhāni aggahesi. Avasesāyapi māraparisāya dve janā ekasadisaṃ āvudhaṃ na gaṇhiṃsu, nānappakāravaṇṇā nānappakāramukhā hutvā mahāsattaṃ ajjhottharamānā āgamiṃsu.

At that time, Māra, the son of a deva, thought, “Prince Siddhattha desires to overcome my domain; I will not let him overcome it.” Having gone to his forces and announced this matter, he had the Māra-proclamation sounded and set out with his army. That army of Māra was twelve yojanas before him, twelve yojanas to his right and to his left, and behind him it stood filling the space to the very edge of the world-system. It was nine yojanas in height, and the roaring sound of its clamor could be heard from a thousand yojanas away, like the sound of the earth splitting. Then Māra, the son of a deva, mounted the elephant named Girimekhala, which was one hundred and fifty yojanas tall, created a thousand arms, and took up various weapons. In the rest of Māra’s retinue, no two people took up a similar weapon; having various colors and various faces, they advanced, overwhelming the Great Being.

Dasasahassacakkavāḷadevatā [M 1.0084] pana mahāsattassa thutiyo vadamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Sakko devarājā vijayuttarasaṅkhaṃ dhamamāno aṭṭhāsi. So kira saṅkho vīsahatthasatiko hoti. Sakiṃ vātaṃ gāhāpetvā dhamanto cattāro māse saddaṃ karitvā nissaddo hoti. Mahākāḷanāgarājā atirekapadasatena vaṇṇaṃ vadanto aṭṭhāsi, mahābrahmā setacchattaṃ dhārayamāno aṭṭhāsi. Mārabale pana bodhimaṇḍaṃ upasaṅkamante tesaṃ ekopi ṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, sammukhasammukhaṭṭhāneneva palāyiṃsu. Kāḷo nāgarājā pathaviyaṃ nimujjitvā pañcayojanasatikaṃ mañjerikanāgabhavanaṃ gantvā ubhohi hatthehi mukhaṃ pidahitvā nipanno. Sakko vijayuttarasaṅkhaṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ katvā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Mahābrahmā setacchattaṃ cakkavāḷakoṭiyaṃ ṭhapetvā brahmalokameva agamāsi. Ekā devatāpi ṭhātuṃ samatthā nāhosi, mahāpuriso ekakova nisīdi.

The deities of the ten thousand world-systems, however, stood uttering praises of the Great Being. Sakka, king of the devas, stood blowing the Vijayuttara conch. That conch, it is said, is one hundred and twenty hands long. When filled with a single breath and blown, it makes a sound for four months before becoming silent. The great Nāga king Mahākāḷa stood reciting praises with more than a hundred verses. Mahābrahmā stood holding a white parasol. But when Māra’s army approached the terrace of the Bodhi tree, not one of them was able to stand their ground; they fled from the very spots where they stood. The Nāga king Kāḷa plunged into the earth, went to the five-hundred-yojana Mañjerika Nāga-palace, and lay down, covering his face with both hands. Sakka, placing the Vijayuttara conch on his back, stood at the rim of the world-system. Mahābrahmā, placing the white parasol at the edge of the world-system, went back to the Brahma-world itself. Not a single deity was able to remain; the Great Being sat all alone.

Māropi attano parisaṃ āha “tātā suddhodanaputtena siddhatthena sadiso añño puriso nāma natthi, mayaṃ sammukhā yuddhaṃ dātuṃ na sakkhissāma, pacchābhāgena dassāmā”ti. Mahāpurisopi tīṇi passāni oloketvā sabbadevatānaṃ palātattā suññāni addasa. Puna uttarapassena mārabalaṃ ajjhottharamānaṃ disvā “ayaṃ ettako jano maṃ ekakaṃ sandhāya mahantaṃ vāyāmaṃ parakkamaṃ karoti, imasmiṃ ṭhāne mayhaṃ mātā vā pitā vā bhātā vā añño vā koci ñātako natthi, imā pana dasa pāramiyova mayhaṃ dīgharattaṃ puṭṭhaparijanasadisā, tasmā pāramiyova [V 1.0082] phalakaṃ katvā pāramisattheneva paharitvā ayaṃ balakāyo mayā viddhaṃsetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti dasa pāramiyo āvajjamāno nisīdi.

Māra, too, said to his assembly, 'Sirs, there is no other man like Siddhattha, the son of Suddhodana. We cannot give battle face to face; we will attack from the rear.' The Great Being looked in the three directions and saw them empty, as all the deities had fled. Then, seeing Māra's army advancing from the northern direction, he thought, 'This great host is exerting great effort and striving against me alone. In this place, I have no mother, father, brother, or any other relative. But these Ten Perfections have long been like my nurtured retinue. Therefore, making the Perfections my shield and striking with the weapon of the Perfections, it is fitting for me to rout this army.' Thus, reflecting on the Ten Perfections, he sat down.

Atha kho māro devaputto “eteneva siddhatthaṃ palāpessāmī”ti vātamaṇḍalaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Taṅkhaṇaṃyeva puratthimādibhedā vātā samuṭṭhahitvā aḍḍhayojanaekayojanadviyojanatiyojanappamāṇāni [P 1.0073] pabbatakūṭāni padāletvā vanagaccharukkhādīni ummūletvā samantā gāmanigame cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ kātuṃ samatthāpi mahāpurisassa puññatejena vihatānubhāvā bodhisattaṃ patvā cīvarakaṇṇamattampi cāletuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Tato “udakena na ajjhottharitvā māressāmī”ti mahāvassaṃ [M 1.0085] samuṭṭhāpesi. Tassānubhāvena uparūpari satapaṭalasahassapaṭalādibhedā valāhakā uṭṭhahitvā vassiṃsu. Vuṭṭhidhārāvegena pathavī chiddā ahosi. Vanarukkhādīnaṃ uparibhāgena mahāmegho āgantvā mahāsattassa cīvare ussāvabinduṭṭhānamattampi temetuṃ nāsakkhi. Tato pāsāṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Mahantāni mahantāni pabbatakūṭāni dhūmāyantāni pajjalantāni ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattaṃ patvā dibbamālāguḷabhāvaṃ āpajjiṃsu. Tato paharaṇavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Ekatodhārāubhatodhārāasisattikhurappādayo dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattaṃ patvā dibbapupphāni ahesuṃ. Tato aṅgāravassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Kiṃsukavaṇṇā aṅgārā ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā vikiriṃsu. Tato kukkuḷavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Accuṇho aggivaṇṇo kukkuḷo ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibbacandanacuṇṇaṃ hutvā nipati. Tato vālukāvassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Atisukhumavālukā dhūmāyantā pajjalantā ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibbapupphāni hutvā nipatiṃsu. Tato kalalavassaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ kalalaṃ dhūmāyantaṃ pajjalantaṃ ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa pādamūle dibbavilepanaṃ hutvā nipati. Tato “iminā bhiṃsetvā siddhatthaṃ palāpessāmī”ti andhakāraṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Taṃ caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ viya mahātamaṃ hutvā bodhisattaṃ patvā sūriyappabhāvihataṃ viya andhakāraṃ antaradhāyi.

Then Māra the deity thought, 'With this I will drive away Siddhattha,' and he stirred up a whirlwind. Instantly, winds arose from the east and other directions, capable of breaking mountain peaks measuring half a yojana, one yojana, two yojanas, and three yojanas, uprooting forest trees and groves, and reducing villages and towns all around to dust; yet, their power nullified by the Great Being's merit, upon reaching the Bodhisatta they could not stir so much as the edge of his robe. Then, thinking, 'I will kill him by overwhelming him with water,' he caused a great rainstorm. By his power, clouds arose in layers of hundreds and thousands and poured down rain. The force of the rain torrents split the earth, but though a great cloud advanced over the tops of the forest trees, it could not wet even a spot the size of a dewdrop on the Great Being's robe. Next, he caused a shower of rocks. Great mountain peaks, smoking and blazing, came through the sky, but upon reaching the Bodhisatta, they turned into divine flower garlands. Then he caused a shower of weapons. Single-edged and double-edged weapons, such as swords, spears, and razor-arrows, smoking and blazing, came through the sky, but upon reaching the Bodhisatta, they became divine flowers. Then he caused a shower of embers. Embers the color of the kiṃsuka flower came through the sky, but at the Bodhisatta's feet, they became divine flowers and scattered. Then he caused a shower of hot ashes. Extremely hot ashes, the color of fire, came through the sky, but at the Bodhisatta's feet, they became divine sandalwood powder and fell. Then he caused a shower of sand. Very fine sand, smoking and blazing, came through the sky, but at the Bodhisatta's feet, it became divine flowers and fell. Then he caused a shower of mud. That mud, smoking and blazing, came through the sky, but at the Bodhisatta's feet, it became divine ointment and fell. Then, thinking, 'With this I will frighten Siddhattha and drive him away,' he created darkness. That darkness, like one with four divisions, became a great gloom, but upon reaching the Bodhisatta, it vanished like darkness dispelled by the sun's radiance.

Evaṃ māro imāhi navahi vātavassapāsāṇapaharaṇaaṅgārakukkuḷavālukākalalaandhakāravuṭṭhīhi bodhisattaṃ palāpetuṃ asakkonto “kiṃ bhaṇe, tiṭṭhatha, imaṃ siddhatthakumāraṃ gaṇhatha hanatha palāpethā”ti parisaṃ āṇāpetvā sayampi girimekhalassa hatthino khandhe nisinno cakkāvudhaṃ ādāya bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “siddhattha uṭṭhāhi etasmā pallaṅkā, nāyaṃ tuyhaṃ pāpuṇāti, mayhaṃ eva pāpuṇātī”ti āha. Mahāsatto tassa vacanaṃ sutvā avoca – “māra, neva tayā dasa pāramiyo pūritā, na upapāramiyo, na paramatthapāramiyo, nāpi pañca mahāpariccāgā pariccattā[V 1.0083], na ñātatthacariyā, na lokatthacariyā, na buddhicariyā pūritā, sabbā [M 1.0086] tā mayāyeva pūritā, tasmā nāyaṃ pallaṅko tuyhaṃ pāpuṇāti[P 1.0074], mayheveso pāpuṇātī”ti.

Thus, Māra, unable to drive away the Bodhisatta with these nine storms of wind, rain, rocks, weapons, embers, hot ashes, sand, mud, and darkness, commanded his assembly, saying, 'Why do you stand there, sirs? Seize this Prince Siddhattha, kill him, drive him away!' Then, mounting the elephant Girimekhala himself, armed with a discus, he approached the Bodhisatta and said, 'Siddhattha, rise from this seat! It does not belong to you—it is mine!' Hearing his words, the Great Being replied, 'Māra, neither have you fulfilled the Ten Perfections, nor the supplementary perfections, nor the ultimate perfections. Nor have you made the Five Great Sacrifices. You have not fulfilled the conduct for the welfare of your kin, nor for the welfare of the world, nor the conduct for enlightenment. All these have been fulfilled by me alone. Therefore, this seat does not belong to you; it is mine!'

Māro kuddho kodhavegaṃ asahanto mahāpurisassa cakkāvudhaṃ vissajjesi. Taṃ tassa dasa pāramiyo āvajjentassa uparibhāge mālāvitānaṃ hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Taṃ kira khuradhāracakkāvudhaṃ aññadā tena kuddhena vissaṭṭhaṃ ekaghanapāsāṇatthambhe vaṃsakaḷīre viya chindantaṃ gacchati, idāni pana tasmiṃ mālāvitānaṃ hutvā ṭhite avasesā māraparisā “idāni pallaṅkato vuṭṭhāya palāyissatī”ti mahantamahantāni selakūṭāni vissajjesuṃ. Tānipi mahāpurisassa dasa pāramiyo āvajjentassa mālāguḷabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā bhūmiyaṃ patiṃsu. Devatā cakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ṭhitā gīvaṃ pasāretvā sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā “naṭṭho vata so siddhatthakumārassa rūpaggappatto attabhāvo, kiṃ nu kho karissatī”ti olokenti.

Māra, enraged and unable to bear his surge of anger, hurled his discus weapon at the Great Being. But as the Great Being reflected upon his ten perfections, it became a canopy of flowers and remained above him. It is said that this razor-edged discus, when hurled by an angered Māra on other occasions, would slice through solid stone pillars as if they were bamboo shoots. But now, as it became a canopy of flowers and remained suspended there, the rest of Māra’s host thought, 'Now he will rise from his seat and flee!' and hurled massive mountain peaks. Yet even these, as the Great Being reflected upon his ten perfections, turned into clusters of flowers and fell to the ground. The deities, standing at the rim of the universe, stretched their necks and lifted their heads, watching and saying, 'Alas, the being of Prince Siddhattha, who has attained the pinnacle of form, is lost! What will he do now?'

Tato mahāpuriso “pūritapāramīnaṃ bodhisattānaṃ abhisambujjhanadivase pattapallaṅko mayhaṃva pāpuṇātī”ti vatvā ṭhitaṃ māraṃ āha – “māra tuyhaṃ dānassa dinnabhāve ko sakkhī”ti. Māro “ime ettakā janā sakkhino”ti mārabalābhimukhaṃ hatthaṃ pasāresi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe māraparisāya “ahaṃ sakkhī, ahaṃ sakkhī”ti pavattasaddo pathaviundriyanasaddasadiso ahosi. Atha māro mahāpurisaṃ āha “siddhattha, tuyhaṃ dānassa dinnabhāve ko sakkhī”ti. Mahāpuriso “tuyhaṃ tāva dānassa dinnabhāve sacetanā sakkhino, mayhaṃ pana imasmiṃ ṭhāne sacetano koci sakkhī nāma natthi, tiṭṭhatu tāva me avasesattabhāvesu dinnadānaṃ, vessantarattabhāve pana ṭhatvā mayhaṃ sattasatakamahādānassa dinnabhāve ayaṃ acetanāpi ghanamahāpathavī sakkhī”ti cīvaragabbhantarato dakkhiṇahatthaṃ abhinīharitvā “vessantarattabhāve ṭhatvā mayhaṃ sattasatakamahādānassa dinnabhāve tvaṃ sakkhī na sakkhī”ti mahāpathaviabhimukhaṃ hatthaṃ pasāresi. Mahāpathavī “ahaṃ te tadā sakkhī”ti viravasatena viravasahassena viravasatasahassena mārabalaṃ avattharamānā viya unnadi.

Then the Great Being said to Māra, who stood there, “The throne attained by Bodhisattas who have fulfilled the perfections on the day of their full enlightenment is mine.” He then asked, “Māra, who is witness to your having given gifts?” Māra said, “These many people are my witnesses,” and stretched out his hand toward his army. At that moment, the sound from Māra’s retinue shouting, “I am a witness! I am a witness!” was like the sound of the earth trembling. Then Māra said to the Great Being, “Siddhattha, who is witness to your having given gifts?” The Great Being replied, “For your gifts, you have conscious witnesses. But here in this place, there is no conscious witness for me. Let alone the gifts I gave in other existences; for the great gift of seven hundreds that I gave in my existence as Vessantara, this inanimate, solid great earth is my witness.” So saying, he drew forth his right hand from within his robe and stretched it toward the great earth, declaring, “In my existence as Vessantara, when I gave the great gift of seven hundreds, were you my witness or not?” The great earth roared with a hundred, a thousand, a hundred thousand roars, as if to overwhelm the army of Māra, proclaiming, “I was your witness then!”

Tato [M 1.0087] mahāpurise “dinnaṃ te siddhattha mahādānaṃ uttamadāna”nti vessantaradānaṃ sammasante diyaḍḍhayojanasatiko girimekhalahatthī jaṇṇukehi pathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi, māraparisā disāvidisā palāyi, dve ekamaggena gatā nāma natthi, sīsābharaṇāni ceva nivatthavatthāni ca pahāya sammukhasammukhadisāhiyeva palāyiṃsu. Tato devasaṅghā palāyamānaṃ mārabalaṃ disvā “mārassa [P 1.0075] parājayo jāto, siddhatthakumārassa jayo, jayapūjaṃ karissāmā”ti nāgā nāgānaṃ, supaṇṇā supaṇṇānaṃ[V 1.0084], devatā devatānaṃ, brahmāno brahmānaṃ, ugghosetvā gandhamālādihatthā mahāpurisassa santikaṃ bodhipallaṅkaṃ agamaṃsu.

Then, as the Great Being reflected upon the Vessantara gift, thinking, “Siddhattha, the great gift, the supreme gift, has been given by you!”, the elephant Girimekhala, one hundred and fifty yojanas in size, knelt upon the earth. Māra’s retinue fled in all directions—not even two went by the same path. Casting off their head ornaments and garments, they fled in opposite directions. Seeing Māra’s forces fleeing, the hosts of gods cried out, “Māra is defeated! Prince Siddhattha is victorious! Let us make a victory offering!” Nāgas proclaimed to nāgas, supaṇṇas to supaṇṇas, deities to deities, and brahmās to brahmās, and bearing perfumes and garlands, they approached the Great Being at the throne of awakening.

Evaṃ gatesu ca pana tesu –

And so, when they had departed—

“Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ, mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā, jayaṃ tadā nāgagaṇā mahesino.

“Victory is indeed the Buddha’s, the glorious one, and defeat is Māra’s, the evil one! Delighted, the hosts of nāgas proclaimed the victory of the Great Sage at the Bodhimaṇḍa.

“Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ, mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā, supaṇṇasaṅghāpi jayaṃ mahesino.

“Victory is indeed the Buddha’s, the glorious one, and defeat is Māra’s, the evil one! Delighted, the hosts of supaṇṇas also proclaimed the victory of the Great Sage at the Bodhimaṇḍa.

“Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ, mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā, jayaṃ tadā devagaṇā mahesino.

“Victory is indeed the Buddha’s, the glorious one, and defeat is Māra’s, the evil one! Delighted, the hosts of deities proclaimed the victory of the Great Sage at the Bodhimaṇḍa.

“Jayo hi buddhassa sirīmato ayaṃ, mārassa ca pāpimato parājayo;

Ugghosayuṃ bodhimaṇḍe pamoditā, jayaṃ tadā brahmagaṇāpi tādino”ti.

“Victory is indeed the Buddha’s, the glorious one, and defeat is Māra’s, the evil one! Delighted, the hosts of brahmās also proclaimed the victory of the Steadfast One at the Bodhimaṇḍa.”

Avasesā dasasu cakkavāḷasahassesu devatā mālāgandhavilepanehi ca pūjayamānā nānappakārā thutiyo ca vadamānā aṭṭhaṃsu. Evaṃ anatthaṅgateyeva [M 1.0088] sūriye mahāpuriso mārabalaṃ vidhametvā cīvarūpari patamānehi bodhirukkhaṅkurehi rattapavāḷapallavehi viya pūjiyamāno paṭhamayāme pubbenivāsañāṇaṃ anussaritvā, majjhimayāme dibbacakkhuṃ visodhetvā, pacchimayāme paṭiccasamuppāde ñāṇaṃ otāresi. Athassa dvādasapadikaṃ paccayākāraṃ vaṭṭavivaṭṭavasena anulomapaṭilomato sammasantassa dasasahassī lokadhātu udakapariyantaṃ katvā dvādasakkhattuṃ sampakampi.

The remaining deities in the ten thousand world-systems stood worshipping with garlands, perfumes, and unguents, and uttering praises of various kinds. Thus, while the sun had not yet set, the Great Being, having vanquished the forces of Māra, was honored by shoots of the Bodhi tree like red coral leaves falling upon his robe. In the first watch of the night, he recollected the knowledge of his past lives. In the middle watch, he purified the divine eye. In the last watch, he directed his knowledge to dependent origination. Then, as he was thoroughly comprehending the twelve-factored dependent origination in terms of continuation and cessation, in forward and reverse order, the ten-thousandfold world-system, up to its watery boundary, quaked twelve times.

Mahāpurise pana dasasahassilokadhātuṃ unnādetvā aruṇuggamanavelāya sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhante [P 1.0076] sakaladasasahassī lokadhātu alaṅkatapaṭiyattā ahosi. Pācīnacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ussāpitānaṃ dhajānaṃ paṭākānaṃ raṃsiyo pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ paharanti, tathā pacchimacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ussāpitānaṃ pācīnacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ, dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ussāpitānaṃ uttaracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ, uttaracakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ ussāpitānaṃ [V 1.0085] dakkhiṇacakkavāḷamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ paharanti, pathavitale ussāpitānaṃ pana dhajānaṃ paṭākānaṃ brahmalokaṃ āhacca aṭṭhaṃsu, brahmaloke baddhānaṃ pathavitale patiṭṭhahiṃsu, dasasahassacakkavāḷesu pupphūpagarukkhā pupphaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, phalūpagarukkhā phalapiṇḍībhārabharitā ahesuṃ. Khandhesu khandhapadumāni pupphiṃsu, sākhāsu sākhāpadumāni, latāsu latāpadumāni, ākāse olambakapadumāni, silātalāni bhinditvā uparūpari satta satta hutvā daṇḍakapadumāni uṭṭhahiṃsu. Dasasahassī lokadhātu vaṭṭetvā vissaṭṭhamālāguḷā viya susanthatapupphasanthāro viya ca ahosi. Cakkavāḷantaresu aṭṭhayojanasahassalokantarikā sattasūriyappabhāyapi anobhāsitapubbā ekobhāsā ahesuṃ, caturāsītiyojanasahassagambhīro mahāsamuddo madhurodako ahosi, nadiyo nappavattiṃsu, jaccandhā rūpāni passiṃsu, jātibadhirā saddaṃ suṇiṃsu, jātipīṭhasappino padasā gacchiṃsu, andubandhanādīni chijjitvā patiṃsu.

Moreover, as the Great Being made the ten-thousandfold world-system resound and penetrated omniscience at the time of dawn, the entire ten-thousandfold world-system became adorned and prepared. The rays of banners and flags raised on the rim of the eastern world-system struck the rim of the western world-system; likewise, those on the western rim struck the eastern, those on the southern rim struck the northern, and those on the northern rim struck the southern. Banners and flags raised on the surface of the earth reached the Brahma world, and those fastened in the Brahma world stood firm on the earth. In the ten-thousandfold world-systems, flowering trees bore flowers, and fruit trees were laden with clusters of fruit. Lotuses bloomed on tree trunks, on branches, and on vines; hanging lotuses appeared in the sky. Breaking through the rocky ground, stalk-lotuses arose one above another in sets of seven. The ten-thousandfold world-system was like a rolled-up garland cast open, and like a well-laid carpet of flowers. The inter-world spaces, eight thousand yojanas in extent, which had never before been illuminated even by the light of seven suns, became a single expanse of light. The great ocean, eighty-four thousand yojanas deep, became sweet water. Rivers ceased to flow. The blind by birth saw forms, the deaf by birth heard sounds, and the lame by birth walked on their own feet. Bonds and shackles were broken and fell away.

Evaṃ aparimāṇena sirivibhavena pūjiyamāno mahāpuriso anekappakāresu acchariyadhammesu pātubhūtesu sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭivijjhitvā sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

Thus, being honored with immeasurable glory and splendor, and with many kinds of wondrous phenomena manifesting, the Great Being penetrated the knowledge of omniscience and uttered the inspired utterance never abandoned by all Buddhas:

“Anekajātisaṃsāraṃ[M 1.0089], sandhāvissaṃ anibbisaṃ;

Gahakāraṃ gavesanto, dukkhā jāti punappunaṃ.

“Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, not finding the builder of this house; painful is birth again and again.

“Gahakāraka diṭṭhosi, puna gehaṃ na kāhasi;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, gahakūṭaṃ visaṅkhataṃ;

Visaṅkhāragataṃ cittaṃ, taṇhānaṃ khayamajjhagā”ti. (dha. pa. 153-154);

“O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build a house again. All your rafters are broken, your ridgepole is shattered. My mind has reached the Unconditioned; the destruction of craving has been attained.”

Iti [P 1.0077] tusitapurato paṭṭhāya yāva ayaṃ bodhimaṇḍe sabbaññutappatti, ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ avidūrenidānaṃ nāmāti veditabbaṃ.

Thus, from Tusita heaven up to the attainment of omniscience at the Bodhi-maṇḍa, this entire section is to be understood as the “Near Origin.”

Avidūrenidānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Account of the Near Origin is concluded.

3. Santikenidānakathā

3. The Account of the Immediate Origin

“Santikenidānaṃ [V 1.0086] pana ‘bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharati jetavane anāthapiṇḍikassa ārāme. Vesāliyaṃ viharati mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāya’nti evaṃ tesu tesu ṭhānesu viharato tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāneyeva labbhatī”ti vuttaṃ. Kiñcāpi evaṃ vuttaṃ, atha kho pana tampi ādito paṭṭhāya evaṃ veditabbaṃ – udānaṃ udānetvā jayapallaṅke nisinnassa hi bhagavato etadahosi “ahaṃ kappasatasahassādhikāni cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni imassa pallaṅkassa kāraṇā sandhāviṃ, ettakaṃ me kālaṃ imasseva pallaṅkassa kāraṇā alaṅkatasīsaṃ gīvāya chinditvā dinnaṃ, suañjitāni akkhīni hadayamaṃsañca ubbaṭṭetvā dinnaṃ, jālīkumārasadisā puttā kaṇhājinakumārisadisā dhītaro maddīdevisadisā bhariyāyo ca paresaṃ dāsatthāya dinnā, ayaṃ me pallaṅko jayapallaṅko varapallaṅko ca. Ettha me nisinnassa saṅkappā paripuṇṇā, na tāva ito uṭṭhahissāmī”ti anekakoṭisatasahassā samāpattiyo samāpajjanto sattāhaṃ tattheva nisīdi. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ “atha kho bhagavā sattāhaṃ ekapallaṅkena nisīdi vimuttisukhapaṭisaṃvedī”ti (udā. 1; mahāva. 1).

Regarding the Immediate Origin, it is said: “The Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Monastery. He was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Hall with the Peaked Roof.” Thus, it is found in each of those places where he was dwelling. Though it is said thus, it should be understood from the beginning as follows. Having uttered the inspired utterance, this thought occurred to the Blessed One as he sat on the throne of victory: “For four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more, I have wandered for the sake of this throne. For all that time, for the sake of this very throne, my adorned head was severed from my neck and given away, my well-anointed eyes and the flesh of my heart were torn out and given away, sons like Prince Jāli, daughters like Princess Kaṇhājinā, and wives like Queen Maddī were given to others for servitude. This throne of mine is the throne of victory, the supreme throne. Seated here, my aspirations are fulfilled. I shall not yet rise from this spot.” Entering into many hundreds of thousands of millions of meditative attainments, he sat there for seven days. With reference to this, it is said: “Then the Blessed One sat for seven days in a single posture, experiencing the bliss of liberation.”

Atha ekaccānaṃ devatānaṃ “ajjāpi nūna siddhatthassa kattabbakiccaṃ atthi, pallaṅkasmiñhi ālayaṃ na vijahatī”ti parivitakko udapādi. Satthā devatānaṃ [M 1.0090] parivitakkaṃ ñatvā tāsaṃ vitakkavūpasamanatthaṃ vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ dassesi. Mahābodhimaṇḍasmiñhi katapāṭihāriyañca, ñātisamāgame katapāṭihāriyañca, pāthikaputtasamāgame katapāṭihāriyañca, sabbaṃ kaṇḍambarukkhamūle yamakapāṭihāriyasadisaṃ ahosi.

Then this thought arose in some deities: “Surely, Siddhattha must still have some duty to perform, for he does not relinquish his attachment to the throne.” The Teacher, knowing the thought of these deities, rose into the air to dispel their doubt and displayed the Twin Miracle. The miracle performed at the Great Bodhi Maṇḍala, the miracle performed at the gathering of his kinsmen, and the miracle performed at the gathering with Pāthikaputta—all were similar to the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree.

Evaṃ satthā iminā pāṭihāriyena devatānaṃ vitakkaṃ vūpasametvā pallaṅkato īsakaṃ pācīnanissite uttaradisābhāge ṭhatvā “imasmiṃ vata me pallaṅke sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭividdha”nti cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni kappasatasahassañca pūritānaṃ pāramīnaṃ phalādhigamaṭṭhānaṃ pallaṅkaṃ bodhirukkhañca animisehi akkhīhi olokayamāno sattāhaṃ vītināmesi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ animisacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Atha pallaṅkassa ca ṭhitaṭṭhānassa ca antarā caṅkamaṃ māpetvā puratthimapacchimato āyate ratanacaṅkame [P 1.0078] caṅkamanto sattāhaṃ vītināmesi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ ratanacaṅkamacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ.

Thus, having pacified the deities' doubt with this miracle, the Teacher stood in a spot slightly to the northeast of the throne. For seven days he gazed with unblinking eyes at the throne and the Bodhi tree—the place where the fruit of the perfections fulfilled over four incalculable aeons and a hundred thousand more was attained—reflecting: 'Indeed, on this throne the knowledge of omniscience was penetrated.' That place became known as the Unblinking Shrine. Then, having had a cloister created between the throne and the place where he had stood, he spent seven days walking upon the Jewel Cloister, which extended from east to west. That place became known as the Jewel Cloister Shrine.

Catutthe pana sattāhe bodhito pacchimuttaradisābhāge devatā ratanagharaṃ māpayiṃsu, tattha pallaṅkena [V 1.0087] nisīditvā abhidhammapiṭakaṃ visesato cettha anantanayaṃ samantapaṭṭhānaṃ vicinanto sattāhaṃ vītināmesi. Ābhidhammikā panāhu “ratanagharaṃ nāma na sattaratanamayaṃ gehaṃ, sattannaṃ pana pakaraṇānaṃ sammasitaṭṭhānaṃ ‘ratanaghara’nti vuccatī”ti. Yasmā panettha ubhopete pariyāyā yujjanti, tasmā ubhayampetaṃ gahetabbameva. Tato paṭṭhāya pana taṃ ṭhānaṃ ratanagharacetiyaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Evaṃ bodhisamīpeyeva cattāri sattāhāni vītināmetvā pañcame sattāhe bodhirukkhamūlā yena ajapālanigrodho tenupasaṅkami, tatrāpi dhammaṃ vicinantoyeva vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvedento nisīdi.

In the fourth week, deities created a jewel house in the northwestern direction from the Bodhi tree. There, seated cross-legged, he spent seven days contemplating the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and especially the Conditional Relations of infinite modes. The Abhidhamma scholars, however, say: “The ‘jewel house’ is not a house made of seven kinds of jewels, but the place where the seven treatises were thoroughly examined is called the ‘jewel house.’” Since both of these interpretations are fitting, both should be accepted. From that time onward, that place became known as the Jewel House Shrine. Having thus spent four weeks near the Bodhi tree, in the fifth week he went from the foot of the Bodhi tree to the Ajapāla Banyan Tree. There too he sat, contemplating the Dhamma and experiencing the bliss of liberation.

Tasmiṃ samaye māro devaputto “ettakaṃ kālaṃ anubandhanto otārāpekkhopi imassa na kiñci khalitaṃ addasaṃ, atikkantodāni esa mama vasa”nti domanassappatto mahāmagge nisīditvā soḷasa kāraṇāni cintento bhūmiyaṃ soḷasa lekhā kaḍḍhi – “ahaṃ eso viya dānapāramiṃ na pūresiṃ, tenamhi iminā sadiso na jāto”ti ekaṃ lekhaṃ kaḍḍhi. Tathā “ahaṃ eso viya sīlapāramiṃ, nekkhammapāramiṃ, paññāpāramiṃ, vīriyapāramiṃ, khantipāramiṃ, saccapāramiṃ, adhiṭṭhānapāramiṃ, mettāpāramiṃ, upekkhāpāramiṃ na pūresiṃ[M 1.0091], tenamhi iminā sadiso na jāto”ti dasamaṃ lekhaṃ kaḍḍhi. Tathā “ahaṃ eso viya asādhāraṇassa indriyaparopariyattañāṇassa paṭivedhāya upanissayabhūtā dasa pāramiyo na pūresiṃ, tenamhi iminā sadiso na jāto”ti ekādasamaṃ lekhaṃ kaḍḍhi. Tathā “ahaṃ eso viya asādhāraṇassa āsayānusayañāṇassa, mahākaruṇāsamāpattiñāṇassa, yamakapāṭihīrañāṇassa, anāvaraṇañāṇassa, sabbaññutaññāṇassa paṭivedhāya upanissayabhūtā dasa pāramiyo na pūresiṃ, tenamhi iminā sadiso na jāto”ti soḷasamaṃ lekhaṃ kaḍḍhi. Evaṃ imehi kāraṇehi mahāmagge soḷasa lekhā kaḍḍhamāno nisīdi.

At that time, Māra the devaputta, thinking, “For so long have I been following him, looking for an opportunity, yet I have seen no fault in him. Now he has gone beyond my control,” became distressed and sat down on the great road, pondering sixteen reasons. He drew sixteen lines on the ground: “I did not fulfill the perfection of giving as he did, therefore I am not like him,” and he drew one line. Similarly, “I did not fulfill the perfection of virtue, the perfection of renunciation, the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of energy, the perfection of patience, the perfection of truthfulness, the perfection of determination, the perfection of loving-kindness, or the perfection of equanimity, as he did, therefore I am not like him,” and he drew the tenth line. Likewise, “I did not fulfill the ten perfections, which serve as the basis for realizing the extraordinary knowledge of the maturity of others' faculties, therefore I am not like him,” and he drew the eleventh line. Similarly, “I did not fulfill the ten perfections, which serve as the basis for realizing the extraordinary knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies, the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion, the knowledge of the twin miracle, unobstructed knowledge, and omniscient knowledge, therefore I am not like him,” and he drew the sixteenth line. Thus, for these reasons, he sat on the great road, drawing sixteen lines.

Tasmiṃ samaye taṇhā, arati, ragāti tisso māradhītaro “pitā no na paññāyati, kahaṃ nu kho etarahī”ti olokayamānā taṃ domanassappattaṃ bhūmiṃ vilekhamānaṃ nisinnaṃ disvā pitu santikaṃ gantvā “kasmā, tāta, dukkhī dummano”ti pucchiṃsu. Ammā, ayaṃ mahāsamaṇo mayhaṃ vasaṃ atikkanto, ettakaṃ kālaṃ olokento otāramassa daṭṭhuṃ nāsakkhiṃ, tenāhaṃ dukkhī dummanoti. Yadi [P 1.0079] evaṃ mā cintayittha, mayametaṃ attano vase katvā ādāya āgamissāmāti. Na sakkā, ammā, eso kenaci vase kātuṃ, acalāya saddhāya patiṭṭhito eso purisoti. “Tāta mayaṃ itthiyo nāma idāneva naṃ rāgapāsādīhi bandhitvā ānessāma, tumhe mā cintayitthā”ti bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “pāde te samaṇa paricāremā”ti āhaṃsu. Bhagavā [V 1.0088] va tāsaṃ vacanaṃ manasi akāsi, na akkhīni ummīletvā olokesi, anuttare upadhisaṅkhaye vimuttamānaso vivekasukhaññeva anubhavanto nisīdi.

At that time, the three daughters of Māra—Taṇhā, Arati, and Rāga—were looking around, thinking, “Our father is not to be seen. Where could he be now?” Seeing him sitting on the ground, overcome with sorrow and scraping at the earth, they approached their father and asked, “Why, dear father, are you suffering and distressed?” “Dear daughters, this great ascetic has slipped from my control. Though I watched for so long, I could not find any opportunity against him. That is why I am suffering and distressed.” “If that is the case, do not worry. We will bring him under our control and take him away.” “It is impossible, dear daughters. No one can bring him under their control. This man is firmly established in unwavering faith.” “Father, we are women. Surely we can bind him with the snares of lust and bring him back. Do not worry.” They approached the Blessed One and said, “Ascetic, let us attend to your feet.” But the Blessed One paid no attention to their words. He did not open his eyes to look at them. With his mind liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the bases of existence, experiencing only the bliss of seclusion, he remained seated.

Puna māradhītaro “uccāvacā kho purisānaṃ adhippāyā, kesañci kumārikāsu pemaṃ hoti, kesañci paṭhamavaye ṭhitāsu, kesañci majjhimavaye ṭhitāsu, yaṃnūna mayaṃ nānappakārehi rūpehi palobheyyāmā”ti ekamekā kumārivaṇṇādivasena sataṃ sataṃ attabhāve abhinimminitvā kumāriyo, avijātā, sakiṃvijātā, duvijātā, majjhimitthiyo, mahitthiyo ca hutvā chakkhattuṃ bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “pāde te samaṇa paricāremā”ti āhaṃsu. Tampi bhagavā na manasākāsi, yathā taṃ anuttare upadhisaṅkhayeva vimutto. Keci panācariyā vadanti “tā mahitthibhāvena [M 1.0092] upagatā disvā bhagavā ‘evamevaṃ etā khaṇḍadantā palitakesā hontū’ti adhiṭṭhāsī”ti, taṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Na hi satthā evarūpaṃ adhiṭṭhānaṃ karoti. Bhagavā pana “apetha tumhe, kiṃ disvā evaṃ vāyamatha, evarūpaṃ nāma avītarāgādīnaṃ purato kātuṃ yuttaṃ, tathāgatassa pana rāgo pahīno, doso pahīno, moho pahīno”ti attano kilesappahānaṃ ārabbha –

Again, Māra’s daughters thought, “Men have various inclinations. Some feel affection for maidens, some for women in their early prime, some for women in their middle prime. Why don’t we tempt him with forms of various kinds?” So, each one created a hundred forms of herself—as maidens, as women who had not yet given birth, who had given birth once, or twice, as middle-aged women, and as elderly women—and approached the Blessed One six times, saying, “Let us serve at your feet, ascetic.” But the Blessed One paid no attention to them, as he was liberated in the unsurpassed destruction of the bases of existence. Some teachers say, “Seeing them approach in their elderly forms, the Blessed One resolved, ‘Let them become broken-toothed and gray-haired!’” This should not be accepted, for the Teacher does not make such resolutions. Instead, the Blessed One said, “Be gone! What have you seen that you strive thus? Such behavior is fitting only for those not free from lust and so on. But in the Tathāgata, lust is abandoned, hatred is abandoned, delusion is abandoned”—thus speaking with reference to his own abandonment of defilements.

“Yassa jitaṃ nāvajīyati, jitamassa noyāti koci loke;

Taṃ buddhamanantagocaraṃ, apadaṃ kena padena nessatha.

He whose victory cannot be undone, whose victory no one in the world can overtake—that Buddha, whose range is boundless, the trackless one, by what track will you lead him?

“Yassa jālinī visattikā, taṇhā natthi kuhiñci netave;

Taṃ buddhamanantagocaraṃ, apadaṃ kena padena nessathā”ti. (dha. pa. 179-180) –

He who has no craving, the ensnaring, the clinging, to lead him anywhere—that Buddha, whose range is boundless, the trackless one, by what track will you lead him?

Imā dhammapade buddhavagge dve gāthā vadanto dhammaṃ kathesi. Tā “saccaṃ kira no pitā avoca, arahaṃ sugato loke na rāgena suvānayo”tiādīni [P 1.0080] vatvā pitu santikaṃ agamaṃsu.

He taught the Dhamma by reciting these two verses from the Buddha Chapter of the Dhammapada. They, saying, "Truly, our father spoke thus: ‘The Arahant, the Sugata in the world, is not easily led by lust,’" and so forth, went to their father’s presence.

Bhagavāpi tattha sattāhaṃ vītināmetvā mucalindamūlaṃ agamāsi. Tattha sattāhavaddalikāya uppannāya sītādipaṭibāhanatthaṃ mucalindena nāgarājena sattakkhattuṃ bhogehi parikkhitto asambādhāya gandhakuṭiyaṃ viharanto viya vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvediyamāno sattāhaṃ vītināmetvā rājāyatanaṃ upasaṅkami, tatthāpi vimuttisukhaṃ paṭisaṃvediyamānoyeva nisīdi. Ettāvatā satta sattāhāni [V 1.0089] paripuṇṇāni. Etthantare neva mukhadhovanaṃ, na sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ, na āhārakiccaṃ ahosi, jhānasukhaphalasukheneva vītināmesi.

The Blessed One, having spent seven days there, went to the foot of the Mucalinda tree. There, when a great storm arose for seven days, the Nāga king Mucalinda encircled him seven times with his coils to ward off the cold and such. The Blessed One, experiencing the bliss of liberation as if dwelling in a perfumed chamber, unconstrained, spent seven days there and then approached the Rājāyatana tree. There too, while experiencing the bliss of liberation, he sat down. Thus, seven full weeks had passed. During this time, there was neither washing the face, nor tending the body, nor attending to meals; he passed the time solely with the bliss of jhāna and fruition.

Athassa tasmiṃ sattasattāhamatthake ekūnapaññāsatime divase tattha nisinnassa “mukhaṃ dhovissāmī”ti cittaṃ udapādi. Sakko devānamindo agadaharīṭakaṃ āharitvā adāsi, satthā taṃ paribhuñji, tenassa sarīravaḷañjaṃ ahosi. Athassa sakkoyeva nāgalatādantakaṭṭhañceva mukhadhovanaudakañca [M 1.0093] adāsi. Satthā taṃ dantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā anotattadahodakena mukhaṃ dhovitvā tattheva rājāyatanamūle nisīdi.

Then, at the end of those seven weeks, on the forty-ninth day, as he sat there, the thought arose in him, "I shall wash my face." Sakka, the king of the gods, brought a medicinal myrobalan fruit and offered it. The Teacher consumed it, and it resulted in a cleansing of his body. Then Sakka himself offered a tooth-cleaning stick made of naga creeper wood and water for washing the face. The Teacher chewed the tooth stick, washed his face with water from Lake Anotatta, and sat right there at the foot of the Rājāyatana tree.

Tasmiṃ samaye tapussabhallikā nāma dve vāṇijā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi ukkalājanapadā majjhimadesaṃ gacchantā attano ñātisālohitāya devatāya sakaṭāni sannirumbhitvā satthu āhārasampādane ussāhitā manthañca madhupiṇḍikañca ādāya “paṭiggaṇhātu no, bhante, bhagavā imaṃ āhāraṃ anukampaṃ upādāyā”ti satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Bhagavā pāyāsapaṭiggahaṇadivaseyeva pattassa antarahitattā “na kho tathāgatā hatthesu paṭiggaṇhanti, kimhi nu kho ahaṃ paṭiggaṇheyya”nti cintesi. Athassa cittaṃ ñatvā catūhi disāhi cattāro mahārājāno indanīlamaṇimaye patte upanāmesuṃ, bhagavā te paṭikkhipi. Puna muggavaṇṇaselamaye cattāro patte upanāmesuṃ. Bhagavā catunnampi devaputtānaṃ anukampāya cattāropi patte paṭiggahetvā uparūpari ṭhapetvā “eko hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi, cattāropi mukhavaṭṭiyaṃ paññāyamānalekhā hutvā majjhimena pamāṇena ekattaṃ upagamiṃsu. Bhagavā tasmiṃ paccagghe selamaye patte āhāraṃ paṭiggaṇhitvā paribhuñjitvā anumodanaṃ akāsi. Dve bhātaro vāṇijā buddhañca dhammañca saraṇaṃ gantvā [P 1.0081] dvevācikā upāsakā ahesuṃ. Atha nesaṃ “ekaṃ no, bhante, paricaritabbaṭṭhānaṃ dethā”ti vadantānaṃ dakkhiṇahatthena attano sīsaṃ parāmasitvā kesadhātuyo adāsi. Te attano nagare tā dhātuyo suvaṇṇasamuggassa anto pakkhipitvā cetiyaṃ patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

At that time, two merchants named Tapussa and Bhallika, traveling with five hundred carts from the Ukkala country to the Middle Country, had their carts brought to a standstill by a deity who was their kinsman. Prompted to provide food for the Teacher, they took parched grain meal and honey cakes and approached the Teacher, saying, "Venerable sir, may the Blessed One accept this food out of compassion for us," and stood before him. As his bowl had disappeared on the very day he accepted the milk-rice, the Blessed One thought, "Tathāgatas do not receive food in their hands. In what, then, should I receive it?" Knowing his thought, the Four Great Kings from the four directions brought bowls made of sapphire. The Blessed One declined them. Then they brought four bowls made of stone the color of mung beans. Out of compassion for the four divine youths, the Blessed One accepted all four bowls, placed them one above the other, and resolved, "Let them become one." The four bowls merged into one of moderate size, with lines remaining visible where the rims met. The Blessed One received the food in that new stone bowl, partook of it, and gave his blessing. The two merchant brothers took refuge in the Buddha and the Dhamma, becoming lay followers with the twofold declaration. Then, when they said, "Venerable sir, please give us something to venerate," the Blessed One stroked his head with his right hand and gave them hair relics. They enshrined those relics in a golden casket in their own city and established a cetiya.

Sammāsambuddhopi kho tato uṭṭhāya puna ajapālanigrodhameva gantvā nigrodhamūle nisīdi. Athassa tattha nisinnamattasseva attanā adhigatassa dhammassa gambhīrataṃ paccavekkhantassa sabbabuddhānaṃ āciṇṇo “adhigato kho myāyaṃ dhammo”ti paresaṃ dhammaṃ adesetukamyatākārapavatto vitakko udapādi. Atha brahmā sahampati “nassati vata bho loko, vinassati vata bho loko”ti dasahi cakkavāḷasahassehi sakkasuyāmasantusitasunimmitavasavattimahābrahmāno [V 1.0090] ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā “desetu, bhante, bhagavā dhamma”ntiādinā nayena dhammadesanaṃ āyāci.

The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, rising from there, went again to the Goatherd's Banyan Tree and sat down at its foot. Then, as soon as he was seated, while reflecting on the profundity of the Dhamma he had realized, a thought arose in him, a train of thought that is the custom of all Buddhas, proceeding in the manner of a disinclination to teach the Dhamma to others: "This Dhamma has been realized by me." Then Brahmā Sahampati, thinking, "Alas, the world is being destroyed! Alas, the world is perishing!" taking with him Sakka, Suyāma, Santusita, Sunimmita, Vasavatti, and the great Brahmās from ten thousand world-systems, approached the Teacher. He requested the teaching of the Dhamma in the manner beginning with, "Venerable sir, let the Blessed One teach the Dhamma."

Satthā [M 1.0094] tassa paṭiññaṃ datvā “kassa nu kho ahaṃ paṭhamaṃ dhammaṃ deseyya”nti cintento “āḷāro paṇḍito, so imaṃ dhammaṃ khippaṃ ājānissatī”ti cittaṃ uppādetvā puna olokento tassa sattāhakālakatabhāvaṃ ñatvā udakaṃ āvajjesi. Tassāpi abhidosakālakatabhāvaṃ ñatvā “bahūpakārā kho me pañcavaggiyā bhikkhū”ti pañcavaggiye ārabbha manasikāraṃ katvā “kahaṃ nu kho te etarahi viharantī”ti āvajjento “bārāṇasiyaṃ isipatane migadāye”ti ñatvā “tattha gantvā dhammacakkaṃ pavattessāmī”ti katipāhaṃ bodhimaṇḍasāmantāyeva piṇḍāya caranto viharitvā āsāḷhipuṇṇamāsiyaṃ “bārāṇasiṃ gamissāmī”ti cātuddasiyaṃ paccūsasamaye vibhātāya rattiyā kālasseva pattacīvaramādāya aṭṭhārasayojanamaggaṃ paṭipanno antarāmagge upakaṃ nāma ājīvakaṃ disvā tassa attano buddhabhāvaṃ ācikkhitvā taṃ divasaṃyeva sāyanhasamaye isipatanaṃ agamāsi.

The Teacher, having given his consent, thought, "To whom should I first teach the Dhamma?" The thought arose, "Āḷāra is wise; he will quickly understand this Dhamma." But upon further reflection, knowing that Āḷāra had passed away seven days earlier, he turned his attention to Uddaka. Knowing that he too had passed away the previous night, he thought, "The five monks were very helpful to me." Focusing his mind on the group of five, he considered, "Where are they staying now?" He knew they were at Isipatana in the Deer Park near Bārāṇasī. "I will go there and set the Wheel of Dhamma in motion," he resolved. For a few days, he stayed there, wandering for alms in the vicinity of the Bodhi tree. Then, intending to go to Bārāṇasī for the Āsāḷhī full moon, he took his bowl and robe early at dawn on the fourteenth day, as the night brightened, and set out on the eighteen-yojana journey. Along the way, he saw an Ājīvaka ascetic named Upaka. After declaring his Buddhahood to him, he reached Isipatana by evening of that same day.

Pañcavaggiyā therā tathāgataṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā “ayaṃ āvuso samaṇo gotamo paccayabāhullāya āvattitvā paripuṇṇakāyo pīṇindriyo suvaṇṇavaṇṇo hutvā āgacchati, imassa abhivādanādīni na karissāma, mahākulapasuto kho panesa āsanābhihāraṃ arahati, tenassa āsanamattaṃ paññāpessāmā”ti katikaṃ akaṃsu. Bhagavā sadevakassa lokassa cittācāraṃ jānanasamatthena ñāṇena “kiṃ nu kho ime cintayiṃsū”ti āvajjetvā cittaṃ aññāsi. Atha ne sabbadevamanussesu anodissakavasena pharaṇasamatthaṃ [P 1.0082] mettacittaṃ saṅkhipitvā odissakavasena mettacittena phari. Te bhagavatā mettacittena phuṭṭhā tathāgate upasaṅkamante sakāya katikāya saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontā abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānādīni sabbakiccāni akaṃsu, sammāsambuddhabhāvaṃ panassa ajānamānā kevalaṃ nāmena ca āvusovādena ca samudācaranti.

The five elders, seeing the Tathāgata approaching from afar, made an agreement among themselves: "Friends, this ascetic Gotama, having reverted to a life of abundance, comes with a well-fed body, plump faculties, and a golden complexion. We shall not perform acts of respect such as greeting him. Yet, being born into a great family, he deserves the offering of a seat. Therefore, we shall prepare just a seat for him." The Blessed One, with his knowledge capable of knowing the mental dispositions of the world with its gods, reflected, "What are they thinking?" and knew their thoughts. Then, concentrating his loving-kindness, which was capable of pervading all gods and humans without specific direction, he pervaded them with loving-kindness with specific direction. Touched by the Blessed One's loving-kindness, they were unable to maintain their agreement as the Tathāgata approached. Instead, they performed all duties of respect, such as greeting and rising. However, unaware of his state of perfect self-enlightenment, they addressed him merely by name and with the term 'friend.'

Atha ne bhagavā “mā vo, bhikkhave, tathāgataṃ nāmena ca āvusovādena ca samudācaratha, arahaṃ, bhikkhave, tathāgato sammāsambuddho”ti attano buddhabhāvaṃ saññāpetvā paññatte varabuddhāsane nisinno uttarāsāḷhanakkhattayoge vattamāne aṭṭhārasahi brahmakoṭīhi parivuto pañcavaggiye [M 1.0095] there āmantetvā dhammacakkappavattanasuttantaṃ desesi. Tesu aññāsikoṇḍaññatthero desanānusārena ñāṇaṃ pesento suttapariyosāne aṭṭhārasahi brahmakoṭīhi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Satthā tattheva vassaṃ upagantvā punadivase vappattheraṃ ovadanto vihāreyeva [V 1.0091] nisīdi, sesā cattāro piṇḍāya cariṃsu. Vappatthero pubbaṇheyeva sotāpattiphalaṃ pāpuṇi. Eteneva upāyena punadivase bhaddiyattheraṃ, punadivase mahānāmattheraṃ, punadivase assajittheranti sabbe sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpetvā pañcamiyaṃ pakkhassa pañcapi jane sannipātetvā anattalakkhaṇasuttantaṃ (saṃ. ni. 3.59; mahāva. 20 ādayo) desesi. Desanāpariyosāne pañcapi therā arahattaphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Atha satthā yasakulaputtassa upanissayaṃ disvā taṃ rattibhāge nibbijjitvā gehaṃ pahāya nikkhantaṃ “ehi yasā”ti pakkositvā tasmiṃyeva rattibhāge sotāpattiphale, punadivase arahatte patiṭṭhāpetvā, aparepi tassa sahāyake catupaṇṇāsa jane ehibhikkhupabbajjāya pabbājetvā arahattaṃ pāpesi.

Then the Blessed One said to them: "Bhikkhus, do not address the Tathāgata by name or with the term 'friend'. The Tathāgata, bhikkhus, is an Arahant, a Perfectly Self-Enlightened One." Having made known his own Buddhahood, he sat on the prepared excellent Buddha-seat while the constellation Uttarāsāḷha was in conjunction, surrounded by eighteen crores of Brahmās, and addressed the group of five bhikkhus, delivering the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Among them, the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña, directing his knowledge in accordance with the discourse, was established in the fruit of stream-entry along with eighteen crores of Brahmās at the conclusion of the sutta. The Teacher entered the rains retreat right there. The next day, while instructing the Elder Vappa, he remained seated in the monastery itself, while the other four went for almsfood. The Elder Vappa attained the fruit of stream-entry in the forenoon. In the same manner, on the next day the Elder Bhaddiya, on the day after that the Elder Mahānāma, and on the day after that the Elder Assaji—all were established in the fruit of stream-entry. Then, on the fifth day of the lunar fortnight, gathering all five, he taught the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta. At the conclusion of the discourse, all five Elders were established in the fruit of arahantship. Then the Teacher, seeing the underlying potential of the clansman Yasa, who, having become disenchanted during the night, had abandoned his home and gone forth, called out to him, “Come, Yasa!” and established him in the fruit of stream-entry that very night, and in arahantship on the next day. Later, he also ordained fifty-four of his companions with the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination, and led them to arahantship.

Evaṃ loke ekasaṭṭhiyā arahantesu jātesu satthā vutthavasso pavāretvā “caratha, bhikkhave, cārika”nti saṭṭhi bhikkhū disāsu pesetvā sayaṃ uruvelaṃ gacchanto antarāmagge kappāsikavanasaṇḍe tiṃsa jane bhaddavaggiyakumāre vinesi. Tesu sabbapacchimako sotāpanno, sabbuttamo anāgāmī ahosi. Tepi sabbe ehibhikkhubhāveneva pabbājetvā disāsu pesetvā uruvelaṃ gantvā aḍḍhuḍḍhāni pāṭihāriyasahassāni dassetvā uruvelakassapādayo sahassajaṭilaparivāre tebhātikajaṭile vinetvā ehibhikkhubhāveneva pabbājetvā gayāsīse nisīdāpetvā ādittapariyāyadesanāya (mahāva. 54) arahatte patiṭṭhāpetvā tena arahantasahassena parivuto “bimbisārarañño dinnaṃ paṭiññaṃ [P 1.0083] mocessāmī”ti rājagahaṃ gantvā nagarūpacāre laṭṭhivanuyyānaṃ agamāsi. Rājā uyyānapālassa santikā “satthā āgato”ti sutvā dvādasanahutehi brāhmaṇagahapatikehi parivuto satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā [M 1.0096] cakkavicittatalesu suvaṇṇapaṭṭavitānaṃ viya pabhāsamudayaṃ vissajjantesu tathāgatassa pādesu sirasā nipatitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi saddhiṃ parisāya.

Thus, when sixty-one Arahants had arisen in the world, the Teacher, having completed the rains retreat and held the Pavāraṇā ceremony, sent sixty bhikkhus into the regions with the words, "Wander forth, bhikkhus, on tour." He himself went to Uruvelā. Along the way, in the Kappāsika forest grove, he tamed the thirty Bhaddavaggiya young men. Among them, the last of them became a stream-enterer, and the foremost became a non-returner. Having ordained them all with the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination, he sent them into the regions. Then, proceeding to Uruvelā, he displayed one and a half thousand feats of psychic power and tamed Uruvela Kassapa and his two brothers, the matted-hair ascetics, along with their thousand followers. Ordaining them too with the 'Come, bhikkhu' ordination, he seated them at Gayāsīsa and, through the discourse on the Fire Sermon, established them in arahantship. Surrounded by that thousand Arahants, he thought, "I shall fulfill the promise given to King Bimbisāra," and went to Rājagaha. He went to the Laṭṭhivana pleasure grove in the vicinity of the city. The king, hearing from the park keeper that "the Teacher has arrived," approached the Teacher accompanied by twelve myriads of brahmins and householders. Prostrating with his head at the feet of the Tathāgata, which were adorned with chakra-marks on their soles and emitted a mass of radiance like a canopy of golden cloth, the king sat down to one side along with his assembly.

Atha kho tesaṃ brāhmaṇagahapatikānaṃ etadahosi “kiṃ nu kho mahāsamaṇo uruvelakassape brahmacariyaṃ carati, udāhu uruvelakassapo mahāsamaṇe”ti. Bhagavā tesaṃ cetasā cetoparivitakkamaññāya theraṃ gāthāya ajjhabhāsi –

Then this thought occurred to those brahmins and householders: "Does the Great Ascetic lead the holy life under Uruvela Kassapa, or does Uruvela Kassapa lead the holy life under the Great Ascetic?" The Blessed One, knowing their mental reflection with his mind, addressed the Elder in verse:

“Kimeva disvā uruvelavāsi, pahāsi aggiṃ kisako vadāno;

Pucchāmi taṃ kassapa etamatthaṃ, kathaṃ pahīnaṃ tava aggihutta”nti. (mahāva. 55);

"What did you see, O dweller of Uruvelā, that you abandoned the fire, you who were once emaciated, saying thus? I ask you, Kassapa, about this matter: how was your fire sacrifice abandoned?"

Theropi [V 1.0092] bhagavato adhippāyaṃ viditvā –

The Elder, too, having understood the Blessed One's intention, replied:

“Rūpe ca sadde ca atho rase ca, kāmitthiyo cābhivadanti yaññā;

Etaṃ malanti upadhīsu ñatvā, tasmā na yiṭṭhe na hute arañji”nti. (mahāva. 55) –

"Sacrifices praise forms and sounds, and also tastes, and women as objects of desire; knowing this to be a stain in the substrata of existence, therefore I delighted not in oblations or sacrifices."

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā attano sāvakabhāvapakāsanatthaṃ tathāgatassa pādapiṭṭhe sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā “satthā me, bhante, bhagavā, sāvakohamasmī”ti vatvā ekatālaṃ dvitālaṃ titālanti yāva sattatālappamāṇaṃ sattakkhattuṃ vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā oruyha tathāgataṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Taṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvā mahājano “aho mahānubhāvā buddhā, evaṃ thāmagatadiṭṭhiko nāma ‘arahā’ti maññamāno uruvelakassapopi diṭṭhijālaṃ bhinditvā tathāgatena damito”ti satthu guṇakathaṃyeva kathesi. Bhagavā “nāhaṃ idāniyeva uruvelakassapaṃ damemi, atītepi esa mayā damitoyevā”ti vatvā imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā mahānāradakassapajātakaṃ (jā. 2.22.545 ādayo) kathetvā cattāri saccāni pakāsesi. Magadharājā ekādasahi nahutehi saddhiṃ sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi, ekaṃ nahutaṃ upāsakattaṃ paṭivedesi. Rājā [P 1.0084] satthu santike nisinnoyeva pañca assāsake pavedetvā [M 1.0097] saraṇaṃ gantvā svātanāya nimantetvā āsanā vuṭṭhāya bhagavantaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

Having spoken this verse, to proclaim his discipleship, he placed his head upon the Tathāgata's feet and said, "Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my Teacher; I am his disciple." Then, rising into the air one palm-span, two palm-spans, three palm-spans, up to seven palm-spans, seven times he ascended into the sky and descended, paid homage to the Tathāgata, and sat down to one side. Seeing this miracle, the great crowd exclaimed, "Ah, the Buddhas are indeed of great power! Even Uruvela Kassapa, who was so firm in his views and thought himself an Arahant, has been tamed by the Tathāgata, having broken through the net of his wrong views." They spoke only in praise of the Teacher's virtues. The Blessed One said, "It is not only now that I have tamed Uruvela Kassapa; in the past, too, he was tamed by me." Then, with reference to this occasion, he narrated the Mahānāradakassapa Jātaka and expounded the Four Noble Truths. The king of Magadha, along with eleven myriads, was established in the fruit of stream-entry, and one myriad declared themselves lay followers. The king, while still seated in the Teacher's presence, declared that his five aspirations had been fulfilled, took refuge, and invited the Blessed One for the next day's meal. Then, rising from his seat, he circumambulated the Blessed One and departed.

Punadivase yehi ca bhagavā diṭṭho, yehi ca adiṭṭho, sabbepi rājagahavāsino aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhā manussā tathāgataṃ daṭṭhukāmā pātova rājagahato laṭṭhivanuyyānaṃ agamaṃsu. Tigāvuto maggo nappahosi, sakalalaṭṭhivanuyyānaṃ nirantaraṃ phuṭaṃ ahosi. Mahājano dasabalassa rūpasobhaggappattaṃ attabhāvaṃ passanto tittiṃ kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Vaṇṇabhūmi nāmesā. Evarūpesu hi ṭhānesu tathāgatassa lakkhaṇānubyañjanādippabhedā sabbāpi rūpakāyasirī vaṇṇetabbā. Evaṃ rūpasobhaggappattaṃ dasabalassa sarīraṃ passamānena mahājanena nirantaraṃ phuṭe uyyāne ca magge ca ekabhikkhussapi nikkhamanokāso nāhosi. Taṃ divasaṃ kira bhagavā chinnabhatto bhaveyya, taṃ mā ahosīti sakkassa nisinnāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So āvajjamāno taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā māṇavakavaṇṇaṃ abhinimminitvā buddhadhammasaṅghapaṭisaṃyuttā thutiyo vadamāno dasabalassa purato otaritvā devatānubhāvena okāsaṃ katvā –

On the following day, all the residents of Rājagaha—eighteen crores of people in number, both those who had seen the Blessed One and those who had not—desiring to see the Tathāgata, went early in the morning from Rājagaha to the Laṭṭhivana garden. The three-gāvuta road was not sufficient, and the entire Laṭṭhivana garden was filled without a gap. The great crowd, seeing the person of the Dasabala, which had attained such beauty and splendor, could not be satisfied. This is called the 'ground for description,' for in such places, all the glory of the Tathāgata’s physical body, distinguished by the major and minor marks and so forth, should be described. As the great crowd beheld the Dasabala’s body, radiant with beauty, the garden and the road were so densely packed that there was no room for even a single bhikkhu to leave. It is said that on that day the Blessed One might have gone without food. So that this would not happen, Sakka's seat showed a sign of heat. He, reflecting and knowing the reason, created the form of a young man and, uttering praises connected with the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, descended before the Dasabala and, by the power of the devas, made space.

“Danto dantehi saha purāṇajaṭilehi, vippamutto vippamuttehi;

Siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo, rājagahaṃ pāvisi bhagavā.

Tamed, together with the tamed ancient matted-hair ascetics; liberated, with the liberated; of the color of refined gold, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.

“Mutto [V 1.0093] muttehi saha purāṇajaṭilehi, vippamutto vippamuttehi;

Siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo, rājagahaṃ pāvisi bhagavā.

Freed, together with the freed ancient matted-hair ascetics; liberated, with the liberated; of the color of refined gold, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.

“Tiṇṇo tiṇṇehi saha purāṇajaṭilehi, vippamutto vippamuttehi;

Siṅgīnikkhasavaṇṇo, rājagahaṃ pāvisi bhagavā.

Crossed over, together with those who have crossed over, the ancient matted-hair ascetics; liberated, with the liberated; of the color of refined gold, the Blessed One entered Rājagaha.

“Dasavāso [M 1.0098] dasabalo, dasadhammavidū dasabhi cupeto;

So dasasataparivāro, rājagahaṃ pāvisi bhagavā”ti. (mahāva. 58) –

Master of ten, possessing ten powers, knowing the ten qualities, and endowed with ten [qualities]; He, surrounded by a thousand, the Blessed One, entered Rājagaha.

Imāhi gāthāhi satthu vaṇṇaṃ vadamāno purato pāyāsi. Tadā mahājano māṇavakassa rūpasiriṃ disvā “ativiya abhirūpo ayaṃ māṇavako, na kho pana amhehi diṭṭhapubbo”ti cintetvā “kuto ayaṃ māṇavako, kassa vāya”nti āha. Taṃ sutvā māṇavo –

With these verses, praising the Teacher's virtues, he proceeded ahead. Then, seeing the young man's beautiful appearance, the crowd thought, "This young man is exceedingly handsome, and we have never seen him before." Thinking thus, they said, "Where does this young man come from, and whose is he?" Hearing that, the young man—

“Yo dhīro sabbadhi danto, suddho appaṭipuggalo;

Arahaṃ sugato loke, tassāhaṃ paricārako”ti. (mahāva. 58) – gāthamāha;

"The wise one, tamed in every way, pure, without peer; the Arahant, the Sugata in the world—I am his attendant."—thus he spoke the verse.

Satthā sakkena katokāsaṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā bhikkhusahassaparivuto [P 1.0085] rājagahaṃ pāvisi. Rājā buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā “ahaṃ, bhante, tīṇi ratanāni vinā vattituṃ na sakkhissāmi, velāya vā avelāya vā bhagavato santikaṃ āgamissāmi, laṭṭhivanuyyānaṃ nāma atidūre, idaṃ pana amhākaṃ veḷuvanaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ nātidūre nāccāsanne gamanāgamanasampannaṃ buddhārahaṃ senāsanaṃ. Idaṃ me bhagavā paṭiggaṇhātū”ti suvaṇṇabhiṅkārena pupphagandhavāsitaṃ maṇivaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ ādāya veḷuvanuyyānaṃ pariccajanto dasabalassa hatthe udakaṃ pātesi. Tasmiṃ ārāmapaṭiggahaṇe “buddhasāsanassa mūlāni otiṇṇānī”ti mahāpathavī kampi. Jambudīpasmiñhi ṭhapetvā veḷuvanaṃ aññaṃ mahāpathaviṃ kampetvā gahitasenāsanaṃ nāma natthi. Tambapaṇṇidīpepi ṭhapetvā mahāvihāraṃ aññaṃ pathaviṃ kampetvā gahitasenāsanaṃ nāma natthi. Satthā veḷuvanārāmaṃ paṭiggahetvā rañño anumodanaṃ katvā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto veḷuvanaṃ agamāsi.

The Teacher, taking the path for which space was made by Sakka, entered Rājagaha surrounded by a thousand bhikkhus. The king, after offering a great alms to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha, said, "Venerable sir, I cannot live without the Three Jewels. Whether it is the proper time or not, I will come to the presence of the Blessed One. The Laṭṭhivana garden is too far, but this Veḷuvana garden of ours is not too far nor too near, suitable for coming and going, a dwelling worthy of the Buddha. May the Blessed One accept this from me." Taking water scented with the fragrance of flowers in a golden vessel, he poured the jewel-colored water into the hands of the Ten-Powered One, relinquishing the Veḷuvana garden. At the acceptance of that park, the great earth trembled, as if to say, "The roots of the Buddha's Dispensation have been established." For in Jambudīpa, except for Veḷuvana, there is no other dwelling accepted with the trembling of the great earth. Similarly, in Tambapaṇṇidīpa, except for the Mahāvihāra, there is no other dwelling accepted with the trembling of the earth. The Teacher, having accepted the Veḷuvana park, expressed his appreciation to the king, rose from his seat, and went to Veḷuvana surrounded by the community of bhikkhus.

Tasmiṃ kho pana samaye sāriputto ca moggallāno cāti dve paribbājakā rājagahaṃ upanissāya viharanti amataṃ pariyesamānā. Tesu sāriputto assajittheraṃ piṇḍāya paviṭṭhaṃ disvā [V 1.0094] pasannacitto payirupāsitvā [M 1.0099] “ye dhammā hetuppabhavā”ti gāthaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya attano sahāyakassa moggallānaparibbājakassapi tameva gāthaṃ abhāsi. Sopi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Te ubhopi janā sañcayaṃ oloketvā attano parisāya saddhiṃ bhagavato santike pabbajiṃsu. Tesu mahāmoggallāno sattāhena arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, sāriputtatthero aḍḍhamāsena. Ubhopi ca ne satthā aggasāvakaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sāriputtattherena arahattappattadivaseyeva sāvakasannipātaṃ akāsi.

At that time, the two wanderers Sāriputta and Moggallāna were staying near Rājagaha, seeking the Deathless. Sāriputta saw the elder Assaji entering for alms and, with a pleased mind, approached him. Upon hearing the verse beginning, "Of things that arise from a cause...," he became established in the fruit of stream-entry. He then recited the same verse to his companion, the wanderer Moggallāna, who also became established in the fruit of stream-entry. Both of them, after speaking with Sañcaya, went forth with their following in the presence of the Blessed One. Among them, Mahāmoggallāna attained arahantship in seven days, while the elder Sāriputta did so in half a month. The Teacher placed both of them in the position of chief disciples. On the very day the elder Sāriputta attained arahantship, the Teacher held the assembly of disciples.

Tathāgate pana tasmiṃyeva veḷuvanuyyāne viharante suddhodanamahārājā “putto kira me chabbassāni dukkarakārikaṃ caritvā paramābhisambodhiṃ patvā pavattavaradhammacakko rājagahaṃ upanissāya veḷuvane viharatī”ti sutvā aññataraṃ amaccaṃ āmantesi “ehi, bhaṇe, purisasahassaparivāro rājagahaṃ gantvā mama vacanena ‘pitā vo suddhodanamahārājā daṭṭhukāmo’ti vatvā puttaṃ me gaṇhitvā ehī”ti āha. So “evaṃ, devā”ti rañño vacanaṃ sirasā sampaṭicchitvā purisasahassaparivāro khippameva saṭṭhiyojanamaggaṃ gantvā dasabalassa catuparisamajjhe nisīditvā dhammadesanāvelāya vihāraṃ pāvisi. So “tiṭṭhatu tāva rañño pahitasāsana”nti pariyante ṭhito satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā yathāṭhitova saddhiṃ purisasahassena [P 1.0086] arahattaṃ patvā pabbajjaṃ yāci. Bhagavā “etha bhikkhavo”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi, sabbe taṅkhaṇaṃyeva iddhimayapattacīvaradharā saṭṭhivassattherā viya ahesuṃ. Arahattaṃ pattakālato paṭṭhāya pana ariyā nāma majjhattāva hontīti so raññā pahitasāsanaṃ dasabalassa na kathesi. Rājā “neva gato āgacchati, na sāsanaṃ suyyatī”ti “ehi, bhaṇe, tvaṃ gacchāhī”ti teneva niyāmena aññaṃ amaccaṃ pesesi. Sopi gantvā purimanayeneva saddhiṃ parisāya arahattaṃ patvā tuṇhī ahosi. Rājā eteneva niyāmena purisasahassaparivāre nava amacce pesesi, sabbe attano kiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā tuṇhībhūtā tattheva vihariṃsu.

Meanwhile, while the Tathāgata was dwelling in that very Bamboo Grove, King Suddhodana heard, “My son, it is said, after practicing severe austerities for six years, attained supreme enlightenment and, having set in motion the excellent Wheel of the Dhamma, is now dwelling near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove.” He then addressed a certain minister, saying, “Go, my good man, taking a retinue of a thousand men to Rājagaha and, with my word, say, ‘Your father, King Suddhodana, wishes to see you,’ and bring my son back here.” The minister replied, “Yes, Your Majesty,” accepted the king’s command with bowed head, and swiftly traveled the sixty-league journey with his retinue of a thousand men. He entered the monastery at the time of the Ten-Powered One's Dhamma discourse, while the Buddha was seated in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Thinking, “Let the king’s message wait for now,” he stood at the edge, listened to the Teacher’s discourse and, just as he stood, together with the thousand men, attained arahantship and requested the going forth. The Blessed One stretched out his hand and said, “Come, monks.” Instantly, they all became like elders of sixty years, wearing robes and carrying bowls created by psychic power. Now, from the moment they attain arahantship, noble ones are impartial, and so he did not convey the king’s message to the Ten-Powered One. The king thought, “The one who went does not return, nor is any message heard.” So he sent another minister in the same manner. He too went and, in the same way as the first, attained arahantship with his retinue and remained silent. In this manner, the king sent nine ministers, each with a retinue of a thousand men; all of them, having accomplished their own purpose, became silent and dwelt right there.

Rājā [M 1.0100] sāsanamattampi āharitvā ācikkhantaṃ alabhitvā cintesi “ettakā janā mayi sinehābhāvena sāsanamattampi na paccāhariṃsu, ko nu kho mama vacanaṃ karissatī”ti sabbaṃ rājabalaṃ olokento kāḷudāyiṃ addasa. So kira rañño sabbatthasādhako amacco abbhantariko ativissāsiko bodhisattena saddhiṃ ekadivase jāto sahapaṃsukīḷako sahāyo. Atha naṃ rājā āmantesi “tāta, kāḷudāyi ahaṃ mama puttaṃ passitukāmo nava purisasahassāni pesesiṃ, ekapurisopi āgantvā sāsanamattaṃ ārocentopi natthi, dujjāno kho pana jīvitantarāyo, ahaṃ jīvamānova puttaṃ daṭṭhuṃ icchāmi, sakkhissasi nu kho me puttaṃ [V 1.0095] dassetu”nti. Sakkhissāmi, deva, sace pabbajituṃ labhissāmīti. Tāta, tvaṃ pabbajitvā vā apabbajitvā vā mayhaṃ puttaṃ dassehīti. So “sādhu, devā”ti rañño sāsanaṃ ādāya rājagahaṃ gantvā satthu dhammadesanāvelāya parisapariyante ṭhito dhammaṃ sutvā saparivāro arahattaphalaṃ patvā ehibhikkhubhāve patiṭṭhāsi.

The king, not finding anyone to bring back and deliver even a mere message, thought: “So many people, due to a lack of affection for me, did not bring back even a message. Who then will do my bidding?” Surveying the entire royal force, he saw Kāḷudāyī. He was, it seems, the king’s minister, successful in all affairs, an intimate, and highly trusted, born on the same day as the Bodhisatta, a friend with whom he had played in the dust. Then the king addressed him: “My dear Kāḷudāyī, wishing to see my son, I sent nine thousand men, but not a single person has returned to deliver even a message. An obstacle to life is indeed hard to know, and I wish to see my son while I am still living. Will you be able to show me my son?” “I will be able, Your Majesty, if I am allowed to go forth.” “My dear, whether you go forth or not, you must show me my son.” “Very well, Your Majesty,” he said. Taking the king’s message, he went to Rājagaha. Standing at the edge of the assembly during the Teacher's Dhamma discourse, he heard the Dhamma and, together with his retinue, attained the fruit of arahantship and was established in the state of a monk through the invitation, “Come, monk.”

Satthā buddho hutvā paṭhamaṃ antovassaṃ isipatane vasitvā vutthavasso pavāretvā uruvelaṃ gantvā tattha tayo māse vasanto tebhātikajaṭile vinetvā bhikkhusahassaparivāro phussamāsapuṇṇamāyaṃ rājagahaṃ gantvā dve māse vasi. Ettāvatā bārāṇasito nikkhantassa pañca māsā jātā, sakalo hemanto atikkanto. Kāḷudāyittherassa āgatadivasato sattaṭṭha divasā vītivattā, so phagguṇīpuṇṇamāsiyaṃ cintesi “atikkanto hemanto, vasantasamayo anuppatto, manussehi sassādīni uddharitvā sammukhasammukhaṭṭhānehi maggā dinnā, haritatiṇasañchannā pathavī, supupphitā vanasaṇḍā, paṭipajjanakkhamā maggā, kālo dasabalassa ñātisaṅgahaṃ kātu”nti. Atha bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā –

The Teacher, having become the Buddha, spent the first rains retreat in Isipatana. Having completed the rains retreat and performed the pavāraṇā ceremony, he went to Uruvelā. Staying there for three months, he disciplined the three matted-hair ascetic brothers and, with a retinue of a thousand monks, on the full moon day of the month of Phussa, he went to Rājagaha and stayed for two months. By then, five months had passed since his departure from Bārāṇasī, and the entire winter season had passed. Seven or eight days had passed since the arrival of the Elder Kāḷudāyī. On the full moon day of Phagguṇa, he thought: “The winter has passed, the spring season has arrived. The crops have been harvested by the people, and the paths are clear from place to place. The earth is covered with green grass, the forest groves are in full bloom, the roads are fit for travel. It is time for the Ten-Powered One to attend to his kinsmen.” Then he approached the Blessed One.

“Aṅgārino [P 1.0087] dāni dumā bhadante, phalesino chadanaṃ vippahāya;

Te accimantova pabhāsayanti, samayo mahāvīra aṅgīrasānaṃ…pe….

“Venerable sir, the trees are now like embers; seeking fruit, they have shed their foliage. They shine as if with flames. It is time, O great hero, for the Aṅgīrasas…

“Nātisītaṃ [M 1.0101] nātiuṇhaṃ, nātidubbhikkhachātakaṃ;

Saddalā haritā bhūmi, esa kālo mahāmunī”ti. –

“It is not too cold, not too hot, not a time of famine or hunger; the ground is grassy and green, this is the time, O great sage.”

Saṭṭhimattāhi gāthāhi dasabalassa kulanagaraṃ gamanatthāya gamanavaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇesi. Atha naṃ satthā “kiṃ nu kho udāyi madhurassarena gamanavaṇṇaṃ vaṇṇesī”ti āha. Bhante, tumhākaṃ pitā suddhodanamahārājā passitukāmo, karotha ñātakānaṃ saṅgahanti. Sādhu udāyi, karissāmi ñātakānaṃ saṅgahaṃ, bhikkhusaṅghassa ārocehi, gamikavattaṃ pūressantīti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti thero tesaṃ ārocesi.

With some sixty verses, he praised the beauty of the journey, for the sake of the Ten-Powered One’s going to his native city. Then the Teacher asked him, “Why, Udāyī, do you praise the journey with such a sweet voice?” “Venerable sir, your father, the great king Suddhodana, wishes to see you; please attend to your kinsmen.” “Good, Udāyī, I will attend to my kinsmen. Inform the Saṅgha of monks that they should fulfill the duties of those who are to travel.” “Very well, venerable sir,” the elder informed them.

Bhagavā aṅgamagadhavāsīnaṃ kulaputtānaṃ dasahi sahassehi, kapilavatthuvāsīnaṃ dasahi sahassehīti sabbeheva vīsatisahassehi khīṇāsavabhikkhūhi parivuto rājagahā nikkhamitvā divase divase yojanaṃ gacchati. “Rājagahato saṭṭhiyojanaṃ kapilavatthuṃ dvīhi māsehi pāpuṇissāmī”ti aturitacārikaṃ pakkāmi. Theropi “bhagavato nikkhantabhāvaṃ rañño ārocessāmī”ti [V 1.0096] vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā rañño nivesane pāturahosi. Rājā theraṃ disvā tuṭṭhacitto mahārahe pallaṅke nisīdāpetvā attano paṭiyāditassa nānaggarasabhojanassa pattaṃ pūretvā adāsi. Thero uṭṭhāya gamanākāraṃ dassesi. Nisīditvā bhuñjatha, tātāti. Satthu santikaṃ gantvā bhuñjissāmi, mahārājāti. Kahaṃ pana, tāta, satthāti? Vīsatisahassabhikkhuparivāro tumhākaṃ dassanatthāya cārikaṃ nikkhanto, mahārājāti. Rājā tuṭṭhamānaso āha “tumhe imaṃ paribhuñjitvā yāva mama putto imaṃ nagaraṃ pāpuṇāti, tāvassa itova piṇḍapātaṃ harathā”ti. Thero adhivāsesi. Rājā theraṃ parivisitvā pattaṃ gandhacuṇṇena ubbaṭṭetvā uttamabhojanassa pūretvā “tathāgatassa dethā”ti therassa hatthe patiṭṭhāpesi. Thero sabbesaṃ passantānaṃyeva pattaṃ ākāse khipitvā sayampi vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā piṇḍapātaṃ āharitvā satthu hatthe ṭhapesi. Satthā taṃ paribhuñji. Etenupāyena thero divase divase āhari, satthāpi antarāmagge raññoyeva piṇḍapātaṃ paribhuñji. Theropi bhattakiccāvasāne divase divase “ajja ettakaṃ bhagavā āgato, ajja ettaka”nti [P 1.0088] buddhaguṇapaṭisaṃyuttāya kathāya sakalaṃ rājakulaṃ satthu dassanaṃ vināyeva satthari sañjātappasādaṃ akāsi. Teneva naṃ bhagavā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ [M 1.0102] bhikkhūnaṃ kulappasādakānaṃ yadidaṃ kāḷudāyī”ti (a. ni. 1.219, 225) etadagge ṭhapesi.

The Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand monks—ten thousand clansmen from Anga and Magadha and ten thousand from Kapilavatthu, all arahants—left Rājagaha and traveled a yojana each day. Thinking, “I will reach Kapilavatthu, sixty yojanas from Rājagaha, in two months,” he set out on an unhurried journey. The elder also thought, “I will inform the king of the Blessed One’s departure.” Rising into the air, he appeared in the king’s palace. The king, delighted at seeing the elder, had him seated on a splendid couch and offered him a bowl filled with various delicious foods prepared for himself. The elder stood up to indicate his intention to leave. The king said, “Sit and eat, dear one.” “I will eat after going to the Teacher, great king,” he replied. “But where, dear one, is the Teacher?” “Great king, surrounded by twenty thousand monks, he has set out on a journey to see you.” The king, overjoyed, said, “After you have eaten this, until my son arrives in this city, bring him almsfood from here.” The elder consented. The king served the elder, rubbed the bowl with fragrant powder, filled it with the finest food, and placed it in the elder’s hands, saying, “Give this to the Tathāgata.” The elder, in full view of everyone, threw the bowl into the sky and, rising into the air himself, brought the almsfood and placed it in the Teacher’s hands. The Teacher ate it. In this way, the elder brought food each day, and the Teacher ate the king’s almsfood along the way. At the end of each meal, the elder daily reported, “Today the Blessed One has come this far, today this far,” and with talk connected to the Buddha’s virtues, he inspired the entire royal family with faith in the Teacher even before they saw him. For this reason, the Blessed One declared, “Monks, among my monk disciples who inspire confidence in families, Kāludāyī is foremost,” and placed him in that foremost position.

Sākiyāpi kho “anuppatte bhagavati amhākaṃ ñātiseṭṭhaṃ passissāmā”ti sannipatitvā bhagavato vasanaṭṭhānaṃ vīmaṃsamānā “nigrodhasakkassa ārāmo ramaṇīyo”ti sallakkhetvā tattha sabbaṃ paṭijagganavidhiṃ kāretvā gandhapupphahatthā paccuggamanaṃ karontā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍite daharadahare nāgaradārake ca nāgaradārikāyo ca paṭhamaṃ pahiṇiṃsu, tato rājakumāre ca rājakumārikāyo ca, tesaṃ anantaraṃ sāmaṃ gandhapupphacuṇṇādīhi pūjayamānā bhagavantaṃ gahetvā nigrodhārāmameva agamaṃsu. Tatra bhagavā vīsatisahassakhīṇāsavaparivuto paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi. Sākiyā nāma mānajātikā mānatthaddhā, te “siddhatthakumāro amhehi daharataro, amhākaṃ kaniṭṭho, bhāgineyyo, putto, nattā”ti cintetvā daharadahare rājakumāre āhaṃsu “tumhe vandatha, mayaṃ tumhākaṃ piṭṭhito nisīdissāmā”ti.

The Sakyans, thinking, “When the Blessed One arrives, we will see our foremost relative,” gathered and, inquiring about the Blessed One’s lodging, determined that “The park of Nigrodha the Sakyan is delightful.” They arranged all the necessary preparations there and, holding perfumes and flowers, went to welcome him. They first sent ahead the very young boys and girls of the city, adorned in all their finery, then the princes and princesses. Following them, they themselves went, honoring the Blessed One with perfumes, flowers, and powders, and led him to the Nigrodha park. There, the Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand arahants, sat on the prepared, excellent Buddha-seat. The Sakyans, being a proud and obstinate people, thought, “Prince Siddhattha is younger than us—our junior, nephew, son, or grandson.” So they told the very young princes, “You bow down; we will sit behind you.”

Tesu evaṃ avanditvā nisinnesu bhagavā tesaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ oloketvā “na maṃ ñātayo vandanti, handa dāni ne vandāpessāmī”ti abhiññāpādakaṃ catutthajjhānaṃ samāpajjitvā tato vuṭṭhāya ākāsaṃ abbhuggantvā tesaṃ sīse pādapaṃsuṃ okiramāno viya kaṇḍambarukkhamūle yamakapāṭihāriyasadisaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ akāsi. Rājā taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā āha – “bhagavā tumhākaṃ [V 1.0097] jātadivase kāḷadevalassa vandanatthaṃ upanītānaṃ pāde vo parivattitvā brāhmaṇassa matthake patiṭṭhite disvāpi ahaṃ tumhe vandiṃ, ayaṃ me paṭhamavandanā. Vappamaṅgaladivase jambucchāyāya sirisayane nisinnānaṃ vo jambucchāyāya aparivattanaṃ disvāpi pāde vandiṃ, ayaṃ me dutiyavandanā. Idāni imaṃ adiṭṭhapubbaṃ pāṭihāriyaṃ disvāpi ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pāde vandāmi, ayaṃ me tatiyavandanā”ti. Raññā pana vandite bhagavantaṃ avanditvā ṭhātuṃ samattho nāma ekasākiyopi nāhosi, sabbe vandiṃsuyeva.

While they sat there without paying homage, the Blessed One, discerning their intention, thought, “My relatives do not pay homage to me. Very well, I will make them pay homage.” Then he entered the fourth jhāna, which is the basis for psychic powers, emerged from it, rose into the air, and performed a miracle similar to the Twin Miracle at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree, as if scattering the dust from his feet upon their heads.
