Seeing this marvel, the king said, “Venerable Sir, on your birthday, when you were brought to pay homage to Kāḷadevala, I paid homage to you when I saw your feet turn and rest upon the brahmin’s head. That was my first act of homage. On the Ploughing Festival day, when I saw the shade of the rose-apple tree not moving while you sat on the royal couch, I paid homage at your feet. That was my second act of homage. Now, seeing this unprecedented miracle, I pay homage at your feet once more. This is my third act of homage.” When the king had paid homage, not a single Sakyan was able to remain standing without paying homage to the Blessed One. All of them paid homage.

Iti bhagavā ñātayo vandāpetvā ākāsato otaritvā paññattāsane nisīdi. Nisinne bhagavati sikhāpatto ñātisamāgamo ahosi[M 1.0103], sabbe ekaggacittā hutvā nisīdiṃsu. Tato mahāmegho pokkharavassaṃ vassi. Tambavaṇṇaṃ udakaṃ heṭṭhā viravantaṃ gacchati, temitukāmova temeti, atemitukāmassa sarīre ekabindumattampi na patati. Taṃ disvā sabbe acchariyabbhutacittajātā “aho acchariyaṃ, aho abbhuta”nti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā “na idāneva [P 1.0089] mayhaṃ ñātisamāgame pokkharavassaṃ vassati, atītepi vassī”ti imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā vessantarajātakaṃ kathesi. Dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sabbe uṭṭhāya vanditvā pakkamiṃsu. Ekopi rājā vā rājamahāmatto vā “sve amhākaṃ bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vatvā gato nāma natthi.

Thus, the Blessed One, having made his relatives pay homage, descended from the sky and sat on the prepared seat. While the Blessed One was seated, the gathering of relatives reached its culmination, and all sat with unified minds. Then a great cloud poured down a lotus-rain. The copper-colored water flowed beneath, making a roaring sound; it moistened those who wished to be moistened, yet not a single drop fell on the body of anyone who did not wish to be moistened. Seeing this, all were filled with wonder and amazement, exclaiming, “How marvelous, how astonishing!” The Teacher said, “Not only now during this gathering of my relatives does a lotus-rain fall—it rained in the past as well,” and to explain this occurrence, he narrated the Vessantara Jātaka. After hearing the Dhamma discourse, all rose, paid homage, and departed. Not a single king or royal minister departed after saying, “Tomorrow, accept alms from us.”

Satthā punadivase vīsatisahassabhikkhuparivuto kapilavatthuṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Taṃ na koci gantvā nimantesi, pattaṃ vā aggahosi. Bhagavā indakhīle ṭhitova āvajjesi “kathaṃ nu kho pubbabuddhā kulanagare piṇḍāya cariṃsu, kiṃ uppaṭipāṭiyā issarajanānaṃ gharāni agamaṃsu, udāhu sapadānacārikaṃ cariṃsū”ti. Tato ekabuddhassapi uppaṭipāṭiyā gamanaṃ adisvā “mayāpi idāni ayameva vaṃso, ayaṃ paveṇī paggahetabbā, āyatiñca me sāvakāpi mamaññeva anusikkhantā piṇḍacārikavattaṃ paripūressantī”ti koṭiyaṃ niviṭṭhagehato paṭṭhāya sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya cari. “Ayyo kira siddhatthakumāro piṇḍāya caratī”ti dvibhūmakatibhūmakādīsu pāsādesu sīhapañjare vivaritvā mahājano dassanabyāvaṭo ahosi.

On the following day, the Teacher, surrounded by twenty thousand monks, entered Kapilavatthu for alms. No one went to invite him, nor did anyone take his bowl. The Blessed One, standing at the city pillar, reflected: “How, indeed, did the Buddhas of the past go for alms in the city of their clan? Did they go out of order to the houses of the elite, or did they go on a continuous almsround?” Then, not seeing even a single Buddha who had gone out of order, he thought, “I too must now take up this same lineage, this same tradition. In the future, my disciples, following my example, will also perfect the practice of the almsround.” Starting from the house situated at the end of the street, he went for alms from house to house in continuous order. “It is said that the noble Prince Siddhattha is going for alms,” and so the great populace, opening the lion-windows in the two- and three-storied mansions, became occupied with seeing him.

Rāhulamātāpi devī “ayyaputto kira imasmiṃyeva nagare mahantena rājānubhāvena suvaṇṇasivikādīhi vicaritvā idāni kesamassuṃ ohāretvā kāsāyavatthavasano kapālahattho piṇḍāya carati, sobhati nu kho”ti sīhapañjaraṃ vivaritvā olokayamānā bhagavantaṃ nānāvirāgasamujjalāya sarīrappabhāya nagaravīthiyo obhāsetvā byāmappabhāparikkhepasamaṅgībhūtāya asītianubyañjanāvabhāsitāya [V 1.0098] dvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitāya anopamāya buddhasiriyā virocamānaṃ disvā uṇhīsato paṭṭhāya yāva pādatalā –

Rāhula’s mother, the queen, also thought, “It is said that my noble son, who once moved about in this very city with great royal splendor in golden palanquins and the like, has now, having shaved his hair and beard and donned ochre robes, goes for alms with a bowl in hand. Does he look splendid, I wonder?” Opening the lion-window and gazing, she saw the Blessed One illuminating the city streets with the brilliant radiance of his body of various hues, endowed with a surrounding fathom-long aura, resplendent with the eighty minor characteristics, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man, shining with incomparable Buddha-glory, from the crown of his head down to the soles of his feet:

“Siniddhanīlamudukuñcitakeso[M 1.0104], sūriyanimmalatalābhinalāṭo;

Yuttatuṅgamudukāyatanāso, raṃsijālavitato narasīho.

“With glossy, dark blue, soft, and curling hair, a forehead lustrous like a spotless sun-disc; with a well-proportioned, prominent, soft, and long nose, the lion among men is covered in a web of rays.”

“Cakkavaraṅkitarattasupādo, lakkhaṇamaṇḍitaāyatapaṇhi;

Cāmarihatthavibhūsitapaṇho, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.

“With excellent feet, red and marked with a wheel, his long heels adorned with auspicious signs; whose heels are adorned like a yak-tail whisk in hand, this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

“Sakyakumāro varado sukhumālo, lakkhaṇavicittapasannasarīro;

Lokahitāya āgato naravīro, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.

“The Sakyan prince, a giver of boons, delicately nurtured, with a body serene and beautifully adorned with auspicious signs; the hero among men has come for the welfare of the world, this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

“Āyatayuttasusaṇṭhitasoto, gopakhumo abhinīlanetto;

Indadhanuabhinīlabhamuko, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.

“With long, well-proportioned, and well-formed ears, with eyelashes like a cow’s, with deep blue eyes; with eyebrows as deep a blue as Indra’s bow, this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

“Puṇṇacandanibho mukhavaṇṇo, devanarānaṃ piyo naranāgo;

Mattagajindavilāsitagāmī, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.

“His facial complexion is like the full moon, beloved of gods and men, a great man; with the graceful gait of a majestic elephant in rut, this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

“Siniddhasugambhīramañjusaghoso, hiṅgulavaṇṇarattasujivho;

Vīsativīsatisetasudanto, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.

“With a voice smooth, very deep, and sweet, a beautiful tongue red as the color of vermilion; with forty beautiful white teeth, this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

“Khattiyasambhavaaggakulindo, devamanussanamassitapādo;

Sīlasamādhipatiṭṭhitacitto, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.

“Born of the Khattiya clan, lord of the highest family, whose feet are revered by devas and humans; whose mind is established in virtue and concentration—this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

“Vaṭṭasuvaṭṭasusaṇṭhitagīvo[M 1.0105], sīhahanumigarājasarīro;

Kañcanasucchaviuttamavaṇṇo, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.

“Whose neck is round, well-rounded, and well-formed; whose jaw is like a lion's, whose upper body is like the king of beasts; whose skin is golden, whose complexion is supreme—this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

“Añjanasamavaṇṇasunīlakeso, kañcanapaṭṭavisuddhanalāṭo;

Osadhipaṇḍarasuddhasuuṇṇo, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho.

“Whose beautiful hair is a deep blue-black, the color of collyrium; whose forehead is pure like a plate of burnished gold; whose beautiful uṇṇā is purely white like the morning star—this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

“Gacchantonilapathe [V 1.0099] viya cando, tārāgaṇaparivaḍḍhitarūpo;

Sāvakamajjhagato samaṇindo, esa hi tuyhaṃ pitā narasīho”ti. –

“Like the moon moving in the blue sky, its beauty enhanced by the host of stars; the king of ascetics, amidst his disciples—this indeed is your father, the lion among men.”

Evamimāhi dasahi narasīhagāthāhi nāma abhitthavitvā “tumhākaṃ putto kira idāni piṇḍāya caratī”ti rañño ārocesi. Rājā saṃviggahadayo hatthena sāṭakaṃ saṇṭhapento turitaturitaṃ nikkhamitvā vegena gantvā bhagavato purato ṭhatvā āha – “kiṃ, bhante, amhe lajjāpetha, kimatthaṃ piṇḍāya caratha, kiṃ ‘ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ na sakkā bhattaṃ laddhu’nti saññaṃ [P 1.0090] karitthā”ti. Vaṃsacārittametaṃ, mahārāja, amhākanti. Nanu, bhante, amhākaṃ mahāsammatakhattiyavaṃso nāma vaṃso, tattha ca ekakhattiyopi bhikkhācaro nāma natthīti. “Ayaṃ, mahārāja, rājavaṃso nāma tava vaṃso, amhākaṃ pana dīpaṅkaro koṇḍañño…pe… kassapoti ayaṃ buddhavaṃso nāma. Ete ca aññe ca anekasahassasaṅkhā buddhā bhikkhācarā, bhikkhācāreneva jīvikaṃ kappesu”nti antaravīthiyaṃ ṭhitova –

Thus having praised him with these ten verses called the ‘Lion of Men,’ she informed the king, saying, “It is said that your son is now going for alms.” The king, with a perturbed heart, adjusting his robe with his hand, went out in great haste, and approaching the Blessed One swiftly, stood before him and said: “Venerable sir, why do you shame us? For what reason do you go for alms? Do you suppose that it is not possible to obtain food for so many monks?” “This, great king, is the custom of our lineage.” “But, venerable sir, is not our lineage called the great Mahāsammata Khattiya lineage? And in it, there has never been a single Khattiya who went for alms.” “This, great king, the royal lineage, is your lineage. But ours is the Buddha lineage of Dīpaṅkara, Koṇḍañña… and so on… up to Kassapa. These and many other thousands of Buddhas were alms-wanderers; they sustained their lives by wandering for alms.” And standing in the middle of the street, he spoke:

“Uttiṭṭhe nappamajjeyya, dhammaṃ sucaritaṃ care;

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi cā”ti. (dha. pa. 168) –

“One should arise and not be heedless; one should practice the Dhamma well. The one who practices the Dhamma dwells happily in this world and in the next.”

Imaṃ gāthamāha. Gāthāpariyosāne rājā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi.

He spoke this verse. At the conclusion of the verse, the king was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

“Dhammaṃ care sucaritaṃ, na naṃ duccaritaṃ care;

Dhammacārī sukhaṃ seti, asmiṃ loke paramhi cā”ti. (dha. pa. 169) –

“One should practice the Dhamma well; one should not practice it badly. The one who practices the Dhamma dwells happily in this world and in the next.”

Imaṃ [M 1.0106] pana gāthaṃ sutvā sakadāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Mahādhammapālajātakaṃ (jā. 1.10.92 ādayo) sutvā anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāsi, maraṇasamaye setacchattassa heṭṭhā sirisayane nipannoyeva arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Araññavāsena pana padhānānuyogakiccaṃ rañño nāhosi. Sotāpattiphalaṃ sacchikatvāyeva pana bhagavato pattaṃ gahetvā saparisaṃ bhagavantaṃ mahāpāsādaṃ āropetvā paṇītena khādanīyena bhojanīyena parivisi. Bhattakiccapariyosāne sabbaṃ itthāgāraṃ āgantvā bhagavantaṃ vandi ṭhapetvā rāhulamātaraṃ. Sā pana “gaccha, ayyaputtaṃ vandāhī”ti parijanena vuccamānāpi “sace mayhaṃ guṇo atthi, sayameva mama santikaṃ ayyaputto āgamissati, āgatameva naṃ vandissāmī”ti vatvā na agamāsi.

Having heard this verse, he was established in the fruit of once-returning. After hearing the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka, he was established in the fruit of non-returning. At the time of his death, while lying on the royal couch beneath the white parasol, he attained Arahantship. For the king, however, there was no duty of applying himself to exertion by living in the forest. Having realized the fruit of stream-entry, he took the Blessed One’s bowl and, with his retinue, led the Blessed One up to the great palace and served him with exquisite hard and soft foods. At the conclusion of the meal, all the women of the inner palace came and paid homage to the Blessed One, with the exception of Rāhula’s mother. Though she was told by her attendants, “Go and pay homage to the noble son,” she said, “If there is any virtue in me, the noble son himself will come to my presence. When he has come, I will pay homage to him,” and she did not go.

Bhagavā [V 1.0100] rājānaṃ pattaṃ gāhāpetvā dvīhi aggasāvakehi saddhiṃ rājadhītāya sirigabbhaṃ gantvā “rājadhītā yathāruci vandamānā na kiñci vattabbā”ti vatvā paññattāsane nisīdi. Sā vegenāgantvā gopphakesu gahetvā pādapiṭṭhiyaṃ sīsaṃ parivattetvā yathāajjhāsayaṃ vandi. Rājā rājadhītāya bhagavati sinehabahumānādiguṇasampattiyo kathesi “bhante, mama dhītā ‘tumhehi kāsāyāni vatthāni nivāsitānī’ti [P 1.0091] sutvā tato paṭṭhāya kāsāyavatthanivatthā jātā, tumhākaṃ ekabhattikabhāvaṃ sutvā ekabhattikāva jātā, tumhehi mahāsayanassa chaḍḍitabhāvaṃ sutvā paṭṭikāmañcakeyeva nipannā, tumhākaṃ mālāgandhādīhi viratabhāvaṃ ñatvā viratamālāgandhāva jātā, attano ñātakehi ‘mayaṃ paṭijaggissāmā’ti sāsane pesitepi ekañātakampi na olokesi, evaṃ guṇasampannā me dhītā bhagavā”ti. “Anacchariyaṃ, mahārāja, yaṃ idāni tayā rakkhiyamānā rājadhītā paripakke ñāṇe attānaṃ rakkheyya, esā pubbe anārakkhā pabbatapāde vicaramānā aparipakke ñāṇe attānaṃ rakkhī”ti vatvā candakinnarījātakaṃ (jā. 1.14.18 ādayo) kathetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi.

The Blessed One had the king take the bowl and, accompanied by his two chief disciples, went to the princess's private chamber. He said, "Let the princess pay homage as she wishes; nothing should be said to her," and then sat down on the prepared seat. She came swiftly, grasped his ankles, placed her head upon the tops of his feet, and paid homage as she wished. The king described the princess's qualities of deep affection, reverence, and so forth to the Blessed One: "Venerable sir, my daughter, upon hearing that you wear saffron robes, has since then worn only saffron robes. Hearing that you eat only one meal a day, she too has taken to eating only one meal. Learning that you have abandoned the luxurious couch, she now lies only on a simple cot. Knowing that you abstain from garlands and perfumes, she has also given them up. Even when her relatives sent word saying, 'We will care for her,' she did not look at a single relative. Such is my daughter’s virtue, Blessed One." "It is no wonder, great king, that now, protected by you, the princess should guard herself with mature wisdom. In the past, even when unprotected and wandering at the foot of the mountain with immature wisdom, she guarded herself." Having spoken thus, the Blessed One recounted the Candakinnari Jātaka (Jātaka 1.14.18, etc.), then rose from his seat and departed.

Dutiyadivase pana nandassa rājakumārassa abhisekagehappavesanavivāhamaṅgalesu vattamānesu tassa gehaṃ gantvā kumāraṃ pattaṃ gāhāpetvā pabbājetukāmo maṅgalaṃ vatvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Janapadakalyāṇī kumāraṃ gacchantaṃ disvā “tuvaṭaṃ kho, ayyaputta, āgaccheyyāsī”ti vatvā [M 1.0107] gīvaṃ pasāretvā olokesi. Sopi bhagavantaṃ “pattaṃ gaṇhathā”ti vattuṃ avisahamāno vihāraṃyeva agamāsi, taṃ anicchamānaṃyeva bhagavā pabbājesi. Iti bhagavā kapilavatthuṃ gantvā tatiyadivase nandaṃ pabbājesi.

On the second day, while Prince Nanda's ceremonies of consecration, house-entry, and marriage were taking place, the Blessed One went to his house, had the prince take the alms bowl, and wishing to ordain him, spoke words of blessing. Then, rising from his seat, he departed. Seeing the prince going away, Janapada Kalyani said, "Come back quickly, my lord!" and stretching out her neck, she gazed at him. He, unable to bring himself to say to the Blessed One, 'Take the bowl,' went to the monastery. Though he was unwilling, the Blessed One ordained him. Thus, having gone to Kapilavatthu, the Blessed One ordained Nanda on the third day.

Sattame divase rāhulamātā kumāraṃ alaṅkaritvā bhagavato santikaṃ pesesi “passa, tāta, etaṃ vīsatisahassasamaṇaparivutaṃ suvaṇṇavaṇṇaṃ brahmarūpavaṇṇaṃ samaṇaṃ, ayaṃ te pitā, etassa mahantā nidhayo ahesuṃ, tyāssa nikkhamanakālato paṭṭhāya na passāma, gaccha, naṃ dāyajjaṃ yācāhi – ‘ahaṃ tāta kumāro abhisekaṃ patvā cakkavattī bhavissāmi, dhanena me attho, dhanaṃ me dehi. Sāmiko hi putto pitu santakassā’ti”. Kumāro ca bhagavato santikaṃ gantvā pitu sinehaṃ paṭilabhitvā haṭṭhatuṭṭho “sukhā te, samaṇa, chāyā”ti vatvā aññañca bahuṃ attano anurūpaṃ vadanto aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā katabhattakicco anumodanaṃ katvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Kumāropi “dāyajjaṃ me, samaṇa, dehi, dāyajjaṃ me, samaṇa, dehī”ti bhagavantaṃ anubandhi. Bhagavā kumāraṃ na nivattāpesi, parijanopi bhagavatā saddhiṃ gacchantaṃ nivattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Iti so bhagavatā saddhiṃ ārāmameva agamāsi.

On the seventh day, Rāhula's mother adorned the prince and sent him to the Blessed One, saying, "Look, dear, at this ascetic surrounded by twenty thousand monks, golden in color, with a complexion like Brahmā—he is your father. He once possessed vast treasures, but since the time of his going forth, we have not seen them. Go, ask him for your inheritance—'Father, I am a prince, and having been consecrated, I will become a wheel-turning monarch. I have need of wealth, give me wealth. For a son is the owner of his father’s property.'" The prince went to the Blessed One and, receiving fatherly affection, stood there joyful and delighted, saying, "Pleasant is your shadow, ascetic," and spoke many other words befitting himself. The Blessed One, having finished his meal and given thanks, rose from his seat and departed. The prince followed the Blessed One, saying, "Give me my inheritance, ascetic! Give me my inheritance, ascetic!" The Blessed One did not turn the prince back, nor could the retinue stop him from going with the Blessed One. Thus, he went to the monastery with the Blessed One.

Tato [V 1.0101] bhagavā cintesi “yaṃ ayaṃ pitu santakaṃ dhanaṃ icchati, taṃ vaṭṭānugataṃ savighātaṃ, handassa bodhimaṇḍe paṭiladdhaṃ sattavidhaṃ ariyadhanaṃ demi, lokuttaradāyajjassa naṃ sāmikaṃ karomī”ti āyasmantaṃ sāriputtaṃ āmantesi “tena hi, tvaṃ [P 1.0092] sāriputta, rāhulakumāraṃ pabbājehī”ti. Thero taṃ pabbājesi. Pabbajite pana kumāre rañño adhimattaṃ dukkhaṃ uppajji. Taṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto bhagavato nivedetvā “sādhu, bhante, ayyā mātāpitūhi ananuññātaṃ puttaṃ na pabbājeyyu”nti varaṃ yāci. Bhagavā tassa taṃ varaṃ datvā punadivase rājanivesane katapātarāso ekamantaṃ nisinnena raññā “bhante, tumhākaṃ dukkarakārikakāle ekā devatā maṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘putto te kālakato’ti āha, tassā vacanaṃ asaddahanto ‘na mayhaṃ putto bodhiṃ appatvā kālaṃ karotī’ti taṃ paṭikkhipi”nti vutte “idāni kiṃ saddahissatha, ye tumhe pubbepi [M 1.0108] aṭṭhikāni dassetvā ‘putto te mato’ti vutte na saddahitthā”ti imissā aṭṭhuppattiyā mahādhammapālajātakaṃ kathesi. Kathāpariyosāne rājā anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhāsi.

Then the Blessed One thought, "This wealth of his father that he desires is subject to the cycle and fraught with ruin. Well then, I shall give him the sevenfold noble wealth obtained at the Bodhi seat and make him the owner of the supramundane inheritance." He addressed the Venerable Sāriputta, "Therefore, Sāriputta, you should ordain Prince Rāhula." The elder ordained him. When the prince was ordained, excessive suffering arose in the king. Unable to endure it, he informed the Blessed One and requested a boon, saying, "Venerable sir, may the noble ones not ordain a son without the permission of his parents." The Blessed One granted him that boon. The next day, after the Blessed One had finished his morning meal at the royal residence, the king, seated to one side, said, "Venerable sir, during the time of your difficult ascetic practices, a deity approached me and said, 'Your son has died.' Not believing her words, I replied, 'My son will not die without attaining enlightenment.'" The Blessed One responded, "Why should you believe it now? Even in the past, when they showed you bones and said, 'Your son is dead,' you did not believe." Then, on this occasion, he recounted the Mahādhammapāla Jātaka. At the conclusion of the discourse, the king was established in the fruit of non-returning.

Iti bhagavā pitaraṃ tīsu phalesu patiṭṭhāpetvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto punadeva rājagahaṃ gantvā veḷuvane vihāsi. Tasmiṃ samaye anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati pañcahi sakaṭasatehi bhaṇḍaṃ ādāya rājagahe attano piyasahāyakassa seṭṭhino gehaṃ gantvā tattha buddhassa bhagavato uppannabhāvaṃ sutvā balavapaccūsasamaye devatānubhāvena vivaṭena dvārena satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammaṃ sutvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya dutiyadivase buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā sāvatthiṃ āgamanatthāya satthu paṭiññaṃ gahetvā antarāmagge pañcacattālīsayojanaṭṭhāne satasahassaṃ satasahassaṃ datvā yojanike yojanike vihāre kāretvā jetavanaṃ koṭisanthārena aṭṭhārasahiraññakoṭīhi kiṇitvā navakammaṃ paṭṭhapesi. So majjhe dasabalassa gandhakuṭiṃ kāresi, taṃ parivāretvā asītimahātherānaṃ pāṭiyekkasannivesane āvāse ekakūṭāgāradvikūṭāgārahaṃsavaṭṭakadīghasālāmaṇḍapādivasena sesasenāsanāni pokkharaṇīcaṅkamanarattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāni cāti aṭṭhārasakoṭipariccāgena ramaṇīye bhūmibhāge manoramaṃ vihāraṃ kārāpetvā dasabalassa āgamanatthāya dūtaṃ pesesi. Satthā dūtassa vacanaṃ sutvā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto rājagahā nikkhamitvā anupubbena sāvatthinagaraṃ pāpuṇi.

Thus, the Blessed One established his father in the three fruits, and surrounded by the community of monks, returned again to Rājagaha and dwelt in the Bamboo Grove. At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, taking goods with five hundred carts, went to the house of his dear friend, the chief merchant in Rājagaha. There, hearing that the Buddha, the Blessed One, had arisen, he approached the Teacher at dawn, the gate having been opened by the power of the devas. After hearing the Dhamma, he became established in the fruit of stream-entry. On the following day, he gave a great offering to the community of monks headed by the Buddha. Then, having obtained the Teacher’s promise to come to Sāvatthī, along the forty-five yojana route, he had monasteries built at every yojana, spending one hundred thousand on each. He purchased the Jetavana by paving it with eighteen crores of gold coins and began the construction work. In the middle, he had a fragrant hut built for the Ten-Powered One. Surrounding it, he had dwellings constructed for the eighty great elders, each with individual residences—single-peaked dwellings, double-peaked dwellings, swan-shaped dwellings, long halls, and pavilions, and so forth—along with the remaining lodgings, lotus ponds, walking paths, night resting places, and day resting places. Thus, with an expenditure of eighteen crores, he had a charming monastery built on the delightful grounds and sent a messenger to invite the Ten-Powered One to come. The Teacher, hearing the messenger's words, left Rājagaha surrounded by a large community of monks and gradually reached the city of Sāvatthī.

Mahāseṭṭhipi kho vihāramahaṃ sajjetvā tathāgatassa jetavanappavisanadivase puttaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ katvā alaṅkatapaṭiyatteheva pañcahi kumārasatehi saddhiṃ pesesi. So saparivāro pañcavaṇṇavatthasamujjalāni pañca dhajasatāni gahetvā dasabalassa [P 1.0093] purato ahosi. Tesaṃ [V 1.0102] pacchato mahāsubhaddā cūḷasubhaddāti dve seṭṭhidhītaro pañcahi kumārikāsatehi saddhiṃ puṇṇaghaṭe gahetvā nikkhamiṃsu. Tāsaṃ pacchato seṭṭhibhariyā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā pañcahi mātugāmasatehi saddhiṃ puṇṇapātiyo gahetvā nikkhami. Sabbesaṃ pacchato sayaṃ mahāseṭṭhi ahatavatthanivattho [M 1.0109] ahatavatthanivattheheva pañcahi seṭṭhisatehi saddhiṃ bhagavantaṃ abbhuggañchi. Bhagavā imaṃ upāsakaparisaṃ purato katvā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto attano sarīrappabhāya suvaṇṇarasasekapiñjarāni viya vanantarāni kurumāno anantāya buddhalīḷāya apaṭisamāya buddhasiriyā jetavanavihāraṃ pāvisi.

The great merchant, having prepared the monastery festival, on the day the Tathāgata was to enter Jetavana, adorned his son with all ornaments and sent him forth with five hundred young men, all finely dressed and prepared. With his retinue, holding up five hundred banners shining with cloths of five colors, he stood before the Ten-Powered One. Behind them, the two merchant’s daughters, Mahāsubhaddā and Cūḷasubhaddā, came forth with five hundred maidens, carrying full pots. Behind them, the merchant’s wife, adorned with all ornaments, came forth with five hundred women, carrying full bowls. Behind them all, the great merchant himself, clad in new robes, along with five hundred merchants clad in new robes, went forth to meet the Blessed One. The Blessed One, placing this assembly of lay followers before him and surrounded by the great community of monks, entered the Jetavana Monastery, making the forest groves golden-hued as if by a sprinkling of golden essence from the radiance of his body, with the boundless grace of a Buddha and the incomparable splendor of a Buddha.

Atha naṃ anāthapiṇḍiko pucchi – “kathāhaṃ, bhante, imasmiṃ vihāre paṭipajjāmī”ti. Tena hi gahapati imaṃ vihāraṃ āgatānāgatassa cātuddisassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dehīti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti mahāseṭṭhi suvaṇṇabhiṅkāraṃ ādāya dasabalassa hatthe udakaṃ pātetvā “imaṃ jetavanavihāraṃ āgatānāgatassa cātuddisassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dammī”ti adāsi. Satthā vihāraṃ paṭiggahetvā anumodanaṃ karonto –

Then Anāthapiṇḍika asked him, "Venerable sir, how should I act with regard to this monastery?" "Then, householder, give this monastery to the Sangha of monks from the four directions, both those who have come and those who have yet to come." "Very well, venerable sir," replied the great merchant. Taking a golden vessel, he poured water onto the hand of the Ten-Powered One and said, "I give this Jetavana monastery to the Sangha of monks from the four directions, both those who have come and those who have yet to come." The Teacher accepted the monastery and, giving a discourse of appreciation, said:

“Sītaṃ uṇhaṃ paṭihanti, tato vāḷamigāni ca;

Sarīsape ca makase, sisire cāpi vuṭṭhiyo.

They ward off cold and heat, and also beasts of prey; and reptiles and mosquitoes, and rains in the cold season.

“Tato vātātapo ghoro, sañjāto paṭihaññati;

Leṇatthañca sukhatthañca, jhāyituñca vipassituṃ.

Then a fierce wind and sun's heat, having arisen, are warded off; for the purpose of shelter and for comfort, for meditating and for insight.

“Vihāradānaṃ saṅghassa, aggaṃ buddhena vaṇṇitaṃ;

Tasmā hi paṇḍito poso, sampassaṃ atthamattano.

The gift of a monastery to the Sangha has been praised by the Buddha as foremost. Therefore, a wise person, seeing their own welfare—

“Vihāre kāraye ramme, vāsayettha bahussute;

Tesaṃ annañca pānañca, vatthasenāsanāni ca.

Build delightful monasteries, and house the learned there; provide them with food and drink, and with robes and lodgings.

“Dadeyya ujubhūtesu, vippasannena cetasā;

Te [P 1.0094] tassa dhammaṃ desenti, sabbadukkhāpanūdanaṃ;

Yaṃ so dhammaṃ idhaññāya, parinibbāti anāsavo”ti. (cūḷava. 295) –

One should give to the upright, with a mind serene and clear; they teach them the Dhamma, which dispels all suffering; understanding that Dhamma here, one who is without influxes attains final Nibbāna.

Vihārānisaṃsaṃ [V 1.0103] kathesi. Anāthapiṇḍiko dutiyadivasato paṭṭhāya vihāramahaṃ ārabhi. Visākhāya pāsādamaho catūhi māsehi niṭṭhito, anāthapiṇḍikassa pana vihāramaho navahi māsehi niṭṭhāsi. Vihāramahepi aṭṭhāraseva koṭiyo pariccāgaṃ agamaṃsu. Iti ekasmiṃyeva vihāre catupaṇṇāsakoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanaṃ pariccaji.

He spoke on the benefits of a monastery. From the second day, Anāthapiṇḍika began the monastery festival. Visākhā's mansion festival was completed in four months, but Anāthapiṇḍika's monastery festival was finished in nine months. For the monastery festival as well, eighteen crores were spent. Thus, for that one monastery, wealth amounting to fifty-four crores was given away.

Atīte [M 1.0110] pana vipassissa bhagavato kāle punabbasumitto nāma seṭṭhi suvaṇṇiṭṭhakāsanthārena kiṇitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne yojanappamāṇaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kāresi. Sikhissa bhagavato kāle sirivaḍḍho nāma seṭṭhi suvaṇṇaphālasanthārena kiṇitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne tigāvutappamāṇaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kāresi. Vessabhussa bhagavato kāle sotthijo nāma seṭṭhi suvaṇṇahatthipadasanthārena kiṇitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne aḍḍhayojanappamāṇaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kāresi. Kakusandhassa bhagavato kāle accuto nāma seṭṭhi suvaṇṇiṭṭhakāsanthārena kiṇitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne gāvutappamāṇaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kāresi. Koṇāgamanassa bhagavato kāle uggo nāma seṭṭhi suvaṇṇakacchapasanthārena kiṇitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne aḍḍhagāvutappamāṇaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kāresi. Kassapassa bhagavato kāle sumaṅgalo nāma seṭṭhi suvaṇṇakaṭṭisanthārena kiṇitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne soḷasakarīsappamāṇaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kāresi. Amhākaṃ pana bhagavato kāle anāthapiṇḍiko nāma seṭṭhi kahāpaṇakoṭisanthārena kiṇitvā tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne aṭṭhakarīsappamāṇaṃ saṅghārāmaṃ kāresi. Idaṃ kira ṭhānaṃ sabbabuddhānaṃ avijahitaṭṭhānameva.

In the past, in the time of the Blessed One Vipassī, a wealthy merchant named Punabbasumitta purchased the land by paving it with golden bricks and built a monastery one yojana in size on that very spot. In the time of the Blessed One Sikhī, a wealthy merchant named Sirivaḍḍha purchased the land by paving it with golden tiles and built a monastery three gāvutas in size on that very spot. In the time of the Blessed One Vessabhū, a wealthy merchant named Sotthija purchased the land by paving it with golden elephant footprints and built a monastery half a yojana in size on that very spot. In the time of the Blessed One Kakusandha, a wealthy merchant named Accuta purchased the land by paving it with golden bricks and built a monastery one gāvuta in size on that very spot. In the time of the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, a wealthy merchant named Ugga purchased the land by paving it with golden tortoises and built a monastery half a gāvuta in size on that very spot. In the time of the Blessed One Kassapa, a wealthy merchant named Sumaṅgala purchased the land by paving it with golden rods and built a monastery sixteen karīsas in size on that very spot. In the time of our Blessed One, the wealthy merchant Anāthapiṇḍika purchased the land by paving it with a crore of kahāpaṇas and built a monastery eight karīsas in size on that very spot. This place, it is said, is indeed a site never abandoned by any of the Buddhas.

Iti mahābodhimaṇḍe sabbaññutappattito yāva mahāparinibbānamañcā yasmiṃ yasmiṃ ṭhāne bhagavā vihāsi, idaṃ santikenidānaṃ nāma, tassa vasena sabbajātakāni vaṇṇayissāma.

Thus, from the attainment of omniscience at the Great Bodhi Terrace up to the couch of the Great Parinibbāna, in whatever place the Blessed One resided, this is called the Proximate Introduction. By means of this, we shall recount all the Jātakas.

Nidānakathā niṭṭhitā.

The Introduction is concluded.

1. Ekakanipāto

1. The Book of Ones

1. Apaṇṇakavaggo

1. The Chapter on the Unerring

1. Apaṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka

Imaṃ [V 1.0104][P 1.0095] tāva [M 1.0111] apaṇṇakadhammadesanaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiṃ upanissāya jetavanamahāvihāre viharanto kathesi. Kaṃ pana ārabbha ayaṃ kathā samuṭṭhitāti? Seṭṭhissa sahāyake pañcasate titthiyasāvake. Ekasmiñhi divase anāthapiṇḍiko seṭṭhi attano sahāyake pañcasate aññatitthiyasāvake ādāya bahuṃ mālāgandhavilepanañceva sappitelamadhuphāṇitavatthacchādanāni ca gāhāpetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā bhesajjāni ceva vatthāni ca bhikkhusaṅghassa vissajjetvā cha nisajjādose vajjetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tepi aññatitthiyasāvakā tathāgataṃ vanditvā satthu puṇṇacandasassirikaṃ mukhaṃ, lakkhaṇānubyañjanapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ byāmappabhāparikkhittaṃ brahmakāyaṃ, āveḷāveḷā yamakayamakā hutvā niccharantiyo ghanabuddharasmiyo ca olokayamānā anāthapiṇḍikassa samīpeyeva nisīdiṃsu.

The Blessed One taught this discourse on the unerring Dhamma while dwelling in the Great Monastery of Jetavana, near Sāvatthī. Concerning whom did this story arise? Concerning five hundred followers of other sects who were friends of the wealthy merchant. For one day, the wealthy merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, taking his five hundred friends who were followers of other sects, and having procured many flowers, perfumes, and ointments, as well as ghee, oil, honey, molasses, cloths, and coverings, went to Jetavana. Having paid homage to the Blessed One and honored him with perfumes, flowers, and so on, he distributed medicines and cloths to the Saṅgha of monks. Avoiding the six faults in sitting, he sat down to one side. Those followers of other sects also paid homage to the Tathāgata. Gazing at the Teacher’s face, resplendent like the full moon; at his body, like that of Brahmā, adorned with the major and minor marks and surrounded by a fathom-wide aura; and at the dense rays of the Buddha that emanated in continuous pairs, they sat down near Anāthapiṇḍika.

Atha nesaṃ satthā manosilātale sīhanādaṃ nadanto taruṇasīho viya gajjanto pāvussakamegho viya ca ākāsagaṅgaṃ otārento [P 1.0096] viya ca ratanadāmaṃ ganthento viya ca aṭṭhaṅgasamannāgatena savanīyena kamanīyena brahmassarena nānānayavicittaṃ madhuradhammakathaṃ kathesi. Te satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannacittā uṭṭhāya dasabalaṃ vanditvā aññatitthiyasaraṇaṃ bhinditvā buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ agamaṃsu. Te tato paṭṭhāya niccakālaṃ anāthapiṇḍikena saddhiṃ gandhamālādihatthā vihāraṃ gantvā dhammaṃ suṇanti, dānaṃ denti, sīlaṃ rakkhanti, uposathakammaṃ karonti.

Then the Teacher, on a slab of red arsenic, roaring a lion’s roar like a young lion, thundering like a monsoon cloud, as if bringing down the celestial Ganges, and as if stringing a jeweled garland, delivered a sweet Dhamma talk, varied in its methods, with a Brahmā-like voice endowed with eight qualities, pleasant to hear and lovely. Hearing the Teacher's discourse on the Dhamma, their minds filled with faith, they rose, paid homage to the One with Ten Powers, abandoned their refuge in other sects, and went for refuge to the Buddha. From that time onwards, they would constantly go to the monastery with Anāthapiṇḍika, their hands bearing perfumes and garlands, listen to the Dhamma, give alms, observe the precepts, and perform the Uposatha ceremony.

Atha bhagavā sāvatthito punadeva rājagahaṃ agamāsi. Te tathāgatassa gatakāle taṃ saraṇaṃ bhinditvā puna aññatitthiyasaraṇaṃ gantvā attano [M 1.0112] mūlaṭṭhāneyeva patiṭṭhitā. Bhagavāpi sattaṭṭha māse [V 1.0105] vītināmetvā puna jetavanameva agamāsi. Anāthapiṇḍiko punapi te ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ gandhamālādīhi pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Tepi bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ tathāgate cārikaṃ pakkante gahitasaraṇaṃ bhinditvā puna aññatitthiyasaraṇameva gahetvā mūle patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ bhagavato ārocesi.

Then the Blessed One went again from Sāvatthī to Rājagaha. When the Tathāgata had departed, they abandoned that refuge, went again for refuge to the other sects, and were re-established in their original position. After passing seven or eight months, the Blessed One returned to Jetavana. Anāthapiṇḍika again took them and went to the Teacher’s presence. Having honored the Teacher with perfumes, garlands, and so on, and having paid homage, he sat down to one side. They too paid homage to the Blessed One and sat down to one side. Then Anāthapiṇḍika informed the Blessed One that when the Tathāgata had departed on tour, they had abandoned the refuge they had taken, had again taken refuge only in the other sects, and had become re-established in their original ways.

Bhagavā aparimitakappakoṭiyo nirantaraṃ pavattitavacīsucaritānubhāvena dibbagandhagandhitaṃ nānāgandhapūritaṃ ratanakaraṇḍakaṃ vivaranto viya mukhapadumaṃ vivaritvā madhurassaraṃ nicchārento “saccaṃ kira tumhe upāsakā tīṇi saraṇāni bhinditvā aññatitthiyasaraṇaṃ gatā”ti pucchi. Atha tehi paṭicchādetuṃ asakkontehi “saccaṃ bhagavā”ti vutte satthā “upāsakā heṭṭhā avīciṃ upari bhavaggaṃ paricchedaṃ katvā tiriyaṃ aparimāṇāsu lokadhātūsu sīlādīhi guṇehi buddhena sadiso nāma natthi, kuto adhikataro”ti. “Yāvatā, bhikkhave, sattā apadā vā dvipadā vā catuppadā vā bahuppadā vā, tathāgato tesaṃ aggamakkhāyati (saṃ. ni. 5.139; a. ni. 4.34), yaṃ kiñci vittaṃ idha vā huraṃ vā…pe… (khu. pā. 6.3; su. ni. 226) aggato ve pasannāna”ntiādīhi (a. ni. 4.34; itivu. 90) suttehi pakāsite ratanattayaguṇe pakāsetvā “evaṃ uttamaguṇehi samannāgataṃ ratanattayaṃ saraṇaṃ gatā upāsakā vā upāsikā vā nirayādīsu nibbattakā nāma natthi, apāyanibbattito pana muccitvā devaloke uppajjitvā mahāsampattiṃ anubhonti, tasmā tumhehi evarūpaṃ saraṇaṃ bhinditvā aññatitthiyasaraṇaṃ gacchantehi ayuttaṃ kata”nti āha.

The Blessed One, by the power of his virtuous speech practiced unceasingly over countless eons, opened his lotus-like mouth as if opening a jeweled casket filled with divine and various fragrances, and in a sweet voice asked, “Is it true, lay devotees, that you have broken the Three Refuges and gone to the refuge of other sectarians?” When they, unable to conceal it, replied, “It is true, Blessed One,” the Teacher said, “Lay devotees, from Avīci below to the highest plane of existence above, and across the immeasurable world-systems, there is none equal to the Buddha in virtues such as morality—how then could there be one superior?” Having expounded the virtues of the Triple Gem as declared in suttas such as, “Monks, of all beings—whether footless, two-footed, four-footed, or many-footed—the Tathāgata is declared the foremost among them” (SN 5.139; AN 4.34), “Whatever treasure there is, here or in the world beyond…” (Khp 6.3; Sn 226), and “For those who have confidence in the supreme…” (AN 4.34; Iti 90), he then said, “Lay devotees or laywomen who have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, endowed with such supreme virtues, are never reborn in hell or other such states. Freed from rebirth in the lower realms, they arise in the heavenly world and enjoy great prosperity. Therefore, by breaking such a refuge and going for refuge to other sectarians, you have done what is improper.”

Ettha ca tīṇi ratanāni mokkhavasena uttamavasena saraṇagatānaṃ apāyesu nibbattiyā abhāvadīpanatthaṃ imāni suttāni dassetabbāni –

Here, to show the absence of rebirth in the lower realms for those who have gone for refuge to the Triple Gem, by virtue of its being a means to liberation and its supremacy, these suttas should be cited:

“Ye [P 1.0097] keci buddhaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse, na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ, devakāyaṃ paripūressanti. (dī. ni. 2.332; saṃ. ni. 1.37);

“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha will not go to the states of woe; having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the divine host.”

“Ye [M 1.0113] keci dhammaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse, na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ, devakāyaṃ paripūressanti.

“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Dhamma will not go to the states of woe; having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the divine host.”

“Ye [V 1.0106] keci saṅghaṃ saraṇaṃ gatāse, na te gamissanti apāyabhūmiṃ;

Pahāya mānusaṃ dehaṃ, devakāyaṃ paripūressanti.

“Whoever has gone for refuge to the Saṅgha will not go to the states of woe; having abandoned the human body, they will fulfill the divine host.”

“Bahuṃ ve saraṇaṃ yanti, pabbatāni vanāni ca;

Ārāmarukkhacetyāni, manussā bhayatajjitā.

“Many indeed, tormented by fear, go for refuge to mountains, forests, groves, trees, and shrines.

“Netaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, netaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ;

Netaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccati.

“Indeed, this is not a secure refuge; this is not the supreme refuge. By resorting to this refuge, one is not released from all suffering.”

“Yo ca buddhañca dhammañca, saṅghañca saraṇaṃ gato;

Cattāri ariyasaccāni, sammappaññāya passati.

“But whoever has gone for refuge to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha, sees the Four Noble Truths with right wisdom:”

“Dukkhaṃ dukkhasamuppādaṃ, dukkhassa ca atikkamaṃ;

Ariyañcaṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ, dukkhūpasamagāminaṃ.

“Suffering, the origin of suffering, the transcending of suffering, and the Noble Eightfold Path leading to the stilling of suffering.”

“Etaṃ kho saraṇaṃ khemaṃ, etaṃ saraṇamuttamaṃ;

Etaṃ saraṇamāgamma, sabbadukkhā pamuccatī”ti. (dha. pa. 188-192);

“This indeed is the secure refuge; this is the supreme refuge. By resorting to this refuge, one is released from all suffering.”

Na kevalañca nesaṃ satthā ettakaṃyeva dhammaṃ desesi, apica kho “upāsakā buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, dhammānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma, saṅghānussatikammaṭṭhānaṃ nāma sotāpattimaggaṃ deti, sotāpattiphalaṃ deti, sakadāgāmimaggaṃ deti, sakadāgāmiphalaṃ deti, anāgāmimaggaṃ deti, anāgāmiphalaṃ deti, arahattamaggaṃ deti, arahattaphalaṃ detī”tievamādīhipi nayehi dhammaṃ desetvā “evarūpaṃ nāma saraṇaṃ bhindantehi ayuttaṃ tumhehi kata”nti āha. Ettha ca buddhānussatikammaṭṭhānādīnaṃ sotāpattimaggādippadānaṃ “ekadhammo, bhikkhave, bhāvito bahulīkato ekantanibbidāya virāgāya nirodhāya upasamāya abhiññāya sambodhāya nibbānāya [M 1.0114] saṃvattati. Katamo ekadhammo? Buddhānussatī”tievamādīhi (a. ni. 1.296) suttehi dīpetabbaṃ.

Not only did the Teacher teach them just this much Dhamma, but having also taught the Dhamma in such ways as, 'Lay disciples, the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha, the meditation on the recollection of the Dhamma, and the meditation on the recollection of the Saṅgha gives the path of stream-entry, gives the fruit of stream-entry, gives the path of once-returning, gives the fruit of once-returning, gives the path of non-returning, gives the fruit of non-returning, gives the path to Arahantship, and gives the fruit of Arahantship,' he then said, 'It was improper for you to break such a refuge.' Here, that the meditation on the recollection of the Buddha and so on bestows the path of stream-entry and so forth should be illustrated by suttas such as: 'Monks, one thing, when developed and cultivated, leads exclusively to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation, to peace, to direct knowledge, to full enlightenment, to Nibbāna. What is that one thing? The recollection of the Buddha' (AN 1.296).

Evaṃ bhagavā nānappakārehi upāsake ovaditvā “upāsakā pubbepi manussā asaraṇaṃ ‘saraṇa’nti takkaggāhena viraddhaggāhena gahetvā amanussapariggahite kantāre yakkhabhakkhā hutvā [V 1.0107] mahāvināsaṃ pattā, apaṇṇakaggāhaṃ pana ekaṃsikaggāhaṃ aviraddhaggāhaṃ gahitamanussā tasmiṃyeva kantāre sotthibhāvaṃ pattā”ti vatvā tuṇhī ahosi. Atha kho anāthapiṇḍiko gahapati uṭṭhāyāsanā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā abhitthavitvā sirasmiṃ añjaliṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā evamāha “bhante, idāni tāva imesaṃ upāsakānaṃ uttamasaraṇaṃ bhinditvā takkaggahaṇaṃ amhākaṃ pākaṭaṃ, pubbe pana amanussapariggahite kantāre takkikānaṃ vināso, apaṇṇakaggāhaṃ gahitamanussānañca sotthibhāvo amhākaṃ paṭicchanno, tumhākameva [P 1.0098] pākaṭo, sādhu vata no bhagavā ākāse puṇṇacandaṃ uṭṭhāpento viya imaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ karotū”ti. Atha bhagavā “mayā kho, gahapati, aparimitakālaṃ dasa pāramiyo pūretvā lokassa kaṅkhacchedanatthameva sabbaññutaññāṇaṃ paṭividdhaṃ, sīhavasāya suvaṇṇanāḷiṃ pūrento viya sakkaccaṃ sotaṃ odahitvā suṇohī”ti seṭṭhino satuppādaṃ janetvā himagabbhaṃ padāletvā puṇṇacandaṃ nīharanto viya bhavantarena paṭicchannakāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

Thus the Blessed One, having advised the lay disciples in various ways, said: “Lay disciples, in the past, people, taking what was not a refuge as a ‘refuge’ through grasping by speculation and misguided grasping, became prey to yakkhas in a wilderness haunted by non-humans and met with great destruction. But those who took the unerring grasp, the certain grasp, the unfailing grasp, attained safety in that very wilderness.” Having said this, he fell silent. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍika rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, extolled him, placed his hands together in reverence on his head, and said: “Venerable sir, that these lay disciples have taken to speculation after breaking the supreme refuge is now clear to us. But in the past, the destruction of the speculators and the safety of those who took the unerring grasp in that wilderness haunted by non-humans was hidden from us; it was clear only to you. It would be good, venerable sir, if you would make this matter clear, just as one might reveal the full moon in the sky.” Then the Blessed One said: “Householder, it was precisely to cut through the world’s doubt that I, for an immeasurable time, fulfilled the ten perfections and realized omniscience. Listen carefully, paying close attention, as one would diligently fill a golden tube with lion’s marrow.” Generating the arising of mindfulness in the great merchant, like splitting open a cloud of hail to reveal the full moon, he made manifest the matter that was hidden by another existence.

Atīte kāsiraṭṭhe bārāṇasinagare brahmadatto nāma rājā ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto satthavāhakule paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā dasamāsaccayena mātukucchito nikkhamitvā anupubbena vayappatto pañcahi sakaṭasatehi vaṇijjaṃ karonto vicarati. So kadāci pubbantato aparantaṃ gacchati, kadāci aparantato pubbantaṃ. Bārāṇasiyaṃyeva aññopi satthavāhaputto atthi bālo abyatto anupāyakusalo. Tadā bodhisatto bārāṇasito mahagghaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ gahetvā pañca sakaṭasatāni pūretvā gamanasajjāni katvā ṭhapesi. Sopi bālasatthavāhaputto tatheva pañca sakaṭasatāni pūretvā gamanasajjāni katvā ṭhapesi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta. At that time, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the family of a caravan leader; after ten months, he emerged from his mother's womb and in due course reached maturity. He went about conducting trade with five hundred carts. Sometimes he went from the east to the west, and sometimes from the west to the east. In Bārāṇasī itself, there was another son of a caravan leader—foolish, unskilled, and lacking in resourcefulness. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having taken valuable goods from Bārāṇasī, filled five hundred carts and made them ready for the journey. That foolish son of a caravan leader also filled five hundred carts in the same way and made them ready for the journey.

Tadā bodhisatto cintesi “sace ayaṃ bālasatthavāhaputto mayā saddhiṃyeva gamissati, sakaṭasahasse ekato maggaṃ gacchante maggopi [M 1.0115] nappahossati, manussānaṃ dārudakādīnipi, balibaddānaṃ tiṇānipi dullabhāni bhavissanti, etena vā mayā vā purato gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So taṃ pakkosāpetvā etamatthaṃ ārocetvā “dvīhipi amhehi ekato gantuṃ na sakkā, kiṃ tvaṃ purato gamissasi, udāhu pacchato”ti āha. So cintesi “mayi purato gacchante bahū ānisaṃsā, maggena abhinneneva gamissāmi, goṇā anāmaṭṭhatiṇaṃ khādissanti, manussānaṃ anāmaṭṭhaṃ sūpeyyapaṇṇaṃ bhavissati, pasannaṃ udakaṃ bhavissati, yathāruciṃ agghaṃ ṭhapetvā bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇissāmī”ti. So “ahaṃ, samma, purato gamissāmī”ti [P 1.0099] āha. Bodhisattopi pacchato gamane bahū ānisaṃse addasa. Evaṃ hissa ahosi – “purato gacchantā magge visamaṭṭhānaṃ samaṃ karissanti, ahaṃ tehi gatamaggena gamissāmi, purato gatehi balibaddehi pariṇatathaddhatiṇe [V 1.0108] khādite mama goṇā puna uṭṭhitāni madhuratiṇāni khādissanti, gahitapaṇṇaṭṭhānato uṭṭhitaṃ manussānaṃ sūpeyyapaṇṇaṃ madhuraṃ bhavissati, anudake ṭhāne āvāṭaṃ khanitvā ete udakaṃ uppādessanti, tehi katesu āvāṭesu mayaṃ udakaṃ pivissāma, agghaṭṭhapanaṃ nāma manussānaṃ jīvitā voropanasadisaṃ, ahaṃ pacchato gantvā etehi ṭhapitagghena bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇissāmī”ti. Atha so ettake ānisaṃse disvā “samma, tvaṃ purato gacchāhī”ti āha. “Sādhu, sammā”ti bālasatthavāho sakaṭāni yojetvā nikkhanto anupubbena manussāvāsaṃ atikkamitvā kantāramukhaṃ pāpuṇi.

Then the Bodhisatta thought: 'If this foolish son of a caravan leader travels with me, when a thousand carts go together on the road, the road will not suffice, and firewood, water, and such for the people, as well as grass for the oxen, will become scarce. Either he or I ought to go first.' So he summoned him, explained this matter, and said, 'It is not possible for both of us to go together. Will you go first, or behind?' The other thought: 'If I go first, there are many advantages. I will travel on an unbroken road. The oxen will eat untouched grass. The people will have untouched greens for relish. The water will be clear. I can set prices as I wish and sell my goods.' So he said, 'Friend, I will go first.' The Bodhisatta, however, saw many advantages in going behind. He thought: 'Those who go first will level the rough spots on the road. I will travel the path they have taken. After the oxen in front have eaten the old, tough grass, my oxen will eat the sweet grass that grows up again. The greens for relish that grow up again in the places where they have been picked will be sweet. In a place without water, they will dig a well and produce water. We will drink from the wells they have dug. Setting prices is like depriving people of their life. I will go behind and sell my goods at the price they have set.' Then, seeing these many advantages, he said, 'Friend, you go first.' 'Very well, friend,' replied the foolish caravan leader. He yoked his carts and set out. Gradually, he passed beyond human habitation and reached the entrance to the wilderness.

Kantāraṃ nāma – corakantāraṃ, vāḷakantāraṃ, nirudakakantāraṃ, amanussakantāraṃ, appabhakkhakantāranti pañcavidhaṃ. Tattha corehi adhiṭṭhitamaggo corakantāraṃ nāma. Sīhādīhi adhiṭṭhitamaggo vāḷakantāraṃ nāma. Yattha nhāyituṃ vā pātuṃ vā udakaṃ natthi, idaṃ nirudakakantāraṃ nāma. Amanussādhiṭṭhitaṃ amanussakantāraṃ nāma. Mūlakhādanīyādivirahitaṃ appabhakkhakantāraṃ nāma. Imasmiṃ pañcavidhe kantāre taṃ kantāraṃ nirudakakantārañceva amanussakantārañca. Tasmā so bālasatthavāhaputto sakaṭesu mahantamahantā cāṭiyo ṭhapetvā udakassa pūrāpetvā saṭṭhiyojanikaṃ kantāraṃ paṭipajji.

A wilderness is of five kinds: the wilderness of thieves, the wilderness of wild beasts, the wilderness without water, the wilderness of non-humans, and the wilderness with little food. Among these, a path occupied by thieves is called the wilderness of thieves. A path occupied by lions and other wild beasts is called the wilderness of wild beasts. Where there is no water for bathing or drinking, this is called the wilderness without water. A place inhabited by non-humans is called the wilderness of non-humans. A place devoid of roots and other edibles is called the wilderness with little food. Of these five kinds, that particular wilderness was both a wilderness without water and a wilderness of non-humans. Therefore, that foolish son of a caravan leader, having placed very large water jars on the carts and filled them with water, entered the sixty-yojana wilderness.

Athassa kantāramajjhaṃ gatakāle kantāre adhivatthayakkho “imehi manussehi gahitaṃ udakaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā dubbale katvā sabbeva ne khādissāmī”ti [M 1.0116] sabbasetataruṇabalibaddayuttaṃ [P 1.0100] manoramaṃ yānakaṃ māpetvā dhanukalāpaphalakāvudhahatthehi dasahi dvādasahi amanussehi parivuto uppalakumudāni piḷandhitvā allakoso allavattho issarapuriso viya tasmiṃ yānake nisīditvā kaddamamakkhitehi cakkehi paṭipathaṃ agamāsi. Parivāraamanussāpissa purato ca pacchato ca gacchantā allakesā allavatthā uppalakumudamālā piḷandhitvā padumapuṇḍarīkakalāpe gahetvā bhisamuḷālāni khādantā udakabindūhi ceva kalalehi ca paggharantehi agamaṃsu. Satthavāhā ca nāma yadā dhuravāto vāyati, tadā yānake nisīditvā upaṭṭhākaparivutā rajaṃ pariharantā purato gacchanti. Yadā pacchato vāto vāyati, tadā teneva nayena pacchato gacchanti. Tadā pana dhuravāto ahosi, tasmā so satthavāhaputto purato agamāsi.

Then, when he had reached the middle of the wilderness, a yakkha dwelling there thought, 'Having made these men discard the water they have taken and weakened them, I will devour them all.' He conjured a delightful carriage yoked with all-white young bulls, and, surrounded by ten or twelve non-humans holding bows, quivers, shields, and weapons, he sat in that carriage like a lordly man, wearing blue and white lotuses and clad in wet garments. With wheels smeared with mud, he came towards them along the path. His non-human attendants, walking in front and behind, had wet hair and wet clothes, wore garlands of blue and white lotuses, held clusters of red and white lotuses, ate lotus roots and shoots, and went along dripping with water drops and mud. Now, it is the custom of caravan leaders that when a headwind blows, they sit in their carriages surrounded by attendants, avoiding the dust, and go in front. When a tailwind blows, they go behind in the same way. At that time, a headwind was blowing, so that son of a caravan leader went in front.

Yakkho taṃ āgacchantaṃ disvā attano yānakaṃ maggā okkamāpetvā “kahaṃ gacchathā”ti tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ akāsi. Satthavāhopi attano yānakaṃ maggā okkamāpetvā sakaṭānaṃ gamanokāsaṃ datvā ekamante ṭhito taṃ yakkhaṃ avoca “bho, amhe tāva [V 1.0109] bārāṇasito āgacchāma. Tumhe pana uppalakumudāni piḷandhitvā padumapuṇḍarīkahatthā bhisamuḷālāni khādantā kaddamamakkhitā udakabindūhi paggharantehi āgacchatha. Kiṃ nu kho tumhehi āgatamagge devo vassati, uppalādisañchannāni vā sarāni atthī”ti pucchi. Yakkho tassa kathaṃ sutvā “samma, kiṃ nāmetaṃ kathesi. Esā nīlavanarāji paññāyati. Tato paṭṭhāya sakalaṃ araññaṃ ekodakaṃ, nibaddhaṃ devo vassati, kandarā pūrā, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne padumādisañchannāni sarāni atthī”ti vatvā paṭipāṭiyā gacchantesu [P 1.0101] sakaṭesu “imāni sakaṭāni ādāya kahaṃ gacchathā”ti pucchi. “Asukajanapadaṃ nāmā”ti. “Imasmiṃ cimasmiñca sakaṭe kiṃ nāma bhaṇḍa”nti? “Asukañca asukañcā”ti. “Pacchato āgacchantaṃ sakaṭaṃ ativiya garukaṃ hutvā āgacchati, etasmiṃ kiṃ bhaṇḍa”nti? “Udakaṃ etthā”ti. “Parato tāva udakaṃ ānentehi vo manāpaṃ kataṃ, ito paṭṭhāya pana udakena kiccaṃ natthi, purato bahu udakaṃ, cāṭiyo bhinditvā udakaṃ chaḍḍetvā sukhena gacchathā”ti āha. Evañca pana vatvā “tumhe gacchatha, amhākaṃ papañco hotī”ti thokaṃ gantvā tesaṃ adassanaṃ patvā attano yakkhanagarameva agamāsi.

Seeing him approaching, the yakkha moved his own small vehicle aside from the road and exchanged friendly greetings with him, asking, 'Where are you going?' The caravan leader also moved his own small vehicle aside from the road, giving the carts room to pass, and standing to one side, said to the yakkha, 'Sir, we are coming from Bārāṇasī. But you, wearing blue lotuses and white water lilies, holding red and white lotuses in your hands, eating lotus roots and stalks, smeared with mud, and with water drops dripping from you—did it rain on the road you came by, or are there ponds covered with blue lotuses and the like?' he asked. Having heard his words, the yakkha said, 'Friend, what is this you say? That dark line of forest is visible. From there onwards, the whole forest is full of water, the rain falls continuously, the ravines are full, and in every place there are ponds covered with lotuses and the like.' Then, as the carts were moving along in succession, he asked, 'Taking these carts, where are you going?' 'To such-and-such a district.' 'And what sort of goods are in this cart and that cart?' 'Such-and-such and such-and-such.' 'The cart coming behind is approaching very heavily laden—what goods are in it?' 'There is water in it.' 'You have done well to bring water this far, but from here onwards, there is no need for water. Ahead there is plenty of water. Break the pots, throw away the water, and go with ease,' he said. And having said this, he added, 'You must go on; we are being delayed,' and after going a short distance, he went out of their sight and proceeded to his own yakkha city.

Sopi [M 1.0117] bālasatthavāho attano bālatāya yakkhassa vacanaṃ gahetvā cāṭiyo bhindāpetvā pasatamattampi udakaṃ anavasesetvā sabbaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā sakaṭāni pājāpesi, purato appamattakampi udakaṃ nāhosi, manussā pānīyaṃ alabhantā kilamiṃsu. Te yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā gantvā sakaṭāni mocetvā parivaṭṭakena ṭhapetvā goṇe cakkesu bandhiṃsu. Neva goṇānaṃ udakaṃ ahosi, na manussānaṃ yāgubhattaṃ vā. Dubbalamanussā tattha tattha nipajjitvā sayiṃsu. Rattibhāgasamanantare yakkhā yakkhanagarato āgantvā sabbepi goṇe ca manusse ca jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā aṭṭhīni avasesetvā agamaṃsu. Evamekaṃ bālasatthavāhaputtaṃ nissāya sabbepi te vināsaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, hatthaṭṭhikādīni disāvidisāsu vippakiṇṇāni ahesuṃ. Pañca sakaṭasatāni yathāpūritāneva aṭṭhaṃsu.

That foolish caravan leader, due to his own foolishness, accepted the yakkha's words, had the water jars broken, and, not leaving even a handful of water, had it all discarded and drove the carts onward. Ahead, there was not even a little water. The people, unable to get drinking water, grew weary. They traveled until sunset, then unyoked the carts, arranged them in a circle, and tied the oxen to the wheels. There was no water for the oxen, nor rice gruel or cooked rice for the people. The weakened people lay down here and there and slept. In the course of the night, the yakkhas came from the yakkha city, brought all the oxen and people to the destruction of their lives, devoured their flesh, left only the bones, and departed. Thus, on account of one foolish caravan leader's son, they all met with destruction. Bones of hands and the like were scattered in all directions. The five hundred carts stood just as they were, fully loaded.

Bodhisattopi kho bālasatthavāhaputtassa nikkhantadivasato māsaḍḍhamāsaṃ vītināmetvā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi nagarā nikkhamma anupubbena kantāramukhaṃ pāpuṇi. So tattha udakacāṭiyo pūretvā bahuṃ udakaṃ ādāya khandhāvāre bheriṃ carāpetvā manusse sannipātetvā [P 1.0102] evamāha “tumhe maṃ anāpucchitvā pasatamattampi udakaṃ mā vaḷañjayittha, kantāre visarukkhā nāma honti, pattaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā tumhehi pure akhāditapubbaṃ maṃ anāpucchitvā mā khāditthā”ti. Evaṃ manussānaṃ ovādaṃ datvā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi kantāraṃ paṭipajji. Tasmiṃ kantāramajjhaṃ sampatte so [V 1.0110] yakkho purimanayeneva bodhisattassa paṭipathe attānaṃ dassesi. Bodhisatto taṃ disvāva aññāsi “imasmiṃ kantāre udakaṃ natthi, nirudakakantāro nāmesa, ayañca nibbhayo rattanetto, chāyāpissa na paññāyati, nissaṃsayaṃ iminā purato gato bālasatthavāhaputto sabbaṃ udakaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā kilametvā sapariso khādito bhavissati, mayhaṃ pana paṇḍitabhāvaṃ upāyakosallaṃ na jānāti maññe”ti. Tato naṃ āha “gacchatha tumhe, mayaṃ vāṇijā nāma aññaṃ udakaṃ adisvā gahitaudakaṃ na chaḍḍema, diṭṭhaṭṭhāne pana chaḍḍetvā sakaṭāni sallahukāni katvā gamissāmā”ti yakkho thokaṃ gantvā adassanaṃ upagamma attano yakkhanagarameva gato.

Now the Bodhisatta, letting a month and a half pass from the day the foolish caravan leader's son had departed, left the city with five hundred carts and in due course reached the entrance to the wilderness. There, he had the water jars filled, took a great quantity of water, had a drum beaten throughout the encampment, assembled the men, and said this: 'Without asking me, you are not to use even a handful of water. In the wilderness, there are poisonous trees. Do not eat any leaf, flower, or fruit that you have not eaten before without asking me.' Having given this instruction to the men, he entered the wilderness with the five hundred carts. When he had reached the middle of the wilderness, that yakkha showed himself on the path before the Bodhisatta in the same manner as before. The Bodhisatta, as soon as he saw him, knew: 'In this wilderness, there is no water; it is called the waterless wilderness. This being is fearless and red-eyed, and his shadow is not visible. Without a doubt, the foolish caravan leader's son who went before was made by this one to discard all his water, and having been exhausted, was devoured along with his company. But I think he does not know of my wisdom and skill in means.' Then he said to him: 'You go on. We who are merchants do not discard the water we have taken without seeing other water. Only at a place where we see it will we discard this water, lighten our carts, and proceed.' The yakkha went a short distance, passed from their sight, and returned to his own yakkha city.

Yakkhe pana gate manussā bodhisattaṃ āhaṃsu “ayya, ete manussā ‘esā nīlavanarāji paññāyati, tato paṭṭhāya nibaddhaṃ devo vassatī’ti vatvā [M 1.0118] uppalakumudamālādhārino padumapuṇḍarīkakalāpe ādāya bhisamuḷālāni khādantā allavatthā allakesā udakabindūhi paggharantehi āgatā, udakaṃ chaḍḍetvā sallahukehi sakaṭehi khippaṃ gacchāmā”ti. Bodhisatto tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā sakaṭāni ṭhapāpetvā sabbe manusse sannipātāpetvā “tumhehi ‘imasmiṃ kantāre saro vā pokkharaṇī vā atthī’ti kassaci sutapubba”nti pucchi. “Na, ayya, sutapubba”nti. Nirudakakantāro nāma eso, idāni ekacce manussā “etāya nīlavanarājiyā purato devo vassatī”ti vadanti, “vuṭṭhivāto nāma kittakaṃ ṭhānaṃ [P 1.0103] vāyatī”ti? “Yojanamattaṃ, ayyā”ti. “Kacci pana vo ekassāpi sarīraṃ vuṭṭhivāto paharatī”ti? “Natthi ayyā”ti. “Meghasīsaṃ nāma kittake ṭhāne paññāyatī”ti? “Tiyojanamatte ayyā”ti. “Atthi pana vo kenaci ekampi meghasīsaṃ diṭṭha”nti? “Natthi, ayyā”ti. “Vijjulatā nāma kittake ṭhāne paññāyatī”ti? “Catuppañcayojanamatte, ayyā”ti. “Atthi pana vo kenaci vijjulatobhāso diṭṭho”ti? “Natthi, ayyā”ti. “Meghasaddo nāma kittake ṭhāne suyyatī”ti? “Ekadviyojanamatte, ayyā”ti. “Atthi pana vo kenaci meghasaddo suto”ti? “Natthi, ayyā”ti. “Na ete manussā, yakkhā ete, amhe udakaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā dubbale katvā khāditukāmā āgatā bhavissanti. Purato gato bālasatthavāhaputto na upāyakusalo. Addhā so etehi udakaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā kilametvā khādito bhavissati, pañca sakaṭasatāni yathāpūritāneva ṭhitāni bhavissanti. Ajja mayaṃ tāni passissāma, pasatamattampi udakaṃ achaḍḍetvā sīghasīghaṃ pājethā”ti pājāpesi.

When the yakkhas had gone, the men said to the Bodhisatta, 'Sir, these men, wearing garlands of blue and white water lilies, holding bunches of red and white lotuses, eating lotus roots and stalks, with wet clothes and wet hair from which drops of water trickle, have come saying, "That dark line of forest is visible; from there onwards, it rains unceasingly. Let us discard our water and proceed quickly with lightened carts."' Hearing their words, the Bodhisatta had the carts stopped and all the men assembled. He asked, 'Have any of you ever heard it said that in this wilderness there is a lake or a pond?' 'No, sir, we have never heard of one.' 'This is called the Waterless Wilderness. Just now, some men said, "It is raining beyond that dark line of forest." How far does a rain-wind blow?' 'About a yojana, sir.' 'But has a rain-wind struck the body of any one of you?' 'No, sir.' 'At what distance does a cloud-bank become visible?' 'At about three yojanas, sir.' 'But has any one of you seen a single cloud-bank?' 'No, sir.' 'At what distance is a flash of lightning visible?' 'At about four or five yojanas, sir.' 'But has any one of you seen the gleam of lightning?' 'No, sir.' 'From what distance is the sound of thunder heard?' 'From about one or two yojanas, sir.' 'But has any one of you heard the sound of thunder?' 'No, sir.' 'These are not men; they are yakkhas. They must have come desiring to devour us after making us discard our water and thus weakening us. The foolish son of a caravan leader who went before was not skilled in strategy. Surely, he must have been made by them to discard his water, and having been exhausted, was devoured. The five hundred carts will be standing just as they were filled. Today we shall see them. Do not discard even a handful of water; drive on with all speed.' Thus, he had them drive on.

So gacchanto yathāpūritāneva pañca sakaṭasatāni goṇamanussānañca hatthaṭṭhikādīni disāvidisāsu vippakiṇṇāni disvā sakaṭāni mocāpetvā sakaṭaparivaṭṭakena khandhāvāraṃ bandhāpetvā [V 1.0111] kālasseva manusse ca goṇe ca sāyamāsabhattaṃ bhojāpetvā manussānaṃ majjhe goṇe nipajjāpetvā sayaṃ balanāyako hutvā khaggahattho tiyāmarattiṃ ārakkhaṃ gahetvā ṭhitakova aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpesi. Punadivase pana pātova [M 1.0119] sabbakiccāni niṭṭhāpetvā goṇe bhojetvā dubbalasakaṭāni chaḍḍāpetvā thirāni gāhāpetvā appagghaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā mahagghaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ āropāpetvā yathādhippetaṃ ṭhānaṃ gantvā diguṇatiguṇena mūlena bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇitvā sabbaṃ parisaṃ ādāya puna attano nagarameva agamāsi.

Proceeding on his way, he saw the five hundred carts standing just as they had been filled, and the hand-bones and so forth of the men and oxen scattered in all directions. He had the carts unyoked, formed a defensive encampment by circling the carts, and in the evening, had both the men and the oxen eat their meal. He had the oxen lie down in the midst of the men, and he himself, as the leader of the troop, stood guard with sword in hand throughout the three watches of the night until dawn arose. The next day, early in the morning, having completed all their duties, he had the oxen fed, the weak carts discarded and the sturdy ones taken, the goods of little value discarded and the highly valuable goods loaded up. Reaching his intended destination, he sold the goods for twice and three times their value and, taking his entire retinue, returned to his own city.

Satthā [P 1.0104] imaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathetvā “evaṃ, gahapati, pubbe takkaggāhagāhino mahāvināsaṃ pattā, apaṇṇakaggāhagāhino pana amanussānaṃ hatthato muccitvā sotthinā icchitaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā puna sakaṭṭhānameva paccāgamiṃsū”ti vatvā dvepi vatthūni ghaṭetvā imissā apaṇṇakadhammadesanāya abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, said: 'Thus, householder, in the past those who grasped what was based on speculation came to great destruction; but those who grasped the infallible, being freed from the hands of non-humans, safely reached their desired destination and returned again to their own place.' Then, having connected both stories, as the Fully Enlightened One, he spoke this verse in this discourse on the Infallible Teaching:

1.

1.

“Apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhānameke, dutiyaṃ āhu takkikā;

Etadaññāya medhāvī, taṃ gaṇhe yadapaṇṇaka”nti.

One position, some declare, is the infallible one; a second, say the speculators. The wise one, having understood this, should grasp that which is infallible.

Tattha apaṇṇakanti ekaṃsikaṃ aviraddhaṃ niyyānikaṃ. Ṭhānanti kāraṇaṃ. Kāraṇañhi yasmā tadāyattavuttitāya phalaṃ tiṭṭhati nāma, tasmā “ṭhāna”nti vuccati, “ṭhānañca ṭhānato aṭṭhānañca aṭṭhānato”tiādīsu (vibha. 809) cassa payogo veditabbo. Iti “apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhāna”nti padadvayenāpi “yaṃ ekantahitasukhāvahattā paṇḍitehi paṭipannaṃ ekaṃsikakāraṇaṃ aviraddhakāraṇaṃ niyyānikakāraṇaṃ, taṃ ida”nti dīpeti. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, pabhedato pana tīṇi saraṇagamanāni, pañca sīlāni, dasa sīlāni, pātimokkhasaṃvaro, indriyasaṃvaro, ājīvapārisuddhi, paccayapaṭisevanaṃ, sabbampi catupārisuddhisīlaṃ; indriyesu guttadvāratā, bhojane mattaññutā, jāgariyānuyogo, jhānaṃ, vipassanā, abhiññā, samāpatti, ariyamaggo, ariyaphalaṃ, sabbampetaṃ apaṇṇakaṭṭhānaṃ apaṇṇakapaṭipadā, niyyānikapaṭipadāti attho.

Herein, 'apaṇṇaka' means certain, unerring, and leading forth. 'Ṭhāna' means cause. For since a result is established by reason of its dependence on that, it is therefore called 'ṭhāna' (basis). Its usage is to be understood in such passages as, 'a possible case as a possible case, and an impossible case as an impossible case' (Vibh. 809). Thus, by the two words 'apaṇṇakaṃ ṭhāna' is shown: 'This is that certain, unerring, and liberating cause which is practiced by the wise because it brings exclusive welfare and happiness.' This is the summary here. In detail, however: the going for the three refuges, the five precepts, the ten precepts, the restraint of the Pātimokkha, the restraint of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, the proper use of the requisites—all of the fourfold purification of virtue; guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, the practice of wakefulness, jhāna, insight, the direct knowledges, the attainments, the noble path, and the noble fruit—all this is the infallible basis, the infallible practice, the practice that leads forth. This is the meaning.

Yasmā ca pana niyyānikapaṭipadāya etaṃ nāmaṃ, tasmāyeva bhagavā apaṇṇakapaṭipadaṃ dassento imaṃ suttamāha –

And since this is the name for the practice that leads forth, the Blessed One, in order to show the infallible practice, spoke this sutta:

“Tīhi, bhikkhave, dhammehi samannāgato bhikkhu apaṇṇakapaṭipadaṃ paṭipanno hoti, yoni cassa āraddhā hoti āsavānaṃ khayāya[M 1.0120]. Katamehi tīhi? Idha, bhikkhave[V 1.0112], bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hoti, bhojane mattaññū hoti, jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti. Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu cakkhunā rūpaṃ disvā na nimittaggāhī hoti…pe… evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu indriyesu guttadvāro hoti.

'Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who possesses three qualities has entered upon the infallible practice, and he has initiated the means for the destruction of the taints. What are the three? Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu guards the doors of his sense faculties, is moderate in eating, and is devoted to wakefulness. And how, bhikkhus, does a bhikkhu guard the doors of his sense faculties? Here, bhikkhus, having seen a form with the eye, a bhikkhu does not grasp at its signs... and so on... In this way, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu guards the doors of his sense faculties.'

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhojane mattaññū hoti? Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso āhāraṃ āhāreti neva davāya na madāya…pe… evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu bhojane mattaññū hoti.

And how, monks, is a monk one who knows moderation in eating? Here, monks, a monk, reflecting properly, partakes of food not for amusement, not for intoxication... Thus, monks, a monk is one who knows moderation in eating.

“Kathañca, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hoti. Idha, bhikkhave, bhikkhu divasaṃ caṅkamena nisajjāya…pe… evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, bhikkhu jāgariyaṃ anuyutto hotī”ti (a. ni. 3.16).

And how, monks, is a monk devoted to wakefulness? Here, monks, during the day, while walking back and forth and sitting... Thus, monks, a monk is devoted to wakefulness.

Imasmiñcāpi sutte tayova dhammā vuttā. Ayaṃ pana apaṇṇakapaṭipadā yāva arahattaphalaṃ labbhateva[P 1.0105]. Tattha arahattaphalampi, phalasamāpattivihārassa ceva, anupādāparinibbānassa ca, paṭipadāyeva nāma hoti.

In this discourse, too, only these three qualities are mentioned. But this infallible practice leads all the way to the attainment of Arahantship. There, even the fruit of Arahantship, as well as the abiding in fruition attainment and final Nibbāna without clinging, is simply called the practice.

Eketi ekacce paṇḍitamanussā. Tattha kiñcāpi “asukā nāmā”ti niyamo natthi, idaṃ pana saparisaṃ bodhisattaṃyeva sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ. Dutiyaṃ āhu takkikāti dutiyanti paṭhamato apaṇṇakaṭṭhānato niyyānikakāraṇato dutiyaṃ takkaggāhakāraṇaṃ aniyyānikakāraṇaṃ. Āhu takkikāti ettha pana saddhiṃ purimapadena ayaṃ yojanā – apaṇṇakaṭṭhānaṃ ekaṃsikakāraṇaṃ aviraddhakāraṇaṃ niyyānikakāraṇaṃ eke bodhisattappamukhā paṇḍitamanussā gaṇhiṃsu. Ye pana bālasatthavāhaputtappamukhā takkikā āhu, te dutiyaṃ sāparādhaṃ anekaṃsikaṭṭhānaṃ viraddhakāraṇaṃ aniyyānikakāraṇaṃ aggahesuṃ. Tesu ye apaṇṇakaṭṭhānaṃ aggahesuṃ, te sukkapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā. Ye dutiyaṃ “purato bhavitabbaṃ udakenā”ti takkaggāhasaṅkhātaṃ aniyyānikakāraṇaṃ aggahesuṃ. Te kaṇhapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā.

`Eke` means some wise people. Here, although there is no fixed rule stating 'it is such and such,' it should be understood that this was spoken with reference to the Bodhisatta and his retinue. `Dutiyaṃ āhu takkikā` means 'the logicians say the second.' Here, `dutiyaṃ` means the second, which, in contrast to the first—the infallible basis, the liberating cause—is the cause of grasping at logic, a non-liberating cause. As for `āhu takkikā`, the connection with the previous phrase is this: The infallible basis—a certain cause, an unerring cause, a liberating cause—was adopted by some wise people headed by the Bodhisatta. But those logicians, headed by the foolish caravan leader, adopted the second position—a faulty, uncertain basis, an erroneous cause, a non-liberating cause. Among them, those who adopted the infallible basis undertook the bright practice. Those who adopted the second—the non-liberating cause known as grasping at logic—undertook the dark practice.

Tattha [M 1.0121] sukkapaṭipadā aparihānipaṭipadā, kaṇhapaṭipadā parihānipaṭipadā. Tasmā ye sukkapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā, te aparihīnā sotthibhāvaṃ pattā. Ye pana kaṇhapaṭipadaṃ paṭipannā, te [V 1.0113] parihīnā anayabyasanaṃ āpannāti imamatthaṃ bhagavā anāthapiṇḍikassa gahapatino vatvā uttari idamāha “etadaññāya medhāvī, taṃ gaṇhe yadapaṇṇaka”nti.

Here, the bright practice is the practice of non-decline; the dark practice is the practice of decline. Therefore, those who have undertaken the bright practice are without decline and have attained well-being. But those who have undertaken the dark practice are in decline and meet with misfortune and ruin. Having told this meaning to the householder Anāthapiṇḍika, the Blessed One further said, "Knowing this, the wise person should take up that which is infallible."

Tattha etadaññāya medhāvīti “medhā”ti laddhanāmāya vipulāya visuddhāya uttamāya paññāya samannāgato kulaputto etaṃ apaṇṇake ceva sapaṇṇake cāti dvīsu atakkaggāhatakkaggāhasaṅkhātesu ṭhānesu guṇadosaṃ vuddhihāniṃ atthānatthaṃ ñatvāti attho. Taṃ gaṇhe yadapaṇṇakanti yaṃ apaṇṇakaṃ ekaṃsikaṃ sukkapaṭipadāaparihāniyapaṭipadāsaṅkhātaṃ niyyānikakāraṇaṃ, tadeva gaṇheyya. Kasmā? Ekaṃsikādibhāvatoyeva. Itaraṃ pana na gaṇheyya. Kasmā? Anekaṃsikādibhāvatoyeva. Ayañhi apaṇṇakapaṭipadā nāma sabbesaṃ buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhaputtānaṃ paṭipadā. Sabbabuddhā hi apaṇṇakapaṭipadāyameva ṭhatvā daḷhena vīriyena pāramiyo pūretvā bodhimūle buddhā nāma honti, paccekabuddhā paccekabodhiṃ uppādenti, buddhaputtā sāvakapāramiñāṇaṃ paṭivijjhanti.

Here, `etadaññāya medhāvī` (knowing this, the wise) means: a clansman endowed with wisdom—vast, purified, and supreme, which has received the name `medhā`—having known the qualities and faults, growth and decline, benefit and harm in these two positions, the infallible and the fallible, designated as 'without grasping at logic' and 'with grasping at logic.' `Taṃ gaṇhe yadapaṇṇaka` (one should take up that which is infallible) means one should take up only that which is infallible, certain, designated as the bright practice, the practice of non-decline, the cause of liberation. Why? Because it is certain and so forth. But one should not take up the other. Why? Because it is uncertain and so forth. For this infallible practice is the practice of all Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and sons of the Buddha. All Buddhas, indeed, standing on this infallible practice, fulfill the perfections with strong effort and become Buddhas at the foot of the Bodhi tree. Paccekabuddhas bring forth individual enlightenment, and sons of the Buddha penetrate the knowledge of the disciple's perfection.

Iti bhagavā tesaṃ upāsakānaṃ tisso kulasampattiyo ca cha kāmasagge brahmalokasampattiyo ca datvāpi pariyosāne arahattamaggaphaladāyikā [P 1.0106] apaṇṇakapaṭipadā nāma, catūsu apāyesu pañcasu ca nīcakulesu nibbattidāyikā sapaṇṇakapaṭipadā nāmāti imaṃ apaṇṇakadhammadesanaṃ dassetvā uttari cattāri saccāni soḷasahi ākārehi pakāsesi. Catusaccapariyosāne sabbepi te pañcasatā upāsakā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu.

Thus, the Blessed One, having explained to those lay followers the three kinds of family prosperity, the six heavens of the sensual realm, and the prosperity of the Brahmā-worlds, ultimately showed them that the infallible practice is that which gives the path and fruit of Arahantship, and the fallible practice is that which gives rebirth in the four states of misery and the five low families. Having shown this teaching on the infallible, he further revealed the four truths in sixteen aspects. At the conclusion of the teaching on the four truths, all five hundred of those lay followers were established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā dassetvā dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānetvā dassesi – “tasmiṃ samaye bālasatthavāhaputto devadatto ahosi, tassa parisā devadattaparisāva, paṇḍitasatthavāhaputtaparisā buddhaparisā, paṇḍitasatthavāhaputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

The Teacher, having brought forth and shown this Dhamma discourse, related the two stories, connected them, and identified the characters of the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the foolish caravan leader was Devadatta, his retinue was Devadatta's retinue, the retinue of the wise caravan leader was the Buddha's retinue, and the wise caravan leader was I myself.' Thus he concluded the discourse.

Apaṇṇakajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first commentary, on the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka.

2. Vaṇṇupathajātakavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Vaṇṇupatha Jātaka

Akilāsunoti [V 1.0114][M 1.0122] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto kathesi. Kaṃ pana ārabbhāti? Ekaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyaṃ bhikkhuṃ. Tathāgate kira sāvatthiyaṃ viharante eko sāvatthivāsī kulaputto jetavanaṃ gantvā satthu santike dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannacitto kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā pabbajitvā upasampadāya pañcavassiko hutvā dve mātikā uggaṇhitvā vipassanācāraṃ sikkhitvā satthu santike attano cittaruciyaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ekaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā vassaṃ upagantvā temāsaṃ vāyamantopi obhāsamattaṃ vā nimittamattaṃ vā uppādetuṃ nāsakkhi.

The Blessed One, while dwelling at Sāvatthī, delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with `Akilāsu`. Concerning whom was it spoken? A certain monk who had abandoned his effort. It is said that while the Tathāgata was dwelling at Sāvatthī, a certain clansman from Sāvatthī went to Jetavana. After hearing a Dhamma discourse in the Teacher's presence, his mind was inspired, and seeing the danger in sensual pleasures, he went forth and received the higher ordination. Having been ordained for five years, he learned the two Mātikās, trained in the practice of insight, and received a meditation subject from the Teacher that suited his own inclination. He then entered a forest and undertook the rains retreat. Though he strove for the three months, he was unable to produce even a glimmer of light or a mere sign.

Athassa etadahosi “satthārā cattāro puggalā kathitā, tesu mayā padaparamena bhavitabbaṃ, natthi maññe mayhaṃ imasmiṃ attabhāve maggo vā phalaṃ vā, kiṃ karissāmi araññavāsena, satthu santikaṃ gantvā rūpasobhaggappattaṃ buddhasarīraṃ olokento madhuraṃ dhammadesanaṃ suṇanto viharissāmī”ti puna jetavanameva paccāgamāsi. Atha naṃ sandiṭṭhasambhattā āhaṃsu – “āvuso, tvaṃ satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā ‘samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī’ti gato, idāni pana āgantvā saṅgaṇikāya abhiramamāno carasi, kiṃ nu kho te pabbajitakiccaṃ matthakaṃ pattaṃ, appaṭisandhiko jātosī”ti? Āvuso, ahaṃ maggaṃ vā phalaṃ vā alabhitvā “abhabbapuggalena mayā bhavitabba”nti vīriyaṃ ossajitvā āgatomhīti. “Akāraṇaṃ te, āvuso, kataṃ daḷhavīriyassa satthu sāsane pabbajitvā vīriyaṃ ossajantena, ayuttaṃ te kataṃ, ehi tathāgatassa [P 1.0107] dassemā”ti taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ agamaṃsu.

Then it occurred to him: 'The Teacher has spoken of four types of individuals. Among them, I must be one whose highest attainment is the word of the text. I think there is no path or fruit for me in this existence. What shall I accomplish by dwelling in the forest? I will go to the Teacher’s presence, gaze upon the Buddha’s body, which has attained the pinnacle of beauty, and dwell listening to the sweet Dhamma teaching.' So he returned once more to Jetavana. Then his friends and companions said to him: 'Friend, you went to the Teacher’s presence, received a meditation subject, and said, ‘I will practice the ascetic's duty.’ But now you have returned and are delighting in company, moving about. Has your renunciate's duty reached its culmination? Have you become one for whom there is no more to be done?' 'Friends, not having attained the path or the fruit, I thought, ‘I must be an incapable person,’ and so I abandoned my effort and returned.' 'Friend, what you have done is unreasonable. Having gone forth in the dispensation of the Teacher of steadfast energy, to abandon that energy is unsuitable. You have acted improperly. Come, let us present you to the Tathāgata.' Taking him, they went to the Teacher’s presence.
