Satthā taṃ disvā evamāha “bhikkhave, tumhe etaṃ bhikkhuṃ anicchamānaṃ ādāya āgatā, kiṃ kataṃ iminā”ti? “Bhante, ayaṃ bhikkhu evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā samaṇadhammaṃ karonto vīriyaṃ ossajitvā āgato”ti āhaṃsu. Atha naṃ satthā āha “saccaṃ kira tayā bhikkhu vīriyaṃ ossaṭṭha”nti? “Saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti. “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ bhikkhu evarūpe mama sāsane pabbajitvā ‘appiccho’ti vā ‘santuṭṭho’ti vā ‘pavivitto’ti vā ‘āraddhavīriyo’ti vā evaṃ attānaṃ ajānāpetvā ‘ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhū’ti jānāpesi. Nanu tvaṃ pubbe vīriyavā ahosi, tayā ekena kataṃ vīriyaṃ nissāya marukantāre pañcasu sakaṭasatesu manussā ca goṇā [M 1.0123] ca pānīyaṃ labhitvā sukhitā jātā[V 1.0115], idāni kasmā vīriyaṃ ossajasī”ti. So bhikkhu ettakena vacanena upatthambhito ahosi.

Seeing him, the Teacher said: 'Monks, you have brought this monk here against his will. What has he done?' 'Venerable sir,' they replied, 'this monk, having gone forth in such a dispensation that leads to liberation, abandoned his effort while practicing the ascetic's duty and has returned.' Then the Teacher asked him: 'Is it true, monk, that you have abandoned your effort?' 'It is true, Blessed One.' 'Why is it, monk, that having gone forth in such a dispensation as mine, you did not make yourself known as one of few desires, or as content, or as secluded, or as one with aroused energy, but instead made yourself known as a monk who has abandoned his effort? Were you not energetic in the past? Relying on the effort made by you alone, the people and oxen of five hundred carts obtained water in the desert and became happy. Why do you now abandon your effort?' That monk was heartened by these words.

Taṃ pana kathaṃ sutvā bhikkhū bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu – “bhante, idāni iminā bhikkhunā vīriyassa ossaṭṭhabhāvo amhākaṃ pākaṭo, pubbe panassa ekassa vīriyaṃ nissāya marukantāre goṇamanussānaṃ pānīyaṃ labhitvā sukhitabhāvo paṭicchanno, tumhākaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇasseva pākaṭo, amhākampetaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathethā”ti. “Tena hi, bhikkhave, suṇāthā”ti bhagavā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ satuppādaṃ janetvā bhavantarena paṭicchannakāraṇaṃ pākaṭamakāsi.

Hearing this account, the monks requested of the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, that this monk has now abandoned his effort is evident to us. But the former matter—that relying on his effort alone, the men and oxen obtained water in the desert and found relief—was hidden from us. It was evident only to your omniscient knowledge. Please tell us this story.' 'In that case, monks, listen,' said the Blessed One, and having aroused mindfulness in those monks, he made manifest the matter that was concealed by another existence.

Atīte kāsiraṭṭhe bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto satthavāhakule paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā vayappatto pañcahi sakaṭasatehi vaṇijjaṃ karonto vicarati. So ekadā saṭṭhiyojanikaṃ marukantāraṃ paṭipajji. Tasmiṃ kantāre sukhumavālukā muṭṭhinā gahitā hatthe na tiṭṭhati, sūriyuggamanato paṭṭhāya aṅgārarāsi viya uṇhā hoti, na sakkā akkamituṃ. Tasmā taṃ paṭipajjantā dārudakatilataṇḍulādīni sakaṭehi ādāya rattimeva gantvā aruṇuggamane sakaṭāni parivaṭṭaṃ katvā matthake maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā kālasseva āhārakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā chāyāya nisinnā divasaṃ khepetvā atthaṅgate sūriye sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā bhūmiyā sītalāya jātāya sakaṭāni yojetvā gacchanti, samuddagamanasadisameva gamanaṃ hoti. Thalaniyāmako nāma laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, so tārakasaññā [P 1.0108] satthaṃ tāreti.

In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the family of a caravan leader. Having come of age, he went about conducting trade with five hundred carts. He once entered upon a desert sixty yojanas in extent. In that desert, the sand is so fine that when grasped by the fist, it does not remain in the hand. From sunrise onwards, it becomes as hot as a heap of embers and cannot be walked upon. Therefore, those who travel through it take firewood, water, oil, rice, and other provisions in their carts and travel only by night. At dawn, they arrange the carts in a circle, erect a canopy overhead, finish their morning meal early, and pass the day sitting in the shade. When the sun has set, they eat their evening meal, and once the ground has cooled, they yoke the carts and proceed. The journey is indeed like a sea voyage. A 'land-pilot,' as he is called, must be obtained; he guides the caravan by the signs of the stars.

Sopi satthavāho tasmiṃ kāle imināva niyāmena taṃ kantāraṃ gacchanto ekūnasaṭṭhi yojanāni gantvā “idāni ekaratteneva marukantārā nikkhamanaṃ bhavissatī”ti sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā sabbaṃ dārudakaṃ khepetvā sakaṭāni yojetvā pāyāsi. Niyāmako pana purimasakaṭe āsanaṃ pattharāpetvā ākāse tārakaṃ olokento “ito pājetha, ito pājethā”ti vadamāno nipajji. So dīghamaddhānaṃ aniddāyanabhāvena kilanto niddaṃ okkami, goṇe nivattitvā āgatamaggameva gaṇhante na [M 1.0124] aññāsi. Goṇā sabbarattiṃ agamaṃsu. Niyāmako aruṇuggamanavelāya pabuddho nakkhattaṃ oloketvā “sakaṭāni nivattetha nivattethā”ti āha. Sakaṭāni nivattetvā paṭipāṭiṃ karontānaññeva aruṇo uggato. Manussā “hiyyo amhākaṃ niviṭṭhakhandhāvāraṭṭhānamevetaṃ, dārudakampi no khīṇaṃ, idāni naṭṭhamhā”ti sakaṭāni mocetvā parivaṭṭakena ṭhapetvā matthake maṇḍapaṃ katvā attano attano sakaṭassa heṭṭhā anusocantā nipajjiṃsu.

That caravan leader, traveling through the desert in this same manner, had gone fifty-nine yojanas and thought, 'Now, in just one more night, we will get out of this desert.' After the evening meal, having used up all the firewood and water, he had the carts yoked and set out. The land-pilot, however, had a seat spread for him on the lead cart and, while observing the stars in the sky and saying, 'Drive this way, drive that way,' he lay down. As he was exhausted from being sleepless for a long time, he fell into a deep sleep and did not notice that the oxen had turned around and taken the very same path by which they had come. The oxen went on for the entire night. At the time of dawn, the land-pilot awoke, and observing the constellations, he cried out, 'Turn the carts around! Turn them around!' Just as they were turning the carts and arranging them in formation, the sun rose. The men realized, 'This is the very same place we camped yesterday! Our firewood and water are gone. Now we are ruined!' They unyoked the carts, arranged them in a circle, erected a canopy overhead, and lay down beneath their respective carts, despairing.

Bodhisatto [V 1.0116] “mayi vīriyaṃ ossajante sabbe vinassissantī”ti pāto sītalavelāyameva āhiṇḍanto ekaṃ dabbatiṇagacchaṃ disvā “imāni tiṇāni heṭṭhā udakasinehena uṭṭhitāni bhavissantī”ti cintetvā kuddālaṃ gāhāpetvā taṃ padesaṃ khaṇāpesi, te saṭṭhihatthaṭṭhānaṃ khaṇiṃsu. Ettakaṃ ṭhānaṃ khaṇitvā paharantānaṃ kuddālo heṭṭhāpāsāṇe paṭihaññi, pahaṭamatte sabbe vīriyaṃ ossajiṃsu. Bodhisatto pana “imassa pāsāṇassa heṭṭhā udakena bhavitabba”nti otaritvā pāsāṇe ṭhito oṇamitvā sotaṃ odahitvā saddaṃ āvajjento heṭṭhā udakassa pavattanasaddaṃ sutvā uttaritvā cūḷupaṭṭhākaṃ āha – “tāta, tayā vīriye ossaṭṭhe sabbe vinassissāma, tvaṃ vīriyaṃ anossajanto imaṃ ayakūṭaṃ gahetvā āvāṭaṃ otaritvā etasmiṃ pāsāṇe pahāraṃ dehī”ti. So tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā sabbesu [P 1.0109] vīriyaṃ ossajitvā ṭhitesupi vīriyaṃ anossajanto otaritvā pāsāṇe pahāraṃ adāsi. Pāsāṇo majjhe bhijjitvā heṭṭhā patitvā sotaṃ sannirumbhitvā aṭṭhāsi, tālakkhandhappamāṇā udakavaṭṭi uggañchi. Sabbe pānīyaṃ pivitvā nhāyiṃsu, atirekāni akkhayugādīni phāletvā yāgubhattaṃ pacitvā bhuñjitvā goṇe ca bhojetvā sūriye atthaṅgate udakāvāṭasamīpe dhajaṃ bandhitvā icchitaṭṭhānaṃ agamaṃsu. Te tattha bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇitvā diguṇaṃ tiguṇaṃ catugguṇaṃ lābhaṃ labhitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamaṃsu. Te tattha yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gatā, bodhisattopi dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammameva gato.

The Bodhisatta thought, 'If I abandon my effort, all will perish.' Early in the cool morning, while wandering about, he saw a clump of dabba grass and thought, 'This grass must have grown due to moisture below.' He had a spade brought and had that spot dug. They dug to a depth of sixty cubits. After digging that far, as they struck, the spade hit a rock below. As soon as it was struck, they all gave up their effort. But the Bodhisatta, thinking, 'There must be water beneath this rock,' descended and stood on the rock. Bending down, he placed his ear to it and, paying attention to the sound, heard the sound of water flowing below. He climbed up and said to his young attendant, 'My dear, if you give up your effort, we will all perish. Do not give up your effort. Take this iron hammer, descend into the pit, and strike this rock.' Accepting his words, although all the others stood by having given up their effort, he did not abandon his. He descended and struck the rock. The rock split in the middle, fell below, and obstructed the current. A column of water the size of a palm trunk gushed forth. Everyone drank the water and bathed. They broke up their extra axles and yokes for firewood, cooked and ate rice porridge, fed the oxen, and when the sun had set, they tied a banner near the water pit and went to their desired destination. There they sold their goods, gaining double, triple, and quadruple profits, and returned to their own dwelling place. They lived there for the rest of their lives and passed away according to their kamma. The Bodhisatta too, having performed meritorious deeds such as generosity, passed away according to his kamma.

Sammāsambuddho imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ kathetvā abhisambuddhova imaṃ gāthaṃ kathesi –

The Perfectly Enlightened One, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, then, being fully enlightened, spoke this verse:

2.

2.

“Akilāsuno [M 1.0125] vaṇṇupathe khaṇantā, udaṅgaṇe tattha papaṃ avinduṃ;

Evaṃ munī vīriyabalūpapanno, akilāsu vinde hadayassa santi”nti.

“Just as the untiring, digging in a sandy tract, found water there in the open ground; even so the sage, endowed with the power of energy, untiring, may find peace of heart.”

Tattha akilāsunoti nikkosajjā āraddhavīriyā. Vaṇṇupatheti vaṇṇu vuccati vālukā, vālukāmaggeti attho. Khaṇantāti bhūmiṃ khaṇamānā. Udaṅgaṇeti ettha udāti nipāto, aṅgaṇeti manussānaṃ sañcaraṇaṭṭhāne, anāvāṭe bhūmibhāgeti attho. Tatthāti tasmiṃ vaṇṇupathe. Papaṃ avindunti udakaṃ paṭilabhiṃsu. Udakañhi papīyanabhāvena “papā”ti vuccati. Pavaddhaṃ vā āpaṃ papaṃ, mahodakanti attho.

Herein, akilāsuno means not indolent, of ardent energy. Vaṇṇupathe means: vaṇṇu is said to be sand; the meaning is 'on a sandy path.' Khaṇantā means digging the earth. Udaṅgaṇe: here uda is a particle; aṅgaṇe means in a place where people travel, that is, in an open area of ground, not in a pit. Tattha means in that sandy path. Papaṃ avinduṃ means they obtained water. For water is called papaṃ because it is to be drunk. Or, papaṃ is abundant water (pavaddhaṃ āpaṃ), meaning a great quantity of water.

Evanti opammapaṭipādanaṃ. Munīti monaṃ vuccati ñāṇaṃ, kāyamoneyyādīsu vā aññataraṃ, tena samannāgatattā puggalo “munī”ti vuccati. So panesa agāriyamuni, anagāriyamuni[V 1.0117], sekkhamuni, asekkhamuni, paccekabuddhamuni, munimunīti anekavidho. Tattha agāriyamunīti gihī āgataphalo viññātasāsano. Anagāriyamunīti tathārūpova pabbajito. Sekkhamunīti satta sekkhā. Asekkhamunīti khīṇāsavo. Paccekabuddhamunīti paccekasambuddho. Munimunīti sammāsambuddho. Imasmiṃ panatthe sabbasaṅgāhakavasena [P 1.0110] moneyyasaṅkhātāya paññāya samannāgato “munī”ti veditabbo. Vīriyabalūpapannoti vīriyena ceva kāyabalañāṇabalena ca samannāgato. Akilāsūti nikkosajjo –

'Evaṃ' ('Thus') indicates the application of the simile. 'Munī': 'mona' is said to be knowledge (ñāṇa), or one of the kinds of sagehood (moneyya) such as sagehood of body; because of being endowed with that, a person is called a 'muni'. Now, this muni is of many kinds: the householder sage (agāriyamuni), the homeless sage (anagāriyamuni), the trainee sage (sekkhamuni), the adept sage (asekkhamuni), the solitary sage (paccekabuddhamuni), and the Sage of sages (munimuni). Herein, the householder sage is a layperson who has attained a fruit and has understood the Teaching. The homeless sage is one of the same attainment who has gone forth. The trainee sage refers to the seven kinds of trainees. The adept sage is one whose cankers are destroyed. The solitary sage is a Paccekabuddha. The Sage of sages is the Perfectly Enlightened One. In this context, however, 'muni' is to be understood in an all-encompassing sense as one endowed with the wisdom called sagehood (moneyya). 'Vīriyabalūpapanno' ('endowed with the power of energy') means endowed with energy and with the power of the body and the power of knowledge. 'Akilāsu' ('untiring') means not indolent—

“Kāmaṃ taco ca nhāru ca, aṭṭhi ca avasissatu;

Upasussatu nissesaṃ, sarīre maṃsalohita”nti. –

“‘Willingly, let only skin, sinews, and bones remain; let the flesh and blood in my body dry up completely.’”

Evaṃ vuttena caturaṅgasamannāgatena vīriyena samannāgatattā analaso. Vinde hadayassa santinti cittassapi hadayarūpassapi sītalabhāvakaraṇena “santi”nti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ jhānavipassanābhiññāarahattamaggañāṇasaṅkhātaṃ ariyadhammaṃ vindati paṭilabhatīti attho. Bhagavatā hi –

—thus, being endowed with the four-factored energy just described, one is not indolent. Vinde hadayassa santiṃ ('may find peace of heart') means: by making cool both the mind (citta) and the heart-basis (hadayarūpa), one finds, one obtains the noble Dhamma designated as 'peace' (santi), which is reckoned as absorption (jhāna), insight (vipassanā), direct knowledges (abhiññā), and the path knowledge of Arahantship. For the Blessed One has said:

“Dukkhaṃ, bhikkhave, kusīto viharati vokiṇṇo pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehi, mahantañca sadatthaṃ parihāpeti. Āraddhavīriyo ca kho, bhikkhave, sukhaṃ viharati pavivitto pāpakehi akusalehi [M 1.0126] dhammehi, mahantañca sadatthaṃ paripūreti, na, bhikkhave, hīnena aggassa patti hotī”ti (saṃ. ni. 2.22) –

“‘Bhikkhus, the indolent person dwells in suffering, mixed up with evil, unwholesome states, and they neglect their own great welfare. But the energetic person, bhikkhus, dwells happily, secluded from evil, unwholesome states, and they fulfill their own great welfare. Bhikkhus, the highest is not attained by that which is inferior.’ (SN 12.22)”

Evaṃ anekehi suttehi kusītassa dukkhavihāro, āraddhavīriyassa ca sukhavihāro saṃvaṇṇito. Idhāpi āraddhavīriyassa akatābhinivesassa vipassakassa vīriyabalena adhigantabbaṃ tameva sukhavihāraṃ dassento “evaṃ munī vīriyabalūpapanno, akilāsu vinde hadayassa santi”nti āha. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā te vāṇijā akilāsuno vaṇṇupathe khaṇantā udakaṃ labhiṃsu, evaṃ imasmimpi sāsane akilāsu hutvā vāyamamāno paṇḍito bhikkhu imaṃ jhānādibhedaṃ hadayassa santiṃ labhati. So tvaṃ bhikkhu pubbe udakamattassa atthāya vīriyaṃ katvā idāni evarūpe maggaphaladāyake niyyānikasāsane kasmā vīriyaṃ ossajasīti evaṃ imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ dassetvā cattāri saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

Thus, in many suttas, the painful dwelling of the indolent and the pleasant dwelling of the energetic are praised. Here too, showing that this same pleasant dwelling is to be attained through the power of energy by an insight meditator who is energetic and not fixated on what is yet to be done, he said: 'Even so the sage, endowed with the power of energy, untiring, may find peace of heart.' This is the meaning: just as those merchants, being untiring, found water by digging in the sandy tract, so too in this Teaching, a wise bhikkhu, striving without indolence, attains this peace of heart which consists of absorption and so on. You, bhikkhu, previously made an effort for the sake of mere water; why do you now relax your effort in such a liberating Teaching that leads to the path and its fruit? Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher revealed the Four Truths. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, the bhikkhu who had relaxed his effort was established in the highest fruit, in Arahantship.

Satthāpi [V 1.0118] dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānetvā dassesi “tasmiṃ samaye vīriyaṃ anossajitvā pāsāṇaṃ bhinditvā mahājanassa udakadāyako cūḷupaṭṭhāko ayaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu ahosi, avasesaparisā idāni buddhaparisā jātā, satthavāhajeṭṭhako pana ahameva ahosi”nti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

The Teacher, having related the two stories and connected the narrative, identified the birth story, saying: 'At that time, the young attendant who, without relaxing his effort, broke the rock and gave water to the great multitude, was this very monk of relaxed effort. The remaining assembly has now become the Buddha's assembly, and the chief caravan leader was I myself.' Thus, he concluded the discourse.

Vaṇṇupathajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Vaṇṇupatha Jātaka, the Second.

3. Serivavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Serivavāṇija Jātaka

Idha ce naṃ virādhesīti imampi dhammadesanaṃ bhagavā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto ekaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyameva bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi purimanayeneva bhikkhūhi ānītaṃ disvā satthā āha – “tvaṃ bhikkhu, evarūpe maggaphaladāyake sāsane [P 1.0111] pabbajitvā vīriyaṃ ossajanto satasahassagghanikāya kañcanapātiyā parihīno serivavāṇijo viya ciraṃ socissasī”ti. Bhikkhū tassatthassa [M 1.0127] āvibhāvatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu, bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannakāraṇaṃ pākaṭamakāsi.

'If he misses it here': this Dhamma discourse the Blessed One delivered while dwelling in Sāvatthī concerning a certain monk of relaxed effort. For, seeing him brought by the monks in the same way as before, the Teacher said: 'Monk, having gone forth in such a Dispensation that gives the path and its fruit, by relaxing your effort you will grieve for a long time, like the merchant of Seriva who was deprived of the golden bowl worth a hundred thousand.' The monks requested the Blessed One to make its meaning clear, and the Blessed One revealed the cause which was hidden by a previous existence.

Atīte ito pañcame kappe bodhisatto serivaraṭṭhe kacchapuṭavāṇijo ahosi. So serivanāmakena ekena lolakacchapuṭavāṇijena saddhiṃ vohāratthāya gacchanto nīlavāhaṃ nāma nadiṃ uttaritvā ariṭṭhapuraṃ nāma nagaraṃ pavisanto nagaravīthiyo bhājetvā attano pattavīthiyā bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇanto vicari. Itaropi attano pattavīthiṃ gaṇhi. Tasmiñca nagare ekaṃ seṭṭhikulaṃ parijiṇṇaṃ ahosi, sabbe puttabhātikā ca dhanañca parikkhayaṃ agamaṃsu, ekā dārikā ayyikāya saddhiṃ avasesā ahosi, tā dvepi paresaṃ bhatiṃ katvā jīvanti. Gehe pana tāsaṃ mahāseṭṭhinā paribhuttapubbā suvaṇṇapāti bhājanantare nikkhittā dīgharattaṃ avalañjiyamānā malaggahitā ahosi, tā tassā suvaṇṇapātibhāvampi na jānanti. So lolavāṇijo tasmiṃ samaye “maṇike gaṇhatha, maṇike gaṇhathā”ti vicaranto taṃ gharadvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Sā kumārikā taṃ disvā ayyikaṃ āha “amma mayhaṃ ekaṃ piḷandhanaṃ gaṇhā”ti. Amma mayaṃ duggatā, kiṃ datvā gaṇhissāmāti. Ayaṃ no pāti atthi, no ca amhākaṃ upakārā, imaṃ datvā gaṇhāti. Sā vāṇijaṃ pakkosāpetvā āsane nisīdāpetvā taṃ pātiṃ datvā “ayya, imaṃ gahetvā tava bhaginiyā kiñcideva dehī”ti āha. Vāṇijo pātiṃ hatthena gahetvāva “suvaṇṇapāti bhavissatī”ti parivattetvā pātipiṭṭhiyaṃ sūciyā lekhaṃ kaḍḍhitvā suvaṇṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā [V 1.0119] “imāsaṃ kiñci adatvāva imaṃ pātiṃ harissāmī”ti “ayaṃ kiṃ agghati, aḍḍhamāsakopissā mūlaṃ na [P 1.0112] hotī”ti bhūmiyaṃ khipitvā uṭṭhāyāsanā pakkāmi. Ekena pavisitvā nikkhantavīthiṃ itaro pavisituṃ labhatīti bodhisatto taṃ vīthiṃ pavisitvā “maṇike gaṇhatha, maṇike gaṇhathā”ti vicaranto tameva gharadvāraṃ pāpuṇi.

In the past, five aeons ago, the Bodhisatta was a peddler in the country of Seriva. Traveling for trade with a greedy peddler named Seriva, he crossed the river Nīlavāha and entered the city named Ariṭṭhapura. They divided the city streets, and he went along his assigned street selling his wares. The other merchant also took his assigned street. In that city, a noble family had fallen into ruin; all the sons and brothers had passed away and their wealth was gone. Only a young girl with her grandmother remained, and the two survived by working for hire. In their house, however, was a golden bowl formerly used by the head of the family. Placed among other vessels and unused for a long time, it was covered with grime. They did not even know it was a golden bowl. At that time, the greedy peddler, wandering about and calling, 'Buy trinkets, buy trinkets!' reached their door. The young girl saw him and said to her grandmother, 'Mother, buy an ornament for me.' 'My dear, we are poor. What can we give to buy one?' 'We have this bowl, which is of no use to us. Give this and get something.' She had the peddler called in, seated him, and gave him the bowl, saying, 'Sir, take this and give your little sister something.' The peddler took the bowl, and suspecting it might be gold, turned it over and scratched a line on the back with a needle. Knowing it was gold, he thought, 'I will take this bowl without giving them anything,' and said, 'What is this worth? It is not even worth half a māsaka!' Throwing it to the ground, he rose from his seat and left. As it was the custom that a second merchant could enter a street that the first had already gone through, the Bodhisatta entered that street, calling, 'Buy trinkets, buy trinkets!' and arrived at the same door.

Puna sā kumārikā tatheva ayyikaṃ āha. Atha naṃ ayyikā “amma, paṭhamaṃ āgatavāṇijo pātiṃ bhūmiyaṃ khipitvā gato, idāni kiṃ datvā gaṇhissāmā”ti āha. Amma, so vāṇijo pharusavāco, ayaṃ pana piyadassano mudusallāpo, appeva nāma naṃ gaṇheyyāti. Amma, tena hi pakkosāhīti. Sā taṃ pakkosi. Athassa gehaṃ pavisitvā nisinnassa [M 1.0128] taṃ pātiṃ adaṃsu. So tassā suvaṇṇapātibhāvaṃ ñatvā “amma, ayaṃ pāti satasahassaṃ agghati, satasahassagghanakabhaṇḍaṃ mayhaṃ hatthe natthī”ti āha. Ayya, paṭhamaṃ āgatavāṇijo “ayaṃ aḍḍhamāsakampi na agghatī”ti vatvā bhūmiyaṃ khipitvā gato, ayaṃ pana tava puññena suvaṇṇapāti jātā bhavissati, mayaṃ imaṃ tuyhaṃ dema, kiñcideva no datvā imaṃ gahetvā yāhīti. Bodhisatto tasmiṃ khaṇe hatthagatāni pañca kahāpaṇasatāni pañcasatagghanakañca bhaṇḍaṃ sabbaṃ datvā “mayhaṃ imaṃ tulañca pasibbakañca aṭṭha ca kahāpaṇe dethā”ti ettakaṃ yācitvā ādāya pakkāmi. So sīghameva nadītīraṃ gantvā nāvikassa aṭṭha kahāpaṇe datvā nāvaṃ abhiruhi.

Again, the young girl spoke to her grandmother in the same way. Then the grandmother said to her, 'My dear, the first peddler who came threw the bowl on the ground and left. Now what can we give to buy anything?' 'Mother, that peddler was harsh-spoken, but this one is pleasant to see and gentle in speech. Perhaps he might take it.' 'In that case, Mother, call him.' She called him. When he had entered the house and was seated, they gave him the bowl. He, knowing it was a golden bowl, said, 'Mother, this bowl is worth a hundred thousand; I do not have goods worth a hundred thousand in my possession.' 'Sir, the first peddler who came said, "This is not worth even half a māsaka," threw it on the ground, and left. Through your merit, it must have become a golden bowl. We give it to you. Just give us something for it, take it, and go.' At that moment, the Bodhisatta gave them the five hundred kahāpanas he had on hand and all his wares, worth another five hundred. He then asked for his scale, his bag, and eight kahāpanas, and taking only these, he departed. Going quickly to the riverbank, he gave the eight kahāpanas to the ferryman and boarded the boat.

Tato lolavāṇijopi puna taṃ gehaṃ gantvā “āharatha taṃ pātiṃ, tumhākaṃ kiñcideva dassāmī”ti āha. Sā taṃ paribhāsitvā “tvaṃ amhākaṃ satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ aḍḍhamāsagghanikampi na akāsi, tuyhaṃ pana sāmikasadiso eko dhammiko vāṇijo amhākaṃ sahassaṃ datvā taṃ ādāya gato”ti āha. Taṃ sutvāva “satasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇapātiyā parihīnomhi, mahājānikaro vata me aya”nti sañjātabalavasoko satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkonto [P 1.0113] visaññī hutvā attano hatthagate kahāpaṇe ceva bhaṇḍikañca gharadvāreyeva vikiritvā nivāsanapārupanaṃ pahāya tulādaṇḍaṃ muggaraṃ katvā ādāya bodhisattassa anupadaṃ pakkanto nadītīraṃ gantvā bodhisattaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā “ambho, nāvika, nāvaṃ nivattehī”ti āha. Bodhisatto pana “tāta, mā nivattayī”ti paṭisedhesi. Itarassapi bodhisattaṃ gacchantaṃ passantasseva balavasoko udapādi, hadayaṃ uṇhaṃ ahosi, mukhato lohitaṃ uggañchi, vāpikaddamo viya hadayaṃ phali. So bodhisatte āghātaṃ bandhitvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi[V 1.0120]. Idaṃ paṭhamaṃ devadattassa bodhisatte āghātabandhanaṃ. Bodhisatto dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Then the greedy merchant went back to that house and said, “Bring that bowl; I will give you something.” She scolded him, saying, “You did not value our golden bowl, worth a hundred thousand, even at half a māsaka; but a righteous merchant, like your master, gave us a thousand and took it away.” Hearing this, he thought, “I have lost a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand—this is indeed a great loss for me!” Overwhelmed by intense grief and unable to regain his composure, he became senseless. Right at the doorstep of the house, he scattered the coins he held and his merchandise, discarded his lower and upper garments, took his balance-beam as a club, and set out following the Bodhisatta. Reaching the riverbank, he saw the Bodhisatta departing and called out, “Ho, boatman, turn the boat back!” But the Bodhisatta forbade it, saying, “Good sir, do not turn it back.” As the other man watched the Bodhisatta departing, intense grief arose in him. His heart grew hot, blood gushed from his mouth, and his heart burst like mud from a pond. Conceiving hatred toward the Bodhisatta, he met his end right there. This was Devadatta’s first instance of forming hatred toward the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds such as generosity, departed according to his kamma.

Sammāsambuddho imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ kathetvā abhisambuddhova imaṃ gāthaṃ kathesi –

The Perfectly Enlightened One, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, then, as one who is fully enlightened, spoke this verse:

3.

3.

“Idha [M 1.0129] ce naṃ virādhesi, saddhammassa niyāmataṃ;

Ciraṃ tvaṃ anutappesi, serivāyaṃva vāṇijo”ti.

“If here you fail to attain it, the fixed path of the True Dhamma, long will you regret it, like the merchant Seriva.”

Tattha idha ce naṃ virādhesi, saddhammassa niyāmatanti imasmiṃ sāsane etaṃ saddhammassa niyāmatāsaṅkhātaṃ sotāpattimaggaṃ virādhesi. Yadi virādhesi, vīriyaṃ ossajanto nādhigacchasi na paṭilabhasīti attho. Ciraṃ tvaṃ anutappesīti evaṃ sante tvaṃ dīghamaddhānaṃ socanto paridevanto anutapessasi, atha vā ossaṭṭhavīriyatāya ariyamaggassa virādhitattā dīgharattaṃ nirayādīsu uppanno nānappakārāni dukkhāni anubhavanto anutappissasi kilamissasīti ayamettha attho. Kathaṃ? Serivāyaṃva vāṇijoti “serivā”ti evaṃnāmako ayaṃ vāṇijo yathā. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – yathā pubbe serivanāmako vāṇijo satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ labhitvā tassā gahaṇatthāya vīriyaṃ akatvā tato parihīno anutappi, evameva tvampi imasmiṃ sāsane paṭiyattasuvaṇṇapātisadisaṃ ariyamaggaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyatāya anadhigacchanto tato parihīno dīgharattaṃ anutappissasi. Sace pana vīriyaṃ na ossajissasi, paṇḍitavāṇijo suvaṇṇapātiṃ viya mama sāsane navavidhampi lokuttaradhammaṃ paṭilabhissasīti.

Herein, if here you fail to attain it, the fixed path of the True Dhamma means: if in this Dispensation you fail to attain this path of stream-entry, designated as the fixed path of the True Dhamma. If you fail to attain it means that by abandoning effort, you do not achieve or obtain it. Long will you regret it means: in that case, you will grieve, lament, and regret for a long time. Or, having failed to attain the Noble Path due to abandoning effort, you will be reborn in states of woe such as hell for a long time, experiencing various kinds of suffering, and you will regret and be exhausted—this is the meaning here. How so? Like the merchant Seriva means: just as this merchant named Seriva. This is what is said: Just as formerly the merchant named Seriva, having had the opportunity to acquire a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, did not make an effort to take it and, being deprived of it, regretted it; so too will you, in this Dispensation, by not attaining the Noble Path—which is like a prepared golden bowl—due to abandoning effort, be deprived of it and regret it for a long time. But if you do not abandon effort, you will obtain the ninefold supramundane Dhamma in my Dispensation, just as the wise merchant obtained the golden bowl.

Evamassa [P 1.0114] satthā arahattena kūṭaṃ gaṇhanto imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ dassetvā cattāri saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

Thus the Teacher, bringing this Dhamma discourse to its climax in Arahantship, revealed it and then explained the Four Truths. At the conclusion of the explanation of the Truths, the monk who had been lax in effort was established in the highest fruit, Arahantship.

Satthāpi dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānetvā dassesi – “tadā bālavāṇijo devadatto ahosi, paṇḍitavāṇijo pana ahameva ahosi”nti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

The Teacher, having related the two stories, connected the threads and identified the characters of the Jātaka, concluding the discourse thus: “At that time, the foolish merchant was Devadatta, and the wise merchant was I myself.”

Serivavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Merchant Seriva, the Third.

4. Cūḷaseṭṭhijātakavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Minor Seṭṭhi

Appakenapi [V 1.0121][M 1.0130] medhāvīti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ bhagavā rājagahaṃ upanissāya jīvakambavane viharanto cūḷapanthakattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi.

The Blessed One delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with the words, “Even with little, a wise person...” while dwelling near Rājagaha in Jīvaka’s Mango Grove, concerning the Elder Cūḷapanthaka.

Tattha cūḷapanthakassa tāva nibbatti kathetabbā. Rājagahe kira dhanaseṭṭhikulassa dhītā attano dāseneva saddhiṃ santhavaṃ katvā “aññepi me imaṃ kammaṃ jāneyyu”nti bhītā evamāha “amhehi imasmiṃ ṭhāne vasituṃ na sakkā, sace me mātāpitaro imaṃ dosaṃ jānissanti, khaṇḍākhaṇḍaṃ karissanti, videsaṃ gantvā vasissāmā”ti hatthasāraṃ gahetvā aggadvārena nikkhamitvā “yattha vā tattha vā aññehi ajānanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vasissāmā”ti ubhopi agamaṃsu.

In this connection, the birth of Cūḷapanthaka is to be related first. In Rājagaha, it is said, the daughter of a wealthy seṭṭhi’s family became intimate with her own slave. Fearing that others might learn of this deed, she said, “We cannot stay in this place. If my parents find out about this transgression, they will cut us to pieces. Let us go to another country and live there.” Taking their valuables, they left by the main gate, thinking, “We will go and live in some place or other where we will not be known by others.” Thus, they both departed.

Tesaṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantānaṃ saṃvāsamanvāya tassā kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhāsi. Sā gabbhaparipākaṃ āgamma sāmikena saddhiṃ mantesi “gabbho me paripākaṃ gato, ñātibandhuvirahite ṭhāne gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ nāma ubhinnampi amhākaṃ dukkhameva, kulagehameva gacchāmā”ti. So “sacāhaṃ gamissāmi, jīvitaṃ me natthī”ti cintetvā “ajja gacchāma, sve gacchāmā”ti divase atikkāmesi. Sā cintesi “ayaṃ bālo attano dosamahantatāya gantuṃ na ussahati, mātāpitaro nāma ekantahitā, ayaṃ gacchatu vā mā vā, mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Sā tasmiṃ gehā nikkhante gehaparikkhāraṃ paṭisāmetvā attano kulagharaṃ gatabhāvaṃ anantaragehavāsīnaṃ ārocetvā maggaṃ paṭipajji.

While they were living in a certain place, as a result of their cohabitation, a child was conceived in her womb. When her pregnancy came to term, she conferred with her husband, saying, “My pregnancy is full-term. To give birth in a place devoid of relatives and friends will be a hardship for us both. Let us go to my family’s home.” But he, thinking, “If I go, my life is forfeit,” let the days pass, saying, “We will go today; we will go tomorrow.” She thought, “This fool does not dare to go because of the gravity of his transgression. Parents, however, are truly well-wishers. Whether he goes or not, I ought to go.” When he had left the house, she put the household goods in order, informed her next-door neighbors that she had gone to her family’s home, and set out on her journey.

Atha so puriso gharaṃ āgato taṃ adisvā paṭivissake pucchitvā “kulagharaṃ gatā”ti sutvā vegena anubandhitvā antarāmagge sampāpuṇi. Tassāpi tattheva gabbhavuṭṭhānaṃ ahosi. So “kiṃ idaṃ bhadde”ti pucchi. “Sāmi, eko putto jāto”ti. “Idāni kiṃ karissāmā”ti? “Yassatthāya mayaṃ kulagharaṃ gaccheyyāma, taṃ kammaṃ antarāva nipphannaṃ, tattha gantvā kiṃ karissāma, nivattāmā”ti dvepi ekacittā hutvā nivattiṃsu. Tassa ca dārakassa panthe jātattā “panthako”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu[P 1.0115]. Tassā na cirasseva aparopi gabbho patiṭṭhahi. Sabbaṃ purimanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Tassāpi dārakassa panthe jātattā paṭhamajātassa “mahāpanthako”ti nāmaṃ [M 1.0131] katvā itarassa “cūḷapanthako”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Te dvepi dārake gahetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva āgatā.

Then that man, having returned home and not seeing her, asked the neighbors. Hearing that she had gone to her family’s house, he quickly followed and caught up with her along the way. For her, the birth occurred right there on the path. He asked, “What is this, my dear?” “Sir, a son has been born,” she replied. “Now what shall we do?” “The purpose for which we were going to my family’s house has been fulfilled along the way. What would we do by going there now? Let us turn back.” Both of them, being of one mind, turned back. And because the boy was born on the path, they named him Panthaka. Not long after, she conceived again. The entire account should be elaborated as before. For that boy too, since he was born on the path, they named the firstborn Mahāpanthaka and the other Cūḷapanthaka. Taking the two boys, they returned to their own dwelling place.

Tesaṃ [V 1.0122] tattha vasantānaṃ ayaṃ mahāpanthakadārako aññe dārake “cūḷapitā mahāpitā”ti, “ayyako ayyikā”ti ca vadante sutvā mātaraṃ pucchi “amma, aññe dārakā ‘cūḷapitā mahāpitā’tipi vadanti, ‘ayyako ayyikā’tipi vadanti, amhākaṃ ñātakā natthī”ti. “Āma, tāta, tumhākaṃ ettha ñātakā natthi, rājagahanagare pana vo dhanaseṭṭhi nāma ayyako, tattha tumhākaṃ bahū ñātakā”ti. “Kasmā tattha na gacchatha, ammā”ti? Sā attano agamanakāraṇaṃ puttassa akathetvā puttesu punappunaṃ kathentesu sāmikaṃ āha – “ime dārakā maṃ ativiya kilamenti, kiṃ no mātāpitaro disvā maṃsaṃ khādissanti, ehi dārakānaṃ ayyakakulaṃ dassessāmā”ti. “Ahaṃ sammukhā bhavituṃ na sakkhissāmi, taṃ pana tattha nayissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, ayya, yena kenaci upāyena dārakānaṃ ayyakakulameva daṭṭhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti dvepi janā dārake ādāya anupubbena rājagahaṃ patvā nagaradvāre ekissā sālāya nivāsaṃ katvā dārakamātā dve dārake gahetvā āgatabhāvaṃ mātāpitūnaṃ ārocāpesi.

While they were living there, the boy Mahāpanthaka, hearing other boys saying, “Younger uncle, elder uncle,” and “Grandfather, grandmother,” asked his mother, “Mother, other boys say ‘younger uncle, elder uncle’ and ‘grandfather, grandmother,’ but do we have no relatives?” “Indeed, dear son, you have no relatives here, but in the city of Rājagaha, you have a grandfather named Dhanaseṭṭhi. There, you have many relatives.” “Why do we not go there, mother?” she asked. Without telling her son the reason for not going, when the children kept asking repeatedly, she said to her husband, “These children are greatly vexing me. What, will my parents eat my flesh if they see me? Come, let us show the children their grandfather’s family.” “I cannot appear before them, but I will take you there.” “Good, sir, by whatever means, it is right for the children to see their grandfather’s family.” Taking both children, the two of them gradually reached Rājagaha. At the city gate, they took up residence in a certain hall. The children’s mother then sent a message to her parents, informing them of her arrival with the two children.

Te taṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā “saṃsāre vicarantānaṃ na putto na dhītā nāma natthi, te amhākaṃ mahāparādhikā, na sakkā tehi amhākaṃ cakkhupathe ṭhātuṃ, ettakaṃ pana dhanaṃ gahetvā dvepi janā phāsukaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā jīvantu, dārake pana idha pesentū”ti. Seṭṭhidhītā mātāpitūhi pesitaṃ dhanaṃ gahetvā dārake āgatadūtānaṃyeva hatthe datvā pesesi, dārakā ayyakakule vaḍḍhanti. Tesu cūḷapanthako atidaharo, mahāpanthako pana ayyakena saddhiṃ dasabalassa dhammakathaṃ sotuṃ gacchati. Tassa niccaṃ satthu sammukhā dhammaṃ suṇantassa pabbajjāya cittaṃ nami. So ayyakaṃ āha “sace tumhe sampaṭicchatha, ahaṃ pabbajeyya”nti. “Kiṃ vadesi, tāta, mayhaṃ sakalalokassapi pabbajjāto taveva pabbajjā bhaddikā, sace sakkosi, pabbaja tātā”ti sampaṭicchitvā satthu santikaṃ gato. Satthā “kiṃ mahāseṭṭhi dārako te laddho”ti. “Āma, bhante ayaṃ dārako mayhaṃ nattā, tumhākaṃ [P 1.0116] santike pabbajāmīti vadatī”ti āha. Satthā aññataraṃ [M 1.0132] piṇḍacārikaṃ bhikkhuṃ “imaṃ dārakaṃ pabbājehī”ti āṇāpesi. Thero tassa tacapañcakakammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhitvā pabbājesi. So bahuṃ buddhavacanaṃ uggaṇhitvā paripuṇṇavasso upasampadaṃ labhi. Upasampanno hutvā yoniso manasikāre kammaṃ karonto arahattaṃ pāpuṇi.

Hearing that message, they said, “For those wandering in saṃsāra, there is no such thing as a son or a daughter. They have committed a great offense against us; they cannot stand in our sight. However, let those two take this much wealth, go to a comfortable place, and live, but let them send the children here.” The merchant's daughter took the wealth sent by her parents, handed the children to the messengers who had come, and sent them away. The children grew up in their grandfather's household. Of the two, Cūḷapanthaka was very young, while Mahāpanthaka would go with his grandfather to listen to the Ten-Powered One's discourse on the Dhamma. Constantly hearing the Dhamma in the presence of the Teacher, his mind inclined toward ordination. He said to his grandfather, “If you consent, I would like to go forth.” “What are you saying, my dear grandson? To me, your going forth is more welcome than that of the entire world. If you are able, go forth, my dear.” Consenting, he took him to the Teacher. The Teacher asked, “Great merchant, have you brought a boy?” “Yes, Venerable Sir, this boy is my grandson. He says he wishes to go forth in your presence.” The Teacher instructed a certain monk who lived on alms-food, “Go and give this boy the going forth.” The elder taught him the meditation subject of the five parts of the body and gave him the going forth. He learned much of the Buddha's word and, having completed twenty years of age, received the higher ordination. Once ordained, he applied himself with wise attention and attained Arahantship.

So jhānasukhena, maggasukhena, phalasukhena vītināmento cintesi “sakkā nu kho imaṃ sukhaṃ cūḷapanthakassa dātu”nti. Tato ayyakaseṭṭhissa santikaṃ gantvā “mahāseṭṭhi sace tumhe sampaṭicchatha, ahaṃ cūḷapanthakaṃ pabbājeyya”nti āha. “Pabbājetha, bhante”ti. Thero cūḷapanthakadārakaṃ [V 1.0123] pabbājetvā dasasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi. Cūḷapanthakasāmaṇero pabbajitvāva dandho ahosi.

As he was spending his time in the bliss of jhāna, the bliss of the path, and the bliss of fruition, he thought, “Might it be possible to give this bliss to Cūḷapanthaka?” Then, going to his grandfather, the great merchant, he said, “Great merchant, if you consent, I will give Cūḷapanthaka the going forth.” “Give him the going forth, Venerable Sir.” The Elder gave the boy Cūḷapanthaka the going forth and established him in the ten precepts. From the moment he had gone forth, the novice Cūḷapanthaka was dull-witted.

“Padumaṃ yathā kokanadaṃ sugandhaṃ, pāto siyā phullamavītagandhaṃ;

Aṅgīrasaṃ passa virocamānaṃ, tapantamādiccamivantalikkhe”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.123; a. ni. 5.195) –

“Just as a fragrant red lotus, blooming at dawn, its scent unfaded; so behold Aṅgīrasa, shining, blazing like the sun in the sky.”

Imaṃ ekagāthaṃ catūhi māsehi gaṇhituṃ nāsakkhi. So kira kassapasammāsambuddhakāle pabbajitvā paññavā hutvā aññatarassa dandhabhikkhuno uddesaggahaṇakāle parihāsakeḷiṃ akāsi. So bhikkhu tena parihāsena lajjito neva uddesaṃ gaṇhi, na sajjhāyamakāsi. Tena kammena ayaṃ pabbajitvāva dandho jāto, gahitagahitaṃ padaṃ uparūpari padaṃ gaṇhantassa nassati. Tassa imameva gāthaṃ gahetuṃ vāyamantassa cattāro māsā atikkantā.

He was unable to grasp this single verse in four months. It is said that in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One, Kassapa, he had gone forth and was intelligent. On one occasion, he playfully mocked a certain dull-witted monk during his recitation lesson. That monk, shamed by the mockery, neither learned the recitation nor did he chant. Due to that kamma, this one became dull-witted from the moment he went forth. As he tried to learn each subsequent word, the word he had just learned would be lost. As he strove to grasp just this one verse, four months passed by.

Atha naṃ mahāpanthako āha “cūḷapanthaka, tvaṃ imasmiṃ sāsane abhabbo, catūhi māsehi ekampi gāthaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkosi, pabbajitakiccaṃ pana tvaṃ kathaṃ matthakaṃ pāpessasi, nikkhama ito”ti vihārā nikkaḍḍhi. Cūḷapanthako buddhasāsane sinehena gihibhāvaṃ na pattheti. Tasmiñca kāle mahāpanthako bhattuddesako hoti. Jīvako komārabhacco bahuṃ gandhamālaṃ ādāya attano ambavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā dhammaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāyāsanā dasabalaṃ vanditvā mahāpanthakaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kittakā[M 1.0133], bhante, satthu santike bhikkhū”ti pucchi. “Pañcamattāni bhikkhusatānī”ti. “Sve, bhante, buddhappamukhāni pañca bhikkhusatāni ādāya amhākaṃ nivesane bhikkhaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. “Upāsaka, cūḷapanthako nāma bhikkhu dandho aviruḷhidhammo, taṃ ṭhapetvā sesānaṃ nimantanaṃ sampaṭicchāmī”ti [P 1.0117] thero āha. Taṃ sutvā cūḷapanthako cintesi “thero ettakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ nimantanaṃ sampaṭicchanto maṃ bāhiraṃ katvā sampaṭicchati, nissaṃsayaṃ mayhaṃ bhātikassa mayi cittaṃ bhinnaṃ bhavissati, kiṃ idāni mayhaṃ iminā sāsanena, gihī hutvā dānādīni puññāni karonto jīvissāmī”ti.

Then Mahāpanthaka said to him, 'Cūḷapanthaka, you are unfit for this Dispensation. You could not master even one verse in four months—how then will you bring the duties of a monastic to completion? Get out of here!' And he expelled him from the monastery. Cūḷapanthaka, out of love for the Buddha’s Dispensation, did not desire to return to the lay life. At that time, Mahāpanthaka was the allocator of meals. Jīvaka Komārabhacca, taking many perfumes and garlands, went to his mango grove, paid homage to the Teacher, listened to the Dhamma, rose from his seat, venerated the One of Ten Powers, and approached Mahāpanthaka, asking, 'Venerable sir, how many monks are in the Teacher's presence?' 'Five hundred monks.' 'Venerable sir, tomorrow, please accept alms at our residence, bringing the five hundred monks headed by the Buddha.' The elder replied, 'Lay devotee, the monk named Cūḷapanthaka is slow and his spiritual qualities are undeveloped. Excluding him, I accept the invitation for the rest.' Hearing this, Cūḷapanthaka thought, 'The elder, in accepting the invitation for so many monks, accepts it while excluding me. Without a doubt, my brother’s heart has turned against me. What use is this Dispensation to me now? I will become a layman and live by performing meritorious deeds such as giving alms.'

So punadivase pātova “gihī bhavissāmī”ti pāyāsi. Satthā paccūsakāleyeva lokaṃ olokento imaṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā paṭhamataraṃ gantvā cūḷapanthakassa gamanamagge dvārakoṭṭhake caṅkamanto aṭṭhāsi. Cūḷapanthako gharaṃ gacchanto satthāraṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā vandi. Atha naṃ satthā “kahaṃ pana, tvaṃ cūḷapanthaka, imāya velāya gacchasī”ti āha. Bhātā maṃ, bhante, nikkaḍḍhati[V 1.0124], tenāhaṃ vibbhamituṃ gacchāmīti. Cūḷapanthaka, tava pabbajjā nāma mama santakā, bhātarā nikkaḍḍhito kasmā mama santikaṃ nāgañchi? Ehi kiṃ te gihibhāvena, mama santike bhavissasī”ti bhagavā cūḷapanthakaṃ ādāya gantvā gandhakuṭippamukhe nisīdāpetvā “cūḷapanthaka, tvaṃ puratthābhimukho hutvā imaṃ pilotikaṃ ‘rajoharaṇaṃ rajoharaṇa’nti parimajjanto idheva hohī”ti iddhiyā abhisaṅkhataṃ parisuddhaṃ pilotikākhaṇḍaṃ datvā kāle ārocite bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto jīvakassa gehaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīdi.

The next day, early in the morning, thinking, 'I will become a layman,' he set out. The Teacher, surveying the world at dawn, saw this matter and, going ahead, stood walking meditation in the gateway on Cūḷapanthaka's path. Cūḷapanthaka, on his way to the house, saw the Teacher, approached, and paid homage. Then the Teacher asked him, 'Cūḷapanthaka, where are you going at this hour?' 'Venerable Sir, my brother is expelling me; therefore, I am going to disrobe.' 'Cūḷapanthaka, your ordination is my responsibility. When expelled by your brother, why did you not come to me? Come, what use is the lay life to you? You shall remain in my presence.' The Blessed One, taking Cūḷapanthaka with him, had him sit at the entrance of the Fragrant Chamber and gave him a piece of perfectly clean cloth created by psychic power, saying, 'Cūḷapanthaka, facing east, remain here rubbing this piece of cloth and repeating, "Remover of dust, remover of dust."' When the time was announced, the Buddha, surrounded by the community of monks, went to Jīvaka’s house and sat on the prepared seat.

Cūḷapanthakopi sūriyaṃ olokento taṃ pilotikākhaṇḍaṃ “rajoharaṇaṃ rajoharaṇa”nti parimajjanto nisīdi, tassa taṃ pilotikākhaṇḍaṃ parimajjantassa parimajjantassa kiliṭṭhaṃ ahosi. Tato cintesi “idaṃ pilotikākhaṇḍaṃ ativiya parisuddhaṃ, imaṃ pana attabhāvaṃ nissāya purimapakatiṃ vijahitvā evaṃ kiliṭṭhaṃ jātaṃ, aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti khayavayaṃ paṭṭhapento vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhesi. Satthā “cūḷapanthakassa cittaṃ vipassanaṃ āruḷha”nti ñatvā “cūḷapanthaka, tvaṃ etaṃ pilotikākhaṇḍameva saṃkiliṭṭhaṃ rajorañjitaṃ jātanti mā saññaṃ kari, abbhantare pana te rāgarajādayo atthi, te harāhī”ti vatvā obhāsaṃ vissajjetvā purato nisinno viya paññāyamānarūpo hutvā imā gāthā abhāsi –

Cūḷapanthaka, looking at the sun, sat rubbing that piece of cloth, repeating, 'Remover of dust, remover of dust.' As he continued to rub it, the piece of cloth became soiled. Then he reflected, 'This piece of cloth was originally exceedingly pure, but depending on this body, it has abandoned its former nature and become soiled. Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned phenomena!' Establishing his mind on arising and passing away, he developed insight. The Teacher, knowing that Cūḷapanthaka's mind had mounted to insight, emitted a radiance and appeared before him as if seated there, saying, 'Cūḷapanthaka, do not think that only this piece of cloth has become soiled and stained by dust. Within you there are dusts such as the dust of lust. Remove them!' Then he spoke these verses:

“Rāgo [M 1.0134] rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati, rāgassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ rajoti;

Etaṃ rajaṃ vippajahitva bhikkhavo, viharanti te vigatarajassa sāsane.

Lust is called 'dust,' but not the dust that is powder. 'Dust' is a name for lust. Having abandoned this dust, O monks, they dwell in the Dispensation of the One who is free from dust.

“Doso [P 1.0118] rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati, dosassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ rajoti;

Etaṃ rajaṃ vippajahitva bhikkhavo, viharanti te vigatarajassa sāsane.

Hatred is called 'dust,' but not the dust that is powder. 'Dust' is a name for hatred. Having abandoned this dust, O monks, they dwell in the Dispensation of the One who is free from dust.

“Moho rajo na ca pana reṇu vuccati, mohassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ rajoti;

Etaṃ rajaṃ vippajahitva bhikkhavo, viharanti te vigatarajassa sāsane”ti. (mahāni. 209; cūḷani. udayamāṇavapucchāniddesa 74);

Delusion is called 'dust,' but not the dust that is powder. 'Dust' is a name for delusion. Having abandoned this dust, O monks, they dwell in the Dispensation of the One who is free from dust.

Gāthāpariyosāne cūḷapanthako saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ pāpuṇi, paṭisambhidāhiyevassa tīṇi piṭakāni āgamaṃsu. So kira pubbe rājā hutvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karonto nalāṭato sede muccante parisuddhena sāṭakena nalāṭantaṃ puñchi, sāṭako kiliṭṭho ahosi. So “imaṃ sarīraṃ [V 1.0125] nissāya evarūpo parisuddho sāṭako pakatiṃ jahitvā kiliṭṭho jāto, aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti aniccasaññaṃ paṭilabhi. Tena kāraṇenassa rajoharaṇameva paccayo jāto.

At the conclusion of the verses, Cūḷapanthaka attained Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. And with the analytical knowledges, the three Piṭakas came to him. It is said that in a previous life, when he was a king circumambulating the city, sweat broke out on his forehead. He wiped it with a clean cloth, and the cloth became soiled. He reflected, 'Depending on this body, such a pure cloth has abandoned its natural state and become soiled. Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned phenomena!' and thus he gained the perception of impermanence. For that reason, the very 'remover of dust' became a supporting condition for his attainment.

Jīvakopi kho komārabhacco dasabalassa dakkhiṇodakaṃ upanāmesi. Satthā “nanu, jīvaka, vihāre bhikkhū atthī”ti hatthena pattaṃ pidahi. Mahāpanthako “bhante, vihāre natthi bhikkhū”ti āha. Satthā “atthi jīvakā”ti āha. Jīvako “tena hi, bhaṇe, gaccha, vihāre bhikkhūnaṃ atthibhāvaṃ vā natthibhāvaṃ vā jānāhī”ti purisaṃ pesesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe cūḷapanthako “mayhaṃ bhātiko ‘vihāre bhikkhū natthī’ti bhaṇati, vihāre bhikkhūnaṃ atthibhāvamassa pakāsessāmī”ti sakalaṃ ambavanaṃ bhikkhūnaṃyeva pūresi. Ekacce bhikkhū cīvarakammaṃ karonti, ekacce rajanakammaṃ, ekacce sajjhāyaṃ karontīti evaṃ aññamaññaṃ asadisaṃ bhikkhusahassaṃ māpesi. So puriso vihāre bahū bhikkhū disvā nivattitvā “ayya[M 1.0135], sakalaṃ ambavanaṃ bhikkhūhi paripuṇṇa”nti jīvakassa ārocesi. Theropi kho tattheva –

Jīvaka Komārabhacca also offered the dedication water to the Ten-Powered One. The Teacher asked, "Jīvaka, are there not monks in the monastery?" and covered the bowl with his hand. Mahāpanthaka replied, "Venerable sir, there are no monks in the monastery." The Teacher said, "There are, Jīvaka." Jīvaka then sent a man, saying, "Go, friend, and find out whether monks are present or absent in the monastery." At that moment, Cūḷapanthaka thought, "My brother says 'there are no monks in the monastery'; I will reveal the presence of monks in the monastery to him," and filled the entire mango grove with monks. Some monks were making robes, some dyeing, and some reciting—thus he created a thousand monks, each dissimilar from the others. The man, seeing many monks in the monastery, returned and reported to Jīvaka, "Sir, the entire mango grove is filled with monks." The Elder also remained there—

“Sahassakkhattumattānaṃ, nimminitvāna panthako;

Nisīdambavane ramme, yāva kālappavedanā”ti. (theragā. 563);

“Panthaka, having created himself a thousand times, sat in the delightful mango grove until the time was announced.”

Atha satthā taṃ purisaṃ āha – “vihāraṃ gantvā ‘satthā cūḷapanthakaṃ nāma pakkosatī’ti vadehī”ti. Tena gantvā tathāvutte “ahaṃ cūḷapanthako, ahaṃ cūḷapanthako”ti mukhasahassaṃ uṭṭhahi. Puriso gantvā “sabbepi kira te, bhante, cūḷapanthakāyeva nāmā”ti āha. Tena hi tvaṃ gantvā yo paṭhamaṃ “ahaṃ cūḷapanthako”ti vadati, taṃ [P 1.0119] hatthe gaṇha, avasesā antaradhāyissantīti. So tathā akāsi, tāvadeva sahassamattā bhikkhū antaradhāyiṃsu. Thero tena purisena saddhiṃ agamāsi. Satthā bhattakiccapariyosāne jīvakaṃ āmantesi “jīvaka, cūḷapanthakassa pattaṃ gaṇha, ayaṃ te anumodanaṃ karissatī”ti. Jīvako tathā akāsi. Thero sīhanādaṃ nadanto taruṇasīho viya tīṇi piṭakāni saṃkhobhetvā anumodanaṃ akāsi.

Then the Teacher said to that man, "Go to the monastery and say, 'The Teacher is calling one named Cūḷapanthaka.'" When he went and said thus, a thousand voices arose, "I am Cūḷapanthaka, I am Cūḷapanthaka." The man went back and said, "Venerable sir, it seems all of them are named Cūḷapanthaka." "Then go, and the first one who says, 'I am Cūḷapanthaka,' take him by the hand; the rest will disappear." He did so, and immediately about a thousand monks vanished. The elder went with that man. After the meal was finished, the Teacher addressed Jīvaka, "Jīvaka, take Cūḷapanthaka's bowl; he will give the discourse of appreciation for you." Jīvaka did so. The elder, roaring a lion's roar like a young lion, stirred up the three baskets and gave the discourse of appreciation.

Satthā uṭṭhāyāsanā bhikkhusaṅghaparivāro vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhūhi vatte dassite uṭṭhāyāsanā gandhakuṭippamukhe ṭhatvā bhikkhusaṅghassa sugatovādaṃ datvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathetvā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ uyyojetvā surabhigandhavāsitaṃ gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ upagato. Atha sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū ito cito ca samosaritvā rattakambalasāṇiṃ parikkhipantā [V 1.0126] viya nisīditvā satthu guṇakathaṃ ārabhiṃsu “āvuso, mahāpanthako cūḷapanthakassa ajjhāsayaṃ ajānanto ‘catūhi māsehi ekagāthaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkoti, dandho aya’nti vihārā nikkaḍḍhi, sammāsambuddho pana attano anuttaradhammarājatāya ekasmiṃyevassa antarabhatte saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ adāsi, tīṇi piṭakāni paṭisambhidāhiyeva āgatāni, aho buddhānaṃ balaṃ nāma mahanta”nti.

The Teacher, rising from his seat and surrounded by the community of monks, went to the monastery. After the monks had performed their duties, he rose from his seat, stood at the entrance of the perfumed chamber, gave the Sugata's exhortation to the community of monks, explained the meditation subject, and dismissed the community. Then, entering the fragrant perfumed chamber, he lay down on his right side in the lion's posture. In the evening, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall from all directions, and sitting down as if a dark red woolen curtain were drawn around them, began to praise the virtues of the Teacher: "Friends, Mahāpanthaka, not knowing Cūḷapanthaka's inclination, expelled him from the monastery, saying, 'He cannot learn a single verse in four months; he is dull!' Yet the Perfectly Enlightened One, by his supreme sovereignty of the Dhamma, granted him arahantship along with the analytical knowledges during a single meal interval. The three baskets also came with the analytical knowledges. Ah, truly great is the power of the Buddhas!"

Atha bhagavā dhammasabhāyaṃ imaṃ kathāpavattiṃ ñatvā “ajja mayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti buddhaseyyāya uṭṭhāya surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā vijjulataṃ viya kāyabandhanaṃ [M 1.0136] bandhitvā rattakambalasadisaṃ sugatamahācīvaraṃ pārupitvā surabhigandhakuṭito nikkhamma mattavāraṇo viya sīhavikkantavilāsena vijambhamāno sīho viya anantāya buddhalīlāya dhammasabhaṃ gantvā alaṅkatamaṇḍapamajjhe supaññattavarabuddhāsanaṃ abhiruyha chabbaṇṇabuddharasmiyo vissajjento aṇṇavakucchiṃ obhāsayamāno yugandharamatthake bālasūriyo viya āsanamajjhe nisīdi. Sammāsambuddhe pana āgatamatte bhikkhusaṅgho kathaṃ pacchinditvā tuṇhī ahosi.

Then the Blessed One, knowing of this conversation taking place in the Dhamma hall, thought, "Today it is fitting for me to go." Rising from the Buddha's bed, he put on a deep red double-layered robe, fastened his belt like a streak of lightning, draped the great Sugata-robe resembling a red blanket, and emerging from his fragrant chamber, like a mighty elephant in rut, like a lion stretching with the majestic grace of a lion's gait, and with endless Buddha-majesty, he went to the Dhamma hall. Ascending the splendidly prepared excellent Buddha-seat at the center of the adorned pavilion, he radiated the six-colored Buddha-rays, illuminating the very heart of the ocean like the morning sun atop Mount Yugandhara, and sat in the middle of the seat. As soon as the Perfectly Enlightened One had arrived, the community of monks, ceasing their discussion, became silent.

Satthā mudukena mettacittena parisaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ parisā ativiya sobhati, ekassapi hatthakukkuccaṃ vā pādakukkuccaṃ vā ukkāsitasaddo vā khipitasaddo vā natthi, sabbepime buddhagāravena sagāravā buddhatejena tajjitā mayi āyukappampi akathetvā nisinne paṭhamaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā na kathessanti, kathāsamuṭṭhāpanavattaṃ nāma mayāva jānitabbaṃ, ahameva paṭhamaṃ kathessāmī”ti madhurena brahmassarena bhikkhū āmantetvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave[P 1.0120], etarahi kathāya sannisinnā, kā ca pana vo antarākathā vippakatā”ti āha. Bhante, na mayaṃ imasmiṃ ṭhāne nisinnā aññaṃ tiracchānakathaṃ kathema, tumhākaṃyeva pana guṇe vaṇṇayamānā nisinnāmha “āvuso mahāpanthako cūḷapanthakassa ajjhāsayaṃ ajānanto ‘catūhi māsehi ekaṃ gāthaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkoti, dandho aya’nti vihārā nikkaḍḍhi, sammāsambuddho pana anuttaradhammarājatāya ekasmiṃyevassa antarabhatte saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ adāsi, aho buddhānaṃ balaṃ nāma mahanta”nti. Satthā bhikkhūnaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “bhikkhave, cūḷapanthako maṃ nissāya idāni tāva dhammesu dhammamahantataṃ patto, pubbe pana maṃ nissāya bhogesupi bhogamahantataṃ pāpuṇī”ti āha. Bhikkhū tassatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu. Bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

The Teacher, with a gentle and loving mind, surveyed the assembly and thought: 'This assembly is exceedingly splendid. There is not a single instance of a restless hand or a restless foot, not a cough or a sneeze. All these monks, out of reverence for the Buddha, are respectful and restrained by the Buddha's majesty. Even if I were to sit for an entire aeon without speaking, they would not be the first to initiate a conversation. The custom of initiating a conversation is for me to know. I shall be the first to speak.' Then, with a sweet, Brahma-like voice, he addressed the monks: 'For what discussion, O monks, are you now gathered? And what was the talk among you that was left unfinished?' 'Venerable sir, we who are seated here do not engage in any worldly talk; rather, we sit praising your virtues: “Friends, Mahāpanthaka, not knowing Cūḷapanthaka’s disposition, expelled him from the monastery, saying, ‘He cannot learn even one verse in four months—he is dull.’ Yet the Perfectly Enlightened One, being the unsurpassed King of the Dhamma, in the interval of a single meal, granted him arahantship together with the analytical knowledges. Ah, how great is the power of the Buddhas!”' Hearing the monks’ discussion, the Teacher said: 'Monks, it is not only now that Cūḷapanthaka, by relying on me, has attained greatness in the Dhamma; in the past, too, by relying on me, he achieved greatness in wealth.' The monks requested the Blessed One to make this matter clear. The Blessed One then made manifest the cause, which was concealed by a previous existence.

Atīte kāsiraṭṭhe bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā vayappatto [V 1.0127] seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhitvā cūḷaseṭṭhi nāma ahosi, so paṇḍito byatto sabbanimittāni jānāti. So ekadivasaṃ rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchanto antaravīthiyaṃ matamūsikaṃ disvā taṅkhaṇaññeva nakkhattaṃ [M 1.0137] samānetvā idamāha “sakkā cakkhumatā kulaputtena imaṃ undūraṃ gahetvā puttadārabharaṇañca kātuṃ kammante ca payojetu”nti? Aññataro duggatakulaputto taṃ seṭṭhissa vacanaṃ sutvā “nāyaṃ ajānitvā kathessatī”ti taṃ mūsikaṃ gahetvā ekasmiṃ āpaṇe biḷālassatthāya vikkiṇitvā kākaṇikaṃ labhitvā tāya kākaṇikāya phāṇitaṃ gahetvā ekena ghaṭena pānīyaṃ gaṇhi. So araññato āgacchante mālākāre disvā thokaṃ thokaṃ phāṇitakhaṇḍaṃ datvā uḷuṅkena pānīyaṃ adāsi, te cassa ekekaṃ pupphamuṭṭhiṃ adaṃsu. So tena pupphamūlena punadivasepi phāṇitañca pānīyaghaṭañca gahetvā pupphārāmameva gato. Tassa taṃ divasaṃ mālākārā aḍḍhocitake pupphagacche datvā agamaṃsu. So na cirasseva iminā upāyena aṭṭha kahāpaṇe labhi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Kāsi, at Bārāṇasī, when Brahmadatta was reigning, the Bodhisatta was born into a treasurer's family. Upon reaching maturity, he obtained the position of treasurer and was known as Cūḷaseṭṭhi. He was wise, astute, and knew all omens. One day, while going to attend upon the king, he saw a dead mouse in the middle of the street. At that very moment, he calculated the stellar positions and said: 'An astute man could take this mouse, support a wife and children, and establish a business.' A certain man from a poor family heard the treasurer's words and thought, 'He would not speak without knowledge.' He took the mouse, sold it in a shop for cat food, and received a kākaṇika. With that kākaṇika, he bought molasses and got a pot of water. Seeing flower-gatherers coming from the forest, he gave them small pieces of molasses and offered them water with a ladle. They each gave him a handful of flowers. With the money from those flowers, the next day he again took molasses and a water pot and went to the flower garden. That day, the flower-gatherers gave him the flowering plants they had half-picked and then departed. Before long, by this method, he had acquired eight kahāpaṇas.

Puna ekasmiṃ vātavuṭṭhidivase rājuyyāne bahū sukkhadaṇḍakā ca sākhā ca palāsañca vātena pātitaṃ hoti, uyyānapālo chaḍḍetuṃ upāyaṃ na passati[P 1.0121]. So tattha gantvā “sace imāni dārupaṇṇāni mayhaṃ dassasi, ahaṃ te imāni sabbāni nīharissāmī”ti uyyānapālaṃ āha, so “gaṇha ayyā”ti sampaṭicchi. Cūḷantevāsiko dārakānaṃ kīḷanamaṇḍalaṃ gantvā phāṇitaṃ datvā muhuttena sabbāni dārupaṇṇāni nīharāpetvā uyyānadvāre rāsiṃ kāresi. Tadā rājakumbhakāro rājakule bhājanānaṃ pacanatthāya dārūni pariyesamāno uyyānadvāre tāni disvā tassa hatthato kiṇitvā gaṇhi. Taṃ divasaṃ cūḷantevāsiko dāruvikkayena soḷasa kahāpaṇe cāṭiādīni ca pañca bhājanāni labhi.

Again, on a day of wind and rain, many dry sticks, branches, and leaves were blown down in the royal garden, and the garden keeper saw no way to dispose of them. The young man went there and said to the garden keeper, 'If you give me this wood and these leaves, I will remove them all for you.' The garden keeper agreed, saying, 'Take them, sir.' The protégé went to the children's playground, gave them molasses, and within a moment had them remove all the wood and leaves, piling them up at the garden gate. At that time, the royal potter, searching for firewood to fire pots for the royal household, saw the pile at the garden gate and bought it from him. That day, from the sale of the firewood, the protégé earned sixteen kahāpaṇas, along with five vessels such as water pots.

So catuvīsatiyā kahāpaṇesu jātesu “atthi ayaṃ upāyo mayha”nti nagaradvārato avidūre ṭhāne ekaṃ pānīyacāṭiṃ ṭhapetvā pañcasate tiṇahārake pānīyena upaṭṭhahi. Te āhaṃsu “samma, tvaṃ amhākaṃ bahūpakāro, kiṃ te karomā”ti? So “mayhaṃ kicce uppanne karissathā”ti vatvā ito cito ca vicaranto thalapathakammikena ca jalapathakammikena ca saddhiṃ mittasanthavaṃ akāsi. Tassa thalapathakammiko “sve imaṃ nagaraṃ assavāṇijako pañca assasatāni gahetvā āgamissatī”ti ācikkhi. So tassa vacanaṃ sutvā tiṇahārake āha “ajja mayhaṃ ekekaṃ tiṇakalāpaṃ detha, mayā ca tiṇe avikkiṇite attano tiṇaṃ mā vikkiṇathā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā [M 1.0138] pañca tiṇakalāpasatāni āharitvā tassa [V 1.0128] ghare pāpayiṃsu. Assavāṇijo sakalanagare assānaṃ gocaraṃ alabhitvā tassa sahassaṃ datvā taṃ tiṇaṃ gaṇhi.

When he had acquired twenty-four kahāpaṇas, he thought, 'This is a good method for me.' Setting up a water pot in a place not far from the city gate, he served five hundred grass-cutters with water. They said, 'Friend, you have been of great service to us. What can we do for you?' He replied, 'When a need arises for me, you shall do it.' Wandering about, he made friends with both a land-route trader and a water-route trader. His friend, the land-route trader, informed him, 'Tomorrow, a horse trader will come to this city bringing five hundred horses.' Hearing this, he told the grass-cutters, 'Today, each of you give me one bundle of grass, and until I have sold my grass, do not sell your own.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and brought five hundred bundles of grass, delivering them to his house. The horse trader, unable to find fodder for his horses in the entire city, gave him a thousand kahāpaṇas and bought the grass.

Tato katipāhaccayenassa jalapathakammiko sahāyako ārocesi “paṭṭanamhi mahānāvā āgatā”ti. So “atthi ayaṃ upāyo”ti aṭṭhahi kahāpaṇehi sabbaparivārasampannaṃ tāvakālikaṃ rathaṃ gahetvā mahantena yasena nāvāpaṭṭanaṃ gantvā ekaṃ aṅgulimuddikaṃ nāvikassa saccakāraṃ datvā avidūre ṭhāne sāṇiyā parikkhipāpetvā nisinno purise āṇāpesi “bāhirato vāṇijesu āgatesu tatiyena paṭihārena maṃ ārocethā”ti[P 1.0122]. “Nāvā āgatā”ti sutvā bārāṇasito satamattā vāṇijā “bhaṇḍaṃ gaṇhāmā”ti āgamiṃsu. Bhaṇḍaṃ tumhe na labhissatha, asukaṭṭhāne nāma mahāvāṇijena saccakāro dinnoti. Te taṃ sutvā tassa santikaṃ āgatā. Pādamūlikapurisā purimasaññāvasena tatiyena paṭihārena tesaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ārocesuṃ. Te satamattā vāṇijā ekekaṃ sahassaṃ datvā tena saddhiṃ nāvāya pattikā hutvā puna ekekaṃ sahassaṃ datvā pattiṃ vissajjāpetvā bhaṇḍaṃ attano santakamakaṃsu.

Then, after a few days, his friend who worked in the shipping trade informed him, 'A great ship has arrived at the port.' Thinking, 'Here is my chance,' he hired a temporary carriage with a full retinue for eight kahāpaṇas and went to the port with great splendor. He gave a signet ring to the ship's captain as a deposit and, having had a canvas screen erected nearby, he sat and instructed his men, 'When merchants arrive from outside, have them announced to me through three intermediaries.' Upon hearing that the ship had arrived, about a hundred merchants from Bārāṇasī came, saying, 'Let us acquire the goods.' They were told, 'You will not get the goods; a great merchant has already given a deposit.' Hearing this, they went to him. His attendants, following the prior instruction, announced their arrival through three intermediaries. The hundred merchants each gave a thousand to become partners with him for the ship's cargo. Then, giving another thousand each, they had him relinquish his share and made the goods their own.

Cūḷantevāsiko dve satasahassāni gaṇhitvā bārāṇasiṃ āgantvā “kataññunā me bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ekaṃ satasahassaṃ gāhāpetvā cūḷaseṭṭhissa samīpaṃ gato. Atha naṃ seṭṭhi “kiṃ te, tāta, katvā idaṃ dhanaṃ laddha”nti pucchi. So “tumhehi kathitaupāye ṭhatvā catumāsambhantareyeva laddha”nti matamūsikaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbaṃ vatthuṃ kathesi. Cūḷaseṭṭhi tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “idāni evarūpaṃ dārakaṃ mama santakaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vayappattaṃ attano dhītaraṃ datvā sakalakuṭumbassa sāmikaṃ akāsi. So seṭṭhino accayena tasmiṃ nagare seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhi. Bodhisattopi yathākammaṃ agamāsi.

The young apprentice, taking two hundred thousand, returned to Bārāṇasī. Thinking, 'It is proper for me to be grateful,' he took one hundred thousand and went to the junior merchant. Then the merchant asked him, 'My dear boy, by what means did you acquire this wealth?' He replied, 'By following the method you described, I acquired it in just four months,' and, beginning with the dead mouse, he related the entire story. Hearing his words, the junior merchant thought, 'It is now fitting to make such a youth my own,' and giving him his grown-up daughter, he made him the master of the entire estate. After the merchant passed away, he obtained the position of chief merchant in that city. The Bodhisatta, too, fared according to his kamma.

Sammāsambuddhopi imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ kathetvā abhisambuddhova imaṃ gāthaṃ kathesi –

The Perfectly Enlightened One, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, then, as the Enlightened One, uttered this verse:

4.

4.

“Appakenapi medhāvī, pābhatena vicakkhaṇo;

Samuṭṭhāpeti attānaṃ, aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhama”nti.

A wise and discerning person, even with small means, can raise themselves up, just like one fanning a tiny fire.

Tattha [M 1.0139] appakenapīti thokenapi parittakenapi. Medhāvīti paññavā. Pābhatenāti bhaṇḍamūlena. Vicakkhaṇoti vohārakusalo. Samuṭṭhāpeti attānanti mahantaṃ dhanañca yasañca uppādetvā tattha attānaṃ saṇṭhāpeti patiṭṭhāpeti. Yathā kiṃ? Aṇuṃ aggiṃva sandhamaṃ, yathā paṇḍitapuriso [V 1.0129] parittaṃ aggiṃ anukkamena gomayacuṇṇādīni pakkhipitvā mukhavātena dhamanto samuṭṭhāpeti vaḍḍheti mahantaṃ aggikkhandhaṃ karoti, evameva paṇḍito thokampi pābhataṃ labhitvā nānāupāyehi payojetvā dhanañca yasañca vaḍḍheti[P 1.0123], vaḍḍhetvā ca pana tattha attānaṃ patiṭṭhāpeti, tāya eva vā pana dhanayasamahantatāya attānaṃ samuṭṭhāpeti, abhiññātaṃ pākaṭaṃ karotīti attho.

Herein, 'even with little' means with a small or trifling amount. 'Wise' means intelligent. 'With means' refers to the initial capital. 'Discerning' means skilled in commerce. 'Raises themselves up' means that having generated great wealth and fame, one establishes and founds oneself therein. How is this? 'Like one fanning a tiny fire': just as a wise person, starting with a small fire and gradually adding things like powdered cow-dung, fanning it with the breath from their mouth, builds it up, increases it, and makes it into a great mass of fire; even so, a wise person, having obtained even a little capital, employing it through various means, increases their wealth and fame. And having increased them, they establish themselves therein. Or, by that very greatness of wealth and fame, they raise themselves up, meaning they make themselves renowned and manifest.

Iti bhagavā “bhikkhave, cūḷapanthako maṃ nissāya idāni dhammesu dhammamahantataṃ patto, pubbe pana bhogesupi bhogamahantataṃ pāpuṇī”ti evaṃ imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ dassetvā dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā cūḷantevāsiko cūḷapanthako ahosi, cūḷakaseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

Thus the Blessed One said: 'Monks, Cūḷapanthaka, by relying on me, has now attained greatness in the Dhamma; but previously, he also attained greatness in wealth.' Having thus presented this Dhamma discourse, related the two stories, connected the link between them, and identified the birth story, he concluded the teaching by saying: 'At that time, the young apprentice was Cūḷapanthaka, and the junior merchant was I myself.'

Cūḷaseṭṭhijātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷaseṭṭhi Jātaka, the Fourth.

5. Taṇḍulanāḷijātakavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Taṇḍulanāḷi Jātaka

Kimagghati taṇḍulanāḷikāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lāludāyittheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiṃ samaye āyasmā dabbo mallaputto saṅghassa bhattuddesako hoti. Tasmiṃ pātova salākabhattāni uddisamāne lāludāyittherassa kadāci varabhattaṃ pāpuṇāti, kadāci lāmakabhattaṃ. So lāmakabhattassa pattadivase salākaggaṃ ākulaṃ karoti, “kiṃ dabbova salākaṃ dātuṃ jānāti, amhe na jānāmā”ti vadati. Tasmiṃ salākaggaṃ ākulaṃ karonte “handa dāni tvameva salākaṃ dehī”ti salākapacchiṃ adaṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya so saṅghassa salākaṃ adāsi. Dento ca pana “idaṃ varabhatta”nti vā “lāmakabhatta”nti vā “asukavassagge varabhatta”nti vā “asukavassagge lāmakabhatta”nti vā na jānāti, ṭhitikaṃ karontopi “asukavassagge ṭhitikā”ti na [M 1.0140] sallakkheti. Bhikkhūnaṃ ṭhitavelāya “imasmiṃ ṭhāne ayaṃ ṭhitikā ṭhitā, imasmiṃ ṭhāne aya”nti bhūmiyaṃ vā bhittiyaṃ vā lekhaṃ kaḍḍhati. Punadivase salākagge bhikkhū mandatarā vā honti bahutarā vā, tesu mandataresu lekhā heṭṭhā hoti, bahutaresu upari. So ṭhitikaṃ ajānanto lekhāsaññāya salākaṃ deti.

'What is a measure of rice worth?' This story the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyī. At that time, the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta was the assigner of meals for the Sangha. When he was distributing the ticket-meals early in the morning, the Elder Lāḷudāyī would sometimes receive a superior meal and sometimes an inferior one. On a day he received an inferior meal, he would create a disturbance at the ticket-distribution hall, saying, 'Does only Dabba know how to distribute the tickets? Do we not know?' As he was creating a disturbance at the ticket-distribution hall, they said, 'Well then, you distribute the tickets yourself,' and gave him the ticket-basket. From then on, he distributed the tickets for the Sangha. But in distributing them, he did not know which was a superior meal and which an inferior one, nor for which seniority-group a superior meal was due, or for which an inferior one. When establishing the order, he could not discern, 'The order is for such-and-such a seniority-group.' At the time when the monks stood in order, he would draw a line on the ground or on a wall, thinking, 'In this place this group stood, in that place that one.' On the next day at the ticket-distribution hall, the monks might be fewer or more numerous. When they were fewer, the line was lower down; when more numerous, it was higher up. Not knowing the established order, he would distribute the tickets according to the sign of the line.

Atha naṃ bhikkhū “āvuso, udāyi, lekhā nāma heṭṭhā vā hoti upari vā, varabhattaṃ pana asukavassagge ṭhitaṃ, lāmakabhattaṃ asukavassagge”ti āhaṃsu. So bhikkhū paṭippharanto “yadi [V 1.0130] evaṃ ayaṃ lekhā kasmā evaṃ ṭhitā, kiṃ ahaṃ tumhākaṃ saddahāmi, imissā lekhāya saddahāmī”ti vadati. Atha naṃ daharā ca sāmaṇerā ca “āvuso lāludāyi [P 1.0124] tayi salākaṃ dente bhikkhū lābhena parihāyanti, na tvaṃ dātuṃ anucchaviko, gaccha ito”ti salākaggato nikkaḍḍhiṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe salākagge mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ ahosi. Taṃ sutvā satthā ānandattheraṃ pucchi “ānanda, salākagge mahantaṃ kolāhalaṃ, kiṃ saddo nāmeso”ti. Thero tathāgatassa tamatthaṃ ārocesi. “Ānanda, na idāneva lāludāyi attano bālatāya paresaṃ lābhahāniṃ karoti, pubbepi akāsiyevā”ti āha. Thero tassatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ yāci. Bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

Then the monks said to him, 'Friend Udāyi, a mark is either below or above; the choice meal is designated for such-and-such a seniority group, and the inferior meal for such-and-such a seniority group.' Retorting to the monks, he said, 'If that is so, why is this mark placed like this? Why should I believe you? I believe this mark.' Then the young monks and novices said to him, 'Friend Lāludāyi, when you distribute the tickets, the monks are deprived of their gains. You are not fit to distribute them. Go away from here!' And they expelled him from the ticket distribution place. At that moment, there was a great uproar at the ticket distribution place. Hearing it, the Teacher asked the Venerable Ānanda, 'Ānanda, there is a great uproar at the ticket distribution place. What is that noise?' The Elder reported the matter to the Tathāgata. 'Ānanda, it is not only now that Lāludāyi, due to his foolishness, causes loss of gain to others; he did so in the past as well.' The Elder requested the Blessed One to make that matter clear. The Blessed One made manifest the cause hidden by a previous existence.

Atīte kāsiraṭṭhe bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto rājā ahosi. Tadā amhākaṃ bodhisatto tassa agghāpaniko ahosi. Hatthiassādīni ceva maṇisuvaṇṇādīni ca agghāpesi, agghāpetvā bhaṇḍasāmikānaṃ bhaṇḍānurūpameva mūlaṃ dāpesi. Rājā pana luddho hoti, so lobhapakatitāya evaṃ cintesi “ayaṃ agghāpaniko evaṃ agghāpento na cirasseva mama gehe dhanaṃ parikkhayaṃ gamessati, aññaṃ agghāpanikaṃ karissāmī”ti. So sīhapañjaraṃ ugghāṭetvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ olokento ekaṃ gāmikamanussaṃ lolabālaṃ rājaṅgaṇena gacchantaṃ disvā “esa mayhaṃ agghāpanikakammaṃ kātuṃ sakkhissatī”ti taṃ pakkosāpetvā “sakkhissasi, bhaṇe, amhākaṃ agghāpanikakammaṃ kātu”nti āha. Sakkhissāmi, devāti. Rājā attano dhanarakkhaṇatthāya taṃ bālaṃ agghāpanikakamme ṭhapesi. Tato paṭṭhāya so bālo hatthiassādīni agghāpento agghaṃ hāpetvā [M 1.0141] yathāruciyā katheti. Tassa ṭhānantare ṭhitattā yaṃ so katheti, tameva mūlaṃ hoti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was king in Bārāṇasī in the Kāsī kingdom, our Bodhisatta was his appraiser. He appraised elephants, horses, gems, gold, and other things, and after appraising them, he had the owners of the goods receive a price commensurate with their goods. The king, however, was greedy. Due to his greedy nature, he thought, 'This appraiser, by appraising in this way, will soon deplete the wealth in my house. I shall appoint another appraiser.' He opened the lion-window and, while observing the royal courtyard, saw a foolish and greedy villager passing through. Thinking, 'This man will be able to do the work of appraising for me,' he had him summoned and said, 'My good man, will you be able to perform the work of appraising for us?' 'I will be able, Your Majesty,' he replied. The king, wishing to protect his own wealth, appointed that fool to the office of appraiser. From then on, that fool, when appraising elephants, horses, and other things, would lower the price and state it as he pleased. Because he was established in that office, whatever price he stated became the actual price.

Tasmiṃ kāle uttarāpathato eko assavāṇijo pañca assasatāni ānesi. Rājā taṃ purisaṃ pakkosāpetvā asse agghāpesi. So pañcannaṃ assasatānaṃ ekaṃ taṇḍulanāḷikaṃ agghamakāsi. Katvā ca pana “assavāṇijassa ekaṃ taṇḍulanāḷikaṃ dethā”ti vatvā asse assasālāyaṃ [P 1.0125] saṇṭhāpesi. Assavāṇijo porāṇaagghāpanikassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “idāni kiṃ kattabba”nti pucchi. So āha “tassa purisassa lañjaṃ datvā evaṃ pucchatha ‘amhākaṃ tāva assā ekaṃ taṇḍulanāḷikaṃ agghantīti ñātametaṃ, tumhe pana nissāya taṇḍulanāḷiyā agghaṃ jānitukāmamhā, sakkhissatha no rañño santike ṭhatvā sā taṇḍulanāḷikā idaṃ nāma agghatīti vattu’nti, sace sakkomīti vadati, taṃ gahetvā rañño santikaṃ gacchatha, ahampi tattha āgamissāmī”ti.

At that time, a horse trader from the northern region brought five hundred horses. The king summoned that man and had the horses appraised. He valued the five hundred horses at one measure of rice. Having done so, he said, 'Give the horse trader one measure of rice,' and had the horses placed in the stables. The horse trader went to the former appraiser, reported the event, and asked, 'What is to be done now?' He replied, 'Give that man a bribe and ask him thus: "It is understood that our horses are worth one measure of rice. However, relying on you, we wish to know the value of a measure of rice. Will you be able to stand in the king's presence and state that the measure of rice is worth such-and-such?" If he says, "I can," then take him and go to the king. I too will come there.'

Assavāṇijo [V 1.0131] “sādhū”ti bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā agghāpanikassa lañjaṃ datvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. So lañjaṃ labhitvāva “sakkhissāmi taṇḍulanāḷiṃ agghāpetu”nti. “Tena hi gacchāma rājakula”nti taṃ ādāya rañño santikaṃ agamāsi. Bodhisattopi aññepi bahū amaccā agamiṃsu. Assavāṇijo rājānaṃ vanditvā āha – “deva, pañcannaṃ assasatānaṃ ekaṃ taṇḍulanāḷiṃ agghanakabhāvaṃ jānāma, sā pana taṇḍulanāḷi kiṃ agghatīti agghāpanikaṃ pucchatha devā”ti. Rājā taṃ pavattiṃ ajānanto “ambho agghāpanika, pañca assasatāni kiṃ agghantī”ti pucchi. Taṇḍulanāḷiṃ, devāti. “Hotu, bhaṇe, assā tāva taṇḍulanāḷiṃ agghantu. Sā pana kiṃ agghati taṇḍulanāḷikā”ti pucchi. So bālapuriso “bārāṇasiṃ santarabāhiraṃ agghati taṇḍulanāḷikā”ti āha. So kira pubbe rājānaṃ anuvattanto ekaṃ taṇḍulanāḷiṃ assānaṃ agghamakāsi. Puna vāṇijassa hatthato lañjaṃ labhitvā tassā taṇḍulanāḷikāya bārāṇasiṃ santarabāhiraṃ agghamakāsi. Tadā pana bārāṇasiyā pākāraparikkhepo dvādasayojaniko hoti. Idamassa antaraṃ, bāhiraṃ pana tiyojanasatikaṃ raṭṭhaṃ. Iti so bālo [M 1.0142] evaṃ mahantaṃ bārāṇasiṃ santarabāhiraṃ taṇḍulanāḷikāya agghamakāsi.

The horse trader, saying 'Very well,' accepted the Bodhisatta's words, gave a bribe to the appraiser, and informed him of the matter. Upon receiving the bribe, he said, 'I will be able to appraise the measure of rice.' 'Then let us go to the royal court.' Taking him, he went to the king. The Bodhisatta and many other ministers also went. The horse trader paid homage to the king and said, 'Your Majesty, we know that five hundred horses are worth one measure of rice. But what is that measure of rice worth? Your Majesty, please ask the appraiser.' The king, not knowing what had transpired, asked, 'My good appraiser, what are five hundred horses worth?' 'A measure of rice, Your Majesty.' 'So be it, my good man. Let the horses be worth a measure of rice. But what is that measure of rice worth?' he asked. That foolish man said, 'The measure of rice is worth Bārāṇasī, with its inner and outer regions.' Indeed, previously, following the king's wish, he had made one measure of rice the value of the horses. Then, having received a bribe from the trader's hand, he made Bārāṇasī, with its inner and outer regions, the value of that measure of rice.
