Now, at that time, the circumference of Bārāṇasī's ramparts was twelve yojanas. This was its inner part. The outer region, however, was a country of three hundred yojanas. Thus that fool made the great city of Bārāṇasī, with its inner and outer regions, the value of a measure of rice.

Taṃ sutvā amaccā pāṇiṃ [P 1.0126] paharitvā hasamānā “mayaṃ pubbe pathaviñca rajjañca anagghanti saññino ahumha, evaṃ mahantaṃ kira sarājakaṃ bārāṇasirajjaṃ taṇḍulanāḷimattaṃ agghati, aho agghāpanikassa ñāṇasampadā. Kahaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ ayaṃ agghāpaniko vihāsi, amhākaṃ rañño eva anucchaviko”ti parihāsaṃ akaṃsu –

Hearing this, the ministers clapped their hands and laughed, mocking him, 'Previously, we were of the opinion that the earth and the kingdom were priceless. Now, it seems, such a great kingdom of Bārāṇasī, together with its king, is worth a mere measure of rice. Oh, the glorious wisdom of the appraiser! Where has this appraiser been all this time? He is truly a fitting man for our king!'

5.

5.

“Kimagghati taṇḍulanāḷikāyaṃ, assāna mūlāya vadehi rāja;

Bārāṇasiṃ santarabāhiraṃ, ayamagghati taṇḍulanāḷikā”ti.

'O king, declare the value of a measure of rice, the price for the horses! Bārāṇasī, with its inner and outer regions—this is what the measure of rice is worth.'

Tasmiṃ kāle rājā lajjito taṃ bālaṃ nikkaḍḍhāpetvā bodhisattasseva agghāpanikaṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. Bodhisattopi yathākammaṃ gato.

At that time, the king, being ashamed, had that fool dismissed and gave the position of appraiser to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, too, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā gāmikabālaagghāpaniko lāludāyī ahosi, paṇḍitaagghāpaniko pana ahameva ahosi”nti desanaṃ niṭṭhāpesi.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, related the two stories, connected them, and identified the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the foolish village appraiser was Lāludāyī, but the wise appraiser was indeed myself.' Thus he concluded the teaching.

Taṇḍulanāḷijātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The fifth, the commentary on the Taṇḍulanāḷi Jātaka.

6. Devadhammajātakavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Devadhamma Jātaka

Hiriottappasampannāti [V 1.0132] idaṃ bhagavā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bahubhaṇḍikaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthivāsī kireko kuṭumbiko bhariyāya kālakatāya pabbaji. So pabbajanto attano pariveṇañca aggisālañca bhaṇḍagabbhañca kāretvā bhaṇḍagabbhaṃ sappitaṇḍulādīhi pūretvā pabbaji. Pabbajitvā ca pana attano dāse pakkosāpetvā yathārucitaṃ āhāraṃ pacāpetvā bhuñjati, bahuparikkhāro ca ahosi[M 1.0143], rattiṃ aññaṃ nivāsanapārupanaṃ hoti, divā aññaṃ. Vihārapaccante vasati. Tassekadivasaṃ cīvarapaccattharaṇādīni nīharitvā pariveṇe pattharitvā sukkhāpentassa sambahulā jānapadā bhikkhū senāsanacārikaṃ āhiṇḍantā pariveṇaṃ gantvā cīvarādīni disvā “kassimānī”ti pucchiṃsu. So “mayhaṃ, āvuso”ti āha. “Āvuso, idampi cīvaraṃ, idampi nivāsanaṃ, idampi paccattharaṇaṃ, sabbaṃ tuyhamevā”ti? “Āma mayhamevā”ti. “Āvuso bhagavatā tīṇi cīvarāni anuññātāni, tvaṃ evaṃ appicchassa buddhassa sāsane pabbajitvā evaṃ bahuparikkhāro jāto, ehi taṃ dasabalassa santikaṃ nessāmā”ti taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ agamaṃsu.

The Blessed One, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this regarding a certain monk with many possessions, beginning with the words 'Endowed with moral shame and moral dread...'. It is said that a certain householder from Savatthi, whose wife had passed away, went forth as a monk. When he went forth, he had his own dwelling, a fire hall, and a storeroom built, and he filled the storeroom with ghee, rice, and other provisions before ordaining. Even after ordaining, he would summon his servants and have them prepare meals according to his liking, which he would then eat. He had many requisites: at night he wore one set of robes, during the day another. He lived on the outskirts of the monastery. One day, while he was airing his robes, sheets, and other belongings outside his dwelling, several country monks wandering on a tour of the lodgings went to his dwelling, saw the robes and other things, and asked, 'Whose are these?' He replied, 'They are mine, friends.' 'Friend, is this robe yours too? And this lower robe? And this sheet? Is everything here yours?' 'Yes, all of it is mine.' 'Friend, the Blessed One has allowed only three robes. Yet you, having gone forth in the Dispensation of the Buddha, who is of few desires, have become one with so many requisites. Come, we will take you to the presence of the One of Ten Powers.' So saying, they took him and went to the Teacher.

Satthā disvāva “kiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave[P 1.0127], anicchamānakaṃyeva bhikkhuṃ gaṇhitvā āgatatthā”ti āha. “Bhante, ayaṃ bhikkhu bahubhaṇḍo bahuparikkhāro”ti. “Saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu bahubhaṇḍo”ti? “Saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti. “Kasmā pana tvaṃ bhikkhu bahubhaṇḍo jāto”? “Nanu ahaṃ appicchatāya santuṭṭhitāya pavivekassa vīriyārambhassa vaṇṇaṃ vadāmī”ti. So satthu vacanaṃ sutvā kupito “iminā dāni nīhārena carissāmī”ti pārupanaṃ chaḍḍetvā parisamajjhe ekacīvaro aṭṭhāsi.

Seeing him, the Teacher said, 'Monks, why have you brought this monk here against his will?' 'Venerable sir, this monk has many belongings and many requisites.' 'Is it true, monk, that you have many belongings?' 'It is true, Blessed One.' 'But why, monk, have you become one with many belongings? Do I not praise the qualities of fewness of wishes, contentment, seclusion, and the arousal of energy?' Hearing the Teacher's words, he became angry. 'Now I will live in this manner!' he exclaimed, throwing off his outer robe and standing in the midst of the assembly wearing only a single robe.

Atha naṃ satthā upatthambhayamāno “nanu tvaṃ bhikkhu pubbe hirottappagavesako dakarakkhasakālepi hirottappaṃ gavesamāno dvādasa saṃvaccharāni vihāsi, atha kasmā idāni evaṃ garuke buddhasāsane pabbajitvā catuparisamajjhe pārupanaṃ chaḍḍetvā hirottappaṃ pahāya ṭhitosī”ti? So satthu vacanaṃ sutvā hirottappaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā taṃ cīvaraṃ pārupitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Bhikkhū tassatthassa āvibhāvatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu, bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

Then the Teacher, encouraging him, said: 'Monk, were you not formerly a seeker after moral shame and moral dread? Even during the time you were a water-demon, you sought after moral shame and moral dread and lived for twelve years. So why now, having gone forth into such a weighty Dispensation of the Buddha, do you, in the midst of the fourfold assembly, stand having discarded your outer robe and abandoned moral shame and moral dread?' Hearing the Teacher's words, he re-established moral shame and moral dread, put on that robe, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down to one side. The monks requested the Blessed One to reveal the meaning of this. The Blessed One then made clear the reason hidden by a previous existence.

Atīte kāsiraṭṭhe bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto nāma rājā ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā [V 1.0133] kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “mahisāsakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tassa ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle rañño aññopi putto jāto, tassa “candakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Tassa pana ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle bodhisattassa mātā kālamakāsi, rājā aññaṃ [M 1.0144] aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Sā rañño piyā ahosi manāpā, sāpi saṃvāsamanvāya ekaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi, “sūriyakumāro”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Rājā puttaṃ disvā tuṭṭhacitto “bhadde, puttassa te varaṃ dammī”ti āha. Devī, varaṃ icchitakāle gahetabbaṃ katvā ṭhapesi. Sā putte vayappatte rājānaṃ āha – “devena mayhaṃ puttassa jātakāle varo dinno, puttassa me rajjaṃ dehī”ti. Rājā “mayhaṃ dve puttā aggikkhandhā viya jalamānā vicaranti, na sakkā tava puttassa rajjaṃ dātu”nti paṭikkhipitvāpi taṃ punappunaṃ yācamānameva disvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ [P 1.0128] puttānaṃ pāpakampi cinteyyā”ti putte pakkosāpetvā āha – “tātā, ahaṃ sūriyakumārassa jātakāle varaṃ adāsiṃ. Idānissa mātā rajjaṃ yācati, ahaṃ tassa na dātukāmo, mātugāmo nāma pāpo, tumhākaṃ pāpakampi cinteyya, tumhe araññaṃ pavisitvā mama accayena kulasantake nagare rajjaṃ kareyyāthā”ti roditvā kanditvā sīse cumbitvā uyyojesi. Te pitaraṃ vanditvā pāsādā otarante rājaṅgaṇe kīḷamāno sūriyakumāro disvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “ahampi bhātikehi saddhiṃ gamissāmī”ti tehi saddhiṃyeva nikkhami. Te himavantaṃ pavisiṃsu.

In the past, in the kingdom of Kasi, in the city of Bārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta. At that time, the Bodhisatta took conception in the womb of his chief queen. On his naming day, they gave him the name 'Prince Mahisāsa.' While he was running and playing, another son was born to the king, and they named him 'Prince Canda.' While he too was running and playing, the Bodhisatta’s mother passed away, and the king appointed another as chief queen. She was dear and pleasing to the king, and in due course, she bore a son, whom they named 'Prince Sūriya.' The king, delighted upon seeing the child, said, 'My dear, I shall grant you a boon for your son.' The queen, deciding to claim the boon at a suitable time, set it aside. When her son came of age, she said to the king, 'Your Majesty, you granted me a boon when my son was born; now give the kingdom to my son.' The king refused, saying, 'My two sons are like blazing masses of fire—it is not possible to give the kingdom to your son.' But seeing her repeatedly pleading, he thought, 'She may even plot evil against my sons.' So he summoned his sons and said, 'My dear sons, I once granted a boon when Prince Sūriya was born. Now his mother is demanding the kingdom for him. I do not wish to give it to him. Womankind is indeed wicked—she may even plot harm against you. Go into the forest, and after my death, you should rule the kingdom in the ancestral city.' Weeping and lamenting, he kissed them on their heads and sent them away. They paid respects to their father and descended from the palace. As they were descending, Prince Sūriya, playing in the royal courtyard, saw them and, learning the reason, said, 'I too shall go with my brothers,' and left with them. They entered the Himalayas.

Bodhisatto [M 1.0145] maggā okkamma rukkhamūle nisīditvā sūriyakumāraṃ āmantesi “tāta sūriyakumāra, etaṃ saraṃ gantvā nhatvā ca pivitvā ca paduminipaṇṇehi amhākampi pānīyaṃ ānehī”ti. Taṃ pana saraṃ vessavaṇassa santikā ekena dakarakkhasena laddhaṃ hoti, vessavaṇo ca taṃ āha – “ṭhapetvā devadhammajānanake ye aññe imaṃ saraṃ otaranti, te khādituṃ labhasi. Anotiṇṇe na labhasī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya so rakkhaso ye taṃ saraṃ otaranti, te devadhamme pucchitvā ye na jānanti, te khādati. Atha kho sūriyakumāro taṃ saraṃ gantvā avīmaṃsitvāva otari. Atha naṃ so rakkhaso gahetvā “devadhamme jānāsī”ti pucchi. So “devadhammā nāma candimasūriyā”ti āha. Atha naṃ “tvaṃ devadhamme na jānāsī”ti vatvā udakaṃ pavesetvā attano vasanaṭṭhāne ṭhapesi. Bodhisattopi taṃ aticirāyantaṃ disvā candakumāraṃ pesesi. Rakkhaso tampi gahetvā “devadhamme jānāsī”ti pucchi. “Āma jānāmi, devadhammā nāma catasso disā”ti. Rakkhaso “na tvaṃ devadhamme jānāsī”ti tampi gahetvā tattheva ṭhapesi.

The Bodhisatta, stepping off the path, sat down at the foot of a tree and addressed Prince Sūriya, saying, 'Dear Prince Sūriya, go to this lake, bathe and drink, and bring us some water in lotus leaves.' Now, that lake had been granted to a water-ogre by Vessavaṇa, and Vessavaṇa had told him, 'Except for those who know the devadhamma, you may devour any others who enter this lake. You may not take those who do not enter.' From that time onward, that ogre would question those who entered the lake about the devadhamma, and those who did not know, he would devour. Then Prince Sūriya went to the lake and, without investigating, entered it. The ogre seized him and asked, 'Do you know the devadhamma?' He replied, 'The devadhamma are the sun and the moon.' The ogre said, 'You do not know the devadhamma,' and leading him into the water, placed him in his own dwelling. The Bodhisatta, seeing that he was taking a very long time, sent Prince Canda. The ogre seized him also and asked, 'Do you know the devadhamma?' 'Yes, I know. The devadhamma are the four directions.' The ogre said, 'You do not know the devadhamma,' and seizing him, placed him in that same place.

Bodhisatto [V 1.0134] tasmimpi cirāyante “ekena antarāyena bhavitabba”nti sayaṃ tattha gantvā dvinnampi otaraṇapadavaḷañjaṃ [P 1.0129] disvā “rakkhasapariggahitena iminā sarena bhavitabba”nti khaggaṃ sannayhitvā dhanuṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. Dakarakkhaso bodhisattaṃ udakaṃ anotarantaṃ disvā vanakammikapuriso viya hutvā bodhisattaṃ āha – “bho, purisa, tvaṃ maggakilanto kasmā imaṃ saraṃ otaritvā nhatvā pivitvā bhisamuḷālaṃ khāditvā pupphāni piḷandhitvā yathāsukhaṃ na gacchasī”ti? Bodhisatto taṃ disvā “eso yakkho bhavissatī”ti ñatvā “tayā me bhātikā gahitā”ti āha. “Āma, gahitā”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Ahaṃ imaṃ saraṃ otiṇṇake labhāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana sabbeva labhasī”ti? “Ye devadhamme jānanti, te ṭhapetvā avasese labhāmī”ti. “Atthi pana te devadhammehi attho”ti? “Āma, atthī”ti. “Yadi evaṃ ahaṃ te devadhamme kathessāmī”ti. “Tena hi kathehi, ahaṃ devadhamme suṇissāmī”ti. Bodhisatto āha “ahaṃ devadhamme katheyyaṃ, kiliṭṭhagatto panamhī”ti. Yakkho bodhisattaṃ nhāpetvā bhojanaṃ bhojetvā pānīyaṃ pāyetvā pupphāni piḷandhāpetvā gandhehi vilimpāpetvā alaṅkatamaṇḍapamajjhe pallaṅkaṃ attharitvā adāsi.

When he too was taking a long time, the Bodhisatta, thinking, 'There must be some danger,' went there himself. Seeing the footprints of both of them leading down into the water, he realized, 'This lake must be possessed by an ogre.' He girded on his sword, took up his bow, and stood there. The water-ogre, seeing that the Bodhisatta was not entering the water, appeared in the guise of a woodsman and said to the Bodhisatta, 'Ho, sir! You are weary from your journey. Why do you not enter this lake to bathe and drink, eat the lotus stalks and roots, adorn yourself with flowers, and go on your way in comfort?' The Bodhisatta saw him and knew, 'This must be a yakkha.' He asked, 'Was it you who seized my brothers?' 'Yes, it was I.' 'For what reason?' 'I get those who enter this lake.' 'Do you get all of them?' 'Except for those who know the devadhamma, I get the rest.' 'Do you have a need for the devadhamma?' 'Yes, I do.' 'If so, I will teach you the devadhamma.' 'Then teach me; I will listen to the devadhamma.' The Bodhisatta said, 'I would teach the devadhamma, but I am travel-stained.' The yakkha had the Bodhisatta bathed, fed him a meal, gave him drink, had him adorned with flowers, anointed with perfumes, and prepared a seat for him in the middle of a decorated pavilion.

Bodhisatto āsane nisīditvā yakkhaṃ pādamūle nisīdāpetvā “tena hi ohitasoto sakkaccaṃ devadhamme suṇāhī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, having seated himself on the seat and having made the yakkha sit at his feet, said, 'Well then, listen attentively and respectfully to the devadhamma,' and spoke this verse:

6.

6.

“Hiriottappasampannā, sukkadhammasamāhitā;

Santo sappurisā loke, devadhammāti vuccare”ti.

Those endowed with moral shame and moral dread, established in pure qualities—the serene and virtuous persons in the world—are said to be the devadhamma.

Tattha hiriottappasampannāti hiriyā ca ottappena ca samannāgatā. Tesu kāyaduccaritādīhi hiriyatīti hirī, lajjāyetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tehiyeva ottappatīti ottappaṃ, pāpato ubbegassetaṃ adhivacanaṃ. Tattha ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī, bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ. Attādhipateyyā hirī, lokādhipateyyaṃ ottappaṃ. Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā hirī, bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ. Sappatissavalakkhaṇā hirī, vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ.

Herein, 'endowed with moral shame and moral dread' means possessed of both moral shame and moral dread. Of these, moral shame is the shame felt regarding bodily misconduct and the like; it is a synonym for modesty. Moral dread is the dread felt regarding those same things; it is a synonym for fear of evil. Of these, moral shame is internally conditioned, while moral dread is externally conditioned. Moral shame has the self as its governing principle; moral dread has the world as its governing principle. Moral shame is founded on the nature of modesty; moral dread is founded on the nature of fear. Moral shame has the characteristic of reverence; moral dread has the characteristic of fear of blame and seeing danger therein.

Tattha ajjhattasamuṭṭhānaṃ hiriṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpeti – jātiṃ paccavekkhitvā vayaṃ paccavekkhitvā [P 1.0130] sūrabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā bāhusaccaṃ paccavekkhitvā[M 1.0146]. Kathaṃ? “Pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ na jātisampannānaṃ kammaṃ, hīnajaccānaṃ kevaṭṭādīnaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa jātisampannassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ tāva jātiṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto [V 1.0135] hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakaraṇaṃ nāmetaṃ daharehi kattabbaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa vaye ṭhitassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ vayaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ dubbalajātikānaṃ kammaṃ, mādisassa sūrabhāvasampannassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ sūrabhāvaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Tathā “pāpakammaṃ nāmetaṃ andhabālānaṃ kammaṃ, na paṇḍitānaṃ, mādisassa paṇḍitassa bahussutassa idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na yutta”nti evaṃ bāhusaccaṃ paccavekkhitvā pāṇātipātādipāpaṃ akaronto hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpeti. Evaṃ ajjhattasamuṭṭhānaṃ hiriṃ catūhi kāraṇehi samuṭṭhāpeti. Samuṭṭhāpetvā ca pana attano citte hiriṃ pavesetvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ hirī ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā nāma hoti.

Herein, one arouses internally-conditioned moral shame through four reasons: by reflecting on one's birth, by reflecting on one's age, by reflecting on one's valor, and by reflecting on one's great learning. How so? 'This act of evil is not the work of the well-born; it is the work of those of low birth, such as fishermen and the like. It is not fitting for one such as I, who is well-born, to do such a deed.' Thus, by reflecting on one's birth, one refrains from evil deeds such as the taking of life and arouses moral shame. Likewise: 'This act of evil is something to be done by the young. It is not fitting for one such as I, who has come of age, to do such a deed.' Thus, by reflecting on one's age, one refrains from evil deeds such as the taking of life and arouses moral shame. Likewise: 'This evil deed is the work of the weak-natured. It is not fitting for one such as I, who is endowed with valor, to do such a deed.' Thus, by reflecting on one's valor, one refrains from evil deeds such as the taking of life and arouses moral shame. Likewise: 'This evil deed is the work of blind fools, not of the wise. It is not fitting for one such as I, who is wise and of great learning, to do such a deed.' Thus, by reflecting on one's great learning, one refrains from evil deeds such as the taking of life and arouses moral shame. In this way, one arouses internally-conditioned moral shame through these four reasons. And having aroused it, establishing moral shame in one's own mind, one does no evil. Thus, moral shame is called internally-conditioned.

Kathaṃ ottappaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma? “Sace tvaṃ pāpakammaṃ karissasi, catūsu parisāsu garahappatto bhavissasi.

How is moral dread called externally-conditioned? 'If you were to do an evil deed, you would become subject to censure in the four assemblies.'

“Garahissanti taṃ viññū, asuciṃ nāgariko yathā;

Vajjito sīlavantehi, kathaṃ bhikkhu karissasī”ti. (dha. sa. aṭṭha. 1 balarāsivaṇṇanā) –

'The wise will censure you, as a townsman would an impure thing; rejected by the virtuous, how will you fare, O monk?'

Evaṃ paccavekkhanto hi bahiddhāsamuṭṭhitena ottappena pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ ottappaṃ bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ nāma hoti.

Thus, by reflecting in this way, one does not commit evil deeds due to moral dread that has arisen externally. Thus, moral dread is called externally arisen.

Kathaṃ hirī attādhipateyyā nāma? Idhekacco kulaputto attānaṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā “mādisassa saddhāpabbajitassa bahussutassa dhutaṅgadharassa na yuttaṃ pāpakammaṃ kātu”nti pāpaṃ na karoti. Evaṃ hirī attādhipateyyā nāma hoti. Tenāha bhagavā –

How is moral shame called 'having self as its authority'? Here, a certain clansman, making himself his master and chief, thinks: 'It is not proper for someone like me, who has gone forth from the household life in faith, is extensively learned, and upholds the ascetic practices, to commit evil deeds.' Thus, he does not commit evil. In this way, moral shame is called 'having self as its authority.' Therefore, the Blessed One has said:

“So attānaṃyeva adhipatiṃ katvā akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti. Sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti. Suddhamattānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 3.40).

'Making oneself the master, one abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; one abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; one keeps oneself pure.' (AN 3.40)

Kathaṃ ottappaṃ lokādhipateyyaṃ nāma? Idhekacco kulaputto lokaṃ adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ katvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Yathāha –

How is moral dread called 'having the world as its authority'? Here, a certain clansman, making the world his master and chief, refrains from evil deeds. As it is said:

“Mahā [V 1.0136][M 1.0147] kho panāyaṃ lokasannivāso. Mahantasmiṃ kho pana lokasannivāse santi samaṇabrāhmaṇā iddhimanto dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduno, te dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṃ jānanti, tepi maṃ evaṃ jānissanti ‘passatha bho, imaṃ kulaputtaṃ, saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti.

'Vast indeed is this world-assembly. In such a vast world-assembly, there are ascetics and brahmins possessing psychic power, having the divine eye, who are knowers of others' minds. They see even from afar, and are not seen even when near. They know mind with their own mind. They too will know me thus: "See, good sirs, this clansman, who has gone forth from the household life into homelessness out of faith, yet dwells intermingled with evil, unwholesome states."

“Santi devatā iddhimantiyo dibbacakkhukā paracittaviduniyo, tā dūratopi passanti, āsannāpi na dissanti, cetasāpi cittaṃ jānanti, tāpi maṃ evaṃ jānissanti ‘passatha bho, imaṃ kulaputtaṃ, saddhā agārasmā anagāriyaṃ pabbajito [P 1.0131] samāno vokiṇṇo viharati pāpakehi akusalehi dhammehī’ti. So lokaṃyeva adhipatiṃ jeṭṭhakaṃ karitvā akusalaṃ pajahati, kusalaṃ bhāveti. Sāvajjaṃ pajahati, anavajjaṃ bhāveti. Suddhamattānaṃ pariharatī”ti (a. ni. 3.40).

'There are deities possessing psychic power, having the divine eye, who are knowers of others' minds. They see even from afar, and are not seen even when near. They know mind with their own mind. They too will know me thus: "See, good sirs, this clansman, who out of faith has gone forth from the household life into homelessness, yet dwells intermingled with evil, unwholesome states." He, making the world itself his master and chief, abandons the unwholesome and develops the wholesome; he abandons the blameworthy and develops the blameless; he keeps himself pure.' (AN 3.40)

Evaṃ ottappaṃ lokādhipateyyaṃ nāma hoti.

Thus, moral dread is called 'having the world as its authority.'

“Lajjāsabhāvasaṇṭhitā hirī, bhayasabhāvasaṇṭhitaṃ ottappa”nti ettha pana lajjāti lajjanākāro, tena sabhāvena saṇṭhitā hirī. Bhayanti apāyabhayaṃ, tena sabhāvena saṇṭhitaṃ ottappaṃ. Tadubhayampi pāpaparivajjane pākaṭaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi yathā nāmeko kulaputto uccārapassāvādīni karonto lajjitabbayuttakaṃ ekaṃ disvā lajjanākārappatto bhaveyya hīḷito, evamevaṃ ajjhattaṃ lajjidhammaṃ okkamitvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Ekacco apāyabhayabhīto hutvā pāpakammaṃ na karoti. Tatridaṃ opammaṃ – yathā hi dvīsu ayoguḷesu eko sītalo bhaveyya gūthamakkhito, eko uṇho āditto. Tattha paṇḍito sītalaṃ gūthamakkhitattā jigucchanto na gaṇhāti, itaraṃ ḍāhabhayena. Tattha sītalassa gūthamakkhitassa jigucchāya agaṇhanaṃ viya ajjhattaṃ lajjidhammaṃ okkamitvā pāpassa akaraṇaṃ, uṇhassa ḍāhabhayena agaṇhanaṃ viya apāyabhayena pāpassa akaraṇaṃ veditabbaṃ.

'Moral shame is established in the nature of modesty; moral dread is established in the nature of fear.' Here, 'modesty' means the mode of being ashamed; moral shame is established in that nature. 'Fear' means fear of the lower realms; moral dread is established in that nature. Both are manifest in the avoidance of evil. For instance, just as a certain clansman, while excreting or urinating, upon seeing someone before whom one should feel shame, might become ashamed and feel humiliated—in the same way, one who has internally entered into the state of shame does not commit evil deeds. Another, having become fearful of the lower realms, does not commit evil deeds. Here is a simile: Just as of two iron balls, one might be cold and smeared with excrement, the other hot and burning, a wise person, disgusted by the cold one being smeared with excrement, does not take it, and he does not take the other out of fear of being burned. Here, not taking the cold one smeared with excrement out of disgust should be understood as being like not committing evil by having internally entered into the state of shame; and not taking the hot one out of fear of being burned should be understood as being like not committing evil out of fear of the lower realms.

“Sappatissavalakkhaṇā [M 1.0148] hirī, vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappa”nti idampi dvayaṃ pāpaparivajjaneyeva pākaṭaṃ hoti. Ekacco hi jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇā, satthumahattapaccavekkhaṇā, dāyajjamahattapaccavekkhaṇā, sabrahmacārimahattapaccavekkhaṇāti catūhi kāraṇehi sappatissavalakkhaṇaṃ hiriṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā pāpaṃ na karoti. Ekacco attānuvādabhayaṃ, parānuvādabhayaṃ[V 1.0137], daṇḍabhayaṃ, duggatibhayanti catūhi kāraṇehi vajjabhīrukabhayadassāvilakkhaṇaṃ ottappaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā pāpaṃ na karoti. Tattha jātimahattapaccavekkhaṇādīni ceva attānuvādabhayādīni ca vitthāretvā kathetabbāni. Tesaṃ vitthāro aṅguttaranikāyaṭṭhakathāyaṃ vutto.

'Moral shame has the characteristic of respectfulness; moral dread has the characteristic of being fearful of blame and seeing danger.' This pair, too, is manifest in the avoidance of evil. Indeed, one person, by reflecting on the greatness of their birth, reflecting on the greatness of the Teacher, reflecting on the greatness of the inheritance, and reflecting on the greatness of their fellow practitioners—for these four reasons—having generated moral shame with the characteristic of respectfulness, does not commit evil. Another person, due to the fear of self-reproach, the fear of others' reproach, the fear of punishment, and the fear of a bad destination—for these four reasons—having generated moral dread with the characteristic of being fearful of blame and seeing danger, does not commit evil. Here, the reflections on the greatness of birth and so forth, and the fears of self-reproach and so forth, should be explained in detail. Their detailed explanation is stated in the Commentary to the Aṅguttara Nikāya.

Sukkadhammasamāhitāti idameva hirottappaṃ ādiṃ katvā kattabbā kusalā dhammā sukkadhammā nāma, te sabbasaṅgāhakanayena catubhūmakalokiyalokuttaradhammā. Tehi samāhitā samannāgatāti attho. Santo sappurisā loketi kāyakammādīnaṃ santatāya santo, kataññukataveditāya sobhanā purisāti sappurisā. Loko pana saṅkhāraloko, sattaloko, okāsaloko, khandhaloko, āyatanaloko, dhātulokoti anekavidho. Tattha “eko loko sabbe sattā āhāraṭṭhitikā…pe… aṭṭhārasa lokā aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo”ti (paṭi. ma. 1.112) ettha saṅkhāraloko vutto. Khandhalokādayo tadantogadhāyeva. “Ayaṃ loko paraloko, devaloko manussaloko”tiādīsu (mahāni. 3; cūḷani. ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2) pana sattaloko vutto.

'Established in white qualities' (sukkadhammasamāhitā): making this very moral shame and moral dread their beginning, the wholesome states to be cultivated are called 'white qualities.' These, by way of comprehensive inclusion, are the mundane and supramundane states of the four planes. The meaning is 'established in them, endowed with them.' 'The peaceful, the good persons in the world' (santo sappurisā loke): they are 'peaceful' (santo) due to the peacefulness of their bodily actions and so forth; they are 'good persons' (sappurisā) because they are grateful and acknowledge what has been done for them, being thus 'excellent persons' (sobhanā purisā). The world (loko), however, is of many kinds: the world of conditioned phenomena, the world of beings, the world of space, the world of aggregates, the world of sense spheres, and the world of elements. Among these, in the passage, 'One world: all beings are sustained by food... eighteen worlds: eighteen elements' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.112), the world of conditioned phenomena is stated. The worlds of aggregates and so forth are included within that. However, in passages such as, 'This world, the other world, the world of devas, the world of humans' (Mahāniddesa 3; Cūḷaniddesa, Ajitamāṇavapucchāniddesa 2), the world of beings is stated.

“Yāvatā [P 1.0132] candimasūriyā, pariharanti disā bhanti virocamānā;

Tāva sahassadhā loko, ettha te vattate vaso”ti. (ma. ni. 1.503) –

“As far as the moon and sun revolve, shining and illuminating the directions, so far extends the thousandfold world where your power prevails.” (MN 120)

Ettha okāsaloko vutto. Tesu idha sattaloko adhippeto. Sattalokasmiñhi ye evarūpā sappurisā, te devadhammāti vuccanti.

Here, the world of space is mentioned. Among these, the world of beings is intended here. For in the world of beings, those good persons of such a kind are called 'those of divine nature.'

Tattha [M 1.0149] devāti sammutidevā, upapattidevā, visuddhidevāti tividhā. Tesu mahāsammatakālato paṭṭhāya lokena “devā”ti sammatattā rājarājakumārādayo sammutidevā nāma. Devaloke uppannā upapattidevā nāma. Khīṇāsavā pana visuddhidevā nāma. Vuttampi cetaṃ –

Herein, gods are of three kinds: conventional gods, gods by rebirth, and purified gods. Among these, kings, princes, and the like are called conventional gods because they have been regarded as “gods” by the world since the time of the great election (Mahā Sammata). Those born in the heavenly realms are called gods by rebirth. But those whose taints are destroyed are called purified gods. And this has been said:

“Sammutidevā nāma rājāno deviyo rājakumārā. Upapattidevā nāma bhummadeve upādāya taduttaridevā. Visuddhidevā nāma buddhā paccekabuddhā khīṇāsavā”ti (cūḷani. dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32; pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 119).

“Conventional gods are kings, queens, and princes. Gods by rebirth are gods beginning with the earth-dwelling gods and those above them. Purified gods are Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and those whose taints are destroyed” (Cūḷaniddesa, Dhotakamāṇavapucchāniddesa 32; Pārāyanānugītigāthāniddesa 119).

Imesaṃ devānaṃ dhammāti devadhammā. Vuccareti vuccanti. Hirottappamūlakā hi kusalā dhammā kulasampadāya [V 1.0138] ceva devaloke nibbattiyā ca visuddhibhāvassa ca kāraṇattā kāraṇaṭṭhena tividhānampi tesaṃ devānaṃ dhammāti devadhammā, tehi devadhammehi samannāgatā puggalāpi devadhammā. Tasmā puggalādhiṭṭhānadesanāya te dhamme dassento “santo sappurisā loke, devadhammāti vuccare”ti āha.

The qualities of these deities are called divine qualities (devadhammā). They are so called (vuccare) because wholesome qualities rooted in moral shame and moral dread are, in the sense of being the cause, the cause for family prosperity, rebirth in the divine realm, and the attainment of purity—thus, in this threefold sense, they are the qualities of those deities. Individuals endowed with these divine qualities are also called divine. Therefore, to illustrate these qualities in a teaching concerning individuals, it is said: “The peaceful, good persons in the world are called divine.”

Yakkho imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pasannacitto bodhisattaṃ āha – “paṇḍita, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pasanno, ekaṃ bhātaraṃ demi, kataraṃ ānemī”ti? “Kaniṭṭhaṃ ānehī”ti. “Paṇḍita, tvaṃ kevalaṃ devadhamme jānāsiyeva, na pana tesu vattasī”ti. “Kiṃ kāraṇā”ti? “Yaṃkāraṇā jeṭṭhakaṃ ṭhapetvā kaniṭṭhaṃ āṇāpento jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammaṃ na karosī”ti. Devadhamme cāhaṃ, yakkha, jānāmi, tesu ca vattāmi. Mayañhi imaṃ araññaṃ etaṃ nissāya paviṭṭhā. Etassa hi atthāya amhākaṃ pitaraṃ etassa mātā rajjaṃ yāci, amhākaṃ pana pitā taṃ varaṃ adatvā amhākaṃ anurakkhaṇatthāya araññavāsaṃ anujāni. So kumāro anuvattitvā amhehi saddhiṃ āgato. “Taṃ araññe eko yakkho khādī”ti vuttepi na koci saddahissati, tenāhaṃ garahabhayabhīto tameva āṇāpemīti. “Sādhu sādhu paṇḍita, tvaṃ devadhamme ca jānāsi, tesu ca vattasī”ti [P 1.0133] pasanno yakkho bodhisattassa sādhukāraṃ datvā dvepi bhātaro ānetvā adāsi.

Having heard this teaching on the Dhamma, the ogre, with a pleased mind, said to the Bodhisatta: “Wise one, I am pleased with you. I will give back one brother—which one shall I bring?” “Bring the youngest,” he replied. “Wise one, you only know the divine principles, but you do not practice them.” “Why is that?” “Because by setting aside the eldest and ordering the youngest to be brought, you fail to perform the act of respecting the elder.” “Ogre, I both know the divine principles and I practice them. For we entered this forest on his account. It was for his sake that his mother asked our father for the kingdom, but our father, not granting that boon, permitted us to live in the forest for our own protection. That prince followed and came with us. Even if it is said, ‘An ogre in the forest devoured him,’ no one would believe it. Therefore, fearing blame, I ask for him.” “Good, good, wise one! You both know the divine principles and practice them,” said the pleased ogre, applauding the Bodhisatta, and he brought both brothers and gave them back.

Atha naṃ bodhisatto āha – “samma, tvaṃ pubbe attanā katena pāpakammena paresaṃ maṃsalohitakhādako yakkho hutvā nibbatto, idānipi pāpameva karosi, idaṃ te pāpakammaṃ nirayādīhi muccituṃ okāsaṃ na dassati[M 1.0150], tasmā ito paṭṭhāya pāpaṃ pahāya kusalaṃ karohī”ti. Asakkhi ca pana taṃ dametuṃ. So taṃ yakkhaṃ dametvā tena saṃvihitārakkho tattheva vasanto ekadivasaṃ nakkhattaṃ oloketvā pitu kālakatabhāvaṃ ñatvā yakkhaṃ ādāya bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rajjaṃ gahetvā candakumārassa oparajjaṃ, sūriyakumārassa senāpatiṭṭhānaṃ, datvā yakkhassa ramaṇīye ṭhāne āyatanaṃ kāretvā, yathā so aggamālaṃ aggapupphaṃ aggabhattañca labhati, tathā akāsi. So dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Then the Bodhisatta said to him: “Friend, formerly, due to an evil deed you yourself committed, you were reborn as an ogre who eats the flesh and blood of others. Even now you continue to do evil. This evil deed of yours will not give you an opportunity to escape from hell and other such states. Therefore, from now on, abandon evil and do good.” And he was able to tame him. Having tamed that ogre, and with protection provided by him, he remained there. One day, observing the constellations, he learned of his father's death. Taking the ogre with him, he went to Benares and assumed kingship. He gave the position of viceroy to Prince Canda, and the position of commander-in-chief to Prince Suriya. For the ogre, he had a dwelling built in a pleasant place, and arranged that he receive the finest garlands, the finest flowers, and the finest food. Having ruled righteously, he passed away according to his deeds.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā dassetvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Sammāsambuddhopi dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dakarakkhaso bahubhaṇḍikabhikkhu ahosi, sūriyakumāro ānando, candakumāro sāriputto, jeṭṭhakabhātā mahisāsakumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this discourse and proclaimed the truths. At the conclusion of the truths, that monk became established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Perfectly Enlightened One, having related the two stories and made the connection, identified the birth, saying: “At that time, the water demon was the monk with many possessions, Prince Sūriya was Ānanda, Prince Canda was Sāriputta, and the eldest brother, Prince Mahisāsa, was none other than myself.”

Devadhammajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Devadhamma Jātaka, the sixth.

7. Kaṭṭhahārijātakavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka

Putto [V 1.0139] tyāhaṃ mahārājāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto vāsabhakhattiyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vāsabhakhattiyāya vatthu dvādasakanipāte bhaddasālajātake āvibhavissati. Sā kira mahānāmassa sakkassa dhītā nāgamuṇḍāya nāma dāsiyā kucchismiṃ jātā kosalarājassa aggamahesī ahosi. Sā rañño puttaṃ vijāyi. Rājā panassā pacchā dāsibhāvaṃ ñatvā ṭhānaṃ parihāpesi, puttassa viṭaṭūbhassāpi ṭhānaṃ parihāpesiyeva. Te ubhopi antonivesaneyeva vasanti. Satthā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā pubbaṇhasamaye pañcasatabhikkhuparivuto [P 1.0134] rañño nivesanaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīditvā “mahārāja, kahaṃ vāsabhakhattiyā”ti āha. “Rājā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ārocesi. Mahārāja vāsabhakhattiyā kassa dhītā”ti? “Mahānāmassa bhante”ti. “Āgacchamānā kassa āgatā”ti? “Mayhaṃ bhante”ti. Mahārāja sā rañño dhītā, raññova āgatā, rājānaṃyeva paṭicca puttaṃ [M 1.0151] labhi, so putto kiṃkāraṇā pitu santakassa rajjassa sāmiko na hoti, pubbe rājāno muhuttikāya kaṭṭhahārikāya kucchismimpi puttaṃ labhitvā puttassa rajjaṃ adaṃsūti. Rājā tassatthassāvibhāvatthāya bhagavantaṃ yāci, bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this, “I am your son, O great king,” concerning Vāsabhakhattiyā. The story of Vāsabhakhattiyā will become clear in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka of the Twelfth Book. She was, it is said, the daughter of the Sakyan Mahānāma, born from the womb of a slave woman named Nāgamuṇḍā, and became the chief queen of the Kosala king. She bore a son to the king. Later, when the king learned of her slave status, he deprived her of her position, and likewise deprived her son Viṭaṭūbha of his position. Both of them lived within the inner palace. Knowing this matter, the Teacher, surrounded by five hundred monks in the forenoon, went to the king’s residence. Seating himself on the prepared seat, he asked, “Great king, where is Vāsabhakhattiyā?” The king explained the matter. “Great king, whose daughter is Vāsabhakhattiyā?” “The daughter of Mahānāma, Venerable Sir.” “When she came, to whom did she come?” “To me, Venerable Sir.” “Great king, she is the daughter of a king, and she came to a king. It was through a king that she bore a son. Why then is that son not the rightful heir to his father’s kingdom? In the past, kings have granted the kingdom even to a son born in the womb of a temporary wood-gathering woman.” The king requested the Blessed One to clarify the matter, and the Blessed One revealed the reason, which had been hidden by a previous existence.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto rājā mahantena yasena uyyānaṃ gantvā tattha pupphaphalalobhena vicaranto uyyānavanasaṇḍe gāyitvā dārūni uddharamānaṃ ekaṃ itthiṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva bodhisatto tassā kucchiyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, tāvadeva tassā vajirapūritā viya garukā kucchi ahosi. Sā gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā “gabbho me, deva, patiṭṭhito”ti āha. Rājā aṅgulimuddikaṃ datvā “sace dhītā hoti, imaṃ vissajjetvā poseyyāsi, sace putto hoti, aṅgulimuddikāya saddhiṃ mama santikaṃ āneyyāsī”ti vatvā pakkāmi.

In the past, in Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta went to a park with a great retinue. There, while wandering in the park's grove, desirous of its flowers and fruits, he saw a woman singing while gathering firewood. His heart became attached, and he cohabited with her. At that very moment, the Bodhisatta took conception in her womb, and at once her womb became heavy, as if filled with adamant. Knowing that she had conceived, she said, “Your Majesty, I have conceived a child.” The king gave her a signet ring and said, “If it is a daughter, sell this and raise her. If it is a son, bring him to me along with the signet ring.” Having said this, he departed.

Sāpi paripakkagabbhā bodhisattaṃ vijāyi. Tassa ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle kīḷāmaṇḍale kīḷantassa evaṃ vattāro honti “nippitikenamhā pahaṭā”ti. Taṃ sutvā bodhisatto mātu santikaṃ gantvā “amma, ko mayhaṃ pitā”ti pucchi. “Tāta, tvaṃ bārāṇasirañño putto”ti. “Amma, atthi pana koci sakkhī”ti? Tāta rājā imaṃ muddikaṃ datvā “sace dhītā hoti, imaṃ vissajjetvā poseyyāsi, sace putto hoti, imāya aṅgulimuddikāya saddhiṃ āneyyāsī”ti vatvā gatoti. “Amma, evaṃ sante kasmā maṃ pitu santikaṃ [V 1.0140] na nesī”ti[P 1.0135]. Sā puttassa ajjhāsayaṃ ñatvā rājadvāraṃ gantvā rañño ārocāpesi. Raññā ca pakkosāpitā pavisitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā “ayaṃ te, deva, putto”ti āha. Rājā jānantopi parisamajjhe lajjāya “na mayhaṃ putto”ti āha. “Ayaṃ te, deva, muddikā, imaṃ sañjānāsī”ti. “Ayampi mayhaṃ muddikā na hotī”ti. “Deva, idāni ṭhapetvā saccakiriyaṃ añño mama sakkhi natthi, sacāyaṃ dārako tumhe paṭicca jāto, ākāse tiṭṭhatu, no ce, bhūmiyaṃ patitvā maratū”ti bodhisattassa pāde gahetvā ākāse khipi. Bodhisatto ākāse pallaṅkamābhujitvā nisinno madhurassarena pitu dhammaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

When her pregnancy came to term, she gave birth to the Bodhisatta. When he was old enough to run about and play in the playground, other children would say, “We are struck by one who has no father.” Hearing this, the Bodhisatta went to his mother and asked, “Mother, who is my father?” “My dear, you are the son of the king of Bārāṇasī.” “Mother, is there any witness?” “My dear, the king gave this signet ring and said, ‘If it is a daughter, sell this and raise her; if it is a son, bring him with this signet ring,’ and then he departed.” “Mother, that being so, why do you not take me to my father?” Understanding her son’s wish, she went to the palace gate and had the king informed. Having been summoned by the king, she entered, paid homage to him, and said, “Your Majesty, this is your son.” The king, though he knew, was ashamed before the assembly and said, “He is not my son.” She said, “Your Majesty, this is your signet ring; do you recognize it?” He replied, “This is not my signet ring either.” She then said, “Your Majesty, apart from an act of truth, I have no other witness. If this child was indeed begotten by you, let him remain in the sky; if not, let him fall to the earth and die.” Then, taking the Bodhisatta by the feet, she tossed him into the air. The Bodhisatta, sitting cross-legged in the sky, preached the Dhamma to his father with a sweet voice, uttering this verse:

7.

7.

“Putto [M 1.0152] tyāhaṃ mahārāja, tvaṃ maṃ posa janādhipa;

Aññepi devo poseti, kiñca devo sakaṃ paja”nti.

“I am your son, O great king; support me, O lord of the people. Your Majesty supports even others; why not then your own child?”

Tattha putto tyāhanti putto te ahaṃ. Putto ca nāmesa atrajo, khettajo, antevāsiko, dinnakoti catubbidho. Tattha attānaṃ paṭicca jāto atrajo nāma. Sayanapiṭṭhe pallaṅke uretievamādīsu nibbatto khettajo nāma. Santike sippuggaṇhanako antevāsiko nāma. Posāvanatthāya dinno dinnako nāma. Idha pana atrajaṃ sandhāya “putto”ti vuttaṃ. Catūhi saṅgahavatthūhi janaṃ rañjetīti rājā, mahanto rājā mahārājā. Tamālapanto āha “mahārājā”ti. Tvaṃ maṃ posa janādhipāti janādhipa mahājanajeṭṭhaka tvaṃ maṃ posa bharassu vaḍḍhehi. Aññepi devo posetīti aññepi hatthibandhādayo manusse, hatthiassādayo tiracchānagate ca bahujane devo poseti. Kiñca devo sakaṃ pajanti ettha pana kiñcāti garahatthe ca anuggahaṇatthe ca nipāto. “Sakaṃ pajaṃ attano puttaṃ maṃ devo na posetī”ti vadanto garahati nāma, “aññe bahujane posetī”ti vadanto anuggaṇhati nāma. Iti bodhisatto garahantopi anuggaṇhantopi “kiñca devo sakaṃ paja”nti āha.

Herein, putto tyāhaṃ means putto te ahaṃ (I am your son). The term 'son' is of four kinds: one born of oneself (atraja), one born in one's domain (khettaja), a pupil (antevāsika), and one who is given (dinnaka). Among these, one born from oneself is called atraja. One born on one's bed, couch, breast, and so forth, is called khettaja. One who learns a craft in one's presence is called an antevāsika. One given for the purpose of being raised is called a dinnaka. Here, however, 'son' is said in reference to one born of oneself. Because he delights (`rañjeti`) the people with the four bases of social harmony, he is a king (`rājā`); a great king is a mahārāja. Addressing him, he said, 'O great king.' Tvaṃ maṃ posa janādhipa means: 'O lord of the people, chief of the great multitude, you must support me, nourish me, and provide for my growth.' Aññepi devo poseti means: 'Your Majesty supports many others, such as elephant keepers and other humans, as well as many creatures like elephants and horses.' As for kiñca devo sakaṃ pajaṃ: here the particle kiñca is used in the sense of censure and in the sense of appreciation. In saying, 'Your Majesty does not support me, his own child,' he expresses censure. In saying, 'He supports many others,' he expresses appreciation. Thus the Bodhisatta, intending both censure and appreciation, said, 'Why not then your own child?'

Rājā bodhisattassa ākāse nisīditvā evaṃ dhammaṃ desentassa sutvā “ehi, tātā”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi, “ahameva posessāmi, ahameva posessāmī”ti hatthasahassaṃ pasāriyittha. Bodhisatto [P 1.0136] aññassa hatthe anotaritvā raññova hatthe otaritvā aṅke nisīdi. Rājā tassa oparajjaṃ datvā mātaraṃ aggamahesiṃ akāsi. So pitu accayena kaṭṭhavāhanarājā nāma hutvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Hearing the Bodhisatta preach the Dhamma while seated in the sky, the king extended his hands, saying, “Come, my dear son! I myself will support you, I myself will support you!” Then a thousand hands from the assembly were also extended. But the Bodhisatta, not descending into the hands of another, came down into the king’s hands and sat upon his lap. The king gave him the rank of viceroy and made his mother the chief queen. After his father’s passing, he became King Kaṭṭhavāhana, ruled righteously, and passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 1.0141] kosalarañño imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā dve vatthūni dassetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātā mahāmāyā ahosi, pitā suddhodanamahārājā, kaṭṭhavāhanarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse to the king of Kosala and having shown the connection between the two stories, identified the birth, saying: “At that time, the mother was Mahāmāyā, the father was King Suddhodana, and King Kaṭṭhavāhana was I myself.”

Kaṭṭhahārijātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Kaṭṭhahāri Jātaka, the Seventh.

8. Gāmaṇijātakavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Gāmaṇi Jātaka

Api [M 1.0153] ataramānānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ossaṭṭhavīriyaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Imasmiṃ pana jātake paccuppannavatthu ca atītavatthu ca ekādasakanipāte saṃvarajātake āvibhavissati. Vatthu hi tasmiñca imasmiñca ekasadisameva, gāthā pana nānā. Gāmaṇikumāro bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā bhātikasatassa kaniṭṭhopi hutvā bhātikasataparivārito setacchattassaheṭṭhā varapallaṅke nisinno attano yasasampattiṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ mayhaṃ yasasampatti amhākaṃ ācariyassa santakā”ti tuṭṭho imaṃ udānaṃ udānesi –

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Jetavana monastery, told this story beginning with the words, “Even for those not hurrying,” concerning a monk who had slackened his effort. In this Jātaka, the story of the present and the story of the past will be made clear in the Saṃvara Jātaka in the Book of the Elevens. For the story is the same in both, but the verses are different. Prince Gāmaṇi, having followed the Bodhisatta’s advice, though he was the youngest of a hundred brothers, was seated on a magnificent couch under a white parasol, surrounded by his hundred brothers. Gazing upon his own glorious fortune, he was pleased and uttered this inspired utterance: “This glorious fortune of mine belongs to our teacher.”

8.

8.

“Api ataramānānaṃ, phalāsāva samijjhati;

Vipakkabrahmacariyosmi, evaṃ jānāhi gāmaṇī”ti.

“Even for those who do not hasten, the aspiration for the fruit is fulfilled. My holy life has come to fruition; know this, O Gāmaṇi.”

Tattha apīti nipātamattaṃ. Ataramānānanti paṇḍitānaṃ ovāde ṭhatvā ataritvā avegāyitvā upāyena kammaṃ karontānaṃ. Phalāsāva samijjhatīti yathāpatthike phale āsā tassa phalassa nipphattiyā samijjhatiyeva. Atha vā phalāsāti āsāphalaṃ, yathāpatthitaṃ phalaṃ samijjhatiyevāti attho. Vipakkabrahmacariyosmīti ettha cattāri saṅgahavatthūni seṭṭhacariyattā brahmacariyaṃ nāma, tañca tammūlikāya yasasampattiyā paṭiladdhattā vipakkaṃ nāma. Yo vāssa yaso nipphanno, sopi seṭṭhaṭṭhena brahmacariyaṃ nāma. Tenāha “vipakkabrahmacariyosmī”ti. Evaṃ jānāhi gāmaṇīti [P 1.0137] katthaci gāmikapurisopi gāmajeṭṭhakopi gāmaṇī. Idha pana sabbajanajeṭṭhakaṃ attānaṃ sandhāyāha. Ambho gāmaṇi, tvaṃ etaṃ kāraṇaṃ evaṃ jānāhi, ācariyaṃ nissāya bhātikasataṃ atikkamitvā idaṃ mahārajjaṃ pattosmīti udānaṃ udānesi.

Here, 'api' is merely a particle. The phrase 'ataramānānaṃ' means for those who, abiding in the advice of the wise, do not act hastily or impetuously, but perform their work with skill. The phrase 'phalāsāva samijjhati' means that the aspiration for the desired fruit is surely fulfilled by the attainment of that fruit. Alternatively, 'phalāsā' means the fruit of aspiration; the meaning is that the desired fruit is indeed achieved. Regarding 'vipakkabrahmacariyosmi': Here, the four bases of sympathy are called 'brahmacariya' because they are the foremost conduct, and because it is attained through the glory rooted in them, it is called 'vipakka' (ripened). Or, the glory that has arisen for him is also called 'brahmacariya' due to its excellence. Hence it is said, 'I have a holy life that has borne its fruit'. Regarding 'evaṃ jānāhi gāmaṇī': In some contexts, a village man or a village elder is called 'gāmaṇī.' Here, however, it refers to himself as the foremost among all people. He uttered this exclamation: 'O Gāmaṇī, understand this reason thus—relying on the teacher, surpassing a hundred brothers, I have attained this great kingdom.'

Tasmiṃ pana rajjaṃ patte sattaṭṭhadivasaccayena sabbepi bhātaro attano attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gatā[V 1.0142]. Gāmaṇirājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā yathākammaṃ gato, bodhisattopi puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

When he had attained the kingdom, after a lapse of seven or eight days, all the brothers went each to his own dwelling. King Gāmaṇi ruled righteously and passed away according to his kamma, and the Bodhisatta also, having performed meritorious deeds, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā dassetvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhito. Satthā dve [M 1.0154] vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā gāmaṇikumāro ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu ahosi, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth and presented this Dhamma discourse, revealed the truths. At the conclusion of the truths, the monk of slackened effort was established in Arahantship. The Teacher, having related the two stories, connected the links, and identified the Jātaka: "At that time Prince Gāmaṇi was the monk of slackened effort, and the teacher was indeed myself."

Gāmaṇijātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Gāmaṇi Jātaka: The Eighth.

9. Maghadevajātakavaṇṇanā

9. The Commentary on the Maghadeva Jātaka

Uttamaṅgaruhā mayhanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto mahābhinikkhamanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ heṭṭhā nidānakathāyaṃ kathitameva. Tasmiṃ pana kāle bhikkhū dasabalassa nekkhammaṃ vaṇṇayantā nisīdiṃsu. Atha satthā dhammasabhaṃ āgantvā buddhāsane nisinno bhikkhū āmantesi “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti. “Bhante, na aññāya kathāya, tumhākaṃyeva pana nekkhammaṃ vaṇṇayamānā nisinnāmhā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato etarahiyeva nekkhammaṃ nikkhanto, pubbepi nikkhantoyevā”ti āha. Bhikkhū tassatthassāvibhāvatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu, bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

Beginning with the words, 'The hairs on my head...,' the Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jetavana concerning the Great Renunciation. That has already been explained in the introductory story. At that time, the monks sat praising the renunciation of the Ten-Powered One. Then the Teacher arrived at the Dhamma hall, sat on the Buddha’s seat, and addressed the monks: 'Monks, with what discussion are you now assembled here?' When they replied, 'Venerable sir, not with any other discussion, but we were sitting here praising your renunciation,' the Teacher then said, 'Monks, the Tathāgata has not only renounced now; he renounced in the past as well.' The monks, desiring the meaning to be revealed, requested the Blessed One. The Blessed One made clear the cause hidden by another existence.

Atīte videharaṭṭhe mithilāyaṃ maghadevo nāma rājā ahosi dhammiko dhammarājā. So caturāsīti vassasahassāni kumārakīḷaṃ kīḷi, tathā oparajjaṃ, tathā mahārajjaṃ katvā dīghamaddhānaṃ khepetvā ekadivasaṃ kappakaṃ āmantesi “yadā me, samma kappaka, sirasmiṃ palitāni passeyyāsi, atha me āroceyyāsī”ti. Kappakopi dīghamaddhānaṃ khepetvā ekadivasaṃ [P 1.0138] rañño añjanavaṇṇānaṃ kesānaṃ antare ekameva palitaṃ disvā “deva, ekaṃ te palitaṃ dissatī”ti ārocesi. “Tena hi me, samma, taṃ palitaṃ uddharitvā pāṇimhi ṭhapehī”ti ca vutte suvaṇṇasaṇḍāsena uddharitvā rañño pāṇimhi patiṭṭhāpesi. Tadā rañño caturāsīti vassasahassāni āyu avasiṭṭhaṃ hoti. Evaṃ santepi palitaṃ disvāva maccurājānaṃ āgantvā samīpe ṭhitaṃ viya attānaṃ ādittapaṇṇasālaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ viya ca maññamāno saṃvegaṃ āpajjitvā [V 1.0143] “bāla maghadeva, yāva palitassuppādāva ime kilese jahituṃ nāsakkhī”ti cintesi.

In the past, in the Videha country, in Mithila, there was a king named Maghadeva, a righteous king who ruled by the Dhamma. He played the games of a prince for eighty-four thousand years, likewise served as viceroy, and likewise ruled as a great king. Having thus spent a long time, one day he addressed his barber, 'Dear barber, when you see gray hairs on my head, you must inform me.' The barber, after a long time had passed, one day saw a single gray hair among the king’s collyrium-black locks and announced, 'Your Majesty, a single gray hair of yours is visible.' When the king said, 'Then, my dear, pluck out that gray hair and place it in my hand,' he plucked it out with golden tweezers and placed it in the king’s palm. At that time, the king had eighty-four thousand years of life remaining. Even so, upon seeing the gray hair, he felt as if the King of Death had come and stood near, or as if he himself had entered a burning leaf-hut. Filled with spiritual urgency, he thought, 'Foolish Maghadeva, you were unable to abandon these defilements even up to the arising of a gray hair.'

Tassevaṃ [M 1.0155] palitapātubhāvaṃ āvajjentassa antoḍāho uppajji, sarīrā sedā mucciṃsu, sāṭakā pīḷetvā apanetabbākārappattā ahesuṃ. So “ajjeva mayā nikkhamitvā pabbajituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti kappakassa satasahassuṭṭhānakaṃ gāmavaraṃ datvā jeṭṭhaputtaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, mama sīse palitaṃ pātubhūtaṃ, mahallakomhi jāto, bhuttā kho pana me mānusakā kāmā, idāni dibbe kāme pariyesissāmi, nekkhammakālo mayhaṃ, tvaṃ imaṃ rajjaṃ paṭipajja, ahaṃ pana pabbajitvā maghadevaambavanuyyāne vasanto samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmī”ti āha. Taṃ evaṃ pabbajitukāmaṃ amaccā upasaṅkamitvā “deva, kiṃ tumhākaṃ pabbajjākāraṇa”nti pucchiṃsu. Rājā palitaṃ hatthena gahetvā amaccānaṃ imaṃ gāthamāha –

As he was thus reflecting on the appearance of the gray hair, an inner burning arose, sweat poured from his body, and his garments reached a state where they had to be wrung out and set aside. He thought: 'It is fitting for me to go forth and renounce this very day.' He gave the barber a choice village with a revenue of one hundred thousand, had his eldest son summoned, and said: 'Dear son, a gray hair has appeared on my head; I have become old. I have enjoyed human sensual pleasures; now I shall seek divine sensual pleasures. The time for my renunciation has come. You take up this kingdom. I, for my part, will renounce and, dwelling in the Maghadeva mango grove, will practice the ascetic's life.' The ministers approached him, who was thus desirous of renouncing, and asked: 'Your Majesty, what is the reason for your renunciation?' The king took the gray hair in his hand and spoke this verse to the ministers:

9.

9.

“Uttamaṅgaruhā mayhaṃ, ime jātā vayoharā;

Pātubhūtā devadūtā, pabbajjāsamayo mamā”ti.

"These hairs on my head have grown, these carriers of old age; Divine messengers have appeared; it is time for my renunciation."

Tattha uttamaṅgaruhāti kesā. Kesā hi sabbesaṃ hatthapādādīnaṃ aṅgānaṃ uttame sirasmiṃ ruhattā “uttamaṅgaruhā”ti vuccanti. Ime jātā vayoharāti passatha, tātā, palitapātubhāvena tiṇṇaṃ vayānaṃ haraṇato [P 1.0139] ime jātā vayoharā. Pātubhūtāti nibbattā. Devadūtāti devo vuccati maccu, tassa dūtāti devadūtā. Sirasmiñhi palitesu pātubhūtesu maccurājassa santike ṭhito viya hoti, tasmā palitāni “maccudevassa dūtā”ti vuccanti. Devā viya dūtātipi devadūtā. Yathā hi alaṅkatapaṭiyattāya devatāya ākāse ṭhatvā “asukadivase tvaṃ marissasī”ti vutte taṃ tatheva hoti, evaṃ sirasmiṃ palitesu pātubhūtesu devatāya byākaraṇasadisameva hoti, tasmā palitāni “devasadisā dūtā”ti vuccanti. Visuddhidevānaṃ dūtātipi devadūtā. Sabbabodhisattā hi jiṇṇabyādhimatapabbajite disvāva saṃvegamāpajjitvā nikkhamma pabbajanti. Yathāha –

Here, 'hairs of the head' (uttamaṅgaruhā) means hairs. Hairs are called 'hairs of the head' because they grow on the head, the highest of all limbs such as the hands and feet. 'These have appeared as robbers of age' (ime jātā vayoharā): See, dear sirs, by the appearance of grayness, these have arisen as robbers of the three stages of life, hence they are called 'robbers of age'. 'They have appeared' (pātubhūtā) means they have arisen. 'Divine messengers' (devadūtā): Here, 'deva' is said to be death, and its messengers are called 'divine messengers'. For when gray hairs appear on the head, it is as if one stands near the king of death. Therefore, gray hairs are called 'messengers of the god of death'. They are also called 'divine messengers' because they are like messengers of the gods. Just as when a celestial being, adorned and prepared, stands in the sky and declares, 'On such-and-such a day, you will die,' it happens exactly as said; likewise, when gray hairs appear on the head, it is just like a declaration made by a deity. Hence, gray hairs are called 'messengers like gods'. They are also called 'divine messengers' as messengers of the pure gods. For all Bodhisattas, upon seeing an old person, a sick person, a dead person, and one who has gone forth, are stirred with a sense of urgency and go forth into homelessness. As it is said—

“Jiṇṇañca disvā dukhitañca byādhitaṃ, matañca disvā gatamāyusaṅkhayaṃ;

Kāsāyavatthaṃ pabbajitañca disvā, tasmā ahaṃ pabbajitomhi rājā”ti. (theragā. 73 thokaṃ visadisaṃ);

Having seen the aged, the afflicted, the sick, Having seen the dead whose lifespan is complete, Having seen one gone forth in the ochre robe, Therefore I have gone forth, O king.

Iminā [V 1.0144][M 1.0156] pariyāyena palitāni visuddhidevānaṃ dūtattā “devadūtā”ti vuccanti. Pabbajjāsamayo mamāti gihibhāvato nikkhantaṭṭhena “pabbajjā”ti laddhanāmassa samaṇaliṅgagahaṇassa kālo mayhanti dasseti.

By this method, gray hairs are called 'divine messengers' because they are messengers of the pure gods. 'The time for renunciation is mine' (pabbajjāsamayo mamā) indicates that the time for me to take on the ascetic garb, which has gained the name 'renunciation' by virtue of going forth from the household life, has come.

So evaṃ vatvā taṃ divasameva rajjaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tasmiṃyeva maghadevaambavane viharanto caturāsīti vassasahassāni cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā aparihīnajjhāne ṭhito kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbattitvā puna tato cuto mithilāyaṃyeva nimi nāma rājā hutvā osakkamānaṃ attano vaṃsaṃ ghaṭetvā tattheva ambavane pabbajitvā brahmavihāre bhāvetvā puna brahmalokūpagova ahosi.

Having spoken thus, he renounced the kingdom that very day and went forth into the ascetic's homelessness. Dwelling in that very Maghadeva mango grove, he developed the four divine abodes for eighty-four thousand years. Established in unwaning absorption, he passed away and was reborn in the Brahma world. Then, having passed away from there, he was reborn as King Nimi in Mithila. He re-established his declining lineage and, having gone forth in that same mango grove, he developed the divine abodes and was again reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthāpi “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto, pubbepi nikkhantoyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā dassetvā cattāri saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne keci sotāpannā ahesuṃ, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino. Iti bhagavā imāni dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā kappako ānando ahosi, putto rāhulo, maghadevarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher also said: "Monks, the Tathagata has not only now gone forth in the Great Renunciation; he went forth before as well." Having brought forth and shown this teaching, he revealed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners. Thus, the Blessed One, having spoken these two accounts and connected the sequence of events, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the barber was Ānanda, the son was Rāhula, and King Maghadeva was none other than myself."

Maghadevajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Maghadeva Jātaka, the Ninth.

10. Sukhavihārijātakavaṇṇanā

10. The Commentary on the Sukhavihārī Jātaka.

Yañca [P 1.0140] aññe na rakkhantīti idaṃ satthā anupiyanagaraṃ nissāya anupiyaambavane viharanto sukhavihāriṃ bhaddiyattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sukhavihārī bhaddiyatthero chakhattiyasamāgame upālisattamo pabbajito. Tesu bhaddiyatthero ca, kimilatthero ca, bhagutthero ca, upālitthero ca arahattaṃ pattā, ānandatthero sotāpanno jāto, anuruddhatthero dibbacakkhuko, devadatto jhānalābhī jāto. Channaṃ pana khattiyānaṃ vatthu yāva anupiyanagarā khaṇḍahālajātake āvibhavissati. Āyasmā pana bhaddiyo rājakāle attano rakkhasaṃvidhānañceva tāva bahūhi [M 1.0157] rakkhāhi rakkhiyamānassa uparipāsādavaratale mahāsayane samparivattamānassāpi attano bhayuppattiñca idāni arahattaṃ patvā araññādīsu yattha katthaci viharantopi attano vigatabhayatañca samanussaranto “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti udānaṃ udānesi. Taṃ sutvā bhikkhū “āyasmā bhaddiyo aññaṃ byākarotī”ti bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā “na, bhikkhave[V 1.0145], bhaddiyo idāneva sukhavihārī, pubbepi sukhavihārīyevā”ti āha. Bhikkhū tassatthassāvibhāvatthāya bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu. Bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

'And what others do not guard' (Yañca aññe na rakkhanti): This the Teacher spoke concerning the Elder Bhaddiya, the Happy Dweller, while residing near the city of Anupiya in the Anupiya mango grove. The Elder Bhaddiya, the Happy Dweller, was the seventh, with Upāli, among the six Sakyan princes who went forth into homelessness. Among them, the Elder Bhaddiya, the Elder Kimila, the Elder Bhagu, and the Elder Upāli attained arahantship; the Elder Ānanda became a stream-enterer; the Elder Anuruddha gained the divine eye; and Devadatta acquired meditative attainments. The story of the six princes will be fully revealed in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka as far as the city of Anupiya. Now, the Venerable Bhaddiya, recalling how during his royal days he was guarded by many protections—and how fear arose in him even while turning on his great bed on the upper terrace of his palace—and now, having attained arahantship, dwelling in the wilderness or anywhere else, he reflected on his freedom from fear and uttered this inspired utterance: "Ah, happiness! Ah, happiness!" Hearing this, the monks reported to the Blessed One: "Venerable Bhaddiya is boasting of his attainment." The Blessed One said: "Monks, Bhaddiya is not just now a happy dweller—he was a happy dweller even before." The monks requested the Blessed One to explain the meaning in detail. The Blessed One then revealed the hidden reason, which had been concealed by a previous existence.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārayamāne bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇamahāsālo hutvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ, nekkhamme cānisaṃsaṃ disvā kāme pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattesi, parivāropissa mahā ahosi pañca tāpasasatāni. So vassakāle himavantato nikkhamitvā tāpasagaṇaparivuto gāmanigamādīsu cārikaṃ caranto bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājānaṃ nissāya rājuyyāne vāsaṃ kappesi. Tattha vassike cattāro māse vasitvā rājānaṃ āpucchi. Atha naṃ rājā “tumhe, bhante, mahallakā, kiṃ vo himavantena, antevāsike himavantaṃ pesetvā [P 1.0141] idheva vasathā”ti yāci. Bodhisatto jeṭṭhantevāsikaṃ pañca tāpasasatāni paṭicchāpetvā “gaccha, tvaṃ imehi saddhiṃ himavante vasa, ahaṃ pana idheva vasissāmī”ti te uyyojetvā sayaṃ tattheva vāsaṃ kappesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a great and wealthy brahmin from the North. Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit of renunciation, he gave up sensual desires, entered the Himalayas, and embraced the ascetic's homelessness. There, he attained the eight meditative attainments, and his following grew to five hundred ascetics. During the rainy season, he left the Himalayas and, surrounded by his group of ascetics, wandered through villages and towns until he arrived in Benares. There, relying on the king, he took up residence in the royal park. After spending the four months of the rains there, he took leave of the king. Then the king pleaded with him, saying: "Venerable sir, you are elderly. What need have you of the Himalayas? Send your disciples to the Himalayas and stay here instead." The Bodhisatta instructed his senior disciple to take charge of the five hundred ascetics, saying: "Go, dwell in the Himalayas with them. But I shall remain here." Having sent them away, he himself stayed right there.

So panassa jeṭṭhantevāsiko rājapabbajito mahantaṃ rajjaṃ pahāya pabbajitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭhasamāpattilābhī ahosi. So tāpasehi saddhiṃ himavante vasamāno ekadivasaṃ ācariyaṃ daṭṭhukāmo hutvā te tāpase āmantetvā “tumhe anukkaṇṭhamānā idheva vasatha, ahaṃ ācariyaṃ vanditvā āgamissāmī”ti ācariyassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā paṭisanthāraṃ katvā ekaṃ kaṭṭhattharikaṃ attharitvā ācariyassa santikeyeva nipajji. Tasmiñca samaye rājā “tāpasaṃ passissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Antevāsikatāpaso rājānaṃ disvā neva vuṭṭhāsi, nipannoyeva pana “aho sukhaṃ, aho sukha”nti udānaṃ udānesi. Rājā “ayaṃ tāpaso maṃ disvāpi na uṭṭhito”ti [M 1.0158] anattamano bodhisattaṃ āha – “bhante, ayaṃ tāpaso yadicchakaṃ bhutto bhavissati, udānaṃ udānento sukhaseyyameva kappetī”ti. Mahārāja, ayaṃ tāpaso pubbe tumhādiso eko rājā ahosi, svāyaṃ “ahaṃ pubbe gihikāle rajjasiriṃ anubhavanto āvudhahatthehi bahūhi rakkhiyamānopi evarūpaṃ sukhaṃ nāma nālattha”nti attano pabbajjāsukhaṃ jhānasukhañca ārabbha imaṃ udānaṃ udānetīti. Evañca pana vatvā bodhisatto rañño dhammakathaṃ kathetuṃ imaṃ gāthamāha –

Now, his senior disciple, who had gone forth from kingship, had abandoned a great kingdom and become an ascetic. After performing the preliminary kasiṇa meditation, he became an attainer of the eight meditative absorptions. While dwelling in the Himalayas with the other ascetics, one day he wished to see his teacher. Addressing those ascetics, he said, 'You may stay here without discontent; I will go to pay my respects to the teacher and return.' He went to his teacher, paid homage, exchanged friendly greetings, spread out a single wooden mat, and lay down near his teacher. At that time, the king, thinking, 'I shall see the ascetic,' went to the park, paid homage, and sat to one side. The disciple-ascetic saw the king but did not rise. Instead, while lying down, he uttered this inspired exclamation: 'Ah, what happiness! Ah, what happiness!' The king, displeased that the ascetic had not risen upon seeing him, said to the Bodhisatta, 'Venerable sir, this ascetic must have eaten as he pleased; uttering exclamations, he simply arranges a comfortable sleep for himself.' 'Great king, this ascetic was formerly a king like you. He utters this inspired exclamation concerning the happiness of renunciation and the happiness of meditative absorption, thinking, "Formerly, in my life as a householder, while enjoying the splendor of kingship and being guarded by many men with weapons in hand, I never attained such happiness as this."' Having said this, the Bodhisatta, in order to give a Dhamma talk to the king, spoke this verse:

10.

10.

“Yañca aññe na rakkhanti, yo ca aññe na rakkhati;

Sa ve rāja sukhaṃ seti, kāmesu anapekkhavā”ti.

He whom others do not guard, and who does not guard others—he, O king, truly sleeps in comfort, being unconcerned with sensual pleasures.

Tattha [V 1.0146] yañca aññe na rakkhantīti yaṃ puggalaṃ aññe bahū puggalā na rakkhanti. Yo ca aññe na rakkhatīti yo ca “ekako ahaṃ rajjaṃ kāremī”ti aññe bahū jane na rakkhati. Sa ve rāja sukhaṃ setīti mahārāja so [P 1.0142] puggalo eko adutiyo pavivitto kāyikacetasikasukhasamaṅgī hutvā sukhaṃ seti. Idañca desanāsīsameva. Na kevalaṃ pana setiyeva, evarūpo pana puggalo sukhaṃ gacchati tiṭṭhati nisīdati sayatīti sabbiriyāpathesu sukhappattova hoti. Kāmesu anapekkhavāti vatthu kāmakilesakāmesu apekkhārahito vigatacchandarāgo nittaṇho evarūpo puggalo sabbiriyāpathesu sukhaṃ viharati mahārājāti.

Herein, 'whom others do not guard' means a person whom many other people do not guard. And 'who does not guard others' means one who, unlike a king thinking 'I alone shall rule,' does not guard many other people. As for the phrase 'He indeed, O king, sleeps in comfort,' it means: O great king, that person, being alone, without a companion, secluded, and endowed with physical and mental happiness, sleeps in comfort. And this is but the pinnacle of the teaching. It is not only that he sleeps in comfort; such a person walks, stands, sits, and lies down in comfort—thus, he has attained happiness in all postures. As for 'unconcerned with sensual pleasures,' it means: being free from attachment to sensual objects and sensual defilements, devoid of sensual desire and passion, without craving—such a person, O great king, dwells happily in all postures.

Rājā dhammadesanaṃ sutvā tuṭṭhamānaso vanditvā nivesanameva gato, antevāsikopi ācariyaṃ vanditvā himavantameva gato. Bodhisatto pana tattheva viharanto aparihīnajjhāno kālaṃ katvā brahmaloke nibbatti.

The king, having heard the Dhamma teaching, was delighted in mind. He paid homage and went to his palace. The disciple also, having paid homage to the teacher, went back to the Himalayas. The Bodhisatta, however, dwelling there with his meditative absorption undiminished, passed away and was reborn in the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā dassetvā dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā antevāsiko bhaddiyatthero ahosi, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having brought forth and presented this Dhamma teaching, told the two stories, connected the sequence, and identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the disciple was the Elder Bhaddiya, and the teacher of the group was I myself.'

Sukhavihārijātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Sukhavihārī Jātaka, the tenth.

Apaṇṇakavaggo paṭhamo.

The Apaṇṇaka Chapter, the first.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Apaṇṇakaṃ [M 1.0159] vaṇṇupathaṃ, serivaṃ cūḷaseṭṭhi ca;

Taṇḍulaṃ devadhammañca, kaṭṭhavāhanagāmaṇi;

Maghadevaṃ vihārīti, piṇḍitā dasa jātakāti.

Apaṇṇaka, Vaṇṇupatha, Seriva, and Cūḷaseṭṭhi; Taṇḍula, Devadhamma, and Kaṭṭhavāhana-Gāmaṇi; Maghadeva, and Vihārī—these ten Jātakas are thus compiled.

2. Sīlavaggo

2. The Chapter on Virtue

[11] 1. Lakkhaṇamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[11] 1. The Commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Deer Jātaka

Hoti [V 1.0147] sīlavataṃ atthoti idaṃ satthā rājagahaṃ upanissāya veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadattassa vatthu yāva abhimārappayojanā khaṇḍahālajātake āvibhavissati, yāva dhanapālakavissajjanā pana cūḷahaṃsajātake āvibhavissati, yāva pathavippavesanā dvādasanipāte samuddavāṇijajātake āvibhavissati.

'There is benefit for the virtuous'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling near Rājagaha, in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta. The story of Devadatta, up to the sending of assassins, will be made clear in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka; up to the unleashing of the elephant Dhanapāla, it will be made clear in the Cūḷahaṃsa Jātaka; and up to his entering the earth, it will be made clear in the Samuddavāṇija Jātaka in the Book of Twelve.

Ekasmiñhi samaye devadatto pañca vatthūni yācitvā alabhanto saṅghaṃ bhinditvā pañca bhikkhusatāni ādāya gayāsīse viharati. Atha tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ agamāsi. Taṃ ñatvā satthā dve aggasāvake āmantesi “sāriputtā, tumhākaṃ nissitakā pañcasatā bhikkhū devadattassa laddhiṃ rocetvā tena saddhiṃ gatā, idāni pana tesaṃ ñāṇaṃ paripākaṃ gataṃ, tumhe bahūhi bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ tattha gantvā tesaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā te bhikkhū maggaphalehi pabodhetvā gahetvā āgacchathā”ti. Te tatheva gantvā tesaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā maggaphalehi pabodhetvā punadivase aruṇuggamanavelāya [P 1.0143] te bhikkhū ādāya veḷuvanameva āgamaṃsu. Āgantvā ca pana sāriputtattherassa bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ṭhitakāle bhikkhū theraṃ pasaṃsitvā bhagavantaṃ āhaṃsu – “bhante, amhākaṃ jeṭṭhabhātiko dhammasenāpati pañcahi bhikkhusatehi parivuto āgacchanto ativiya sobhati, devadatto pana parihīnaparivāro jāto”ti. Na, bhikkhave, sāriputto idāneva ñātisaṅghaparivuto āgacchanto sobhati, pubbepi sobhiyeva. Devadattopi [M 1.0160] na idāneva gaṇato parihīno, pubbepi parihīnoyevāti. Bhikkhū tassatthassāvibhāvatthāya bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu, bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

On one occasion, Devadatta, having requested the five points and not receiving them, created a schism in the Saṅgha and, taking five hundred monks, dwelt at Gayāsīsa. Then the knowledge of those monks matured. Knowing this, the Teacher addressed his two chief disciples: 'Sāriputta and Moggallāna, five hundred monks, your followers, having approved of Devadatta’s doctrine, have gone with him. But now their knowledge has matured. You should go there with many monks, teach them the Dhamma, awaken them with the path and its fruit, and bring them back.' They went accordingly, taught them the Dhamma, awakened them with the path and its fruit, and at dawn the next day, brought those monks back to the Veḷuvana monastery. Upon their arrival, while the Elder Sāriputta was standing there after paying homage to the Blessed One, the monks praised the elder, saying to the Blessed One: 'Venerable sir, our elder brother, the General of the Dhamma, is exceedingly resplendent, arriving surrounded by five hundred monks. Devadatta, however, is now left with a diminished retinue.' 'Monks, it is not only now that Sāriputta is resplendent arriving surrounded by his retinue of kinsmen; he was resplendent in the past as well. And it is not only now that Devadatta is diminished in his following; he was diminished in the past as well.' The monks requested the Blessed One to make this matter clear, and the Blessed One made manifest the reason that was concealed by another existence.

Atīte magadharaṭṭhe rājagahanagare eko magadharājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto migayoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā vuddhippatto migasahassaparivāro araññe vasati. Tassa lakkhaṇo ca kāḷo cāti dve puttā ahesuṃ. So attano mahallakakāle “tātā, ahaṃ idāni mahallako, tumhe imaṃ gaṇaṃ pariharathā”ti pañca pañca migasatāni ekekaṃ puttaṃ paṭicchāpesi[V 1.0148]. Tato paṭṭhāya te dve janā migagaṇaṃ pariharanti. Magadharaṭṭhasmiñca sassapākasamaye kiṭṭhasambādhe araññe migānaṃ paripantho hoti. Manussā sassakhādakānaṃ migānaṃ māraṇatthāya tattha tattha opātaṃ khaṇanti, sūlāni ropenti, pāsāṇayantāni sajjenti, kūṭapāsādayo pāse oḍḍenti, bahū migā vināsaṃ āpajjanti. Bodhisatto kiṭṭhasambādhasamayaṃ ñatvā dve putte pakkosāpetvā āha – “tātā, ayaṃ kiṭṭhasambādhasamayo, bahū migā vināsaṃ pāpuṇanti, mayaṃ mahallakā yena kenaci upāyena ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vītināmessāma, tumhe tumhākaṃ migagaṇe gahetvā araññe pabbatapādaṃ pavisitvā sassānaṃ uddhaṭakāle āgaccheyyāthā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti pitu vacanaṃ sutvā saparivārā nikkhamiṃsu. Tesaṃ pana gamanamaggaṃ manussā jānanti “imasmiṃ kāle migā pabbatamārohanti, imasmiṃ kāle orohantī”ti. Te tattha tattha paṭicchannaṭṭhāne [P 1.0144] nilīnā bahū mige vijjhitvā mārenti.

In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, in the city of Rājagaha, a certain king of Magadha reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having taken rebirth as a deer and reached maturity, lived in the forest with a retinue of a thousand deer. He had two sons named Lakkhaṇa and Kāḷa. In his old age, he said to them, 'Sons, I am now old. You must look after this herd.' He entrusted five hundred deer to each son. From then on, the two managed the herd of deer. During the season of ripening grain in the kingdom of Magadha, there was danger for the deer in the forest near the dense cornfields. To kill the deer that ate the crops, men would dig pits here and there, plant stakes, prepare stone-traps, and lay treacherous snares and the like. Many deer met with destruction. The Bodhisatta, knowing it was the season of ripening grain, called his two sons and said, 'Sons, this is the season of ripening grain. Many deer are meeting with destruction. We who are old will somehow pass the time in one place. You must take your herds, enter the foothills of the mountains, and return only when the crops have been harvested.' They replied, 'Very well,' and, heeding their father’s word, they departed with their retinues. However, men knew the path the deer took, saying, 'At this time, the deer climb the mountain; at this time, they descend.' Hiding in concealed places here and there, they shot and killed many deer.

Kāḷamigo attano dandhatāya “imāya nāma velāya gantabbaṃ, imāya velāya na gantabba”nti ajānanto migagaṇaṃ ādāya pubbaṇhepi sāyanhepi padosepi paccūsepi gāmadvārena gacchati. Manussā tattha tattha pakatiyā ṭhitā ca nilīnā ca bahū mige vināsaṃ pāpenti. Evaṃ so attano dandhatāya bahū mige vināsaṃ pāpetvā appakeheva migehi araññaṃ pāvisi. Lakkhaṇamigo pana paṇḍito byatto upāyakusalo “imāya velāya gantabbaṃ, imāya velāya na gantabba”nti jānāti. So gāmadvārenapi na gacchati[M 1.0161], divāpi na gacchati, padosepi na gacchati, paccūsepi na gacchati, migagaṇaṃ ādāya aḍḍharattasamayeyeva gacchati. Tasmā ekampi migaṃ avināsetvā araññaṃ pāvisi. Te tattha cattāro māse vasitvā sassesu uddhaṭesu pabbatā otariṃsu.

The deer Kāḷa, on account of his foolishness, not knowing 'at such a time one should go, at such a time one should not go,' took the herd of deer and went near the village gate in the morning, in the evening, at nightfall, and at dawn. Men, standing about openly or lying in ambush here and there, brought many deer to destruction. Thus, on account of his foolishness, having brought many deer to destruction, he entered the forest with only a few deer. The deer Lakkhaṇa, however, was wise, astute, and skilled in strategy; he knew, 'at such a time one should go, at such a time one should not go.' He did not go near the village gate, nor did he go by day, nor at nightfall, nor at dawn; taking the herd of deer, he went only at midnight. Therefore, without allowing even a single deer to be destroyed, he entered the forest. Having lived there for four months, they descended from the mountain when the crops had been harvested.

Kāḷo paccāgacchantopi purimanayeneva avasesamige vināsaṃ pāpento ekakova āgami. Lakkhaṇo pana ekamigampi avināsetvā pañcahi migasatehi parivuto mātāpitūnaṃ santikaṃ āgami. Bodhisatto dvepi putte āgacchante disvā migagaṇena saddhiṃ mantento imaṃ gāthaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi –

When Kāḷa was returning, in the very same manner as before, he brought the remaining deer to destruction and came back all alone. Lakkhaṇa, however, without allowing even one deer to be destroyed, returned to his parents' presence surrounded by five hundred deer.
