The Bodhisatta, seeing both his sons returning and conferring with the herd of deer, uttered this verse:

11.

11.

“Hoti sīlavataṃ attho, paṭisanthāravuttinaṃ;

Lakkhaṇaṃ passa āyantaṃ, ñātisaṅghapurakkhataṃ;

Atha passasimaṃ kāḷaṃ, suvihīnaṃva ñātibhī”ti.

Success comes to the virtuous, to those who practice hospitality; Behold Lakkhaṇa approaching, escorted by his host of kinsmen. And then behold this Kāḷa, utterly bereft of his kin.

Tattha [V 1.0149] sīlavatanti sukhasīlatāya sīlavantānaṃ ācārasampannānaṃ. Atthoti vuḍḍhi. Paṭisanthāravuttinanti dhammapaṭisanthāro ca āmisapaṭisanthāro ca etesaṃ vuttīti paṭisanthāravuttino, tesaṃ paṭisanthāravuttinaṃ. Ettha ca pāpanivāraṇaovādānusāsanivasena dhammapaṭisanthāro ca, gocaralābhāpanagilānupaṭṭhānadhammikarakkhāvasena āmisapaṭisanthāro ca veditabbo. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – imesu dvīsu paṭisanthāresu ṭhitānaṃ ācārasampannānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ vuḍḍhi nāma hotīti. Idāni taṃ vuḍḍhiṃ dassetuṃ puttamātaraṃ ālapanto viya “lakkhaṇaṃ passā”tiādimāha. Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – ācārapaṭisanthārasampannaṃ attano puttaṃ [P 1.0145] ekamigampi avināsetvā ñātisaṅghena purakkhataṃ parivāritaṃ āgacchantaṃ passa. Tāya pana ācārapaṭisanthārasampadāya vihīnaṃ dandhapaññaṃ atha passasimaṃ kāḷaṃ ekampi ñātiṃ anavasesetvā suvihīnameva ñātīhi ekakaṃ āgacchantanti. Evaṃ puttaṃ abhinanditvā pana bodhisatto yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Herein, virtuous means those who are virtuous through good conduct, accomplished in right behavior. Success means growth. Those who practice hospitality means those whose practice consists of hospitality in the Dhamma and material hospitality; of these practitioners of hospitality. Herein, hospitality in the Dhamma is to be understood as giving advice and instruction to prevent evil, and material hospitality is to be understood as securing pasture, attending to the sick, and providing righteous protection. This is the meaning: for the wise who are accomplished in right behavior and established in these two kinds of hospitality, there is indeed growth. Now, to illustrate that growth, as if addressing the son's mother, he spoke the words beginning, 'Behold Lakkhaṇa.' The concise meaning is this: Behold your son, accomplished in right behavior and hospitality, approaching, honored and surrounded by his host of kinsmen, without having allowed even one deer to be destroyed. Then behold this Kāḷa, who is deficient in that accomplishment of right behavior and hospitality, a dull-witted one, approaching all alone, utterly bereft of his kin, not having a single kinsman left. Having thus rejoiced in his son, the Bodhisatta lived for the remainder of his lifespan and passed on according to his kamma.

Satthāpi “na, bhikkhave, sāriputto idāneva ñātisaṅghaparivārito sobhati, pubbepi sobhatiyeva. Na ca devadatto etarahiyeva gaṇamhā parihīno, pubbepi parihīnoyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ dassetvā dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā [M 1.0162] kāḷo devadatto ahosi, parisāpissa devadattaparisāva, lakkhaṇo sāriputto, parisā panassa buddhaparisā, mātā rāhulamātā, pitā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Bhikkhus, it is not only now that Sāriputta is glorious, surrounded by a host of kinsmen; he was glorious in the past as well. And it is not only now that Devadatta is bereft of a following; he was bereft in the past as well.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse and related the two stories, he made the connection and identified the birth, saying: 'At that time, Kāḷa was Devadatta, and his retinue was Devadatta's retinue. Lakkhaṇa was Sāriputta, and his retinue was the Buddha's retinue. The mother was Rāhula's mother, and the father was none other than myself.'

Lakkhaṇamigajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Lakkhaṇa Deer Jātaka, the First.

[12] 2. Nigrodhamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[12] 2. The Commentary on the Nigrodha Deer Jātaka.

Nigrodhameva seveyyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kumārakassapattherassa mātaraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kira rājagahanagare mahāvibhavassa seṭṭhino dhītā ahosi ussannakusalamūlā parimadditasaṅkhārā pacchimabhavikā, antoghaṭe padīpo viya tassā hadaye arahattūpanissayo jalati. Sā attānaṃ jānanakālato paṭṭhāya gehe anabhiratā pabbajitukāmā hutvā mātāpitaro āha – “ammatātā, mayhaṃ gharāvāse cittaṃ nābhiramati, ahaṃ niyyānike buddhasāsane pabbajitukāmā, pabbājetha ma”nti. Amma, kiṃ vadesi, idaṃ kulaṃ bahuvibhavaṃ, tvañca amhākaṃ ekadhītā, na labbhā tayā pabbajitunti. Sā punappunaṃ yācitvāpi mātāpitūnaṃ santikā pabbajjaṃ alabhamānā cintesi “hotu, patikulaṃ gatā sāmikaṃ ārādhetvā [V 1.0150] pabbajissāmī”ti. Sā vayappattā patikulaṃ gantvā patidevatā hutvā sīlavatī kalyāṇadhammā agāraṃ ajjhāvasi.

The Teacher spoke this, beginning with the verse 'Nigrodhameva seveyya,' while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the mother of the Elder Kumārakassapa. She was, it is said, the daughter of a wealthy merchant in the city of Rājagaha, with abundant roots of merit, having thoroughly comprehended the formations, and destined for her final existence. Like a lamp within a pot, the potential for Arahantship burned in her heart. From the time she became self-aware, she found no delight in household life and, desiring to go forth, said to her parents, 'Mother and father, my mind finds no joy in the household life. I wish to go forth into the Buddha’s teaching, which leads to liberation. Please let me go forth.' 'Child, what are you saying? This family is very wealthy, and you are our only daughter. It is not possible for you to go forth.' Though she repeatedly asked, she could not obtain permission to go forth from her parents. She then thought, 'So be it. Having gone to my husband’s family, I will please my husband and then go forth.' When she came of age, she went to her husband’s family. There, revering her husband as a deity, she lived the household life, virtuous and endowed with noble qualities.

Athassā saṃvāsamanvāya kucchiyaṃ gabbho patiṭṭhahi. Sā gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ na aññāsi. Atha tasmiṃ nagare nakkhattaṃ ghosayiṃsu, sakalanagaravāsino [P 1.0146] nakkhattaṃ kīḷiṃsu, nagaraṃ devanagaraṃ viya alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ ahosi. Sā pana tāva uḷārāyapi nakkhattakīḷāya vattamānāya attano sarīraṃ na vilimpati nālaṅkaroti, pakativeseneva vicarati.

Then, through their cohabitation, a fetus was established in her womb. She did not know that a fetus had been established. Then in that city they announced a festival. All the city-dwellers celebrated the festival, and the city was adorned and prepared like a city of the gods. But even as the magnificent festival was underway, she neither anointed nor adorned her body, but went about in her natural state.

Atha naṃ sāmiko āha – “bhadde, sakalanagaraṃ nakkhattanissitaṃ, tvaṃ pana sarīraṃ nappaṭijaggasī”ti. Ayyaputta, dvattiṃsāya me kuṇapehi pūritaṃ sarīraṃ, kiṃ iminā alaṅkatena, ayañhi kāyo neva devanimmito, na brahmanimmito, na suvaṇṇamayo, na maṇimayo, na haricandanamayo, na puṇḍarīkakumuduppalagabbhasambhūto[M 1.0163], na amatosadhapūrito, atha kho kuṇape jāto, mātāpettikasambhavo, aniccucchādanaparimaddanabhedanaviddhaṃsanadhammo, kaṭasivaḍḍhano, taṇhūpādinno, sokānaṃ nidānaṃ, paridevānaṃ vatthu, sabbarogānaṃ ālayo, kammakaraṇānaṃ paṭiggaho, antopūti, bahi niccapaggharaṇo, kimikulānaṃ āvāso, sivathikapayāto, maraṇapariyosāno, sabbalokassa cakkhupathe vattamānopi –

Then her husband said to her: 'Dear one, the entire city is engaged in the festival, yet you do not attend to your body.' 'Dear husband, my body is filled with thirty-two foul things. What is the use of adorning it? For this body is not created by gods, nor by Brahma; it is not made of gold, nor of jewels, nor of yellow sandalwood; it is not born from the heart of a white lotus, water lily, or blue lotus, nor is it filled with the medicine of immortality. Rather, it is born from a foul thing, originating from mother and father. It is subject to impermanence, anointing, massaging, breaking, and destruction. It increases the charnel ground, is grasped by craving, is a source of sorrow, a basis for lamentation, a dwelling for all diseases, a recipient of the consequences of action, putrid within, constantly oozing without, a habitat for worms, bound for the charnel ground, and ending in death. Though it exists in the sight of the whole world—'

“Aṭṭhinahārusaṃyutto, tacamaṃsāvalepano;

Chaviyā kāyo paṭicchanno, yathābhūtaṃ na dissati.

Bound together with bones and sinews, plastered with skin and flesh; covered by the outer skin, the body is not seen as it truly is.

“Antapūro udarapūro, yakanapeḷassa vatthino;

Hadayassa papphāsassa, vakkassa pihakassa ca.

Full of entrails, full of belly; of the liver's mass and of the bladder; of the heart, lungs, kidneys, and spleen.

“Siṅghāṇikāya kheḷassa, sedassa ca medassa ca;

Lohitassa lasikāya, pittassa ca vasāya ca.

Of snot, of saliva, of sweat, and of solid fat; of blood, of synovial fluid, of bile, and of liquid fat.

“Athassa navahi sotehi, asucī savati sabbadā;

Akkhimhā akkhigūthako, kaṇṇamhā kaṇṇagūthako.

Then from its nine openings, impurity always flows; from the eye, eye-excrement; from the ear, ear-excrement.

“Siṅghāṇikā [V 1.0151] ca nāsato, mukhena vamatekadā;

Pittaṃ semhañca vamati, kāyamhā sedajallikā.

And snot from the nose; from the mouth one sometimes vomits; one vomits bile and phlegm; from the body, sweat and grime.

“Athassa susiraṃ sīsaṃ, matthaluṅgassa pūritaṃ;

Subhato naṃ maññati bālo, avijjāya purakkhato. (su. ni. 196-201);

Then its hollow head, filled with the brain; a fool, led on by ignorance, thinks it beautiful.

“Anantādīnavo kāyo, visarukkhasamūpamo;

Āvāso sabbarogānaṃ, puñjo dukkhassa kevalo. (apa. thera 2.54.55);

The body has endless perils, comparable to a poisonous tree; it is the dwelling place of all diseases, a mere heap of suffering.

“Sace imassa kāyassa, anto bāhirako siyā;

Daṇḍaṃ nūna gahetvāna, kāke soṇe ca vāraye.

If the inside of this body were on the outside, one would surely have to take a stick to ward off the crows and dogs.

“Duggandho asuci kāyo, kuṇapo ukkarūpamo;

Nindito cakkhubhūtehi, kāyo bālābhinandito.

Foul-smelling and impure is the body, a carcass comparable to a rubbish heap; censured by those who have become the eye, the body is delighted in by fools.

“Allacammapaṭicchanno, navadvāro mahāvaṇo;

Samantato paggharati, asucī pūtigandhiyo”ti. (visuddhi. 1.122);

Covered with wet skin, it is a great wound with nine openings; from all around it oozes impurity, putrid and foul-smelling.

Ayyaputta[P 1.0147][M 1.0164], imaṃ kāyaṃ alaṅkaritvā kiṃ karissāmi? Nanu imassa alaṅkatakaraṇaṃ gūthapuṇṇaghaṭassa bahi cittakammakaraṇaṃ viya hotīti? Seṭṭhiputto tassā vacanaṃ sutvā āha “bhadde, tvaṃ imassa sarīrassa ime dose passamānā kasmā na pabbajasī”ti? “Ayyaputta, ahaṃ pabbajjaṃ labhamānā ajjeva pabbajeyya”nti. Seṭṭhiputto “sādhu, ahaṃ taṃ pabbājessāmī”ti vatvā mahādānaṃ pavattetvā mahāsakkāraṃ katvā mahantena parivārena bhikkhunupassayaṃ netvā taṃ pabbājento devadattapakkhiyānaṃ bhikkhunīnaṃ santike pabbājesi. Sā pabbajjaṃ labhitvā paripuṇṇasaṅkappā attamanā ahosi.

'Dear husband, what shall I do by adorning this body? Is not the act of adorning it like decorating the outside of a pot full of excrement?' The merchant's son, hearing her words, said, 'Good lady, seeing these faults of this body, why do you not go forth?' 'Dear husband, if I could obtain the going forth, I would go forth this very day.' The merchant's son said, 'Good, I will have you go forth.' Having arranged a great offering of alms, paid great honor, and taken her with a large retinue to the nuns' residence, he had her go forth in the presence of the nuns who were of Devadatta's faction. Having obtained the going forth, her aspiration was fulfilled, and she was joyful.

Athassā gabbhe paripākaṃ gacchante indriyānaṃ aññathattaṃ hatthapādapiṭṭhīnaṃ bahalattaṃ udarapaṭalassa ca mahantataṃ disvā bhikkhuniyo taṃ pucchiṃsu “ayye, tvaṃ gabbhinī viya paññāyasi, kiṃ eta”nti? Ayye, “idaṃ nāma kāraṇa”nti na jānāmi, sīlaṃ pana me paripuṇṇanti[V 1.0152]. Atha naṃ tā bhikkhuniyo devadattassa santikaṃ netvā devadattaṃ pucchiṃsu “ayya, ayaṃ kuladhītā kicchena sāmikaṃ ārādhetvā pabbajjaṃ labhi, idāni panassā gabbho paññāyati, mayaṃ imassa gabbhassa gihikāle vā pabbajitakāle vā laddhabhāvaṃ na jānāma, kiṃdāni karomā”ti? Devadatto attano abuddhabhāvena ca khantimettānuddayānañca natthitāya evaṃ cintesi “devadattapakkhikā bhikkhunī kucchinā gabbhaṃ pariharati, devadatto ca taṃ ajjhupekkhatiyevāti mayhaṃ garahā uppajjissati, mayā imaṃ uppabbājetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So avīmaṃsitvāva selaguḷaṃ pavaṭṭayamāno viya pakkhanditvā “gacchatha, imaṃ uppabbājethā”ti āha. Tā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā uṭṭhāya vanditvā upassayaṃ gatā.

When her pregnancy was advancing, the change in her faculties, the swelling of her hands, feet, and back, and the enlargement of her abdominal area became noticeable. Seeing this, the nuns asked her, "Venerable, you appear to be pregnant—what is this?" "Venerables, I do not know the cause of this, but my virtue is complete," she replied. Then those nuns took her to Devadatta and asked him, "Venerable, this daughter of a good family, after great difficulty, won her husband’s consent and went forth. Now, however, she appears to be pregnant. We do not know whether this conception occurred while she was still a laywoman or after her ordination. What should we do now?" Devadatta, because of his lack of wisdom and absence of patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, thought thus: "A nun belonging to Devadatta’s faction is carrying a child in her womb, and Devadatta simply overlooks it—this will bring blame upon me. It is proper for me to have her disrobed." Without proper reflection, like one rolling a stone downhill, he rashly declared, "Go, disrobe her!" Hearing his words, they rose, paid homage, and returned to their dwelling.

Atha sā daharā tā bhikkhuniyo āha – “ayye, na devadattatthero buddho, nāpi mayhaṃ tassa santike pabbajjā, loke pana aggapuggalassa sammāsambuddhassa santike mayhaṃ pabbajjā, sā ca pana me dukkhena laddhā, mā naṃ antaradhāpetha, etha maṃ gahetvā satthu santikaṃ jetavanaṃ gacchathā”ti. Tā taṃ ādāya rājagahā pañcacattālīsayojanikaṃ maggaṃ atikkamma anupubbena jetavanaṃ patvā satthāraṃ vanditvā tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā cintesi – “kiñcāpi gihikāle etissā gabbho patiṭṭhito, evaṃ santepi ‘samaṇo gotamo devadattena [P 1.0148] jahitaṃ ādāya caratī’ti titthiyānaṃ okāso bhavissati. Tasmā imaṃ kathaṃ pacchindituṃ sarājikāya parisāya [M 1.0165] majjhe imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ vinicchituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Punadivase rājānaṃ pasenadikosalaṃ mahāanāthapiṇḍikaṃ cūḷaanāthapiṇḍikaṃ visākhaṃ mahāupāsikaṃ aññāni ca abhiññātāni mahākulāni pakkosāpetvā sāyanhasamaye catūsu parisāsu sannipatitāsu upālittheraṃ āmantesi “gaccha, tvaṃ catuparisamajjhe imissā daharabhikkhuniyā kammaṃ sodhehī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti thero parisamajjhaṃ gantvā attano paññattāsane nisīditvā rañño purato visākhaṃ upāsikaṃ pakkosāpetvā imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ paṭicchāpesi “gaccha visākhe, ‘ayaṃ daharā asukamāse asukadivase pabbajitā’ti tathato ñatvā imassa gabbhassa pure vā pacchā vā laddhabhāvaṃ jānāhī”ti. Upāsikā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā sāṇiṃ parikkhipāpetvā antosāṇiyaṃ daharabhikkhuniyā hatthapādanābhiudarapariyosānādīni oloketvā māsadivase samānetvā gihibhāve gabbhassa laddhabhāvaṃ tathato ñatvā therassa santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Thero catuparisamajjhe taṃ bhikkhuniṃ suddhaṃ akāsi. Sā suddhā hutvā bhikkhusaṅghañca satthārañca vanditvā bhikkhunīhi saddhiṃ upassayameva gatā. Sā gabbhaparipākamanvāya padumuttarapādamūle patthitapatthanaṃ mahānubhāvaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi.

Then the young nun said to those nuns: "Venerable ones, the Elder Devadatta is not the Buddha, nor did I receive the going forth in his presence. I received the going forth in the presence of the Supreme Person in the world, the Perfectly Enlightened One. And that going forth was obtained by me with difficulty—do not let it be lost. Come, take me and go to the Teacher at Jetavana." Taking her, they left Rājagaha, traversed the forty-five yojana road, and gradually reached Jetavana. They paid homage to the Teacher and reported the matter to him. The Teacher considered: "Although this pregnancy was established while she was still a laywoman, still, the sectarians will have an opportunity to say, 'The ascetic Gotama accepts what Devadatta has rejected.' Therefore, it is proper to settle this matter in the midst of an assembly including the king, in order to cut off this talk." The next day, he had King Pasenadi of Kosala, the Great Anāthapiṇḍika, the Lesser Anāthapiṇḍika, Visākhā the Great Laywoman, and other well-known great families summoned. In the evening, when the fourfold assembly had convened, he addressed the Elder Upāli: "Go, clear this young nun’s case in the midst of the fourfold assembly." "Yes, Venerable Sir," the Elder replied. Going into the midst of the assembly, he sat on the seat prepared for him and had the laywoman Visākhā summoned before the king. He entrusted her with this matter: "Go, Visākhā, find out the truth of when this young nun went forth—in such and such a month, on such and such a day—and determine whether this pregnancy was conceived before or after that." The laywoman accepted, saying, "Yes, Venerable Sir." She had a screen arranged and, inside the screen, examined the young nun’s hands, feet, navel, abdomen, and so on. Comparing the months and days, she determined that the pregnancy had occurred during her lay life and reported the facts to the Elder. The Elder declared the nun pure in the midst of the fourfold assembly. Having been cleared, she paid homage to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha and the Teacher, then returned to the nunnery with the nuns. In due course, when the pregnancy came to term, she gave birth to a son of great power, as she had aspired at the feet of the Buddha Padumuttara.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0153] rājā bhikkhunupassayasamīpena gacchanto dārakasaddaṃ sutvā amacce pucchi. Amaccā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “deva, daharabhikkhunī puttaṃ vijātā, tasseso saddo”ti āhaṃsu. “Bhikkhunīnaṃ, bhaṇe, dārakapaṭijagganaṃ nāma palibodho, mayaṃ naṃ paṭijaggissāmā”ti rājā taṃ dārakaṃ nāṭakitthīnaṃ dāpetvā kumāraparihārena vaḍḍhāpesi. Nāmaggahaṇadivase cassa “kassapo”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Atha naṃ kumāraparihārena vaḍḍhitattā “kumārakassapo”ti sañjāniṃsu. So sattavassikakāle satthu santike pabbajitvā paripuṇṇavasso upasampadaṃ labhitvā gacchante gacchante kāle dhammakathikesu citrakathī ahosi. Atha naṃ satthā “etadaggaṃ, bhikkhave, mama sāvakānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ cittakathikānaṃ yadidaṃ kumārakassapo”ti (a. ni. 1.209, 217) etadagge ṭhapesi. So pacchā vammikasutte (ma. ni. 1.249 ādayo) arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Mātāpissa bhikkhunī vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā aggaphalaṃ pattā. Kumārakassapatthero buddhasāsane gaganamajjhe [P 1.0149] puṇṇacando viya pākaṭo jāto.

Then one day, the king, while passing near the nuns' residence, heard the sound of a child and asked his ministers. The ministers, knowing the reason, replied, "Your Majesty, the young nun has given birth to a son; that is his sound." The king said, "Looking after a child is an impediment for nuns; we will look after him." The king then entrusted the boy to actresses and had him raised with the care befitting a prince. On the naming day, they named him Kassapa. As he had been raised with the care befitting a prince, he came to be known as Kumārakassapa. At the age of seven, he went forth in the presence of the Teacher and, upon reaching full age, received the higher ordination. As time went by, he became a skilled speaker of elaborate discourses among the preachers of the Dhamma. Then the Teacher established him in the foremost position, declaring, "Monks, among my monk disciples who are skilled in elaborate discourse, the foremost is this Kumārakassapa." Later, in connection with the Vammika Sutta, he attained arahantship. His mother, the nun, also developed insight and attained the highest fruit. The Elder Kumārakassapa became renowned in the Buddha’s dispensation, shining like the full moon in the midst of the sky.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 1.0166] tathāgato pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto bhikkhūnaṃ ovādaṃ datvā gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Bhikkhū ovādaṃ gahetvā attano attano rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu divasabhāgaṃ khepetvā sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitvā “āvuso, devadattena attano abuddhabhāvena ceva khantimettādīnañca abhāvena kumārakassapatthero ca therī ca ubho nāsitā, sammāsambuddho pana attano dhammarājatāya ceva khantimettānuddayasampattiyā ca ubhinnampi tesaṃ paccayo jāto”ti buddhaguṇe vaṇṇayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā buddhalīlāya dhammasabhaṃ āgantvā paññattāsane nisīditvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchi. “Bhante, tumhākameva guṇakathāyā”ti sabbaṃ ārocayiṃsu. Na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva imesaṃ ubhinnaṃ paccayo ca patiṭṭhā ca jāto, pubbepi ahosiyevāti. Bhikkhū tassatthassāvibhāvatthāya bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu. Bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi.

Then one day, the Tathāgata, having returned from his alms-round after the meal, gave an exhortation to the monks and entered his fragrant chamber. The monks, having received the exhortation, spent the day in their respective day and night quarters. In the evening, they gathered in the Hall of Dhamma and sat discussing: 'Friends, Devadatta, on account of his own foolishness and his lack of patience, loving-kindness, and other virtues, has brought ruin upon both the Elder Kumārakassapa and the Elder Nun. The Perfectly Enlightened One, however, on account of being the King of Dhamma and his endowment with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, has become a support for them both.' Thus they sat, extolling the virtues of the Buddha. The Teacher, with the grace of a Buddha, came to the Hall of Dhamma, sat upon the prepared seat, and asked, 'Monks, for the sake of what discussion are you now gathered together?' 'Venerable Sir,' they replied, 'it is for a discussion of your own virtues,' and they related the entire matter. 'Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata has become a support and a refuge for these two; in the past, also, he was so.' The monks requested the Blessed One to make this matter clear. The Blessed One then made manifest the reason that was concealed by another existence.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārayamāne bodhisatto migayoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. So mātukucchito nikkhanto suvaṇṇavaṇṇo ahosi, akkhīni panassa maṇiguḷasadisāni ahesuṃ, siṅgāni rajatavaṇṇāni, mukhaṃ rattakambalapuñjavaṇṇaṃ, hatthapādapariyantā lākhārasaparikammakatā viya, vāladhi camarassa viya ahosi, sarīraṃ panassa mahantaṃ assapotakappamāṇaṃ ahosi. So pañcasatamigaparivāro araññe vāsaṃ kappesi nāmena nigrodhamigarājā [V 1.0154] nāma. Avidūre panassa aññopi pañcasatamigaparivāro sākhamigo nāma vasati, sopi suvaṇṇavaṇṇova ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of a doe. When he came forth from his mother’s womb, he was of a golden hue. His eyes were like jewel-orbs, his horns were the color of silver, his mouth was the color of a cluster of red wool, the tips of his hooves were as if finished with lacquer, and his tail was like that of a chowry bull. His body was large, the size of a colt. With a retinue of five hundred deer, he dwelt in the forest and was known by the name Nigrodha, the king of the deer. Not far from him dwelt another deer named Sākha, also with a retinue of five hundred deer; he, too, was of a golden hue.

Tena samayena bārāṇasirājā migavadhappasuto hoti, vinā maṃsena na bhuñjati, manussānaṃ kammacchedaṃ katvā sabbe negamajānapade sannipātetvā devasikaṃ migavaṃ gacchati. Manussā cintesuṃ – “ayaṃ rājā amhākaṃ kammacchedaṃ karoti, yaṃnūna mayaṃ uyyāne [P 1.0150] migānaṃ nivāpaṃ vapitvā pānīyaṃ sampādetvā bahū mige uyyānaṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ bandhitvā rañño niyyādeyyāmā”ti. Te sabbe uyyāne migānaṃ nivāpatiṇāni ropetvā udakaṃ sampādetvā dvāraṃ yojetvā vāgurāni ādāya muggarādinānāvudhahatthā [M 1.0167] araññaṃ pavisitvā mige pariyesamānā “majjhe ṭhite mige gaṇhissāmā”ti yojanamattaṃ ṭhānaṃ parikkhipitvā saṅkhipamānā nigrodhamigasākhamigānaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ majjhe katvā parikkhipiṃsu. Atha naṃ migagaṇaṃ disvā rukkhagumbādayo ca bhūmiñca muggarehi paharantā migagaṇaṃ gahanaṭṭhānato nīharitvā asisattidhanuādīni āvudhāni uggiritvā mahānādaṃ nadantā taṃ migagaṇaṃ uyyānaṃ pavesetvā dvāraṃ pidhāya rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, nibaddhaṃ migavaṃ gacchantā amhākaṃ kammaṃ nāsetha, amhehi araññato mige ānetvā tumhākaṃ uyyānaṃ pūritaṃ, ito paṭṭhāya tesaṃ maṃsāni khādathā”ti rājānaṃ āpucchitvā pakkamiṃsu.

At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī was devoted to the hunting of deer; he would not eat his meal without meat. Causing an interruption to the people's work, he would assemble all the town and country folk and go hunting daily. The people thought: 'This king causes an interruption to our work. What if we were to sow fodder in the royal park, provide water, drive many deer into the park, close the gate, and hand them over to the king?' Accordingly, they all planted fodder grass for the deer in the park, made water available, and fitted a gate. Taking nets, clubs, and various other weapons in hand, they entered the forest. Searching for the deer and thinking, 'We will catch the deer that are in the middle,' they encircled an area of one yojana. Gradually closing in, they made the dwelling place of the deer of Nigrodha and Sākha the center of their encirclement. Then, having spotted the herd of deer, they beat upon the trees, bushes, and the ground with their clubs, driving the herd from its thicket. Brandishing swords, spears, bows, and other weapons and raising a great cry, they drove that herd of deer into the park, shut the gate, and approaching the king, said: 'Your Majesty, by constantly going to hunt deer, you destroy our work. We have brought deer from the forest and filled your park. From this day forward, may you eat their flesh.' Having thus taken their leave of the king, they departed.

Rājā tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā uyyānaṃ gantvā mige olokento dve suvaṇṇamige disvā tesaṃ abhayaṃ adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya pana kadāci sayaṃ gantvā ekaṃ migaṃ vijjhitvā āneti, kadācissa bhattakārako gantvā vijjhitvā āharati. Migā dhanuṃ disvāva maraṇabhayena tajjitā palāyanti, dve tayo pahāre labhitvā kilamantipi, gilānāpi honti, maraṇampi pāpuṇanti. Migagaṇo taṃ pavattiṃ bodhisattassa ārocesi. So sākhaṃ pakkosāpetvā āha – “samma, bahū migā nassanti, ekaṃsena maritabbe sati ito paṭṭhāya mā kaṇḍena mige vijjhantu, dhammagaṇḍikaṭṭhāne migānaṃ vāro hotu. Ekadivasaṃ mama parisāya vāro pāpuṇātu, ekadivasaṃ tava parisāya, vārappatto migo gantvā dhammagaṇḍikāya gīvaṃ ṭhapetvā nipajjatu, evaṃ sante migā kilantā na bhavissantī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Tato paṭṭhāya vārappattova migo gantvā dhammagaṇḍikāya [P 1.0151] gīvaṃ ṭhapetvā nipajjati, bhattakārako āgantvā tattha nipannakameva gahetvā gacchati.

The king, having heard their words, went to the park. While observing the deer, he saw the two golden deer and granted them immunity. From that time onwards, sometimes the king himself would go, shoot one deer, and have it brought back; at other times his cook would go, shoot one, and bring it back. The deer, as soon as they saw a bow, would flee, terrified by the fear of death. Some, receiving two or three wounds, would become exhausted, fall sick, and even die. The herd of deer reported this matter to the Bodhisatta. He had Sākha summoned and said: 'Friend, many deer are being destroyed. Since death is inevitable, from now on, let them not shoot the deer with arrows. Let the deer take their turn at the execution block. One day let the turn fall to my retinue, and one day to your retinue. The deer whose turn it is should go, place its neck upon the block, and lie down. In this way, the deer will not be needlessly afflicted.' Sākha consented, saying, 'It is well.' From that time onwards, the deer whose turn it was would go, place its neck upon the execution block, and lie down. The cook would come and take only the one that was lying there.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0155] sākhamigassa parisāya ekissā gabbhinimigiyā vāro pāpuṇi. Sā sākhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “sāmi, ahaṃ gabbhinī, puttaṃ vijāyitvā dve janā vāraṃ gamissāma, mayhaṃ vāraṃ atikkāmehī”ti āha. So “na sakkā tava vāraṃ aññesaṃ pāpetuṃ, tvameva tuyhaṃ vāraṃ jānissasi, gacchāhī”ti āha. Sā tassa santikā anuggahaṃ alabhamānā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. So tassā vacanaṃ sutvā “hotu gaccha tvaṃ, ahaṃ te vāraṃ atikkāmessāmī”ti sayaṃ [M 1.0168] gantvā dhammagaṇḍikāya sīsaṃ katvā nipajji. Bhattakārako taṃ disvā “laddhābhayo migarājā dhammagaṇḍikāya nipanno, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti vegena gantvā rañño ārocesi.

Then one day, the turn came for a pregnant doe in the herd of the Sākha deer. She approached the Sākha deer and said, 'Lord, I am pregnant. After giving birth to my young one, the two of us shall take our turn. Please let my turn pass.' He replied, 'It is not possible to assign your turn to others. You yourself must know your turn. Go.' Unable to obtain favor from him, she approached the Bodhisatta and explained the matter. Hearing her words, he said, 'So be it. You may go. I shall take your turn.' He went himself, placed his head on the block of execution, and lay down. The cook, seeing him, thought, 'The deer-king, to whom safety has been granted, is lying on the block of execution. What could be the reason?' He hurried to inform the king.

Rājā tāvadeva rathaṃ āruyha mahantena parivārena āgantvā bodhisattaṃ disvā āha “samma migarāja, nanu mayā tuyhaṃ abhayaṃ dinnaṃ, kasmā tvaṃ idha nipanno”ti. Mahārāja, gabbhinī migī āgantvā “mama vāraṃ aññassa pāpehī”ti āha, na sakkā kho pana mayā ekassa maraṇadukkhaṃ aññassa upari nikkhipituṃ, svāhaṃ attano jīvitaṃ tassā datvā tassā santakaṃ maraṇaṃ gahetvā idha nipanno, mā aññaṃ kiñci āsaṅkittha, mahārājāti. Rājā āha – “sāmi, suvaṇṇavaṇṇamigarāja, mayā na tādiso khantimettānuddayasampanno manussesupi diṭṭhapubbo, tena te pasannosmi, uṭṭhehi, tuyhañca tassā ca abhayaṃ dammī”ti. “Dvīhi abhaye laddhe avasesā kiṃ karissanti, narindā”ti? “Avasesānampi abhayaṃ dammi, sāmī”ti. “Mahārāja, evampi uyyāneyeva migā abhayaṃ labhissanti, sesā kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Etesampi abhayaṃ dammi, sāmī”ti. “Mahārāja, migā tāva abhayaṃ labhantu, sesā catuppadā kiṃ karissantī”ti[P 1.0152]? “Etesampi abhayaṃ dammi, sāmī”ti. “Mahārāja, catuppadā tāva abhayaṃ labhantu, dijagaṇā kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Etesampi abhayaṃ dammi, sāmī”ti. “Mahārāja, dijagaṇā tāva abhayaṃ labhantu, udake vasantā macchā kiṃ karissantī”ti? “Etesampi abhayaṃ dammi, sāmī”ti. Evaṃ mahāsatto rājānaṃ sabbasattānaṃ abhayaṃ yācitvā uṭṭhāya rājānaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā “dhammaṃ cara, mahārāja, mātāpitūsu puttadhītāsu brāhmaṇagahapatikesu negamajānapadesu dhammaṃ caranto samaṃ caranto kāyassa bhedā paraṃ maraṇā sugatiṃ saggaṃ lokaṃ gamissasī”ti rañño buddhalīlāya dhammaṃ desetvā katipāhaṃ uyyāne vasitvā rañño ovādaṃ datvā migagaṇaparivuto araññaṃ pāvisi. Sāpi kho migadhenu pupphakaṇṇikasadisaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. So kīḷamāno sākhamigassa santikaṃ gacchati. Atha naṃ mātā tassa santikaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā “putta, ito paṭṭhāya mā etassa santikaṃ gaccha, nigrodhasseva santikaṃ gaccheyyāsī”ti ovadantī imaṃ gāthamāha –

The king immediately mounted his chariot and arrived with a great retinue. Seeing the Bodhisatta, he said, 'My good deer-king, did I not grant you safety? Why are you lying here?' 'Great king, a pregnant doe came and said, "Let my turn pass to another." But I could not place the suffering of death upon another. Therefore, I gave my own life to her, took upon myself the death that was hers, and now lie here. Do not suspect anything else, great king.' The king said, 'Lord, golden-hued deer-king, never before have I seen such a being endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, even among humans. Therefore, I am pleased with you. Arise; I grant safety both to you and to her.' 'With safety granted to two, what will the remaining ones do, O lord of men?' 'I grant safety to the remaining ones as well, lord.' 'Great king, even so, only the deer in the park will obtain safety. What will the others do?' 'I grant safety to those as well, lord.' 'Great king, let the deer have safety. What will the remaining quadrupeds do?' 'I grant safety to those as well, lord.' 'Great king, let the quadrupeds have safety. What will the flocks of birds do?' 'I grant safety to those as well, lord.' 'Great king, let the flocks of birds have safety. What will the fish dwelling in the water do?' 'I grant safety to those as well, lord.' Thus, the Great Being requested safety for all beings from the king. Then, rising, he established the king in the five precepts and said, 'Practice righteousness, great king. By practicing righteousness toward your parents, sons and daughters, brahmins and householders, and the people of town and country—by living justly—upon the dissolution of the body, after death, you will go to a good destination, the heavenly world.' Having taught the king the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha, he stayed in the park for some days. Then, after advising the king, he returned to the forest surrounded by his herd of deer. That doe gave birth to a fawn resembling a flower's pericarp. While playing, he went near the Sākha deer. Then his mother, seeing him going near him, admonished him, speaking this verse:

12.

12.

“Nigrodhameva [V 1.0156][M 1.0169] seveyya, na sākhamupasaṃvase;

Nigrodhasmiṃ mataṃ seyyo, yañce sākhasmi jīvita”nti.

“One should associate only with Nigrodha; one should not live with Sākha. Better is death with Nigrodha than the life that is with Sākha.”

Tattha nigrodhameva seveyyāti tāta tvaṃ vā añño vā attano hitakāmo nigrodhameva seveyya bhajeyya upasaṅkameyya, na sākhamupasaṃvaseti sākhamigaṃ pana na upasaṃvase upagamma na saṃvaseyya, etaṃ nissāya jīvikaṃ na kappeyya. Nigrodhasmiṃ mataṃ seyyoti nigrodharañño pādamūle maraṇampi seyyo varaṃ uttamaṃ. Yañce sākhasmi jīvitanti yaṃ pana sākhassa santike jīvitaṃ, taṃ neva seyyo na varaṃ na uttamanti attho.

Herein, 'One should associate only with Nigrodha' means: Dear one, whether it is you or another who seeks their own welfare, you should associate only with Nigrodha, attend upon him, and approach him. 'One should not live with Sākha' means: one should not live with the Sākha deer, one should not approach and dwell with him, nor should one make a living depending on him. 'Better is death with Nigrodha' means: even death at the feet of King Nigrodha is better, more choice, more excellent. 'Than the life that is with Sākha' means: but that life which is in the presence of Sākha is not better, not choice, not excellent. This is the meaning.

Tato paṭṭhāya ca pana abhayaladdhakā migā manussānaṃ sassāni khādanti, manussā “laddhābhayā ime migā”ti mige paharituṃ vā palāpetuṃ vā na visahanti, te rājaṅgaṇe sannipatitvā rañño tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Rājā “mayā pasannena nigrodhamigarājassa [P 1.0153] varo dinno, ahaṃ rajjaṃ jaheyyaṃ, na ca taṃ paṭiññaṃ bhindāmi, gacchatha na koci mama vijite mige paharituṃ labhatī”ti āha. Nigrodhamigo taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā migagaṇaṃ sannipātāpetvā “ito paṭṭhāya paresaṃ sassaṃ khādituṃ na labhissathā”ti mige ovaditvā manussānaṃ ārocāpesi “ito paṭṭhāya sassakārakā manussā sassarakkhaṇatthaṃ vatiṃ mā karontu, khettaṃ pana āvijjhitvā paṇṇasaññaṃ bandhantū”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya kira khettesu paṇṇabandhanasaññā udapādi. Tato paṭṭhāya paṇṇasaññaṃ atikkamanamigo nāma natthi. Ayaṃ kira nesaṃ bodhisattato laddhaovādo. Evaṃ migagaṇaṃ ovaditvā bodhisatto yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā saddhiṃ migehi yathākammaṃ gato, rājāpi bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

From that time onward, the deer who had been granted safety began to eat the people's crops. The people, thinking, 'These deer have been granted safety,' did not dare to strike or chase them away. They gathered in the royal courtyard and reported the matter to the king. The king said, 'Being pleased, I granted a boon to the Nigrodha deer-king. I would give up my kingdom, but I will not break that promise. Go; no one in my domain is to harm the deer.' Hearing of this, the Nigrodha deer assembled the herd and advised them, 'From now on, you are not to eat the crops of others.' He then had a message proclaimed to the people: 'From now on, let those who cultivate crops not make fences for crop protection, but let them enclose the field by tying a leaf as a sign.' From that time, it is said, the sign of the tied leaf came into being in the fields. And from then on, there was no deer that would transgress a leaf-sign. This, it is said, was the instruction they received from the Bodhisatta. Having thus advised the herd of deer, the Bodhisatta lived for the remainder of his lifespan and then passed on according to his kamma, together with the deer. The king, too, having abided by the Bodhisatta’s advice and performed meritorious deeds, passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idānevāhaṃ theriyā ca kumārakassapassa ca avassayo, pubbepi avassayo evā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā catusaccadhammadesanaṃ vinivaṭṭetvā dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā sākhamigo devadatto ahosi, parisāpissa devadattaparisāva, migadhenu therī ahosi, putto kumārakassapo, rājā ānando, nigrodhamigarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that I am a refuge for the Theri and for Kumārakassapa; in the past, too, I was their refuge.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse and connected the link, he identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the Sākha deer was Devadatta, his retinue was Devadatta's retinue, the doe was the Theri, her son was Kumārakassapa, the king was Ānanda, but the Nigrodha deer-king was indeed myself.'

Nigrodhamigajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Second Nigrodhamiga Jātaka.

[13] 3. Kaṇḍijātakavaṇṇanā

[13] 3. The Commentary on the Kaṇḍi Jātaka

Dhiratthu [V 1.0157][M 1.0170] kaṇḍinaṃ sallanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ aṭṭhakanipāte indriyajātake āvibhavissati. Bhagavā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ etadavoca “bhikkhu, pubbepi tvaṃ etaṃ mātugāmaṃ nissāya jīvitakkhayaṃ patvā vītaccitesu aṅgāresu pakko”ti. Bhikkhū tassatthassāvibhāvatthāya bhagavantaṃ yāciṃsu, bhagavā bhavantarena paṭicchannakāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ akāsi. Ito paraṃ pana bhikkhūnaṃ yācanaṃ [P 1.0154] bhavantarapaṭicchannatañca avatvā “atītaṃ āharī”ti ettakameva vakkhāma, ettake vuttepi yācanañca valāhakagabbhato candanīharaṇūpamāya bhavantarapaṭicchannakāraṇabhāvo cāti sabbametaṃ heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yojetvā veditabbaṃ.

This discourse, beginning with the words 'Fie upon the arrowed dart,' the Teacher delivered while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the luring by a former wife. That will be made clear in the Indriya Jātaka in the Book of Eights. The Blessed One said to that monk: 'Monk, in a former time as well, on account of this woman, you reached the end of your life and were roasted on smokeless embers.' The monks requested the Blessed One to make the meaning of this clear, and the Blessed One made manifest the cause that was hidden by another existence. Hereafter, however, without mentioning the monks' request and the fact of it being hidden by another existence, we shall say only this much: 'He related a story of the past.' Even when only this much is said, the request, and the fact of the cause being hidden by another existence—by the simile of drawing the moon from the belly of a cloud—all this should be understood by connecting it with the method previously stated.

Atīte magadharaṭṭhe rājagahe magadharājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Magadhavāsikānaṃ sassasamaye migānaṃ mahāparipantho hoti. Te araññe pabbatapādaṃ pavisanti. Tattha eko araññavāsī pabbateyyamigo ekāya gāmantavāsiniyā migapotikāya saddhiṃ santhavaṃ katvā tesaṃ migānaṃ pabbatapādato oruyha puna gāmantaṃ otaraṇakāle migapotikāya paṭibaddhacittattā tehi saddhiṃyeva otari. Atha naṃ sā āha – “tvaṃ khosi, ayya, pabbateyyo bālamigo, gāmanto ca nāma sāsaṅko sappaṭibhayo, mā amhehi saddhiṃ otarī”ti. So tassā paṭibaddhacittattā anivattitvā saddhiṃyeva agamāsi. Magadhavāsino “idāni migānaṃ pabbatapādā otaraṇakālo”ti ñatvā magge paṭicchannakoṭṭhakesu tiṭṭhanti. Tesampi dvinnaṃ āgamanamagge eko luddako paṭicchannakoṭṭhake ṭhito hoti. Migapotikā manussagandhaṃ ghāyitvā “eko luddako ṭhito bhavissatī”ti taṃ bālamigaṃ purato katvā sayaṃ pacchato ahosi. Luddako ekeneva sarappahārena migaṃ tattheva pāteti. Migapotikā tassa viddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā uppatitvā vātagatiyāva palāyi. Luddako koṭṭhakato nikkhamitvā migaṃ okkantitvā aggiṃ katvā vītaccitesu aṅgāresu madhuramaṃsaṃ pacitvā khāditvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā avasesaṃ lohitabindūhi paggharantehi kājenādāya dārake tosento gharaṃ agamāsi.

In the past, when the king of Magadha was ruling in Rājagaha, during the harvest time of the people of Magadha, there was great danger for the deer. They would stay at the foot of the mountain in the forest. There, a mountain-dwelling deer formed an attachment to a young doe that lived near a village. When those deer were descending from the foot of the mountain to the outskirts of the village, because his mind was bound to the young doe, he descended along with them. Then she said to him, 'Sir, you are a foolish mountain deer. The village outskirts are fraught with suspicion and danger; do not come down with us.' But because his mind was bound to her, he did not turn back and went along with her. The people of Magadha, knowing, 'Now is the time for the deer to descend from the foot of the mountain,' would wait in concealed pits along the path. On the path these two were taking, a hunter was situated in a concealed pit. The young doe, smelling the scent of a human, thought, 'There must be a hunter here,' and putting the foolish deer in front of her, she herself followed behind. The hunter, with a single shot of his arrow, felled the deer right there. The young doe, knowing he had been shot, leaped up and fled with the speed of the wind. The hunter, coming out of the pit, butchered the deer, made a fire, and roasted the tender meat on the smokeless embers. Having eaten and drunk water, he took the rest of the meat on a carrying pole and went home to please his children.

Tadā [M 1.0171] bodhisatto tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatto hoti. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ disvā “imassa bālamigassa maraṇaṃ neva mātaraṃ nissāya, na pitaraṃ nissāya, atha kho kāmaṃ nissāya. Kāmanimittañhi [P 1.0155] sattā sugatiyaṃ hatthacchedādikaṃ, duggatiyañca pañcavidhabandhanādinānappakārakaṃ dukkhaṃ pāpuṇanti, paresaṃ maraṇadukkhuppādanampi nāma imasmiṃ loke [V 1.0158] garahitameva. Yaṃ janapadaṃ mātugāmo vicāreti anusāsati, so itthipariṇāyako janapadopi garahitoyeva. Ye sattā mātugāmassa vasaṃ gacchanti, tepi garahitāyevā”ti ekāya gāthāya tīṇi garahavatthūni dassetvā vanadevatāsu sādhukāraṃ datvā gandhapupphādīhi pūjayamānāsu madhurena sarena taṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ unnādento imāya gāthāya dhammaṃ desesi –

At that time, the Bodhisatta had been reborn as a tree deity in that forest grove. Seeing that event, he reflected: 'This foolish deer's death was not on account of its mother, nor on account of its father, but on account of sensual desire. For it is because of sensual desire that beings, in a good destination, attain suffering such as having their hands cut off, and in a bad destination, various kinds of suffering such as the fivefold bondage. Causing the suffering of death to others is indeed censured in this world. A country that a woman administers and rules, a country with a female leader, is also to be censured. And those beings who fall under the power of women are also to be censured.' Having thus pointed out three objects of censure, while the forest deities gave cries of approval and worshipped him with perfumes, flowers, and so on, making the forest grove resound with his sweet voice, he taught the Dhamma with this verse:

13.

13.

“Dhiratthu kaṇḍinaṃ sallaṃ, purisaṃ gāḷhavedhinaṃ;

Dhiratthu taṃ janapadaṃ, yatthitthī pariṇāyikā;

Te cāpi dhikkitā sattā, ye itthīnaṃ vasaṃ gatā”ti.

“Fie on the arrowed dart and the man who pierces deeply! Fie on that country where a woman is the leader! And censured, too, are those beings who have fallen under the power of women.”

Tattha dhiratthūti garahaṇatthe nipāto, svāyamidha uttāsubbegavasena garahaṇe daṭṭhabbo. Uttasitubbiggo hi honto bodhisatto evamāha. Kaṇḍamassa atthīti kaṇḍī, taṃ kaṇḍinaṃ. Taṃ pana kaṇḍaṃ anupavisanaṭṭhena “salla”nti vuccati, tasmā kaṇḍinaṃ sallanti ettha sallakaṇḍinanti attho. Sallaṃ vā assatthītipi sallo, taṃ sallaṃ. Mahantaṃ vaṇamukhaṃ katvā balavappahāraṃ dento gāḷhaṃ vijjhatīti gāḷhavedhī, taṃ gāḷhavedhinaṃ. Nānappakārena kaṇḍena, kumudapattasaṇṭhānathalena ujukagamaneneva sallena ca samannāgataṃ gāḷhavedhinaṃ purisaṃ dhiratthūti ayamettha attho. Pariṇāyikāti issarā saṃvidhāyikā. Dhikkitāti garahitā. Sesamettha uttānatthameva. Ito paraṃ pana ettakampi avatvā yaṃ yaṃ anuttānaṃ, taṃ tadeva vaṇṇayissāma. Evaṃ ekāya gāthāya tīṇi garahavatthūni dassetvā bodhisatto vanaṃ unnādetvā buddhalīlāya dhammaṃ desesi.

Herein, 'dhiratthu' is a particle in the sense of censure; here it should be understood as censure arising from agitation and distress. For it was while being agitated and distressed that the Bodhisatta spoke thus. 'He has an arrow (kaṇḍa),' thus he is an archer (kaṇḍī); 'of the archer' is 'kaṇḍinaṃ'. That arrow (kaṇḍa), because it penetrates, is called a 'dart' (salla); therefore, 'kaṇḍinaṃ sallaṃ' here means 'the archer's dart'. Or, 'he has a dart (salla),' thus he is a darter (sallo); 'the darter' is 'sallaṃ'. 'He pierces deeply (gāḷhaṃ vijjhati),' making a large wound and delivering a powerful blow, thus he is a 'deep-piercer' (gāḷhavedhī); 'the deep-piercer' is 'gāḷhavedhinaṃ'. This is the meaning here: 'Fie!' on the man who pierces deeply, endowed with various kinds of arrows and with a dart that has a shaft shaped like a water-lily petal and flies straight. 'Pariṇāyikā' means a sovereign, an administrator. 'Dhikkitā' means censured. The rest here has a clear meaning. Hereafter, however, without saying even this much, we will explain only that which is not clear. Thus, having shown three objects of censure in a single verse, the Bodhisatta, making the forest resound, taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Satthā dve vatthūni [P 1.0156] kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. Ito paraṃ pana “dve [M 1.0172] vatthūni kathetvā”ti idaṃ avatvā “anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā”ti ettakameva vakkhāma, avuttampi pana heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva yojetvā gahetabbaṃ.

The Teacher delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher related the two stories, connected them, and identified the Jātaka. From now on, instead of saying, "He related the two stories," we will simply say, "He connected them," but what is not stated should be understood and construed in the same way as stated before.

Tadā pabbateyyamigo ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, migapotikā purāṇadutiyikā, kāmesu dosaṃ dassetvā dhammadesakadevatā pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the mountain deer was the discontented monk, the young doe was his former wife, and I myself was the deity who showed the fault in sensual pleasures and taught the Dhamma.

Kaṇḍijātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Kaṇḍi Jātaka, the third.

[14] 4. Vātamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[14] 4. The Commentary on the Vātamiga Jātaka

Na [V 1.0159] kiratthi rasehi pāpiyoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Satthari kira rājagahaṃ upanissāya veḷuvane viharante tissakumāro nāma mahāvibhavassa seṭṭhikulassa putto ekadivasaṃ veḷuvanaṃ gantvā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbajitukāmo pabbajjaṃ yācitvā mātāpitūhi ananuññātattā paṭikkhitto sattāhaṃ bhattacchedaṃ katvā raṭṭhapālatthero viya mātāpitaro anujānāpetvā satthu santike pabbaji. Satthā taṃ pabbājetvā aḍḍhamāsamattaṃ veḷuvane viharitvā jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Tatrāyaṃ kulaputto terasa dhutaṅgāni samādāya sāvatthiyaṃ sapadānaṃ piṇḍāya caramāno kālaṃ vītināmeti, “cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissatthero nāmā”ti vutte gaganatale puṇṇacando viya buddhasāsane pākaṭo paññāto ahosi.

“Truly, there is nothing more evil than tastes.” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika-Tissa. It is said that when the Teacher was dwelling near Rājagaha at the Veḷuvana monastery, a young man named Tissa, the son of a very wealthy merchant family, went to Veḷuvana one day. Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, he wished to go forth and requested ordination. Because he was not given permission by his parents, he was refused. Like the elder Raṭṭhapāla, he abstained from food for seven days, thereby causing his parents to give their consent, and he went forth in the Teacher's presence. The Teacher ordained him and, after dwelling in Veḷuvana for about half a month, went to Jetavana. There, this son of a good family, having undertaken the thirteen ascetic practices, spent his time going for alms from house to house in Sāvatthī. He became famous and well-known in the Buddha’s Dispensation as 'the elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika-Tissa,' like the full moon in the sky.

Tasmiṃ kāle rājagahe nakkhattakīḷāya vattamānāya therassa mātāpitaro yaṃ tassa gihikāle ahosi ābharaṇabhaṇḍakaṃ, taṃ ratanacaṅkoṭake nikkhipitvā ure ṭhapetvā “aññāsu nakkhattakīḷāsu amhākaṃ putto iminā alaṅkārena alaṅkato nakkhattaṃ kīḷati, taṃ no ekaputtaṃ gahetvā samaṇo gotamo sāvatthinagaraṃ gato, kahaṃ nu kho so etarahi nisinno, kahaṃ ṭhito”ti vatvā rodanti.

At that time, while a festival was being held in Rājagaha, the elder’s parents took the ornaments that had belonged to him in his lay life, placed them in a jeweled casket, and held it to their chests. They wept, saying, “At other festivals, our son, adorned with these ornaments, used to enjoy the festivities. But the ascetic Gotama has taken our only son to the city of Sāvatthī. Where might he be sitting now? Where might he be standing?”

Athekā vaṇṇadāsī taṃ kulaṃ gantvā seṭṭhibhariyaṃ rodantiṃ disvā pucchi “kiṃ pana, ayye, rodasī”ti? “Sā tamatthaṃ ārocesi”. “Kiṃ pana, ayye, ayyaputto piyāyatī”ti? “Asukañca asukañcā”ti. “Sace tumhe [M 1.0173] imasmiṃ gehe sabbaṃ issariyaṃ mayhaṃ detha, ahaṃ vo puttaṃ ānessāmī”ti. Seṭṭhibhariyā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā paribbayaṃ datvā mahantena parivārena taṃ uyyojesi “gaccha, attano balena mama puttaṃ ānehī”ti. Sā paṭicchannayāne nisinnā sāvatthiṃ gantvā therassa bhikkhācāravīthiyaṃ nivāsaṃ gahetvā seṭṭhikulā āgate manusse [P 1.0157] therassa adassetvā attano parivāreneva parivutā therassa piṇḍāya paviṭṭhassa āditova uḷuṅkayāguñca rasakabhikkhañca datvā rasataṇhāya bandhitvā anukkamena gehe nisīdāpetvā bhikkhaṃ dadamānā ca attano vasaṃ upagatabhāvaṃ ñatvā gilānālayaṃ dassetvā antogabbhe nipajji. Theropi bhikkhācāravelāya sapadānaṃ caranto gehadvāraṃ agamāsi. Parijano therassa pattaṃ gahetvā theraṃ ghare nisīdāpesi. Thero nisīditvāva “kahaṃ upāsikā”ti pucchi. “Gilānā, bhante, tumhākaṃ dassanaṃ icchatī”ti. So rasataṇhāya baddho attano vatasamādānaṃ [V 1.0160] bhinditvā tassā nipannaṭṭhānaṃ pāvisi. Sā attano āgatakāraṇaṃ kathetvā taṃ palobhetvā rasataṇhāya bandhitvā uppabbājetvā attano vase ṭhapetvā yāne nisīdāpetvā mahantena parivārena rājagahameva agamāsi. Sā pavatti pākaṭā jātā.

Then a certain courtesan went to that household and, seeing the merchant's wife weeping, asked, “Why, madam, do you weep?” The wife told her the matter. The courtesan asked, “And what, madam, is the young master fond of?” “He is fond of such and such foods,” she replied. “If you give me full authority in this house, I will bring your son back to you.” The merchant's wife agreed, saying, “Very well.” Giving her provisions for the journey, she sent her off with a large retinue, saying, “Go, and by your own power, bring my son back.” Seated in a covered carriage, the courtesan went to Sāvatthī and took up residence on the elder's alms-round path. Keeping the people who came from the merchant's family from the elder's sight, and surrounded only by her own attendants, she first gave the elder, when he entered for alms, a special kind of gruel and savory food, thus binding him with craving for tastes. Gradually, having him take his seat inside the house when she gave him alms, she realized he had come under her power. Then, feigning illness, she lay down in an inner chamber. At the time of the alms-round, the elder, going from house to house, came to her door. Her attendant took the elder's bowl and had him sit inside the house. Having sat down, the elder asked, “Where is the female lay supporter?” “She is ill, venerable sir, and wishes to see you.” Bound by craving for tastes, he broke his ascetic vow and entered the place where she lay. She told him the reason for her coming, and having enticed him and bound him with craving for tastes, she made him leave the Order. Taking him under her control and seating him in the carriage, she returned to Rājagaha with her large retinue. This affair became widely known.

Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā “cūḷapiṇḍapātikatissattheraṃ kira ekā vaṇṇadāsī rasataṇhāya bandhitvā ādāya gatā”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā dhammasabhaṃ upagantvā alaṅkatadhammāsane nisīditvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti āha. Te taṃ pavattiṃ kathayiṃsu. “Na, bhikkhave, idāneva eso bhikkhu rasataṇhāya bajjhitvā tassā vasaṃ gato, pubbepi tassā vasaṃ gatoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The monks, gathered in the Hall of Dhamma, started a discussion, saying: “It is said that the elder Cūḷapiṇḍapātika-Tissa was bound by craving for tastes and taken away by a certain courtesan.” The Teacher came to the Hall of Dhamma, sat down on the prepared and adorned Dhamma seat, and asked, “For what discussion are you gathered together here now, monks?” They told him of that affair. The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that this monk, bound by craving for tastes, has fallen under her sway; in the past, too, he fell under her sway.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ rañño brahmadattassa sañjayo nāma uyyānapālo ahosi. Atheko vātamigo taṃ uyyānaṃ āgantvā sañjayaṃ disvā palāyati, sañjayopi na taṃ tajjetvā nīharati. So punappunaṃ āgantvā uyyāneyeva carati. Uyyānapālo uyyāne nānappakārāni pupphaphalāni gahetvā divase divase rañño abhiharati. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ rājā pucchi “samma uyyānapāla, uyyāne kiñci acchariyaṃ [M 1.0174] passasī”ti? “Deva, aññaṃ na passāmi, eko pana vātamigo āgantvā uyyāne carati, etaṃ passāmī”ti. “Sakkhissati pana taṃ gahetu”nti. “Thokaṃ madhuṃ labhanto anto rājanivesanampi naṃ ānetuṃ sakkhissāmi, devā”ti. Rājā tassa madhuṃ dāpesi. So taṃ gahetvā uyyānaṃ gantvā vātamigassa caraṇaṭṭhāne tiṇāni madhunā [P 1.0158] makkhetvā nilīyi. Migo āgantvā madhumakkhitāni tiṇāni khāditvā rasataṇhāya baddho aññatra agantvā uyyānameva āgacchati. Uyyānapālo tassa madhumakkhitatiṇesu paluddhabhāvaṃ ñatvā anukkamena attānaṃ dassesi. So taṃ disvā katipāhaṃ palāyitvā punappunaṃ passanto vissāsaṃ āpajjitvā anukkamena uyyānapālassa hatthe ṭhitatiṇāni khādituṃ ārabhi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there was a park keeper named Sañjaya. Then a wind-deer came to that park, saw Sañjaya, and fled, but Sañjaya did not threaten it and drive it away. It kept coming back and roamed in the park itself. The park keeper gathered various flowers and fruits from the park and presented them to the king daily. One day, the king asked him, 'Friend park keeper, do you see anything wonderful in the park?' 'My lord, I see nothing else, but a wind-deer comes and roams in the park—that is what I see.' 'Can you capture it?' 'If I obtain a little honey, I shall be able to bring it even inside the royal residence, my lord.' The king had honey given to him. Taking it, he went to the park, smeared grass with honey in the wind-deer’s grazing area, and hid. The wind-deer came, ate the honey-smeared grass, and, bound by craving for tastes, it did not go elsewhere but came only to the park. The park keeper, knowing its enticement to the honey-smeared grass, gradually revealed himself. Seeing him, it fled for a few days but, seeing him repeatedly, developed trust and gradually began to eat the grass held in the park keeper’s hand.

So tassa vissāsaṃ āpannabhāvaṃ ñatvā yāva rājanivesanā vīthiṃ kilañjehi parikkhipitvā tahiṃ tahiṃ sākhābhaṅgaṃ pātetvā madhulābukaṃ aṃse laggetvā tiṇakalāpaṃ upakacchake ṭhapetvā madhumakkhitāni tiṇāni migassa purato purato vikiranto antorājanivesanaṃyeva agamāsi. Mige anto paviṭṭhe dvāraṃ pidahiṃsu. Migo manusse disvā kampamāno maraṇabhayatajjito antonivesanaṅgaṇe ādhāvati paridhāvati. Rājā pāsādā oruyha taṃ kampamānaṃ disvā “vātamigo nāma manussānaṃ diṭṭhaṭṭhānaṃ sattāhaṃ na gacchati, tajjitaṭṭhānaṃ [V 1.0161] yāvajīvaṃ na gacchati, so evarūpo gahananissito vātamigo rasataṇhāya baddho idāni evarūpaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgato, natthi vata bho loke rasataṇhāya pāpataraṃ nāmā”ti imāya gāthāya dhammadesanaṃ paṭṭhapesi –

Knowing that it had developed trust, the park keeper fenced off the path up to the royal residence with reed mats, dropped broken branches here and there, hung a honey gourd on his shoulder, placed a bundle of grass under his arm, and, scattering honey-smeared grass right in front of the deer, went right into the royal residence. When the deer had entered inside, they closed the gate. Seeing the people, the deer, trembling and terrified by the fear of death, ran hither and thither in the inner courtyard of the residence. The king, descending from his palace, saw it trembling and thought, 'A wind-deer, it is said, does not go to a place where it has been seen by humans for seven days, nor to a place where it has been frightened for as long as it lives. Yet such a wind-deer, dependent on the wilderness, bound by craving for tastes, has now come to such a place. Truly, sirs, there is nothing in the world worse than craving for tastes.' He then commenced his discourse on the Dhamma with this verse:

14.

14.

“Na kiratthi rasehi pāpiyo, āvāsehiva santhavehi vā;

Vātamigaṃ gahananissitaṃ, vasamānesi rasehi sañjayo”ti.

“Truly, there is nothing worse than tastes, or than dwellings or friendships. Sañjaya, by means of tastes, brought under his sway the wind-deer that dwelt in the deep forest.”

Tattha kirāti anussavanatthe nipāto. Rasehīti jivhāviññeyyehi madhurambilādīhi. Pāpiyoti pāpataro. Āvāsehiva santhavehi vāti nibaddhavasanaṭṭhānasaṅkhātesu hi āvāsesupi mittasanthavesupi chandarāgo pāpakova, tehi pana sacchandarāgaparibhogehi āvāsehi vā mittasanthavehi [M 1.0175] vā sataguṇena ca sahassaguṇena ca satasahassaguṇena ca dhuvapaṭisevanaṭṭhena āhāraṃ vinā jīvitindriyapālanāya abhāvena ca sacchandarāgaparibhogarasāva pāpatarāti. Bodhisatto pana anussavāgataṃ [P 1.0159] viya imamatthaṃ katvā “na kiratthi rasehi pāpiyo, āvāsehiva santhavehi vā”ti āha. Idāni tesaṃ pāpiyabhāvaṃ dassento “vātamiga”ntiādimāha. Tattha gahananissitanti gahanaṭṭhānanissitaṃ. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – passatha rasānaṃ pāpiyabhāvaṃ, idaṃ nāma araññāyatane gahananissitaṃ vātamigaṃ sañjayo uyyānapālo madhurasehi attano vasaṃ ānesi, sabbathāpi sacchandarāgaparibhogehi rasehi nāma aññaṃ pāpataraṃ lāmakataraṃ natthīti rasataṇhāya ādīnavaṃ kathesi. Kathetvā ca pana taṃ migaṃ araññameva pesesi.

Herein, `kira` is a particle in the sense of 'it is said'. `Rasehi` refers to tastes cognizable by the tongue, such as sweet and sour. `Pāpiyo` means 'worse'. As for `āvāsehiva santhavehi vā`: sensual desire is indeed evil in regard to dwellings, which are reckoned as places of constant abode, and in regard to friendships. However, tastes indulged with sensual desire are a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred thousandfold worse than those dwellings or friendships indulged with sensual desire, because of constant partaking and because of the impossibility of maintaining the life faculty without food. The Bodhisatta, however, presented this matter as if it were a traditional saying and said, 'Truly, there is nothing worse than tastes, or than dwellings or friendships.' Now, to show their evil nature, he said, 'the wind-deer,' and so on. Here, `gahananissitaṃ` means 'dwelling in a dense place'. This is what was said: 'Behold the evil nature of tastes! This wind-deer, dwelling in the wilderness of the forest, was brought under his sway by Sañjaya the park keeper through sweet tastes. In every way, there is nothing more evil or base than tastes indulged with sensual desire.' Thus he spoke on the danger of craving for tastes. And having spoken, he sent that deer back to the forest.

Satthāpi “na, bhikkhave, sā vaṇṇadāsī idāneva etaṃ rasataṇhāya bandhitvā attano vase karoti, pubbepi akāsiyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. “Tadā sañjayo ayaṃ vaṇṇadāsī ahosi, vātamigo cūḷapiṇḍapātiko, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that this courtesan has bound him with craving for tastes and brought him under her sway; she did so in the past as well.' Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, he made the connection and identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, Sañjaya was this courtesan, the wind-deer was Cūḷapiṇḍapātika, and the King of Benares was I myself.'

Vātamigajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Wind-Deer Jātaka, the Fourth.

[15] 5. Kharādiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[15] 5. The Commentary on the Kharādiya Jātaka

Aṭṭhakkhuraṃ [V 1.0162] kharādiyeti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira bhikkhu dubbaco ovādaṃ na gaṇhāti. Atha naṃ satthā pucchi “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu dubbaco ovādaṃ na gaṇhāsī”ti? “Saccaṃ bhagavā”ti. Satthā “pubbepi tvaṃ dubbacatāya paṇḍitānaṃ ovādaṃ aggahetvā pāsena baddho jīvitakkhayaṃ patto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story, which begins 'Aṭṭhakkhuraṃ kharādiya,' concerning a certain intractable monk. That monk, it is said, was intractable and would not accept admonition. Then the Teacher asked him, 'Is it true, monk, that you are intractable and do not accept admonition?' 'It is true, Blessed One.' The Teacher said, 'In the past, too, due to your intractability, you did not heed the admonition of the wise and, being caught in a snare, you met your end,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto migo hutvā migagaṇaparivuto araññe vasati. Athassa bhaginimigī puttakaṃ dassetvā “bhātika, ayaṃ te bhāgineyyo, etaṃ migamāyaṃ uggaṇhāpehī”ti paṭicchāpesi. So taṃ bhāgineyyaṃ “asukavelāya nāma āgantvā uggaṇhāhī”ti āha. So vuttavelāya nāgacchati. Yathā [M 1.0176] ca ekadivasaṃ, evaṃ satta divase sattovāde atikkanto so migamāyaṃ anuggaṇhitvāva vicaranto pāse bajjhi. Mātāpissa bhātaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ te, bhātika, bhāgineyyo migamāyaṃ uggaṇhāpito”ti pucchi. Bodhisatto ca “tassa anovādakassa mā cintayi, na [P 1.0160] te puttena migamāyā uggahitā”ti vatvā idānipi taṃ anovaditukāmova hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a deer living in the forest, surrounded by a herd of deer. Then his sister, a doe, showing him her fawn, entrusted it to him, saying, 'Brother, this is your nephew; teach him the wiles of the deer.' He told his nephew, 'Come at such and such a time to learn.' But he did not come at the appointed time. Just as on one day, so for seven days he transgressed the seven admonitions. Wandering about without having learned the wiles of the deer, he was caught in a snare. His mother approached her brother and asked, 'Brother, was your nephew taught the wiles of the deer?' The Bodhisatta said, 'Do not worry about that disobedient one; your son has not learned the wiles of the deer.' And even then, being unwilling to admonish him, he spoke this verse:

15.

15.

“Aṭṭhakkhuraṃ kharādiye, migaṃ vaṅkātivaṅkinaṃ;

Sattahi kālātikkantaṃ, na naṃ ovaditussahe”ti.

O Kharādiyā, the eight-hoofed deer with very crooked antlers, who has transgressed the seven appointed times—I am unable to admonish him.

Tattha aṭṭhakkhuranti ekekasmiṃ pāde dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ vasena aṭṭhakkhuraṃ. Kharādiyeti taṃ nāmena ālapati. Miganti sabbasaṅgāhikavacanaṃ. Vaṅkātivaṅkinanti mūle vaṅkāni, agge ativaṅkānīti vaṅkātivaṅkāni, tādisāni siṅgāni assa atthīti vaṅkātivaṅkī, taṃ vaṅkātivaṅkinaṃ. Sattahi kālātikkantanti sattahi ovādakālehi ovādaṃ atikkantaṃ. Na naṃ ovaditussaheti etaṃ dubbacamigaṃ ahaṃ ovadituṃ na ussahāmi, etassa me ovādatthāya cittampi na uppajjatīti dasseti. Atha naṃ dubbacamigaṃ pāse baddhaṃ luddo māretvā maṃsaṃ ādāya pakkāmi.

Herein, 'eight-hoofed' means having eight hooves, in the sense of two on each foot. By 'Kharādiyā,' he addresses her by name. 'Deer' is an all-inclusive term. 'With very crooked antlers' means its antlers are crooked at the base and exceedingly crooked at the tips; having such antlers, it is called 'one with very crooked antlers.' 'Having transgressed the seven times' means having transgressed the admonition on the seven occasions for admonition. 'I am unable to admonish him' shows: 'I am not able to admonish this intractable deer; not even the thought to admonish him arises in me.' Then a hunter killed that intractable deer, which was bound in the snare, took its meat, and departed.

Satthāpi [V 1.0163] “na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva dubbaco, pubbepi dubbacoyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. “Tadā bhāgineyyo migo dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, bhaginī uppalavaṇṇā, ovādamigo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher also said, 'Monk, you are not intractable only now; you were intractable in the past as well.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse and connected the narrative, he identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the nephew deer was the intractable monk, the sister was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the admonishing deer was I myself.'

Kharādiyajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Kharādiya Jātaka, the Fifth.

[16] 6. Tipallatthamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[16] 6. The Commentary on the Tipallatthamiga Jātaka

Migaṃ [M 1.0177] tipallatthanti idaṃ satthā kosambiyaṃ badarikārāme viharanto sikkhākāmaṃ rāhulattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi kāle satthari āḷavinagaraṃ upanissāya aggāḷave cetiye viharante bahū upāsakā upāsikā bhikkhū bhikkhuniyo ca vihāraṃ dhammassavanatthāya gacchanti, divā dhammassavanaṃ hoti. Gacchante pana kāle upāsikāyo bhikkhuniyo ca na gacchiṃsu, bhikkhū ceva upāsakā ca ahesuṃ. Tato paṭṭhāya rattiṃ dhammassavanaṃ jātaṃ. Dhammassavanapariyosāne therā bhikkhū attano attano vasanaṭṭhānāni gacchanti. Daharā sāmaṇerā ca upāsakehi saddhiṃ upaṭṭhānasālāyaṃ sayanti. Tesu niddaṃ upagatesu ekacce ghurughurupassāsā kākacchamānā dante khādantā nipajjiṃsu, ekacce [P 1.0161] muhuttaṃ niddāyitvā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Te taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā “yo pana bhikkhu anupasampannena sahaseyyaṃ kappeyya pācittiya”nti (pāci. 49) sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetvā kosambiṃ agamāsi.

The Teacher told this story, which begins 'Migaṃ tipallatthaṃ,' while dwelling in the Badarikārāma at Kosambi, concerning the Venerable Rāhula, who was desirous of training. For at one time, while the Teacher was dwelling at the Aggāḷava Shrine near Āḷavī, many laymen, laywomen, monks, and nuns would go to the monastery to listen to the Dhamma. The Dhamma-talk was held during the day. When night fell, the laywomen and nuns would depart, and only the monks and laymen remained. From that time on, the Dhamma-talk came to be held at night. At the conclusion of the Dhamma-talk, the elder monks would go to their respective dwellings. The young monks and novices, however, would sleep in the attendance hall with the laymen. When they fell asleep, some lay snoring loudly, cawing like crows, and grinding their teeth, while others would wake up after sleeping for only a moment. Seeing this improper conduct, they reported it to the Blessed One. The Blessed One then laid down the training rule: 'Whatever monk should lie down together in the same lodging with an unordained person, it is an offense of expiation.' Having established this training rule, he went to Kosambi.

Tattha bhikkhū āyasmantaṃ rāhulaṃ āhaṃsu – “āvuso rāhula, bhagavatā sikkhāpadaṃ paññattaṃ, idāni tvaṃ attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ jānāhī”ti. Pubbe pana te bhikkhū bhagavati ca gāravaṃ tassa cāyasmato sikkhākāmataṃ paṭicca taṃ attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ ativiya saṅgaṇhanti, khuddakamañcakaṃ paññapetvā ussīsakakaraṇatthāya cīvaraṃ denti. Taṃ divasaṃ pana sikkhāpadabhayena vasanaṭṭhānampi na adaṃsu. Rāhulabhaddopi “pitā me”ti dasabalassa vā, “upajjhāyo me”ti dhammasenāpatino vā, “ācariyo me”ti mahāmoggallānassa vā, “cūḷapitā me”ti ānandattherassa vā santikaṃ agantvā dasabalassa vaḷañjanavaccakuṭiṃ brahmavimānaṃ pavisanto viya pavisitvā vāsaṃ kappesi. Buddhānañhi vaḷañjanakuṭiyaṃ dvāraṃ supihitaṃ hoti, gandhaparibhaṇḍakatā bhūmi, gandhadāmamālādāmāni osāritāneva honti, sabbarattiṃ dīpo jhāyati. Rāhulabhaddo pana na tassā kuṭiyā imaṃ sampattiṃ paṭicca tattha vāsaṃ upagato, bhikkhūhi pana “vasanaṭṭhānaṃ jānāhī”ti vuttattā ovādagāravena sikkhākāmatāya [V 1.0164] tattha vāsaṃ upagato. Antarantarā hi bhikkhū taṃ āyasmantaṃ dūratova āgacchantaṃ disvā tassa vīmaṃsanatthāya muṭṭhisammajjaniṃ vā kacavarachaḍḍanakaṃ vā bahi khipitvā tasmiṃ āgate [M 1.0178] “āvuso, imaṃ kena chaḍḍita”nti vadanti. Tattha kehici “rāhulo iminā maggena gato”ti vutte so āyasmā “nāhaṃ, bhante, etaṃ jānāmī”ti avatvāva taṃ paṭisāmetvā “khamatha me, bhante”ti khamāpetvā gacchati. Evamesa sikkhākāmo.

There, the monks said to the Venerable Rāhula, 'Friend Rāhula, the Blessed One has laid down a training rule. Now you must find your own lodging.' Previously, however, out of respect for the Blessed One and for that venerable one's desire for training, those monks would greatly accommodate him when he came to their lodging, preparing a small cot and giving him a robe to use as a pillow. But on that day, out of fear of the training rule, they did not even offer him a place to stay. The good Rāhula, however, did not go to the Ten-Powered One, thinking, 'He is my father,' nor to the General of the Dhamma, thinking, 'He is my preceptor,' nor to Mahāmoggallāna, thinking, 'He is my teacher,' nor to the Elder Ānanda, thinking, 'He is my uncle.' Instead, he entered the Blessed One's personal latrine as if entering a Brahma-mansion and took up his lodging there. For in the Buddhas' latrine, the door is well-shut, the floor is prepared with perfumes, garlands of scents and flowers are hung about, and a lamp burns throughout the night. The good Rāhula, however, did not take up lodging there on account of this splendor, but rather because the monks had told him, 'Find your own lodging,' and out of respect for the instruction and his desire for training. From time to time, seeing the venerable one coming from afar, the monks, in order to test him, would throw out a broom or a dustpan. When he arrived, they would ask, 'Friend, who threw this out?' When some said, 'Rāhula came by this way,' the venerable one, without saying, 'Venerable sirs, I do not know,' would put them away, and saying, 'Venerable sirs, please forgive me,' he would ask for their pardon and then depart. Such was his desire for training.

So taṃ sikkhākāmataṃyeva paṭicca tattha vāsaṃ upagato. Atha satthā purearuṇaṃyeva vaccakuṭidvāre ṭhatvā ukkāsi, sopāyasmā ukkāsi. “Ko eso”ti? “Ahaṃ rāhulo”ti nikkhamitvā vandi. “Kasmā tvaṃ rāhula idha nipannosī”ti? “Vasanaṭṭhānassa abhāvato”. “Pubbe hi, bhante, bhikkhū mama saṅgahaṃ karonti, idāni attano āpattibhayena vasanaṭṭhānaṃ [P 1.0162] na denti, svāhaṃ ‘idaṃ aññesaṃ asaṅghaṭṭanaṭṭhāna’nti iminā kāraṇena idha nipannosmīti. Atha bhagavato “rāhulaṃ tāva bhikkhū evaṃ pariccajanti, aññe kuladārake pabbājetvā kiṃ karissantī”ti dhammasaṃvego udapādi.

He went to stay there solely on account of his desire for the training. Then, just before dawn, the Teacher stood at the door of the latrine and coughed. The venerable one also coughed. 'Who is that?' 'It is I, Rāhula,' he said, and coming out, he paid homage. 'Why are you lying here, Rāhula?' 'Due to the lack of a place to stay.' 'Previously, venerable sir, the monks supported me, but now, out of fear of their own offense, they do not give me a place to stay. So I, thinking, "This is a place of non-conflict with others," am lying here for this reason.' Then a sense of spiritual urgency arose in the Blessed One, who thought: 'The monks abandon even Rāhula in this way; what will they do after having ordained other young men of good family?'

Atha bhagavā pātova bhikkhū sannipātāpetvā dhammasenāpatiṃ pucchi “jānāsi pana tvaṃ, sāriputta, ajja katthaci rāhulassa vutthabhāva”nti? “Na jānāmi, bhante”ti. “Sāriputta, ajja rāhulo vaccakuṭiyaṃ vasi, sāriputta, tumhe rāhulaṃ evaṃ pariccajantā aññe kuladārake pabbājetvā kiṃ karissatha? Evañhi sante imasmiṃ sāsane pabbajitā na patiṭṭhā bhavissanti, ito dāni paṭṭhāya anupasampannena ekaṃ dve divase attano santike vasāpetvā tatiyadivase tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ ñatvā bahi vāsethā”ti imaṃ anupaññattiṃ katvā puna sikkhāpadaṃ paññapesi.

Then the Blessed One, having assembled the monks early in the morning, asked the General of the Dhamma: 'Do you know, Sāriputta, where Rāhula has stayed today?' 'I do not know, venerable sir.' 'Sāriputta, today Rāhula stayed in the latrine. Sāriputta, if you abandon Rāhula in this way, what will you do after having ordained other young men of good family? If this is so, those who have gone forth in this Dispensation will not be established. From now on, you are to have one who is not fully ordained stay near you for one or two days, and on the third day, having ascertained their lodging, you are to have them stay outside.' Having made this supplementary regulation, he then laid down a training rule.

Tasmiṃ samaye dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā bhikkhū rāhulassa guṇakathaṃ kathenti “passathāvuso, yāva sikkhākāmo vatāyaṃ rāhulo, ‘tava vasanaṭṭhānaṃ jānāhī’ti vutto nāma ‘ahaṃ dasabalassa putto, tumhākaṃ senāsanasmā tumheyeva nikkhamathā’ti ekaṃ bhikkhumpi appaṭippharitvā vaccakuṭiyaṃ vāsaṃ kappesī”ti. Evaṃ tesu kathayamānesu satthā dhammasabhaṃ gantvā alaṅkatāsane nisīditvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti āha. “Bhante, rāhulassa sikkhākāmakathāya, na aññāya kathāyā”ti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, rāhulo idāneva sikkhākāmo, pubbe tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattopi sikkhākāmoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

At that time, monks assembled in the Dhamma hall were discussing the virtues of Rāhula: 'See, friends, how desirous of the training this Rāhula is! When told, "Find your own place to stay," he did not retort against even a single monk, saying, "I am the son of the One with Ten Powers; you yourselves get out of your lodgings," but instead took up his dwelling in the latrine.' While they were speaking thus, the Teacher went to the Dhamma hall, sat on the decorated seat, and asked, 'Monks, for the sake of what discussion are you now assembled here?' 'Venerable sir, for the sake of a discussion about Rāhula's desire for the training, not for any other discussion.' The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Rāhula is desirous of the training. In the past, even when born in the animal realm, he was just as desirous of the training.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0165][M 1.0179] rājagahe eko magadharājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto migayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā migagaṇaparivuto araññe vasati. Athassa bhaginī attano puttakaṃ upanetvā “bhātika, imaṃ te bhāgineyyaṃ migamāyaṃ sikkhāpehī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā “gaccha, tāta, asukavelāya nāma āgantvā sikkheyyāsī”ti āha. So mātulena vuttavelaṃ anatikkamitvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā migamāyaṃ sikkhi. So ekadivasaṃ vane vicaranto pāsena baddho baddharavaṃ ravi, migagaṇo palāyitvā “putto te pāsena baddho”ti tassa mātuyā ārocesi. Sā bhātu santikaṃ gantvā “bhātika, bhāgineyyo te migamāyaṃ sikkhāpito”ti pucchi. Bodhisatto “mā tvaṃ puttassa [P 1.0163] kiñci pāpakaṃ āsaṅki, suggahitā tena migamāyā, idāni taṃ hāsayamāno āgacchissatī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, a king of Magadha reigned in Rājagaha. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the deer realm and lived in the forest surrounded by a herd of deer. Then his sister brought her young son to him and said, 'Brother, please teach this nephew of yours the deer's wile.' The Bodhisatta consented, saying, 'Go, my dear boy; come at such and such a time to learn.' Without transgressing the time spoken by his maternal uncle, he approached him and learned the deer's wile. One day, while wandering in the forest, he was caught in a snare and cried out the cry of the captured. The herd of deer fled and informed his mother, 'Your son has been caught in a snare.' She went to her brother and asked, 'Brother, was your nephew taught the deer's wile?' The Bodhisatta said, 'Do not suspect any harm for your son. The deer's wile has been well learned by him. He will soon come, causing you to rejoice.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

16.

16.

“Migaṃ tipallatthamanekamāyaṃ, aṭṭhakkhuraṃ aḍḍharattāpapāyiṃ;

Ekena sotena chamāssasanto, chahi kalāhitibhoti bhāgineyyo”ti.

'The nephew overcomes with six arts, breathing on the ground through a single opening—that deer of three resting postures, of manifold wiles, with eight hooves, who drinks water at midnight.'

Tattha miganti bhāgineyyamigaṃ. Tipallatthanti pallatthaṃ vuccati sayanaṃ, ubhohi passehi ujukameva ca nipannakavasenāti tīhākārehi pallatthaṃ assa, tīṇi vā pallatthāni assāti tipallattho, taṃ tipallatthaṃ. Anekamāyanti bahumāyaṃ bahuvañcanaṃ. Aṭṭhakkhuranti ekekasmiṃ pāde dvinnaṃ dvinnaṃ vasena aṭṭhahi khurehi samannāgataṃ. Aḍḍharattāpapāyinti purimayāmaṃ atikkamitvā majjhimayāme araññato āgamma pānīyassa pivanato aḍḍharatte āpaṃ pivatīti aḍḍharattāpapāyī. Taṃ aḍḍharatte apāyinti attho. Mama bhāgineyyaṃ migaṃ ahaṃ sādhukaṃ migamāyaṃ uggaṇhāpesiṃ. Kathaṃ? Yathā ekena sotena chamāssasanto, chahi kalāhitibhoti bhāgineyyoti. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ahañhi tava puttaṃ tathā uggaṇhāpesiṃ, yathā ekasmiṃ uparimanāsikāsote vātaṃ sannirumbhitvā pathaviyā allīnena ekena heṭṭhimasotena tattheva chamāyaṃ assasanto chahi kalāhi [M 1.0180] luddakaṃ atibhoti, chahi koṭṭhāsehi ajjhottharati vañcetīti attho. Katamāhi chahi? Cattāro pāde pasāretvā ekena passena seyyāya, khurehi tiṇapaṃsukhaṇanena, jivhāninnāmanena udarassa uddhumātabhāvakaraṇena, uccārapassāvavissajjanena, vātasannirumbhanenāti.

Therein, 'migaṃ' refers to the nephew deer. 'Tipallatthaṃ': `pallattha` means a way of lying down. Since it lies on both sides and also straight, its posture is of three kinds; or, it has three postures, hence `tipallattha`. 'Anekamāyaṃ' means many wiles, much deception. 'Aṭṭhakkhuraṃ' means endowed with eight hooves, two on each foot. 'Aḍḍharattāpapāyiṃ': one who, after the first watch has passed, comes from the forest in the middle watch and drinks water; one who drinks water at midnight. The meaning is 'one who drinks at midnight'. I caused my nephew deer to learn the deer's wile well. How? In such a way that 'breathing on the ground with one opening, the nephew overcomes with six arts.' This is what was said: I taught your son in such a way that by restraining the breath in the upper nostril and breathing on the ground through the lower opening pressed to the earth, he overcomes the hunter with six arts; he overwhelms with six parts, meaning he deceives him. With which six? By lying on one side with the four feet stretched out; by digging up grass and dust with the hooves; by letting the tongue hang down; by making the belly appear swollen; by releasing excrement and urine; and by restraining the breath.

Aparo [V 1.0166] nayo – pādena paṃsuṃ gahetvā abhimukhākaḍḍhanena, paṭipaṇāmanena, ubhosu passesu sañcaraṇena, udaraṃ uddhaṃ pakkhipanena, adho avakkhipanenāti imāhi chahi kalāhi yathā atibhoti, “mato aya”nti saññaṃ uppādetvā vañceti, evaṃ taṃ migamāyaṃ uggaṇhāpesinti dīpeti.
