Another interpretation: by taking dust with the foot and drawing it forward, by pushing it back, by scattering it on both sides, by thrusting the belly upwards, and by casting it downwards—it is by these six arts that he overcomes. He deceives by producing the perception, 'This one is dead.' In this way, it shows: 'Thus I caused him to learn that deer's wile.'

Aparo nayo – tathā naṃ uggaṇhāpesiṃ, yathā ekena sotena chamāssasanto chahi kalāhiti dvīsupi nayesu dassitehi chahi kāraṇehi kalāhiti kalāyissati, luddaṃ vañcessatīti [P 1.0164] attho. Bhotīti bhaginiṃ ālapati. Bhāgineyyoti evaṃ chahi kāraṇehi vañcanakaṃ bhāgineyyaṃ niddisati. Evaṃ bodhisatto bhāgineyyassa migamāyāya sādhukaṃ uggahitabhāvaṃ dassento bhaginiṃ samassāseti.

Another method: 'I have taught him in such a way that, breathing on the ground through one nostril, with six arts...'—this means that with the six reasons shown in both methods, he will practice the arts, that is, he will deceive the hunter. By 'bhoti' he addresses his sister. By 'bhāgineyyo' he indicates the nephew skilled in deception with these six reasons. In this way, the Bodhisatta comforts his sister by showing that his nephew has thoroughly learned the deer's wile.

Sopi migapotako pāse baddho avipphanditvāyeva bhūmiyaṃ mahāphāsukapassena pāde pasāretvā nipanno pādānaṃ āsannaṭṭhāne khureheva paharitvā paṃsuñca tiṇāni ca uppāṭetvā uccārapassāvaṃ vissajjetvā sīsaṃ pātetvā jivhaṃ ninnāmetvā sarīraṃ kheḷakilinnaṃ katvā vātaggahaṇena udaraṃ uddhumātakaṃ katvā akkhīni parivattetvā heṭṭhā nāsikāsotena vātaṃ sañcarāpento uparimanāsikāsotena vātaṃ sannirumbhitvā sakalasarīraṃ thaddhabhāvaṃ gāhāpetvā matākāraṃ dassesi. Nīlamakkhikāpi naṃ samparivāresuṃ, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne kākā nilīyiṃsu. Luddo āgantvā udaraṃ hatthena paharitvā “atipātova baddho bhavissati, pūtiko jāto”ti tassa bandhanarajjukaṃ mocetvā “etthevadāni naṃ ukkantitvā maṃsaṃ ādāya gamissāmī”ti nirāsaṅko hutvā sākhāpalāsaṃ gahetuṃ āraddho. Migapotakopi uṭṭhāya catūhi pādehi ṭhatvā kāyaṃ vidhunitvā gīvaṃ pasāretvā mahāvātena chinnavalāhako viya vegena mātu santikaṃ agamāsi.

The young deer, caught in the snare, lay on the ground without struggling, stretching out its legs and lying on its side as if in great comfort. It struck the ground near its feet with its hooves, tearing up dust and grass. It released feces and urine, dropped its head, let its tongue hang out, and made its body wet with saliva. Taking in wind, it made its belly swell up, rolled its eyes, let air pass through its lower nostril while blocking the upper one, and made its entire body become stiff, showing the appearance of being dead. Blue flies swarmed around it, and crows perched in various places. The hunter came, struck its belly with his hand, and thought, 'It must have been caught a long time ago; it has become putrid.' He untied the rope that bound it and, now without suspicion, started to gather branches and leaves, thinking, 'I will cut it up right here and take the meat.' But the young deer got up, stood on its four feet, shook its body, stretched out its neck, and, like a cloud scattered by a great wind, sped to its mother's side.

Satthāpi [M 1.0181] “na, bhikkhave, rāhulo idāneva sikkhākāmo, pubbepi sikkhākāmoyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bhāgineyyamigapotako rāhulo ahosi, mātā uppalavaṇṇā, mātulamigo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: 'Bhikkhus, it is not only now that Rāhula is eager for training; in the past, too, he was eager for training.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he made the connection and identified the birth: 'At that time, the nephew, the young deer, was Rāhula; the mother was Uppalavaṇṇā; and the maternal uncle, the deer, was myself.'

Tipallatthamigajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Tipallatthamiga Jātaka, the Sixth.

[17] 7. Mālutajātakavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Māluta Jātaka

Kāḷe [V 1.0167] vā yadi vā juṇheti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dve vuḍḍhapabbajite ārabbha kathesi. Te kira kosalajanapade [P 1.0165] ekasmiṃ araññāvāse vasanti. Eko kāḷatthero nāma, eko juṇhatthero nāma. Athekadivasaṃ juṇho kāḷaṃ pucchi “bhante kāḷa, sītaṃ nāma kasmiṃ kāle hotī”ti. So “kāḷe hotī”ti āha. Athekadivasaṃ kāḷo juṇhaṃ pucchi – “bhante juṇha, sītaṃ nāma kasmiṃ kāle hotī”ti. So “juṇhe hotī”ti āha. Te ubhopi attano kaṅkhaṃ chindituṃ asakkontā satthu santikaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā “bhante, sītaṃ nāma kasmiṃ kāle hotī”ti pucchiṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “pubbepi ahaṃ, bhikkhave, tumhākaṃ imaṃ pañhaṃ kathesiṃ, bhavasaṅkhepagatattā pana na sallakkhayitthā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'In the dark fortnight or the bright…' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning two elderly monastics. They, it seems, were living in a forest dwelling in the country of Kosala. One was named the Elder Kāḷa, the other the Elder Juṇha. Then one day, Juṇha asked Kāḷa: 'Venerable Kāḷa, during what time does it get cold?' He replied: 'It gets cold during the dark fortnight.' Then on another day, Kāḷa asked Juṇha: 'Venerable Juṇha, during what time does it get cold?' He replied: 'It gets cold during the bright fortnight.' Unable to resolve their doubt, they both went to the Teacher, paid homage to him, and asked: 'Venerable sir, during what time does it get cold?' Having heard their talk, the Teacher said: 'Bhikkhus, in the past, too, I answered this question for you, but because it has been obscured by rebirth, you do not remember it.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte ekasmiṃ pabbatapāde sīho ca byaggho ca dve sahāyā ekissāyeva guhāya vasanti. Tadā bodhisattopi isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tasmiṃyeva pabbatapāde vasati. Athekadivasaṃ tesaṃ sahāyakānaṃ sītaṃ nissāya vivādo udapādi. Byaggho “kāḷeyeva sītaṃ hotī”ti āha. Sīho “juṇheyeva sītaṃ hotī”ti āha. Te ubhopi attano kaṅkhaṃ chindituṃ asakkontā bodhisattaṃ pucchiṃsu. Bodhisatto imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, at the foot of a mountain, a lion and a tiger, two friends, lived together in a single cave. At that time the Bodhisatta had gone forth as an ascetic and was living at the foot of that same mountain. Then one day a dispute arose between those friends on account of the cold. The tiger said, 'It is cold only in the dark fortnight.' The lion said, 'It is cold only in the bright fortnight.' Unable to resolve their doubt, they both asked the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta spoke this verse:

17.

17.

“Kāḷe vā yadi vā juṇhe, yadā vāyati māluto;

Vātajāni hi sītāni, ubhotthamaparājitā”ti.

Whether in the dark fortnight or the bright, whenever the wind blows; for cold spells are born of the wind, you are both undefeated in this matter.

Tattha [M 1.0182] kāḷe vā yadi vā juṇheti kāḷapakkhe vā juṇhapakkhe vā. Yadā vāyati mālutoti yasmiṃ samaye puratthimādibhedo vāto vāyati, tasmiṃ samaye sītaṃ hoti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Vātajāni hi sītāni, yasmā vāte vijjanteyeva sītāni honti, kāḷapakkho vā juṇhapakkho vā ettha apamāṇanti vuttaṃ hoti. Ubhotthamaparājitāti ubhopi tumhe imasmiṃ pañhe aparājitāti. Evaṃ bodhisatto te sahāyake saññāpesi.

Herein, 'whether in the dark fortnight or the bright' means in the dark lunar fortnight or the bright lunar fortnight. 'Whenever the wind blows' means at whatever time a wind from the east or another direction blows, at that time it becomes cold. For what reason? 'For cold spells are born of the wind': since cold spells occur only when the wind is present, it is said that whether it is the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight is not the measure here. 'You are both undefeated in this matter' means you are both undefeated in this question. Thus the Bodhisatta made those friends understand.

Satthāpi “bhikkhave, pubbepi mayā tumhākaṃ ayaṃ pañho kathito”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne [P 1.0166] dvepi therā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Satthā anusandhiṃ [V 1.0168] ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā byaggho kāḷo ahosi, sīho juṇho, pañhavissajjanakatāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher also said: 'Bhikkhus, in the past, too, this question was explained by me to you.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he declared the Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse on the Truths, both elders were established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher then made the connection and identified the birth: 'At that time the tiger was Kāḷa, the lion was Juṇha, and the ascetic who answered the question was myself.'

Mālutajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Māluta Jātaka, the Seventh.

[18] 8. Matakabhattajātakavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Matakabhatta Jātaka

Evaṃ ce sattā jāneyyunti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto matakabhattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi kāle manussā bahū ajeḷakādayo māretvā kālakate ñātake uddissa matakabhattaṃ nāma denti. Bhikkhū te manusse tathā karonte disvā satthāraṃ pucchiṃsu “etarahi, bhante, manussā bahū pāṇe jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā matakabhattaṃ nāma denti. Atthi nu kho, bhante, ettha vuḍḍhī”ti? Satthā “na, bhikkhave, ‘matakabhattaṃ dassāmā’ti katepi pāṇātipāte kāci vuḍḍhi nāma atthi, pubbe paṇḍitā ākāse nisajja dhammaṃ desetvā ettha ādīnavaṃ kathetvā sakalajambudīpavāsike etaṃ kammaṃ jahāpesuṃ. Idāni pana bhavasaṅkhepagatattā puna pātubhūta”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“If beings only knew this…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the meal for the dead. For at that time, people would kill many goats, sheep, and other animals and give what is called a “meal for the dead” on behalf of their deceased relatives. Seeing people acting thus, the bhikkhus asked the Teacher: “Venerable sir, nowadays people deprive many living beings of life and give what is called a ‘meal for the dead.’ Is there any benefit in this?” The Teacher said: “No, bhikkhus, there is no benefit at all in the destruction of life, even when it is done with the thought, ‘We will give a meal for the dead.’ In the past, wise ones, seated in the sky, taught the Dhamma, explained the danger in this, and made all the inhabitants of Jambudīpa abandon this practice. But now, because of the change of existence, it has reappeared.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente eko tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū disāpāmokkho ācariyabrāhmaṇo “matakabhattaṃ dassāmī”ti ekaṃ eḷakaṃ gāhāpetvā antevāsike āha – “tātā, imaṃ eḷakaṃ nadiṃ [M 1.0183] netvā nhāpetvā kaṇṭhe mālaṃ parikkhipitvā pañcaṅgulikaṃ datvā maṇḍetvā ānethā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā taṃ ādāya nadiṃ gantvā nhāpetvā maṇḍetvā nadītīre ṭhapesuṃ. So eḷako attano pubbakammaṃ disvā “evarūpā nāma dukkhā ajja muccissāmī”ti somanassajāto mattikāghaṭaṃ bhindanto viya mahāhasitaṃ hasitvā puna “ayaṃ brāhmaṇo maṃ ghātetvā mayā laddhadukkhaṃ labhissatī”ti brāhmaṇe kāruññaṃ uppādetvā mahantena saddena parodi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, a certain brahmin teacher, a master of the three Vedas and a world-renowned professor, intending to give a meal for the dead, had a goat procured. He told his pupils: “My dears, take this goat to the river, bathe it, hang a garland around its neck, give it the five-finger mark, adorn it, and bring it here.” Saying, “Very well,” they consented, took it to the river, bathed and adorned it, and set it down on the riverbank. The goat, seeing its own past kamma, became joyful, thinking, “Today I will be released from such suffering as this!” and it laughed a great laugh like the smashing of a clay pot. Then, thinking, “This brahmin, by killing me, will receive the same suffering that I received,” it felt compassion for the brahmin and cried with a loud sound.

Atha naṃ te māṇavā pucchiṃsu “samma eḷaka[P 1.0167], tvaṃ mahāsaddena hasi ceva rodi ca, kena nu kho kāraṇena hasi, kena kāraṇena parodī”ti? “Tumhe maṃ imaṃ kāraṇaṃ attano ācariyassa santike puccheyyāthā”ti. Te taṃ ādāya gantvā idaṃ kāraṇaṃ ācariyassa ārocesuṃ. Ācariyo tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā eḷakaṃ pucchi “kasmā tvaṃ eḷaka, hasi, kasmā rodī”ti? Eḷako attanā katakammaṃ jātissarañāṇena anussaritvā brāhmaṇassa kathesi “ahaṃ, brāhmaṇa, pubbe tādisova mantajjhāyakabrāhmaṇo hutvā ‘matakabhattaṃ dassāmī’ti ekaṃ eḷakaṃ māretvā matakabhattaṃ adāsiṃ, svāhaṃ ekassa eḷakassa ghātitattā ekenūnesu pañcasu attabhāvasatesu sīsacchedaṃ pāpuṇiṃ, ayaṃ me [V 1.0169] koṭiyaṃ ṭhito pañcasatimo attabhāvo, svāhaṃ ‘ajja evarūpā dukkhā muccissāmī’ti somanassajāto iminā kāraṇena hasiṃ. Rodanto pana ‘ahaṃ tāva ekaṃ eḷakaṃ māretvā pañca jātisatāni sīsacchedadukkhaṃ patvā ajja tamhā dukkhā muccissāmi, ayaṃ pana brāhmaṇo maṃ māretvā ahaṃ viya pañca jātisatāni sīsacchedadukkhaṃ labhissatī’ti tayi kāruññena rodi”nti. “Eḷaka, mā bhāyi, nāhaṃ taṃ māressāmī”ti. “Brāhmaṇa, kiṃ vadesi, tayi mārentepi amārentepi na sakkā ajja mayā maraṇā muccitu”nti. “Eḷaka, mā bhāyi, ahaṃ te ārakkhaṃ gahetvā tayā saddhiṃyeva vicarissāmī”ti. “Brāhmaṇa, appamattako tava ārakkho, mayā katapāpaṃ pana mahantaṃ balava”nti.

Then those young men asked it: “Friend goat, you both laughed and cried loudly. For what reason did you laugh, and for what reason did you cry?” “You should ask me about this matter in the presence of your teacher.” Taking it along, they went and reported this matter to their teacher. Hearing their words, the teacher asked the goat: “Why did you laugh, goat, and why did you cry?” Recalling its own past deeds with the knowledge of remembering past lives, the goat said to the brahmin: “Brahmin, in a past life, I was just such a brahmin who recited sacred verses. Thinking, ‘I will give a meal for the dead,’ I killed a single goat and gave the meal. Because I killed that one goat, I suffered beheading in four hundred and ninety-nine existences. This is my five hundredth and final existence. Today, I rejoiced, thinking, ‘Now I will be freed from such suffering,’ and for that reason I laughed. But I cried out of compassion for you, thinking: ‘Having killed just one goat, I have experienced the suffering of beheading for five hundred births and will be freed from that suffering today. But this brahmin, by killing me, will, like me, incur the suffering of beheading for five hundred births.’” “Goat, do not be afraid, I will not kill you.” “Brahmin, what are you saying? Whether you kill me or not, it is not possible for me to escape death today.” “Goat, do not be afraid, I will take up your protection and wander about together with you.” “Brahmin, your protection is insignificant, but the evil I have done is great and powerful.”

Brāhmaṇo eḷakaṃ muñcitvā “imaṃ eḷakaṃ kassacipi māretuṃ na dassāmī”ti antevāsike ādāya eḷakeneva saddhiṃ vicari. Eḷako vissaṭṭhamattova ekaṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭhiṃ nissāya jātagumbe gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā paṇṇāni khādituṃ āraddho. Taṅkhaṇaññeva tasmiṃ pāsāṇapiṭṭhe asani pati, tato [M 1.0184] ekā pāsāṇasakalikā chijjitvā eḷakassa pasāritagīvāya patitvā sīsaṃ chindi, mahājano sannipati. Tadā bodhisatto [P 1.0168] tasmiṃ ṭhāne rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatto. So passantasseva tassa mahājanassa devatānubhāvena ākāse pallaṅkena nisīditvā “ime sattā evaṃ pāpassa phalaṃ jānamānā appevanāma pāṇātipātaṃ na kareyyu”nti madhurassarena dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin released the goat and, saying, “I will not let anyone kill this goat,” he took his pupils and wandered about with the goat. As soon as it was released, the goat went to a thicket growing by a stone slab, stretched out its neck, and began to eat the leaves. At that very moment, a thunderbolt struck the stone slab. A splinter of rock broke off and fell on the goat’s outstretched neck, severing its head. A great crowd gathered. At that time, the Bodhisatta had been reborn as a tree deity in that place. By his divine power, he appeared seated cross-legged in the sky in full view of the great crowd. Thinking, “If only these beings, knowing thus the fruit of evil, would not engage in the destruction of life!” he taught the Dhamma in a sweet voice, speaking this verse:

18.

18.

“Evaṃ ce sattā jāneyyuṃ, dukkhāyaṃ jātisambhavo;

Na pāṇo pāṇinaṃ haññe, pāṇaghātī hi socatī”ti.

“If beings were to know that this rebirth is suffering, no living being would kill another; for the killer of life surely grieves.”

Tattha evaṃ ce sattā jāneyyunti ime sattā evaṃ ce jāneyyuṃ. Kathaṃ? Dukkhāyaṃ jātisambhavoti ayaṃ tattha tattha jāti ca jātassa anukkamena vaḍḍhisaṅkhāto sambhavo ca jarābyādhimaraṇaappiyasampayogapiyavippayogahatthapādacchedādīnaṃ dukkhānaṃ vatthubhūtattā “dukkho”ti yadi jāneyyuṃ. Na pāṇo pāṇinaṃ haññeti “paraṃ vadhanto jātisambhave vadhaṃ labhati, pīḷento pīḷaṃ labhatī”ti jātisambhavassa dukkhavatthutāya dukkhabhāvaṃ jānanto koci pāṇo aññaṃ pāṇinaṃ na haññe, satto sattaṃ na haneyyāti attho. Kiṃkāraṇā? Pāṇaghātī hi socatīti, yasmā sāhatthikādīsu chasu payogesu yena kenaci payogena parassa jīvitindriyupacchedanena pāṇaghātī puggalo aṭṭhasu mahānirayesu soḷasasu ussadanirayesu nānappakārāya tiracchānayoniyā pettivisaye asurakāyeti imesu catūsu apāyesu mahādukkhaṃ anubhavamāno dīgharattaṃ antonijjhāyanalakkhaṇena sokena [V 1.0170] socati. Yathā vāyaṃ eḷako maraṇabhayena socati, evaṃ dīgharattaṃ socatītipi ñatvā na pāṇo pāṇinaṃ haññe, koci pāṇātipātakammaṃ nāma na kareyya. Mohena pana mūḷhā avijjāya andhīkatā imaṃ ādīnavaṃ apassantā pāṇātipātaṃ karontīti.

Herein, If beings were to know means: if these beings were to know thus. How? This birth and arising is suffering means: if they were to know as “suffering” this birth here and there and this arising—designated as the gradual growth of one who is born—because it is the ground for such sufferings as aging, sickness, death, association with the unloved, separation from the loved, the cutting off of hands and feet, and so on. No living being would kill another means: knowing that birth and arising are suffering because they are a basis for suffering, and that “one who kills another will in turn be killed in a future birth, and one who injures another will in turn be injured,” no living being would kill another living being; this is the meaning. For what reason? For the killer of life grieves means: because a person who destroys life—by any of the six methods of application such as by one's own hand—by cutting off the life faculty of another, experiences great suffering for a long time in the four planes of misery—the eight great hells, the sixteen subsidiary hells, the various kinds of animal wombs, the realm of ghosts, and the host of asuras—and thus grieves with a sorrow characterized by internal burning. And just as this goat grieved from fear of death, so too, knowing that one will grieve for a long time, a living being would not kill another; no one would commit the act of destroying life. But, deluded by delusion, blinded by ignorance, not seeing this danger, they destroy life.

Evaṃ mahāsatto nirayabhayena tajjetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Manussā taṃ dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nirayabhayabhītā pāṇātipātā viramiṃsu. Bodhisattopi dhammaṃ desetvā mahājanaṃ sīle patiṭṭhāpetvā yathākammaṃ gato, mahājanopi bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā [M 1.0185] devanagaraṃ pūresi. Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “ahaṃ tena samayena rukkhadevatā ahosi”nti.

Thus the Great Being, having terrified them with the fear of hell, taught the Dhamma. Hearing that Dhamma teaching, the people, frightened by the fear of hell, refrained from destroying life. The Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma and established the great crowd in virtue, departed according to his kamma. The great crowd, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and filled the city of the gods. The Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, made the connection and identified the Jātaka: “At that time, I was the tree deity.”

Matakabhattajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Matakabhattajātaka, the eighth.

[19] 9. Āyācitabhattajātakavaṇṇanā

[19] 9. The Commentary on the Āyācitabhattajātaka

Sace [P 1.0169] mucce pecca mucceti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto devatānaṃ āyācanabalikammaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā kira manussā vaṇijjāya gacchantā pāṇe vadhitvā devatānaṃ balikammaṃ katvā “mayaṃ anantarāyena atthasiddhiṃ patvā āgantvā puna tumhākaṃ balikammaṃ karissāmā”ti āyācitvā gacchanti. Tatthānantarāyena atthasiddhiṃ patvā āgatā “devatānubhāvena idaṃ jāta”nti maññamānā bahū pāṇe vadhitvā āyācanato muccituṃ balikammaṃ karonti, taṃ disvā bhikkhū “atthi nu kho, bhante, ettha attho”ti bhagavantaṃ pucchiṃsu. Bhagavā atītaṃ āhari.

“If one is to be freed, be freed hereafter…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the practice of making vowed offerings to deities. At that time, it seems, people going on trading journeys would kill living beings, make offerings to the deities, and make a vow: “If we achieve our goal and return without mishap, we will make offerings to you again.” Then, having achieved their goal and returned without mishap, thinking, “This has come about through the power of the deities,” they would kill many living beings and make offerings to be released from their vow. Seeing this, the bhikkhus asked the Blessed One, “Venerable sir, is there any benefit in this?” The Blessed One related a story from the past.

Atīte kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ gāmake kuṭumbiko gāmadvāre ṭhitanigrodharukkhe devatāya balikammaṃ paṭijānitvā anantarāyena āgantvā bahū pāṇe vadhitvā “āyācanato muccissāmī”ti rukkhamūlaṃ gato. Rukkhadevatā khandhaviṭape ṭhatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, in a village in the Kāsi country, a householder promised an offering to the deity dwelling in a banyan tree at the village gate. Having returned without mishap, he killed many living beings and went to the foot of the tree, thinking, “I shall be freed from my vow.” The tree deity, standing on a fork of the trunk, spoke this verse:

19.

19.

“Sace mucce pecca mucce, muccamāno hi bajjhati;

Na hevaṃ dhīrā muccanti, mutti bālassa bandhana”nti.

“If you are to be freed, be freed after death; for one being freed is bound. The wise are not freed in this way; for the fool, release is bondage.”

Tattha sace mucce pecca mucceti bho purisa, tvaṃ sace mucce yadi muccitukāmosi. Pecca mucceti yathā paraloke na bajjhasi, evaṃ muccāhi. Muccamāno hi bajjhatīti yathā pana tvaṃ [V 1.0171] pāṇaṃ vadhitvā muccituṃ icchasi, evaṃ muccamāno hi pāpakammena bajjhati. Tasmā na hevaṃ dhīrā muccantīti ye paṇḍitapurisā, te evaṃ paṭissavato na muccanti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Evarūpā hi mutti bālassa bandhanaṃ, esā pāṇātipātaṃ katvā mutti nāma bālassa bandhanameva hotīti dhammaṃ desesi. Tato [M 1.0186] paṭṭhāya manussā evarūpā pāṇātipātakammā viratā dhammaṃ caritvā devanagaraṃ pūrayiṃsu.

Herein, If you are to be freed, be freed after death means: O man, if you wish to be freed, then be freed in such a way that you are not bound in the world beyond. For one being freed is bound means: just as you wish to be freed by killing a living being, one being freed in this way is bound by an evil deed. Therefore, The wise are not freed thus means: wise people are not freed from a vow in this way. For what reason? Such a release is the fool's bondage; this so-called release obtained by destroying life is truly the fool's bondage—thus he taught the Dhamma. From then on, people, having refrained from such acts of destroying life, practiced the Dhamma and filled the city of the gods.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “ahaṃ tena samayena rukkhadevatā ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, made the connection and identified the Jātaka: “At that time, I was the tree deity.”

Āyācitabhattajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Āyācitabhattajātaka, the ninth.

[20] 10. Naḷapānajātakavaṇṇanā

[20] 10. The Commentary on the Naḷapāna Jātaka

Disvā [P 1.0170] padamanuttiṇṇanti idaṃ satthā kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno naḷakapānagāmaṃ patvā naḷakapānapokkharaṇiyaṃ ketakavane viharanto naḷadaṇḍake ārabbha kathesi. Tadā kira bhikkhū naḷakapānapokkharaṇiyaṃ nhatvā sūcigharatthāya sāmaṇerehi naḷadaṇḍake gāhāpetvā te sabbatthakameva chidde disvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, mayaṃ sūcigharatthāya naḷadaṇḍake gaṇhāpema, te mūlato yāva aggā sabbatthakameva chiddā, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti pucchiṃsu. Satthā “idaṃ, bhikkhave, mayhaṃ porāṇakaadhiṭṭhāna”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Seeing the footprints that had not come out…” This the Teacher spoke while wandering on tour in the Kosala country. Having reached the village of Naḷakapāna, he was dwelling in a Ketaka grove by the Naḷakapāna pond, and he spoke concerning the reed-stalks. At that time, it seems, the bhikkhus, after bathing in the Naḷakapāna pond, had the novices fetch some reed-stalks for making needle-cases. Seeing that they were perforated all the way through, they approached the Teacher and asked, “Venerable sir, we had some reed-stalks fetched for making needle-cases, but they are perforated from root to tip. What can be the reason for this?” The Teacher replied, “Bhikkhus, this is due to an ancient resolution of mine,” and he related a story from the past.

Pubbe kira so vanasaṇḍo arañño ahosi. Tassāpi pokkharaṇiyā eko dakarakkhaso otiṇṇotiṇṇe khādati. Tadā bodhisatto rohitamigapotakappamāṇo kapirājā hutvā asītisahassamattavānaraparivuto yūthaṃ pariharanto tasmiṃ araññe vasati. So vānaragaṇassa ovādaṃ adāsi “tātā, imasmiṃ araññe visarukkhāpi amanussapariggahitapokkharaṇiyopi honti, tumhe akhāditapubbaṃ phalāphalaṃ khādantā vā apītapubbaṃ pānīyaṃ pivantā vā maṃ paṭipuccheyyāthā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā ekadivasaṃ agatapubbaṭṭhānaṃ gatā tattha bahudeva divasaṃ caritvā pānīyaṃ gavesamānā ekaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ disvā pānīyaṃ apivitvāva bodhisattassāgamanaṃ olokayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Bodhisatto āgantvā “kiṃ tātā, pānīyaṃ na pivathā”ti āha. “Tumhākaṃ āgamanaṃ olokemā”ti. “Suṭṭhu, tātā”ti bodhisatto pokkharaṇiṃ āvijjhitvā padaṃ paricchindanto otiṇṇameva [V 1.0172] passi, na uttiṇṇaṃ. So “nissaṃsayaṃ esā amanussapariggahitā”ti ñatvā “suṭṭhu vo kataṃ, tātā, pānīyaṃ apivantehi, amanussapariggahitā aya”nti āha.

In the past, it is said, that grove was a wilderness. In its pond lived a water-ogre who devoured all who entered. At that time, the Bodhisatta, about the size of a young roe deer, was a monkey king who, surrounded by a retinue of eighty thousand monkeys, led his troop while living in that wilderness. He gave this advice to the troop of monkeys: "Sirs, in this wilderness there are poisonous trees and ponds possessed by non-human beings. Before eating any fruit you have not eaten before, or drinking any water you have not drunk before, you should ask me first." They agreed, replying, "Very well." One day, having gone to a place they had not been before, they roamed there for many days. Searching for water, they saw a pond, but without drinking the water, they sat watching for the Bodhisatta's arrival. The Bodhisatta arrived and asked, "Sirs, why do you not drink the water?" They replied, "We are watching for your arrival." "Well done, sirs," said the Bodhisatta. Examining the pond and scrutinizing the footprints, he saw only those that had gone in, not those that had come out. Realizing, "Without a doubt, this pond is possessed by a non-human being," he said, "You have done well, sirs, by not drinking the water. This pond is possessed by a non-human being."

Dakarakkhasopi [M 1.0187] tesaṃ anotaraṇabhāvaṃ [P 1.0171] ñatvā nīlodaro paṇḍaramukho surattahatthapādo bībhacchadassano hutvā udakaṃ dvidhā katvā nikkhamitvā “kasmā nisinnāttha, otaritvā pānīyaṃ pivathā”ti āha. Atha naṃ bodhisatto pucchi “tvaṃ idha nibbattadakarakkhasosī”ti? “Āma, aha”nti. “Tvaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ otiṇṇake labhasī”ti? “Āma, labhāmi, ahaṃ idhotiṇṇaṃ antamaso sakuṇikaṃ upādāya na kiñci muñcāmi, tumhepi sabbe khādissāmī”ti. “Na mayaṃ attānaṃ tuyhaṃ khādituṃ dassāmā”ti. “Pānīyaṃ pana pivissathā”ti. “Āma, pānīyaṃ pivissāma, na ca te vasaṃ gamissāmā”ti. “Atha kathaṃ pānīyaṃ pivissathā”ti? Kiṃ pana tvaṃ maññasi “otaritvā pivissantī”ti. “Mayañhi anotaritvā asītisahassānipi ekamekaṃ naḷadaṇḍakaṃ gahetvā uppalanāḷena udakaṃ pivantā viya tava pokkharaṇiyā pānīyaṃ pivissāma, evaṃ no tvaṃ khādituṃ na sakkhissasī”ti. Etamatthaṃ viditvā satthā abhisambuddho hutvā imissā gāthāya purimapadadvayaṃ abhāsi –

The water-ogre, knowing that they were not entering, became blue-bellied, pale-faced, with bright red hands and feet, and of terrifying appearance. Splitting the water in two, he emerged and said, "Why do you sit there? Come down and drink the water." Then the Bodhisatta asked him, "Are you the water-ogre who has arisen here?" "Yes, I am." "Do you get those who enter the pond?" "Yes, I do. I do not release anything that enters here, not even so much as a small bird. I will devour all of you, too." "We will not give ourselves to you to be devoured." "But will you drink the water?" "Yes, we will drink the water, but we will not fall under your power." "Then how will you drink the water?" "What do you think? That we will enter and drink? We, all eighty thousand of us, without entering, will each take a single reed stalk and drink the water from your pond as if drinking through a lotus stalk. In this way, you will not be able to devour us." Understanding this matter, the Teacher, having become perfectly enlightened, spoke the first two lines of this verse:

20.

20.

“Disvā padamanuttiṇṇaṃ, disvānotaritaṃ pada”nti.

“Having seen the footprints not come up [out of the water], having seen the footprints gone down [into it].”

Tassattho – bhikkhave, so kapirājā tassā pokkharaṇiyā ekampi uttiṇṇapadaṃ nāddasa, otaritaṃ pana otiṇṇapadameva addasa. Evaṃ disvā padaṃ anuttiṇṇaṃ disvāna otaritaṃ padaṃ “addhāyaṃ pokkharaṇī amanussapariggahitā”ti ñatvā tena saddhiṃ sallapanto sapariso āha –

The meaning of this is as follows, monks: that monkey king did not see even a single footprint that had come out of that pond; he saw only the footprint that had gone in. Thus, having seen the footprint not come out and having seen the footprint gone in, he knew, "Surely this pond is possessed by a non-human being." Knowing this, while conversing with him, he, with his retinue, said:

“Naḷena vāriṃ pissāmā”ti;

Through a reed we will drink the water;

Tassattho – mayaṃ tava pokkharaṇiyaṃ naḷena pānīyaṃ pivissāmāti. Puna mahāsatto āha –

The meaning of that is: 'We will drink water from your pond with a reed.' Then the Great Being said:

“Neva maṃ tvaṃ vadhissasī”ti;

You will not kill me.

Evaṃ naḷena pānīyaṃ pivantaṃ saparisampi maṃ tvaṃ neva vadhissasīti attho.

The meaning is: 'Thus, as I drink water with a reed together with my retinue, you will not kill me.'

Evañca pana vatvā bodhisatto ekaṃ naḷadaṇḍakaṃ āharāpetvā pāramiyo āvajjetvā saccakiriyaṃ katvā mukhena dhami, naḷo [P 1.0172] anto kiñci gaṇṭhiṃ asesetvā sabbatthakameva susiro ahosi[V 1.0173]. Iminā niyāmena aparampi aparampi āharāpetvā mukhena dhamitvā adāsi. Evaṃ santepi na sakkā niṭṭhāpetuṃ, tasmā evaṃ na gahetabbaṃ. Bodhisatto pana “imaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ parivāretvā jātā sabbepi naḷā ekacchiddā hontū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi[M 1.0188]. Bodhisattānañhi hitūpacārassa mahantatāya adhiṭṭhānaṃ samijjhati. Tato paṭṭhāya sabbepi taṃ pokkharaṇiṃ parivāretvā uṭṭhitanaḷā ekacchiddā jātā. Imasmiñhi kappe cattāri kappaṭṭhiyapāṭihāriyāni nāma. Katamāni cattāri? Cande sasalakkhaṇaṃ sakalampi imaṃ kappaṃ ṭhassati, vaṭṭakajātake aggino nibbutaṭṭhānaṃ sakalampi imaṃ kappaṃ aggi na jhāyissati, ghaṭīkāranivesanaṭṭhānaṃ sakalampi imaṃ kappaṃ anovassakaṃ ṭhassati, imaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ parivāretvā uṭṭhitanaḷā sakalampi imaṃ kappaṃ ekacchiddā bhavissantīti imāni cattāri kappaṭṭhiyapāṭihāriyāni nāma.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta had a single reed stalk brought, reflected on the perfections, made an act of truth, and blew through it with his mouth. The reed became completely hollow throughout, without any knot remaining inside. In this way, he had more and more brought, blew through them with his mouth, and gave them out. But even so, it was not possible to finish the task; therefore, this method was not to be adopted. The Bodhisatta then made a resolution: "May all the reeds that have grown surrounding this pond become single-holed." For the resolutions of Bodhisattas succeed due to the greatness of their beneficial conduct. From that time onwards, all the reeds that grew surrounding that pond became single-holed. Indeed, in this auspicious aeon, there are four marvels that endure for the entire aeon. What are the four? The mark of the hare on the moon will last for this entire aeon. The place where the fire was extinguished in the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka will not be burned by fire for this entire aeon. The site of Ghaṭīkāra’s residence will remain without rain for this entire aeon. The reeds that have grown surrounding this pond will be single-holed for this entire aeon. These are the four marvels that endure for the aeon.

Bodhisatto evaṃ adhiṭṭhahitvā ekaṃ naḷaṃ ādāya nisīdi. Tepi asītisahassavānarā ekekaṃ ādāya pokkharaṇiṃ parivāretvā nisīdiṃsu. Tepi bodhisattassa naḷena ākaḍḍhitvā pānīyaṃ pivanakāle sabbe tīre nisinnāva piviṃsu. Evaṃ tehi pānīye pivite dakarakkhaso kiñci alabhitvā anattamano sakanivesanameva gato. Bodhisattopi saparivāro araññameva pāvisi.

Having made this resolution, the Bodhisatta took a reed and sat down. Those eighty thousand monkeys also each took one and sat down surrounding the pond. At the time when the Bodhisatta drew up water with a reed and drank, all of them also drank while seated on the bank. When they had thus drunk the water, the water-ogre, having gotten nothing, was displeased and went back to his own dwelling. The Bodhisatta, too, with his retinue, entered the forest.

Satthā pana “imesaṃ, bhikkhave, naḷānaṃ ekacchiddabhāvo nāma mayhamevetaṃ porāṇakaadhiṭṭhāna”nti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dakarakkhaso devadatto ahosi, asītisahassavānarā buddhaparisā, upāyakusalo pana kapirājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse: "Monks, this single-holed nature of these reeds is indeed my own ancient resolve." Then, having made the connection, he identified the birth story: "At that time, the water-ogre was Devadatta, the eighty thousand monkeys were the Buddha’s assembly, and the monkey king skilled in means was I myself."

Naḷapānajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The tenth is the Commentary on the Naḷapāna Jātaka.

Sīlavaggo dutiyo.

The second is the Sīla Chapter.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Nigrodhaṃ lakkhaṇaṃ kaṇḍi, vātamigaṃ kharādiyaṃ;

Tipallatthaṃ mālutañca, matabhatta ayācitaṃ;

Naḷapānanti te dasāti.

Nigrodha, Lakkhaṇa, Kaṇḍi, Vātamiga, Kharādiya, Tipallattha, Māluta, Matabhatta, Ayācita, and Naḷapāna—these are the ten.

3. Kuruṅgavaggo

3. The Kuruṅga Chapter

[21] 1. Kuruṅgamigajātakavaṇṇanā

[21] 1. The Commentary on the Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka

Ñātametaṃ [V 1.0174][P 1.0173][M 1.0189] kuruṅgassāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā bhikkhū “āvuso devadatto tathāgatassa ghātanatthāya dhanuggahe payojesi, silaṃ pavijjhi, dhanapālaṃ vissajjesi, sabbathāpi dasabalassa vadhāya parisakkatī”ti devadattassa avaṇṇaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā paññattāsane nisinno “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchi. Bhante, devadatto tumhākaṃ vadhāya parisakkatīti tassa aguṇakathāya sannisinnāmhāti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva mama vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi mama vadhāya parisakkiyeva, na ca pana maṃ vadhituṃ asakkhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, spoke this discourse beginning, 'This was known to the Kuruṅga,' concerning Devadatta. For at one time, the monks, having gathered in the Hall of Dhamma, sat speaking in dispraise of Devadatta, saying, 'Venerable sirs, Devadatta employed archers to kill the Tathāgata, he hurled a rock, he unleashed the elephant Dhanapāla; in every way he strives for the death of the one of Ten Powers.' The Teacher arrived and, having sat down on the prepared seat, asked, 'For what discussion, monks, are you now gathered?' 'Venerable Sir, we are gathered to discuss the faults of Devadatta, for he strives for your death.' The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta strives for my death; in the past, too, he strove for it, yet he was unable to kill me.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kuruṅgamigo hutvā ekasmiṃ araññāyatane phalāni khādanto vasati. So ekasmiṃ kāle phalasampanne sepaṇṇirukkhe sepaṇṇiphalāni khādati. Atheko gāmavāsī aṭṭakaluddako phalarukkhamūlesu migānaṃ padāni upadhāretvā uparirukkhe aṭṭakaṃ bandhitvā tattha nisīditvā phalāni khādituṃ āgatāgate mige sattiyā vijjhitvā tesaṃ maṃsaṃ vikkiṇanto jīvikaṃ kappeti. So ekadivasaṃ tasmiṃ rukkhamūle bodhisattassa padavaḷañjaṃ disvā tasmiṃ sepaṇṇirukkhe aṭṭakaṃ bandhitvā pātova bhuñjitvā sattiṃ ādāya vanaṃ pavisitvā taṃ rukkhaṃ āruhitvā aṭṭake nisīdi. Bodhisattopi pātova vasanaṭṭhānā nikkhamitvā “sepaṇṇiphalāni khādissāmī”ti āgamma taṃ rukkhamūlaṃ sahasāva apavisitvā “kadāci aṭṭakaluddakā rukkhesu aṭṭakaṃ bandhanti, atthi nu kho evarūpo upaddavo”ti pariggaṇhanto bāhiratova aṭṭhāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a Kuruṅga deer, living in a certain forest region and eating fruits. At one time, he was eating the fruits of a sepaṇṇi tree that was laden with fruit. Now, a certain village-dwelling hunter who used a platform, having observed the tracks of deer at the foot of fruit trees, would build a platform up in a tree. Sitting there, he would spear the deer that came to eat the fruit, and he made his living by selling their flesh. One day, seeing the Bodhisatta’s tracks at the foot of that tree, he built a platform in that sepaṇṇi tree. Having eaten early in the morning, he took his spear, entered the forest, climbed the tree, and sat on the platform. The Bodhisatta also came forth from his dwelling place early in the morning, intending to eat the sepaṇṇi fruits. Approaching the foot of that tree, he did not enter hastily, but stood just outside, considering, 'Sometimes hunters build platforms in trees. Might there be such a danger here?'

Luddakopi bodhisattassa anāgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā aṭṭake nisinnova [P 1.0174] sepaṇṇiphalāni khipitvā khipitvā tassa purato pātesi. Bodhisatto “imāni phalāni āgantvā mayhaṃ purato patanti, atthi nu kho upari luddako”ti punappunaṃ ullokento luddakaṃ disvā apassanto [V 1.0175] viya hutvā “ambho, rukkha-pubbe tvaṃ olambakaṃ cārento [M 1.0190] viya ujukameva phalāni pātesi, ajja pana te rukkhadhammo pariccatto, evaṃ tayā rukkhadhamme pariccatte ahampi aññaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ upasaṅkamitvā mayhaṃ āhāraṃ pariyesissāmī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The hunter, knowing that the Bodhisatta was not approaching, remained seated on the platform and repeatedly threw sepaṇṇi fruits, causing them to fall in front of him. The Bodhisatta, thinking, 'These fruits are coming and falling before me; could there be a hunter above?' looked up again and again. Seeing the hunter, yet acting as if he had not seen him, he said, 'O tree! Formerly, you would drop your fruits straight down, as if letting them hang. But today you have abandoned the nature of a tree. Since you have abandoned the nature of a tree, I shall approach the foot of another tree to seek my food.' So saying, he spoke this verse:

21.

21.

“Ñātametaṃ kuruṅgassa, yaṃ tvaṃ sepaṇṇi seyyasi;

Aññaṃ sepaṇṇi gacchāmi, na me te ruccate phala”nti.

This is known to the Kuruṅga, O Sepaṇṇi, how you are behaving. I shall go to another sepaṇṇi tree; your fruit does not please me.

Tattha ñātanti pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Etanti idaṃ. Kuruṅgassāti kuruṅgamigassa. Yaṃ tvaṃ sepaṇṇi seyyasīti yaṃ tvaṃ ambho sepaṇṇirukkha purato phalāni pātayamāno seyyasi viseyyasi visiṇṇaphalo hosi, taṃ sabbaṃ kuruṅgamigassa pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Na me te ruccate phalanti evaṃ phalaṃ dadamānāya na me tava phalaṃ ruccati, tiṭṭha tvaṃ, ahaṃ aññattha gacchissāmīti agamāsi.

Therein, known means it has become manifest. This means this. Of the Kuruṅga means of the Kuruṅga deer. That you, O Sepaṇṇi, are behaving means: 'O sepaṇṇi tree, that you lie there causing fruits to fall before me, that you lie scattered, that your fruit is strewn about—all this has become manifest to the Kuruṅga deer.' Your fruit does not please me means: 'From you who gives fruit in this manner, your fruit does not please me. You may stay; I shall go elsewhere.' And so he went.

Athassa luddako aṭṭake nisinnova sattiṃ khipitvā “gaccha, viraddho dānimhi ta”nti āha. Bodhisatto nivattitvā ṭhito āha “ambho purisa, idānīsi kiñcāpi maṃ viraddho, aṭṭha pana mahāniraye soḷasaussadaniraye pañcavidhabandhanādīni ca kammakāraṇāni aviraddhoyevāsī”ti. Evañca pana vatvā palāyitvā yathāruciṃ gato, luddopi otaritvā yathāruciṃ gato.

Then the hunter, still seated on the platform, threw his spear and said, 'Go! I have missed you now!' The Bodhisatta, turning back, stood and said, 'Friend, though you have missed me now, you have certainly not missed the eight great hells, the sixteen Ussada hells, the five kinds of bondage, and other karmic torments.' Having said this, he fled and went where he pleased. The hunter, too, descended and went where he pleased.

Satthāpi “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva mama vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi parisakkiyeva, na ca pana maṃ vadhituṃ asakkhī”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā aṭṭakaluddako devadatto ahosi, kuruṅgamigo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, saying, 'Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta strives for my death; in the past, too, he strove for it, yet he was unable to kill me,' connected the narrative and identified the birth-story: 'At that time, the platform hunter was Devadatta, and the Kuruṅga deer was I myself.'

Kuruṅgamigajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first is the Commentary on the Kuruṅgamiga Jātaka.

[22] 2. Kukkurajātakavaṇṇanā

[22] 2. The Commentary on the Kukkura Jātaka

Ye [V 1.0176][P 1.0175] kukkurāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ñātatthacariyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā dvādasakanipāte bhaddasālajātake āvibhavissati. Idaṃ pana vatthuṃ patiṭṭhapetvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this discourse beginning, 'Those dogs,' concerning his conduct for the welfare of his relatives. That story will be made clear in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka in the Book of Twelve. Here, however, having set forth the present story, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 1.0191] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tathārūpaṃ kammaṃ paṭicca kukkurayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā anekasatakukkuraparivuto mahāsusāne vasati. Athekadivasaṃ rājā setasindhavayuttaṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ rathaṃ āruyha uyyānaṃ gantvā tattha divasabhāgaṃ kīḷitvā atthaṅgate sūriye nagaraṃ pāvisi. Tassa taṃ rathavarattaṃ yathānaddhameva rājaṅgaṇe ṭhapayiṃsu, so rattibhāge deve vassante tinto. Uparipāsādato koleyyakasunakhā otaritvā tassa cammañca naddhiñca khādiṃsu. Punadivase rañño ārocesuṃ “deva, niddhamanamukhena sunakhā pavisitvā rathassa cammañca naddhiñca khādiṃsū”ti. Rājā sunakhānaṃ kujjhitvā “diṭṭhadiṭṭhaṭṭhāne sunakhe ghātethā”ti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya sunakhānaṃ mahābyasanaṃ udapādi. Te diṭṭhidiṭṭhaṭṭhāne ghātiyamānā palāyitvā susānaṃ gantvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta, on account of a certain deed, was reborn as a dog and lived in a great cemetery surrounded by many hundreds of dogs. One day, the king, mounting a chariot adorned with all ornaments and yoked with white Sindh horses, went to the park. After enjoying himself there for the day, he entered the city as the sun set. That excellent chariot was left just as it was in the royal courtyard, and when it rained during the night, it became soaked. From the upper palace, the well-bred dogs descended and chewed its leather and fastenings. The next day, they reported to the king, "Your Majesty, dogs entered through the drainage outlet and chewed the chariot's leather and fastenings." Enraged at the dogs, the king ordered, "Kill every dog in every place you see them." From then on, a great calamity arose for the dogs. Being killed wherever they were seen, they fled and went to the cemetery, approaching the Bodhisatta.

Bodhisatto ‘tumhe bahū sannipatitā, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti pucchi. Te “antepure kira rathassa cammañca naddhi ca sunakhehi khāditā’ti kuddho rājā sunakhavadhaṃ āṇāpesi, bahū sunakhā vinassanti, mahābhayaṃ uppanna”nti āhaṃsu. Bodhisatto cintesi “ārakkhaṭṭhāne bahi sunakhānaṃ okāso natthi, antorājanivesane koleyyakasunakhānameva taṃ kammaṃ bhavissati. Idāni pana corānaṃ kiñci bhayaṃ natthi, acorā maraṇaṃ labhanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ core rañño dassetvā ñātisaṅghassa jīvitadānaṃ dadeyya”nti. So ñātake samassāsetvā “tumhe mā bhāyittha, ahaṃ vo abhayaṃ āharissāmi, yāva [P 1.0176] rājānaṃ passāmi, tāva idheva hothā”ti pāramiyo āvajjetvā mettābhāvanaṃ purecārikaṃ katvā “mayhaṃ upari leḍḍuṃ vā muggaraṃ vā mā koci khipituṃ ussahī”ti adhiṭṭhāya ekakova antonagaraṃ pāvisi. Atha naṃ disvā ekasattopi kujjhitvā olokento nāma nāhosi. Rājāpi sunakhavadhaṃ āṇāpetvā sayaṃ vinicchaye nisinno hoti. Bodhisatto tattheva gantvā pakkhanditvā rañño āsanassa heṭṭhā pāvisi. Atha naṃ rājapurisā nīharituṃ āraddhā, rājā pana vāresi.

The Bodhisatta asked, "You have gathered in great numbers—what is the reason?" They replied, "It is said that in the inner palace, the leather and fastenings of a chariot have been chewed by dogs. The angry king ordered the killing of dogs. Many dogs are being destroyed; great danger has arisen." The Bodhisatta thought, "There is no access for dogs outside the guarded area. Only the well-bred dogs inside the royal residence could have done that deed. Now, the thieves have no fear, while the innocent receive death. Why should I not show the king the thieves and give the gift of life to my kinsfolk?" Comforting his kinsfolk, he said, "Do not fear. I will bring you safety. Stay right here until I see the king." Reflecting on his perfections and making loving-kindness his forerunner, he resolved, "Let no one dare to throw a clod or mallet at me," and entered the city alone. Seeing him, not a single being so much as looked at him angrily. The king, having ordered the killing of dogs, was seated in the hall of justice. The Bodhisatta went right there, rushed forward, and went beneath the king’s seat. Then, as the king’s men began to drag him out, the king forbade them.

So thokaṃ vissamitvā heṭṭhāsanā nikkhamitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā “deva, tumhe kukkure mārāpethā”ti pucchi. “Āma, mārāpemaha”nti[M 1.0192]. “Ko nesaṃ aparādho narindā”ti? “Rathassa me [V 1.0177] parivāracammañca naddhiñca khādiṃsū”ti. “Ye khādiṃsu, te jānāthā”ti? “Na jānāmā”ti. “‘Ime nāma cammakhādakacorā’ti tathato ajānitvā diṭṭhadiṭṭhaṭṭhāneyeva mārāpanaṃ na yuttaṃ, devā”ti. “Rathacammassa kukkurehi khāditattā ‘diṭṭhadiṭṭhe sabbeva mārethā’ti sunakhavadhaṃ āṇāpesi”nti. “Kiṃ pana vo manussā sabbeva kukkure mārenti, udāhu maraṇaṃ alabhantāpi atthī”ti? “Atthi, amhākaṃ ghare koleyyakā maraṇaṃ na labhantī”ti. Mahārāja idāneva tumhe “rathacammassa kukkurehi khāditattā ‘diṭṭhadiṭṭhe sabbeva mārethā’ti sunakhavadhaṃ āṇāpesi”nti avocuttha, idāni pana “amhākaṃ ghare koleyyakā maraṇaṃ na labhantī”ti vadetha. “Nanu evaṃ sante tumhe chandādivasena agatigamanaṃ gacchatha, agatigamanañca nāma na yuttaṃ, na ca rājadhammo, raññā nāma kāraṇagavesakena tulāsadisena bhavituṃ vaṭṭati, idāni ca koleyyakā maraṇaṃ na labhanti, dubbalasunakhāva labhanti, evaṃ sante nāyaṃ sabbasunakhaghaccā, dubbalaghātikā nāmesā”ti. Evañca pana vatvā mahāsatto madhurassaraṃ nicchāretvā “mahārāja, yaṃ tumhe karotha, nāyaṃ dhammo”ti rañño dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

After resting a while, he came out from under the seat, paid homage to the king, and asked, "Your Majesty, are you having dogs killed?" "Yes, we are having them killed." "What is their offense, O king?" "They chewed the leather coverings and straps of my chariot." "Do you know which ones did it?" "We do not know." "Without knowing for certain, 'These are the leather-chewing thieves,' it is not right to have them killed wherever they are seen, Your Majesty." "Because the chariot's leather was chewed by dogs, I ordered, 'Kill all dogs wherever they are seen.'" "But do your people kill every dog, or are there some who do not meet with death?" "There are. In our house, the well-bred dogs do not meet with death." "Great king, just now you said, 'Because the chariot's leather was chewed by dogs, I ordered, 'Kill all dogs wherever they are seen,'' but now you say, 'In our house, the well-bred dogs do not meet with death.' Does this not mean you are following a wrong course of action due to desire and other biases? Such a wrong course is not proper, nor is it the way of a king. A king should be like a balance, seeking the cause. Now, the well-bred dogs do not meet with death, but only the weak dogs do. In that case, this is not a slaughter of all dogs; this is called a slaughter of the weak." Having spoken thus, the Great Being, emitting a sweet voice, declared, "Great king, what you do is not righteous," and teaching the king the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

22.

22.

“Ye [P 1.0177] kukkurā rājakulamhi vaddhā, koleyyakā vaṇṇabalūpapannā;

Teme na vajjhā mayamasma vajjhā, nāyaṃ saghaccā dubbalaghātikāya”nti.

Those dogs raised in the royal household, the well-bred ones, endowed with beauty and strength—they are not to be killed, but we are to be killed. This is not a slaughter of all; it is a slaughter of the weak.

Tattha ye kukkurāti ye sunakhā. Yathā hi dhāruṇhopi passāvo “pūtimutta”nti, tadahujātopi siṅgālo “jarasiṅgālo”ti, komalāpi galocilatā “pūtilatā”ti, suvaṇṇavaṇṇopi kāyo “pūtikāyo”ti vuccati, evamevaṃ vassasatikopi sunakho “kukkuro”ti vuccati. Tasmā mahallakā kāyabalūpapannāpi te “kukkurā”tveva vuttā. Vaddhāti vaḍḍhitā. Koleyyakāti rājakule jātā sambhūtā saṃvaḍḍhā. Vaṇṇabalūpapannāti sarīravaṇṇena ceva kāyabalena ca sampannā. Teme na vajjhāti te ime sassāmikā sārakkhā na vajjhā. Mayamasma vajjhāti assāmikā anārakkhā mayaṃ vajjhā nāma jātā. Nāyaṃ saghaccāti evaṃ sante ayaṃ avisesena saghaccā nāma na hoti. Dubbalaghātikāyanti [M 1.0193] ayaṃ pana dubbalānaṃyeva ghātanato dubbalaghātikā nāma hoti. Rājūhi nāma corā niggaṇhitabbā, no acorā. Idha pana corānaṃ kiñci bhayaṃ natthi, acorā maraṇaṃ labhanti. Aho imasmiṃ loke ayuttaṃ vattati, aho adhammo vattatīti.

Therein, 'kukkurā' means dogs. For just as even harsh urine is called 'foul urine,' a jackal just born is called an 'old jackal,' a tender galocī creeper is called a 'rotten creeper,' and a body of golden color is called a 'foul body,' in the same way, even a dog a hundred years old is called a 'kukkura.' Therefore, even those who are old and endowed with bodily strength are simply called 'kukkurā.' 'Vaddhā' means reared. 'Koleyyakā' means those born, originated, and reared in the royal family. 'Vaṇṇabalūpapannā' means endowed with beauty of form and bodily strength. 'These are not to be killed'—these, being owned and protected, are not to be killed. 'But we are to be killed'—we, being ownerless and unprotected, are born to be killed. 'This is not indiscriminate slaughter'—in such a situation, this is not an indiscriminate slaughter. 'Only the weak are killed'—this, however, is called the 'killing of the weak' (dubbalaghātikā) because it is only the weak who are slain. Kings ought to punish thieves, not non-thieves. But here, thieves have no fear at all, while non-thieves meet death. Alas, in this world what is unjust prevails; alas, unrighteousness prevails!

Rājā [V 1.0178] bodhisattassa vacaraṃ sutvā āha – “jānāsi tvaṃ, paṇḍita, asukehi nāma rathacammaṃ khādita”nti? “Āma, jānāmī”ti. “Kehi khādita”nti? “Tumhākaṃ gehe vasanakehi koleyyakasunakhehī”ti. “Kathaṃ tehi khāditabhāvo jānitabbo”ti? “Ahaṃ tehi khāditabhāvaṃ dassesāmī”ti. “Dassehi paṇḍitā”ti. “Tumhākaṃ ghare koleyyakasunakhe āharāpetvā thokaṃ takkañca dabbatiṇāni ca āharāpethā”ti. Rājā tathā akāsi. Atha naṃ mahāsatto “imāni tiṇāni takkena maddāpetvā ete sunakhe pāyethā”ti āha. Rājā tathā katvā pāyāpesi, pītā pītā sunakhā saddhiṃ cammehi vamiṃsu. Rājā “sabbaññubuddhassa byākaraṇaṃ viyā”ti tuṭṭho bodhisattassa setacchattena pūjaṃ akāsi. Bodhisatto “dhammaṃ cara, mahārāja, mātāpitūsu khattiyā”tiādīhi (jā. 2.17.39) tesakuṇajātake āgatāhi dasahi dhammacariyagāthāhi rañño dhammaṃ desetvā “mahārāja, ito paṭṭhāya appamatto hohī”ti rājānaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā setacchattaṃ raññova paṭiadāsi.

The king, hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, said: “Do you know, wise one, by which dogs the chariot leather was eaten?” “Yes, I know.” “By whom was it eaten?” “By the high-bred dogs living in your house.” “How can it be known that they ate it?” “I will demonstrate that they ate it.” “Demonstrate it, wise one.” “Have the high-bred dogs from your house brought here, and also fetch a little buttermilk and some dabba grass.” The king did so. Then the Great Being said, “Have this grass crushed with the buttermilk and give it to these dogs to drink.” The king did so and had them drink it. As soon as they drank, the dogs vomited, along with the leather. The king, delighted as if it were the pronouncement of an omniscient Buddha, honored the Bodhisatta with a white parasol. The Bodhisatta, teaching the king the Dhamma with the ten verses on righteous conduct from the Tesakuṇa Jātaka, beginning with, “Practice righteousness, great king, towards your mother and father, O Khattiya,” and saying, “Great king, from now on be diligent,” established the king in the five precepts and returned the white parasol to the king himself.

Rājā mahāsattassa dhammakathaṃ [P 1.0178] sutvā sabbasattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā bodhisattaṃ ādiṃ katvā sabbasunakhānaṃ attano bhojanasadisameva niccabhattaṃ paṭṭhapetvā bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhito yāvatāyukaṃ dānādīni puññāni katvā kālaṃ katvā devaloke uppajji. Kukkurovādo dasa vassasahassāni pavatti. Bodhisattopi yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Hearing the Great Being's discourse on the Dhamma, the king granted safety to all beings. Beginning with the Bodhisatta, he established for all the dogs a regular provision of food equal to his own. Abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving for as long as he lived, and after passing away, he arose in the celestial world. The Dog’s Admonition prevailed for ten thousand years. The Bodhisatta also, having lived out his lifespan, passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva ñātakānaṃ atthaṃ carati, pubbepi cariyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, avasesā parisā buddhaparisā, kukkurapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Bhikkhus, it is not only now that the Tathāgata acts for the welfare of his relatives; he did so in the past as well.' Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he made the connection and concluded the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the king was Ānanda, the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and the wise dog was none other than myself.'

Kukkurajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The commentary on the Kukkura Jātaka, the second, is concluded.

[23] 3. Bhojājānīyajātakavaṇṇanā

[23] 3. The Commentary on the Bhojājānīya Jātaka

Api [M 1.0194] passena semānoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi samaye satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantetvā “bhikkhu, pubbe paṇḍitā anāyatanepi vīriyaṃ akaṃsu, pahāraṃ laddhāpi neva ossajiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this story, beginning 'Api passena semāno,' concerning a monk who had slackened his effort. At that time, the Teacher addressed that monk, saying, 'Bhikkhu, in the past, the wise exerted effort even in an untenable position, and even when struck, they did not give up.' Having said this, he recounted a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0179] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bhojājānīyasindhavakule nibbatto sabbālaṅkārasampanno bārāṇasirañño maṅgalasso ahosi. So satasahassagghanikāya suvaṇṇapātiyaṃyeva nānaggarasasampannaṃ tivassikagandhasālibhojanaṃ bhuñjati, cātujjātikagandhūpalittāyameva bhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhati, taṃ ṭhānaṃ rattakambalasāṇiparikkhittaṃ upari suvaṇṇatārakakhacitacelavitānaṃ samosaritagandhadāmamālādāmaṃ avijahitagandhatelapadīpaṃ hoti. Bārāṇasirajjaṃ pana apatthentā rājāno nāma natthi. Ekaṃ samayaṃ satta rājāno bārāṇasiṃ parikkhipitvā “amhākaṃ rajjaṃ vā detu, yuddhaṃ vā”ti bārāṇasirañño paṇṇaṃ pesesuṃ. Rājā amacce sannipātetvā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā “idāni kiṃ karoma, tātā”ti pucchi. “Deva, tumhehi tāva āditova yuddhāya na gantabbaṃ, asukaṃ [P 1.0179] nāma assārohaṃ pesetvā yuddhaṃ kāretha, tasmiṃ asakkonte pacchā jānissāmā”ti. Rājā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “sakkhissasi, tāta, sattahi rājūhi saddhiṃ yuddhaṃ kātu”nti āha. “Deva, sace bhojājānīyasindhavaṃ labhāmi, tiṭṭhantu satta rājāno, sakalajambudīpe rājūhipi saddhiṃ yujjhituṃ sakkhissāmī”ti. “Tāta, bhojājānīyasindhavo vā hotu añño vā, yaṃ icchasi, taṃ gahetvā yuddhaṃ karohī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the lineage of Bhojājānīya thoroughbreds. Endowed with all adornments, he became the auspicious state horse of the King of Bārāṇasī. He ate fragrant three-year-old rice with various exquisite flavors from a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand. The ground where he stood was anointed with perfumes of four kinds, and the place was enclosed by a curtain of red blankets and hemp, with a canopy above made of cloth adorned with golden stars, hung with fragrant garlands and wreaths, and with perfumed oil lamps that were never extinguished. Now, there were no kings who did not covet the kingdom of Bārāṇasī. On one occasion, seven kings surrounded Bārāṇasī and sent a letter to the king, saying: 'Either give us your kingdom, or give battle!' The king assembled his ministers, explained the situation, and asked, 'Sirs, what shall we do now?' They replied, 'Your Majesty, you should not go into battle at the outset. Send a certain horseman and have him do battle. If he is unable, we will know what to do next.' The king summoned him and asked, 'Sir, will you be able to do battle with the seven kings?' He replied, 'Your Majesty, if I can get the Bhojājānīya thoroughbred, let alone the seven kings—I will be able to fight even with all the kings in the whole of Jambudīpa!' The king said, 'Sir, whether it be the Bhojājānīya thoroughbred or another, take whichever you wish and do battle.'

So “sādhu, devā”ti rājānaṃ vanditvā pāsādā oruyha bhojājānīyasindhavaṃ āharāpetvā suvammitaṃ katvā attanāpi sabbasannāhasannaddho khaggaṃ bandhitvā sindhavapiṭṭhivaragato nagarā nikkhamma vijjulatā viya caramāno paṭhamaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā ekaṃ rājānaṃ jīvaggāhameva gahetvā āgantvā nagare balassa niyyādetvā puna gantvā dutiyaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā tathā tatiyanti evaṃ pañca rājāno jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvā chaṭṭhaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ [M 1.0195] bhinditvā chaṭṭhassa rañño gahitakāle bhojājānīyo pahāraṃ labhati, lohitaṃ paggharati, vedanā balavatiyo vattanti. Assāroho tassa pahaṭabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhojājānīyasindhavaṃ rājadvāre nipajjāpetvā sannāhaṃ sithilaṃ katvā aññaṃ assaṃ sannayhituṃ āraddho. Bodhisatto mahāphāsukapassena nipannova akkhīni ummiletvā assārohaṃ disvā “ayaṃ aññaṃ assaṃ sannayhati, ayañca asso sattamaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā sattamaṃ rājānaṃ gaṇhituṃ na sakkhissati, mayā katakammañca nassissati, appaṭisamo assārohopi nassissati, rājāpi parahatthaṃ gamissati, ṭhapetvā maṃ añño asso sattamaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā sattamaṃ rājānaṃ gahetuṃ samattho nāma natthī”ti nipannakova assārohaṃ pakkosāpetvā “samma assāroha, sattamaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā sattamaṃ rājānaṃ gahetuṃ samattho ṭhapetvā maṃ añño asso nāma natthi, nāhaṃ mayā katakammaṃ nāsessāmi, mamaññeva uṭṭhāpetvā sannayhāhī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

"Very well, Your Majesty," he said, and having paid homage to the king, he descended from the palace. He had the Bhojājānīya thoroughbred brought and well-armored. He himself, fully clad in armor and with his sword fastened, mounted the back of the excellent thoroughbred. Moving like a flash of lightning, he sallied forth from the city, first breaking through a stronghold and capturing one king alive. Returning to the city, he delivered the captive to the army, then went forth again and broke through a second stronghold. In this manner he captured five kings alive. While breaking through the sixth stronghold and capturing the sixth king, the Bhojājānīya thoroughbred received a blow. Blood flowed, and severe pains arose. The horseman, knowing it had been struck, had the Bhojājānīya thoroughbred lie down at the royal gate, loosened its armor, and began to harness another horse. The Bodhisatta, lying on his great flank, opened his eyes and saw the horseman, thinking: "This man is harnessing another horse, but that horse will not be able to break through the seventh stronghold and capture the seventh king. The deed I have done will be lost, the peerless horseman will also be lost, and the king will fall into the hands of others. Apart from me, there is no other horse capable of breaking through the seventh stronghold and capturing the seventh king." While still lying down, he had the horseman summoned and said, "Friend horseman, apart from me, there is no other horse capable of breaking through the seventh stronghold and capturing the seventh king. I will not allow the deed I have done to be lost. Raise me up and harness me." Then he spoke this verse:

23.

23.

“Api [V 1.0180][P 1.0180] passena semāno, sallebhi sallalīkato;

Seyyova vaḷavā bhojjho, yuñja maññeva sārathī”ti.

"Though lying on my side, riddled with arrows, the Bhojja is still better than a common steed; therefore, yoke me and me alone, O charioteer!"

Tattha api passena semānoti ekena passena sayamānakopi. Sallebhi sallalīkatoti sallehi viddhopi samāno. Seyyova vaḷavā bhojjhoti vaḷavāti sindhavakulesu ajāto khaluṅkasso. Bhojjhoti bhojājānīyasindhavo. Iti etasmā vaḷavā sallehi viddhopi bhojājānīyasindhavova seyyo varo uttamo. Yuñja maññeva sārathīti yasmā eva gatopi ahameva seyyo, tasmā mamaññeva yojehi, maṃ vammehīti vadati.

Herein, 'Though lying on my side' means even while lying on one side. 'Riddled with arrows' means even while pierced by arrows. 'The Bhojja is still better than a common steed': 'common steed' refers to a low-bred horse not born in the lineage of Sindh thoroughbreds. 'Bhojja' refers to the Bhojājānīya thoroughbred. Thus, the Bhojājānīya thoroughbred, though pierced by arrows, is still better, more excellent, and supreme than that common steed. 'Therefore, yoke me and me alone, O charioteer!' means: because even in this state I am still better, he says, 'Yoke me alone, armor me!'

Assāroho bodhisattaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā vaṇaṃ bandhitvā susannaddhaṃ sannayhitvā tassa piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīditvā sattamaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā sattamaṃ rājānaṃ jīvaggāhaṃ gahetvā rājabalassa niyyādesi, bodhisattampi rājadvāraṃ ānayiṃsu. Rājā tassa dassanatthāya nikkhami. Mahāsatto rājānaṃ āha – “mahārāja, satta rājāno mā ghātayittha, sapathaṃ kāretvā vissajjetha, mayhañca assārohassa ca dātabbaṃ yasaṃ assārohasseva detha[M 1.0196], satta rājāno gahetvā dinnayodhaṃ nāma nāsetuṃ na vaṭṭati. Tumhepi dānaṃ detha, sīlaṃ rakkhatha, dhammena samena rajjaṃ kārethā”ti. Evaṃ bodhisattena rañño ovāde dinne bodhisattassa sannāhaṃ mocayiṃsu, so sannāhe muttamatteyeva nirujjhi. Rājā tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā assārohassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā satta rājāno puna attanno adubbhāya sapathaṃ kāretvā sakasakaṭṭhānāni pesetvā dhammena samena rajjaṃ kāretvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.

The horseman raised the Bodhisatta, bandaged his wound, securely fastened his armor, mounted his back, broke through the seventh stronghold, captured the seventh king alive, and handed him over to the king's army. They brought the Bodhisatta to the royal gate. The king came out to see him. The Great Being said to the king, "Great King, do not kill the seven kings. Make them swear an oath and release them. The honor that is to be given to me and the horseman, give to the horseman alone. It is not right to destroy the warrior who has captured and delivered seven kings. You too should give alms, observe the moral precepts, and rule with justice and equity." When the Bodhisatta had thus advised the king, they removed the Bodhisatta’s armor. The moment his armor was removed, he passed away. The king had his funeral rites performed, bestowed great honor upon the horseman, made the seven kings swear an oath not to act with treachery against him again, and sent them back to their own places. He ruled with justice and equity, and at the end of his life, he passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā “evaṃ bhikkhu pubbe paṇḍitā anāyatanepi vīriyaṃ akaṃsu, evarūpaṃ pahāraṃ laddhāpi na ossajiṃsu, tvaṃ pana evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā kasmā vīriyaṃ ossajasī”ti vatvā cattāri saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu arahattaphale patiṭṭhāsi.

The Teacher said, "Thus, bhikkhu, in the past the wise exerted effort even in a hopeless situation; though having received such a blow, they did not relinquish their effort. But you, having gone forth in such a liberating teaching, why do you relinquish your effort?" Having spoken thus, he proclaimed the Four Noble Truths. At the conclusion of the proclamation of the Truths, the bhikkhu who had relinquished his effort became established in the fruit of Arahantship.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ [P 1.0181] ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, assāroho sāriputto, bhojājānīyasindhavo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the links and identified the birth, saying: "At that time, the king was Ānanda, the horseman was Sāriputta, but the Bhojājānīya thoroughbred was none other than myself."

Bhojājānīyajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Bhojājānīya Jātaka, the Third.

[24] 4. Ājaññajātakavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Ājañña Jātaka

Yadā [V 1.0181] yadāti idampi satthā jetavane viharanto ossaṭṭhavīriyameva bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ pana bhikkhuṃ satthā āmantetvā “bhikkhu pubbe paṇḍitā anāyatanepi laddhappahārāpi hutvā vīriyaṃ akaṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This discourse beginning "Whenever, whenever" was also told by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a bhikkhu who had relinquished his effort. The Teacher addressed that bhikkhu, saying, "Bhikkhu, in the past the wise exerted effort even in a hopeless situation and though having received blows." Thus he related the story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente purimanayeneva satta rājāno nagaraṃ parivārayiṃsu. Atheko rathikayodho dve bhātikasindhave rathe yojetvā nagarā nikkhamma cha balakoṭṭhake bhinditvā cha rājāno aggahesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe jeṭṭhakaasso pahāraṃ labhi. Rathiko rathaṃ pesento rājadvāraṃ āgantvā jeṭṭhabhātikaṃ rathā mocetvā sannāhaṃ sithilaṃ katvā ekeneva passena nipajjāpetvā [M 1.0197] aññaṃ assaṃ sannayhituṃ āraddho. Bodhisatto taṃ disvā purimanayeneva cintetvā rathikaṃ pakkosāpetvā nipannakova imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, seven kings surrounded the city in the same manner as before. Then a chariot-warrior yoked two brother thoroughbreds of Sindh to his chariot, left the city, broke through six strongholds, and captured six kings. At that moment, the elder horse received a wound. The charioteer, driving the chariot, arrived at the royal gate, unyoked the elder brother from the chariot, loosened its armor, and made it lie down on one side while he began to harness another horse. The Bodhisatta, seeing this, reflected as before, had the charioteer summoned, and while still lying down, spoke this verse:

24.

24.

“Yadā yadā yattha yadā, yattha yattha yadā yadā;

Ājañño kurute vegaṃ, hāyanti tattha vāḷavā”ti.

"Whenever and wherever, wherever and whenever a thoroughbred shows its speed, right there the common steeds fall behind."

Tattha yadā yadāti pubbaṇhādīsu yasmiṃ yasmiṃ kāle. Yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne magge vā saṅgāmasīse vā. Yadāti yasmiṃ khaṇe. Yattha yatthāti sattannaṃ balakoṭṭhakānaṃ vasena bahūsu yuddhamaṇḍalesu. Yadā yadāti yasmiṃ yasmiṃ kāle pahāraṃ laddhakāle vā aladdhakāle vā. Ājañño kurute veganti sārathissa cittarucitaṃ kāraṇaṃ ājānanasabhāvo ājañño varasindhavo vegaṃ karoti vāyamati vīriyaṃ ārabhati. Hāyanti tattha vāḷavāti tasmiṃ vege kariyamāne itare vaḷavasaṅkhātā khaḷuṅkassā hāyanti parihāyanti, tasmā imasmiṃ rathe maṃyeva yojehīti āha.

Herein, 'yadā yadā' refers to any time, such as dawn and so on. 'Yattha' means in any place, on a path or at the head of the battle. 'Yadā' means at any moment. 'Yattha yattha' refers to the many battlefields, by way of the seven strongholds. 'Yadā yadā' means at any time, whether a blow is received or not. 'Ājañño kurute vegaṃ' means the noble thoroughbred, understanding the charioteer’s intent, exerts effort, strives, and initiates energy. 'Hāyanti tattha vāḷavā' means when this effort is made, the others, the inferior horses, weaken and decline. Therefore, he said, 'In this chariot, yoke only me.'

Sārathi bodhisattaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā rathe yojetvā sattamaṃ balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā sattamaṃ rājānaṃ ādāya rathaṃ pesento rājadvāraṃ [P 1.0182] āgantvā sindhavaṃ mocesi. Bodhisatto ekena passena nipanno purimanayeneva rañño ovādaṃ datvā nirujjhi. Rājā tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā sārathissa sammānaṃ katvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā yathākammaṃ gato.

The charioteer roused the Bodhisatta, yoked him to the chariot, broke through the seventh stronghold, captured the seventh king, and, sending the chariot onward, arrived at the royal gate and released the Sindh horse. The Bodhisatta, lying on one side, gave the king counsel as before and passed away. The king, having performed his funeral rites, honored the charioteer, ruled the kingdom righteously, and departed according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 1.0182] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Satthā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā rājā ānandatthero ahosi, asso sammāsambuddho”ti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, that monk was established in arahantship. The Teacher connected the birth story: 'At that time, the king was the Elder Ānanda, and the horse was the Perfectly Enlightened One.'

Ājaññajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Ājañña Jātaka, the Fourth.

[25] 5. Titthajātakavaṇṇanā

[25] 5. The Commentary on the Tittha Jātaka

Aññamaññehi [M 1.0198] titthehīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dhammasenāpatissa saddhivihārikaṃ ekaṃ suvaṇṇakārapubbakaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Āsayānusayañāṇañhi buddhānaṃyeva hoti, na aññesaṃ. Tasmā dhammasenāpati attano āsayānusayañāṇassa natthitāya saddhivihārikassa āsayānusayaṃ ajānanto asubhakammaṭṭhānameva kathesi, tassa taṃ na sappāyamahosi. Kasmā? So kira paṭipāṭiyā pañca jātisatāni suvaṇṇakārageheyeva paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi, athassa dīgharattaṃ parisuddhasuvaṇṇadassanavasena paricitattā asubhaṃ na sappāyamahosi. So tattha nimittamattampi uppādetuṃ asakkonto cattāro māse khepesi.

'By various fords'—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who was formerly a goldsmith, a disciple living with the General of the Dhamma. Indeed, the knowledge of inclinations and underlying tendencies belongs only to the Buddhas, not to others. Therefore, the General of the Dhamma, unaware of his disciple's inclinations and underlying tendencies due to the absence of such knowledge himself, taught him only the meditation on the repulsive. But this was not suitable for him. Why? It is said that for five hundred consecutive lives, he had taken rebirth in goldsmiths' households, and due to long familiarity with seeing pure gold, the repulsive was not agreeable to him. Unable to produce even the slightest mental sign, he passed four months.

Dhammasenāpati attano saddhivihārikassa arahattaṃ dātuṃ asakkonto “addhā ayaṃ buddhaveneyyo bhavissati, tathāgatassa santikaṃ nessāmī”ti cintetvā pātova taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ agamāsi. Satthā “kiṃ nu kho, sāriputta, ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ ādāya āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ, bhante, imassa kammaṭṭhānaṃ adāsiṃ, ayaṃ pana catūhi māsehi nimittamattampi na uppādesi, svāhaṃ ‘buddhaveneyyo eso bhavissatī’ti cintetvā tumhākaṃ santikaṃ ādāya āgato”ti. “Sāriputta, kataraṃ pana te kammaṭṭhānaṃ saddhivihārikassa dinna”nti? “Asubhakammaṭṭhānaṃ bhagavā”ti. “Sāriputta, natthi tava santāne āsayānusayañāṇaṃ, gaccha, tvaṃ sāyanhasamaye āgantvā tava saddhivihārikaṃ ādāya gaccheyyāsī”ti. Evaṃ satthā theraṃ uyyojetvā tassa bhikkhussa manāpaṃ cīvarañca nivāsanañca dāpetvā taṃ ādāya gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā paṇītaṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ dāpetvā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro puna vihāraṃ āgantvā gandhakuṭiyaṃ divasabhāgaṃ khepetvā [P 1.0183] sāyanhasamaye taṃ bhikkhuṃ gahetvā vihāracārikaṃ caramāno ambavane ekaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ māpetvā tattha mahantaṃ paduminigacchaṃ, tatrāpi ca mahantaṃ ekaṃ padumapupphaṃ māpetvā “bhikkhu imaṃ pupphaṃ olokento nisīdā”ti nisīdāpetvā gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi.

The General of the Dhamma, unable to lead his disciple to the attainment of arahantship, thought, 'Surely, this one must be trained by the Buddha; I will take him to the presence of the Tathāgata.' Early in the morning, he took him and went to the Teacher. The Teacher asked, 'Why, Sāriputta, have you come bringing a monk?' 'Venerable sir, I gave him a meditation subject, but even after four months, he has not produced even the slightest mental sign. Thinking, "This one must be trained by the Buddha," I have brought him to your presence.' 'Sāriputta, what meditation subject did you give to your disciple?' 'The meditation on the unattractive, Blessed One.' 'Sāriputta, you do not possess the knowledge of inclinations and latent tendencies. Go, and in the evening, return and take your disciple with you.' Having thus dismissed the elder, the Teacher had pleasing robes and an undergarment given to that monk. Taking him, he entered the village for alms and had fine food and delicacies offered. Surrounded by a great assembly of monks, he returned to the monastery. After spending the day in the perfumed chamber, in the evening, he took that monk and went on a walk around the monastery grounds. He magically created a lotus pond in the mango grove, and in it, a large clump of lotus plants, and among them, a large lotus flower. He had the monk sit down, saying, 'Monk, sit here looking at this flower.' Then he entered the perfumed chamber.

So [V 1.0183] bhikkhu taṃ pupphaṃ punappunaṃ oloketi. Bhagavā taṃ pupphaṃ jaraṃ pāpesi, taṃ tassa passantasseva jaraṃ patvā vivaṇṇaṃ ahosi. Athassa pariyantato paṭṭhāya [M 1.0199] pattāni patantāni muhuttena sabbāni patiṃsu. Tato kiñjakkhaṃ pati, kaṇṇikāva avasissi. So bhikkhu taṃ passanto cintesi “idaṃ padumapupphaṃ idāneva abhirūpaṃ ahosi dassanīyaṃ, athassa vaṇṇo pariṇato, pattāni ca kiñcakkhañca patitaṃ, kaṇṇikāmattameva avasiṭṭhaṃ, evarūpassa nāma padumassa jarā pattā, mayhaṃ sarīrassa kiṃ na pāpuṇissati, sabbe saṅkhārā aniccā”ti vipassanaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Satthā “tassa cittaṃ vipassanaṃ āruḷha”nti ñatvā gandhakuṭiyaṃ nisinnova obhāsaṃ pharitvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

That monk kept looking at the flower again and again. The Blessed One caused that flower to age, and as he watched, it aged and became discolored. Then, starting from the periphery, its petals began to fall, and in a moment they had all dropped. Next, the filaments fell, leaving only the seed pod behind. Seeing this, the monk reflected: 'This lotus flower was just now beautiful and delightful to see, but now its color has changed, its petals and filaments have fallen, and only the seed pod remains. If such a lotus is subject to aging, how can my body not be subject to it? All conditioned phenomena are impermanent.' Thus he established insight. The Teacher, knowing that his mind had ascended to insight, while seated in the perfumed chamber, radiated light and spoke this verse:

“Ucchinda sinehamattano, kumudaṃ sāradikaṃva pāṇinā;

Santimaggameva brūhaya, nibbānaṃ sugatena desita”nti. (dha. pa. 285);

'Cut off affection for yourself, as one plucks an autumn water lily with the hand. Cultivate only the path of peace, Nibbāna taught by the Sugata.'

So bhikkhu gāthāpariyosāne arahattaṃ patvā “mutto vatamhi sabbabhavehī”ti cintetvā –

That monk, at the end of the verse, attained Arahantship and reflected, 'Indeed, I am freed from all states of existence,' and uttered these verses:

“So vutthavāso paripuṇṇamānaso, khīṇāsavo antimadehadhārī;

Visuddhasīlo susamāhitindriyo, cando yathā rāhumukhā pamutto.

'He has lived the holy life, with mind fulfilled, with taints destroyed, bearing his final body; pure in virtue, with senses well-composed, like the moon freed from Rāhu's mouth.

“Samotataṃ mohamahandhakāraṃ, vinodayiṃ sabbamalaṃ asesaṃ;

Ālokapajjotakaro pabhaṅkaro, sahassaraṃsī viya bhāṇumā nabhe”ti. –

I have dispelled the dense, great darkness of delusion, and all defilements without remainder. A maker of light, a bringer of radiance, I am like the thousand-rayed sun in the sky.'

Ādīhi gāthāhi udānaṃ udānesi. Udānetvā ca pana gantvā bhagavantaṃ vandi. Theropi āgantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā attano saddhivihārikaṃ gahetvā agamāsi. Ayaṃ pavatti bhikkhūnaṃ antare pākaṭā jātā. Bhikkhū [P 1.0184] dhammasabhāyaṃ dasabalassa guṇe vaṇṇayamānā nisīdiṃsu – “āvuso, sāriputtatthero āsayānusayañāṇassa abhāvena attano saddhivihārikassa āsayaṃ na jānāti, satthā pana ñatvā ekadivaseneva tassa saha paṭisambhidāhi arahattaṃ adāsi, aho buddhā nāma mahānubhāvā”ti.

With verses such as these, he uttered an inspired utterance. Having uttered this utterance, he went and paid homage to the Blessed One. The Elder also came, paid homage to the Teacher, took his own co-resident monk, and departed. This event became well-known among the monks. The monks, sitting in the hall of Dhamma, extolled the virtues of the One with Ten Powers, saying: 'Venerable sirs, the Elder Sāriputta, due to his lack of the knowledge of dispositions and underlying tendencies, did not know the inclination of his own co-resident. The Teacher, however, knowing it, bestowed upon him Arahantship together with the analytical knowledges in a single day. Oh, how great is the power of the Buddhas!'

Satthā [M 1.0200] āgantvā paññattāsane nisīditvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchi. “Na bhagavā aññāya kathāya, tumhākaññeva pana dhammasenāpatino saddhivihārikassa āsayānusayañāṇakathāyā”ti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, etaṃ acchariyaṃ, svāhaṃ [V 1.0184] etarahi buddho hutvā tassa āsayaṃ jānāmi, pubbepāhaṃ tassa āsayaṃ jānāmiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher arrived, sat down on the prepared seat, and asked, 'For what discussion, monks, are you now assembled?' 'For no other discussion, Blessed One, but for the discussion concerning the knowledge of the dispositions and underlying tendencies of the co-resident of your General of the Dhamma.' The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not astonishing that I, having now become a Buddha, know his disposition. I knew his disposition in the past as well.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto taṃ rājānaṃ atthe ca dhamme ca anusāsati. Tadā rañño maṅgalaassanhānatitthe aññataraṃ vaḷavaṃ khaḷuṅkassaṃ nhāpesuṃ. Maṅgalasso vaḷavena nhānatitthaṃ otāriyamāno jigucchitvā otarituṃ na icchi. Assagopako gantvā rañño ārocesi “deva, maṅgalasso titthaṃ otarituṃ na icchatī”ti. Rājā bodhisattaṃ pesesi – “gaccha, paṇḍita, jānāhi kena kāraṇena asso titthaṃ otāriyamāno na otaratī”ti. Bodhisatto “sādhu, devā”ti nadītīraṃ gantvā assaṃ oloketvā nirogabhāvamassa ñatvā “kena nu kho kāraṇena ayaṃ imaṃ titthaṃ na otaratī”ti upadhārento “paṭhamataraṃ ettha añño nhāpito bhavissati, tenesa jigucchamāno titthaṃ na otarati maññe”ti cintetvā assagopake pucchi “ambho, imasmiṃ titthe kaṃ paṭhamaṃ nhāpayitthā”ti? “Aññataraṃ vaḷavassaṃ, sāmī”ti.
