In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta advised that king in matters temporal and spiritual. Now at that time, at the bathing ford of the king's state horse, they bathed a certain common mare. The state horse, Maṅgala, when being led down to the ford where the mare had been bathed, was disgusted and did not wish to enter. The horse groom went and informed the king, 'Your Majesty, the state horse Maṅgala does not wish to enter the ford.' The king sent the Bodhisatta, saying, 'Go, wise one, and find out for what reason the horse does not enter when being led to the ford.' The Bodhisatta replied, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' and went to the riverbank. Observing the horse and knowing it to be free from disease, he considered, 'For what reason does it not enter this ford?' Reflecting, he thought, 'Another must have been bathed here first; I imagine it is because it is disgusted that it does not enter.' He then asked the horse grooms, 'Sirs, whom did you bathe first in this ford?' 'A certain common mare, master,' they replied.

Bodhisatto “esa attano sindhavatāya jigucchanto ettha nhāyituṃ na icchati, imaṃ aññatitthe nhāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tassa āsayaṃ ñatvā “bho assagopaka, sappimadhuphāṇitādibhisaṅkhatapāyāsampi tāva punappunaṃ bhuñjantassa titti hoti. Ayaṃ asso bahū vāre idha titthe nhāto, aññampi tāva naṃ titthaṃ [P 1.0185] otāretvā nhāpetha ca pāyetha cā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, knowing the horse's disposition, thought, 'Being of the Sindhava breed, it is disgusted and does not wish to bathe here. It is proper to bathe it at another ford.' Then he said to the horse groom, 'Sir, even one who repeatedly eats rice-porridge prepared with ghee, honey, molasses, and so forth, becomes satiated. This horse has bathed at this ford many times. Now, lead it down to another ford, and let it bathe and drink.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

25.

25.

“Aññamaññehi titthehi, assaṃ pāyehi sārathi;

Accāsanassa puriso, pāyāsassapi tappatī”ti.

“At different fords, O charioteer, let the horse drink; a man, from overeating, grows weary even of rice-porridge.”

Tattha aññamaññehīti aññehi aññehi. Pāyehīti desanāsīsametaṃ, nhāpehi ca pāyehi cāti attho. Accāsanassāti karaṇatthe sāmivacanaṃ[M 1.0201], atiasanena atibhuttenāti attho. Pāyāsassapi tappatīti sappiādīhi abhisaṅkhatena madhurapāyāsena tappati titto hoti, dhāto suhito na puna bhuñjitukāmataṃ āpajjati. Tasmā ayampi asso imasmiṃ titthe nibaddhaṃ nhānena pariyattiṃ āpanno bhavissati, aññattha naṃ nhāpethāti.

Herein, 'with different fords' means with one ford after another. 'Let it drink' is a summary of the instruction; the meaning is 'let it bathe and let it drink.' 'Of overeating' is a genitive used in the sense of the instrumental, meaning 'by overeating' or 'by having eaten too much.' 'Grows weary even of rice-porridge' means one becomes satisfied and full from sweet rice-porridge prepared with ghee and so on; being nourished and well-satisfied, one no longer desires to eat. Therefore, this horse too, by constantly bathing at this ford, must have had enough; bathe it elsewhere.

Te tassa vacanaṃ sutvā assaṃ aññatitthaṃ otāretvā pāyiṃsu ceva nhāpayiṃsu ca. Bodhisatto [V 1.0185] assassa pānīyaṃ pivitvā nhānakāle rañño santikaṃ agamāsi. Rājā “kiṃ, tāta, asso nhāto ca pīto cā”ti pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Paṭhamaṃ kiṃ kāraṇā na icchatī”ti? “Iminā nāma kāraṇenā”ti sabbaṃ ācikkhi. Rājā “evarūpassa tiracchānassāpi nāma āsayaṃ jānāti, aho paṇḍito”ti bodhisattassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ datvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato. Bodhisattopi yathākammameva gato.

Hearing his words, they led the horse to another ford, and they let it drink and bathe. While the horse was drinking and bathing, the Bodhisatta went to the king. The king asked, 'Well, my dear sir, has the horse bathed and drunk?' 'Yes, Your Majesty.' 'For what reason did it not wish to at first?' 'For this and that reason,' he replied, and explained everything. The king said, 'He knows the disposition even of such an animal! Oh, what a wise man!' and he bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta. At the end of his life, the king passed away according to his kamma. The Bodhisatta also passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, ahaṃ etassa idāneva āsayaṃ jānāmi, pubbepi jānāmiyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā maṅgalaasso ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, rājā ānando, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that I know this monk's disposition; I knew it in the past as well.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he connected the narrative and identified the birth-story, saying: 'At that time, the state horse was this monk, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was none other than myself.'

Titthajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Tittha Jātaka, the fifth.

[26] 6. Mahiḷāmukhajātakavaṇṇanā

[26] 6. The Commentary on the Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka

Purāṇacorāna vaco nisammāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadatto ajātasattukumāraṃ pasādetvā lābhasakkāraṃ nipphādesi. Ajātasattukumāro devadattassa gayāsīse vihāraṃ kāretvā nānaggarasehi tivassikagandhasālibhojanassa [P 1.0186] divase divase pañca thālipākasatāni abhihari. Lābhasakkāraṃ nissāya devadattassa parivāro mahanto jāto, devadatto parivārena saddhiṃ vihāreyeva hoti. Tena samayena rājagahavāsikā dve sahāyā. Tesu eko satthu santike pabbajito, eko devadattassa. Te aññamaññaṃ tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhānepi passanti, vihāraṃ gantvāpi passantiyeva.

While dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, the Teacher told this story concerning Devadatta, which begins with the words, 'Having heard the words of ancient thieves...' Devadatta, having inspired faith in Prince Ajātasattu, brought about much gain and honor for himself. Prince Ajātasattu had a monastery built for Devadatta at Gayāsīsa and daily supplied five hundred pots of food, made from three-year-old fragrant Sāli rice with various choice flavors. On account of this gain and honor, Devadatta’s following became large, and he stayed in that monastery with his retinue. At that time, there were two friends living in Rājagaha. One of them went forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher, the other in the presence of Devadatta. They would see each other in various places, and they would also see each other when going to the monastery.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 1.0202] devadattassa nissitako itaraṃ āha – “āvuso, kiṃ tvaṃ devasikaṃ sedehi muccamānehi piṇḍāya carasi, devadatto gayāsīsavihāre nisīditvāva nānaggarasehi subhojanaṃ bhuñjati, evarūpo upāyo natthi, kiṃ tvaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhosi, kiṃ te pātova gayāsīsaṃ āgantvā sauttaribhaṅgaṃ yāguṃ pivitvā aṭṭhārasavidhaṃ khajjakaṃ khāditvā nānaggarasehi subhojanaṃ bhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti? So punappunaṃ vuccamāno gantukāmo hutvā tato paṭṭhāya gayāsīsaṃ gantvā bhuñjitvā kālasseva veḷuvanaṃ āgacchati. So sabbakālaṃ paṭicchādetuṃ nāsakkhi, “gayāsīsaṃ gantvā devadattassa paṭṭhapitaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjatī”ti na cirasseva pākaṭo jāto[V 1.0186]. Atha naṃ sahāyā pucchiṃsu “saccaṃ kira, tvaṃ āvuso, devadattassa paṭṭhapitaṃ bhattaṃ bhuñjasī”ti. “Ko evamāhā”ti? “Asuko ca asuko cā”ti. “Saccaṃ ahaṃ āvuso gayāsīsaṃ gantvā bhuñjāmi, na pana me devadatto bhattaṃ deti, aññe manussā dentī”ti. “Āvuso, devadatto buddhānaṃ paṭikaṇṭako dussīlo ajātasattuṃ pasādetvā adhammena attano lābhasakkāraṃ uppādesi, tvaṃ evarūpe niyyānike buddhasāsane pabbajitvā devadattassa adhammena uppannaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjasi, ehi taṃ satthu santikaṃ nessāmā”ti taṃ bhikkhuṃ ādāya dhammasabhaṃ āgamiṃsu.

One day, a follower of Devadatta said to another, “Friend, why do you wander for alms every day, drenched in sweat, while Devadatta sits in the Gayāsīsa monastery and enjoys fine food of various flavors? There is no need for such a method. Why do you endure hardship? Why should you not go to Gayāsīsa early in the morning, drink gruel with accompaniments, eat the eighteen kinds of delicacies, and enjoy fine food of various flavors?” Being repeatedly urged, he became inclined to go. From then on, he went to Gayāsīsa, ate there, and returned to Veḷuvana early. He could not conceal it for long, and it soon became known: “He goes to Gayāsīsa and eats the meal provided by Devadatta.” Then his companions asked him, “Is it true, friend, that you eat the meal provided by Devadatta?” “Who says so?” “So-and-so and so-and-so,” they replied. “It is true, friends. I go to Gayāsīsa and eat, but Devadatta does not give me the meal; other people give it,” he said. “Friend, Devadatta is an adversary of the Buddhas, an immoral person. Having won the confidence of Ajātasattu, he has unrighteously produced gain and honor for himself. You, having gone forth in this salvific dispensation of the Buddha, eat food unrighteously obtained by Devadatta. Come, we will take you to the Teacher.” Taking that monk, they went to the Hall of Truth.

Satthā disvāva “kiṃ, bhikkhave, etaṃ bhikkhuṃ anicchantaññeva ādāya āgatatthā”ti? “Āma bhante, ayaṃ bhikkhu tumhākaṃ santike pabbajitvā devadattassa adhammena uppannaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjatī”ti. “Saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu devadattassa adhammena uppannaṃ bhojanaṃ bhuñjasī”ti? “Na bhante, devadatto mayhaṃ deti, aññe manussā denti, tamahaṃ bhuñjāmī”ti. Satthā “mā bhikkhu ettha parihāraṃ kari, devadatto anācāro dussīlo, kathañhi nāma tvaṃ idha pabbajitvā mama sāsanaṃ bhajantoyeva devadattassa bhattaṃ bhuñjasi, niccakālampi bhajanasīlakova tvaṃ diṭṭhadiṭṭheyeva bhajasī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Upon seeing them, the Teacher asked, “Monks, why have you brought this monk here against his will?” “Yes, Venerable Sir. This monk, having gone forth in your presence, eats food unrighteously obtained by Devadatta.” The Teacher asked, “Monk, is it true that you eat food unrighteously obtained by Devadatta?” “Venerable Sir, Devadatta does not give it to me; other people give it, and that is what I eat.” The Teacher said, “Monk, make no excuses here. Devadatta is of bad conduct and immoral. How is it that you, having gone forth here and entered my dispensation, eat Devadatta’s food? You have always been one to associate with whomever you happen to see.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa amacco ahosi. Tadā rañño mahiḷāmukho nāma [P 1.0187] maṅgalahatthī ahosi sīlavā ācārasampanno, na kañci viheṭheti. Athekadivasaṃ tassa sālāya samīpe rattibhāgasamanantare corā āgantvā tassa avidūre [M 1.0203] nisinnā coramantaṃ mantayiṃsu “evaṃ ummaṅgo bhinditabbo, evaṃ sandhicchedakammaṃ kattabbaṃ, ummaṅgañca sandhicchedañca maggasadisaṃ titthasadisaṃ nijjaṭaṃ niggumbaṃ katvā bhaṇḍaṃ harituṃ vaṭṭati, harantena māretvāva haritabbaṃ, evaṃ uṭṭhātuṃ samattho nāma na bhavissati, corena ca nāma sīlācārayuttena na bhavitabbaṃ, kakkhaḷena pharusena sāhasikena bhavitabba”nti. Evaṃ mantetvā aññamaññaṃ uggaṇhāpetvā agamaṃsu. Eteneva upāyena punadivasepi punadivasepīti bahū divase tattha āgantvā mantayiṃsu. So tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “te maṃ sikkhāpentī”ti saññāya “idāni mayā kakkhaḷena pharusena sāhasikena bhavitabba”nti tathārūpova ahosi. Pātova āgataṃ hatthigopakaṃ soṇḍāya gahetvā bhūmiyaṃ pothetvā māresi. Aparampi tathā aparampi tathāti āgatāgataṃ māretiyeva.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister. At that time, the king had a state elephant named Mahiḷāmukha, who was virtuous and of good conduct, harming no one. Then one day, during the night, thieves came near its stable and, sitting not far from it, plotted their theft: “This is how a tunnel should be dug; this is how a wall should be breached. Having made the tunnel and the breach like a road or a ford, clear of thickets and undergrowth, one may carry away the goods. One who steals should do so only after killing; in that way, no one will be able to rise up in opposition. A thief should not be endowed with virtue and good conduct; he must be harsh, cruel, and violent.” Having plotted thus and instructed one another, they departed. In this same way they came and plotted for many days. Hearing their words, the elephant formed the perception, “They are instructing me,” and concluded, “Now I must become harsh, cruel, and violent.” And he became just so. Early in the morning, he seized the approaching elephant keeper with his trunk, dashed him to the ground, and killed him. He did the same to the next one, and the one after that, killing each one who came.

“Mahiḷāmukho [V 1.0187] ummattako jāto diṭṭhadiṭṭhe māretī”ti rañño ārocayiṃsu. Rājā bodhisattaṃ pahiṇi “gaccha paṇḍita, jānāhi kena kāraṇena so duṭṭho jāto”ti. Bodhisatto gantvā tassa sarīre arogabhāvaṃ ñatvā “kena nu kho kāraṇena esa duṭṭho jāto”ti upadhārento “addhā avidūre kesañci vacanaṃ sutvā ‘maṃ ete sikkhāpentī’ti saññāya duṭṭho jāto”ti sanniṭṭhānaṃ katvā hatthigopake pucchi “atthi nu kho hatthisālāya samīpe rattibhāge kehici kiñci kathitapubba”nti? “Āma, sāmi, corā āgantvā kathayiṃsū”ti. Bodhisatto gantvā rañño ārocesi “deva, añño hatthissa sarīre vikāro natthi, corānaṃ kathaṃ sutvā duṭṭho jāto”ti. “Idāni kiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Sīlavante samaṇabrāhmaṇe hatthisālāyaṃ nisīdāpetvā sīlācārakathaṃ kathāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Evaṃ kārehi, tātā”ti.

“Mahiḷāmukha has gone mad; he kills everyone he sees,” they reported to the king. The king dispatched the Bodhisatta, saying, “Go, wise one, and find out for what reason he has become vicious.” The Bodhisatta went and, seeing that the elephant’s body was free from disease, he considered, “For what reason could he have become vicious?” He came to the conclusion: “Surely, he has become vicious after hearing the words of someone nearby, perceiving, ‘They are instructing me.’” He then asked the elephant keepers, “Has anything ever been spoken by anyone near the elephant stable at night?” “Yes, my lord, thieves came and spoke here.” The Bodhisatta went and reported to the king, “Your Majesty, there is no physical ailment in the elephant; he became vicious after hearing the talk of thieves.” “What should be done now?” asked the king. “It would be proper to have virtuous ascetics and brahmins sit in the elephant stable and discourse on virtue and good conduct.” “Then do so, my dear,” said the king.

Bodhisatto gantvā sīlavante samaṇabrāhmaṇe hatthisālāyaṃ nisīdāpetvā “sīlakathaṃ [P 1.0188] kathetha, bhante”ti āha. Te hatthissa avidūre nisinnā “na koci parāmasitabbo na māretabbo, sīlācārasampannena khantimettānuddayayuttena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti sīlakathaṃ kathayiṃsu. So taṃ sutvā “maṃ ime sikkhāpenti, ito dāni paṭṭhāya sīlavantena bhavitabba”nti sīlavā ahosi. Rājā bodhisattaṃ pucchi “kiṃ, tāta, sīlavā jāto”ti[M 1.0204]? Bodhisatto “āma, devā”ti. “Evarūpo duṭṭhahatthī paṇḍite nissāya porāṇakadhammeyeva patiṭṭhito”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta went and seated virtuous ascetics and brahmins in the elephant stable, saying, "Venerable sirs, speak on virtue." Seated not far from the elephant, they spoke on virtue, saying, "No one should be assaulted, no one should be killed; one should be endowed with virtuous conduct, patience, loving-kindness, and compassion." Hearing this, the elephant thought, "These are teaching me; from now on I must be virtuous," and he became virtuous. The king asked the Bodhisatta, "My dear, has he become virtuous?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Yes, Your Majesty." Intending to say, "Such a vicious elephant, by relying on the wise, has become established in its former good nature," he spoke this verse:

26.

26.

“Purāṇacorāna vaco nisamma, mahiḷāmukho pothayamanvacārī;

Susaññatānañhi vaco nisamma, gajuttamo sabbaguṇesu aṭṭhā”ti.

"Having heard the words of the former thieves, Mahiḷāmukha went about striking others; But having heard the words of the well-restrained, The supreme elephant was established in all virtues."

Tattha purāṇacorānanti porāṇacorānaṃ. Nisammāti sutvā, paṭhamaṃ corānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvāti attho. Mahiḷāmukhoti hatthinimukhena sadisamukho. Yathā mahiḷā purato olokiyamānā sobhati, na pacchato, tathā sopi purato olokiyamāno sobhati. Tasmā “mahiḷāmukho”tissa nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Pothayamanvacārīti pothayanto mārento anucārī. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Susaññatānanti suṭṭhu saññatānaṃ sīlavantānaṃ. Gajuttamoti uttamagajo maṅgalahatthī. Sabbaguṇesu aṭṭhāti sabbesu porāṇaguṇesu patiṭṭhito. Rājā “tiracchānagatassāpi āsayaṃ jānātī”ti bodhisattassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi. So yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā saddhiṃ bodhisattena yathākammaṃ gato.

Here, purāṇacorāna means 'of the former thieves'. Nisamma means 'having heard'; the meaning is 'having first heard the words of the thieves'. Mahiḷāmukha means 'one with a face like a female elephant'. Just as a woman is beautiful when looked at from the front, but not from behind, so too was he beautiful when looked at from the front. Therefore, they gave him the name 'Mahiḷāmukha'. Pothayamanvacārī means 'striking and killing, he went about'. Or this is the reading. Susaññatānaṃ means 'of the well-restrained, the virtuous'. Gajuttamo means 'the supreme elephant', the state elephant. Sabbaguṇesu aṭṭhā means 'he was established in all his former virtues'. The king, thinking, "He knows the disposition even of an animal," bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta. He remained for his lifespan and, together with the Bodhisatta, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 1.0188] “pubbepi tvaṃ bhikkhu diṭṭhadiṭṭheyeva bhaji, corānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā core bhaji, dhammikānaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā dhammike bhajī”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mahiḷāmukho vipakkhasevakabhikkhu ahosi, rājā ānando, amacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Monk, in the past, too, you associated with whomever you saw. Having heard the words of thieves, you associated with thieves; having heard the words of the righteous, you associated with the righteous." Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and made the connection, he identified the characters of the Jātaka: "At that time, the monk who associates with bad company was Mahiḷāmukha, the king was Ānanda, and the minister was myself."

Mahiḷāmukhajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka, the Sixth.

[27] 7. Abhiṇhajātakavaṇṇanā

[27] 7. The Commentary on the Abhiṇha Jātaka

Nālaṃ [M 1.0205] kabaḷaṃ padātaveti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ upāsakañca mahallakattherañca ārabbha kathesi[P 1.0189]. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira dve sahāyakā. Tesu eko pabbajitvā devasikaṃ itarassa gharaṃ gacchati. So tassa bhikkhaṃ datvā sayampi bhuñjitvā teneva saddhiṃ vihāraṃ gantvā yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā ālāpasallāpena nisīditvā nagaraṃ pavisati, itaropi naṃ yāva nagaradvārā anugantvā nivattati. So tesaṃ vissāso bhikkhūnaṃ antare pākaṭo jāto. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū tesaṃ vissāsakathaṃ kathentā dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchi, te “imāya nāma, bhante”ti kathayiṃsu. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva ime vissāsikā, pubbepi vissāsikāyeva ahesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"He is not able to take a mouthful..." This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain lay follower and an elderly Thera. In Sāvatthī, it is said, there were two friends. One of them went forth as a monk and would daily go to the house of the other. The lay follower would give him alms-food, and after eating himself, would go with the monk to the monastery. There he would sit in conversation until sunset, and then enter the city. The monk, in turn, would accompany him as far as the city gate before returning. Their great attachment became well-known among the monks. Then one day, as the monks were sitting in the Hall of Dhamma discussing this attachment, the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" They replied, "Venerable sir, for this very one." The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that these two are so attached; they were attached in the past as well," and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa amacco ahosi. Tadā eko kukkuro maṅgalahatthisālaṃ gantvā maṅgalahatthissa bhuñjanaṭṭhāne patitāni bhattasitthāni khādati. So teneva bhojanena saṃvaddhamāno maṅgalahatthissa vissāsiko jāto hatthisseva santike bhuñjati, ubhopi vinā vattituṃ na sakkonti. So hatthī naṃ soṇḍāya gahetvā aparāparaṃ karonto kīḷati, ukkhipitvā kumbhe patiṭṭhāpeti. Athekadivasaṃ eko gāmikamanusso hatthigopakassa mūlaṃ datvā taṃ kukkuraṃ ādāya attano gāmaṃ agamāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya so hatthī kukkuraṃ apassanto neva khādati na pivati na nhāyati. Tamatthaṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā bodhisattaṃ pahiṇi “gaccha paṇḍita, jānāhi kiṃkāraṇā hatthī evaṃ karotī”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister. At that time, a certain dog went to the state elephant's stable and ate the morsels of rice that had fallen in the state elephant's feeding place. Being nourished by that food, he became attached to the state elephant and would eat right beside the elephant; neither could bear to be without the other. The elephant would take the dog with its trunk and play, tossing it back and forth, and would lift it up and place it on its frontal globes. Then one day, a certain villager, having paid the elephant keeper, took the dog and went to his own village. From then on, the elephant, not seeing the dog, would neither eat, nor drink, nor bathe. They reported this matter to the king. The king sent the Bodhisatta, saying, "Go, wise one, and find out for what reason the elephant is acting thus."

Bodhisatto [V 1.0189] hatthisālaṃ gantvā hatthissa dummanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “imassa sarīre rogo na paññāyati, kenaci panassa saddhiṃ mittasanthavena bhavitabbaṃ, taṃ apassanto esa maññe sokābhibhūto”ti hatthigopake pucchi “atthi nu kho imassa kenaci saddhiṃ vissāso”ti? “Āma, atthi sāmi ekena sunakhena saddhiṃ balavā mettī”ti. “Kahaṃ so etarahī”ti? “Ekena manussena nīto”ti. “Jānātha panassa nivāsanaṭṭhāna”nti? “Na jānāma, sāmī”ti. Bodhisatto rañño santikaṃ gantvā “natthi, deva, hatthissa koci ābādho[M 1.0206], ekena panassa sunakhena saddhiṃ balavavissāso[P 1.0190], taṃ apassanto na bhuñjati maññe”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta went to the elephant stable and, perceiving the elephant's dejection, thought, "No disease is apparent in its body, but it must have formed a friendship with some creature. Not seeing that creature, I believe it is overcome by sorrow." He asked the elephant keepers, "Does this elephant have a close attachment to anyone?" "Yes, lord, it has a strong bond of affection with a certain dog." "Where is he now?" "He was taken by a certain man." "Do you know where that man lives?" "We do not know, lord." The Bodhisatta went to the king and said, "Your Majesty, the elephant has no ailment, but it has a strong attachment to a certain dog. I believe that it does not eat because it cannot see him." Having said this, he spoke this verse:

27.

27.

“Nālaṃ kabaḷaṃ padātave, na ca piṇḍaṃ na kuse na ghaṃsituṃ;

Maññāmi abhiṇhadassanā, nāgo snehamakāsi kukkure”ti.

"He is not able to take a mouthful, nor a morsel, nor grass, nor to eat; I think from constant sight, the great elephant has formed an affection for the dog."

Tattha nālanti na samattho. Kabaḷanti bhojanakāle paṭhamameva dinnaṃ kaṭukakabaḷaṃ. Padātaveti paādātave, sandhivasena ākāralopo veditabbo, gahetunti attho. Na ca piṇḍanti vaḍḍhetvā dīyamānaṃ bhattapiṇḍampi nālaṃ gahetuṃ. Na kuseti khādanatthāya dinnāni tiṇānipi nālaṃ gahetuṃ. Na ghaṃsitunti nhāpiyamāno sarīrampi ghaṃsituṃ nālaṃ. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ so hatthī kātuṃ na samattho, taṃ taṃ sabbaṃ rañño ārocetvā tassa asamatthabhāve attanā sallakkhitakāraṇaṃ ārocento “maññāmī”tiādimāha.

Herein, 'nālaṃ' means 'is not capable.' 'Kabaḷa' refers to the morsel given first at mealtime. 'Padātaveti' is for 'ādātave' (to take); the elision of the vowel 'ā' is to be understood as due to sandhi. It is unable to take even a ball of rice that is being served. It is unable to take even the grass given to eat. It is unable to endure its body being rubbed while being bathed. Thus, after reporting to the king all that the elephant was unable to do, the Bodhisatta, explaining the reason for its incapacity which he himself had perceived, said, 'I think,' and so on.

Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “idāni kiṃ kātabbaṃ paṇḍitā”ti pucchi. “‘Amhākaṃ kira maṅgalahatthissa sahāyaṃ sunakhaṃ eko manusso gahetvā gato, yassa ghare taṃ sunakhaṃ passanti, tassa ayaṃ nāma daṇḍo’ti bheriṃ carāpetha devā”ti. Rājā tathā kāresi. Taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā so puriso sunakhaṃ vissajjesi, sunakho vegenāgantvā hatthissa santikameva agamāsi. Hatthī taṃ soṇḍāya gahetvā kumbhe ṭhapetvā roditvā paridevitvā kumbhā otāretvā tena bhutte pacchā attanāpi bhuñji. “Tiracchānagatassa āsayaṃ jānātī”ti rājā bodhisattassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi.

Hearing his words, the king asked, 'What should be done now, wise one?' 'Have it announced by drum, Your Majesty: "It is said a certain man has taken the companion dog of our auspicious elephant. For any man in whose house the dog is found, this shall be his punishment."' The king did so. Hearing this news, that man released the dog. The dog ran swiftly and went straight to the elephant. The elephant took it with its trunk, placed it on its head, wept and lamented, then lowered it. After the dog had eaten, the elephant ate as well. Thinking, 'He knows the disposition of an animal,' the king bestowed great honor upon the Bodhisatta.

Satthā [V 1.0190] “na, bhikkhave, ime idāneva vissāsikā, pubbepi vissāsikāyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā catusaccakathāya vinivaṭṭetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. Idaṃ catusaccakathāya vinivaṭṭanaṃ nāma sabbajātakesupi atthiyeva. Mayaṃ pana yatthassa ānisaṃso paññāyati[M 1.0207], tattheva dassayissāma.

The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that these two are intimate; they were intimate in the past as well.' Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he concluded it with a discourse on the Four Noble Truths, connected the sequence, and identified the Jataka. This concluding with a discourse on the Four Noble Truths is present in all Jatakas, but we shall show it only where its benefit is apparent.

Tadā sunakho upāsako ahosi, hatthī mahallakatthero, rājā ānando, amaccapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the dog was the lay follower, the elephant was the elder monk, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was indeed myself.

Abhiṇhajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Explanation of the Abhiṇha Jātaka, the Seventh.

[28] 8. Nandivisālajātakavaṇṇanā

8. The Explanation of the Nandivisāla Jātaka

Manuññameva [P 1.0191] bhāseyyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto chabbaggiyānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ omasavādaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi samaye chabbaggiyā kalahaṃ karontā pesale bhikkhū khuṃsenti vambhenti ovijjhanti, dasahi akkosavatthūhi akkosanti. Bhikkhū bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā chabbaggiye pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira bhikkhavo”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte vigarahitvā “bhikkhave, pharusavācā nāma tiracchānagatānampi amanāpā, pubbepi eko tiracchānagato attānaṃ pharusena samudācarantaṃ sahassaṃ parājesī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'One should speak pleasantly...' — this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the abusive speech of the group-of-six monks. At that time, the group-of-six monks, being quarrelsome, harassed, insulted, and belittled the well-behaved monks, reviling them with the ten grounds for abuse. The monks reported this to the Blessed One. The Blessed One summoned the group-of-six monks and asked, 'Is it true, monks?' When they admitted it was true, he rebuked them, saying, 'Monks, harsh speech is displeasing even to animals. In the past, an animal caused the one who treated it harshly to lose a thousand.' Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilāyaṃ gandhārarājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto goyoniyaṃ nibbatti. Atha naṃ taruṇavacchakakāleyeva eko brāhmaṇo godakkhiṇādāyakānaṃ santikā labhitvā “nandivisālo”ti nāmaṃ katvā puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā sampiyāyamāno yāgubhattādīni datvā posesi. Bodhisatto vayappatto cintesi “ahaṃ iminā brāhmaṇena kicchena paṭijaggito, mayā ca saddhiṃ sakalajambudīpe añño samadhuro goṇo nāma natthi, yaṃnūnāhaṃ attano balaṃ dassetvā brāhmaṇassa posāvaniyaṃ dadeyya”nti so ekadivasaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ āha “gaccha, brāhmaṇa, ekaṃ govittakaseṭṭhiṃ upasaṅkamitvā ‘mayhaṃ balibaddo atibaddhaṃ sakaṭasataṃ pavaṭṭetī’ti vatvā sahassena abbhutaṃ karohī”ti. So brāhmaṇo seṭṭhissa santikaṃ gantvā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi “imasmiṃ nagare kassa goṇo thāmasampanno”ti. Atha naṃ seṭṭhi “asukassa ca asukassa cā”ti vatvā “sakalanagare pana amhākaṃ goṇehi sadiso nāma natthī”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo [V 1.0191] “mayhaṃ eko [M 1.0208] goṇo atibaddhaṃ sakaṭasataṃ pavaṭṭetuṃ samattho atthī”ti āha. Seṭṭhi gahapati “kuto evarūpo goṇo”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo “mayhaṃ gehe atthī”ti. “Tena hi abbhutaṃ karohī”ti. “Sādhu karomī”ti sahassena abbhutaṃ [P 1.0192] akāsi.

In the past, in the Gandhāra kingdom, at Takkasilā, the king of Gandhāra reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born as an ox. Then, while he was still a young calf, a certain brahmin obtained him from those who give cows as a religious gift and, naming him 'Nandivisāla,' kept him in the place of a son, treating him with affection and nourishing him with rice gruel and other foods. When the Bodhisatta came of age, he thought, 'This brahmin has taken great pains to look after me, and there is no other bull in all of Jambudīpa as strong as I am. I should demonstrate my strength and give the brahmin payment for my upkeep.' One day, he said to the brahmin, 'Go, brahmin, approach a certain wealthy cattle merchant and say, "My bull can pull a hundred carts that are tightly bound together," and make a wager for a thousand.' The brahmin went to the merchant and initiated a conversation: 'In this city, whose bull is the most powerful?' The merchant replied, 'So-and-so’s and so-and-so’s,' adding, 'But in the entire city, there is none equal to our bulls.' The brahmin said, 'I have a bull who is able to pull a hundred carts that are tightly bound together.' The merchant asked, 'Where is such a bull?' The brahmin replied, 'He is at my house.' 'Then make the wager!' said the merchant. 'Very well, I will,' said the brahmin, and he made the wager for a thousand.

So sakaṭasataṃ vālukāsakkharapāsāṇānaṃyeva pūretvā paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapetvā sabbāni akkhabandhanayottena ekato bandhitvā nandivisālaṃ nhāpetvā gandhapañcaṅgulikaṃ katvā kaṇṭhe mālaṃ piḷandhitvā purimasakaṭadhure ekakameva yojetvā sayaṃ dhure nisīditvā patodaṃ ukkhipitvā “gaccha kūṭa, vahassu kūṭā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “ayaṃ maṃ akūṭaṃ kūṭavādena samudācaratī”ti cattāro pāde thambhe viya niccale katvā aṭṭhāsi. Seṭṭhi taṅkhaṇaññeva brāhmaṇaṃ sahassaṃ āharāpesi. Brāhmaṇo sahassaparājito goṇaṃ muñcitvā gharaṃ gantvā sokābhibhūto nipajji. Nandivisālo caritvā āgato brāhmaṇaṃ sokābhibhūtaṃ disvā upasaṅkamitvā “kiṃ, brāhmaṇa, niddāyasī”ti āha. “Kuto me, niddā, sahassaparājitassāti, brāhmaṇa, mayā ettakaṃ kālaṃ tava gehe vasantena atthi kiñci bhājanaṃ vā bhinditapubbaṃ, koci vā madditapubbo, aṭṭhāne vā pana uccārapassāvo katapubbo”ti? “Natthi tātā”ti. Atha tvaṃ maṃ kasmā kūṭavādena samudācarasi, taveveso doso, mayhaṃ doso natthi, gaccha, tena saddhiṃ dvīhi sahassehi abbhutaṃ karohi, kevalaṃ maṃ akūṭaṃ kūṭavādena mā samudācarasīti.

He filled a hundred carts with only sand, gravel, and stones, arranged them in a row, tied them all together with an axle-rope, bathed Nandivisāla, made a five-fingered mark of perfume upon him, placed a garland around his neck, yoked him alone to the foremost cart, sat himself on the pole, raised his goad, and said, 'Go, you rogue! Pull, you rogue!' The Bodhisatta thought, 'This man addresses me, who am no rogue, with the word "rogue."' So he made his four feet as immovable as pillars and stood still. The merchant immediately made the brahmin pay the thousand. The brahmin, having lost the thousand, unyoked the bull and went home, where he lay down, overcome with sorrow. Nandivisāla, having returned from grazing, saw the brahmin overcome with sorrow, approached him, and asked, 'Why, brahmin, are you sleeping?' 'How can I sleep, having lost a thousand?' 'Brahmin, in all the time I have lived in your house, have I ever broken any pot, or trampled upon anything, or passed excrement or urine in an improper place?' 'No, my dear.' 'Then why do you address me with the word "rogue"? This is your fault alone; there is no fault in me. Go, make a wager for two thousand with him, but do not address me, who am no rogue, with the word "rogue."'

Brāhmaṇo tassa vacanaṃ sutvā gantvā dvīhi sahassehi abbhutaṃ katvā purimanayeneva sakaṭasataṃ atibandhitvā nandivisālaṃ maṇḍetvā purimasakaṭadhure yojesi. Kathaṃ yojesīti? Yugaṃ dhure niccalaṃ bandhitvā ekāya koṭiyā nandivisālaṃ yojetvā ekaṃ koṭiṃ dhurayottena paliveṭhetvā yugakoṭiñca akkhapādañca nissāya muṇḍarukkhadaṇḍakaṃ datvā tena yottena niccalaṃ bandhitvā ṭhapesi. Evañhi kate yugaṃ etto vā ito vā na gacchati, sakkā hoti ekeneva goṇena ākaḍḍhituṃ. Athassa brāhmaṇo dhure nisīditvā nandivisālassa piṭṭhiṃ parimajjitvā “gaccha bhadra, vahassu, bhandrā”ti āha. Bodhisatto atibaddhaṃ sakaṭasataṃ ekavegeneva ākaḍḍhitvā pacchā ṭhitaṃ sakaṭaṃ purato ṭhitassa sakaṭassa [P 1.0193] ṭhāne ṭhapesi[M 1.0209]. Govittakaseṭṭhi parājito brāhmaṇassa dve sahassāni adāsi. Aññepi manussā bodhisattassa bahuṃ dhanaṃ adaṃsu, sabbaṃ brāhmaṇasseva ahosi. Evaṃ so bodhisattaṃ nissāya bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhi.

Hearing his words, the brahmin went and made a wager for two thousand, and in the same manner as before, he bound the hundred carts very tightly, adorned Nandivisāla, and yoked him to the pole of the foremost cart. How did he yoke him? He fastened the yoke firmly to the pole, attached Nandivisāla to one end, wrapped the other end with the pole-rope, and placing a short wooden prop against the yoke-end and the axle-base, he bound it immovably with that rope. When this was done, the yoke could not move from side to side, and it was possible for a single bull to pull it. Then the brahmin, sitting on the pole, stroked Nandivisāla’s back and said, 'Go, my good fellow! Pull, my good fellow!' With a single pull, the Bodhisatta dragged the hundred tightly bound carts, placing the last cart in the spot where the first cart had stood. The merchant Govittaka, being defeated, gave the brahmin two thousand. Other people also gave much wealth to the Bodhisatta, and all of it went to the brahmin. Thus, on account of the Bodhisatta, he obtained great wealth.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, pharusavacanaṃ nāma kassaci manāpa”nti chabbaggiye bhikkhū garahitvā sikkhāpadaṃ paññapetvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, saying, 'Monks, harsh speech is pleasing to no one,' rebuked the group-of-six monks, laid down a training rule, and, as the Fully Awakened One, spoke this verse:

28.

28.

“Manuññameva [V 1.0192] bhāseyya, nāmanuññaṃ kudācanaṃ;

Manuññaṃ bhāsamānassa, garuṃ bhāraṃ udaddhari;

Dhanañca naṃ alābhesi, tena cattamano ahū”ti.

'One should speak only what is pleasing, never what is displeasing. For the one who spoke pleasingly, he (the bull) lifted the heavy burden. And he caused him to obtain wealth, and because of that, he was gladdened.'

Tattha manuññameva bhāseyyāti parena saddhiṃ bhāsamāno catudosavirahitaṃ madhuraṃ manāpaṃ saṇhaṃ mudukaṃ piyavacanameva bhāseyya. Garuṃ bhāraṃ udaddharīti nandivisālo balibaddo amanāpaṃ bhāsamānassa bhāraṃ anuddharitvā pacchā manāpaṃ piyavacanaṃ bhāsamānassa brāhmaṇassa garuṃ bhāraṃ uddhari, uddharitvā kaḍḍhitvā pavaṭṭesīti attho, da-kāro panettha byañjanasandhivasena padasandhikaro.

Herein, 'one should speak only what is pleasing' means that when speaking with another, one should speak only words that are sweet, agreeable, gentle, soft, and endearing. 'He lifted the heavy burden' means that Nandivisāla, the strong bull, did not lift the burden for the one who spoke unpleasantly, but later, for the brahmin who spoke agreeable and endearing words, he lifted the heavy burden. The meaning is that having lifted it and pulled it, he set it in motion. The letter 'd' here is a word-joiner by means of consonant sandhi.

Iti satthā “manuññameva bhāseyyā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo ānando ahosi, nandivisālo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse beginning with 'One should speak only what is pleasing,' made the connection to the Jātaka: 'At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, and Nandivisāla was I myself.'

Nandivisālajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Eighth: The Commentary on the Nandivisāla Jātaka.

[29] 9. Kaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā

[29] 9. The Commentary on the Kaṇha Jātaka

Yato yato garu dhuranti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ saddhiṃ devorohaṇena terasakanipāte sarabhamigajātake (jā. 1.13.134 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Sammāsambuddhe pana yamakapāṭihāriyaṃ katvā devaloke temāsaṃ vasitvā mahāpavāraṇāya saṅkassanagaradvāre oruyha mahantena parivārena jetavanaṃ paviṭṭhe bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitvā “āvuso, tathāgato nāma asamadhuro, tathāgatena vuḷhadhuraṃ añño vahituṃ samattho nāma natthi, cha satthāro ‘mayameva [M 1.0210] pāṭihāriyaṃ karissāma, mayameva pāṭihāriyaṃ karissāmā’ti vatvā ekampi pāṭihāriyaṃ na akaṃsu, aho satthā asamadhuro”ti satthu guṇakathaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti [P 1.0194] pucchi. “Mayaṃ, bhante, na aññāya kathāya, evarūpāya nāma tumhākameva guṇakathāyā”ti. Satthā “bhikkhave, idāni mayā vuḷhadhuraṃ ko vahissati, pubbe tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattopi ahaṃ attanā samadhuraṃ kañci nālattha”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this Jātaka beginning 'Wherever the yoke is heavy,' with reference to the Twin Miracle. That miracle, along with the descent from the deva-world, will be made clear in the thirteenth book, in the Sarabhamiga Jātaka. Now, when the Perfectly Enlightened One, having performed the Twin Miracle, dwelt in the deva-world for three months, descended at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa on the day of the Great Pavāraṇā, and entered Jetavana with a great retinue, the monks gathered in the Hall of Dhamma. They sat praising the Teacher's virtues, saying: 'Sirs, the Tathāgata is indeed unequalled in shouldering burdens. There is no one else capable of bearing the burden borne by the Tathāgata. The six teachers, though they said, "We shall perform a miracle, we shall perform a miracle," could not perform a single one. Ah, the Teacher is unequalled in shouldering burdens!' The Teacher approached and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?' 'Venerable Sir, not for any other discussion, but for one of this very kind: a discussion of your virtues.' The Teacher said, 'Monks, who now can bear the burden borne by me? In the past, even when born in the animal realm, I could not find anyone equal to myself in shouldering a burden.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0193] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto goyoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Atha naṃ sāmikā taruṇavacchakakāleyeva ekissā mahallikāya ghare vasitvā tassā nivāsavetanato paricchinditvā adaṃsu. Sā taṃ yāgubhattādīhi paṭijaggamānā puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā vaḍḍhesi. So “ayyikākāḷako” tveva nāmaṃ paññāyittha. Vayappatto ca añjanavaṇṇo hutvā gāmagoṇehi saddhiṃ carati, sīlācārasampanno ahosi. Gāmadārakā siṅgesupi kaṇṇesupi galepi gahetvā olambanti, naṅguṭṭhepi gahetvā kīḷanti, piṭṭhiyampi nisīdanti. So ekadivasaṃ cintesi “mayhaṃ mātā duggatā, maṃ puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā dukkhena posesi, yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhatiṃ katvā imaṃ duggatabhāvato moceyya”nti. So tato paṭṭhāya bhatiṃ upadhārento carati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as an ox. Then his owners, while he was still a young calf, gave him to an old woman, assigning him as payment for her lodging. She nurtured him with rice porridge and other foods, raising him as her own son. He became known by the name 'Grandmother’s Blackie.' When he grew up, he was the color of antimony and grazed with the village cattle; he was virtuous and well-behaved. The village children would hang from his horns, ears, and neck; they would play by holding onto his tail and would also sit on his back. One day, he thought, 'My mother is poor. She raised me with hardship, treating me as her own son. I should work for wages and free her from this poverty.' From that day onward, he went about seeking work for hire.

Athekadivasaṃ eko satthavāhaputto pañcahi sakaṭasatehi visamatitthaṃ sampatto, tassa goṇā sakaṭāni uttāretuṃ na sakkonti, pañcasu sakaṭasatesu goṇā yugaparamparāya yojitā ekampi sakaṭaṃ uttāretuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Bodhisattopi gāmagoṇehi saddhiṃ tattha samīpe carati. Satthavāhaputtopi gosuttavittako, so “atthi nu kho etesaṃ gunnaṃ antare imāni sakaṭāni uttāretuṃ samattho usabhājānīyo”ti upadhārayamāno bodhisattaṃ disvā “ayaṃ ājānīyo sakkhissati mayhaṃ sakaṭāni uttāretuṃ, ko nu kho assa sāmiko”ti gopālake pucchi “ko nu kho bho imassa sāmiko, ahaṃ imaṃ sakaṭe yojetvā sakaṭesu uttāritesu vetanaṃ dassāmī”ti. Te āhaṃsu “gahetvā naṃ yojetha, natthi imassa imasmiṃ ṭhāne sāmiko”ti. So naṃ nāsāya rajjukena bandhitvā [P 1.0195] ākaḍḍhento cāletumpi nāsakkhi. Bodhisatto kira “bhatiyā kathitāya [M 1.0211] gamissāmī”ti na agamāsi. Satthavāhaputto tassādhippāyaṃ ñatvā “sāmi, tayā pañcasu sakaṭasatesu uttāritesu ekekassa sakaṭassa dve dve kahāpaṇe bhatiṃ katvā sahassaṃ dassāmī”ti āha. Tadā bodhisatto sayameva agamāsi. Atha naṃ purisā purimasakaṭesu yojesuṃ. Atha naṃ ekavegeneva ukkhipitvā thale patiṭṭhāpesi. Etenupāyena sabbasakaṭāni uttāresi.

One day, the son of a caravan leader arrived at a difficult ford with five hundred carts. His oxen were unable to pull the carts across. Even when the oxen from all five hundred carts were yoked in succession, they could not pull even a single cart across. The Bodhisatta was grazing nearby with the village cattle. The caravan leader's son was an expert in the lore of oxen. He looked among the cattle, thinking, 'Is there a thoroughbred bull among these oxen capable of pulling these carts across?' Seeing the Bodhisatta, he thought, 'This thoroughbred will be able to pull my carts across. Who might be his owner?' He asked the cowherds, 'Sirs, who is the owner of this one? I will yoke him to the carts, and when the carts are pulled across, I will give a wage.' They replied, 'Take him and yoke him. He has no owner in this place.' The man tied a rope through the ox's nose and tried to pull him, but could not even make him budge. The Bodhisatta, it seems, resolved, 'I will go only when the wage has been stated,' and so he did not go. The caravan leader's son, understanding his intention, said, 'Sir, when you have pulled the five hundred carts across, I will give you a wage of two kahāpaṇas for each cart, a thousand in total.' Then the Bodhisatta went of his own accord. The men yoked him to the first of the carts. Then, with a single effort, he pulled it up and set it on dry land. In this way, he pulled all the carts across.

Satthavāhaputto ekekassa sakaṭassa ekekaṃ katvā pañcasatāni bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā tassa gale bandhi. So “ayaṃ mayhaṃ yathāparicchinnaṃ bhatiṃ na deti, na dānissa gantuṃ dassāmī”ti gantvā sabbapurimasakaṭassa purato maggaṃ nivāretvā aṭṭhāsi. Apanetuṃ vāyamantāpi naṃ apanetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Satthavāhaputto “jānāti maññe esa attano bhatiyā ūnabhāva”nti ekekasmiṃ sakaṭe dve dve katvā sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ bandhitvā “ayaṃ te sakaṭuttaraṇabhatī”ti gīvāyaṃ laggesi. So sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ ādāya mātu santikaṃ agamāsi. Gāmadārakā “kiṃ nāmetaṃ [V 1.0194] ayyikākāḷakassa gale”ti bodhisattassa santikaṃ āgacchanti. So te anubandhitvā dūratova palāpento mātu santikaṃ gato. Pañcannaṃ pana sakaṭasatānaṃ uttāritattā rattehi akkhīhi kilantarūpo paññāyittha. Ayyikā tassa gīvāya sahassatthavikaṃ disvā “tāta, ayaṃ te kahaṃ laddhā”ti gopālakadārake pucchitvā tamatthaṃ sutvā “tāta, kiṃ ahaṃ tayā laddhabhatiyā jīvitukāmā, kiṃkāraṇā evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhosī”ti vatvā bodhisattaṃ uṇhodakena nhāpetvā sakalasarīraṃ telena makkhetvā pānīyaṃ pāyetvā sappāyaṃ bhojanaṃ bhojetvā jīvitapariyosāne saddhiṃ bodhisattena yathākammaṃ gatā.

The caravan leader's son, making a bundle of five hundred coins—one for each cart—tied it around his neck. The Bodhisatta thought, 'This man is not giving me the wage as agreed. I will not let him go now.' He went and stood in front of the very first cart, blocking the way. Although they tried to make him move, they could not. The caravan leader's son thought, 'I suppose he knows that his wage is deficient.' Making a bundle of a thousand coins—two for each cart—he hung it on the Bodhisatta's neck, saying, 'This is your wage for pulling the carts.' Taking the purse containing a thousand, the Bodhisatta went to his mother. The village children came towards the Bodhisatta, saying, 'What is this on Grandmother’s Blackie’s neck?' He chased them, making them flee from a distance, and went to his mother. From having pulled five hundred carts across, he appeared weary, with reddened eyes. The old woman, seeing the purse of a thousand on his neck, asked the cowherd boys where he had gotten it. Having heard the matter, she said to the Bodhisatta, 'My dear, do I wish to live on the wages you have earned? Why did you endure such hardship?' Then she bathed the Bodhisatta with warm water, anointed his whole body with oil, gave him water to drink, fed him suitable food, and at the end of her life, she passed away according to her kamma, as did the Bodhisatta.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva asamadhuro, pubbepi asamadhuroyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata is unequalled in bearing burdens; he was unequalled in bearing burdens in the past as well.' Having brought forth this Dhamma teaching and connected the story, being fully enlightened, he spoke this verse:

29.

29.

“Yato [P 1.0196] yato garu dhuraṃ, yato gambhīravattanī;

Tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjanti, svāssu taṃ vahate dhura”nti.

Wherever the burden is heavy, wherever the track is deep, then it is the black one they yoke; and he is the one who bears that burden.

Tattha yato yato garu dhuranti yasmiṃ yasmiṃ ṭhāne dhuraṃ garu bhāriyaṃ hoti, aññe balibaddā ukkhipituṃ na sakkonti. Yato gambhīravattanīti [M 1.0212] vattanti etthāti vattanī, maggassetaṃ nāmaṃ, yasmiṃ ṭhāne udakacikkhallamahantatāya vā visamacchinnataṭabhāvena vā maggo gambhīro hotīti attho. Tadāssu kaṇhaṃ yuñjantīti ettha assūti nipātamattaṃ, tadā kaṇhaṃ yuñjantīti attho. Yadā dhurañca garu hoti maggo ca gambhīro, tadā aññe balibadde apanetvā kaṇhameva yojentīti vuttaṃ hoti. Svāssu taṃ vahate dhuranti etthāpi assūti nipātamattameva, so taṃ dhuraṃ vahatīti attho.

Herein, 'Wherever the burden is heavy' means: in whatever place the burden is heavy and weighty, so that other oxen cannot lift it. 'Wherever the track is deep': a track (vattanī) is so called because one proceeds (vattanti) on it; this is a name for a path. The meaning is: in whatever place the path is deep, either because of much water and mud, or because its banks are uneven and broken. 'Then it is the black one they yoke': here 'assu' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'then they yoke the black one.' The meaning is that when the burden is heavy and the path is deep, they remove the other oxen and yoke only the black one. 'And he is the one who bears that burden': here too 'assu' is merely a particle; the meaning is 'he bears that burden.'

Evaṃ bhagavā “tadā, bhikkhave, kaṇhova taṃ dhuraṃ vahatī”ti dassetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mahallikā uppalavaṇṇā ahosi, ayyikākāḷako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Blessed One, having shown that 'At that time, monks, it was the black one who bore that burden,' connected the story and identified the birth: 'At that time, the old woman was Uppalavaṇṇā, and Grandmother’s Blackie was I myself.'

Kaṇhajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Kaṇha Jātaka, the ninth.

[30] 10. Munikajātakavaṇṇanā

[30] 10. The Commentary on the Munika Jātaka

Mā [V 1.0195] munikassa pihayīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto thullakumārikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Taṃ terasakanipāte cūḷanāradakassapajātake (jā. 1.13.40 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ nissāyā”ti? “Thullakumārikāpalobhanaṃ bhante”ti. Satthā “bhikkhu esā tava anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ imissā vivāhadivase jīvitakkhayaṃ patvā mahājanassa uttaribhaṅgabhāvaṃ patto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This, 'Do not envy Munika,' the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the luring by a plump young woman. This will be revealed in the thirteenth section, in the Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka (Jā. 1.13.40, etc.). The Teacher then asked that monk, “Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?” “Yes, Venerable Sir.” “On what account?” “Because of the luring by a plump young woman, Venerable Sir.” The Teacher said, “Monk, this woman is a doer of harm to you. In the past too, on account of her, on the day of her wedding, you met your death and became a special dish for the multitude.” Having said this, he recounted a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ gāmake ekassa kuṭumbikassa gehe goyoniyaṃ nibbatti “mahālohito”ti nāmena, kaniṭṭhabhātāpissa cūḷalohito nāma ahosi. Teyeva dve bhātike nissāya tasmiṃ kule kammadhuraṃ vattati. Tasmiṃ pana kule ekā kumārikā atthi, taṃ eko nagaravāsī kulaputto attano puttassa vāresi. Tassā mātāpitaro “kumārikāya vivāhakāle āgatānaṃ pāhunakānaṃ [P 1.0197] uttaribhaṅgo bhavissatī”ti yāgubhattaṃ datvā munikaṃ nāma sūkaraṃ posesuṃ. Taṃ disvā cūḷalohito [M 1.0213] bhātaraṃ pucchi “imasmiṃ kule kammadhuraṃ vattamānaṃ amhe dve bhātike nissāya vattati, ime pana amhākaṃ tiṇapalālādīneva denti, sūkaraṃ yāgubhattena posenti, kena nu kho kāraṇena esa etaṃ labhatī”ti. Athassa bhātā “tāta cūḷalohita, mā tvaṃ etassa bhojanaṃ pihayi, ayaṃ sūkaro maraṇabhattaṃ bhuñjati. Etissā hi kumārikāya vivāhakāle āgatānaṃ pāhunakānaṃ uttaribhaṅgo bhavissatīti ime etaṃ sūkaraṃ posenti, ito katipāhaccayena te manussā āgamissanti, atha naṃ sūkaraṃ pādesu gahetvā kaḍḍhentā heṭṭhāmañcato nīharitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā pāhunakānaṃ sūpabyañjanaṃ kariyamānaṃ passissasī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the ox-kind in the house of a certain householder in a village. He was named 'Mahālohita,' and his younger brother was named 'Cūḷalohita.' The burden of work in that family was carried on depending on these two brothers. Now in that family there was a young girl, and a townsman from a good family asked for her for his son. Her parents, thinking, 'This will be a special dish for the guests who come for the maiden's wedding,' fed a pig named Munika with rice-gruel and rice. Seeing this, Cūḷalohita asked his brother: 'The burden of work in this family is carried on depending on us two brothers, yet they give us only grass, straw, and the like, while they feed the pig with rice-gruel and rice. For what reason does he get this?' Then his brother said: 'Dear Cūḷalohita, do not envy this one's food. This pig is eating the meal of death. For thinking, "This will be a special dish for the guests who come for this maiden's wedding," they are rearing this pig. In a few days from now those people will come. Then you will see this pig seized by the feet, dragged out from under the couch, deprived of life, and made into soup and curry for the guests.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

30.

30.

“Mā munikassa pihayi, āturannāni bhuñjati;

Appossukko bhusaṃ khāda, etaṃ dīghāyulakkhaṇa”nti.

“Do not envy Munika; he eats the food of one doomed to die. Eat your chaff without anxiety; this is the mark of a long life.”

Tattha mā munikassa pihayīti munikassa bhojane pihaṃ mā uppādayi, “esa muniko subhojanaṃ bhuñjatī”ti mā munikassa pihayi, “kadā nu kho ahampi evaṃ sukhito bhaveyya”nti mā munikabhāvaṃ patthayi. Ayañhi āturannāni bhuñjati. Āturannānīti maraṇabhojanāni. Appossukko bhusaṃ khādāti tassa bhojane nirussukko hutvā attanā laddhaṃ bhusaṃ [V 1.0196] khāda. Etaṃ dīghāyulakkhaṇanti etaṃ dīghāyubhāvassa kāraṇaṃ. Tato na cirasseva te manussā āgamiṃsu, munikaṃ ghātetvā nānappakārehi paciṃsu. Bodhisatto cūḷalohitaṃ āha “diṭṭho te, tāta, muniko”ti. Diṭṭhaṃ me, bhātika, munikassa bhojanaphalaṃ, etassa bhojanato sataguṇena sahassaguṇena amhākaṃ tiṇapalālabhusamattameva uttamañca anavajjañca dīghāyulakkhaṇañcāti.

Herein, Do not envy Munika means: do not arouse desire for Munika's food; do not envy Munika, thinking, 'This Munika eats fine food'; do not wish for the state of being Munika, longing, 'When will I too be so fortunate?' For he eats the food of the afflicted. The food of the afflicted means the food of death. Eat your chaff without anxiety means: being unconcerned about his food, eat the chaff you have received. This is the mark of a long life means: this is the cause of having a long life. Not long after that, those people came, killed Munika, and cooked him in various ways. The Bodhisatta said to Cūḷalohita: 'Dear one, have you seen Munika?' 'I have seen, brother, the fruit of Munika's food. Our mere portion of grass, straw, and chaff is a hundred times, a thousand times better than his food; it is supreme, blameless, and the mark of a long life.'

Satthā “evaṃ kho tvaṃ bhikkhu pubbepi imaṃ kumārikaṃ nissāya jīvitakkhayaṃ patvā mahājanassa uttaribhaṅgabhāvaṃ gato”ti [P 1.0198] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhito bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Satthā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi [M 1.0214] – “tadā munikasūkaro ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, thullakumārikā esā eva, cūḷalohito ānando, mahālohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: 'Thus, bhikkhu, in the past too, on account of this young girl, you met with the destruction of your life and became a special dish for the great crowd.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he declared the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the dissatisfied bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher connected the threads and identified the birth: 'At that time, the pig Munika was the dissatisfied bhikkhu, the plump young girl was this very one, Cūḷalohita was Ānanda, and Mahālohita was myself.'

Munikajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Munika Jātaka, the Tenth.

Kuruṅgavaggo tatiyo.

The Kuruṅga Chapter, the Third.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse:

Kuruṅgaṃ kukkurañceva, bhojājānīyañca ājaññaṃ;

Titthaṃ mahiḷāmukhābhiṇhaṃ, nandikaṇhañca munikanti.

The Antelope, the Dog, the Noble Steed Bhoja, and the Thoroughbred; The Ford, Mahiḷāmukha, Abhiṇha; Nandivisāla, Kaṇha, and Munika.

4. Kulāvakavaggo

4. The Kulāvaka Chapter

[31] 1. Kulāvakajātakavaṇṇanā

[31] 1. The Commentary on the Kulāvaka Jātaka

Kulāvakāti [V 1.0197] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aparissāvetvā pānīyaṃ pītaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthito kira dve sahāyakā daharabhikkhū janapadaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ phāsukaṭṭhāne yathājjhāsayaṃ vasitvā “sammāsambuddhaṃ passissāmā”ti puna tato nikkhamitvā jetavanābhimukhā pāyiṃsu. Ekassa hatthe parissāvanaṃ atthi, ekassa natthi. Dvepi ekato pānīyaṃ parissāvetvā pivanti. Te ekadivasaṃ vivādaṃ akaṃsu. Parissāvanasāmiko itarassa parissāvanaṃ adatvā sayameva pānīyaṃ parissāvetvā pivi, itaro pana parissāvanaṃ alabhitvā pipāsaṃ sandhāretuṃ asakkonto aparissāvetvā pānīyaṃ pivi. Te ubhopi anupubbena jetavanaṃ patvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ kathetvā “kuto āgatatthā”ti pucchi. “Bhante, mayaṃ kosalajanapade ekasmiṃ gāmake vasitvā tato nikkhamitvā tumhākaṃ dassanatthāya āgatā”ti. “Kacci pana vo samaggā āgatatthā”ti? Aparissāvanako āha “ayaṃ, bhante, antarāmagge mayā saddhiṃ vivādaṃ katvā parissāvanaṃ nādāsī”ti. Itaropi āha “ayaṃ, bhante, aparissāvetvāva jānaṃ sapāṇakaṃ udakaṃ pivī”ti. “Saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu jānaṃ sapāṇakaṃ udakaṃ pivī”ti? “Āma, bhante, aparissāvitaṃ udakaṃ pivinti[M 1.0215]. Satthā “bhikkhu pubbe paṇḍitā devanagare rajjaṃ kārentā yuddhaparājitā samuddapiṭṭhena palāyantā ‘issariyaṃ nissāya pāṇavadhaṃ na karissāmā’ti tāva mahantaṃ yasaṃ pariccajitvā supaṇṇapotakānaṃ jīvitaṃ datvā rathaṃ nivattayiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Kulāvaka. This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a bhikkhu who drank water without straining it. It is said that two young companion bhikkhus from Sāvatthī went to the countryside and, after dwelling as they pleased in a comfortable place, set out again for Jetavana, thinking, 'We will see the Perfectly Enlightened One.' One had a water-strainer in his hand; the other did not. They would both strain water together and drink. One day they had a quarrel. The owner of the strainer did not give it to the other but strained the water and drank by himself. The other, however, unable to obtain a strainer and unable to endure his thirst, drank water without straining it. Both of them in due course reached Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down. The Teacher exchanged friendly greetings with them and asked, 'From where have you come?' 'Venerable sir, we dwelt in a small village in the Kosalan country and have come from there for the sake of seeing you.' 'But I trust you have come in harmony?' The one without a strainer said, 'Venerable sir, on the way this one quarreled with me and did not give me the strainer.' The other also said, 'Venerable sir, this one knowingly drank water containing living creatures.' 'Is it true, bhikkhu, that you knowingly drank water containing living creatures?' 'Yes, venerable sir, I drank unstrained water.' The Teacher said, 'Bhikkhu, in the past, wise men, while ruling in the city of the devas, were defeated in battle and were fleeing over the surface of the ocean. Thinking, "We will not take life for the sake of sovereignty," they renounced such great glory, gave life to the young supaṇṇas, and turned back their chariot.' Then he related the past story.

Atīte [P 1.0199] magadharaṭṭhe rājagahe eko māgadharājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto yathā etarahi sakko purimattabhāve magadharaṭṭhe macalagāmake nibbatti, evaṃ tasmiṃyeva macalagāmake mahākulassa putto hutvā nibbatti. Nāmaggahaṇadivase cassa “maghakumāro”tveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto “maghamāṇavo”ti paññāyittha. Athassa mātāpitaro samānajātikakulato dārikaṃ ānayiṃsu. So puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhamāno dānapati ahosi, pañca sīlāni rakkhati. Tasmiñca gāme tettiṃseva kulāni honti, tepi tettiṃsa kulā manussā ekadivasaṃ gāmamajjhe ṭhatvā gāmakammaṃ [V 1.0198] karonti. Bodhisatto ṭhitaṭṭhāne pādehi paṃsuṃ viyūhitvā taṃ padesaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ katvā aṭṭhāsi, athañño eko āgantvā tasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhito. Bodhisatto aparaṃ ṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ katvā aṭṭhāsi, tatrāpi añño ṭhito. Bodhisatto aparampi aparampīti sabbesampi ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ katvā aparena samayena tasmiṃ ṭhāne maṇḍapaṃ kāresi, maṇḍapampi apanetvā sālaṃ kāresi, tattha phalakāsanāni santharitvā pānīyacāṭiṃ ṭhapesi.

In the past, a king of Magadha reigned in Rājagaha in the country of Magadha. At that time the Bodhisatta—just as the present Sakka was born in a former existence in the village of Macala in the country of Magadha—was similarly born in that very village of Macala as the son of a great family. On his naming day, they gave him the name 'Maghakumāra.' When he came of age, he became known as 'the young man Magha.' Then his parents brought a girl from a family of equal birth. As he prospered with sons and daughters, he became a master of giving and observed the five precepts. In that village there were just thirty-three families. One day, these thirty-three men stood in the middle of the village to do the village work. The Bodhisatta, at the spot where he stood, cleared away the dust with his feet, made the place pleasant, and stood there. Then another man came and stood in that spot. The Bodhisatta made another spot pleasant and stood there, and another man stood there too. The Bodhisatta continued making one spot after another pleasant for all of them, and after some time he built a pavilion in that place. He then removed the pavilion and built a hall, where he spread out plank seats and set up a pot of drinking water.

Aparena samayena tepi tettiṃsajanā bodhisattena samānacchandā ahesuṃ. Te bodhisatto pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā tato paṭṭhāya tehi saddhiṃ puññāni karonto vicarati. Tepi teneva saddhiṃ puññāni karontā kālasseva vuṭṭhāya vāsipharasumusalahatthā catumahāpathādīsu musalena pāsāṇe ubbattetvā pavaṭṭenti, yānānaṃ akkhapaṭighātarukkhe haranti, visamaṃ samaṃ karonti, setuṃ attharanti, pokkharaṇiyo khaṇanti, sālaṃ karonti, dānāni denti, sīlāni rakkhanti. Evaṃ yebhuyyena sakalagāmavāsino bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā sīlāni rakkhiṃsu.

After some time, those thirty-three men became of like mind with the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta established them in the five precepts, and from then on, he went about with them, performing meritorious deeds. They too, performing meritorious deeds along with him, would rise early in the morning and, with adzes, axes, and clubs in hand, would go to the four great highways and other places, dislodge stones with their clubs and roll them away. They cleared away trees that would strike the axles of vehicles, leveled uneven ground, built causeways, dug ponds, built a hall, gave alms, and observed the precepts. Thus, for the most part, all the villagers abided by the Bodhisatta's instruction and observed the precepts.

Atha [M 1.0216] nesaṃ gāmabhojako cintesi “ahaṃ pubbe etesu suraṃ pivantesu pāṇātipātādīni karontesu cāṭikahāpaṇādivasena ceva daṇḍabalivasena ca dhanaṃ labhāmi, idāni pana magho māṇavo sīlaṃ rakkhāpeti, tesaṃ pāṇātipātādīni kātuṃ [P 1.0200] na deti, idāni pana te pañca sīlāni na rakkhāpessāmī”ti kuddho rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, bahū corā gāmaghātādīni karontā vicarantī”ti āha. Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “gaccha, te ānehī”ti āha. So gantvā sabbepi te bandhitvā ānetvā “ānītā, deva, corā”ti rañño ārocesi. Rājā tesaṃ kammaṃ asodhetvāva “hatthinā ne maddāpethā”ti āha. Tato sabbepi te rājaṅgaṇe nipajjāpetvā hatthiṃ ānayiṃsu. Bodhisatto tesaṃ ovādaṃ adāsi “tumhe sīlāni āvajjetha, pesuññakārake ca raññe ca hatthimhi ca attano sarīre ca ekasadisameva mettaṃ bhāvethā”ti. Te tathā akaṃsu. Atha nesaṃ maddanatthāya hatthiṃ upanesuṃ. So upanīyamānopi na upagacchati, mahāviravaṃ viravitvā palāyati. Aññaṃ aññaṃ hatthiṃ ānayiṃsu, tepi tatheva palāyiṃsu.

Then the village headman thought: 'Formerly, when these people drank liquor and committed acts such as taking life, I gained wealth through fines and punishments. But now, the young man Magha has them observe the moral precepts and does not allow them to take life and so on. Now I will see to it that they do not observe the five precepts.' Angrily, he approached the king and said, 'Your Majesty, many thieves are roaming about, committing village raids and the like.' Hearing his words, the king said, 'Go, bring them here.' He went, bound them all, brought them back, and reported to the king, 'Your Majesty, the thieves have been brought.' Without investigating their deeds, the king ordered, 'Have them crushed by an elephant.' Then they laid them all down in the royal courtyard and brought an elephant. The Bodhisatta advised them: 'Reflect on your moral precepts, and develop loving-kindness equally toward the slanderer, the king, the elephant, and your own bodies.' They did so. Then they brought the elephant to crush them. But even when it was led forward, it would not approach. Trumpeting loudly, it fled. They brought one elephant after another, and they too fled in the same way.

Rājā “etesaṃ hatthe kiñci osadhaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā “vicinathā”ti āha. Vicinantā adisvā “natthi, devā”ti āhaṃsu. Tena hi kiñci mantaṃ parivattessanti, pucchatha ne “atthi vo parivattanamanto”ti? Rājapurisā pucchiṃsu, bodhisatto “atthī”ti āha. Rājapurisā “atthi kira, devā”ti ārocayiṃsu, rājā sabbepi te pakkosāpetvā “tumhākaṃ [V 1.0199] jānanamantaṃ kathethā”ti āha. Bodhisatto avoca “deva, añño amhākaṃ manto nāma natthi, amhe pana tettiṃsamattā janā pāṇaṃ na hanāma, adinnaṃ nādiyāma, micchācāraṃ na carāma, musāvādaṃ na bhaṇāma, majjaṃ na pivāma, mettaṃ bhāvema, dānaṃ dema, maggaṃ samaṃ karoma, pokkharaṇiyo khaṇāma, sālaṃ karoma, ayaṃ amhākaṃ manto ca parittañca vuḍḍhi cā”ti. Rājā tesaṃ pasanno pesuññakārakassa sabbaṃ gehavibhavaṃ tañca tesaṃyeva dāsaṃ katvā adāsi, taṃ hatthiñca gāmañca tesaṃyeva adāsi.

The king thought, “There must be some medicine in their hands,” and he ordered, “Search them.” After searching and finding nothing, they said, “There is nothing, Your Majesty.” “Then they must be reciting some charm. Ask them, ‘Do you have a charm to recite?’” The king’s men asked, and the Bodhisatta replied, “We do.” The king’s men reported, “It seems they do, Your Majesty.” The king summoned them all and said, “Tell me the charm that you know.” The Bodhisatta said: “Your Majesty, we have no other charm. But we, the thirty-three of us, do not destroy life, we do not take what is not given, we do not engage in sexual misconduct, we do not speak falsehood, we do not drink intoxicating drink; we develop loving-kindness, we give gifts, we level roads, we dig ponds, and we build a public hall. This is our charm, our protection, and our prosperity.” The king was pleased with them and gave them all the slanderer’s household wealth, made the slanderer their slave, and also gave them that elephant and the village.

Te tato paṭṭhāya yathāruciyā puññāni karontā “catumahāpathe mahantaṃ sālaṃ kāressāmā”ti vaḍḍhakiṃ pakkosāpetvā sālaṃ [M 1.0217] paṭṭhapesuṃ. Mātugāmesu pana vigatacchandatāya [P 1.0201] tassā sālāya mātugāmānaṃ pattiṃ nādaṃsu. Tena ca samayena bodhisattassa gehe sudhammā, cittā, nandā, sujāti catasso itthiyo honti. Tāsu sudhammā vaḍḍhakinā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā “bhātika, imissā sālāya maṃ jeṭṭhikaṃ karohī”ti vatvā lañjaṃ adāsi. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā paṭhamameva kaṇṇikārukkhaṃ sukkhāpetvā tacchetvā vijjhitvā kaṇṇikaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā vatthena paliveṭhetvā ṭhapesi. Atha sālaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā kaṇṇikāropanakāle “aho, ayyā, ekaṃ na sarimhā”ti āha. “Kiṃ nāma, bho”ti. “Kaṇṇikā laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Hotu āharissāmā”ti? “Idāni chinnarukkhena kātuṃ na sakkā, pubbeyeva chinditvā tacchetvā vijjhitvā ṭhapitakaṇṇikā laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. “Idāni kiṃ kātabba”nti? “Sace kassaci gehe niṭṭhāpetvā ṭhapitā vikkāyikakaṇṇikā atthi, sā pariyesitabbā”ti. Te pariyesantā sudhammāya gehe disvā mūlena na labhiṃsu. “Sace maṃ sālāya pattikaṃ karotha, dassāmī”ti vutte “na mayaṃ mātugāmānaṃ pattiṃ damhā”ti āhaṃsu.

From that time on, they performed meritorious deeds as they wished and decided, “We will have a great hall built at the main crossroads.” They summoned a carpenter and had the work on the hall started. But because they were disinclined toward women, they did not give women a share in that hall. Now at that time there were four women in the Bodhisatta’s household: Sudhammā, Cittā, Nandā, and Sujāti. Among them, Sudhammā colluded with the carpenter, saying, “Brother, make me the chief benefactor of this hall,” and she gave him a bribe. He agreed, saying, “Very well.” He first had the wood for the pinnacle seasoned, then he shaped it, bored it, finished the pinnacle, wrapped it in a cloth, and set it aside. Then, when the hall was finished and it was time to set up the pinnacle, he said: “Oh, sirs, there is one thing we did not remember.” “What is that, sir?” “A pinnacle needs to be obtained.” “So be it, we will bring one.” “It cannot be made now from a freshly cut tree. A pinnacle that was cut, shaped, and bored beforehand must be obtained.” “What is to be done now?” “If there is a finished pinnacle for sale in anyone’s house, that must be sought.” Searching, they saw one in Sudhammā’s house but could not get it for a price. When she said, “If you make me a partner in the hall, I will give it,” they replied, “We do not give a share to women.”

Atha ne vaḍḍhakī āha “ayyā, tumhe kiṃ kathetha, ṭhapetvā brahmalokaṃ aññaṃ mātugāmarahitaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthi, gaṇhatha kaṇṇikaṃ, evaṃ sante amhākaṃ kammaṃ niṭṭhaṃ gamissatī”ti. Te “sādhū”ti kaṇṇikaṃ gahetvā sālaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā āsanaphalakāni santharitvā pānīyacāṭiyo ṭhapetvā yāgubhattaṃ nibandhiṃsu. Sālaṃ pākārena parikkhipitvā dvāraṃ yojetvā antopākāre vālukaṃ ākiritvā bahipākāre tālapantiyo ropesuṃ. Cittāpi tasmiṃ ṭhāne uyyānaṃ kāresi, “pupphūpagaphalūpagarukkho asuko nāma tasmiṃ natthī”ti nāhosi. Nandāpi tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne pokkharaṇiṃ kāresi pañcavaṇṇehi padumehi sañchannaṃ ramaṇīyaṃ. Sujā na kiñci akāsi.

Then the carpenter said to them: “Sirs, what are you saying? Except for the Brahma-world, there is no place without women. Take the pinnacle; in that way our work will be completed.” Saying, “Very well,” they took the pinnacle, finished the hall, spread out planks for seats, set up pots of drinking water, and arranged for a regular supply of rice gruel and cooked rice. They enclosed the hall with a wall, fitted it with a door, scattered sand within the enclosure, and planted rows of palmyra palms outside the enclosure. Cittā also had a park made in that place, such that there was no tree in it that was not either flower-bearing or fruit-bearing. Nandā, too, had a delightful lotus pond made in that very place, covered with lotuses of five colors. Sujātā did nothing.

Bodhisatto [V 1.0200] mātu upaṭṭhānaṃ pitu upaṭṭhānaṃ kule jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammaṃ saccavācaṃ apharusavācaṃ [P 1.0202] apisuṇavācaṃ maccheravinayanti imāni satta vatapadāni pūretvā –

The Bodhisatta fulfilled these seven vows: attendance upon his mother, attendance upon his father, honoring the elders of the clan, truthful speech, gentle speech, non-slanderous speech, and the dispelling of stinginess—

“Mātāpettibharaṃ jantuṃ, kule jeṭṭhāpacāyinaṃ;

Saṇhaṃ sakhilasambhāsaṃ, pesuṇeyyappahāyinaṃ.

“The person who supports his mother and father,

Who honors the elders in his clan,

Whose speech is gentle and courteous,

Who has abandoned slander;

“Maccheravinaye [M 1.0218] yuttaṃ, saccaṃ kodhābhibhuṃ naraṃ;

Taṃ ve devā tāvatiṃsā, āhu sappuriso itī”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.257) –

“Who is engaged in dispelling stinginess,

Is truthful, and has vanquished anger—

That one the Tāvatiṃsa gods

Truly call a superior person.” (SN 11.12)

Evaṃ pasaṃsiyabhāvaṃ āpajjitvā jīvitapariyosāne tāvatiṃsabhavane sakko devarājā hutvā nibbatti, tepissa sahāyā tattheva nibbattiṃsu. Tasmiṃ kāle tāvatiṃsabhavane asurā paṭivasanti. Sakko devarājā “kiṃ no sādhāraṇena rajjenā”ti asure dibbapānaṃ pāyetvā matte samāne pādesu gāhāpetvā sinerupabbatapāde khipāpesi. Te asurabhavanameva sampāpuṇiṃsu.

Having thus become worthy of praise, at the end of his life he was reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa realm as Sakka, king of the devas. His companions were also reborn there. At that time, the asuras were dwelling in the Tāvatiṃsa realm. Sakka, king of the devas, thought, “What is the good of a kingdom shared with others?” He had the asuras drink a divine beverage, and when they were intoxicated, he had them seized by the feet and thrown down to the foot of Mount Sineru. They thus arrived at the realm of the asuras.

Asurabhavanaṃ nāma sinerussa heṭṭhimatale tāvatiṃsadevalokappamāṇameva, tattha devānaṃ pāricchattako viya cittapāṭali nāma kappaṭṭhiyarukkho hoti. Te cittapāṭaliyā pupphitāya jānanti “nāyaṃ amhākaṃ devaloko, devalokasmiñhi pāricchattako pupphatī”ti. Atha te “jarasakko amhe matte katvā mahāsamuddapiṭṭhe khipitvā amhākaṃ devanagaraṃ gaṇhi, te mayaṃ tena saddhiṃ yujjhitvā amhākaṃ devanagarameva gaṇhissāmā”ti kipillikā viya thambhaṃ sineruṃ anusañcaramānā uṭṭhahiṃsu. Sakko “asurā kira uṭṭhitā”ti sutvā samuddapiṭṭheyeva abbhuggantvā yujjhamāno tehi parājito diyaḍḍhayojanasatikena vejayantarathena dakkhiṇasamuddassa matthakena palāyituṃ āraddho. Athassa ratho samuddapiṭṭhena vegena gacchanto simbalivanaṃ pakkhanto, tassa gamanamagge simbalivanaṃ naḷavanaṃ viya chijjitvā chijjitvā samuddapiṭṭhe patati. Supaṇṇapotakā samuddapiṭṭhe paripatantā mahāviravaṃ raviṃsu. Sakko mātaliṃ pucchi “samma mātali, kiṃ saddo nāmesa, atikāruññaravo [P 1.0203] vattatī”ti? “Deva, tumhākaṃ rathavegena vicuṇṇite simbalivane patante supaṇṇapotakā maraṇabhayatajjitā ekaviravaṃ viravantī”ti.

The realm of the asuras is at the base of Sineru, equal in extent to the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world. There, like the Pāricchattaka tree of the devas, they have a tree called the Cittapāṭali, which lasts for an aeon. When the Cittapāṭali blossoms, they know, “This is not our deva-world, for in the deva-world the Pāricchattaka blossoms.” Then they think: “That old Sakka made us intoxicated, cast us upon the surface of the great ocean, and seized our deva-city. We will fight with him and take back our deva-city!” Like ants climbing up a pillar, they ascended Sineru. When Sakka heard, “It seems the asuras have risen up,” he went out over the surface of the ocean and gave battle. Being defeated by them, he began to flee over the southern ocean in his Vejayanta chariot, which was one hundred and fifty yojanas long. As his chariot sped over the surface of the ocean, it entered a silk-cotton tree forest. The trees in its path were snapped and fell upon the ocean’s surface like a forest of reeds. The young supaṇṇas falling onto the ocean’s surface cried out with a great shriek. Sakka asked Mātali: “Friend Mātali, what is this sound? A most piteous cry is heard.” “Sire, because of the speed of your chariot, the silk-cotton tree forest is being smashed, and the young supaṇṇas, terrified by the fear of death, are crying out in unison.”

Mahāsatto [V 1.0201] “samma mātali, mā amhe nissāya ete kilamantu, na mayaṃ issariyaṃ nissāya pāṇavadhakammaṃ karoma, etesaṃ pana atthāya mayaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā asurānaṃ dassāma, nivattayetaṃ ratha”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Great Being said: “Friend Mātali, let not these beings suffer on our account. We do not commit the act of destroying life for the sake of sovereignty. For their sake, we will give up our own lives to the asuras. Turn back the chariot.” Having said this, he uttered this verse:

31.

31.

“Kulāvakā [M 1.0219] mātali simbalismiṃ, īsāmukhena parivajjayassu;

Kāmaṃ cajāma asuresu pāṇaṃ, māme dijā vikulāvā ahesu”nti.

“Mātali, there are nestlings in the silk-cotton tree;

avoid them with the chariot pole.

Let us willingly give up our life to the asuras,

but let not these twice-born be without their nests.”

Tattha kulāvakāti supaṇṇapotakā. Mātalīti sārathiṃ āmantesi. Simbalisminti passa ete simbalirukkhe olambantā ṭhitāti dasseti. Īsāmukhena parivajjayassūti ete etassa rathassa īsāmukhena yathā na haññanti, evaṃ te parivajjayassu. Kāmaṃ cajāma asuresu pāṇanti yadi amhesu asurānaṃ pāṇaṃ cajantesu etesaṃ sotthi hoti, kāmaṃ cajāma ekaṃseneva mayaṃ asuresu amhākaṃ pāṇaṃ cajāma. Māme dijā vikulāvā ahesunti ime pana dijā ime garuḷapotakā viddhastavicuṇṇitakulāvakatāya vikulāvā mā ahesuṃ, mā amhākaṃ dukkhaṃ etesaṃ upari khipa, nivattaya nivattaya rathanti. Mātalisaṅgāhako tassa vacanaṃ sutvā rathaṃ nivattetvā aññena maggena devalokābhimukhaṃ akāsi. Asurā pana taṃ nivattayamānameva disvā “addhā aññehipi cakkavāḷehi sakkā āgacchanti, balaṃ labhitvā ratho nivatto bhavissatī”ti maraṇabhayabhītā palāyitvā asurabhavanameva pavisiṃsu.

Here, 'kulāvakā' means young supaṇṇa birds. 'Mātali' is an address to his charioteer. 'In the silk-cotton tree'—he points out, 'Look, they are there, hanging from these silk-cotton trees.' 'Avoid them with the chariot pole'—'Avoid them so that they are not struck by the pole of this chariot.' 'Willingly we give up our lives to the asuras'—'If there is safety for these while we give up our lives to the asuras, then let us by all means willingly give up our lives to the asuras.' 'Let these twice-born not be without nests'—'These twice-born, these young garuḷas, may not become without nests because their nests have been destroyed and crushed; do not cast our suffering upon them. Turn back, turn back the chariot.' Mātali the charioteer, hearing his words, turned the chariot around and took another path toward the world of the devas. The asuras, however, seeing it turning back, thought, 'Surely other Sakkas are coming from other world-systems; having gained reinforcements, the chariot must have turned back,' and, terrified by the fear of death, they fled and entered the abode of the asuras.

Sakkopi devanagaraṃ pavisitvā dvīsu devalokesu devagaṇena parivuto nagaramajjhe aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe pathaviṃ bhinditvā yojanasahassubbedho vejayantapāsādo uṭṭhahi. Vijayante uṭṭhitattā “vejayanto” tveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Atha sakko puna asurānaṃ anāgamanatthāya pañcasu ṭhānesu ārakkhaṃ ṭhapesi. Yaṃ sandhāya vuttaṃ –

Sakka, having entered the city of the devas, stood in the middle of the city surrounded by a host of devas from the two deva worlds. At that moment, splitting the earth, the Vejayanta Palace arose, a thousand yojanas high. Because it arose when victory was won, they gave it the name 'Vejayanta.' Then Sakka, to prevent the asuras from coming again, established guards in five places. In reference to which it was said:

“Antarā [P 1.0204] dvinnaṃ ayujjhapurānaṃ, pañcavidhā ṭhapitā abhirakkhā;

Uragakaroṭipayassa ca hārī, madanayutā caturo ca mahantā”ti. (saṃ. ni. aṭṭha. 1.1.247);

“Between the two unconquerable cities, a fivefold guard was established: the serpents, the Supaṇṇas, the Kumbhaṇḍas, the frenzied ones, and the four great ones.”

Dve [V 1.0202] nagarānipi yuddhena gahetuṃ asakkuṇeyyatāya ayujjhapurāni nāma jātāni devanagarañca asuranagarañca. Yadā hi asurā balavantā honti, atha devehi palāyitvā devanagaraṃ pavisitvā dvāre pihite asurānaṃ satasahassampi [M 1.0220] kiñci kātuṃ na sakkoti. Yadā devā balavantā honti, atha asurehi palāyitvā asuranagaraṃ pavisitvā dvāre pihite sakkānaṃ satasahassampi kiñci kātuṃ na sakkoti. Iti imāni dve nagarāni ayujjhapurāni nāma. Tesaṃ antarā etesu uragādīsu pañcasu ṭhānesu sakkena ārakkhā ṭhapitā. Tattha uraga-saddena nāgā gahitā. Te udake balavantā honti, tasmā sinerussa paṭhamālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Karoṭi-saddena supaṇṇā gahitā. Tesaṃ kira karoṭi nāma pānabhojanaṃ, tena taṃ nāmaṃ labhiṃsu, dutiyālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Payassahāri-saddena kumbhaṇḍā gahitā. Dānavarakkhasā kirete, tatiyālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Madanayuta-saddena yakkhā gahitā. Visamacārino kira te yuddhasoṇḍā, catutthālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Caturo ca mahantāti cattāro mahārājāno vuttā, pañcamālinde tesaṃ ārakkhā. Tasmā yadi asurā kupitā āvilacittā devapuraṃ upayanti, pañcavidhesu yaṃ girino paṭhamaṃ paribhaṇḍaṃ, taṃ uragā paribāhiya tiṭṭhanti. Evaṃ sesesu sesā.

The two cities—the city of the devas and the city of the asuras—came to be named Ayujjhapura (Unconquerable Cities) because they could not be captured by war. For when the asuras are powerful, the devas flee, enter their city, and close the gates, and then even a hundred thousand asuras cannot do anything. When the devas are powerful, the asuras flee, enter their city, and close the gates, and then even a hundred thousand Sakkas cannot do anything. Thus, these two cities are called Ayujjhapura. Between them, in these five places beginning with the uragas, Sakka established guards. Here, by the term 'uraga,' the nāgas are meant. They are powerful in water, so their guard is stationed at the first terrace of Sineru. By the term 'karoṭi,' the supaṇṇas are meant. It is said their drink and food is called 'karoṭi,' hence they got that name; their guard is stationed at the second terrace. By the term 'payassahāri,' the kumbhaṇḍas are meant. They are said to be dānava-rakkhasas; their guard is stationed at the third terrace. By the term 'madanayuta,' the yakkhas are meant. They are said to be of erratic conduct and fond of battle; their guard is stationed at the fourth terrace. And by 'the four great ones,' the Four Great Kings are meant; their guard is stationed at the fifth terrace.
