Therefore, if the asuras, angry and with agitated minds, approach the city of the devas, the uragas stand guarding the first terrace of the mountain. Similarly, the others guard the remaining terraces.

Imesu pana pañcasu ṭhānesu ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā sakke devānaminde dibbasampattiṃ anubhavamāne sudhammā cavitvā tasseva pādaparicārikā hutvā nibbatti, kaṇṇikāya dinnanissandena cassā pañcayojanasatikā sudhammā nāma devasabhā udapādi, yattha dibbasetacchattassa heṭṭhā yojanappamāṇe kañcanapallaṅke nisinno sakko devānamindo devamanussānaṃ kattabbakiccāni karoti. Cittāpi cavitvā tasseva pādaparicārikā hutvā nibbatti, uyyānassa karaṇanissandena cassā cittalatāvanaṃ nāma uyyānaṃ udapādi. Nandāpi cavitvā tasseva pādaparicārikā hutvā nibbatti, pokkharaṇiyā nissandena cassā nandā nāma pokkharaṇī udapādi.

Now, while Sakka, king of the devas, was enjoying divine fortune after having established guards in these five places, Sudhammā passed away and was reborn as his foot-attendant. As a result of the gift of a pinnacle, the deva-assembly hall named Sudhammā, five hundred yojanas in extent, arose for her. There, seated on a golden couch a yojana in size beneath a divine white parasol, Sakka, king of the devas, attends to the duties to be done for devas and humans. Cittā, too, passed away and was reborn as his foot-attendant. As a result of her having made a park, the pleasure grove named Cittalatāvana arose for her. Nandā, too, passed away and was reborn as his foot-attendant. As a result of the pond she had made, the pond named Nandā arose for her.

Sujā pana [P 1.0205] kusalakammassa akatattā ekasmiṃ araññe kandarāya bakasakuṇikā hutvā nibbattā. Sakko “sujā na paññāyati, kattha nu kho nibbattā”ti āvajjento taṃ disvā tattha gantvā taṃ ādāya devalokaṃ āgantvā tassā ramaṇīyaṃ devanagaraṃ sudhammaṃ devasabhaṃ cittalatāvanaṃ nandāpokkharaṇiñca dassetvā “etā kusalaṃ katvā mayhaṃ pādaparicārikā hutvā nibbattā, tvaṃ pana kusalaṃ akatvā tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattā[M 1.0221], ito paṭṭhāya sīlaṃ rakkhāhī”ti taṃ ovaditvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā tattheva netvā vissajjesi. Sāpi tato [V 1.0203] paṭṭhāya sīlaṃ rakkhati. Sakko katipāhaccayena “sakkā nu kho sīlaṃ rakkhitu”nti gantvā maccharūpena uttāno hutvā purato nipajji, sā “matamacchako”ti saññāya sīse aggahesi, maccho naṅguṭṭhaṃ cālesi, atha naṃ “jīvati maññe”ti vissajjesi. Sakko “sādhu sādhu, sakkhissasi sīlaṃ rakkhitu”nti agamāsi. Sā tato cutā bārāṇasiyaṃ kumbhakāragehe nibbatti.

Sujā, however, because she had not performed any meritorious deeds, was reborn as a female heron in a certain forest ravine. Sakka, adverting his mind and thinking, 'Sujā is not to be seen; where can she have been reborn?' saw her. He went there, took her, and brought her to the world of the devas. There, he showed her the delightful city of the devas, the Sudhammā deva-assembly hall, the Cittalatā grove, and the Nandā lotus pond. Then he said: 'These women, having performed meritorious deeds, were reborn as my foot-attendants. But you, having done no merit, were reborn in the animal realm. From now on, observe the precepts.' Having advised her thus, he established her in the five precepts and then took her back and released her in that very place. From then on, she observed the precepts. After a few days, Sakka thought, 'Is she able to observe the precepts?' and went there in the form of a fish, lying on its back in front of her. She, thinking, 'It is a dead fish,' took it by the head. The fish flicked its tail, and then she thought, 'I suppose it is alive,' and let it go. Sakka said, 'Good, good! You will be able to observe the precepts,' and departed. After passing away from there, she was reborn in a potter's household in Bārāṇasī.

Sakko “kahaṃ nu kho nibbattā”ti tattha nibbattabhāvaṃ ñatvā suvaṇṇaeḷālukānaṃ yānakaṃ pūretvā majjhe gāmassa mahallakavesena nisīditvā “eḷālukāni gaṇhatha, eḷālukāni gaṇhathā”ti ugghosesi. Manussā āgantvā “dehi, tātā”ti āhaṃsu. “Ahaṃ sīlarakkhakānaṃ dammi, tumhe sīlaṃ rakkhathā”ti? “Mayaṃ sīlaṃ nāma na jānāma, mūlena dehī”ti. “Na mayhaṃ mūlena attho, sīlarakkhakānaññevāhaṃ dammī”ti. Manussā “ko cāyaṃ eḷāluko”ti pakkamiṃsu. Sujā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “mayhaṃ ānītaṃ bhavissatī”ti cintetvā gantvā taṃ “dehi, tātā”ti āha. “Sīlaṃ rakkhasi, ammā”ti? “Āma, rakkhāmī”ti. “Idaṃ mayā tuyhameva atthāya ābhata”nti saddhiṃ yānakena gehadvāre ṭhapetvā pakkāmi.

Sakka, wondering, 'Where can she have been reborn?' and knowing that she had been reborn there, filled a small cart with golden cucumbers and sat in the middle of the village in the guise of an old man, calling out: 'Take cucumbers, take cucumbers!' People came and said, 'Give us some, father.' 'I give them to those who observe the precepts. Do you observe the precepts?' 'We do not know what precepts are. Give them to us for a price.' 'I have no need for a price; I give them only to those who observe the precepts.' The people left, saying, 'What kind of cucumber-seller is this?' Sujā, hearing the news, thought, 'He must have brought them for me.' She went and said, 'Give me some, father.' 'Do you observe the precepts, mother?' 'Yes, I observe them.' 'I have brought these just for you.' He left them, together with the cart, at her door and departed.

Sāpi yāvajīvaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhitvā tato cutā vepacittissa asurindassa dhītā hutvā nibbatti, sīlānisaṃsena abhirūpā ahosi. So tassā vayappattakāle “mayhaṃ dhītā attano cittarucitaṃ sāmikaṃ gaṇhatū”ti asure sannipātesi[P 1.0206]. Sakko “kahaṃ nu kho sā nibbattā”ti olokento tattha nibbattabhāvaṃ ñatvā “sujā cittarucitaṃ sāmikaṃ gaṇhantī maṃ gaṇhissatī”ti asuravaṇṇaṃ māpetvā tattha agamāsi. Sujaṃ alaṅkaritvā sannipātaṭṭhānaṃ ānetvā “cittarucitaṃ sāmikaṃ gaṇhā”ti āhaṃsu. Sā olokentī sakkaṃ disvā pubbepi sinehavasena uppannapemena mahoghena viya ajjhotthaṭahadayā hutvā “ayaṃ me sāmiko”ti vatvā tassa upari pupphadāmaṃ khipitvā aggahesi. Asurā “amhākaṃ rājā ettakaṃ kālaṃ dhītu anucchavikaṃ alabhitvā idāni labhati[M 1.0222], ayamevassā dhītu pitāmahato mahallako anucchaviko”ti lajjamānā pakkamiṃsu. So taṃ devanagaraṃ ānetvā aḍḍhateyyānaṃ nāṭikākoṭīnaṃ jeṭṭhikaṃ katvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gato.

She, having observed the precepts throughout her life, passed away from there and was reborn as the daughter of Vepacitti, king of the asuras. As a benefit of her virtue, she was exceedingly beautiful. When she came of age, he assembled the asuras, saying, 'Let my daughter choose a husband to her own liking.' Sakka, wondering, 'Where can she have been reborn?' and seeing she had been reborn there, thought: 'When choosing a husband to her own liking, Sujā will choose me.' Disguising himself as an asura, he went there. They adorned Sujā and brought her to the assembly, saying, 'Choose a husband to your own liking.' As she looked around, she saw Sakka. With her heart overwhelmed by love that arose from past-life affection, as if by a great flood, she said, 'This is my husband,' and chose him by throwing a garland of flowers over him. The asuras, ashamed, departed, saying: 'Our king, having been unable to find a suitable husband for his daughter for so long, now gets this one; this old man, older than his daughter's grandfather, is unsuitable for her!' He took her to the city of the devas and made her chief among twenty-five million dancing girls. She lived there for the extent of her lifespan before passing on according to her kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “evaṃ bhikkhu pubbe paṇḍitā devanagare rajjaṃ kārayamānā attano jīvitaṃ pariccajantāpi pāṇātipātaṃ na kariṃsu, tvaṃ nāma evarūpe niyyānike [V 1.0204] sāsane pabbajitvā aparissāvitaṃ sapāṇakaṃ udakaṃ pivissasī”ti taṃ bhikkhuṃ garahitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātalisaṅgāhako ānando ahosi, sakko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said: 'Thus, bhikkhu, in the past the wise, while exercising sovereignty in the city of the devas, did not destroy life even when giving up their own lives. But you, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, have drunk unstrained water containing living beings!' Having rebuked that bhikkhu and made the connection, he identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, Mātali the charioteer was Ānanda, and Sakka was I myself.'

Kulāvakajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kulāvaka Jātaka, the First.

[32] 2. Naccajātakavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Nacca Jātaka

Rudaṃ manuññanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ bahubhaṇḍikaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā devadhammajātake (jā. 1.1.6) vuttasadisameva. Satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu bahubhaṇḍo”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā tvaṃ bhikkhu bahubhaṇḍo jātosī”ti? So ettakaṃ sutvāva kuddho nivāsanapārupanaṃ chaḍḍetvā “iminā dāni nīhārena vicarāmī”ti satthu purato naggo aṭṭhāsi. Manussā “dhī dhī”ti āhaṃsu. So tato palāyitvā hīnāyāvatto. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā “satthu nāma purato evarūpaṃ karissatī”ti tassa aguṇakathaṃ kathesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti bhikkhū pucchi. Bhante, “so hi nāma bhikkhu tumhākaṃ purato catuparisamajjhe hirottappaṃ pahāya gāmadārako viya naggo ṭhatvā manussehi jigucchiyamāno hīnāyāvattitvā sāsanā parihīno”ti tassa aguṇakathāya nisinnāmhāti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva so bhikkhu hirottappābhāvena ratanasāsanā parihīno, pubbe itthiratanapaṭilābhatopi parihīnoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Your cry is delightful…” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a monk with many possessions. The story is similar to the one told in the Devadhamma Jātaka. The Teacher asked that monk: “Is it true, monk, that you have many possessions?” “Yes, venerable sir.” “For what reason, monk, have you become one with many possessions?” Hearing just this, he became angry, and casting off his lower and upper robes, he stood naked before the Teacher, saying: “Now I will go about in this manner!” People cried out, “Shame, shame!” He then fled from there and returned to the lower life. The monks, gathered in the Hall of Dhamma, were discussing his faults, saying: “To think that he would do such a thing in front of the Teacher!” The Teacher came and asked: “For what talk, monks, are you now gathered together?” “Venerable sir, we are gathered discussing the faults of that monk who, abandoning shame and moral dread, stood naked before you in the midst of the fourfold assembly like a village boy. Being reviled by people, he has reverted to the lower life and has fallen away from the Dispensation.” The Teacher said: “Monks, it is not only now that this monk, through his lack of shame and moral dread, has fallen away from the precious Dispensation. In the past, too, he fell away from obtaining the jewel of a woman.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 1.0207][M 1.0223] paṭhamakappe catuppadā sīhaṃ rājānaṃ akaṃsu, macchā ānandamacchaṃ, sakuṇā suvaṇṇahaṃsaṃ. Tassa pana suvaṇṇahaṃsarājassa dhītā haṃsapotikā abhirūpā ahosi. So tassā varaṃ adāsi, sā attano cittarucitaṃ sāmikaṃ vāresi. Haṃsarājā tassā varaṃ datvā himavante sabbe sakuṇe sannipātāpesi, nānappakārā haṃsamorādayo sakuṇagaṇā samāgantvā ekasmiṃ mahante pāsāṇatale sannipatiṃsu. Haṃsarājā “attano cittarucitaṃ sāmikaṃ āgantvā gaṇhātū”ti dhītaraṃ pakkosāpesi. Sā sakuṇasaṅghaṃ olokentī maṇivaṇṇagīvaṃ citrapekhuṇaṃ moraṃ disvā “ayaṃ me sāmiko hotū”ti ārocesi. Sakuṇasaṅghā moraṃ upasaṅkamitvā āhaṃsu “samma mora, ayaṃ rājadhītā ettakānaṃ sakuṇānaṃ majjhe sāmikaṃ rocentī tayi ruciṃ uppādesī”ti. Moro “ajjāpi tāva me balaṃ na passatī”ti atituṭṭhiyā hirottappaṃ bhinditvā [V 1.0205] tāva mahato sakuṇasaṅghassa majjhe pakkhe pasāretvā naccituṃ ārabhi, naccanto appaṭicchanno ahosi.

In the past, during the first aeon, the quadrupeds made the lion their king, the fish made the Ānanda fish their king, and the birds made the golden goose their king. Now, that golden goose king had a very beautiful daughter, a young goose. He gave her a boon, that she could choose a husband to her own heart's liking. Having given her the boon, the goose king had all the birds in the Himalayas assemble. Flocks of various kinds of birds, such as geese, peacocks, and others, came together and gathered on a great stone slab. The goose king had his daughter summoned, saying: “Let her come and choose a husband to her own heart's liking.” Surveying the assembly of birds, she saw a peacock with a neck the color of a jewel and with colorful tail-feathers and announced: “Let this one be my husband.” The assembly of birds approached the peacock and said: “Friend peacock, this king’s daughter, choosing a husband from among so many birds, has taken a liking to you.” The peacock, overjoyed, said, “She has not yet seen my strength!” and breaking through shame and moral dread, he spread his wings in the midst of that great assembly of birds and began to dance. While dancing, he became exposed.

Suvaṇṇahaṃsarājā lajjito “imassa neva ajjhattasamuṭṭhānā hirī atthi, na bahiddhāsamuṭṭhānaṃ ottappaṃ, nāssa bhinnahirottappassa mama dhītaraṃ dassāmī”ti sakuṇasaṅghamajjhe imaṃ gāthamāha –

The golden goose king was ashamed and thought: “This one has no inner sense of shame, nor any outer moral dread. I will not give my daughter to this one who has broken through shame and moral dread.” In the midst of the assembly of birds, he spoke this verse:

32.

32.

“Rudaṃ manuññaṃ rucirā ca piṭṭhi, veḷuriyavaṇṇūpanibhā ca gīvā;

Byāmamattāni ca pekhuṇāni, naccena te dhītaraṃ no dadāmī”ti.

“Your cry is delightful, your back is beautiful, your neck has the hue of beryl, and your tail-feathers are a fathom long; but because of your dance, I will not give you my daughter.”

Tattha rudaṃ manuññanti ta-kārassa da-kāro kato, rutaṃ manāpaṃ, vassitasaddo madhuroti attho. Rucirā ca piṭṭhīti piṭṭhipi te citrā ceva sobhanā ca. Veḷuriyavaṇṇūpanibhāti veḷuriyamaṇivaṇṇasadisā. Byāmamattānīti ekabyāmappamāṇāni. Pekhuṇānīti piñchāni. Naccena te dhītaraṃ no dadāmīti hirottappaṃ bhinditvā naccitabhāveneva te evarūpassa nillajjassa dhītaraṃ no dadāmīti vatvā haṃsarājā tasmiṃyeva parisamajjhe attano bhāgineyyassa haṃsapotakassa dhītaraṃ adāsi. Moro haṃsapotikaṃ alabhitvā [P 1.0208] lajjitvā tatova uppatitvā palāyi. Haṃsarājāpi attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gato.

Herein, rudaṃ manuññaṃ: the ‘t’ has become a ‘d’; it means the cry is pleasing, the call is sweet. Rucirā ca piṭṭhi means your back is both colorful and beautiful. Veḷuriyavaṇṇūpanibhā means like the color of a beryl gem. Byāmamattāni means measuring one fathom. Pekhuṇāni means tail-feathers. Naccena te dhītaraṃ no dadāmi means: ‘Because you have broken through shame and moral dread by dancing, I will not give my daughter to such a shameless one.’ Having said this, the goose king, right there in the midst of the assembly, gave his daughter to his own nephew, a young goose. The peacock, having failed to get the young goose maiden, was ashamed and flew away from there. The goose king also went back to his own dwelling place.

Satthā [M 1.0224] “na, bhikkhave, idāneva esa hirottappaṃ bhinditvā ratanasāsanā parihīno, pubbepi itthiratanapaṭilābhato parihīnoyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā moro bahubhaṇḍiko ahosi, haṃsarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: “Monks, it is not only now that this one, having broken through shame and moral dread, has fallen away from the jewel of the Dispensation. In the past, too, he fell away from obtaining the jewel of a woman.” Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he made the connection and identified the birth: “At that time, the peacock was the monk with many possessions, and the goose king was myself.”

Naccajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Nacca Jātaka, the Second.

[33] 3. Sammodamānajātakavaṇṇanā

[33] 3. The Commentary on the Sammodamāna Jātaka

Sammodamānāti idaṃ satthā kapilavatthuṃ upanissāya nigrodhārāme viharanto cumbaṭakakalahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kuṇālajātake (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana satthā ñātake āmantetvā “mahārājā ñātakānaṃ aññamaññaṃ viggaho nāma na yutto, tiracchānagatāpi [V 1.0206] hi pubbe samaggakāle paccāmitte abhibhavitvā sotthiṃ pattā yadā vivādamāpannā, tadā mahāvināsaṃ pattā”ti vatvā ñātirājakulehi āyācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Living in concord…” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling near Kapilavatthu in the Banyan Grove concerning a quarrel over a head-rest. This will be made clear in the Kuṇāla Jātaka. At that time, the Teacher addressed his kinsmen, saying: “O great king, a quarrel among kinsmen is not fitting. In the past, even animals, when they were in harmony, overcame their enemies and achieved security; but when they fell into dispute, they met with great destruction.” Then, having been requested by his royal kinsmen, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto vaṭṭakayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā anekavaṭṭakasahassaparivāro araññe paṭivasati. Tadā eko vaṭṭakaluddako tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vaṭṭakavassitaṃ katvā tesaṃ sannipatitabhāvaṃ ñatvā tesaṃ upari jālaṃ khipitvā pariyantesu maddanto sabbe ekato katvā pacchiṃ pūretvā gharaṃ gantvā te vikkiṇitvā tena mūlena jīvikaṃ kappeti. Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto te vaṭṭake āha – “ayaṃ sākuṇiko amhākaṃ ñātake vināsaṃ pāpeti, ahaṃ ekaṃ upāyaṃ jānāmi, enesa amhe gaṇhituṃ na sakkhissati, ito dāni paṭṭhāya etena tumhākaṃ upari jāle khittamatte ekeko ekekasmiṃ jālakkhike sīsaṃ ṭhapetvā jālaṃ ukkhipitvā icchitaṭṭhānaṃ haritvā ekasmiṃ kaṇṭakagumbe pakkhipatha, evaṃ sante heṭṭhā tena tena ṭhānena palāyissāmā”ti. Te sabbe “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇiṃsu. Dutiyadivase upari jāle khitte te bodhisattena vuttanayeneva jālaṃ ukkhipitvā [P 1.0209] ekasmiṃ [M 1.0225] kaṇṭakagumbe khipitvā sayaṃ heṭṭhābhāgena tato tato palāyiṃsu. Sākuṇikassa gumbato jālaṃ mocentasseva vikālo jāto, so tucchahatthova agamāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a quail and lived in the forest with a retinue of many thousands of quails. At that time, a quail-trapper would go to their dwelling place, imitate the call of a quail, and when he knew they had gathered, he would cast a net over them. Pressing down on the edges, he would gather them all together, fill his basket, and go home. He sold them and made his living from the proceeds. One day, the Bodhisatta addressed the quails: “This fowler is bringing ruin upon our kinsfolk. I know a stratagem by which he will not be able to catch us. From now on, as soon as he has cast the net over you, each of you should stick your head through one of the meshes, lift up the net together, carry it to a place of your choosing, and drop it on a thorn-bush. In this way, we can escape from underneath through the openings.” They all agreed, saying, “Very good.” The next day, when the net was cast over them, they lifted it up just as the Bodhisatta had instructed, dropped it on a thorn-bush, and escaped from underneath. By the time the fowler had disentangled his net from the bush, it was late, and he went away empty-handed.

Punadivasato paṭṭhāyapi vaṭṭakā tatheva karonti. Sopi yāva sūriyatthaṅgamanā jālameva mocento kiñci alabhitvā tucchahatthova gehaṃ gacchati. Athassa bhariyā kujjhitvā “tvaṃ divase divase tucchahattho āgacchasi, aññampi te bahi positabbaṭṭhānaṃ atthi maññe”ti āha. Sākuṇiko “bhadde, mama aññaṃ positabbaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, apica kho pana te vaṭṭakā samaggā hutvā caranti, mayā khittamatte jālaṃ ādāya kaṇṭakagumbe khipitvā gacchanti, na kho panete sabbakālameva sammodamānā viharissanti, tvaṃ mā cintayi, yadā te vivādamāpajjissanti, tadā te sabbeva ādāya tava mukhaṃ hāsayamāno āgacchissāmī”ti vatvā bhariyāya imaṃ gāthamāha –

From the next day onwards, the quails continued to do the same. The fowler, too, spent his time until sunset just disentangling his net, and getting nothing, he would go home empty-handed. Then his wife grew angry and said: “Day after day you come home empty-handed. I suppose you have another household to support somewhere else!” The fowler replied: “My dear, I have no other household to support. But those quails are now acting in harmony. As soon as I cast my net, they lift it up, drop it on a thorn-bush, and get away. However, they will not live in concord forever. Do not worry. When they fall into a dispute, I will bring them all back and come to you, making your face light up with a smile.” Then he spoke this verse to his wife:

33.

33.

“Sammodamānā gacchanti, jālamādāya pakkhino;

Yadā te vivadissanti, tadā ehinti me vasa”nti.

“While living in concord, the birds fly off with the net; but when they start to quarrel, they will come into my power.”

Tattha [V 1.0207] yadā te vivadissantīti yasmiṃ kāle te vaṭṭakā nānāladdhikā nānāgāhā hutvā vivadissanti, kalahaṃ karissantīti attho. Tadā ehinti me vasanti tasmiṃ kāle sabbepi te mama vasaṃ āgacchissanti. Athāhaṃ te gahetvā tava mukhaṃ hāsento āgacchissāmīti bhariyaṃ samassāsesi.

Herein, ‘yadā te vivadissanti’ means: at the time when those quails, holding different views and opinions, will dispute and quarrel. ‘Tadā ehinti me vasaṃ’ means: at that time, they will all come under my control. He comforted his wife, saying: “Then I will catch them and come back, making your face light up with a smile.”

Katipāhasseva pana accayena eko vaṭṭako gocarabhūmiṃ otaranto asallakkhetvā aññassa sīsaṃ akkami, itaro “ko maṃ sīse akkamī”ti kujjhiṃ. “Ahaṃ asallakkhetvā akkamiṃ, mā kujjhī”ti vuttepi kujjhiyeva. Te punappunaṃ kathentā “tvameva maññe jālaṃ ukkhipasī”ti aññamaññaṃ vivādaṃ kariṃsu. Tesu vivadantesu bodhisatto cintesi “vivādake sotthibhāvo nāma natthi, idāneva te jālaṃ na ukkhipissanti, tato mahantaṃ vināsaṃ pāpuṇissanti, sākuṇiko okāsaṃ labhissati, mayā imasmiṃ ṭhāne na sakkā vasitu”nti. So attano parisaṃ ādāya aññattha gato. Sākuṇikopi kho katipāhaccayena [P 1.0210] āgantvā vaṭṭakavassitaṃ vassitvā tesaṃ sannipatitānaṃ upari jālaṃ [M 1.0226] khipi. Atheko vaṭṭako “tuyhaṃ kira jālaṃ ukkhipantasseva matthake lomāni patitāni, idāni ukkhipā”ti āha. Aparo “tuyhaṃ kira jālaṃ ukkhipantasseva dvīsu pakkhesu pattāni patitāni, idāni ukkhipā”ti āha. Iti tesaṃ “tvaṃ ukkhipa, tvaṃ ukkhipā”ti vadantānaññeva sākuṇiko jālaṃ ukkhipitvā sabbeva te ekato katvā pacchiṃ pūretvā bhariyaṃ hāsayamāno gehaṃ agamāsi.

After a few days, a quail, descending into the feeding ground, inadvertently stepped on another's head. The other, angered, said, 'Who stepped on my head?' Though the first said, 'I stepped on you inadvertently, do not be angry,' the other remained angry. As they argued back and forth, they quarreled with each other, saying, 'I suppose it's you who lifts the net!' While they were quarreling, the Bodhisatta thought: 'There is no safety for those who quarrel. Now they will not lift the net, and so they will meet with great destruction. The fowler will get his chance. I cannot stay in this place.' So he took his flock and went elsewhere. After a few days, the fowler returned and, imitating the quail's call, cast the net over them as they gathered. One quail said, 'They say the feathers on your head fell out while you were lifting the net. Now you lift it!' Another said, 'They say the feathers on your two wings fell out while you were lifting the net. Now you lift it!' As they were arguing thus, 'You lift it, you lift it,' the fowler lifted the net himself. Gathering them all together, he filled his basket and, delighting his wife, went home.

Satthā “evaṃ mahārājā ñātakānaṃ kalaho nāma na yutto, kalaho vināsamūlameva hotī”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā apaṇḍitavaṭṭako devadatto ahosi, paṇḍitavaṭṭako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: 'Thus, great king, a quarrel among kinsmen is not fitting, for a quarrel is the very root of destruction.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse and connected the story, he identified the birth, saying: 'At that time, the foolish quail was Devadatta, but the wise quail was I myself.'

Sammodamānajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Sammodamāna Jātaka: The Third.

[34] 4. Macchajātakavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Fish Jātaka

Na maṃ sītaṃ na maṃ uṇhanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchi. “Saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti. “Kenāsi ukkaṇṭhāpito”ti? “Purāṇadutiyikā me, bhante madhurahattharasā, taṃ jahituṃ na sakkomī”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “bhikkhu esā itthī tava anatthakārikā[V 1.0208], pubbepi tvaṃ etaṃ nissāya maraṇaṃ pāpuṇanto maṃ āgamma maraṇā mutto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Neither cold nor heat…' This the Teacher said while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the enticement by a former wife. At that time, the Teacher asked a certain bhikkhu, 'Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are dissatisfied?' 'It is true, Blessed One.' 'What has made you dissatisfied?' 'Venerable sir, my former wife has a sweet touch, and I am unable to abandon her.' Then the Teacher said to him: 'Bhikkhu, this woman is harmful to you. In the past, too, on her account you were about to meet death, but you were freed from death by coming to me.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa purohito ahosi. Tadā kevaṭṭā nadiyaṃ jālaṃ khipiṃsu. Atheko mahāmaccho rativasena attano macchiyā saddhiṃ kīḷamāno āgacchati. Tassa sā macchī purato gacchamānā jālagandhaṃ ghāyitvā jālaṃ pariharamānā gatā. So pana kāmagiddho lolamaccho jālakucchimeva paviṭṭho. Kevaṭṭā tassa jālaṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā jālaṃ ukkhipitvā macchaṃ gahetvā amāretvāva vālikāpiṭṭhe khipitvā [P 1.0211] “imaṃ aṅgāresu pacitvā khādissāmā”ti aṅgāre karonti, sūlaṃ tacchenti. Maccho “etaṃ aṅgāratāpanaṃ vā sūlavijjhanaṃ vā aññaṃ vā pana dukkhaṃ na maṃ kilameti, yaṃ [M 1.0227] panesā macchī ‘aññaṃ so nūna ratiyā gato’ti mayi domanassaṃ āpajjati, tameva maṃ bādhatī”ti paridevamāno imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his chaplain. At that time, some fishermen cast a net in the river. Then a great fish, driven by passion, came along playing with his mate. The female fish, going ahead, smelled the net and swam away, avoiding it. But that lustful, greedy fish entered right into the belly of the net. The fishermen, realizing that the fish had entered, lifted the net, seized the fish, and without killing it, threw it on a sandbank. Thinking, 'We will roast this on the coals and eat it,' they prepared the coals and sharpened a spit. The fish lamented: 'It is not the heat from these coals, nor the piercing by the spit, nor any other pain that torments me. But that my mate will be distressed about me, thinking, "Surely he has gone to another for pleasure"—that is what torments me.' And lamenting, he uttered this verse:

34.

34.

“Na maṃ sītaṃ na maṃ uṇhaṃ, na maṃ jālasmi bādhanaṃ;

Yañca maṃ maññate macchī, aññaṃ so ratiyā gato”ti.

Neither cold nor heat torments me, nor my confinement in the net; but what the female fish thinks of me—'He has gone to another for pleasure'—that is what torments me.

Tattha na maṃ sītaṃ na maṃ uṇhanti macchānaṃ udakā nīhaṭakāle sītaṃ hoti, tasmiṃ vigate uṇhaṃ hoti, tadubhayampi sandhāya “na maṃ sītaṃ na maṃ uṇhaṃ bādhatī”ti paridevati. Yampi aṅgāresu paccanamūlakaṃ dukkhaṃ bhavissati, tampi sandhāya “na maṃ uṇha”nti paridevateva. Na maṃ jālasmi bādhananti yampi me jālasmiṃ bādhanaṃ ahosi, tampi maṃ na bādhetīti paridevati. “Yañca ma”ntiādīsu ayaṃ piṇḍattho – sā macchī mama jāle patitassa imehi kevaṭṭehi gahitabhāvaṃ ajānantī maṃ apassamānā “so maccho idāni aññaṃ macchiṃ kāmaratiyā gato bhavissatī”ti cinteti, taṃ tassā domanassappattāya cintanaṃ maṃ bādhatīti vālikāpiṭṭhe nipanno paridevati.

Herein, by 'Neither cold nor heat': when fish are taken from the water, they feel cold; when that passes, they feel heat. Referring to both, he laments, 'Neither cold nor heat torments me.' And referring also to the future suffering rooted in being roasted on coals, he laments, 'nor heat.' By 'nor my confinement in the net': he laments, 'Even the confinement I experienced in the net does not torment me.' In 'But what...' and so on, the summary meaning is this: 'That female fish, not knowing that I have fallen into the net and been caught by these fishermen, and not seeing me, thinks: "That fish must now have gone to another female fish for sensual pleasure." That thought of hers, who has become dejected, is what torments me.' Thus he laments, lying on the sandbank.

Tasmiṃ samaye purohito dāsaparivuto nhānatthāya nadītīraṃ āgato. So pana sabbarutaññū hoti. Tenassa macchaparidevanaṃ sutvā etadahosi “ayaṃ maccho kilesavasena paridevati, evaṃ āturacitto kho panesa mīyamāno nirayeyeva nibbattissati, ahamassa avassayo bhavissāmī”ti kevaṭṭānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “ambho tumhe amhākaṃ ekadivasampi byañjanatthāya macchaṃ na dethā”ti āha. Kevaṭṭā “kiṃ vadetha, sāmi, tumhākaṃ ruccanakamacchaṃ gaṇhitvā [V 1.0209] gacchathā”ti āhaṃsu. “Amhākaṃ aññena kammaṃ natthi, imaññeva dethā”ti. “Gaṇhatha sāmī”ti. Bodhisatto taṃ ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā nadītīre nisīditvā “ambho maccha, sace tāhaṃ ajja na passeyyaṃ, jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇeyyāsi, idāni ito paṭṭhāya mā kilesavasiko ahosī”ti ovaditvā udake vissajjetvā nhatvā nagaraṃ pāvisi.

At that time, the chaplain, surrounded by his retinue of slaves, came to the riverbank to bathe. Now, he was one who understood all sounds. Hearing the fish's lament, he thought: 'This fish is lamenting because of defilements. If it dies with such an afflicted mind, it will surely be reborn in hell. I will become its refuge.' He went to the fishermen and said: 'Sirs, won't you give us a fish for just one day's curry?' The fishermen replied: 'What are you saying, master? Take any fish you like and go.' 'We have no need for any other; just give us this one.' 'Take it, master.' The Bodhisatta took the fish with both hands, sat on the riverbank, and advised it: 'Friend fish, if I had not seen you today, you would have lost your life. From now on, do not be under the sway of defilements.' Having given this advice, he released it into the water, bathed, and returned to the city.

Satthā [P 1.0212] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Satthāpi anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā [M 1.0228] jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā macchī purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, maccho ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu purohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse and then declared the Truths. At the conclusion of the talk on the Truths, the dissatisfied bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher then connected the story and identified the birth, saying: 'At that time, the female fish was the former wife, the fish was the dissatisfied bhikkhu, and the chaplain was I myself.'

Macchajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Fish Jātaka: The Fourth.

[35] 5. Vaṭṭakajātakavaṇṇanā

5. The Commentary on the Quail Jātaka

Santi pakkhā apatanāti idaṃ satthā magadhesu cārikaṃ caramāno dāvagginibbānaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye satthā magadhesu cārikaṃ caramāno aññatarasmiṃ magadhagāmake piṇḍāya caritvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto bhikkhugaṇaparivuto maggaṃ paṭipajji. Tasmiṃ samaye mahāḍāho uṭṭhahi, purato ca pacchato ca bahū bhikkhū dissanti, sopi kho aggi ekadhūmo ekajālo hutvā avattharamāno āgacchateva. Tattheke puthujjanabhikkhū maraṇabhayabhītā “paṭaggiṃ dassāma, tena daḍḍhaṭṭhānaṃ itaro aggi na ottharissatī”ti araṇisahitaṃ nīharitvā aggiṃ karonti. Apare āhaṃsu “āvuso, tumhe kiṃ nāma karotha, gaganamajjhe ṭhitaṃ candamaṇḍalaṃ, pācīnalokadhātuto uggacchantaṃ sahassaraṃsipaṭimaṇḍitaṃ sūriyamaṇḍalaṃ, velāya tīre ṭhitā samuddaṃ, sineruṃ nissāya ṭhitā sineruṃ apassantā viya sadevake loke aggapuggalaṃ attanā saddhiṃ gacchantameva sammāsambuddhaṃ anoloketvā ‘paṭaggiṃ demā’ti vadatha, buddhabalaṃ nāma na jānātha, etha satthu santikaṃ gamissāmā”ti. Te purato ca pacchato ca gacchantā sabbepi ekato hutvā dasabalassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Satthā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivāro aññatarasmiṃ padese aṭṭhāsi. Dāvaggi abhibhavanto viya viravanto āgacchati. Āgantvā tathāgatassa ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ patvā tassa padesassa samantā soḷasakarīsamattaṭṭhānaṃ patto udake opilāpitatiṇukkā viya nibbāyi, vinibbedhato dvattiṃsakarīsamattaṭṭhānaṃ avattharituṃ nāsakkhi.

'I have wings, but cannot fly…' This the Teacher said while wandering in Magadha, with reference to the extinguishing of a forest fire. On one occasion, the Teacher was wandering in Magadha. Having walked for alms in a certain Magadhan village and returned from his alms round after the meal, he set out on the road surrounded by the assembly of bhikkhus. At that time, a great forest fire arose. Many bhikkhus were seen both in front and behind, and that fire, becoming a single column of smoke and a single flame, advanced, spreading continuously. There, some ordinary bhikkhus, terrified by the fear of death, said: 'Let us set a counter-fire. Then the main fire will not spread over the area we have burned.' Taking out fire-sticks, they kindled a fire. Others said: 'Friends, what are you doing? It is as if you do not see the moon in the middle of the sky, or the sun with its thousand rays rising from the eastern world-system, or the ocean while standing on the shore, or Mount Sineru while standing at its base. In the same way, you fail to see the Perfectly Enlightened One, the foremost person in the world with its gods, who is walking right along with you, and yet you say, "Let us set a counter-fire." You do not know the power of the Buddha. Come, let us go to the Teacher's presence.' Those walking in front and behind all gathered together and approached the one with the Ten Powers. The Teacher, surrounded by the great assembly of bhikkhus, stood in a certain place. The forest fire came on, roaring as if to overwhelm everything. But upon reaching the place where the Tathāgata stood, when it came within a perimeter of sixteen karīsas, it was extinguished like a grass-torch plunged into water, and it was unable to penetrate the thirty-two karīsa area.

Bhikkhū [V 1.0210] satthu guṇakathaṃ ārabhiṃsu – “aho buddhānaṃ guṇā nāma, ayañhi nāma acetano aggi buddhānaṃ ṭhitaṭṭhānaṃ avattharituṃ na sakkoti, udake [M 1.0229] tiṇukkā viya nibbāyati, aho buddhānaṃ [P 1.0213] ānubhāvo nāmā”ti. Satthā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “na, bhikkhave, etaṃ etarahi mayhaṃ balaṃ, yaṃ imaṃ bhūmippadesaṃ patvā esa aggi nibbāyati. Idaṃ pana mayhaṃ porāṇakasaccabalaṃ. Imasmiñhi padese sakalampi imaṃ kappaṃ aggi na jalissati, kappaṭṭhiyapāṭihāriyaṃ nāmeta”nti āha. Athāyasmā ānando satthu nisīdanatthāya catugguṇaṃ saṅghāṭiṃ paññapesi, nisīdi satthā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā. Bhikkhusaṅghopi tathāgataṃ vanditvā parivāretvā nisīdi. Atha satthā “idaṃ tāva, bhante, amhākaṃ pākaṭaṃ, atītaṃ paṭicchannaṃ, taṃ no pākaṭaṃ karothā”ti bhikkhūhi āyācito atītaṃ āhari.

The bhikkhus began a discussion on the Teacher's virtues: "Oh, the virtues of the Buddhas! Indeed, this mindless fire cannot spread over the place where a Buddha has stood; it is extinguished like a grass torch in water. Oh, the spiritual power of the Buddhas!" Hearing their discussion, the Teacher said: "Bhikkhus, it is not by my present power that this fire is extinguished upon reaching this spot of ground. This, rather, is the power of an ancient act of truth of mine. In this place, fire will not burn for this entire aeon; this is called the 'eon-standing miracle.'" Then the Venerable Ānanda prepared the outer robe folded in four as a seat for the Teacher. The Teacher sat down, folding his legs crosswise. The Sangha of bhikkhus also paid homage to the Tathāgata, surrounded him, and sat down. Then, having been requested by the bhikkhus, "Venerable sir, this is manifest to us, but the past is concealed; please make it manifest for us," the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte magadharaṭṭhe tasmiṃyeva padese bodhisatto vaṭṭakayoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā mātukucchito jāto aṇḍakosaṃ padāletvā nikkhantakāle mahāgeṇḍukappamāṇo vaṭṭakapotako ahosi. Atha naṃ mātāpitaro kulāvake nipajjāpetvā mukhatuṇḍakena gocaraṃ āharitvā posenti. Tassa pakkhe pasāretvā ākāse gamanabalaṃ vā pāde ukkhipitvā thale gamanabalaṃ vā natthi. Tañca padesaṃ saṃvacchare saṃvacchare dāvaggi gaṇhāti, so tasmimpi samaye mahāravaṃ ravanto taṃ padesaṃ gaṇhi, sakuṇasaṅghā attano attano kulāvakehi nikkhamitvā maraṇabhayabhītā viravantā palāyanti, bodhisattassapi mātāpitaro maraṇabhayabhītā bodhisattaṃ chaḍḍetvā palāyiṃsu. Bodhisatto kulāvake nipannakova gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā avattharitvā āgacchantaṃ aggiṃ disvā cintesi “sace mayhaṃ pakkhe pasāretvā ākāsena gamanabalaṃ bhaveyya, uppatitvā aññattha gaccheyyaṃ. Sace pāde ukkhipitvā gamanabalaṃ bhaveyya, padavārena aññattha gaccheyyaṃ. Mātāpitaropi kho me maraṇabhayabhītā maṃ ekakaṃ pahāya attānaṃ parittāyantā palātā. Idāni me aññaṃ paṭisaraṇaṃ natthi, atāṇomhi asaraṇo, kiṃ nu kho ajja mayā kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti.

In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, in that very place, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a quail. When he hatched from the eggshell and emerged, he was a young quail the size of a large ball. His parents laid him in the nest and, fetching food with their beaks, nourished him. He had no strength to fly through the air by spreading his wings, nor to walk on the ground by lifting his feet. Every year, a forest fire would sweep through that area. At that time, roaring loudly, the fire consumed that place. Flocks of birds, terrified by the fear of death, cried out and fled from their nests. The Bodhisatta’s parents, too, terrified by the fear of death, abandoned the Bodhisatta and fled. Lying in the nest, the Bodhisatta raised his neck and saw the fire approaching. He thought: "If I had the strength to fly through the air by spreading my wings, I could fly up and go elsewhere. If I had the strength to walk on the ground by lifting my feet, I could go elsewhere on foot. But my parents, terrified by the fear of death, have left me alone and fled to save themselves. Now I have no other refuge; I am helpless and without protection. What, now, should I do today?"

Athassa etadahosi “imasmiṃ loke sīlaguṇo nāma atthi, saccaguṇo nāma atthi, atīte pāramiyo pūretvā bodhimūle nisīditvā abhisambuddhā sīlasamādhipaññāvimuttivimuttiñāṇadassanasampannā [P 1.0214] saccānuddayakāruññakhantisamannāgatā sabbasattesu samappavattamettābhāvanā sabbaññubuddhā [M 1.0230] nāma atthi, tehi ca paṭividdhā dhammaguṇā nāma atthi, mayi cāpi ekaṃ saccaṃ atthi, saṃvijjamāno eko sabhāvadhammo paññāyati, tasmā atīte buddhe ceva tehi paṭividdhaguṇe ca āvajjetvā mayi vijjamānaṃ saccasabhāvadhammaṃ gahetvā saccakiriyaṃ katvā aggiṃ [V 1.0211] paṭikkamāpetvā ajja mayā attano ceva sesasakuṇānañca sotthibhāvaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Tena vuttaṃ –

Then it occurred to him: "In this world, there exists the virtue of morality and the virtue of truthfulness. In the past, having fulfilled the perfections and seated at the foot of the Bodhi tree, there were fully enlightened ones, endowed with morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; possessed of truth, compassion, pity, and patience; developers of impartial loving-kindness towards all beings—such All-Knowing Buddhas exist. And there exist the qualities of the Dhamma realized by them. In me, too, there is a certain truth; an existing natural principle is evident. Therefore, by reflecting on the past Buddhas and the qualities they realized, and by grasping the true natural principle existing in me, I should perform an act of truth, make the fire recede, and today bring about the well-being of both myself and the remaining birds." Thus it is said:

“Atthi loke sīlaguṇo, saccaṃ soceyyanuddayā;

Tena saccena kāhāmi, saccakiriyamanuttaraṃ.

There is in the world the virtue of morality, truth, purity, and compassion. By this truth, I shall perform a supreme act of truth.

“Āvajjetvā dhammabalaṃ, saritvā pubbake jine;

Saccabalamavassāya, saccakiriyamakāsaha”nti. (cariyā. 3.79-80);

Having reflected on the power of the Dhamma, remembering the former Victors, relying on the power of truth, I performed an act of truth.

Atha bodhisatto atīte parinibbutānaṃ buddhānaṃ guṇe āvajjetvā attani vijjamānaṃ saccasabhāvaṃ ārabbha saccakiriyaṃ karonto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, reflecting on the virtues of the Buddhas who had attained final Nibbāna in the past, and taking as his basis the true nature existing in himself, performed an act of truth and spoke this verse:

35.

35.

“Santi pakkhā apatanā, santi pādā avañcanā;

Mātāpitā ca nikkhantā, jātaveda paṭikkamā”ti.

I have wings, but they cannot fly; I have feet, but they cannot walk. My mother and father have departed; O Jātaveda, retreat!

Tattha santi pakkhā apatanāti mayhaṃ pakkhā nāma atthi upalabbhanti, no ca kho sakkā etehi uppatituṃ ākāsena gantunti apatanā. Santi pādā avañcanāti pādāpi me atthi, tehi pana vañcituṃ padavāragamanena gantuṃ na sakkāti avañcanā. Mātāpitā ca nikkhantāti ye ca maṃ aññattha neyyuṃ, tepi maraṇabhayena mātāpitaro nikkhantā. Jātavedāti aggiṃ ālapati. So hi jātova vedayati paññāyati, tasmā “jātavedo”ti vuccati. Paṭikkamāti paṭigaccha nivattāti jātavedaṃ āṇāpeti.

Herein, 'I have wings, but they cannot fly' means: I have wings, they exist, but it is not possible to fly up and go through the sky with them; hence 'they cannot fly.' 'I have feet, but they cannot walk' means: I do have feet, but it is not possible to go by walking step by step with them; hence 'they cannot walk.' 'Mother and father have departed' means: those who would carry me elsewhere, my parents, have departed out of fear of death. 'Jātaveda': he addresses the fire. For as soon as it is born (jāta), it makes itself known (vedayati), it is perceived; therefore it is called 'Jātaveda.' 'Retreat!': he commands Jātaveda, "Go back! Turn away!"

Iti mahāsatto “sace mayhaṃ pakkhānaṃ atthibhāvo, te ca pasāretvā ākāse apatanabhāvo, pādānaṃ atthibhāvo, te ca ukkhipitvā avañcanabhāvo, mātāpitūnaṃ maṃ kulāvakeyeva chaḍḍetvā palātabhāvo ca sacco sabhāvabhūtoyeva, jātaveda, etena [M 1.0231] saccena tvaṃ ito paṭikkamā”ti kulāvake nipannakova saccakiriyaṃ akāsi. Tassa saha saccakiriyāya soḷasakarīsamatte ṭhāne jātavedo paṭikkami. Paṭikkamanto ca na jhāyamānova aññaṃ gato, udake pana opilāpitā ukkā viya tattheva nibbāyi. Tena vuttaṃ –

Thus the Great Being, lying in the nest, made an act of truth: "If it is a fact, a true state of things, that I have wings but cannot fly by spreading them; that I have feet but cannot walk by lifting them; and that my mother and father have abandoned me right in the nest and fled—if this is true, O Jātaveda, by this truth, you retreat from here!" Simultaneously with his act of truth, the fire retreated for a space of sixteen karīsas. As it retreated, it did not spread elsewhere burning, but was extinguished right there, like a torch plunged into water. Hence it is said:

“Saha [V 1.0212][P 1.0215] sacce kate mayhaṃ, mahāpajjalito sikhī;

Vajjesi soḷasa karīsāni, udakaṃ patvā yathā sikhī”ti. (cariyā. 3.82);

Simultaneously with my act of truth, the greatly blazing fire avoided a space of sixteen karīsas, just as a fire does upon reaching water.

Taṃ pana ṭhānaṃ sakalepi imasmiṃ kappe agginā anabhibhavanīyattā kappaṭṭhiyapāṭihāriyaṃ nāma jātaṃ. Evaṃ bodhisatto saccakiriyaṃ katvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.

That place, because it was not overcome by fire throughout this entire aeon, became known as the 'Miracle of Enduring for the Aeon.' Thus, having performed this act of truth, the Bodhisatta, at the end of his life, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, imassa vanassa agginā anajjhottharaṇaṃ etarahi mayhaṃ balaṃ, porāṇaṃ panetaṃ vaṭṭapotakakāle mayhameva saccabala”nti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi. Saccapariyosāne keci sotāpannā ahesuṃ, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahattaṃ pattāti. Satthāpi anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātāpitaro etarahi mātāpitarova ahesuṃ, vaṭṭakarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: "Bhikkhus, that this forest is not overwhelmed by fire is not by my power now; rather, this is the power of my act of truth from the time when I was a young quail." Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he expounded the Truths. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some attained arahantship. The Teacher then connected the story and identified the birth: "At that time, the parents were the present-day parents, and the quail king was I myself."

Vaṭṭakajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Vaṭṭaka Jātaka, the Fifth.

[36] 6. Sakuṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[36] 6. The Commentary on the Sakuṇa Jātaka

Yaṃ nissitāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto daḍḍhapaṇṇasālaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira bhikkhu satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā jetavanato nikkhamma kosalesu ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ nissāya ekasmiṃ araññasenāsane vasati. Athassa paṭhamamāseyeva paṇṇasālā ḍayhittha. So “paṇṇasālā me daḍḍhā, dukkhaṃ vasāmī”ti manussānaṃ ācikkhi. Manussā “idāni no khettaṃ parisukkhaṃ, kedāre pāyetvā karissāma”, tasmiṃ pāyite “bījaṃ vapitvā”, bīje vutte “vatiṃ katvā”, vatiyā katāya “niddāyitvā, lāyitvā, madditvā”ti evaṃ taṃ taṃ kammaṃ apadisantāyeva temāsaṃ vītināmesuṃ. So bhikkhu temāsaṃ ajjhokāse dukkhaṃ vasanto [M 1.0232] kammaṭṭhānaṃ vaḍḍhetvā visesaṃ nibbattetuṃ nāsakkhi. Pavāretvā pana satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kiṃ bhikkhu sukhena vassaṃvutthosi, kammaṭṭhānaṃ te matthakaṃ patta”nti pucchi. So taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā “senāsanasappāyassa me abhāvena kammaṭṭhānaṃ matthakaṃ na patta”nti āha. Satthā “pubbe bhikkhu tiracchānagatāpi attano sappāyāsappāyaṃ jāniṃsu, tvaṃ kasmā na aññāsī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Whom one depends upon…" This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a bhikkhu whose leaf-hut had burned down. It seems a certain bhikkhu received a meditation subject from the Teacher, left Jetavana, and took up residence in a forest lodging dependent on a border village in Kosala. Then, in the very first month, his leaf-hut burned down. He told the people, "My leaf-hut has burned down; I am living in discomfort." The people said, "Now our fields are dry; we will do it after watering the plots." When the plots were watered, they said, "After sowing the seeds." When the seeds were sown, "After making the fence." When the fence was made, "After weeding, reaping, and threshing." Thus, citing one task after another, they let three months pass. That bhikkhu, living uncomfortably in the open for three months, was unable to develop his meditation subject and attain a spiritual distinction. After the Pavāraṇā, he went to the Teacher, paid homage, and sat to one side. The Teacher exchanged friendly greetings with him and asked, "Bhikkhu, did you spend the Rains comfortably? Has your meditation subject reached its culmination?" The bhikkhu explained what had happened and said, "Due to the lack of a suitable dwelling, my meditation subject did not reach its culmination." The Teacher said, "In the past, bhikkhu, even animals knew what was suitable and unsuitable for themselves. Why did you not know?" and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0213][P 1.0216] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakuṇayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā sakuṇasaṅghaparivuto araññāyatane sākhāviṭapasampannaṃ mahārukkhaṃ nissāya vasati. Athekadivasaṃ tassa rukkhassa sākhāsu aññamaññaṃ ghaṃsantīsu cuṇṇaṃ patati, dhūmo uṭṭhāti. Taṃ disvā bodhisatto cintesi “imā dve sākhā evaṃ ghaṃsamānā aggiṃ vissajjessanti, so patitvā purāṇapaṇṇāni gaṇhissati, tato paṭṭhāya imampi rukkhaṃ jhāpessati, na sakkā idha amhehi vasituṃ, ito palāyitvā aññattha gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So sakuṇasaṅghassa imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a bird. Surrounded by a flock of birds, he lived in a forest, relying on a great tree endowed with branches and twigs. Then one day, as the branches of that tree rubbed against each other, powder fell and smoke arose. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta thought: “When these two branches rub together like this, they will produce fire. When it falls, it will catch the old leaves, and from there it will burn down this very tree. It is not possible for us to live here; we should flee from here and go elsewhere.” He then addressed this verse to the flock of birds:

36.

36.

“Yaṃ nissitā jagatiruhaṃ vihaṅgamā, svāyaṃ aggiṃ pamuñcati;

Disā bhajatha vakkaṅgā, jātaṃ saraṇato bhaya”nti.

“This tree on which we birds depend is now itself producing fire. Flee to the quarters, O crooked-limbed ones! Fear has arisen from our very refuge.”

Tattha jagatiruhanti jagati vuccati pathavī, tattha jātattā rukkho “jagatiruho”ti vuccati. Vihaṅgamāti vihaṃ vuccati ākāsaṃ, tattha gamanato pakkhī “vihaṅgamā”ti vuccanti. Disā bhajathāti imaṃ rukkhaṃ muñcitvā ito palāyantā catasso disā bhajatha. Vakkaṅgāti sakuṇe ālapati. Te hi uttamaṅgaṃ galaṃ kadāci kadāci vaṅkaṃ karonti, tasmā “vakkaṅgā”ti vuccanti. Vaṅkā vā tesaṃ ubhosu passesu pakkhā jātāti vakkaṅgā. Jātaṃ saraṇato bhayanti amhākaṃ avassayarukkhatoyeva bhayaṃ nibbattaṃ, etha aññattha gacchāmāti.

Herein, `jagatiruhaṃ` (grown on the ground): `jagati` means the earth; because it grows there, a tree is called a `jagatiruha`. `Vihaṅgamā` (sky-goers): `vihaṃ` means the sky; because they go there, birds are called `vihaṅgamā`. `Disā bhajatha` (Flee to the quarters) means: having abandoned this tree and fled from here, resort to the four quarters. `Vakkaṅgā` (crooked-limbed) is an address to the birds. For they sometimes make their chief limb, the neck, crooked; therefore they are called `vakkaṅgā`. Or their wings grow crookedly on both sides, thus they are `vakkaṅgā`. `Jātaṃ saraṇato bhayaṃ` (Fear has arisen from our refuge) means: fear has arisen from the very tree that is our support; come, let us go elsewhere.

Bodhisattassa vacanakarā paṇḍitasakuṇā tena saddhiṃ ekappahāreneva uppatitvā aññattha gatā. Ye pana apaṇḍitā, te “evameva esa bindumatte udake kumbhīle passatī”ti tassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā tattheva vasiṃsu. Tato na cirasseva bodhisattena cintitākāreneva aggi nibbattitvā taṃ rukkhaṃ aggahesi. Dhūmesu ca jālāsu ca uṭṭhitāsu dhūmandhā [M 1.0233] sakuṇā aññattha gantuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, aggimhi patitvā patitvā vināsaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

The wise birds who did the Bodhisatta’s bidding flew up all at once with him and went elsewhere. But the foolish ones, thinking, “He sees crocodiles in a mere drop of water,” did not heed his words and remained right there. Before long, just as the Bodhisatta had thought, a fire broke out and seized the tree. When the smoke and flames arose, the birds, blinded by the smoke, were unable to go elsewhere. Falling into the fire again and again, they met with destruction.

Satthā “evaṃ bhikkhu pubbe tiracchānagatāpi rukkhagge vasantā attano sappāyāsappāyaṃ jānanti, tvaṃ kasmā na aññāsī”ti imaṃ [P 1.0217] dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi. Saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhito. Satthāpi anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bodhisattassa vacanakarā sakuṇā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, paṇḍitasakuṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, saying: “Bhikkhu, in the past even animals dwelling in treetops knew what was suitable and unsuitable for them; why did you not know?” Then he declared the truths. At the conclusion of the truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher connected the story and identified the birth: “At that time, the birds who followed the Bodhisatta’s advice were the Buddha’s assembly, and the wise bird was I myself.”

Sakuṇajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Sakuṇa Jātaka, the Sixth.

[37] 7. Tittirajātakavaṇṇanā

[37] 7. The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka

Ye [V 1.0214] vuḍḍhamapacāyantīti idaṃ satthā sāvatthiṃ gacchanto sāriputtattherassa senāsanapaṭibāhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Anāthapiṇḍikena hi vihāraṃ kāretvā dūte pesite satthā rājagahā nikkhamma vesāliṃ patvā tattha yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā “sāvatthiṃ gamissāmī”ti maggaṃ paṭipajji. Tena ca samayena chabbaggiyānaṃ antevāsikā purato purato gantvā therānaṃ senāsanesu aggahitesveva “idaṃ senāsanaṃ amhākaṃ upajjhāyassa, idaṃ ācariyassa, idaṃ amhākameva bhavissatī”ti senāsanāni palibundhenti. Pacchā āgatā therā senāsanāni na labhanti. Sāriputtattherassāpi antevāsikā therassa senāsanaṃ pariyesantā na labhiṃsu. Thero senāsanaṃ alabhanto satthu senāsanassa avidūre ekasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisajjāya ca caṅkamena ca rattiṃ vītināmesi. Satthā paccūsasamaye nikkhamitvā ukkāsi, theropi ukkāsi. “Ko eso”ti? “Ahaṃ, bhante, sāriputto”ti. “Sāriputta, imāya velāya idha kiṃ karosī”ti? “So taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi”. Satthā therassa vacanaṃ sutvā “idāni tāva mayi jīvanteyeva bhikkhū aññamaññaṃ agāravā apatissā viharanti, parinibbute kiṃ nu kho karissantī”ti āvajjentassa dhammasaṃvego udapādi.

“Those who honor the elders….” This the Teacher spoke while traveling to Sāvatthī concerning the obstruction of the Venerable Sāriputta’s lodging. When Anāthapiṇḍika had the monastery built and sent messengers, the Teacher departed from Rājagaha, reached Vesālī, and after dwelling there as long as he wished, he set out on the road, thinking, “I will go to Sāvatthī.” At that time, the disciples of the group of six bhikkhus went on ahead and, before the lodgings were taken by the elder bhikkhus, they reserved them, saying: “This lodging is for our preceptor, this for our teacher, and this will be for us.” The elders who arrived later could not get lodgings. The Venerable Sāriputta’s disciples, too, searched for a lodging for the elder but could not find one. Having failed to obtain a lodging, the elder spent the night near the Teacher’s quarters, at the foot of a tree, sometimes sitting, sometimes walking. At dawn, the Teacher came out and cleared his throat; the elder also cleared his throat. “Who is that?” “It is I, Sāriputta, venerable sir.” “Sāriputta, what are you doing here at this hour?” He related the incident. When the Teacher heard the elder’s words, a sense of spiritual urgency arose in him as he reflected: “If bhikkhus dwell with such lack of respect and deference for one another even while I am alive, what will they do when I have attained final Nibbāna?”

So pabhātāya rattiyā bhikkhusaṅghaṃ sannipātāpetvā bhikkhū pucchi “saccaṃ kira, bhikkhave, chabbaggiyā bhikkhū purato purato gantvā therānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ [M 1.0234] senāsanaṃ paṭibāhantī”ti. “Saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti? Tato chabbaggiye garahitvā dhammiṃ kathaṃ katvā bhikkhū āmantesi “ko nu kho, bhikkhave, aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ arahatī”ti? Ekacce “khattiyakulā pabbajito”ti āhaṃsu, ekacce “brāhmaṇakulā, gahapatikulā pabbajito”ti, apare “vinayadharo, dhammakathiko, paṭhamassa jhānassa lābhī, dutiyassa, tatiyassa, catutthassa jhānassa lābhī”ti. Apare “sotāpanno, sakadāgāmī, anāgāmī, arahā, tevijjo, chaḷabhiñño”ti āhaṃsu. Evaṃ tehi bhikkhūhi attano attano rucivasena aggāsanādirahānaṃ kathitakāle satthā āha – “na, bhikkhave, mayhaṃ [P 1.0218] sāsane aggāsanādīni patvā khattiyakulā pabbajito pamāṇaṃ, na brāhmaṇakulā pabbajito, na gahapatikulā pabbajito, na vinayadharo, na suttantiko, na ābhidhammiko, na paṭhamajjhānādilābhino, na sotāpannādayo pamāṇaṃ, atha kho, bhikkhave, imasmiṃ sāsane yathāvuḍḍhaṃ abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ añjalikammaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ kātabbaṃ, aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍo laddhabbo. Idamettha pamāṇaṃ. Tasmā vuḍḍhataro bhikkhu etesaṃ anucchaviko. Idāni kho pana, bhikkhave, sāriputto mayhaṃ [V 1.0215] aggasāvako anudhammacakkappavattako mamānantaraṃ senāsanaṃ laddhuṃ arahati, so imaṃ rattiṃ senāsanaṃ alabhanto rukkhamūle vītināmesi, tumhe idāneva evaṃ agāravā apatissā, gacchante gacchante kāle kinti katvā viharissathā”ti. Atha nesaṃ ovādadānatthāya “pubbe, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatāpi ‘na kho panetaṃ amhākaṃ patirūpaṃ, yaṃ mayaṃ aññamaññaṃ agāravā apatissā asabhāgavuttino vihareyyāma, amhesu mahallakataraṃ jānitvā tassa abhivādanādīni karissāmā’ti sādhukaṃ vīmaṃsitvā ‘ayaṃ no mahallako’ti ñatvā tassa abhivādanādīni katvā devapathaṃ pūrayamānā gatā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

When the night grew bright, he had the Saṅgha of bhikkhus assembled and asked them: “Is it true, bhikkhus, that the group of six bhikkhus go on ahead and reserve the lodgings of the elder bhikkhus?” “It is true, Blessed One.” Then, after rebuking the group of six bhikkhus and giving a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus, who is worthy of the chief seat, the chief water, and the chief portion of almsfood?” Some said: “One who has gone forth from a khattiya family.” Others said: “One who has gone forth from a brahmin family or a householder family.” Others said: “A master of the Vinaya, a preacher of the Dhamma, one who has attained the first jhānas, the second, the third, or the fourth jhānas.” Still others said: “A stream-enterer, a once-returner, a non-returner, an arahant, one with the threefold true knowledge, or one with the six supernormal powers.” When the bhikkhus had thus spoken according to their own inclinations about who is worthy of the chief seat and so on, the Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, in my Dispensation, the measure is not that one has gone forth from a khattiya family, a brahmin family, or a householder family; nor is it that one is a master of the Vinaya, the Suttas, or the Abhidhamma; nor that one is an attainer of the first jhānas and so on; nor that one is a stream-enterer or the like. Rather, bhikkhus, in this Dispensation, salutation, rising up, reverential salutation, and proper conduct should be done according to seniority; the chief seat, the chief water, and the chief portion of almsfood should be received according to seniority. This is the measure here. Therefore, the most senior bhikkhu is the one fit for these things. But now, bhikkhus, Sāriputta is my chief disciple, one who turns the wheel of Dhamma in conformity with the Dhamma; he deserves to receive the lodging next to mine. Yet tonight, being unable to get a lodging, he spent the time at the foot of a tree. If you are so disrespectful and undeferential now, how will you conduct yourselves as time goes on?” Then, in order to admonish them, he related a past incident, saying: “In the past, bhikkhus, even those of animal birth, having reflected, ‘It is not proper for us to live without respect and deference for one another, with unsuitable conduct; we should find out who is the eldest among us and pay respects to him,’ carefully investigated. Having determined, ‘This one is our eldest,’ they paid him respects and thus fulfilled the path to the deva world.”

Atīte himavantappadese ekaṃ mahānigrodhaṃ upanissāya tayo sahāyā vihariṃsu – tittiro, makkaṭo, hatthīti. Te aññamaññaṃ agāravā apatissā asabhāgavuttino ahesuṃ. Atha nesaṃ etadahosi “na yuttaṃ amhākaṃ evaṃ viharituṃ, yaṃnūna mayaṃ yo no mahallakataro, tassa [M 1.0235] abhivādanādīni karontā vihareyyāmā”ti. “Ko pana no mahallakataro”ti cintentā ekadivasaṃ “attheso upāyo”ti tayopi janā nigrodhamūle nisīditvā tittiro ca makkaṭo ca hatthiṃ pucchiṃsu “samma hatthi, tvaṃ imaṃ nigrodharukkhaṃ kīvappamāṇakālato paṭṭhāya jānāsī”ti? So āha “sammā, ahaṃ taruṇapotakakāle imaṃ nigrodhagacchaṃ antarasatthīsu katvā gacchāmi, avattharitvā ṭhitakāle ca pana me etassa aggasākhā nābhiṃ ghaṭṭeti, evāhaṃ imaṃ gacchakālato paṭṭhāya jānāmī”ti puna ubhopi janā purimanayeneva makkaṭaṃ pucchiṃsu. So āha “ahaṃ sammā makkaṭacchāpako samāno bhūmiyaṃ nisīditvā gīvaṃ [P 1.0219] anukkhipitvāva imassa nigrodhapotakassa aggaṅkure khādāmi, evāhaṃ imaṃ khuddakakālato paṭṭhāya jānāmī”ti. Atha itare ubhopi purimanayeneva tittiraṃ pucchiṃsu. So āha “sammā, pubbe asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne mahānigrodharukkho ahosi, ahaṃ tassa phalāni khāditvā imasmiṃ ṭhāne vaccaṃ pātesiṃ, tato esa rukkho jāto, evāhaṃ imaṃ ajātakālato paṭṭhāya jānāmi, tasmā ahaṃ tumhehi jātiyā mahallakataro”ti.

In the past, in the Himalayan region, three friends lived depending on a great banyan tree—a partridge, a monkey, and an elephant. They lived without respect for one another, without deference, and in disharmony. Then it occurred to them: 'It is not proper for us to live like this. Let us find out who is the eldest among us and then live paying him homage and so forth.' As they were considering, 'But who among us is the eldest?' one day they thought, 'Here is a way.' All three sat down at the foot of the banyan tree, and the partridge and the monkey asked the elephant: 'Friend elephant, since what time have you known this banyan tree?' He replied: 'Friends, when I was a young calf, I would walk over this banyan sapling, passing with it between my thighs. And when I stood over it, its topmost branch would touch my navel. Thus I have known this tree since it was a sapling.' Then the other two asked the monkey in the same way. He replied: 'Friends, when I was a baby monkey, I would sit on the ground and, without stretching my neck, I could eat the topmost shoots of this banyan sapling. Thus I have known this tree since it was small.' Then the other two asked the partridge in the same way. He replied: 'Friends, formerly in a certain place there was a great banyan tree. I ate its fruits and dropped my excrement in this spot. From that, this tree grew. Thus I have known this tree since before it was born. Therefore, I am the eldest of you by birth.'

Evaṃ vutte makkaṭo ca hatthī ca tittirapaṇḍitaṃ āhaṃsu “samma, tvaṃ amhehi mahallakataro, ito paṭṭhāya mayaṃ tava sakkāragarukāramānanavandanapūjanāni ceva abhivādanapaccuṭṭhānaañjalikammasāmīcikammāni ca karissāma, ovāde ca te ṭhassāma, tvaṃ pana ito paṭṭhāya amhākaṃ ovādānusāsaniṃ dadeyyāsī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya tittiro tesaṃ ovādaṃ adāsi, sīlesu patiṭṭhāpesi, sayampi sīlāni samādiyi. Te tayopi janā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāya aññamaññaṃ sagāravā sappatissā sabhāgavuttino hutvā jīvitapariyosāne [V 1.0216] devalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ. Tesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ samādānaṃ tittiriyaṃ brahmacariyaṃ nāma ahosi.

When this was said, the monkey and the elephant said to the wise partridge: 'Friend, you are the eldest of us. From now on, we will offer you honor, respect, reverence, and veneration, and we will perform the duties of paying homage, rising up, making the añjali salutation, and proper service. We will stand by your advice, and may you, from now on, give us counsel and instruction.' From that time on, the partridge gave them advice and established them in the moral precepts, and he himself undertook the precepts. Those three, established in the five precepts, lived with mutual respect, deference, and in harmony. At the end of their lives, they were destined for the deva world. The undertaking of these three came to be known as the Tittiriya holy life.

Te hi nāma, bhikkhave, tiracchānagatā aññamaññaṃ sagāravā sappatissā vihariṃsu, tumhe evaṃ svākhāte dhammavinaye pabbajitvā kasmā aññamaññaṃ agāravā apatissā viharatha. Anujānāmi, bhikkhave, ito paṭṭhāya tumhākaṃ yathāvuḍḍhaṃ abhivādanaṃ paccuṭṭhānaṃ añjalikammaṃ sāmīcikammaṃ, yathāvuḍḍhaṃ aggāsanaṃ aggodakaṃ aggapiṇḍaṃ, na ito paṭṭhāya ca navakatarena vuḍḍhataro [M 1.0236] senāsanena paṭibāhitabbo, yo paṭibāheyya, āpattidukkaṭassāti evaṃ satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

'Monks, if even those born as animals could live with mutual respect and deference, why do you, having gone forth in this well-expounded Dhamma and Discipline, live without respect and deference for one another? Monks, from now on I allow you paying homage, rising up, making the añjali salutation, and performing proper duties according to seniority; and the chief seat, the chief water, and the chief almsfood according to seniority. And from now on, a junior monk should not keep a senior monk from a lodging. Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing.' Thus the Teacher delivered this Dhamma discourse, and then, as the Fully Enlightened One, he spoke this verse:

37.

37.

“Ye vuḍḍhamapacāyanti, narā dhammassa kovidā;

Diṭṭheva dhamme pāsaṃsā, samparāye ca suggatī”ti.

Those persons who revere the elders, who are skilled in the Dhamma, are praised in this very life and find a good destination in the life to come.

Tattha ye vuḍḍhamapacāyantīti jātivuḍḍho, vayovuḍḍho, guṇavuḍḍhoti tayo vuḍḍhā. Tesu jātisampanno jātivuḍḍho nāma, vaye ṭhito vayovuḍḍho nāma[P 1.0220], guṇasampanno guṇavuḍḍho nāma. Tesu guṇasampanno vayovuḍḍho imasmiṃ ṭhāne “vuḍḍho”ti adhippeto. Apacāyantīti jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammena pūjenti. Dhammassa kovidāti jeṭṭhāpacāyanadhammassa kovidā kusalā. Diṭṭheva dhammeti imasmiṃyeva attabhāve. Pāsaṃsāti pasaṃsārahā. Samparāye ca suggatīti samparetabbe imaṃ lokaṃ hitvā gantabbe paralokepi tesaṃ sugatiyeva hotīti. Ayaṃ panettha piṇḍattho – bhikkhave, khattiyā vā hontu brāhmaṇā vā vessā vā suddā vā gahaṭṭhā vā pabbajitā vā tiracchānagatā vā, ye keci sattā jeṭṭhāpacitikamme chekā kusalā guṇasampannānaṃ vayovuḍḍhānaṃ apacitiṃ karonti, te imasmiñca attabhāve jeṭṭhāpacitikārakāti pasaṃsaṃ vaṇṇanaṃ thomanaṃ labhanti, kāyassa ca bhedā sagge nibbattantīti.

Herein, those who revere the elders: there are three kinds of elders: an elder by birth, an elder by age, and an elder by virtue. One of high birth is called an elder by birth; one advanced in age is called an elder by age; one endowed with virtue is called an elder by virtue. Among these, the elder by virtue and the elder by age are intended here by 'elder.' Revere means they honor them with acts of respect for seniority. Skilled in the Dhamma means they are skilled and expert in the Dhamma of revering elders. In this very life means in this very existence. Are praised means they are worthy of praise. And a good destination in the life to come means that in the future, when they have left this world and gone to the next, their destination is a good one. This is the summary meaning here: Monks, whether they are khattiyas, brahmins, vessas, or suddas, householders or those gone forth, or even animals—whatever beings are clever and skilled in the act of revering elders and show respect to those who are elders by virtue and by age, they gain praise, commendation, and acclaim in this very life as 'those who show respect to their elders,' and with the breakup of the body, they are reborn in heaven.

Evaṃ satthā jeṭṭhāpacitikammassa guṇaṃ kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā hatthināgo moggallāno ahosi, makkaṭo sāriputto, tittirapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, having spoken on the virtue of the act of revering elders, connected the links and identified the birth: 'At that time, the great elephant was Moggallāna, the monkey was Sāriputta, and the wise partridge was myself.'

Tittirajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka, the Seventh.

[38] 8. Bakajātakavaṇṇanā

[38] 8. The Commentary on the Baka Jātaka

Nāccantaṃ [V 1.0217][M 1.0237] nikatippaññoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto cīvaravaḍḍhakaṃ bhikkhu ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira jetavanavāsiko bhikkhu yaṃkiñci cīvare kattabbaṃ chedanaghaṭṭanavicāraṇasibbanādikaṃ kammaṃ, tattha sukusalo. So tāya kusalatāya cīvaraṃ vaḍḍheti, tasmā “cīvaravaḍḍhako” tveva paññāyittha. Kiṃ panesa karotīti? Jiṇṇapilotikāsu hatthakammaṃ dassetvā suphassikaṃ manāpaṃ cīvaraṃ katvā rajanapariyosāne piṭṭhodakena rajitvā saṅkhena ghaṃsitvā ujjalaṃ manuññaṃ katvā nikkhipati. Cīvarakammaṃ kātuṃ ajānantā bhikkhū ahate sāṭake gahetvā tassa santikaṃ āgantvā “mayaṃ cīvaraṃ kātuṃ na jānāma, cīvaraṃ no katvā dethā”ti vadanti. So “cīvaraṃ āvuso kariyamānaṃ cirena niṭṭhāti, mayā katacīvarameva atthi, ime sāṭake ṭhapetvā taṃ gaṇhitvā gacchathā”ti nīharitvā dasseti. Te tassa vaṇṇasampattimeva disvā antaraṃ ajānantā “thira”nti saññāya ahatasāṭake cīvaravaḍḍhakassa datvā taṃ gaṇhitvā gacchanti. Taṃ tehi thokaṃ kiliṭṭhakāle uṇhodakena dhoviyamānaṃ attano pakatiṃ dasseti, tattha tattha jiṇṇaṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati, te vippaṭisārino honti. Evaṃ āgatāgate pilotikāhi vañcento so bhikkhu sabbattha pākaṭo jāto.

“Not entirely by deceitful wisdom…” This the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who was an enhancer of robes. It seems a certain monk dwelling at Jetavana was very skilled in whatever work needed to be done on a robe: cutting, joining, arranging, sewing, and so on. Through this skill he would ‘enhance’ robes, and for that reason he became known as ‘the Robe-Enhancer.’ What did he do? Showing his handiwork on old rags, he would make a soft, pleasing robe. At the end of the dyeing process, he would glaze it with rice-water and polish it with a conch shell, making it bright and attractive, and then set it aside. Monks who did not know how to make robes would take new cloths and come to him, saying: “We do not know how to make a robe; please make a robe for us.” He would say: “Friends, making a robe takes a long time. I have a robe already made. Leave these cloths here, take that one, and go.” He would bring it out and show it to them. Seeing only its fine appearance and not knowing its inner substance, they would think it was durable. Giving their new cloths to the Robe-Enhancer, they would take his robe and go. When it became a little soiled and they washed it with warm water, it would reveal its true nature; the worn-out places would become apparent here and there, and they would become regretful. By thus deceiving all who came to him with old rags, that monk became notorious everywhere.

Yathā cesa jetavane, tathā aññatarasmiṃ gāmakepi eko cīvaravaḍḍhako lokaṃ vañceti. Tassa [P 1.0221] sambhattā bhikkhū “bhante, jetavane kira eko cīvaravaḍḍhako evaṃ lokaṃ vañcetī”ti ārocesuṃ. Athassa etadahosi “handāhaṃ, taṃ nagaravāsikaṃ vañcemī”ti pilotikacīvaraṃ atimanāpaṃ katvā surattaṃ rajitvā taṃ pārupitvā jetavanaṃ agamāsi. Itaro taṃ disvāva lobhaṃ uppādetvā “bhante, imaṃ cīvaraṃ tumhehi kata”nti pucchi. “Āmāvuso”ti. “Bhante, imaṃ cīvaraṃ mayhaṃ detha, tumhe aññaṃ labhissathā”ti? “Āvuso, mayaṃ gāmavāsikā dullabhapaccayā, imāhaṃ tuyhaṃ datvā attanā kiṃ pārupissāmī”ti? “Bhante, mama santike ahatasāṭakā atthi, te gahetvā tumhākaṃ cīvaraṃ karothā”ti. “Āvuso, mayā ettha hatthakammaṃ dassitaṃ, tayi pana evaṃ vadante kiṃ sakkā kātuṃ, gaṇhāhi na”nti tassa pilotikacīvaraṃ datvā ahatasāṭake ādāya taṃ vañcetvā pakkāmi. Jetavanavāsikopi [M 1.0238] taṃ cīvaraṃ pārupitvā katipāhaccayena uṇhodakena dhovanto jiṇṇapilotikabhāvaṃ disvā lajjito “gāmavāsicīvaravaḍḍhakena kira jetavanavāsiko vañcito”ti tassa vañcitabhāvo saṅghamajjhe pākaṭo jāto.

Just as this one was in Jetavana, so too in a certain village another Robe-Enhancer was deceiving people. Monks who were his companions reported to him: “Venerable sir, it is said that in Jetavana a Robe-Enhancer is deceiving people in this way.” Then it occurred to him: “Come now, I will deceive that city-dweller!” He made a robe of old rags look very pleasing, dyed it a bright red, put it on, and went to Jetavana. The other saw it and, conceiving a desire for it, asked: “Venerable sir, was this robe made by you?” “Yes, friend.” “Venerable sir, give this robe to me; you will get another.” “Friend, we are village-dwellers, and requisites are hard for us to get. If I give this to you, what will I myself wear?” “Venerable sir, I have some new cloths. Take them and make a robe for yourself.” “Friend, I have put my handiwork into this, but since you speak thus, what can be done? Take it.” Giving him the robe of old rags and taking the new cloths, he deceived him and departed. The Jetavana-dweller wore that robe, but after a few days, when he washed it with hot water, he saw that it was just old rags and felt ashamed. The fact that the Jetavana-dweller had been deceived by the village-dwelling Robe-Enhancer became well-known in the midst of the Sangha.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0218] bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ taṃ kathaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchi. Te tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, jetavanavāsī cīvaravaḍḍhako idāneva aññe vañceti, pubbepi vañcesiyeva. Na gāmavāsikenāpi idāneva esa jetavanavāsī cīvaravaḍḍhako vañcito, pubbepi vañcitoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

One day, the bhikkhus were sitting in the Hall of Dhamma discussing this matter. The Teacher came and asked: “For what discussion, bhikkhus, are you now gathered together?” They told him the matter. The Teacher said: “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this Robe-Enhancer of Jetavana deceives others; he deceived them in the past as well. And it is not only now that this Robe-Enhancer of Jetavana has been deceived by the villager; he was deceived in the past as well.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte ekasmiṃ araññāyatane bodhisatto aññataraṃ padumasaraṃ nissāya ṭhite varaṇarukkhe rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tadā aññatarasmiṃ nātimahante sare nidāghasamaye udakaṃ mandaṃ ahosi, bahū cettha macchā honti. Atheko bako te macche disvā “ekena upāyena ime macche vañcetvā khādissāmī”ti gantvā udakapariyante cintento nisīdi. Atha naṃ macchā disvā “kiṃ, ayya, cintento nisinnosī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Tumhākaṃ cintento nisinnomhī”ti. “Kiṃ amhākaṃ cintesi, ayyā”ti? “‘Imasmiṃ sare udakaṃ parittaṃ, gocaro mando, nidāgho ca mahanto, idānime macchā kiṃ nāma karissantī’ti tumhākaṃ cintento nisinnomhī”ti. “Atha kiṃ karoma, ayyā”ti? “Tumhe sace mayhaṃ vacanaṃ kareyyātha[P 1.0222], ahaṃ vo ekekaṃ mukhatuṇḍakena gahetvā ekaṃ pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchannaṃ mahāsaraṃ netvā vissajjeyya”nti. “Ayya, paṭhamakappikato paṭṭhāya macchānaṃ cintanakabako nāma natthi, tvaṃ amhesu ekekaṃ khāditukāmosī”ti. “Nāhaṃ tumhe mayhaṃ saddahante khādissāmi”. “Sace pana sarassa atthibhāvaṃ mayhaṃ na saddahatha, ekaṃ macchaṃ mayā saddhiṃ saraṃ passituṃ pesethā”ti. Macchā tassa saddahitvā “ayaṃ jalepi thalepi samattho”ti ekaṃ kāḷamahāmacchaṃ adaṃsu “imaṃ gahetvā gacchathā”ti. So taṃ gahetvā netvā sare vissajjetvā sabbaṃ saraṃ dassetvā puna ānetvā tesaṃ macchānaṃ santike vissajjesi. So tesaṃ macchānaṃ sarassa sampattiṃ vaṇṇesi. Te [M 1.0239] tassa kathaṃ sutvā gantukāmā hutvā “sādhu, ayya, amhe gaṇhitvā gacchāhī”ti āhaṃsu.

In the past, in a certain stretch of forest, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree-deity in a varaṇa tree by a lotus lake. At that time, in a certain lake of no great size, the water was low during the hot season, and there were many fish in it. Then a heron, seeing those fish, thought: “By some stratagem I will deceive and eat these fish.” He went and sat on the water’s edge, absorbed in thought. The fish saw him and asked: “Sir, what are you sitting and thinking about?” “I am thinking about you.” “What are you thinking about us, sir?” “I am thinking about you: ‘In this lake the water is low, the feeding ground is scanty, and the heat is great. What will these fish do now?’” “Then what should we do, sir?” “If you would do my bidding, I would take you one by one in my beak, bring you to a great lake covered with five-colored lotuses, and release you there.” “Sir, from the beginning of the world-cycle, there has never been a heron concerned about fish. You want to eat us one by one!” “I will not eat you who trust me. But if you do not trust me about the existence of the lake, send one fish with me to see it.” The fish trusted him and, thinking, “This one is capable both in water and on land,” they gave him a large black fish, saying: “Take this one and go.” The heron took it, brought it to the lake and released it, showed it the entire lake, and then brought it back and released it in the presence of the other fish. That fish described to them the splendors of the lake. Hearing its words, they became eager to go and said: “Very well, sir, take us and go.”

Bako paṭhamaṃ taṃ kāḷamahāmacchameva gahetvā saratīraṃ netvā saraṃ dassetvā saratīre jāte varaṇarukkhe nilīyitvā taṃ viṭapantare pakkhipitvā tuṇḍena vijjhanto jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā kaṇṭake rukkhamūle pātetvā puna gantvā “vissaṭṭho, me so maccho, añño āgacchatū”ti etenupāyena ekekaṃ gahetvā sabbe macche khāditvā puna āgato ekaṃ macchampi nāddasa. Eko panettha kakkaṭako avasiṭṭho. Bako tampi khāditukāmo hutvā “bho, kakkaṭaka, mayā sabbete macchā netvā padumasañchanne mahāsare vissajjitā, ehi tampi nessāmī”ti. “Maṃ gahetvā gacchanto kathaṃ gaṇhissasī”ti? “Ḍaṃsitvā gaṇhissāmī”ti. “Tvaṃ [V 1.0219] evaṃ gahetvā gacchanto maṃ pātessasi, nāhaṃ tayā saddhiṃ gamissāmī”ti. “Mā bhāyi, ahaṃ taṃ suggahitaṃ gahetvā gamissāmī”ti. Kakkaṭako cintesi “imassa macche netvā sare vissajjanaṃ nāma natthi. Sace pana maṃ sare vissajjessati, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce vissajjessati, gīvamassa chinditvā jīvitaṃ harissāmī”ti.

The heron first took that very large black fish, and having carried it to the lake shore and shown it the lake, he alighted on a varaṇa tree growing on the shore. He placed the fish in a fork of the branches, and pecking it with his beak, he brought about its death. He ate its flesh and dropped the bones at the foot of the tree. Then he went back and said, “That fish has been released by me; let another come.” By this stratagem, he took all the fish one by one and ate them. When he came back again, he did not see even a single fish. Only one crab was left there. The heron, wanting to eat it too, said, “O crab, I have taken all those fish and released them in a great lake covered with lotuses. Come, I will take you too.” The crab asked, “While carrying me, how will you take hold of me?” “I will take hold of you by biting,” said the heron. “Carrying me like that, you will drop me. I will not go with you.” “Do not be afraid. I will take you, holding you securely.” The crab thought, “For this one, there is no such thing as taking fish and releasing them in a lake. If, however, he should release me in the lake, that would be excellent. If he does not release me, I will sever his neck and take his life.”

Atha naṃ evamāha “samma baka, na kho tvaṃ suggahitaṃ gahetuṃ sakkhissasi, amhākaṃ pana gahaṇaṃ suggahaṇaṃ[P 1.0223], sacāhaṃ aḷehi tava gīvaṃ gahetuṃ labhissāmi, tava gīvaṃ suggahitaṃ katvā tayā saddhiṃ gamissāmī”ti. So taṃ “vañcetukāmo esa ma”nti ajānanto “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Kakkaṭako attano aḷehi kammārasaṇḍāsena viya tassa gīvaṃ suggahitaṃ katvā “idāni gacchā”ti āha. So taṃ netvā saraṃ dassetvā varaṇarukkhābhimukho pāyāsi. Kakkaṭako āha “mātula, ayaṃ saro etto, tvaṃ pana ito kiṃ nesī”ti? Bako “na te mātulo ahaṃ, na bhaginiputtosi vata me tva”nti vatvā “tvaṃ ‘esa maṃ ukkhipitvā vicaranto mayhaṃ dāso’ti saññaṃ karosi maññe, passetaṃ varaṇarukkhassa mūle kaṇṭakarāsiṃ, yathā me te sabbe macchā khāditā, tampi tatheva khādissāmī”ti āha. Kakkaṭako “ete macchā attano bālatāya tayā khāditā, ahaṃ pana te maṃ khādituṃ na dassāmi, taññeva pana vināsaṃ pāpessāmi. Tvañhi [M 1.0240] bālatāya mayā vañcitabhāvaṃ na jānāsi, marantā ubhopi marissāma, ahaṃ te sīsaṃ chinditvā bhūmiyaṃ khipissāmī”ti vatvā kammārasaṇḍāsena viya aḷehi tassa gīvaṃ nippīḷesi. So vivaṭena mukhena akkhīhi assunā paggharantena maraṇabhayatajjito “sāmi, ahaṃ taṃ na khādissāmi, jīvitaṃ me dehī”ti āha. “Yadi evaṃ otaritvā maṃ sarasmiṃ vissajjehī”ti. So nivattitvā sarameva otaritvā kakkaṭakaṃ sarapariyante paṅkapiṭṭhe ṭhapesi, kakkaṭako kattarikāya kumudanāḷaṃ kappento viya tassa gīvaṃ kappetvā udakaṃ pāvisi.

Then the crab said to him, “Friend heron, you will not be able to take a secure hold of me, but our grip is very secure. If I might take hold of your neck with my pincers, I will make my grip secure on your neck and go with you.” The heron, not realizing, “This one wants to deceive me,” agreed, saying, “Very well.” The crab, with its pincers, took a secure hold of the heron’s neck as if with a blacksmith’s tongs and said, “Now, go.” The heron carried him, showed him the lake, and then proceeded towards the varaṇa tree. The crab asked, “Uncle, this lake is over here, but where are you taking me from here?” The heron replied, “I am not your uncle, and you are certainly not my nephew! You seem to think, ‘This one who carries me about is my slave.’ Look at that pile of bones at the foot of the varaṇa tree. Just as I ate all those fish, so I will eat you too.” The crab said, “Those fish were eaten by you because of their own folly, but I will not let you eat me.
