Instead, I will bring about your destruction. In your folly, you did not realize that you were being deceived by me. If we are to die, we shall both die. I will cut off your head and cast it upon the ground.” Saying this, he squeezed the heron’s neck with his pincers as if with a blacksmith’s tongs. With his mouth gaping open, tears streaming from his eyes, and terrified by the fear of death, the heron pleaded, “Master, I will not eat you! Grant me my life!” “If that is so, then descend and release me in the lake.” The heron turned back, descended to the lake, and placed the crab on the mud at the water’s edge. The crab, as if snipping a water lily stalk with shears, severed the heron’s neck and entered the water.

Taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā varaṇarukkhe adhivatthā devatā sādhukāraṃ dadamānā vanaṃ unnādayamānā madhurassarena imaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing this wonderful event, the deity dwelling in the varaṇa tree gave a cry of approval and, making the forest resound with a sweet voice, spoke this verse:

38.

38.

“Nāccantaṃ nikatippañño, nikatyā sukhamedhati;

Ārādheti nikatippañño, bako kakkaṭakāmivā”ti.

“One of treacherous wisdom does not find lasting happiness through deceit; the treacherous one reaps his due, just as the heron did from the crab.”

Tattha nāccantaṃ nikatippañño, nikatyā sukhamedhatīti nikati vuccati vañcanā, nikatippañño [V 1.0220] vañcanapañño puggalo tāya nikatyā nikatiyā vañcanāya [P 1.0224] na accantaṃ sukhamedhati, niccakāle sukhasmiṃyeva patiṭṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, ekaṃsena pana vināsaṃ pāpuṇātiyevāti attho. Ārādhetīti paṭilabhati. Nikatippaññoti kerāṭikabhāvaṃ sikkhitapañño pāpapuggalo attanā katassa pāpassa phalaṃ ārādheti paṭilabhati vindatīti attho. Kathaṃ? Bako kakkaṭakāmiva, yathā bako kakkaṭakā gīvacchedaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ pāpapuggalo attanā katapāpato diṭṭhadhamme vā samparāye vā bhayaṃ ārādheti paṭilabhatīti imamatthaṃ pakāsento mahāsatto vanaṃ unnādento dhammaṃ desesi.

Herein, 'one of treacherous wisdom does not find lasting happiness through deceit': 'treachery' means deception; a person of treacherous wisdom, of deceptive wisdom, does not find lasting happiness through that treachery, that deception. He is unable to remain established in happiness forever; the meaning is that he inevitably meets with destruction. 'Reaps': this means he obtains. 'The treacherous one': an evil person whose wisdom is trained in roguery. The meaning is that such an evil person reaps, obtains, and experiences the fruit of the evil he himself has done. How? 'As the heron did from the crab': just as the heron met with the severing of its neck from the crab, so an evil person, on account of the evil he has done, reaps and obtains fear either in this present life or in the life to come. Expounding this meaning, the Great Being taught the Dhamma, making the forest resound.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva gāmavāsicīvaravaḍḍhakenesa vañcito, atītepi vañcitoyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā so bako jetavanavāsī cīvaravaḍḍhako ahosi, kakkaṭako gāmavāsī cīvaravaḍḍhako, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this one has been deceived by the village-dwelling robe-maker; he was deceived in the past as well.” Then he made the connection and identified the birth: “At that time, the heron was the robe-maker dwelling in Jetavana, the crab was the village-dwelling robe-maker, and the tree-deity was I myself.”

Bakajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Baka Jātaka, the Eighth.

[39] 9. Nandajātakavaṇṇanā

[39] 9. The Commentary on the Nanda Jātaka

Maññe [M 1.0241] sovaṇṇayo rāsīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sāriputtattherassa saddhivihārikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira bhikkhu subbaco ahosi vacanakkhamo, therassa mahantenussāhena upakāraṃ karoti. Athekaṃ samayaṃ thero satthāraṃ āpucchitvā cārikaṃ caranto dakkhiṇāgirijanapadaṃ agamāsi. So bhikkhu tattha gatakāle mānatthaddho hutvā therassa vacanaṃ na karoti “āvuso, idaṃ nāma karohī”ti vutte pana therassa paṭipakkho hoti. Thero tassa āsayaṃ na jānāti. So tattha cārikaṃ caritvā puna jetavanaṃ āgato. So bhikkhu therassa jetavanavihāraṃ āgatakālato paṭṭhāya puna tādisova jāto. Thero tathāgatassa ārocesi “bhante, mayhaṃ eko saddhivihāriko ekasmiṃ ṭhāne satena kītadāso viya hoti, ekasmiṃ ṭhāne mānatthaddho hutvā ‘idaṃ nāma karohī’ti vutte paṭipakkho hotī”ti. Satthā “nāyaṃ, sāriputta, bhikkhu idāneva evaṃsīlo, pubbepesa ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ gato satena kītadāso viya hoti. Ekaṃ ṭhānaṃ gato paṭipakkho paṭisattu hotī”ti vatvā therena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“I think it is a heap of gold.” This the Teacher said while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a co-resident of the Venerable Sāriputta. It seems that bhikkhu was compliant and easy to speak to, and he served the Venerable Elder with great diligence. Then on one occasion, the Venerable Elder took leave of the Teacher and, while wandering on tour, went to the Dakkhiṇāgiri country. When that bhikkhu went there, he became proud and stubborn and would not do what the Venerable Elder said. When told, “Friend, do this,” he would become hostile to the Venerable Elder. The Venerable Elder did not know his disposition. After wandering on tour there, he returned to Jetavana. From the time that bhikkhu arrived back at the Jetavana monastery, he became just as he was before. The Venerable Elder reported this to the Tathāgata: “Venerable sir, a certain co-resident of mine is like a slave bought for a hundred coins in one place, but in another place he becomes proud and stubborn, and when told, ‘Do this,’ he becomes hostile.” The Teacher said: “Sāriputta, it is not only now that this bhikkhu has such a nature; in the past, too, when he went to one place he was like a slave bought for a hundred coins, and when he went to another place he became an opposing enemy.” Having said this, at the Venerable Elder's request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0221] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ kuṭumbiyakule paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tasseko sahāyako kuṭumbiko sayaṃ mahallako, bhariyā panassa [P 1.0225] taruṇī. Sā taṃ nissāya puttaṃ paṭilabhi. So cintesi “ayaṃ itthī taruṇattā mamaccayena kañcideva purisaṃ gahetvā imaṃ dhanaṃ vināseyya, puttassa me na dadeyya, yaṃnūnāhaṃ imaṃ dhanaṃ pathavigataṃ kareyya”nti ghare nandaṃ nāma dāsaṃ gahetvā araññaṃ gantvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne taṃ dhanaṃ nidahitvā tassa ācikkhitvā “tāta, nanda, imaṃ dhanaṃ mamaccayena mayhaṃ puttassa ācikkheyyāsi, mā ca naṃ pariccajasī”ti ovaditvā kālamakāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in a householder's family. He had a householder friend who was himself elderly, but his wife was young. Through him, she conceived a son. He thought: “This woman is young. After my death, she might take some other man, squander this wealth, and not give it to my son. What if I were to bury this wealth in the ground?” Taking a slave in his household named Nanda, he went to the forest, buried the wealth in a certain place, and informed him of it. He then advised him: “My dear Nanda, after my death, you must tell my son about this wealth, and do not abandon him.” Then he passed away.

Puttopissa anukkamena vayappatto jāto. Atha naṃ mātā āha – “tāta, tava pitā nandaṃ dāsaṃ gahetvā dhanaṃ nidhesi, taṃ āharāpetvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapehī”ti. So ekadivasaṃ nandaṃ āha – “mātula, atthi kiñci mayhaṃ pitarā dhanaṃ nidahita”nti. “Āma, sāmī”ti. “Kuhiṃ [M 1.0242] taṃ nidahita”nti. “Araññe, sāmī”ti. “Tena hi gacchāmā”ti kuddālapiṭakaṃ ādāya nidhiṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “kahaṃ mātula, dhana”nti āha. Nando āruyha dhanamatthake ṭhatvā dhanaṃ nissāya mānaṃ uppādetvā “are dāsiputta ceṭaka, kuto te imasmiṃ ṭhāne dhana”nti kumāraṃ akkosati. Kumāro tassa pharusavacanaṃ sutvā asuṇanto viya “tena hi gacchāmā”ti taṃ gahetvā paṭinivattitvā puna dve tayo divase atikkamitvā agamāsi, nando tatheva akkosati. Kumāro tena saddhiṃ pharusavacanaṃ avatvāva nivattitvā “ayaṃ dāso ito paṭṭhāya ‘dhanaṃ ācikkhissāmī’ti gacchati, gantvā pana maṃ akkosati, tattha kāraṇaṃ na jānāmi, atthi kho pana me pitu sahāyo kuṭumbiko, taṃ paṭipucchitvā jānissāmī”ti bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “kiṃ nu kho, tāta, kāraṇa”nti pucchi.

In due course, his son came of age. Then his mother said to him: “My dear, your father took the slave Nanda and buried some wealth. Have it brought here and establish the household.” One day he said to Nanda: “Uncle, is there any wealth that was buried by my father?” “Yes, master.” “Where was it buried?” “In the forest, master.” “Then let us go.” Taking a spade and a basket, he went to the place of the buried treasure and asked: “Where is the wealth, uncle?” Nanda climbed up and stood on top of the wealth, and becoming filled with pride on account of the wealth, he reviled the young man: “You there, you son of a slave woman, you wretch! From where would there be wealth for you in this place?” Hearing his harsh words, the young man, as if he had not heard, said, “Then let us go,” and taking him along, he returned. After two or three days had passed, he went again, and Nanda reviled him in the very same way. Without speaking a harsh word in return, the young man turned back and thought: “This slave goes along saying, ‘I will point out the wealth,’ but having gone there, he reviles me. I do not know the reason for this. But there is a householder who was a friend of my father; I will ask him and find out.” He went to the Bodhisatta, related the entire matter to him, and asked: “My dear, what could be the reason?”

Bodhisatto “yasmiṃ te, tāta, ṭhāne ṭhito nando akkosati, tattheva te pitu santakaṃ dhanaṃ, tasmā yadā te nando akkosati, tadā naṃ ‘ehi re dāsa, kiṃ akkosasī’ti ākaḍḍhitvā taṃ ṭhānaṃ bhinditvā kulasantakaṃ dhanaṃ nīharitvā dāsaṃ ukkhipāpetvā dhanaṃ āharā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta said: “My dear, in the very place where Nanda stands and reviles you, there is your father's wealth. Therefore, when Nanda reviles you, drag him away, saying, ‘Come now, slave, why do you revile me?’ Then break open that spot, take out the family wealth, have the slave carry it, and bring the wealth home.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

39.

39.

“Maññe [P 1.0226] sovaṇṇayo rāsi, sovaṇṇamālā ca nandako;

Yattha dāso āmajāto, ṭhito thullāni gajjatī”ti.

“I think there is a heap of golden things,

and golden garlands, where the slave Nandaka,

born of a slave-woman, stands

and roars out coarse words.”

Tattha [V 1.0222] maññeti evaṃ ahaṃ jānāmi. Sovaṇṇayoti sundaro vaṇṇo etesanti sovaṇṇāni. Kāni tāni? Rajatamaṇikañcanapavāḷādīni ratanāni. Imasmiñhi ṭhāne sabbānetāni “suvaṇṇānī”ti adhippetāni, tesaṃ rāsi sovaṇṇayo rāsi. Sovaṇṇamālā cāti tuyhaṃ pitusantakā suvaṇṇamālā ca etthevāti maññāmi. Nandako yattha dāsoti yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhito nandako dāso. Āmajātoti “āma, ahaṃ vo dāsī”ti evaṃ dāsabyaṃ upagatāya āmadāsisaṅkhātāya dāsiyā putto. Ṭhito thullāni gajjatīti “so yasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhito thullāni pharusavacanāni vadati, tattheva te kulasantakaṃ dhanaṃ, evaṃ ahaṃ taṃ maññāmī”ti bodhisatto kumārassa dhanaggahaṇūpāyaṃ ācikkhi.

Herein, I think means: thus I know. Golden things: Golden things are those that have a beautiful color. What are they? Jewels such as silver, gems, gold, and coral. In this context, all these are intended by “golden things,” and a heap of them is a heap of golden things. And golden garlands means: I think that the golden garlands belonging to your father are also here. Where Nandaka the slave means: the place where Nandaka the slave stands. Born of a slave-woman means: the son of a slave-woman called an “āmadāsī” (a “yes-slave”) because she has entered servitude by saying, “Yes, I am your slave.” Stands and roars coarse words means: “In the very place where he stands and speaks coarse, harsh words, there is your family's wealth; thus I think.” In this way the Bodhisatta explained to the young man the method for retrieving the wealth.

Kumāro [M 1.0243] bodhisattaṃ vanditvā gharaṃ gantvā nandaṃ ādāya nidhiṭṭhānaṃ gantvā yathānusiṭṭhaṃ paṭipajjitvā taṃ dhanaṃ āharitvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhito dānādīni puññāni katvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.

The young man paid homage to the Bodhisatta and returned home. He took Nanda, went to the place of the buried treasure, and acted according to the instructions. He retrieved the wealth, established his household, and, abiding by the Bodhisatta’s advice, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms. At the end of his life, he passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā “pubbepesa evaṃsīloyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā nando sāriputtassa saddhivihāriko ahosi, paṇḍitakuṭumbiko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, saying, “In the past, too, he was of such a nature,” delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection, and identified the birth: “At that time, Nanda was Sāriputta's co-resident, and the wise householder was myself.”

Nandajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Nanda Jātaka, the Ninth.

[40] 10. Khadiraṅgārajātakavaṇṇanā

[40] 10. The Commentary on the Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka

Kāmaṃ patāmi nirayanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Anāthapiṇḍiko hi vihārameva ārabbha catupaññāsakoṭidhanaṃ buddhasāsane pariccajitvā vikiritvā ṭhapetvā tīṇi ratanāni aññattha ratanasaññameva anuppādetvā satthari jetavane viharante devasikaṃ tīṇi mahāupaṭṭhānāni gacchati. Pātova ekavāraṃ gacchati, katapātarāso ekavāraṃ, sāyanhe ekavāraṃ. Aññānipi antarantarupaṭṭhānāni hontiyeva. Gacchanto ca “kiṃ nu kho ādāya āgatoti sāmaṇerā vā daharā vā hatthampi me olokeyyu”nti tucchahattho nāma na gatapubbo. Pātova gacchanto yāguṃ gāhāpetvā [P 1.0227] gacchati, katapātarāso sappinavanītamadhuphāṇitādīnipi, sāyanhasamaye gandhamālāvatthādihatthoti. Evaṃ divase divase pariccajantassa panassa pariccāge pamāṇaṃ natthi.

“Willingly I would fall into hell.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning Anāthapiṇḍika. For Anāthapiṇḍika, on account of the monastery alone, had given up and scattered fifty-four crores of wealth for the Buddha's Dispensation, and apart from the Three Jewels, he did not conceive of anything else as a jewel. When the Teacher was dwelling at Jetavana, he would attend upon him with three great services daily. He went once in the early morning, once after his morning meal, and once in the evening. There were also other intermittent services. And when he went, he never went empty-handed, thinking, “The novices or young monks might look at my hands to see what I have brought.” When going in the early morning, he would have rice gruel brought; after his morning meal, such things as ghee, fresh butter, honey, and molasses; and in the evening, he would have perfumes, garlands, and cloth in his hands. Thus, as he gave day after day, there was no measure to his giving.

Bahū [V 1.0223] vohārūpajīvinopissa hatthato paṇṇe āropetvā aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanaṃ iṇaṃ gaṇhiṃsu, te mahāseṭṭhi na āharāpeti. Aññā panassa kulasantakā aṭṭhārasa koṭiyo nadītīre nidahitvā ṭhapitā aciravatodakena nadīkūle bhinne mahāsamuddaṃ paviṭṭhā, tā yathāpihitalañchi tāva lohacāṭiyo aṇḍavakucchiyaṃ pavaṭṭantā vicaranti. Gehe [M 1.0244] panassa pañcannaṃ bhikkhusatānaṃ niccabhattaṃ nibaddhameva hoti. Seṭṭhino hi gehaṃ bhikkhusaṅghassa catumahāpathe khatapokkharaṇisadisaṃ, sabbabhikkhūnaṃ mātāpituṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ. Tenassa gharaṃ sammāsambuddhopi gacchati, asītimahātherāpi gacchantiyeva. Sesabhikkhūnaṃ pana gacchantānañca āgacchantānañca pamāṇaṃ natthi. Taṃ pana gharaṃ sattabhūmakaṃ sattadvārakoṭṭhakapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ, tassa catutthe dvārakoṭṭhake ekā micchādiṭṭhikā devatā vasati, sā sammāsambuddhe gehaṃ pavisante attano vimāne ṭhātuṃ na sakkoti, dārake gahetvā otaritvā bhūmiyaṃ tiṭṭhati. Asītimahātheresupi avasesattheresupi pavisantesu ca nikkhamantesu ca tatheva karoti. Sā cintesi “samaṇe gotame ca sāvakesu cassa imaṃ gehaṃ pavisantesu mayhaṃ sukhaṃ nāma natthi, niccakālaṃ otaritvā otaritvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhātuṃ na sakkhissāmi. Yathā ime etaṃ gharaṃ na pavisanti, tathā mayā kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Athekadivasaṃ sayanūpagatasseva mahākammantikassa santikaṃ gantvā obhāsaṃ pharitvā aṭṭhāsi. “Ko etthā”ti ca vutte “ahaṃ catutthadvārakoṭṭhake nibbattadevatā”ti āha. “Kasmā āgatāsī”ti? “Kiṃ tumhe seṭṭhissa kiriyaṃ na passatha, attano pacchimakālaṃ anoloketvā dhanaṃ nīharitvā samaṇaṃ gotamaṃyeva pūjeti, neva vaṇijjaṃ payojeti, na kammante paṭṭhapeti, tumhe seṭṭhiṃ tathā ovadatha, yathā attano kammantaṃ karoti. Yathā ca samaṇo gotamo sasāvako imaṃ gharaṃ na pavisati, tathā karothā”ti. Atha naṃ so āha “bāladevate, seṭṭhi dhanaṃ vissajjento niyyānike buddhasāsane vissajjeti, so sace maṃ cūḷāyaṃ gahetvā vikkiṇissati, nevāhaṃ kiñci kathessāmi, gaccha tvaṃ”nti. Sā punekadivasaṃ seṭṭhino jeṭṭhaputtaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tatheva ovadi, sopi taṃ purimanayeneva tajjesi. Seṭṭhinā pana saddhiṃ kathetuṃyeva na sakkoti.

Many who lived by trade, having deposited promissory notes in his hand, took loans amounting to eighteen crores, but the great merchant did not call them in. Another eighteen crores of his family wealth, which had been buried on the riverbank, entered the great ocean when the bank was broken by the water of the Aciravatī river. Those iron pots, still sealed just as they had been hidden, now roll about and drift in the belly of the ocean. In his house, a regular meal for five hundred bhikkhus was always established. Indeed, the merchant’s house was like a lotus pond dug at a great crossroads for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus; it stood in the place of mother and father for all the bhikkhus. Therefore, the Perfectly Enlightened One would go to his house, and the eighty great elders would also go. As for the other bhikkhus coming and going, there was no measure. That house was seven stories high, adorned with seven gate-chambers. In its fourth gate-chamber dwelt a devatā of wrong view. When the Perfectly Enlightened One entered the house, she was unable to remain in her celestial mansion; taking her children, she would descend and stand on the ground. She did the same when the eighty great elders and the remaining elders entered and left. She thought: ‘When the ascetic Gotama and his disciples enter this house, there is no happiness for me. I will not be able to keep descending and standing on the ground all the time. I must act in such a way that they do not enter this house.’ Then one day, she went to the chief steward while he was lying down to sleep, suffused him with light, and stood there. When he asked, ‘Who is there?’ she replied, ‘I am the devatā who has arisen in the fourth gate-chamber.’ ‘Why have you come?’ ‘Do you not see what the merchant is doing? Without considering his own future, he takes out his wealth and honors only the ascetic Gotama. He neither engages in trade nor establishes businesses. You should advise the merchant so that he attends to his own business, and you should act so that the ascetic Gotama and his disciples do not enter this house.’ Then he said to her: ‘Foolish devatā, the merchant dispenses his wealth in the Buddha’s Dispensation, which leads to release. If he were to seize me by the topknot and sell me, I would not say a thing. Go away!’ Another day, she approached the merchant’s eldest son and advised him in the same way. He too rebuked her in the same manner. But with the merchant himself, she was unable even to speak.

Seṭṭhinopi nirantaraṃ dānaṃ dentassa [P 1.0228] vohāre akarontassa āye mandībhūte dhanaṃ parikkhayaṃ agamāsi. Athassa anukkamena dāliddiyappattassa paribhogasāṭakasayanabhojanānipi purāṇasadisāni na bhaviṃsu. Evaṃbhūtopi bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ deti, paṇītaṃ pana katvā dātuṃ na sakkoti[M 1.0245]. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ vanditvā nisinnaṃ satthā “dīyati pana te, gahapati, kule dāna”nti pucchi. So “dīyati, bhante, tañca kho kaṇājakaṃ bilaṅgadutiya”nti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “gahapati, ‘lūkhaṃ dānaṃ demī’ti mā cittaṃ saṅkocayittha[V 1.0224]. Cittasmiñhi paṇīte buddhapaccekabuddhabuddhasāvakānaṃ dinnadānaṃ lūkhaṃ nāma na hoti. Kasmā? Vipākamahantattā”ti āha. Cittañhi paṇītaṃ kātuṃ sakkontassa dānaṃ lūkhaṃ nāma natthīti cetaṃ evaṃ veditabbaṃ –

As the merchant was constantly giving alms and not engaging in trade, his income dwindled and his wealth came to an end. Then, as he gradually fell into poverty, his clothing, bedding, and food were no longer as they were before. Even in this state, he still gave alms to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, but he was unable to prepare and give anything refined. Then one day, as he was sitting after having paid homage, the Teacher asked him: ‘Householder, is alms-giving still carried on in your family?’ He replied: ‘It is given, venerable sir, but it is only broken rice with sour gruel as the second item.’ Then the Teacher said to him: ‘Householder, do not be disheartened thinking, “I am giving a coarse gift.” For when the mind is refined, a gift given to Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and the disciples of a Buddha is not called coarse. Why? Because of the greatness of its result.’ For one who is able to make the mind refined, there is no such thing as a coarse gift. This should be understood thus:

“Natthi citte pasannamhi, appakā nāma dakkhiṇā;

Tathāgate vā sambuddhe, atha vā tassa sāvake. (vi. va. 804);

“When the mind is serene, no offering is small, whether to the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Enlightened One, or to his disciple.”

“Na kiratthi anomadassisu, pāricariyā buddhesu appakā;

Sukkhāya aloṇikāya ca, passa phalaṃ kummāsapiṇḍiyā”ti.

“Indeed, no service to the Buddhas of noble vision is small. See the fruit of a lump of barley-meal, dry and without salt!”

Aparampi naṃ āha “gahapati, tvaṃ tāva lūkhaṃ dānaṃ dadamāno aṭṭhannaṃ ariyapuggalānaṃ desi, ahaṃ velāmakāle sakalajambudīpaṃ unnaṅgalaṃ katvā satta ratanāni dadamāno pañca mahānadiyo ekoghapuṇṇaṃ katvā viya ca mahādānaṃ pavattayamāno tisaraṇagataṃ vā pañcasīlarakkhanakaṃ vā kañci nālatthaṃ, dakkhiṇeyyapuggalā nāma evaṃ dullabhā. Tasmā ‘lūkhaṃ me dāna’nti mā cittaṃ saṅkocayitthā”ti evañca pana vatvā velāmasuttaṃ (a. ni. 9.20) kathesi.

He said to him further: ‘Householder, though you give a coarse gift, you give it to the eight noble persons. When I was the brahmin Velāma, I gave a great gift, making the whole of Jambudīpa plowless, giving the seven kinds of gems, and making the five great rivers flow as a single stream, yet I did not find anyone who had gone for refuge to the Three Jewels or who observed the five precepts. So rare are persons worthy of offerings. Therefore, do not be disheartened thinking, “My gift is coarse.”’ And having said this, he delivered the Velāma Sutta (AN 9.20).

Atha kho sā devatā issarakāle seṭṭhinā saddhiṃ kathetumpi asakkontī “idānāyaṃ duggatattā mama vacanaṃ gaṇhissatī”ti maññamānā aḍḍharattasamaye sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā obhāsaṃ pharitvā ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Seṭṭhi taṃ disvā “ko eso”ti āha. “Ahaṃ mahāseṭṭhi catutthadvārakoṭṭhake adhivatthā, devatā”ti. “Kimatthamāgatāsī”ti? “Tuyhaṃ ovādaṃ kathetukāmā hutvā āgacchāmī”ti. “Tena hi kathehī”ti. Mahāseṭṭhi tvaṃ pacchimakālaṃ na cintesi, puttadhītaro na olokesi, samaṇassa te gotamassa sāsane bahuṃ dhanaṃ vippakiṇṇaṃ, so tvaṃ ativelaṃ dhanavissajjanena [P 1.0229] vā vaṇijjādikammānaṃ akaraṇena vā [M 1.0246] samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ nissāya duggato jāto, evaṃbhūtopi samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ na muñcasi, ajjapi te samaṇā gharaṃ pavisantiyeva. Yaṃ tāva tehi nītaṃ, taṃ na sakkā paccāharāpetuṃ, gahitaṃ gahitameva hotu, ito paṭṭhāya pana sayañca samaṇassa gotamassa santikaṃ mā gamittha, sāvakānañcassa imaṃ gharaṃ pavisituṃ mā adāsi, samaṇaṃ gotamaṃ nivattitvāpi anolokento attano vohāre ca vaṇijjañca katvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapehī”ti. Atha naṃ so evamāha “ayaṃ tayā mayhaṃ dātabbaovādo”ti. “Āma, ayyā”ti. Tādisānaṃ devatānaṃ satenapi sahassenapi satasahassenapi [V 1.0225] akampanīyo ahaṃ dasabalena kato. Mama hi saddhā sineru viya acalā suppatiṭṭhitā, mayā niyyānike ratanasāsane dhanaṃ vissajjitaṃ, ayuttaṃ te kathitaṃ, buddhasāsane pahāro dinno, evarūpāya anācārāya dussīlāya kāḷakaṇṇiyā saddhiṃ tayā mama ekagehe vasanakiccaṃ natthi, sīghaṃ mama gehā nikkhamitvā aññattha gacchāti.

Now that devatā, who had been unable even to speak with the merchant in the time of his prosperity, thought, ‘Now that he is destitute, he will take my word.’ At midnight, she entered his magnificent chamber, suffused it with light, and stood in the air. Seeing her, the merchant asked, ‘Who is that?’ ‘Great merchant, I am the devatā who dwells in the fourth gate-chamber.’ ‘For what purpose have you come?’ ‘I have come wishing to give you advice.’ ‘Then speak.’ ‘Great merchant, you do not think of the future, you do not look after your sons and daughters. You have scattered much wealth in the Dispensation of the ascetic Gotama. Through excessive giving of wealth and neglect of trade and business, you have become destitute on account of the ascetic Gotama. Even in this state, you do not give up the ascetic Gotama. Even today the ascetics still enter your house. What has been taken by them cannot be brought back; let what is taken be taken. But from now on, do not yourself go to the ascetic Gotama, and do not allow his disciples to enter this house. Turning away from the ascetic Gotama and paying him no heed, attend to your own affairs and trade and re-establish your household.’ Then he said to her: ‘Is this the advice you have to give me?’ ‘Yes, master.’ ‘I have been made unshakeable by the one with the Ten Powers, not to be swayed by a hundred, a thousand, or a hundred thousand such devatās as you. My faith is as immoveable and well-established as Mount Sineru. I have dispensed my wealth in the Jewel Dispensation, which leads to release. What you have said is improper; you have struck a blow against the Buddha’s Dispensation. There is no reason for an ill-behaved, immoral, wretched creature like you to live in the same house with me. Leave my house at once and go elsewhere!’

Sā sotāpannassa ariyasāvakassa vacanaṃ sutvā ṭhātuṃ asakkontī attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā dārake hatthena gahetvā nikkhami. Nikkhamitvā ca pana aññattha vasanaṭṭhānaṃ alabhamānā “seṭṭhiṃ khamāpetvā tattheva vasissāmī”ti cintetvā nagarapariggāhakadevaputtassa santikaṃ gantvā taṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. “Kenaṭṭhena āgatāsī”ti ca vutte “ahaṃ sāmi, attano bālatāya anupadhāretvā anāthapiṇḍikena seṭṭhinā saddhiṃ kathesiṃ, so maṃ kujjhitvā vasanaṭṭhānā nikkaḍḍhi, maṃ seṭṭhissa santikaṃ netvā khamāpetvā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ me dethā”ti. “Kiṃ pana tayā seṭṭhi vutto”ti “ito paṭṭhāya buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ saṅghupaṭṭhānaṃ mā kari, samaṇassa gotamassa gharappavesanaṃ mā adāsī”ti “evaṃ me vutto, sāmī”ti. Ayuttaṃ tayā vuttaṃ, sāsane pahāro dinno, “ahaṃ taṃ ādāya seṭṭhino santikaṃ gantuṃ na ussahāmī”ti. Sā tassa santikā saṅgahaṃ alabhitvā catunnaṃ mahārājānaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi.

Unable to remain after hearing the words of the noble disciple, a stream-enterer, she went to her dwelling place, took her children by the hand, and left. Having left, but unable to find another place to live, she thought, ‘I will ask the merchant’s forgiveness and live right there.’ Then she went to the devaputta who was guardian of the city, paid homage to him, and stood there. When he asked, ‘For what reason have you come?’ she replied, ‘Lord, out of my own foolishness and without reflection, I spoke with the merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. He became angry with me and drove me out of my dwelling place. Please take me to the merchant, have him forgive me, and give me back my dwelling place.’ ‘But what did you say to the merchant?’ ‘I said, “From now on, do not attend upon the Buddha, do not attend upon the Sangha, do not allow the ascetic Gotama to enter the house.” That is what I said, lord.’ ‘What you said was improper; you have struck a blow against the Dispensation. I do not dare to take you to the merchant.’ Receiving no help from him, she went to the Four Great Kings.

Tehipi tatheva paṭikkhittā sakkaṃ devarājaṃ upasaṅkamitvā taṃ pavattiṃ ācikkhitvā “ahaṃ, deva, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ alabhamānā dārake hatthena gahetvā anāthā vicarāmi, tumhākaṃ siriyā mayhaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ dāpethā”ti suṭṭhutaraṃ [M 1.0247] yāci. Sopi naṃ āha “tayā ayuttaṃ kataṃ, jinasāsane pahāro dinno, ahampi taṃ nissāya seṭṭhinā saddhiṃ kathetuṃ na sakkomi, ekaṃ pana te seṭṭhissa khamanūpāyaṃ [P 1.0230] kathessāmī”ti. “Sādhu, deva, kathehī”ti. Mahāseṭṭhissa hatthato manussehi paṇṇe āropetvā aṭṭhārasakoṭisaṅkhyaṃ dhanaṃ gahitaṃ atthi, tvaṃ tassa āyuttakavesaṃ gahetvā kañci ajānāpetvā tāni paṇṇāni ādāya katipayehi yakkhataruṇehi parivāritā ekena hatthena paṇṇaṃ, ekena lekhaniṃ gahetvā tesaṃ gehaṃ gantvā gehamajjhe ṭhitā attano yakkhānubhāvena te uttāsetvā “idaṃ tumhākaṃ iṇapaṇṇaṃ, amhākaṃ seṭṭhi attano issarakāle tumhe na kiñci āha, idāni duggato jāto, tumhehi gahitakahāpaṇāni dethā”ti attano yakkhānubhāvaṃ dassetvā sabbāpi tā aṭṭhārasa hiraññakoṭiyo sādhetvā seṭṭhissa tucchakoṭṭhake pūretvā aññaṃ aciravatinadītīre nidahitaṃ dhanaṃ nadīkūle bhinne samuddaṃ paviṭṭhaṃ atthi, tampi attano ānubhāvena āharitvā tucchakoṭṭhake pūretvā, aññampi asukaṭṭhāne nāma assāmikaṃ aṭṭhārasakoṭimattameva [V 1.0226] dhanaṃ atthi, tampi āharitvā tucchakoṭṭhake pūrehi, imāhi catupaññāsakoṭīhi imaṃ tucchakoṭṭhakapūrakaṃ daṇḍakammaṃ katvā mahāseṭṭhiṃ khamāpehīti.

Rejected by them as well, she approached Sakka, king of the devas, and told him what had happened, pleading most earnestly: 'Lord, unable to find a place to live, I wander about helplessly, holding my children by the hand. Please, by your glory, provide me with a place to stay.' He replied: 'You have acted improperly by striking a blow against the Victor's Dispensation. On your account, I too cannot speak to the great merchant. However, I will tell you a way to gain the great merchant's forgiveness.' 'Very well, lord, please tell me,' she said. 'People have taken wealth worth eighteen crores from the great merchant by means of promissory notes. You should take the guise of a collector, and without informing anyone, take those notes. Then, surrounded by a few young yakkhas, go to their houses. Stand in the middle of the house with a promissory note in one hand and a stylus in the other. Frighten them with your yakkha power and say: “This is your promissory note of debt. Our great merchant said nothing to you during his prosperous days. Now he has become poor—give back the kahāpanas you took!” By displaying your yakkha power, recover all eighteen crores of gold. Fill the great merchant’s empty storerooms with it. There is also wealth buried on the bank of the Aciravati River, which was washed into the sea when the riverbank collapsed. Bring that too by your power and fill the empty storerooms. Furthermore, in such-and-such a place, there is another eighteen crores worth of ownerless wealth. Bring that as well and fill the empty storerooms. With these fifty-four crores, perform this punitive task of filling the empty storerooms and ask for the great merchant's forgiveness.'

Sā “sādhu, devā”ti tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā vuttanayeneva sabbaṃ dhanaṃ āharitvā koṭṭhake pūretvā aḍḍharattasamaye seṭṭhissa sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā obhāsaṃ pharitvā ākāse aṭṭhāsi. “Ko eso”ti vutte “ahaṃ te mahāseṭṭhi catutthadvārakoṭṭhake adhivatthā andhabāladevatā, mayā mahāmohamūḷhāya buddhaguṇe ajānitvā purimesu divasesu tumhehi saddhiṃ kiñci kathitaṃ atthi, taṃ me dosaṃ khamatha. Sakkassa hi me devarājassa vacanena tumhākaṃ iṇaṃ sodhetvā aṭṭhārasa koṭiyo, samuddaṃ gatā aṭṭhārasa koṭiyo, tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne assāmikadhanassa aṭṭhārasa koṭiyoti catupaṇṇāsa koṭiyo āharitvā tucchakoṭṭhakapūraṇena daṇḍakammaṃ kataṃ, jetavanavihāraṃ ārabbha parikkhayaṃ gatadhanaṃ sabbaṃ sampiṇḍitaṃ, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ alabhamānā kilamāmi, mayā [M 1.0248] aññāṇatāya kathitaṃ manasi akatvā khamatha mahāseṭṭhī”ti āha.

She replied, 'Very well, lord,' and accepting his words, in the manner described she gathered all the wealth, filled the storerooms, and at midnight entered the great merchant’s splendid chamber. Suffusing it with light, she stood in the air. When asked, 'Who is that?' she said, 'Great merchant, I am the blind and foolish deity dwelling in the fourth gatehouse. Deluded by great delusion, not recognizing the qualities of the Buddha, I said certain things to you on previous days—please forgive me for that offense. By the command of Sakka, king of the devas, I have performed the punitive task of filling your empty storerooms by bringing fifty-four crores: eighteen crores from collecting your debts, eighteen crores that had gone into the sea, and eighteen crores of ownerless wealth from various places. The entire sum of wealth that was exhausted on account of the Jetavana monastery has been restored. Unable to find a dwelling place, I am weary. Great merchant, please do not take to heart what was said out of ignorance—forgive me.'

Anāthapiṇḍiko tassā vacanaṃ sutvā cintesi “ayaṃ devatā ‘daṇḍakammañca me kata’nti vadati, attano ca dosaṃ paṭijānāti, satthā imaṃ vinetvā attano guṇe jānāpessati, sammāsambuddhassa naṃ dassessāmī”ti. Atha naṃ āha “amma, devate, sacesi maṃ khamāpetukāmā, satthu santike maṃ khamāpehī”ti. Sādhu evaṃ karissāmi, “satthu pana maṃ santikaṃ gahetvā gacchāhī”ti. So “sādhū”ti vatvā vibhātāya rattiyā pātova taṃ gahetvā satthu santikaṃ gantvā tāya katakammaṃ sabbaṃ tathāgatassa ārocesi. Satthā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “idha, gahapati, pāpapuggalopi yāva pāpaṃ na paccati[P 1.0231], tāva bhadrāni passati. Yadā panassa pāpaṃ paccati, tadā pāpameva passati. Bhadrapuggalopi yāva bhadraṃ na paccati, tāva pāpāni passati. Yadā panassa bhadraṃ paccati, tadā bhadrameva passatī”ti vatvā imā dhammapade dve gāthā abhāsi –

Having heard her words, Anāthapiṇḍika thought: 'This deity says, “A punitive task has been done by me,” and she confesses her own fault. The Teacher will discipline her and make her recognize his own qualities. I will present her to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One.' Then he said to her: 'Mother deity, if you wish to ask for my forgiveness, ask for it in the Teacher's presence.' 'Very well, I will do so,' she replied, 'but you must take me into the Teacher's presence.' Saying, 'Good,' at the break of dawn he took her and went to the Teacher. There, he recounted to the Tathāgata all that she had done. After hearing his words, the Teacher said: 'Here, householder, so long as an evil person's evil deed does not ripen, they experience good things. But when their evil deed ripens, then they experience evil things. Similarly, so long as a virtuous person's good deed does not ripen, they may experience evil things. But when their good deed ripens, then they experience good things.' Having said this, he spoke these two verses from the Dhammapada:

“Pāpopi passatī bhadraṃ, yāva pāpaṃ na paccati;

Yadā ca paccatī pāpaṃ, atha pāpo pāpāni passati.

Even an evil person experiences good, so long as the evil has not ripened; but when the evil ripens, then that evil person experiences evil things.

“Bhadropi [V 1.0227] passatī pāpaṃ, yāva bhadraṃ na paccati;

Yadā ca paccatī bhadraṃ, atha bhadro bhadrāni passatī”ti. (dha. pa. 119-120);

Even a good person experiences evil, so long as the good has not ripened; but when the good ripens, then that good person experiences good things.

Imāsañca pana gāthānaṃ pariyosāne sā devatā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Sā cakkaṅkitesu satthu pādesu nipatitvā “mayā, bhante, rāgarattāya dosapaduṭṭhāya mohamūḷhāya avijjandhāya tumhākaṃ guṇe ajānantiyā pāpakaṃ vacanaṃ vuttaṃ, taṃ me khamathā”ti satthāraṃ khamāpetvā mahāseṭṭhimpi khamāpesi.

At the conclusion of these verses, that deity was established in the fruit of stream-entry. She fell at the feet of the Teacher, which were marked with wheels, and said: 'Venerable sir, impassioned with lust, corrupted by hatred, deluded by delusion, and blinded by ignorance, not knowing your qualities, I spoke an evil word. Please forgive me for that.' Having asked the Teacher for forgiveness, she also asked for the great merchant's forgiveness.

Tasmiṃ samaye anāthapiṇḍiko satthu purato attano guṇaṃ kathesi “bhante, ayaṃ devatā ‘buddhupaṭṭhānādīni mā karohī’ti vārayamānāpi maṃ vāretuṃ nāsakkhi, ‘dānaṃ na dātabba’nti imāya vāriyamānopahaṃ dānaṃ adāsimeva, nūna esa, bhante, mayhaṃ guṇo”ti. Satthā “tvaṃ khosi gahapati sotāpanno ariyasāvako acalasaddho visuddhadassano, tuyhaṃ imāya appesakkhadevatāya vārentiyā avāritabhāvo na acchariyo[M 1.0249]. Yaṃ pana pubbe paṇḍitā anuppanne buddhe aparipakkañāṇe ṭhitā kāmāvacarissarena mārena ākāse ṭhatvā ‘sace dānaṃ dassasi, imasmiṃ niraye paccissasī’ti asītihatthagambhīraṃ aṅgārakāsuṃ dassetvā ‘mā dānaṃ adāsī’ti vāritāpi padumakaṇṇikāmajjhe ṭhatvā dānaṃ adaṃsu, idaṃ acchariya”nti vatvā anāthapiṇḍikena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

At that time, Anāthapiṇḍika, standing before the Teacher, spoke of his own virtue: 'Venerable sir, though this deity tried to stop me, saying, “Do not perform services for the Buddha and so on,” she was unable to stop me. Though I was hindered by her from giving, with her saying, “Alms should not be given,” I still gave alms. Surely, venerable sir, this is my virtue.' The Teacher replied: 'Householder, you are a stream-enterer, a noble disciple of unshakable faith and purified vision; it is no wonder that you were not stopped by this deity of little power. But that in the past, when a Buddha had not yet arisen and their knowledge was still immature, wise ones were hindered by Māra, the lord of the sense-sphere, who stood in the sky, showed them a pit of burning coals eighty cubits deep, and said, “If you give alms, you will be cooked in this hell! Do not give alms!”—that even then they gave alms while standing in the middle of a lotus calyx, this is what is truly astonishing.' And at Anāthapiṇḍika's request, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiseṭṭhissa kule nibbattitvā nānappakārehi sukhūpakaraṇehi devakumāro viya saṃvaḍḍhiyamāno anukkamena viññutaṃ patvā soḷasavassakāleyeva sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patto. So pitu accayena seṭṭhiṭṭhāne ṭhatvā catūsu nagaradvāresu catasso dānasālāyo, majjhe nagarassa ekaṃ, attano nivesanadvāre ekanti cha dānasālāyo kāretvā mahādānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ [P 1.0232] rakkhati, uposathakammaṃ karoti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of the great merchant of Bārāṇasī. Growing up like a young deva, surrounded by various comforts, he gradually attained discernment and, by the age of sixteen, was proficient in all the crafts. After his father's death, he was established in the position of great merchant. He had four alms halls built at the city's four gates, one in the center of the city, and one at the gate of his own house—six alms halls in total—and gave great alms, observed the moral precepts, and undertook the Uposatha observance.

Athekadivasaṃ pātarāsavelāya bodhisattassa nānaggarase manuññabhojane upanīyamāne eko paccekabuddho sattāhaccayena nirodhā vuṭṭhāya bhikkhācāravelaṃ sallakkhetvā “ajja mayā bārāṇasiseṭṭhissa gehadvāraṃ gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti nāgalatādantakaṭṭhaṃ khāditvā anotattadahe mukhadhovanaṃ katvā manosilātale ṭhito nivāsetvā vijjulatāsadisaṃ kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā cīvaraṃ pārupitvā iddhimayamattikāpattaṃ ādāya ākāsenāgantvā bodhisattassa bhatte upanītamatte gehadvāre [V 1.0228] aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto taṃ disvāva āsanā vuṭṭhāya nipaccakāraṃ dassetvā parikammakārakaṃ olokesi. “Kiṃ karomi, sāmī”ti ca vutte “ayyassa pattaṃ āharathā”ti āha. Taṅkhaṇaññeva māro pāpimā vikampamāno uṭṭhāya “ayaṃ paccekabuddho ito sattame divase āhāraṃ labhi, ajja alabhamāno vinassissati, imañca vināsessāmi, seṭṭhino ca dānantarāyaṃ karissāmī”ti taṅkhaṇaññeva āgantvā antaravatthumhi asītihatthamattaṃ aṅgārakāsuṃ nimmini. Sā khadiraṅgārapuṇṇā sampajjalitā sajotibhūtā avīcimahānirayo viya khāyittha. Taṃ pana māpetvā sayaṃ ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Pattāharaṇatthāya gacchamāno puriso taṃ disvā mahābhayappatto nivatti. Bodhisatto “kiṃ, tāta, nivattosī”ti pucchi. Ayaṃ sāmi antaravatthumhi mahatī aṅgārakāsu sampajjalitā sajotibhūtāti[M 1.0250]. Athañño athaññoti evaṃ āgatāgatā sabbepi bhayappattā vegena palāyiṃsu.

One day, at the time of the morning meal, when a delightful meal of various choice flavors was being brought to the Bodhisatta, a paccekabuddha, having emerged from the attainment of cessation after seven days, took note of the time for the almsround. Thinking, 'Today it is proper for me to go to the door of the great merchant of Bārāṇasī,' he chewed a nāgalatā tooth-stick, washed his face in the Anotatta Lake, stood on the Manosilā plateau, put on his lower robe, fastened his belt that was like a flash of lightning, draped his upper robe, took his miraculous earthen bowl, and arrived through the air. Just as the meal was brought to the Bodhisatta, he stood at the house door. The Bodhisatta, upon seeing him, rose from his seat, showed reverence, and looked for an attendant. When asked, 'What shall I do, master?' he replied, 'Bring the noble one’s bowl.' At that very moment, the evil Māra, trembling, arose and thought: 'This paccekabuddha obtained food seven days ago. If he does not obtain it today, he will perish. I will destroy him and create an obstacle to the great merchant’s generosity.' Instantly, he came and created in the courtyard a pit of burning coals eighty cubits deep. Filled with acacia-wood embers, it blazed fiercely, appearing like the great Avīci hell. After creating it, Māra himself stood in the sky. The man going to fetch the bowl saw it and, struck with great fear, turned back. The Bodhisatta asked, 'Why have you turned back, my good man?' He replied, 'Master, in the courtyard there is a great pit of burning coals blazing fiercely!' Then another and another—thus all who came were struck with fear and fled with haste.

Bodhisatto cintesi “ajja mayhaṃ dānantarāyaṃ kātukāmo vasavattī māro uyyutto bhavissati, na kho pana jānāti mārasatena mārasahassenapi mayhaṃ akampiyabhāvaṃ, ajja dāni mayhaṃ vā mārassa vā balamahantataṃ, ānubhāvamahantataṃ jānissāmī”ti taṃ yathāsajjitameva bhattapātiṃ sayaṃ ādāya gehā nikkhamma aṅgārakāsutaṭe ṭhatvā ākāsaṃ ulloketvā māraṃ disvā “kosi tva”nti āha. “Ahaṃ, māro”ti. “Ayaṃ aṅgārakāsu tayā nimmitā”ti? “Āma, mayā”ti[P 1.0233]. “Kimatthāyā”ti. “Tava dānassa antarāyakaraṇatthāya ca paccekabuddhassa ca jīvitanāsanatthāyā”ti. Bodhisatto “neva te ahaṃ attano dānassa antarāyaṃ, na paccekabuddhassa jīvitantarāyaṃ kātuṃ dassāmi, ajja dāni mayhaṃ vā tuyhaṃ vā balamahantataṃ, ānubhāvamahantataṃ jānissāmī”ti aṅgārakāsutaṭe ṭhatvā “bhante, paccekabuddha ahaṃ imissā aṅgārakāsuyā adhosīso patamānopi na nivattissāmi, kevalaṃ tumhe mayā dinnaṃ bhojanaṃ paṭiggaṇhathā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta thought: “Today, Māra the sovereign, desiring to create an obstacle to my giving, will be ready. But he does not know my unshakable nature, even against a hundred or a thousand Māras. Today, indeed, I will know whether my great strength and power or Māra’s is greater.” Taking the food bowl himself just as it was prepared, he left the house and stood on the edge of the pit of coals. Looking up to the sky, he saw Māra and said: “Who are you?” “I am Māra.” “Was this pit of coals created by you?” “Yes, by me.” “For what purpose?” “To create an obstacle to your giving and to destroy the life of the Paccekabuddha.” The Bodhisatta said: “I will not allow you to create an obstacle to my giving, nor an obstacle to the life of the Paccekabuddha. Today, indeed, I will know whether my great strength and power or yours is greater.” Standing on the edge of the pit of coals, he said: “Venerable Paccekabuddha, even if I fall headfirst into this pit of coals, I will not turn back. Just accept the food given by me.” Then he spoke this verse:

40.

40.

“Kāmaṃ patāmi nirayaṃ, uddhaṃpādo avaṃsiro;

Nānariyaṃ karissāmi, handa piṇḍaṃ paṭiggahā”ti.

“Though I should fall into hell, feet up and head down, I will not do an ignoble deed; come now, accept this alms-food.”

Tatthāyaṃ piṇḍattho – bhante, paccekavarabuddha sacepahaṃ tumhākaṃ piṇḍapātaṃ dento ekaṃseneva imaṃ nirayaṃ uddhaṃpādo avaṃsiro hutvā patāmi, tathāpi yadidaṃ adānañca asīlañca ariyehi akattabbattā anariyehi ca kattabbattā “anariya”nti vuccati, “na taṃ anariyaṃ karissāmi[V 1.0229], handa imaṃ mayā dīyamānaṃ piṇḍaṃ paṭiggaha paṭiggaṇhāhī”ti. Ettha ca handāti vossaggatthe nipāto.

Here is the meaning of the verse: “Venerable, excellent Paccekabuddha, if by giving you alms-food I should certainly fall into this hell, feet up and head down, still I will not do that which is ignoble—that is, not giving and immorality, which are called ‘ignoble’ because they should not be done by noble ones but are done by the ignoble. I will not do that ignoble thing. Come now, accept this alms-food being given by me; please accept it!” Here, handa is a particle with the sense of offering.

Evaṃ vatvā bodhisatto daḷhasamādānena bhattapātiṃ gahetvā aṅgārakāsumatthakena pakkhanto, tāvadeva asītihatthagambhīrāya aṅgārakāsuyā talato uparūparijātaṃ satapattapupphitaṃ ekaṃ mahāpadumaṃ uggantvā bodhisattassa pāde sampaṭicchi. Tato mahātumbamattā reṇu uggantvā [M 1.0251] mahāsattassa muddhani ṭhatvā sakalasarīraṃ suvaṇṇacuṇṇasamokiṇṇamiva akāsi. So padumakaṇṇikāya ṭhatvā nānaggarasabhojanaṃ paccekabuddhassa patte patiṭṭhāpesi. So taṃ paṭiggahetvā anumodanaṃ katvā pattaṃ ākāse khipitvā passantasseva mahājanassa sayampi vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā nānappakāraṃ valāhakapantiṃ maddamāno viya himavantameva gato. Māropi parājito domanassaṃ patvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gato. Bodhisatto pana padumakaṇṇikāya ṭhitakova mahājanassa dānasīlasaṃvaṇṇanena [P 1.0234] dhammaṃ desetvā mahājanena parivuto attano nivesanameva pavisitvā yāvajīvaṃ dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta, with firm resolve, took the bowl of food and set out over the burning coals. Instantly, from the bottom of the eighty-cubit-deep pit of coals, a great hundred-petalled lotus, in full bloom, sprang up and received the Bodhisatta's feet. Then, pollen the size of a large gourd rose up and settled upon the Great Being's head, making his whole body appear as if sprinkled with gold powder. Standing on the pericarp of the lotus, he placed the food of various excellent flavors in the Paccekabuddha's bowl. The Paccekabuddha accepted it, expressed his appreciation, and threw the bowl into the sky; then, as the great crowd looked on, he himself rose into the air and, as if treading upon a line of various clouds, went to the Himālaya. Māra, defeated and dejected, went to his own dwelling place. The Bodhisatta, however, remaining standing on the pericarp of the lotus, taught the Dhamma to the great crowd, extolling generosity and virtue. Surrounded by the crowd, he entered his own dwelling and, after performing meritorious deeds such as giving for as long as he lived, passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā “nayidaṃ, gahapati, acchariyaṃ, yaṃ tvaṃ evaṃ dassanasampanno etarahi devatāya na kampito, pubbe paṇḍitehi katameva acchariya”nti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā paccekabuddho tattheva parinibbāyi, māraṃ parājetvā padumakaṇṇikāya ṭhatvā paccekabuddhassa piṇḍapātadāyako bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: “Householder, it is no wonder that you, so endowed with vision, are now unshaken by a deity. What was done by the wise in the past is the real wonder.” Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher made the connection and identified the birth, saying: “At that time, the Paccekabuddha attained final Nibbāna right there. The merchant of Bārāṇasī who defeated Māra and, standing on the pericarp of the lotus, gave alms-food to the Paccekabuddha was I myself.”

Khadiraṅgārajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Khadiraṅgāra Jātaka, the Tenth.

Kulāvakavaggo catuttho.

The Kulāvaka Chapter, the Fourth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary of its contents:

Kulāvakañca naccañca, sammodamacchavaṭṭakaṃ;

Sakuṇaṃ tittiraṃ bakaṃ, nandañca khadiraṅgāranti.

Kulāvaka, the Dance, Friendly Talk, the Fish, the Quail, the Bird, the Partridge, the Crane, Nanda, and Khadiraṅgāra.

5. Atthakāmavaggo

5. The Chapter on Desiring What is Beneficial

[41] 1. Losakajātakavaṇṇanā

[41] 1. The Commentary on the Losaka Jātaka

Yo [V 1.0230] atthakāmassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto losakatissattheraṃ nāma ārabbha kathesi. Ko panesa losakatissatthero nāmāti? Kosalaraṭṭhe eko attano kulanāsako kevaṭṭaputtako [M 1.0252] alābhī bhikkhu. So kira nibbattaṭṭhānetā cavitvā kosalaraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ kulasahassavāse kevaṭṭagāme ekissā kevaṭṭiyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa paṭisandhiggahaṇadivase taṃ kulasahassaṃ jālahatthaṃ nadiyañca taḷākādīsu ca macche pariyesantaṃ ekaṃ khuddakamacchampi nālattha. Tato paṭṭhāya ca te kevaṭṭā parihāyantiyeva. Tasmiñhi kucchigateyeva nesaṃ gāmo satta vāre agginā daḍḍho, satta vāre raññā daṇḍito. Evaṃ anukkamena duggatā jātā. Te cintayiṃsu “pubbe amhākaṃ evarūpaṃ natthi, idāni pana parihāyāma, amhākaṃ antare ekāya kāḷakaṇṇiyā bhavitabbaṃ, dve bhāgā homā”ti pañca pañca kulasatāni ekato ahesuṃ. Tato yattha tassa mātāpitaro, sova koṭṭhāso parihāyati, itaro vaḍḍhati. Te tampi koṭṭhāsaṃ dvidhā, tampi dvidhāti evaṃ yāva tameva kulaṃ ekaṃ ahosi, tāva vibhajitvā tesaṃ kāḷakaṇṇibhāvaṃ ñatvā pothetvā nikkaḍḍhiṃsu.

“One who desires what is beneficial…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Losaka Tissa. Now who was this Elder Losaka Tissa? In the country of Kosala there was a monk of little gain, the son of a fisherman, who was the ruin of his own family. It is said that, having passed away from his former state of existence, he took conception in the womb of a fisherwoman in a fishing village of a thousand families in the country of Kosala. On the day he was conceived, that thousand of families, searching for fish in the river, lakes, and so on with nets in hand, did not get even a single tiny fish. From then on, those fishermen only declined. While he was in the womb, their village was burned by fire seven times and fined by the king seven times. Thus they gradually became destitute. They thought: “Previously we had no such trouble, but now we are declining. There must be an ill-omened one among us. Let us divide into two parts.” They formed two groups of five hundred families each. Then, the section where his parents were declined, while the other prospered. They divided that section in two, and that one in two again, and so on, until only that one family remained. Having divided thus and realized that this family was the ill-omened one, they beat them and drove them out.

Athassa [P 1.0235] mātā kicchena jīvamānā paripakke gabbhe ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vijāyi. Pacchimabhavikasattaṃ na sakkā nāsetuṃ, antoghaṭe padīpo viya tassa hadaye arahattassa upanissayo jalati. Sā taṃ dārakaṃ paṭijaggitvā ādhāvitvā paridhāvitvā vicaraṇakāle ekamassa kapālakaṃ hatthe datvā “putta, etaṃ gharaṃ pavisā”ti pesetvā palātā. So tato paṭṭhāya ekakova hutvā tattha tattha bhikkhaṃ pariyesitvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sayati, na nhāyati, na sarīraṃ paṭijaggati, paṃsupisācako viya kicchena jīvikaṃ kappeti. So anukkamena sattavassiko hutvā ekasmiṃ gehadvāre ukkhalidhovanassa chaḍḍitaṭṭhāne kāko viya ekekaṃ bhattasitthaṃ uccinitvā khādati.

Then his mother, living with difficulty, gave birth in a certain place when her womb was mature. A being in his final existence cannot be destroyed; like a lamp inside a pot, the supporting condition for arahantship was burning in his heart. She looked after the boy, but when he was old enough to run about, she put a potsherd in his hand, said, “Son, enter this house,” sent him off, and fled. From then on, he was all alone. He begged here and there and slept in one place. He did not bathe or look after his body, and sustained his life with difficulty, like a dust-goblin. Gradually, having become seven years old, at a house door, in the place where the water from washing the pot was thrown out, he would pick up and eat single grains of rice like a crow.

Atha naṃ dhammasenāpati sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caramāno disvā “ayaṃ satto atikāruññappatto[V 1.0231], kataragāmavāsiko nu kho”ti tasmiṃ mettacittaṃ vaḍḍhetvā “ehi, re”ti āha. So āgantvā theraṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ thero “kataragāmavāsikosi, kahaṃ vā te mātāpitaro”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ, bhante, nippaccayo, mayhaṃ mātāpitaro maṃ nissāya ‘kilantamhā’ti maṃ chaḍḍetvā palātā”ti. “Api pana pabbajissasī”ti. “Bhante, ahaṃ tāva pabbajeyyaṃ, mādisaṃ pana kapaṇaṃ ko pabbājessasī”ti? “Ahaṃ [M 1.0253] pabbājessāmī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante, pabbājethā”ti. Thero tassa khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ datvā taṃ vihāraṃ netvā sahattheneva nhāpetvā pabbājetvā paripuṇṇavassaṃ upasampādesi. So mahallakakāle “losakatissatthero”ti paññāyittha appapuñño appalābho. Tena kira asadisadānepi kucchipūro na laddhapubbo, jīvitaghaṭanamattameva labhati. Tassa hi patte ekasmiṃyeva yāguuḷuṅke dinne patto samatittiko viya hutvā paññāyati. Atha manussā “imassa patto pūro”ti heṭṭhā yāguṃ denti. Tassa patte yāguṃ dānakāle manussānaṃ bhājane yāgu antaradhāyatītipi vadanti. Khajjakādīsupi eseva nayo.

Then the General of the Dhamma, while walking for alms in Sāvatthī, saw him and thought, “This being is in a most pitiable state. From what village is he?” Developing a mind of loving-kindness towards him, he said, “Come here, boy.” The boy came, paid homage to the elder, and stood by. Then the elder asked him, “From what village are you? Where are your parents?” “Venerable sir, I am without support. My parents abandoned me on my account, saying, ‘We are worn out,’ and fled.” “Will you go forth?” “Venerable sir, I would go forth, but who would give the going forth to one as wretched as I?” “I will give you the going forth.” “Excellent, venerable sir, please give me the going forth.” The elder gave him food to eat, took him to the monastery, bathed him with his own hands, gave him the going forth and, when he came of age, the higher ordination. In his old age, he became known as the Elder Losaka Tissa, one of little merit and little gain. It is said that even at the incomparable almsgiving he had never received a bellyful; he obtained only enough to sustain life. For when just a single ladleful of rice-gruel was given into his bowl, the bowl would appear to be full to the brim. Then people, thinking, “His bowl is full,” would give rice-gruel only at the bottom. It is also said that when people were giving rice-gruel into his bowl, the rice-gruel in their own vessels would disappear. The same was the case with hard foods and so on.

So aparena samayena vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā aggaphale arahatte patiṭṭhitopi appalābhova ahosi. Athassa anupubbena āyusaṅkhāresu parihīnesu parinibbānadivaso sampāpuṇi. Dhammasenāpati āvajjento tassa parinibbānabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃ losakatissatthero ajja parinibbāyissati, ajja mayā etassa yāvadatthaṃ āhāraṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti taṃ ādāya sāvatthiṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Thero taṃ nissāya tāva bahumanussāya sāvatthiyā hatthaṃ pasāretvā vandanamattampi nālattha. Atha naṃ thero “gacchāvuso, āsanasālāya nisīdā”ti uyyojetvā gato. Taṃ āgatameva manussā “ayyo, āgato”ti āsane nisīdāpetvā bhojesi. Theropi “imaṃ losakassa dethā”ti [P 1.0236] laddhāhāraṃ pesesi. Taṃ gahetvā gatā losakatissattheraṃ asaritvā sayameva bhuñjiṃsu. Atha therassa uṭṭhāya vihāraṃ gamanakāle losakatissatthero āgantvā theraṃ vandi, thero nivattitvā ṭhitakova “laddhaṃ te, āvuso, bhatta”nti pucchi. Labhissāma no, bhanteti. Thero saṃvegapatto kālaṃ olokesi, kālo atikkanto. Thero “hotāvuso, idheva nisīdā”ti losakattheraṃ āsanasālāyaṃ nisīdāpetvā kosalarañño nivesanaṃ agamāsi. Rājā therassa pattaṃ gāhāpetvā “bhattassa akālo”ti pattapūraṃ catumadhuraṃ dāpesi. Thero taṃ ādāya gantvā “ehāvuso, tissa imaṃ catumadhuraṃ bhuñjā”ti vatvā pattaṃ gahetvā aṭṭhāsi. So there gāravena lajjanto na paribhuñjati. Atha naṃ thero “ehāvuso tissa, ahaṃ imaṃ pattaṃ gahetvāva ṭhassāmi, tvaṃ nisīditvā paribhuñja. Sace ahaṃ pattaṃ hatthato [M 1.0254] muñceyyaṃ, kiñci na bhaveyyā”ti āha. Athāyasmā losakatissatthero aggasāvake dhammasenāpatimhi pattaṃ gahetvā ṭhite [V 1.0232] catumadhuraṃ paribhuñji. Taṃ therassa ariyiddhibalena parikkhayaṃ na agamāsi. Tadā losakatissatthero yāvadatthaṃ udarapūraṃ katvā paribhuñji, taṃ divasaṃyeva ca anupādisesāya nibbānadhātuyā parinibbāyi. Sammāsambuddho santike ṭhatvā sarīranikkhepaṃ kāresi, dhātuyo gahetvā cetiyaṃ kariṃsu.

Then, after some time, having developed insight and become established in the highest fruit, arahantship, he was still one of little gain. As his life-formations gradually declined, the day of his final Nibbāna arrived. The General of the Dhamma, reflecting and knowing of his impending final Nibbāna, thought, 'Today the Elder Losaka Tissa will attain final Nibbāna. It is fitting that I give him as much food as he needs today.' Taking him along, he entered Sāvatthī for almsfood. In his company, the elder stretched out his hand in the populous city of Sāvatthī but did not receive so much as a gesture of respect. Then the elder sent him away, saying, 'Go, friend, and sit in the assembly hall,' and continued on his way. As soon as the elder arrived, the people said, 'The venerable one has come,' seated him, and served him. The elder, too, saying, 'Give this to Losaka,' sent the food he had received. Those who took it went, but without remembering the Elder Losaka Tissa, they ate it themselves. Then, at the time when the elder was rising to go to the monastery, the Elder Losaka Tissa came and paid homage to him. The elder turned back, stood still, and asked, 'Friend, did you get any almsfood?' 'I have not received any, venerable sir.' Struck with a sense of urgency, the elder looked at the time; the time had passed. The elder said, 'Very well, friend, sit right here.' Having seated the Elder Losaka in the assembly hall, he went to the residence of the king of Kosala. The king had the elder’s bowl taken and, as it was not the time for a meal, had it filled to the brim with the four sweets. The elder took it, went back, and said, 'Come, friend Tissa, eat these four sweets,' and he stood there holding the bowl. Out of respect for the elder, he was ashamed and did not eat. Then the elder said to him, 'Come, friend Tissa, I will stand here holding this bowl. You sit and eat. If I were to let the bowl go from my hand, there would be nothing left.' Then the Venerable Losaka Tissa, while the General of the Dhamma, the chief disciple, stood holding the bowl, partook of the four sweets. Through the elder’s noble psychic power, it did not become exhausted. On that day, the Elder Losaka Tissa ate as much as he desired to his belly’s fill, and on that very day he attained final Nibbāna with the Nibbāna-element with no residue remaining. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, standing nearby, had his bodily remains disposed of. They took the relics and built a cetiya.

Tadā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitvā “āvuso, aho losakatissatthero appapuñño appalābhī, evarūpena nāma appapuññena appalābhinā kathaṃ ariyadhammo laddho”ti kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā dhammasabhaṃ gantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchi. Te “imāya nāma, bhante”ti ārocayiṃsu. Satthā “bhikkhave, eso bhikkhu attano alābhibhāvañca ariyadhammalābhibhāvañca attanāva akāsi. Ayañhi pubbe paresaṃ lābhantarāyaṃ katvā appalābhī jāto, “aniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ, anattā”ti vipassanāya yuttabhāvassa balena ariyadhammalābhī jāto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then the monks, having gathered in the Hall of the Dhamma, sat discussing: 'Friends, the Elder Losaka Tissa was of little merit and of little gain. How could the noble Dhamma have been attained by one of such little merit and little gain?' The Teacher went to the Hall of the Dhamma and asked, 'For what discussion are you now gathered here, monks?' They replied, 'Concerning this topic, venerable sir.' The Teacher said, 'Monks, this monk by himself created both his state of being without gain and his attainment of the noble Dhamma. For in the past, having created an obstacle to the gains of others, he was born with little gain; but through the power of his application to insight meditation on “impermanent, suffering, non-self,” he became an attainer of the noble Dhamma.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte kira kassapasammāsambuddhakāle aññataro bhikkhu ekaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ nissāya gāmakāvāse vasati pakatatto sīlavā vipassanāya yuttappayutto. Atheko khīṇāsavatthero samavattavāsaṃ vasamāno anupubbena tassa bhikkhuno upaṭṭhākakuṭumbikassa vasanagāmaṃ sampatto. Kuṭumbiko therassa [P 1.0237] iriyāpatheyeva pasīditvā pattaṃ ādāya gharaṃ pavesetvā sakkaccaṃ bhojetvā thokaṃ dhammakathaṃ sutvā theraṃ vanditvā “bhante, amhākaṃ dhuravihārameva gacchatha, mayaṃ sāyanhasamaye āgantvā passissāmā”ti āha. Thero vihāraṃ gantvā nevāsikattheraṃ vanditvā āpucchitvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Sopi tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “laddho te, āvuso, bhikkhāhāro”ti pucchi. “Āma, laddho”ti. “Kahaṃ laddho”ti? “Tumhākaṃ dhuragāme kuṭumbikaghare”ti. Evañca pana vatvā attano senāsanaṃ pucchitvā paṭijaggitvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā jhānasukhena phalasukhena ca vītināmento nisīdi.

In the past, it is said, during the time of the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One Kassapa, a certain monk lived in a village residence, dependent on a householder. He was self-possessed, virtuous, and diligently engaged in insight meditation. Then an elder whose taints were destroyed, while abiding in a suitable manner, gradually arrived at the village where that monk’s supporting householder lived. The householder, gaining confidence simply from the elder’s deportment, took his bowl, led him into the house, respectfully served him a meal, listened to a short discourse on the Dhamma, and after paying homage, said: 'Venerable sir, please go to the monastery we support. We will come in the evening to see you.' The elder went to the monastery, paid homage to the resident elder, took his leave, and sat down to one side. The resident elder exchanged friendly greetings with him and asked: 'Friend, did you obtain almsfood?' 'Yes, I did.' 'Where did you obtain it?' 'At a householder’s home in your supporting village.' Having said this, the visiting elder inquired about his lodging, tidied it up, put away his bowl and robes, and sat down, passing the time with the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition.

Sopi [M 1.0255] kuṭumbiko sāyanhe gandhamālañceva padīpeyyañca gāhāpetvā vihāraṃ gantvā nevāsikattheraṃ vanditvā “bhante, eko āgantukatthero atthi, āgato nu kho”ti pucchi. “Āma, āgato”ti. “Idāni kaha”nti. “Asukasenāsane nāmā”ti. So tassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno dhammakathaṃ sutvā sītalavelāya cetiyañca bodhiñca pūjetvā dīpe jāletvā ubhopi jane nimantetvā gato. Nevāsikattheropi kho “ayaṃ kuṭumbiko paribhinno, sacāyaṃ bhikkhu imasmiṃ vihāre vasissati, na maṃ esa kismiñci gaṇayissatī”ti [V 1.0233] there anattamanataṃ āpajjitvā “imasmiṃ vihāre etassa avasanākāro mayā kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti tena upaṭṭhānavelāya āgatena saddhiṃ kiñci na kathesi. Khīṇāsavatthero tassa ajjhāsayaṃ jānitvā “ayaṃ thero mama kule vā gaṇe vā apalibuddhabhāvaṃ na jānātī”ti attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā jhānasukhena phalasukhena vītināmesi.

That householder, in the evening, had scents, garlands, and lamp oil brought, and went to the monastery. He paid homage to the resident elder and asked: 'Venerable sir, has a visiting elder arrived?' 'Yes, he has arrived.' 'Where is he now?' 'In such-and-such a lodging.' The householder went to his presence, paid homage, and sat down to one side. After listening to a discourse on the Dhamma, during the cool of the evening, he paid homage at the cetiya and the Bodhi tree, lit the lamps, invited both monks for the next day, and departed. The resident elder, for his part, became displeased with the visiting elder, thinking: 'This householder has been won over. If this monk stays in this monastery, he will hold me in no esteem. I must find a way to prevent him from staying in this monastery.' When the visiting elder came at the time for paying respects, the resident elder said nothing at all to him. The elder whose taints were destroyed, knowing his intention, thought: 'This elder does not know that I am unattached to his family or following.' He went to his own lodging and passed the time with the bliss of jhāna and the bliss of fruition.

Nevāsikopi punadivase nakhapiṭṭhena gaṇḍiṃ paharitvā nakhena dvāraṃ ākoṭetvā kuṭumbikassa gehaṃ agamāsi. So tassa pattaṃ gahetvā paññattāsane nisīdāpetvā “āgantukatthero kahaṃ, bhante”ti pucchi. “Nāhaṃ tava kulūpakassa pavattiṃ jānāmi, gaṇḍiṃ paharantopi dvāraṃ ākoṭentopi pabodhetuṃ nāsakkhiṃ, hiyyo tava gehe paṇītabhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā [P 1.0238] jīrāpetuṃ asakkonto idāni niddaṃ okkantoyeva bhavissati, tvaṃ pasīdamāno evarūpesuyeva ṭhānesu pasīdasī”ti āha – “khīṇāsavattheropi attano bhikkhācāravelaṃ sallakkhetvā sarīraṃ paṭijaggitvā pattacīvaramādāya ākāse uppatitvā aññattha agamāsi. So kuṭumbiko nevāsikattheraṃ sappimadhusakkharābhisaṅkhataṃ pāyāsaṃ pāyetvā pattaṃ gandhacuṇṇehi ubbaṭṭetvā puna pūretvā “bhante, so thero maggakilanto bhavissati, idamassa harathā”ti adāsi. Itaro apaṭikkhipitvāva gahetvā gacchanto “sace so bhikkhu imaṃ pāyāsaṃ pivissati, gīvāyaṃ gahetvā nikkaḍḍhiyamānopi na gamissati. Sace panāhaṃ imaṃ pāyāsaṃ manussānaṃ dassāmi, pākaṭaṃ me kammaṃ bhavissati. Sace udake opilāpessāmi, udakapiṭṭhe sappi paññāyissati[M 1.0256]. Sace bhūmiyaṃ chaḍḍessāmi, kākasannipātena paññāyissati. Kattha nu kho imaṃ chaḍḍeyya”nti upadhārento ekaṃ jhāmakkhettaṃ disvā aṅgāre viyūhitvā tattha pakkhipitvā upari aṅgārehi paṭicchādetvā vihāraṃ gato taṃ bhikkhuṃ adisvā cintesi “addhā so bhikkhu khīṇāsavo mama ajjhāsayaṃ viditvā aññattha gato bhavissati, aho mayā udarahetu ayuttaṃ kata”nti tāvadevassa mahantaṃ domanassaṃ udapādi. Tato paṭṭhāyeva ca manussapeto hutvā na cirasseva kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbatti.

The next day, the resident monk struck the gong with the back of his fingernail and knocked on the door with his nail, and then went to the householder’s home. The householder took his bowl, seated him on the prepared seat, and asked: 'Venerable sir, where is the visiting elder?' 'I do not know what has become of that intimate of your family. Though I struck the gong and knocked on the door, I was unable to wake him. Having eaten that rich food at your house yesterday, he was unable to digest it and must have fallen fast asleep. You place your confidence in just such types!' Meanwhile, the elder whose taints were destroyed, noting that it was his time for the alms round, attended to his bodily needs, took his bowl and robes, rose up into the air, and went elsewhere. The householder had the resident elder drink rice-porridge prepared with ghee, honey, and sugar, and after rubbing the bowl with fragrant powders, he filled it again and gave it to him, saying: 'Venerable sir, that elder must be weary from his journey. Please take this to him.' The other, without refusing, took it and went. As he was going, he thought: 'If that monk drinks this rice-porridge, he will not leave even if he is seized by the neck and dragged out. But if I give this rice-porridge to other people, my deed will become known. If I pour it into water, the ghee will be visible on the surface. If I throw it on the ground, it will be revealed by a gathering of crows. Where can I possibly throw it away?' Looking about, he saw a field of burnt stubble, pushed aside the embers, threw the porridge in, and covered it with embers. He then went to the monastery. Not seeing that monk, he thought: 'Surely that monk, an Arahant, has perceived my intention and gone elsewhere. Alas, for the sake of my belly I have done a wrong thing!' At that very moment, great remorse arose in him. From that time on he became like a human ghost, and not long afterwards he passed away and was reborn in hell.

So bahūni vassasatasahassāni niraye paccitvā pakkāvasesena paṭipāṭiyā pañcajātisatesu yakkho hutvā ekadivasampi udarapūraṃ āhāraṃ na labhi. Ekadivasaṃ pana gabbhamalaṃ udarapūraṃ labhi. Puna pañcajātisatesu sunakho ahosi. Tadāpi ekadivasaṃ bhattavamanaṃ udarapūraṃ labhi, sesakāle pana tena udarapūro āhāro nāma na laddhapubbo. Sunakhayonito pana cavitvā kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ gāme duggatakule nibbatti. Tassa nibbattito paṭṭhāya taṃ kulaṃ paramaduggatameva jātaṃ, jātito uddhaṃ udakakañjikāmattampi na labhi. Tassa pana [V 1.0234] “mittavindako”ti nāmaṃ ahosi. Mātāpitaro [P 1.0239] chātakadukkhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkontā “gaccha kāḷakaṇṇī”ti taṃ pothetvā nīhariṃsu. So apaṭisaraṇo vicaranto bārāṇasiṃ agamāsi. Tadā bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañca māṇavakasatāni sippaṃ vāceti. Tadā bārāṇasivāsino duggatānaṃ paribbayaṃ datvā sippaṃ sikkhāpenti. Ayampi mittavindako bodhisattassa santike sippaṃ sikkhati. So pharuso anovādakkhamo taṃ taṃ paharanto vicarati, bodhisattena ovadiyamānopi ovādaṃ na gaṇhāti. Taṃ nissāya āyopissa mando jāto.

Having been tormented in hell for many hundreds of thousands of years, as a residual result of that kamma, he was reborn in sequence as a yakkha for five hundred births, but not even for a single day did he get a bellyful of food. One day, however, he got a bellyful of uterine filth. Again, for five hundred births he was a dog. Even then, only on one day did he get a bellyful of vomit; at other times he never got a bellyful of food. Passing away from the dog existence, he was reborn in a poor family in a village in the Kāsi country. From his birth, that family became utterly destitute; after he was born they did not get so much as a measure of rice gruel. His name was Mittavindaka. Unable to endure the suffering of hunger, his parents beat him, saying, “Go, you ill-omened one!” and drove him out. Without refuge, he wandered about and came to Benares. At that time the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher in Benares, teaching the arts to five hundred young men. The people of Benares would provide for the expenses of the poor and have them taught a craft. This Mittavindaka, too, studied a craft under the Bodhisatta. But he was harsh and intolerant of admonition, and went about striking this one and that. Even when admonished by the Bodhisatta, he would not accept the advice. On his account, the teacher's income also became meager.

Atha so māṇavakehi saddhiṃ bhaṇḍitvā ovādaṃ aggaṇhanto tato palāyitvā āhiṇḍanto ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ patvā bhatiṃ katvā jīvati. So tattha ekāya duggatitthiyā saddhiṃ saṃvāsaṃ kappesi. Sā taṃ nissāya dve dārake vijāyi. Gāmavāsino “amhākaṃ susāsanaṃ dussāsanaṃ āroceyyāsī”ti mittavindakassa bhatiṃ datvā taṃ gāmadvāre kuṭikāya [M 1.0257] vasāpesuṃ. Taṃ pana mittavindakaṃ nissāya te paccantagāmavāsino sattakkhattuṃ rājadaṇḍaṃ agamaṃsu, sattakkhattuṃ nesaṃ gehāni jhāyiṃsu, sattakkhattuṃ taḷākaṃ bhijji. Te cintayiṃsu “amhākaṃ pubbe imassa mittavindakassa anāgamanakāle evarūpaṃ natthi, idāni panassa āgatakālato paṭṭhāya parihāyāmā”ti taṃ pothetvā nīhariṃsu.

Then, having quarreled with the young men and refusing to accept advice, he fled from there and, while wandering about, reached a border village where he lived by working for wages. There he lived together with a poor woman, and she bore him two children. The villagers gave Mittavindaka a wage and had him live in a hut at the village gate, thinking, “You will inform us of good and bad tidings.” But on account of Mittavindaka, those border villagers incurred the king’s punishment seven times, their houses were burned down seven times, and their reservoir burst seven times. They thought, “Formerly, before this Mittavindaka came, nothing like this happened to us, but now, since he has come, we are declining.” So they beat him and drove him out.

So attano dārake gahetvā aññattha gacchanto ekaṃ amanussapariggahaṃ aṭaviṃ pāvisi. Tatthassa amanussā dārake ca bhariyañca māretvā maṃsaṃ khādiṃsu. So tato palāyitvā tato tato āhiṇḍanto ekaṃ gambhīraṃ nāma paṭṭanagāmaṃ nāvāvissajjanadivaseyeva patvā kammakārako hutvā nāvaṃ abhiruhi. Nāvā samuddapiṭṭhe sattāhaṃ gantvā sattame divase samuddamajjhe ākoṭetvā ṭhapitā viya aṭṭhāsi. Te kāḷakaṇṇisalākaṃ cāresuṃ, sattakkhattuṃ mittavindakasseva pāpuṇi. Manussā tassekaṃ veḷukalāpaṃ datvā hatthe gahetvā samuddapiṭṭhe khipiṃsu, tasmiṃ khittamatte nāvā agamāsi. Mittavindako [P 1.0240] veḷukalāpe nipajjitvā samuddapiṭṭhe gacchanto kassapasammāsambuddhakāle rakkhitasīlassa phalena samuddapiṭṭhe ekasmiṃ phalikavimāne catasso devadhītaro paṭilabhitvā tāsaṃ santike sukhaṃ anubhavamāno sattāhaṃ vasi. Tā pana vimānapetiyo sattāhaṃ sukhaṃ anubhavanti, sattāhaṃ dukkhaṃ. Sattāhaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhavituṃ gacchamānā “yāva mayaṃ āgacchāma, tāva idheva hohī”ti vatvā agamaṃsu.

Taking his children, he went elsewhere and entered a forest possessed by non-human beings. There, the non-human beings killed his children and his wife and ate their flesh. Fleeing from there and wandering about, he reached a port village named Gambhīra on the very day a ship was being launched. Becoming a laborer, he boarded the ship. The ship sailed on the ocean for seven days, but on the seventh day it stood still in the middle of the ocean as if brought to a halt. They cast lots to find the person of ill-luck, and seven times the lot fell to Mittavindaka. The men gave him a raft of bamboo and threw him onto the surface of the ocean. As soon as he was thrown, the ship moved on. Lying on the raft of bamboo and floating on the ocean, Mittavindaka, as a result of the virtue he had protected in the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, obtained four celestial nymphs in a crystal mansion on the surface of the ocean. He dwelt there for seven days, enjoying happiness in their presence. These female spirits of the mansion, however, experience happiness for seven days and suffering for seven days. As they were leaving to experience their seven days of suffering, they said, “Stay right here until we return,” and departed.

Mittavindako [V 1.0235] tāsaṃ gatakāle veḷukalāpe nipajjitvā purato gacchanto rajatavimāne aṭṭha devadhītaro labhi. Tatopi paraṃ gacchanto maṇivimāne soḷasa, kanakavimāne dvattiṃsa devadhītaro labhi. Tāsampi vacanaṃ akatvā parato gacchanto antaradīpake ekaṃ yakkhanagaraṃ addasa. Tatthekā yakkhinī ajarūpena vicarati. Mittavindako tassā yakkhinibhāvaṃ ajānanto “ajamaṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti taṃ pāde aggahesi, sā yakkhānubhāvena taṃ ukkhipitvā khipi. So tāya khitto samuddamatthakena gantvā bārāṇasiyaṃ parikhāpiṭṭhe ekasmiṃ kaṇṭakagumbamatthake patitvā pavaṭṭamāno bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi. Tasmiñca samaye tasmiṃ parikhāpiṭṭhe rañño ajikā caramānā corā haranti. Ajikagopakā “core gaṇhissāmā”ti [M 1.0258] ekamantaṃ nilīnā aṭṭhaṃsu. Mittavindako pavaṭṭitvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhito tā ajikā disvā cintesi “ahaṃ samudde ekasmiṃ dīpake ajikaṃ pāde gahetvā tāya khitto idha patito. Sace idāni ekaṃ ajikaṃ pāde gahessāmi, sā maṃ parato samuddapiṭṭhe vimānadevatānaṃ santike khipissatī”ti. So evaṃ ayoniso manasikaritvā ajikaṃ pāde gaṇhi, sā gahitamattā viravi. Ajikagopakā ito cito ca āgantvā taṃ gahetvā “ettakaṃ kālaṃ rājakule ajikakhādako esa coro”ti taṃ koṭṭetvā bandhitvā rañño santikaṃ nenti.

When they had gone, Mittavindaka lay down on his raft of bamboo and, floating onward, came to a silver mansion where he obtained eight celestial nymphs. Going further still, he came to a jeweled mansion with sixteen, and then to a golden mansion with thirty-two. Disregarding their words as well, he went further and saw a city of yakkhas on an island in the middle of the ocean. There a female yakkha was wandering about in the form of a she-goat. Not knowing she was a yakkha, Mittavindaka thought, “I will eat goat’s meat,” and seized her by the foot. With her yakkha-power, she lifted him up and flung him away. Thrown by her, he flew over the surface of the sea and fell on top of a thorny bush on the bank of the moat at Benares; rolling off, he landed on the ground. At that time, thieves had been stealing the king’s she-goats that were grazing on the bank of the moat. The goatherds were hiding in a secluded spot, thinking, “We will catch the thieves.” Mittavindaka, having rolled onto the ground and stood up, saw the she-goats and thought: “On an island in the sea, I seized a she-goat by the foot and was thrown here by her. If I now seize a she-goat by the foot, she will throw me further, over the sea, to the vicinity of the deities of the mansions.” So, reflecting unwisely, he seized a she-goat by the foot. As soon as he seized it, it bleated. The goatherds came from all sides, seized him, and said, “So this is the thief who has been eating the royal family’s she-goats all this time!” They beat him, bound him, and led him to the king.

Tasmiṃ khaṇe bodhisatto pañcasatamāṇavakaparivuto nagarā nikkhamma nhāyituṃ gacchanto mittavindakaṃ disvā sañjānitvā te manusse āha – “tātā, ayaṃ amhākaṃ antevāsiko, kasmā naṃ gaṇhathā”ti? “Ajikacorako, ayya, ekaṃ ajikaṃ pāde gaṇhi, tasmā gahito”ti. “Tena hetaṃ [P 1.0241] amhākaṃ dāsaṃ katvā detha, amhe nissāya jīvissatī”ti. Te, “sādhu ayyā”ti taṃ vissajjetvā agamaṃsu. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “mittavindaka, tvaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ kahaṃ vasī”ti pucchi. So sabbaṃ attanā katakammaṃ ārocesi. Bodhisatto “atthakāmānaṃ vacanaṃ akaronto evaṃ dukkhaṃ pāpuṇātī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that moment, the Bodhisatta, surrounded by five hundred young men, was departing from the city to bathe. Seeing Mittavindaka, he recognized him and said to those men, “My good men, this is a pupil of ours. Why have you seized him?” “Sir, he is a goat thief. He seized a she-goat by the foot; that is why he was seized.” “In that case, make him our servant and give him to us. He will make his living in dependence on us.” “Very well, sirs,” they said, and releasing him, they went away. Then the Bodhisatta asked him, “Mittavindaka, where have you been living all this time?” He related all the deeds he had done. The Bodhisatta, thinking, “One who does not follow the word of those who wish for one's welfare meets with such suffering,” spoke this verse:

41.

41.

“Yo atthakāmassa hitānukampino, ovajjamāno na karoti sāsanaṃ;

Ajiyā pādamolamba, mittako viya socatī”ti.

“He who, when admonished by one who seeks his welfare, one compassionate for his good, does not follow the instruction, grieves like Mittaka, clinging to the she-goat’s foot.”

Tattha atthakāmassāti vuḍḍhiṃ icchantassa. Hitānukampinoti hitena anukampamānassa. Ovajjamānoti mudukena hitacittena ovadiyamāno. Na karoti sāsananti anusiṭṭhaṃ na karoti, dubbaco anovādako hoti. Mittako viya socatīti yathāyaṃ mittavindako ajikāya [V 1.0236] pādaṃ gahetvā socati kilamati, evaṃ niccakālaṃ socatīti imāya gāthāya bodhisatto dhammaṃ desesi.

Herein, of one who seeks his welfare means: of one who desires his prosperity. Compassionate for his good means: one who is compassionate with what is beneficial. Being admonished means: being advised with a gentle and benevolent mind. Does not follow the instruction means: he does not do what he is taught; he is obstinate and intolerant of admonition. Grieves like Mittaka means: just as this Mittavindaka, having seized the she-goat’s foot, grieves and becomes weary, so one like him grieves perpetually. With this verse the Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma.

Evaṃ tena therena ettake addhāne tīsuyeva attabhāvesu kucchipūro laddhapubbo. Yakkhena hutvā ekadivasaṃ gabbhamalaṃ laddhaṃ, sunakhena hutvā ekadivasaṃ [M 1.0259] bhattavamanaṃ, parinibbānadivase dhammasenāpatissānubhāvena catumadhuraṃ laddhaṃ. Evaṃ parassa lābhantarāyakaraṇaṃ nāma mahādosanti veditabbaṃ. Tasmiṃ pana kāle sopi ācariyo mittavindakopi yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, in all that long time, that elder had obtained a bellyful on only three occasions in three of his lifetimes. As a yakkha, he obtained uterine filth for one day; as a dog, he obtained vomited food for one day; and on the day of his final Nibbāna, through the spiritual power of the General of the Dhamma, he obtained the four sweet things. Thus it should be understood that causing an obstruction to another’s gain is a great fault. At that time, both the teacher and Mittavindaka passed away according to their kamma.
