Satthā “evaṃ, bhikkhave, attano appalābhibhāvañca ariyadhammalābhibhāvañca sayameva esa akāsī”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mittavindako losakatissatthero ahosi, disāpāmokkhācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: “Thus, bhikkhus, this one himself brought about his own lack of gain and his lack of gain in the noble Dhamma.” Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he connected the links and identified the birth: “At that time, Mittavindaka was the Elder Losaka Tissa, and the world-renowned teacher was myself.”

Losakajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Losaka Jātaka, the First.

[42] 2. Kapotajātakavaṇṇanā

[42] 2. The Commentary on the Kapota Jātaka

Yo atthakāmassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ lolabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa lolabhāvo navakanipāte kākajātake āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana taṃ bhikkhū “ayaṃ, bhante, bhikkhu lolo”ti satthu ārocesuṃ. Atha naṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira [P 1.0242] tvaṃ bhikkhu lolosī”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante”ti. Satthā “pubbepi tvaṃ bhikkhu lolo lolakāraṇā jīvitakkhayaṃ patto, paṇḍitāpi taṃ nissāya attano vasanaṭṭhānā parihīnā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher told this story, which begins, “He who, of one who seeks his welfare,” concerning a certain fickle bhikkhu. His fickleness will become manifest in the Kāka Jātaka in the Book of Nines. At that time, the bhikkhus reported to the Teacher: “Venerable sir, this bhikkhu is fickle.” The Teacher asked him, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are fickle?” “Yes, venerable sir.” The Teacher said: “Bhikkhu, in the past, too, you were fickle, and on account of that fickleness you met with the destruction of your life. And on your account, even wise beings were deprived of their dwelling place.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto pārāvatayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Tadā bārāṇasivāsino puññakāmatāya tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne sakuṇānaṃ sukhavasanatthāya thusapacchiyo olambenti. Bārāṇasiseṭṭhinopi bhattakārako attano mahānase ekaṃ thusapacchiṃ olambetvā ṭhapesi, bodhisatto tattha vāsaṃ kappesi. So pātova nikkhamitvā gocare caritvā sāyaṃ āgantvā tattha vasanto kālaṃ khepesi. Athekadivasaṃ eko kāko mahānasamatthakena gacchanto ambilānambilamacchamaṃsānaṃ dhūpanavāsaṃ ghāyitvā lobhaṃ uppādetvā “kaṃ nu kho nissāya imaṃ macchamaṃsaṃ labhissāmī”ti avidūre [M 1.0260] nisīditvā pariggaṇhanto sāyaṃ bodhisattaṃ āgantvā mahānasaṃ [V 1.0237] pavisantaṃ disvā “imaṃ pārāvataṃ nissāya macchamaṃsaṃ labhissāmī”ti punadivase pātova āgantvā bodhisattassa nikkhamitvā gocaratthāya gamanakāle piṭṭhito piṭṭhito agamāsi. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “kasmā tvaṃ, samma, amhehi saddhiṃ carasī”ti āha. “Sāmi, tumhāhaṃ kiriyā mayhaṃ ruccati, ito paṭṭhāya tumhe upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti. “Samma, tumhe aññagocarā, mayaṃ aññagocarā, tumhehi amhākaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ dukkara”nti. “Sāmi, tumhākaṃ gocaraggahaṇakāle ahampi gocaraṃ gahetvā tumhehi saddhiṃyeva gamissāmī”ti. “Sādhu, kevalaṃ te appamattena bhavitabba”nti evaṃ bodhisatto kākaṃ ovaditvā gocaraṃ caranto tiṇabījādīni khādati. Bodhisattassa pana gocaraggahaṇakāle kāko gantvā gomayapiṇḍaṃ apanetvā pāṇake khāditvā udaraṃ pūretvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ āgantvā “sāmi, tumhe ativelaṃ caratha, atibahubhakkhena nāma bhavituṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā bodhisattena gocaraṃ gahetvā sāyaṃ āgacchantena saddhiṃyeva mahānasaṃ pāvisi. Bhattakārako [P 1.0243] “amhākaṃ kapoto aññampi gahetvā āgato”ti kākassapi pacchiṃ ṭhapesi. Tato paṭṭhāya dve janā vasanti.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a pigeon. At that time, the residents of Benares, out of a desire for merit, hung up chaff-baskets in various places for birds to live comfortably. The cook of the Benares chief merchant also hung a chaff-basket in his great kitchen, and the Bodhisatta took up residence there. He would go out early in the morning to forage and, returning in the evening, would pass his time dwelling there. One day, a crow, passing over the great kitchen, caught the scent of the smoke from sour and non-sour fish and meat and became greedy. Thinking, “By relying on whom might I get this fish and meat?” he sat nearby and observed. In the evening, he saw the Bodhisatta returning and entering the great kitchen. “By relying on this pigeon, I will get the fish and meat,” he thought. The next day, he came early in the morning and followed close behind the Bodhisatta as he went out to forage. The Bodhisatta asked him, “Friend, why are you foraging with us?” The crow replied, “Master, your conduct pleases me. From now on, I will attend upon you.” “Friend, your foraging grounds are different, and ours are different; it is difficult for you to attend upon us,” said the Bodhisatta. “Master, when you gather your food, I too will gather food and go along with you,” the crow said. “Very well, but you must be heedful,” the Bodhisatta advised, and then went on foraging, eating grass seeds and the like. But when the Bodhisatta was gathering his food, the crow would go, break apart a lump of cow dung, and eat the insects, filling its belly. It would then come to the Bodhisatta and say, “Master, you forage for too long; one should not be so gluttonous.” Then, when the Bodhisatta had gathered his food and was returning in the evening, the crow entered the great kitchen along with him. The cook thought, “Our pigeon has brought another,” and he also set up a basket for the crow. From then on, the two of them dwelt there.

Athekadivasaṃ seṭṭhissa bahuṃ macchamaṃsaṃ āhariṃsu. Taṃ ādāya bhattakārako mahānase tattha tattha olambesi. Kāko taṃ disvā lobhaṃ uppādetvā “sve gocarabhūmiṃ agantvā mayā idameva khāditabba”nti rattiṃ nitthunanto nipajji. Punadivase bodhisatto gocarāya gacchanto “ehi, samma, kākā”ti āha. “Sāmi, tumhe gacchatha, mayhaṃ kucchirogo atthī”ti. “Samma, kākānaṃ kucchirogo nāma na kadāci bhūtapubbo, rattiṃ tīsu yāmesu ekekasmiṃ yāme mucchitā honti, dīpavaṭṭiṃ gilitakāle pana nesaṃ muhuttaṃ titti hoti, tvaṃ imaṃ macchamaṃsaṃ khāditukāmo bhavissasi, ehi manussaparibhogo nāma tumhākaṃ dupparibhuñjiyo, mā evarūpaṃ akāsi, mayā saddhiṃyeva gocarāya gacchāhī”ti. “Na sakkomi, sāmī”ti. “Tena hi paññāyissasi sakena kammena, lobhavasaṃ agantvā appamatto hohī”ti taṃ ovaditvā bodhisatto gocarāya gato.

One day, they brought a large amount of fish and meat for the chief merchant. Taking it, the cook hung it here and there in the great kitchen. Seeing this, the crow, having become greedy, thought, 'Tomorrow, without going to the feeding grounds, I must eat this,' and spent the night groaning as he lay down. The next day, the Bodhisatta, going out to forage, said, 'Come, friend crow!' 'Master, you go ahead, I have a stomach ache,' he replied. 'Friend, crows have never had stomach aches before. At night, during each of the three watches, their food is digested; but when they swallow a lamp wick, they feel satisfied for a moment. You must be wanting to eat this fish and meat. Come, that which is for human consumption is difficult for you to partake of; do not do such a thing. Come forage with me.' 'I cannot, master.' 'Well then, you will be known by your own deed. Do not fall under the sway of greed; be heedful!' advised the Bodhisatta before going off to forage.

Bhattakārako [M 1.0261] nānappakāraṃ macchamaṃsavikatiṃ sampādetvā usumanikkhamanatthaṃ bhājanāni thokaṃ vivaritvā rasaparissāvanakaroṭiṃ bhājanamatthake ṭhapetvā bahi nikkhamitvā sedaṃ puñchamāno aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe kāko pacchito sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā bhattagehaṃ olokento tassa nikkhantabhāvaṃ ñatvā “ayaṃdāni mayhaṃ manorathaṃ pūretvā maṃsaṃ khādituṃ kālo, kiṃ nu kho mahāmaṃsaṃ khādāmi, udāhu cuṇṇikamaṃsa”nti cintetvā “cuṇṇikamaṃsena nāma khippaṃ kucchiṃ pūretuṃ na sakkā, mahantaṃ maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ āharitvā pacchiyaṃ nikkhipitvā khādamāno nipajjissāmī”ti [V 1.0238] pacchito uppatitvā rasakaroṭiyaṃ nilīyi. Sā “kirī”ti saddamakāsi. Bhattakārako taṃ saddaṃ sutvā “kiṃ nu kho eta”nti paviṭṭho kākaṃ disvā “ayaṃ duṭṭhakāko mahāseṭṭhino pakkamaṃsaṃ khāditukāmo, ahaṃ kho pana seṭṭhiṃ nissāya jīvāmi, na imaṃ bālaṃ, kiṃ me iminā”ti dvāraṃ pidhāya kākaṃ gahetvā sakalasarīre pattāni [P 1.0244] luñcitvā allasiṅgīveraloṇajīrakādayo koṭṭetvā ambilatakkena āloḷetvā tenassa sakalasarīraṃ makkhetvā taṃ kākaṃ pacchiyaṃ khipi. So adhimattavedanābhibhūto nitthunanto nipajji.

The cook, having prepared various kinds of fish and meat dishes, slightly opened the containers for the steam to escape and placed a straining bowl for the broth on top of the vessels. He then stepped outside and stood there wiping off his sweat. At that moment, the crow, lifting its head from its basket and looking into the kitchen, noticed the cook's departure and thought, 'Now is the time for me to fulfill my desire and eat some meat. Should I eat a large piece of meat, or just some minced meat?' After considering, it decided, 'With minced meat, one cannot quickly fill the stomach. I will take a large piece of meat, place it in the basket, and eat while lying down.' So, it flew up from the basket and alighted on the broth bowl. The bowl made a 'kiri' sound. Hearing the noise, the cook wondered, 'What is this?' and upon entering, saw the crow. He thought, 'This wicked crow wants to eat the chief merchant's cooked meat. I, however, depend on the chief merchant for my livelihood, not on this fool. What use is this fool to me?' So, he closed the door, caught the crow, and plucked all the feathers from its entire body. He ground together fresh ginger, salt, cumin, and other spices, mixed them with sour buttermilk, smeared the crow's entire body with this paste, and threw the crow into the basket. Overwhelmed by intense pain, it lay there moaning.

Bodhisatto sāyaṃ āgantvā taṃ byasanappattaṃ disvā “lolakāka, mama vacanaṃ akatvā tava lobhaṃ nissāya mahādukkhaṃ pattosī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, arriving in the evening and seeing it had fallen into misfortune, said, 'O greedy crow, by not heeding my words, you have met with great suffering on account of your greed.' Then he spoke this verse:

42.

42.

“Yo atthakāmassa hitānukampino, ovajjamāno na karoti sāsanaṃ;

Kapotakassa vacanaṃ akatvā, amittahatthatthagatova setī”ti.

Whoever, being advised by one who desires his welfare and is compassionate for his benefit, does not follow that instruction, lies fallen into the hands of an enemy, like one who did not heed the pigeon's word.

Tattha kapotakassa vacanaṃ akatvāti pārāvatassa hitānusāsanavacanaṃ akatvā. Amittahatthatthagatova setīti amittānaṃ anatthakārakānaṃ dukkhuppādakapuggalānaṃ hatthatthaṃ hatthapathaṃ gato ayaṃ kāko viya so puggalo mahantaṃ byasanaṃ patvā anusocamāno setīti.

Herein, 'not having followed the pigeon's word' means not having followed the beneficial, instructive word of the pigeon. 'Lies as one who has fallen into the hands of the enemy' means that just as this crow, having come into the hands, into the reach, of enemies—of persons who cause harm and produce suffering—so too that person, having met with great calamity, lies lamenting.

Bodhisatto [M 1.0262] imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā “idāni mayā ca imasmiṃ ṭhāne na sakkā vasitu”nti aññattha gato. Kākopi tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patto. Atha naṃ bhattakārako saddhiṃ pacchiyā gahetvā saṅkāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍesi.

Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta, thinking, 'Now it is not possible for me either to dwell in this place,' went elsewhere. The crow, too, met the end of its life right there. Then the cook, taking it along with the basket, threw it on the refuse heap.

Satthāpi “na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva lolo, pubbepi loloyeva, tañca pana te lolyaṃ nissāya paṇḍitāpi sakāvāsā parihīnā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu anāgāmiphalaṃ patto. Satthā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kāko lolabhikkhu ahosi, pārāvato pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher also said, 'Monk, you are not greedy only now; in the past, too, you were greedy. And on account of that greed of yours, even a wise one was deprived of his own dwelling.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse on the Truths, that monk attained the fruit of a Non-Returner. The Teacher connected the story and identified the birth: 'At that time, the crow was the greedy monk, and the pigeon was none other than myself.'

Kapotajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The commentary on the second Kapota Jātaka is concluded.

[43] 3. Veḷukajātakavaṇṇanā

[43] 3. The Commentary on the Veḷuka Jātaka

Yo [V 1.0239] atthakāmassāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhagavā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu dubbacosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva dubbaco, pubbepi dubbacoyeva, dubbacattāyeva [P 1.0245] ca paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā sappamukhe jīvitakkhayaṃ patto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this, beginning with the words 'Whoever desires his welfare...', in reference to a certain monk who was difficult to admonish. The Blessed One asked him, 'Is it true, monk, that you are difficult to admonish?' When he replied, 'It is true, Venerable Sir,' the Blessed One said, 'Monk, you are not difficult to admonish only now; in the past, too, you were difficult to admonish. And it was precisely because you were difficult to admonish and did not follow the words of the wise that you met the end of your life in the mouth of a snake.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe mahābhogakule nibbatto viññutaṃ patvā kāmesu ādīnavaṃ nekkhamme cānisaṃsaṃ disvā kāme pahāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā pañcābhiññā aṭṭha samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā jhānasukhena vītināmento aparabhāge mahāparivāro pañcahi tāpasasatehi parivuto gaṇassa satthā hutvā vihāsi. Atheko āsivisapotako attano dhammatāya caranto aññatarassa tāpasassa assamapadaṃ patto. Tāpaso tasmiṃ puttasinehaṃ uppādetvā taṃ ekasmiṃ veḷupabbe sayāpetvā paṭijaggati. Tassa veḷupabbe sayanato “veḷuko”tveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Taṃ puttasinehena paṭijagganato tāpasassa “veḷukapitā”tveva nāmaṃ akaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth in the kingdom of Kāsi. Having come to an age of discretion, he saw the danger in sensual pleasures and the benefit in renunciation. Abandoning sensual pleasures, he entered the Himalayas and went forth into the ascetic life. Having practiced the preliminary kasiṇa exercises, he brought forth the five supernormal knowledges and the eight attainments, and passed his time in the bliss of meditative absorption. In time, he became the teacher of a group, surrounded by a large retinue of five hundred ascetics. Now, a young viper, wandering according to its nature, came to the hermitage of a certain ascetic. The ascetic, developing a paternal affection for it, had it sleep in a section of bamboo and took care of it. Because it slept in a section of bamboo, they gave it the name 'Veḷuka.' And because he cared for it with paternal affection, they gave the ascetic the name 'Veḷuka's Father.'

Tadā [M 1.0263] bodhisatto “eko kira tāpaso āsivisaṃ paṭijaggatī”ti sutvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ āsivisaṃ paṭijaggasī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte “āsivisena saddhiṃ vissāso nāma natthi, mā evaṃ jaggāhī”ti āha. “So me ācariya putto, nāhaṃ tena vinā vattituṃ sakkhissāmī”ti. “Tena hi etasseva santikā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇissasī”ti. Tāpaso bodhisattassa vacanaṃ na gaṇhi, āsivisampi jahituṃ nāsakkhi. Tato katipāhaccayeneva sabbe tāpasā phalāphalatthāya gantvā gataṭṭhāne phalāphalassa sulabhabhāvaṃ disvā dve tayo divase tattheva vasiṃsu, veḷukapitāpi tehi saddhiṃ gacchanto āsivisaṃ veḷupabbeyeva sayāpetvā pidahitvā gato. So puna tāpasehi saddhiṃ dvīhatīhaccayena āgantvā “veḷukassa gocaraṃ dassāmī”ti veḷupabbaṃ ugghāṭetvā “ehi, puttaka, chātakosī”ti hatthaṃ pasāresi. Āsiviso dvīhatīhaṃ nirāhāratāya kujjhitvā pasāritahatthaṃ ḍaṃsitvā tāpasaṃ tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā araññaṃ pāvisi. Tāpasā taṃ disvā bodhisattassa ārocesuṃ. Bodhisatto [P 1.0246] tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā isigaṇassa majjhe nisīditvā isīnaṃ ovādavasena imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta, hearing, “It seems a certain ascetic is tending a poisonous snake,” summoned him and asked, “Is it true that you are tending a poisonous snake?” When he replied, “It is true,” the Bodhisatta said: “No trust can be placed in a poisonous snake; do not tend it.” The ascetic replied: “He is my son, Teacher; I cannot live without him.” The Bodhisatta said: “Then you will meet your death because of him.” The ascetic did not heed the Bodhisatta’s words and could not bring himself to abandon the snake. A few days later, all the ascetics went to gather fruits and roots. Seeing that these were plentiful where they had gone, they stayed there for two or three days. The bamboo-father, who went with them, had put the snake to sleep in a bamboo tube and covered it before he left. When he returned with the other ascetics after two or three days, he said, “I will give the bamboo-dweller his food,” uncovered the bamboo tube, and extended his hand, calling out: “Come, little son, you must be hungry.” But the snake, enraged from being without food for two or three days, bit his outstretched hand and caused the ascetic’s death on the spot, then entered the forest. Seeing this, the ascetics reported it to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta had the funeral rites performed for him and, sitting in the midst of the assembly of seers, spoke this verse as an admonition to them:

43.

43.

“Yo [V 1.0240] atthakāmassa hitānukampino, ovajjamāno na karoti sāsanaṃ;

Evaṃ so nihato seti, veḷukassa yathā pitā”ti.

“He who, being admonished by one who seeks his good, one compassionate for his welfare, does not follow the instruction, lies slain just like the bamboo’s father.”

Tattha evaṃ so nihato setīti yo hi isīnaṃ ovādaṃ na gaṇhāti, so yathā esa tāpaso āsivisamukhe pūtibhāvaṃ patvā nihato seti, evaṃ mahāvināsaṃ patvā nihato setīti attho. Evaṃ bodhisatto isigaṇaṃ ovaditvā cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā āyupariyosāne brahmaloke uppajji.

Herein, Thus he lies slain: whoever does not accept the admonition of the seers, he, like this ascetic who met with ruin from the viper’s fangs and lies slain, meets with great destruction and lies slain. This is the meaning. Thus the Bodhisatta, having admonished the assembly of seers and developed the four divine abidings, at the end of his lifespan was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā “na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva dubbaco, pubbepi dubbacoyeva, dubbacabhāveneva ca āsivisamukhe pūtibhāvaṃ patto”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā [M 1.0264] anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā veḷukapitā dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: “Bhikkhu, it is not only now that you are difficult to admonish; in the past, too, you were difficult to admonish. And it was because you were difficult to admonish that you met with ruin from the fangs of a viper.” Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he connected the links and identified the birth: “At that time, the bamboo-father was the monk who is difficult to admonish, the remaining assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and the teacher of the group was myself.”

Veḷukajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Veḷuka Jātaka, the Third.

[44] 4. Makasajātakavaṇṇanā

[44] 4. The Commentary on the Makasa Jātaka

Seyyo amittoti idaṃ satthā magadhesu cārikaṃ caramāno aññatarasmiṃ gāmake bālagāmikamanusse ārabbha kathesi. Tathāgato kira ekasmiṃ samaye sāvatthito magadharaṭṭhaṃ gantvā tattha cārikaṃ caramāno aññataraṃ gāmakaṃ sampāpuṇi. So ca gāmako yebhuyyena andhabālamanussehiyeva ussanno. Tatthekadivasaṃ te andhabālamanussā sannipatitvā “bho, amhe araññaṃ pavisitvā kammaṃ karonte makasā khādanti, tappaccayā amhākaṃ kammacchedo hoti, sabbeva dhanūni ceva āvudhāni ca ādāya gantvā makasehi saddhiṃ yujjhitvā sabbamakase vijjhitvā chinditvā ca māressāmā”ti mantayitvā araññaṃ gantvā “makase vijjhissāmā”ti aññamaññaṃ vijjhitvā ca paharitvā ca dukkhappattā āgantvā antogāme ca gāmamajjhe ca gāmadvāre ca nipajjiṃsu.

The Teacher spoke this verse beginning, “Better an enemy,” while wandering on tour in the Magadhan country, concerning some foolish villagers. It is said that the Tathagata, on one occasion, went from Sāvatthī to the country of Magadha. While wandering on tour there, he came to a certain small village. That village was filled mostly with blind, foolish people. One day, those blind, foolish people assembled and conferred, saying: “Sirs, when we enter the forest to work, mosquitoes bite us, and because of that our work is interrupted. Let us all take our bows and weapons, go and fight with the mosquitoes, and kill all of them by shooting and cutting them down.” Having gone to the forest, intending, “We will shoot the mosquitoes,” they shot and struck one another. Having come to grief, they returned and lay down inside the village, in the middle of the village, and at the village gate.

Satthā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto taṃ gāmaṃ piṇḍāya pāvisi. Avasesā paṇḍitamanussā bhagavantaṃ disvā gāmadvāre maṇḍapaṃ kāretvā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa [P 1.0247] mahādānaṃ datvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne patitamanusse disvā te upāsake pucchi [V 1.0241] “bahū ime gilānā manussā, kiṃ etehi kata”nti? “Bhante, ete manussā ‘makasayuddhaṃ karissāmā’ti gantvā aññamaññaṃ vijjhitvā sayaṃ gilānā jātā”ti. Satthā “na idāneva andhabālamanussā ‘makase paharissāmā’ti attānaṃ paharanti, pubbepi ‘makasaṃ paharissāmā’ti paraṃ paharaṇakamanussā ahesuṃyevā”ti vatvā tehi manussehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, surrounded by the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, entered that village for alms-food. The remaining wise people, seeing the Blessed One, had a pavilion erected at the village gate and gave a great offering to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus with the Buddha at its head. Having paid homage to the Teacher, they sat down. The Teacher, seeing the people who had fallen in various places, asked the lay followers: “There are many sick people here. What have they done?” “Venerable sir, these people went off, thinking, ‘We will wage war on the mosquitoes,’ and ended up wounding one another and becoming sick themselves.” The Teacher said: “It is not only now that these blind, foolish people, intending to strike mosquitoes, strike themselves. In the past, too, there were people who, intending to strike a mosquito, struck another person.” And being requested by those people, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto vaṇijjāya jīvikaṃ kappeti. Tadā kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ paccantagāme bahū [M 1.0265] vaḍḍhakī vasanti. Tattheko khalitavaḍḍhakī rukkhaṃ tacchati, athassa eko makaso tambalohathālakapiṭṭhisadise sīse nisīditvā sattiyā paharanto viya sīsaṃ mukhatuṇḍakena vijjhi. So attano santike nisinnaṃ puttaṃ āha – “tāta, mayhaṃ sīsaṃ makaso sattiyā paharanto viya vijjhati, vārehi na”nti. “Tāta, adhivāsehi, ekappahāreneva taṃ māressāmī”ti. Tasmiṃ samaye bodhisattopi attano bhaṇḍaṃ pariyesamāno taṃ gāmaṃ patvā tassā vaḍḍhakisālāya nisinno hoti. Atha so vaḍḍhakī puttaṃ āha – “tāta, imaṃ makasaṃ vārehī”ti. So “vāressāmi, tātā”ti tikhiṇaṃ mahāpharasuṃ ukkhipitvā pitu piṭṭhipasse ṭhatvā “makasaṃ paharissāmī”ti pitu matthakaṃ dvidhā bhindi, vaḍḍhakī tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patto.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta earned his living by trade. At that time, in a border village in the Kāsi country, many carpenters were living. There, a certain bald carpenter was hewing a tree when a mosquito landed on his head, which was like the back of a copper plate, and pierced it with its proboscis as if striking it with a spear. He said to his son, who was sitting near him: “Son, a mosquito is piercing my head as if striking it with a spear. Drive it away.” “Bear with it, father. I will kill it with a single blow.” At that time, the Bodhisatta, who was seeking his merchandise, had arrived at that village and was sitting in the carpenter’s workshop. Then the carpenter said to his son: “Son, drive this mosquito away.” “I will drive it away, father,” he said. He raised a sharp, large axe, stood behind his father, and thinking, “I will strike the mosquito,” he split his father’s head in two. The carpenter met his end right there.

Bodhisatto tassa taṃ kammaṃ disvā “paccāmittopi paṇḍitova seyyo. So hi daṇḍabhayenapi manusse na māressatī”ti cintetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, seeing that deed of his, thought, “Even an enemy is better if he is wise, for through fear of punishment he would not kill a person,” and he spoke this verse:

44.

44.

“Seyyo amitto matiyā upeto, na tveva mitto mativippahīno;

‘Makasaṃ vadhissa’nti hi eḷamūgo, putto pitu abbhidā uttamaṅga”nti.

“Better an enemy endowed with intelligence than a friend who is devoid of sense. For the foolish son, thinking, ‘I will kill the mosquito,’ split his father’s head.”

Tattha [P 1.0248] seyyoti pavaro uttamo. Matiyā upetoti paññāya samannāgato. Eḷamūgoti lālāmukho bālo. Putto pitu abbhidā uttamaṅganti attano bālatāya puttopi hutvā pitu uttamaṅgaṃ matthakaṃ “makasaṃ paharissāmī”ti dvidhā bhindi. Tasmā bālamittato paṇḍitaamittova seyyoti imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā bodhisatto uṭṭhāya yathākammaṃ gato. Vaḍḍhakissapi ñātakā sarīrakiccaṃ akaṃsu.

Herein, better means superior, excellent. Endowed with intelligence means possessed of wisdom. Foolish son: a slobbering-mouthed fool. The son split his father’s head: because of his foolishness, though he was his son, thinking, “I will strike the mosquito,” he split his father’s head—the top of his body—in two. Therefore a wise enemy is better than a foolish friend. Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta rose and went about his business. The carpenter’s relatives performed the funeral rites.

Satthā [V 1.0242] “evaṃ upāsakā pubbepi ‘makasaṃ paharissāmā’ti paraṃ paharaṇakamanussā ahesuṃyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā gāthaṃ vatvā pakkanto paṇḍitavāṇijo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: “Thus, lay followers, in the past, too, there were people who, intending to strike a mosquito, struck another person.” Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he connected the links and identified the birth: “At that time, the wise merchant who spoke the verse and departed was myself.”

Makasajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Makasa Jātaka, the Fourth.

[45] 5. Rohiṇijātakavaṇṇanā

[45] 5. The Commentary on the Rohiṇī Jātaka

Seyyo [M 1.0266] amittotiidaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ anāthapiṇḍikaseṭṭhino dāsiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Anāthapiṇḍikassa kira ekā rohiṇī nāma dāsī ahosi. Tassā vīhipaharaṇaṭṭhāne āgantvā mahallikā mātā nipajji, taṃ makkhikā parivāretvā sūciyāvijjhamānā viya khādanti. Sā dhītaraṃ āha – “amma, makkhikā maṃ khādanti, etā vārehī”ti. Sā “vāressāmi, ammā”ti musalaṃ ukkhipitvā “mātu sarīre makkhikā māretvā vināsaṃ pāpessāmī”ti mātaraṃ musalena paharitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Taṃ disvā “mātā me matā”ti rodituṃ ārabhi. Taṃ pavattiṃ seṭṭhissa ārocesuṃ. Seṭṭhi tassā sarīrakiccaṃ kāretvā vihāraṃ gantvā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ satthu ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, gahapati, esā ‘mātu sarīre makkhikā māressāmī’ti idāneva musalena paharitvā mātaraṃ māresi, pubbepi māresiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this verse beginning, “Better an enemy,” concerning a slave girl of the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika. It seems Anāthapiṇḍika had a slave girl named Rohiṇī. Her elderly mother came and lay down at the place where she was husking rice. Flies swarmed around her and bit her as if piercing her with needles. The mother said to her daughter: “Dear, flies are biting me; drive them away.” She replied, “I will drive them away, mother.” Then, lifting a pestle and thinking, “I will kill the flies on my mother’s body and destroy them,” she struck her mother with the pestle and killed her. Seeing this, she began to cry, “My mother is dead!” They reported the matter to the great merchant. The merchant had the funeral rites performed for her, went to the monastery, and reported the entire matter to the Teacher. The Teacher said: “Householder, it is not only now that this girl, thinking, ‘I will kill the flies on my mother’s body,’ struck her mother with a pestle and killed her. She killed her in the past as well.” And being requested by him, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto seṭṭhikule nibbattitvā pituaccayena seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi. Tassāpi rohiṇīyeva nāma dāsī ahosi. Sāpi attano vīhipaharaṇaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā nipannaṃ mātaraṃ “makkhikā me, amma, vārehī”ti vuttā evameva musalena paharitvā mātaraṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā rodituṃ ārabhi. Bodhisatto taṃ pavattiṃ [P 1.0249] sutvā “amittopi hi imasmiṃ loke paṇḍitova seyyo”ti cintetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a merchant's family and, after his father's death, attained the position of a merchant. He too had a slave girl named Rohiṇī. Her mother also came to the place where she threshed rice and lay down. Being told by her, “Shoo the flies away from me, dear,” she similarly struck her mother with a pestle, causing her death, and began to weep. Hearing of this incident, the Bodhisatta reflected, “Even an enemy in this world, if wise, is better,” and spoke this verse:

45.

45.

“Seyyo amitto medhāvī, yañce bālānukampako;

Passa rohiṇikaṃ jammiṃ, mātaraṃ hantvāna socatī”ti.

“Better a wise enemy than a foolish sympathizer; Behold Rohiṇī, the wretch, who, having slain her mother, now grieves.”

Tattha medhāvīti paṇḍito ñāṇī vibhāvī. Yañce bālānukampakoti ettha yanti liṅgavipallāso kato, ceti nāmatthe nipāto. Yo nāma bālo anukampako, tato sataguṇena sahassaguṇena [V 1.0243] paṇḍito amitto hontopi seyyoyevāti attho. Atha vā yanti paṭisedhanatthe nipāto, no ce bālānukampakoti attho. Jamminti lāmikaṃ dandhaṃ. Mātaraṃ hantvāna socatīti “makkhikā māressāmī”ti mātaraṃ hantvā idāni ayaṃ bālā sayameva rodati paridevati. Iminā kāraṇena [M 1.0267] imasmiṃ loke amittopi paṇḍito seyyoti bodhisatto paṇḍitaṃ pasaṃsanto imāya gāthāya dhammaṃ desesi.

Herein, “wise” means intelligent, discerning, and perspicacious. Regarding the phrase “than a foolish sympathizer” (`yañce bālānukampako`), `yaṃ` is used with a change of gender, and `ce` is a particle in the sense of ‘indeed.’ The meaning is that a wise enemy is a hundredfold, a thousandfold better than any foolish sympathizer. Alternatively, `yaṃ` is a particle in the sense of negation, meaning “not a foolish sympathizer.” “Wretch” (`jammiṃ`) means lowly, slow. “Who, having slain her mother, now grieves” means that, thinking, “I will kill the flies,” she killed her mother, and now this fool weeps and laments by herself. For this reason, the Bodhisatta, praising the wise, taught the Dhamma with this verse, saying that in this world even an enemy, if wise, is better.

Satthā “na kho, gahapati, esā idāneva ‘makkhikā māressāmī’ti mātaraṃ ghātesi, pubbepi ghātesiyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātāyeva mātā ahosi, dhītāyeva dhītā, mahāseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, “Householder, it was not only now that she killed her mother thinking, ‘I will kill the flies.’ She had killed her before as well.” Having brought forth this teaching, connected the sequence of events, he identified the birth: “At that time, the mother was indeed the mother, the daughter was indeed the daughter, but the great merchant was none other than I.”

Rohiṇijātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Rohiṇī Jātaka, the Fifth.

[46] 6. Ārāmadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā

[46] 6. The Commentary on the Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka

Na ve anatthakusalenāti idaṃ satthā aññatarasmiṃ kosalagāmake viharanto uyyānadūsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Satthā kira kosalesu cārikaṃ caramāno aññataraṃ gāmakaṃ sampāpuṇi. Tattheko kuṭumbiko tathāgataṃ nimantetvā attano uyyāne nisīdāpetvā buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa mahādānaṃ datvā “bhante, yathāruciyā imasmiṃ uyyāne vicarathā”ti āha. Bhikkhū uṭṭhāya uyyānapālaṃ gahetvā uyyāne vicarantā ekaṃ aṅgaṇaṭṭhānaṃ disvā uyyānapālaṃ pucchiṃsu “upāsaka, imaṃ uyyānaṃ aññattha sandacchāyaṃ, imasmiṃ pana ṭhāne na koci rukkho vā gaccho vā atthi, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti? “Bhante, imassa uyyānassa ropanakāle eko gāmadārako udakaṃ siñcanto imasmiṃ ṭhāne rukkhapotake ummūlaṃ katvā mūlappamāṇena udakaṃ siñci[P 1.0250]. Te rukkhapotakā milāyitvā matā. Iminā kāraṇena idaṃ ṭhānaṃ aṅgaṇaṃ jāta”nti. Bhikkhū satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, so gāmadārako idāneva ārāmadūsako, pubbepi ārāmadūsakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher spoke this while staying in a certain village in Kosala, concerning a park-vandal. It is said that while the Teacher was wandering in Kosala, he arrived at a certain village. There, a householder invited the Tathāgata and had him sit in his park. After offering a great alms-giving to the Sangha headed by the Buddha, he said, “Venerable sir, please wander in this park as you wish.” The monks, rising and taking the park-keeper with them, wandered in the park. Seeing a barren place, they asked the park-keeper, “Lay follower, this park is shady elsewhere, but in this place, there is neither tree nor shrub. What is the reason for this?” “Venerable sirs, when this park was being planted, a village boy, while watering, uprooted the saplings in this place and watered them according to the size of their roots. Those saplings withered and died. Because of this, this place became barren.” The monks approached the Teacher and reported the matter. The Teacher said, “Monks, that village boy is not just now a park-vandal; he was a park-vandal before as well.” Having said this, he related a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasiyaṃ nakkhattaṃ ghosayiṃsu. Nakkhattabherisaddasavanakālato paṭṭhāya sakalanagaravāsino nakkhattanissitakā hutvā vicaranti. Tadā rañño uyyāne bahū makkaṭā vasanti. Uyyānapālo cintesi “nagare nakkhattaṃ ghuṭṭhaṃ, ime vānare ‘udakaṃ siñcathā’ti vatvā ahaṃ nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmī”ti jeṭṭhakavānaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā [V 1.0244][M 1.0268] “samma vānarajeṭṭhaka, imaṃ uyyānaṃ tumhākampi bahūpakāraṃ, tumhe ettha pupphaphalapallavāni khādatha, nagare nakkhattaṃ ghuṭṭhaṃ, ahaṃ nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmi. Yāvāhaṃ āgacchāmi, tāva imasmiṃ uyyāne rukkhapotakesu udakaṃ siñcituṃ sakkhissathā”ti pucchi. “Sādhu, siñcissāmī”ti. “Tena hi appamattā hothā”ti udakasiñcanatthāya tesaṃ cammakuṭe ca dārukuṭe ca datvā gato. Vānarā cammakuṭe ceva dārukuṭe ca gahetvā rukkhapotakesu udakaṃ siñcanti. Atha ne vānarajeṭṭhako evamāha “bhonto vānarā, udakaṃ nāma rakkhitabbaṃ, tumhe rukkhapotakesu udakaṃ siñcantā uppāṭetvā uppāṭetvā mūlaṃ oloketvā gambhīragatesu mūlesu bahuṃ udakaṃ siñcatha, agambhīragatesu appaṃ, pacchā amhākaṃ udakaṃ dullabhaṃ bhavissatī”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tathā akaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, a festival was proclaimed in the city. From the time the sound of the festival drum was heard, all the city-dwellers, devoted to the festival, went about enjoying themselves. At that time, many monkeys lived in the king’s park. The park-keeper thought, “A festival has been proclaimed in the city. I will tell these monkeys to water the saplings, and then I will go and enjoy the festival.” Approaching the chief monkey, he said, “Friend, chief of monkeys, this park is of great service to you. Here you eat the flowers, fruits, and tender leaves. A festival has been proclaimed in the city, and I am going to enjoy it. Until I return, will you be able to water the young trees in this park?” The chief monkey replied, “Very well, we will water them.” “In that case, be diligent,” said the park-keeper, and giving them leather bags and wooden pots for watering, he departed. The monkeys took the leather bags and wooden pots and began to water the young trees. Then the chief monkey addressed them, saying, “Friends, water must be conserved. As you water the young trees, uproot each one, examine its roots, and pour much water on those with deep roots and little water on those with shallow roots. Afterwards, water will be difficult for us to obtain.” They agreed, saying, “Very well,” and did as he said.

Tasmiṃ samaye eko paṇḍitapuriso rājuyyāne te vānare tathā karonte disvā evamāha “bhonto vānarā, kasmā tumhe rukkhapotake uppāṭetvā uppāṭetvā mūlappamāṇena udakaṃ siñcathā”ti? Te “evaṃ no vānarajeṭṭhako ovadatī”ti āhaṃsu. So taṃ vacanaṃ sutvā “aho vata bho bālā apaṇḍitā, ‘atthaṃ karissāmā’ti anatthameva karontī”ti cintetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, a certain wise man, seeing the monkeys acting thus in the royal park, asked them, “Sirs, why are you uprooting these young trees and watering them according to the measure of their roots?” They replied, “Thus our chief monkey instructs us.” Hearing their words, he thought, “Alas, these fools, these unwise ones! Thinking to do good, they only do harm.” And thinking thus, he spoke this verse:

46.

46.

“Na [P 1.0251] ve anatthakusalena, atthacariyā sukhāvahā;

Hāpeti atthaṃ dummedho, kapi ārāmiko yathā”ti.

“Truly, a beneficial action does not lead to happiness when performed by one skilled in what is harmful. The fool destroys the benefit, just as the monkey in the park did.”

Tattha veti nipātamattaṃ. Anatthakusalenāti anatthe anāyatane kusalena, atthe āyatane kāraṇe akusalena vāti attho. Atthacariyāti vuḍḍhikiriyā. Sukhāvahāti evarūpena anatthakusalena kāyikacetasikasukhasaṅkhātassa atthassa cariyā na sukhāvahā, na sakkā āvahitunti attho. Kiṃkāraṇā? Ekanteneva hi hāpeti atthaṃ dummedhoti, bālapuggalo “atthaṃ karissāmī”ti atthaṃ hāpetvā anatthameva karoti. Kapi ārāmiko yathāti yathā ārāme niyutto ārāmarakkhanako makkaṭo “atthaṃ karissāmī”ti anatthameva karoti, evaṃ yo koci anatthakusalo, tena na sakkā atthacariyaṃ āvahituṃ, so ekaṃsena atthaṃ hāpetiyevāti. Evaṃ so paṇḍito puriso imāya [M 1.0269] gāthāya vānarajeṭṭhakaṃ garahitvā attano parisaṃ ādāya uyyānā nikkhami.

Herein, `ve` is merely a particle. `Anatthakusalena` means: by one skilled in what is unbeneficial, in the wrong sphere; or, by one unskilled in what is beneficial, in the right sphere, in the right cause. `Atthacariyā` means an action for welfare. `Sukhāvahā` means: by such a one skilled in what is unbeneficial, the practice of what is beneficial, which is defined as physical and mental happiness, does not bring happiness; it cannot be brought about—this is the meaning. For what reason? Because `a fool destroys the benefit`. A foolish person, thinking, “I will bring about a benefit,” destroys that benefit and brings about only what is harmful. `Just as the monkey who was the park-keeper`: just as a monkey appointed in the park as a park-guardian, thinking, “I will bring about a benefit,” brings about only what is harmful, so too anyone who is skilled in what is unbeneficial cannot bring about a beneficial action; he will certainly destroy the benefit. Thus that wise man, having rebuked the chief monkey with this verse, took his retinue and departed from the park.

Satthāpi [V 1.0245] “na, bhikkhave, esa gāmadārako idāneva ārāmadūsako, pubbepi ārāmadūsakoyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vānarajeṭṭhako ārāmadūsakagāmadārako ahosi, paṇḍitapuriso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this village boy is a spoiler of parks; he was a spoiler of parks in the past as well.” Having delivered this Dhamma discourse and made the connection, he identified the birth story: “At that time, the park-spoiling village boy was the chief monkey, and the wise man was I myself.”

Ārāmadūsakajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Ārāmadūsaka Jātaka, the sixth.

[47] 7. Vāruṇidūsakajātakavaṇṇanā

7. The Commentary on the Vāruṇidūsaka Jātaka

Na ve anatthakusalenāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto vāruṇidūsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Anāthapiṇḍikassa kira sahāyo eko vāruṇivāṇijo tikhiṇaṃ vāruṇiṃ yojetvā hiraññasuvaṇṇādīni gahetvā vikkiṇanto mahājane sannipatite “tāta, tvaṃ mūlaṃ gahetvā vāruṇiṃ dehī”ti antevāsikaṃ āṇāpetvā sayaṃ nhāyituṃ agamāsi. Antevāsiko mahājanassa vāruṇiṃ dento manusse antarantarā loṇasakkharā āharāpetvā khādante disvā “ayaṃ surā aloṇikā bhavissati, loṇamettha pakkhipissāmī”ti surācāṭiyaṃ nāḷimattaṃ loṇaṃ pakkhipitvā tesaṃ suraṃ adāsi. Te mukhaṃ pūretvā pūretvā chaḍḍetvā “kiṃ te kata”nti pucchiṃsu. “Tumhe suraṃ pivitvā loṇaṃ āharāpente disvā loṇena yojesi”nti. “Evarūpaṃ nāma manāpaṃ vāruṇiṃ nāsesi bālā”ti taṃ garahitvā uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya pakkantā. Vāruṇivāṇijo āgantvā ekampi adisvā [P 1.0252] “vāruṇipāyakā kahaṃ gatā”ti pucchi, so tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ ācariyo “bāla, evarūpā nāma te surā nāsitā”ti garahitvā imaṃ kāraṇaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa ārocesi. Anāthapiṇḍiko “atthidāni me idaṃ kathāpābhata”nti jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na esa, gahapati, idāneva vāruṇidūsako, pubbepi vāruṇidūsakoyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Indeed, for one skilled in what is unbeneficial…”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, with reference to the spoiler of liquor. It is said that a friend of Anāthapiṇḍika, a liquor merchant, prepared some strong vāruṇī liquor and was selling it for gold, silver, and so on. When a large crowd had gathered, he instructed his apprentice, “My dear, take the payment and give them the vāruṇī,” and went to bathe. While the apprentice was giving the vāruṇī to the crowd, he saw people from time to time having lumps of salt brought to them and eating them. Thinking, “This liquor must be unsalted; I will add salt to it,” he threw a measure of salt into the liquor jar and gave the liquor to them. They filled their mouths with it, spat it out, and asked, “What have you done?” He replied, “Seeing you drinking the liquor and having salt brought, I mixed it with salt.” “Fool! You have ruined such delightful vāruṇī!” they said, and scolding him, they got up and left. When the liquor merchant returned and saw no one, he asked, “Where have the vāruṇī drinkers gone?” The apprentice told him what had happened. Then his master rebuked him, “Fool, you have ruined such fine liquor!” and he related this matter to Anāthapiṇḍika. Anāthapiṇḍika thought, “Now I have a topic to bring to the Teacher,” and went to Jetavana. Having paid homage to the Teacher, he related the matter. The Teacher said, “Householder, it is not only now that this person is a spoiler of liquor; he was a spoiler of liquor in the past as well.” And being requested by him, He related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 1.0270] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ seṭṭhi ahosi. Taṃ upanissāya eko vāruṇivāṇijo jīvati. So tikhiṇaṃ suraṃ yojetvā “imaṃ vikkiṇāhī”ti antevāsikaṃ vatvā nhāyituṃ gato. Antevāsiko tasmiṃ gatamatteyeva surāya loṇaṃ pakkhipitvā imināva nayena suraṃ vināsesi. Athassa ācariyo āgantvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā seṭṭhissa ārocesi. Seṭṭhi “anatthakusalā nāma bālā ‘atthaṃ karissāmā’ti anatthameva karontī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was the chief merchant in Benares. A liquor merchant lived dependent on him. Having prepared strong liquor, he told his apprentice, “Sell this,” and went to bathe. The apprentice, as soon as he had gone, ruined the liquor by mixing salt into it in this very manner. Then his master returned, and knowing that matter, reported it to the chief merchant. The chief merchant said, “Fools unskilled in what is beneficial, thinking ‘we will do what is beneficial,’ only do what is harmful,” and spoke this verse –

47.

47.

“Na [V 1.0246] ve anatthakusalena, atthacariyā sukhāvahā;

Hāpeti atthaṃ dummedho, koṇḍañño vāruṇiṃ yathā”ti.

“Indeed, for one skilled in what is harmful, the practice of what is beneficial brings no happiness; the fool diminishes what is beneficial, as Koṇḍañña did the Vāruṇī liquor.”

Tattha koṇḍañño vāruṇiṃ yathāti yathā ayaṃ koṇḍaññanāmako antevāsiko “atthaṃ karissāmī”ti loṇaṃ pakkhipitvā vāruṇiṃ hāpesi parihāpesi vināsesi, evaṃ sabbopi anatthakusalo atthaṃ hāpetīti bodhisatto imāya gāthāya dhammaṃ desesi.

Therein, 'as Koṇḍañña did the Vāruṇī liquor' means: just as this apprentice named Koṇḍañña, thinking, ‘I will do what is beneficial,’ ruined, diminished, and destroyed the Vāruṇī liquor by adding salt to it, so too does anyone skilled in what is harmful diminish what is beneficial. Thus the Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma by means of this verse.

Satthāpi “na esa gahapati idāneva vāruṇidūsako, pubbepi vāruṇidūsakoyevā”ti vatvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vāruṇidūsako idānipi vāruṇidūsakova ahosi, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher also said, “Householder, this one is not a liquor-spoiler only now; he was a liquor-spoiler in the past as well.” Having made the connection, he identified the Jātaka: “The liquor-spoiler at that time was this very liquor-spoiler of today, but the chief merchant of Benares was I myself.”

Vāruṇidūsakajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The commentary on the Vāruṇidūsaka Jātaka is the seventh.

[48] 8. Vedabbajātakavaṇṇanā

[48] 8. Commentary on the Vedabba Jātaka

Anupāyena yo atthanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva dubbaco, pubbepi dubbacoyeva, teneva [P 1.0253] ca kāraṇena paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā tiṇhena asinā dvidhā katvā chinno hutvā magge nipatittha, tañca ekakaṃ nissāya purisasahassaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ patta”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This verse beginning with ‘Anupāyena yo atthaṃ’ the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a recalcitrant monk. For that monk, the Teacher said, “Monk, you are not only recalcitrant now; you were recalcitrant even in the past. And for that very reason, not having followed the word of the wise ones, you were cut in two by a sharp sword and fell on the road. And relying on you alone, a thousand men met the destruction of their lives.” Having said this, he recounted a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente ekasmiṃ gāmake aññataro brāhmaṇo vedabbaṃ nāma mantaṃ jānāti. So kira manto anaggho [M 1.0271] mahāraho, nakkhattayoge laddhe taṃ mantaṃ parivattetvā ākāse ullokite ākāsato sattaratanavassaṃ vassati. Tadā bodhisatto tassa brāhmaṇassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhāti. Athekadivasaṃ brāhmaṇo bodhisattaṃ ādāya kenacideva karaṇīyena attano gāmā nikkhamitvā cetaraṭṭhaṃ agamāsi, antarāmagge ca ekasmiṃ araññaṭṭhāne pañcasatā pesanakacorā nāma panthaghātaṃ karonti. Te bodhisattañca vedabbabrāhmaṇañca gaṇhiṃsu. Kasmā panete “pesanakacorā”ti vuccanti? Te kira dve jane gahetvā ekaṃ dhanāharaṇatthāya pesenti, tasmā “pesanakacorā”tveva vuccanti. Tepi ca pitāputte gahetvā pitaraṃ “tvaṃ amhākaṃ dhanaṃ āharitvā puttaṃ gahetvā yāhī”ti vadanti. Etenupāyena [V 1.0247] mātudhītaro gahetvā mātaraṃ vissajjenti, jeṭṭhakaniṭṭhe gahetvā jeṭṭhabhātikaṃ vissajjenti, ācariyantevāsike gahetvā antevāsikaṃ vissajjenti. Te tasmiṃ kāle vedabbabrāhmaṇaṃ gahetvā bodhisattaṃ vissajjesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, a certain brahmin in a certain village knew a spell called Vedabba. It is said that this spell was priceless and very precious. When a favorable conjunction of stars was obtained, by reciting that spell and looking up at the sky, a rain of the seven treasures would fall from the sky. At that time, the Bodhisatta was learning the craft from that brahmin. Then one day, the brahmin, taking the Bodhisatta, left his own village for some business and went to the Ceta country. On the way, in a certain forest area, five hundred robbers called “Pesanaka-robbers” were committing highway robbery. They seized the Bodhisatta and the Vedabba brahmin. Why, then, were they called “Pesanaka-robbers”? It is said that when they captured two people, they would send one to fetch wealth; therefore, they were called “Pesanaka-robbers.” They also captured fathers and sons, saying to the father, “You go and bring us wealth, and then take your son and leave.” By this method, they would capture mothers and daughters and release the mother, or capture elder and younger brothers and release the elder brother, or capture teachers and pupils and release the pupil. At that time, they seized the Vedabba brahmin and released the Bodhisatta.

Bodhisatto ācariyaṃ vanditvā “ahaṃ ekāhadvīhaccayena āgamissāmi, tumhe mā bhāyittha, apica kho pana mama vacanaṃ karotha, ajja dhanavassāpanakanakkhattayogo bhavissati, mā kho tumhe dukkhaṃ asahantā mantaṃ parivattetvā dhanaṃ vassāpayittha. Sace vassāpessatha, tumhe ca vināsaṃ pāpuṇissatha, ime ca pañcasatā corā”ti evaṃ ācariyaṃ ovaditvā dhanatthāya agamāsi. Corāpi sūriye atthaṅgate brāhmaṇaṃ bandhitvā nipajjāpesuṃ. Taṅkhaṇaññeva pācīnalokadhātuto paripuṇṇacandamaṇḍalaṃ uṭṭhahi. Brāhmaṇo nakkhattaṃ olokento “dhanavassāpanakanakkhattayogo [P 1.0254] laddho, kiṃ me dukkhena anubhūtena, mantaṃ parivattetvā ratanavassaṃ vassāpetvā corānaṃ dhanaṃ datvā yathāsukhaṃ gamissāmī”ti cintetvā core āmantesi “bhonto corā, tumhe maṃ kimatthāya gaṇhathā”ti? “Dhanatthāya, ayyā”ti. “Sace vo, dhanena attho, khippaṃ maṃ bandhanā mocetvā sīsaṃ nhāpetvā ahatavatthāni acchādetvā gandhehi vilimpāpetvā pupphāni pilandhāpetvā ṭhapethā”ti. “Corā tassa kathaṃ sutvā tathā akaṃsu”.

The Bodhisatta paid homage to his teacher and said, “I will return in a day or two; do not be afraid. But do follow my words: today the conjunction for making wealth rain will occur. Do not, unable to bear suffering, recite the spell and make wealth rain down. If you do make it rain, you will meet destruction, and so will these five hundred thieves.” Having thus advised his teacher, he left in search of wealth. When the sun set, the thieves bound the brahmin and made him lie down. At that very moment, a full moon arose from the eastern quarter. The brahmin, observing the constellation, thought, “The conjunction for making wealth rain has arrived. Why should I endure suffering? I will recite the spell, make a rain of jewels fall, give the wealth to the thieves, and go as I please.” Then he addressed the thieves, “Honorable thieves, why have you seized me?” “For wealth, sir,” they replied. “If you need wealth, quickly release me from my bonds, bathe my head, dress me in fresh clothes, anoint me with perfumes, and adorn me with flowers, and then set me up.” Hearing this, the thieves did as he instructed.

Brāhmaṇo [M 1.0272] nakkhattayogaṃ ñatvā mantaṃ parivattetvā ākāsaṃ ullokesi, tāvadeva ākāsato ratanāni patiṃsu. Corā taṃ dhanaṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā uttarāsaṅgesu bhaṇḍikaṃ katvā pāyiṃsu. Brāhmaṇopi tesaṃ pacchatova agamāsi. Atha te core aññe pañcasatā corā gaṇhiṃsu. “Kimatthaṃ amhe gaṇhathā”ti ca vuttā “dhanatthāyā”ti āhaṃsu. “Yadi vo dhanena attho, etaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ gaṇhatha, eso ākāsaṃ ulloketvā dhanaṃ vassāpesi, amhākampetaṃ eteneva dinna”nti. Corā core vissajjetvā “amhākampi dhanaṃ dehī”ti brāhmaṇaṃ gaṇhiṃsu. Brāhmaṇo “ahaṃ tumhākaṃ dhanaṃ dadeyyaṃ, dhanavassāpanakanakkhattayogo pana ito saṃvaccharamatthake bhavissati. Yadi vo dhanenattho, adhivāsetha, tadā dhanavassaṃ vassāpessāmī”ti āha. Corā kujjhitvā “ambho, duṭṭhabrāhmaṇa, aññesaṃ idāneva dhanaṃ vassāpetvā amhe aññaṃ saṃvaccharaṃ adhivāsāpesī”ti tiṇhena asinā brāhmaṇaṃ dvidhā chinditvā magge chaḍḍetvā vegena anubandhitvā tehi corehi saddhiṃ yujjhitvā te sabbepi māretvā dhanaṃ ādāya puna dve koṭṭhāsā hutvā aññamaññaṃ yujjhitvā aḍḍhateyyāni purisasatāni ghātetvā etena upāyena yāva dve janā avasiṭṭhā ahesuṃ, tāva aññamaññaṃ ghātayiṃsu. Evaṃ taṃ purisasahassaṃ vināsaṃ pattaṃ.

The brahmin, knowing the conjunction of the stars, recited the spell and gazed at the sky. Instantly, jewels fell from the sky. The thieves collected that wealth, made bundles in their upper garments, and departed. The brahmin also went right behind them. Then another five hundred thieves seized those thieves. When asked, “For what reason have you seized us?” they replied, “For the sake of wealth.” “If wealth is what you desire, then seize this brahmin—he made riches rain down by gazing at the sky. This wealth was given to us by him.” The thieves released the other thieves and seized the brahmin, demanding, “Give us wealth too!” The brahmin said, “I would give you wealth, but the stellar conjunction for making wealth rain will occur at the end of a year from now. If you desire wealth, be patient; then I will make it rain riches.” Enraged, the thieves shouted, “O wicked brahmin! You made wealth rain for others just now, yet you make us wait for another year?” They sliced the brahmin in two with a sharp sword, left him on the road, and quickly pursued and fought with those thieves, killing them all, and took the wealth. Then, having become two factions, they fought each other, slaughtering two hundred and fifty men. In this way, they kept killing one another until only two men remained. Thus, those thousand men met their destruction.

Te [V 1.0248] pana dve janā upāyena taṃ dhanaṃ āharitvā ekasmiṃ gāmasamīpe gahanaṭṭhāne dhanaṃ paṭicchādetvā eko khaggaṃ gahetvā [P 1.0255] rakkhanto nisīdi, eko taṇḍule gahetvā bhattaṃ pacāpetuṃ gāmaṃ pāvisi. Lobho ca nāmesa vināsamūlamevāti dhanasantike nisinno cintesi “tasmiṃ āgate idaṃ dhanaṃ dve koṭṭhāsā bhavissanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ taṃ āgatamattameva khaggena paharitvā ghāteyya”nti. So khaggaṃ sannayhitvā tassa āgamanaṃ olokento nisīdi. Itaropi cintesi “taṃ dhanaṃ dve koṭṭhāsā bhavissanti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ bhatte visaṃ pakkhipitvā taṃ purisaṃ bhojetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā ekakova dhanaṃ gaṇheyya”nti. So niṭṭhite bhatte sayaṃ bhuñjitvā sesake visaṃ pakkhipitvā taṃ ādāya tattha agamāsi. Taṃ bhattaṃ otāretvā ṭhitamattameva itaro khaggena dvidhā chinditvā taṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne chaḍḍetvā tañca bhattaṃ bhuñjitvā sayampi tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Evañca taṃ dhanaṃ nissāya sabbeva vināsaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu.

Those two men, having brought that wealth by some means, hid it in a dense thicket near a certain village. One, taking a sword, sat guarding it, while the other, taking rice, entered the village to have food cooked. For greed, it is said, is indeed the very root of destruction. The one sitting by the wealth thought: “When he returns, this wealth will be divided into two portions. What if I were to strike him with the sword as soon as he arrives and kill him?” So, preparing his sword, he sat watching for his arrival. The other also thought: “That wealth will be divided into two portions. What if I were to put poison in the food, feed that man, cause him to reach the end of his life, and take the wealth all by myself?” When the food was ready, he ate some himself, put poison in the remainder, and taking it, went there. As soon as he had set down the food, the other man cut him in two with his sword, threw him into the hiding place, and then, eating that food, he himself also met his end right there. Thus, on account of that wealth, they all met with destruction.

Bodhisattopi [M 1.0273] kho ekāhadvīhaccayena dhanaṃ ādāya āgato tasmiṃ ṭhāne ācariyaṃ adisvā vippakiṇṇaṃ pana dhanaṃ disvā “ācariyena mama vacanaṃ akatvā dhanaṃ vassāpitaṃ bhavissati, sabbehi vināsaṃ pattehi bhavitabba”nti mahāmaggena pāyāsi. Gacchanto ācariyaṃ mahāmagge dvidhā chinnaṃ disvā “mama vacanaṃ akatvā mato”ti dārūni uddharitvā citakaṃ katvā ācariyaṃ jhāpetvā vanapupphehi pūjetvā purato gacchanto jīvitakkhayaṃ patte pañcasate, purato aḍḍhateyyasateti anukkamena avasāne dve jane jīvitakkhayaṃ patte disvā cintesi “imaṃ dvīhi ūnaṃ purisasahassaṃ vināsaṃ pattaṃ, aññehi dvīhi corehi bhavitabbaṃ, tepi santhambhituṃ na sakkhissanti, kahaṃ nu kho te gatā”ti gacchanto tesaṃ dhanaṃ ādāya gahanaṭṭhānaṃ paviṭṭhamaggaṃ disvā gacchanto bhaṇḍikabaddhassa dhanassa rāsiṃ disvā ekaṃ bhattapātiṃ avattharitvā mataṃ addasa. Tato “idaṃ nāma tehi kataṃ bhavissatī”ti sabbaṃ ñatvā “kahaṃ nu kho so puriso”ti vicinanto tampi paṭicchannaṭṭhāne apaviddhaṃ disvā “amhākaṃ [P 1.0256] ācariyo mama vacanaṃ akatvā attano dubbacabhāvena attanāpi vināsaṃ patto, aparampi tena purisasahassaṃ vināsitaṃ, anupāyena vata akāraṇena attano vuḍḍhiṃ patthayamānā amhākaṃ ācariyo viya mahāvināsameva pāpuṇissantī”ti cintetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, after a day or two had passed, came bringing the wealth. Arriving at that place and not seeing his teacher, but seeing the wealth scattered about, he thought: “My teacher, not heeding my words, must have caused the wealth to be rained down; all must have met with destruction.” He then set out along the main road. As he went, he saw his teacher cut in two on the road. Thinking, “He died for not heeding my words,” he gathered wood, made a pyre, cremated his teacher, honored him with forest flowers, and proceeded onward. He saw five hundred men who had met their end, then two hundred and fifty more ahead, and so on in succession until, at the end, he saw two men who had met their end. He thought: “These thousand men, less two, have met with destruction. There must have been two other thieves, but they too could not have endured. Where could they have gone?” As he went on, he saw the path they had taken into a dense thicket, carrying the wealth. Proceeding, he saw a heap of wealth tied in bundles, and then he saw one man dead with a food bowl overturned beside him. Then, realizing, “This must have been their doing,” and understanding it all, he wondered: “Where could the other man be?” Searching, he saw him also, cast into the hiding place. He reflected: “Our teacher, by not heeding my words, through his own intractability, has met with destruction himself and has also destroyed a thousand other men. Indeed, those who, through improper means and without cause, desire their own advancement will, like our teacher, surely meet with great destruction.” Having thought thus, he spoke this verse:

48.

48.

“Anupāyena yo atthaṃ, icchati so vihaññati;

Cetā haniṃsu vedabbaṃ, sabbe te byasanamajjhagū”ti.

“He who seeks a benefit by improper means is afflicted; the Ceta thieves slew Vedabba, and all of them met with disaster.”

Tattha [V 1.0249] so vihaññatīti so anupāyena “attano atthaṃ vuḍḍhiṃ sukhaṃ icchāmī”ti akāle vāyāmaṃ karonto puggalo vihaññati kilamati mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇāti. Cetāti cetaraṭṭhavāsino corā. Haniṃsu vedabbanti vedabbamantavasena “vedabbo”ti laddhanāmaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ haniṃsu. Sabbe te byasanamajjhagūti tepi ca anavasesā aññamaññaṃ ghātayamānā byasanaṃ adhigacchiṃsu paṭilabhiṃsūti.

Therein, ‘is afflicted’ means that a person, striving improperly and at the wrong time, wishing for his own benefit, prosperity, and happiness, is afflicted, becomes exhausted, and meets with great destruction. ‘The Ceta thieves’ means the robbers dwelling in the Ceta country. ‘Slew Vedabba’ means they slew the brahmin who had gained the name ‘Vedabba’ by means of the Vedabba spell. ‘All of them met with disaster’ means that all of them, without exception, killing one another, came to disaster.

Evaṃ bodhisatto “yathā amhākaṃ ācariyo anupāyena aṭṭhāne parakkamaṃ karonto dhanaṃ vassāpetvā attanāpi jīvitakkhayaṃ patto, aññesañca [M 1.0274] vināsapaccayo jāto, evameva yo aññopi anupāyena attano atthaṃ icchanto vāyāmaṃ karissati, sabbo so attanā ca vinassissati, paresañca vināsapaccayo bhavissatī”ti vanaṃ unnādento devatāsu sādhukāraṃ dadamānāsu imāya gāthāya dhammaṃ desetvā taṃ dhanaṃ upāyena attano gehaṃ āharitvā dānādīni puññāni karonto yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā jīvitapariyosāne saggapathaṃ pūrayamāno agamāsi.

Thus the Bodhisatta, making the forest resound while the deities gave their applause, taught the Dhamma with this verse, saying: 'Just as our teacher, striving by wrong means in the wrong place, caused wealth to rain down and thereby met his own end and became a cause of ruin for others, even so, whoever else, desiring their own gain, strives by wrong means, will both perish themselves and become a cause of ruin for others.' Then, having brought that wealth to his own house by proper means, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and having lived for the full extent of his life, at its end, he went on to fulfill the path to the celestial realm.

Satthāpi “na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva dubbaco, pubbepi dubbacova, dubbacattā pana mahāvināsaṃ patto”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vedabbabrāhmaṇo dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, antevāsiko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said: 'Bhikkhu, it is not only now that you are difficult to admonish; you were difficult to admonish in the past as well. And because you were difficult to admonish, you met with great ruin.' Having delivered this Dhamma teaching and connected the sequence, he identified the birth, saying: 'At that time, the Vedabba Brahmin was the bhikkhu who is difficult to admonish, and the pupil was I myself.'

Vedabbajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The eighth is the commentary on the Vedabba Jātaka.

[49] 9. Nakkhattajātakavaṇṇanā

[49] 9. Commentary on the Nakkhatta Jātaka

Nakkhattaṃ [P 1.0257] patimānentanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ ājīvakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kirekaṃ kuladhītaraṃ janapade eko kulaputto attano puttassa vāretvā “asukadivase nāma gaṇhissāmī”ti divasaṃ ṭhapetvā tasmiṃ divase sampatte attano kulūpakaṃ ājīvakaṃ pucchi “bhante, ajja mayaṃ ekaṃ maṅgalaṃ karissāma, sobhanaṃ nu kho nakkhatta”nti. So “ayaṃ maṃ paṭhamaṃ apucchitvāva divasaṃ ṭhapetvā idāni paṭipucchati, hotu, sikkhāpessāmi na”nti kujjhitvā “ajja asobhanaṃ nakkhattaṃ, mā ajja maṅgalaṃ karittha, sace karissatha, mahāvināso bhavissatī”ti āha. Tasmiṃ kule manussā tassa saddahitvā taṃ divasaṃ na gacchiṃsu. Nagaravāsino sabbaṃ maṅgalakiriyaṃ katvā tesaṃ anāgamanaṃ disvā “tehi ajja divaso ṭhapito, no [V 1.0250] ca kho āgatā, amhākampi bahu vayakammaṃ kataṃ, kiṃ no tehi, amhākaṃ dhītaraṃ aññassa dassāmā”ti yathākateneva maṅgalena dhītaraṃ aññassa kulassa adaṃsu.

'Awaiting the constellation...' This the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain Ājīvaka. It is said that in Sāvatthī, a certain clansman from the countryside, having arranged a marriage for his son with a daughter of a good family, fixed a date, saying: 'On such-and-such a day we shall take her.' When that day arrived, he asked the Ājīvaka who frequented his family: 'Venerable sir, today we are to perform a ceremony. Is the constellation auspicious?' The Ājīvaka, becoming angry, thought: 'This man fixed the date without first asking me, and only now consults me. So be it, I shall teach him a lesson!' And he said: 'Today the constellation is inauspicious. Do not perform the ceremony today. If you do, there will be great ruin.' The people of that family, believing him, did not go on that day. The city-dwellers, having made all the ceremonial preparations and seeing their non-arrival, said: 'They fixed today as the date, yet they have not come. We too have incurred much expense. What are they to us? We shall give our daughter to another!' And with the very ceremony they had prepared, they gave their daughter to another family.

Itare punadivase āgantvā “detha no dārika”nti āhaṃsu. Atha ne sāvatthivāsino “janapadavāsino nāma tumhe gahapatikā pāpamanussā divasaṃ ṭhapetvā avaññāya na āgatā, āgatamaggeneva paṭigacchatha[M 1.0275], amhehi aññesaṃ dārikā dinnā”ti paribhāsiṃsu. Te tehi saddhiṃ kalahaṃ katvā dārikaṃ alabhitvā yathāgatamaggeneva gatā. Tenapi ājīvakena tesaṃ manussānaṃ maṅgalantarāyassa katabhāvo bhikkhūnaṃ antare pākaṭo jāto. Te bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā “āvuso, ājīvakena kulassa maṅgalantarāyo kato”ti kathayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchi. Te “imāya nāmā”ti kathayiṃsu. “Na, bhikkhave, idāneva ājīvako tassa kulassa maṅgalantarāyaṃ karoti, pubbepi esa tesaṃ kujjhitvā maṅgalantarāyaṃ akāsiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The others, coming on the next day, said: 'Give us the girl!' Then the residents of Sāvatthī rebuked them, saying: 'You country-dwelling householders are wicked people! Having fixed the day, you did not come out of contempt. Go back the way you came! We have given the girl to others.' After quarreling with them and failing to get the girl, they went back the way they had come. The fact that the Ājīvaka had caused an obstruction to those people's ceremony became known among the bhikkhus. Those bhikkhus, having gathered in the hall of Dhamma, sat discussing it, saying: 'Venerable sirs, the Ājīvaka has caused an obstruction to the family's ceremony.' The Teacher arrived and asked: 'Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now gathered together?' They told him: 'For this one.' 'Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this Ājīvaka causes an obstruction to that family's ceremony; in the past, too, becoming angry with them, he did indeed cause an obstruction to their ceremony.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente nagaravāsino janapadavāsīnaṃ dhītaraṃ vāretvā divasaṃ ṭhapetvā attano kulūpakaṃ ājīvakaṃ pucchiṃsu “bhante, ajja amhākaṃ ekā maṅgalakiriyā, sobhanaṃ nu kho nakkhatta”nti. So “ime attano ruciyā divasaṃ ṭhapetvā idāni maṃ pucchantī”ti kujjhitvā “ajja nesaṃ maṅgalantarāyaṃ karissāmī”ti cintetvā “ajja asobhanaṃ [P 1.0258] nakkhattaṃ, sace karotha, mahāvināsaṃ pāpuṇissathā”ti āha. Te tassa saddahitvā na gamiṃsu. Janapadavāsino tesaṃ anāgamanaṃ ñatvā “te ajja divasaṃ ṭhapetvāpi na āgatā, kiṃ no tehi, aññesaṃ dhītaraṃ dassāmā”ti aññesaṃ dhītaraṃ adaṃsu. Nagaravāsino punadivase āgantvā dārikaṃ yāciṃsu. Janapadavāsino “tumhe nagaravāsino nāma chinnahirikā gahapatikā, divasaṃ ṭhapetvā dārikaṃ na gaṇhittha, mayaṃ tumhākaṃ anāgamanabhāvena aññesaṃ adamhā”ti. Mayaṃ ājīvakaṃ paṭipucchitvā “‘nakkhattaṃ na sobhana’nti nāgatā, detha no dārika”nti. “Amhehi tumhākaṃ anāgamanabhāvena aññesaṃ dinnā, idāni dinnadārikaṃ kathaṃ puna ānessāmā”ti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the city-dwellers arranged a marriage with the daughter of some country-dwellers and fixed a date. They then asked the Ājīvaka who frequented their family: 'Venerable sir, today we have a ceremony; is the constellation auspicious?' He, becoming angry, thought: 'They fixed the date according to their own liking and only now ask me. Today I will create an obstruction to their ceremony!' And he said: 'Today the constellation is inauspicious. If you proceed, you will meet with great ruin.' Believing him, they did not go. The country-dwellers, knowing of their non-arrival, said: 'Although they fixed today as the date, they have not come. What are they to us? We shall give our daughter to others,' and they gave their daughter to others. The next day, the city-dwellers came and asked for the girl. The country-dwellers said: 'You city-dwellers are shameless householders! Having fixed the date, you did not come to take the girl. Because of your non-arrival, we have given her to others.' The city-dwellers replied: 'We consulted the Ājīvaka and did not come because he said, "The constellation is not auspicious." Give us the girl!' The country-dwellers answered: 'Because of your non-arrival, we have given her to others. Now, how can we bring back a girl who has already been given away?'

Evaṃ tesu aññamaññaṃ kalahaṃ karontesu eko nagaravāsī paṇḍitapuriso ekena kammena janapadaṃ gato tesaṃ nagaravāsīnaṃ “mayaṃ ājīvakaṃ pucchitvā nakkhattassa asobhanabhāvena nāgatā”ti kathentānaṃ sutvā “nakkhattena ko attho, nanu dārikāya laddhabhāvova nakkhatta”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

While they were thus quarreling with one another, a wise man from the city, who had gone to the countryside on some business, heard those city-dwellers saying, 'We consulted an Ājīvaka and did not come because the constellation was inauspicious.' Hearing this, he said, 'What is the use of a constellation? Is not the very attainment of the girl the constellation?' and spoke this verse:

49.

49.

“Nakkhattaṃ [V 1.0251][M 1.0276] patimānentaṃ, attho bālaṃ upaccagā;

Attho atthassa nakkhattaṃ, kiṃ karissanti tārakā”ti.

For one who awaits the constellation, the goal passes by the fool. The goal itself is the constellation of the goal; what will the stars do?

Tattha patimānentanti olokentaṃ, “idāni nakkhattaṃ bhavissati, idāni nakkhattaṃ bhavissatī”ti āgamayamānaṃ. Attho bālaṃ upaccagāti etaṃ nagaravāsikaṃ bālaṃ dārikāpaṭilābhasaṅkhāto attho atikkanto. Attho atthassa nakkhattanti yaṃ atthaṃ pariyesanto carati, so paṭiladdho atthova atthassa nakkhattaṃ nāma. Kiṃ karissanti tārakāti itare pana ākāse tārakā kiṃ karissanti, kataraṃ atthaṃ sādhessantīti attho. Nagaravāsino kalahaṃ katvā dārikaṃ alabhitvāva agamaṃsu.

Here, 'awaiting the constellation' means observing, expecting, "Now the auspicious time will come, now the auspicious time will come." 'The goal passes by the fool' means that the foolish city-dweller missed the opportunity called obtaining the girl. 'The goal itself is the constellation of the goal' means that the very goal one seeks, that obtained goal, is indeed the auspicious time. 'What will the stars do?' implies that the other stars in the sky, what will they do, what purpose will they accomplish? The city-dwellers, having quarreled, left without obtaining the girl.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, esa ājīvako idāneva kulassa maṅgalantarāyaṃ karoti, pubbepi akāsiyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ājīvako etarahi [P 1.0259] ājīvakova ahosi, tānipi kulāni etarahi kulāniyeva, gāthaṃ vatvā ṭhito paṇḍitapuriso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that this Ājīvaka brings misfortune to a family; he did so in the past as well." Having given this discourse, he connected the story and identified the birth: "The Ājīvaka then was the same as the Ājīvaka now, those families were the same as the families now, and the wise man who spoke the verse was none other than myself."

Nakkhattajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The commentary on the Nakkhatta Jātaka, the ninth, is concluded.

[50] 10. Dummedhajātakavaṇṇanā

[50] 10. The Commentary on the Dummedha Jātaka.

Dummedhānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lokatthacariyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā dvādasakanipāte mahākaṇhajātake (jā. 1.12.61 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

Regarding 'Dummedhānaṃ,' this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning conduct for the benefit of the world. It will appear in the Mahākaṇha Jātaka in the Book of Twelve (Jātaka 1.12.61, etc.).

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa rañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tassa mātukucchito nikkhantassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “brahmadattakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So soḷasavassuddesiko hutvā takkasilāyaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ [M 1.0277] pāraṃ gantvā aṭṭhārasannaṃ vijjaṭṭhānānaṃ nipphattiṃ pāpuṇi, athassa pitā oparajjaṃ adāsi. Tasmiṃ samaye bārāṇasivāsino devatāmaṅgalikā honti, devatā namassanti, bahū ajeḷakakukkuṭabhūkarādayo vadhitvā nānappakārehi pupphagandhehi ceva maṃsalohitehi ca balikammaṃ karonti. Bodhisatto cintesi “idāni sattā devatāmaṅgalikā, bahuṃ pāṇavadhaṃ karonti, mahājano yebhuyyena adhammasmiṃyeva niviṭṭho, ahaṃ pitu accayena rajjaṃ [V 1.0252] labhitvā ekampi akilametvā upāyeneva pāṇavadhaṃ kātuṃ na dassāmī”ti. So ekadivasaṃ rathaṃ abhiruyha nagarā nikkhanto addasa ekasmiṃ mahante vaṭarukkhe mahājanaṃ sannipatitaṃ, tasmiṃ rukkhe nibbattadevatāya santike puttadhītuyasadhanādīsu yaṃ yaṃ icchati, taṃ taṃ patthentaṃ. So taṃ disvā rathā oruyha taṃ rukkhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā gandhapupphehi pūjetvā udakena abhisekaṃ katvā rukkhaṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā devatāmaṅgaliko viya hutvā devataṃ namassitvā rathaṃ abhiruyha nagaraṃ pāvisi. Tato paṭṭhāya imināva niyāmena antarantare tattha gantvā devatāmaṅgaliko [P 1.0260] viya pūjaṃ karoti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the king’s chief queen. When he emerged from his mother’s womb, on the naming day, they gave him the name "Prince Brahmadatta." At sixteen years of age, he went to Takkasilā to learn the arts, mastered the three Vedas, and became proficient in the eighteen branches of knowledge. Then his father gave him the viceroyalty. At that time, the people of Benares were devoted to deities, worshipping them and making offerings. They would slaughter many goats, fowl, pigs, and other animals, performing sacrifices with various flowers, perfumes, meat, and blood. The Bodhisatta thought, "Nowadays, beings are devoted to deities and commit much slaughter. The majority are deeply entrenched in unrighteousness. When I inherit the kingdom after my father’s death, I will not allow even a single creature to be killed, but will prevent it by some skillful means." One day, while riding out of the city in his chariot, he saw a large crowd gathered around a great banyan tree. In that tree dwelt a deity, and whatever one desired—sons, daughters, wealth, or prosperity—one would pray for it. Seeing this, he descended from his chariot, approached the tree, worshipped it with fragrant flowers, sprinkled it with water, circumambulated the tree, and, like one devoted to deities, paid homage to the deity. Then he mounted his chariot and returned to the city. From then on, he would go there from time to time in the same manner, performing worship as if devoted to the deity.

So aparena samayena pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya catasso agatiyo vajjetvā dasa rājadhamme akopento dhammena rajjaṃ kārento cintesi “mayhaṃ manoratho matthakaṃ patto, rajje patiṭṭhitomhi. Yaṃ panāhaṃ pubbe ekaṃ atthaṃ cintayiṃ, idāni taṃ matthakaṃ pāpessāmī”ti amacce ca brāhmaṇagahapatikādayo ca sannipātāpetvā āmantesi “jānātha bho mayā kena kāraṇena rajjaṃ patta”nti? “Na jānāma, devā”ti. “Api vohaṃ asukaṃ nāma vaṭarukkhaṃ gandhādīhi pūjetvā añjaliṃ paggahetvā namassamāno diṭṭhapubbo”ti. “Āma, devā”ti. Tadāhaṃ patthanaṃ akāsiṃ “sace rajjaṃ pāpuṇissāmi, balikammaṃ te karissāmī”ti. “Tassā me devatāya ānubhāvena idaṃ rajjaṃ laddhaṃ, idānissā balikammaṃ karissāmi, tumhe papañcaṃ akatvā khippaṃ devatāya balikammaṃ sajjethā”ti. “Kiṃ kiṃ gaṇhāma, devā”ti? Bho ahaṃ devatāya āyācamāno “ye mayhaṃ rajje pāṇātipātādīni pañca dussīlakammāni dasa akusalakammapathe samādāya vattissanti, te ghātetvā antavaṭṭimaṃsalohitādīhi balikammaṃ karissāmī”ti āyāciṃ. Tasmā tumhe evaṃ bheriṃ carāpetha “amhākaṃ rājā uparājakāleyeva evaṃ āyāci ‘sacāhaṃ rajjaṃ pāpuṇissāmi, ye [M 1.0278] me rajje dussīlā bhavissanti, te sabbe ghātetvā balikammaṃ karissāmī’ti, so idāni pañcavidhaṃ dussīlakammaṃ dasavidhaṃ akusalakammapathaṃ samādāya vattamānānaṃ dussīlānaṃ sahassaṃ ghātetvā tesaṃ hadayamaṃsādīni gāhāpetvā devatāya balikammaṃ kātukāmo, evaṃ nagaravāsino jānantū”ti. Evañca pana vatvā “yedāni ito paṭṭhāya dussīlakamme vattissanti, tesaṃ sahassaṃ ghātetvā yaññaṃ yajitvā āyācanato muccissāmī”ti etamatthaṃ pakāsento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, after some time, when his father had passed away and he had ascended the throne, avoiding the four wrong courses and not violating the ten royal virtues, he ruled righteously and thought: "My heart’s desire has been fulfilled; I have ascended the throne. But that one wish I had before—now I shall bring it to completion." Having assembled his ministers, brahmins, householders, and others, he addressed them: "Do you know, sirs, by what means I obtained the kingdom?" "We do not know, lord." "Have you ever seen me honoring a certain banyan tree with perfumes and so on, and paying homage with joined hands?" "Yes, lord." "At that time, I made a vow: 'If I obtain the kingdom, I will perform an offering for you.' By the power of that deity, I have gained this kingdom. Now I shall perform the offering for her. Without delay, prepare the offering for the deity." "What should we gather, lord?" "Sirs, when I entreated the deity, I vowed: 'Those who, in my kingdom, commit the five immoral acts—killing living beings and so on—or follow the ten unwholesome courses of action, I will slay them and perform an offering with their entrails, flesh, blood, and so on.' Therefore, have the drum proclaimed thus: 'Our king, even while still a prince, vowed thus: "If I obtain the kingdom, I will slay all the immoral ones in my realm and perform an offering." Now, wishing to perform an offering for the deity by slaying a thousand immoral persons who engage in the five kinds of immoral acts and the ten kinds of unwholesome courses, he will take their heart-flesh, and so forth. Let the city-dwellers know this.'" And having said this, to make this meaning clear, he declared: "From now on, those who engage in immoral acts—a thousand of them will be slain, and after performing the offering, I shall be freed from my vow," and spoke this verse:

50.

50.

“Dummedhānaṃ sahassena, yañño me upayācito;

Idāni khohaṃ yajissāmi, bahu adhammiko jano”ti.

"A sacrifice with a thousand foolish ones was vowed by me; now indeed I shall perform the sacrifice, for many people are unrighteous."

Tattha [V 1.0253][P 1.0261] dummedhānaṃ sahassenāti “idaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭati, idaṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti ajānanabhāvena, dasasu vā pana akusalakammapathesu samādāya vattanabhāvena duṭṭhā medhā etesanti dummedhā, tesaṃ dummedhānaṃ nippaññānaṃ bālapuggalānaṃ gaṇitvā gahitena sahassena. Yañño me upayācitoti mayā devataṃ upasaṅkamitvā “evaṃ yajissāmī”ti yañño yācito. Idāni khohaṃ yajissāmīti so ahaṃ iminā āyācanena rajjassa paṭiladdhattā idāni yajissāmi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Idāni hi bahu adhammiko jano, tasmā idāneva naṃ gahetvā balikammaṃ karissāmīti.

Therein, 'by a thousand fools' means: because they do not know 'this action is proper to perform, this is not proper,' or because they conduct themselves by undertaking the ten unwholesome courses of action, their wisdom is corrupted, hence they are 'fools' (dummedhā). It refers to a thousand such foolish, unwise individuals, counted and seized. 'A sacrifice was entreated by me' means: having approached a deity, I made a vow thinking, 'I will sacrifice thus.' 'Now I shall sacrifice' means: I, having obtained the kingdom through this entreaty, will now perform the sacrifice. For what reason? Because now there are many unrighteous people; therefore, I will seize them right now and perform the sacrificial offering.

Amaccā bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sādhu, devā”ti dvādasayojanike bārāṇasinagare bheriṃ carāpesuṃ. Bheriyā āṇaṃ sutvā ekampi dussīlakammaṃ samādāya ṭhito ekapurisopi nāhosi. Iti yāva bodhisatto rajjaṃ kāresi, tāva ekapuggalopi pañcasu dasasu vā dussīlakammesu ekampi kammaṃ karonto na paññāyittha. Evaṃ bodhisatto ekapuggalampi akilamento sakalaraṭṭhavāsino sīlaṃ rakkhāpetvā sayampi dānādīni puññāni katvā jīvitapariyosāne attano parisaṃ ādāya devanagaraṃ pūrento agamāsi.

The ministers, hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, said, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' and had a drum beaten throughout the twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī. Upon hearing the drum’s proclamation, there was not a single person who stood by having undertaken even one immoral deed. Thus, for as long as the Bodhisatta reigned, not a single person was known to be committing even one of the five or ten immoral actions. In this way, the Bodhisatta, without causing hardship to a single person, had all the inhabitants of the kingdom observe morality, and himself performed meritorious deeds such as generosity. At the end of his life, taking his retinue with him, he went on to fill the city of the gods.

Satthāpi “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva lokassa atthaṃ carati, pubbepi cariyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ [M 1.0279] samodhānesi – “tadāparisā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, bārāṇasirājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata acts for the welfare of the world; he acted so in the past as well.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse and connected the narrative, he concluded the Jātaka, saying: 'The assembly at that time became the Buddha’s assembly, and the king of Bārāṇasī was I myself.'

Dummedhajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.
