The Commentary on the Dummedha Jātaka is the tenth.

Atthakāmavaggo pañcamo.

The Atthakāmavagga, the fifth section.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Losakatissakapota, veḷukaṃ makasampi ca;

Rohiṇī ārāmadūsaṃ, vāruṇīdūsavedabbaṃ;

Nakkhattaṃ dummedhaṃ dasāti.

Losaka, Kapota, Veḷuka, and also Makasa; Rohiṇī, Ārāmadūsaka, Vāruṇidūsaka, Vedabba; Nakkhatta, Dummedha—these are the ten.

Paṭhamo paṇṇāsako.

The First Fifty.

6. Āsīsavaggo

6. The Chapter of Aspiration

[51] 1. Mahāsīlavajātakavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Mahāsīlava Jātaka

Āsīsetheva [V 1.0254] purisoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ossaṭṭhavīriyaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ossaṭṭhavīriyosī”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante”ti [P 1.0262] ca vutte “kasmā tvaṃ bhikkhu evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā vīriyaṃ ossaji, pubbe paṇḍitā rajjā parihāyitvāpi attano vīriye ṭhatvāva naṭṭhampi yasaṃ puna uppādayiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'A person should indeed aspire...' This was spoken by the Teacher while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a monk who had slackened his effort. The Teacher asked him, 'Is it true, monk, that you have slackened your effort?' When he replied, 'Yes, venerable sir,' the Teacher said, 'Why, monk, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, have you slackened your effort? In the past, the wise, even after losing their kingdoms, by standing firm in their own effort, regained their lost glory.' Having said this, he related a story from the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto rañño aggamahesiyā kucchimhi nibbatto. Tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase “sīlavakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So soḷasavassuddesikova sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā aparabhāge pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhito mahāsīlavarājā nāma ahosi dhammiko dhammarājā. So nagarassa catūsu dvāresu catasso, majjhe ekaṃ, nivesanadvāre ekanti niccaṃ cha dānasālāyo kārāpetvā kapaṇaddhikānaṃ dānaṃ deti, sīlaṃ rakkhati, uposathakammaṃ karoti, khantimettānuddayasampanno aṅke nisinnaṃ puttaṃ paritosayamāno [M 1.0280] viya sabbasatte paritosayamāno dhammena rajjaṃ kāreti. Tasseko amacco antepure padubbhitvā aparabhāge pākaṭo jāto. Amaccā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā pariggaṇhanto attanā paccakkhato ñatvā taṃ amaccaṃ pakkosāpetvā “andhabāla ayuttaṃ te kataṃ, na tvaṃ mama vijite vasituṃ arahasi, attano dhanañca puttadāre ca gahetvā aññattha yāhī”ti raṭṭhā pabbājesi. So nikkhamitvā kāsiraṭṭhaṃ atikkamma kosalajanapadaṃ gantvā kosalarājānaṃ upaṭṭhahanto anukkamena rañño abbhantariko vissāsiko jāto.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the king’s chief queen. On his naming day, they gave him the name Prince Sīlava. When he was sixteen years of age, having achieved mastery in all the arts, he was later, upon his father’s passing, established in the kingship and became the great king named Sīlava, a righteous king who ruled with justice. He had six permanent alms-halls built—four at the four city gates, one in the center of the city, and one at his palace gate—and gave alms to the poor and to travellers. He observed the moral precepts, undertook the Uposatha observance, and was endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion. Ruling righteously, he brought delight to all beings, just as one would delight a child seated on one's lap. One of his ministers committed an offense in the inner palace and was later discovered. The other ministers informed the king. The king, investigating the matter and knowing it to be true firsthand, had that minister summoned and said, 'Blind fool, you have done what is improper. You are not fit to live in my domain. Take your wealth, your wife and children, and go elsewhere.' Thus, he banished him from the country. Leaving, he crossed the kingdom of Kāsī and went to the country of Kosala. While serving the king of Kosala, he gradually became an intimate and trusted courtier.

So ekadivasaṃ kosalarājānaṃ āha – “deva bārāṇasirajjaṃ nāma nimmakkhikamadhupaṭalasadisaṃ, rājā atimuduko, appeneva balavāhanena sakkā bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhitu”nti. Rājā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “bārāṇasirajjaṃ nāma mahā, ayañca ‘appeneva balavāhanena sakkā bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhitu’nti āha, kiṃ nu kho pana payuttakacoro siyā”ti [V 1.0255] cintetvā “payuttakosi maññe”ti āha. “Nāhaṃ, deva, payuttako, saccameva vadāmi. Sace me na saddahatha, manusse pesetvā paccantagāmaṃ hanāpetha, te manusse gahetvā attano santikaṃ nīte dhanaṃ datvā vissajjessatī”ti. Rājā “ayaṃ ativiya sūro hutvā vadati, vīmaṃsissāmi tāvā”ti [P 1.0263] attano purise pesetvā paccantagāmaṃ hanāpesi. Manussā te core gahetvā bārāṇasirañño dassesuṃ. Rājā te disvā “tātā, kasmā gāmaṃ hanathā”ti pucchi. “Jīvituṃ asakkontā, devā”ti vutte rājā “atha kasmā mama santikaṃ nāgamittha, itodāni paṭṭhāya evarūpaṃ kammaṃ mā karitthā”ti tesaṃ dhanaṃ datvā vissajjesi. Te gantvā kosalarañño taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. So ettakenāpi gantuṃ avisahanto puna majjhejanapadaṃ hanāpesi. Tepi core rājā tatheva dhanaṃ datvā vissajjesi. So ettakenāpi agantvā puna pesetvā antaravīthiyaṃ vilumpāpesi, rājā tesampi corānaṃ dhanaṃ datvā vissajjesiyeva. Tadā kosalarājā “ativiya dhammiko rājā”ti ñatvā “bārāṇasirajjaṃ gahessāmī”ti balavāhanaṃ ādāya niyyāsi.

One day, he said to the king of Kosala: 'Sire, the kingdom of Benares is like a honeycomb free of bees. The king is very gentle, and with but a small military force, the kingdom of Benares can be taken.' Hearing his words, the king thought, 'The kingdom of Benares is vast, yet this man says it can be taken with but a small military force. Could he be a spy?' Reflecting thus, he said, 'I suppose you are a spy.' 'I am not a spy, sire; I speak the truth. If you do not believe me, send men to raid a border village. When those men are captured and brought into his presence, he will give them wealth and release them.' The king thought, 'This man speaks with great boldness. I shall first investigate.' He sent his own men to raid a border village. The inhabitants captured those thieves and presented them to the king of Benares. Seeing them, the king asked, 'My dears, why do you raid the village?' When they replied, 'We are unable to make a living, sire,' the king said, 'Then why did you not come to me? From this day forward, do not commit such an act.' He gave them wealth and released them. They went and reported the matter to the king of Kosala. Still not daring to go, he again had a village in the interior of the country raided. The king likewise gave those thieves wealth and released them. Still not venturing forth, he again sent men and had them plunder within the city streets, and the king gave wealth to those thieves as well and released them. Then the king of Kosala, knowing, 'The king is exceedingly righteous,' took his forces and set out, thinking, 'I shall take the kingdom of Benares.'

Tadā pana bārāṇasirañño mattavāraṇepi abhimukhaṃ āgacchante anivattanadhammā asaniyāpi sīse patantiyā asantasanasabhāvā sīlavamahārājassa [M 1.0281] ruciyā sati sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ gahetuṃ samatthā sahassamattā abhejjavarasūrā mahāyodhā honti. Te “kosalarājā āgacchatī”ti sutvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, kosalarājā kira ‘bārāṇasirajjaṃ gaṇhissāmī’ti āgacchati, gacchāma, naṃ amhākaṃ rajjasīmaṃ anokkantameva pothetvā gaṇhāmā”ti vadiṃsu. Rājā “tātā, maṃ nissāya aññesaṃ kilamanakiccaṃ natthi, rajjatthiko rajjaṃ gaṇhātu, māgamitthā”ti nivāresi. Kosalarājā rajjasīmaṃ atikkamitvā janapadamajjhaṃ pāvisi. Amaccā punapi rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tatheva vadiṃsu, rājā purimanayeneva nivāresi. Kosalarājā bahinagare ṭhatvā “rajjaṃ vā detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti sīlavamahārājassa sāsanaṃ pesesi. Rājā taṃ sutvā “natthi mayā saddhiṃ yuddhaṃ, rajjaṃ gaṇhātū”ti paṭisāsanaṃ pesesi. Punapi amaccā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, na mayaṃ kosalarañño nagaraṃ pavisituṃ dema, bahinagareyeva naṃ pothetvā gaṇhāmā”ti āhaṃsu, rājā purimanayeneva nivāretvā nagaradvārāni vivarāpetvā saddhiṃ [P 1.0264] amaccasahassena mahātale pallaṅkamajjhe nisīdi.

Now, at that time, the king of Benares had a thousand great warriors—unbreakable, excellent, and brave—who were of a nature not to retreat even when a rutting elephant came charging, who were of a nature not to tremble even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon their heads, and who, should it be King Sīlava's wish, were capable of seizing the kingship of all Jambudīpa. Hearing that the king of Kosala was coming, they approached the king and said, 'Sire, the king of Kosala is reportedly coming to take the kingdom of Benares. Let us go and crush and capture him before he even crosses our border.' The king forbade them, saying, 'My dears, on my account there is no need for others to suffer hardship. Let him who desires the kingdom take it. Do not go.' The king of Kosala crossed the border and entered the interior of the country. The ministers again approached the king and spoke in the same manner, and the king forbade them as before. The king of Kosala, standing outside the city, sent a message to the great King Sīlava: 'Either give up the kingdom or give battle!' Hearing this, the king sent back a reply: 'There is no battle with me; let him take the kingdom.' Again the ministers approached the king and said, 'Sire, we will not allow the king of Kosala to enter the city. We shall crush and capture him right outside the city.' The king forbade them as before, had the city gates opened, and sat upon his throne on the great terrace, together with his thousand ministers.

Kosalarājā mahantena balavāhanena bārāṇasiṃ pāvisi. So ekampi paṭisattuṃ apassanto rañño nivesanadvāraṃ gantvā amaccagaṇaparivuto apārutadvāre nivesane alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ [V 1.0256] mahātalaṃ āruyha nisinnaṃ nirāparādhaṃ sīlavamahārājānaṃ saddhiṃ amaccasahassena gaṇhāpetvā “gacchatha, imaṃ rājānaṃ saddhiṃ amaccehi pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā āmakasusānaṃ netvā galappamāṇe āvāṭe khanitvā yathā ekopi hatthaṃ ukkhipituṃ na sakkoti, evaṃ paṃsuṃ pakkhipitvā nikhanatha, rattiṃ siṅgālā āgantvā etesaṃ kātabbayuttakaṃ karissantī”ti āha. Manussā corarañño āṇaṃ sutvā rājānaṃ saddhiṃ amaccehi pacchābāhaṃ gāḷhabandhanaṃ bandhitvā nikkhamiṃsu. Tasmimpi kāle sīlavamahārājā corarañño āghātamattampi nākāsi. Tesupi amaccesu evaṃ bandhitvā nīyamānesu ekopi rañño vacanaṃ bhindituṃ samattho nāma nāhosi. Evaṃ suvinītā kirassa parisā. Atha te rājapurisā sāmaccaṃ sīlavamahārājānaṃ āmakasusānaṃ netvā galappamāṇe āvāṭe khanitvā sīlavamahārājānaṃ majjhe[M 1.0282], ubhosu passesu sesaamacceti evaṃ sabbepi āvāṭesu otāretvā paṃsuṃ ākiritvā ghanaṃ ākoṭetvā agamaṃsu. Tadā sīlavamahārājā amacce āmantetvā “corarañño upari kopaṃ akatvā mettaṃ eva bhāvetha, tātā”ti ovadi.

The king of Kosala entered Benares with a great army. Seeing not a single opponent, he went to the gate of the king’s residence. Surrounded by his retinue of ministers, he entered the palace with its open doors, ascended the great, adorned, and prepared terrace, and had the blameless great King Sīlava, who was seated there, seized along with his thousand ministers, saying: 'Go, take this king with his ministers, bind their hands tightly behind their backs, lead them to the charnel ground, and dig pits neck-deep. Then, fill the pits with earth and bury them so that not one can lift a hand. At night, the jackals will come and do to them what must be done.' Hearing the command of the robber king, his men bound the king and his ministers tightly with their hands behind their backs and led them away. Even at that moment, the great King Sīlava did not harbor so much as a trace of malice toward the robber king. And among those ministers being led away thus bound, not a single one was capable of disobeying the king’s word. So well-disciplined, it is said, was his assembly. Then those royal men took the great King Sīlava with his ministers to the charnel ground, dug pits neck-deep, and having lowered the great King Sīlava into the middle one and the remaining ministers into those on both sides, they filled them all with earth, stamped it down firmly, and departed. Then the great King Sīlava addressed his ministers, giving this counsel: 'My dears, do not harbor anger toward the robber king, but cultivate only loving-kindness.'

Atha aḍḍharattasamaye “manussamaṃsaṃ khādissāmā”ti siṅgālā āgamiṃsu. Te disvā rājā ca amaccā ca ekappahāreneva saddamakaṃsu, siṅgālā bhītā palāyiṃsu. Te nivattitvā olokentā pacchato kassaci anāgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā puna paccāgamiṃsu. Itarepi tatheva saddamakaṃsu. Evaṃ yāvatatiyaṃ palāyitvā puna olokentā tesu ekassapi anāgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “vajjhappattā ete bhavissantī”ti sūrā hutvā nivattitvā puna tesu saddaṃ karontesupi na palāyiṃsu. Jeṭṭhakasiṅgālo rājānaṃ upagañchi, sesā siṅgālā sesānaṃ amaccānaṃ santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Upāyakusalo [P 1.0265] rājā tassa attano santikaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā ḍaṃsituṃ okāsaṃ dento viya gīvaṃ ukkhipitvā taṃ gīvāya ḍaṃsamānaṃ hanukaṭṭhikena ākaḍḍhitvā yante pakkhipitvā viya gāḷhaṃ gaṇhi, nāgabalena raññā hanukaṭṭhikena ākaḍḍhitvā gīvāya gāḷhaṃ gahitasiṅgālo attānaṃ mocetuṃ asakkonto maraṇabhayatajjito mahāviravaṃ viravi. Avasesā siṅgālā tassa taṃ aṭṭassaraṃ sutvā “ekena purisena suggahito bhavissatī”ti amacce upasaṅkamituṃ asakkontā maraṇabhayatajjitā sabbe palāyiṃsu. Rañño hanukaṭṭhikena daḷhaṃ katvā gahitasiṅgāle aparāparaṃ sañcarante paṃsu sithilā ahosi. Sopi siṅgālo maraṇabhayabhīto catūhi pādehi rañño uparibhāge paṃsuṃ apabyūhi, rājā paṃsuno sithilabhāvaṃ ñatvā siṅgālaṃ vissajjetvā nāgabalo thāmasampanno aparāparaṃ sañcaranto ubho hatthe ukkhipitvā āvāṭamukhavaṭṭiyaṃ olubbha vātacchinnavalāhako viya nikkhamitvā ṭhito amacce assāsetvā paṃsuṃ viyūhitvā sabbe uddharitvā amaccaparivuto āmakasusāne aṭṭhāsi.

At midnight, jackals came, thinking, 'We will eat human flesh.' Seeing them, the king and his ministers made a loud noise together, and the frightened jackals fled. They turned back to look and, realizing that no one had followed, returned again. The others also made the same noise. Thus, up to the third time they fled and then, looking back and seeing that not even one was following, they thought, 'These men must be doomed,' and, growing bold, turned back. Even when the men made noise again, they did not flee. The eldest jackal approached the king, while the other jackals went near the ministers. The king, skilled in stratagem, knowing that the jackal had come close to him, as if giving it an opportunity to bite, raised his neck. As it bit his neck, the king, with his jawbone, pulled it in as if putting it into a machine, and held it tightly. The jackal, tightly held by the neck and pulled by the king's jawbone with the strength of an elephant, unable to free itself and terrified by the fear of death, let out a great cry. The remaining jackals, hearing that loud sound and thinking, 'He must have been firmly seized by a man,' were unable to approach the ministers and fled in terror of death. As the jackal, firmly held by the king's jawbone, struggled back and forth, the earth became loose. The jackal, frightened by the fear of death, kicked up earth with its four feet onto the king's upper body. Realizing the earth had loosened, the king released the jackal. Then, the mighty king, endowed with the strength of an elephant, moving back and forth, raising both hands and clinging to the edge of the pit, emerged like a cloud torn by the wind. He stood up, reassured his ministers, cleared away the earth, and lifted them all out. Surrounded by his ministers, he stood in the charnel ground.

Tasmiṃ [V 1.0257] samaye manussā ekaṃ matamanussaṃ āmakasusāne chaḍḍentā dvinnaṃ yakkhānaṃ sīmantarikāya chaḍḍesuṃ. Te yakkhā taṃ matamanussaṃ bhājetuṃ asakkontā “na mayaṃ imaṃ bhājetuṃ sakkoma, ayaṃ sīlavarājā dhammiko, esa no bhājetvā dassati, etassa santikaṃ gacchāmā”ti [M 1.0283] taṃ matamanussaṃ pāde gahetvā ākaḍḍhantā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “deva, amhākaṃ imaṃ matakaṃ bhājetvā dehī”ti āhaṃsu. “Bho yakkhā, ahaṃ imaṃ tumhākaṃ bhājetvā dadeyyaṃ, aparisuddho panamhi, nhāyissāmi tāvā”ti. Yakkhā corarañño ṭhapitaṃ vāsitaudakaṃ attano ānubhāvena āharitvā rañño nhānatthāya adaṃsu. Nhatvā ṭhitassa saṃharitvā ṭhapite corarañño sāṭake āharitvā adaṃsu, te nivāsetvā ṭhitassa catujjātiyagandhasamuggaṃ āharitvā adaṃsu, gandhe vilimpitvā ṭhitassa suvaṇṇasamugge maṇitālavaṇṭesu ṭhapitāni nānāpupphāni āharitvā adaṃsu. Pupphāni piḷandhitvā ṭhitakāle “aññaṃ kiṃ karomā”ti pucchiṃsu. Rājā attano chātakākāraṃ [P 1.0266] dassesi, te gantvā corarañño sampāditaṃ nānaggarasabhojanaṃ āharitvā adaṃsu, rājā nhātānulitto sumaṇḍitappasādhito nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhuñji. Yakkhā corarañño ṭhapitaṃ vāsitapānīyaṃ suvaṇṇabhiṅkāreneva suvaṇṇasarakenapi saddhiṃ āhariṃsu. Athassa pānīyaṃ pivitvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā hatthe dhovitvā ṭhitakāle corarañño sampāditaṃ pañcasugandhikasuparibhāvitaṃ tambūlaṃ āharitvā adaṃsu. Taṃ khāditvā ṭhitakāle “aññaṃ kiṃ karomā”ti pucchiṃsu. Gantvā corarañño ussīsake nikkhittaṃ maṅgalakhaggaṃ āharathāti. Tampi gantvā āhariṃsu. Rājā taṃ khaggaṃ gahetvā taṃ matamanussaṃ ujukaṃ ṭhapāpetvā matthakamajjhe asinā paharitvā dve koṭṭhāse katvā dvinnaṃ yakkhānaṃ samavibhattameva vibhajitvā adāsi, datvā ca pana khaggaṃ dhovitvā sannayhitvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha te yakkhā manussamaṃsaṃ khāditvā suhitā hutvā tuṭṭhacittā “aññaṃ te, mahārāja, kiṃ karomā”ti pucchiṃsu. Tena hi tumhe attano ānubhāvena maṃ corarañño sirigabbhe otāretha, ime ca amacce attano attano gehesu patiṭṭhāpethāti. Te “sādhu devā”ti sampaṭicchitvā tathā akaṃsu.

At that time, people, abandoning a dead body in a charnel ground, left it in the boundary area between the territories of two yakkhas. Unable to divide the corpse between themselves, the yakkhas said, 'We cannot divide this body. This King Sīlava is righteous; he will divide it for us. Let us go to him.' So, dragging the corpse by its feet, they went to the king and said, 'O king, divide this dead body for us.' The king replied, 'O yakkhas, I would divide it for you, but I am unclean—let me bathe first.' The yakkhas, by their own power, brought scented water that had been prepared for the robber king and gave it to the king for his bathing. After he had bathed and was standing, they brought robes that had been folded and set aside for the robber king and gave them to him. After he had dressed and was standing, they brought a casket of the four kinds of perfumes and gave it to him. After he had anointed himself with the perfumes and was standing, they brought various flowers placed in golden caskets and on jeweled fans and gave them to him. When he had adorned himself with the flowers and was standing, they asked, 'What else shall we do?' The king indicated that he was hungry. They went and brought various choice and delicious foods prepared for the robber king and gave them to him. The king, having bathed, anointed himself, and being beautifully adorned, ate the choice and delicious food. The yakkhas then brought scented drinking water prepared for the robber king in a golden pitcher along with a golden cup. After he had drunk the water, rinsed his mouth, and washed his hands, they brought betel prepared for the robber king, well-infused with the five kinds of fragrances, and gave it to him. When he had eaten the betel and was standing, they asked, 'What else shall we do?' 'Go and bring the auspicious sword placed at the head of the robber king’s bed,' he said. They went and brought that as well. Taking the sword, the king had the corpse laid straight, and striking it in the middle of the head with the blade, he made two portions and divided it equally between the two yakkhas. Having given it, he washed the sword, sheathed it, and stood. Then the yakkhas, having eaten the human flesh, were satisfied and, with pleased minds, asked, 'Great king, what else shall we do for you?' 'Then, by your own power, place me in the robber king’s royal bedchamber, and establish these ministers in their respective homes,' he said. They consented, saying, 'Very well, O king,' and did as instructed.

Tasmiṃ samaye corarājā alaṅkatasirigabbhe sirisayanapiṭṭhe nipanno niddāyati. Rājā tassa pamattassa niddāyantassa khaggatalena udaraṃ pahari. So bhīto pabujjhitvā dīpālokena sīlavamahārājānaṃ sañjānitvā sayanā uṭṭhāya satiṃ upaṭṭhapetvā ṭhito rājānaṃ āha “mahārāja, evarūpāya [M 1.0284] rattiyā gahitārakkhe pihitadvāre bhavane ārakkhamanussehi nirokāse ṭhāne khaggaṃ sannayhitvā alaṅkatapaṭiyatto kathaṃ nāma tvaṃ imaṃ sayanapiṭṭhaṃ āgatosī”ti. Rājā attano āgamanākāraṃ sabbaṃ vitthārato kathesi. Taṃ sutvā corarājā saṃviggamānaso “mahārāja, ahaṃ manussabhūtopi samāno tumhākaṃ guṇe na jānāmi, paresaṃ lohitamaṃsakhādakehi [V 1.0258] pana kakkhaḷehi pharusehi yakkhehi tava guṇā ñātā, na dānāhaṃ, narinda[P 1.0267], evarūpe sīlasampanne tayi dubbhissāmī”ti khaggaṃ ādāya sapathaṃ katvā rājānaṃ khamāpetvā mahāsayane nipajjāpetvā attanā khuddakamañcake nipajjitvā pabhātāya rattiyā uṭṭhite sūriye bheriṃ carāpetvā sabbaseniyo ca amaccabrāhmaṇagahapatike ca sannipātāpetvā tesaṃ purato ākāse puṇṇacandaṃ ukkhipanto viya sīlavarañño guṇe kathetvā parisamajjheyeva puna rājānaṃ khamāpetvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā “mahārāja, ito paṭṭhāya tumhākaṃ uppanno corūpaddavo mayhaṃ bhāro, mayā gahitārakkhā tumhe rajjaṃ karothā”ti vatvā pesuññakārakassa āṇaṃ kāretvā attano balavāhanaṃ ādāya sakaraṭṭhameva gato.

At that time, the robber king was asleep, lying on a royal bed in an ornamented chamber. King Mahāsīlava struck his belly with the flat of his sword as he lay heedless and sleeping. Startled, he awoke and, recognizing the great King Sīlava by the lamplight, rose from his bed, composed himself, and stood, saying to the king: “Great King, on such a night, in a palace with guards posted and doors locked, in a place inaccessible to the watchmen, how have you come to this very bed, girt with a sword and fully adorned?” The king related in full detail the manner of his arrival. Hearing this, the robber king, with a stirred mind, said: “Great King, though I am a human being, I did not know your virtues; but your virtues are known by the harsh, cruel yakkhas who eat the flesh and blood of others. Now, O Lord of men, I shall not act with malice toward you who are so endowed with virtue.” Taking his sword, he made an oath, asked for the king’s forgiveness, had him lie down on the great bed, and himself lay down on a small couch. When the night had passed and the sun had risen, he had the drum sounded, assembled all his armies, ministers, brahmins, and householders, and before them, as if raising the full moon in the sky, he declared the virtues of King Sīlava. Then, in the midst of the assembly, he again asked for the king’s forgiveness, handed back the kingdom, and said: “Great King, from this day forward, any danger from robbers that arises for you shall be my responsibility. Rule your kingdom with the protection I have provided.” Having had the slandering minister punished, he took his own army and retinue and departed for his own country.

Sīlavarājāpi kho alaṅkatapaṭiyatto setacchattassa heṭṭhā sarabhapādake kañcanapallaṅke nisinno attano sampattiṃ oloketvā “ayañca evarūpā sampatti amaccasahassassa ca jīvitapaṭilābho mayi vīriyaṃ akaronte na kiñci abhavissa, vīriyabalena panāhaṃ naṭṭhañca imaṃ yasaṃ paṭilabhiṃ, amaccasahassassa ca jīvitadānaṃ adāsiṃ, āsacchedaṃ vata akatvā vīriyameva kattabbaṃ. Katavīriyassa hi phalaṃ nāma evaṃ samijjhatī”ti cintetvā udānavasena imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then King Sīlava, fully adorned, seated on a sarabha-footed golden throne beneath the white parasol, surveyed his good fortune and thought: “This great fortune and the restoration of life for a thousand ministers would not have come to be at all had I not made an effort. By the power of my effort, I have regained this lost glory and have given the gift of life to a thousand ministers. Truly, one should not give up hope, but should make an effort. For one who has made an effort, the fruit is indeed accomplished in this way.” Thinking thus, he uttered this verse as a solemn utterance:

51.

51.

“Āsīsetheva puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito;

Passāmi vohaṃ attānaṃ, yathā icchiṃ tathā ahū”ti.

“A man should indeed maintain hope; a wise person should not despair. Behold, I see myself: as I wished, so it has become.”

Tattha āsīsethevāti “evāhaṃ vīriyaṃ ārabhanto imamhā dukkhā muccissāmī”ti attano vīriyabalena āsaṃ karotheva. Na nibbindeyya paṇḍitoti paṇḍito upāyakusalo yuttaṭṭhāne vīriyaṃ karonto “ahaṃ imassa vīriyassa phalaṃ na labhissāmī”ti na ukkaṇṭheyya, āsacchedaṃ kareyyāti attho. Passāmi vohaṃ attānanti ettha voti nipātamattaṃ[M 1.0285], ahaṃ ajja attānaṃ passāmi. Yathā icchiṃ tathā ahūti ahañhi āvāṭe nikhāto tamhā dukkhā muccitvā puna attano rajjasampattiṃ icchiṃ, so ahaṃ imaṃ sampattiṃ pattaṃ attānaṃ passāmi. Yathevāhaṃ pubbe icchiṃ, tatheva me attā jātoti. Evaṃ bodhisatto “aho vata bho sīlasampannānaṃ vīriyaphalaṃ nāma samijjhatī”ti imāya gāthāya udānaṃ udānetvā yāvajīvaṃ puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Herein, A man should indeed maintain hope means: one should indeed create hope by the power of one’s own effort, thinking, ‘By initiating this effort, I shall be freed from this suffering.’ A wise person should not despair means: a wise person, skilled in means, making an effort in a suitable matter, should not become disheartened, thinking, ‘I will not obtain the fruit of this effort,’ nor should they give up hope—this is the meaning. In Behold, I see myself, the word ‘behold’ is a mere particle; it means, ‘Today I see myself.’ As I wished, so it has become means: I, who was thrown into a pit, wished to be freed from that suffering and to regain my royal fortune. I now see myself as having attained that fortune. Just as I wished before, so has it become for me. Thus the Bodhisatta, having made the solemn utterance, “Oh, indeed, for those endowed with virtue, the fruit of effort is truly accomplished!” with this verse, performed meritorious deeds for the rest of his life and passed on according to his kamma.

Satthāpi [V 1.0259][P 1.0268] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhāsi. Satthā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paduṭṭhāmacco devadatto ahosi, amaccasahassaṃ buddhaparisā, sīlavamahārājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, expounded the Truths. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, the monk of lax effort was established in Arahantship. The Teacher connected the links of the story and identified the characters of the Jātaka: “At that time, the malevolent minister was Devadatta, the thousand ministers were the Buddha’s assembly, and I myself was King Sīlava.”

Mahāsīlavajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Mahāsīlava Jātaka, the First.

[52] 2. Cūḷajanakajātakavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Cūḷajanaka Jātaka

Vāyametheva purisoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ossaṭṭhavīriyamevārabbha kathesi. Tattha yaṃ vattabbaṃ, taṃ sabbaṃ mahājanakajātake (jā. 2.22.123 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Janakarājā pana setacchattassa heṭṭhā nisinno imaṃ gāthamāha –

“A man should indeed strive…”: This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana with reference to a monk of lax effort. Whatever is to be said concerning this will be made clear in the Mahājanaka Jātaka. King Janaka, seated beneath the white parasol, uttered this verse:

52.

52.

“Vāyametheva puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito;

Passāmi vohaṃ attānaṃ, udakā thalamubbhata”nti.

“A man should indeed strive; a wise person should not despair. Behold, I see myself, lifted from the water onto dry land.”

Tattha vāyamethevāti vāyāmaṃ karotheva. Udakā thalamubbhatanti udakato thalamuttiṇṇaṃ thale patiṭṭhitaṃ attānaṃ passāmīti. Idhāpi ossaṭṭhavīriyo bhikkhu arahattaṃ patto, janakarājā sammāsambuddhova ahosīti.

Herein, A man should indeed strive means: one should indeed make an effort. Lifted from the water onto dry land means: I see myself having crossed over from the water and become established on dry land. In this case as well, the monk of lax effort attained Arahantship. And King Janaka was the Perfectly Enlightened One himself.

Cūḷajanakajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Cūḷajanaka Jātaka, the Second.

[53] 3. Puṇṇapātijātakavaṇṇanā

3. The Commentary on the Puṇṇapāti Jātaka

Tatheva [M 1.0286] puṇṇā pātiyoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto visavāruṇiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekaṃ samayaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ surādhuttā sannipatitvā mantayiṃsu – “surāmūlaṃ no khīṇaṃ, kahaṃ nu kho labhissāmā”ti. Atheko kakkhaḷadhutto āha “mā cintayittha, attheko upāyo”ti. “Kataro upāyo nāmā”ti? “Anāthapiṇḍiko aṅgulimuddikā piḷandhitvā maṭṭhasāṭakanivattho rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati, mayaṃ surāpātiyaṃ visaññīkaraṇaṃ bhesajjaṃ pakkhipitvā āpānaṃ sajjetvā nisīditvā anāthapiṇḍikassa āgamanakāle ‘ito ehi mahāseṭṭhī’ti pakkositvā taṃ suraṃ pāyetvā visaññībhūtassa [V 1.0260] aṅgulimuddikā ca sāṭake ca gahetvā surāmūlaṃ karissāmā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā tathā katvā seṭṭhissa āgamanakāle paṭimaggaṃ gantvā “sāmi, ito tāva āgacchatha[P 1.0269], ayaṃ amhākaṃ santike atimanāpā surā, thokaṃ pivitvā gacchathā”ti vadiṃsu. Sotāpanno ariyasāvako kiṃ suraṃ pivissati, anatthiko samānopi pana “ime dhutte pariggaṇhissāmī”ti tesaṃ āpānabhūmiṃ gantvā tesaṃ kiriyaṃ oloketvā “ayaṃ surā imehi iminā nāma kāraṇena yojitā”ti ñatvā “ito dāni paṭṭhāya ime ito palāpessāmī”ti cintetvā āha – “hare duṭṭhadhuttā, tumhe ‘surāpātiyaṃ bhesajjaṃ pakkhipitvā āgatāgate pāyetvā visaññī katvā vilumpissāmā’ti āpānamaṇḍalaṃ sajjetvā nisinnā kevalaṃ imaṃ suraṃ vaṇṇetha, ekopi taṃ ukkhipitvā pivituṃ na ussahati. Sace ayaṃ ayojitā assa, imaṃ tumheva piveyyāthā”ti te dhutte tajjetvā tato palāpetvā attano gehaṃ gantvā “dhuttehi katakāraṇaṃ tathāgatassa ārocessāmī”ti cintento jetavanaṃ gantvā ārocesi. Satthā “idāni tāva gahapati te dhuttā taṃ vañcetukāmā jātā, pubbe pana paṇḍitepi vañcetukāmā ahesu”nti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“The bowls are full just as before”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a poisoned liquor. Once in Sāvatthī, a group of drunkards gathered and discussed: “Our money for liquor is exhausted—where can we get more?” Then one brazen rogue said, “Do not worry, there is a plan.” “What plan?” they asked. “Anāthapiṇḍika wears a finger-ring and a fine cloak when he goes to attend upon the king. We will mix a stupefying medicine into a liquor bowl, prepare a drinking place, and sit there. When Anāthapiṇḍika comes, we will call out, ‘Come here, great merchant!’ Then we will make him drink that liquor, and once he is unconscious, we will take his finger-ring and cloak and make that our money for liquor.” They agreed, saying, ‘Good!’ and did just that. When the merchant arrived, they went to meet him on the road and said, ‘Sir, please come this way! We have some very pleasant liquor here; please drink a little and then go.’ Would a stream-enterer, a noble disciple, drink liquor? But though he had no desire for it, he thought, ‘I will deal with these rogues,’ and went to their drinking place. Observing their actions, he realized, ‘This liquor has been prepared by them for a certain reason.’ Thinking, ‘From this day forward, I will drive them away from here,’ he said, ‘Hey, you wicked rogues! You have set up this drinking stall and are sitting here, having mixed a medicine into the liquor bowl, intending to make those who come drink it, render them unconscious, and rob them. You merely praise this liquor, but not one of you dares to lift it and drink it. If this were unadulterated, you yourselves would drink it!’ Scolding those rogues, he drove them away from there and returned to his own house. Thinking, ‘I will report what these rogues did to the Tathāgata,’ he went to Jetavana and told him. The Teacher said, ‘Now, householder, these rogues have sought to deceive you. But in the past, they also sought to deceive the wise.’ Being asked by him, he related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiseṭṭhi ahosi. Tadāpete dhuttā evameva sammantetvā suraṃ yojetvā bārāṇasiseṭṭhissa āgamanakāle paṭimaggaṃ gantvā evameva kathayiṃsu. Seṭṭhi anatthikopi hutvā te pariggaṇhitukāmo gantvā tesaṃ [M 1.0287] kiriyaṃ oloketvā “idaṃ nāmete kātukāmā, palāpessāmi ne ito”ti cintetvā evamāha “bhonto, dhuttā suraṃ pivitvā rājakulaṃ gantuṃ nāma ayuttaṃ, rājānaṃ disvā puna āgacchanto jānissāmi, tumhe idheva nisīdathā”ti rājupaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā paccāgañchi. Dhuttā “ito etha, sāmī”ti. Sopi tattha gantvā bhesajjena saṃyojitā surāpātiyo oloketvā evamāha “bhonto dhuttā tumhākaṃ kiriyā mayhaṃ na ruccati, tumhākaṃ surāpātiyo yathāpūritāva ṭhitā, tumhe kevalaṃ suraṃ vaṇṇetha, na pana pivatha. Sacāyaṃ manāpā assa, tumhepi piveyyātha, imāya pana visasaṃyuttāya bhavitabba”nti tesaṃ manorathaṃ bhindanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was the great merchant of Bārāṇasī. At that time, those rogues, having conspired in the same way and prepared the liquor, went to meet him on the road at the time of the great merchant’s arrival and spoke in the same manner. Though the merchant had no desire for it, he wished to take them in hand, so he went and observed their actions. Thinking, ‘This is what they intend to do; I will drive them away from here,’ he said, ‘Sirs, it is not proper to drink liquor and go to the royal court. Having seen the king, I will know upon my return. You just sit here.’ He went to attend upon the king and returned. The rogues said, ‘Come here, master.’ He went there and, seeing the liquor bowls mixed with medicine, said, ‘Sirs, your actions do not please me. Your liquor bowls remain just as they were filled. You merely praise the liquor but do not drink it. If this were pleasant, you too would drink it. This must be mixed with poison.’ Thus, crushing their hopes, he spoke this verse:

53.

53.

“Tatheva puṇṇā pātiyo, aññāyaṃ vattate kathā;

Ākāraṇena jānāmi, na cāyaṃ bhaddikā surā”ti.

“The bowls are full just as before; this talk of yours is false. By this sign I know: this is certainly no good liquor.”

Tattha [P 1.0270] tathevāti yathā mayā gamanakāle diṭṭhā, idānipi imā surāpātiyo tatheva puṇṇā. Aññāyaṃ vattate kathāti yā ayaṃ tumhākaṃ surāvaṇṇanakathā vattati, sā aññāva abhūtā [V 1.0261] atacchā. Yadi hi esā surā manāpā assa, tumhepi piveyyātha, upaḍḍhapātiyo avasisseyyuṃ. Tumhākaṃ pana ekenāpi surā na pītā. Ākāraṇena jānāmīti tasmā iminā kāraṇena jānāmi. Na cāyaṃ bhaddikā surāti “nevāyaṃ bhaddikā surā, visasaṃyojitāya etāya bhavitabba”nti dhutte niggaṇhitvā yathā na puna evarūpaṃ karonti, tathā te tajjetvā vissajjesi. So yāvajīvaṃ dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Herein, ‘just as before’ means: just as they were seen by me at the time of my departure, now too these liquor bowls are full in that very same way. ‘This talk is false’ means: this talk of yours praising the liquor is other, unreal, and untrue. For if this liquor were pleasing, you too would drink it, and half-full bowls would remain. But not even one of you has drunk the liquor. ‘By this sign I know’ means: therefore, by this sign I know. ‘This is no good liquor’ means: ‘this is indeed no good liquor; it must be mixed with poison.’ Having rebuked the rogues and threatened them so that they would not do such a thing again, he dismissed them. He performed meritorious deeds such as giving throughout his life and passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dhuttā etarahi dhuttā, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Birth Story: “The rogues at that time are the rogues now, but the great merchant of Bārāṇasī was I myself.”

Puṇṇapātijātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Puṇṇapāti Jātaka, the Third.

[54] 4. Kiṃphalajātakavaṇṇanā

[54] 4. The Commentary on the Kiṃphala Jātaka.

Nāyaṃ [M 1.0288] rukkho durāruhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ phalakusalaṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira sāvatthivāsī kuṭumbiko buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā attano ārāme nisīdāpetvā yāgukhajjakaṃ datvā uyyānapālaṃ āṇāpesi “bhikkhūhi saddhiṃ uyyāne vicaritvā ayyānaṃ ambādīni nānāphalāni dehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā bhikkhūsaṅghamādāya uyyāne vicaranto rukkhaṃ ulloketvāva “etaṃ phalaṃ āmaṃ, etaṃ na supakkaṃ, etaṃ supakka”nti jānāti. Yaṃ so vadati, taṃ tatheva hoti. Bhikkhū gantvā tathāgatassa ārocesuṃ “bhante, ayaṃ uyyānapālo phalakusalo bhūmiyaṃ ṭhitova rukkhaṃ ulloketvā ‘etaṃ phalaṃ āmaṃ, etaṃ na supakkaṃ, etaṃ supakka’nti jānāti. Yaṃ so vadati, taṃ tatheva hotī”ti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, ayameva uyyānapālo phalakusalo, pubbe paṇḍitāpi phalakusalāyeva ahesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This tree is not hard to climb”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, with reference to a certain lay follower skilled in fruits. It seems a certain householder living in Sāvatthī invited the Sangha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha, seated them in his park, and after giving them rice gruel and solid food, ordered the park-keeper: ‘Having walked in the park with the bhikkhus, give the venerable ones mangoes and various other fruits.’ He, replying ‘Very well,’ and taking the Sangha of bhikkhus, while walking in the park, just by looking up at a tree, would know: ‘This fruit is unripe, this is not quite ripe, this is fully ripe.’ Whatever he said was exactly so. The bhikkhus went and reported it to the Tathāgata: ‘Venerable sir, this park-keeper is skilled in fruits. Standing on the ground and just by looking up at a tree, he knows: “This fruit is unripe, this is not quite ripe, this is fully ripe.” Whatever he says is exactly so.’ The Teacher said, ‘Not only now, bhikkhus, is this park-keeper skilled in fruits; in the past, wise men were also skilled in fruits.’ Having said this, he related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto satthavāhakule nibbattitvā vayappatto pañcahi sakaṭasatehi vaṇijjaṃ karonto ekasmiṃ kāle mahāvattaniaṭaviṃ patvā [P 1.0271] aṭavimukhe ṭhatvā sabbe manusse sannipātāpetvā “imissā aṭaviyā visarukkhā nāma honti, visapattāni, visapupphāni, visaphalāni, visamadhūni hontiyeva, pubbe tumhehi aparibhuttaṃ, yaṃ kiñci pattaṃ vā pupphaṃ vā phalaṃ vā pallavaṃ vā maṃ aparipucchitvā mā khādathā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā aṭaviṃ otariṃsu. Aṭavimukhe ca ekasmiṃ gāmadvāre [V 1.0262] kiṃphalarukkho nāma atthi, tassa khandhasākhāpalāsapupphaphalāni sabbāni ambasadisāneva honti. Na kevalaṃ vaṇṇasaṇṭhānatova, gandharasehipissa āmapakkāni phalāni ambaphalasadisāneva, khāditāni pana halāhalavisaṃ viya taṅkhaṇaññeva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpenti. Purato gacchantā ekacce lolapurisā “amburukkho aya”nti saññāya phalāni khādiṃsu, ekacce “satthavāhaṃ pucchitvāva khādissāmā”ti hatthena gahetvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Te satthavāhe āgate “ayya, imāni ambaphalāni khādāmā”ti pucchiṃsu. Bodhisatto “nāyaṃ [M 1.0289] ambarukkho”ti ñatvā “kiṃ phalarukkho nāmesa, nāyaṃ ambarukkho, mā khāditthā”ti vāretvā ye khādiṃsu. Tepi vamāpetvā catumadhuraṃ pāyetvā niroge akāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a caravan leader's family. When he came of age, while conducting trade with five hundred carts, on one occasion he arrived at a great wilderness. Stopping at the edge of the forest, he gathered all the people together and said, "In this forest, there are so-called poisonous trees, poisonous leaves, poisonous flowers, poisonous fruits, and even poisonous honey. Since you have never before consumed them, do not eat any leaf, flower, fruit, or shoot without first asking me." They agreed, saying "Very well," and entered the forest. At the edge of the forest, near a village gate, there was a tree called the Kimphala tree. Its trunk, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits all resembled those of a mango tree. Not only in appearance and shape, but also in scent and taste, its unripe and ripe fruits were just like mangoes. However, when eaten, they acted like a deadly poison, causing instant loss of life. As they went ahead, some greedy men, thinking, "This is a mango tree," ate the fruits. Others, thinking, "We will ask the caravan leader first," held the fruits in their hands and waited. When the caravan leader arrived, they asked, "Sir, may we eat these mango fruits?" The Bodhisatta, knowing it was not a mango tree, forbade them: "This is called the Kimphala tree; it is not a mango tree. Do not eat!" He then made those who had already eaten vomit, and after giving them the four sweet remedies, he restored them to health.

Pubbe pana imasmiṃ rukkhamūle manussā nivāsaṃ kappetvā “ambaphalānī”ti saññāya imāni visaphalāni khāditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇanti. Punadivase gāmavāsino nikkhamitvā matamanusse disvā pāde gaṇhitvā paṭicchannaṭṭhāne chaḍḍetvā sakaṭehi saddhiṃyeva sabbaṃ tesaṃ santakaṃ gahetvā gacchanti. Te taṃ divasampi aruṇuggamanakāleyeva “mayhaṃ balibaddo bhavissati, mayhaṃ sakaṭaṃ, mayhaṃ bhaṇḍa”nti vegena taṃ rukkhamūlaṃ gantvā manusse niroge disvā “kathaṃ tumhe imaṃ rukkhaṃ ‘nāyaṃ ambarukkho’ti jānitthā”ti pucchiṃsu. Te “mayaṃ na jānāma, satthavāhajeṭṭhako no jānātī”ti āhaṃsu. Manussā bodhisattaṃ pucchiṃsu “paṇḍita, kinti katvā tvaṃ imassa rukkhassa anambarukkhabhāvaṃ aññāsī”ti? So “dvīhi kāraṇehi aññāsi”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Previously, people who camped at the foot of this tree, perceiving the fruits to be mangoes, ate these poisonous fruits and met their end. The next day, the villagers would come out, see the dead bodies, seize them by the feet, discard them in a hidden place, and depart, taking all their possessions along with the carts. On this day too, at dawn, they hurried to the foot of that tree, each thinking, "The ox will be mine, the cart will be mine, the goods will be mine!" When they saw the people unharmed, they asked, "How did you know that this tree was not a mango tree?" They replied, "We did not know; our caravan leader knew." The people then asked the Bodhisatta, "Wise one, by what means did you know that this tree was not a mango tree?" He said, "I knew for two reasons," and spoke this verse:

54.

54.

“Nāyaṃ [P 1.0272] rukkho durāruho, napi gāmato ārakā;

Ākāraṇena jānāmi, nāyaṃ sāduphalo dumo”ti.

"This tree is not hard to climb, nor is it far from the village; by these signs I know this is not a tree with sweet fruit."

Tattha nāyaṃ rukkho durāruhoti ayaṃ visarukkho na dukkhāruho, ukkhipitvā ṭhapitanisseṇī viya sukhenārohituṃ sakkāti vadati. Napi gāmato ārakāti gāmato dūre ṭhitopi na hoti, gāmadvāre ṭhitoyevāti dīpeti. Ākāraṇena jānāmīti iminā duvidhena kāraṇenāhaṃ imaṃ rukkhaṃ jānāmi. Kinti? Nāyaṃ sāduphalo dumoti. Sace hi ayaṃ madhuraphalo ambarukkho abhavissa, evaṃ sukhāruḷhe avidūre ṭhite etasmiṃ ekampi phalaṃ na tiṭṭheyya, phalakhādakamanussehi niccaṃ parivutova assa. Evaṃ ahaṃ attano ñāṇena paricchinditvā imassa visarukkhabhāvaṃ aññāsinti mahājanassa dhammaṃ desetvā sotthigamanaṃ gato.

Here, "This tree is not hard to climb" means this poisonous tree is not difficult to ascend; it can be climbed with ease, as if a ladder were placed against it. "Nor is it far from the village" means it is not located far from the village; it stands right at the village gate. "By these signs I know" means: by these two reasons I know that "this is not a tree with sweet fruit." For if this were a mango tree with sweet fruit, being so easily climbable and standing so near, not a single fruit would remain on it; it would always be surrounded by people eating the fruit. Thus, discerning with my own wisdom, I knew its nature as a poisonous tree. After teaching the Dhamma to the great crowd, he departed safely.

Satthāpi [V 1.0263] “evaṃ, bhikkhave, pubbe paṇḍitāpi phalakusalā ahesu”nti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā parisā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, satthavāho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Thus, bhikkhus, in the past, the wise were also skilled in fruits." Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he connected the events and concluded the Jātaka: "The assembly of that time is now the Buddha's assembly, and the caravan leader was I myself."

Kiṃphalajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Kiṃphala Jātaka, the Fourth.

[55] 5. Pañcāvudhajātakavaṇṇanā

[55] 5. The Commentary on the Pañcāvudha Jātaka.

Yo [M 1.0290] alīnena cittenāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ossaṭṭhavīriyaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā āmantetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ossaṭṭhavīriyosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti vutte “bhikkhu pubbe paṇḍitā vīriyaṃ kātuṃ yuttaṭṭhāne vīriyaṃ katvā rajjasampattiṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“With an unsluggish mind”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who had given up his effort. The Teacher addressed that monk and asked, “Is it true, monk, that you have given up your effort?” When the monk replied, “It is true, Blessed One,” the Teacher said, “Monk, in the past, wise men exerted effort where effort was due and attained royal prosperity,” and he told a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa rañño aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbatti. Tassa nāmaggahaṇadivase aṭṭhasate brāhmaṇe sabbakāmehi santappetvā lakkhaṇāni pucchiṃsu. Lakkhaṇakusalā brāhmaṇā lakkhaṇasampattiṃ disvā “puññasampanno, mahārāja, kumāro tumhākaṃ accayena rajjaṃ pāpuṇissati, pañcāvudhakamme paññāto pākaṭo jambudīpe aggapuriso bhavissatī”ti byākariṃsu. Rājā brāhmaṇānaṃ [P 1.0273] vacanaṃ sutvā kumārassa nāmaṃ gaṇhanto “pañcāvudhakumāro”ti nāmaṃ akāsi. Atha naṃ viññutaṃ patvā soḷasavassuddese ṭhitaṃ rājā āmantetvā “tāta, sippaṃ uggaṇhāhī”ti āha. “Kassa santike uggaṇhāmi, devā”ti? “Gaccha, tāta, gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilanagare disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike uggaṇha, idañcassa ācariyabhāgaṃ dajjeyyāsī”ti sahassaṃ datvā uyyojesi. So tattha gantvā sippaṃ sikkhitvā ācariyena dinnaṃ pañcāvudhaṃ gahetvā ācariyaṃ vanditvā takkasilanagarato nikkhamitvā sannaddhapañcāvudho bārāṇasimaggaṃ paṭipajji.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of the king’s chief queen. On the day of his naming ceremony, they satisfied eight hundred brahmins with all their desires and asked them about his marks. The brahmins, skilled in reading marks and seeing the excellence of his marks, declared: “Great king, your son is endowed with merit. After your passing, he will attain the throne. Famed for his skill with the five weapons, he will become renowned as the foremost man in Jambudipa.” Hearing the brahmins’ words, the king, when naming the prince, gave him the name “Prince Pañcāvudha.” When the prince came of age, at about sixteen years old, the king summoned him and said, “Dear son, learn the arts.” “From whom shall I learn, sire?” “Go, dear son, to the world-renowned teacher in the city of Takkasilā in the Gandhāra country. Learn from him, and give him this as the teacher’s fee.” Giving him a thousand coins, he sent him off. The prince went there, mastered the arts, received the five weapons given by his teacher, paid homage to the teacher, and left Takkasilā. Armed with the five weapons, he set out on the road to Benares.

So antarāmagge silesalomayakkhena nāma adhiṭṭhitaṃ ekaṃ aṭaviṃ pāpuṇi. Atha naṃ aṭavimukhe manussā disvā “bho māṇava, mā imaṃ aṭaviṃ pavisa, silesalomayakkho nāmettha atthi, so diṭṭhadiṭṭhe manusse jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetī”ti vārayiṃsu. Bodhisatto attānaṃ takkento asambhītakesarasīho viya aṭaviṃ pāvisiyeva. Tasmiṃ aṭavimajjhaṃ sampatte so yakkho tālamatto hutvā kūṭāgāramattaṃ sīsaṃ pattappamāṇāni akkhīni, dakalimakuḷamattā dve dāṭhā [V 1.0264] ca māpetvā setamukho kabarakucchi nīlahatthapādo hutvā bodhisattassa attānaṃ dassetvā “kahaṃ yāsi, tiṭṭha bhakkhosi me”ti āha. Atha naṃ bodhisatto [M 1.0291] “yakkha, ahaṃ attānaṃ takketvā idha paviṭṭho, tvaṃ appamatto hutvā maṃ upagaccheyyāsi. Visapītena hi sarena taṃ vijjhitvā ettheva pātessāmī”ti santajjetvā halāhalavisapītaṃ saraṃ sannayhitvā muñci, so yakkhassa lomesuyeva allīyi. Tato aññaṃ, tato aññanti evaṃ paññāsa sare muñci, sabbe tassa lomesuyeva allīyiṃsu. Yakkho sabbepi te sare phoṭetvā attano pādamūleyeva pātetvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkami.

On his way, he came to a forest inhabited by a demon named Silesaloma. At the forest's edge, people saw him and warned, “Young man, do not enter this forest! There is a demon here called Silesaloma who brings death to any man he sees.” But the Bodhisatta, trusting in his own strength, entered the forest as fearlessly as a lion. When he reached the middle of the forest, the demon made himself appear, as tall as a palm tree, with a head the size of a gabled house, eyes the size of bowls, two fangs the size of water-lily buds, a white face, a mottled belly, and blue hands and feet. He showed himself to the Bodhisatta and said, “Where are you going? Stop! You are my food!” The Bodhisatta replied, “Demon, I entered this forest trusting in myself. Approach me with caution, for I will strike you with a poison-tipped arrow and fell you right here!” Threatening him thus, he fitted a deadly poison-tipped arrow and shot it. The arrow merely stuck to the demon’s hair. He then shot another, and another, until he had shot fifty arrows, but every one of them just stuck to the demon's hair. The demon shook off all the arrows, letting them fall at his feet, and then advanced toward the Bodhisatta.

Bodhisatto punapi taṃ tajjetvā khaggaṃ kaḍḍhitvā pahari, tettiṃsaṅgulāyato khaggo lomesuyeva allīyi. Atha naṃ kaṇayena pahari, sopi lomesuyeva allīyi. Tassa allīnabhāvaṃ ñatvā muggarena pahari, sopi lomesuyeva allīyi. Tassa allīnabhāvaṃ ñatvā kuntena pahari, sopi lomesuyeva allīyi. Tassa allīnabhāvaṃ ñatvā “bho yakkhana, te ahaṃ ‘pañcāvudhakumāro [P 1.0274] nāmā’ti sutapubbo, ahaṃ tayā adhiṭṭhitaṃ aṭaviṃ pavisanto na dhanuādīni takketvā paviṭṭho, attānaṃyeva pana takketvā paviṭṭho, ajja taṃ pothetvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karissāmī”ti unnādento attānaṃ takketvā dakkhiṇahatthena yakkhaṃ pahari, hattho lomesuyeva allīyi. Vāmahatthena pahari, sopi allīyi. Dakkhiṇapādena pahari, sopi allīyi. Vāmapādena pahari, sopi allīyi. “Sīsena taṃ pothetvā cuṇṇavicuṇṇaṃ karissāmī”ti sīsena pahari, tampi lomesuyeva allīyi. So pañcoḍḍito pañcasu ṭhānesu baddho olambantopi nibbhayo nissārajjova ahosi.

The Bodhisatta, threatening him again, drew his sword and struck, but the thirty-three-inch-long sword merely stuck to the hair. He then struck the demon with a spear, and that too stuck to the hair. Knowing it was stuck, he struck with a club, and that too stuck. Knowing it was also stuck, he struck with a lance, and that too stuck. Realizing that this too was stuck, he cried out, “O demon, have you not heard of me before? I am called Prince Pañcāvudha! When I entered this forest that you inhabit, I did not rely on my bow and other weapons; rather, I entered relying on myself alone. Today, I will pound you to dust!” Shouting thus and trusting in his own strength, he struck the demon with his right hand, but his hand stuck to the hair. He struck with his left hand, and that too stuck. He struck with his right foot, and that too stuck. He struck with his left foot, and that too stuck. Then, intending to crush him to dust with his head, he struck him with his head, and that too stuck to the hair. Thus, caught and bound in five places, he hung there, yet he remained fearless and undaunted.

Yakkho cintesi “ayaṃ eko purisasīho purisājānīyo, na purisamattova, mādisena nāmassa yakkhena gahitassa santāsamattampi na bhavissati, mayā imaṃ maggaṃ hanantena ekopi evarūpo puriso na diṭṭhapubbo, kasmā nu kho esa na bhāyatī”ti. So taṃ khādituṃ avisahanto “kasmā nu kho, tvaṃ māṇava, maraṇabhayaṃ na bhāyasī”ti pucchi. “Kiṃkāraṇā, yakkha, bhāyissāmi. Ekasmiñhi attabhāve ekaṃ maraṇaṃ niyatameva, apica mayhaṃ kucchimhi vajirāvudhaṃ atthi. Sace maṃ khādissasi, taṃ āvudhaṃ jīrāpetuṃ na sakkhissasi, taṃ te antāni khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chinditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ [M 1.0292] pāpessati. Iti ubhopi nassissāma, iminā kāraṇenāhaṃ na bhāyāmī”ti. Idaṃ kira bodhisatto attano abbhantare ñāṇāvudhaṃ sandhāya kathesi. Taṃ sutvā yakkho cintesi “ayaṃ māṇavo saccameva bhaṇati, imassa purisasīhassa sarīrato muggabījamattampi maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ mayhaṃ kucchi jīretuṃ na sakkhissati, vissajjessāmi na”nti [V 1.0265] maraṇabhayatajjito bodhisattaṃ vissajjetvā “māṇava, purisasīho tvaṃ, na te ahaṃ maṃsaṃ khādissāmi, tvaṃ ajja rāhumukhā muttacando viya mama hatthato muccitvā ñātisuhajjamaṇḍalaṃ tosento yāhī”ti āha.

The yakkha thought, "This is a lion among men, a thoroughbred of a man, not merely an ordinary man. Even though captured by a yakkha like me, not even the slightest fear arises in him. In all my time striking down travellers on this path, I have never before seen such a man. Why is he not afraid?" Unable to devour him, he asked, "Why, young man, do you not fear death?" "For what reason, yakkha, should I fear? In a single lifetime, one death is indeed certain. Moreover, I have a diamond weapon in my belly. If you eat me, you will not be able to digest that weapon. It will cut your intestines into pieces and bring about the destruction of your life. Thus, we both will perish. For this reason, I am not afraid." The Bodhisatta, it is said, spoke this with reference to the weapon of wisdom within himself. Hearing this, the yakkha thought, "This young man speaks the truth. My stomach would be unable to digest even a piece of flesh the size of a mung bean from this lion among men. I shall release him." Terrified by the fear of death, he released the Bodhisatta, saying, "Young man, you are a lion among men. I will not eat your flesh. Today, like the moon freed from Rāhu’s mouth, escape from my grasp and go, gladdening your circle of relatives and friends."

Atha naṃ bodhisatto āha – “yakkha, ahaṃ tāva gacchissāmi, tvaṃ pana pubbepi akusalaṃ katvā luddo lohitapāṇi pararuhiramaṃsabhakkho yakkho hutvā nibbatto. Sace idhāpi [P 1.0275] ṭhatvā akusalameva karissasi, andhakārā andhakārameva gamissasi, maṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya pana na sakkā tayā akusalaṃ kātuṃ, pāṇātipātakammaṃ nāma niraye tiracchānayoniyaṃ pettivisaye asurakāye ca nibbatteti, manussesu nibbattanibbattaṭṭhāne appāyukasaṃvattanikaṃ hotī”ti evamādinā nayena pañcannaṃ dussīlyakammānaṃ ādīnavaṃ, pañcannaṃ sīlānaṃ ānisaṃsañca kathetvā nānākāraṇehi yakkhaṃ tajjetvā dhammaṃ desetvā dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā tassāyeva naṃ aṭaviyā balipaṭiggāhakaṃ devataṃ katvā appamādena ovaditvā aṭavito nikkhamitvā aṭavimukhe manussānaṃ ācikkhitvā sannaddhapañcāvudho bārāṇasiṃ gantvā mātāpitaro disvā aparabhāge rajje patiṭṭhāya dhammena rajjaṃ kārento dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Then the Bodhisatta said to him: "Yakkha, I shall now depart. But you, having previously done unwholesome deeds, were reborn as a cruel, blood-handed yakkha, feeding on the flesh and blood of others. If you remain here and continue to do only unwholesome deeds, you will go from darkness to deeper darkness. However, from the time you have seen me, it is not proper for you to commit unwholesome deeds. The act of taking life leads to rebirth in hell, in the animal realm, in the sphere of spirits, and in the domain of asuras; and when reborn among humans, it leads to a short life." In this way, he explained the dangers of the five kinds of immoral conduct and the benefits of the five precepts. Through various reasons, he admonished the yakkha, taught him the Dhamma, tamed him, humbled him, and established him in the five precepts. He appointed him as the offering-receiving deity of that very forest. Having exhorted him to be heedful, the Bodhisatta left the forest. At the entrance to the forest, he informed the people, and then, girt with his five weapons, he went to Bārāṇasī. There, he saw his parents and later was established in the kingdom. Ruling righteously, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and passed away according to his kamma.

Satthāpi imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having brought forth this discourse and attained perfect enlightenment, spoke this verse:

55.

55.

“Yo alīnena cittena, alīnamanaso naro;

Bhāveti kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, yogakkhemassa pattiyā;

Pāpuṇe anupubbena, sabbasaṃyojanakkhaya”nti.

The person who, with an unshrinking mind and an unwavering heart, cultivates the wholesome Dhamma for the attainment of security from the yokes, will gradually reach the destruction of all fetters.

Tatrāyaṃ piṇḍattho – yo puriso alīnena asaṃkuṭitena cittena pakatiyāpi alīnamano alīnajjhāsayova hutvā anavajjaṭṭhena kusalaṃ sattatiṃ sabodhipakkhiyabhedaṃ dhammaṃ bhāveti vaḍḍheti, visālena cittena vipassanaṃ [M 1.0293] anuyuñjati catūhi yogehi khemassa nibbānassa pattiyā, so evaṃ sabbasaṅkhāresu “aniccaṃ dukkhaṃ anattā”ti tilakkhaṇaṃ āropetvā taruṇavipassanato paṭṭhāya uppanne bodhipakkhiyadhamme bhāvento anupubbena ekasaṃyojanampi anavasesetvā sabbasaṃyojanakkhayakarassa catutthamaggassa pariyosāne uppannattā “sabbasaṃyojanakkhayo”ti saṅkhyaṃ gataṃ arahattaṃ pāpuṇeyyāti.

Here is the summary meaning: That person who, with an unshrinking, uncontracted mind, being by nature of an unshrinking mind and disposition, cultivates and develops the wholesome Dhamma—that is, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—which is blameless; who with an expansive mind engages in insight meditation for the attainment of Nibbāna, the security from the four yokes; that person, by thus applying the three characteristics of impermanence, suffering, and non-self to all conditioned phenomena, and by developing the factors of enlightenment that have arisen beginning with tender insight, would gradually, leaving not even a single fetter behind, attain Arahantship, which is reckoned as ‘the destruction of all fetters’ because it arises at the conclusion of the fourth path, the destroyer of all fetters.

Evaṃ [V 1.0266] satthā arahattena dhammadesanāya kūṭaṃ gahetvā matthake cattāri saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Satthā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā yakkho aṅgulimālo ahosi, pañcāvudhakumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

In this way, the Teacher, taking Arahantship as the pinnacle of the Dhamma teaching, revealed the Four Noble Truths at its climax. At the conclusion of the teaching on the truths, that monk attained Arahantship. The Teacher then made the connection and concluded the Jātaka: "At that time, the yakkha was Aṅgulimāla, and Prince Pañcāvudha was I myself."

Pañcāvudhajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Pañcāvudha Jātaka is the fifth.

[56] 6. Kañcanakkhandhajātakavaṇṇanā

[56] 6. The Commentary on the Kañcanakkhandha Jātaka.

Yo [P 1.0276] pahaṭṭhena cittenāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā ratanasāsane uraṃ datvā pabbaji. Athassa ācariyupajjhāyā “āvuso, ekavidhena sīlaṃ nāma, duvidhena, tividhena, catubbidhena, pañcavidhena, chabbidhena, sattavidhena, aṭṭhavidhena, navavidhena, dasavidhena, bahuvidhena sīlaṃ nāma. Idaṃ cūḷasīlaṃ nāma, idaṃ majjhimasīlaṃ nāma, idaṃ mahāsīlaṃ nāma. Idaṃ pātimokkhasaṃvarasīlaṃ nāma, idaṃ indriyasaṃvarasīlaṃ nāma, idaṃ ājīvapārisuddhisīlaṃ nāma, idaṃ paccayapaṭisevanasīlaṃ nāmā”ti sīlaṃ ācikkhanti. So cintesi “idaṃ sīlaṃ nāma atibahu, ahaṃ ettakaṃ samādāya vattituṃ na sakkhissāmi, sīlaṃ pūretuṃ asakkontassa ca nāma pabbajjāya ko attho, ahaṃ gihī hutvā dānādīni puññāni ca karissāmi, puttadārañca posessāmī”ti. Evañca pana cintetvā “bhante, ahaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkhissāmi, asakkontassa ca nāma pabbajjāya ko attho, ahaṃ hīnāyāvattissāmi, tumhākaṃ pattacīvaraṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this, beginning with 'Whoever, with a delighted mind,' concerning a certain monk. It seems a certain man of good family from Savatthi, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Teacher, devoted himself to the precious Dispensation and went forth. Then his teachers and preceptors instructed him in virtue, saying: 'Friend, virtue is of one kind, of two kinds, of three kinds, of four kinds, of five kinds, of six kinds, of seven kinds, of eight kinds, of nine kinds, of ten kinds, of many kinds. This is called minor virtue, this is called intermediate virtue, this is called great virtue. This is called virtue of restraint according to the Patimokkha, this is called virtue of restraint of the senses, this is called virtue of purity of livelihood, this is called virtue concerning the use of the requisites.' He thought: 'This thing called virtue is too much. I will not be able to undertake and practice so much. What is the use of going forth for one who cannot fulfill virtue? I will return to lay life, perform meritorious deeds like giving, and support my wife and children.' Having reflected thus, he said: 'Venerable sirs, I will not be able to maintain virtue. What is the use of going forth for one who cannot? I will return to the lower life. Take your bowl and robe.'

Atha [M 1.0294] naṃ āhaṃsu “āvuso evaṃ sante dasabalaṃ vanditvāva yāhī”ti te taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ dhammasabhaṃ agamaṃsu. Satthā disvāva “kiṃ, bhikkhave, anatthikaṃ bhikkhuṃ ādāya āgatatthā”ti āha. Bhante, ayaṃ bhikkhu “ahaṃ sīlaṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti pattacīvaraṃ niyyādeti, atha naṃ mayaṃ gahetvā āgatamhāti. “Kasmā pana tumhe, bhikkhave, imassa bhikkhuno bahuṃ sīlaṃ ācikkhatha. Yattakaṃ esa rakkhituṃ sakkoti, tattakameva rakkhissati. Ito paṭṭhāya tumhe etaṃ mā kiñci avacuttha, ahamettha kattabbaṃ jānissāmi, ehi tvaṃ bhikkhu, kiṃ te bahunā sīlena, tīṇiyeva sīlāni rakkhituṃ sakkhissasī”ti? “Rakkhissāmi, bhante”ti. Tena hi tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya kāyadvāraṃ vacīdvāraṃ manodvāranti tīṇi dvārāni [V 1.0267] rakkha, mā kāyena pāpakammaṃ kari, mā vācāya, mā manasā. “Gaccha mā hīnāyāvatti, imāni tīṇiyeva sīlāni rakkhā”ti. Ettāvatā so bhikkhu tuṭṭhamānaso “sādhu, bhante, rakkhissāmi imāni tīṇi sīlānī”ti satthāraṃ vanditvā ācariyupajjhāyehi saddhiṃyeva agamāsi. So tāni tīṇi sīlāni pūrentova aññāsi “ācariyupajjhāyehi mayhaṃ ācikkhitaṃ sīlampi ettakameva, te pana attano abuddhabhāvena maṃ bujjhāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu, sammāsambuddho [P 1.0277] attano buddhasubuddhatāya anuttaradhammarājatāya ettakaṃ sīlaṃ tīsuyeva dvāresu pakkhipitvā maṃ gaṇhāpesi, avassayo vata me satthā jāto”ti vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā katipāheneva arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

Then they said to him, 'Friend, if that is the case, pay homage to the Ten-Powered One and then go.' Taking him, they went to the Dhamma hall in the presence of the Teacher. As soon as the Teacher saw him, he said, 'Monks, why have you brought this unwilling monk here?' 'Venerable sir, this monk says, "I cannot maintain the precepts," and is relinquishing his bowl and robe. So we have brought him here.' 'But why, monks, do you instruct this monk in many precepts? He will keep only as much as he is able to. From now on, do not say anything more to him. I will know what should be done here. Come, monk, what need have you for many precepts? Can you maintain just three precepts?' 'I can, Venerable sir.' 'Then from now on, guard the three doors: the door of the body, the door of speech, and the door of the mind. Do no evil with the body, with speech, or with the mind. Go, do not revert to the lower life. Maintain just these three precepts.' At that, the monk, pleased in mind, said, 'Good, Venerable sir, I will maintain these three precepts,' paid homage to the Teacher, and went away with his teachers and preceptors. Fulfilling those three precepts, he realized, 'The virtue taught to me by my teachers and preceptors is also just this much. However, because they are not Buddhas, they were unable to make me understand. The Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, by his own perfect awakening and as the unsurpassed King of the Dhamma, having placed this much virtue within just the three doors, enabled me to grasp it. Truly, the Teacher has become my refuge.' Developing insight, in just a few days he was established in arahantship.

Taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā bhikkhū “āvuso, taṃ kira bhikkhuṃ ‘bahusīlāni rakkhituṃ na sakkomī’ti hīnāyāvattantaṃ sabbāni sīlāni tīhi koṭṭhāsehi saṅkhipitvā gāhāpetvā satthā arahattaṃ pāpesi, aho buddhānaṃ balaṃ nāma acchariya”nti buddhaguṇe kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Atha satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “bhikkhave, atigarukopi bhāro koṭṭhāsavasena bhājetvā dinno lahuko viya hoti, pubbepi paṇḍitā mahantaṃ kañcanakkhandhaṃ labhitvā ukkhipituṃ asakkontā vibhāgaṃ katvā ukkhipitvā agamaṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Knowing this event, the monks who had gathered in the Dhamma hall said, "Friends, it is said that the Teacher made that monk, who declared, 'I cannot maintain many precepts,' and was about to revert to a lower state, uphold all the precepts, having condensed them into three sections, and then led him to arahantship. Ah, the power of the Buddhas is indeed marvelous!" Speaking thus of the virtues of the Buddha, they sat down. Then the Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, what discussion are you seated here engaged in now?" When they replied, "About this," he said, "Monks, even a very heavy burden becomes light when divided into sections and given. In the past, wise men who were unable to lift a large mass of gold they had found, divided it and lifted it up, then went on their way." And he related a past incident.

Atīte [M 1.0295] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ gāmake kassako ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ aññatarasmiṃ chaḍḍitagāmake khette kasiṃ kasati. Pubbe ca tasmiṃ gāme eko vibhavasampanno seṭṭhi ūrumattapariṇāhaṃ catuhatthāyāmaṃ kañcanakkhandhaṃ nidahitvā kālamakāsi. Tasmiṃ bodhisattassa naṅgalaṃ lagitvā aṭṭhāsi. So “mūlasantānakaṃ bhavissatī”ti paṃsuṃ viyūhanto taṃ disvā paṃsunā paṭicchādetvā divasaṃ kasitvā atthaṅgate sūriye yuganaṅgalādīni ekamante nikkhipitvā “kañcanakkhandhaṃ gaṇhitvā gacchissāmī”ti taṃ ukkhipituṃ nāsakkhi. Asakkonto nisīditvā “ettakaṃ kucchibharaṇāya bhavissati, ettakaṃ nidahitvā ṭhapessāmi, ettakena kammante payojessāmi, ettakaṃ dānādipuññakiriyāya bhavissatī”ti cattāro koṭṭhāse akāsi. Tassevaṃ vibhattakāle so kañcanakkhandho sallahuko viya ahosi. So taṃ ukkhipitvā gharaṃ netvā catudhā vibhajitvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a farmer in a certain village. One day, while ploughing a field in a certain abandoned village, his plough got stuck. Previously, in that village, a wealthy merchant had buried a golden ingot, thigh-thick and four cubits long, and then passed away. The Bodhisatta, thinking, 'This must be a root,' cleared away the soil, and seeing it, covered it again with earth. After ploughing all day, when the sun set, he put aside his yoke, plough, and so forth, thinking, 'I will take this golden ingot and go.' But when he tried to lift it, he was unable. Being unable, he sat down and divided it into four portions: 'This much will be for sustenance, this much I will put aside, this much I will use for my business, and this much will be for meritorious deeds such as charity.' As soon as he thus divided it, the golden ingot became as if light. He lifted it, took it home, divided it into four, performed charitable and other meritorious deeds, and then passed away according to his kamma.

Iti [V 1.0268] bhagavā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus the Blessed One, having delivered this discourse, and having become fully enlightened, spoke this verse:

56.

56.

“Yo [P 1.0278] pahaṭṭhena cittena, pahaṭṭhamanaso naro;

Bhāveti kusalaṃ dhammaṃ, yogakkhemassa pattiyā;

Pāpuṇe anupubbena, sabbasaṃyojanakkhaya”nti.

Whoever, with a gladdened heart, with a delighted mind, develops wholesome states for the attainment of security from bondage, will gradually reach the destruction of all fetters.

Tattha pahaṭṭhenāti vinīvaraṇena. Pahaṭṭhamanasoti tāya eva vinīvaraṇatāya pahaṭṭhamānaso, suvaṇṇaṃ viya pahaṃsitvā samujjotitasappabhāsacitto hutvāti attho.

Herein, 'with a gladdened heart' means free from hindrances. 'With a delighted mind' means with a mind delighted by that very freedom from hindrances; that is, with a mind bright and radiant like polished gold, having become a mind shining with its own brilliance.

Evaṃ satthā arahattakūṭena desanaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kañcanakkhandhaladdhapuriso ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, having concluded the discourse with the pinnacle of Arahantship, connected the sequence of events and identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the man who obtained the mass of gold was I myself.'

Kañcanakkhandhajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The sixth is the Commentary on the Mass of Gold Jātaka.

[57] 7. Vānarindajātakavaṇṇanā

[57] 7. The Commentary on the Vānarinda Jātaka.

Yassete [M 1.0296] caturo dhammāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi samaye satthā “devadatto vadhāya parisakkatī”ti sutvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi parisakkiyeva, tāsamattampi pana kātuṃ nāsakkhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher spoke this, beginning with 'Whoever possesses these four qualities,' while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s efforts to kill him. At that time, having heard that Devadatta was making an effort to kill him, the Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta makes an effort to kill me; he has done so before. But he was not able to cause me even a fright.' And he related a story from the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kapiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vuḍḍhimanvāya assapotakappamāṇo thāmasampanno ekacaro hutvā nadītīre viharati. Tassā pana nadiyā vemajjhe eko dīpako nānappakārehi ambapanasādīhi phalarukkhehi sampanno. Bodhisatto nāgabalo thāmasampanno nadiyā orimatīrato uppatitvā dīpakassa orato nadīmajjhe eko piṭṭhipāsāṇo atthi, tasmiṃ nipatati, tato uppatitvā tasmiṃ dīpake patati. Tattha nānappakārāni phalāni khāditvā sāyaṃ teneva upāyena paccāgantvā attano vasanaṭṭhāne vasitvā punadivasepi tatheva karoti. Iminā niyāmena tattha vāsaṃ kappeti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a monkey. Growing up, he became as large as a young horse, full of strength, and lived alone on the riverbank. In the middle of that river, there was an island abundant with various kinds of fruit trees, such as mangoes and jackfruit. The Bodhisatta, possessing the strength of an elephant and great power, would leap from the near shore of the river to a flat rock in the middle of the river, and from there, leap again to reach the island. There, he would eat various fruits and return in the evening by the same method, dwelling in his own abode. The next day, he would do the same. In this way, he made his dwelling there.

Tasmiṃ pana kāle eko kumbhīlo sapajāpatiko tassā nadiyā vasati. Tassa bhariyā bodhisattaṃ aparāparaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā bodhisattassa hadayamaṃse dohaḷaṃ [P 1.0279] uppādetvā kumbhīlaṃ āha [V 1.0269] – “mayhaṃ kho, ayya, imassa vānarindassa hadayamaṃse dohaḷo uppanno”ti. Kumbhīlo “sādhu, bhadde, lacchasī”ti vatvā “ajja taṃ sāyaṃ dīpakato āgacchantameva gaṇhissāmī”ti gantvā piṭṭhipāsāṇe nipajji.

At that time, a crocodile with his mate lived in that river. His wife, seeing the Bodhisatta going back and forth, developed a craving for the Bodhisatta's heart-flesh and said to the crocodile, 'My lord, I have developed a craving for the heart-flesh of this monkey king.' The crocodile replied, 'Very well, my dear, you shall have it,' and said, 'Today, when he comes from the island in the evening, I will catch him.' Then he went and lay down on the flat rock.

Bodhisatto divasaṃ caritvā sāyanhasamaye dīpake ṭhitova pāsāṇaṃ oloketvā – “ayaṃ pāsāṇo idāni uccataro khāyati, kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti cintesi. Tassa kira udakappamāṇañca pāsāṇappamāṇañca suvavatthāpitameva hoti. Tenassa etadahosi “ajja imissā nadiyā udakaṃ neva hāyati, na ca vaḍḍhati, atha ca panāyaṃ pāsāṇo mahā hutvā paññāyati, kacci nu kho ettha mayhaṃ gahaṇatthāya kumbhīlo nipanno”ti. So “vīmaṃsāmi tāva na”nti tattheva [M 1.0297] ṭhatvā pāsāṇena saddhiṃ kathento viya “bho pāsāṇā”ti vatvā paṭivacanaṃ alabhanto yāvatatiyaṃ “bho pāsāṇā”ti āha. Pāsāṇo kiṃ paṭivacanaṃ dassati. Punapi vānaro “kiṃ bho pāsāṇa, ajja mayhaṃ paṭivacanaṃ na desī”ti āha. Kumbhīlo “addhā aññesu divasesu ayaṃ pāsāṇo vānarindassa paṭivacanaṃ adāsi, dassāmi dānissa paṭivacana”nti cintetvā “kiṃ, bho vānarindā”ti āha. “Kosi tva”nti? “Ahaṃ kumbhīlo”ti. “Kimatthaṃ ettha nipannosī”ti? “Tava hadayamaṃsaṃ patthayamāno”ti. Bodhisatto cintesi “añño me gamanamaggo natthi, ajja mayā esa kumbhīlo vañcetabbo”ti. Atha naṃ evamāha “samma kumbhīla, ahaṃ attānaṃ tuyhaṃ pariccajissāmi, tvaṃ mukhaṃ vivaritvā maṃ tava santikaṃ āgatakāle gaṇhāhī”ti. Kumbhīlānañhi mukhe vivaṭe akkhīni nimmīlanti. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ asallakkhetvā mukhaṃ vivari, athassa akkhīni pithīyiṃsu. So mukhaṃ vivaritvā akkhīni nimmīletvā nipajji. Bodhisatto tathābhāvaṃ ñatvā dīpakā uppatito gantvā kumbhīlassa matthake akkamitvā tato uppatito vijjulatā viya vijjotamāno paratīre aṭṭhāsi.

The Bodhisatta, having roamed during the day, stood on the island in the evening and, looking at the rock, thought: 'This rock now appears higher; what could be the reason?' For him, both the water level and the size of the rock were well-established. Then it occurred to him: 'Today, the water in this river neither decreases nor increases, yet this rock appears larger. Could it be that a crocodile is lying here to catch me?' He thought, 'I will investigate it first,' and standing right there, he spoke to the rock as if conversing: 'O rock!' Receiving no reply, he repeated it up to a third time: 'O rock!' How could the rock give an answer? Again, the monkey said, 'What is this, O rock? Why do you not answer me today?' The crocodile thought, 'Surely, on other days, this rock answered the monkey king. I will give him an answer now,' and said, 'What is it, O monkey king?' 'Who are you?' 'I am a crocodile.' 'For what purpose are you lying here?' 'Desiring your heart-flesh.' The Bodhisatta reflected, 'There is no other path for me to take. Today, I must deceive this crocodile.' Then he said to him, 'Friend crocodile, I will surrender myself to you. Open your mouth, and when I come near you, seize me.' For when crocodiles open their mouths, their eyes close. Not noticing this fact, the crocodile opened its mouth, and its eyes shut. With its mouth open and eyes closed, it lay there. The Bodhisatta, knowing this to be the case, leaped from the island, stepped on the crocodile’s head, and then, shining like a flash of lightning, sprang to the opposite shore.

Kumbhīlo taṃ acchariyaṃ disvā “iminā vānarindena atiaccherakaṃ kata”nti cintetvā “bho vānarinda, imasmiṃ loke catūhi dhammehi samannāgato [P 1.0280] puggalo paccāmitte adhibhavati. Te sabbepi tuyhaṃ abbhantare atthi maññe”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing this marvel, the crocodile thought, 'This monkey king has done a truly astonishing thing.' Then he said, 'O monkey king, in this world a person endowed with four qualities overcomes enemies. I think all of them are within you.' And he spoke this verse:

57.

57.

“Yassete caturo dhammā, vānarinda yathā tava;

Saccaṃ dhammo dhiti cāgo, diṭṭhaṃ so ativattatī”ti.

'O monkey king, whoever possesses these four qualities, as you do—truthfulness, wisdom, fortitude, and renunciation—that person overcomes the enemy.'

Tattha [V 1.0270] yassāti yassa kassaci puggalassa. Eteti idāni vattabbe paccakkhato niddisati. Caturo dhammāti cattāro guṇā. Saccanti vacīsaccaṃ, “mama santikaṃ āgamissāmī”ti vatvā musāvādaṃ akatvā āgatoyevāti etaṃ te vacīsaccaṃ. Dhammoti vicāraṇapaññā, “evaṃ kate idaṃ nāma bhavissatī”ti esā te vicāraṇapaññā atthi. Dhitīti abbocchinnaṃ vīriyaṃ vuccati, etampi te atthi. Cāgoti attapariccāgo, tvaṃ attānaṃ pariccajitvā [M 1.0298] mama santikaṃ āgato. Yaṃ panāhaṃ gaṇhituṃ nāsakkhiṃ, mayhamevesa doso. Diṭṭhanti paccāmittaṃ. So ativattatīti yassa puggalassa yathā tava, evaṃ ete cattāro dhammā atthi, so yathā maṃ ajja tvaṃ atikkanto, tatheva attano paccāmittaṃ atikkamati abhibhavatīti. Evaṃ kumbhīlo bodhisattaṃ pasaṃsitvā attano vasaṭṭhānaṃ gato.

Here, 'of whom' (yassa) refers to any individual. 'These' (ete) directly indicates what is now to be stated. 'Four qualities' (caturo dhammā) means four virtues. 'Truthfulness' (saccaṃ) refers to truthfulness in speech: having said, 'I will come to you,' and not speaking falsely, you indeed came. This is your truthfulness in speech. 'Wisdom' (dhammo) means discerning wisdom: 'If this is done, such will be the result'—this discerning wisdom you possess. 'Fortitude' (dhiti) is called unbroken effort; this too you possess. 'Renunciation' (cāgo) means self-sacrifice: you sacrificed yourself and came to me. That I was not able to seize you is my own fault. 'The seen' (diṭṭhaṃ) refers to an adversary. 'He overcomes' (so ativattati) means that any individual who possesses these four qualities as you do, just as you surpassed me today, likewise overcomes and conquers his own adversary. Having thus praised the Bodhisatta, the crocodile returned to his own abode.

Satthāpi “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi parisakkiyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kumbhīlo devadatto ahosi, bhariyāssa ciñcamāṇavikā, vānarindo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher also said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta strives to kill me; he has striven before.' Having delivered this discourse and made the connection, the Teacher identified the Jātaka: 'At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, his wife was Ciñcamāṇavikā, and the monkey king was I myself.'

Vānarindajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Vānarinda Jātaka, the seventh.

[58] 8. Tayodhammajātakavaṇṇanā

[58] 8. The Commentary on the Tayodhamma Jātaka

Yassa ete tayo dhammāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanamevārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher spoke this, beginning with 'He who possesses these three qualities,' while dwelling at Veḷuvana, concerning Devadatta’s striving to kill him.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente devadatto vānarayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā himavantappadese yūthaṃ pariharanto attānaṃ paṭicca jātānaṃ vānarapotakānaṃ “vuḍḍhippattā ime yūthaṃ parihareyyu”nti bhayena dantehi ḍaṃsitvā tesaṃ [P 1.0281] bījāni uppāṭeti. Tadā bodhisattopi taññeva paṭicca ekissā vānariyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Atha sā vānarī gabbhassa patiṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā attano gabbhaṃ anurakkhamānā aññaṃ pabbatapādaṃ agamāsi. Sā paripakkagabbhā bodhisattaṃ vijāyi. So vuḍḍhimanvāya viññutaṃ patto thāmasampanno ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ mātaraṃ pucchi “amma, mayhaṃ pitā kaha”nti? “Tāta, asukasmiṃ nāma pabbatapāde yūthaṃ pariharanto vasatī”ti. “Amma, tassa maṃ santikaṃ nehī”ti. “Tāta, na sakkā [V 1.0271] tayā pitu santikaṃ gantuṃ. Pitā hi te attānaṃ paṭicca jātānaṃ vānarapotakānaṃ yūthapariharaṇabhayena dantehi ḍaṃsitvā bījāni uppāṭetī”ti. “Amma, nehi maṃ tattha, ahaṃ jānissāmī”ti. Sā puttaṃ ādāya tassa santikaṃ agamāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, Devadatta was reborn in a monkey existence. Leading a troop in the Himalayan region, he would bite the young monkeys born from himself with his teeth and tear out their testicles, fearing that they might grow up and take over the troop. At that time, the Bodhisatta was also conceived in the womb of a certain female monkey, sired by that same one. Then, knowing that her pregnancy had taken root, that female monkey, protecting her womb, went to another mountainside. When her pregnancy was fully matured, she gave birth to the Bodhisatta. He grew up and, having attained discernment, became endowed with strength. One day, he asked his mother, "Mother, where is my father?" "Dear, he lives leading a troop at such-and-such a mountainside." "Mother, take me to him." "Dear, you cannot go to your father.
