For your father, fearing that the young monkeys born from himself might take over the troop, bites them with his teeth and tears out their testicles." "Mother, take me there, I will know." She took her son and went to his presence.

So [M 1.0299] vānaro attano puttaṃ disvāva “ayaṃ vaḍḍhanto mayhaṃ yūthaṃ pariharituṃ na dassati, idāneva māretabbo”ti “etaṃ āliṅganto viya gāḷhaṃ pīḷetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessāmī”ti cintetvā “ehi, tāta, ettakaṃ kālaṃ kahaṃ gatosī”ti bodhisattaṃ āliṅganto viya nippīḷesi. Bodhisatto pana nāgabalo thāmasampanno, sopi naṃ nippīḷesi, athassa aṭṭhīni bhijjanākārappattāni ahesuṃ. Athassa etadahosi “ayaṃ vaḍḍhanto maṃ māressati, kena nu kho upāyena puretaraññeva māreyya”nti. Tato cintesi “ayaṃ avidūre rakkhasapariggahito saro atthi, tattha naṃ rakkhasena khādāpessāmī”ti. Atha naṃ evamāha “tāta, ahaṃ mahallako, imaṃ yūthaṃ tuyhaṃ niyyādemi, ajjeva taṃ rājānaṃ karomi, asukasmiṃ nāma ṭhāne saro atthi, tattha dve kumudiniyo, tisso uppaliniyo, pañca paduminiyo ca pupphanti, gaccha, tato pupphāni āharā”ti. So “sādhu, tāta, āharissāmī”ti gantvā sahasā anotaritvā samantā padaṃ paricchindanto otiṇṇapadaññeva addasa, na uttiṇṇapadaṃ. So “iminā sarena rakkhasapariggahitena bhavitabbaṃ, mayhaṃ pitā attanā māretuṃ asakkonto rakkhasena maṃ khādāpetukāmo bhavissati[P 1.0282], ahaṃ imañca saraṃ na otarissāmi, pupphāni ca gahessāmī”ti nirudakaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā vegaṃ gahetvā uppatitvā parato gacchanto nirudake okāse ṭhitāneva dve pupphāni gahetvā paratīre pati. Paratīratopi orimatīraṃ āgacchanto tenevupāyena dve gaṇhi. Evaṃ ubhosu passesu rāsiṃ karonto pupphāni ca gaṇhi, rakkhasassa ca āṇaṭṭhānaṃ na otari.

Seeing his own son, that monkey thought, "As he grows, this one will not allow me to lead the troop. He must be killed now." Thinking, "I will squeeze him tightly as if embracing him and bring about his death," he said, "Come, dear, where have you been all this time?" and squeezed the Bodhisatta as if embracing him. The Bodhisatta, however, possessed the strength of an elephant and was endowed with great firmness; he squeezed back, and the other's bones were on the verge of breaking. Then it occurred to him, "As he grows, this one will kill me. By what means can I kill him first?" Then he thought, "Not far from here is a lake possessed by a rakkhasa. I will have him devoured by the rakkhasa." So he said to him, "Dear, I am old. I am handing over this troop to you. Today, I will make you king. In such-and-such a place, there is a lake where two white water-lilies, three blue water-lilies, and five red lotuses bloom. Go and bring the flowers from there." He replied, "Very well, father, I will bring them." Going there, without hastily entering the water, he carefully examined the footprints all around and saw only footprints going in, and none coming out. He realized, "This lake must be possessed by a rakkhasa. My father, unable to kill me himself, wants me to be eaten by the rakkhasa. I will not enter this lake, but I will still get the flowers." Going to a dry spot on the bank, he took a running start and leaped across. While in mid-air, he plucked two flowers and landed on the far bank. Returning from the far bank to this bank, he took two more in the same way. Thus, making a pile on each bank, he gathered the flowers without entering the rakkhasa's dominion.

Athassa “ito uttari ukkhipituṃ na sakkhissāmī”ti tāni pupphāni gahetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne rāsiṃ karontassa so rakkhaso “mayā ettakaṃ kālaṃ evarūpo paññavā acchariyapuriso na diṭṭhapubbo, pupphāni ca nāma yāvadicchakaṃ gahitāni, mayhañca āṇaṭṭhānaṃ na otarī”ti udakaṃ dvidhā bhindanto udakato uṭṭhāya bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “vānarinda, imasmiṃ loke yassa tayo dhammā atthi, so paccāmittaṃ abhibhavati, te sabbepi tava abbhantare atthi maññe”ti vatvā bodhisattassa thutiṃ karonto imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, as he was gathering those flowers into a pile in one place, thinking, 'I will not be able to carry any more than this,' the water-ogre thought, "In all this time, I have never before seen such a wise and marvelous being. He has taken as many flowers as he wished, yet he has not entered my dominion." Splitting the water in two, he rose from the water and approached the Bodhisatta. "O king of monkeys, in this world, whoever possesses three qualities overcomes his enemies. I think that all these qualities are within you," he said, and praising the Bodhisatta, he spoke this verse:

58.

58.

“Yassa [V 1.0272][M 1.0300] ete tayo dhammā, vānarinda yathā tava;

Dakkhiyaṃ sūriyaṃ paññā, diṭṭhaṃ so ativattatī”ti.

"O king of monkeys, in whom these three qualities exist, as they do in you—dexterity, courage, and wisdom—that one overcomes his foe."

Tattha dakkhiyanti dakkhabhāvo, sampattabhayaṃ vidhamituṃ jānanapaññāya sampayuttauttamavīriyassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sūriyanti sūrabhāvo, nibbhayabhāvassetaṃ nāmaṃ. Paññāti paññāpadaṭṭhānāya upāyapaññāyetaṃ nāmaṃ.

Herein, 'dexterity' means the state of being deft; it is a name for that supreme effort, conjoined with the wisdom that knows how to dispel a danger that has arisen. 'Courage' means the state of being heroic; it is a name for fearlessness. 'Wisdom' means wisdom; it is a name for the wisdom of means, which is the basis for wisdom.

Evaṃ so dakarakkhaso imāya gāthāya bodhisattassa thutiṃ katvā “imāni pupphāni kimatthaṃ harasī”ti pucchi. “Pitā maṃ rājānaṃ kātukāmo, tena kāraṇena harāmī”ti. “Na sakkā tādisena uttamapurisena pupphāni vahituṃ ahaṃ vahissāmī”ti ukkhipitvā tassa pacchato pacchato agamāsi. Athassa pitā dūratova taṃ disvā “ahaṃ imaṃ ‘rakkhasabhattaṃ bhavissatī’ti pahiṇiṃ, so dānesa rakkhasaṃ pupphāni gāhāpento āgacchati, idānimhi naṭṭho”ti cintento sattadhā hadayaphālanaṃ [P 1.0283] patvā tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patto. Sesavānarā sannipatitvā bodhisattaṃ rājānaṃ akaṃsu.

Thus the water-ogre, having praised the Bodhisatta with this verse, asked, 'For what purpose do you carry these flowers?' 'My father wishes to make me king; for that reason I carry them.' 'It is not proper for such an excellent man to carry flowers. I shall carry them.' So saying, he took them and followed behind him. Then his father, seeing him from afar, thought, 'I sent him away, thinking, "He will become food for the ogre," but now he returns, making the ogre carry the flowers. Now I am ruined!' As he thought this, his heart broke into seven pieces, and he died on that very spot. The remaining monkeys assembled and made the Bodhisatta their king.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā yūthapati devadatto ahosi, yūthapatiputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and connected the links, identified the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the herd-leader was Devadatta, and the herd-leader's son was none other than myself.'

Tayodhammajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Tayodhamma Jātaka, the Eighth.

[59] 9. Bherivādakajātakavaṇṇanā

[59] 9. The Commentary on the Bherivādaka Jātaka

Dhame dhameti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tañhi bhikkhuṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu dubbacosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti vutte “na tvaṃ bhikkhu idāneva dubbaco, pubbepi dubbacoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this, beginning with the words 'Dhame dhame,' concerning a certain intractable monk. The Teacher asked that monk, 'Is it true, monk, that you are intractable?' When he replied, 'It is true, Blessed One,' the Teacher said, 'Monk, you are not intractable only now; in the past, too, you were intractable.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bherivādakakule nibbattitvā gāmake vasati. So “bārāṇasiyaṃ nakkhattaṃ [M 1.0301] ghuṭṭha”nti sutvā “samajjamaṇḍale bheriṃ vādetvā dhanaṃ āharissāmī”ti puttaṃ ādāya tattha gantvā bheriṃ vādetvā bahudhanaṃ labhi. So taṃ ādāya attano gāmaṃ gacchanto corāṭaviṃ patvā puttaṃ nirantaraṃ bheriṃ vādentaṃ vāresi “tāta, nirantaraṃ [V 1.0273] avādetvā maggapaṭipannassa issarassa bheriṃ viya antarantarā vādehī”ti so pitarā vāriyamānopi “bherisaddeneva core palāpessāmī”ti vatvā nirantarameva vādesi. Corā paṭhamaññeva bherisaddaṃ sutvā “issarabherī bhavissatī”ti palāyitvā ati viya ekābaddhaṃ saddaṃ sutvā “nāyaṃ issarabherī bhavissatī”ti āgantvā upadhārentā dveyeva jane disvā pothetvā vilumpiṃsu. Bodhisatto “kicchena vata no laddhaṃ dhanaṃ ekābaddhaṃ katvā vādento nāsesī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of drummers and lived in a small village. Hearing that a festival had been proclaimed in Bārāṇasī, he thought, 'I will earn wealth by playing the drum in the festival assembly.' Taking his son, he went there, played the drum, and obtained much wealth. While returning to his own village with it, he came to a forest infested with thieves. He stopped his son, who was beating the drum continuously, saying, 'My dear, do not beat it continuously. Beat it intermittently, like the drum of a lord on a journey.' Although restrained by his father, the son said, 'I will frighten the thieves away with the very sound of the drum,' and beat it without interruption. At first, the thieves heard the drum sound and fled, thinking, 'It must be a lord's drum.' But hearing the excessively continuous sound, they thought, 'This cannot be a lord's drum.' They came back, and upon investigating, saw only two people, whom they beat and plundered. The Bodhisatta, saying, 'The wealth we gained with difficulty has been destroyed by this continuous beating,' spoke this verse:

59.

59.

“Dhame dhame nātidhame, atidhantañhi pāpakaṃ;

Dhantena hi sataṃ laddhaṃ, atidhantena nāsita”nti.

"Beat, beat, but do not over-beat, for over-beating is evil. By beating, a hundred was gained; by over-beating, it was lost."

Tattha [P 1.0284] dhame dhameti dhameyya no na dhameyya, bheriṃ vādeyya no na vādeyyāti attho. Nātidhameti atikkamitvā pana nirantarameva katvā na vādeyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Atidhantañhi pāpakaṃ, nirantaraṃ bherivādanaṃ idāni amhākaṃ pāpakaṃ lāmakaṃ jātaṃ. Dhantena hi sataṃ laddhanti nagare dhamantena bherivādanena kahāpaṇasataṃ laddhaṃ. Atidhantena nāsitanti idāni pana me puttena vacanaṃ akatvā yadidaṃ aṭaviyaṃ atidhantaṃ, tena atidhantena sabbaṃ nāsitanti.

Herein, 'beat, beat' means one should beat, not that one should not beat; that is, one should play the drum, not that one should not play it. 'Do not over-beat' means one should not go to excess and play continuously. Why? Because 'over-beating is evil'; continuous drumming has now become evil and wretched for us. 'By beating, a hundred was gained' means a hundred kahāpaṇas were gained by beating the drum in the city. 'By over-beating, it was lost' means that now, because my son did not follow my words and over-beat in the forest, by that over-beating, all was lost.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā putto dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, pitā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and connected the links, identified the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the son was the intractable monk, and the father was none other than myself.'

Bherivādakajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Bherivādaka Jātaka, the Ninth.

[60] 10. Saṅkhadhamajātakavaṇṇanā

[60] 10. The Commentary on the Saṅkhadhama Jātaka

Dhame [M 1.0302] dhameti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dubbacamevārabbha kathesi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this, beginning with the words 'Dhame dhame,' concerning that same intractable monk.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto saṅkhadhamakakule nibbattitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ nakkhatte ghuṭṭhe pitaraṃ ādāya saṅkhadhamanakammena dhanaṃ labhitvā āgamanakāle corāṭaviyaṃ pitaraṃ nirantaraṃ saṅkhaṃ dhamantaṃ vāresi. So “saṅkhasaddena core palāpessāmī”ti nirantarameva dhami, corā purimanayeneva āgantvā vilumpiṃsu. Bodhisatto purimanayeneva gāthaṃ abhāsi –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of conch-blowers. When a festival was proclaimed in Bārāṇasī, he took his father, and having obtained wealth through the act of conch-blowing, he was returning. In a forest infested with thieves, he tried to stop his father, who was blowing the conch continuously. The father, thinking, 'I will frighten the thieves away with the sound of the conch,' blew it without interruption. The thieves came just as before and plundered them. The Bodhisatta then spoke the verse in the same manner as before:

60.

60.

“Dhame [V 1.0274] dhame nātidhame, atidhantañhi pāpakaṃ;

Dhantenādhigatā bhogā, te tāto vidhamī dhama”nti.

"Blow, blow, but do not over-blow, for over-blowing is evil. The riches acquired by blowing, O father, you destroy by your blowing."

Tattha te tāto vidhamī dhamanti te saṅkhaṃ dhamitvā laddhabhoge mama pitā punappunaṃ dhamanto vidhami viddhaṃsesi vināsesīti.

Herein, 'the riches... you destroy by your blowing' means: 'Those riches gained by blowing the conch, my father, by blowing again and again, has destroyed, scattered, and ruined.'

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā pitā dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, putto panassa ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and connected the links, identified the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the father was the intractable monk, and his son was none other than myself.'

Saṅkhadhamajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Saṅkhadhama Jātaka, the Tenth.

Āsīsavaggo chaṭṭho.

The Chapter on Aspirations, the Sixth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Mahāsīlavajanakaṃ, puṇṇapāti ca kiṃphalaṃ;

Pañcāvudhakañcanakkhandhaṃ, vānarindaṃ tayodhammaṃ;

Bherivādasaṅkhadhamanti.

Mahāsīlava and Vajanaka, Puṇṇapāti and Kiṃphala; Pañcāvudha, Kañcanakkhandha, Vānarinda, Tayodhamma; Bherivāda and Saṅkhadhama.

7. Itthivaggo

7. The Chapter on Women

[61] 1. Asātamantajātakavaṇṇanā

[61] 1. The Commentary on the Asātamanta Jātaka

Asā [V 1.0275][P 1.0285][M 1.0303] lokitthiyo nāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa vatthu ummādantijātake āvi bhavissati. Taṃ pana bhikkhuṃ satthā “bhikkhu itthiyo nāma asātā asatiyo lāmikā pacchimikā, tvaṃ evarūpaṃ lāmikaṃ itthiṃ nissāya kasmā ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Women in this world are indeed unpleasant”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a discontented monk. The story of this monk will be made clear in the Ummādantijātaka. The Teacher said to that monk: “Monk, women are indeed unpleasant, unmindful, base, and vile. Why are you discontented on account of such a base woman?” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilāyaṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto tīsu vedesu sabbasippesu ca nipphattiṃ patto disāpāmokkho ācariyo ahosi. Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ ekasmiṃ brāhmaṇakule puttassa jātadivase aggiṃ gahetvā anibbāyantaṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇakumāraṃ soḷasavassakāle mātāpitaro āhaṃsu “putta, mayaṃ tava jātadivase aggiṃ gahetvā ṭhapayimha. Sace brahmalokaparāyaṇo bhavitukāmo, tvaṃ aggiṃ ādāya araññaṃ pavisitvā aggiṃ bhagavantaṃ namassamāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo hohi. Sace agāraṃ ajjhāvasitukāmo, takkasilaṃ gantvā disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapehī”ti. Māṇavo “nāhaṃ sakkhissāmi araññe aggiṃ paricarituṃ, kuṭumbameva saṇṭhapessāmī”ti mātāpitaro vanditvā ācariyabhāgaṃ sahassaṃ gahetvā takkasilaṃ gantvā sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā paccāgamāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a brahmin family in Takkasilā, in the Gandhāra country. Having come of age and mastered the three Vedas and all the arts, he became a world-renowned teacher. At that time, in a brahmin family in Benares, on the day of their son’s birth, they took up a fire and kept it from being extinguished. When the brahmin youth was sixteen years old, his parents said to him: “Son, on the day of your birth, we took up a fire and have kept it. If you wish to be destined for the Brahma world, take this fire, enter the forest, and paying homage to the Lord Fire, be one destined for the Brahma world. If you wish to live the household life, go to Takkasilā, learn the arts in the presence of the world-renowned teacher, and establish a household.” The young brahmin replied: “I will not be able to tend the fire in the forest; I will establish a household instead.” He paid respects to his parents, took a thousand coins as the teacher’s fee, went to Takkasilā, learned the arts, and returned.

Mātāpitaro panassa anatthikā gharāvāsena, araññe aggiṃ paricarāpetukāmā honti. Atha naṃ mātā itthīnaṃ dosaṃ dassetvā araññaṃ pesetukāmā “so ācariyo paṇḍito byatto sakkhissati me puttassa itthīnaṃ dosaṃ kathetu”nti cintetvā āha – “uggahitaṃ te, tāta, sippa”nti. “Āma, ammā”ti. “Asātamantopi [P 1.0286] te uggahito”ti. “Na uggahito, ammā”ti. “Tāta, yadi te asātamanto na uggahito, kiṃ nāma te sippaṃ uggahitaṃ, gaccha, uggaṇhitvā ehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti puna takkasilābhimukho pāyāsi. Tassapi ācariyassa mātā mahallikā vīsativassasatikā[M 1.0304]. So taṃ sahatthā nhāpento bhojento pāyento [V 1.0276] paṭijaggati. Aññe manussā naṃ tathā karontaṃ jigucchanti. So cintesi “yaṃnūnāhaṃ araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha mātaraṃ paṭijagganto vihareyya”nti. Athekasmiṃ vivitte araññe udakaphāsukaṭṭhāne paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā sappitaṇḍulādīni āharāpetvā mātaraṃ ukkhipitvā tattha gantvā mātaraṃ paṭijagganto vāsaṃ kappesi.

But his parents were not pleased with the household life and wished for him to tend the fire in the forest. Then his mother, wanting to show him the faults of women and send him to the forest, thought: “That teacher is wise and skilled; he will be able to explain the faults of women to my son.” She asked him: “Son, have you learned the art?” “Yes, mother.” “Have you also learned the Asātamanta?” “No, mother, I have not.” “Son, if you have not learned the Asātamanta, what art have you learned? Go, learn it and return.” He said, “Very well,” and set out again towards Takkasilā. Now, his teacher’s mother was very old, one hundred and twenty years of age. He would attend to her with his own hands, bathing her, feeding her, and giving her drink. Other people were disgusted with him for doing so. He thought: “It would be best for me to enter the forest and live there, attending to my mother.” So, in a secluded forest, in a place with convenient water, he had a leaf-hut built, had provisions like ghee and rice brought, and carrying his mother, he went there and took up residence, attending to her.

Sopi kho māṇavo takkasilaṃ gantvā ācariyaṃ apassanto “kahaṃ ācariyo”ti pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā tattha gantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ ācariyo “kiṃ nu kho, tāta, atisīghaṃ āgatosī”ti? “Nanu ahaṃ tumhehi asātamanto nāma na uggaṇhāpito”ti? “Ko pana te asātamante uggaṇhitabbe katvā kathesī”ti? “Mayhaṃ mātā ācariyā”ti. Bodhisatto cintesi “asātamanto nāma koci natthi, imassa pana mātā imaṃ itthidose jānāpetukāmā bhavissatī”ti. Atha naṃ “sādhu, tāta, dassāmi te asātamante, tvaṃ ajja ādiṃ katvā mama ṭhāne ṭhatvā mama mātaraṃ sahatthā nhāpento bhojento pāyento paṭijaggāhi, hatthapādasīsapiṭṭhisambāhanādīni cassā karonto ‘ayye jaraṃ pattakālepi tāva te evarūpaṃ sarīraṃ, daharakāle kīdisaṃ ahosī’ti hatthapādaparikammādikaraṇakāle hatthapādādīnaṃ vaṇṇaṃ katheyyāsi. Yañca te mama mātā katheti, taṃ alajjanto aniguhanto mayhaṃ āroceyyāsi, evaṃ karonto asātamante lacchasi, akaronto na lacchasī”ti āha. So “sādhu ācariyā”ti tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā tato paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ yathāvuttavidhānaṃ akāsi.

The young brahmin, upon arriving at Takkasilā and not seeing his teacher, asked, “Where is the teacher?” Hearing what had happened, he went there, paid his respects, and stood to one side. Then the teacher asked him: “Dear one, why have you returned so quickly?” “Sir, was I not left untaught by you concerning the so-called Asātamanta?” “But who told you that the Asātamanta was to be learned?” “My mother, O teacher.” The Bodhisatta thought: “There is no such thing as an Asātamanta. This young man’s mother must want to make him understand the faults of women.” Then he said to him: “Very well, dear one, I will give you the Asātamanta. Starting today, take my place and attend to my mother, bathing her with your own hands, feeding her, giving her drink, and massaging her hands, feet, head, and back. While doing so, say: ‘Lady, even in old age your body is like this—what must it have been like when you were young?’ And while attending to her hands and feet, you should praise their beauty. Whatever my mother tells you, report it to me without shame or concealment. By doing so, you will receive the Asātamanta; if you do not do so, you will not.” The young man said, “Very well, teacher,” and accepting his instruction, from that day forward he did everything according to the prescribed method.

Athassā tasmiṃ māṇave punappunaṃ vaṇṇayamāne “ayaṃ mayā saddhiṃ abhiramitukāmo bhavissatī”ti andhāya jarājiṇṇāya abbhantare kileso uppajji[P 1.0287]. Sā ekadivasaṃ attano sarīravaṇṇaṃ kathayamānaṃ māṇavaṃ āha “mayā saddhiṃ abhiramituṃ icchasī”ti? “Ayye, ahaṃ tāva iccheyyaṃ, ācariyo pana garuko”ti. “Sace maṃ icchasi, puttaṃ me mārehī”ti. “Ahaṃ ācariyassa santike ettakaṃ sippaṃ uggaṇhitvā kilesamattaṃ nissāya kinti katvā ācariyaṃ māressāmī”ti. “Tena hi sace tvaṃ maṃ na pariccajasi, ahameva naṃ māressāmī”ti. Evaṃ itthiyo nāma asātā [M 1.0305] lāmikā pacchimikā, tathārūpe nāma vaye ṭhitā rāgacittaṃ uppādetvā kilesaṃ anuvattamānā evaṃ upakārakaṃ puttaṃ māretukāmā jātā. Māṇavo sabbaṃ taṃ kathaṃ bodhisattassa ārocesi.

Then, as the young man repeatedly praised her, a defilement arose within the blind and age-worn woman, who thought, “This man must wish to take his pleasure with me.” One day, as the young man was speaking of the beauty of her body, she asked him: “Do you wish to take your pleasure with me?” “Lady, I would wish to, but the teacher is venerable.” “If you desire me, kill my son.” “Having learned so much skill in the presence of the teacher, how could I kill him on account of a mere defilement?” “In that case, if you do not abandon me, I myself will kill him.” Thus, women are indeed unpleasant, base, and vile. Standing at such an age, she gave rise to a lustful thought and, following that defilement, became willing to kill such a helpful son. The young man reported the entire conversation to the Bodhisatta.

Bodhisatto [V 1.0277] “suṭṭhu te, māṇava, kataṃ mayhaṃ ārocentenā”ti vatvā mātu āyusaṅkhāraṃ olokento “ajjeva marissatī”ti ñatvā “ehi, māṇava, vīmaṃsissāma na”nti ekaṃ udumbararukkhaṃ chinditvā attano pamāṇena kaṭṭharūpakaṃ katvā sasīsaṃ pārupitvā attano sayanaṭṭhāne uttānaṃ nipajjāpetvā rajjukaṃ bandhitvā antevāsikaṃ āha – “tāta, pharasuṃ ādāya gantvā mama mātu saññaṃ dehī”ti. Māṇavo gantvā “ayye, ācariyo paṇṇasālāyaṃ attano sayanaṭṭhāne nipanno, rajjusaññā me baddhā, imaṃ pharasuṃ ādāya gantvā sace sakkosi, mārehi na”nti āha. “Tvaṃ pana maṃ na pariccajissasī”ti? “Kiṃkāraṇā pariccajissāmī”ti? Sā pharasuṃ ādāya pavedhamānā uṭṭhāya rajjusaññāya gantvā hatthena parāmasitvā “ayaṃ me putto”ti saññāya kaṭṭharūpakassa mukhato sāṭakaṃ apanetvā pharasuṃ ādāya “ekappahāreneva māressāmī”ti gīvāyameva paharitvā “dha”nti sadde uppanne rukkhabhāvaṃ aññāsi. Atha bodhisattena “kiṃ karosi, ammā”ti vutte sā “vañcitāmhī”ti tattheva maritvā patitā. Attano kira paṇṇasālāya nipannāyapi taṅkhaṇaññeva tāya maritabbameva.

The Bodhisatta said: “You have done well, young man, in informing me.” Then, observing his mother's life-span, he knew: “She will die this very day.” He said: “Come, young man, let us test her.” He cut down an udumbara tree, fashioned a wooden image of his own size, covered it including the head, and laid it face up in his own sleeping place. He tied a rope to it and told his pupil: “My dear, take an axe and go give my mother the signal.” The young man went and said: “Madam, the teacher is lying in his sleeping place in the leaf-hut. I have tied a rope as a signal. Take this axe, go, and if you can, kill him.” She asked: “But you will not abandon me?” He replied: “For what reason would I abandon you?” Taking the axe, she rose up trembling, followed the rope signal, and felt it with her hand. Thinking, “This is my son,” she removed the cloth from the face of the wooden image, took the axe, and thinking, “I will kill him with a single blow,” she struck it on the neck. When the sound “thud” arose, she realized it was wood. Then, when the Bodhisatta said, “What are you doing, mother?” she replied, “I have been deceived,” and died and fell right there. Indeed, even if she had been lying in her own leaf-hut, she was destined to die at that very moment.

So tassā matabhāvaṃ ñatvā sarīrakiccaṃ katvā āḷāhanaṃ nibbāpetvā vanapupphehi pūjetvā māṇavaṃ ādāya paṇṇasāladvāre nisīditvā “tāta, pāṭiyekko asātamanto [P 1.0288] nāma natthi, itthiyo asātā nāma, tava mātā ‘asātamantaṃ uggaṇhā’ti mama santikaṃ pesayamānā itthīnaṃ dosaṃ jānanatthaṃ pesesi. Idāni pana te paccakkhameva mama mātu doso diṭṭho, iminā kāraṇena ‘itthiyo nāma asātā lāmikā pacchimikā’ti jāneyyāsī”ti taṃ ovaditvā uyyojesi. Sopi ācariyaṃ vanditvā mātāpitūnaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ mātā pucchi “tāta, uggahito te asātamanto”ti? “Āma, ammā”ti. “Idāni kiṃ karissasi, pabbajitvā aggiṃ vā paricarissasi, agāramajjhe vā vasissasī”ti? Māṇavo “mayā, amma, paccakkhato itthīnaṃ dosā diṭṭhā[M 1.0306], agārena me kiccaṃ natthi, pabbajissāmaha”nti attano adhippāyaṃ pakāsento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Knowing she had died, he performed the funeral rites, extinguished the funeral pyre, made an offering of forest flowers, and taking the young man, he sat at the door of the leaf-hut and said: “My dear, there is no such thing as a separate ‘Mantra of Displeasure’; women themselves are what is called displeasure. Your mother, in sending you to me to ‘learn the Mantra of Displeasure,’ sent you so that you would understand the faults of women. Now, however, you have witnessed with your own eyes the fault of my mother. For this reason, you should know that women are displeasing, base, and vile.” Having advised him thus, he sent him on his way. The young man paid his respects to the teacher and went to his parents. Then his mother asked him, “My dear, have you learned the Mantra of Displeasure?” “Yes, mother.” “Now what will you do? Will you go forth and tend the sacred fire, or will you live in the midst of the household?” The young man replied, “Mother, I have seen with my own eyes the faults of women. I have no use for the household life; I shall go forth.” Declaring his intention, he spoke this verse:

61.

61.

“Asā lokitthiyo nāma, velā tāsaṃ na vijjati;

Sārattā ca pagabbhā ca, sikhī sabbaghaso yathā;

Tā hitvā pabbajissāmi, vivekamanubrūhaya”nti.

“Women in this world are indeed unpleasant; no restraint is found in them. They are full of passion and bold, like an all-consuming fire. Having abandoned them, I shall go forth, developing seclusion.”

Tattha [V 1.0278] asāti asatiyo lāmikā. Atha vā sātaṃ vuccati sukhaṃ, taṃ tāsu natthi. Attani paṭibaddhacittānaṃ asātameva dentītipi asā, dukkhā dukkhavatthubhūtāti attho. Imassa panatthassa sādhanatthāya idaṃ suttaṃ āharitabbaṃ –

Herein, `asā` means unfaithful and base. Or, `sāta` is said to be pleasure, which is not found in them. And because they give only displeasure to those whose minds are attached to them, they are called `asā`; the meaning is that they are suffering and the ground for suffering. To establish this meaning, this discourse should be brought forth:

“Māyā cetā marīcī ca, soko rogo cupaddavo;

Kharā ca bandhanā cetā, maccupāsā guhāsayā;

Tāsu yo vissase poso, so naresu narādhamo”ti. (jā. 2.21.118);

“They are illusion and a mirage, sorrow, disease, and calamity; they are harsh bonds, the snares of Death, a hidden danger. Whatever man puts his trust in them, he, among men, is the vilest of men.”

Lokitthiyoti loke itthiyo. Velā tāsaṃ na vijjatīti amma, tāsaṃ itthīnaṃ kilesuppattiṃ patvā velā saṃvaro mariyādā pamāṇaṃ nāma natthi. Sārattā ca pagabbhā cāti velā ca etāsaṃ natthi, pañcasu kāmaguṇesu sārattā allīnā, tathā kāyapāgabbhiyena, vācāpāgabbhiyena, manopāgabbhiyenāti tividhena pāgabbhiyena samannāgatattā pagabbhā cetā. Etāsañhi abbhantare kāyadvārādīni patvā saṃvaro nāma natthi, lolā kākapaṭibhāgāti dasseti. Sikhī sabbaghaso yathāti amma, yathā jālasikhāya “sikhī”ti saṅkhaṃ gato aggi nāma gūthagatādibhedaṃ asucimpi, sappimadhuphāṇitādibhedaṃ sucimpi, iṭṭhampi aniṭṭhampi yaṃ yadeva labhati, sabbaṃ ghasati khādati, tasmā “sabbaghaso”ti vuccati. Tatheva tā itthiyopi hatthimeṇḍagomeṇḍādayo vā hontu hīnajaccā hīnakammantā, khattiyādayo vā hontu uttamakammantā, hīnukkaṭṭhabhāvaṃ acintetvā lokassādavasena [P 1.0289] kilesasanthave uppanne yaṃ yaṃ labhanti, sabbameva sevantīti sabbaghasasikhisadisā honti. Tasmā sikhī sabbaghaso yathā, tathevetāti veditabbā.

‘Women in the world’ means women who are in the world. ‘No restraint is found in them’ means, my dear, that with regard to the arising of defilements in these women, there is no such thing as a limit, restraint, boundary, or measure. ‘They are full of passion and bold’ means they have no restraint, are passionately attached to and immersed in the five strands of sensual pleasure, and are likewise possessed of the threefold boldness: boldness of body, boldness of speech, and boldness of mind. For within them, with regard to the sense-doors and so on, there is no restraint; this shows they are fickle, like crows. ‘Like an all-consuming fire’ means, my dear, just as fire—which is known as `sikhī` because it has a crest of flame—devours and consumes everything it gets, whether impure things like dung or pure things like ghee, honey, and molasses, whether pleasant or unpleasant, and is therefore called ‘all-consuming’; in the very same way, these women, without considering high or low status—whether men are of low birth and low trade, such as keepers of elephants, rams, or cattle, or of high birth and noble trade, such as warriors—when an attachment to defilements arises through worldly taste, they associate with whomever they get. Thus they are like the all-consuming fire. Therefore, it should be understood that they are just like an all-consuming fire.

Tā [M 1.0307] hitvā pabbajissāmīti ahaṃ tā lāmikā dukkhavatthubhūtā itthiyo hitvā araññaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajissāmi. Vivekamanubrūhayanti kāyaviveko cittaviveko upadhivivekoti tayo vivekā, tesu idha kāyavivekopi vaṭṭati cittavivekopi. Idaṃ vuttaṃ hoti – ahaṃ, amma, pabbajitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā aṭṭha samāpattiyo ca pañcābhiññā ca uppādetvā gaṇato kāyaṃ, kilesehi ca cittaṃ vivecetvā imaṃ vivekaṃ brūhento vaḍḍhento brahmalokaparāyaṇo bhavissāmi, alaṃ me agārenāti. Evaṃ itthiyo garahitvā mātāpitaro vanditvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pabbajitvā vuttappakāraṃ vivekaṃ brūhento brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

‘Having abandoned them, I shall go forth’ means: having abandoned those base women who are the ground for suffering, I shall enter the forest and undertake the going-forth of a seer. ‘Developing seclusion’: there are three kinds of seclusion—seclusion of body, seclusion of mind, and seclusion from the substrates of existence. Here, both seclusion of body and seclusion of mind are applicable. This is what is said: “Mother, having gone forth and performed the preliminary work on the kasiṇas, having produced the eight attainments and the five supernormal knowledges, having secluded the body from company and the mind from defilements, and by developing and increasing this seclusion, I shall be one whose destination is the Brahma-world. Enough of the household life for me!” Thus, having censured women and paid respect to his parents, he entered the Himalayas, went forth, and by developing seclusion in the way described, he became one whose destination is the Brahma-world.

Satthāpi [V 1.0279] “evaṃ bhikkhu itthiyo nāma asātā lāmikā pacchimikā dukkhadāyikā”ti itthīnaṃ aguṇaṃ kathetvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāsi. Satthā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mātā bhaddakāpilānī, pitā mahākassapo ahosi, antevāsiko ānando, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher also declared the truths, saying, 'Indeed, monk, women are disagreeable, base, inferior, and bringers of suffering,' thus speaking of women's faults. At the conclusion of the exposition of the truths, that monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher connected the story and identified the birth: 'At that time, the mother was Bhaddakāpilānī, the father was Mahākassapa, the disciple was Ānanda, and I myself was the teacher.'

Asātamantajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first, the commentary on the Asātamanta Jātaka.

[62] 2. Aṇḍabhūtajātakavaṇṇanā

[62] 2. Commentary on the Aṇḍabhūta Jātaka

Yaṃ brāhmaṇo avādesīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitamevārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte “bhikkhu itthiyo nāma arakkhiyā, pubbe paṇḍitā itthiṃ gabbhato paṭṭhāya rakkhantāpi rakkhituṃ nāsakkhiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this discourse beginning, 'What the brahmin advised,' concerning a certain monk who was discontented. The Teacher asked him, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' When he replied, 'It is true,' the Teacher said, 'Monk, women are indeed unguardable. In the past, even the wise, though guarding a woman from the womb onwards, were unable to protect her,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā pitu accayena rajje patiṭṭhāya dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. So purohitena saddhiṃ jūtaṃ kīḷati. Kīḷanto pana –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. Having reached maturity and mastered all arts, he ascended the throne after his father's passing and ruled righteously. He would play dice with his chaplain. While playing, he would recite:

“Sabbā [M 1.0308] nadī vaṅkagatī, sabbe kaṭṭhamayā vanā;

Sabbitthiyo kare pāpaṃ, labhamāne nivātake”ti. (jā. 2.21.308) –

"All rivers have a winding course, all forests are made of wood; All women would do evil, should they find a private place."

Imaṃ [P 1.0290] jūtagītaṃ gāyanto rajataphalake suvaṇṇapāsake khipati. Evaṃ kīḷanto pana rājā niccaṃ jināti, purohito parājīyati.

Singing this gambling-song, he would throw the golden dice upon a silver board. When they played in this way, the king always won, and the chaplain was always defeated.

So anukkamena ghare vibhave parikkhayaṃ gacchante cintesi “evaṃ sante sabbaṃ imasmiṃ ghare dhanaṃ khīyissati, pariyesitvā purisantaraṃ agataṃ ekaṃ mātugāmaṃ ghare karissāmī”ti. Athassa etadahosi “aññaṃ purisaṃ diṭṭhapubbaṃ itthiṃ rakkhituṃ na sakkhissāmi, gabbhato paṭṭhāyekaṃ mātugāmaṃ rakkhitvā taṃ vayappattaṃ vase ṭhapetvā ekapurisikaṃ katvā gāḷhaṃ ārakkhaṃ saṃvidahitvā rājakulato dhanaṃ āharissāmī”ti. So ca aṅgavijjāya cheko hoti, athekaṃ duggatitthiṃ gabbhiniṃ disvā “dhītaraṃ vijāyissatī”ti ñatvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā paribbayaṃ datvā [V 1.0280] ghareyeva vasāpetvā vijātakāle dhanaṃ datvā uyyojetvā taṃ kumārikaṃ aññesaṃ purisānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ adatvā itthīnaṃyeva hatthe datvā posāpetvā vayappattakāle taṃ attano vase ṭhapesi. Yāva cesā vaḍḍhati, tāva raññā saddhiṃ jūtaṃ na kīḷi. Taṃ pana vase ṭhapetvā brāhmaṇo “mahārāja, jūtaṃ kīḷāmā”ti āha. Rājā “sādhū”ti purimaniyāmeneva kīḷi. Purohito rañño gāyitvā pāsakaṃ khipanakāle “ṭhapetvā mama māṇavika”nti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya purohito jināti, rājā parājīyati.

As his household wealth gradually declined, he thought, 'If this continues, all the wealth in this house will be exhausted. I must find a woman who has not known another man and make her my wife.' Then it occurred to him, 'I will not be able to guard a woman who has previously seen another man. But if I guard a woman from the time she is in the womb, raise her until she comes of age, keep her under my control, make her faithful to one man only, and arrange a strict guard, then I can bring wealth from the royal court.' He was skilled in the science of physiognomy. Seeing a poor pregnant woman, he knew, 'She will give birth to a daughter.' He summoned her, gave her provisions, and had her stay in his house. When she gave birth, he gave her money and sent her away. He had the young girl raised by women only, not allowing her to be seen by other men. When she came of age, he brought her under his own control. As long as she was growing up, he did not gamble with the king. But after bringing her under his control, the brahmin said, 'Great king, let us gamble.' The king agreed, and they played as before. When the king, having sung his verse, threw the dice, the chaplain said, 'Except for my young maiden.' From that time on, the chaplain won, and the king was defeated.

Bodhisatto “imassa ghare ekapurisikāya ekāya itthiyā bhavitabba”nti pariggaṇhāpento atthibhāvaṃ ñatvā “sīlamassā bhindāpessāmī”ti ekaṃ dhuttaṃ pakkosāpetvā “sakkhissasi purohitassa itthiyā sīlaṃ bhinditu”nti āha. “Sakkomi, devā”ti. Athassa rājā dhanaṃ datvā “tena hi khippaṃ niṭṭhāpehī”ti taṃ pahiṇi. So rañño santikā dhanaṃ ādāya gandhadhūmacuṇṇakappūrādīni gahetvā tassa gharato avidūre sabbagandhāpaṇaṃ pasāresi. Purohitassapi gehaṃ sattabhūmakaṃ sattadvārakoṭṭhakaṃ hoti, sabbesu dvārakoṭṭhakesu itthīnaṃyeva ārakkhā. Ṭhapetvā pana brāhmaṇaṃ añño puriso gehaṃ pavisituṃ labhanto nāma [M 1.0309] natthi, kacavarachaḍḍanapacchimpi [P 1.0291] sodhetvāyeva pavesenti. Taṃ māṇavikaṃ purohitoyeva daṭṭhuṃ labhati. Tassā ca ekā paricārikā itthī atthi. Athassā sā paricārikā gandhapupphamūlaṃ gahetvā gacchantī tassa dhuttassa āpaṇasamīpena gacchati. So “ayaṃ tassā paricārikā”ti suṭṭhu ñatvā ekadivasaṃ taṃ āgacchantiṃ disvā āpaṇā uṭṭhāya gantvā tassā pādamūle patitvā ubhohi hatthehi pāde gāḷhaṃ gahetvā “amma, ettakaṃ kālaṃ kahaṃ gatāsī”ti paridevi, avasesāpi payuttakadhuttā ekamantaṃ ṭhatvā “hatthapādamukhasaṇṭhānehi ca ākappena ca mātāputtā ekasadisāyevā”ti āhaṃsu. Sā itthī tesu tesu kathentesu attano asaddahitvā “ayaṃ me putto bhavissatī”ti sayampi rodituṃ ārabhi. Te ubhopi kanditvā roditvā aññamaññaṃ āliṅgetvā aṭṭhaṃsu.

The Bodhisatta, having investigated and learned that 'in this household there must be a woman faithful to one man,' thought, 'I shall have her virtue broken.' He summoned a rogue and asked, 'Will you be able to corrupt the chaplain's wife?' 'I am able, Your Majesty,' he replied. Then the king gave him money and said, 'In that case, accomplish it quickly,' and sent him away. Taking the money from the king, the rogue procured perfumes, incense, powders, camphor, and the like, and set up a perfumery not far from the brahmin's house. The chaplain's house was seven-storied with seven gatehouses, and in every gatehouse, only women stood guard. Except for the brahmin, no other man was allowed to enter the house; even a basket for discarding rubbish was inspected before being brought in. Only the chaplain was able to see the young woman. She had one female attendant. Now, this attendant, when going to fetch perfumes and flowers, would pass by the rogue's shop. Recognizing her as the attendant, the rogue saw her approaching one day, rose from his shop, went and fell at her feet, grasped them firmly with both hands, and lamented, 'Mother, where have you been all this time?' The other rogues who had been posted there stood to one side and said, 'By the shape of their hands, feet, and face, and by their general appearance, they are the very image of mother and son.' When they said this, the attendant woman was convinced, thinking, 'This must be my son,' and she herself began to weep. Then they both wept and cried, and stood embracing one another.

Atha so dhutto āha “amma, kahaṃ vasasī”ti? “Kinnarilīlāya vasamānāya rūpasobhaggappattāya purohitassa daharitthiyā upaṭṭhānaṃ kurumānā vasāmi, tātā”ti. “Idāni kahaṃ yāsi, ammā”ti? “Tassā gandhamālādīnaṃ atthāyā”ti. “Amma, kiṃ te aññattha gatāya, ito paṭṭhāya mameva santikā harā”ti mūlaṃ aggahetvāva bahūni tambūlatakkolakādīni ceva nānāpupphāni ca adāsi. Māṇavikā bahūni gandhapupphādīni disvā “kiṃ, amma, ajja amhākaṃ brāhmaṇo pasanno”ti āha. “Kasmā evaṃ vadasī”ti? “Imesaṃ bahubhāvaṃ disvā”ti. Na brāhmaṇo bahumūlaṃ adāsi, mayā panetaṃ mayhaṃ puttassa [V 1.0281] santikā ābhatanti. Tato paṭṭhāya sā brāhmaṇena dinnamūlaṃ attanā gahetvā tasseva santikā gandhapupphādīni āharati. Dhutto katipāhaccayena gilānālayaṃ katvā nipajji. Sā tassa āpaṇadvāraṃ gantvā taṃ adisvā “kahaṃ me putto”ti pucchi. “Puttassa te aphāsukaṃ jāta”nti? Sā tassa nipannaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā nisīditvā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjantī “kiṃ te, tāta, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. So tuṇhī ahosi. “Kiṃ na kathesi puttā”ti? “Amma, marantenāpi tuyhaṃ kathetuṃ na sakkā”ti. “Tāta, mayhaṃ akathetvā [P 1.0292] kassa katheyyāsi, kathehi, tātā”ti. “Amma, mayhaṃ aññaṃ aphāsukaṃ natthi, tassā pana māṇavikāya vaṇṇaṃ sutvā paṭibaddhacittosmi[M 1.0310], taṃ labhanto jīvissāmi, alabhanto idheva marissāmī”ti. “Tāta, mayhaṃ esa bhāro, mā tvaṃ etaṃ nissāya cintayī”ti taṃ assāsetvā bahūni gandhapupphādīni ādāya māṇavikāya santikaṃ gantvā “putto me, amma, mama santikā tava vaṇṇaṃ sutvā paṭibaddhacitto jāto, kiṃ kātabba”nti? “Sace ānetuṃ sakkotha, mayā katokāsoyevā”ti.

Then the rogue said, 'Mother, where do you live?' 'I live serving the young wife of the brahmin, who is endowed with beauty and grace, possessing the elegance of a Kinnarī, my son.' 'Where are you going now, mother?' 'For her perfumes, garlands, and the like.' 'Mother, why go elsewhere? From now on, take them only from me.' Without taking any payment, he gave her many betel leaves, areca nuts, and various flowers. Seeing the abundance of perfumes and flowers, the young woman said, 'Why, mother, is our brahmin pleased today?' 'Why do you say so?' 'Seeing such abundance.' 'The brahmin did not give so much money; I brought these from my son.' From then on, she took the money given by the brahmin for herself and brought perfumes and flowers from her son. After a few days, the rogue feigned illness and lay down. She went to his shop door and, not seeing him, asked, 'Where is my son?' They replied, 'Your son is unwell.' She went to where he was lying, sat down, and stroking his back, asked, 'What is wrong, my son?' He remained silent. 'Why do you not speak, son?' 'Mother, even if I were dying, I could not tell you.' 'My son, if you do not tell me, whom will you tell? Speak, my son.' 'Mother, I have no other affliction, but having heard of the young woman's beauty, my heart is bound to her. If I obtain her, I will live; if not, I will die right here.' 'My son, this burden is mine; do not worry on her account.' Comforting him, she took many perfumes and flowers and went to the young woman. 'My son, my dear, has become infatuated with you after hearing of your beauty from me. What is to be done?' 'If you can bring him, I give my consent.'

Sā tassā vacanaṃ sutvā tato paṭṭhāya tassa gehassa kaṇṇakaṇṇehi bahuṃ kacavaraṃ saṅkaḍḍhitvā ārakkhitthiyā upari chaḍḍesi. Sā tena aṭṭīyamānā apeti. Itarā teneva niyāmena yā yā kiñci katheti, tassā tassā upari kacavaraṃ chaḍḍesi. Tato paṭṭhāya pana sā yaṃ yaṃ āharati vā harati vā, taṃ taṃ na kāci sodhetuṃ ussahati. Tasmiṃ kāle sā taṃ dhuttaṃ pupphapacchiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā māṇavikāya santikaṃ abhihari. Dhutto māṇavikāya sīlaṃ bhinditvā ekāhadvīhaṃ pāsādeyeva ahosi. Purohite bahi nikkhante ubho abhiramanti. Tasmiṃ āgate dhutto nilīyati.

Hearing her words, from that time onward, she began to sweep up much refuse from every corner of the house and dumped it on the guardian woman. Distressed by this, the guardian woman departed. Then, in the same manner, she would dump refuse on whichever woman said anything. From then on, whatever she brought in or carried out, no one dared to inspect. At that time, she had the rogue lie down in a flower basket and brought him to the young woman. The rogue violated the young woman's virtue and stayed in the palace for a day or two. When the brahmin went out, the two enjoyed themselves. When he returned, the rogue hid.

Atha naṃ sā ekāhadvīhaccayena “sāmi, idāni tayā gantuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti āha. “Ahaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ paharitvā gantukāmo”ti. Sā “evaṃ hotū”ti dhuttaṃ nilīyāpetvā brāhmaṇe āgate evamāha “ahaṃ, ayya, tumhesu vīṇaṃ vādentesu naccituṃ icchāmī”ti. “Sādhu, bhadde, naccassū”ti vīṇaṃ vādesi. “Tumhesu olokentesu lajjāmi, mukhaṃ pana vo sāṭakena bandhitvā naccissāmī”ti. “Sace lajjasi, evaṃ karohī”ti. Māṇavikā ghanasāṭakaṃ gahetvā tassa akkhīni pidahamānā mukhaṃ bandhi. Brāhmaṇo mukhaṃ bandhāpetvā vīṇaṃ vādesi. Sā muhuttaṃ naccitvā “ayya, ahaṃ te ekavāraṃ sīse paharitukāmā”ti āha. Itthilolo brāhmaṇo kiñci kāraṇaṃ ajānanto “paharāhī”ti āha, māṇavikā dhuttassa saññaṃ adāsi. So saṇikaṃ āgantvā brāhmaṇassa piṭṭhipasse ṭhatvā [P 1.0293] sīse kapparena pahari, akkhīni [V 1.0282] patanākārappattāni ahesuṃ, sīse gaṇḍo uṭṭhahi. So vedanāṭṭo hutvā “āhara te hattha”nti āha. Māṇavikā attano hatthaṃ ukkhipitvā tassa hatthe ṭhapesi. Brāhmaṇo “hattho muduko, pahāro pana thaddho”ti āha[M 1.0311]. Dhutto brāhmaṇaṃ paharitvā nilīyi. Māṇavikā tasmiṃ nilīne brāhmaṇassa mukhato sāṭakaṃ mocetvā telaṃ ādāya sīsaṃ parisambāhi. Brāhmaṇe bahi nikkhante puna sā itthī dhuttaṃ pacchiyaṃ nipajjāpetvā nīhari.

Then, after a day or two, she said to him, 'Sir, it is now time for you to depart.' 'I wish to strike the brahmin before I depart,' he said. 'So be it,' she said. Hiding the rogue, when the brahmin arrived, she spoke thus: 'Sir, while you play the lute, I wish to dance.' 'Good, my lady, dance then,' and he played the lute. 'I feel shy while you watch me; I will dance after binding your face with a cloth.' 'If you are shy, do so.' The young woman took a thick cloth and, covering his eyes, bound his face. The brahmin, with his face bound, played the lute. She danced for a moment and then said, 'Sir, I wish to strike your head once.' The lustful brahmin, not knowing any reason, said, 'Strike.' The young woman gave the signal to the rogue. He came quietly and, standing behind the brahmin, struck his head with his elbow. His eyes seemed about to fall out, and a lump rose on his head. Overcome with pain, he said, 'Give me your hand.' The young woman raised her own hand and placed it in his. The brahmin said, 'The hand is soft, but the blow was hard.' The rogue, having struck the brahmin, hid again. When he was hidden, the young woman removed the cloth from the brahmin's face, took some oil, and massaged his head. When the brahmin had gone out, the servant woman again had the rogue lie down in the basket and carried him out.

So rañño santikaṃ gantvā sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Rājā attano upaṭṭhānaṃ āgataṃ brāhmaṇaṃ āha “jūtaṃ kīḷāma brāhmaṇā”ti? “Sādhu, mahārājā”ti. Rājā jūtamaṇḍalaṃ sajjāpetvā purimanayeneva jūtagītaṃ gāyitvā pāsake khipati. Brāhmaṇo māṇavikāya tapassa bhinnabhāvaṃ ajānanto “ṭhapetvā mama māṇavika”nti āha. Evaṃ vadantopi parājitoyeva. Rājā jinitvā “brāhmaṇa, kiṃ vadesi, māṇavikāya te tapo bhinno, tvaṃ ‘mātugāmaṃ gabbhato paṭṭhāya rakkhanto sattasu ṭhānesu ārakkhaṃ karonto rakkhituṃ sakkhissāmī’ti maññasi, mātugāmo nāma kucchiyaṃ pakkhipitvā carantenāpi rakkhituṃ na sakkā, ekapurisikā itthī nāma natthi, tava māṇavikā ‘naccitukāmāmhī’ti vatvā vīṇaṃ vādentassa tava sāṭakena mukhaṃ bandhitvā attano jāraṃ tava sīse kapparena paharāpetvā uyyojesi, idāni kiṃ kathesī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

He went to the king and reported all that had happened. The king, seeing the brahmin who had come to attend on him, said, 'Brahmin, shall we play at dice?' 'Very well, great king,' he replied. The king had the dice board prepared and, as before, sang the dice song and threw the dice. The brahmin, unaware that the young woman's virtue had been broken, said, 'Except for my young woman.' Even as he spoke thus, he was defeated. Having won, the king said, 'Brahmin, what do you say? Your vow has been broken by the young woman. You think, "I can guard a woman by protecting her in seven places from the time she is in the womb." But a woman cannot be guarded even if placed inside one's belly and carried about. There is no such thing as a woman faithful to one man. Your young woman, saying, "I wish to dance," while you played the lute, had your face covered with a cloth, had her lover strike you on the head with his elbow, and sent him away. Now, what do you say?' Having spoken thus, he uttered this verse:

62.

62.

“Yaṃ brāhmaṇo avādesi, vīṇaṃ samukhaveṭhito;

Aṇḍabhūtābhatā bhariyā, tāsu ko jātu vissase”ti.

'The brahmin played the lute with his face covered. A wife is reared from the embryonic stage—who indeed could place trust in them?'

Tattha yaṃ brāhmaṇo avādesi, vīṇaṃ samukhaveṭhitoti yena kāraṇena brāhmaṇo ghanasāṭakena saha mukhena veṭhito hutvā vīṇaṃ vādesi, taṃ kāraṇaṃ na jānātīti attho. Tañhi sā vañcetukāmā evamakāsi. Brāhmaṇo pana taṃ itthiṃ bahumāyābhāvaṃ ajānanto mātugāmassa saddahitvā “maṃ esā lajjatī”ti evaṃsaññī ahosi, tenassa aññāṇabhāvaṃ pakāsento rājā evamāha, ayametthādhippāyo[P 1.0294]. Aṇḍabhūtābhatā bhariyāti aṇḍaṃ vuccati bījaṃ, bījabhūtā mātukucchito anikkhantakāleyeva ābhatā ānītā, bhatāti vā puṭṭhāti attho. Kā sā? Bhariyā pajāpati pādaparicārikā. Sā hi bhattavatthādīhi [M 1.0312] bharitabbatāya, bhinnasaṃvaratāya, lokadhammehi bharitatāya vā “bhariyā”ti vuccati. Tāsu ko jātu vissaseti jātūti ekaṃsādhivacanaṃ, tāsu mātukucchito paṭṭhāya rakkhiyamānāsupi evaṃ vippakāraṃ āpajjantīsu bhariyāsu ko nāma paṇḍito puriso ekaṃsena vissase, “nibbikārā esā mayī”ti ko saddaheyyāti [V 1.0283] attho. Asaddhammavasena hi āmantakesu nimantakesu vijjamānesu mātugāmo nāma na sakkā rakkhitunti.

Therein, regarding the line, 'The brahmin played the lute with his face covered': the meaning is that he does not know the reason why the brahmin, with his face covered by a thick cloth, played the lute. For she, wishing to deceive him, acted thus. But the brahmin, not knowing that woman's great deceitfulness, trusted her and thought, 'She is shy of me.' To reveal his ignorance, the king spoke thus—this is the intended meaning here. Regarding 'A wife is reared from the embryonic stage': an 'egg' (aṇḍa) refers to a seed. 'Reared from the embryonic stage' means she was brought and taken care of from the time she was a seed-being, before she had even emerged from her mother's womb. Or, bhatā means 'nourished.' Who is she? The wife (bhariyā), the consort, the one who attends to his feet. She is called bhariyā because she is to be supported (bharitabbā) with food and clothing, because her restraint is broken (bhinna-saṃvarā), or because she is burdened (bharitā) with worldly conditions. Regarding 'who indeed could place trust in them?': jātu is an emphatic term. The meaning is: among such wives who, even when guarded from their mother's womb, fall into such misconduct, what wise man could place absolute trust, thinking, 'She is unwavering towards me'? Who could have faith? For it is said that, due to their unrighteous nature, when there are men who call and invite them, a woman cannot be guarded.

Evaṃ bodhisatto brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desesi. Brāhmaṇo bodhisattassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā nivesanaṃ gantvā taṃ māṇavikaṃ āha – “tayā kira evarūpaṃ pāpakammaṃ kata”nti? “Ayya, ko evamāha, na karomi, ‘ahameva pahariṃ, na añño koci’. Sace na saddahatha, ahaṃ ‘tumhe ṭhapetvā aññassa purisassa hatthasamphassaṃ na jānāmī’ti saccakiriyaṃ katvā aggiṃ pavisitvā tumhe saddahāpessāmī”ti. Brāhmaṇo “evaṃ hotū”ti mahantaṃ dārurāsiṃ kāretvā aggiṃ katvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “sace attano saddahasi, aggiṃ pavisāhī”ti āha.

Thus the Bodhisatta taught the Dhamma to the brahmin. Having heard the Bodhisatta's teaching, the brahmin went to his residence and said to the young woman, 'Is it true that you have done such an evil deed?' 'Sir, who says so? I did not do it. It was I myself who struck you, not anyone else. If you do not believe me, I will perform an act of truth, stating, "Apart from you, I know not the touch of another man's hand," and enter the fire to make you believe.' The brahmin said, 'So be it.' He had a great pile of wood prepared, lit a fire, summoned her, and said, 'If you trust in yourself, enter the fire.'

Māṇavikā attano paricārikaṃ paṭhamameva sikkhāpesi “amma, tava puttaṃ tattha gantvā mama aggiṃ pavisanakāle hatthaggahaṇaṃ kātuṃ vadehī”ti. Sā gantvā tathā avaca. Dhutto āgantvā parisamajjhe aṭṭhāsi. Sā māṇavikā brāhmaṇaṃ vañcetukāmā mahājanamajjhe ṭhatvā “brāhmaṇa, taṃ ṭhapetvā aññassa purisassa hatthasamphassaṃ nāma na jānāmi, iminā saccena ayaṃ aggi mā maṃ jhāpesī”ti aggiṃ pavisituṃ āraddhā. Tasmiṃ khaṇe dhutto “passatha bho purohitabrāhmaṇassa kammaṃ, evarūpaṃ mātugāmaṃ aggiṃ pavesāpetī”ti gantvā taṃ māṇavikaṃ hatthe gaṇhi. Sā hatthaṃ vissajjāpetvā purohitaṃ āha – “ayya, mama saccakiriyā bhinnā, na sakkā aggiṃ pavisitu”nti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Ajja mayā evarūpā saccakiriyā katā ‘ṭhapetvā mama sāmikaṃ aññassa purisassa hatthasamphassaṃ na jānāmī’ti[P 1.0295], idāni camhi iminā purisena hatthe gahitā”ti. Brāhmaṇo “vañcito ahaṃ imāyā”ti ñatvā taṃ pothetvā nīharāpesi. Evaṃ asaddhammasamannāgatā kiretā itthiyo tāva mahantampi pāpakammaṃ katvā attano sāmikaṃ vañcetuṃ “nāhaṃ evarūpaṃ kammaṃ karomī”ti divasampi sapathaṃ kurumānā nānācittāva honti. Tena vuttaṃ –

The young woman had already instructed her attendant, saying, 'Mother, go to your son and tell him to seize my hand at the moment I am to enter the fire.' She went and spoke accordingly. The rogue came and stood in the midst of the assembly. That young woman, wishing to deceive the brahmin, stood in the middle of the great crowd and declared, 'Brahmin, apart from you, I know not the touch of another man's hand. By this truth, may this fire not burn me!' and she began to enter the fire. At that very moment, the rogue went and seized the young woman by the hand, crying out, 'Behold, sirs, the deed of the purohita brahmin! He makes such a woman enter the fire!' She had him release her hand and said to the purohita, 'Sir, my act of truth has been broken; it is not possible to enter the fire.' 'For what reason?' he asked. 'Today I made an act of truth of this nature: "Apart from my husband, I know not the touch of another man's hand." But now I have been seized by the hand by this man.' The brahmin, realizing, 'I have been deceived by this woman,' had her beaten and driven out. Thus, it is said, are women who possess an unrighteous nature: having committed even a great evil deed, in order to deceive their own husband, they will swear oaths even for a day, saying, 'I did not do such a deed,' and are indeed of fickle minds. Therefore it was said:

“Corīnaṃ [M 1.0313] bahubuddhīnaṃ, yāsu saccaṃ sudullabhaṃ;

Thīnaṃ bhāvo durājāno, macchassevodake gataṃ. (jā. 2.21.347);

'Of thievish women of many wiles, among whom truth is most hard to find; the nature of women is as difficult to know as the path of a fish in the water.'

“Musā tāsaṃ yathā saccaṃ, saccaṃ tāsaṃ yathā musā;

Gāvo bahi tiṇasseva, omasanti varaṃ varaṃ.

'To them, falsehood is as truth, and truth as falsehood; like cows grazing on grass, they ever seek a better choice.'

“Coriyo [V 1.0284] kathinā hetā, vāḷā ca lapasakkharā;

Na tā kiñci na jānanti, yaṃ manussesu vañcana”nti. (jā. 2.21.332, 334);

'These women are cruel thieves, fierce and harsh-spoken; there is nothing they do not know of the deception that exists among humans.'

Satthā “evaṃ arakkhiyo mātugāmo”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Satthāpi anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā bārāṇasirājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, 'Thus, a woman is impossible to guard,' revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher then made the connection and concluded the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the king of Benares was I myself.'

Aṇḍabhūtajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Aṇḍabhūta Jātaka is the second.

[63] 3. Takkapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā

[63] 3. The Commentary on the Takkapaṇḍita Jātaka

Kodhanā akataññū cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuññevārabbha kathesi. Tañhi satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “sacca”nti vutte “itthiyo nāma bhikkhu akataññū mittadubbhā, kasmā tā nissāya ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke this, beginning with 'Angry and ungrateful,' concerning a certain discontented monk. For the Teacher asked him, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' When he replied, 'It is true,' the Teacher said, 'Women, monk, are ungrateful and betrayers of friends. Why then are you discontented on their account?' and then he related a story from the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā gaṅgātīre assamaṃ māpetvā samāpattiyo ceva abhiññāyo ca nibbattetvā jhānasukhena viharati. Tasmiṃ samaye bārāṇasiseṭṭhino dhītā duṭṭhakumārī nāma caṇḍā ahosi pharusā, dāsakammakare akkosati paribhāsati paharati. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ parivāramanussā gahetvā “gaṅgāya kīḷissāmā”ti [P 1.0296] agamaṃsu. Tesaṃ kīḷantānaññeva sūriyatthaṅgamanavelā jātā, megho uṭṭhahi, manussā meghaṃ disvā [M 1.0314] ito cito ca vegena palāyiṃsu. Seṭṭhidhītāyapi dāsakammakarā “ajja amhehi etissā piṭṭhiṃ passituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti taṃ antoudakasmiṃyeva chaḍḍetvā uttariṃsu. Devo pāvassi, sūriyopi atthaṅgato, andhakāro jāto. Te tāya vināva gehaṃ gantvā “kahaṃ sā”ti vutte “gaṅgāto tāva uttiṇṇā, atha naṃ na jānāma kahaṃ gatā”ti. Ñātakā vicinitvāpi na passiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta renounced the world to become an ascetic. He built a hermitage on the banks of the Ganges and, having attained meditative absorptions and supernatural knowledges, dwelt in the bliss of meditation. At that time, the daughter of a wealthy merchant in Benares, named Duṭṭhakumārī, was a wicked and violent girl. She was harsh, abusing, reviling, and striking the servants and workers. One day, her attendants took her, saying, 'We will play in the Ganges,' and went to the river. While they were playing, the time of sunset arrived, and a cloud arose. Seeing the cloud, the people fled quickly in all directions. The servants and workers of the merchant's daughter, thinking, 'Today we shall be rid of her,' abandoned her in the water and came ashore. It rained, the sun set, and darkness fell. They returned home without her, and when asked, 'Where is she?' they replied, 'She came out of the Ganges, but after that we do not know where she went.' Her relatives searched but could not find her.

Sā mahāviravaṃ viravantī udakena vuyhamānā aḍḍharattasamaye bodhisattassa paṇṇasālāsamīpaṃ pāpuṇi. So tassā saddaṃ sutvā “mātugāmassa saddo eso, parittāṇamassā karissāmī”ti tiṇukkaṃ ādāya nadītīraṃ gantvā taṃ disvā “mā bhāyi, mā bhāyī”ti assāsetvā [V 1.0285] nāgabalo thāmasampanno bodhisatto nadiṃ taramāno gantvā taṃ ukkhipitvā assamapadaṃ ānetvā aggiṃ katvā adāsi. Sīte vigate madhurāni phalāphalāni upanāmesi. Tāni khāditvā ṭhitaṃ “kattha vāsikāsi, kathañca gaṅgāya patitāsī”ti pucchi. Sā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Atha naṃ “tvaṃ idheva vasā”ti paṇṇasālāya vasāpento dvīhatīhaṃ sayaṃ abbhokāse vasitvā “idāni gacchā”ti āha. Sā “imaṃ tāpasaṃ sīlabhedaṃ pāpetvā gahetvā gamissāmī”ti na gacchati. Atha gacchante kāle itthikuttaṃ itthilīlaṃ dassetvā tassa sīlabhedaṃ katvā jhānaṃ antaradhāpesi. So taṃ gahetvā araññeyeva vasati. Atha naṃ sā āha “ayya, kiṃ no araññavāsena, manussapathaṃ gamissāmā”ti? So taṃ ādāya ekaṃ paccantagāmakaṃ gantvā takkabhatiyā jīvikaṃ kappetvā taṃ poseti. Tassa takkaṃ vikkiṇitvā jīvatīti “takkapaṇḍito”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. Athassa gāmavāsino paribbayaṃ datvā “amhākaṃ suyuttaduyuttakaṃ ācikkhanto ettha vasā”ti gāmadvāre kuṭiyaṃ vāsesuṃ.

She, wailing loudly while being carried away by the water, reached the vicinity of the Bodhisatta’s leaf-hut at midnight. Hearing her cry, he thought, 'This is the sound of a woman; I shall rescue her.' Taking a grass torch, he went to the riverbank and, seeing her, reassured her, saying, 'Do not fear, do not fear.' The Bodhisatta, endowed with the strength and power of an elephant, crossed the river, lifted her up, and brought her to his hermitage. He made a fire for her. When the cold had subsided, he offered her sweet fruits. After she had eaten them, he asked, 'Where do you live, and how did you fall into the Ganges?' She told him what had happened. Then he said, 'You may stay here,' and let her stay in the leaf-hut while he himself stayed in the open for two or three days, after which he said, 'Now you may go.' But she thought, 'I will make this ascetic break his virtue, take him with me, and then depart,' and so she did not leave. Then, as time went on, displaying feminine wiles and charms, she caused him to break his virtue and made his meditative attainment disappear. He took her and lived with her in the forest. Then she said to him, 'Sir, what use is this forest life to us? Let us go to a place of human habitation.' Taking her, he went to a border village, made a living by selling buttermilk, and supported her. Because he made his living by selling buttermilk, they gave him the name 'Takkapaṇḍita.' Then the villagers, giving him provisions, said, 'Live here and advise us on what is proper and improper,' and they had him live in a hut at the village gate.

Tena ca samayena corā pabbatā oruyha paccantaṃ paharanti. Te ekadivasaṃ taṃ gāmaṃ paharitvā [P 1.0297] gāmavāsikehiyeva bhaṇḍikā ukkhipāpetvā gacchantā tampi seṭṭhidhītaraṃ gahetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā sesajane vissajjesuṃ. Corajeṭṭhako pana tassā rūpe bajjhitvā taṃ attano bhariyaṃ akāsi. Bodhisatto “itthannāmā kaha”nti pucchi. “Corajeṭṭhakena gahetvā attano bhariyā katā”ti ca sutvāpi “na sā [M 1.0315] tattha mayā vinā vasissati, palāyitvā āgacchissatī”ti tassā āgamanaṃ olokento tattheva vasi.

At that time, bandits descended from the mountains and raided the borderlands. One day, they raided that village and, forcing the villagers themselves to carry away the goods, they departed, taking the merchant’s daughter with them. They went to their own dwelling place and released the other people. But the bandit chief, captivated by her beauty, made her his wife. The Bodhisatta asked, 'Where is the woman?' Hearing, 'She was taken by the bandit chief and made his wife,' he still thought, 'She will not stay there without me; she will escape and come back.' Watching for her return, he stayed right there.

Seṭṭhidhītāpi cintesi “ahaṃ idha sukhaṃ vasāmi, kadāci maṃ takkapaṇḍito kiñcideva nissāya āgantvā ito ādāya gaccheyya, atha etasmā sukhā parihāyissāmi, yannūnāhaṃ sampiyāyamānā viya taṃ pakkosāpetvā ghātāpeyya”nti. Sā ekaṃ manussaṃ pakkositvā “ahaṃ idha dukkhaṃ jīvāmi, takkapaṇḍito āgantvā maṃ ādāya gacchatū”ti sāsanaṃ pesesi. So taṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā saddahitvā tattha gantvā gāmadvāre ṭhatvā sāsanaṃ pesesi. Sā nikkhamitvā taṃ disvā “ayya, sace mayaṃ idāni gacchissāma, corajeṭṭhako anubandhitvā ubhopi amhe ghātessati, rattibhāge gacchissāmā”ti taṃ ānetvā bhojetvā koṭṭhake nisīdāpetvā sāyaṃ corajeṭṭhakassa āgantvā suraṃ pivitvā mattakāle “sāmi, sace imāya velāya tava sattuṃ passeyyāsi, kinti naṃ kareyyāsī”ti āha. “Idañcidañca karissāmīti”. “Kiṃ pana so dūre, nanu koṭṭhake nisinno”ti? Corajeṭṭhako ukkaṃ ādāya tattha gantvā taṃ disvā gahetvā gehamajjhe pātetvā kapparādīhi yathāruciṃ pothesi. So [V 1.0286] pothiyamānopi aññaṃ kiñci avatvā “kodhanā akataññū ca, pisuṇā mittabhedikā”ti ettakameva vadati. Coro taṃ pothetvā bandhitvā nipajjāpetvā sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā sayi. Pabuddho jiṇṇāya surāya puna taṃ pothetuṃ ārabhi, sopi tāneva cattāri padāni vadati.

The merchant's daughter also thought, "I live happily here, but someday Takkapaṇḍita might come on some pretext and take me away from here, and then I would lose this happiness. What if I, pretending to be affectionate, were to summon him and have him killed?" She called a man and sent a message: "I live in misery here; let Takkapaṇḍita come and take me away." Hearing and believing the message, he went there and, standing at the village gate, sent word to her. She came out and, seeing him, said, "Sir, if we go now, the bandit chief will follow and kill us both. Let us go at night." She brought him in, fed him, and had him sit in the storeroom. In the evening, when the bandit chief came and drank liquor until he was drunk, she asked him, "Master, if you saw your enemy at this moment, what would you do to him?" "I would do this and that," he replied. "But is he far away? Is he not sitting in the storeroom?" The bandit chief took a torch, went there, and upon seeing him, seized him, threw him down in the middle of the house, and beat him as he pleased with his elbows and so forth. Even while being beaten, he said nothing else but these words: "They are angry and ungrateful, slanderous and betrayers of friends." The robber, having beaten him, bound him, and made him lie down. After eating his evening meal, he went to sleep. Upon waking, when he had sobered up, he began to beat him again, and he repeated the same four lines.

Coro cintesi “ayaṃ evaṃ pothiyamānopi aññaṃ kiñci avatvā imāneva cattāri padāni vadati, pucchissāmi na”nti tassā suttabhāvaṃ ñatvā taṃ pucchi “ambho tvaṃ evaṃ pothiyamānopi kasmā [P 1.0298] etāneva padāni vadasī”ti? Takkapaṇḍito “tena hi suṇāhī”ti taṃ kāraṇaṃ ādito paṭṭhāya kathesi. “Ahaṃ pubbe araññavāsiko eko tāpaso jhānalābhī, svāhaṃ etaṃ gaṅgāya vuyhamānaṃ uttāretvā paṭijaggiṃ. Atha maṃ esā palobhetvā jhānā parihāpesi, svāhaṃ araññaṃ pahāya etaṃ posento paccantagāmake vasāmi, athesā corehi idhānītā ‘ahaṃ dukkhaṃ vasāmi, āgantvā maṃ netū’ti mayhaṃ sāsanaṃ pesetvā idāni [M 1.0316] tava hatthe pātesi, iminā kāraṇenāhaṃ evaṃ kathemī”ti. Coro cintesi “yā esā evarūpe guṇasampanne upakārake evaṃ vippaṭipajji, sā mayhaṃ kataraṃ nāma upaddavaṃ na kareyya, māretabbā esā”ti so takkapaṇḍitaṃ assāsetvā taṃ pabodhetvā khaggaṃ ādāya nikkhamma “etaṃ purisaṃ gāmadvāre ghātessāmī”ti vatvā tāya saddhiṃ bahigāmaṃ gantvā “etaṃ hatthe gaṇhā”ti taṃ tāya hatthe gāhāpetvā khaggaṃ ādāya takkapaṇḍitaṃ paharanto viya taṃ dvidhā chinditvā sasīsaṃ nhāpetvā takkapaṇḍitaṃ katipāhaṃ paṇītena bhojanena santappetvā idāni kahaṃ gamissasī”ti āha. Takkapaṇḍito “gharāvāsena me kiccaṃ natthi, isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā tattheva araññe vasissāmī”ti āha. “Tena hi ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti ubhopi pabbajitvā taṃ araññāyatanaṃ gantvā pañca abhiññā aṭṭha ca samāpattiyo nibbattetvā jīvitapariyosāne brahmalokūpagā ahesuṃ.

The thief thought, 'Even though he is being beaten like this, he says nothing else but these four phrases. I shall ask him.' Perceiving that she was asleep, he asked him, 'Friend, even when being beaten like this, why do you say only these phrases?' Takka Paṇḍita replied, 'In that case, listen,' and he related the reason from the beginning: 'Formerly, I was a forest-dwelling ascetic who had attained meditative absorption. I rescued this woman as she was being swept away by the Ganges and cared for her. Then she seduced me and caused me to fall from my meditative attainment. I then abandoned the forest and lived in a border village, supporting her. Then, having been brought here by thieves, she sent a message to me, saying, "I am living in misery; come and take me away," and now she has delivered me into your hands. For this reason, I speak thus.' The thief thought, 'If she has acted so wrongly towards such a virtuous and helpful person, what kind of harm would she not do to me? She must be killed.' He comforted Takka Paṇḍita, woke the woman up, and taking his sword, he went out, saying, 'I will kill this man at the village gate.' Going with her outside the village, he said, 'Take this man by the hand.' Having made her take Takka Paṇḍita by the hand, he took his sword and, as if to strike Takka Paṇḍita, he cut her in two. He then bathed Takka Paṇḍita's head and for several days satisfied him with fine food, after which he asked, 'Where will you go now?' Takka Paṇḍita replied, 'I have no use for the household life. I will go forth into the ascetic life and dwell in that same forest.' 'In that case, I too will go forth.' Both went forth, went to that forest hermitage, and developed the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments. At the end of their lives, they were destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imāni dve vatthūni kathetvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having related these two stories and connected them, then, as the Fully Enlightened One, spoke this verse:

63.

63.

“Kodhanā akataññū ca, pisuṇā mittabhedikā;

Brahmacariyaṃ cara bhikkhu, so sukhaṃ na vihāhisī”ti.

“They are angry and ungrateful, slanderous and divisive of friends. Practice the holy life, O monk; thus you will not lose happiness.”

Tatrāyaṃ piṇḍattho – bhikkhu itthiyo nāmetā kodhanā, uppannaṃ kodhaṃ nivāretuṃ na sakkonti. Akataññū ca, atimahantampi upakāraṃ na jānanti. Pisuṇā [P 1.0299] ca, piyasuññabhāvakaraṇameva kathaṃ kathenti. Mittabhedikā, mitte bhindanti, mittabhedanakathaṃ kathanasīlāyeva[V 1.0287], evarūpehi pāpadhammehi samannāgatā etā. Kiṃ te etāhi, brahmacariyaṃ cara bhikkhu, ayañhi methunavirati parisuddhaṭṭhena brahmacariyaṃ nāma, taṃ cara. So sukhaṃ na vihāhisīti so tvaṃ etaṃ brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasanto jhānasukhaṃ maggasukhaṃ phalasukhañca na vihāhisi, etaṃ sukhaṃ na vijahissati, etasmā sukhā na parihāyissasīti attho. “Na parihāhisī”tipi pāṭho, ayamevattho.

Here is the summary meaning: O monk, these beings called women are prone to anger; they are unable to restrain their anger once it has arisen. They are also ungrateful; they do not recognize even the greatest of favors. They are also slanderous; they speak words that create an absence of affection. They are divisive of friends; they break friendships and are disposed to speaking words that cause division among friends. They are possessed of such evil qualities. What have you to do with them? Practice the holy life, O monk. For this abstinence from sexual intercourse is called the holy life on account of its purity; practice that. As for 'thus you will not lose happiness,' it means that you, while living this holy life, will not abandon the happiness of meditative absorption, the happiness of the path, and the happiness of the fruit. You will not give up this happiness; you will not fall away from this happiness. There is also the reading 'na parihāhisi,' which has the same meaning.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Satthā jātakaṃ [M 1.0317] samodhānesi – “tadā corajeṭṭhako ānando ahosi, takkapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher delivered this discourse and revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the revelation of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the chief of the thieves was Ānanda, but Takka Paṇḍita was I myself.'

Takkapaṇḍitajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Takkapaṇḍita Jātaka, the Third.

[64] 4. Durājānajātakavaṇṇanā

4. The Commentary on the Durājāna Jātaka

Māsu nandi icchati manti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira sāvatthivāsī upāsako tīsu saraṇesu pañcasu ca sīlesu patiṭṭhito buddhamāmako, dhammamāmako, saṅghamāmako, bhariyā panassa dussīlā pāpadhammā. Yaṃ divasaṃ micchācāraṃ carati, taṃ divasaṃ satakītadāsī viya hoti, micchācārassa pana akatadivase sāminī viya hoti caṇḍā pharusā. So tassā bhāvaṃ jānituṃ na sakkoti, atha tāya ubbāḷho buddhūpaṭṭhānaṃ na gacchati. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ gandhapupphādīni ādāya āgantvā vanditvā nisinnaṃ satthā āha – “kiṃ nu kho tvaṃ, upāsaka, sattaṭṭha divase buddhūpaṭṭhānaṃ nāgacchasī”ti. Gharaṇī me, bhante, ekasmiṃ divase satakītadāsī viya hoti, ekasmiṃ divase sāminī viya caṇḍā pharusā. Ahaṃ tassā bhāvaṃ jānituṃ na sakkomi, svāhaṃ tāya ubbāḷho buddhūpaṭṭhānaṃ nāgacchāmīti. Athassa vacanaṃ sutvā satthā “upāsaka, ‘mātugāmassa bhāvo nāma dujjāno’ti pubbepi te paṇḍitā kathayiṃsu, tvaṃ pana taṃ bhavasaṅkhepagatattā sallakkhetuṃ na sakkosī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, related this story, beginning with the words 'Māsu nandi icchati maṃ,' concerning a certain lay follower. It is said that a lay follower living in Sāvatthī was established in the three refuges and the five precepts, and was devoted to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha. His wife, however, was immoral and of wicked character. On a day she engaged in misconduct, she was like a slave bought for a hundred coins. But on a day she did not engage in misconduct, she was like a harsh and cruel mistress. He was unable to understand her nature, and being troubled by her, he did not go to attend upon the Buddha. Then one day, having come with perfumes, flowers, and so on, he paid homage and sat down. The Teacher said to him, 'Why is it, lay follower, that you have not come to attend upon the Buddha for seven or eight days?' 'Venerable sir, my wife on one day is like a slave bought for a hundred coins, and on another day is like a harsh and cruel mistress. I am unable to understand her nature, and being troubled by her, I do not come to attend upon the Buddha.' Having heard his words, the Teacher said, 'Lay follower, the wise of old also said, "The nature of a woman is indeed hard to understand." But you are unable to perceive it because it is concealed by another existence.' And being requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañca māṇavakasatāni [P 1.0300] sippaṃ sikkhāpeti. Atheko tiroraṭṭhavāsiko brāhmaṇamāṇavako āgantvā tassa santike sippaṃ uggaṇhanto ekāya itthiyā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā taṃ bhariyaṃ katvā [V 1.0288] tasmiṃyeva bārāṇasinagare vasanto dve tisso velāyo ācariyassa upaṭṭhānaṃ na gacchati. Sā panassa bhariyā dussīlā pāpadhammā. Micchācāraṃ ciṇṇadivase dāsī viya hoti, aciṇṇadivase sāminī viya hoti caṇḍā pharusā. So tassā bhāvaṃ jānituṃ asakkonto tāya ubbāḷho ākulacitto ācariyassa upaṭṭhānaṃ na gacchati. Atha naṃ sattaṭṭha divase atikkamitvā āgataṃ “kiṃ, māṇava[M 1.0318], na paññāyasī”ti ācariyo pucchi. So “bhariyā maṃ, ācariya, ekadivasaṃ icchati pattheti, dāsī viya nihatamānā hoti. Ekadivasaṃ sāminī viya thaddhā caṇḍā pharusā, ahaṃ tassā bhāvaṃ jānituṃ na sakkomi, tāya ubbāḷho ākulacitto tumhākaṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ nāgatomhī”ti. Ācariyo “evametaṃ, māṇava, itthiyo nāma anācāraṃ ciṇṇadivase sāmikaṃ anuvattanti, dāsī viya nihatamānā honti. Anāciṇṇadivase pana mānatthaddhā hutvā sāmikaṃ na gaṇenti. Evaṃ itthiyo nāmetā anācārā dussīlā, tāsaṃ bhāvo nāma dujjāno, tāsu icchantīsupi anicchantīsupi majjhatteneva bhavitabba”nti vatvā tassovādavasena imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher, instructing five hundred young men in the arts. Then a young brahmin from another country came to learn under him. Becoming infatuated with a certain woman, he married her and settled in Benares itself. Consequently, he failed to attend upon his teacher on two or three occasions. Now, his wife was immoral and of a wicked nature. On days when she engaged in misconduct, she was like a female slave; on days she did not, she was like a mistress—fierce and harsh. Unable to understand her disposition and being vexed and agitated by her, he did not go to attend upon his teacher. After seven or eight days had passed, the teacher asked him when he came, “Why, young man, are you not seen?” He replied, “Teacher, on one day my wife desires and longs for me, and is humble in pride like a female slave. On another day, she is stubborn, fierce, and harsh like a mistress. I am unable to understand her disposition; being vexed and agitated by her, I have not come to attend upon you.” The teacher said, “So it is, young man. Women, on the day they engage in misconduct, are compliant with their husbands and are humble in pride like a female slave. But on the day they do not, they become stiff with pride and pay no regard to their husbands. Thus, these women are of improper conduct and immoral; their nature is hard to know. Towards them, whether they are desiring or not desiring, one should remain equanimous.” Having spoken this advice to him, he uttered this verse:

64.

64.

“Mā su nandi icchati maṃ, mā su soci na micchati;

Thīnaṃ bhāvo durājāno, macchassevodake gata”nti.

“Do not rejoice, thinking, ‘She desires me,’ nor grieve, thinking, ‘She does not desire me.’ The nature of women is hard to know, like the path of a fish in the water.”

Tattha mā su nandi icchati manti su-kāro nipātamattaṃ, “ayaṃ itthī maṃ icchati pattheti, mayi sinehaṃ karotī”ti mā tussi. Mā su soci na micchatīti “ayaṃ maṃ na icchatī”tipi mā soci, tassā icchamānāya nandiṃ, na icchamānāya ca sokaṃ akatvā majjhattova hohīti dīpeti. Thīnaṃ bhāvo durājānoti itthīnaṃ bhāvo nāma itthimāyāya paṭicchannattā durājāno. Yathā kiṃ? Macchassevodake gatanti yathā macchassa gamanaṃ udakena paṭicchannattā dujjānaṃ, teneva so kevaṭṭe āgate udakena gamanaṃ paṭicchādetvā palāyati, attānaṃ gaṇhituṃ na deti, evameva itthiyo mahantampi dussīlakammaṃ katvā “mayaṃ evarūpaṃ na karomā”ti attanā katakammaṃ itthimāyāya paṭicchādetvā sāmike vañcenti[P 1.0301]. Evaṃ itthiyo nāmetā pāpadhammā durājānā, tāsu majjhattoyeva sukhito hotīti.

Therein, mā su nandi icchati maṃ means: do not be pleased, thinking, ‘This woman desires me, longs for me, shows affection towards me.’ The particle su is a mere expletive. Mā su soci na micchati means: do not grieve, thinking, ‘This woman does not desire me.’ This shows that one should remain equanimous, neither delighting when she is desiring nor sorrowing when she is not. Thīnaṃ bhāvo durājāno means: the nature of women is hard to know because it is concealed by feminine wiles. How so? Macchassevodake gataṃ means: just as the path of a fish is hard to know because it is concealed by the water—for that reason, when fishermen approach, it conceals its path with the water and flees, not allowing itself to be caught—in the very same way, women, even after committing a great immoral act, conceal the deed they have done with feminine wiles, deceiving their husbands by saying, ‘We do not do such a thing.’ Thus, these women are of a wicked nature and hard to know. Only by being equanimous towards them does one become happy.

Evaṃ bodhisatto antevāsikassa ovādaṃ adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya so tassā upari majjhattova ahosi. Sāpissa bhariyā “ācariyena kira me dussīlabhāvo ñāto”ti tato paṭṭhāya na anācāraṃ cari. Sāpi tassa upāsakassa itthī “sammāsambuddhena kira mayhaṃ durācārabhāvo ñāto”ti tato paṭṭhāya pāpakammaṃ nāma na akāsi.

Thus the Bodhisatta gave advice to his pupil. From that time onward, he remained equanimous towards her. And his wife, thinking, 'It seems the teacher knows of my immoral nature,' from then on did not engage in misconduct. That lay follower's wife also, thinking, 'It seems the Perfectly Enlightened One knows of my misconduct,' from that time onward did no evil deed whatsoever.

Satthāpi [V 1.0289] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne so upāsako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi, satthā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā [M 1.0319] jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jayampatikāyeva idāni jayampatikā, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the discourse on the Truths, that lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher then made the connection and identified the characters of the Jātaka: 'The husband and wife of that time were the husband and wife of today, and the teacher was I myself.'
