Durājānajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Durājāna Jātaka, the fourth.

[65] 5. Anabhiratijātakavaṇṇanā

[65] 5. Commentary on the Anabhirati Jātaka

Yathā nadī ca pantho cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto tathārūpaṃyeva upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So pana pariggaṇhanto tassā dussīlabhāvaṃ ñatvā bhaṇḍito cittabyākulatāya sattaṭṭha divase upaṭṭhānaṃ nāgamāsi. So ekadivasaṃ vihāraṃ gantvā tathāgataṃ vanditvā nisinno “kasmā sattaṭṭha divasāni nāgatosī”ti vutte “bhariyā me, bhante, dussīlā, tassā upari byākulacittatāya nāgatomhī”ti āha. Satthā “upāsaka, itthīsu ‘anācārā etā’ti kopaṃ akatvā majjhatteneva bhavituṃ vaṭṭatīti pubbepi te paṇḍitā kathayiṃsu, tvaṃ pana bhavantarena paṭicchannattā taṃ kāraṇaṃ na sallakkhesī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Just as a river and a path…” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a lay follower of that same kind. Having investigated and learned of his wife's immoral nature, that lay follower became angered, and due to his agitated mind, he did not come to attend upon the Teacher for seven or eight days. One day, having gone to the monastery, he paid homage to the Tathāgata and sat down. When asked, “Why have you not come for seven or eight days?” he replied, “Venerable Sir, my wife is immoral. I have not come because my mind was agitated over her.” The Teacher said, “Lay follower, it is fitting to remain equanimous towards women without becoming angry, thinking, ‘They are of improper conduct.’ The wise men of the past also told you this, but you, because it is concealed by another existence, do not recall this matter.” Then, being requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto purimanayeneva disāpāmokkho ācariyo ahosi. Athassa antevāsiko bhariyāya dosaṃ disvā byākulacittatāya katipāhaṃ anāgantvā ekadivasaṃ ācariyena pucchito taṃ kāraṇaṃ nivedesi. Athassa ācariyo “tāta, itthiyo nāma sabbasādhāraṇā[P 1.0302], tāsu ‘dussīlā etā’ti paṇḍitā kopaṃ na karontī”ti vatvā ovādavasena imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was, in the same way as before, a world-renowned teacher. Then his pupil, having seen a fault in his wife, did not come for some days due to his agitated mind. One day, being asked by his teacher, he related the reason. Then his teacher, wishing to advise him, said, “My dear, women are common to all. The wise do not become angry with them, thinking, ‘They are immoral,’” and spoke this verse:

65.

65.

“Yathā nadī ca panto ca, pānāgāraṃ sabhā papā;

Evaṃ lokitthiyo nāma, nāsaṃ kujjhanti paṇḍitā”ti.

“Just as a river and a path, a tavern, a public hall, and a water-stand; so are women in the world. The wise are not angry with them.”

Tattha yathā nadīti yathā anekatitthā nadī nhānatthāya sampattasampattānaṃ caṇḍālādīnampi khattiyādīnampi sādhāraṇā, na tattha koci nhāyituṃ na labhati nāma. “Pantho”tiādīsupi yathā mahāmaggopi sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇo[M 1.0320], na koci tena gantuṃ na labhati. Pānāgārampi surāgehaṃ sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇaṃ, yo yo pātukāmo, sabbo tattha pavisateva. Puññatthikehi tattha tattha manussānaṃ nivāsatthāya katā sabhāpi sādhāraṇā, na tattha koci pavisituṃ na labhati. Mahāmagge [V 1.0290] pānīyacāṭiyo ṭhapetvā katā papāpi sabbesaṃ sādhāraṇā, na tattha koci pānīyaṃ pivituṃ na labhati. Evaṃ lokitthiyo nāmāti evameva tāta māṇava imasmiṃ loke itthiyopi sabbasādhāraṇāva, teneva ca sādhāraṇaṭṭhena nadīpanthapānāgārasabhāpapāsadisā. Tasmā nāsaṃ kujjhanti paṇḍitā, etāsaṃ itthīnaṃ “lāmikā etā anācārā dussīlā sabbasādhāraṇā”ti cintetvā paṇḍitā chekā buddhisampannā na kujjhantīti.

Here, 'like a river' means that just as a river with many bathing places is common to all for bathing—whether outcasts or nobles—and no one is denied the chance to bathe there; and 'path' and the rest mean that even a great highway is common to all, and no one is denied the chance to travel on it; and a tavern, a drinking house, is common to all—whoever wishes to drink may enter there; and halls built by those desiring merit for people to stay in are common to all, and no one is denied entry there; and water pots set up along great roads for drinking water are common to all, and no one is denied the chance to drink water there—even so, dear student, women in this world are common to all. And through being common in that way, they are like rivers, paths, taverns, halls, and water pots. Therefore, the wise do not get angry. With regard to these women, the wise, the skilled, the intelligent, do not get angry, thinking: 'These are contemptible, ill-behaved, immoral, and common to all.'

Evaṃ bodhisatto antevāsikassa ovādaṃ adāsi, so taṃ ovādaṃ sutvā majjhatto ahosi. Bhariyāpissa “ācariyena kiramhi ñātā”ti tato paṭṭhāya pāpakammaṃ na akāsi. Tassapi upāsakassa bhariyā “satthārā kiramhi ñātā”ti tato paṭṭhāya pāpakammaṃ na akāsi.

Thus, the Bodhisatta gave advice to his pupil, who, hearing this advice, became equanimous. And his wife, thinking, 'The teacher knows about me,' from then on did no evil. Likewise, that lay disciple's wife, thinking, 'The Teacher knows about me,' from then on did no evil.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne upāsako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Satthāpi anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jayampatikāva etarahi jayampatikā, ācariyabrāhmaṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the Truths, the lay follower was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher then made the connection and identified the characters of the Jātaka: 'The couple at that time were the couple of the present day, but the brahmin teacher was myself.'

Anabhiratijātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Anabhirati Jātaka, the fifth.

[66] 6. Mudulakkhaṇajātakavaṇṇanā

6. The Commentary on the Mudulakkhaṇa Jātaka

Ekā icchā pure āsīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto saṃkilesaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto satthu dhammadesanaṃ [P 1.0303] sutvā ratanasāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajitvā paṭipannako yogāvacaro avissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhāno hutvā ekadivasaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caranto ekaṃ alaṅkatapaṭiyattaṃ itthiṃ disvā subhavasena indriyāni bhinditvā olokesi. Tassa abbhantare kileso cali, vāsiyā ākoṭitakhīrarukkho viya ahosi. So tato paṭṭhāya [M 1.0321] kilesavasiko hutvā neva kāyassādaṃ na cittassādaṃ labhati, bhantamigasappaṭibhāgo sāsane anabhirato parūḷhakesalomanakho kiliṭṭhacīvaro ahosi. Athassa indriyavikāraṃ disvā sahāyakā bhikkhū “kiṃ nu kho te, āvuso, na yathā porāṇāni indriyānī”ti pucchiṃsu. Anabhiratosmi, āvusoti.

“Once there was a single desire…” The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this in connection with a defiled monk. It seems that a certain young man of good family, a resident of Sāvatthī, having heard the Teacher's Dhamma teaching, placed his faith in the precious Dispensation and went forth. A practitioner devoted to meditation who had not relinquished his meditation subject, one day while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a woman beautifully adorned and dressed. Breaking his sense restraint, he gazed at her, perceiving her as beautiful. Within him, defilement arose, like a latex-tree struck by an adze. From then on, being controlled by defilement, he obtained no pleasure of body or mind. Resembling a startled deer, he was dissatisfied with the Dispensation, with overgrown hair, body hair, and nails, and soiled robes. Then, seeing the change in his faculties, his fellow monks asked him, 'Why, friend, are your faculties not as they were before?' He replied, 'I am dissatisfied, friends.'

Atha [V 1.0291] naṃ te satthu santikaṃ nayiṃsu. Satthā “kiṃ, bhikkhave, anicchamānaṃ bhikkhuṃ ādāya āgatatthā”ti pucchi. “Ayaṃ, bhante, bhikkhu anabhirato”ti? “Saccaṃ bhikkhū”ti. “Saccaṃ bhagavā”ti. “Ko taṃ ukkaṇṭhāpesī”ti? “Ahaṃ, bhante, piṇḍāya caranto ekaṃ itthiṃ disvā indriyāni bhinditvā olokesiṃ, atha me kileso cali, tenamhi ukkaṇṭhito”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “anacchariyametaṃ bhikkhu, yaṃ tvaṃ indriyāni bhinditvā visabhāgārammaṇaṃ subhavasena olokento kilesehi kampito, pubbe pañcābhiññā aṭṭhasamāpattilābhino jhānabalena kilese vikkhambhetvā visuddhacittā gaganatalacarā bodhisattāpi indriyāni bhinditvā visabhāgārammaṇaṃ olokayamānā jhānā parihāyitvā kilesehi kampitā mahādukkhaṃ anubhaviṃsu. Na hi sineruuppāṭanakavāto hatthimattaṃ muṇḍapabbataṃ, mahājambuummūlakavāto chinnataṭe virūḷhagacchakaṃ, mahāsamuddaṃ vā pana sosanakavāto khuddakataḷākaṃ kismiñcideva gaṇeti, evaṃ uttamabuddhīnaṃ nāma visuddhacittānaṃ bodhisattānaṃ aññāṇabhāvakarā kilesā tayi kiṃ lajjissanti, visuddhāpi sattā saṃkilissanti, uttamayasasamaṅginopi āyasakyaṃ pāpuṇantī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then they led him to the Teacher. The Teacher asked, 'Why, monks, have you brought this unwilling monk here?' 'Venerable sir, this monk is discontent,' they replied. 'Is it true, monk?' 'It is true, Blessed One.' 'Who made you discontent?' 'Venerable sir, while I was walking for alms, I saw a woman. Breaking my sense restraint, I gazed at her. Then my defilements stirred, and so I became discontent.' Then the Teacher said to him, 'It is no surprise, monk, that you—having broken your sense restraint and gazed upon an unsuitable object as if it were beautiful—were shaken by defilements. Even in the past, Bodhisattas who possessed the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments, who had suppressed defilements with the power of jhāna and whose minds were purified, who moved through the sky—even they, breaking their sense restraint and gazing upon unsuitable objects, fell from jhāna and, shaken by defilements, experienced great suffering. For a wind capable of uprooting Mount Sineru would not reckon a bare mountain the size of an elephant; a wind capable of uprooting a great rose-apple tree would not reckon a small bush grown on a broken bank; and a wind capable of drying up the great ocean would not reckon a tiny pond. So too, defilements that cause ignorance even in supremely wise Bodhisattas with purified minds—why would they be ashamed before you? Even purified beings become defiled, and those endowed with supreme glory may meet with misfortune.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe ekassa mahāvibhavassa brāhmaṇassa kule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto sabbasippānaṃ pāraṃ gantvā kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā pañca abhiññā ca aṭṭha samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā jhānasukhena vītināmento himavantappadese vāsaṃ kappesi. So ekasmiṃ kāle loṇambilasevanatthāya [P 1.0304] himavantā otaritvā bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase katasarīrapaṭijaggano rattavākamayaṃ nivāsanapārupanaṃ saṇṭhāpetvā ajinacammaṃ ekasmiṃ aṃse katvā jaṭāmaṇḍalaṃ bandhitvā bhikkhābhājanamādāya bārāṇasiyaṃ bhikkhāya caramāno rañño gharadvāraṃ sampāpuṇi. Rājā tassa iriyāpatheyeva pasīditvā [M 1.0322] pakkosāpetvā mahārahe āsane nisīdāpetvā paṇītena khādanīyabhojanīyena santappetvā katānumodanaṃ uyyāne vasanatthāya yāci. So sampaṭicchitvā rājagehe bhuñjitvā rājakulaṃ ovadamāno tasmiṃ uyyāne soḷasa vassāni vasi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into the family of a very wealthy brahmin in the Kāsī country. Having attained maturity and mastered all crafts, he renounced sensual pleasures, embraced the ascetic life, developed the kasiṇa meditation, and produced the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments. Passing his time in the bliss of jhāna, he dwelt in the Himalayan region. On one occasion, he descended from the Himalayas to Bārāṇasī to obtain salt and sour provisions. Arriving there, he stayed in the royal pleasure park. The next day, after attending to his bodily needs, he arranged his lower and upper robes of red bark, draped a deer skin over one shoulder, tied his matted hair into a topknot, and taking his alms bowl, he went for alms in Bārāṇasī and arrived at the king’s gate. The king, pleased by his mere deportment, summoned him, had him seated on a magnificent seat, and satisfied him with choice food and drink. After he had given his thanks, the king requested him to dwell in the pleasure park. He accepted and stayed there for sixteen years, eating at the king’s house and advising the royal family.

Athekadivasaṃ rājā kupitaṃ paccantaṃ vūpasametuṃ gacchanto mudulakkhaṇaṃ nāma aggamahesiṃ “appamattā ayyassa upaṭṭhānaṃ karohī”ti vatvā agamāsi. Bodhisatto rañño gatakālato paṭṭhāya attano ruccanavelāya rājagehaṃ gacchati. Athekadivasaṃ mudulakkhaṇā bodhisattassa āhāraṃ sampādetvā – “ajja ayyo cirāyatī”ti gandhodakena nhāyitvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā [V 1.0292] mahātale cūḷasayanaṃ paññāpetvā bodhisattassa āgamanaṃ olokayamānā nipajji. Bodhisattopi attano velaṃ sallakkhetvā jhānā vuṭṭhāya ākāseneva rājanivesanaṃ agamāsi. Mudulakkhaṇā vākacīrasaddaṃ sutvāva “ayyo, āgato”ti vegena uṭṭhahi, tassā vegena uṭṭhahantiyā maṭṭhasāṭako bhassi. Tāpasopi sīhapañjarena pavisanto deviyā visabhāgarūpārammaṇaṃ indriyāni bhinditvā subhavasena olokesi. Athassa abbhantare kileso cali, vāsiyā pahaṭakhīrarukkho viya ahosi. Tāvadevassa jhānaṃ antaradhāyi, chinnapakkho kāko viya ahosi. So ṭhitakova āhāraṃ gahetvā abhuñjitvāva kilesakampito pāsādā oruyha uyyānaṃ gantvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā phalakattharaṇasayanassa heṭṭhā āhāraṃ ṭhapetvā visabhāgārammaṇena baddho kilesagginā ḍayhamāno nirāhāratāya sussamāno satta divasāni phalakattharaṇe nipajji.

One day, when a border region was agitated, the king went to pacify it. Before leaving, he said to his chief queen, Mudulakkhaṇā, “Be heedful in attending to the venerable one,” and departed. From the time the king left, the Bodhisatta would go to the royal palace at his preferred time. One day, after preparing food for the Bodhisatta, Mudulakkhaṇā thought, “Today the venerable one is late.” She bathed in fragrant water, adorned herself with all ornaments, prepared a small bed on the great terrace, and lay down, watching for the Bodhisatta’s arrival. The Bodhisatta, noticing his time, emerged from jhāna and went through the air to the royal residence. Hearing the rustle of his bark garment, Mudulakkhaṇā quickly rose, thinking, “The venerable one has come!” As she hurriedly stood up, her smooth garment slipped off. The ascetic, entering through the lion-window, looked at the queen’s form, an unsuitable object, and his senses were shattered, for he looked at it as beautiful. Immediately, defilements arose within him, like a milk-exuding tree struck by an axe. Instantly, his jhāna vanished, and he became like a crow with clipped wings. Standing there, he took the food but did not eat it. Shaken by defilements, he descended from the palace, went to the pleasure park, entered his leaf hut, and placed the food beneath the wooden platform-bed. Bound by the unsuitable object and burning with the fire of defilements, he lay on that wooden platform for seven days, wasting away from lack of food.

Sattame divase rājā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā āgato nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā nivesanaṃ agantvāva “ayyaṃ [P 1.0305] passissāmī”ti uyyānaṃ gantvā paṇṇasālaṃ pavisitvā taṃ nipannakaṃ disvā “ekaṃ aphāsukaṃ jātaṃ maññe”ti paṇṇasālaṃ sodhāpetvā pāde parimajjanto “kiṃ, ayya, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. “Mahārāja aññaṃ me aphāsukaṃ natthi, kilesavasena panamhi paṭibaddhacitto jāto”ti. “Kahaṃ paṭibaddhaṃ te, ayya, citta”nti? “Mudulakkhaṇāya, mahārājā”ti. “Sādhu ayya, ahaṃ mudulakkhaṇaṃ tumhākaṃ dammī”ti [M 1.0323] tāpasaṃ ādāya nivesanaṃ pavisitvā deviṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ katvā tāpasassa adāsi. Dadamānoyeva ca mudulakkhaṇāya saññamadāsi “tayā attano balena ayyaṃ rakkhituṃ vāyamitabba”nti. “Sādhu, deva, rakkhissāmī”ti. Tāpaso deviṃ gahetvā rājanivesanā otari.

On the seventh day, the king, having pacified the border region, returned. After circumambulating the city, without going to his own residence, thinking, “I shall see the venerable one,” he went to the pleasure park, entered the leaf hut, and seeing him lying down, thought, “I think he is unwell.” He had the leaf hut swept clean and, while massaging his feet, asked, “What is the matter, venerable one? Are you unwell?” “Great king, I have no other ailment, but my mind has become bound by defilements.” “To what is your mind bound, venerable one?” “To Mudulakkhaṇā, great king.” “Very well, venerable one, I shall give Mudulakkhaṇā to you.” Taking the ascetic, he entered the royal residence, had the queen adorned with all ornaments, and gave her to the ascetic. As he gave her, he gave Mudulakkhaṇā an instruction, saying, “You must strive to protect the venerable one with your own strength.” “Very well, Your Majesty, I shall protect him.” The ascetic took the queen and descended from the royal residence.

Atha naṃ mahādvārato nikkhantakāle “ayya, amhākaṃ ekaṃ gehaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, gaccha, rājānaṃ gehaṃ yācāhī”ti āha. Tāpaso gantvā gehaṃ yāci. Rājā manussānaṃ vaccakuṭikiccaṃ sādhayamānaṃ ekaṃ chaḍḍitagehaṃ dāpesi. So deviṃ gahetvā tattha agamāsi, sā pavisituṃ na icchati. “Kiṃkāraṇā na pavisasī”ti? “Asucibhāvenā”ti. Idāni “kiṃ karomī”ti. “Paṭijaggāhi na”nti vatvā rañño santikaṃ pesetvā “gaccha, kuddālaṃ āhara, pacchiṃ āharā”ti āharāpetvā asuciñca saṅkārañca chaḍḍāpetvā gāmayaṃ āharāpetvā limpāpetvā punapi “gaccha, mañcaṃ āhara, pīṭhaṃ āhara, attharaṇaṃ āhara, cāṭiṃ āhara, ghaṭaṃ āharā”ti ekamekaṃ āharāpetvā puna udakāharaṇādīnaṃ atthāya āṇāpesi. So ghaṭaṃ ādāya udakaṃ āharitvā cāṭiṃ pūretvā nhānodakaṃ sajjetvā sayanaṃ atthari. Atha naṃ sayane ekato [V 1.0293] nisinnaṃ dāṭhikāsu gahetvā “tava samaṇabhāvaṃ vā brāhmaṇabhāvaṃ vā na jānāsī”ti oṇametvā attano abhimukhaṃ ākaḍḍhi. So tasmiṃ kāle satiṃ paṭilabhi, ettakaṃ pana kālaṃ aññāṇī ahosi. Evaṃ aññāṇakaraṇā kilesā nāma. “Kāmacchandanīvaraṇaṃ, bhikkhave, andhakaraṇaṃ [P 1.0306] aññāṇakaraṇa”ntiādi (saṃ. ni. 5.221) cettha vattabbaṃ.

Then, as they were leaving through the great gate, she said, “Venerable one, we should get a house. Go, ask the king for a house.” The ascetic went and asked for a house. The king gave him an abandoned house that had served as a public latrine. He took the queen and went there, but she would not enter. “Why will you not enter?” he asked. “Because it is unclean,” she said. “What am I to do now?” he asked. “Clean it,” she said. She sent him to the king, saying, “Go, bring a spade and a basket.” She had him bring them, remove the filth and rubbish, bring cow-dung and plaster the floor. Then again she commanded, “Go, bring a bed, bring a stool, bring a mat, bring a large pot, bring a water jar,” having him bring each item one by one. Then she ordered him to do things like fetching water. He took the water jar, brought water, filled the large pot, prepared water for bathing, and spread the bedding. Then, as they sat together on the bed, she grabbed him by the beard, pulled him down towards her and said, “Do you not know your state as a recluse or a brahmin!” At that moment, he regained mindfulness; until then he had been ignorant. Thus, defilements are indeed a cause of ignorance. Here, it should be said: “The hindrance of sensual desire, bhikkhus, is blinding, a cause of ignorance,” and so on (Saṃyutta Nikāya 5.221).

So satiṃ paṭilabhitvā cintesi “ayaṃ taṇhā vaḍḍhamānā mama catūhi apāyehi sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na dassati, ajjeva mayā imaṃ rañño niyyādetvā himavantaṃ pavisituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So taṃ ādāya rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mahārāja, tava deviyā mayhaṃ attho natthi, kevalaṃ me imaṃ nissāya taṇhā vaḍḍhitā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Regaining mindfulness, he reflected, “This craving, growing stronger, will not allow me to lift my head out of the four woeful states. Today, I must hand her back to the king and enter the Himalayas.” Taking her, he approached the king and said, “Great king, I have no need of your queen; it was merely due to her that my craving has grown.” Then he spoke this verse:

66.

66.

“Ekā icchā pure āsi, aladdhā mudulakkhaṇaṃ;

Yato laddhā aḷārakkhī, icchā icchaṃ vijāyathā”ti.

“Formerly there was but one desire, when Mudulakkhaṇā was not obtained; but once the one with alluring eyes was obtained, desire gave birth to desire.”

Tatrāyaṃ [M 1.0324] piṇḍattho – mahārāja, mayhaṃ imaṃ tava deviṃ mudulakkhaṇaṃ alabhitvā pure “aho vatāhaṃ etaṃ labheyya”nti ekā icchā āsi, ekāva taṇhā uppajji. Yato pana me ayaṃ aḷārakkhī visālanettā sobhanalocanā laddhā, atha me sā purimikā icchā gehataṇhaṃ upakaraṇataṇhaṃ upabhogataṇhanti uparūpari aññaṃ nānappakāraṃ icchaṃ vijāyatha janesi uppādesi. Sā kho pana me evaṃ vaḍḍhamānā icchā apāyato sīsaṃ ukkhipituṃ na dassati, alaṃ me imāya, tvaññeva tava bhariyaṃ gaṇha, ahaṃ pana himavantaṃ gamissāmīti tāvadeva naṭṭhaṃ jhānaṃ uppādetvā ākāse nisinno dhammaṃ desetvā rañño ovādaṃ datvā ākāseneva himavantaṃ gantvā puna manussapathaṃ nāma nāgamāsi, brahmavihāre pana bhāvetvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmaloke nibbatti.

Herein is the condensed meaning: “Great king, before I obtained your queen Mudulakkhaṇā, there was formerly a single desire for me, ‘Oh, if only I could obtain her!’ A single craving arose. But when I obtained this one with alluring eyes, with wide eyes, with beautiful eyes, then that former desire gave birth to and produced other various desires, such as craving for a home, craving for possessions, and craving for enjoyment, one after another. Yet this ever-growing desire would not allow me to lift my head from the woeful states. Enough of this for me! You yourself take your wife, and I will go to the Himalayas.” Having thus produced his lost jhāna, he sat in the sky, taught the Dhamma, gave advice to the king, and then went through the sky to the Himalayas. He never again came to the human world but, having cultivated the divine abodes and without decline of his jhāna, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu arahattaphale patiṭṭhahi. Satthāpi anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, mudulakkhaṇā uppalavaṇṇā, isi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher expounded the Truths. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, that monk was established in the fruit of arahantship. The Teacher, making the connection, identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, Mudulakkhaṇā was Uppalavaṇṇā, and the ascetic was myself.”

Mudulakkhaṇajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Mudulakkhaṇa Jātaka, the Sixth.

[67] 7. Ucchaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā

[67] 7. The Commentary on the Ucchaṅga Jātaka

Ucchaṅge [V 1.0294] deva me puttoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ jānapaditthiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye kosalaraṭṭhe tayo janā aññatarasmiṃ aṭavimukhe kasanti. Tasmiṃ samaye antoaṭaviyaṃ corā manusse vilumpitvā palāyiṃsu. Manussā te [P 1.0307] core pariyesitvā apassantā taṃ ṭhānaṃ āgamma “tumhe aṭaviyaṃ vilumpitvā idāni kassakā viya hothā”ti “te corā ime”ti bandhitvā ānetvā kosalarañño adaṃsu. Athekā itthī āgantvā “acchādanaṃ me detha, acchādanaṃ me dethā”ti paridevantī punappunaṃ rājanivesanaṃ pariyāti. Rājā tassā saddaṃ sutvā “gacchatha, detha imissā acchādana”nti āha. Manussā sāṭakaṃ gahetvā adaṃsu. Sā taṃ disvā “nāhaṃ etaṃ acchādanaṃ yācāmi[M 1.0325], sāmikacchādanaṃ yācāmī”ti āha. Manussā gantvā rañño ārocayiṃsu “na kiresā idaṃ acchādanaṃ katheti, sāmikacchādanaṃ kathetī”ti. Atha naṃ rājā pakkosāpetvā “tvaṃ kira sāmikacchādanaṃ yācasī”ti pucchi. Āma, deva, itthiyā hi sāmiko acchādanaṃ nāma, sāmike hi asati sahassamūlampi sāṭakaṃ nivatthā itthī naggāyeva nāma. Imassa panatthassa sādhanatthaṃ –

“My son is in my lap, O king…” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain countrywoman. At one time, in the Kosala country, three men were plowing near the edge of a certain forest. At that time, robbers inside the forest plundered people and fled. The people searched for those robbers, and not finding them, came to that place and said, “You plundered in the forest and now act like farmers.” Thinking, “These are the robbers,” they bound them, brought them, and presented them to the King of Kosala. Then a certain woman came, lamenting repeatedly, “Give me a covering, give me a covering,” and went around the royal residence again and again. The king, hearing her cry, said, “Go, give her a covering.” The men took a cloak and gave it to her. Seeing it, she said, “I do not ask for this covering; I ask for the covering that is my husband.” The men went and reported to the king, “It is said she is not speaking of this covering; she is speaking of the covering that is her husband.” Then the king had her summoned and asked, “Is it true that you are asking for the covering that is your husband?” “Yes, Your Majesty,” she replied. “For a woman, her husband is indeed a covering. For when there is no husband, a woman, even if she wears a garment worth a thousand coins, is truly naked.” To illustrate this meaning—

“Naggā nadī anūdakā, naggaṃ raṭṭhaṃ arājakaṃ;

Itthīpi vidhavā naggā, yassāpi dasa bhātaro”ti. (jā. 2.22.1840) –

“Naked is a river without water; naked is a kingdom without a king; a woman, too, is naked when widowed, even if she has ten brothers.”

Idaṃ suttaṃ āharitabbaṃ.

This verse should be cited.

Rājā tassā pasanno “ime te tayo janā ke hontī”ti pucchi. “Eko me, deva, sāmiko, eko bhātā, eko putto”ti. Rājā “ahaṃ te tuṭṭho, imesu tīsu ekaṃ demi, kataraṃ icchasī”ti pucchi. Sā āha “ahaṃ, deva, jīvamānā ekaṃ sāmikaṃ labhissāmi, puttampi labhissāmiyeva, mātāpitūnaṃ pana me matattā bhātāva dullabho, bhātaraṃ me dehi, devā”ti. Rājā tussitvā tayopi vissajjesi. Evaṃ taṃ ekikaṃ nissāya te tayo janā dukkhato muttā. Taṃ kāraṇaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā “āvuso, ekaṃ itthiṃ nissāya tayo janā dukkhato muttā”ti tassā guṇakathāya nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya [V 1.0295] nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, esā itthī idāneva te tayo jane dukkhā moceti, pubbepi mocesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The king, pleased with her, asked, “Who are these three men to you?” “One, Your Majesty, is my husband, one is my brother, and one is my son,” she replied. The king said, “I am pleased with you. I will give you one of these three. Which one do you wish for?” She answered, “Your Majesty, while I live, I can find another husband and will surely have another son. But since my parents have died, a brother is difficult to obtain. Please give me my brother, Your Majesty.” Delighted, the king released all three. Thus, on account of that one woman, those three men were freed from suffering. This matter became known among the community of monks. Then one day, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and sat discussing her virtues, saying, “Friends, because of one woman, three men were freed from suffering.” When the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the topic of your discussion now, as you are gathered here?” and they told him, he said, “Monks, this woman did not free these three men from suffering only now; she did so in the past as well,” and he recounted a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tayo janā aṭavimukhe kasantīti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Tadā pana raññā “tīsu janesu kaṃ icchasī”ti vutte sā āha – “tayopi dātuṃ na sakkotha, devā”ti? “Āma, na sakkomī”ti. “Sace [P 1.0308] tayo dātuṃ na sakkotha, bhātaraṃ me dethā”ti. “Puttaṃ vā sāmikaṃ vā gaṇha, kiṃ te bhātarā”ti ca vuttā “ete nāma deva sulabhā, bhātā pana dullabho”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, three men were plowing near the forest—everything is the same as before. Then, when the king said, “Among these three men, whom do you wish for?” she replied, “Are you not able to give all three, Your Majesty?” “Indeed, I am not able,” he said. “If you are not able to give all three, then give me my brother.” When told, “Take either your son or your husband; what use is a brother to you?” she said, “These, Your Majesty, are easily obtained, but a brother is difficult to obtain,” and then she spoke this verse:

67.

67.

“Ucchaṅge [M 1.0326] deva me putto, pathe dhāvantiyā pati;

Tañca desaṃ na passāmi, yato sodariyamānaye”ti.

“My son, O king, is in my lap; my husband is on the path I travel; but I see no place from which I could bring a brother born of the same womb.”

Tattha ucchaṅge, deva, me puttoti deva, mayhaṃ putto ucchaṅgeyeva. Yathā hi araññaṃ pavisitvā ucchaṅge katvā ḍākaṃ uccinitvā tattha pakkhipantiyā ucchaṅge ḍākaṃ nāma sulabhaṃ hoti, evaṃ itthiyā puttopi sulabho ucchaṅge ḍākasadisova. Tena vuttaṃ “ucchaṅge, deva, me putto”ti. Pathe dhāvantiyā patīti maggaṃ āruyha ekikāya gacchamānāyapi hi itthiyā pati nāma sulabho, diṭṭhadiṭṭhoyeva hoti. Tena vuttaṃ “pathe dhāvantiyā patī”ti. Tañca desaṃ na passāmi, yato sodariyamānayeti yasmā pana me mātāpitaro natthi, tasmā idāni taṃ mātukucchisaṅkhātaṃ aññaṃ desaṃ na passāmi. Yato ahaṃ samāne udare jātattā saudariyasaṅkhātaṃ bhātaraṃ āneyyaṃ, tasmā bhātaraṃyeva me dethāti.

Here, 'My son, O king, is in my lap' means, 'O king, my son is indeed in my lap.' Just as for a woman who enters the forest, picks edible greens, and puts them in her lap-fold, greens are indeed easily found in the lap, so too for a woman, a son is as easily found as greens in the lap. Hence it is said, 'My son, O king, is in my lap.' 'For a woman going along the path, a husband' means that even for a woman going alone on the road, a husband is indeed easily found—he is seen at every turn. Hence it is said, 'For a woman going along the path, a husband.' 'But I see no place from which to bring a brother' means that since I have no mother and father, I do not now see any other place, namely, my mother’s womb, from which I could bring a brother, one born of the same womb, because we were born from the same belly. Therefore, give me my brother.

Rājā “saccaṃ esā vadatī”ti tuṭṭhacitto tayopi jane bandhanāgārato ānetvā adāsi, sā tayopi te gahetvā gatā.

The king, pleased, thinking, "She speaks the truth," had those three men brought from the prison and gave them to her. She took those three and left.

Satthāpi “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesā ime tayo jane dukkhato mocesiyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “atīte cattārova etarahi cattāro, rājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher then, having brought forth this Dhamma talk, "Monks, this woman did not free these three men from suffering only now; she did so in the past as well," connected the sequence and identified the Jātaka: "The four in the past were the four now, but the king was I myself."

Ucchaṅgajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The commentary on the Ucchaṅga Jātaka, the seventh, is concluded.

[68] 8. Sāketajātakavaṇṇanā

[68] 8. The Commentary on the Sāketa Jātaka

Yasmiṃ [V 1.0296] mano nivisatīti idaṃ satthā sāketaṃ nissāya añjanavane viharanto ekaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Bhagavato kira bhikkhusaṅghaparivutassa sāketaṃ piṇḍāya pavisanakāle eko sāketanagaravāsī mahallakabrāhmaṇo nagarato bahi gacchanto antaradvāre dasabalaṃ disvā pādesu patitvā gopphakesu gāḷhaṃ gahetvā “tāta, nanu nāma puttehi jiṇṇakāle mātāpitaro paṭijaggitabbā, kasmā ettakaṃ [P 1.0309][M 1.0327] kālaṃ amhākaṃ attānaṃ na dassesi? Mayā tāva diṭṭhosi, mātaraṃ pana passituṃ ehī”ti satthāraṃ gahetvā attano gehaṃ agamāsi. Satthā tattha gantvā nisīdi paññatte āsane saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Brāhmaṇīpi āgantvā satthu pādesu patitvā “tāta, ettakaṃ kālaṃ kahaṃ gatosi, nanu nāma mātāpitaro mahallakakāle upaṭṭhātabbā”ti paridevi. Puttadhītaropi “etha, bhātaraṃ vandathā”ti vandāpesi. Ubho tuṭṭhamānasā mahādānaṃ adaṃsu. Satthā bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā tesaṃ dvinnampi janānaṃ jarāsuttaṃ (su. ni. 810 ādayo) kathesi. Suttapariyosāne ubhopi anāgāmiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Satthā uṭṭhāyāsanā añjanavanameva agamāsi.

In whom the mind settles—this the Teacher spoke concerning a certain brahmin while dwelling in the Añjana Grove near Sāketa. It seems that when the Blessed One, surrounded by the community of monks, was entering Sāketa for alms, an elderly brahmin, a resident of Sāketa, going out of the city, saw the Ten-Powered One at the city gate. Falling at his feet and grasping his ankles tightly, he said, "Dear one, should not parents indeed be cared for by their children in old age? Why have you not shown yourself to us for so long? Now that I have seen you, please come and see your mother." Taking the Teacher, he went to his own house. The Teacher went there and sat on the prepared seat together with the community of monks. The brahmin’s wife also came, fell at the Teacher’s feet, and lamented, "Dear one, where have you been all this time? Should not parents indeed be attended to in their old age?" She also had their sons and daughters pay homage, saying to them, "Come, pay respects to your brother." Both, with joyful minds, gave a great offering. The Teacher, having finished the meal, taught both of them the Discourse on Old Age (Jarāsutta, Snp 810ff.). At the end of the discourse, both were established in the fruit of non-returning. The Teacher then rose from his seat and returned to the Añjana Grove.

Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, brāhmaṇo ‘tathāgatassa pitā suddhodano, mātā mahāmāyā’ti jānāti, jānantova saddhiṃ brāhmaṇiyā tathāgataṃ ‘amhākaṃ putto’ti vadati, satthāpi adhivāseti. Kiṃ nu kho kāraṇa”nti? Satthā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā “bhikkhave, ubhopi te attano puttameva ‘putto’ti vadantī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and started this discussion: "Friends, the brahmin knows that the Tathāgata's father was Suddhodana and his mother was Mahāmāyā. Yet, knowing this, he and his wife call the Tathāgata 'our son,' and the Teacher accepts it. What indeed is the reason for this?" Hearing their discussion, the Teacher said, "Monks, both of them call him 'son' because he is indeed their son," and then he related a past event.

Bhikkhave, ayaṃ brāhmaṇo atīte nirantaraṃ pañca jātisatāni mayhaṃ pitā ahosi, pañca jātisatāni cūḷapitā, pañca jātisatāni mahāpitā. Esāpi brāhmaṇī nirantarameva pañca jātisatāni mātā ahosi, pañca jātisatāni cūḷamātā, pañca jātisatāni mahāmātā. Evāhaṃ diyaḍḍhajātisahassaṃ brāhmaṇassa hatthe saṃvaḍḍho, diyaḍḍhajātisahassaṃ brāhmaṇiyā hatthe saṃvaḍḍhoti tīṇi jātisahassāni kathetvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

"Monks, in the past this brahmin was my father for five hundred consecutive lives, my younger paternal uncle for five hundred lives, and my elder paternal uncle for five hundred lives. This brahmin woman was also my mother for five hundred consecutive lives, my younger maternal aunt for five hundred lives, and my elder maternal aunt for five hundred lives. Thus, I was raised by the brahmin for one and a half thousand lives, and by the brahmin woman for another one and a half thousand lives." Having spoken of three thousand lives and having become fully enlightened, he uttered this verse:

68.

68.

“Yasmiṃ mano nivisati, cittañcāpi pasīdati;

Adiṭṭhapubbake pose, kāmaṃ tasmimpi vissase”ti.

"In whom the mind settles down, and the heart is also gladdened; in a person never seen before, one may indeed place trust."

Tattha [V 1.0297] yasmiṃ mano nivisatīti yasmiṃ puggale diṭṭhamatteyeva cittaṃ patiṭṭhāti. Cittañcāpi pasīdatīti yasmiṃ diṭṭhamatte cittaṃ pasīdati, mudukaṃ hoti. Adiṭṭhapubbake poseti pakatiyā tasmiṃ attabhāve adiṭṭhapubbepi [M 1.0328] puggale. Kāmaṃ tasmimpi vissaseti anubhūtapubbasineheneva tasmimpi puggale ekaṃsena vissase, vissāsaṃ āpajjatiyevāti attho.

Here, 'in whom the mind settles' means a person in whom the mind becomes established merely upon sight. 'And the mind is also gladdened' means that upon sight, the mind becomes serene and gentle. The phrase 'in a person never seen before' refers to a person not previously seen in that particular existence. 'One may indeed place trust in him' means that even in such a person, one should certainly place trust, precisely because of affection experienced in the past; one indeed comes to trust them—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ [P 1.0310] satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo ca brāhmaṇī ca ete eva ahesuṃ, putto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus, the Teacher, having brought forth this Dhamma talk and connected the sequence, identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the brahmin and his wife were these very same people, and the son was I myself."

Sāketajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The commentary on the Sāketa Jātaka, the eighth, is concluded.

[69] 9. Visavantajātakavaṇṇanā

[69] 9. The Commentary on the Visavanta Jātaka

Dhiratthu taṃ visaṃ vantanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dhammasenāpatiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Therassa kira piṭṭhakhajjakakhādanakāle manussā saṅghassa bahuṃ piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ gahetvā vihāraṃ agamaṃsu, bhikkhusaṅghassa gahitāvasesaṃ bahu atirittaṃ ahosi. Manussā “bhante, antogāmagatānampi gaṇhathā”ti āhaṃsu. Tasmiṃ khaṇe therassa saddhivihāriko daharo antogāme hoti, tassa koṭṭhāsaṃ gahetvā tasmiṃ anāgacchante “atidivā hotī”ti therassa adaṃsu. Therena tasmiṃ paribhutte daharo agamāsi. Atha naṃ thero “mayaṃ, āvuso, tuyhaṃ ṭhapitakhādanīyaṃ paribhuñjimhā”ti āha. So “madhuraṃ nāma, bhante, kassa appiya”nti āha. Mahātherassa saṃvego uppajji. So ito paṭṭhāya “piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ na khādissāmī”ti adhiṭṭhāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya kira sāriputtattherena piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ nāma na khāditapubbaṃ. Tassa piṭṭhakhādanīyaṃ akhādanabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo jāto. Bhikkhū taṃ kathaṃ kathentā dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīdiṃsu. Atha satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “bhikkhave, sāriputto ekavāraṃ jahitakaṃ jīvitaṃ pariccajantopi puna na gaṇhātiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Fie on that vomited poison…”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the General of the Dhamma. It is said that at a time when the Elder was eating cakes, people brought many cakes to the monastery for the Sangha. After the community of monks had taken their share, much was left over. The people said, “Venerable sirs, please take some for those who have gone into the village.” At that moment, the Elder’s young co-resident was in the village; they took his portion, but as he did not return, they said, “It is late in the day,” and gave it to the Elder. After the Elder had eaten it, the young monk arrived. Then the Elder said to him, “Friend, we have eaten the food set aside for you.” He replied, “Venerable sir, to whom is something sweet disagreeable?” A sense of spiritual urgency arose in the great Elder. From that day forward, he made a formal resolution, “I will not eat cakes.” It is said that from that time onward, the Elder Sāriputta never again ate cakes. His abstention from cakes became well-known among the community of monks. The monks, discussing this matter, were seated in the Hall of Dhamma. Then the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?” When they told him what it was, he said, “Monks, Sāriputta would not take back what he has once relinquished, even if it meant giving up his life,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto visavejjakule nibbattitvā vejjakammena jīvikaṃ kappesi. Athekaṃ janapadamanussaṃ sappo ḍaṃsi, tassa ñātakā pamādaṃ akatvā khippaṃ vejjaṃ ānayiṃsu[M 1.0329]. Vejjo āha “kiṃ tāva osadhena, paribhāvetvā visaṃ harāmi, daṭṭhasappaṃ āvāhetvā daṭṭhaṭṭhānato teneva visaṃ ākaḍḍhāpemī”ti. “Sappaṃ āvāhetvā visaṃ [V 1.0298] ākaḍḍhāpehī”ti. So sappaṃ āvāhetvā “tayā ayaṃ daṭṭho”ti āha. “Āma, mayā”ti[P 1.0311]. “Tayā daṭṭhaṭṭhānato tvaññeva mukhena visaṃ ākaḍḍhāhī”ti. “Mayā ekavāraṃ jahitakaṃ puna na gahitapubbaṃ, nāhaṃ mayā jahitavisaṃ ākaḍḍhissāmī”ti. So dārūni āharāpetvā aggiṃ katvā āha “sace attano visaṃ nākaḍḍhasi, imaṃ aggiṃ pavisā”ti. Sappo “api aggiṃ pavisissāmi, nevattanā ekavāraṃ jahitavisaṃ paccāharissāmī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of poison-healers and made his living by the practice of medicine. Then, a snake bit a man from the countryside. His relatives, not being negligent, quickly brought the healer. The healer asked, “Shall I first remove the poison by applying medicine and using incantations, or shall I summon the snake that bit him and have it draw the poison from the very spot of the bite?” They replied, “Summon the snake and have it draw out the poison.” So he summoned the snake and asked, “Did you bite this man?” “Yes, I did,” it replied. “Then from the place you bit, you yourself must draw the poison back with your mouth.” “I have never taken back what I have once relinquished. I will not draw back the poison I have discharged,” said the snake. The healer then had wood brought, made a fire, and said, “If you do not draw back your own poison, enter this fire.” The snake replied, “I would rather enter the fire; I will not take back the poison I have once discharged,” and spoke this verse:

69.

69.

“Dhiratthu taṃ visaṃ vantaṃ, yamahaṃ jīvitakāraṇā;

Vantaṃ paccāharissāmi, mataṃ me jīvitā vara”nti.

“Fie on that vomited poison, which I, for the sake of life, would take back after having discharged it! Death is better for me than life.”

Tattha dhiratthūti garahatthe nipāto. Taṃ visanti yamahaṃ jīvitakāraṇā vantaṃ visaṃ paccāharissāmi, taṃ vantaṃ visaṃ dhiratthu. Mataṃ me jīvitā varanti tassa visassa apaccāharaṇakāraṇā yaṃ aggiṃ pavisitvā maraṇaṃ, taṃ mama jīvitato varanti attho.

Herein, dhiratthu is a particle used in the sense of censure. That poison means: Fie on that vomited poison, which I would take back for the sake of life. Death is better for me than life means: the death that comes from entering the fire, because of not taking back that poison, is better for me than living.

Evañca pana vatvā aggiṃ pavisituṃ pāyāsi. Atha naṃ vejjo nivāretvā taṃ purisaṃ osadhehi ca mantehi ca nibbisaṃ arogaṃ katvā sappassa sīlāni datvā “ito paṭṭhāya mā kañci viheṭhesī”ti vatvā vissajjesi.

Having spoken thus, it went forth to enter the fire. But the healer prevented it and, using medicines and incantations, made the man poison-free and healthy. He then administered the moral precepts to the snake and, saying, “From this day forward, do not harm anyone,” he released it.

Satthāpi “na, bhikkhave, sāriputto ekavāraṃ jahitakaṃ jīvitampi pariccajanto puna gaṇhātī”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā sappo sāriputto ahosi, vejjo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said: “Monks, Sāriputta would not take back what he has once relinquished, even while giving up his life.” Then, making the connection, he identified the birth story: “At that time, the snake was Sāriputta, and the healer was none other than myself.”

Visavantajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Visavanta Jātaka, the Ninth.

[70] 10. Kuddālajātakavaṇṇanā

[70] 10. The Commentary on the Kuddāla Jātaka

Na [M 1.0330] taṃ jitaṃ sādhu jitanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto cittahatthasāriputtaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthiyaṃ eko kuladārako. Athekadivasaṃ kasitvā āgacchanto vihāraṃ pavisitvā ekassa therassa pattato siniddhaṃ madhuraṃ paṇītabhojanaṃ labhitvā cintesi “mayaṃ rattindivaṃ sahatthena nānākammāni kurumānāpi evarūpaṃ madhurāhāraṃ na labhāma, mayāpi samaṇena bhavitabba”nti[V 1.0299]. So pabbajitvā māsaḍḍhamāsaccayena ayoniso manasikaronto kilesavasiko hutvā vibbhamitvā puna bhattena kilamanto [P 1.0312] āgantvā pabbajitvā abhidhammaṃ uggaṇhi. Imināva upāyena cha vāre vibbhamitvā pabbajito. Tato sattame bhikkhubhāve sattappakaraṇiko hutvā bahū bhikkhū dhammaṃ vācento vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ pāpuṇi. Athassa sahāyakā bhikkhū “kiṃ nu kho, āvuso cittahattha, pubbe viya te etarahi kilesā na vaḍḍhantī”ti parihāsaṃ kariṃsu. “Āvuso, abhabbo dāni ahaṃ ito paṭṭhāya gihibhāvāyā”ti.

“That is not a victory well won…”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder Cittahattha. He, it is said, was a young man of good family in Sāvatthī. One day, as he was returning from plowing, he entered the monastery and received some rich, sweet, and excellent food from an elder's bowl. He thought, “Though we work day and night with our own hands at various tasks, we do not get such delicious food. I too should become a recluse.” Having ordained, after a month and a half had passed, through giving unwise attention to things, he fell under the sway of the defilements and left the Order. Then again, wearied by the toil for food, he returned, ordained, and studied the Abhidhamma. In this way, he left the Order and reordained six times. Then, on his seventh time as a monk, he became a master of the seven treatises, taught the Dhamma to many monks, developed insight, and attained Arahantship. Then his companion monks teased him, saying, “Friend Cittahattha, how is it that your defilements do not arise now as they did before?” He replied, “Friends, from this day forward, I am incapable of returning to the lay state.”

Evaṃ tasmiṃ arahattaṃ patte dhammasabhāyaṃ kathā udapādi “āvuso, evarūpassa nāma arahattassa upanissaye sati āyasmā cittahatthasāriputto chakkhattuṃ uppabbajito, aho mahādoso puthujjanabhāvo”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “bhikkhave, puthujjanacittaṃ nāma lahukaṃ dunniggahaṃ, ārammaṇavasena gantvā allīyati, ekavāraṃ allīnaṃ na sakkā hoti khippaṃ mocetuṃ, evarūpassa cittassa damatho sādhu. Dantameva hi taṃ sukhaṃ āvahati.

Thus, when he attained arahantship, a discussion arose in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, even with such predisposing conditions for arahantship, Venerable Cittahattha disrobed six times. Alas, great is the fault of the state of a worldling!" The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you now sitting together here?" When they replied, "With this one," he said: "Monks, the mind of a worldling is fickle and hard to control. It goes and clings according to its object. Once it has clung, it cannot quickly be freed. Taming such a mind is good, for the tamed mind surely brings happiness."

“Dunniggahassa lahuno, yatthakāmanipātino;

Cittassa damatho sādhu, cittaṃ dantaṃ sukhāvahaṃ”. (dha. pa. 35);

"Hard to control, fickle, alighting wherever it likes; the taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness."

Tassa pana dunniggahatāya pubbe paṇḍitā ekaṃ kuddālakaṃ nissāya taṃ jahituṃ asakkontā lobhavasena chakkhattuṃ uppabbajitvā sattame pabbajitabhāve jhānaṃ uppādetvā taṃ lobhaṃ niggaṇhiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Because the mind is difficult to control, wise ones in the past, relying on a single hoe and being unable to abandon it, disrobed six times due to greed. In their seventh time as renunciates, they developed jhāna and subdued that greed." Having said this, he related a past story.

Atīte [M 1.0331] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto paṇṇikakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ pāpuṇi, “kuddālapaṇḍito”tissa nāmaṃ ahosi. So kuddālakena bhūmiparikammaṃ katvā ḍākañceva alābukumbhaṇḍaeḷālukādīni ca vapitvā tāni vikkiṇanto kapaṇajīvikaṃ kappesi. Tañhissa ekaṃ kuddālakaṃ ṭhapetvā aññaṃ dhanaṃ nāma natthi. So ekadivasaṃ cintesi “kiṃ me gharāvāsena, nikkhamitvā pabbajissāmī”ti. Athekadivasaṃ kuddālakaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā taṃ kuddālakaṃ anussaritvā lobhaṃ chindituṃ asakkonto kuṇṭhakuddālakaṃ [P 1.0313] nissāya uppabbaji. Evaṃ dutiyampi, tatiyampīti cha vāre taṃ kuddālakaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne nikkhipitvā pabbajito ceva uppabbajito ca.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of vegetable sellers and reached maturity. He was known as "Kuddālapaṇḍita." Using a hoe, he tilled the soil and planted vegetables, gourds, pumpkins, cucumbers, and other things, selling them to make a meager living. Apart from that one hoe, he had no other wealth. One day, he thought, "What use is this household life to me? I shall go forth and become a renunciate." Then one day, he placed the hoe in a concealed place and took up the ascetic life. But being unable to cut off his craving, remembering the hoe, he disrobed, on account of that worn-out hoe. This happened a second time, and a third—for six times he left the hoe in a concealed place, went forth, and then disrobed.

Sattame [V 1.0300] pana vāre cintesi “ahaṃ imaṃ kuṇṭhakuddālakaṃ nissāya punappunaṃ uppabbajito, idāni naṃ mahānadiyaṃ pakkhipitvā pabbajissāmī”ti nadītīraṃ gantvā “sacassa patitaṭṭhānaṃ passissāmi, punāgantvā uddharitukāmatā bhaveyyā”ti taṃ kuddālakaṃ daṇḍe gahetvā nāgabalo thāmasampanno sīsassa uparibhāge tikkhattuṃ āvijjhitvā akkhīni nimmīletvā nadīmajjhe khipitvā “jitaṃ me jitaṃ me”ti tikkhattuṃ sīhanādaṃ nadi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bārāṇasirājā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā āgato nadiyā sīsaṃ nhāyitvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍito hatthikkhandhena gacchamāno taṃ bodhisattassa saddaṃ sutvā “ayaṃ puriso ‘jitaṃ me jitaṃ me’ti vadati, ko nu kho etena jito, pakkosatha na”nti pakkosāpetvā “bho purisa, ahaṃ tāva vijitasaṅgāmo idāni jayaṃ gahetvā āgacchāmi, tayā pana ko jito”ti pucchi. Bodhisatto “mahārāja, tayā saṅgāmasatampi saṅgāmasahassampi saṅgāmasatasahassampi jinantena dujjitameva kilesānaṃ ajitattā. Ahaṃ pana mama abbhantare lobhaṃ niggaṇhanto kilese jini”nti kathentoyeva mahānadiṃ oloketvā āpokasiṇārammaṇaṃ jhānaṃ nibbattetvā sampattānubhāvo ākāse nisīditvā rañño dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

On the seventh occasion, he thought, "Relying on this worn-out hoe, I have repeatedly disrobed. Now, I will throw it into the great river and then go forth." Going to the riverbank, he considered, "If I see the place where it falls, I might wish to return and retrieve it." Taking the hoe by its handle, with the strength of an elephant and great power, he whirled it three times above his head, closed his eyes, and hurled it into the middle of the river, roaring three times like a lion, "Victory is mine! Victory is mine!" At that moment, the king of Bārāṇasī, having pacified the borderlands, was returning. Having bathed his head in the river and adorned himself with all his ornaments, he was traveling on the back of an elephant when he heard the Bodhisatta’s cry. He said, "This man declares, 'Victory is mine! Victory is mine!' Who has he conquered? Summon him." When he was summoned, the king asked, "Good man, I have just returned victorious from battle. But who has been conquered by you?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Great king, though you may conquer a hundred battles, a thousand battles, or a hundred thousand battles, it is a poor victory indeed, since the defilements are not conquered. But I, restraining greed within myself, have conquered the defilements." As he spoke, he gazed upon the great river and, with the water-kasiṇa as his object, generated meditative absorption. Having attained this spiritual power, he sat in the air and taught the king the Dhamma, speaking this verse:

70.

70.

“Na taṃ jitaṃ sādhu jitaṃ, yaṃ jitaṃ avajīyati;

Taṃ kho jitaṃ sādhu jitaṃ, yaṃ jitaṃ nāvajīyatī”ti.

"That victory is not well-won which can be won back; but that victory is well-won which cannot be won back."

Tattha [M 1.0332] na taṃ jitaṃ sādhu jitaṃ, yaṃ jitaṃ avajīyatīti yaṃ paccāmitte parājinitvā raṭṭhaṃ jitaṃ paṭiladdhaṃ punapi tehi paccāmittehi avajīyati, taṃ jitaṃ sādhujitaṃ nāma na hoti. Kasmā? Puna avajīyanato. Aparo nayo – jitaṃ vuccati jayo. Yo paccāmittehi saddhiṃ yujjhitvā adhigato jayo puna tesu jinantesu[P 1.0314], parājayo hoti, so na sādhu na sobhano. Kasmā? Yasmā puna parājayova hoti. Taṃ kho jitaṃ sādhu jitaṃ, yaṃ jitaṃ nāvajīyatīti yaṃ kho pana paccāmitte nimmathetvā jitaṃ puna tehi nāvajīyati, yo vā ekavāraṃ laddho jayo na puna parājayo hoti, taṃ jitaṃ sādhu jitaṃ sobhanaṃ, so jayo sādhu sobhano nāma hoti. Kasmā? Puna nāvajīyanato. Tasmā, tvaṃ mahārāja, satakkhattumpi sahassakkhattumpi satasahassakkhattumpi saṅgāmasīsaṃ jinitvāpi saṅgāmayodho nāma na hosi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Attano kilesānaṃ ajitattā. Yo pana ekavārampi attano abbhantare kilese jināti, ayaṃ uttamo saṅgāmasīsayodhoti ākāse nisinnakova buddhalīlāya rañño dhammaṃ desesi. Uttamasaṅgāmayodhabhāvo panettha –

Therein, 'That victory is not well-won which can be won back' means that when a kingdom is conquered and won by defeating enemies, if it is won back again by those same enemies, that victory is not called a good victory. Why? Because it is won back again. Another way: 'jitaṃ' is called 'jayo' (victory). The victory that is gained by fighting with enemies, if it becomes a defeat when they win again, is not good, not excellent. Why? Because it becomes a defeat again. 'But that victory is well-won which cannot be won back' means that a victory won by crushing enemies, which is not won back by them again, or a victory gained once that does not become a defeat again, that victory is called a good and excellent victory. Why? Because it is not won back again. Therefore, great king, even if you were to conquer the field of battle a hundred times, a thousand times, or a hundred thousand times, you would not be called a warrior of battle. For what reason? Because your own defilements are not conquered. But one who conquers the defilements within themselves even once, this is the supreme warrior of battle. Thus, seated in the air, he taught the Dhamma to the king with the grace of a Buddha. Here, the state of being the supreme warrior of battle is:

“Yo [V 1.0301] sahassaṃ sahassena, saṅgāme mānuse jine;

Ekañca jeyyamattānaṃ, sa ve saṅgāmajuttamo”ti. (dha. pa. 103) –

"Though one may conquer a thousand times a thousand men in battle, yet he who conquers his single self is the supreme victor in battle."

Idaṃ suttaṃ sādhakaṃ.

This verse is the authority here.

Rañño pana dhammaṃ suṇantasseva tadaṅgappahānavasena kilesā pahīnā, pabbajjāya cittaṃ nami. Rājabalassapi tatheva kilesā pahīyiṃsu. Rājā “idāni tumhe kahaṃ gamissathā”ti bodhisattaṃ pucchi. “Himavantaṃ pavisitvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajissāmi, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi ahampi pabbajissāmī”ti bodhisatteneva saddhiṃ nikkhami, balakāyo brāhmaṇagahapatikā sabbā seniyoti sabbopi tasmiṃ ṭhāne sannipatito mahājanakāyo raññā saddhiṃyeva nikkhami. Bārāṇasivāsinopi “amhākaṃ kira rājā kuddālapaṇḍitassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbajjābhimukho hutvā saddhiṃ balakāyena nikkhanto, mayaṃ idha kiṃ karissāmā”ti dvādasayojanikāya bārāṇasiyā sakalanagaravāsino nikkhamiṃsu. Dvādasayojanikā parisā ahosi. Taṃ ādāya bodhisatto himavantaṃ pāvisi.

While the king was listening to the Dhamma, his defilements were abandoned by way of momentary abandonment, and his mind inclined toward renunciation. The defilements of the king's forces were likewise abandoned. The king asked the Bodhisatta, “Where will you go now?” “I will enter the Himalayas and go forth into the life of a sage, great king,” he replied. “In that case, I too shall go forth,” said the king, and he departed together with the Bodhisatta. The army, brahmins and householders, all the guilds—indeed, the entire great populace assembled in that place—departed together with the king. The inhabitants of Bārāṇasī also, thinking, “It is said our king, after listening to the Dhamma discourse of Kuddālapaṇḍita, has departed with his army, intent on renunciation; what shall we do here?” all the residents of the twelve-yojana city of Bārāṇasī departed. The assembly was twelve yojanas in extent. Taking them with him, the Bodhisatta entered the Himalayas.

Tasmiṃ [M 1.0333] khaṇe sakkassa devarañño nisinnāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So āvajjamāno “kuddālapaṇḍito mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto”ti disvā “mahāsamāgamo bhavissati, vasanaṭṭhānaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vissakammaṃ āmantetvā “tāta, kuddālapaṇḍito mahābhinikkhamanaṃ nikkhanto[P 1.0315], vasanaṭṭhānaṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, tvaṃ himavantappadesaṃ gantvā same bhūmibhāge dīghato tiṃsayojanaṃ vitthārato pannarasayojanaṃ assamapadaṃ māpehī”ti āha. So “sādhu, devā”ti paṭissuṇitvā gantvā tathā akāsi. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana hatthipālajātake āvi bhavissati. Idañca hi tañca ekaparicchedameva. Vissakammopi assamapade paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā dussadde mige ca sakuṇe ca amanusse ca paṭikkamāpetvā tena tena disābhāgena ekapadikamaggaṃ māpetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Kuddālapaṇḍitopi taṃ parisaṃ ādāya himavantaṃ pavisitvā sakkadattiyaṃ assamapadaṃ gantvā vissakammena māpitaṃ pabbajitaparikkhāraṃ gahetvā paṭhamaṃ attanā pabbajitvā pacchā parisaṃ pabbājetvā assamapadaṃ bhājetvā adāsi. Satta rājāno satta rajjāni chaḍḍayiṃsu. Tiṃsayojanaṃ assamapadaṃ pūri. Kuddālapaṇḍito sesakasiṇesupi parikammaṃ katvā brahmavihāre bhāvetvā parisāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ ācikkhi. Sabbe samāpattilābhino hutvā brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ. Ye pana tesaṃ pāricariyaṃ akaṃsu, te devalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

At that moment, the seat of Sakka, king of the gods, showed a sign of heat. Reflecting, he saw, “Kuddālapaṇḍita has gone forth in the Great Renunciation. There will be a great gathering; it is necessary to provide a dwelling place.” Summoning Vissakamma, he said, “My dear, Kuddālapaṇḍita has gone forth in the Great Renunciation. It is necessary to provide a dwelling place. You must go to the region of the Himalayas and on level ground create a hermitage, thirty yojanas in length and fifteen yojanas in width.” Vissakamma replied, “Very well, lord,” and went and did so. This is the summary here; the full account will become clear in the Hatthipāla Jātaka. For the extent of the hermitage in this Jātaka and in that one is indeed the same. Vissakamma also, having created leaf-huts in the hermitage, and having driven away noisy beasts, birds, and non-human beings, made a footpath leading from each direction and then returned to his own abode. Kuddālapaṇḍita, taking that assembly, entered the Himalayas, went to the hermitage given by Sakka, and taking the requisites of one gone forth created by Vissakamma, he first went forth himself and afterwards caused the assembly to go forth. He then divided the hermitage and gave it to them. Seven kings abandoned seven kingdoms. The thirty-yojana hermitage was filled. Kuddālapaṇḍita, having performed the preliminary practice on the remaining kasiṇas and developed the divine abodes, taught the meditation subjects to the assembly. All of them, having attained meditative absorptions and developed the divine abodes, were destined for the Brahma world. Those, however, who attended on them, were destined for the deva world.

Satthā [V 1.0302] “evaṃ, bhikkhave, cittaṃ nāmetaṃ kilesavasena allīnaṃ dummocayaṃ hoti, uppannā lobhadhammā duppajahā, evarūpepi paṇḍite aññāṇe karontī”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne keci sotāpannā ahesuṃ, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahattaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Satthāpi anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, parisā buddhaparisā, kuddālapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Thus, monks, this so-called mind, clinging through the power of defilements, is difficult to release; arisen states of greed are difficult to abandon; they make even such a wise person ignorant.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some attained Arahantship. The Teacher, connecting the links, identified the birth story: 'At that time, the king was Ānanda, the assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Kuddālapaṇḍita was I myself.'

Kuddālajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Kuddāla Jātaka, the Tenth.

Itthivaggo sattamo.

The Chapter on Women, the Seventh.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Asātamantaṇḍabhūtaṃ[M 1.0334], takkapaṇḍi durājānaṃ;

Anabhirati mudulakkhaṇaṃ, ucchaṅgampi ca sāketaṃ;

Visavantaṃ kuddālakanti.

Asātamanta, Aṇḍabhūta; Takkapaṇḍita, Durājāna; Anabhirati, Mudulakkhaṇa; Ucchaṅga, Sāketa; Visavanta, Kuddālaka.

8. Varuṇavaggo

8. The Varuṇa Chapter

[71] 1. Varuṇajātakavaṇṇanā

1. The Commentary on the Varuṇa Jātaka

Yo [V 1.0303][P 1.0316][M 1.0335] pubbe karaṇīyānīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kuṭumbikaputtatissattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiṃ kira divase sāvatthivāsino aññamaññasahāyakā tiṃsamattā kulaputtā gandhapupphavatthādīni gahetvā “satthu dhammadesanaṃ suṇissāmā”ti mahājanaparivutā jetavanaṃ gantvā nāgamāḷakasālamāḷakādīsu thokaṃ nisīditvā sāyanhasamaye satthari surabhigandhavāsitāya gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā dhammasabhaṃ gantvā alaṅkatabuddhāsane nisinne saparivārā dhammasabhaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ gandhapupphehi pūjetvā cakkaṅkitatalesu phullapadumasassirikesu pādesu vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinnā dhammaṃ suṇiṃsu.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story concerning the elder Tissa, son of a householder, beginning with the words, “He who formerly had duties to perform.” It is said that one day, about thirty young men of good family, residents of Sāvatthī and friends of one another, took perfumes, flowers, cloth, and other things, and thinking, “We will listen to the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse,” surrounded by a great crowd, they went to Jetavana. After sitting for a while on the Nāga terrace, the Sāla terrace, and other such places, in the evening, when the Teacher had emerged from his fragrant chamber, perfumed with sweet scents, gone to the Dhamma hall, and was seated on the adorned Buddha-seat, they, with their retinue, approached the Dhamma hall. They honored the Teacher with perfumes and flowers, paid homage at his feet—which were marked with wheels and glorious like full-blown lotuses—and, having sat down to one side, listened to the Dhamma.

Atha nesaṃ etadahosi “yathā yathā kho mayaṃ bhagavatā dhammaṃ desitaṃ ājānāma, pabbajeyyāmā”ti. Te tathāgatassa dhammasabhāto nikkhantakāle tathāgataṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yāciṃsu, satthā tesaṃ pabbajjaṃ adāsi. Te ācariyupajjhāye ārādhetvā upasampadaṃ labhitvā pañca vassāni ācariyupajjhāyānaṃ santike vasitvā dve mātikā paguṇaṃ katvā kappiyākappiyaṃ ñatvā tisso anumodanā uggaṇhitvā cīvarāni sibbetvā rajitvā “samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmā”ti ācariyupajjhāye āpucchitvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā “mayaṃ, bhante, bhavesu ukkaṇṭhitā jātijarābyādhimaraṇabhayabhītā, tesaṃ no saṃsāraparimocanatthāya kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathethā”ti yāciṃsu. Satthā tesaṃ aṭṭhatiṃsāya kammaṭṭhānesu sappāyaṃ vicinitvā kammaṭṭhānaṃ kathesi. Te satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā satthāraṃ vanditvā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pariveṇaṃ gantvā ācariyupajjhāye oloketvā pattacīvaramādāya “samaṇadhammaṃ karissāmā”ti nikkhamiṃsu.

Then it occurred to them, 'Inasmuch as we understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, we should go forth.' When the Tathāgata departed from the Dhamma hall, they approached him, paid homage, and requested the going forth. The Teacher granted them the going forth. Having satisfied their teachers and preceptors, they received the higher ordination. After living in the presence of their teachers and preceptors for five years, having mastered the two codes of monastic rules, knowing what is proper and improper, having learned the three types of blessings, and having sewn and dyed their robes, they took leave of their teachers and preceptors, saying, 'We will practice the duties of a recluse.' They approached the Teacher, paid homage, sat to one side, and requested, 'Venerable sir, we are weary of existences, fearful of the dangers of birth, aging, sickness, and death. For the sake of our liberation from saṃsāra, please teach us a meditation subject.' The Teacher, having discerned a suitable meditation subject for them from among the thirty-eight, taught them a meditation subject. Having received the meditation subject from the Teacher, they paid homage, circumambulated him, and went to their monastic dwelling. After seeing their teachers and preceptors, they took their bowls and robes and set out, saying, 'We will practice the duties of a recluse.'

Atha nesaṃ abbhantare eko bhikkhu nāmena kuṭumbikaputtatissatthero nāma kusīto hīnavīriyo rasagiddho. So evaṃ cintesi “ahaṃ neva araññe vasituṃ, na padhānaṃ padahituṃ, na bhikkhācariyāya yāpetuṃ sakkhissāmi, ko me gamanena attho, nivattissāmī”ti so vīriyaṃ [V 1.0304] ossajitvā te bhikkhū anugantvā nivatti. Tepi kho bhikkhū kosalesu cārikaṃ caramānā aññataraṃ paccantagāmaṃ [P 1.0317] gantvā taṃ upanissāya ekasmiṃ araññāyatane vassaṃ upagantvā antotemāsaṃ appamattā ghaṭentā vāyamantā vipassanāgabbhaṃ gāhāpetvā pathaviṃ unnādayamānā arahattaṃ patvā vutthavassā pavāretvā “paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ satthu ārocessāmā”ti tato nikkhamitvā anupubbena jetavanaṃ patvā pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā ācariyupajjhāye disvā tathāgataṃ daṭṭhukāmā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā tehi saddhiṃ madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ akāsi. Te katapaṭisanthārā attanā paṭiladdhaguṇaṃ tathāgatassa ārocesuṃ, satthā te bhikkhū pasaṃsi. Kuṭumbikaputtatissatthero satthāraṃ tesaṃ guṇakathaṃ kathentaṃ disvā sayampi samaṇadhammaṃ kātukāmo jāto. Tepi kho bhikkhū “mayaṃ, bhante, tameva araññavāsaṃ gantvā vasissāmā”ti satthāraṃ āpucchiṃsu. Satthā “sādhū”ti anujāni. Te satthāraṃ vanditvā pariveṇaṃ agamaṃsu.

Now, among them was a monk named Elder Kuṭumbikaputtatissa, who was lazy, lacking in energy, and greedy for tastes. He thought thus: 'I will not be able to live in the forest, nor to strive in exertion, nor to sustain myself by gathering alms. What is the use of my going? I shall turn back.' So, abandoning his effort, he accompanied those monks for a short way and then turned back. Those monks, wandering on tour in the Kosala country, went to a certain border village. Dwelling near it in a forest hermitage, they entered the rains retreat. For the three months, being diligent, striving, and making an effort, they developed insight, making the earth resound, and attained Arahantship. Having completed the rains retreat and performed the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they thought, 'We will announce the quality we have attained to the Teacher.' Departing from there, they arrived in due course at Jetavana. Having put away their bowls and robes and seen their teachers and preceptors, desiring to see the Tathāgata, they went into the Teacher's presence, paid homage, and sat down. The Teacher exchanged pleasant greetings with them. After the courteous exchange, they announced to the Tathāgata the quality they had attained. The Teacher praised those monks. Seeing the Teacher speaking in praise of their qualities, Elder Kuṭumbikaputtatissa himself became desirous of practicing the duties of a recluse. Those monks then asked the Teacher, 'Venerable sir, we will go and live in that same forest dwelling.' The Teacher consented, saying, 'Very well.' They paid homage to the Teacher and went to their monastic dwelling.

Atha so kuṭumbikaputtatissatthero rattibhāgasamanantare accāraddhavīriyo hutvā ativegena samaṇadhammaṃ karonto majjhimayāmasamanantare ālambanaphalakaṃ nissāya ṭhitakova niddāyanto parivattitvā pati, ūruṭṭhikaṃ bhijji, vedanā mahantā jātā. Tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ taṃ paṭijaggantānaṃ gamanaṃ na sampajji. Atha ne upaṭṭhānavelāyaṃ āgate satthā pucchi “nanu tumhe, bhikkhave, ‘sve gamissāmā’ti hiyyo āpucchitthā”ti? “Āma, bhante, apica kho pana amhākaṃ sahāyako kuṭumbikaputtatissatthero akāle ativegena samaṇadhammaṃ karonto niddābhibhūto parivattitvā patito, ūruṭṭhissa bhinnaṃ, taṃ nissāya amhākaṃ gamanaṃ na sampajjī”ti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa attano hīnavīriyabhāvena akāle [M 1.0336] ativegena vīriyaṃ karonto tumhākaṃ gamanantarāyaṃ karoti, pubbepesa tumhākaṃ gamanantarāyaṃ akāsiyevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then that Elder Kuṭumbikaputtatissa, having become one of extreme exertion just after the beginning of the night, was practicing the duties of a recluse with great haste. Just after the middle watch, while standing leaning against a support board, he dozed off, turned over, and fell. His thigh bone was broken, and great pain arose. For those monks who were tending to him, their journey could not proceed. Then, when they came at the time of attendance, the Teacher asked them, 'Monks, did you not take leave of me yesterday, saying, "We will go tomorrow"?' 'Yes, venerable sir. However, our companion, Elder Kuṭumbikaputtatissa, while practicing the duties of a recluse with great haste at an improper time, was overcome by drowsiness, turned over, and fell. His thigh bone is broken. On his account, our journey could not proceed.' The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that this one, due to his deficient energy, making an effort with great haste at an improper time, creates an obstacle to your journey. In the past, too, he created an obstacle to your journey.' And, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.

Atīte gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilāyaṃ bodhisatto disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañca māṇavakasatāni sippaṃ uggaṇhāpesi. Athassa te māṇavā ekadivasaṃ dāruṃ āharaṇatthāya araññaṃ gantvā dārūni uddhariṃsu. Tesaṃ antare eko kusītamāṇavo mahantaṃ varuṇarukkhaṃ disvā “sukkharukkho eso”ti saññāya “muhuttaṃ tāva nipajjitvā pacchā rukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā [P 1.0318] dārūni pātetvā ādāya gamissāmī”ti uttarisāṭakaṃ pattharitvā nipajjitvā kākacchamāno niddaṃ okkami. Itare māṇavakā dārukalāpe bandhitvā ādāya gacchantā taṃ pādena piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā pabodhetvā agamaṃsu. Kusītamāṇavo uṭṭhāya akkhīni puñchitvā puñchitvā [V 1.0305] avigataniddova varuṇarukkhaṃ abhiruhitvā sākhaṃ gahetvā attano abhimukhaṃ ākaḍḍhitvā bhañjanto bhijjitvā uṭṭhitakoṭiyā attano akkhiṃ bhindāpetvā ekena hatthena taṃ pidhāya ekena hatthena alladārūni bhañjitvā rukkhato oruyha dārukalāpaṃ bandhitvā ukkhipitvā vegena gantvā tehi pātitānaṃ dārūnaṃ upari pātesi.

In the past, in the country of Gandhāra, in the city of Takkasilā, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher who taught arts to five hundred young men. One day, those young men went to the forest to gather firewood and collected wood. Among them, a lazy young man saw a large Varuṇa tree and, perceiving it to be a dry tree, thought, 'I will first lie down for a moment, and afterwards I will climb the tree, break off some firewood, and take it with me.' Spreading out his upper robe, he lay down and, snoring like a crow, he fell asleep. The other young men tied their bundles of firewood, and as they were leaving, they struck him on the back with a foot to wake him up, and then departed. The lazy young man got up and, rubbing his eyes again and again, still not free from drowsiness, climbed the Varuṇa tree. Grasping a branch, he pulled it towards himself to break it. As it broke, the end of it sprang up and pierced his eye. Covering it with one hand, he broke off wet firewood with the other, climbed down from the tree, tied the bundle of firewood, lifted it up, and went quickly and dropped it on top of the firewood that had been gathered by the others.

Taṃ divasañca janapadagāmake ekaṃ kulaṃ “sve brāhmaṇavācanakaṃ karissāmā”ti ācariyaṃ nimantesi. Ācariyo māṇavake āha “tātā, sve ekaṃ gāmakaṃ gantabbaṃ, tumhe pana nirāhārā na sakkhissatha gantuṃ, pātova yāguṃ pacāpetvā tattha gantvā attanā laddhakoṭṭhāsañca amhākaṃ pattakoṭṭhāsañca sabbamādāya āgacchathā”ti. Te pātova yāgupacanatthāya dāsiṃ uṭṭhāpetvā “khippaṃ no yāguṃ pacāhī”ti āhaṃsu. Sā dārūni gaṇhantī upari ṭhitāni allavaruṇadārūni gahetvā punappunaṃ mukhavātaṃ dadamānāpi aggiṃ ujjāletuṃ asakkontī sūriyaṃ uṭṭhāpesi. Māṇavakā “atidivā jāto, idāni na sakkā gantu”nti ācariyassa santikaṃ agamiṃsu. Ācariyo “kiṃ, tātā, na gatatthā”ti? “Āma, ācariya na gatamhā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Asuko nāma kusītamāṇavo amhehi saddhiṃ dārūnamatthāya araññaṃ gantvā varuṇarukkhamūle niddāyitvā pacchā [M 1.0337] vegena rukkhaṃ āruyha akkhiṃ bhindāpetvā allavaruṇadārūni āharitvā amhehi ānītadārūnaṃ upari pakkhipi. Yāgupācikā tāni sukkhadārusaññāya gahetvā yāva sūriyuggamanā ujjāletuṃ nāsakkhi. Iminā no kāraṇena gamanantarāyo jāto”ti. Ācariyo māṇavena katakammaṃ sutvā “andhabālānaṃ kammaṃ nissāya evarūpā parihāni hotī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi –

And on that day, in a country village, a certain family invited the teacher, saying, 'Tomorrow we will have a recitation by the Brahmins.' The teacher told the young men, 'My dears, tomorrow we must go to a certain village. You, however, will not be able to go without sustenance. Therefore, have gruel cooked early in the morning, go there, and taking both the portion you receive and the portion we are to receive, bring it all back.' Early in the morning, for the purpose of cooking the gruel, they roused a servant girl and said, 'Quickly, cook gruel for us.' While gathering firewood, she took some wet Varuṇa wood that was on top, and though she blew on it again and again, she was unable to make the fire blaze, and the sun rose. The young men said, 'It has become too late in the day; now it is not possible to go,' and went to the teacher. The teacher asked, 'What is it, my dears, have you not gone?' They replied, 'Indeed, teacher, we have not gone.' 'For what reason?' 'A certain lazy young man went with us to the forest for firewood, slept at the foot of a Varuṇa tree, then later, climbing the tree in haste and injuring his eye, brought back wet Varuṇa wood and threw it on top of the wood we had brought. The girl cooking the gruel, mistaking it for dry wood, took it and was unable to make the fire blaze until sunrise. For this reason, our journey was obstructed.' Hearing what the young man had done, the teacher said, 'Such a loss occurs because of the actions of blind fools,' and he uttered this verse:

71.

71.

“Yo [P 1.0319] pubbe karaṇīyāni, pacchā so kātumicchati;

Varuṇakaṭṭhabhañjova, sa pacchā manutappatī”ti.

He who wishes to do later what should be done before, like the breaker of the Varuṇa wood, that person afterwards grieves.

Tattha sa pacchā manutappatīti yo koci puggalo “idaṃ pubbe kattabbaṃ, idaṃ pacchā”ti avīmaṃsitvā pubbe karaṇīyāni paṭhamameva kattabbakammāni pacchā karoti, ayaṃ varuṇakaṭṭhabhañjo amhākaṃ māṇavako viya so bālapuggalo pacchā anutappati socati paridevatīti attho.

Therein, 'that person afterwards grieves' means: any person who, without reflecting, 'This should be done before, this later,' does afterwards those deeds that should be done first—that foolish person, like our young man who broke the Varuṇa wood, afterwards grieves, sorrows, and laments. This is the meaning.

Evaṃ bodhisatto antevāsikānaṃ imaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathetvā dānādīni puññāni karitvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having explained this reason to his pupils, performed meritorious deeds such as generosity, and at the end of his life, passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 1.0306] “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa tumhākaṃ antarāyaṃ karoti, pubbepi akāsiyevā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā akkhibhedaṃ patto māṇavo ūrubhedaṃ pattabhikkhu ahosi, sesamāṇavā buddhaparisā, ācariyabrāhmaṇo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Monks, it is not only now that this one causes you an obstruction; he did so in the past as well.' Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection, and identified the birth story, he said: 'At that time, the young man who suffered the eye injury was the monk who has suffered the thigh injury, the remaining young men were the Buddha's assembly, and the Brahmin teacher was indeed myself.'

Varuṇajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Varuṇa Jātaka, the First.

[72] 2. Sīlavanāgarājajātakavaṇṇanā

2. The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Virtuous Elephant King

Akataññussa posassāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dhammasabhāyañhi bhikkhū “āvuso, devadatto akataññū tathāgatassa guṇe na jānātī”ti kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto [M 1.0338] akataññū, pubbepi akataññūyeva, na kadāci mayhaṃ guṇaṃ jānātī”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'For the ungrateful person...' This the Teacher spoke concerning Devadatta while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove. For in the Hall of Dhamma, the monks were seated discussing, 'Friends, Devadatta is ungrateful; he does not recognize the virtues of the Tathāgata.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled here?' When they replied, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, Devadatta is not only now ungrateful; he was ungrateful in the past as well. He has never recognized my virtues.' Then, at their request, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavantappadese hatthiyoniyaṃ nibbatti. So mātukucchito nikkhanto sabbaseto ahosi rajatapuñjasannibho, akkhīni panassa maṇiguḷasadisāni, paññāyamānāni pañca pasādāni ahesuṃ, mukhaṃ rattakambalasadisaṃ, soṇḍā rattasuvaṇṇabindupaṭimaṇḍitaṃ rajatadāmaṃ viya, cattāro pādā katalākhārasaparikammā viya. Evamassa dasahi pāramīhi alaṅkato rūpasobhaggappatto attabhāvo ahosi. Atha naṃ viññutaṃ pattaṃ sakalahimavante [P 1.0320] vāraṇā sannipatitvā upaṭṭhahantā vicariṃsu. Evaṃ so asītisahassavāraṇaparivāro himavantappadese vasamāno aparabhāge gaṇe dosaṃ disvā gaṇamhā kāyavivekāya ekakova araññe vāsaṃ kappesi. Sīlavantatāya ca panassa “sīlavanāgarājā” tveva nāmaṃ ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the Himalayan region into an elephant species. Emerging from his mother's womb, he was entirely white, resembling a heap of silver. His eyes were like jewel orbs, shining, and his five sense faculties were manifestly clear. His mouth was like a red cloth, his trunk was like a silver garland adorned with spots of red gold, and his four feet were as if prepared with red lacquer. Thus his being, adorned with the ten perfections, attained radiant beauty. When he reached maturity, all the elephants in the entire Himalayas gathered and attended upon him. Thus, dwelling in the Himalayan region with a retinue of eighty thousand elephants, he later saw fault in the herd and, seeking physical solitude from the herd, resolved to live alone in the forest. And because of his virtue, he was given the name 'Sīlavanāgarājā,' the Virtuous Elephant King.

Atheko bārāṇasivāsiko vanacarako himavantaṃ pavisitvā attano ājīvabhaṇḍakaṃ gavesamāno disā vavatthāpetuṃ asakkonto maggamūḷho hutvā maraṇabhayabhīto bāhā paggayha paridevamāno vicarati. Bodhisatto tassa taṃ balavaparidevitaṃ sutvā “imaṃ purisaṃ dukkhā mocessāmī”ti kāruññena codito tassa santikaṃ agamāsi. So taṃ disvāva bhīto palāyi. Bodhisatto taṃ palāyantaṃ disvā tattheva aṭṭhāsi. So puriso bodhisattaṃ ṭhitaṃ disvā aṭṭhāsi[V 1.0307]. Bodhisatto puna agamāsi, so puna palāyitvā tassa ṭhitakāle ṭhatvā cintesi “ayaṃ vāraṇo mama palāyanakāle tiṭṭhati, ṭhitakāle āgacchati, nāyaṃ mayhaṃ anatthakāmo, imamhā pana maṃ dukkhā mācetukāmo bhavissatī”ti sūro hutvā aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “kasmā bho tvaṃ purisa, paridevamāno vicarasī”ti pucchi. “Sāmi, disā vavatthāpetuṃ asakkonto maggamūḷho hutvā maraṇabhayenā”ti. Atha naṃ bodhisatto attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ netvā katipāhaṃ phalāphalehi santappetvā “bho, purisa, mā bhāyi, ahaṃ taṃ manussapathaṃ [M 1.0339] nessāmī”ti attano piṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā manussapathaṃ pāyāsi.

At that time, a certain hunter from Bārāṇasī entered the Himālaya to seek his livelihood. Unable to determine the directions, he became lost on the path. Terrified by the fear of death, he wandered about, wailing with outstretched arms. The Bodhisatta, hearing his loud lamentation, was urged by compassion and thought, 'I shall free this man from suffering,' and so approached him. The man, upon seeing him, fled in fear. Seeing him flee, the Bodhisatta stood still right there. The man, seeing the Bodhisatta standing still, also stopped. The Bodhisatta approached again; the man fled again, but stopped when the Bodhisatta stood still, and he reflected: 'This elephant stands still when I flee and approaches when I stop. He must not wish me harm; rather, he must wish to free me from this suffering.' Becoming courageous, he stood his ground. The Bodhisatta approached him and asked, 'Good man, why do you wander about wailing?'
