'Sir,' he replied, 'being unable to determine the directions, I have become lost on the path and am terrified by the fear of death.' Then the Bodhisatta led him to his own dwelling place, satisfied him with various fruits for some days, and said, 'Good man, do not be afraid. I will take you to the path of men.' Having him sit upon his back, he set out for the path of men.

Atha kho so mittadubbhī puriso “sace koci pucchissati, ācikkhitabbaṃ bhavissatī”ti bodhisattassa piṭṭhe nisinnoyeva rukkhanimittaṃ pabbatanimittaṃ upadhārentova gacchati. Atha naṃ bodhisatto araññā nīharitvā bārāṇasigāmimahāmagge ṭhapetvā “bho purisa, iminā maggena gaccha, mayhaṃ pana vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pucchitopi apucchitopi mā kassaci ācikkhī”ti taṃ uyyojetvā attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃyeva agamāsi. Atha so puriso bārāṇasiṃ gantvā anuvicaranto dantakāravīthiṃ patvā dantakāre dantavikatiyo kurumāne disvā “kiṃ pana bho, jīvadantampi [P 1.0321] labhitvā gaṇheyyāthā”ti? “Bho, kiṃ vadesi, jīvadanto nāma matahatthidantato mahagghataro”ti. “Tena hi ahaṃ vo jīvadantaṃ āharissāmī”ti pātheyyaṃ gahetvā kharakakacaṃ ādāya bodhisattassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi.

Then that treacherous man, while still seated on the Bodhisatta's back, went along noting the landmarks of trees and mountains, thinking, 'If anyone should ask, it will have to be told.' Then the Bodhisatta, having led him out of the forest and placed him on the great road to Bārāṇasī, said, 'Good man, go by this road. But whether asked or not, do not tell anyone of my dwelling place.' Having sent him on his way, he returned to his own dwelling. Then that man, having gone to Bārāṇasī and wandering about, came to the street of the ivory carvers. Seeing the ivory carvers making various ivory articles, he asked, 'Sirs, if you could get the tusk of a living elephant, would you take it?' 'Good man, what are you saying? The tusk of a living elephant is far more valuable than that of a dead elephant.' 'In that case, I will bring you the tusk of a living elephant,' he said. Taking provisions and a sharp saw, he went to the Bodhisatta's dwelling place.

Bodhisatto taṃ disvā “kimatthaṃ āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ, sāmi, duggato kapaṇo jīvituṃ asakkonto tumhe dantakhaṇḍaṃ yācitvā sace dassatha, taṃ ādāya gantvā vikkiṇitvā tena mūlena jīvissāmī”ti āgatoti. “Hotu bho, dantaṃ te dassāmi, sace dantakappanatthāya kakacaṃ atthī”ti. “Kakacaṃ gahetvā āgatomhi sāmī”ti. “Tena hi dante kakacena kantitvā ādāya gacchā”ti bodhisatto pāde samiñjitvā gonisinnakaṃ nisīdi. So dvepi aggadante chindi. Bodhisatto te dante soṇḍāya gahetvā “bho purisa, nāhaṃ ‘ete dantā mayhaṃ appiyā amanāpā’ti dammi, imehi pana me dantehi sataguṇena sahassaguṇena satasahassaguṇena sabbadhammapaṭivedhanasamatthā sabbaññutaññāṇadantāva piyatarā, tassa me idaṃ dantadānaṃ sabbaññutaññāṇapaṭivijjhanatthāya hotū”ti sabbaññutaññāṇassa ārādhanaṃ katvā dantayugalaṃ adāsi.

The Bodhisatta, seeing him, asked, 'For what reason have you come?' 'Sir, I am poor and wretched, unable to make a living. I have come to beg you for a piece of tusk. If you give it, I will take it, sell it, and live on that income.' 'So be it, good man. I will give you the tusks, if you have a saw for cutting them.' 'I have brought a saw, sir.' 'Then cut the tusks with the saw and take them,' said the Bodhisatta, and drawing in his feet, he sat down in the posture of a cow. The man cut off the tips of both tusks. The Bodhisatta, taking the tusks with his trunk, said, 'Good man, it is not because these tusks are unloved or displeasing to me that I give them. Rather, the tusk of omniscient knowledge, which is capable of penetrating all phenomena, is a hundred times, a thousand times, a hundred thousand times dearer to me than these. May this gift of my tusks be for the attainment of omniscient knowledge!' Having thus made an aspiration for omniscient knowledge, he gave the pair of tusks.

So [V 1.0308] taṃ ādāya gantvā vikkiṇitvā tasmiṃ mūle khīṇe puna bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “sāmi, tumhākaṃ dante vikkiṇitvā laddhamūlaṃ mayhaṃ [M 1.0340] iṇasodhanamattameva jātaṃ, avasesadante dethā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā purimanayeneva kappāpetvā avasesadante adāsi. So tepi vikkiṇitvā puna āgantvā “sāmi, jīvituṃ na sakkomi, mūladāṭhā me dethā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā purimanayeneva nisīdi. So pāpapuriso mahāsattassa rajatadāmasadisaṃ soṇḍaṃ maddamāno kelāsakūṭasadisaṃ kumbhaṃ abhiruhitvā ubho dantakoṭiyo paṇhiyā paharanto maṃsaṃ viyūhitvā kumbhaṃ āruyha kharakakacena mūladāṭhā kappetvā pakkāmi. Bodhisattassa dassanūpacāraṃ vijahanteyeva pana tasmiṃ pāpapurise catunahutādhikadviyojanasatasahassabahalā ghanapathavī [P 1.0322] sineruyugandharādayo mahābhāre duggandhajegucchāni gūthamuttādīni ca dhāretuṃ samatthāpi tassa aguṇarāsiṃ dhāretuṃ asakkontī viya bhijjitvā vivaraṃ adāsi. Tāvadeva avīcimahānirayato aggijālā nikkhamitvā taṃ mittadubbhipurisaṃ kulasantakena kambalena pārupantī viya parikkhipitvā gaṇhi.

He took the tusks, went and sold them. When that money was spent, he went again to the Bodhisatta and said, 'Sir, the money I received from selling your tusks was only enough to clear my debts. Please give me the remaining tusks.' The Bodhisatta agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and in the same way as before, had him cut and take the remaining tusks. The man sold those as well, and returning again, said, 'Sir, I cannot make a living. Give me the very roots of the tusks.' The Bodhisatta agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and sat down as before. That evil man, treading on the Great Being's trunk which was like a silver chain, climbed upon his head which was like the peak of Mount Kelāsa. Kicking the flesh away from the two tusk sockets with his heels, he climbed onto the head, cut out the roots of the tusks with the sharp saw, and departed. But just as that evil man was passing out of the Bodhisatta's range of sight, the solid earth—two hundred and forty thousand yojanas thick, capable of bearing the great weights of Sineru, Yugandhara, and other mountains, as well as foul-smelling and repulsive things like excrement and urine—as if unable to bear the mass of his demerit, split apart and gave way. At that very moment, flames from the great Avīci hell shot up and seized that treacherous man, wrapping around him as if covering him with a family blanket.

Evaṃ tassa pāpapuggalassa pathaviṃ paviṭṭhakāle tasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe adhivatthā rukkhadevatā “akataññū mittadubbhī puggalo cakkavattirajjaṃ datvāpi tosetuṃ na sakkā”ti vanaṃ unnādetvā dhammaṃ desayamānā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Thus, at the time that evil person entered the earth, the tree-deity dwelling in that forest grove, teaching the Dhamma and making the forest resound, said: 'An ungrateful, treacherous person cannot be satisfied even if given the kingdom of a universal monarch,' and spoke this verse:

72.

72.

“Akataññussa posassa, niccaṃ vivaradassino;

Sabbaṃ ce pathaviṃ dajjā, neva naṃ abhirādhaye”ti.

For a person who is ungrateful, always finding fault, even if one were to give the whole earth, one could never satisfy him.

Tattha akataññussāti attano kataguṇaṃ ajānantassa. Posassāti purisassa. Vivaradassinoti chiddameva okāsameva olokentassa. Sabbaṃ ce pathaviṃ dajjāti sacepi tādisassa puggalassa sakalaṃ cakkavattirajjaṃ, imaṃ vā pana mahāpathaviṃ parivattetvā pathavojaṃ dadeyya. Neva naṃ abhirādhayeti evaṃ karontopi evarūpaṃ kataguṇaviddhaṃsakaṃ koci paritosetuṃ vā pasādetuṃ vā na sakkuṇeyyāti attho.

Here, 'ungrateful' means one who does not recognize a kindness done to him. 'Man' refers to a person. 'Seeing faults' means one who only looks for flaws and openings. 'Even if one gave the whole earth' means even if such a person were given the entire kingdom of a universal monarch, or if this great earth were transformed and its very essence given to him. 'He would not be pleased' means that even by doing so, no one could satisfy or please such a destroyer of gratitude—this is the meaning.

Evaṃ sā devatā vanaṃ unnādetvā dhammaṃ desesi. Bodhisatto yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ agamāsi.

Thus, the deity, having made the forest resound, taught the Dhamma. The Bodhisatta, having lived out his lifespan, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 1.0309][M 1.0341] “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva akataññū, pubbepi akataññūyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā mittadubbhī puggalo devadatto ahosi, rukkhadevatā sāriputto, sīlavanāgarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, 'Monks, Devadatta is not ungrateful only now; in the past, too, he was ungrateful.' Having said this, he delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the narrative, and identified the birth thus: 'At that time, the treacherous person was Devadatta, the tree deity was Sāriputta, and the virtuous elephant king was I myself.'

Sīlavanāgarājajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Sīlavanāgarāja Jātaka, the second.

[73] 3. Saccaṃkirajātakavaṇṇanā

[73] 3. The Commentary on the Saccaṃkira Jātaka

Saccaṃ kirevamāhaṃsūti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Bhikkhusaṅghasmiñhi dhammasabhāyaṃ nisīditvā “āvuso, devadatto satthu guṇaṃ na jānāti, vadhāyayeva parisakkatī”ti devadattassa aguṇaṃ kathente satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti [P 1.0323] pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi parisakkiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'They spoke the truth indeed.' The Teacher spoke this while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta's attempt to kill him. For when the community of monks was seated in the Dhamma hall, discussing Devadatta's faults and saying, 'Friends, Devadatta does not recognize the Teacher's virtues; he only attempts to kill him,' the Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you gathered together now?' When they told him what it was, he said, 'Monks, not only now does Devadatta attempt to kill me; he attempted to do so in the past as well.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa duṭṭhakumāro nāma putto ahosi kakkhaḷo pharuso pahaṭāsīvisūpamo, anakkositvā vā apaharitvā vā kenaci saddhiṃ na katheti. So antojanassa ca bahijanassa ca akkhimhi patitarajaṃ viya, khādituṃ āgatapisāco viya ca amanāpo ahosi ubbejanīyo. So ekadivasaṃ nadīkīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmo mahantena parivārena nadītīraṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe mahāmegho uṭṭhahi, disā andhakārā jātā. So dāsapessajanaṃ āha “etha bhaṇe, maṃ gahetvā nadīmajjhaṃ netvā nhāpetvā ānethā”ti. Te taṃ tattha netvā “kiṃ no rājā karissati, imaṃ pāpapurisaṃ ettheva māremā”ti mantayitvā “ettha gaccha kāḷakaṇṇī”ti udake naṃ opilāpetvā paccuttaritvā tīre aṭṭhaṃsu. “Kahaṃ kumāro”ti ca vutte “na mayaṃ kumāraṃ passāma, meghaṃ uṭṭhitaṃ disvā udake nimujjitvā purato āgato [M 1.0342] bhavissatī”ti. Amaccā rañño santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Rājā “kahaṃ me putto”ti pucchi. Na jānāma deva, meghe uṭṭhite “purato āgato bhavissatī”ti saññāya āgatamhāti. Rājā dvāraṃ vivarāpetvā “nadītīraṃ gantvā vicinathā”ti tattha tattha vicināpesi, koci kumāraṃ nāddasa.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, he had a son named Duṭṭhakumāra, who was harsh, cruel, and like a venomous snake that has been struck. He would not speak to anyone without first reviling or striking them. He was as unwelcome to the people of the inner and outer court as a speck of dust in the eye or a flesh-eating demon come to devour—a cause of dread. One day, wishing to play in the river, he went to the riverbank with a large retinue. At that moment, a great cloud arose, and the directions were plunged into darkness. He said to his servants, 'Come, sirs, take me to the middle of the river, bathe me, and bring me back.' They took him there and conspired, 'What can the king do to us? Let us kill this wicked man right here!' Saying, 'Be gone, you wretch!' they plunged him into the water, then crossed back and stood on the bank. When asked, 'Where is the prince?' they replied, 'We do not see the prince. Seeing the cloud arise, he must have dived into the water and gone on ahead.' The ministers went to the king. The king asked, 'Where is my son?' They answered, 'We do not know, Your Majesty. When the cloud arose, we came with the thought that he must have gone on ahead.' The king had the gates opened and said, 'Go to the riverbank and search!' He had them search everywhere, but no one saw the prince.

Sopi kho meghandhakāre deve vassante nadiyā vuyhamāno ekaṃ dārukkhandhaṃ disvā tattha nisīditvā [V 1.0310] maraṇabhayatajjito paridevamāno gacchati. Tasmiṃ pana kāle bārāṇasivāsī eko seṭṭhi nadītīre cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ nidahitvāva maranto dhanataṇhāya dhanapiṭṭhe sappo hutvā nibbatti. Aparo tasmiṃyeva padese tiṃsa koṭiyo nidahitvā dhanataṇhāya tattheva undūro hutvā nibbatti. Tesaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ udakaṃ pāvisi. Te udakassa paviṭṭhamaggeneva nikkhamitvā sotaṃ chindantā gantvā taṃ rājakumārena abhinisinnaṃ [P 1.0324] dārukkhandhaṃ patvā eko ekaṃ koṭiṃ, itaro itaraṃ āruyha khandhapiṭṭheyeva nipajjiṃsu. Tassāyeva kho pana nadiyā tīre eko simbalirukkho atthi, tattheko suvapotako vasati. Sopi rukkho udakena dhotamūlo nadīpiṭṭhe pati, suvapotako deve vassante uppatitvā gantuṃ asakkonto gantvā tasseva khandhassa ekapasse nilīyi. Evaṃ te cattāro janā ekato vuyhamānā gacchanti.

In the thick darkness, while the rain poured down, he was swept away by the river. Seeing a log floating by, he sat upon it, trembling with fear of death, wailing as he went. At that very time, a wealthy merchant from Bārāṇasī, who had buried forty crores of wealth by the riverbank before dying, was reborn as a snake on the treasure mound due to his craving for wealth. Another man, who had buried thirty crores in the same place, was reborn there as a rat due to his craving for wealth. The water flooded their dwelling places. They emerged through the opening where the water entered, cutting through the current, and reached the log where the prince was sitting. One climbed onto one end of the log, the other onto the other end, and they lay down upon the log itself. On the bank of that same river stood a silk-cotton tree, where a young parrot lived. The tree, its roots washed away by the water, fell into the river. Unable to fly away in the heavy rain, the parrot flew up and hid on one side of the same log. Thus, these four beings floated together down the river.

Bodhisattopi kho tasmiṃ kāle kāsiraṭṭhe udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vuḍḍhippatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā ekasmiṃ nadīnivattane paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā vasati. So aḍḍharattasamaye caṅkamamāno tassa rājakumārassa balavaparidevanasaddaṃ sutvā cintesi “mādise nāma mettānuddayasampanne tāpase passante etassa purisassa maraṇaṃ ayuttaṃ, udakato uddharitvā tassa jīvitadānaṃ dassāmī”ti. So taṃ “mā bhāyi, mā bhāyī”ti assāsetvā udakasotaṃ chindanto gantvā taṃ dārukkhandhaṃ ekāya koṭiyā gahetvā ākaḍḍhanto nāgabalo thāmasampanno ekavegena tīraṃ patvā kumāraṃ ukkhipitvā tīre patiṭṭhāpesi. Tepi sappādayo disvā ukkhipitvā assamapadaṃ netvā aggiṃ jāletvā “ime dubbalatarā”ti paṭhamaṃ sappādīnaṃ sarīraṃ sedetvā pacchā rājakumārassa sarīraṃ sedetvā tampi arogaṃ katvā āhāraṃ dentopi paṭhamaṃ sappādīnaṃyeva datvā pacchā tassa phalāphalāni upanāmesi. Rājakumāro “ayaṃ kūṭatāpaso maṃ rājakumāraṃ agaṇetvā tiracchānagatānaṃ sammānaṃ karotī”ti bodhisatte āghātaṃ bandhi.

At that time, the Bodhisatta was born in the Udicca brahmin clan in the Kāsi kingdom. Having come of age, he renounced the world to become an ascetic and, having built a leaf-hut by a river bend, he dwelt there. While walking at midnight, he heard the prince’s loud lamentation and thought, “While an ascetic like myself, full of loving-kindness and compassion, is present, it is not fitting that this man should die. I will pull him from the water and give him the gift of life.” So, comforting him with the words, “Do not fear, do not fear,” he cut through the water’s current, took hold of the log by one end, and, being endowed with the strength of an elephant, swiftly reached the shore. He lifted the prince and set him on the bank. Seeing the snake and the others as well, he picked them up and carried them to his hermitage, lit a fire, and thinking, “These are weaker,” he first warmed the bodies of the snake and the others and then warmed the prince’s body, restoring him to health. When offering food, he first gave it to the snake and the others, and only afterward presented fruits to the prince. The prince, thinking, “This deceitful ascetic disregards me, a prince, and gives honor to mere animals,” harbored resentment toward the Bodhisatta.

Tato [M 1.0343] katipāhaccayena sabbesupi tesu thāmabalappattesu nadiyā oghe pacchinne sappo tāpasaṃ vanditvā āha “bhante, tumhehi mayhaṃ mahāupakāro kato, na kho panāhaṃ daliddo, asukaṭṭhāne me cattālīsa hiraññakoṭiyo nidahitvā ṭhapitā, tumhākaṃ dhanena kicce sati sabbampetaṃ dhanaṃ tumhākaṃ dātuṃ sakkomi, taṃ ṭhānaṃ āgantvā ‘dīghā’ti pakkoseyyāthā”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Undūropi tatheva tāpasaṃ nimantetvā “asukaṭṭhāne ṭhatvā ‘undūrā’ti pakkoseyyāthā”ti [P 1.0325] vatvā pakkāmi. Suvapotako pana tāpasaṃ vanditvā “bhante, mayhaṃ dhanaṃ natthi, rattasālīhi pana vo atthe sati asukaṃ nāma mayhaṃ vasanaṭṭhānaṃ, tattha gantvā ‘suvā’ti pakkoseyyātha, ahaṃ ñātakānaṃ ārocetvā anekasakaṭapūramattā rattasāliyo āharāpetvā dātuṃ sakkomī”ti [V 1.0311] vatvā pakkāmi. Itaro pana mittadubbhī “dhammasudhammatāya kiñci avatvā gantuṃ ayuttaṃ, evaṃ taṃ attano santikaṃ āgataṃ māressāmī”ti cintetvā “bhante, mayi rajje patiṭṭhite āgaccheyyātha, ahaṃ vo catūhi paccayehi upaṭṭhahissāmī”ti vatvā pakkāmi. So gantvā na cirasseva rajje patiṭṭhāsi.

After a few days, when all of them had regained their strength and the river’s flood had subsided, the snake bowed to the ascetic and said, “Venerable sir, you have done me a great service. I am not poor; in a certain place, I have forty crores of gold buried. If you have need of wealth, I can give all this treasure to you. Come to that place and call out ‘Dīgha.’” Having said this, he departed. The mouse also invited the ascetic in the same way, saying, “Stand in a certain place and call out ‘Undūra.’” Having said this, he left. The young parrot then bowed to the ascetic and said, “Venerable sir, I have no wealth, but if you have need of red rice, go to my dwelling place and call out ‘Suvā.’ I will inform my relatives and have them bring many cartloads of red rice to give to you.” Having said this, he departed. But the treacherous friend thought, “It is not proper to depart without saying anything. Thus, when he comes into my presence, I will kill him.” So he said, “Venerable sir, when I am established in the kingdom, you must come. I will attend to you with the four requisites.” Having said this, he left. Not long after, he was established in the kingdom.

Bodhisatto “vīmaṃsissāmi tāva ne”ti paṭhamaṃ sappassa santikaṃ gantvā avidūre ṭhatvā “dīghā”ti pakkosi. So ekavacaneneva nikkhamitvā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā “bhante, imasmiṃ ṭhāne cattālīsa hiraññakoṭiyo, tā sabbāpi nīharitvā gaṇhathā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “evamatthu, uppanne kicce jānissāmī”ti taṃ nivattetvā undūrassa santikaṃ gantvā saddamakāsi. Sopi tatheva paṭipajji. Bodhisatto tampi nivattetvā suvassa santikaṃ gantvā “suvā”ti pakkosi. Sopi ekavacaneneva rukkhaggato otaritvā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā “kiṃ, bhante, mayhaṃ ñātakānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā himavantappadesato tumhākaṃ sayaṃjātasālī āharāpemī”ti pucchi. Bodhisatto “atthe sati jānissāmī”ti tampi nivattetvā “idāni rājānaṃ pariggaṇhissāmī”ti gantvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase ākappasampattiṃ katvā bhikkhācāravattena nagaraṃ pāvisi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe so mittadubbhī rājā alaṅkatahatthikkhandhavaragato mahantena parivārena [M 1.0344] nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ karoti. So bodhisattaṃ dūratova disvā “ayaṃ so kūṭatāpaso mama santike bhuñjitvā vasitukāmo āgato, yāva parisamajjhe attano mayhaṃ kataguṇaṃ nappakāseti, tāvadevassa sīsaṃ chindāpessāmī”ti purise olokesi. “Kiṃ karoma, devā”ti ca vutte “esa kūṭatāpaso maṃ kiñci yācitukāmo āgacchati maññe, etassa kāḷakaṇṇitāpasassa maṃ passituṃ adatvāva etaṃ gahetvā pacchābāhaṃ [P 1.0326] bandhitvā catukke catukke paharantā nagarā nikkhāmetvā āghātane sīsamassa chinditvā sarīraṃ sūle uttāsethā”ti āha. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā gantvā niraparādhaṃ mahāsattaṃ bandhitvā catukke catukke paharantā āghātanaṃ netuṃ ārabhiṃsu. Bodhisatto pahaṭapahaṭaṭṭhāne “amma, tātā”ti akanditvā nibbikāro imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta thought, “I will first test them,” and went to the snake. Standing not far off, he called out, “Dīgha!” The snake came out at a single call, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and said, “Venerable sir, in this place there are forty crores of gold; take it all away.” The Bodhisatta replied, “So be it. I will know when the need arises,” and dismissed him. Then he went to the mouse and made a sound. He too responded in the same way. The Bodhisatta dismissed him too and went to the parrot, calling out, “Suvā!” He too, at a single call, descended from the treetop, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, and asked, “What is it, venerable sir? Shall I go to my relatives and have them bring you self-grown rice from the Himalayan region?” The Bodhisatta said, “I will know when the need arises,” and dismissed him as well. Then he thought, “Now I will test the king,” and went to stay in the royal garden. The next day, having prepared himself with the proper attire of an ascetic, he entered the city on his alms round. At that moment, that treacherous king, adorned and mounted on a splendid elephant, was circumambulating the city with a large retinue. Seeing the Bodhisatta from afar, he thought, “This deceitful ascetic has come, wishing to eat and stay with me. Before he can proclaim in the midst of the assembly the good deed he did for me, I will have his head cut off.” He looked at his men. When they asked, “What shall we do, Your Majesty?” he replied, “This deceitful ascetic, I suppose, has come to ask something of me. Do not let this wretched ascetic see me. Seize him, bind his hands behind his back, strike him at every crossroads, drive him out of the city, cut off his head at the execution ground, and impale his body on a stake.” They agreed, “Very well,” and went to seize the innocent Great Being. Binding him, they began to lead him to the execution ground, striking him at every crossroads. Though beaten at every spot, the Bodhisatta, without crying out, “Oh mother! Oh father!” remained unperturbed and uttered this verse:

73.

73.

“Saccaṃ kirevamāhaṃsu, narā ekacciyā idha;

Kaṭṭhaṃ niplavitaṃ seyyo, na tvevekacciyo naro”ti.

“Indeed, some people in this world have spoken truly: ‘It is better to rescue a floating log than a certain kind of person.’”

Tattha [V 1.0312] saccaṃ kirevamāhaṃsūti avitathameva kira evaṃ vadanti. Narā ekacciyā idhāti idhekacce paṇḍitapurisā. Kaṭṭhaṃ niplavitaṃ seyyoti nadiyā vuyhamānaṃ sukkhadāruṃ niplavitaṃ uttāretvā thale ṭhapitaṃ seyyo sundarataro. Evañhi vadamānā te purisā saccaṃ kira vadanti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Tañhi yāgubhattādīnaṃ pacanatthāya, sītāturānaṃ visibbanatthāya, aññesampi ca parissayānaṃ haraṇatthāya upakāraṃ hoti. Na tvevekacciyo naroti ekacco pana mittadubbhī akataññū pāpapuriso oghena vuyhamāno hatthena gahetvā uttārito na tveva seyyo. Tathā hi ahaṃ imaṃ pāpapurisaṃ uttāretvā imaṃ attano dukkhaṃ āharinti. Evaṃ pahaṭapahaṭaṭṭhāne imaṃ gāthamāha.

Therein, ‘Indeed, they spoke thus truly’ means that they speak thus, and it is indeed not false. ‘Some people here’ means certain wise men here. ‘A floating piece of wood is better’ means a dry piece of wood carried by the river, when rescued and placed on the shore, is better, more excellent. Indeed, those men who speak thus speak the truth. Why is that? Because it is useful for cooking rice porridge and other foods, for warming those suffering from cold, and for warding off other misfortunes. ‘But not a certain kind of person’ means that a certain wicked person, a betrayer of friends, ungrateful, even when rescued from the flood by hand, is not better. For indeed, [one might say,] ‘Having rescued this wicked man, I brought this suffering upon myself.’ Thus, at every spot where he was struck, he spoke this verse.

Taṃ sutvā ye tattha paṇḍitapurisā, te āhaṃsu “kiṃ pana, bho pabbajita, tayā amhākaṃ rañño atthi koci guṇo kato”ti? Bodhisatto taṃ pavattiṃ ārocetvā “evamimaṃ mahoghato uttārento ahameva attano dukkhaṃ akāsiṃ, ‘na vata me porāṇakapaṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ kata’nti anussaritvā evaṃ vadāmī”ti āha. Taṃ [M 1.0345] sutvā khattiyabrāhmaṇādayo nagaravāsino “svāyaṃ mittadubbhī rājā evaṃ guṇasampannassa attano jīvitadāyakassa guṇamattampi na jānāti, taṃ nissāya kuto amhākaṃ vuḍḍhi, gaṇhatha na”nti kupitā samantato uṭṭhahitvā ususattipāsāṇamuggarādippahārehi hatthikkhandhagatameva naṃ ghātetvā pāde gahetvā kaḍḍhitvā parikhāpiṭṭhe chaḍḍetvā bodhisattaṃ abhisiñcitvā rajje patiṭṭhāpesuṃ.

Hearing this, the wise men there said, "But, venerable ascetic, what good have you done for our king?" The Bodhisatta, recounting the incident, replied, "Indeed, while rescuing him from this great flood, I myself brought suffering upon myself, recalling that 'I did not heed the words of the ancient sages,' I speak thus." Hearing this, the khattiyas, brahmins, and other city-dwellers, angry, exclaimed, "This king is a betrayer of friends! He does not recognize even a fraction of the merit of the one who gave him his life. Relying on him, how can we prosper? Seize him!" Rising up on all sides, they killed him with blows from arrows, spears, stones, clubs, and other weapons, right there on the elephant's back, dragged him by the feet, and threw him onto the moat bank. Then, they anointed the Bodhisatta and established him on the throne.

So dhammena rajjaṃ kārento puna ekadivasaṃ sappādayo [P 1.0327] pariggaṇhitukāmo mahantena parivārena sappassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “dīghā”ti pakkosi. Sappo āgantvā vanditvā “idaṃ te sāmi dhanaṃ gaṇhā”ti āha. Rājā cattālīsahiraññakoṭidhanaṃ amacce paṭicchāpetvā undūrassa santikaṃ gantvā “undūrā”ti pakkosi. Sopi āgantvā vanditvā tiṃsakoṭidhanaṃ niyyādesi. Rājā tampi amacce paṭicchāpetvā suvassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā “suvā”ti pakkosi. Sopi āgantvā pāde vanditvā “kiṃ, sāmi, sāliṃ āharāmī”ti āha. Rājā “sālīhi atthe sati āharissasi, ehi gacchāmā”ti sattatiyā hiraññakoṭīhi saddhiṃ te tayopi jane gāhāpetvā nagaraṃ gantvā pāsādavare mahātalaṃ āruyhaṃ dhanaṃ saṅgopetvā sappassa vasanatthāya suvaṇṇanāḷiṃ, undūrassa phalikaguhaṃ, suvassa suvaṇṇapañjaraṃ kārāpetvā sappassa ca suvassa ca bhojanatthāya devasikaṃ kañcanataṭṭake madhulāje, undūrassa gandhasālitaṇḍule dāpesi, dānādīni ca puññāni karoti. Evaṃ te cattāropi janā yāvajīvaṃ samaggā sammodamānā viharitvā jīvitakkhaye yathākammaṃ agamaṃsu.

Ruling righteously, one day he wished to gather his allies again. With a great retinue, he went to the snake’s dwelling and called out, “Dīgha!” The snake came, paid homage, and said, “Lord, take this wealth.” The king had forty crores of gold accepted by his ministers and then went to the mouse’s abode, calling, “Undūra!” He too came, paid homage, and offered thirty crores of wealth. The king had that also accepted by his ministers and then went to the parrot’s dwelling, calling, “Suva!” He too came, bowed at his feet, and asked, “Lord, shall I bring rice?” The king replied, “When there is need for rice, you shall bring it. Come, let us go.” Taking those three along with seventy crores of gold, he returned to the city. Ascending the splendid palace’s upper floor, he stored the wealth and had a golden tube made for the snake’s dwelling, a crystal cave for the mouse, and a golden cage for the parrot. Daily, he provided golden plates of honeyed parched rice for the snake and parrot, and fragrant rice for the mouse. He also performed meritorious deeds such as giving. Thus, those four lived in harmony and joy all their lives, and at life’s end, they passed on according to their deeds.

Satthā [V 1.0313] “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi parisakkiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā duṭṭharājā devadatto ahosi, sappo sāriputto, undūro moggallāno, suvo ānando, pacchā rajjappatto dhammarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, “Monks, not only now does Devadatta try to kill me; he also tried in the past.” Having brought forth this teaching, he connected the sequence of events and identified the Jātaka: “Then, the wicked king was Devadatta, the snake was Sāriputta, the mouse was Moggallāna, the parrot was Ānanda, but the righteous king who later attained sovereignty was I myself.”

Saccaṃkirajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The third story, the Commentary on the Saccaṃkira Jātaka, is concluded.

[74] 4. Rukkhadhammajātakavaṇṇanā

[74] 4. Commentary on the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka

Sādhū [M 1.0346] sambahulā ñātīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto udakakalahe attano ñātakānaṃ mahāvināsaṃ paccupaṭṭhitaṃ ñatvā ākāsena gantvā rohiṇīnadiyā upari pallaṅkena nisīditvā nīlaraṃsiṃ vissajjetvā ñātake saṃvejetvā ākāsā oruyha nadītīre nisinno taṃ kalahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ayamettha saṅkhepo, vitthāro pana kuṇālajātake (jā. 2.21.kuṇālajātaka) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana satthā ñātake āmantetvā “mahārājā[P 1.0328], tumhe ñātakā, ñātakehi nāma samaggehi sammodamānehi bhavituṃ vaṭṭati. Ñātakānañhi sāmaggiyā sati paccāmittā okāsaṃ na labhanti, tiṭṭhantu tāva manussabhūtā, acetanānaṃ rukkhānampi sāmaggiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭati. Atītasmiñhi himavantappadese mahāvāto sālavanaṃ pahari, tassa pana sālavanassa aññamaññaṃ rukkhagacchagumbalatāhi sambandhattā ekarukkhampi pātetuṃ asakkonto matthakamatthakeneva agamāsi. Ekaṃ pana aṅgaṇe ṭhitaṃ sākhāviṭapasampannampi mahārukkhaṃ aññehi rukkhehi asambandhattā ummūletvā bhūmiyaṃ pātesi, iminā kāraṇena tumhehipi samaggehi sammodamānehi bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Good are many kinsmen…”—This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, knowing that a great destruction was imminent for his own relatives due to a water dispute. He went through the air and sat cross-legged above the Rohiṇī River. Emitting a blue ray, he stirred his relatives to a sense of urgency. Descending from the sky, he sat on the riverbank and spoke about that dispute. This is the summary here; the details will be clear in the Kuṇāla Jātaka. At that time, the Teacher addressed his relatives: “Great kings, you are relatives. Relatives should live in harmony and mutual joy. When relatives are united, enemies find no opportunity. Let alone human beings, it is proper even for insentient trees to achieve unity. In the past, in the region of the Himalayas, a great wind struck a grove of sal trees. Because the sal trees in that grove were interconnected with one another by trees, shrubs, thickets, and creepers, the wind could not fell even a single tree and had to pass over their tops. But a great tree standing alone in an open space, though full of branches and foliage, was uprooted and thrown to the ground because it was not connected to other trees. For this reason, you too should live in harmony and mutual joy.” Having spoken thus, he responded to their request by bringing forth a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente paṭhamaṃ uppanno vessavaṇo mahārājā cavi, sakko aññaṃ vessavaṇaṃ ṭhapesi. Etasmiṃ vessavaṇe parivatte pacchā nibbattavessavaṇo “rukkhagacchagumbalatānaṃ attano attano ruccanaṭṭhāne vimānaṃ gaṇhantū”ti sāsanaṃ pesesi. Tadā bodhisatto himavantappadese ekasmiṃ sālavane rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. So ñātake āha “tumhe vimānāni gaṇhantā aṅgaṇe ṭhitarukkhesu mā gaṇhatha, imasmiṃ pana sālavane mayā gahitavimānaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitavimānāni gaṇhathā”ti. Tattha bodhisattassa vacanakarā paṇḍitadevatā bodhisattassa vimānaṃ parivāretvā ṭhitavimānāni gaṇhiṃsu. Apaṇḍitā pana devatā “kiṃ amhākaṃ attho araññavimānehi, mayaṃ manussapathe gāmanigamarājadhānidvāresu vimānāni [V 1.0314] gaṇhissāma. Gāmādayo hi upanissāya vasamānā devatā lābhaggayasaggappattā hontī”ti manussapathe aṅgaṇaṭṭhāne nibbattamahārukkhesu vimānāni gaṇhiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the first great King Vessavaṇa passed away, and Sakka appointed another. This new Vessavaṇa sent out a decree: 'Let the deities of trees, shrubs, bushes, and creepers each take a mansion in a place pleasing to them.' At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a certain grove of sal trees in the Himalayan region. He addressed his kinsfolk: 'When you take mansions, do not take them on trees standing in open spaces. Instead, in this sal grove, take mansions standing around the mansion I have taken.' There, the wise deities who followed the Bodhisatta's word took mansions standing around the Bodhisatta's mansion. But the foolish deities thought, 'What use are forest mansions to us? We will take mansions along human paths, at the gates of villages, towns, and royal capitals. For deities dwelling near villages and such attain the highest gain and fame.' So they took mansions on great trees that had grown along human paths and in open spaces.

Athekasmiṃ [M 1.0347] divase mahatī vātavuṭṭhi uppajji. Vātassa atibalavatāya daḷhamūlā vanajeṭṭhakarukkhāpi saṃbhaggasākhāviṭapā samūlā nipatiṃsu. Taṃ pana aññamaññaṃ sambandhanena ṭhitaṃ sālavanaṃ patvā ito cito ca paharanto ekarukkhampi pātetuṃ nāsakkhi. Bhaggavimānā devatā nippaṭisaraṇā dārake hatthesu gahetvā himavantaṃ gantvā attano pavattiṃ sālavanadevatānaṃ [P 1.0329] kathayiṃsu. Tā tāsaṃ evaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ bodhisattassa ārocesuṃ. Bodhisatto “paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ aggahetvā nippaccayaṭṭhānaṃ gatā nāma evarūpāva hontī”ti vatvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, on a certain day, a great storm of wind and rain arose. Due to the exceeding force of the wind, even the sturdy-rooted, chief trees of the forest, with their branches and boughs broken, fell uprooted. But when the wind reached that sal grove, which stood firm through mutual connection, though it struck from every side, it could not fell even a single tree. The deities whose mansions were shattered, being without refuge and taking their children by the hand, went to the Himalayas and recounted their situation to the deities of the sal grove. These in turn reported their arrival to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, saying, 'Those who, not heeding the words of the wise, go to a place without support, indeed meet such a fate,' taught the Dhamma and spoke this verse:

74.

74.

“Sādhū sambahulā ñātī, api rukkhā araññajā;

Vāto vahati ekaṭṭhaṃ, brahantampi vanappati”nti.

Good are many kinsfolk, and so too are trees of the forest; the wind overthrows a tree that stands alone, even a mighty one.

Tattha sambahulā ñātīti cattāro upādāya tatuttari satasahassampi sambahulā nāma, evaṃ sambahulā aññamaññaṃ nissāya vasantā ñātakā. Sādhūti sobhanā pasatthā, parehi appadhaṃsiyāti attho. Api rukkhā araññajāti tiṭṭhantu manussabhūtā, araññe jātarukkhāpi sambahulā aññamaññūpatthambhena ṭhitā sādhuyeva. Rukkhānampi hi sapaccayabhāvo laddhuṃ vaṭṭati. Vāto vahati ekaṭṭhanti puratthimādibhedo vāto vāyanto aṅgaṇaṭṭhāne ṭhitaṃ ekaṭṭhaṃ ekakameva ṭhitaṃ brahantampi vanappatiṃ sākhāviṭapasampannaṃ mahārukkhampi vahati, ummūletvā pātetīti attho. Bodhisatto imaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathetvā āyukkhaye yathākammaṃ gato.

Herein, 'many kinsfolk' means from four upwards, even to a hundred thousand; thus many kinsfolk are they who live depending on one another. 'Good' means excellent and praiseworthy; the meaning is that they are not easily assailed by others. 'And so too are trees of the forest' means, let alone human beings, even trees born in the forest, when there are many, stand well by supporting one another. For it should be understood that even trees have a condition of mutual dependence. 'The wind overthrows a tree that stands alone' means that the wind, blowing from various directions such as the east, overthrows a great lord of the forest, a mighty tree endowed with branches and boughs, that stands solitary, all alone, in an open space; the meaning is, it uproots and fells it. Having explained this reason, the Bodhisatta, at the end of his lifespan, passed on according to his karma.

Satthāpi “evaṃ, mahārājā, ñātakānaṃ tāva sāmaggiyeva laddhuṃ vaṭṭati, samaggā sammodamānā piyasaṃvāsameva vasathā”ti imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā devatā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, paṇḍitadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher also said, 'Thus, great king, it is fitting above all that kinsfolk should achieve concord. Being united and rejoicing together, you should dwell in pleasant harmony.' Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, he made the connection and identified the birth: 'At that time, the deities were the Buddha's assembly, and the wise deity was I myself.'

Rukkhadhammajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Rukkhadhamma Jātaka, the Fourth.

[75] 5. Macchajātakavaṇṇanā

[75] 5. The Commentary on the Maccha Jātaka

Abhitthanaya [V 1.0315][M 1.0348] pajjunnāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto attanā vassāpitavassaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiṃ kira samaye kosalaraṭṭhe devo na vassi, sassāni milāyanti, tesu tesu ṭhānesu taḷākapokkharaṇisarāni sussanti. Jetavanadvārakoṭṭhakasamīpe jetavanapokkharaṇiyāpi udakaṃ chijji. Kalalagahanaṃ pavisitvā nipanne macchakacchape kākakulalādayo kaṇayaggasadisehi tuṇḍehi koṭṭetvā nīharitvā nīharitvā vipphandamāne khādanti.

'Thunder, Pajjunna...' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning the rain he had caused to fall. For at one time, it is said, it did not rain in the kingdom of Kosala; the crops withered, and in various places ponds, pools, and lakes dried up. Even the water in the Jetavana pond near the gatehouse was gone. Fish and turtles lay in the thick mud, and crows, hawks, and other birds pecked at them with their spear-like beaks, dragged them out again and again, and devoured them as they writhed.

Satthā macchakacchapānaṃ taṃ byasanaṃ disvā mahākaruṇāya ussāhitahadayo “ajja mayā devaṃ [P 1.0330] vassāpetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti pabhātāya rattiyā sarīrapaṭijagganaṃ katvā bhikkhācāravelaṃ sallakkhetvā mahābhikkhusaṅghaparivuto buddhalīlāya sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya pavisitvā pacchābhattaṃ piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto sāvatthito vihāraṃ gacchanto jetavanapokkharaṇiyā sopāne ṭhatvā ānandattheraṃ āmantesi “ānanda, udakasāṭikaṃ āhara, jetavanapokkharaṇiyaṃ nhāyissāmī”ti. “Nanu, bhante, jetavanapokkharaṇiyaṃ udakaṃ chinnaṃ, kalalamattameva avasiṭṭha”nti? “Ānanda, buddhabalaṃ nāma mahantaṃ, āhara tvaṃ udakasāṭika”nti. Thero āharitvā adāsi. Satthā ekenantena udakasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvā ekenantena sarīraṃ pārupitvā “jetavanapokkharaṇiyaṃ nhāyissāmī”ti sopāne aṭṭhāsi. Taṅkhaṇaññeva sakkassa paṇḍukambalasilāsanaṃ uṇhākāraṃ dassesi. So “kiṃ nu kho”ti āvajjento taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā vassavalāhakadevarājānaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, satthā ‘jetavanapokkharaṇiyaṃ nhāyissāmī’ti dhurasopāne ṭhito, khippaṃ sakalakosalaraṭṭhaṃ ekameghaṃ katvā vassāpehī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā ekaṃ valāhakaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā meghagītaṃ gāyanto pācīnalokadhātuabhimukho pakkhandi. Pācīnadisābhāge khalamaṇḍalamattaṃ ekaṃ meghapaṭalaṃ uṭṭhāya satapaṭalaṃ sahassapaṭalaṃ hutvā abhitthanantaṃ vijjulatā nicchārentaṃ adhomukhaṃ ṭhapitaudakakumbhākārena vassamānaṃ sakalakosalaraṭṭhaṃ mahoghena viya ajjhotthari. Devo acchinnadhāraṃ vassanto muhutteneva [M 1.0349] jetavanapokkharaṇiṃ pūresi, dhurasopānaṃ āhacca udakaṃ aṭṭhāsi.

The Teacher, seeing the calamity of the fish and turtles, his heart stirred by great compassion, thought, 'Today it is fitting for me to cause it to rain.' When the night had dawned, having attended to his person and observed the time for the alms-round, surrounded by a great assembly of monks, he entered Sāvatthī for alms with the grace of a Buddha. After the meal, having returned from the alms-round, as he was going from Sāvatthī to the monastery, he stood on the steps of the Jetavana pond and addressed the Venerable Ānanda: 'Ānanda, bring a bathing cloth; I shall bathe in the Jetavana pond.' 'But, venerable sir, is not the water in the Jetavana pond cut off, with only mud remaining?' 'Ānanda, the power of a Buddha is great. Bring the bathing cloth.' The elder brought it and gave it to him. The Teacher put on the bathing cloth with one end and covered his body with the other, then stood on the steps, saying, 'I shall bathe in the Jetavana pond.' At that very moment, Sakka’s Paṇḍukambala stone throne showed signs of heat. Wondering, 'What can this be?' he adverted and, knowing the reason, had the king of the rain-cloud devas summoned, saying: 'My dear, the Teacher stands on the main steps intending to bathe in the Jetavana pond. Quickly, making the whole of the Kosala country into a single cloud, cause it to rain.' Consenting with 'Very well,' the deva put on one cloud-garment and draped another over himself and, singing a cloud-song, rushed towards the eastern world-sphere. In the eastern quarter, a cloud-bank the size of a threshing floor arose, becoming a hundred-layered, then a thousand-layered, thundering, flashing forth lightning, and pouring rain in the manner of an overturned water pot, it inundated the entire Kosala country as if with a great flood. The rain god poured an unbroken stream, filling the Jetavana pond in a moment. The water, having reached the main steps, stood still.

Satthā pokkharaṇiyaṃ nhāyitvā surattadupaṭṭaṃ nivāsetvā kāyabandhanaṃ bandhitvā sugatamahācīvaraṃ ekaṃsaṃ katvā bhikkhusaṅghaparivuto gantvā gandhakuṭipariveṇe paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīditvā bhikkhusaṅghena vatte dassite uṭṭhāya maṇisopānaphalake ṭhatvā bhikkhusaṅghassa ovādaṃ datvā [V 1.0316] uyyojetvā surabhigandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā dakkhiṇena passena sīhaseyyaṃ kappetvā sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ “passathāvuso, dasabalassa khantimettānuddayasampattiṃ, vividhasassesu milāyantesu nānājalāsayesu sussantesu macchakacchapesu mahādukkhaṃ pāpuṇantesu kāruññaṃ paṭicca ‘mahājanaṃ dukkhā mocessāmī’ti udakasāṭikaṃ nivāsetvā jetavanapokkharaṇiyā dhurasopāne ṭhatvā muhuttena sakalakosalaraṭṭhaṃ mahoghena opilāpento viya devaṃ vassāpetvā mahājanaṃ kāyikacetasikadukkhato mocetvā [P 1.0331] vihāraṃ paviṭṭho”ti kathāya vattamānāya gandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā dhammasabhaṃ āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva mahājane kilamante devaṃ vassāpeti, pubbe tiracchānayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā maccharājakālepi vassāpesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, having bathed in the pond, put on a deep red double-layered under-robe, fastened his waistband, and arranged the great robe of the Sugata over one shoulder. Surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, he went and sat on the excellent Buddha-seat prepared in the precinct of the Gandhakuṭi. When the Saṅgha of monks had performed their duties, he arose, stood on the jeweled landing of the stairs, gave the exhortation to the Saṅgha of monks, and dismissed them. He then entered the fragrant Gandhakuṭi and lay down on his right side, assuming the lion's posture. In the evening, as the monks were gathered in the Hall of Dhamma, this conversation arose among them: 'Behold, friends, the accomplishment in patience, loving-kindness, and compassion of the one with Ten Powers! When the various crops were withering, when the various reservoirs were drying up, when the fish and turtles were meeting with great suffering, out of compassion, thinking, "I will free the great multitude from suffering," he put on a bathing cloth, stood on the main steps of the Jetavana pond, and in a moment, as if submerging the entire Kosala country with a great flood, he caused it to rain, freeing the great multitude from physical and mental suffering before entering the monastery.' While this conversation was proceeding, the Teacher emerged from the Gandhakuṭi, went to the Hall of Dhamma, and asked, 'For the sake of what talk, monks, are you now gathered together?' When it was said, 'For the sake of this talk,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata causes it to rain when the great multitude is weary; in the past, too, when born in the animal womb as the king of the fish, he also caused it to rain.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte imasmiṃyeva kosalaraṭṭhe imissā sāvatthiyā imasmiṃyeva jetavanapokkharaṇiṭṭhāne ekā valligahanaparikkhittā kandarā ahosi. Tadā bodhisatto macchayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā macchagaṇaparivuto tattha paṭivasati. Yathā pana idāni, evameva tadāpi tasmiṃ raṭṭhe devo na vassi, manussānaṃ sassāni milāyiṃsu, vāpitaḷākakandarādīsu udakaṃ chijji, macchakacchapā kalalagahanaṃ pavisiṃsu. Imissāpi kandarāya macchakacchapā kalalagahanaṃ pavisitvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃ ṭhāne nilīyiṃsu. Kākādayo tuṇḍena koṭṭetvā nīharitvā khādiṃsu.

In the past, in this very Kosala country, in this Sāvatthī, at the very site of the Jetavana pond, there was a natural lake surrounded by a thicket of vines. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into the fish womb and lived there, surrounded by a shoal of fish. Then, just as now, the god did not rain in that country; the people's crops withered; the water in reservoirs, lakes, natural pools, and so on, was cut off; and the fish and turtles entered the thick mud. In this lake, too, the fish and turtles entered the thick mud and hid themselves in this or that place. Crows and other birds, pecking them with their beaks, pulled them out and ate them.

Bodhisatto ñātisaṅghassa taṃ byasanaṃ disvā “imaṃ tesaṃ dukkhaṃ ṭhapetvā maṃ añño mocetuṃ samattho nāma natthi, saccakiriyaṃ katvā devaṃ [M 1.0350] vassāpetvā ñātake maraṇadukkhā mocessāmī”ti kāḷavaṇṇaṃ kaddamaṃ dvidhā viyūhitvā nikkhamitvā añjanarukkhasāraghaṭikavaṇṇo mahāmaccho sudhotalohitaṅgamaṇiguḷasadisāni akkhīni ummīletvā ākāsaṃ ulloketvā pajjunnadevarājassa saddaṃ datvā “bho pajjunna, ahaṃ ñātake nissāya dukkhito, tvaṃ mayi sīlavante kilamante kasmā devaṃ na vassāpesi? Mayā samānajātikānaṃ khādanaṭṭhāne nibbattitvā taṇḍulappamāṇampi macchaṃ ādiṃ katvā khāditapubbo nāma natthi, aññopi me pāṇo jīvitā na voropitapubbo, iminā saccena devaṃ vassāpetvā ñātisaṅghaṃ me dukkhā mocehī”ti vatvā paricārakaceṭakaṃ āṇāpento viya pajjunnadevarājānaṃ ālapanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, seeing that calamity of his host of kinsmen, thought, 'Setting me aside, there is no one else capable of freeing them from this suffering. Having performed an act of truth, I shall cause the god to rain and free my kinsmen from the suffering of death.' Parting the black mud in two, the great fish, the color of a block of heartwood from an anjana tree, emerged. Opening his eyes, which were like well-polished ruby gems, he looked up at the sky and called out to Pajjunna, the king of the devas: 'O Pajjunna, I am afflicted on account of my kinsmen. While I, a virtuous one, am weary, why do you not cause the god to rain? Though I was born into a species that eats its own kind, I have never eaten any fish, not even one the size of a grain of rice. Nor have I ever deprived any other living being of life. By this truth, cause the god to rain and free my host of kinsmen from suffering!' Then, as if commanding a serving boy, he addressed Pajjunna, the king of the devas, and spoke this verse:

75.

75.

“Abhitthanaya [V 1.0317][P 1.0332] pajjunna, nidhiṃ kākassa nāsaya;

Kākaṃ sokāya randhehi, mañca sokā pamocayā”ti.

Thunder forth, O Pajjunna; destroy the treasure of the crow. Subject the crow to sorrow, and from sorrow set me free.

Tattha abhitthanaya pajjunnāti pajjunno vuccati megho, ayaṃ pana meghavasena laddhanāmaṃ vassavalāhakadevarājānaṃ ālapati. Ayaṃ kirassa adhippāyo – devo nāma anabhitthananto vijjulatā anicchārento vassantopi na sobhati, tasmā tvaṃ abhitthananto vijjulatā nicchārento vassāpehīti. Nidhiṃ kākassa nāsayāti kākā kalalaṃ pavisitvā ṭhite macche tuṇḍena koṭṭetvā nīharitvā khādanti, tasmā tesaṃ antokalale macchā “nidhī”ti vuccanti, taṃ kākasaṅghassa nidhiṃ devaṃ vassāpento udakena paṭicchādetvā nāsehīti. Kākaṃ sokāya randhehīti kākasaṅgho imissā kandarāya udakena puṇṇāya macche alabhamāno socissati, taṃ kākagaṇaṃ tvaṃ imaṃ kandaraṃ pūrento sokāya randhehi, sokassatthāya macchassa assāsatthāya devaṃ vassāpehi. Yathā antonijjhānalakkhaṇaṃ sokaṃ pāpuṇāti, evaṃ karohīti attho, mañca sokā pamocayāti ettha ca-kāro sampiṇḍanattho, mañca mama ñātake ca sabbeva imamhā maraṇasokā mocehīti.

Therein, regarding 'Thunder, Pajjunna!': 'Pajjunna' is said to be a cloud. But here, he addresses the king of the rain-cloud devas, who has obtained that name by being a cloud. This, it seems, is his intention: a deva, indeed, even while raining, is not splendid if he does not thunder and does not send forth lightning flashes. Therefore, you, thundering and sending forth lightning flashes, cause it to rain. Regarding 'Destroy the treasure of the crow': crows enter the mud, and when fish are present, they peck at them with their beaks, pull them out, and eat them. Therefore, the fish in that mud are called their 'treasure'. You, causing it to rain, cover them with water and destroy that treasure of the crow assembly. Regarding 'Afflict the crow with sorrow': the assembly of crows, unable to find fish in this ravine filled with water, will grieve. You, filling this ravine, afflict that flock of crows with sorrow; cause it to rain for the sake of their sorrow and for the sake of the fish's relief. The meaning is: act so that they may attain a sorrow characterized by inner burning. Regarding 'And free me from sorrow': here, the particle 'ca' is for the purpose of inclusion. It means: 'Free me and all my kinsfolk from this sorrow of death.'

Evaṃ [M 1.0351] bodhisatto paricārakaceṭakaṃ āṇāpento viya pajjunnaṃ ālapitvā sakalakosalaraṭṭhe mahāvassaṃ vassāpetvā mahājanaṃ maraṇadukkhā mocetvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, as if giving an order to his attendant servant, addressed Pajjunna and caused a great rain to fall throughout the entire Kosala kingdom, liberating the great multitude from the suffering of death, and at the end of his life, passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, tathāgato idāneva devaṃ vassāpeti, pubbe macchayoniyaṃ nibbattopi vassāpesiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā macchagaṇā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, pajjunnadevarājā ānando, maccharājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that the Tathāgata causes it to rain; even in the past, when born in the womb of a fish, he caused it to rain." Having spoken thus, he delivered this Dhamma teaching, made the connection, and concluded the Jātaka: "At that time, the shoal of fish was the Buddha's assembly, the deva-king Pajjunna was Ānanda, and the king of the fish was none other than myself."

Macchajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Fish Jātaka, the Fifth.

[76] 6. Asaṅkiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[76] 6. The Commentary on the Asaṅkiya Jātaka

Asaṅkiyomhi [V 1.0318] gāmamhīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ sāvatthivāsiṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sotāpanno ariyasāvako kenacideva karaṇīyena ekena sakaṭasatthavāhena saddhiṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā ekasmiṃ araññaṭṭhāne sakaṭāni mocetvā khandhāvārabandhe kate satthavāhassa avidūre aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle caṅkamati. Athattano kālaṃ sallakkhetvā pañcasatā corā “khandhāvāraṃ vilumpissāmā”ti dhanumuggarādihatthā taṃ ṭhānaṃ [P 1.0333] parivārayiṃsu. Upāsakopi caṅkamatiyeva. Corā naṃ disvā “addhā esa khandhāvārarakkhako bhavissati, imassa niddaṃ okkantakāle vilumpissāmā”ti ajjhottharituṃ asakkontā tattha tattheva aṭṭhaṃsu. Sopi upāsako paṭhamayāmepi majjhimayāmepi pacchimayāmepi caṅkamantoyeva aṭṭhāsi. Paccūsakāle jāte corā okāsaṃ alabhantā gahite pāsāṇamuggarādayo chaḍḍetvā palāyiṃsu.

"I am free from suspicion in the village." The Teacher said this while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain lay disciple from Sāvatthī. It is said that this stream-enterer, a noble disciple, was traveling on a road with a certain cart-caravan for some business. Having unyoked the carts in a certain forest area and set up camp, he was performing walking meditation at the foot of a tree not far from the caravan. Then, perceiving their opportunity, five hundred robbers, armed with bows, clubs, and so on, surrounded the place, thinking, "We will plunder the camp." The lay disciple, however, continued his walking meditation. Seeing him, the robbers thought, "Surely, this must be the guard of the camp. We will plunder it when he falls asleep." Unable to overpower him, they remained standing right where they were. That lay disciple continued performing walking meditation during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch of the night. At dawn, finding no opportunity, the robbers threw down the stones, clubs, and so on that they had taken up, and fled.

Upāsakopi attano kammaṃ niṭṭhāpetvā puna sāvatthiṃ āgantvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, attānaṃ rakkhamānā pararakkhakā hontī”ti pucchi. “Āma, upāsaka, attānaṃ rakkhanto parampi rakkhati, paraṃ rakkhanto attānampi rakkhatī”ti. So “yāva subhāsitañcidaṃ, bhante, bhagavatā, ahaṃ ekena [M 1.0352] satthavāhena saddhiṃ maggaṃ paṭipanno rukkhamūle caṅkamanto ‘maṃ rakkhissāmī’ti sakalasatthaṃ rakkhi”nti āha. Satthā “upāsaka, pubbepi paṇḍitā attānaṃ rakkhantā paraṃ rakkhiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The lay disciple, having completed his business, returned to Sāvatthī and approached the Teacher. He asked, "Venerable sir, are those who protect themselves also protectors of others?" "Yes, lay disciple, one who protects oneself also protects others, and one who protects others also protects oneself," the Teacher replied. The lay disciple said, "How well-spoken this is, venerable sir, by the Blessed One! While traveling on a road with a caravan leader, I was performing walking meditation at the foot of a tree, thinking, 'I will protect myself,' and thus protected the entire caravan." The Teacher said, "Lay disciple, in the past too, the wise, by protecting themselves, protected others," and being requested by him, he related a story from the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto kāmesu ādīnavaṃ disvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavante vasanto loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadaṃ āgantvā janapadacārikaṃ caranto ekena satthavāhena saddhiṃ maggaṃ paṭipajjitvā ekasmiṃ araññaṭṭhāne satthe niviṭṭhe satthato avidūre jhānasukhena vītināmento aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle caṅkamanto aṭṭhāsi. Atha kho pañcasatā corā “sāyamāsabhattassa bhuttakāle taṃ sakaṭasatthaṃ vilumpissāmā”ti āgantvā parivārayiṃsu. Te taṃ tāpasaṃ disvā “sace ayaṃ amhe passissati, satthavāsikānaṃ ārocessati, etassa niddūpagatavelāya vilumpissāmā”ti tattheva aṭṭhaṃsu. Tāpaso sakalampi rattiṃ caṅkamiyeva. Corā okāsaṃ alabhitvā gahitagahite muggarapāsāṇe chaḍḍetvā sakaṭasatthavāsīnaṃ saddaṃ datvā “bhonto, satthavāsino [V 1.0319] sace esa rukkhamūle caṅkamanakatāpaso ajja nābhavissa, sabbe mahāvilopaṃ pattā abhavissatha, sve tāpasassa mahāsakkāraṃ kareyyāthā”ti vatvā pakkamiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family. Having come of age and seeing the peril in sensual pleasures, he went forth into the life of a sage-ascetic. Dwelling in the Himalayas, he came to the countryside to obtain salt and sour condiments. While wandering through the countryside, he traveled along a road with a caravan. When the caravan had encamped in a certain forest area, not far from it, the Bodhisatta stood performing walking meditation at the foot of a tree, passing the time in the bliss of jhāna. Then five hundred robbers, thinking, "At the time of the evening meal, when they have finished eating, we will plunder that cart-caravan," came and surrounded them. Seeing the ascetic, they thought, "If he sees us, he will alert the members of the caravan. Let us plunder them when he has fallen asleep." So they stood right there. The ascetic, however, performed walking meditation all night long. The robbers, finding no opportunity, threw down the clubs and stones they had taken up, and shouted to the members of the caravan, "Sirs, members of the caravan! If this ascetic performing walking meditation at the foot of the tree had not been here today, you would all have suffered a great plundering. Tomorrow, you should pay great honor to the ascetic!" Having said this, they departed.

Te pabhātāya rattiyā corehi chaḍḍite muggarapāsāṇādayo [P 1.0334] disvā bhītā bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā “bhante, diṭṭhā vo corā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Āmāvuso, diṭṭhā”ti. “Bhante, ettakevo core disvā bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā na uppajjī”ti? Bodhisatto “āvuso core disvā bhayaṃ nāma sadhanassa hoti, ahaṃ pana niddhano, svāhaṃ kiṃ bhāyissāmi. Mayhañhi gāmepi araññepi vasantassa bhayaṃ vā sārajjaṃ vā natthī”ti vatvā tesaṃ dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

At the break of dawn, seeing the clubs, stones, and other things left behind by the thieves, the frightened caravan members went to the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and asked, "Venerable sir, did you see the thieves?" "Yes, friends, I saw them." "Venerable sir, seeing so many thieves, did no fear or dread arise in you?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Friends, fear of thieves arises for those who have wealth. But I am without possessions, so why should I be afraid? For me, whether dwelling in a village or in the forest, there is neither fear nor dread." Then, teaching them the Dhamma, he spoke this verse:

76.

76.

“Asaṅkiyomhi gāmamhi, araññe natthi me bhayaṃ;

Ujumaggaṃ samāruḷho, mettāya karuṇāya cā”ti.

"I am without apprehension in the village; in the forest I have no fear. I have ascended the straight path with loving-kindness and compassion."

Tattha [M 1.0353] asaṅkiyomhi gāmamhīti saṅkāya niyutto patiṭṭhitoti saṅkiyo, na saṅkiyo asaṅkiyo. Ahaṃ gāme vasantopi saṅkāya appatiṭṭhitattā asaṅkiyo nibbhayo nirāsaṅkoti dīpeti. Araññeti gāmagāmūpacāravinimutte ṭhāne. Ujumaggaṃ samāruḷho, mettāya karuṇāya cāti ahaṃ tikacatukkajjhānikāhi mettākaruṇāhi kāyavaṅkādivirahitaṃ ujuṃ brahmalokagāmimaggaṃ āruḷhoti vadati. Atha vā parisuddhasīlatāya kāyavacīmanovaṅkavirahitaṃ ujuṃ devalokamaggaṃ āruḷhomhīti dassetvā tato uttari mettāya karuṇāya ca patiṭṭhitattā ujuṃ brahmalokamaggampi āruḷhomhītipi dasseti. Aparihīnajjhānassa hi ekantena brahmalokaparāyaṇattā mettākaruṇādayo ujumaggā nāma.

Therein, 'I am without apprehension in the village' means: one who is bound and established by apprehension is 'apprehensive'; not being apprehensive, one is 'without apprehension'. It explains: 'Though I dwell in the village, because of not being established in apprehension, I am without apprehension, fearless, and free from anxiety.' 'In the forest' refers to a place free from the vicinity of villages. 'Having ascended the straight path, with loving-kindness and compassion' means he declares, 'I have ascended the straight path leading to the Brahma-world, which is free from bodily crookedness and so forth, by means of the loving-kindness and compassion of the three-fold and four-fold jhānas.' Alternatively, having shown, 'Through purified virtue I have ascended the straight path to the heavenly world, free from bodily, verbal, and mental crookedness,' it is then further shown, 'Because of being established in loving-kindness and compassion, I have also ascended the straight path to the Brahma-world.' For one whose jhāna has not declined, since their final destination is certainly the Brahma-world, loving-kindness, compassion, and so on are indeed called 'straight paths'.

Evaṃ bodhisatto imāya gāthāya dhammaṃ desetvā tuṭṭhacittehi tehi manussehi sakkato pūjito yāvajīvaṃ cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmaloke nibbatti.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma with this verse, was honored and revered by those people with delighted hearts. Having cultivated the four divine abidings throughout his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā satthavāsino buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, established the connection and identified the Jātaka: "At that time, the caravan dwellers were the Buddha's assembly, and the ascetic was I myself."

Asaṅkiyajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Asaṅkiya Jātaka, the Sixth.

[77] 7. Mahāsupinajātakavaṇṇanā

[77] 7. The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Great Dreams

Lābūni [V 1.0320] sīdantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto soḷasa mahāsupine ārabbha kathesi. Ekadivasaṃ kira kosalamahārājā rattiṃ niddūpagato pacchimayāme soḷasa mahāsupine disvā bhītatasito [P 1.0335] pabujjhitvā “imesaṃ supinānaṃ diṭṭhattā kiṃ nu kho me bhavissatī”ti maraṇabhayatajjito sayanapiṭṭhe nisinnakova rattiṃ vītināmesi.

"Gourds sink," this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the sixteen great dreams. One day, it is said, the great king of Kosala, having fallen asleep at night, saw sixteen great dreams in the last watch. Frightened and terrified, he awoke and, tormented by the fear of death, wondering, "What will happen to me because I have seen these dreams?" he spent the rest of the night sitting upon his bed.

Atha naṃ pabhātāya rattiyā brāhmaṇapurohitā upasaṅkamitvā “sukhaṃ sayittha, mahārājā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Kuto me ācariyā sukhaṃ, ajjāhaṃ paccūsasamaye soḷasa mahāsupine passiṃ, somhi tesaṃ diṭṭhakālato paṭṭhāya bhayappatto”ti. “Vadetha, mahārāja, sutvā jānissāmā”ti vuttaṃ [M 1.0354] brāhmaṇānaṃ diṭṭhasupine kathetvā “kiṃ nu kho me imesaṃ diṭṭhakāraṇā bhavissatī”ti pucchi. Brāhmaṇā hatthe vidhuniṃsu. “Kasmā hatthe vidhunathā”ti ca vutte “kakkhaḷā, mahārāja, supinā”ti. “Kā tesaṃ nipphatti bhavissatī”ti? “Rajjantarāyo jīvitantarāyo bhogantarāyoti imesaṃ tiṇṇaṃ antarāyānaṃ aññataro”ti. “Sappaṭikammā, appaṭikammā”ti? “Kāmaṃ ete supinā atipharusattā appaṭikammā, mayaṃ pana te sappaṭikamme karissāma, ete paṭikkamāpetuṃ asakkontānaṃ amhākaṃ sikkhitabhāvo nāma kiṃ karissatī”ti. “Kiṃ pana katvā paṭikkamāpessathā”ti? “Sabbacatukkena yaññaṃ yajissāma, mahārājā”ti. Rājā bhītatasito “tena hi ācariyā mama jīvitaṃ tumhākaṃ hatthe hotu, khippaṃ me sotthiṃ karothā”ti āha. Brāhmaṇā “bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhissāma, bahuṃ khajjabhojjaṃ āharāpessāmā”ti haṭṭhatuṭṭhā “mā cintayittha, mahārājā”ti rājānaṃ samassāsetvā rājanivesanā nikkhamitvā bahinagare yaññāvāṭaṃ katvā bahū catuppadagaṇe thūṇūpanīte katvā pakkhigaṇe samāharitvā “idañcidañca laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti punappunaṃ sañcaranti.

Then, at the break of dawn, the brahmin royal priests approached him and asked, "Did you sleep well, great king?" "How could I have slept well, teachers? This morning at dawn, I saw sixteen great dreams. From the moment I saw them, I have been overcome with fear." "Tell us, great king; upon hearing them, we will know." The king told the brahmins the dreams he had seen and asked, "What will happen to me as a result of seeing these?" The brahmins wrung their hands. When he asked, "Why do you wring your hands?" they replied, "The dreams are terrible, great king." "What will be their outcome?" "A danger to the kingdom, a danger to your life, or a danger to your wealth—one of these three dangers will befall you." "Is there a remedy, or is there no remedy?" "Although these dreams are extremely harsh and irremediable, we shall make them remediable for you. If we are unable to counteract them, of what use is our learning?" "And what will you do to counteract them?" "We will perform a sacrifice with all sets of four, great king." The king, frightened and terrified, said, "Then, teachers, my life is in your hands. Quickly bring me safety!" The brahmins, delighted and pleased at the thought, "We will receive much wealth and have much food, both hard and soft, brought to us," reassured the king, saying, "Do not worry, great king." Leaving the royal palace, they prepared a sacrificial ground outside the city, had many herds of four-footed animals brought to the sacrificial post, gathered flocks of birds, and bustled about repeatedly, saying, "This and that must be obtained."

Atha kho mallikā devī taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā pucchi “kiṃ nu kho, mahārāja, brāhmaṇā punappunaṃ sañcarantī”ti? “Sukhitā, tvaṃ bhadde, amhākaṃ kaṇṇamūle āsīvisaṃ carantaṃ na jānāsī”ti. “Kiṃ etaṃ, mahārājā”ti? Mayā evarūpā dussupinā diṭṭhā, brāhmaṇā “tiṇṇaṃ antarāyānaṃ aññataro paññāyatī”ti vatvā “‘tesaṃ paṭighātāya yaññaṃ yajissāmā’ti vatvā punappunaṃ sañcarantī”ti. “Kiṃ pana te, mahārāja, sadevake loke aggabrāhmaṇo supinapaṭikammaṃ pucchito”ti? “Kataro panesa, bhadde, sadevake loke aggabrāhmaṇo”ti. “Sadevake loke aggapuggalaṃ sabbaññuṃ visuddhaṃ nikkilesaṃ mahābrāhmaṇaṃ na [V 1.0321] jānāsi. So hi bhagavā supinantaraṃ jāneyya, gaccha tvaṃ puccha taṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Sādhu, devī”ti rājā vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā nisīdi.

Then Queen Mallikā, understanding the situation, approached the king and asked, "Why, great king, do the brahmins bustle about so?" "You are fortunate, my dear; you do not know of the viper moving at our ear." "What is this, great king?" "I have seen such evil dreams, and the brahmins, saying, 'One of three dangers is apparent,' and declaring, 'We will perform a sacrifice for their prevention,' are bustling about repeatedly." "But, great king, have you asked the foremost brahmin in the world with its devas about a remedy for the dreams?" "And who, my dear, is the foremost brahmin in the world with its devas?" "Do you not know the great brahmin who is the supreme person in the world with its devas, the all-knowing, the pure, the stainless one? That Blessed One would know the meaning of the dreams. Go, great king, and ask him." "Very well, queen," said the king. He went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat down.

Satthā madhurassaraṃ nicchāretvā “kiṃ nu kho, mahārāja, atippagova āgatosī”ti āha. Ahaṃ, bhante, paccūsasamaye soḷasa mahāsupine [P 1.0336] disvā bhīto brāhmaṇānaṃ ārocesiṃ. Brāhmaṇā “kakkhaḷā, mahārāja[M 1.0355], supinā, etesaṃ paṭighātatthāya sabbacatukkena yaññaṃ yajissāmā”ti yaññaṃ sajjenti, bahū pāṇā maraṇabhayatajjitā, tumhe ca sadevake loke aggapuggalā, atītānāgatapaccuppannaṃ upādāya natthi so ñeyyadhammo, yo vo ñāṇamukhe āpāthaṃ nāgacchati. “Etesaṃ me supinānaṃ nipphattiṃ kathetha bhagavā”ti. “Evametaṃ, mahārāja, sadevake loke maṃ ṭhapetvā añño etesaṃ supinānaṃ antaraṃ vā nipphattiṃ vā jānituṃ samattho nāma natthi, ahaṃ te kathessāmi, apica kho tvaṃ diṭṭhadiṭṭhaniyāmeneva supine kathehī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā diṭṭhaniyāmeneva kathento –

The Teacher, emitting a sweet voice, said, 'Why, great king, have you come so very early?' 'Venerable sir, at dawn I saw sixteen great dreams and, being frightened, I told them to the brahmins. The brahmins said, "These dreams are harsh, great king. To counteract them, we will perform a sacrifice with four of every kind of creature," and they are preparing the sacrifice. Many living beings are terrified by the fear of death. You, venerable sir, are the foremost person in the world with its devas. Concerning the past, future, and present, there is no knowable thing that does not come into the range of your knowledge. May the Blessed One tell me the result of these dreams.' 'It is so, great king. In the world with its devas, setting me aside, there is no one else capable of knowing the significance or the result of these dreams. I will explain them to you. However, you should relate the dreams in the very manner you saw them.' 'Very well, venerable sir,' said the king, preparing to relate them in the very manner he had seen them—

“Usabhā rukkhā gāviyo gavā ca,

Asso kaṃso siṅgālī ca kumbho;

Pokkharaṇī ca apākacandanaṃ.

"Bulls, trees, and cows; a horse, a bronze bowl, a she-jackal, and a pot; a pond, and uncooked sandalwood.

“Lābūni sīdanti silā plavanti, maṇḍūkiyo kaṇhasappe gilanti;

Kākaṃ suvaṇṇā parivārayanti, tasā vakā eḷakānaṃ bhayā hī”ti. –

Gourds sink, and stones float; female frogs swallow black serpents; golden swans attend upon a crow; and wolves are terrified of goats."

Imaṃ mātikaṃ nikkhipitvā kathesi.

Having set forth this summary, he spoke.

(1) Ahaṃ, bhante, ekaṃ tāva supinaṃ evaṃ addasaṃ – cattāro añjanavaṇṇā kāḷausabhā “yujjhissāmā”ti catūhi disāhi rājaṅgaṇaṃ āgantvā “usabhayuddhaṃ passissāmā”ti mahājane sannipatite yujjhanākāraṃ dassetvā naditvā gajjitvā ayujjhitvāva paṭikkantā. Imaṃ paṭhamaṃ supinaṃ addasaṃ, imassa ko vipākoti? “Mahārāja, imassa vipāko neva tava, na mama kāle bhavissati, anāgate pana adhammikānaṃ kapaṇarājūnaṃ adhammikānañca manussānaṃ kāle loke viparivattamāne kusale ossanne, akusale ussanne, lokassa parihāyanakāle devo na sammā vassissati, meghapādā pacchijjissanti, sassāni milāyissanti, dubbhikkhaṃ bhavissati, vassitukāmā viya catūhi disāhi meghā uṭṭhahitvā itthikāhi [V 1.0322] ātape patthaṭānaṃ vīhiādīnaṃ temanabhayena antopavesitakāle purisesu kuddālapiṭakahatthesu āḷibandhanatthāya nikkhantesu vassanākāraṃ [M 1.0356] dassetvā gajjitvā vijjulatā nicchāretvā te usabhā viya ayujjhitvā avassitvāva palāyissanti. Ayametassa vipāko. Tuyhaṃ pana tappaccayā koci antarāyo natthi, anāgataṃ [P 1.0337] ārabbha diṭṭho supino esa, brāhmaṇā pana attano jīvitavuttiṃ nissāya kathayiṃsū”ti evaṃ satthā supinassa nipphattiṃ kathetvā āha “dutiyaṃ kathehi, mahārājā”ti.

"(1) Venerable sir, I saw the first dream thus: four black bulls, the color of collyrium, came from the four directions to the royal courtyard, intending to fight. When a great crowd had gathered, thinking, 'We will see a bullfight,' the bulls displayed the appearance of fighting, roaring and bellowing, but without actually fighting, they departed. This was the first dream I saw. What is its result?' 'Great king, the result of this dream will occur neither in your time nor in mine. But in the future, in the time of unrighteous and miserly kings and unrighteous people, when the world is turning upside down, when the wholesome is in decline and the unwholesome is rampant, during a time of the world's decay, the heavens will not rain properly, the downpours will be cut off, the crops will wither, and there will be a famine. As if wishing to rain, clouds will rise from the four directions. When women, fearing that the paddy and other grains spread in the sun will get wet, have brought them inside, and when men, with hoes and baskets in hand, have gone out to bind the dikes, the clouds will display the appearance of raining, thundering and flashing with lightning, but just like those bulls, they will flee without having rained at all. This is its result. For you, however, there is no danger from it. This is a dream seen concerning the future. The brahmins, on the other hand, spoke depending on their own livelihood.' Thus the Teacher, having explained the result of the dream, said, 'Tell the second, great king.'"

(2) Dutiyāhaṃ, bhante, evaṃ addasaṃ – khuddakā rukkhā ceva gacchā ca pathaviṃ bhinditvā vidatthimattampi ratanamattampi anuggantvāva pupphanti ceva phalanti ca. Imaṃ dutiyaṃ addasaṃ, imassa ko vipākoti? Mahārāja, imassāpi vipāko lokassa parihāyanakāle manussānaṃ parittāyukakāle bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi sattā tibbarāgā bhavissanti, asampattavayāva kumāriyo purisantaraṃ gantvā utuniyo ceva gabbhiniyo ca hutvā puttadhītāhi vaḍḍhissanti. Khuddakarukkhānaṃ pupphaṃ viya hi tāsaṃ utunibhāvo, phalaṃ viya ca puttadhītaro bhavissanti. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, tatiyaṃ kathehi, mahārājāti.

"(2) Secondly, venerable sir, I saw this: tiny trees and shrubs broke through the earth, and without growing even a span or a cubit high, they flowered and bore fruit. This is the second dream I saw. What is its result?' 'Great king, the result of this too will occur during a time of the world's decay, when the lifespan of humans is short. For in the future, beings will have intense passion. Young girls, not yet having reached the proper age, will go to live with men, menstruate, become pregnant, and give birth to sons and daughters. Indeed, their menstruation will be like the flowers of the tiny trees, and their sons and daughters will be like the fruit. From this, too, there is no danger to you. Tell the third, great king.'"

(3) Gāviyo, bhante, tadahujātānaṃ vacchakānaṃ khīraṃ pivantiyo addasaṃ. Ayaṃ me tatiyo supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi vipāko anāgate eva manussānaṃ jeṭṭhāpacāyikakammassa naṭṭhakāle bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi sattā mātāpitūsu vā sassusasuresu vā lajjaṃ anupaṭṭhāpetvā sayameva kuṭumbaṃ saṃvidahantāva ghāsacchādanamattampi mahallakānaṃ dātukāmā dassanti, adātukāmā na dassanti. Mahallakā anāthā asayaṃvasī dārake ārādhetvā jīvissanti tadahujātānaṃ vacchakānaṃ khīraṃ pivantiyo mahāgāviyo viya. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, catutthaṃ kathehi, mahārājāti.

"(3) Venerable sir, I saw cows drinking the milk of their own calves born that very day. This is my third dream. What is its result?' 'The result of this too will occur in the future, at a time when the custom of honoring elders has vanished among humans. In the future, people will show no deference to their own mothers and fathers or to their parents-in-law. They themselves will manage the family estate, and if they wish, they will give the elders mere food and clothing; if they do not wish, they will not give. The elders, helpless and dependent, will have to live by gratifying their own children, just like the great cows drinking the milk of the calves to which they had given birth that day. From this, too, there is no danger to you. Tell the fourth, great king.'"

(4) Dhuravāhe, bhante, ārohapariṇāhasampanne mahāgoṇeyugaparamparāya ayojetvā taruṇe godamme dhure yojente addasaṃ. Te dhuraṃ vahituṃ asakkontā chaḍḍetvā aṭṭhaṃsu, sakaṭāni nappavaṭṭiṃsu. Ayaṃ me catuttho supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi vipāko [M 1.0357] anāgate eva adhammikarājūnaṃ kāle bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi adhammikakapaṇarājāno paṇḍitānaṃ paveṇikusalānaṃ kammaṃ nittharaṇasamatthānaṃ mahāmattānaṃ yasaṃ na dassanti. Dhammasabhāyaṃ vinicchayaṭṭhānepi paṇḍite vohārakusale mahallake amacce na ṭhapessanti, tabbiparītānaṃ pana taruṇataruṇānaṃ yasaṃ dassanti, tathārūpe eva vinicchayaṭṭhāne ṭhapessanti, te rājakammāni ceva yuttāyuttañca [V 1.0323] ajānantā neva taṃ yasaṃ ukkhipituṃ sakkhissanti, na rājakammāni nittharituṃ. Te asakkontā kammadhuraṃ chaḍḍessanti, mahallakāpi paṇḍitāmaccā yasaṃ alabhantā kiccāni nittharituṃ samatthāpi “kiṃ amhākaṃ etehi, mayaṃ bāhirakā jātā, abbhantarikā taruṇadārakā jānissantī”ti [P 1.0338] uppannāni kammāni na karissanti, evaṃ sabbathāpi tesaṃ rājūnaṃ hāniyeva bhavissati, dhuraṃ vahituṃ asamatthānaṃ vacchadammānaṃ dhure yojitakālo viya, dhuravāhānañca mahāgoṇānaṃ yugaparamparāya ayojitakālo viya bhavissati. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, pañcamaṃ kathehi, mahārājāti.

(4) 'Venerable sir, I saw young bullocks, not yet broken in, being yoked to the pole, while great, strong, burden-bearing oxen were not yoked in their proper succession. Unable to bear the load, the young bullocks cast it off and stood still, and the carts did not move. This is my fourth dream. What is its result?' 'The result of this too, great king, will manifest in the future, in the time of unrighteous kings. In the future, unrighteous and base kings will not bestow honor upon wise ministers, skilled in tradition and capable of accomplishing their duties. In the hall of justice and places of judgment, they will not appoint wise, elder ministers skilled in legal affairs. Instead, they will bestow honor upon the very young, and they will appoint such persons to positions of judgment. These, not knowing royal affairs nor what is right and wrong, will be unable to uphold that honor or to accomplish their duties. Unable to do so, they will cast off the yoke of their responsibilities. The elder, wise ministers, though capable of accomplishing their duties, will receive no honor and will think, "What is this to us? We are outsiders. Let the young ones within the court attend to it." Thus, they will not perform the duties that arise. In this way, those kings will suffer decline in every respect. It will be like a time when young bullocks, unable to bear the burden, are yoked to the pole, and when great, burden-bearing oxen are not yoked in their proper succession. From this dream, too, there is no danger for you. Relate the fifth, great king.'

(5) Bhante, ekaṃ ubhatomukhaṃ assaṃ addasaṃ, tassa dvīsu passesu yavasaṃ denti, so dvīhi mukhehi khādati. Ayaṃ me pañcamo supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi anāgate adhammikarājakāleyeva vipāko bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi adhammikā bālarājāno adhammike lolamanusse vinicchaye ṭhapessanti, te pāpapuññesu anādarā bālā sabhāyaṃ nisīditvā vinicchayaṃ dentā ubhinnampi atthapaccatthikānaṃ hatthato lañjaṃ gahetvā khādissanti asso viya dvīhi mukhehi yavasaṃ. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, chaṭṭhaṃ kathehi, mahārājāti.

(5) 'Venerable sir, I saw a horse with a mouth on both sides. Fodder was given to it on both sides, and it ate with both mouths. This is my fifth dream. What is its result?' 'The result of this too, great king, will manifest in the future, in the time of unrighteous kings. In the future, unrighteous and foolish kings will appoint unrighteous and greedy men to pass judgment. Those fools, heedless of good and evil, will sit in the assembly and, while giving judgment, will take bribes from the hands of both litigants and devour them, just as the horse eats fodder with both mouths. From this dream, too, there is no danger for you. Relate the sixth, great king.'

(6) Bhante, mahājano satasahassagghanikaṃ suvaṇṇapātiṃ sammajjitvā “idha passāvaṃ karohī”ti ekassa jarasiṅgālassa upanāmesi, taṃ tattha passāvaṃ karontaṃ addasaṃ. Ayaṃ me chaṭṭho supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi vipāko anāgateyeva bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi [M 1.0358] adhammikā vijātirājāno jātisampannānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ āsaṅkāya yasaṃ na dassanti, akulīnānaṃyeva dassanti. Evaṃ mahākulāni duggatāni bhavissanti, lāmakakulāni issarāni. Te ca kulīnapurisā jīvituṃ asakkontā “ime nissāya jīvissāmā”ti akulīnānaṃ dhītaro dassanti, iti tāsaṃ kuladhītānaṃ akulīnehi saddhiṃ saṃvāso jarasiṅgālassa suvaṇṇapātiyaṃ passāvakaraṇasadiso bhavissati. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, sattamaṃ kathehīti.

(6) 'Venerable sir, a great crowd of people cleaned a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand and presented it to an old jackal, saying, "Pray, urinate in this." I saw it urinating therein. This is my sixth dream. What is its result?' 'The result of this too, great king, will manifest in the future. In the future, unrighteous kings of base lineage will, out of suspicion, not bestow honor upon the well-born sons of noble families, but will give it only to those of low birth. Thus, the great families will fall into poverty, while the lowly families will rise to power. And those men of noble birth, unable to support themselves, will give their daughters in marriage to those of low birth, thinking, "We shall live by depending on them." This union of the daughters of noble families with men of low birth will be like the old jackal urinating in the golden bowl. From this dream, too, there is no danger for you. Relate the seventh.'

(7) Bhante, eko puriso rajjuṃ vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā pādamūle nikkhipati, tena nisinnapīṭhassa heṭṭhā sayitā ekā chātasiṅgālī tassa ajānantasseva taṃ khādati, evāhaṃ addasaṃ. Ayaṃ me sattamo supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi anāgateyeva vipāko bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi itthiyo purisalolā surālolā alaṅkāralolā visikhālolā āmisalolā bhavissanti dussīlā durācārā, tā sāmikehi kasigorakkhādīni kammāni katvā [V 1.0324] kicchena kasirena sambhataṃ dhanaṃ jārehi saddhiṃ suraṃ pivantiyo mālāgandhavilepanaṃ dhārayamānā antogehe accāyikampi kiccaṃ anoloketvā gehe parikkhepassa uparibhāgenapi chiddaṭṭhānehipi jāre upadhārayamānā sve vapitabbayuttakaṃ bījampi koṭṭetvā yāgubhattakhajjakādīni sampādetvā khādamānā vilumpissanti heṭṭhāpīṭhake nipannachātasiṅgālī viya vaṭṭetvā vaṭṭetvā [P 1.0339] pādamūle nikkhittarajjuṃ. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, aṭṭhamaṃ kathehīti.

(7) 'Venerable sir, a man was twisting a rope, and as he finished each length, he placed it at his feet.
