Beneath the stool on which he sat, a hungry she-jackal lay, and without his knowledge, she kept eating the rope. This I saw. This is my seventh dream. What is its result?' 'The result of this too, great king, will manifest in the future. In the future, women will be wanton, given to strong drink, obsessed with adornment, roaming the streets, and greedy for material things; they will be immoral and of evil conduct. While their husbands toil at farming, herding, and other work, gathering wealth with great difficulty and hardship, these women will drink spirits with their lovers, adorning themselves with garlands, perfumes, and ointments. Neglecting urgent household duties, they will watch for their lovers from the upper parts of the house and through crevices. They will plunder the wealth their husbands have earned, pounding even the seed grain set aside for the next day's sowing and consuming it after preparing porridge, rice, and other foods. They will squander their household's substance just as the hungry she-jackal, lying beneath the stool, devoured the rope that the man twisted and laid at his feet. From this dream, too, there is no danger for you. Relate the eighth.'

(8) Bhante, rājadvāre bahūhi tucchakumbhehi parivāretvā ṭhapitaṃ ekaṃ mahantaṃ pūritakumbhaṃ addasaṃ. Cattāropi pana vaṇṇā catūhi disāhi catūhi anudisāhi ca ghaṭehi udakaṃ āharitvā āharitvā pūritakumbhameva pūrenti, pūritapūritaṃ udakaṃ uttaritvā palāyati, tepi punappunaṃ tattheva udakaṃ āsiñcanti, tucchakumbhe pana olokentāpi natthi. Ayaṃ me aṭṭhamo supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi anāgateyeva vipāko bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi loko parihāyissati, raṭṭhaṃ [M 1.0359] nirojaṃ bhavissati, rājāno duggatā kapaṇā bhavissanti. Yo issaro bhavissati, tassa bhaṇḍāgāre satasahassamattā kahāpaṇā bhavissanti, te evaṃ duggatā sabbe jānapade attanova kamme kāressanti, upaddutā manussā sake kammante chaḍḍetvā rājūnaññeva atthāya pubbaṇṇāparaṇṇāni vapantā rakkhantā lāyantā maddantā pavesentā ucchukhettāni karontā yantāni karontā yantāni vāhentā phāṇitādīni pacantā pupphārāme ca phalārāme ca karontā tattha tattha nipphannāni pubbaṇṇādīni āharitvā rañño koṭṭhāgārameva pūressanti, attano gehesu tucchakoṭṭhe olokentāpi na bhavissanti, tucchakumbhe anoloketvā pūritakumbhe pūraṇasadisameva bhavissati. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, navamaṃ kathehīti.

Venerable sir, I saw at the king's gate a single large, full water pot surrounded by many empty pots. People of all four castes brought water from the four cardinal and four intermediate directions and poured it only into the full pot. The water poured into the already full pot overflowed and ran away, yet they repeatedly poured more into that very pot, while not even glancing at the empty ones. This was my eighth dream. What is its result? The result of this too will manifest only in the future. For in the future, the world will decline, the kingdom will become barren, and kings will become poor and wretched. Whoever is the ruler, his treasury will hold only about a hundred thousand coins. Being so impoverished, they will make all the people of the land work for their own purposes. Oppressed, the people will abandon their own work and, for the sake of the kings alone, will sow, guard, reap, thresh, and store various grains; they will cultivate sugarcane fields, make and operate mills, boil molasses and the like, and make flower and fruit gardens. Bringing the grains and other produce from those places, they will fill only the king's granaries. They will not even look at the empty granaries in their own homes. It will be just like filling the full pot without looking at the empty ones. From this cause also, there is no danger to you. Tell the ninth.

(9) Bhante, ekaṃ pañcavaṇṇapadumasañchannaṃ gambhīraṃ sabbato titthaṃ pokkharaṇiṃ addasaṃ. Samantato dvipadacatuppadā otaritvā tattha pānīyaṃ pivanti. Tassā majjhe gambhīraṭṭhāne udakaṃ āvilaṃ, tīrappadesesu dvipadacatuppadānaṃ akkamaṭṭhāne acchaṃ vippasannaṃ anāvilaṃ. Evāhaṃ addasaṃ. Ayaṃ me navamo supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi anāgateyeva vipāko bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi rājāno adhammikā bhavissanti, chandādivasena agatiṃ gacchantā rajjaṃ kāressanti, dhammena vinicchayaṃ nāma na dassanti, lañjavittakā bhavissanti dhanalolā, raṭṭhavāsikesu nesaṃ khantimettānuddayā nāma na bhavissanti, kakkhaḷā pharusā ucchuyante ucchugaṇṭhikā viya manusse pīḷentā nānappakārena baliṃ uppādentā dhanaṃ gaṇhissanti. Manussā balipīḷitā kiñci dātuṃ asakkontā gāmanigamādayo chaḍḍetvā paccantaṃ gantvā vāsaṃ [V 1.0325] kappessanti, majjhimajanapado suñño bhavissati, paccanto ghanavāso seyyathāpi pokkharaṇiyā majjhe udakaṃ āvilaṃ pariyante vippasannaṃ. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, dasamaṃ [P 1.0340] kathehīti.

Venerable sir, I saw a deep pond covered with lotuses of five colors, with bathing places on all sides. From all around, two-footed and four-footed creatures descended to drink water there. In the middle of the pond, in the deep part, the water was turbid; but in the areas near the banks where the creatures trod, the water was clear, bright, and undisturbed. Thus I saw. This was my ninth dream. What is its result? The result of this too will manifest only in the future. For in the future, kings will be unrighteous. Acting on impulse, such as desire, they will go astray onto wrong paths while ruling. They will not give judgments in accordance with the Dhamma. They will take bribes and be greedy for wealth. They will have no patience, loving-kindness, or compassion for the inhabitants of the land. They will be harsh and cruel. Oppressing the people as sugarcane is crushed in a mill, they will levy taxes in various ways and seize their wealth. Oppressed by taxes and unable to pay, the people will abandon their villages, towns, and so forth, and go to live in the borderlands. The central region will become deserted, and the border regions will be densely populated—just as the water in the middle of the pond was turbid, while at the edges it was clear. From this cause also, there is no danger to you. Tell the tenth.

(10) Bhante, ekissāyeva kumbhiyā paccamānaṃ odanaṃ apākaṃ addasaṃ “apāka”nti vicāretvā vibhajitvā ṭhapitaṃ viya tīhākārehi paccamānaṃ, ekasmiṃ [M 1.0360] passe atikilinno hoti, ekasmiṃ uttaṇḍulo, ekasmiṃ supakkoti. Ayaṃ me dasamo supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi anāgateyeva vipāko bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi rājāno adhammikā bhavissanti, tesu adhammikesu rājayuttāpi brāhmaṇagahapatikāpi negamajānapadāpīti samaṇabrāhmaṇe upādāya sabbe manussā adhammikā bhavissanti, tato tesaṃ ārakkhadevatā, balipaṭiggāhikā devatā, rukkhadevatā, ākāsaṭṭhadevatāti evaṃ devatāpi adhammikā bhavissanti. Adhammikarājūnañca rajje vātā visamā kharā vāyissanti, te ākāsaṭṭhavimānāni kampessanti, tesu kampitesu devatā kupitā devaṃ vassituṃ na dassanti, vassamānopi sakalaraṭṭhe ekappahārena na vassissati, vassamānopi sabbattha kasikammassa vā vappakammassa vā upakārako hutvā na vassissati. Yathā ca raṭṭhe, evaṃ janapadepi gāmepi ekataḷākepi ekasarepi ekappahāreneva na vassissati, taḷākassa uparibhāge vassanto heṭṭhābhāge na vassissati, heṭṭhā vassanto upari na vassissati. Ekasmiṃ bhāge sassaṃ ativassena nassissati, ekasmiṃ avassanena milāyissati, ekasmiṃ sammā vassamāno sampādessati. Evaṃ ekassa rañño rajje vuttasassā tippakārā bhavissanti ekakumbhiyā odano viya. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, ekādasamaṃ kathehīti.

Venerable sir, I saw rice cooking in a single pot, and it was cooking in three different ways, as if it had been divided into sections. In one section, it was mushy; in another, it was hard and uncooked; and in a third, it was perfectly cooked. This was my tenth dream. What is its result? The result of this too will manifest only in the future. For in the future, kings will be unrighteous. When they are unrighteous, their royal officials, brahmins and householders, town and country folk—indeed, all people, including ascetics and brahmins—will become unrighteous. Then their guardian deities, the deities who receive offerings, tree deities, and sky-dwelling deities—all these deities will also become unrighteous. In the kingdoms of unrighteous kings, the winds will blow unevenly and fiercely, shaking the celestial mansions in the sky. When these are shaken, the angered deities will not let the rain fall. Or if it does rain, it will not fall over the whole kingdom at once. Nor will it fall everywhere in a way that is beneficial for ploughing or sowing. Just as in the kingdom, so too in a district, a village, a single reservoir, or a single lake, it will not rain everywhere at once. Raining on the upper part of a reservoir, it will not rain on the lower part; raining on the lower part, it will not rain on the upper. In one region, the crops will be ruined by too much rain; in another, they will wither for lack of rain; and in another, they will be perfected by just the right amount of rain. Thus, the crops sown in the kingdom of a single king will be of three kinds, like the rice in the single pot. From this cause also, there is no danger to you. Tell the eleventh.

(11) Bhante, satasahassagghanikaṃ candanasāraṃ pūtitakkena vikkiṇante addasaṃ. Ayaṃ me ekādasamo supino, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi anāgateyeva mayhaṃ sāsane parihāyante vipāko bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi paccayalolā alajjī bhikkhū bahū bhavissanti, te mayā paccayaloluppaṃ nimmathetvā kathitadhammadesanaṃ cīvarādicatupaccayahetu paresaṃ desessanti, paccayehi mucchitā nissaraṇapakkhe ṭhitā nibbānābhimukhaṃ katvā desetuṃ na sakkhissanti, kevalaṃ “padabyañjanasampattiñceva madhurasaddañca sutvā mahagghāni cīvarādīni dassanti” iccevaṃ desessanti. Apare [M 1.0361] antaravīthicatukkarājadvārādīsu nisīditvā kahāpaṇaaḍḍhakahāpaṇapādamāsakarūpādīnipi nissāya desessanti. Iti mayā nibbānagghanakaṃ katvā desitaṃ dhammaṃ catupaccayatthāya ceva kahāpaṇaḍḍhakahāpaṇādīnaṃ atthāya ca vikkiṇitvā desentā [V 1.0326] satasahassagghanakaṃ candanasāraṃ pūtitakkena vikkiṇantā [P 1.0341] viya bhavissanti. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, dvādasamaṃ kathehīti.

"Venerable sir, I saw sandalwood core worth a hundred thousand being sold for spoiled buttermilk. This was my eleventh dream; what is its result?" "The result of this too will be in the future when my dispensation declines. For in the future, there will be many shameless monks, greedy for requisites. They will teach the Dhamma which I taught for the crushing of greed, for the sake of the four requisites—robes and so on—to others. Infatuated with requisites, they will not stand on the side of liberation and will be unable to teach in a way that leads towards Nibbāna. They will teach merely with the thought, 'Having heard the excellence of the words and phrases and the sweet sound, they will give valuable robes and so on.' Others, sitting at crossroads, royal gates, and so on, will teach for the sake of kahāpaṇas, half-kahāpaṇas, quarter-kahāpaṇas, māsakas, and other such currency. Thus, teaching and selling the Dhamma, which I taught as having the priceless value of Nibbāna, for the sake of the four requisites and for kahāpaṇas, half-kahāpaṇas, and so on, they will be like those who sell sandalwood core worth a hundred thousand for spoiled buttermilk. From this cause too, there is no danger for you. Tell the twelfth."

(12) Bhante, tucchalābūni udake sīdantāni addasaṃ, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassapi anāgate adhammikarājakāle loke viparivattanteyeva vipāko bhavissati. Tadā hi rājāno jātisampannānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ yasaṃ na dassanti, akulīnānaṃyeva dassanti, te issarā bhavissanti, itare daliddā. Rājasammukhepi rājadvārepi amaccasammukhepi vinicchayaṭṭhānepi tucchalābusadisānaṃ akulīnānaṃyeva kathā osīditvā ṭhitā viya niccalā suppatiṭṭhitā bhavissati. Saṅghasannipātesupi saṅghakammagaṇakammaṭṭhānesu ceva pattacīvarapariveṇādivinicchayaṭṭhānesu ca dussīlānaṃ pāpapuggalānaṃyeva kathā niyyānikā bhavissati, na lajjibhikkhūnanti evaṃ sabbathāpi tucchalābusīdanakālo viya bhavissati. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, terasamaṃ kathehīti.

"Venerable sir, I saw empty gourds sinking in water; what is its result?" "The result of this, too, will be in the future, during the time of unrighteous kings when the world is in turmoil. At that time, kings will not give honor to clansmen of noble birth, but only to those of low birth. The latter will become powerful, while the former will be poor. In the presence of the king, at the royal court, in the presence of ministers, and in places of judgment, the words of those of low birth, who are like empty gourds, will sink in and stand firm, as it were, unmoving and well-established. In monastic assemblies, in places for Sangha acts and group acts, and in places for settling matters concerning bowls, robes, lodgings, and so forth, the words of immoral and wicked individuals will be decisive, not those of conscientious monks. Thus, in every way, it will be like a time when empty gourds sink. From this cause, too, there is no danger for you. Tell the thirteenth."

(13) Bhante, mahantamahantā kūṭāgārappamāṇā ghanasilā nāvā viya udake plavamānā addasaṃ, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassapi tādiseyeva kāle vipāko bhavissati. Tadā hi adhammikarājāno akulīnānaṃ yasaṃ dassanti, te issarā bhavissanti, kulīnā duggatā. Tesu na keci gāravaṃ karissanti, itaresuyeva karissanti. Rājasammukhe vā amaccasammukhe vā vinicchayaṭṭhāne vā vinicchayakusalānaṃ ghanasilāsadisānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ kathā na ogāhitvā patiṭṭhahissati. Tesu kathentesu “kiṃ ime kathentī”ti itare parihāsameva karissanti. Bhikkhusannipātesupi vuttappakāresu ṭhānesu neva pesale bhikkhū garukātabbe maññissanti, nāpi tesaṃ kathā pariyogāhitvā patiṭṭhahissati, silānaṃ plavanakālo viya bhavissati. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, cuddasamaṃ kathehīti.

"Venerable sir, I saw great, solid rocks, the size of gabled mansions, floating on water like boats. What is the result of this?" "The result of this too will occur at a similar time. For then, unrighteous kings will give honor to those of ignoble families; they will become powerful, while those of noble families will be destitute. No one will pay respect to the noble, but will respect the ignoble instead. In the presence of the king or his ministers, or in courts of justice, the words of sons of good family, who are skilled in judgment and solid as rock, will not sink in and become established. While they are speaking, the others will merely mock them, saying, 'What are these people saying?' Even in assemblies of monks, in the aforementioned situations, they will not consider that virtuous monks ought to be respected, nor will their words be thoroughly grasped and upheld. It will be like a time when rocks float. From this cause, too, there is no danger for you. Tell the fourteenth."

(14) Bhante[M 1.0362], khuddakamadhukapupphappamāṇā maṇḍūkiyo mahantamahante kaṇhasappe vegena anubandhitvā uppalanāḷe viya chinditvā chinditvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā gilantiyo addasaṃ, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassapi loke parihāyante anāgate eva vipāko bhavissati. Tadā hi manussā tibbarāgajātikā kilesānuvattakā hutvā taruṇataruṇānaṃ attano bhariyānaṃ vase vattissanti, gehe dāsakammakarādayopi gomahiṃsādayopi hiraññasuvaṇṇampi sabbaṃ tāsaññeva āyattaṃ bhavissati. “Asukaṃ hiraññasuvaṇṇaṃ vā paricchadādijātaṃ vā kaha”nti vutte “yattha vā tattha vā hotu, kiṃ tuyhiminā byāpārena, tvaṃ mayhaṃ ghare santaṃ vā asantaṃ vā jānitukāmo [V 1.0327] jāto”ti vatvā nānappakārehi akkositvā mukhasattīhi koṭṭetvā dāsaceṭake viya attano vase katvā attano issariyaṃ pavattessanti. Evaṃ madhukapupphappamāṇānaṃ [P 1.0342] maṇḍūkapotikānaṃ āsīvise kaṇhasappe gilanakālo viya bhavissati. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, pannarasamaṃ kathehīti.

"Venerable sir, I saw tiny female frogs, the size of madhuka flowers, swiftly pursuing enormous black snakes, and, cutting them to pieces like lotus stalks, devouring their flesh and swallowing them. What is the result of this?" "The result of this too will occur in the future when the world is in decline. For at that time, men will be of intense passion, followers of their defilements, and will live under the sway of their very young wives. In the household, the male and female servants, the workers, the cattle and buffalo, the gold and silver—everything will be under their wives' control. If a husband should ask, 'Where is such-and-such gold or silver, or such-and-such property?' his wife will reply, 'Let it be wherever it is! What business is this of yours? Do you seek to know what is and what is not in my house?' Then, reviling him in various ways and striking him with verbal darts, they will bring him under their power like a slave or servant and will establish their own authority. Thus, it will be like a time when tiny female frogs, the size of madhuka flowers, devour venomous black snakes. From this cause, too, there is no danger for you. Tell the fifteenth."

(15) Bhante, dasahi asaddhammehi samannāgataṃ gāmagocaraṃ kākaṃ kañcanavaṇṇatāya “suvaṇṇā”ti laddhanāme suvaṇṇarājahaṃse parivārente addasaṃ, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassāpi anāgate dubbalarājakāleyeva vipāko bhavissati. Anāgatasmiñhi rājāno hatthisippādīsu akusalā yuddhesu avisāradā bhavissanti, te attano rajjavipattiṃ āsaṅkamānā samānajātikānaṃ kulaputtānaṃ issariyaṃ adatvā attano pādamūlikanhāpakakappakādīnaṃ dassanti, jātigottasampannā kulaputtā rājakule patiṭṭhaṃ alabhamānā jīvikaṃ kappetuṃ asamatthā hutvā issariye ṭhite jātigottahīne akulīne upaṭṭhahantā vicarissanti, suvaṇṇarājahaṃsehi kākassa parivāritakālo viya bhavissati. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi, soḷasamaṃ kathehīti.

"Venerable sir, I saw a village-dwelling crow, possessed of ten unwholesome qualities, being attended upon by royal golden swans, who are so named on account of their golden hue. What is the result of this?" "The result of this too will be in the future, during a time of weak kings. For in the future, kings will be unskilled in arts such as elephant-lore and inexpert in battle. Fearing the ruin of their own kingdoms, they will not grant authority to men of good family of equal birth, but will instead give it to their own personal attendants, such as bath attendants and barbers. Then men of good family, endowed with noble birth and lineage, being unable to find a position in the royal court and thus unable to support themselves, will wander about attending upon those of low birth and ignoble lineage who have been established in authority. It will be like the time when the royal golden swans attended upon the crow. From this cause, too, there is no danger for you. Tell the sixteenth."

(16) Bhante, pubbe dīpino eḷake khādanti, ahaṃ pana eḷake dīpino anubandhitvā murumurūti khādante addasaṃ. Athaññe tasā vakā eḷake dūratova disvā tasitā tāsappattā hutvā eḷakānaṃ bhayāpalāyitvā gumbagahanādīni [M 1.0363] pavisitvā nilīyiṃsu, evāhaṃ addasaṃ, imassa ko vipākoti? Imassapi anāgate adhammikarājakāleyeva vipāko bhavissati. Tadā hi akulīnā rājavallabhā issarā bhavissanti, kulīnā apaññātā duggatā. Te rājavallabhā rājānaṃ attano kathaṃ gāhāpetvā vinicchayaṭṭhānādīsu balavanto hutvā kulīnānaṃ paveṇiāgatāni khettavatthādīni “amhākaṃ santakāni etānī”ti abhiyuñjitvā tesu “na tumhākaṃ, amhāka”nti āgantvā vinicchayaṭṭhānādīsu vivadantesu vettalatādīhi paharāpetvā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā apakaḍḍhāpetvā “attano pamāṇaṃ na jānātha, amhehi saddhiṃ vivadatha, idāni vo rañño kathetvā hatthapādacchedanādīni kāressāmā”ti santajjessanti. Te tesaṃ bhayena attano santakāni vatthūni “tumhākaṃyevetāni gaṇhathā”ti niyyādetvā attano gehāni pavisitvā bhītā nipajjissanti. Pāpabhikkhūpi pesale bhikkhū yathāruci viheṭhessanti, te pesalā bhikkhū paṭisaraṇaṃ alabhamānā araññaṃ pavisitvā gahanaṭṭhānesu nilīyissanti. Evaṃ hīnajaccehi ceva pāpabhikkhūhi ca upaddutānaṃ jātimantakulaputtānañceva pesalabhikkhūnañca eḷakānaṃ bhayena tasavakānaṃ palāyanakālo viya bhavissati. Itonidānampi te bhayaṃ natthi. Ayampi hi supino anāgataṃyeva [V 1.0328] ārabbha diṭṭho. Brāhmaṇā pana na [P 1.0343] dhammasudhammatāya tayi sinehena kathayiṃsu, “bahudhanaṃ labhissāmā”ti āmisāpekkhatāya jīvitavuttiṃ nissāya kathayiṃsūti.

(16) Venerable sir, formerly leopards ate goats, but I saw goats pursuing leopards and devouring them with a crunching sound. Then, other trembling wolves, seeing the goats from afar, became terrified and filled with fear. Fleeing from the goats, they entered thickets and dense groves and hid. This is what I saw. What is the result of this? The result of this, too, will come to pass in the future, during the time of unrighteous kings. For at that time, the low-born, favorites of the king, will be powerful, while the high-born will be obscure and destitute. These royal favorites, having made the king accept their word, will become powerful in the courts of justice and other such places. They will lay claim to the ancestral fields and properties of the high-born, saying, ‘These belong to us.’ When the high-born come to the courts of justice to dispute this, saying, ‘They are not yours, they are ours,’ the royal favorites will have them beaten with rattan canes and the like, seized by the neck, and dragged away, threatening them, ‘You do not know your own measure, you dispute with us! Now we will speak to the king and have your hands and feet cut off!’ Out of fear of them, the high-born will hand over their own properties, saying, ‘They are yours, take them,’ and entering their own homes, they will lie down in fear. Evil monks, too, will harass virtuous monks as they please. Those virtuous monks, finding no refuge, will enter the forest and hide in dense places. Thus, for the high-born sons of good families and for the virtuous monks oppressed by the low-born and by evil monks, it will be like the time when the trembling wolves fled in fear of the goats. From this, however, there is no danger to you. This dream, too, was seen concerning the future. The brahmins, however, did not speak out of love for you from the goodness of the Dhamma; they spoke depending on their livelihood, with an expectation of material gain, thinking, ‘We will obtain much wealth.’”

Evaṃ satthā soḷasannaṃ mahāsupinānaṃ nipphattiṃ kathetvā “na kho, mahārāja, etarahi tvaññeva ime supine addasa, porāṇakarājānopi addasaṃsu. Brāhmaṇāpi nesaṃ evameva ime supine gahetvā yaññamatthake khipiṃsu, tato paṇḍitehi dinnanayena gantvā bodhisattaṃ pucchiṃsu. Porāṇakā paṇḍitāpi nesaṃ ime supine kathentā imināva niyāmena kathesu”nti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Thus the Teacher, having explained the outcome of the sixteen great dreams, said: “Great King, it is not only you who has now seen these dreams; kings of old also saw them. The brahmins also, taking these dreams in the same way, made them a matter for sacrifice. Then, following the method given by the wise, they went and asked the Bodhisatta. The wise of old, too, when explaining these dreams to them, spoke in this very same manner.” Having said this, being requested by the king, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ceva [M 1.0364] samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā himavantappadese jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto viharati. Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatto imināva niyāmena ime supine disvā brāhmaṇe pucchi. Brāhmaṇā evameva yaññaṃ yajituṃ ārabhiṃsu. Tesu purohitassa antevāsikamāṇavo paṇḍito byatto ācariyaṃ āha – “ācariya, tumhehi mayaṃ tayo vede uggaṇhāpitā, nanu tesu ekaṃ māretvā ekassa sotthikammassa kāraṇaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Tāta, iminā upāyena amhākaṃ bahudhanaṃ uppajjissati, tvaṃ pana rañño dhanaṃ rakkhitukāmo maññeti. Māṇavo “tena hi, ācariya, tumhe tumhākaṃ kammaṃ karotha, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ santike kiṃ karissāmī”ti vicaranto rañño uyyānaṃ agamāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a northern brahmin family. Having come of age, he went forth into the life of an ascetic, developed the higher spiritual knowledges and meditative attainments, and dwelt in the Himalayan region, delighting in the bliss of jhāna. At that time in Bārāṇasī, King Brahmadatta saw these same dreams in the very same way and asked the brahmins. The brahmins, in the very same way, began to prepare a sacrifice. Among them, the royal chaplain’s disciple, a wise and clever youth, said to his teacher: “Teacher, you have had us learn the three Vedas. Surely, in them there is no such thing as causing the well-being of one by killing another.” “My dear boy, by this means much wealth will come to us, but you, I think, wish to protect the king’s wealth.” The youth said, “In that case, teacher, you do your work. What shall I do in your presence?” And wandering off, he went to the king’s park.

Taṃ divasameva bodhisattopi taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “ajja mayi manussapathaṃ gate mahājanassa bandhanā mokkho bhavissatī”ti ākāsena gantvā uyyāne otaritvā suvaṇṇapaṭimā viya maṅgalasilātale nisīdi. Māṇavo bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā paṭisanthāramakāsi. Bodhisattopi tena saddhiṃ madhurapaṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kiṃ nu kho, māṇava, rājā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretī”ti pucchi. “Bhante, rājā nāma dhammiko, apica kho taṃ brāhmaṇā atitthe pakkhandāpe”nti. Rājā soḷasa supine disvā brāhmaṇānaṃ ārocesi. Brāhmaṇā “yaññaṃ yajissāmā”ti [P 1.0344] āraddhā. Kiṃ nu kho, bhante, “ayaṃ nāma imesaṃ supinānaṃ nipphattī”ti rājānaṃ saññāpetvā tumhākaṃ mahājanaṃ bhayā mocetuṃ na vaṭṭatīti. Mayaṃ kho, māṇava, rājānaṃ na jānāma, rājāpi amhe na jānāti. Sace pana idhāgantvā puccheyya, katheyyāmassa mayanti. Māṇavo “ahaṃ, bhante, taṃ ānessāmi, tumhe mamāgamanaṃ udikkhantā muhuttaṃ nisīdathā”ti bodhisattaṃ paṭijānāpetvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “mahārāja, eko [V 1.0329] ākāsacāriko tāpaso tumhākaṃ uyyāne otaritvā ‘tumhehi diṭṭhasupinānaṃ nipphattiṃ kathessāmī’ti tumhe pakkosatī”ti āha.

On that very day, the Bodhisatta, knowing the situation, thought, “Today, if I go to the world of humans, there will be a release from bondage for the great populace.” He traveled through the sky, descended into the park, and sat on the auspicious stone slab like a golden statue. The youth approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, sat to one side, and exchanged friendly greetings. The Bodhisatta also exchanged pleasantries with him and asked, “Tell me, youth, does the king rule righteously?” “Venerable sir, the king is indeed righteous, but the brahmins are causing him to go astray.” The king had seen sixteen dreams and told them to the brahmins, and the brahmins had begun to prepare a sacrifice. The youth then asked, “Venerable sir, would it not be proper for you to inform the king, saying, ‘This is the result of these dreams,’ and thereby free the great populace from fear?” “Youth, I do not know the king, nor does the king know me. But if he were to come here and ask, I would tell him.” The youth said, “Venerable sir, I will bring him. Please wait here for a moment, expecting my return.” Having secured the Bodhisatta's agreement, he went to the king and said, “Great King, a sky-faring ascetic has descended into your park and summons you, saying, ‘I will explain the result of the dreams you have seen.’”

Rājā tassa kathaṃ sutvā tāvadeva mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ gantvā tāpasaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno pucchi “tumhe kira, bhante, mayā diṭṭhasupinānaṃ nipphattiṃ jānāthā”ti? “Āma, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi kathethā”ti. “Kathemi, mahārāja, yathādiṭṭhe tāva supine maṃ sāvehī”ti. “Sādhu, bhante”ti rājā –

The king, having heard his words, immediately went to the park with a large retinue, paid homage to the ascetic, and, sitting to one side, asked, “Venerable sir, is it true that you know the outcome of the dreams I have seen?” “Yes, Great King.” “Then please explain them.” “I will explain, Great King. First, relate to me the dreams just as you saw them.” “Very well, venerable sir,” said the king.

77.

77.

“Usabhā [M 1.0365] rukkhā gāviyo gavā ca,

Asso kaṃso siṅgālī ca kumbho;

Pokkharaṇī ca apākacandanaṃ.

“Bulls, trees, cows, and oxen; a horse, a bowl, a she-jackal, and a pot; a lotus pond, and uncooked sandalwood.”

“Lābūni sīdanti silā plavanti, maṇḍūkiyo kaṇhasappe gilanti;

Kākaṃ suvaṇṇā parivārayanti, tasā vakā eḷakānaṃ bhayā hī”ti. –

“Gourds sink while stones float; small female frogs swallow black snakes; a crow is attended by golden swans; and wolves are terrified of goats.”

Vatvā pasenadiraññā kathitaniyāmeneva supine kathesi.

Having spoken, he recounted the dreams in the same manner as they were related by King Pasenadi.

Bodhisattopi tesaṃ idāni satthārā kathitaniyāmeneva vitthārato nipphattiṃ kathetvā pariyosāne sayaṃ idaṃ kathesi –

The Bodhisatta, too, then explained the fulfillment of those dreams in detail, in the same manner as the Teacher had just related them, concluding by declaring this himself:

“Vipariyāso vattati nayidha matthī”ti;

“A reversal is taking place; there is no truth here.”

Tatrāyamattho – ayaṃ, mahārāja, imesaṃ supinānaṃ nipphatti. Yaṃ panetaṃ tesaṃ paṭighātatthāya yaññakammaṃ vattati, taṃ vipariyāso vattati viparītato vattati, vipallāsena vattatīti vuttaṃ hoti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Imesañhi nipphatti nāma lokassa viparivattanakāle, akāraṇassa kāraṇanti gahaṇakāle, kāraṇassa akāraṇanti chaḍḍanakāle, abhūtassa bhūtanti gahaṇakāle, bhūtassa abhūtanti jahanakāle, alajjīnaṃ ussannakāle, lajjīnañca parihīnakāle bhavissati. Nayidha matthīti idāni pana tava vā mama [P 1.0345] vā kāle idha imasmiṃ purisayuge vattamāne etesaṃ nipphatti natthi. Tasmā etesaṃ paṭighātāya vattamānaṃ yaññakammaṃ vipallāsena vattati, alaṃ tena. Natthi te itonidānaṃ bhayaṃ vā chambhitattaṃ vāti mahāpuriso rājānaṃ samassāsetvā mahājanaṃ [V 1.0330] bandhanā mocetvā puna ākāse ṭhatvā rañño ovādaṃ datvā pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā “ito paṭṭhāya, mahārāja, brāhmaṇehi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā pasughātayaññaṃ mā yajī”ti dhammaṃ desetvā ākāseneva attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Rājāpi tassa ovāde ṭhito dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Herein is the meaning: This, great king, is the future fulfillment of those dreams. As for the sacrificial rite being performed to counteract them, that is a perversion; it is proceeding in a contrary way, through distortion—so it is said. Why? Because the fulfillment of these dreams will occur at a time when the world is being overturned: when a non-cause is taken as a cause, and a cause is rejected as a non-cause; when the unreal is grasped as real, and the real is abandoned as unreal; when the shameless are in the ascendant, and the modest are in decline. As for the words, ‘its fulfillment is not here,’ this means that now, in your time or mine, here in this present human age, the fulfillment of these dreams does not exist. Therefore, the sacrificial rite being performed to counteract them proceeds from distortion. Enough of it! There is no danger or terror for you from this cause.” Thus the great being reassured the king. He freed the great multitude from their bonds and, standing again in the sky, gave the king his counsel, establishing him in the five precepts. He taught the Dhamma, saying, “From now on, great king, do not, in concert with the brahmins, perform animal sacrifices.” Having taught the Dhamma, he departed through the sky to his own dwelling place. The king, abiding in his counsel, performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “supinapaccayā te bhayaṃ natthi, haretaṃ yañña”nti yaññaṃ hāretvā mahājanassa jīvitadānaṃ datvā anusandhiṃ [M 1.0366] ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, māṇavo sāriputto, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, said, “There is no danger to you on account of the dreams; put an end to this sacrifice!” Having thus caused the sacrifice to be stopped and given the gift of life to the great multitude, he connected the narrative and identified the Jātaka: “At that time, the king was Ānanda, the young man was Sāriputta, and the ascetic was none other than myself.”

Parinibbute pana bhagavati saṅgītikārakā “usabhā”tiādīni tīṇi padāni aṭṭhakathaṃ āropetvā “lābūnī”tiādīni cattāri padāni ekaṃ gāthaṃ katvā ekakanipātapāḷiṃ āropesunti.

After the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, the reciters at the Council, having placed the three phrases beginning with 'usabhā' into the commentary, and having formed one verse from the four phrases beginning with 'lābūnī,' included it in the Pāli canon of the Ekanipāta.

Mahāsupinajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Mahāsupina Jātaka, the Seventh.

[78] 8. Illisajātakavaṇṇanā

[78] 8. The Commentary on the Illisa Jātaka

Ubho khañjāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto macchariyakosiyaseṭṭhiṃ ārabbha kathesi. Rājagahanagarassa kira avidūre sakkāraṃ nāma nigamo ahosi, tattheko macchariyakosiyo nāma seṭṭhi asītikoṭivibhavo paṭivasati. So tiṇaggena telabindumattampi neva paresaṃ deti, na attanā paribhuñjati. Iti tassa taṃ vibhavajātaṃ neva puttadārādīnaṃ, na samaṇabrāhmaṇānaṃ atthaṃ anubhoti, rakkhasapariggahitapokkharaṇī viya aparibhogaṃ tiṭṭhati.

The Teacher related this story beginning “Both are lame” while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the miserly merchant Kosiyaseṭṭhi. It is said that not far from the city of Rājagaha there was a market town named Sakkāra, where a merchant named Macchariyakosiyaseṭṭhi, who possessed a fortune of eighty crores, resided. He would not give to others so much as a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass, nor would he consume it himself. Thus, his great wealth was of no benefit to his wife and children, nor to ascetics and brahmins; it remained unenjoyed, like a lotus pond possessed by demons.

Satthā ekadivasaṃ paccūsasamaye mahākaruṇāsamāpattito vuṭṭhāya sakalalokadhātuyaṃ bodhaneyyabandhave olokento pañcacattālīsayojanamatthake vasantassa tassa seṭṭhino sapajāpatikassa sotāpattiphalassa upanissayaṃ addasa. Tato purimadivase pana rājānaṃ upaṭṭhātuṃ rājagehaṃ gantvā rājūpaṭṭhānaṃ katvā āgacchanto ekaṃ chātajjhattaṃ janapadamanussaṃ kummāsapūraṃ kapallapūvaṃ khādantaṃ disvā tattha pipāsaṃ uppādetvā attano gharaṃ [P 1.0346] gantvā cintesi “sacāhaṃ ‘kapallapūvaṃ khāditukāmomhī’ti vakkhāmi, bahū mayā saddhiṃ khāditukāmā bhavissanti, evaṃ me bahūni taṇḍulasappimadhuphāṇitādīni parikkhayaṃ gamissanti, na kassaci kathessāmī”ti [V 1.0331] taṇhaṃ adhivāsento vicarati. So gacchante gacchante kāle uppaṇḍupaṇḍukajāto dhamanisanthatagatto jāto[M 1.0367]. Tato taṇhaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto gabbhaṃ pavisitvā mañcakaṃ upagūhitvā nipajji. Evaṃgatopi dhanahānibhayena kassaci kiñci na kathesi.

One day at dawn, the Teacher, having arisen from the attainment of great compassion and surveying the entire world-system for beings who could be guided, perceived the potential for the fruit of stream-entry in that merchant and his wife, who lived forty-five yojanas away. On the preceding day, the merchant had gone to the royal palace to wait upon the king. Having attended to the king and while returning, he saw a man from the countryside, overcome with hunger, eating a griddle-cake filled with barley-meal. At this sight, a craving arose in him. Upon returning home, he thought, 'If I say, “I desire to eat a griddle-cake,” many people will want to eat with me. In that case, much of my rice, ghee, honey, and molasses will be consumed. I will tell no one.' Enduring his craving, he went about his way. As time went on, he became pale and sallow, and his body grew gaunt, with veins standing out. Then, unable to endure his craving any longer, he entered his private chamber, lay down, and clung to his bed. Yet even in this state, for fear of losing his wealth, he said nothing of this to anyone.

Atha naṃ bhariyā upasaṅkamitvā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjitvā “kiṃ te sāmi, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. “Na me kiñci aphāsukaṃ atthī”ti. “Kiṃ nu kho te rājā kupito”ti? “Rājāpi me na kuppatī”ti. “Atha kiṃ te puttadhītāhi vā dāsakammakarādīhi vā kiñci amanāpaṃ kataṃ atthī”ti? “Evarūpampi natthī”ti. “Kismiñci pana te taṇhā atthī”ti? Evaṃ vuttepi dhanahānibhayena kiñci avatvā nissaddova nipajji. Atha naṃ bhariyā “kathehi, sāmi, kismiṃ te taṇhā”ti āha. So vacanaṃ parigilanto viya “atthi me ekā taṇhā”ti āha. “Kiṃ taṇhā, sāmī”ti? “Kapallapūvaṃ khāditukāmomhī”ti. “Atha kimatthaṃ na kathesi, kiṃ tvaṃ daliddo, idāni sakalasakkāranigamavāsīnaṃ pahonake kapallapūve pacissāmī”ti? “Kiṃ te etehi, te attano kammaṃ katvā khādissantī”ti? “Tena hi ekaracchavāsīnaṃ pahonake pacāmī”ti. Jānāmahaṃ tava mahaddhanabhāvanti. “Tena hi imasmiṃ gehamatte sabbesaṃ pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Jānāmahaṃ tava mahajjhāsayabhāva”nti. “Tena hi te puttadāramattasseva pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana te etehī”ti? “Tena hi tuyhañca mayhañca pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Tvaṃ kiṃ karissasī”ti? “Tena hi ekasseva te pahonakaṃ katvā pacāmī”ti. “Imasmiṃ ṭhāne paccamānaṃ bahū paccāsīsanti, sakalataṇḍule ṭhapetvā bhinnataṇḍule ca uddhanakapallādīni ca ādāya thokaṃ khīrasappimadhuphāṇitañca gahetvā sattabhūmikassa pāsādassa uparimatalaṃ āruyha paca, tatthāhaṃ ekakova nisīditvā khādissāmī”ti. Sā “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā gahetabbaṃ gāhāpetvā pāsādaṃ āruyha dāsiyo vissajjetvā seṭṭhiṃ pakkosāpesi. So ādito paṭṭhāya dvārāni pidahanto sabbadvāresu sūcighaṭikāni datvā sattamatalaṃ abhiruhitvā tatthapi dvāraṃ pidahitvā nisīdi. Bhariyāpissa uddhane aggiṃ jāletvā kapallakaṃ āropetvā pūve pacituṃ ārabhi.

Then his wife approached him, stroked his back, and asked, "What troubles you, my lord?" "Nothing troubles me," he replied. "Is the king angry with you?" "The king is not angry with me." "Then have your sons, daughters, or servants and workers done something displeasing?" "Nothing of that sort." "But do you have some craving for something?" Even when asked this, fearing the loss of wealth, he lay down and remained silent. Then his wife said, "Tell me, my lord, what do you crave?" As if swallowing his words, he replied, "I have one craving." "What is it, my lord?" "I wish to eat a griddle-cake." "Then why did you not say so? Are you poor? I will now prepare griddle-cakes enough for all the residents of the market town of Sakkāra." "What have they to do with you? They will do their own work and eat." "Then I will prepare them enough for the residents of our street." "I know how wealthy you are!" "Then I will prepare them enough for everyone in this house." "I know how generous you are!" "Then I will prepare them enough for just your wife and children." "And what have they to do with you?" "Then I will prepare them enough for you and me." "And what about you?" "Then I will prepare them enough for you alone." "If they are cooked in this place, many will expect some. Setting aside the whole rice grains, take the broken rice, a stove, a pan, and a little milk, ghee, honey, and molasses, go up to the top floor of the seven-storied mansion to cook. There I will sit alone and eat." She agreed, saying, "Very well," and after having the necessary things brought, she went up to the mansion, dismissed the female servants, and summoned the setthi. He, closing all the doors from the very first and placing needle-locks on them, ascended to the seventh floor, closed the door there as well, and sat down. His wife lit the fire in the stove, placed the pan on it, and began to cook the cakes.

Atha [M 1.0368] satthā pātova mahāmoggallānattheraṃ āmantesi, “eso, moggallāna, rājagahanagarassa avidūre [P 1.0347] sakkāranigame macchariyakosiyaseṭṭhi ‘kapallapūve khādissāmī’ti aññesaṃ dassanabhayena sattabhūmike pāsāde kapallapūve pacāpeti. Tvaṃ tattha gantvā taṃ seṭṭhiṃ dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā ubhopi jayampatike pūve ca khīrasappimadhuphāṇitādīni ca gāhāpetvā [V 1.0332] attano balena jetavanaṃ ānehi. Ajjāhaṃ pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ vihāreyeva nisīdissāmi, pūveheva bhattakiccaṃ karissāmī”ti. Thero “sādhu, bhante”ti satthu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā tāvadeva iddhibalena taṃ nigamaṃ gantvā tassa pāsādassa sīhapañjaradvāre sunivattho supāruto ākāseyeva maṇirūpakaṃ viya aṭṭhāsi.

Then the Teacher, early in the morning, addressed the Elder Mahāmoggallāna: “Moggallāna, not far from the city of Rājagaha, in the market town of Sakkāra, the miserly setthi Kosiya, fearing others might see him, is having griddle-cakes cooked in a seven-storied mansion, thinking, ‘I will eat griddle-cakes.’ You go there, subdue that setthi, make him humble, and bring the husband and wife, along with the cakes and the milk, ghee, honey, and molasses, to Jetavana by your own power. Today, I will remain in the monastery with five hundred monks and we will make our meal with these cakes.” The Elder replied, “Very well, Venerable Sir,” and accepting the Teacher’s words, he immediately went to that market town by his psychic power. Standing in the sky at the lion-window of the mansion, well-dressed and well-robed, he appeared like a jeweled statue.

Mahāseṭṭhino theraṃ disvāva hadayamaṃsaṃ kampi. So “ahaṃ evarūpānaññeva bhayena imaṃ ṭhānaṃ āgato, ayañca āgantvā vātapānadvāre ṭhito”ti gahetabbagahaṇaṃ apassanto aggimhi pakkhittaloṇasakkharā viya dosena taṭataṭāyanto evamāha “samaṇa, ākāse ṭhatvā tvaṃ kiṃ labhissasi, ākāse apade padaṃ dassetvā caṅkamantopi neva labhissasī”ti. Thero tasmiṃyeva ṭhāne aparāparaṃ caṅkami. Seṭṭhi “caṅkamanto kiṃ labhissasi, ākāse pallaṅkena nisīdamānopi na labhissasiyevā”ti āha. Thero pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā nisīdi. Atha naṃ “nisinno kiṃ labhissasi, āgantvā vātapānaummāre ṭhitopi na labhissasī”ti āha. Atha thero ummāre aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ “ummāre ṭhito kiṃ labhissasi, dhūmāyantopi na labhissasiyevā”ti āha. Thero dhūmāyi, sakalapāsādo ekadhūmo ahosi, seṭṭhino akkhīnaṃ sūciyā vijjhanakālo viya jāto. Gehajjhāyanabhayena pana naṃ “pajjalantopi na labhissasī”ti avatvā cintesi “ayaṃ samaṇo suṭṭhu laggo, aladdhā na gamissati, ekamassa pūvaṃ dāpessāmī”ti bhariyaṃ āha – “bhadde, ekaṃ khuddakapūvaṃ pacitvā samaṇassa datvā uyyojehi na”nti. Sā thokaññeva piṭṭhaṃ kapallapātiyaṃ pakkhipi, mahāpūvo hutvā sakalapātiṃ pūretvā uddhumāto aṭṭhāsi.

Upon seeing the Elder, the great setthi’s heart trembled. He thought, “I came to this place fearing just such people, and now this one has arrived and stands at the window.” Seeing no way to seize him, he crackled with anger like salt thrown into a fire, and said, “Monk, what will you gain by standing in the sky? Even if you walk back and forth in the sky where there is no path, you will gain nothing!” The Elder then walked back and forth right there. The setthi said, “What will you gain by walking? Even if you sit cross-legged in the sky, you will still gain nothing!” The Elder folded his legs and sat. Then the setthi said, “What will you gain by sitting? Even if you stand on the window ledge, you will gain nothing!” The Elder stood on the ledge. Then the setthi said, “What will you gain by standing on the ledge? Even if you emit smoke, you will still gain nothing!” The Elder emitted smoke, and the entire mansion became a single mass of smoke, making the setthi’s eyes sting as if pierced by needles. Fearing the house might burn down, he did not say, “Even if you blaze, you will gain nothing!” but thought, “This monk is very persistent; he won’t leave without getting something. I will have one cake given to him.” He told his wife, “My dear, bake a small cake, give it to the monk, and send him away.” She put just a little flour into the pan, but it swelled into a large cake, filling the entire pan and rising up.

Seṭṭhi taṃ disvā “bahu tayā piṭṭhaṃ gahitaṃ bhavissatī”ti sayameva dabbikaṇṇena thokataraṃ piṭṭhaṃ gahetvā pakkhipi, pūvo purimapūvato mahantataro [M 1.0369] jāto. Evaṃ yaṃ yaṃ pacati, so so mahantamahantova hoti. So nibbinno bhariyaṃ āha “bhadde, imassa ekaṃ pūvaṃ dehī”ti. Tassā pacchito ekaṃ pūvaṃ gaṇhantiyā sabbe ekābaddhā allīyiṃsu. Sā seṭṭhiṃ āha “sāmi, sabbe pūvā ekato laggā, visuṃ kātuṃ na sakkomī”ti. “Ahaṃ karissāmī”ti sopi kātuṃ nāsakkhi. Ubho janā koṭiyaṃ gahetvā kaḍḍhantāpi viyojetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsuyeva. Athassa pūvehi saddhiṃ vāyamantasseva sarīrato sedā mucciṃsu, pipāsā ca pacchijji. Tato bhariyaṃ āha “bhadde, na me pūvehi attho[P 1.0348], pacchiyā saddhiṃyeva imassa bhikkhussa dehī”ti. Sā pacchiṃ ādāya theraṃ upasaṅkamitvā sabbe pūve therassa adāsi. Thero [V 1.0333] ubhinnampi dhammaṃ desesi, tiṇṇaṃ ratanānaṃ guṇe kathesi, “atthi dinnaṃ, atthi yiṭṭha”nti dānādīnaṃ phalaṃ gaganatale puṇṇacandaṃ viya dassesi.

Seeing this, the merchant said, “You must have taken a lot of flour,” and he himself took a little flour with the tip of a ladle and put it in. The cake became larger than the previous one. In this way, whatever cake he fried, it became larger and larger. Becoming weary, he said to his wife, “My dear, give this one a cake.” As she was taking one cake from the basket, all of them stuck together as one. She said to the merchant, “My lord, all the cakes are stuck together; I cannot separate them.” “I will do it,” he said, but he too could not. Though both of them held an edge and pulled, they could not separate them. Then, as he struggled with the cakes, sweat broke out from his body, and his craving was extinguished. He then said to his wife, “My dear, I have no need for the cakes; give them to this monk along with the basket.” She took the basket, approached the Elder, and gave all the cakes to him. The Elder taught the Dhamma to both of them, spoke of the virtues of the Three Jewels, and, saying, “There is fruit in what is given, there is fruit in what is offered,” he revealed the fruit of giving and so forth, like the full moon in the sky.

Taṃ sutvā pasannacitto seṭṭhi “bhante, āgantvā imasmiṃ pallaṅke nisīditvā pūve paribhuñjathā”ti āha. Thero “mahāseṭṭhi, sammāsambuddho ‘pūve khādissāmī’ti pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ vihāre nisinno, tumhākaṃ ruciyā sati seṭṭhibhariyaṃ pūve ca khīrādīni ca gaṇhāpetha, satthu santikaṃ gamissāmā”ti āha. “Kahaṃ pana, bhante, etarahi satthā”ti? “Ito pañcacattālīsayojanamatthake jetavanamahāvihāre”ti. “Bhante, kālaṃ anatikkamitvā ettakaṃ addhānaṃ kathaṃ gamissāmā”ti? “Mahāseṭṭhi tumhākaṃ ruciyā sati ahaṃ vo attano iddhibalena nessāmi, tumhākaṃ pāsāde sopānasīsaṃ attano ṭhāneyeva bhavissati, sopānapariyosānaṃ pana jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake bhavissati, uparipāsādā heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ otaraṇakālamattena vo jetavanaṃ nessāmī”ti. So “sādhu, bhante”ti sampaṭicchi. Thero sopānasīsaṃ tattheva katvā “sopānapādamūlaṃ jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake hotū”ti adhiṭṭhāsi, tathevāhosi.

Hearing this, the merchant, with a gladdened mind, said, “Venerable sir, please come and sit on this couch and partake of the cakes.” The Elder replied, “Great merchant, the Perfectly Enlightened One is seated in the monastery with five hundred monks, intending to eat the cakes. If it pleases you, have the merchant’s wife take the cakes and milk and so forth, and we shall go to the Teacher’s presence.” “Where, venerable sir, is the Teacher now?” “At the great monastery of Jetavana, forty-five yojanas from here.” “Venerable sir, how can we travel such a distance without the proper time passing?” “Great merchant, if it pleases you, I will take you by my psychic power. The head of the staircase of your mansion will remain in its own place, but the foot of the staircase will be at the gatehouse of Jetavana. I will take you to Jetavana in the time it takes to descend from the upper mansion to the lower.” He agreed, saying, “Very well, venerable sir.” The Elder, keeping the head of the staircase where it was, made a determination: “Let the foot of the staircase be at the gatehouse of Jetavana,” and so it came to be.

Iti thero seṭṭhiñca seṭṭhibhariyañca uparipāsādā heṭṭhāotaraṇakālato khippataraṃ jetavanaṃ sampāpesi. Te ubhopi satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā kālaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā bhattaggaṃ pavisitvā paññattavarabuddhāsane nisīdi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Mahāseṭṭhi buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa [M 1.0370] dakkhiṇodakaṃ adāsi, seṭṭhibhariyā tathāgatassa patte pūve patiṭṭhāpesi. Satthā attano yāpanamattaṃ gaṇhi, pañcasatā bhikkhūpi tatheva gaṇhiṃsu. Seṭṭhi khīrasappimadhuphāṇitasakkharādīni dadamāno agamāsi. Satthā pañcahi bhikkhusatehi saddhiṃ bhattakiccaṃ niṭṭhāpesi. Mahāseṭṭhipi saddhiṃ bhariyāya yāvadatthaṃ khādi, pūvānaṃ pariyosānameva na paññāyati, sakalavihāre bhikkhūnañca vighāsādānañca dinnepi na pariyanto paññāyati. “Bhante, pūvā parikkhayaṃ na gacchantī”ti bhagavato ārocesuṃ. Tena hi jetavanadvārakoṭṭhake chaḍḍethāti. Atha ne dvārakoṭṭhakassa avidūre pabbhāraṭṭhāne chaḍḍayiṃsu. Ajjatanāpi taṃ ṭhānaṃ “kapallapūvapabbhāro”tveva paññāyati. Mahāseṭṭhi saddhiṃ bhariyāya bhagavantaṃ upasaṅkamitvā ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi. Bhagavā anumodanaṃ akāsi. Anumodanāpariyosāne ubhopi sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāya satthāraṃ vanditvā dvārakoṭṭhake sopānaṃ āruyha attano pāsādeyeva patiṭṭhahiṃsu[P 1.0349]. Tato paṭṭhāya mahāseṭṭhi asītikoṭidhanaṃ buddhasāsaneyeva vikiri.

Thus, the Elder conveyed the great merchant and his wife to Jetavana more quickly than the time it takes to descend from the upper mansion. Both of them approached the Teacher, paid homage, and announced that it was time. The Teacher entered the refectory and sat on the excellent, prepared Buddha-seat together with the Saṅgha of monks. The great merchant poured the water of dedication for the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha, while the merchant’s wife placed the cakes in the Tathāgata’s bowl. The Teacher took just enough for his sustenance, and the five hundred monks did likewise. The merchant went on offering milk, ghee, honey, molasses, sugar, and so forth, and the supply was not exhausted. The Teacher, together with the five hundred monks, finished his meal. The great merchant and his wife also ate to their satisfaction, yet no end to the cakes could be seen. Even when they were given to all the monks in the monastery and to those who eat leftovers, no end was apparent. “Venerable sir, the cakes are not being exhausted,” they reported to the Blessed One. “In that case, discard them at the gatehouse of Jetavana.” Then they discarded them in a sloping place not far from the gatehouse. To this day, that place is known as the ‘Slope of the Pan-Cakes.’ The great merchant, together with his wife, approached the Blessed One and stood to one side. The Blessed One gave a discourse of appreciation. At the conclusion of the discourse, both were established in the fruit of stream-entry, and after paying homage to the Teacher, they ascended the staircase at the gatehouse and were established once more in their own mansion. From that time on, the great merchant distributed his fortune of eighty crores in the Dispensation of the Buddha.

Punadivase [V 1.0334] sammāsambuddhe sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caritvā jetavanaṃ āgamma bhikkhūnaṃ sugatovādaṃ datvā gandhakuṭiṃ pavisitvā paṭisallīne sāyanhasamaye dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā bhikkhū “passathāvuso, mahāmoggallānattherassānubhāvaṃ, anupahacca saddhaṃ anupahacca bhoge macchariyaseṭṭhiṃ muhutteneva dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā pūve gāhāpetvā jetavanaṃ ānetvā satthu sammukhaṃ katvā sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhāpesi, aho mahānubhāvo thero”ti therassa guṇakathaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “bhikkhave, kuladamakena nāma bhikkhunā kule aviheṭhetvā akilametvā pupphato reṇuṃ gaṇhantena bhamarena viya upasaṅkamitvā buddhaguṇe jānāpetabba”nti vatvā theraṃ pasaṃsanto –

On the following day, the Perfectly Enlightened One, having gone for alms in Sāvatthī and returned to Jetavana, gave the monks the admonition of the Sugata. Then, having entered the Fragrant Chamber, he went into seclusion. In the evening, the monks gathered in the Hall of Dhamma and were saying: “Behold, friends, the power of the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna! Without damaging their faith and without damaging their wealth, in a single moment he tamed the miserly merchant, made him free from avarice, had him take the cakes, brought him to Jetavana, placed him in the presence of the Teacher, and established him in the fruit of stream-entry. Ah, how great is the Elder’s power!” As they sat speaking of the Elder’s virtues, the Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?” When this was told to him, he said, “Monks, a monk who tames families should approach them without causing harm or weariness, like a bee gathering pollen from a flower, and should make known the virtues of the Buddha.” Then, praising the Elder, he spoke this verse:

“Yathāpi bhamaro pupphaṃ, vaṇṇagandhamaheṭhayaṃ;

Paleti rasamādāya, evaṃ gāme munī care”ti. (dha. pa. 49) –

“Just as a bee, without harming the flower’s color or scent, takes the nectar and flies away, so should the sage wander in the village.”

Imaṃ [M 1.0371] dhammapade gāthaṃ vatvā uttaripi therassa guṇaṃ pakāsetuṃ “na bhikkhave, idāneva moggallānena macchariyaseṭṭhi damito, pubbepi taṃ dametvā kammaphalasambandhaṃ jānāpesiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Having spoken this verse, and in order to further reveal the elder's virtues, the Teacher said, "Monks, it was not only now that Moggallāna tamed the stingy merchant; in the past too, he tamed him and made him understand the connection of kamma and its result." Then he recounted a story from the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasiyaṃ illiso nāma seṭṭhi ahosi asītikoṭivibhavo purisadosasamannāgato khañjo kuṇī visamakkhimaṇḍalo assaddho appasanno maccharī, neva aññesaṃ deti, na sayaṃ paribhuñjati. Rakkhasapariggahitapokkharaṇī viyassa gehaṃ ahosi. Mātāpitaro panassa yāva sattamā kulaparivaṭṭā dāyakā dānapatino. So seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ labhitvāyeva kulavaṃsaṃ nāsetvā dānasālaṃ jhāpetvā yācake pothetvā nikkaḍḍhitvā dhanameva saṇṭhāpesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there lived a merchant named Illisa. He was worth eighty crores but was possessed of many faults—he was lame, had a crippled hand, and had uneven eyes; he was faithless, ungracious, and miserly. He neither gave to others nor enjoyed his wealth himself. His house was like a pond guarded by a demon. His parents and ancestors, for seven generations, had been generous donors, but once he obtained the position of merchant, he destroyed his family lineage, burned down the alms-hall, beat and drove away the beggars, and only accumulated wealth.

So ekadivasaṃ rājūpaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā attano gharaṃ āgacchanto ekaṃ maggakilantaṃ jānapadamanussaṃ, ekaṃ surāvārakaṃ, ādāya pīṭhake nisīditvā ambilasurāya kosakaṃ pūretvā pūretvā pūtimacchakena uttaribhaṅgena pivantaṃ disvā suraṃ pātukāmo [P 1.0350] hutvā cintesi “sacāhaṃ suraṃ pivissāmi, mayi pivante bahū pivitukāmā bhavissanti, evaṃ me dhanaparikkhayo bhavissatī”ti. So taṇhaṃ adhivāsento vicaritvā gacchante gacchante kāle adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto vihatakappāso viya paṇḍusarīro ahosi dhammanisanthatagatto jāto. Athekadivasaṃ gabbhaṃ [V 1.0335] pavisitvā mañcakaṃ upagūhitvā nipajji. Tamenaṃ bhariyā upasaṅkamitvā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjitvā “kiṃ te, sāmi, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. Sabbaṃ heṭṭhā kathitaniyāmeneva veditabbaṃ. “Tena hi ekasseva te pahonakaṃ suraṃ karomī”ti pana vutte “gehe surāya kāriyamānāya bahū paccāsīsanti, antarāpaṇato āharāpetvāpi na sakkā idha nisinnena pivitu”nti māsakamattaṃ datvā antarāpaṇato surāvārakaṃ āharāpetvā ceṭakena gāhāpetvā nagarā nikkhamma nadītīraṃ gantvā mahāmaggasamīpe ekaṃ gumbaṃ pavisitvā surāvārakaṃ ṭhapāpetvā “gaccha tva”nti ceṭakaṃ dūre nisīdāpetvā kosakaṃ pūretvā suraṃ pātuṃ ārabhi.

One day, after attending upon the king and while returning home, he saw a weary man from the countryside who, having taken a flask of liquor, was sitting on a stool, repeatedly filling a cup with sour liquor and drinking it with a piece of rotten fish as a relish. A desire to drink liquor arose in him, and he thought, 'If I drink liquor, many others will want to drink, and in this way my wealth will be depleted.' He went about enduring his craving, but as time went on, he was unable to bear it any longer and became pale like beaten cotton, with veins standing out on his body. Then one day, he entered his chamber, embraced his bed, and lay down. His wife approached him, massaged his back, and asked, 'What ails you, my lord?' After she learned the cause, she said, 'In that case, I will prepare just enough liquor for you alone.' But he thought, 'If liquor is prepared in the house, many will expect some. Even if it is brought from the tavern, it is not possible to sit here and drink it.' Giving a māsaka, he had a flask of liquor brought from the tavern, had a servant take it, and left the city. Going to the riverbank, he entered a thicket near the main road, had the flask of liquor set down, and telling the servant, 'You go,' made him sit at a distance. He then filled a cup and began to drink the liquor.

Pitā [M 1.0372] panassa dānādīnaṃ puññānaṃ katattā devaloke sakko hutvā nibbatti. So tasmiṃ khaṇe “pavattati nu kho me dānaggaṃ, udāhu no”ti āvajjento tassa appavattiṃ ñatvā, puttassa kulavaṃsaṃ nāsetvā dānasālaṃ jhāpetvā yācake nikkaḍḍhitvā macchariyabhāve patiṭṭhāya “aññesaṃ dātabbaṃ bhavissatī”ti bhayena gumbaṃ pavisitvā ekakasseva suraṃ pivanabhāvañca disvā “gacchāmi, naṃ saṅkhobhetvā dametvā kammaphalasambandhaṃ jānāpetvā dānaṃ dāpetvā devaloke nibbattanārahaṃ karomī”ti manussapathaṃ otaritvā illisaseṭṭhinā sadisaṃ khañjaṃ kuṇiṃ visamacakkhumaṇḍalaṃ attabhāvaṃ nimminitvā bārāṇasinagaraṃ pavisitvā rañño nivesanadvāre ṭhatvā attano āgatabhāvaṃ ārocāpetvā “pavisatū”ti vutte pavisitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Rājā “kiṃ, mahāseṭṭhi, avelāya āgatosī”ti āha. “Āma, āgatomhi, deva ghare me asītikoṭimattaṃ dhanaṃ atthi, taṃ devo āharāpetvā attano bhaṇḍāgāraṃ pūrāpetū”ti. “Alaṃ mahāseṭṭhi, tava dhanato [P 1.0351] amhākaṃ gehe bahutaraṃ dhana”nti. “Sace, deva, tumhākaṃ kammaṃ natthi, yathāruciyā dhanaṃ gahetvā dānaṃ dammī”ti. “Dehi, mahāseṭṭhī”ti. So “sādhu, devā”ti rājānaṃ vanditvā nikkhamitvā illisaseṭṭhino gehaṃ agamāsi, sabbe upaṭṭhākamanussā parivāresuṃ, ekopi “nāyaṃ, illiso”ti jānituṃ samattho nāma natthi.

Now, his father, on account of having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, had been reborn as Sakka in the celestial realm. At that moment, reflecting, 'Is my tradition of giving still continuing, or not?' and discerning that it was not, he saw that his son had destroyed the family lineage, burned down the alms-hall, driven away the beggars, and become established in miserliness. He also saw that his son, out of fear that 'it would have to be given to others,' had entered a thicket and was drinking liquor alone. He thought, 'I shall go, agitate him, tame him, make him understand the connection of kamma and its result, have him give alms, and make him worthy of rebirth in a celestial realm.' Descending to the human world, he created for himself a form resembling Illisa the merchant—lame, with a crippled hand, and with uneven eyes—and entered the city of Bārāṇasī. Standing at the gate of the king’s residence, he had his arrival announced. When told, 'You may enter,' he entered, paid homage to the king, and stood there. The king asked, 'Why, great merchant, have you come at this untimely hour?' 'Indeed I have, Your Majesty. In my house there is wealth amounting to eighty crores. Let Your Majesty have it brought and fill your treasury.' 'That is not necessary, great merchant. In our house there is much more wealth than yours.' 'If, Your Majesty, you have no use for it, I shall take the wealth and give it as alms according to my wish.' 'Give it, great merchant.' Saying, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' he paid homage to the king, departed, and went to the house of Illisa the merchant. All the attendants surrounded him, and there was not a single one who was able to know, 'This is not Illisa.'

So gehaṃ pavisitvā antoummāre ṭhatvā dovārikaṃ pakkosāpetvā “yo añño mayā samānarūpo āgantvā ‘mametaṃ geha’nti pavisituṃ āgacchati, taṃ piṭṭhiyaṃ paharitvā nīhareyyāthā”ti vatvā pāsādaṃ āruyha mahārahe āsane nisīditvā seṭṭhibhariyaṃ pakkosāpetvā sitākāraṃ dassetvā “bhadde, dānaṃ demā”ti āha. Tassa taṃ vacanaṃ sutvāva seṭṭhibhariyā ca puttadhītaro ca dāsakammakarā ca “ettakaṃ kālaṃ dānaṃ dātuṃ cittameva natthi, ajja pana suraṃ pivitvā muducitto hutvā dātukāmo jāto bhavissatī”ti vadiṃsu. Atha naṃ seṭṭhibhariyā “yathāruciyā [V 1.0336] detha, sāmī”ti āha. Tena hi bherivādakaṃ pakkosāpetvā “‘suvaṇṇarajatamaṇimuttādīhi atthikā illisaseṭṭhissa gharaṃ gacchantū’nti sakalanagare bheriṃ carāpehī”ti. Sā ca tathā kāresi. Mahājano pacchipasibbakādīni gahetvā gehadvāre sannipati. Sakko sattaratanapūre [M 1.0373] gabbhe vivarāpetvā “tumhākaṃ dammi, yāvadicchakaṃ gahetvā gacchathā”ti āha. Mahājano dhanaṃ nīharitvā mahātale rāsiṃ katvā ābhatabhājanāni pūretvā gacchati.

Entering the house and standing at the inner threshold, he had the doorkeeper summoned and said, 'If anyone else with a form similar to mine comes and tries to enter, claiming, "This house is mine," you are to strike him on the back and drive him out.' Then, ascending to the upper story of the mansion and sitting on a magnificent seat, he had the merchant's wife summoned. Showing a smiling face, he said, 'Good lady, let us give alms.' Upon hearing his words, the merchant's wife, his sons and daughters, and the servants and workers said among themselves, 'For all this time, there has not even been the thought of giving alms. But today, having drunk liquor, he must have become soft-hearted and desirous of giving.' Then the merchant's wife said to him, 'Give as you wish, master.' 'In that case,' he said, 'have the town crier summoned and have him beat the drum throughout the entire city, proclaiming: "Let those who are in need of gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth, go to the house of Illisa the merchant!"' And she had it done just so. A great crowd of people, taking baskets, bags, and the like, gathered at the door of the house. Sakka had the chambers filled with the seven kinds of treasures opened and said, 'I give to you. Take as much as you desire and go.' The people carried out the wealth, made heaps of it in the great courtyard, filled the containers they had brought, and departed.

Aññataro janapadamanusso illisaseṭṭhino goṇe tasseva rathe yojetvā sattahi ratanehi pūretvā nagarā nikkhamma mahāmaggaṃ paṭipajjitvā tassa gumbassa avidūrena rathaṃ pesento “vassasataṃ jīva, sāmi, illisaseṭṭhi, taṃ nissāya idāni me yāvajīvaṃ kammaṃ akatvā jīvitabbaṃ jātaṃ, taveva ratho, taveva goṇā, taveva gehe satta ratanāni, neva mātarā dinnāni, na pitarā, taṃ nissāya laddhāni, sāmī”ti seṭṭhino guṇakathaṃ kathento gacchati. So taṃ saddaṃ sutvā bhītatasito cintesi “ayaṃ mama nāmaṃ gahetvā [P 1.0352] idañcidañca vadati, kacci nu kho mama dhanaṃ raññā lokassa dinna”nti gumbā nikkhamitvā goṇe ca rathañca sañjānitvā “are, ceṭaka, mayhaṃ goṇā, mayhaṃ ratho”ti vatvā gantvā goṇe nāsārajjuyaṃ gaṇhi, gahapatiko rathā oruyha “are, duṭṭhaceṭaka, illisamahāseṭṭhi sakalanagarassa dānaṃ deti, tvaṃ kiṃ ahosī”ti pakkhanditvā asaniṃ pātento viya khandhe paharitvā rathaṃ ādāya agamāsi. So puna kampamāno uṭṭhāya paṃsuṃ puñchitvā puñchitvā vegena gantvā rathaṃ gaṇhi, gahapatiko rathā otaritvā kesesu gahetvā oṇāmetvā kapparapahārehi koṭṭetvā gale gahetvā āgatamaggābhimukhaṃ khipitvā pakkāmi. Ettāvatāssa surāmado chijji. So kampamāno vegena nivesanadvāraṃ gantvā dhanaṃ ādāya gacchante mahājane disvā “ambho kiṃ nāmetaṃ, kiṃ rājā mama dhanaṃ vilumpāpetī”ti taṃ taṃ gantvā gaṇhāti, gahitagahitā paharitvā pādamūleyeva pātenti. So vedanāppatto gehaṃ pavisituṃ ārabhi. Dvārapālā “are, duṭṭhagahapati, kahaṃ pavisasī”ti vaṃsapesikāhi pothetvā gīvāyaṃ gahetvā nīhariṃsu.

A certain man from the countryside yoked the oxen of the merchant Illisa to that very chariot, filled it with the seven treasures, and departed from the city. Proceeding along the main road, he drove the chariot near that thicket. As he went, he spoke in praise of the merchant, saying, 'May you live a hundred years, master, merchant Illisa! On your account, it has now come about that I may live my entire life without working. Yours is the chariot, yours are the oxen, yours are the seven treasures. They were not given by my mother, nor by my father; they were obtained on account of you, master!' Hearing this sound, Illisa, frightened and agitated, thought, 'This man is taking my name and saying this and that. Can it be that my wealth has been given away to the people by the king?' Emerging from the thicket, he recognized the oxen and the chariot and said, 'Hey, you wretch, my oxen, my chariot!' Going forward, he took hold of the oxen by the nose-rope. The householder, alighting from the chariot, shouted, 'Hey, you wicked wretch! The great merchant Illisa is giving alms to the entire city. What is the matter with you?' and rushing at him as if casting a thunderbolt, he struck him on the neck. Then he took the chariot and went away. Again, trembling, Illisa got up, dusted himself off again and again, and quickly ran after the chariot and seized it. The householder, alighting from the chariot, grabbed him by the hair, forced him down, struck him with blows of his elbows, seized him by the throat, and threw him back toward the way he had come, then departed. With just that, his intoxication from liquor was dispelled. Trembling, he hurried to the door of his residence. Seeing the great crowd of people carrying away his wealth, he cried, 'Sirs, what is this? Is the king having my wealth plundered?' He went and seized them one by one, but each person he seized struck him and knocked him down at their feet. Afflicted with pain, he tried to enter the house. The gatekeepers shouted, 'Hey, you wicked householder, where are you entering?' and beat him with bamboo staves, seized him by the neck, and dragged him out.

So “ṭhapetvā idāni rājānaṃ natthi me añño koci paṭisaraṇo”ti rañño santikaṃ gantvā “deva, mama gehaṃ tumhe vilumpāpethā”ti āha. Nāhaṃ seṭṭhi vilumpāpemi, nanu tvameva āgantvā “sace tumhe na gaṇhatha, ahaṃ mama dhanaṃ dānaṃ dassāmī”ti nagare bheriṃ carāpetvā dānaṃ adāsīti. Nāhaṃ[M 1.0374], deva, tumhākaṃ santikaṃ āgacchāmi, kiṃ tumhe mayhaṃ macchariyabhāvaṃ na jānātha, ahaṃ tiṇaggena telabindumpi na kassaci demi. Yo dānaṃ deti, taṃ pakkosāpetvā [V 1.0337] vīmaṃsatha, devāti. Rājā sakkaṃ pakkosāpesi, dvinnaṃ janānaṃ visesaṃ neva rājā jānāti, na amaccā. Macchariyaseṭṭhi “kiṃ, deva, ayaṃ seṭṭhi, ahaṃ seṭṭhī”ti āha. “Mayaṃ na sañjānāma, atthi te koci sañjānanako”ti? “Bhariyā me, devā”ti. Bhariyaṃ pakkosāpetvā “kataro te sāmiko”ti pucchiṃsu. Sā “aya”nti sakkasseva santike aṭṭhāsi. Puttadhītaro dāsakammakare [P 1.0353] ca pakkosāpetvā pucchiṃsu, sabbepi sakkasseva santike tiṭṭhanti.

He thought, 'Now, apart from the king, there is no other refuge for me,' and going to the king, he said, 'Your Majesty, are you having my house plundered?' 'Merchant, I am not having it plundered. Was it not you yourself who came and said, "If you do not take it, I myself will give my wealth as a gift," and then had a drum beaten in the city and gave the gift?' 'I did not come to you, Your Majesty. Do you not know my miserly nature? I would not give anyone so much as a drop of oil on the tip of a blade of grass. Summon the one who is giving the gift and investigate him, Your Majesty.' The king had Sakka summoned. Neither the king nor the ministers knew the difference between the two men. The miserly merchant said, 'What is this, Your Majesty? Is this man the merchant? I am the merchant.' 'We do not recognize you. Is there anyone who recognizes you?' 'My wife, Your Majesty.' They had his wife summoned and asked, 'Which one is your husband?' She stood by Sakka's side and said, 'This one.' They summoned his sons, daughters, servants, and workers and questioned them. All of them stood by Sakka's side.

Puna seṭṭhi cintesi “mayhaṃ sīse piḷakā atthi, kesehi paṭicchannā, taṃ kho pana kappako eva jānāti, taṃ pakkosāpessāmī”ti. So “kappako maṃ, deva, sañjānāti, taṃ pakkosāpethā”ti āha. Tasmiṃ pana kāle bodhisatto tassa kappako ahosi. Rājā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “illisaseṭṭhiṃ jānāsī”ti pucchi. “Sīsaṃ oloketvā jānissāmi, devā”ti. “Tena hi dvinnampi sīsaṃ olokehī”ti. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko sīse piḷakaṃ māpesi. Bodhisatto dvinnampi sīsaṃ olokento piḷakā disvā “mahārāja, dvinnampi sīse piḷakā attheva, nāhaṃ etesu ekassāpi illisabhāvaṃ sañjānituṃ sakkomī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Again the merchant thought, 'On my head there is a mole, covered by my hair. Only the barber knows of it. I will have him summoned.' He said, 'Your Majesty, the barber recognizes me. Please have him summoned.' Now at that time, the Bodhisatta was his barber. The king had him summoned and asked, 'Do you know the merchant Illisa?' 'I will know after looking at the head, Your Majesty.' 'In that case, look at the heads of both.' At that moment, Sakka created a mole on his head. The Bodhisatta, looking at the heads of both and seeing the moles, said, 'Great King, there are moles on both heads. I am not able to recognize which of them is Illisa.' Having said this, he spoke this verse:

78.

78.

“Ubho khañjā ubho kuṇī, ubho visamacakkhukā;

Ubhinnaṃ piḷakā jātā, nāhaṃ passāmi illisa”nti.

'Both are lame, both are crippled, both are squint-eyed; Moles have appeared on both; I do not see Illisa.'

Tattha ubhoti dvepi janā. Khañjāti kuṇṭhapādā. Kuṇīti kuṇṭhahatthā. Visamacakkhukāti visamakkhimaṇḍalā kekarā. Piḷakāti dvinnampi ekasmiṃyeva sīsapadese ekasaṇṭhānāva piḷakā jātā. Nāhaṃ passāmīti ahaṃ “imesu ayaṃ nāma illiso”ti na passāmi, ekassāpi illisabhāvaṃ na jānāmīti avoca.

Therein, 'both' means both persons. 'Lame' means with a crippled foot. 'Crippled' means with a crippled hand. 'Squint-eyed' means with uneven eye-orbs, cross-eyed. 'Moles' means that for both of them, moles of the very same shape have appeared on the very same spot on the head. 'I do not see' means: I do not see, 'This one among these is Illisa,' that is, I do not know the identity of Illisa in even one of them.

Bodhisattassa vacanaṃ sutvā seṭṭhi kampamāno dhanasokena satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkonto tattheva pati. Tasmiṃ khaṇe sakko “nāhaṃ, mahārāja[M 1.0375], illiso, sakkohamasmī”ti mahatiyā sakkalīlāya ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Illisassa mukhaṃ puñchitvā udakena siñciṃsu, so uṭṭhāya sakkaṃ devarājānaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ sakko āha “illisa, idaṃ dhanaṃ mama santakaṃ, na tava. Ahañhi te pitā, tvaṃ mama putto. Ahaṃ dānādīni puññāni katvā sakkattaṃ patto, tvaṃ pana me vaṃsaṃ upacchinditvā adānasīlo hutvā macchariye patiṭṭhāya dānasālāyo jhāpetvā yācake nikkaḍḍhitvā dhanameva saṇṭhāpesi. Taṃ neva tvaṃ paribhuñjasi, na [V 1.0338] aññesaṃ desi, rakkhasapariggahitaṃ viya [P 1.0354] tiṭṭhati. Sace me dānasālā pākatikā katvā dānaṃ dassasi, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce dassasi, sabbaṃ te dhanaṃ antaradhāpetvā iminā indavajirena te sīsaṃ chinditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessāmī”ti. Illisaseṭṭhi maraṇabhayena santajjito “ito paṭṭhāya dānaṃ dassāmī”ti paṭiññaṃ adāsi. Sakko tassa paṭiññaṃ gahetvā ākāse nisinnova dhammaṃ desetvā taṃ sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā sakaṭṭhānameva agamāsi. Illisopi dānādīni puññāni katvā saggaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Hearing the Bodhisatta’s words, the merchant, trembling with grief over his wealth, collapsed right there, unable to regain his composure. At that moment, Sakka declared, “Great king, I am not Illisa, I am Sakka!” and stood in the sky with great divine splendor. They wiped Illisa's face and sprinkled water on him. Rising, he paid homage to Sakka, the king of gods, and stood there. Then Sakka said to him, “Illisa, this wealth is mine, not yours. For I am your father, and you are my son. I attained the state of Sakka by performing meritorious deeds such as generosity, but you, cutting off my lineage, became ungenerous and, established in stinginess, burned down the alms-halls, drove away beggars, and only accumulated wealth. You neither enjoy it yourself nor give it to others—it remains as if possessed by a demon. If you restore my alms-halls to their original state and give alms, that would be good. If you do not, I will make all your wealth vanish, and with this thunderbolt of Indra, I will cut off your head and bring your life to an end.” The merchant Illisa, terrified by the fear of death, gave his promise, “From this day forward, I will give alms.” Sakka, accepting his pledge, while seated in the sky, taught him the Dhamma, established him in virtue, and returned to his own abode. Illisa, too, performed meritorious deeds such as generosity and was destined for heaven.

Satthā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva moggallāno macchariyaseṭṭhiṃ dameti, pubbepesa iminā damitoyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā illiso macchariyaseṭṭhi ahosi, sakko devarājā mahāmoggallāno, rājā ānando, kappako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that Moggallāna tames the stingy merchant; he was tamed by him in the past as well." Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection, and identified the characters of the Jātaka, he said: "At that time, the stingy merchant was Illisa, Sakka, the king of the gods, was Mahāmoggallāna, the king was Ānanda, and the barber was I myself."

Illisajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The explanation of the Illisa Jātaka, the eighth.

[79] 9. Kharassarajātakavaṇṇanā

[79] 9. The Explanation of the Kharassara Jātaka

Yato viluttā ca hatā ca gāvoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ amaccaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kosalarañño kira eko amacco rājānaṃ ārādhetvā paccantagāme rājabaliṃ labhitvā corehi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā “ahaṃ manusse ādāya araññaṃ pavisissāmi, tumhe gāmaṃ vilumpitvā upaḍḍhaṃ mayhaṃ dadeyyāthā”ti vatvā pageva manusse sannipātetvā araññaṃ gantvā coresu āgantvā gāviyo ghātetvā [M 1.0376] maṃsaṃ khāditvā gāmaṃ vilumpitvā gatesu sāyanhasamaye mahājanaparivuto āgacchati. Tassa na cirasseva taṃ kammaṃ pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Manussā rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā taṃ pakkosāpetvā dosaṃ patiṭṭhāpetvā suniggahitaṃ niggahetvā aññaṃ gāmabhojakaṃ pesetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Bhagavā “na, mahārāja, idāneva esa evaṃsīlo, pubbepi evaṃsīloyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“When the cattle were plundered and slain...” The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this concerning a certain minister. It is said that a minister of the Kosala king, having pleased the king, obtained the royal revenue in a border village. Then, having joined with robbers, he said, "I will take the people and enter the forest; you are to plunder the village and give me half." Having gathered the people early in the morning, he went to the forest. When the robbers had come, slaughtered the cattle, eaten the meat, plundered the village, and departed, he returned in the evening surrounded by a large crowd. Before long, his deed became known. The people reported it to the king. The king had him summoned, established his guilt, punished him severely, and sent another to govern the village. Then he went to Jetavana and reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said, "Great king, it is not only now that he is of such character; he was of the same character in the past as well." And being requested by the king, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente ekassa amaccassa paccantagāmaṃ adāsi. Sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Tadā pana bodhisatto vaṇijjāya paccante vicaranto [P 1.0355] tasmiṃ gāmake nivāsaṃ kappesi. So tasmiṃ gāmabhojake sāyanhasamaye mahājanaparivārena bheriyā vajjamānāya [V 1.0339] āgacchante “ayaṃ duṭṭhagāmabhojako corehi saddhiṃ ekato hutvā gāmaṃ vilumpāpetvā coresu palāyitvā aṭaviṃ paviṭṭhesu idāni upasantūpasanto viya bheriyā vajjamānāya āgacchatī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, he gave a border village to a certain minister. Everything was just as in the present story. At that time, the Bodhisatta, traveling for trade in the border regions, took up residence in that small village. When that village headman was returning in the evening surrounded by a large crowd, with a drum being beaten, the Bodhisatta said, "This wicked village headman, having joined with robbers and had the village plundered, now that the robbers have fled and entered the forest, comes as if he were very peaceful, with a drum being beaten," and he spoke this verse:

79.

79.

“Yato viluttā ca hatā ca gāvo, daḍḍhāni gehāni jano ca nīto;

Athāgamā puttahatāya putto, kharassaraṃ ḍiṇḍimaṃ vādayanto”ti.

“When the cattle were plundered and slain, the houses burned, and the people carried off; then came the son of one whose son is slain, beating a harsh-sounding drum.”

Tattha yatoti yadā. Viluttā ca hatā cāti vilumpitvā bandhitvā ca nītā, maṃsaṃ khādanatthāya ca hatā. Gāvoti gorūpāni. Daḍḍhānīti aggiṃ datvā jhāpitāni. Jano ca nītoti karamaraggāhaṃ gahetvā nīto. Puttahatāya puttoti hataputtāya putto, nillajjoti attho. Chinnahirottappassa hi mātā nāma natthi, iti so tassā jīvantopi hataputtaṭṭhāne tiṭṭhatīti hataputtāya putto nāma hoti. Kharassaranti thaddhasaddaṃ. Ḍiṇḍimanti paṭahabheriṃ.

Herein, 'yato' means 'when'. 'Viluttā ca hatā ca' means plundered, bound, and carried away, and also slain for the purpose of eating their flesh. 'Gāvo' means cattle. 'Daḍḍhāni' means set on fire and burned. 'Jano ca nīto' means the people were seized and carried away. 'Puttahatāya putto' means 'the son of one whose son is slain'; the meaning is 'shameless one'. For one who has cut off shame and moral dread, there is no mother, so to speak; thus, even while she lives, he stands in the place of a slain son to her, and so he is called 'the son of one whose son is slain'. 'Kharassaram' means a harsh sound. 'Ḍiṇḍimam' means a kettledrum.

Evaṃ bodhisatto imāya gāthāya taṃ paribhāsi. Na cireneva ca tassa taṃ kammaṃ pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ, athassa rājā dosānurūpaṃ niggahaṃ akāsi.

Thus the Bodhisatta reproached him with this verse. And not long after, that deed of his became manifest, and the king inflicted a punishment upon him that corresponded to his offense.

Satthā [M 1.0377] “na, mahārāja, idānevesa evaṃsīlo, pubbepi evaṃsīloyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā amacco idāni amaccoyeva, gāthāya udāhārakapaṇḍitamanusso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Great king, he is not only of such character now, but he was also of such character in the past." Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he made the connection and identified the characters of the birth story: "At that time, the minister was the same as the minister now; but the wise man who uttered the verse was I myself."

Kharassarajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The explanation of the Kharassara Jātaka, the ninth.

[80] 10. Bhīmasenajātakavaṇṇanā

[80] 10. The Explanation of the Bhīmasena Jātaka

Yaṃ te pavikatthitaṃ pureti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ vikatthitaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira bhikkhu “āvuso, amhākaṃ jātisamā jāti, gottasamaṃ gottaṃ nāma natthi, mayaṃ evarūpe nāma mahākhattiyakule jātā, gottena vā dhanena vā kulappadesena vā amhehi sadiso nāma natthi, amhākaṃ suvaṇṇarajatādīnaṃ anto natthi, dāsakammakarāpi no sālimaṃsodanaṃ bhuñjanti, kāsikavatthaṃ nivāsenti, kāsikavilepanaṃ vilimpanti. Mayaṃ pabbajitabhāvena etarahi [P 1.0356] evarūpāni lūkhāni bhojanāni bhuñjāma, lūkhāni cīvarāni dhāremā”ti [V 1.0340] theranavamajjhimānaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ antare vikatthento jātiādivasena vambhento khuṃsento vicarati. Athassa eko bhikkhu kulappadesaṃ pariggaṇhitvā taṃ vikatthanabhāvaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ārocesi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā vikatthento vambhento khuṃsento vicaratī”ti etassa aguṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, so bhikkhu idāneva vikatthento vambhento khuṃsento vicarati, pubbepi vikatthento vambhento khuṃsento vicarī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This story, beginning with the words, 'What you boasted of before...', the Teacher told while dwelling in Jetavana concerning a certain boastful monk. It is said that one monk went about boasting among the elder, new, and middle monks, saying: 'Friends, there is no birth equal to our birth, no clan equal to our clan. We were born in such a great warrior clan. There is no one like us in clan, wealth, or lineage. Our gold and silver and so on are without limit.
