Even our slaves and servants eat fine rice with meat, wear Kāsi cloth, and anoint themselves with Kāsi perfumes. But now, having gone forth, we eat such coarse food and wear such coarse robes.' Thus, he went about boasting, disparaging, and belittling others on account of birth and so forth. Then, one monk, having ascertained his family background, reported his boastful behavior to the monks. The monks gathered in the Hall of Dhamma and said, 'Friends, this monk, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, goes about boasting, disparaging, and belittling,' and they spoke of his faults. The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, this monk does not only go about boasting, disparaging, and belittling now; he went about boasting, disparaging, and belittling in the past as well,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ nigamagāme udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ disāpāmokkhassa ācariyassa santike tayo vede aṭṭhārasa vijjaṭṭhānāni uggahetvā sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patvā cūḷadhanuggahapaṇḍito nāma [M 1.0378] ahosi. So takkasilāto nikkhamitvā sabbasamayasippāni pariyesamāno mahiṃsakaraṭṭhaṃ agamāsi. Imasmiṃ pana jātake bodhisatto thokaṃ rasso oṇatākāro ahosi. So cintesi “sacāhaṃ kañci rājānaṃ upasaṅkamissāmi, so ‘evaṃ rassasarīro tvaṃ kiṃ amhākaṃ kammaṃ karissasī’ti vakkhati, yaṃnūnāhaṃ ārohapariṇāhasampannaṃ abhirūpaṃ ekaṃ purisaṃ phalakaṃ katvā tassa piṭṭhicchāyāya jīvikaṃ kappeyya”nti. So tathārūpaṃ purisaṃ pariyesamāno bhīmasenassa nāmekassa tantavāyassa tantavītaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “samma, tvaṃ kinnāmosī”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ bhīmaseno nāmā”ti? “Kiṃ pana tvaṃ evaṃ abhirūpo upadhisampanno hutvā imaṃ lāmakakammaṃ karosī”ti? “Jīvituṃ asakkonto”ti. “Samma, mā etaṃ kammaṃ kari, sakalajambudīpe mayā sadiso dhanuggaho nāma natthi. Sace panāhaṃ kañci rājānaṃ passeyyaṃ, so maṃ ‘evaṃrasso ayaṃ kiṃ amhākaṃ kammaṃ karissatī’ti kopeyya, tvaṃ rājānaṃ disvā ‘ahaṃ dhanuggaho’ti vakkhasi. Rājā te paribbayaṃ datvā vuttiṃ [P 1.0357] nibaddhaṃ dassati. Ahaṃ te uppannakammaṃ karonto tava piṭṭhicchāyāya jīvissāmi. Evaṃ ubhopi sukhitā bhavissāma. Karohi mama vacana”nti āha. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a northern Brahmin family in a certain market town. Having come of age, he learned the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge from a world-renowned teacher in Takkasilā. Having attained proficiency in all the arts, he became known as Cūḷadhanuggahapaṇḍita. Leaving Takkasilā and searching for all kinds of arts, he went to the country of Mahiṃsaka. In this Jātaka, however, the Bodhisatta was somewhat short and stooped in form. He thought, 'If I approach any king, he will say, “Being so short of body, what work can you do for us?” What if I were to find a man of fine stature and appearance, make him my shield, and earn a living in the shadow of his back?' Searching for such a man, he went to the weaving place of a weaver named Bhīmasena. After exchanging greetings with him, he asked, 'Friend, what is your name?' 'I am called Bhīmasena.' 'Why do you, being so handsome and well-formed, engage in such wretched work?' 'Because I am unable to make a living.' 'Friend, do not do this work. In all of Jambudīpa, there is no archer equal to me. But if I were to approach a king, he might scorn me, saying, “This man is so short, what work can he do for us?” You should see the king and say, “I am an archer.” The king will give you a regular income and provide for your expenses. I will do whatever work arises for you and live in the shadow of your back. In this way, we shall both be prosperous. Do as I say.' He agreed, saying, 'Very well.'

Atha naṃ ādāya bārāṇasiṃ gantvā sayaṃ cūḷūpaṭṭhāko hutvā taṃ purato katvā rājadvāre ṭhatvā rañño ārocāpesi. “Āgacchantū”ti vutte ubhopi pavisitvā rājānaṃ vanditvā aṭṭhaṃsu. “Kiṃkāraṇā āgatatthā”ti ca vutte bhīmaseno āha – “ahaṃ dhanuggaho, mayā sadiso sakalajambudīpe dhanuggaho natthī”ti. “Kiṃ pana labhanto maṃ upaṭṭhahissasī”ti? “Aḍḍhamāse [V 1.0341] sahassaṃ labhanto upaṭṭhahissāmi, devā”ti. “Ayaṃ te puriso kiṃ hotī”ti? “Cūḷūpaṭṭhāko, devā”ti. “Sādhu upaṭṭhahā”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya bhīmaseno rājānaṃ upaṭṭhahati. Uppannakiccaṃ panassa bodhisattova nittharati.

Then, taking him, he went to Benares. Becoming a junior attendant himself and placing Bhīmasena in front, he stood at the king's gate and had their presence announced to the king. When it was said, 'Let them enter,' both went in, paid homage to the king, and stood there. When asked, 'For what reason have you come?' Bhīmasena said, 'I am an archer; in all of Jambudīpa there is no archer equal to me.' 'For what payment will you serve me?' 'Receiving a thousand every half-month, I will serve you, Your Majesty.' 'And this man, what is he to you?' 'He is my junior attendant, Your Majesty.' 'Very well, you may serve.' From that time on, Bhīmasena served the king. But it was the Bodhisatta who accomplished for him whatever task arose.

Tena kho pana samayena kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ araññe bahūnaṃ manussānaṃ sañcaraṇamaggaṃ byaggho chaḍḍāpeti, bahū manusse gahetvā gahetvā khādati. Taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā bhīmasenaṃ pakkosāpetvā “sakkhissasi, tāta, naṃ byagghaṃ gaṇhitu”nti āha. “Deva, kiṃ dhanuggaho nāmāhaṃ[M 1.0379], yadi byagghaṃ gahetuṃ na sakkomī”ti. Rājā tassa paribbayaṃ datvā uyyojesi. So gharaṃ gantvā bodhisattassa kathesi. Bodhisatto “sādhu, samma, gacchā”ti āha. “Tvaṃ pana na gamissasī”ti? “Āma na gamissāmi, upāyaṃ pana te ācikkhissāmī”ti. “Ācikkha, sammā”ti. Tvaṃ byagghassa vasanaṭṭhānaṃ sahasā ekakova mā agamāsi, janapadamanusse pana sannipātetvā ekaṃ vā dve vā dhanusahassāni gāhāpetvā tattha gantvā byagghassa uṭṭhitabhāvaṃ ñatvā palāyitvā ekaṃ gumbaṃ pavisitvā urena nipajjeyyāsi, jānapadāva byagghaṃ pothetvā gaṇhissanti, tehi byagghe gahite tvaṃ dantehi ekaṃ valliṃ chinditvā koṭiyaṃ gahetvā matabyagghassa santikaṃ gantvā “bho, kenesa, byaggho mārito, ahaṃ imaṃ byagghaṃ goṇaṃ viya [P 1.0358] valliyā bandhitvā rañño santikaṃ nessāmī’ti valliatthāya gumbaṃ paviṭṭho, mayā valliyā anābhatāya eva kenesa mārito”ti katheyyāsi. Atha te jānapadā bhītatasitā “sāmi, mā rañño ācikkhī”ti bahuṃ dhanaṃ dassanti, byaggho tayā gahito bhavissati, raññopi santikā bahuṃ dhanaṃ labhissasīti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā bodhisattena kathitaniyāmeneva byagghaṃ gahetvā araññaṃ khemaṃ katvā mahājanaparivuto bārāṇasiṃ āgantvā rājānaṃ disvā “gahito me, deva, byaggho, araññaṃ khemaṃ kata”nti āha. Rājā tuṭṭho bahuṃ dhanaṃ adāsi. Punekadivasaṃ “ekamaggaṃ mahiṃso chaḍḍāpetī”ti ārocesuṃ, rājā tatheva bhīmasenaṃ pesesi. Sopi bodhisattena dinnanayena byagghaṃ viya tampi gahetvā āgañchi, rājā puna bahuṃ dhanaṃ adāsi, mahantaṃ issariyaṃ jātaṃ. So issariyamadamatto bodhisattaṃ avamaññaṃ katvā tassa vacanaṃ na gaṇhāti, “nāhaṃ taṃ nissāya jīvāmi, kiṃ tvaññeva puriso”tiādīni pharusavacanāni vadati.

At that time, in a certain forest in the Kāsi country, a tiger had made a frequented path impassable, seizing and devouring many people. They reported this matter to the king. The king summoned Bhīmasena and said, "Dear son, can you capture that tiger?" "My lord, what kind of archer would I be if I could not capture a tiger?" The king gave him provisions and sent him off. He went home and told the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta said, "Good, friend, go." "But will you not go?" "No, I will not go, but I will tell you a method." "Tell me, friend." "Do not go alone suddenly to the tiger’s dwelling place. Instead, gather the villagers and have them bring one or two thousand bows. Go there, and when you know the tiger has risen, flee and enter a thicket. Lie down on your chest. The villagers will strike the tiger and capture it. Once they have caught the tiger, you should cut a vine with your teeth, take one end, go near the dead tiger, and say, ‘Sirs, who killed this tiger? I was going to tie this tiger with a vine like an ox and bring it to the king. I entered the thicket for a vine, but before I could fetch it, someone killed it.’ Then those villagers, frightened and trembling, will say, ‘Master, do not tell the king,’ and give you much wealth. The tiger will be considered caught by you, and you will also receive much wealth from the king." He said, "Good," and accepted the advice. Following the method explained by the Bodhisatta, he captured the tiger, made the forest safe, and returned to Bārāṇasī surrounded by a great crowd. Seeing the king, he said, "My lord, I have captured the tiger; the forest has been made safe." The king, pleased, gave him much wealth. Another day, they reported, "A buffalo is blocking a path." The king sent Bhīmasena in the same way. He, too, following the Bodhisatta's method, captured that buffalo just like the tiger and returned. The king again gave him much wealth, and great prosperity arose. Intoxicated by his prosperity, he looked down upon the Bodhisatta and did not heed his words, saying harsh things like, "I do not depend on you for my livelihood. Are you the only man?"

Atha [V 1.0342] katipāhaccayena eko sāmantarājā āgantvā bārāṇasiṃ uparundhitvā “rajjaṃ vā detu, yuddhaṃ vā”ti rañño sāsanaṃ pesesi. Rājā “yujjhāhī”ti bhīmasenaṃ pesesi. So sabbasannāhasannaddho rājavesaṃ gahetvā susannaddhassa vāraṇassa piṭṭhe nisīdi. Bodhisattopi tassa maraṇabhayena sabbasannāhasannaddho bhīmasenasseva pacchimāsane nisīdi. Vāraṇo mahājanaparivuto nagaradvārena nikkhamitvā saṅgāmasīsaṃ pāpuṇi. Bhīmaseno yuddhabherisaddaṃ sutvāva kampituṃ āraddho. Bodhisatto “idānesa [M 1.0380] hatthipiṭṭhito patitvā marissatī”ti hatthikkhandhato apatanatthaṃ bhīmasenaṃ yottena parikkhipitvā gaṇhi, bhīmaseno sampahāraṭṭhānaṃ disvā maraṇabhayatajjito sarīravaḷañjena hatthipiṭṭhiṃ dūsesi. Bodhisatto “na kho te bhīmasena purimena pacchimaṃ sameti, tvaṃ pubbe saṅgāmayodho viya ahosi, idāni hatthipiṭṭhiṃ dūsesī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, after a few days, a neighboring king came and besieged Bārāṇasī, sending a message to the king: "Either give up the kingdom or fight!" The king replied, "Fight!" and sent Bhīmasena. Fully armed and equipped, taking on the appearance of a king, he sat on the back of a well-armored elephant. The Bodhisatta, fearing for his life, also fully armed, sat on the back seat behind Bhīmasena. The elephant, surrounded by a great crowd, went out through the city gate and reached the battlefront. As soon as he heard the sound of the war drum, Bhīmasena began to tremble. The Bodhisatta thought, "Now he will fall from the elephant’s back and die," so to prevent him from falling from the elephant's back, he bound Bhīmasena with a strap and held him. Bhīmasena, seeing the place of combat, terrified by the fear of death, fouled the elephant's back with his bodily waste. The Bodhisatta said, "Bhīmasena, your present state does not agree with your former state. Formerly, you were like a warrior in battle, but now you foul the elephant's back." Then he spoke this verse:

80.

80.

“Yaṃ [P 1.0359] te pavikatthitaṃ pure, atha te pūtisarā sajanti pacchā;

Ubhayaṃ na sameti bhīmasena, yuddhakathā ca idañca te vihañña”nti.

Your boasts of old, and then your foul streams issue forth afterwards; the two do not agree, Bhīmasena: your talk of war and this your affliction.

Tattha yaṃ te pavikatthitaṃ pureti yaṃ tayā pubbe “kiṃ tvaṃyeva puriso, nāhaṃ puriso, ahampi saṅgāmayodho”ti vikatthitaṃ vambhanavacanaṃ vuttaṃ, idaṃ tāva ekaṃ. Atha te pūtisarā sajanti pacchāti atha te ime pūtibhāvena saraṇabhāvena ca “pūtisarā”ti laddhanāmā sarīravaḷañjadhārā sajanti vaḷañjanti paggharanti. Pacchāti tato pure vikatthitato aparabhāge, idāni imasmiṃ saṅgāmasīseti attho. Ubhayaṃ na sameti bhīmasenāti idaṃ bhīmasena ubhayaṃ na sameti. Kataraṃ? Yuddhakathā ca idañca te vihaññanti, yā ca pure kathitā yuddhakathā, yañca te idāni vihaññaṃ kilamatho hatthipiṭṭhidūsanākārappatto vighātoti attho.

Here, "that which you boasted before" refers to that which you previously declared in boastful speech, "Are you the only man? Am I not a man? I too am a warrior in battle." This, indeed, is the first point. Then, "your foul streams issue forth afterwards": these streams of bodily filth, called "foul streams" due to their putrid nature and flowing nature, now issue forth, flow, and drip. "Afterwards" means after that earlier boasting, at this later time, here on the battlefield—this is the meaning. "Bhīmasena, these two do not agree": Bhīmasena, these two do not agree. Which two? "The talk of battle and this, your affliction." This refers to both the talk of battle spoken before and your present affliction, the exhaustion you now suffer, which has reached the state of fouling the elephant's back.

Evaṃ bodhisatto taṃ garahitvā “mā bhāyi, samma, kasmā mayi ṭhite vihaññasī”ti bhīmasenaṃ hatthipiṭṭhito otāretvā “nhāyitvā gehameva gacchā”ti uyyojetvā “ajja mayā pākaṭena bhavituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti saṅgāmaṃ pavisitvā unnaditvā balakoṭṭhakaṃ bhinditvā sapattarājānaṃ jīvaggāhaṃ gāhāpetvā bārāṇasirañño santikaṃ agamāsi. Rājā tuṭṭho bodhisattassa mahantaṃ yasaṃ adāsi. Tato paṭṭhāya “cūḷadhanuggahapaṇḍito”ti sakalajambudīpe pākaṭo ahosi. So bhīmasenassa paribbayaṃ datvā sakaṭṭhānameva pesetvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having rebuked him, said, "Do not fear, friend. Why are you distressed while I am here?" Then he took Bhīmasena down from the elephant's back and sent him away, saying, "Go home after bathing." Thinking, "Today it is right for me to become manifest," he entered the battle, roared, broke through the army's stronghold, had the enemy king captured alive, and went to the king of Bārāṇasī. The king, pleased, bestowed great fame upon the Bodhisatta. From that time onward, he became renowned throughout all of Jambudīpa as "Cūḷadhanuggahapaṇḍita." After providing for Bhīmasena's expenses, he sent him back to his own place, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 1.0343][M 1.0381] “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa bhikkhu vikattheti, pubbepi vikatthiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bhīmaseno vikatthitabhikkhu ahosi, cūḷadhanuggahapaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, "Monks, it is not only now that this monk is boastful; he was boastful in the past as well." Having delivered this discourse, he made the connection and concluded the Jātaka: "At that time, Bhīmasena was the boastful monk, but I myself was the wise archer Cūḷadhanuggaha."

Bhīmasenajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Bhīmasena Jātaka, the Tenth.

Varuṇavaggo aṭṭhamo.

The Varuṇa Chapter, the Eighth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Varuṇaṃ sīlavanāgaṃ, saccaṃkira rukkhadhammaṃ;

Maccharājā asaṅkiyaṃ, mahāsupinaillisaṃ;

Kharassaraṃ bhīmasenanti.

Varuṇa, Sīlavanāga, Saccankira, Rukkhadhamma; Maccharājā, Asaṅkiya, Mahāsupina, Illisa; Kharassara, and Bhīmasena.

9. Apāyimhavaggo

9. The Chapter Beginning 'We Drank'

[81] 1. Surāpānajātakavaṇṇanā

[81] 1. The Commentary on the Surāpāna Jātaka

Apāyimha [V 1.0344][P 1.0360] anaccimhāti idaṃ satthā kosambiṃ upanissāya ghositārāme viharanto sāgatattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Bhagavati hi sāvatthiyaṃ vassaṃ vasitvā cārikāgamanena bhaddavatikaṃ nāma nigamaṃ sampatte gopālakā pasupālakā kassakā pathāvino ca satthāraṃ disvā vanditvā “mā, bhante, bhagavā ambatitthaṃ agamāsi, ambatitthe jaṭilassa assame ambatitthako nāma nāgo āsīviso ghoraviso, so bhagavantaṃ viheṭheyyā”ti vārayiṃsu. Bhagavāpi tesaṃ kathaṃ asuṇanto viya tesu yāvatatiyaṃ vārayamānesupi agamāsiyeva.

The Teacher, while residing near Kosambī in the Ghositārāma, spoke this, beginning with 'Apāyimha anaccimha,' concerning the elder Sāgata. When the Blessed One, having spent the rainy season in Sāvatthī, arrived at a market town named Bhaddavatika while on tour, cowherds, shepherds, farmers, and travelers saw the Teacher, paid homage, and warned him, saying, 'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One not go to Ambatittha. At Ambatittha, in the hermitage of a matted-hair ascetic, there is a nāga named Ambatitthaka, of deadly and terrible venom. He may harm the Blessed One.' But the Blessed One, as if not hearing their words, went on, even though they warned him up to a third time.

Tatra sudaṃ bhagavā bhaddavatikāya avidūre aññatarasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe viharati. Tena kho pana samayena buddhūpaṭṭhāko sāgato nāma thero pothujjanikāya iddhiyā samannāgato taṃ assamaṃ upasaṅkamitvā tassa nāgarājassa vasanaṭṭhāne tiṇasanthārakaṃ paññāpetvā pallaṅkena nisīdi. Nāgo makkhaṃ asahamāno dhūmāyi, theropi dhūmāyi. Nāgo pajjali, theropi pajjali. Nāgassa tejo theraṃ na bādhati, therassa tejo nāgaṃ [M 1.0382] bādhati. Evaṃ so khaṇena taṃ nāgarājānaṃ dametvā saraṇesu ca sīlesu ca patiṭṭhāpetvā satthu santikaṃ agamāsi.

There, the Blessed One was dwelling not far from Bhaddavatika in a certain grove. At that time, the Buddha's attendant, an elder named Sāgata, was endowed with mundane psychic power. He approached that hermitage and, having prepared a grass mat in the dwelling place of the nāga king, sat down cross-legged. Unable to endure the affront, the nāga emitted smoke; the elder also emitted smoke. The nāga burst into flames; the elder also burst into flames. The nāga’s fire did not harm the elder, but the elder’s fire harmed the nāga. Thus, in an instant, he tamed that nāga king, established him in the refuges and precepts, and went to the Teacher’s presence.

Satthā bhaddavatikāyaṃ yathābhirantaṃ viharitvā kosambiṃ agamāsi. Sāgatattherena nāgassa damitabhāvo sakalajanapadaṃ patthari. Kosambinagaravāsino satthu paccuggamanaṃ katvā satthāraṃ vanditvā sāgatattherassa santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ ṭhitā evamāhaṃsu “bhante, yaṃ tumhākaṃ dullabhaṃ, taṃ vadeyyātha, tadeva mayaṃ paṭiyādessāmā”ti. Thero tuṇhī ahosi. Chabbaggiyā panāhaṃsu “āvuso, pabbajitānaṃ nāma kāpotikā surā dullabhā ceva manāpā ca. Sace tumhe therassa pasannā, kāpotikaṃ suraṃ paṭiyādethā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā satthāraṃ svātanāya nimantetvā nagaraṃ pavisitvā attano attano gehe “therassa dassāmā”ti kāpotikaṃ suraṃ pasannaṃ paṭiyādetvā theraṃ nimantetvā ghare ghare pasannaṃ suraṃ adaṃsu. Thero pivitvā surāmadamatto nagarato nikkhamanto dvārantare patitvā vilapamāno nipajji.

After staying in Bhaddavatika as long as he pleased, the Teacher went to Kosambi. The news of the elder Sāgata's taming of the nāga spread throughout the entire region. The inhabitants of Kosambi went out to welcome the Teacher, paid homage to him, and then went to the elder Sāgata. Having paid homage to the elder, they stood to one side and said: 'Venerable sir, whatever is difficult for you to obtain, please tell us, and we will provide it.' The elder remained silent. But the group of six monks said: 'Friends, for monastics, pigeon-colored liquor is both difficult to obtain and pleasing. If you are devoted to the elder, provide pigeon-colored liquor.' They agreed, saying, 'Very well,' and having invited the Teacher for the next day, they entered the city. In their own homes, thinking, 'We will give it to the elder,' they prepared fine, clear liquor. They invited the elder and gave him the fine liquor in each house. The elder drank it and, intoxicated by the liquor, as he was leaving the city, he fell down in the gateway, muttering as he lay there.

Satthā [V 1.0345] katabhattakicco nagarā nikkhamanto theraṃ tenākārena nipannaṃ disvā “gaṇhatha, bhikkhave, sāgata”nti gāhāpetvā ārāmaṃ agamāsi[P 1.0361]. Bhikkhū therassa sīsaṃ tathāgatassa pādamūle katvā taṃ nipajjāpesuṃ, so parivattitvā pāde tathāgatābhimukhe katvā nipajji. Satthā bhikkhū paṭipucchi “kiṃ nu kho, bhikkhave, yaṃ pubbe sāgatassa mayi gāravaṃ, taṃ idāni atthī”ti? “Natthi, bhante”ti. “Bhikkhave, ambatitthakaṃ nāgarājānaṃ ko damesī”ti. “Sāgato, bhante”ti. “Kiṃ panetarahi, bhikkhave, sāgato udakadeḍḍūbhakampi dametuṃ sakkuṇeyyā”ti. “No hetaṃ, bhante”. “Api nu kho, bhikkhave, evarūpaṃ pātuṃ yuttaṃ, yaṃ pivitvā evaṃvisaññī hotī”ti. “Ayuttaṃ, bhante”ti. Atha kho bhagavā theraṃ garahitvā bhikkhū āmantetvā “surāmerayapāne pācittiya”nti (pāci. 327) sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi.

The Teacher, having finished his meal and leaving the city, saw the elder lying there in that state and said, 'Monks, take Sāgata.' Having had him carried to the monastery, the monks placed the elder's head at the Tathāgata's feet and laid him down. He turned around and lay with his feet facing the Tathāgata. The Teacher asked the monks, 'Monks, does Sāgata now have the respect for me that he had before?' 'No, venerable sir.' 'Monks, who tamed the nāga king Ambatitthaka?' 'Sāgata, venerable sir.' 'But now, monks, could Sāgata tame even a water snake?' 'He could not, venerable sir.' 'Is it then proper, monks, to drink that which, when drunk, makes one so senseless?' 'It is not proper, venerable sir.' Then the Blessed One rebuked the elder, addressed the monks, and established the training rule: 'In the drinking of fermented and distilled intoxicants, there is an offense requiring expiation.' (Pāc. 327) Then he rose from his seat and entered the Fragrant Chamber.

Dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā bhikkhū surāpānassa avaṇṇaṃ kathayiṃsu “yāva mahādosañcetaṃ, āvuso, surāpānaṃ nāma, tāva paññāsampannaṃ nāma iddhimantaṃ [M 1.0383] sāgataṃ yathā satthu guṇamattampi na jānāti, tathā akāsī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva suraṃ pivitvā pabbajitā visaññino honti, pubbepi ahesuṃyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and spoke of the demerits of drinking liquor: 'Friends, so great a fault is the drinking of liquor that it made even one as wise and powerful as Sāgata unable to recognize the Teacher's virtues.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When they told him, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that monastics who drink liquor become senseless; they were so in the past as well.' Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kāsiraṭṭhe udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto himavantappadese vasati pañcahi antevāsikasatehi parivuto. Atha naṃ vassānasamaye sampatte antevāsikā āhaṃsu “ācariya, manussapathaṃ gantvā loṇambilaṃ sevitvā āgacchāmā”ti. “Āvuso, ahaṃ idheva vasissāmi, tumhe pana gantvā sarīraṃ santappetvā vassaṃ vītināmetvā āgacchathā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti ācariyaṃ vanditvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase bahidvāragāmeyeva bhikkhāya caritvā suhitā hutvā punadivase nagaraṃ pavisiṃsu. Manussā sampiyāyamānā bhikkhaṃ adaṃsu. Katipāhaccayena ca raññopi ārocesuṃ “deva, himavantato pañcasatā isayo āgantvā uyyāne vasanti ghoratapā paramadhitindriyā sīlavanto”ti. Rājā tesaṃ guṇe sutvā uyyānaṃ gantvā vanditvā katapaṭisanthāro vassānaṃ [P 1.0362] catumāsaṃ tattheva vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gahetvā nimantesi, te tato paṭṭhāya rājageheyeva bhuñjitvā uyyāne vasanti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a brahmin family in the northern region of Kasi country. Having come of age, he took up the ascetic life of a sage, developed supernormal knowledge and meditative attainments, and lived in the Himalayan region, enjoying the bliss of absorption, surrounded by five hundred disciples. Then, when the rainy season arrived, his disciples said to him, 'Teacher, let us go to the inhabited regions, partake of salt and sour things, and then return.' 'Friends, I will stay here. You, however, may go, nourish your bodies, spend the rainy season, and then return.' They said, 'Very well,' paid homage to the teacher, and went to Benares, where they stayed in the royal park. The next day, they went for alms only in the villages outside the city gate and were satisfied. The following day, they entered the city. The people, being well-disposed towards them, gave them alms. After a few days, they informed the king, 'Your Majesty, five hundred ascetics have come from the Himalayas and are staying in the park. They are of austere practice, supremely controlled in their faculties, and virtuous.' Hearing of their virtues, the king went to the park, paid homage to them, and after exchanging courteous greetings, invited them to stay there for the four months of the rainy season, having received their promise. From then on, they ate in the royal palace and stayed in the park.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0346] nagare surānakkhattaṃ nāma ahosi. Rājā “pabbajitānaṃ surā dullabhā”ti bahuṃ uttamasuraṃ dāpesi. Tāpasā suraṃ pivitvā uyyānaṃ gantvā surāmadamattā hutvā ekacce uṭṭhāya nacciṃsu, ekacce gāyiṃsu, naccitvā gāyitvā khārikādīni avattharitvā niddāyitvā surāmade chinne pabujjhitvā taṃ attano vippakāraṃ disvā “na amhehi pabbajitasāruppaṃ kata”nti roditvā paridevitvā “mayaṃ ācariyena vinābhūtattā evarūpaṃ pāpakammaṃ karimhā”ti taṅkhaṇaññeva uyyānaṃ pahāya himavantaṃ gantvā paṭisāmitaparikkhārā ācariyaṃ vanditvā nisīditvā “kiṃ nu kho, tātā, manussapathe bhikkhāya akilamamānā sukhaṃ vasittha, samaggavāsañca pana vasitthā”ti [M 1.0384] pucchitā “ācariya, sukhaṃ vasimha, apica kho pana mayaṃ apātabbayuttakaṃ pivitvā visaññībhūtā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetuṃ asakkontā naccimha ceva gāyimha cā”ti etamatthaṃ ārocentā imaṃ gāthaṃ samuṭṭhāpetvā āhaṃsu –

One day in the city, there was a liquor festival. The king, thinking, 'Liquor is hard to come by for ascetics,' had much excellent liquor given to them. The ascetics drank the liquor, went to the park, and intoxicated by the liquor, some got up and danced, some sang. Having danced and sung, they scattered their belongings and fell asleep. When the intoxication ceased, they awoke, saw their misconduct, and lamented, 'We have acted in a way unbecoming of ascetics!' Weeping and wailing, they thought, 'Because we were without our teacher, we committed such an evil deed.' At that very moment, they left the park, went to the Himalayas, put their requisites in order, paid homage to their teacher, and sat down. When asked, 'Dear ones, did you live happily in the inhabited regions, without difficulty in begging for alms? And did you dwell in harmony?' they replied, 'Teacher, we lived happily. However, we drank what should not be drunk, became senseless, and unable to establish mindfulness, we both danced and sang.' Explaining this matter, they recited this verse:

81.

81.

“Apāyimha anaccimha, agāyimha rudimha ca;

Visaññīkaraṇiṃ pitvā, diṭṭhā nāhumha vānarā”ti.

'We drank, we danced, we sang, and we wept; having drunk that which makes one senseless, fortunately we did not become monkeys.'

Tattha apāyimhāti suraṃ pivimha. Anaccimhāti taṃ pivitvā hatthapāde lāḷentā naccimha. Agāyimhāti mukhaṃ vivaritvā āyatakena sarena gāyimha. Rudimha cāti puna vippaṭisārino “evarūpaṃ nāma amhehi kata”nti rodimha ca. Visaññīkaraṇiṃ pitvā, diṭṭhā nāhumha vānarāti evarūpaṃ saññāvināsanato visaññīkaraṇiṃ suraṃ pivitvā “etadeva sādhu, yaṃ vānarā nāhumhā”ti. Evaṃ te attano aguṇaṃ kathesuṃ.

Therein, 'we drank' means we drank liquor. 'We danced' means that after drinking it, we danced, flailing our hands and feet. 'We sang' means we sang with open mouths in a drawn-out voice. 'And we wept' means that afterwards, filled with remorse, we wept, thinking, 'Such a thing have we done.' As for 'having drunk that which makes one senseless, fortunately we did not become monkeys,' it means: having drunk liquor that causes senselessness because it destroys perception, they meant, 'This is indeed good, that we did not become monkeys.' In this way, they confessed their own faults.

Bodhisatto “garusaṃvāsarahitānaṃ nāma evarūpaṃ hotiyevā”ti te tāpase garahitvā “puna evarūpaṃ mākaritthā”ti tesaṃ ovādaṃ datvā aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

The Bodhisatta, rebuking those ascetics, said, 'Indeed, such things happen to those who are without the guidance of a teacher.' Having given them the advice, 'Do not act like this again,' he, with undiminished meditative absorption, was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā [P 1.0363] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. Ito paṭṭhāya hi “anusandhiṃ ghaṭetvā”ti idampi na vakkhāma. Tadā isigaṇo buddhaparisā ahosi, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosinti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher made the connection and identified the birth. (A commentator's note: From this point onwards, we will not say, 'making the connection.') 'At that time, the group of ascetics was the Buddha's assembly, and the leader of the group was I myself.'

Surāpānajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first is the commentary on the Jātaka on Drinking Liquor.

[82] 2. Mittavindakajātakavaṇṇanā

[82] 2. The Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka

Atikkamma [V 1.0347] ramaṇakanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Imassa pana jātakassa kassapasammāsambuddhakālikaṃ vatthu, taṃ dasakanipāte mahāmittavindakajātake (jā. 1.1.82; 1.5.100 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana bodhisatto imaṃ gāthamāha –

'Having gone beyond Ramaṇaka.' The Teacher told this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning a certain monk who was difficult to admonish. The story of this Jātaka, however, is from the time of the Perfectly Enlightened One Kassapa, and it will be made clear in the Mahāmittavindaka Jātaka in the Book of Ten. At that time, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse:

82.

82.

“Atikkamma [M 1.0385] ramaṇakaṃ, sadāmattañca dūbhakaṃ;

Svāsi pāsāṇamāsīno, yasmā jīvaṃ na mokkhasī”ti.

'Having gone beyond Ramaṇaka, and Sadāmatta, and Dūbhaka, you are now seated on the stone, from which you will not be freed while you live.'

Tattha ramaṇakanti tasmiṃ kāle phalikassa nāmaṃ, phalikapāsādañca atikkantosīti dīpeti. Sadāmattañcāti rajatassa nāmaṃ, rajatapāsādañca atikkantosīti dīpeti. Dūbhakanti maṇino nāmaṃ, maṇipāsādañca atikkantosīti dīpeti. Svāsīti so asi tvaṃ. Pāsāṇamāsīnoti khuracakkaṃ nāma pāsāṇamayaṃ vā hoti rajatamayaṃ vā maṇimayaṃ vā, taṃ pana pāsāṇamayameva. So ca tena āsīno atiniviṭṭho ajjhotthaṭo. Tasmā pāsāṇena āsīnattā “pāsāṇāsīno”ti vattabbe byañjanasandhivasena makāraṃ ādāya “pāsāṇamāsīno”ti vuttaṃ. Pāsāṇaṃ vā āsīno, taṃ khuracakkaṃ āsajja pāpuṇitvā ṭhitoti attho. Yasmā jīvaṃ na mokkhasīti yasmā khuracakkā yāva te pāpaṃ na khīyati, tāva jīvantoyeva na muccissasi, taṃ āsīnosīti.

Therein, 'Ramaṇaka' was the name for crystal at that time; it indicates, 'You have gone beyond the crystal palace.' 'Sadāmatta' was the name for silver; it indicates, 'You have gone beyond the silver palace.' 'Dūbhaka' was the name for a jewel; it indicates, 'You have gone beyond the jewel palace.' 'Svāsi' means 'you are.' 'Pāsāṇamāsīno' refers to the razor-wheel, which may be made of stone, silver, or jewels, but in this case, it is made of stone. And he was seated on it, deeply embedded and overwhelmed by it. Therefore, because he was seated on stone (pāsāṇena āsīna), while it should be said as 'pāsāṇāsīno,' due to euphonic combination, the letter 'm' is inserted, and it is said as 'pāsāṇamāsīno.' Or, it means 'seated on the stone,' that is, having reached and attached himself to that razor-wheel, he stood there. 'From which you will not be freed while you live' means: from that razor-wheel, for as long as your evil is not exhausted, you will not be released while still alive; on that you are seated.

Imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā bodhisatto attano vasanaṭṭhānaṃyeva gato. Mittavindakopi khuracakkaṃ ukkhipitvā mahādukkhaṃ anubhavamāno pāpakamme parikkhīṇe yathākammaṃ gato.

Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta went to his own dwelling place. And Mittavindaka, bearing the razor-wheel and experiencing great suffering, went according to his karma when his evil deed was exhausted.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mittavindako dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, devarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka thus: "At that time, the intractable monk was Mittavindaka, and the king of the devas was indeed myself."

Mittavindakajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Second Mittavindaka Jātaka.

[83] 3. Kāḷakaṇṇijātakavaṇṇanā

[83] 3. The Commentary on the Kāḷakaṇṇī Jātaka

Mitto [V 1.0348][P 1.0364] have sattapadena hotīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ anāthapiṇḍikassa mittaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira anāthapiṇḍikena saddhiṃ sahapaṃsukīḷiko ekācariyasseva santike uggahitasippo nāmena kāḷakaṇṇī nāma. So gacchante kāle duggato hutvā [M 1.0386] jīvituṃ asakkonto seṭṭhissa santikaṃ agamāsi. So taṃ samassāsetvā paribbayaṃ datvā attano kuṭumbaṃ paṭicchāpesi. So seṭṭhino upakārako hutvā sabbakiccāni karoti. Taṃ seṭṭhissa santikaṃ āgatakāle “tiṭṭha, kāḷakaṇṇi, nisīda, kāḷakaṇṇi, bhuñja kāḷakaṇṇī”ti vadanti. Athekadivasaṃ seṭṭhino mittāmaccā seṭṭhiṃ upasaṅkamitvā evamāhaṃsu “mahāseṭṭhi, mā etaṃ tava santike kari, ‘tiṭṭha, kāḷakaṇṇi, nisīda kāḷakaṇṇi, bhuñja kāḷakaṇṇī’ti hi iminā saddena yakkhopi palāyeyya, na cesa tayā samāno, duggato durūpeto, kiṃ te iminā”ti. Anāthapiṇḍiko “nāmaṃ nāma vohāramattaṃ, na taṃ paṇḍitā pamāṇaṃ karonti, sutamaṅgalikena nāma bhavituṃ na vaṭṭati, na sakkā mayā nāmamattaṃ nissāya sahapaṃsukīḷikaṃ sahāyaṃ pariccajitu”nti tesaṃ vacanaṃ anādāya ekadivasaṃ attano bhogagāmaṃ gacchanto taṃ geharakkhakaṃ katvā agamāsi.

"A friend is known by walking seven steps together," the Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke concerning a friend of Anāthapiṇḍika. It seems that this man, named Kāḷakaṇṇī, had played in the dust with Anāthapiṇḍika and had studied a craft under the same teacher. In the course of time, having become poor and unable to make a living, he went to the merchant. The merchant comforted him, gave him an allowance, and put him in charge of his household. He became helpful to the merchant, performing all his duties. Whenever he came into the merchant's presence, they would say, "Stand, Kāḷakaṇṇī, sit, Kāḷakaṇṇī, eat, Kāḷakaṇṇī." Then one day the merchant's friends and advisors approached him and said, "Great merchant, do not keep this man in your presence. With such words as 'Stand, Kāḷakaṇṇī, sit, Kāḷakaṇṇī, eat, Kāḷakaṇṇī,' even a yaksha would flee. And he is not your equal; he is poor and ill-favored. What good is he to you?" Anāthapiṇḍika said, "A name is merely a conventional designation; the wise do not consider that important. It is not proper to be superstitious about what one hears. I cannot abandon a companion I played in the dust with, relying merely on a name." Disregarding their words, one day while going to his estate, he appointed him as the guardian of his house and departed.

Corā “seṭṭhi kira bhogagāmaṃ gato, gehamassa vilumpissāmā”ti nānāvudhahatthā rattibhāge āgantvā gehaṃ parivāresuṃ. Itaropi corānaññeva āgamanaṃ āsaṅkamāno aniddāyantova nisīdi. So corānaṃ āgatabhāvaṃ ñatvā manusse pabodhetuṃ “tvaṃ saṅkhaṃ dhama, tvaṃ mudiṅgaṃ vādehī”ti mahāsamajjaṃ karonto viya sakalanivesanaṃ ekasaddaṃ kāresi. Corā “suññaṃ gehanti dussutaṃ amhehi, attheva idha mahāseṭṭhī”ti pāsāṇamuggarādīni tattheva chaḍḍetvā palāyiṃsu.

The thieves thought, "The merchant has supposedly gone to his estate, so we will plunder his house." Armed with various weapons, they arrived at night and surrounded the house. But the other man, suspecting the arrival of thieves, sat without sleeping. Knowing the thieves had come, to rouse the people he made a great noise as if for a festival, shouting, "You blow the conch, you beat the drum!" and made the entire dwelling resound with one sound. The thieves, thinking, "We were misinformed that the house was empty; the great merchant is indeed here," left their stones, clubs, and the like right there and fled.

Punadivase manussā tattha tattha chaḍḍite pāsāṇamuggarādayo disvā saṃvegappattā hutvā “sace ajja evarūpo buddhisampanno gharavicārako nābhavissa, corehi yathāruciyā pavisitvā sabbaṃ gehaṃ viluttaṃ assa, imaṃ daḷhamittaṃ nissāya seṭṭhino vuḍḍhi jātā”ti taṃ pasaṃsitvā seṭṭhissa bhogagāmato āgatakāle sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocayiṃsu. Atha ne seṭṭhi avoca “tumhe evarūpaṃ mama geharakkhakaṃ mittaṃ nikkaḍḍhāpetha, sacāyaṃ tumhākaṃ vacanena mayā nikkaḍḍhito assa, ajja me kuṭumbaṃ kiñci nābhavissa, nāmaṃ nāma appamāṇaṃ, hitacittameva pamāṇa”nti tassa uttaritaraṃ paribbayaṃ datvā “atthi dāni me idaṃ kathāpābhata”nti [V 1.0349][P 1.0365] satthu santikaṃ gantvā ādito [M 1.0387] paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, gahapati, idāneva kāḷakaṇṇimitto attano mittassa ghare kuṭumbaṃ rakkhati, pubbepi rakkhiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The next day, people saw the stones, clubs, and the like discarded here and there. Alarmed, they thought, "If today there had not been such a wise household manager, thieves would have entered as they pleased and plundered the entire house. Thanks to this steadfast friend, the merchant’s prosperity has increased." They praised him and, when the merchant returned from his estate, they reported the whole incident to him. Then the merchant said to them, "You would have me dismiss such a friend, the guardian of my home? If he had been dismissed by me on your word, today I would have no property left. A name is of no account; a benevolent mind is the true measure." He gave him an even greater reward and, thinking, "Now I have this ‘gift of a story’," he went to the Teacher and recounted the entire incident from the beginning. The Teacher said, "Not only now, householder, has the friend Kāḷakaṇṇi protected his friend’s household—he did so in the past as well." At his request, the Teacher then related a past incident.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mahāyaso seṭṭhi ahosi. Tassa kāḷakaṇṇī nāma mittoti sabbaṃ paccuppannavatthusadisameva. Bodhisatto bhogagāmato āgato taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “sace mayā tumhākaṃ vacanena evarūpo mitto nikkaḍḍhito assa, ajja me kuṭumbaṃ kiñci nābhavissā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a wealthy merchant of great renown. He had a friend named Kāḷakaṇṇī, and the whole story is just like the present one. When the Bodhisatta returned from his estate and heard that account, he said, "If, on your word, I had dismissed such a friend, today I would have no property left." Then he spoke this verse:

83.

83.

“Mitto have sattapadena hoti, sahāyo pana dvādasakena hoti;

Māsaḍḍhamāsena ca ñāti hoti, tatuttariṃ attasamopi hoti;

Sohaṃ kathaṃ attasukhassa hetu, cirasanthutaṃ kāḷakaṇṇiṃ jaheyya”nti.

"A friend, indeed, is made in seven steps, a companion in twelve. In a month or half a month, one becomes a kinsman, and beyond that, one is like oneself. So how, for the sake of my own happiness, could I abandon Kāḷakaṇṇī, with whom I have been long acquainted?"

Tattha haveti nipātamattaṃ. Mettāyatīti mitto, mettaṃ paccupaṭṭhāpeti, sinehaṃ karotīti attho. So panesa sattapadena hoti, ekato sattapadavītihāragamanamattena hotīti attho. Sahāyo pana dvādasakena hotīti sabbakiccāni ekato karaṇavasena sabbiriyāpathesu saha gacchatīti sahāyo. So panesa dvādasakena hoti, dvādasāhaṃ ekato nivāsena hotīti attho. Māsaḍḍhamāsena cāti māsena vā aḍḍhamāsena vā. Ñāti hotīti ñātisamo hoti. Tatuttarinti tato uttariṃ ekato vāsena attasamopi hotiyeva. Jaheyyanti “evarūpaṃ sahāyaṃ kathaṃ jaheyya”nti mittassa guṇaṃ kathesi. Tato paṭṭhāya puna koci tassa antare vattā nāma nāhosīti.

Here, `have` is merely a particle. 'One who is friendly (`mettāyati`) is a friend (`mitto`)'; this means one establishes friendliness, one creates affection. This friendship comes to be in seven steps, meaning it comes to be simply by walking together for a distance of seven steps. A 'companion' (`sahāyo`) is one who goes together (`saha gacchati`) in all postures, by way of doing all activities together. This companionship comes to be in twelve, meaning it comes to be by living together for twelve days. 'In a month or half a month' means in a month or in half a month. 'One becomes a kinsman' means one becomes like a kinsman. 'Beyond that' means that by living together longer, one becomes even like oneself. 'Should I abandon?'—thus he spoke of his friend's quality, thinking, "How could I abandon such a companion?" From then on, no one dared to speak on that matter again.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kāḷakaṇṇī ānando ahosi, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: "At that time, Kāḷakaṇṇī was Ānanda, and the merchant of Benares was indeed myself."

Kāḷakaṇṇijātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Third Kāḷakaṇṇī Jātaka.

[84] 4. Atthassadvārajātakavaṇṇanā

[84] 4. The Commentary on the Atthassadvāra Jātaka

Ārogyamicche [V 1.0350][P 1.0366][M 1.0388] paramañca lābhanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ atthakusalaṃ kulaputtaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi ekassa mahāvibhavassa seṭṭhino putto jātiyā sattavasso paññavā atthakusalo. So ekadivasaṃ pitaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā atthassa dvārapañhaṃ nāma pucchi, so taṃ na jānāti. Athassa etadahosi “ayaṃ pañho atisukhumo, ṭhapetvā sabbaññubuddhaṃ añño upari bhavaggena, heṭṭhā ca avīcinā paricchinne lokasannivāse etaṃ pañhaṃ kathetuṃ samattho nāma natthī”ti. So puttamādāya bahuṃ mālāgandhavilepanaṃ gāhāpetvā jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno bhagavantaṃ etadavoca “ayaṃ, bhante, dārako paññavā atthakusalo maṃ atthassa dvārapañhaṃ nāma pucchi, ahaṃ taṃ pañhaṃ ajānanto tumhākaṃ santikaṃ āgato, sādhu me, bhante, bhagavā taṃ pañhaṃ kathetū”ti. Satthā “pubbepāhaṃ, upāsaka, iminā kumārakenetaṃ pañhaṃ puṭṭho, mayā cassa kathito, tadā naṃ esa jānāti, idāni pana bhavasaṅkhepagatattā na sallakkhetī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

While residing at Jetavana, the Teacher spoke this Dhamma teaching concerning a certain young man of good family skilled in welfare, beginning with the words, "One should desire health, the supreme gain." In Sāvatthī, the son of a very wealthy merchant, seven years of age, was wise and skilled in welfare. One day, he approached his father and asked the question called "the gateway to welfare," but his father did not know the answer. Then it occurred to him, "This question is very subtle; apart from the All-Knowing Buddha, there is no one in this world-system, bounded above by the highest state of existence and below by the Avīci hell, who is capable of explaining this question." Taking his son, and having procured many flowers, perfumes, and ointments, he went to Jetavana, honored the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. He then addressed the Blessed One: "Venerable Sir, this boy is wise and skilled in welfare. He asked me the question called 'the gateway to welfare,' but I did not know the answer. Therefore, I have come to you. Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One kindly explain that question to me." The Teacher said, "Lay follower, in the past I was asked this very question by this boy, and I answered it for him; at that time, he understood it. But now, due to the covering of repeated existence, he does not recollect it." Being thus entreated by him, the Teacher recounted a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mahāvibhavo seṭṭhi ahosi. Athassa putto sattavassiko jātiyā paññavā atthakusalo. So ekadivasaṃ pitaraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “tāta, atthassa dvāraṃ nāma ki”nti atthassa dvārapañhaṃ pucchi. Athassa pitā taṃ pañhaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a wealthy merchant of great means. His son, seven years of age, was wise and skilled in welfare. One day, he approached his father and asked the question of the gateway to welfare, saying, "Father, what is the gateway to welfare?" Then his father, explaining that question to him, spoke this verse:

84.

84.

“Ārogyamicche paramañca lābhaṃ, sīlañca vuddhānumataṃ sutañca;

Dhammānuvattī ca alīnatā ca, atthassa dvārā pamukhā chaḷete”ti.

"One should desire health, the supreme gain; virtue, that which is approved by the elders, and learning; adherence to the Dhamma and diligence—these six are the foremost gateways to welfare."

Tattha ārogyamicche paramañca lābhanti ca-kāro nipātamattaṃ. Tāta, paṭhamameva ārogyasaṅkhātaṃ paramaṃ lābhaṃ iccheyyāti imamatthaṃ dīpento evamāha. Tattha ārogyaṃ nāma sarīrassa ceva cittassa ca arogabhāvo anāturatā. Sarīre hi rogāture neva aladdhaṃ bhogalābhaṃ uppādetuṃ sakkoti, na [P 1.0367] laddhaṃ paribhuñjituṃ, anāture pana ubhayampetaṃ sakkoti. Citte ca kilesāture neva aladdhaṃ jhānādibhedaṃ lābhaṃ uppādetuṃ [M 1.0389] sakkoti, na laddhaṃ puna samāpattivasena paribhuñjituṃ. Etasmiṃ anārogye sati aladdhopi lābho na labbhati, laddhopi niratthako hoti, asati panetasmiṃ aladdhopi lābho labbhati, laddhopi sātthako hotīti ārogyaṃ [V 1.0351] paramo lābho nāma. Taṃ sabbapaṭhamaṃ icchitabbaṃ. Idamekaṃ atthassa dvāranti ayamettha attho. Sīlañcāti ācārasīlaṃ. Iminā lokacārittaṃ dasseti. Vuddhānumatanti guṇavuddhānaṃ paṇḍitānaṃ anumataṃ. Iminā ñāṇasampannānaṃ garūnaṃ ovādaṃ dasseti. Sutañcāti kāraṇanissitaṃ sutaṃ. Iminā imasmiṃ loke atthanissitaṃ bāhusaccaṃ dasseti. Dhammānuvattī cāti tividhassa sucaritadhammassa anuvattanaṃ. Iminā duccaritadhammaṃ vajjetvā sucaritadhammassa anuvattanabhāvaṃ dasseti. Alīnatā cāti cittassa alīnatā anīcatā. Iminā cittassa asaṅkocataṃ paṇītabhāvaṃ uttamabhāvaṃ dasseti. Atthassa dvārā pamukhā chaḷeteti attho nāma vuḍḍhi, tassa vuḍḍhisaṅkhātassa lokiyalokuttarassa atthassa ete pamukhā uttamā cha dvārā upāyā adhigamamukhānīti.

Therein, regarding 'One should desire health, the supreme gain,' the particle 'ca' is merely an enclitic. He spoke thus to explain this meaning: "My dear son, one should first of all desire the supreme gain known as health." Herein, 'health' means the state of being free from disease, the absence of affliction, in both body and mind. For when the body is afflicted by disease, one can neither generate unattained material gains nor enjoy what has been attained. But when free from affliction, one can do both. Similarly, when the mind is afflicted by defilements, one can neither attain gains such as jhāna and the like, nor enjoy what has been attained by way of repeated absorption. When there is ill health, even unattained gains are not obtained, and even attained gains are useless. But when there is no ill health, even unattained gains are obtained, and even attained gains are meaningful. Thus, health is called the supreme gain. This should be desired first of all. This is one gateway to welfare—this is the meaning here. 'And virtue' refers to moral conduct. By this, he indicates worldly custom. 'Approved by the elders' refers to what is approved by the virtuous and wise elders. By this, he indicates the counsel of wise teachers. 'And learning' refers to learning based on reason. By this, he indicates extensive learning related to what is beneficial in this world. 'And adherence to the Dhamma' means following the threefold good conduct. By this, he indicates the state of avoiding bad conduct and adhering to good conduct. 'And diligence' means the mind's diligence, its non-inferiority. By this, he indicates the mind's unconstrictedness, its refined state, its excellent state. 'These six are the foremost gateways to welfare' means that welfare is growth; for that welfare, characterized as growth, which is both mundane and supramundane, these six are the foremost, the supreme gateways, means, and entrances to its attainment.

Evaṃ bodhisatto puttassa atthassa dvārapañhaṃ kathesi. So tato paṭṭhāya tesu chasu dhammesu vatti. Bodhisattopi dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus the Bodhisatta explained the question of the gateway to welfare to his son. From that time onwards, the son conducted himself according to those six principles. The Bodhisatta too, having performed meritorious deeds such as generosity, passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā puttova paccuppannaputto, mahāseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher connected the Jātaka, saying: "The son at that time was the present son, and the great merchant was I myself."

Atthassadvārajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Atthassadvāra Jātaka, the fourth.

[85] 5. Kiṃpakkajātakavaṇṇanā

[85] 5. The Commentary on the Kiṃpakka Jātaka

Āyatiṃ dosaṃ nāññāyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Aññataro kira kulaputto buddhasāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajito ekadivasaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ piṇḍāya caranto ekaṃ alaṅkataitthiṃ disvā ukkaṇṭhi. Atha naṃ ācariyupajjhāyā satthu santikaṃ ānayiṃsu. Satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā [M 1.0390] “sacca”nti vutte “pañca kāmaguṇā nāmete bhikkhu paribhogakāle ramaṇīyā. So pana tesaṃ paribhogo nirayādīsu paṭisandhidāyakattā kiṃpakkaphalaparibhogasadiso hoti. Kiṃpakkaphalaṃ nāma vaṇṇagandharasasampannaṃ, khāditaṃ pana antāni khaṇḍitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpeti. Pubbe bahū bālajanā tassa dosaṃ adisvā [P 1.0368] vaṇṇagandharasesu bajjhitvā taṃ phalaṃ paribhuñjitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇiṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling in Jetavana, spoke this teaching, beginning with "Not having understood the future danger," concerning a certain discontented monk. It is said that a certain man of good family, having dedicated himself to the Buddha's Dispensation, went forth as a monk. One day, while wandering for alms in Sāvatthī, he saw a finely adorned woman and became discontented. Then his teachers and preceptors brought him to the Teacher. The Teacher asked him, "Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?" When he replied, "It is true," the Teacher said, "Monk, these five strands of sensual pleasure are delightful at the time of enjoyment. But the enjoyment of them, because it gives rebirth in hell and other woeful states, is like consuming a kiṃpakka fruit. The kiṃpakka fruit is endowed with color, fragrance, and taste, but when eaten, it severs the intestines and brings about the destruction of life. In the past, many foolish people, not seeing the danger in it, became attached to its color, fragrance, and taste. Having consumed that fruit, they met with the destruction of their lives." Having said this, being requested by them, he recounted a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0352] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto satthavāho hutvā pañcahi sakaṭasatehi pubbantāparantaṃ gacchanto aṭavimukhaṃ patvā manusse sannipātetvā “imissā aṭaviyā visarukkhā nāma atthi, mā kho maṃ anāpucchā pubbe akhāditapubbāni phalāphalāni khāditthā”ti ovadi. Manussā aṭaviṃ atikkamitvā aṭavimukhe ekaṃ kiṃpakkarukkhaṃ phalabhāraoṇamitasākhaṃ addasaṃsu. Tassa khandhasākhāpattaphalāni saṇṭhānavaṇṇarasagandhehi ambasadisāneva. Tesu ekacce vaṇṇagandharasesu bajjhitvā ambaphalasaññāya phalāni khādiṃsu, ekacce “satthavāhaṃ pucchitvā khādissāmā”ti gahetvā aṭṭhaṃsu. Bodhisatto taṃ ṭhānaṃ patvā ye gahetvā ṭhitā, te phalāni chaḍḍāpetvā, ye khādamānā aṭṭhaṃsu, te vamanaṃ kāretvā tesaṃ bhesajjaṃ adāsi. Tesu ekacce arogā jātā, paṭhamameva khāditvā ṭhitā pana jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā. Bodhisattopi icchitaṭṭhānaṃ sotthinā gantvā lābhaṃ labhitvā puna sakaṭṭhānameva āgantvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a caravan leader. Traveling with five hundred carts from east to west, he reached the entrance to a wilderness. Having gathered the people, he advised them, 'In this wilderness, there are indeed poison trees. Do not eat any fruits you have not eaten before without consulting me.' The people, having crossed the wilderness, saw at the entrance to the wilderness a kiṃpakka tree, its branches bending under the weight of fruit. Its trunk, branches, leaves, and fruits resembled mangoes in form, color, taste, and fragrance. Some, captivated by their color, fragrance, and taste, mistook them for mangoes and ate the fruits. Others, thinking, 'We will ask the caravan leader before eating,' took them and waited. When the Bodhisatta arrived at the spot, he made those who had taken them discard the fruits, and induced vomiting in those who had eaten them, then gave them medicine. Some became healthy, but those who had eaten them first met their death. The Bodhisatta safely reached his desired destination, obtained gain, and returned to his own place. After performing meritorious deeds such as generosity, he passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā taṃ vatthuṃ kathetvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Having narrated that story, the Teacher, having become perfectly enlightened, spoke this verse:

85.

85.

“Āyatiṃ dosaṃ nāññāya, yo kāme paṭisevati;

Vipākante hananti naṃ, kiṃpakkamiva bhakkhita”nti.

Not knowing the fault in the future, whoever partakes of sensual pleasures—at the time of their fruition, they destroy him, like a kiṃpakka fruit when eaten.

Tattha āyatiṃ dosaṃ nāññāyāti anāgate dosaṃ na aññāya, ajānitvāti attho. Yo kāme paṭisevatīti yo vatthukāme ca kilesakāme ca paṭisevati. Vipākante hananti nanti te kāmā taṃ purisaṃ attano vipākasaṅkhāte ante nirayādīsu uppannaṃ nānappakārena dukkhena saṃyojayamānā hananti. Kathaṃ? Kiṃpakkamiva bhakkhitanti, yathā paribhogakāle [M 1.0391] vaṇṇagandharasasampattiyā manāpaṃ kiṃpakkaphalaṃ anāgatadosaṃ adisvā bhakkhitaṃ ante hanati, jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpeti, evaṃ paribhogakāle manāpāpi kāmā vipākakāle hanantīti desanaṃ yathānusandhiṃ pāpetvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphalaṃ [P 1.0369] pāpuṇi. Sesaparisāyapi keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino, keci arahanto ahesuṃ.

Herein, 'Not knowing the fault in the future' means not knowing the fault in time to come, not being aware of it—that is the meaning. 'Whoever partakes of sensual pleasures' refers to one who partakes of both sensual pleasures of the object and sensual pleasures of defilement. 'At the time of their fruition, they destroy him' means those sensual pleasures destroy that person at the end, which is called their fruition, by connecting him with various kinds of suffering after he has arisen in hell and so on. How? 'Like a kiṃpakka fruit when eaten'—just as a kiṃpakka fruit, which is agreeable at the time of consumption due to its endowment with color, fragrance, and taste, when eaten without seeing the future fault, destroys one in the end, causing the destruction of life; so too, sensual pleasures, though agreeable at the time of enjoyment, destroy one at the time of their fruition. Having thus drawn the connection in the teaching, he revealed the truths. At the conclusion of the revelation of the truths, the discontented bhikkhu attained the fruit of stream-entry. Among the rest of the assembly, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, some non-returners, and some arahants.

Satthāpi imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā parisā buddhaparisā ahosi, satthavāho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma teaching, made the connection of the Jātaka: 'The assembly of that time is now the Buddha's assembly, and I myself was the caravan leader.'

Kiṃpakkajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The commentary on the Kiṃpakka Jātaka, the fifth.

[86] 6. Sīlavīmaṃsakajātakavaṇṇanā

[86] 6. The Commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka

Sīlaṃ [V 1.0353] kireva kalyāṇanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ sīlavīmaṃsakaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira kosalarājānaṃ nissāya jīvati tisaraṇaṃ gato akhaṇḍapañcasīlo tiṇṇaṃ vedānaṃ pāragū. Rājā “ayaṃ sīlavā”ti tassa atirekasammānaṃ karoti. So cintesi “ayaṃ rājā mayhaṃ aññehi brāhmaṇehi atirekasammānaṃ karoti, ativiya maṃ garuṃ katvā passati, kiṃ nu kho esa mama jātigottakulappadesasippasampattiṃ nissāya imaṃ sammānaṃ karoti, udāhu sīlasampattiṃ, vīmaṃsissāmi tāvā”ti. So ekadivasaṃ rājūpaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā gharaṃ āgacchanto ekassa heraññikassa phalakato anāpucchitvā ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ gahetvā agamāsi, heraññiko brāhmaṇe garubhāvena kiñci avatvā nisīdi. Punadivase dve kahāpaṇe gaṇhi, heraññiko tatheva adhivāsesi. Tatiyadivase kahāpaṇamuṭṭhiṃ aggahesi, atha naṃ heraññiko “ajja te tatiyo divaso rājakuṭumbaṃ vilumpantassā”ti “rājakuṭumbavilumpakacoro me gahito”ti tikkhattuṃ viravi. Atha naṃ manussā ito cito ca āgantvā “ciraṃdāni tvaṃ sīlavā viya vicarī”ti dve tayo pahāre datvā bandhitvā rañño dassesuṃ.

While dwelling in Jetavana, the Teacher spoke this, beginning with 'Virtue indeed is beautiful,' concerning a certain brahmin who was examining virtue. This brahmin, it is said, lived dependent on the king of Kosala, had gone to the Triple Gem for refuge, possessed the five precepts unbroken, and was a master of the three Vedas. The king, thinking, 'This one is virtuous,' showed him excessive honor. The brahmin reflected, 'This king honors me more than other brahmins, regarding me with extreme reverence. Does he bestow this honor on me based on my accomplishment in birth, lineage, family, and skill, or is it based on my accomplishment in virtue? I shall first investigate this.' One day, after attending upon the king and while returning home, he took one coin from a goldsmith’s counter without asking and left. The goldsmith, out of respect for the brahmin, said nothing and remained seated. The next day, he took two coins, and the goldsmith tolerated it just as before. On the third day, he grabbed a handful of coins. Then the goldsmith shouted three times, 'Today is the third day you have been plundering the king's property!' and 'A thief plundering the king's property has been caught by me!' Then people came from all directions, saying, 'For a long time now you have gone about as if you were virtuous!' They struck him two or three blows, bound him, and presented him to the king.

Rājā [M 1.0392] vippaṭisārī hutvā “kasmā, brāhmaṇa, evarūpaṃ dussīlakammaṃ karosī”ti vatvā “gacchatha, tassa rājāṇaṃ karothā”ti āha. Brāhmaṇo “nāhaṃ, mahārāja, coro”ti āha. Atha “kasmā rājakuṭumbikassa phalakato kahāpaṇe gaṇhī”ti? “Etaṃ mayā tayi mama atisammānaṃ karonte ‘kiṃ nu kho rājā mama jātiādīni nissāya atisammānaṃ karoti, udāhu sīlaṃ nissāyā’ti vīmaṃsanatthāya kataṃ, idāni pana mayā ekaṃsena ñātaṃ. Yathā sīlameva nissāya tayā mama sammāno kato, na jātiādīni. Tathā hi me idāni rājāṇaṃ kāresi, svāhaṃ iminā kāraṇena ‘imasmiṃ loke sīlameva uttamaṃ sīlaṃ pamukha’nti sanniṭṭhānaṃ gato. Imassa panāhaṃ sīlassa anucchavikaṃ [P 1.0370] karonto gehe ṭhito kilese paribhuñjanto na sakkhissāmi kātuṃ, ajjeva jetavanaṃ gantvā satthu santike pabbajissāmi, pabbajjaṃ me detha, devā”ti vatvā rājānaṃ anujānāpetvā jetavanābhimukho pāyāsi.

The king, becoming remorseful, said, 'Why, brahmin, do you commit such an unvirtuous act?' and then commanded, 'Go, inflict the royal punishment upon him.' The brahmin replied, 'I am not a thief, great king.' Then the king asked, 'Why then did you take coins from the royal treasurer's counter?' The brahmin explained, 'When you were showing me excessive honor, I did this for the sake of investigation, wondering: "Does the king honor me based on my birth and so on, or is it based on my virtue?" Now, however, I have understood this for certain: that the honor you showed me was based solely on virtue, not on birth and so on. For you are now having the royal punishment inflicted upon me. For this reason, I have reached the conclusion that in this world, virtue alone is excellent, virtue is foremost. But I will not be able to act in a way befitting this virtue while living at home and enjoying sensual pleasures. This very day I will go to Jetavana and go forth into homelessness in the presence of the Teacher. Grant me leave to go forth, Your Majesty.' Having obtained the king's permission, he set out in the direction of Jetavana.

Atha naṃ ñātisuhajjabandhavā sannipatitvā nivāretuṃ asakkontā nivattiṃsu. So satthu santikaṃ gantvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhitvā avissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhāno vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā arahattaṃ patvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, mayhaṃ pabbajjā matthakaṃ pattā”ti [V 1.0354] aññaṃ byākāsi. Tassa taṃ aññabyākaraṇaṃ bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭaṃ jātaṃ. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā bhikkhū “āvuso, asuko nāma rañño upaṭṭhākabrāhmaṇo attano sīlaṃ vīmaṃsitvā rājānaṃ āpucchitvā pabbajitvā arahatte patiṭṭhito”ti tassa guṇaṃ kathayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāni ayameva brāhmaṇo attano sīlaṃ vīmaṃsitvā pabbajitvā attano patiṭṭhaṃ akāsi, pubbepi paṇḍitā attano sīlaṃ vīmaṃsitvā pabbajitvā attano patiṭṭhaṃ kariṃsū”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then his relatives, friends, and acquaintances gathered to prevent him, but being unable to do so, they desisted. He went to the Teacher, requested ordination, and having received both the going forth and full ordination, he, without neglecting his meditation subject, developed insight and attained arahantship. He approached the Teacher and declared, 'Venerable sir, my going forth has reached its culmination.' This declaration of his attainment became known in the Sangha of monks. Then one day, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and sat discussing his virtues, saying, 'Friends, that brahmin attendant of the king, after examining his own virtue, having taken leave of the king, went forth, and is established in arahantship.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, what discussion are you currently engaged in?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that this brahmin, having examined his own virtue, went forth and established a refuge for himself. In the past too, the wise, having examined their own virtue, went forth and established a refuge for themselves.' Then, being requested by them, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa purohito ahosi dānādhimutto sīlajjhāsayo akhaṇḍapañcasīlo. Rājā sesabrāhmaṇehi atirekaṃ tassa sammānaṃ karotīti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva. Bodhisatte pana bandhitvā rañño santikaṃ nīyamāne [M 1.0393] ahituṇḍikā antaravīthiyaṃ sappaṃ kīḷāpentā naṅguṭṭhe gaṇhanti, gīvāya gaṇhanti, gale veṭhenti. Bodhisatto te disvā “mā, tātā, evaṃ sappaṃ naṅguṭṭhe gaṇhatha, mā gīvāya gaṇhatha, mā gale veṭhetha. Ayañhi vo ḍaṃsitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpeyyā”ti āha. Ahituṇḍikā “ayaṃ, brāhmaṇa, sappo sīlavā ācārasampanno tādiso dussīlo na hoti, tvaṃ pana attano dussīlatāya anācārena rājakuṭumbavilumpakacoroti bandhitvā nīyasī”ti āhaṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his chaplain, devoted to generosity, with a mind inclined to virtue, observing the five precepts unbrokenly. The king honored him more than the other brahmins; all this is just as in the previous story. But when the Bodhisatta was bound and being led to the king, snake charmers on the street were playing with a snake, grabbing it by the tail, seizing it by the neck, and coiling it around their throats. Seeing this, the Bodhisatta said, 'Sirs, do not grab the snake by the tail, do not seize it by the neck, do not coil it around your throat. It might bite you and bring you to the destruction of life.' The snake charmers replied, 'This snake, brahmin, is virtuous and well-behaved—it is not immoral like you. But you, due to your own immorality and misconduct, are being bound and led away as a thief who plunders the royal family's wealth.'

So cintesi “sappāpi tāva aḍaṃsantā aviheṭhentā ‘sīlavanto’ti nāmaṃ labhanti, kimaṅgaṃ pana manussabhūtā. Sīlameva imasmiṃ loke uttamaṃ, natthi [P 1.0371] tato uttaritara”nti. Atha naṃ netvā rañño dassesuṃ. Rājā “kiṃ idaṃ, tātā”ti pucchi. “Rājakuṭumbavilumpako coro, devā”ti. “Tena hissa rājāṇaṃ karothā”ti. Brāhmaṇo “nāhaṃ, mahārāja, coro”ti āha. “Atha kasmā kahāpaṇe aggahesī”ti ca vutte purimanayeneva sabbaṃ ārocento “svāhaṃ iminā kāraṇena ‘imasmiṃ loke sīlameva uttamaṃ, sīlaṃ pāmokkha’nti sanniṭṭhānaṃ gato”ti vatvā “tiṭṭhatu tāva idaṃ, āsīvisopi tāva aḍaṃsanto aviheṭhento ‘sīlavā’ti vattabbataṃ labhati. Imināpi kāraṇena sīlameva uttamaṃ, sīlaṃ pavara”nti sīlaṃ vaṇṇento imaṃ gāthamāha –

He thought, 'Even snakes, if they do not bite or harm, obtain the name "virtuous." How much more so for human beings? Virtue is indeed the highest in this world; there is nothing superior to it.' Then they took him and showed him to the king. The king asked, 'What is this, sirs?' 'A thief, Your Majesty, who plunders the royal family's wealth.' 'Then inflict the royal penalty on him,' the king said. The brahmin replied, 'I am not a thief, great king.' When asked, 'Then why did you take the coins?' he recounted everything as before, declaring, 'For this reason, I have come to the firm conclusion that in this world, virtue is indeed the highest; virtue is paramount.' Speaking thus, he said, 'Let this matter be for now. Even a venomous snake, if it does not bite or harm, deserves to be called "virtuous." For this reason too, virtue is the highest; virtue is excellent.' Extolling virtue, he spoke this verse:

86.

86.

“Sīlaṃ kireva kalyāṇaṃ, sīlaṃ loke anuttaraṃ;

Passa ghoraviso nāgo, sīlavāti na haññatī”ti.

'Virtue, it is said, is truly auspicious; virtue is supreme in the world. See the fierce venomous serpent; because it is virtuous, it is not harmed.'

Tattha [V 1.0355] sīlaṃ kirevāti kāyavācācittehi avītikkamasaṅkhātaṃ ācārasīlameva. Kirāti anussavavasena vadati. Kalyāṇanti sundarataraṃ. Anuttaranti jeṭṭhakaṃ sabbaguṇadāyakaṃ. Passāti attanā diṭṭhakāraṇaṃ abhimukhaṃ karonto katheti. Sīlavāti na haññatīti ghoravisopi samāno aḍaṃsanaaviheṭhanamattakena sīlavāti pasaṃsaṃ labhati, na haññati na vihaññatīti. Imināpi kāraṇena sīlameva uttamanti.

Herein, 'virtue, it is said' refers to the virtue of conduct, defined as non-transgression by way of body, speech, and mind. 'It is said' (kira) is spoken in the sense of a report. 'Auspicious' (kalyāṇaṃ) means most beautiful. 'Supreme' (anuttaraṃ) means pre-eminent, the giver of all good qualities. 'See' (passa) means he speaks while making the reason he has seen directly evident. 'Because it is virtuous, it is not harmed' means that even though it is a fierce venomous snake, merely by not biting or harming, it obtains praise as 'virtuous,' and it is not harmed, not injured. For this reason too, virtue alone is supreme.

Evaṃ bodhisatto imāya gāthāya rañño dhammaṃ desetvā kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavantaṃ pavisitvā pañcābhiññā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having taught the king the Dhamma with this verse, renounced sensual pleasures and embraced the ascetic life, entered the Himalayas, developed the five higher knowledges and the eight attainments, and was destined for the Brahma-world.

Satthā [M 1.0394] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, rājaparisā buddhaparisā, purohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka thus: 'At that time, the king was Ānanda, the royal assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and the chaplain was none other than myself.'

Sīlavīmaṃsakajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The commentary on the Sīlavīmaṃsaka Jātaka, the sixth.

[87] 7. Maṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā

[87] 7. The Commentary on the Maṅgala Jātaka

Yassa maṅgalā samūhatāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ekaṃ sāṭakalakkhaṇabrāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Rājagahavāsiko [P 1.0372] kireko brāhmaṇo kotuhalamaṅgaliko tīsu ratanesu appasanno micchādiṭṭhiko aḍḍho mahaddhano mahābhogo, tassa samugge ṭhapitaṃ sāṭakayugaṃ mūsikā khādiṃsu. Athassa sīsaṃ nhāyitvā “sāṭake āharathā”ti vuttakāle mūsikāya khāditabhāvaṃ ārocayiṃsu. So cintesi “sace idaṃ mūsikādaṭṭhaṃ sāṭakayugaṃ imasmiṃ gehe bhavissati, mahāvināso bhavissati. Idañhi avamaṅgalaṃ kāḷakaṇṇisadisaṃ puttadhītādīnaṃ vā dāsakammakarādīnaṃ vā na sakkā dātuṃ. Yo hi idaṃ gaṇhissati, sabbassa mahāvināso bhavissati, āmakasusāne taṃ chaḍḍāpessāmi, na kho pana sakkā dāsakammakarādīnaṃ hatthe dātuṃ. Te hi ettha lobhaṃ uppādetvā imaṃ gahetvā vināsaṃ pāpuṇeyyuṃ, puttassa taṃ hatthe dassāmī”ti. So puttaṃ pakkosāpetvā tamatthaṃ ārocetvā “tvampi naṃ, tāta, hatthena aphusitvā daṇḍakena gahetvā āmakasusāne chaḍḍetvā sīsaṃ nhāyitvā ehī”ti pesesi.

This discourse, beginning with the words 'Whose omens are uprooted,' was delivered by the Teacher while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning a certain brahmin who divined omens from cloth. It is said that a certain brahmin, a resident of Rājagaha, was superstitious about omens, had little faith in the Three Jewels, and held wrong views. He was prosperous, very wealthy, and of great means. A pair of cloths that he had placed in a casket was gnawed by mice. Then, when he had bathed his head and said, 'Bring the cloths,' they informed him that they had been gnawed by a mouse. He thought, 'If this mouse-bitten pair of cloths remains in this house, there will be great ruin. Indeed, this is inauspicious, like a jinx. It cannot be given to my sons and daughters, nor to my servants and workers. For whoever takes this, great ruin will befall them all. I will have it discarded in the charnel ground. But it cannot be placed in the hands of servants and workers, for they might become greedy for it, take it, and meet with ruin. I will give it into my son's hands.' Having summoned his son and explained the matter to him, he sent him, saying, 'You, my dear, without touching it with your hand, take it with a stick, discard it in the charnel ground, and then, having bathed your head, return.'

Satthāpi [V 1.0356] kho taṃ divasaṃ paccūsasamaye bodhaneyyabandhave olokento imesaṃ pitāputtānaṃ sotāpattiphalassa upanissayaṃ disvā migavīthiṃ gahetvā migaluddako viya gantvā āmakasusānadvāre nisīdi chabbaṇṇabuddharasmiyo vissajjento. Māṇavopi pitu vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā ajagarasappaṃ viya taṃ yugasāṭakaṃ yaṭṭhikoṭiyā gahetvā āmakasusānadvāraṃ pāpuṇi. Atha naṃ satthā “kiṃ karosi māṇavā”ti āha. “Bho gotama, idaṃ sāṭakayugaṃ mūsikādaṭṭhaṃ kāḷakaṇṇisadisaṃ halāhalavisūpamaṃ, mama pitā ‘añño etaṃ chaḍḍento lobhaṃ uppādetvā gaṇheyyā’ti [M 1.0395] bhayena maṃ pahiṇi, ahametaṃ chaḍḍetvā sīsaṃ nhāyissāmīti āgatomhi, bho gotamā”ti. “Tena hi chaḍḍehī”ti. Māṇavo chaḍḍesi, satthā “amhākaṃ dāni vaṭṭatī”ti tassa sammukhāva gaṇhi. “Avamaṅgalaṃ, bho gotama, etaṃ kāḷakaṇṇisadisaṃ, mā gaṇhi mā gaṇhī”ti tasmiṃ vārayamāneyeva taṃ gahetvā veḷuvanābhimukho pāyāsi.

On that day, at dawn, the Teacher, surveying the world for those who could be enlightened, saw the supporting condition for the fruit of stream-entry in this father and son. Taking a deer path, he went like a deer hunter and sat at the gate of the charnel ground, emitting the six-hued Buddha-rays. The young brahmin, having accepted his father’s word, took that pair of cloths with the tip of a stick as if it were a python, and reached the gate of the charnel ground. Then the Teacher asked him, 'What are you doing, young man?' 'Venerable Gotama, this pair of cloths is mouse-bitten, like a jinx, comparable to deadly poison. My father, fearing that someone else discarding it might become greedy and take it, sent me. I have come to discard this and bathe my head, Venerable Gotama.' 'In that case, discard it.' The young man discarded it. The Teacher then said, 'Now it is suitable for us,' and picked it up right in front of him. 'It is inauspicious, Venerable Gotama, like a jinx! Do not take it! Do not take it!' Even while the young man was trying to prevent him, the Teacher took it and departed in the direction of the Bamboo Grove.

Māṇavo vegena gantvā pitu ārocesi “tāta, mayā āmakasusāne chaḍḍitaṃ sāṭakayugaṃ samaṇo gotamo ‘amhākaṃ vaṭṭatī’ti mayā vāriyamānopi gahetvā veḷuvanaṃ gato”ti. Brāhmaṇo cintesi “taṃ sāṭakayugaṃ avamaṅgalaṃ kāḷakaṇṇisadisaṃ, taṃ vaḷañjento samaṇopi gotamo nassissati, vihāropi nassissati, tato amhākaṃ garahā bhavissati, samaṇassa gotamassa aññe bahū sāṭake datvā taṃ chaḍḍāpessāmī”ti. So bahū sāṭake gāhāpetvā puttena saddhiṃ veḷuvanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ disvā ekamantaṃ ṭhito evamāha “saccaṃ kira vo, bho gotama, āmakasusāne [P 1.0373] sāṭakayugaṃ gahita”nti? “Saccaṃ, brāhmaṇā”ti. “Bho gotama, taṃ sāṭakayugaṃ avamaṅgalaṃ, tumhe taṃ paribhuñjamānā nassissatha, sakalavihāropi nassissati. Sace vo nivāsanaṃ vā pārupanaṃ vā nappahoti, ime sāṭake gahetvā taṃ chaḍḍāpethā”ti. Atha naṃ satthā “mayaṃ brāhmaṇa pabbajitā nāma, amhākaṃ āmakasusāne antaravīthiyaṃ saṅkāraṭṭhāne nhānatitthe mahāmaggeti evarūpesu ṭhānesu chaḍḍitā vā patitā vā pilotikā vaṭṭati, tvaṃ pana na idāneva evaṃladdhiko, pubbepi evaṃladdhikoyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The young man went quickly and reported to his father, 'Father, the pair of cloths I discarded in the charnel ground, the ascetic Gotama took, saying, "It is suitable for us," even though I tried to prevent him, and he has gone to the Bamboo Grove.' The brahmin thought, 'That pair of cloths is inauspicious, like a jinx. Using it, the ascetic Gotama will perish, and the monastery will also perish. Then blame will fall upon us. I will give the ascetic Gotama many other cloths and have him discard that one.' So he had many cloths brought, and together with his son, he went to the Bamboo Grove. Seeing the Teacher, he stood to one side and said, 'Venerable Gotama, is it true that you took a pair of cloths in the charnel ground?' 'It is true, brahmin.' 'Venerable Gotama, that pair of cloths is inauspicious. If you use it, you will perish, and the entire monastery will also perish. If you do not have enough for a lower garment or an upper garment, take these cloths and discard that one.' Then the Teacher said to him, 'Brahmin, for us who have gone forth, a rag discarded or fallen in such places as a charnel ground, an alley, a rubbish heap, a bathing place, or on the highway is suitable. You, however, are not of such a view only now; in the past, too, you were of the very same view.' Having said this, being requested by the brahmin, he related a story of the past.

Atīte magadharaṭṭhe rājagahanagare dhammiko magadharājā rajjaṃ kāresi. Tadā bodhisatto ekasmiṃ udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā himavante vasamāno ekasmiṃ kāle himavantato nikkhamitvā rājagahanagare rājuyyānaṃ patvā tattha vasitvā dutiyadivase bhikkhācāratthāya nagaraṃ pāvisi. Rājā [V 1.0357] taṃ disvā pakkosāpetvā pāsāde nisīdāpetvā bhojetvā uyyāneyeva vasanatthāya paṭiññaṃ gaṇhi. Bodhisatto rañño nivesane bhuñjitvā uyyāne vasati. Tasmiṃ kāle rājagahanagare dussalakkhaṇabrāhmaṇo [M 1.0396] nāma ahosi. Tassa samugge ṭhapitaṃ sāṭakayuganti sabbaṃ purimasadisameva.

In the past, in the city of Rājagaha in the kingdom of Magadha, a king of Magadha named Dhammika reigned. At that time, the Bodhisatta was born into a northern brahmin family. Upon reaching maturity, he went forth into the life of a seer, produced the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, and dwelt in the Himalayas. On one occasion, leaving the Himalayas, he came to the royal park in Rājagaha and stayed there. On the second day, he entered the city for alms. The king, seeing him, had him summoned, seated him in the palace, offered him food, and secured his promise to reside in the park. The Bodhisatta, having eaten at the king's residence, dwelt in the park. At that time in Rājagaha, there was a brahmin named Dussalakkhaṇa. The entire story, beginning with the pair of cloths placed in his casket, is just as the one before.

Māṇave pana susānaṃ gacchante bodhisatto paṭhamataraṃ gantvā susānadvāre nisīditvā tena chaḍḍitaṃ sāṭakayugaṃ gahetvā uyyānaṃ agamāsi. Māṇavo gantvā pitu ārocesi. Pitā “rājakulūpako tāpaso nasseyyā”ti bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “tāpasa, tayā gahitasāṭake chaḍḍehi, mā nassī”ti āha. Tāpaso “amhākaṃ susāne chaḍḍitapilotikā vaṭṭati, na mayaṃ kotuhalamaṅgalikā, kotuhalamaṅgalaṃ nāmetaṃ na buddhapaccekabuddhabodhisattehi vaṇṇitaṃ, tasmā paṇḍitena nāma kotuhalamaṅgalikena na bhavitabba”nti brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desesi. Brāhmaṇo dhammaṃ sutvā diṭṭhiṃ bhinditvā bodhisattaṃ saraṇaṃ gato. Bodhisattopi aparihīnajjhāno brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

When the young man was going to the charnel ground, the Bodhisatta went ahead, sat down at the entrance of the charnel ground, took the pair of cloths the young man had discarded, and went to the park. The young man went and informed his father. The father, thinking, “Lest the ascetic who attends on the royal family perish,” went to the Bodhisatta and said, “Ascetic, discard the cloths you have taken, lest you perish.” The ascetic replied, “For us, rags discarded in the charnel ground are suitable; we are not superstitious about omens. This so-called auspicious omen is not praised by Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, or Bodhisattas. Therefore, a wise person should not be superstitious about omens.” He then taught the Dhamma to the brahmin. Hearing the Dhamma, the brahmin shattered his wrong views and went to the Bodhisatta for refuge. The Bodhisatta, with his meditative absorption undiminished, was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthāpi [P 1.0374] imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having related this past event and having become fully enlightened, while teaching the Dhamma to the brahmin, spoke this verse:

87.

87.

“Yassa maṅgalā samūhatā, uppātā supinā ca lakkhaṇā ca;

So maṅgaladosavītivatto, yugayogādhigato na jātumetī”ti.

“For whom omens are eradicated, along with portents, dreams, and signs; he has overcome the flaws of omens, has mastered the pairs and yokes, and never comes to be again.”

Tattha yassa maṅgalā samūhatāti yassa arahato khīṇāsavassa diṭṭhamaṅgalaṃ, sutamaṅgalaṃ, mutamaṅgalanti ete maṅgalā samucchinnā. Uppātā supinā ca lakkhaṇā cāti “evarūpo candaggāho bhavissati, evarūpo sūriyaggāho bhavissati, evarūpo nakkhattaggāho bhavissati, evarūpo ukkāpāto bhavissati, evarūpo disāḍāho bhavissatī”ti ime pañca mahāuppātā, nānappakārā supinā, subhagalakkhaṇaṃ, dubbhagalakkhaṇaṃ, itthilakkhaṇaṃ, purisalakkhaṇaṃ, dāsilakkhaṇaṃ, dāsalakkhaṇaṃ, asilakkhaṇaṃ, hatthilakkhaṇaṃ, assalakkhaṇaṃ, usabhalakkhaṇaṃ, āvudhalakkhaṇaṃ, vatthalakkhaṇanti evamādikāni lakkhaṇāni ime ca diṭṭhiṭṭhānā yassa samūhatā, na etehi uppātādīhi attano maṅgalaṃ vā avamaṅgalaṃ vā pacceti. So maṅgaladosavītivattoti [M 1.0397] so khīṇāsavo sabbamaṅgaladose vītivatto atikkanto pajahitvā ṭhito. Yugayogādhigatoti “kodho ca upanāho ca, makkho ca paḷāso cā”tiādinā [V 1.0358] (vibha. 833) nayena dve dve ekato āgatakilesā yugā nāma. Kāmayogo, bhavayogo, diṭṭhiyogo, avijjāyogoti ime saṃsāre yojanabhāvato cattāro yogā nāma. Te yuge ca yoge cāti yugayoge adhigato abhibhavitvā gato vītivatto samatikkanto khīṇāsavo bhikkhu. Na jātumetīti puna paṭisandhivasena ekaṃseneva imaṃ lokaṃ na eti nāgacchatīti.

Therein, for whom omens are eradicated means that for that Arahant with cankers destroyed, the seen omen, the heard omen, and the sensed omen—these omens are uprooted. Portents, dreams, and signs refers to these five great portents: “There will be an eclipse of the moon like this, an eclipse of the sun like this, an eclipse of a star like this, a meteor shower like this, a conflagration in a cardinal direction like this”; it also refers to various kinds of dreams, and signs such as auspicious signs, inauspicious signs, signs concerning women, men, female slaves, male slaves, swords, elephants, horses, bulls, weapons, and garments. For him, these and other such signs, which are grounds for views, are eradicated. He does not believe that these portents and so on are good or bad omens for himself. He has overcome the faults of omens means that Arahant with cankers destroyed has transcended, gone beyond, and stands having abandoned all faults of omens.
