He has mastered the pairs and the yokes refers to the defilements that come together in pairs, such as “anger and resentment, hypocrisy and spite,” etc., according to the method stated in the Vibhaṅga (833); these are called ‘pairs.’ The yoke of sensual desire, the yoke of existence, the yoke of views, and the yoke of ignorance—these four are called ‘yokes’ because they bind one to the cycle of existence. The Arahant monk has mastered, overcome, transcended, and gone beyond both the pairs and the yokes. He never comes to be again means he certainly does not come to this world again through rebirth.

Evaṃ satthā imāya gāthāya brāhmaṇassa dhammaṃ desetvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne brāhmaṇo saddhiṃ puttena sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. Satthā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā eteva pitāputtā idāni pitāputtā ahesuṃ, tāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus, the Teacher, having taught the Dhamma to the brahmin with this verse, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the revelation of the Truths, the brahmin, together with his son, was established in the fruition of stream-entry. The Teacher connected the Jātaka: “The father and son of that time were the father and son of the present; but the ascetic was none other than myself.”

Maṅgalajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Maṅgala Jātaka, the Seventh.

[88] 8. Sārambhajātakavaṇṇanā

[88] 8. The Commentary on the Sārambha Jātaka

Kalyāṇimeva muñceyyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto omasavādasikkhāpadaṃ (pāci. 15) ārabbha kathesi. Dvepi vatthūni heṭṭhā nandivisālajātake vuttasadisāneva. Imasmiṃ pana jātake bodhisatto [P 1.0375] gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilāyaṃ aññatarassa brāhmaṇassa sārambho nāma balibaddo ahosi. Satthā idaṃ atītavatthuṃ kathetvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

“One should utter only what is virtuous”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the training rule on abusive speech (Pācittiya 15). Both the present and past stories are similar to those told in the Nandivisāla Jātaka below. In this birth story, however, the Bodhisatta was a bull named Sārambha belonging to a certain brahmin in Takkasilā in the Gandhāra country. The Teacher, having related this past story and having become fully enlightened, spoke this verse:

88.

88.

“Kalyāṇimeva muñceyya, na hi muñceyya pāpikaṃ;

Mokkho kalyāṇiyā sādhu, mutvā tappati pāpika”nti.

“One should utter only what is virtuous, and surely not what is evil; the utterance of the virtuous is good; having uttered the evil, one is tormented.”

Tattha kalyāṇimeva muñceyyāti catudosavinimuttaṃ kalyāṇiṃ sundaraṃ anavajjaṃ vācameva muñceyya vissajjeyya katheyya. Na hi muñceyya pāpikanti pāpikaṃ lāmikaṃ paresaṃ appiyaṃ amanāpaṃ na muñceyya na katheyya. Mokkho [M 1.0398] kalyāṇiyā sādhūti kalyāṇavācāya vissajjanameva imasmiṃ loke sādhu sundaraṃ bhaddakaṃ. Mutvā tappati pāpikanti pāpikaṃ pharusavācaṃ muñcitvā vissajjetvā kathetvā so puggalo tappati socati kilamatīti.

Therein, one should utter only what is virtuous means one should utter, release, and speak only speech that is free from the four faults—virtuous, beautiful, and blameless speech. And surely not what is evil means one should not utter or speak what is evil, base, unpleasant, and disagreeable to others. The utterance of the virtuous is good means that the release of virtuous speech is indeed good, beautiful, and auspicious in this world. Having uttered the evil, one is tormented means that having uttered, released, and spoken evil, harsh speech, that person is tormented, grieves, and becomes weary.

Evaṃ satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇo ānando ahosi, brāhmaṇī uppalavaṇṇā, sārambho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the brahmin was Ānanda, the brahmin woman was Uppalavaṇṇā, but Sārambha was none other than myself.”

Sārambhajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Sārambha Jātaka, the Eighth.

[89] 9. Kuhakajātakavaṇṇanā

[89] 9. The Commentary on the Kuhaka Jātaka

Vācāva [V 1.0359] kira te āsīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Kuhakavatthu uddālakajātake āvi bhavissati.

“It seems it was only your speech”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a deceitful monk. The story of the deceitful monk will become clear in the Uddālaka Jātaka.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente ekaṃ gāmakaṃ upanissāya eko kūṭajaṭilo kuhakatāpaso vasati. Eko kuṭumbiko tassa araññe paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā tattha naṃ vāsento attano gehe paṇītāhārena paṭijaggati. So taṃ kūṭajaṭilaṃ “sīlavā eso”ti saddahitvā corabhayena suvaṇṇanikkhasataṃ tassa paṇṇasālaṃ netvā bhūmigataṃ katvā “idaṃ olokeyyāsi, bhante”ti āha. Atha naṃ tāpaso “pabbajitānaṃ nāma, āvuso, evarūpaṃ kathetuṃ, na vaṭṭati, amhākaṃ pana parasantake lobho nāma natthī”ti āha. So “sādhu, bhante”ti tassa vacanaṃ saddahitvā pakkāmi. Duṭṭhatāpaso “sakkā ettakena jīvitu”nti [P 1.0376] katipāhaṃ atikkamitvā taṃ suvaṇṇaṃ gahetvā antarāmagge ekasmiṃ ṭhāne ṭhapetvā āgantvā paṇṇasālāyameva vasitvā punadivase tassa gehe bhattakiccaṃ katvā evamāha “āvuso, mayaṃ tumhe nissāya ciraṃ vasimha, aticiraṃ ekasmiṃ ṭhāne vasantānaṃ manussehi saddhiṃ saṃsaggo hoti, saṃsaggo ca nāma pabbajitānaṃ malaṃ, tasmā gacchāmaha”nti vatvā tena punappunaṃ yāciyamānopi nivattituṃ na icchi. Atha naṃ so “evaṃ sante gacchatha, bhante”ti yāva gāmadvāraṃ anugantvā nivatti. Tāpasopi thokaṃ gantvāva “imaṃ kuṭumbikaṃ mayā vañcetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā [M 1.0399] jaṭānaṃ antare tiṇaṃ ṭhapetvā paṭinivatti. Kuṭumbiko “kiṃ, bhante, nivattitthā”ti pucchi. Āvuso tumhākaṃ gehacchadanato me jaṭāsu ekatiṇaṃ laggaṃ, adinnādānañca nāma pabbajitānaṃ na vaṭṭati, taṃ ādāya āgatomhīti. Kuṭumbiko “chaḍḍetvā gacchatha, bhante”ti vatvā “tiṇasalākampi nāma parasantakaṃ na gaṇhāti, aho kukkuccako me ayyo”ti pasīditvā vanditvā uyyojesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, a deceitful, matted-hair ascetic, a hypocrite, lived near a certain village. A householder had a leaf-hut built for him in the forest and, having him dwell there, looked after him with fine food in his own home. Trusting that this ascetic was virtuous, the householder, for fear of thieves, took one hundred nikkhas of gold to his leaf-hut, buried it in the ground, and said, “Venerable sir, please watch over this.” The ascetic replied, “Friend, it is not proper to speak of such things to renunciants. We have no greed for others' possessions.” The householder, believing his words, said, “Very well, venerable sir,” and departed. The wicked ascetic thought, “It is possible to make a living with this much,” and after a few days, he took the gold, placed it in a certain spot along the road, and returning, stayed in the leaf-hut. The next day, after taking his meal at the householder’s house, he said, “Friend, we have lived depending on you for a long time. For those who stay too long in one place, association with people arises, and association is a stain for renunciants. Therefore, we shall go.” Though the householder repeatedly pleaded with him, he was unwilling to turn back. Then the householder said, “If that is so, venerable sir, you may go,” and accompanied him as far as the village gate before turning back. The ascetic, having gone only a short distance, thought, “It is right for me to deceive this householder,” and placing a blade of grass within his matted hair, he returned. The householder asked, “Why, venerable sir, have you returned?” “Friend, a blade of grass from your roof became lodged in my matted hair. Taking what is not given is not proper for renunciants, so I have come back, bringing it with me.” The householder said, “Discard it and go, venerable sir,” and being pleased, he thought, “He does not take even a blade of grass belonging to another—oh, how scrupulous my master is!” He then paid homage and sent him on his way.

Tadā pana bodhisattena bhaṇḍatthāya paccantaṃ gacchantena tasmiṃ nivesane nivāso gahito hoti. So tāpasassa vacanaṃ sutvāva “addhā iminā duṭṭhatāpasena imassa kiñci gahitaṃ bhavissatī”ti kuṭumbikaṃ pucchi “atthi pana te, samma, kiñci etassa tāpasassa santike nikkhitta”nti? “Atthi, samma, suvaṇṇanikkhasata”nti. “Tena hi gaccha, taṃ upadhārehī”ti[V 1.0360]. So paṇṇasālaṃ gantvā taṃ adisvā vegenāgantvā “natthi, sammā”ti āha. “Na te suvaṇṇaṃ aññena gahitaṃ, teneva kuhakatāpasena gahitaṃ, ehi, taṃ anubandhitvā gaṇhāmā”ti vegena gantvā kūṭatāpasaṃ gaṇhitvā hatthehi ca pādehi ca pothetvā suvaṇṇaṃ āharāpetvā gaṇhiṃsu. Bodhisatto suvaṇṇaṃ disvā “nikkhasataṃ haramāno asajjitvā tiṇamatte sattosī”ti vatvā taṃ garahanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, the Bodhisatta, traveling to the border for trade, had taken lodging in that very house. Hearing the ascetic’s words, he thought, “Surely this wicked ascetic must have taken something from him.” So he asked the householder, “Friend, is there anything you have entrusted to this ascetic?” “Yes, friend, one hundred nikkhas of gold,” he replied. “Then go and check on it,” said the Bodhisatta. The householder went to the leaf-hut, and not finding it, hurried back and said, “It is gone, friend.” “Your gold was not taken by anyone else—it was taken by that very hypocritical ascetic. Come, let us follow and catch him.” They quickly pursued the fraudulent ascetic, seized him, and after beating him with their hands and feet, made him produce the gold, and they took it. Seeing the gold, the Bodhisatta, rebuking him, spoke this verse:

89.

89.

“Vācāva kira te āsi, saṇhā sakhilabhāṇino;

Tiṇamatte asajjittho, no ca nikkhasataṃ hara”nti.

“Your speech was indeed soft, you of gentle words; you were attached to a mere blade of grass, yet not so while stealing a hundred nikkhas.”

Tattha [P 1.0377] vācāva kira te āsi, saṇhā sakhilabhāṇinoti “pabbajitānaṃ tiṇamattampi adinnaṃ ādātuṃ na vaṭṭatī”ti evaṃ sakhilaṃ muduvacanaṃ vadantassa vācā eva kira te saṇhā āsi, vacanamattameva maṭṭhaṃ ahosīti attho. Tiṇamatte asajjitthoti kūṭajaṭila ekissā tiṇasalākāya kukkuccaṃ kurumāno tvaṃ satto āsatto laggo ahosi. No ca nikkhasataṃ haranti imaṃ pana nikkhasataṃ haranto asatto nillaggova jātosīti.

Herein, Your speech was indeed soft, you of gentle words means: your speech alone was indeed soft, as you spoke such gentle, tender words as, ‘For renunciants, it is not proper to take even a mere blade of grass that has not been given’; only your speech was polished, that is the meaning. You were attached to a mere blade of grass means: O fraudulent ascetic, making a scruple over a single blade of grass, you were attached and clinging. Yet not so while stealing a hundred nikkhas means: however, in stealing these hundred nikkhas of gold, you became unattached and unconcerned.

Evaṃ bodhisatto taṃ garahitvā “mā puna, kūṭajaṭila, evarūpamakāsī”ti ovādaṃ datvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Having thus rebuked him, the Bodhisatta advised, “Never again, fraudulent ascetic, act in such a way,” and then departed according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa bhikkhu kuhako, pubbepi kuhakoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā [M 1.0400] kūṭatāpaso kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, paṇḍitapuriso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, said, “Monks, this monk is not a hypocrite only now—he was a hypocrite in the past as well.” Then he made the connection for the Jātaka: “At that time, the fraudulent ascetic was the hypocritical monk, but the wise man was none other than myself.”

Kuhakajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Kuhaka Jātaka, the Ninth.

[90] 10. Akataññujātakavaṇṇanā

[90] 10. The Commentary on the Akataññu Jātaka

Yo pubbe katakalyāṇoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa kireko paccantavāsiko seṭṭhi adiṭṭhasahāyo ahosi. So ekadā paccante uṭṭhānakabhaṇḍassa pañca sakaṭasatāni pūretvā kammantikamanusse āha – “gacchatha, bho, imaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ sāvatthiṃ netvā amhākaṃ sahāyakassa anāthapiṇḍikamahāseṭṭhissa paccagghena vikkiṇitvā paṭibhaṇḍaṃ [V 1.0361] āharathā”ti. Te “sādhū”ti tassa vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā sāvatthiṃ gantvā mahāseṭṭhiṃ disvā paṇṇākāraṃ datvā taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Mahāseṭṭhi “svāgataṃ vo”ti tesaṃ āvāsañca paribbayañca dāpetvā sahāyakassa sukhaṃ pucchitvā bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇitvā paṭibhaṇḍaṃ dāpesi. Te paccantaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ attano seṭṭhissa ārocesuṃ.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this story beginning with the words, Yo pubbe katakalyāṇo, concerning Anāthapiṇḍika. It is said that a certain merchant who was a border-dweller was his unseen friend. One day, he loaded five hundred carts with merchandise and instructed his workers: “Go, sirs, take this merchandise to Sāvatthī, sell it at a good price to our friend, the great merchant Anāthapiṇḍika, and bring back goods in return.” They accepted his words with “Very well,” went to Sāvatthī, and upon seeing the great merchant, presented gifts and reported the matter. The great merchant welcomed them, had lodging and expenses provided, inquired about his friend's well-being, sold the merchandise, and had goods given in return. They returned to the border and reported the matter to their own merchant.

Aparabhāge anāthapiṇḍikopi tatheva pañca sakaṭasatāni tattha pesesi. Manussā tattha gantvā paṇṇākāraṃ ādāya paccantavāsikaseṭṭhiṃ passiṃsu. So “kuto āgacchathā”ti pucchitvā “sāvatthito tumhākaṃ sahāyakassa anāthapiṇḍikassa santikā”ti vutte “anāthapiṇḍikoti kassaci purisassa nāmaṃ bhavissatī”ti parihāsaṃ katvā paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā “gacchatha tumhe”ti uyyojesi, neva nivāsaṃ, na paribbayaṃ dāpesi. Te sayameva bhaṇḍaṃ vikkiṇitvā paṭibhaṇḍaṃ ādāya sāvatthiṃ āgantvā seṭṭhissa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ.

Subsequently, Anāthapiṇḍika also sent five hundred carts there in the same manner. His men went there, took the gift, and saw the merchant of the border region. He asked, “From where have you come?” When they replied, “From Sāvatthī, from your friend Anāthapiṇḍika,” he said mockingly, “Anāthapiṇḍika must be the name of some man.” Then, taking the gift, he dismissed them, saying, “You may go,” and had neither lodging nor provisions given to them. They sold the goods themselves, took merchandise in return, returned to Sāvatthī, and reported the matter to the merchant.

Atha so paccantavāsī [P 1.0378] punapi ekavāraṃ tatheva pañca sakaṭasatāni sāvatthiṃ pesesi, manussā paṇṇākāraṃ ādāya mahāseṭṭhiṃ passiṃsu. Te [M 1.0401] pana disvā anāthapiṇḍikassa manussā “mayaṃ, sāmi, etesaṃ nivāsañca bhattañca paribbayañca jānissāmā”ti vatvā tesaṃ sakaṭāni bahinagare tathārūpe ṭhāne mocāpetvā “tumhe idheva vasatha, amhākaṃ vo ghare yāgubhattañca paribbayo ca bhavissatī”ti gantvā dāsakammakare sannipātetvā majjhimayāmasamanantare pañca sakaṭasatāni vilumpitvā nivāsanapārupanānipi nesaṃ acchinditvā goṇe palāpetvā sakaṭāni vicakkāni katvā bhūmiyaṃ ṭhapetvā cakkānipi gaṇhitvāva agamaṃsu. Paccantavāsino nivāsanamattassapi sāmikā ahutvā bhītā vegena palāyitvā paccantameva gatā. Seṭṭhimanussāpi tamatthaṃ mahāseṭṭhino ārocesuṃ. So “atthi dānidaṃ kathāpābhata”nti satthu santikaṃ gantvā ādito paṭṭhāya sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Satthā “na kho, gahapati, so paccantavāsī idāneva evaṃsīlo, pubbepi evaṃsīloyeva ahosī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then that merchant of the border region once again sent five hundred carts to Sāvatthī in the same manner. His men, taking a gift, saw the great merchant. Seeing them, Anāthapiṇḍika’s men said, “Master, we will see to their lodging, food, and provisions.” Having said this, they had the carts unyoked in a suitable place outside the city and said, “You stay right here; you will have gruel, rice, and provisions at our house.” Then, having gone and gathered the servants and workers, immediately after the middle watch of the night, they plundered the five hundred carts, snatched away their lower and upper garments, drove off the oxen, made the carts wheel-less, set them on the ground, and departed, taking the wheels with them. The men from the border region, left without mastery over even a loincloth, fled in fear and went straight back to the border. The merchant’s men reported the matter to the great merchant. He thought, “Now this is a topic for a story,” and went to the Teacher. He recounted the entire incident from the beginning. The Teacher said, “Householder, it is not only now that this merchant of the border region is of such a character; in the past, too, he was of the same character.” And being requested by him, He brought forth a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ mahāvibhavo seṭṭhi ahosi. Tasseko paccantavāsiko seṭṭhi adiṭṭhasahāyo ahosi. Sabbaṃ atītavatthu paccuppannavatthusadisameva bodhisatto pana attano manussehi “ajja amhehi idaṃ nāma kata”nti ārocite “paṭhamaṃ attano kataṃ upakāraṃ ajānantā pacchā evarūpaṃ labhantiyevā”ti vatvā sampattaparisāya dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a merchant of great wealth in Bārāṇasī. He had a merchant dwelling in the border region who was a friend he had never seen. The entire story of the past is just like the story of the present. However, when his men reported to the Bodhisatta, “Today we have done such-and-such,” he said, “Those who do not acknowledge a favor previously done to them will indeed receive such a result later.” Then, teaching the Dhamma to the assembled company, he spoke this verse:

90.

90.

“Yo [V 1.0362] pubbe katakalyāṇo, katattho nāvabujjhati;

Pacchā kicce samuppanne, kattāraṃ nādhigacchatī”ti.

“He for whom a good deed was previously done, a benefit accomplished, yet does not recognize it, will not find a helper when a need arises later.”

Tatrāyaṃ piṇḍattho – khattiyādīsu yo koci puriso pubbe paṭhamataraṃ aññena katakalyāṇo katūpakāro katattho nipphāditakicco hutvā taṃ parena attani kataṃ kalyāṇañceva atthañca na jānāti, so pacchā attano kicce samuppanne tassa kiccassa kattāraṃ nādhigacchati na labhatīti.

Herein, this is the summary meaning: Whoever, among nobles or others, having previously had a good deed done for him, a favor rendered, a benefit conferred, and a task accomplished for him by another, does not recognize that good deed and benefit done for him by that other; he, when a need of his own arises later, does not find, does not obtain, a doer for that task.

Evaṃ bodhisatto imāya gāthāya dhammaṃ desetvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma with this verse and performed meritorious deeds such as giving, passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā [P 1.0379][M 1.0402] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paccantavāsī idānīpi paccantavāsīyeva, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the Jātaka: “The merchant of the border region at that time was the same merchant of the border region now, but the merchant of Bārāṇasī was I myself.”

Akataññujātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Akataññu Jātaka, the Tenth.

Apāyimhavaggo navamo.

The Apāyimha Vagga, the Ninth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Surāpānaṃ mittavindaṃ, kāḷakaṇṇī atthadvāraṃ;

Kiṃpakkasīlavīmaṃsaṃ, maṅgalañcāpi sārambhaṃ;

Kuhakaṃ akataññū cāti.

Surāpāna, Mittavinda, Kāḷakaṇṇī, Atthadvāra; Kiṃpakka, Sīlavīmaṃsa, Maṅgala, and Sārambha; Kuhaka, and Akataññū.

10. Littavaggo

10. The Littavagga

[91] 1. Littajātakavaṇṇanā

[91] 1. The Commentary on the Litta Jātaka

Littaṃ [V 1.0363] paramena tejasāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto apaccavekkhitaparibhogaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiṃ kira kāle bhikkhū cīvarādīni labhitvā yebhuyyena apaccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanti. Te cattāro paccaye apaccavekkhitvā paribhuñjamānā yebhuyyena nirayatiracchānayonito na muccanti. Satthā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā bhikkhūnaṃ anekapariyāyena dhammiṃ kathaṃ kathetvā apaccavekkhitaparibhoge ādīnavaṃ dassetvā “bhikkhave, bhikkhunā nāma cattāro paccaye labhitvā apaccavekkhitvā paribhuñjituṃ na vaṭṭati, tasmā ito paṭṭhāya cattāro paccaye paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjeyyāthā”ti paccavekkhanavidhiṃ dassento “idha pana, bhikkhave, bhikkhu paṭisaṅkhā yoniso cīvaraṃ paṭisevati sītassa paṭighātāyā”tiādinā (ma. ni. 1.23; a. ni. 6.58) nayena tantiṃ ṭhapetvā “bhikkhave, cattāro paccaye evaṃ paccavekkhitvā paribhuñjituṃ vaṭṭati, apaccavekkhitvā paribhogo nāma halāhalavisaparibhogasadiso. Porāṇakā hi apaccavekkhitvā dosaṃ ajānitvā visaṃ paribhuñjitvā vipākante mahādukkhaṃ anubhaviṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Smeared with the highest potency…” This discourse the Teacher gave while dwelling in the Jeta Grove, concerning the use of requisites without reflection. At that time, it is said, the monks, having received robes and other requisites, for the most part used them without reflection. Those who used the four requisites without reflection were, for the most part, not freed from hell or the animal realm. The Teacher, knowing this reason, gave a Dhamma talk to the monks in various ways, showing the danger in using requisites without reflection. He said: “Monks, it is not fitting for a monk, having received the four requisites, to use them without reflection. Therefore, from now on, you should use the four requisites only after reflecting.” Then, showing the method of reflection, He laid down the textual authority in the manner beginning: “Here, monks, a monk reflects wisely and uses the robe only for protection from the cold…” (MN 2; AN 6.58). He continued: “Monks, it is fitting to use the four requisites after reflecting in this way. Using them without reflection is like consuming deadly poison. For the ancients, not knowing the danger, consumed poison without reflection and experienced great suffering when the result ripened.” Having said this, He brought forth a story of the past.

Atīte [M 1.0403] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto aññatarasmiṃ mahābhogakule nibbattitvā vayappatto akkhadhutto ahosi. Athāparo kūṭakkhadhutto bodhisattena saddhiṃ kīḷanto attano jaye vattamāne keḷimaṇḍalaṃ na bhindati, parājayakāle pana akkhaṃ mukhe pakkhipitvā “akkho naṭṭho”ti keḷimaṇḍalaṃ bhinditvā pakkamati. Bodhisatto [P 1.0380] tassa taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “hotu, jānissāmettha patirūpakāraṇa”nti akkhe ādāya attano ghare halāhalavisena rañjitvā punappunaṃ sukkhāpetvā te ādāya tassa santikaṃ gantvā “ehi, samma, akkhehi kīḷāmā”ti āha. So “sādhu, sammā”ti keḷimaṇḍalaṃ sajjetvā tena saddhiṃ kīḷanto attano parājayakāle ekaṃ akkhaṃ mukhe pakkhipi. Atha naṃ bodhisatto tathā karontaṃ disvā “gilāhi tāva, pacchā idaṃ nāmetanti jānissasī”ti codetuṃ imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of great wealth. When he came of age, he became an avid dice-player. Now, another deceitful dice-player, while playing with the Bodhisatta, would not break up the game when he was winning; but when he was losing, he would put a die in his mouth, say, “The die is lost,” break up the game, and leave. The Bodhisatta, knowing his tactic, thought, “So be it, I shall find a suitable remedy for this.” He took the dice, and at his home, he smeared them with deadly poison and dried them repeatedly. Taking these, he went to that gambler and said, “Come, friend, let us play dice.” The other replied, “Very well, friend,” set up the gaming circle, and while playing with him, put one die in his mouth when he was losing. Then the Bodhisatta, seeing him do this and intending to admonish him, thought, “Swallow it for now; afterwards you will learn what this means!” and spoke this verse:

91.

91.

“Littaṃ [V 1.0364] paramena tejasā, gilamakkhaṃ puriso na bujjhati;

Gila re gila pāpadhuttaka, pacchā te kaṭukaṃ bhavissatī”ti.

“A man swallowing the die, anointed with the most potent venom, does not realize. Swallow, O wicked gambler, swallow! Afterwards, it will be bitter for you.”

Tattha littanti makkhitaṃ rañjitaṃ. Paramena tejasāti uttamatejasampannena halāhalavisena. Gilanti gilanto. Akkhanti guḷakaṃ. Na bujjhatīti “ayaṃ me gilato idaṃ nāma karissatī”ti na jānāti. Gila reti gilāhi are. Gilāti punapi codento vadati. Pacchā te kaṭukaṃ bhavissatīti imasmiṃ te akkhe gilite pacchā etaṃ visaṃ tikhiṇaṃ bhavissatīti attho.

Herein, ‘littaṃ’ means smeared, dyed. ‘Paramena tejasā’ means by the supremely potent halāhala poison. ‘Gilam’ means swallowing. ‘Akkhaṃ’ means the die. ‘Na bujjhati’ means: he does not know, ‘This will do such-and-such to me as I swallow it.’ ‘Gila re’ means ‘Swallow, O you!’ ‘Gila’ is said again, urging him. ‘Pacchā te kaṭukaṃ bhavissati’ means: after this die has been swallowed by you, this poison will later become potent—this is the meaning.

So bodhisattassa kathentasseva visavegena mucchito akkhīni parivattetvā khandhaṃ nāmetvā pati. Bodhisatto “idānissa jīvitadānaṃ dātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti osadhaparibhāvitaṃ vamanayogaṃ datvā vametvā sappiphāṇitamadhusakkarādayo khādāpetvā arogaṃ katvā “puna evarūpaṃ mā akāsī”ti ovaditvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Even as the Bodhisatta was speaking, that man, overcome by the force of the poison, fainted, his eyes rolled, his head drooped, and he fell. The Bodhisatta thought, “Now it is right to give him the gift of life,” and gave him an emetic prepared with medicinal herbs. After making him vomit, he had him eat ghee, molasses, honey, sugar, and the like, restoring him to health. Then he admonished him, “Do not do such a thing again,” and after performing meritorious deeds such as giving alms, he passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “bhikkhave, apaccavekkhitaparibhogo nāma apaccavekkhitvā katavisaparibhogasadiso hotī”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā paṇḍitadhutto ahameva ahosiṃ, kūṭadhutto [M 1.0404] panettha na kathīyati, yathā ca ettha, evaṃ sabbattha. Yo pana imasmiṃ kāle na paññāyati, so na kathīyatevā”ti.

The Teacher, having presented this Dhamma discourse, said, “Monks, the use of requisites without reflection is like the use of poison without reflection.” He then made the connection to the Jātaka: “At that time, I myself was the wise gambler. The deceitful gambler is not identified here. And as it is here, so it is everywhere: whoever is not apparent at the present time is not identified.”

Littajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Litta Jātaka, the first.

[92] 2. Mahāsārajātakavaṇṇanā

[92] 2. The Commentary on the Mahāsāra Jātaka

Ukkaṭṭhe [P 1.0381] sūramicchantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto āyasmantaṃ ānandattheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye kosalarañño itthiyo cintayiṃsu “buddhuppādo nāma dullabho, tathā manussapaṭilābho, paripuṇṇāyatanatā ca. Mayañca imaṃ dullabhaṃ khaṇasamavāyaṃ labhitvāpi attano ruciyā vihāraṃ gantvā dhammaṃ vā sotuṃ buddhapūjaṃ vā kātuṃ dānaṃ vā dātuṃ na labhāma, mañjūsāya pakkhittā viya vasāma, rañño kathetvā amhākaṃ dhammaṃ desetuṃ anucchavikaṃ ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā tassa santike dhammaṃ sossāma, tato yaṃ sakkhissāma, taṃ uggaṇhissāma, dānādīni ca puññāni karissāma. Evaṃ no ayaṃ khaṇapaṭilābho saphalo bhavissatī”ti. Tā sabbāpi rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā attanā cintitakāraṇaṃ kathayiṃsu. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi.

The Teacher spoke this, beginning with ‘Ukkaṭṭhe sūramicchantī,’ while dwelling in Jetavana, with reference to the Venerable Ānanda. For at one time, the royal ladies of the King of Kosala thought: “The arising of a Buddha is rare, as is the attainment of a human birth, and the possession of unimpaired faculties. And we, though we have gained this rare conjunction of opportunities, are not able to go to the monastery according to our own wishes to hear the Dhamma, to make offerings to the Buddha, or to give alms. We live as though packed in a chest. Let us speak to the king and have him summon a suitable monk to teach us the Dhamma. In his presence, we shall hear the Dhamma, learn what we can from it, and perform meritorious deeds such as giving alms. In this way, our attainment of this opportunity will be fruitful.” They all approached the king and told him what they had considered. The king consented, saying, “Very well.”

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0365] rājā uyyānakīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmo uyyānapālaṃ pakkosāpetvā “uyyānaṃ sodhehī”ti āha. Uyyānapālo uyyānaṃ sodhento satthāraṃ aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle nisinnaṃ disvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “suddhaṃ, deva, uyyānaṃ, apicettha aññatarasmiṃ rukkhamūle bhagavā nisinno”ti āha. Rājā “sādhu, samma, satthu santike dhammampi sossāmā”ti alaṅkatarathaṃ abhiruhitvā uyyānaṃ gantvā satthu santikaṃ agamāsi.

Then one day, the king, desiring to amuse himself in the royal park, summoned the park-keeper and said, “Prepare the park.” While preparing the park, the park-keeper saw the Teacher seated at the foot of a certain tree. He went to the king and said, “The park is prepared, Your Majesty, and furthermore, the Blessed One is seated there at the foot of a certain tree.” The king replied, “Excellent, my good man. We shall also hear the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence.” He mounted an ornamented chariot, went to the park, and approached the Teacher.

Tasmiñca samaye chattapāṇi nāmeko anāgāmī upāsako satthu santike dhammaṃ suṇamāno nisinno hoti. Rājā taṃ disvā āsaṅkamāno muhuttaṃ ṭhatvā puna “sacāyaṃ pāpako bhaveyya, na satthu santike nisīditvā dhammaṃ suṇeyya, apāpakena iminā bhavitabba”nti cintetvā satthāraṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Upāsako buddhagāravena rañño [M 1.0405] paccuṭṭhānaṃ vā vandanaṃ vā na akāsi, tenassa rājā anattamano ahosi. Satthā tassa anattamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā upāsakassa guṇaṃ kathesi “ayaṃ, mahārāja, upāsako bahussuto āgatāgamo kāmesu vītarāgo”ti rājā “na iminā orakena bhavitabbaṃ, yassa satthā guṇaṃ vaṇṇetī”ti cintetvā “upāsaka, vadeyyāsi yena te attho”ti āha. Upāsako “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchi. Rājā satthu santike dhammaṃ sutvā satthāraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi.

And at that time, a lay disciple named Chattapāṇi, who was a non-returner, was seated in the Teacher's presence, listening to the Dhamma. Seeing him, the king became suspicious and stood for a moment. Then he thought, “If this man were of low character, he would not be sitting in the Teacher's presence listening to the Dhamma. He must be a good man.” He then approached the Teacher, paid homage, and sat down to one side. Out of reverence for the Buddha, the lay disciple did not rise to greet the king or pay homage to him, and for this reason, the king was displeased with him. The Teacher, knowing his displeasure, spoke of the lay disciple’s qualities: “Great King, this lay disciple is very learned, has mastered the traditions, and is free from sensual desire.” The king thought, “This cannot be an ordinary person, for the Teacher himself praises his qualities,” and he said, “Lay disciple, you may state whatever you have need of.” The lay disciple consented, saying, “Very well.” The king, after listening to the Dhamma in the Teacher's presence, circumambulated him respectfully and departed.

So ekadivasaṃ uparipāsāde mahāvātapānaṃ vivaritvā ṭhito taṃ upāsakaṃ bhuttapātarāsaṃ chattamādāya jetavanaṃ gacchantaṃ disvā pakkosāpetvā evamāha “tvaṃ kira, upāsaka, bahussuto, amhākañca itthiyo dhammaṃ sotukāmā ceva uggahetukāmā ca, sādhu vatassa sace tāsaṃ dhammaṃ vāceyyāsī”ti. “Deva, gihīnaṃ nāma rājantepure [P 1.0382] dhammaṃ desetuṃ vā vācetuṃ vā nappatirūpaṃ, ayyānaṃ eva patirūpa”nti. Rājā “saccaṃ esa vadatī”ti uyyojetvā itthiyo pakkosāpetvā “bhadde, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ dhammadesanatthāya ca dhammavācanatthāya ca satthu santikaṃ gantvā ekaṃ bhikkhuṃ yācāmi, asītiyā mahāsāvakesu kataraṃ yācāmī”ti āha. Tā sabbāpi mantetvā dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaṃ ānandattherameva ārocesuṃ. Rājā satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno evamāha “bhante, amhākaṃ gehe itthiyo ānandattherassa santike dhammaṃ sotuñca uggaṇhituñca icchanti, sādhu vata sace thero amhākaṃ gehe dhammaṃ deseyya ceva vāceyya cā”ti. Satthā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā theraṃ āṇāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya rañño itthiyo therassa santike dhammaṃ suṇanti ceva uggaṇhanti ca.

One day, having opened a large window in the upper palace and standing there, he saw that lay devotee, having eaten his morning meal, taking an umbrella and going to Jetavana. He summoned him and said, "Lay devotee, it seems you are very learned, and our women wish both to hear and to learn the Dhamma. It would be good if you would teach them the Dhamma." "Your Majesty, it is not proper for a householder to teach or recite the Dhamma in the royal palace; it is proper only for the noble ones," he replied. The king, thinking, "He speaks the truth," dismissed him and summoned the women, saying, "Ladies, I will go to the Teacher's presence and request a monk to teach and recite the Dhamma for you. Among the eighty great disciples, whom shall I request?" After consulting together, they all requested the Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma. The king went to the Teacher's presence, paid homage, sat to one side, and said, "Venerable sir, the women in our household wish to hear and learn the Dhamma in the presence of the Venerable Ānanda. It would be good if the Elder would teach and recite the Dhamma in our home." The Teacher consented, saying "Good," and instructed the Elder. From then on, the king's women listened to and learned the Dhamma in the presence of the Elder.

Athekadivasaṃ rañño cūḷāmaṇi naṭṭho. Rājā tassa naṭṭhabhāvaṃ sutvā amacce āṇāpesi “sabbe [V 1.0366] antovaḷañjanake manusse gahetvā cūḷāmaṇiṃ āharāpethā”ti. Amaccā mātugāme ādiṃ katvā cūḷāmaṇiṃ paripucchantā adisvā mahājanaṃ kilamenti. Taṃ divasaṃ ānandatthero rājanivesanaṃ paviṭṭho. Yathā tā itthiyo pubbe theraṃ disvāva haṭṭhatuṭṭhā dhammaṃ suṇanti ceva uggaṇhanti ca, tathā akatvā sabbā domanassappattāva ahesuṃ. Tato therena “kasmā tumhe ajja evarūpā [M 1.0406] jātā”ti pucchitā evamāhaṃsu “bhante, rañño cūḷāmaṇiṃ pariyesāmāti amaccā mātugāme upādāya antovaḷañjanake kilamenti, na jānāma kassa ‘kiṃ bhavissatī’ti, tenamha domanassappattā”ti. Thero “mā cintayitthā”ti tā samassāsetvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīditvā “maṇi kira te, mahārāja, naṭṭho”ti pucchi. “Āma, bhante”ti. “Asakkhi pana taṃ āharāpetu”nti. “Bhante, sabbaṃ antojanaṃ gahetvā kilamentopi na sakkomi āharāpetu”nti. “Mahārāja, mahājanaṃ akilametvāva āharaṇūpāyo atthī”ti. “Kataro, bhante”ti? “Piṇḍadānaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Kataraṃ piṇḍadānaṃ, bhante”ti? “Mahārāja, yattakesu āsaṅkā atthi, te gahetvā ekekassa ekekaṃ palālapiṇḍaṃ vā mattikāpiṇḍaṃ vā datvā ‘imaṃ paccūsakāle āharitvā asukaṭṭhāne nāma pātethā’ti vattabbaṃ. Yena gahito bhavissati, so tasmiṃ pakkhipitvā āharissati. Sace paṭhamadivaseyeva pātenti, iccetaṃ kusalaṃ. No ce pātenti, dutiyadivasepi tatiyadivasepi tatheva kātabbaṃ. Evaṃ mahājano ca na kilamissati, maṇiñca labhissasī”ti evaṃ vatvā thero agamāsi.

Then one day, the king's crest-jewel was lost. Upon hearing of its loss, the king ordered his ministers, "Seize all the people who serve within the palace and have them bring back the crest-jewel." The ministers, beginning with the women, questioned them about the crest-jewel, but not seeing it, they afflicted the many people. That day, the Venerable Ānanda entered the royal residence. Whereas previously, upon seeing the Elder, those women would joyfully and delightedly listen to and learn the Dhamma, they did not do so, and all were overcome with sorrow. Then, when asked by the Elder, "Why have you become like this today?" they said, "Venerable sir, saying, 'We are searching for the king's crest-jewel,' the ministers are afflicting those who serve within the palace, beginning with the women. We do not know what will happen to whom; that is why we are overcome with sorrow." The Elder, having consoled them by saying, "Do not worry," went to the king's presence, sat down on the prepared seat, and asked, "Great King, is it true that your jewel is lost?" "Yes, venerable sir." "But were you able to have it brought back?" "Venerable sir, even after seizing and afflicting everyone in the inner household, I am not able to have it brought back." "Great King, there is a way to bring it back without afflicting the many people." "What is that, venerable sir?" "The giving of lumps, Great King." "What giving of lumps, venerable sir?" "Great King, as many as are under suspicion, they should be gathered, and to each one should be given a lump of straw or a lump of clay, and they should be told, 'Bring this at dawn and drop it in such-and-such a place.' The one by whom it was taken will place it inside and bring it back. If they drop it on the first day, that is good. If they do not drop it, the same should be done on the second and third days. In this way, the many people will not be afflicted, and you will get the jewel." Having said this, the Elder departed.

Rājā vuttanayeneva tayo divase dāpesi, neva maṇiṃ āhariṃsu. Thero [P 1.0383] tatiyadivase āgantvā “kiṃ, mahārāja, pātito maṇī”ti pucchi. “Na pātenti, bhante”ti. “Tena hi, mahārāja, mahātalasmiṃyeva paṭicchannaṭṭhāne mahācāṭiṃ ṭhapāpetvā udakassa pūrāpetvā sāṇiṃ parikkhipāpetvā ‘sabbe antovaḷañjanakamanussā ca itthiyo ca uttarāsaṅgaṃ katvā ekekova antosāṇiṃ pavisitvā hatthaṃ dhovitvā āgacchantū’ti vadehī”ti thero imaṃ upāyaṃ ācikkhitvā pakkāmi. Rājā tathā kāresi. Maṇicoro cintesi “dhammabhaṇḍāgāriko imaṃ adhikaraṇaṃ ādāya maṇiṃ adassetvā osakkissatīti aṭṭhānametaṃ, pātetuṃ dāni vaṭṭatī”ti maṇiṃ paṭicchannaṃ katvā ādāya antosāṇiṃ pavisitvā cāṭiyaṃ pātetvā nikkhami. Sabbesaṃ nikkhantakāle udakaṃ chaḍḍetvā maṇiṃ addasaṃsu. Rājā “theraṃ nissāya mahājanaṃ akilametvāva me maṇi laddho”ti tussi, antovaḷañjanakamanussāpi “theraṃ nissāya mahādukkhato muttamhā”ti tussiṃsu. “Therassānubhāvena rañño [M 1.0407] cūḷāmaṇi laddho”ti therassānubhāvo sakalanagare ceva bhikkhusaṅghe ca pākaṭo jāto.

The king had the lumps given for three days in the manner described, but they did not bring the jewel. On the third day, the Elder came and asked, "What, Great King, has the jewel been dropped?" "They do not drop it, venerable sir." "In that case, Great King, have a large pot placed in a concealed spot on the great terrace, have it filled with water, have a screen placed around it, and say, 'Let all the men and women who serve within the palace, having arranged their upper robes, enter inside the screen one by one, wash their hands, and come out.'" Having explained this method, the Elder departed. The king had it done so. The jewel thief thought, "It is impossible that the Treasurer of the Dhamma, having taken up this case, will withdraw without the jewel being revealed; it is now time to drop it." Having concealed the jewel and taken it, he entered inside the screen, dropped it in the pot, and came out. When everyone had come out, they emptied the water and saw the jewel. The king was pleased, thinking, "Relying on the Elder, my jewel has been found without afflicting the many people." The people who served within the palace were also pleased, thinking, "Relying on the Elder, we have been freed from great suffering." The Elder's power became renowned throughout the entire city and among the community of monks: "Through the Elder's power, the king's crest-jewel was found."

Dhammasabhāyaṃ [V 1.0367] sannisinnā bhikkhū therassa guṇaṃ vaṇṇayiṃsu “āvuso, ānandatthero attano bahussutatāya paṇḍiccena upāyakusalatāya mahājanaṃ akilametvā upāyeneva rañño maṇiṃ dassesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāni ānandeneva parahatthagataṃ bhaṇḍaṃ dassitaṃ, pubbepi paṇḍitā mahājanaṃ akilametvā upāyeneva tiracchānahatthagataṃ bhaṇḍaṃ dassayiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The monks, seated together in the Dhamma hall, extolled the Elder's virtue, saying: "Friends, the Venerable Ānanda, through his great learning, wisdom, and skillfulness in means, revealed the king's jewel by a stratagem, without afflicting the many people." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now seated together?" When it was said, "For this one," he replied, "Monks, it is not only now that Ānanda has revealed an item that had gone into another's hand. In the past, too, the wise revealed an item that had gone into the hand of an animal by a stratagem, without afflicting the many people." Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sabbasippesu nipphattiṃ patto tasseva amacco ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ rājā mahantena parivārena uyyānaṃ gantvā vanantarāni vicaritvā udakakīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmo maṅgalapokkharaṇiṃ otaritvā itthāgārampi pakkosi. Itthiyo attano attano sīsūpagagīvūpagādīni ābharaṇāni omuñcitvā uttarāsaṅgesu pakkhipitvā samuggapiṭṭhesu ṭhapetvā dāsiyo paṭicchāpetvā pokkharaṇiṃ otariṃsu. Athekā uyyānamakkaṭī sākhantare nisinnā deviṃ piḷandhanāni omuñcitvā uttarāsaṅge pakkhipitvā samuggapiṭṭhe ṭhapayamānaṃ disvā tassā muttāhāraṃ piḷandhitukāmā hutvā dāsiyā [P 1.0384] pamādaṃ olokayamānā nisīdi, dāsīpi taṃ rakkhamānā tahaṃ tahaṃ oloketvā nisinnāyeva niddāyituṃ ārabhi. Makkaṭī tassā pamādabhāvaṃ ñatvā vātavegena otaritvā mahāmuttāhāraṃ gīvāya paṭimuñcitvā vātavegena uppatitvā sākhantare nisīditvā aññāsaṃ makkaṭīnaṃ dassanabhayena ekasmiṃ rukkhasusiraṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā upasantūpasantā viya taṃ rakkhamānā nisīdi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having attained proficiency in all the arts, was his advisor. One day, the king, with a large retinue, went to the park. After wandering through the woods, wishing to play in the water, he descended into the Royal Lotus Pond and also summoned the women of his harem. The women removed their ornaments for the head, neck, and so forth, placed them in their upper garments, put them on casket-stools, and having entrusted them to the maidservants, they entered the pond. At that moment, a female monkey in the park, sitting on a branch, saw the queen removing her ornaments, placing them in her upper garment, and putting them on a casket-stool. Desiring to wear her pearl necklace, she sat watching for the maidservant’s negligence. The maidservant, while guarding the ornaments, looked about here and there, and as she sat, began to doze off. The monkey, knowing her to be negligent, descended with the speed of the wind, fastened the great pearl necklace on her neck, leaped up with the speed of the wind, and sat on a branch. Fearing being seen by the other monkeys, she placed it in a hollow of a tree and sat guarding it, as if perfectly calm.

Sāpi kho dāsī paṭibujjhitvā muttāhāraṃ apassantī kampamānā aññaṃ upāyaṃ adisvā “puriso deviyā muttāhāraṃ gahetvā palāto”ti mahāviravaṃ viravi. Ārakkhamanussā tato tato sannipatitvā tassā vacanaṃ sutvā rañño ārocayiṃsu. Rājā “coraṃ gaṇhathā”ti āha. Purisā uyyānā [M 1.0408] nikkhamitvā “coraṃ gaṇhatha, coraṃ gaṇhathā”ti ito cito ca olokenti. Atheko jānapado balikārakapuriso taṃ saddaṃ sutvā kampamāno palāyi. Taṃ disvā rājapurisā “ayaṃ coro bhavissatī”ti anubandhitvā taṃ gahetvā pothetvā “are, duṭṭhacora, evaṃ mahāsāraṃ nāma piḷandhanaṃ avaharissasī”ti paribhāsiṃsu. So cintesi “sacāhaṃ ‘na gaṇhāmī’ti vakkhāmi, ajja me jīvitaṃ natthi, pothentāyeva maṃ māressanti, sampaṭicchāmi na”nti. So “āma, sāmi, gahitaṃ me”ti āha. Atha naṃ bandhitvā rañño santikaṃ ānayiṃsu. Rājāpi naṃ pucchi “gahitaṃ te mahāsārapiḷandhana”nti? “Āma, devā”ti[V 1.0368]. “Idāni taṃ kaha”nti. “Deva, mayā mahāsāraṃ nāma mañcapīṭhampi na diṭṭhapubbaṃ, seṭṭhi pana maṃ mahāsārapiḷandhanaṃ gaṇhāpesi, sohaṃ taṃ gahetvāva tassa adāsiṃ, so naṃ jānātī”ti.

Then that maidservant, waking up and not seeing the pearl necklace, trembled. Seeing no other recourse, she cried out loudly, 'A man has taken the queen's pearl necklace and fled!' The guards gathered from all directions and, hearing her words, reported to the king. The king said, 'Catch the thief!' The men left the garden, shouting, 'Catch the thief, catch the thief!' as they searched here and there. At that moment, a man from the countryside who collected taxes, hearing the noise, trembled and fled. Seeing him, the king's men thought, 'This must be the thief!' They chased him, caught him, beat him, and scolded him, 'You wicked thief, to steal such a valuable ornament!' He thought, 'If I say, “I did not take it,” I will not live today—they will beat me to death. I shall confess to it.' So he said, 'Yes, sirs, I took it.' Then they bound him and brought him before the king. The king asked him, 'Did you take the valuable ornament?' 'Yes, Your Majesty,' he replied. 'Where is it now?' 'Your Majesty, I have never before seen so much as a bed or a stool of great value. The merchant, however, made me take the valuable ornament; I took it and gave it to him. He knows of it.'

Rājā seṭṭhiṃ pakkosāpetvā “gahitaṃ te imassa hatthato mahāsārapiḷandhana”nti pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Kahaṃ ta”nti. “Purohitassa me dinna”nti. Purohitampi pakkosāpetvā tatheva pucchi, sopi sampaṭicchitvā “gandhabbassa me dinna”nti āha. Tampi pakkosāpetvā “purohitassa hatthato te mahāsārapiḷandhanaṃ gahita”nti pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Kahaṃ ta”nti. “Kilesavasena me vaṇṇadāsiyā [P 1.0385] dinna”nti. Tampi pakkosāpetvā pucchi, sā “na gaṇhāmī”ti āha. Te pañca jane pucchantānaññeva sūriyo atthaṃ gato. Rājā “idāni vikālo jāto, sve jānissāmā”ti te pañca jane amaccānaṃ datvā nagaraṃ pāvisi.

The king summoned the merchant and asked, 'Did you take the valuable ornament from this man's hand?' 'Yes, Your Majesty,' he replied. 'Where is it?' 'I gave it to the royal chaplain.' The king then summoned the royal chaplain and asked him the same. He too confessed, saying, 'I gave it to the musician.' The musician was also summoned, and the king asked, 'Did you take the valuable ornament from the royal chaplain’s hand?' 'Yes, Your Majesty,' he replied. 'Where is it?' 'Driven by defilement, I gave it to a courtesan.' She too was summoned and questioned, but she said, 'I did not take it.' While these five people were being questioned, the sun set. The king said, 'It is now an improper time; we will find out tomorrow,' and handing the five over to his ministers, he entered the city.

Bodhisatto cintesi – “idaṃ piḷandhanaṃ antovaḷañje naṭṭhaṃ, ayañca gahapatiko bahivaḷañjo, dvārepi balavārakkho, tasmā antovaḷañjanakānampi taṃ gahetvā palāyituṃ na sakkā. Evaṃ neva bahivaḷañjanakānaṃ, na anto, uyyāne vaḷañjanakānaṃ gahaṇūpāyo dissati. Iminā duggatamanussena ‘seṭṭhissa me dinna’nti kathentena attano mokkhatthāya kathitaṃ bhavissati, seṭṭhināpi ‘purohitassa me dinna’nti kathentena ‘ekato hutvā nittharissāmī’ti cintetvā kathitaṃ bhavissati, purohitenāpi ‘gandhabbassa me dinna’nti kathentena ‘bandhanāgāre gandhabbaṃ nissāya sukhena vasissāmā’ti cintetvā [M 1.0409] kathitaṃ bhavissati, gandhabbenāpi ‘vaṇṇadāsiyā me dinna’nti kathentena ‘ekantena anukkaṇṭhitā bhavissāmā’ti cintetvā kathitaṃ bhavissati, imehi pañcahipi corehi na bhavitabbaṃ, uyyāne makkaṭā bahū, piḷandhanena ekissā makkaṭiyā hatthe āruḷhena bhavitabba”nti. So rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mahārāja, core amhākaṃ niyyādetha, mayaṃ taṃ kiccaṃ sodhessāmā”ti āha. Rājā “sādhu, paṇḍita, sodhehī”ti tassa niyyādesi.

The Bodhisatta reflected: 'This ornament was lost within the palace grounds. This householder is an outsider, and the gates are heavily guarded; therefore, not even those within the palace grounds could have taken it and escaped. Thus, no means of taking it is apparent for those outside, nor for those inside, nor for those who frequent the garden. This poor man, saying, “I gave it to the merchant,” must have spoken to save himself. The merchant, saying, “I gave it to the royal chaplain,” must have thought, “Together we will get out of this,” and spoken thus. The royal chaplain, saying, “I gave it to the musician,” must have thought, “In prison, relying on the musician, we will live comfortably,” and spoken thus. The musician, saying, “I gave it to a courtesan,” must have thought, “We will be entirely without anxiety,” and spoken thus. These five cannot be the thieves. There are many monkeys in the garden; the ornament must have fallen into the hands of a female monkey.' He then approached the king and said, 'Great King, entrust the accused to us; we will resolve this matter.' The king replied, 'Very well, wise one, resolve it,' and entrusted them to him.

Bodhisatto attano dāsapurise pakkosāpetvā te pañca jane ekasmiṃyeva ṭhāne vasāpetvā samantā ārakkhaṃ katvā kaṇṇaṃ datvā “yaṃ te aññamaññaṃ kathenti, taṃ mayhaṃ ārocethā”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Te tathā akaṃsu. Tato manussānaṃ sannisinnavelāya seṭṭhi taṃ gahapatikaṃ āha – “are, duṭṭhagahapati, tayā ahaṃ, mayā vā tvaṃ kahaṃ diṭṭhapubbo, kadā te mayhaṃ [V 1.0369] piḷandhanaṃ dinna”nti āha. So “sāmi mahāseṭṭhi, ahaṃ mahāsāraṃ nāma rukkhasārapādakaṃ mañcapīṭhampi na jānāmi, ‘taṃ nissāya pana mokkhaṃ labhissāmī’ti evaṃ avacaṃ, mā me kujjha, sāmī”ti āha. Purohitopi [P 1.0386] seṭṭhiṃ āha “mahāseṭṭhi, tvaṃ iminā attano adinnakameva mayhaṃ kathaṃ adāsī”ti? “Mayampi dve issarā, amhākaṃ ekato hutvā ṭhitakāle kammaṃ khippaṃ nipphajjissatī”ti kathesinti. Gandhabbopi purohitaṃ āha “brāhmaṇa, kadā tayā mayhaṃ piḷandhanaṃ dinna”nti? “Ahaṃ taṃ nissāya vasanaṭṭhāne sukhaṃ vasissāmī”ti kathesinti. Vaṇṇadāsīpi gandhabbaṃ āha “are duṭṭhagandhabba, ahaṃ kadā tava santikaṃ gatapubbā, tvaṃ vā mama santikaṃ āgatapubbo, kadā te mayhaṃ piḷandhanaṃ dinna”nti? Bhagini kiṃkāraṇā kujjhasi, “amhesu pañcasu ekato vasantesu gharāvāso bhavissati, anukkaṇṭhamānā sukhaṃ vasissāmā”ti kathesinti. Bodhisatto payojitamanussānaṃ santikā taṃ kathaṃ sutvā tesaṃ tathato acorabhāvaṃ ñatvā “makkaṭiyā gahitapiḷandhanaṃ upāyeneva pātessāmī”ti geṇḍumayāni bahūni piḷandhanāni kāretvā uyyāne makkaṭiyo gāhāpetvā hatthapādagīvāsu geṇḍupiḷandhanāni piḷandhāpetvā vissajjesi. Itarā makkaṭī piḷandhanaṃ rakkhamānā uyyāne eva nisīdi.

The Bodhisatta summoned his servants and had those five people dwell in one place, setting guards all around. He instructed them to listen in and said, 'Whatever you discuss among yourselves, report it to me,' then left. They did so. Then, when the people were gathered, the merchant said to that householder: 'Hey, you wretched householder, where have you ever seen me before, or I you? When did you give me the ornament?' He replied, 'Great merchant, I do not even know a bed or stool with legs of heartwood called Mahāsāra. I only said thus, thinking, “Relying on you, I will gain my freedom.” Do not be angry with me, sir.' The chaplain also said to the merchant, 'Great merchant, how did you give me what this householder had not given to you?' 'We are two powerful men,' he replied. 'I said this thinking, “When we stand united, our task will be quickly accomplished.”' The musician said to the chaplain, 'Brahmin, when did you give me the ornament?' 'I said this thinking, “Relying on you, I will dwell happily in my residence.”' The courtesan said to the musician, 'Hey, you wretched musician, when have I ever come to you, or you to me? When did you give me the ornament?' 'Sister, why are you angry?' he replied. 'I said this thinking, “When the five of us dwell together, it will be like a household; without discontent, we will live happily.”' The Bodhisatta, having heard their conversation from the men he had employed, understood that they were truly not thieves. Thinking, 'I will make the monkey drop the ornament she took, but only by a stratagem,' he had many ornaments made of knotted string. Then, he had monkeys caught in the garden, had the string ornaments fastened to their hands, feet, and necks, and released them. The other monkey, guarding the ornament, remained sitting in the garden.

Bodhisatto manusse āṇāpesi “gacchatha tumhe, uyyāne sabbā makkaṭiyo upadhāretha, yassā taṃ piḷandhanaṃ passatha, taṃ uttāsetvā piḷandhanaṃ gaṇhathā”ti. Tāpi kho makkaṭiyo “piḷandhanaṃ no laddha”nti tuṭṭhapahaṭṭhā [M 1.0410] uyyāne vicarantiyo tassā santikaṃ gantvā “passa amhākaṃ piḷandhana”nti āhaṃsu. Sā makkaṭī asahamānā “kiṃ iminā geṇḍupiḷandhanenā”ti muttāhāraṃ piḷandhitvā nikkhami. Atha naṃ te purisā disvā piḷandhanaṃ chaḍḍāpetvā āharitvā bodhisattassa adaṃsu. So taṃ ādāya rañño dassetvā “idaṃ te deva piḷandhanaṃ, te pañcapi acorā, idaṃ pana uyyāne makkaṭiyā ābhata”nti āha. “Kathaṃ pana te, paṇḍita, makkaṭiyā hatthaṃ āruḷhabhāvo ñāto, kathaṃ te gahita”nti? So sabbaṃ ācikkhi. Rājā tuṭṭhamānaso “saṅgāmasīsādīsu [P 1.0387] nāma sūrādayo icchitabbā hontī”ti bodhisattassa thutiṃ karonto imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta commanded the men, 'Go, observe all the monkeys in the garden. Whichever one you see with that ornament, frighten her and take the ornament.' Those other monkeys, delighted and overjoyed, thinking, 'We have received ornaments,' went wandering in the garden. Approaching that one monkey, they said, 'Look at our ornaments!' Unable to bear the comparison, that monkey thought, 'What is this string ornament to me?' and came out wearing the pearl necklace. Then those men, seeing her, made her drop the ornament, and bringing it, they gave it to the Bodhisatta. He took it, showed it to the king, and said, 'Your Majesty, this is your ornament. Those five are not thieves; this was taken by a monkey in the garden.' The king asked, 'But how, wise one, did you know it had fallen into a monkey’s hands, and how was it recovered?' The Bodhisatta explained everything. The king, with a pleased mind, wishing to praise the Bodhisatta, said, 'Indeed, in the forefront of battle and so on, heroes are to be desired,' and spoke this verse:

92.

92.

“Ukkaṭṭhe sūramicchanti, mantīsu akutūhalaṃ;

Piyañca annapānamhi, atthe jāte ca paṇḍita”nti.

“In a crisis, they desire a hero; in counsel, one who is discreet; in matters of food and drink, a dear companion; and when a problem arises, a wise man.”

Tattha ukkaṭṭheti upakaṭṭhe, ubhatobyūḷhe saṅgāme sampahāre vattamāneti attho. Sūramicchantīti [V 1.0370] asaniyāpi matthake patamānāya apalāyinaṃ sūraṃ icchanti, tasmiṃ khaṇe evarūpo saṅgāmayodho patthetabbo hoti. Mantīsu akutūhalanti kattabbākattabbakiccaṃ sammantanakāle uppanne mantīsu yo akutūhalo avikiṇṇavāco mantaṃ na bhindati, taṃ icchanti, tādiso tesu ṭhānesu patthetabbo hoti. Piyañca annapānamhīti madhure annapāne paccupaṭṭhite sahaparibhuñjanatthāya piyapuggalaṃ patthenti, tādiso tasmiṃ kāle patthetabbo hoti. Atthe jāte ca paṇḍitanti atthagambhīre dhammagambhīre kismiñcideva kāraṇe vā pañhe vā uppanne paṇḍitaṃ vicakkhaṇaṃ icchanti. Tathārūpo hi tasmiṃ samaye patthetabbo hotīti.

Herein, in a crisis means when a battle is drawn up on both sides and the fighting is underway. They desire a hero means they desire a hero who would not flee even if a thunderbolt were to fall upon his head; such a warrior is to be sought at that moment. In counsel, one who is discreet means that when the time comes for consultation on what should and should not be done, they desire one who is not loose-tongued, whose speech is not scattered, and who does not betray the counsel; such a person is to be sought in those situations. And in matters of food and drink, a dear companion means that when sweet food and drink are served, they seek a dear person to enjoy it with; such a person is to be sought at that time. And when a problem arises, a wise man means that when some matter or question arises that is profound in meaning or profound in Dhamma, they desire a wise and discerning person. For such a person is to be sought at that time.

Evaṃ rājā bodhisattaṃ vaṇṇetvā thometvā ghanavassaṃ vassento mahāmegho viya sattāhi ratanehi pūjetvā tassovāde ṭhatvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato, bodhisattopi yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus the king, having praised and extolled the Bodhisatta, honored him with the seven kinds of jewels, like a great cloud pouring down a heavy rain. Abiding in his counsel and performing meritorious deeds such as giving, the king passed away according to his karma. The Bodhisatta also passed away according to his karma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā therassa guṇaṃ kathetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājā ānando ahosi, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and spoken of the elder's virtue, made the connection for the Jātaka: 'At that time, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was none other than myself.'

Mahāsārajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Mahāsāra Jātaka, the Second.

[93] 3. Vissāsabhojanajātakavaṇṇanā

3. Commentary on the Vissāsabhojana Jātaka

Na [M 1.0411] vissase avissattheti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto vissāsabhojanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiṃ kira samaye yebhuyyena bhikkhū “mātarā no dinnaṃ, pitarā no dinnaṃ, bhātarā, bhaginiyā, cūḷamātarā, cūḷapitarā, mātulena, mātulāniyā dinnaṃ. Amhākaṃ gihikālepi bhikkhukālepi ete dātuṃ yuttarūpāvā”ti ñātīhi dinne cattāro paccaye vissatthā hutvā apaccavekkhitvā paribhuñjanti. Satthā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “bhikkhūnaṃ mayā dhammadesanaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti bhikkhū sannipātāpetvā “bhikkhave, bhikkhunā nāma ñātīhipi aññātīhipi [P 1.0388] dinnake cattāro paccaye paccavekkhitvāva paribhogo kātabbo. Apaccavekkhitvā paribhogaṃ katvā hi kālaṃ kurumāno bhikkhu yakkhapetaattabhāvato na muccati, apaccavekkhitaparibhogo nāmesa visaparibhogasadiso. Visañhi vissāsikena dinnakampi avissāsikena dinnakampi māretiyeva. Pubbepi vissāsena dinnaṃ visaṃ paribhuñjitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

This discourse beginning, 'Do not trust the untrustworthy,' the Teacher delivered while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning food accepted out of trust. At that time, the majority of monks, thinking, "This was given by our mother, father, brother, sister, or by our aunts and uncles. These are the proper ones to give to us both in household life and in monastic life," would consume the four requisites given by relatives without reflection, placing trust in them. Knowing this reason, the Teacher thought, "It is fitting for me to give a Dhamma talk to the monks." He then assembled the monks and said, "Monks, a monk should use the four requisites given by relatives or strangers only after reflecting on them. For if a monk consumes them without reflection and dies, he cannot escape the states of existence as a yakkha or peta. Consumption without reflection is like consuming poison. For poison, whether given by someone trusted or untrusted, kills just the same. In the past, too, some met their end from consuming poison given out of trust." Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0371] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mahāvibhavo seṭṭhi ahosi. Tasseko gopālako kiṭṭhasambādhasamaye gāvo gahetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā tattha gosālaṃ katvā rakkhanto vasati. Seṭṭhino ca kālena kālaṃ gorasaṃ āharati. Athassa gosālāya avidūre sīho nivāsaṃ gaṇhi. Gāvīnaṃ sīhasantāsena milātānaṃ khīraṃ mandaṃ ahosi. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ sappiṃ ādāya āgataṃ seṭṭhi pucchi “kiṃ nu kho, samma gopālaka, mandaṃ sappī”ti? So taṃ kāraṇaṃ ācikkhi. “Atthi pana, samma, tassa sīhassa katthaci paṭibandho”ti? “Atthissa sāmi, ekāya migamātukāya saddhiṃ saṃsaggo”ti. “Sakkā pana taṃ gāhāpetu”nti? “Sakkā, sāmī”ti. “Tena hi taṃ gahetvā tassā nalāṭato paṭṭhāya sarīre lomāni visena punappunaṃ rajitvā sukkhāpetvā dve tayo divase atikkāmetvā taṃ migamātukaṃ vissajjehi, so tassā sinehena sarīraṃ lehitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇissati. Athassa cammanakhadāṭhā ceva vasañca maṃsañca gahetvā āgaccheyyāsī”ti halāhalavisaṃ datvā uyyojesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a very wealthy merchant. He had a cowherd who, during the season when the crops were dense, would take the cattle into the forest, build a cowshed there, and stay guarding them. From time to time, he would bring milk products to the merchant. Now, not far from the cowshed, a lion had taken up residence. The cows, terrified by the lion’s presence, became distressed and gave little milk. One day, when the cowherd brought ghee, the merchant asked, "Friend cowherd, why is there so little ghee?" The cowherd explained the reason. "Friend, does that lion have any attachment?" "Yes, master—he has an association with a certain female deer." "Can you capture it?" "Yes, master." "Then catch it, and from its forehead downwards, repeatedly smear its fur with poison. Let it dry for two or three days, and then release the female deer. The lion, licking its body out of affection, will meet its end. Then bring back its skin, claws, teeth, fat, and flesh." Giving him deadly poison, he sent him off.

So [M 1.0412] gopālako jālaṃ khipitvā upāyena taṃ migamātukaṃ gaṇhitvā tathā akāsi. Sīho taṃ disvāva balavasinehena tassā sarīraṃ lehitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇi. Gopālakopi cammādīni gahetvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ agamāsi. Bodhisatto taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “paresu sineho nāma na kātabbo, evaṃ balasampannopi sīho migarājā kilesavasena saṃsaggaṃ nissāya migamātukāya sarīraṃ lehanto visaparibhogaṃ katvā jīvitakkhayaṃ patto”ti vatvā sampattaparisāya dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The cowherd cast a net and skillfully captured the female deer, and did as instructed. The lion, as soon as it saw her, licked her body with intense affection and met its death. The cowherd took the skin and other parts and went to the Bodhisatta. Understanding the situation, the Bodhisatta said, "One should not form an affection for others; for even a mighty lion, the king of beasts, overcome by defilements due to his association, met his death by consuming poison while licking the female deer's body." Then, teaching the Dhamma to the assembled company, he spoke this verse:

93.

93.

“Na [P 1.0389] vissase avissatthe, vissatthepi na vissase;

Vissāsā bhayamanveti, sīhaṃva migamātukā”ti.

"Do not trust the untrustworthy, nor trust even the trustworthy; from trust, danger comes, as to the lion from the female deer."

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – yo pubbe sabhayo attani avissattho ahosi, tasmiṃ avissatthe, yo pubbepi nibbhayo attani vissāsikoyeva, tasmiṃ vissatthepi na vissase, neva vissāsaṃ kareyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Vissāsā bhayamanveti, yo hi mittepi amittepi vissāso, tato bhayameva āgacchati. Kathaṃ? Sīhaṃva migamātukā, yathā mittasanthavavasena katavissāsāya migamātukāya santikā sīhassa bhayaṃ anveti, upagataṃ sampattanti attho. Yathā vā vissāsavasena sīhaṃ migamātukā anvetā upagatātipi attho.

Here is the brief meaning: One should not trust an untrustworthy person, one who was previously fearful and distrustful. Nor should one trust even a trustworthy person, one who was previously fearless and confident. One should never place trust. Why? Because from trust, danger comes. Indeed, from trust in both friends and foes, only danger arises. How so? Like the lion and the female deer. Just as danger came to the lion from the female deer, in whom he had placed trust due to friendly intimacy—that is to say, it befell him, it came upon him. Or, the meaning is that the female deer approached the lion because of his trust.

Evaṃ [V 1.0372] bodhisatto sampattaparisāya dhammaṃ desetvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma to the assembled company and performed meritorious deeds such as giving, passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mahāseṭṭhi ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth: "At that time, the great merchant was none other than myself."

Vissāsabhojanajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The third, the commentary on the Vissāsabhojana Jātaka.

[94] 4. Lomahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[94] 4. The Commentary on the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka

Sotatto [M 1.0413] sosinno cevāti idaṃ satthā vesāliṃ upanissāya pāṭikārāme viharanto sunakkhattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Ekasmiñhi samaye sunakkhatto satthu upaṭṭhāko hutvā pattacīvaramādāya vicaramāno korakkhattiyassa dhammaṃ rocento dasabalassa pattacīvaraṃ niyyādetvā korakkhattiyaṃ nissāya vasati. Tassa kālakañjikaasurayoniyaṃ nibbattakāle gihi hutvā “natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttari manussadhammā alamariyañāṇadassanaviseso, takkapariyāhataṃ samaṇo gotamo dhammaṃ deseti vīmaṃsānucaritaṃ sayaṃpaṭibhānaṃ. Yassa ca khvāssa atthāya dhammo desito, na so niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā”ti (ma. ni. 1.146) vesāliyaṃ tiṇṇaṃ pākārānaṃ antare vicaranto satthu avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati.

This discourse beginning, 'Scorched by heat, drenched by cold,' the Teacher delivered while dwelling near Vesālī in the Pāṭikārāma, concerning Sunakkhatta. At one time, Sunakkhatta, having been an attendant of the Teacher, took his bowl and robe and wandered about, taking delight in the doctrine of Korakkhattiya. He then returned the bowl and robe to the Ten-Powered One and lived in dependence on Korakkhattiya. When Korakkhattiya was reborn in the realm of the Kālakañjika Asuras, Sunakkhatta, having reverted to the lay life, wandered within the triple walls of Vesālī, disparaging the Teacher, saying: "The ascetic Gotama possesses no superior human states, no distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones. The ascetic Gotama teaches a doctrine hammered out by reasoning, based on investigation, and born of his own invention. And that doctrine, for the sake of which it is taught, does not lead the one who practises it to the complete destruction of suffering." (MN 1.146)

Athāyasmā sāriputto piṇḍāya caranto tassevaṃ avaṇṇaṃ bhāsantassa sutvā piṇḍapātapaṭikkanto tamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocesi. Bhagavā “kodhano, sāriputta, sunakkhatto moghapuriso, kodhavasenevamāha, kodhavasenāpi pana ‘na so niyyāti takkarassa sammā dukkhakkhayāyā’ti vadanto ajānitvāpi mayhaṃ guṇameva bhāsati. Na kho pana so moghapuriso mayhaṃ guṇaṃ [P 1.0390] jānāti. Mayhañhi, sāriputta, cha abhiññā nāma atthi, ayampi me uttarimanussadhammova. Dasabalañāṇāni atthi, catuvesārajjañāṇaṃ atthi, catuyoniparicchedakañāṇaṃ atthi, pañcagatiparicchedakañāṇaṃ atthi, ayampi me uttarimanussadhammova. Evaṃ uttarimanussadhammasamannāgataṃ pana maṃ yo evaṃ vadeyya ‘natthi samaṇassa gotamassa uttarimanussadhammo’ti, so taṃ vācaṃ appahāya taṃ cittaṃ appahāya taṃ diṭṭhiṃ appaṭinissajjitvā yathābhataṃ nikkhitto evaṃ niraye”ti evaṃ attano vijjamānaṃ uttarimanussadhammassa guṇaṃ kathetvā “sunakkhatto kira, sāriputta, korakkhattiyassa dukkarakārikāya [V 1.0373] micchātape pasanno, micchātape pasīdantena pana mayi eva pasīdituṃ vaṭṭati. Ahañhi ito ekanavutikappamatthake ‘atthi nu kho ettha sāro’ti bāhirakaṃ micchātapaṃ vīmaṃsanto caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ brahmacariyavāsaṃ vasiṃ, tapassī sudaṃ homi paramatapassī, lūkho [M 1.0414] sudaṃ homi paramalūkho, jegucchī sudaṃ homi paramajegucchī, pavivitto sudaṃ homi paramapavivitto”ti vatvā therena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then the Venerable Sāriputta, while going for alms, heard him speaking such dispraise, returned from the alms round, and reported the matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: "Sāriputta, Sunakkhatta, that foolish man, is angry; it is out of anger that he speaks thus. Even speaking out of anger, when he says, ‘The doctrine he teaches does not lead its practitioner to the complete destruction of suffering,’ he unknowingly speaks praise of me. However, that foolish man does not know my qualities. For, Sāriputta, I possess six kinds of direct knowledge—this too is my superhuman state. I possess the ten powers of the Tathāgata, the four kinds of fearlessness, the knowledge that discerns the four types of birth, and the knowledge that discerns the five destinations—this too is my superhuman state. Now, Sāriputta, anyone who would say of me, endowed with such superhuman states, ‘The ascetic Gotama has no superhuman states,’ would, unless he abandons that speech, abandons that thought, and relinquishes that view, be cast into hell as surely as if he had been carried off and placed there." Having thus spoken of the qualities of his own superhuman states, the Blessed One said: "Sāriputta, it seems Sunakkhatta is pleased with Korakkhattiya's wrong asceticism, which involves difficult practices. But one who is pleased with wrong asceticism should be pleased with me. For ninety-one eons ago, examining the external wrong asceticism, wondering, ‘Is there any essence here?,’ I lived a holy life endowed with four factors. I was an ascetic, the highest ascetic; I was austere, the most austere; I was scrupulous, the most scrupulous; I was secluded, the most secluded." Having spoken thus, being requested by the elder, he recounted the past.

Atīte ekanavutikappamatthake bodhisatto “bāhirakatapaṃ vīmaṃsissāmī”ti ājīvakapabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā acelako ahosi rajojalliko, pavivitto ahosi ekavihārī. Manusse disvā migo viya palāyi, mahāvikatibhojano ahosi, vacchakagomayādīni paribhuñji, appamādavihāratthāya araññe ekasmiṃ bhiṃsanake vanasaṇḍe vihāsi. Tasmimpi viharanto himapātasamaye antaraṭṭhake rattiṃ vanasaṇḍā nikkhamitvā abbhokāse viharitvā sūriye uggate vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati. So yathā rattiṃ abbhokāse himodakena tinto, tatheva divā vanasaṇḍato paggharantehi udakabindūhi temayi. Evaṃ ahorattaṃ sītadukkhaṃ anubhoti. Gimhānaṃ pana pacchime māse divā abbhokāse viharitvā rattiṃ vanasaṇḍaṃ pavisati. So yathā divā abbhokāse ātapena pariḷāhappatto, tatheva rattiṃ nivāte vanasaṇḍe pariḷāhaṃ pāpuṇāti, sarīrā sedadhārā muccanti. Athassa pubbe assutapubbā ayaṃ gāthā paṭibhāsi –

In the past, ninety-one eons ago, the Bodhisatta, thinking, "I will investigate external ascetic practices," took up the Ājīvaka ascetic life, becoming a naked ascetic covered in dust and dirt, living in seclusion, dwelling alone. Seeing people, he would flee like a deer. He ate very coarse food, consumed the dung of young calves and the like, and for the purpose of diligent living, he lived in a terrifying grove in the forest. While living there, during the eight days of deep winter in the cold season, at night he would leave the grove and stay in the open, then enter the grove when the sun rose. Just as he was drenched by the icy water at night in the open, so too during the day he was soaked by the water dripping from the trees in the grove. Thus, day and night, he experienced the suffering of cold. But in the last month of the hot season, he would stay in the open during the day and enter the grove at night. Just as during the day in the open he was scorched by the heat, so too at night in the windless grove, he suffered from the heat, and streams of sweat flowed from his body. Then, this verse, never heard before, occurred to him:

94.

94.

“Sotatto sosinno ceva, eko bhiṃsanake vane;

Naggo na caggimāsīno, esanāpasuto munī”ti.

“Scorched by heat and drenched by sweat, alone in the dreadful forest, naked, not sitting by the fire, the sage is intent on the quest.”

Tattha [P 1.0391] sotattoti sūriyasantāpena suṭṭhu tatto. Sosinnoti himodakena susinno suṭṭhu tinto. Eko bhiṃsanake vaneti yattha paviṭṭhānaṃ yebhuyyena lomāni haṃsanti, tathārūpe bhiṃsanakevanasaṇḍe eko adutiyova ahosinti dīpeti. Naggo na caggimāsīnoti naggo ca na ca aggimāsīno. Tathā sītena pīḷiyamānopi neva nivāsanapārupanaṃ vā ādiyiṃ, na ca aggiṃ āgamma nisīdinti dīpeti. Esanāpasutoti abrahmacariyepi tasmiṃ brahmacariyasaññī hutvā “brahmacariyamevetaṃ esanā gavesanā upāyo brahmalokassā”ti evaṃ tāya brahmacariyesanāya pasuto anuyutto ussukkaṃ āpanno ahosinti dasseti. Munīti [M 1.0415] “muni kho esa monatthāya paṭipanno”ti evaṃ lokena sambhāvito ahosinti dīpeti.

Therein, 'scorched by heat' means thoroughly scorched by the heat of the sun. 'Drenched by cold' means thoroughly drenched by icy water. 'Alone in a terrifying forest' explains that he lived alone without a companion in a frightening forest grove where the hair of most who entered would stand on end. 'Naked and not sitting by the fire' means he was naked and did not sit by a fire; it shows that even though oppressed by the cold, he did not take up any clothing or covering, nor did he sit by a fire. 'Intent on the quest' shows that even though it was not the holy life, he perceived it as such, thinking, "This is the holy life, the quest, the search, the way to the Brahma-world." Thus, he was devoted and diligently engaged in that quest for the holy life. 'Sage' shows that he was esteemed by the world as 'one who has undertaken the practice for the sake of sagehood.'

Evaṃ [V 1.0374] caturaṅgasamannāgataṃ brahmacariyaṃ caritvā bodhisatto maraṇakāle upaṭṭhitaṃ nirayanimittaṃ disvā “idaṃ vatasamādānaṃ niratthaka”nti ñatvā taṅkhaṇaññeva taṃ laddhiṃ bhinditvā sammādiṭṭhiṃ gahetvā devaloke nibbatti.

Having practiced the holy life endowed with these four factors, the Bodhisatta, at the time of death, saw the sign of hell appearing and, realizing, "This undertaking of vows is fruitless," he immediately shattered that doctrine, embraced right view, and was reborn in the heavenly world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “ahaṃ tena samayena so ājīvako ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the birth by saying: "At that time, I was that Ājīvaka ascetic."

Lomahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Lomahaṃsa Jātaka, the Fourth.

[95] 5. Mahāsudassanajātakavaṇṇanā

[95] 5. The Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Jātaka

Aniccā vata saṅkhārāti idaṃ satthā parinibbānamañce nipanno ānandattherassa “mā, bhante, bhagavā imasmiṃ khuddakanagarake”tyādivacanaṃ (dī. ni. 2.210) ārabbha kathesi. Tathāgate hi jetavane viharante sāriputtatthero kattikapuṇṇamāyaṃ nāḷakagāmake jātovarake parinibbāyi, mahāmoggallāno kattikamāsasseva kāḷapakkhaamāvasiyaṃ. Evaṃ parinibbute aggasāvakayuge “ahampi kusinārāyaṃ parinibbāyissāmī”ti anupubbena cārikaṃ caramāno tattha gantvā yamakasālānamantare uttarasīsake mañcake anuṭṭhānaseyyāya nipajji. Atha naṃ āyasmā ānandatthero “mā, bhante, bhagavā imasmiṃ khuddakanagarake visame ujjaṅgalanagarake, sākhānagarake parinibbāyi, aññesaṃ campārājagahādīnaṃ mahānagarānaṃ aññatarasmiṃ bhagavā parinibbāyatū”ti yāci. Satthā “mā, ānanda, imaṃ ‘khuddakanagarakaṃ, ujjaṅgalanagarakaṃ sākhānagaraka’nti vadehi, ahañhi pubbe sudassanacakkavattirājakāle imasmiṃ nagare vasiṃ, tadā idaṃ dvādasayojanikena ratanapākārena parikkhittaṃ [P 1.0392] mahānagaraṃ ahosī”ti vatvā therena yācito atītaṃ āharanto mahāsudassanasuttaṃ (dī. ni. 2.241 ādayo) kathesi.

"Impermanent indeed are all conditioned things." This the Teacher spoke while lying on the couch for his final passing away, prompted by Venerable Ānanda's words, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One not pass away in this small town," and so on. For while the Tathāgata was dwelling in Jetavana, the Elder Sāriputta attained his final passing away in Nāḷaka village on the full-moon day of Kattika, and Mahāmoggallāna on the new-moon day of the dark fortnight of the same month. Thus, when the pair of chief disciples had passed away, thinking, "I too shall attain my final passing away in Kusinārā," he journeyed by stages and arrived there, lying down between the twin sāla trees on a couch with his head to the north, in the lion's posture from which he would not rise again. Then the Venerable Ānanda entreated him, "Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One not pass away in this small town, this rough wilderness town, this branch town. Let the Blessed One attain his final passing away in one of the great cities like Campā or Rājagaha." The Teacher replied, "Do not, Ānanda, call this a 'small town, a wilderness town, a branch town.' For in the past, during the time of King Sudassana, the Wheel-Turning Monarch, I dwelt in this city. Then it was a great city, twelve leagues in extent, surrounded by a rampart of jewels." And being entreated by the Elder, he, bringing forth the past, related the Mahāsudassana Sutta.

Tadā pana mahāsudassanaṃ sudhammapāsādā otaritvā avidūre sattaratanamaye tālavane paññattasmiṃ kappiyamañcake dakkhiṇena passena [M 1.0416] anuṭṭhānaseyyāya nipannaṃ disvā “imāni te, deva, caturāsīti nagarasahassāni kusāvatirājadhānippamukhāni, ettha chandaṃ karohī”ti subhaddāya deviyā vutte mahāsudassano “mā devi evaṃ avaca, atha kho ‘ettha chandaṃ vinehi, mā apekkhaṃ akāsī’ti evaṃ maṃ ovadā”ti vatvā “kiṃkāraṇā, devā”ti pucchito “ajjāhaṃ kālakiriyaṃ karissāmī”ti. Atha naṃ devī rodamānā akkhīni puñchitvā kicchena [V 1.0375] kasirena tathā vatvā rodi paridevi. Sesāpi caturāsītisahassaitthiyo rodiṃsu parideviṃsu. Amaccādīsupi ekopi adhivāsetuṃ nāsakkhi, sabbepi rodiṃsu. Bodhisatto “alaṃ, bhaṇe, mā saddamakatthā”ti sabbe nivāretvā deviṃ āmantetvā “mā tvaṃ devi rodi, mā paridevi. Tilaphalamattopi hi saṅkhāro nicco nāma natthi, sabbepi aniccā bhedanadhammā evā”ti vatvā deviṃ ovadanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, King Mahāsudassana descended from the Sudhammā palace and lay down on his right side, never to rise again, on a suitable couch prepared in a palm grove adorned with the seven treasures not far away. Seeing him thus, Queen Subhaddā said, "Your Majesty, these are your eighty-four thousand cities, with the royal capital Kusāvatī as the foremost. Please set your heart on them." King Mahāsudassana replied, "Do not speak thus, O Queen. Rather, advise me in this way: ‘Relinquish your desire for these; do not have any longing.’" When asked, "For what reason, Your Majesty?" he said, "Today I shall die." Then the queen, weeping, wiped her eyes and with great difficulty and sorrow, spoke as he had said, and then she wept and lamented. The remaining eighty-four thousand women also wept and lamented. Among the ministers and others, not even one could endure it; all of them wept. The Bodhisatta, saying, "Enough, sirs, do not make a sound," restrained them all and addressed the queen: "Do not weep, O Queen, do not lament. For not even a conditioned thing the size of a sesame seed is permanent. All are impermanent, subject to breaking up." And advising the queen, he spoke this verse:

95.

95.

“Aniccā vata saṅkhārā, uppādavayadhammino;

Uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, tesaṃ vūpasamo sukho”ti.

"Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned things, subject to arising and passing away. Having arisen, they cease; their stilling is happiness."

Tattha aniccā vata saṅkhārāti bhadde subhaddādevi, yattakā kehici paccayehi samāgantvā katā khandhāyatanādayo saṅkhārā, sabbe te aniccāyeva nāma. Etesu hi rūpaṃ aniccaṃ…pe… viññāṇaṃ aniccaṃ. Cakkhu aniccaṃ…pe… dhammā aniccā. Yaṃkiñci saviññāṇakaṃ aviññāṇakaṃ ratanaṃ, sabbaṃ taṃ aniccameva. Iti “aniccā vata saṅkhārā”ti gaṇha. Kasmā? Uppādavayadhamminoti, sabbe hete uppādadhammino ceva vayadhammino ca uppajjanabhijjanasabhāvāyeva, tasmā “aniccā”ti veditabbā. Yasmā ca aniccā, tasmā uppajjitvā nirujjhanti, uppajjitvā ṭhitiṃ patvāpi nirujjhantiyeva. Sabbeva hete nibbattamānā uppajjanti nāma, bhijjamānā nirujjhanti nāma. Tesaṃ uppāde satiyeva ca ṭhiti nāma hoti, ṭhitiyā satiyeva bhaṅgo nāma hoti, na hi anuppannassa ṭhiti nāma[P 1.0393], nāpi ṭhitaṃ abhijjanakaṃ nāma atthi. Iti sabbepi saṅkhārā tīṇi lakkhaṇāni patvā tattha tattheva nirujjhanti, tasmā sabbepime aniccā khaṇikā ittarā adhuvā pabhaṅguno calitā samīritā anaddhaniyā payātā tāvakālikā nissārā, tāvakālikaṭṭhena māyāmarīcipheṇasadisā. Tesu bhadde subhaddādevi, kasmā sukhasaññaṃ uppādesi, evaṃ pana gaṇha tesaṃ vūpasamo sukhoti, sabbavaṭṭavūpasamanato tesaṃ vūpasamo nāma nibbānaṃ, tadevekaṃ ekantato sukhaṃ, tato aññaṃ sukhaṃ nāma natthīti.

Herein, ‘Impermanent, indeed, are conditioned things’ means this: O noble Queen Subhaddā, whatever conditioned things—such as the aggregates and sense bases—are formed, having come together through various causes, all of them are indeed impermanent. For among these, form is impermanent… consciousness is impermanent. The eye is impermanent… mental objects are impermanent. Whatever treasure there is, whether sentient or insentient, all of it is impermanent. Thus, take it to heart that ‘conditioned things are impermanent.’ Why? Because they are ‘subject to arising and passing away.’ For all of them have the nature of arising and the nature of passing away; they are inherently of a nature to arise and break apart. Therefore, they should be known as ‘impermanent.’ And because they are impermanent, ‘having arisen, they cease.’ Even after arising and reaching a state of duration, they still cease. For all of them, when they are produced, are said to arise; when they break apart, they are said to cease. And only when there is their arising is there what is called duration; only when there is duration is there what is called dissolution.
