For what has not arisen has no duration, nor is there anything that has duration that does not break apart. Thus, all conditioned things, having reached the three characteristics, cease right then and there. Therefore, all these are impermanent, momentary, fleeting, not lasting, fragile, trembling, shaken, not eternal, transient, temporary, and without essence. Due to their temporary nature, they are like an illusion, a mirage, and foam. In these things, O noble Queen Subhaddā, why do you give rise to a perception of happiness? Rather, take it to heart that ‘their stilling is happiness.’ Because it is the stilling of the entire round of existence, their stilling is called Nibbāna. That alone is absolute happiness; apart from that, there is no such thing as happiness.

Evaṃ [M 1.0417] mahāsudassano amatamahānibbānena desanāya kūṭaṃ gahetvā avasesassapi mahājanassa “dānaṃ detha, sīlaṃ rakkhatha, uposathakammaṃ karothā”ti ovādaṃ datvā devalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus Mahāsudassana, having brought his teaching to a peak with the deathless, great Nibbāna, gave this advice to the rest of the great assembly: "Give alms, protect your virtue, and perform the Uposatha observance." Then he was destined for the heavenly world.

Satthā [V 1.0376] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā subhaddā devī rāhulamātā ahosi, pariṇāyakaratanaṃ rāhulo, sesaparisā buddhaparisā, mahāsudassano pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the birth story: "At that time, Queen Subhaddā was Rāhula's mother, the counselor-jewel was Rāhula, the remaining assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and Mahāsudassana was none other than myself."

Mahāsudassanajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Mahāsudassana Jātaka, the Fifth.

[96] 6. Telapattajātakavaṇṇanā

[96] 6. The Commentary on the Oil Bowl Jātaka

Samatittikaṃ anavasesakanti idaṃ satthā sumbharaṭṭhe sedakaṃ nāma nigamaṃ upanissāya aññatarasmiṃ vanasaṇḍe viharanto janapadakalyāṇisuttaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tatra hi bhagavā –

"Full to the brim, without leaving any space." This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in a certain forest grove near a market town named Sedaka in the Sumbha country, in connection with the Janapadakalyāṇī Sutta. For there the Blessed One said:

“Seyyathāpi, bhikkhave, ‘janapadakalyāṇī janapadakalyāṇī’ti kho, bhikkhave, mahājanakāyo sannipateyya, sā kho panassa janapadakalyāṇī paramapāsāvinī nacce, paramapāsāvinī gīte. ‘Janapadakalyāṇī naccati gāyatī’ti kho, bhikkhave, bhiyyosomattāya mahājanakāyo sannipateyya. Atha puriso āgaccheyya jīvitukāmo amaritukāmo sukhakāmo dukkhapaṭikūlo. Tamenaṃ evaṃ vadeyya “ayaṃ te, ambho purisa, samatittiko telapatto antarena ca mahājanakāyassa antarena ca janapadakalyāṇiyā pariharitabbo, puriso ca taṃ ukkhittāsiko piṭṭhito piṭṭhito anubandhissati ‘yattheva naṃ thokampi chaḍḍessasi, tattheva te sīsaṃ pātessāmī’”ti. “Taṃ kiṃ maññatha, bhikkhave, api nu so puriso amuṃ telapattaṃ amanasikaritvā bahiddhā pamādaṃ āhareyyā”ti? “No hetaṃ, bhante”. Upamā kho myāyaṃ, bhikkhave, [P 1.0394] katā atthassa viññāpanāya. Ayamevettha attho – ‘samatittiko telapatto’ti kho, bhikkhave, kāyagatāyetaṃ satiyā adhivacanaṃ. Tasmātiha[M 1.0418], bhikkhave, evaṃ sikkhitabbaṃ ‘kāyagatā no sati bhāvitā bhavissati susamāraddhā’ti evañhi vo, bhikkhave, sikkhitabba”nti (saṃ. ni. 5.386) –

“Just as, monks, if a great crowd were to gather, saying, ‘The beauty of the land! The beauty of the land!’ And that beauty of the land was a supremely captivating dancer and a supremely captivating singer. If it were said, ‘The beauty of the land is dancing and singing!’ then an even greater crowd would gather. Then a man might come along, desiring to live and not to die, desiring happiness and averse to suffering. Someone might say to him, ‘Here, good man, you must carry this bowl filled to the brim with oil between the great crowd and the beauty of the land. A man with a drawn sword will follow close behind you and say, “Wherever you spill even a little of it, right there I will make your head fall!”’ What do you think, monks? Would that man, disregarding that bowl of oil, direct his attention outwardly and become heedless?” “Certainly not, venerable sir.” “This simile, monks, I have made to make the meaning clear. And this is the meaning here: ‘The bowl filled to the brim with oil’—this, monks, is a designation for mindfulness directed to the body. Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: ‘Our mindfulness directed to the body will be developed and well-undertaken.’ This is how you should train yourselves.”

Idaṃ janapadakalyāṇisuttaṃ sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ kathesi.

He spoke this Discourse on the Beauty of the Land, complete with its meaning and phrasing.

Tatrāyaṃ [V 1.0377] saṅkhepattho – janapadakalyāṇīti janapadamhi kalyāṇī uttamā chasarīradosarahitā pañcakalyāṇasamannāgatā. Sā hi yasmā nātidīghā, nātirassā, nātikisā, nātithūlā, nātikāḷā, nāccodātā, atikkantā mānusakavaṇṇaṃ, apattā dibbavaṇṇaṃ, tasmā chasarīradosarahitā. Chavikalyāṇaṃ, maṃsakalyāṇaṃ, nhārukalyāṇaṃ, aṭṭhikalyāṇaṃ, vayokalyāṇanti imehi pana pañcahi kalyāṇehi samannāgatattā pañcakalyāṇasamannāgatā nāma. Tassā hi āgantukobhāsakiccaṃ nāma natthi, attano sarīrobhāseneva dvādasahatthe ṭhāne ālokaṃ karoti, piyaṅgusāmā vā hoti suvaṇṇasāmā vā. Ayamassā chavikalyāṇatā. Cattāro panassā hatthapādā mukhapariyosānañca lākhārasaparikammakataṃ viya rattapavāḷarattakambalasadisaṃ hoti. Ayamassā maṃsakalyāṇatā. Vīsati nakhapattāni maṃsato amuttaṭṭhāne lākhārasapūritāni viya, muttaṭṭhāne khīradhārāsadisāni. Ayamassā nhārukalyāṇatā. Dvattiṃsa dantā suphusitā sudhotavajirapanti viya khāyanti. Ayamassā aṭṭhikalyāṇatā. Vīsativassasatikāpi pana samānā soḷasavassuddesikā viya hoti nibbalipalitā. Ayamassā vayokalyāṇatā.

Herein, the brief meaning is this: ‘Janapadakalyāṇī’ means the supreme beauty of the land, free from six bodily defects and endowed with five kinds of beauty. For she is neither too tall nor too short, neither too thin nor too stout, neither too dark nor too fair; having surpassed the human complexion but not yet attained a divine complexion, she is thus free from the six bodily defects. And because she is endowed with these five kinds of beauty—beauty of skin, beauty of flesh, beauty of sinews, beauty of bones, and beauty of youth—she is called ‘endowed with the five kinds of beauty’. For her, there is no need for external radiance; with her own bodily radiance she illuminates a space of twelve cubits. She has a golden complexion, like the priyaṅgu flower or like gold. This is her beauty of skin. Her palms and soles, and her lips, are like red coral or a red blanket, as if treated with lacquer. This is her beauty of flesh. Her twenty nails, where they are attached to the flesh, are as if filled with lacquer, and where they are detached, they are like streams of milk. This is her beauty of sinews. Her thirty-two teeth are well-set and appear like a row of well-polished diamonds. This is her beauty of bones. Even at one hundred and twenty years of age, she appears like a sixteen-year-old, without wrinkles or grey hair. This is her beauty of youth.

Paramapāsāvinīti ettha pana pasavanaṃ pasavo, pavattīti attho. Pasavo eva pāsāvo, paramo pāsāvo paramapāsāvo, so assā atthīti paramapāsāvinī. Nacce ca gīte ca uttamappavatti seṭṭhakiriyā. Uttamameva naccaṃ naccati, gītañca gāyatīti vuttaṃ hoti.

In the word ‘Paramapāsāvinī’, ‘pasavana’ means ‘pasavo’, which means ‘occurrence’. ‘Pasavo’ itself is ‘pāsāva’. The supreme ‘pāsāva’ is ‘paramapāsāva’; she who possesses this is ‘paramapāsāvinī’. In dance and song, this signifies supreme performance and excellent action. It means that she dances the supreme dance and sings the supreme song.

Atha puriso āgaccheyyāti na attano ruciyā āgaccheyya, ayaṃ panettha adhippāyo – athevaṃ mahājanamajjhe janapadakalyāṇiyā naccamānāya “sādhu sādhū”ti sādhukāresu aṅguliphoṭanesu celukkhepesu ca pavattamānesu taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā rājā bandhanāgārato ekaṃ corapurisaṃ pakkosāpetvā [M 1.0419] nigaḷāni chinditvā samatittikaṃ suparipuṇṇaṃ telapattaṃ tassa hatthe datvā ubhohi hatthehi daḷhaṃ gāhāpetvā ekaṃ asihatthaṃ purisaṃ āṇāpesi “etaṃ gahetvā janapadakalyāṇiyā samajjaṭṭhānaṃ gaccha. Yattheva cesa pamādaṃ āgamma ekampi telabinduṃ chaḍḍeti, tatthevassa sīsaṃ chindā”ti. So puriso asiṃ ukkhipitvā taṃ tajjento tattha nesi. So maraṇabhayatajjito jīvitukāmatāya pamādavasena taṃ amanasikaritvā sakimpi akkhīni ummīletvā taṃ janapadakalyāṇiṃ na olokesi. Evaṃ bhūtapubbamevetaṃ vatthu, sutte pana parikappavasenetaṃ vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

“Then a man might come”—this means he would not come of his own accord. This is the intention here: While the beauty of the land was dancing in the midst of that great crowd, and while cries of ‘Excellent! Excellent!’, snapping of fingers, and waving of cloths were occurring, the king, hearing of this event, had a thief summoned from prison. After having his fetters cut, he placed a bowl filled to the brim with oil in his hands, having him hold it firmly with both hands. The king then commanded a man with a sword: ‘Take this man and go to the performance place of the beauty of the land. Wherever, through heedlessness, he spills even a single drop of oil, cut off his head right there!’ That man, raising his sword and threatening him, led him there. Terrified by the fear of death and desiring to live, he, disregarding the spectacle, did not even once open his eyes to look at the beauty of the land. This is a story of something that has actually happened in the past, but it should be understood that in the sutta it is stated by way of a hypothetical scenario.

Upamā [V 1.0378] kho myāyanti ettha pana telapattassa tāva kāyagatāsatiyā opammasaṃsandanaṃ katameva. Ettha pana rājā viya kammaṃ daṭṭhabbaṃ, asi viya kilesā, ukkhittāsikapuriso viya māro, telapattahattho puriso viya kāyagatāsatibhāvako vipassakayogāvacaro. Iti [P 1.0395] bhagavā “kāyagatāsatiṃ bhāvetukāmena bhikkhunā telapattahatthena tena purisena viya satiṃ avissajjetvā appamattena kāyagatāsati bhāvetabbā”ti imaṃ suttaṃ āharitvā dassesi.

“‘This simile is mine’—here, first, the comparison of the oil bowl to mindfulness directed to the body has already been made. In this context, kamma should be seen as the king, the defilements as the sword, Māra as the man with the raised sword, and the yogi, the insight meditator who develops mindfulness directed to the body, as the man holding the oil bowl. Thus the Blessed One, presenting this sutta, showed that: ‘A bhikkhu wishing to develop mindfulness directed to the body should develop it with diligence, without letting go of mindfulness, just like that man holding the oil bowl.’”

Bhikkhū imaṃ suttañca atthañca sutvā evamāhaṃsu – “dukkaraṃ, bhante, tena purisena kataṃ tathārūpiṃ janapadakalyāṇiṃ anoloketvā telapattaṃ ādāya gacchantenā”ti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, tena dukkaraṃ kataṃ, sukaramevetaṃ. Kasmā? Ukkhittāsikena purisena santajjetvā nīyamānatāya. Yaṃ pana pubbe paṇḍitā appamādena satiṃ avissajjetvā abhisaṅkhataṃ dibbarūpampi indriyāni bhinditvā anoloketvāva gantvā rajjaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu, etaṃ dukkara”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Having heard this discourse and its meaning, the monks said: 'Venerable sir, what that man did was difficult—carrying the oil bowl without looking at such a village beauty.' The Teacher replied: 'Monks, what he did was not difficult; it was easy. Why? Because he was threatened and led by a man with a raised sword. But what the wise in the past did—who, through diligence, without abandoning mindfulness, even when faced with a conjured divine form, broke the power of their senses, did not look, and so going, attained kingship—that was difficult.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa rañño puttasatassa sabbakaniṭṭho hutvā nibbatti, so anupubbena viññutaṃ pāpuṇi. Tadā ca rañño gehe paccekabuddhā bhuñjanti, bodhisatto tesaṃ veyyāvaccaṃ karoti. So ekadivasaṃ cintesi “mama bahū bhātaro, lacchāmi nu kho ahaṃ imasmiṃ nagare kulasantakaṃ rajjaṃ, udāhu no”ti? Athassa etadahosi “paccekabuddhe pucchitvā jānissāmī”ti. So dutiyadivase paccekabuddhesu āgatesu dhamakaraṇaṃ ādāya pānīyaṃ parissāvetvā pāde dhovitvā telena makkhetvā tesaṃ antarakhajjakaṃ khāditvā [M 1.0420] nisinnakāle vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno tamatthaṃ pucchi. Atha naṃ te avocuṃ – kumāra, na tvaṃ imasmiṃ nagare rajjaṃ labhissasi, ito pana vīsayojanasatamatthake gandhāraraṭṭhe takkasilānagaraṃ nāma atthi, tattha gantuṃ sakkonto ito sattame divase rajjaṃ lacchasi. Antarāmagge pana mahāvattaniaṭaviyaṃ paripantho atthi, taṃ aṭaviṃ pariharitvā gacchantassa yojanasatiko maggo hoti, ujukaṃ gacchantassa paññāsa yojanāni honti. So hi amanussakantāro nāma. Tattha yakkhiniyo antarāmagge gāme ca sālāyo ca māpetvā upari suvaṇṇatārakavicittavitānaṃ mahārahaseyyaṃ paññāpetvā nānāvirāgapaṭasāṇiyo parikkhipitvā dibbālaṅkārehi attabhāvaṃ maṇḍetvā sālāsu nisīditvā āgacchante purise madhurāhi vācāhi [P 1.0396] saṅgaṇhitvā “kilantarūpā viya paññāyatha, idhāgantvā nisīditvā pānīyaṃ pivitvā gacchathā”ti pakkositvā āgatāgatānaṃ āsanāni datvā attano rūpalīlāvilāsehi palobhetvā kilesavasike katvā attanā saddhiṃ ajjhācāre kate tattheva [V 1.0379] ne lohitena paggharantena khāditvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpenti. Rūpagocaraṃ sattaṃ rūpeneva gaṇhanti, saddagocaraṃ madhurena gītavāditasaddena, gandhagocaraṃ dibbagandhehi, rasagocaraṃ dibbena nānaggarasabhojanena, phoṭṭhabbagocaraṃ ubhatolohitakūpadhānehi dibbasayanehi gaṇhanti. Sace indriyāni bhinditvā tā anoloketvā satiṃ paccupaṭṭhāpetvā gamissasi, sattame divase tattha rajjaṃ lacchasīti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the youngest of the king’s hundred sons, and in due course, he attained wisdom. At that time, Paccekabuddhas would take their meals in the king’s palace, and the Bodhisatta attended to their needs. One day, he thought, 'I have many brothers—will I obtain the ancestral kingdom in this city, or not?' Then it occurred to him, 'I will ask the Paccekabuddhas and find out.' The next day, when the Paccekabuddhas arrived, he took a water filter, filtered water for them, washed their feet, and anointed them with oil. While they were seated after partaking of refreshments, he paid homage, sat to one side, and asked them about the matter. They replied, 'Prince, you will not obtain the kingdom in this city. However, a hundred and twenty yojanas from here, in the land of Gandhāra, there is a city called Takkasilā. If you can go there, you will obtain the kingdom on the seventh day from today. But along the way, in a great wilderness, there is danger. For one who goes around that forest, the path is a hundred yojanas long; for one who goes straight, it is fifty yojanas. It is called the Wilderness of Non-Humans. There, along the path, ogresses conjure up villages and halls, preparing costly beds with canopies above, adorned with golden stars, and surrounding them with curtains of various colors. They adorn themselves with divine ornaments and sit in the halls. When men approach, they greet them with sweet words, saying, ‘You seem weary. Come, sit here, drink some water, and then go.’ Having invited them, they offer seats and entice them with their beauty and charm, making them subject to their defilements. Once they have engaged in misconduct with them, the ogresses devour them right there as their blood streams, bringing their lives to an end. A being whose domain is form, they capture with form. One whose domain is sound, they capture with sweet songs and music. One whose domain is smell, they capture with divine fragrances. One whose domain is taste, they capture with divine food of various excellent flavors. One whose domain is touch, they capture with divine beds having red cushions at both ends. If you can go, having broken the power of your senses, not looking at them, and establishing mindfulness, you will obtain the kingdom there on the seventh day.'

Bodhisatto “hotu, bhante, tumhākaṃ ovādaṃ gahetvā kiṃ tā olokessāmī”ti paccekabuddhehi parittaṃ kārāpetvā parittavālukañceva parittasuttañca ādāya paccekabuddhe ca mātāpitaro ca vanditvā nivesanaṃ gantvā attano purise āha – “ahaṃ takkasilāyaṃ rajjaṃ gahetuṃ gacchāmi, tumhe idheva tiṭṭhathā”ti. Atha naṃ pañca janā āhaṃsu “mayampi anugacchāmā”ti. “Na sakkā tumhehi anugantuṃ, antarāmagge kira yakkhiniyo rūpādigocare manusse evañcevañca rūpādīhi palobhetvā gaṇhanti, mahā paripantho, ahaṃ pana attānaṃ takketvā gacchāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana, deva, mayaṃ tumhehi saddhiṃ gacchantā attano piyāni rūpādīni olokessāma, mayampi [M 1.0421] tatheva gamissāmā”ti. Bodhisatto “tena hi appamattā hothā”ti te pañca jane ādāya maggaṃ paṭipajji.

The Bodhisatta said, 'So be it, venerable sirs. Having received your advice, why would I look at them?' Having had a protective charm recited by the Paccekabuddhas, he took the protective sand and the protective thread. After paying homage to the Paccekabuddhas and his parents, he went to his residence and said to his men, 'I am going to Takkasilā to take the kingdom. You stay here.' Then five men said to him, 'We too will follow you.' 'You cannot follow. Along the way, it is said that ogresses entice and capture humans who are attached to sense-objects like forms and so on. The danger is great. I, however, will go, relying on my own wits.' 'But, lord, if we go with you, would we look at our beloved forms and so on? We too will go in the same way.' The Bodhisatta said, 'In that case, be diligent.' Taking those five men, he set out on the path.

Yakkhiniyo gāmādīni māpetvā nisīdiṃsu. Tesu rūpagocaro puriso tā yakkhiniyo oloketvā rūpārammaṇe paṭibaddhacitto thokaṃ ohīyi. Bodhisatto “kiṃ bho, thokaṃ ohīyasī”ti āha. “Deva, pādā me rujjanti, thokaṃ sālāyaṃ nisīditvā āgacchāmī”ti. “Ambho, etā yakkhiniyo, mā kho patthesī”ti. “Yaṃ hoti, taṃ hotu, na sakkomi, devā”ti. “Tena hi paññāyissasī”ti itare cattāro ādāya agamāsi. Sopi rūpagocarako tāsaṃ santikaṃ agamāsi. Tā attanā saddhiṃ [P 1.0397] ajjhācāre kate taṃ tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā purato gantvā aññaṃ sālaṃ māpetvā nānātūriyāni gahetvā gāyamānā nisīdiṃsu, tattha saddagocarako ohīyi. Purimanayeneva tampi khāditvā purato gantvā nānappakāre gandhakaraṇḍake pūretvā āpaṇaṃ pasāretvā nisīdiṃsu, tattha gandhagocarako ohīyi. Tampi khāditvā purato gantvā nānaggarasānaṃ dibbabhojanānaṃ bhājanāni pūretvā odanikāpaṇaṃ pasāretvā nisīdiṃsu, tattha rasagocarako ohīyi. Tampi khāditvā purato gantvā dibbasayanāni paññāpetvā nisīdiṃsu, tattha phoṭṭhabbagocarako ohīyi. Tampi khādiṃsu, bodhisatto ekakova ahosi.

The demonesses created villages and so on and waited. Among them, the man whose sphere was forms saw those demonesses and, his mind captivated by the object of form, lagged behind somewhat. The Bodhisatta asked, 'Why, friend, are you lagging behind?' 'Lord, my feet ache. Let me sit for a while in this hall and then I will come.' 'Friend, these are demonesses. Do not crave them.' 'Whatever happens, let it happen; I cannot, lord.' 'Then you will know the consequence!' Taking the other four, he went his way. That man whose sphere was forms went to them. After he had engaged in misconduct with them, they brought about his death right there. Then they went ahead, created another hall, took various musical instruments, and sat singing. There, the man whose sphere was sounds lagged behind. In the same way as before, they devoured him too. Then they went ahead, filled various perfume boxes, set up a perfume stall, and sat there. There, the man whose sphere was scents lagged behind. They devoured him too. Then they went ahead, filled dishes with various delicious and divine foods, set up a cooked-rice stall, and sat there. There, the man whose sphere was tastes lagged behind. They devoured him too. Then they went ahead, arranged divine beds, and sat there. There, the man whose sphere was touch lagged behind. They devoured him too. The Bodhisatta was left alone.

Athekā [V 1.0380] yakkhinī “atikharamanto vatāyaṃ, ahaṃ taṃ khāditvāva nivattissāmī”ti bodhisattassa pacchato pacchato agamāsi. Aṭaviyā parabhāge vanakammikādayo yakkhiniṃ disvā “ayaṃ te purato gacchanto puriso kiṃ hotī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Komārasāmiko me, ayyā”ti. “Ambho, ayaṃ evaṃ sukumālā pupphadāmasadisā suvaṇṇavaṇṇā kumārikā attano kulaṃ chaḍḍetvā bhavantaṃ takketvā nikkhantā, kasmā etaṃ akilametvā ādāya na gacchasī”ti? “Nesā, ayyā, mayhaṃ pajāpati, yakkhinī esā, etāya me pañca manussā khāditā”ti. “Ayyā, purisā nāma kuddhakāle attano pajāpatiyo yakkhiniyopi karonti petiniyopī”ti. Sā gacchamānā gabbhinivaṇṇaṃ dassetvā puna sakiṃ vijātavaṇṇaṃ katvā puttaṃ aṅkena ādāya bodhisattaṃ anubandhi, diṭṭhadiṭṭhā [M 1.0422] purimanayeneva pucchanti. Bodhisattopi tatheva vatvā gacchanto takkasilaṃ pāpuṇi. Sā puttaṃ antaradhāpetvā ekikāva anubandhi. Bodhisatto nagaradvāraṃ gantvā ekissā sālāya nisīdi. Sā bodhisattassa tejena pavisituṃ asakkontī dibbarūpaṃ māpetvā sālādvāre aṭṭhāsi.

Then a demoness thought, 'This one is very sharp-witted indeed. I will devour him and then return.' So she followed right behind the Bodhisatta. In the latter part of the forest, some forest workers and others saw the demoness and asked, 'Who is this man who goes before you?' 'He is my young husband, sirs,' she replied. 'Good sir, this delicate maiden, like a garland of flowers, golden-complexioned, has left her family, thinking of you, and gone forth. Why do you not take her along without tiring her?' 'Sirs, she is not my wife; she is a demoness. She has devoured five men of mine.' 'Sirs, men, when angry, sometimes call their wives demonesses or even female ghosts.' As she walked on, she displayed the appearance of a pregnant woman, then again assumed the appearance of one who had just given birth, carrying a child in her arms, and pursued the Bodhisatta. Those who saw her questioned him in the same way as before, and the Bodhisatta, speaking in the same way, continued on his journey until he reached Takkasilā. She made the child disappear and followed alone. The Bodhisatta went to the city gate and sat down in a hall. Unable to enter due to the Bodhisatta’s power, the demoness assumed a divine form and stood at the hall entrance.

Tasmiṃ samaye takkasilarājā uyyānaṃ gacchanto taṃ disvā paṭibaddhacitto hutvā “gaccha, imissā sassāmikaassāmikabhāvaṃ jānāhī”ti [P 1.0398] manussaṃ pesesi. So taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “sassāmikāsī”ti pucchi. “Āma, ayya, ayaṃ me sālāya nisinno sāmiko”ti. Bodhisatto “nesā mayhaṃ pajāpati, yakkhinī esā, etāya me pañca manussā khāditā”ti āha. Sāpi “purisā nāma ayyā kuddhakāle yaṃ icchanti, taṃ vadantī”ti āha. So ubhinnampi vacanaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā “assāmikabhaṇḍaṃ nāma rājasantakaṃ hotī”ti yakkhiniṃ pakkosāpetvā ekahatthipiṭṭhe nisīdāpetvā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pāsādaṃ abhiruyha taṃ aggamahesiṭṭhāne ṭhapesi.

At that time, the King of Takkasilā, while going to the park, saw her and his mind became attached. He sent a man, saying, 'Go and find out whether she is married or unmarried.' The man approached her and asked, 'Are you married?' She replied, 'Yes, sir, this man sitting in the hall is my husband.' The Bodhisatta said, 'She is not my wife; she is a demoness. She has devoured five men of mine.' She also said, 'Sirs, men, when angry, say whatever they wish.' He reported the statements of both to the king. The king declared, 'Ownerless property belongs to the king,' and had the demoness summoned. He had her sit on the back of a single elephant, circumambulated the city, ascended the palace, and placed her in the position of chief queen.

So nhātavilitto sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā sirīsayanaṃ abhiruhi. Sāpi yakkhinī attano upakappanakaṃ āhāraṃ āharitvā alaṅkatapaṭiyattā sirisayane raññā saddhiṃ nipajjitvā rañño rativasena sukhaṃ samappitassa nipannakāle ekena passena parivattitvā parodi. Atha naṃ rājā “kiṃ, bhadde, rodasī”ti pucchi. “Deva, ahaṃ tumhehi magge disvā ānītā, tumhākañca gehe bahū itthiyo, ahaṃ sapattīnaṃ antare vasamānā kathāya uppannāya ‘ko tuyhaṃ mātaraṃ vā pitaraṃ vā gottaṃ vā jātiṃ vā jānāti, tvaṃ antarāmagge disvā ānītā nāmā’ti sīse gahetvā nippīḷiyamānā viya maṅku bhavissāmi. Sace tumhe sakalarajje issariyañca āṇañca mayhaṃ dadeyyātha, koci mayhaṃ cittaṃ kopetvā kathetuṃ na sakkhissatī”ti[V 1.0381]. “Bhadde, mayhaṃ sakalaraṭṭhavāsino na kiñci honti, nāhaṃ etesaṃ sāmiko. Ye pana rājāṇaṃ kopetvā akattabbaṃ karonti, tesaññevāhaṃ sāmiko. Iminā kāraṇena na sakkā tuyhaṃ sakalaraṭṭhe vā nagare vā issariyañca āṇañca dātu”nti. “Tena hi, deva, sace raṭṭhe vā nagare vā āṇaṃ dātuṃ na sakkotha, antonivesane [M 1.0423] antovaḷañjanakānaṃ upari mama vasaṃ vattanatthāya āṇaṃ dethā”ti. Rājā dibbaphoṭṭhabbena baddho tassā vacanaṃ atikkamituṃ asakkonto “sādhu, bhadde, antovaḷañjanakesu tuyhaṃ āṇaṃ dammi, tvaṃ ete attano vase vattāpehī”ti [P 1.0399] āha. Sā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā rañño niddaṃ okkantakāle yakkhanagaraṃ gantvā yakkhe pakkositvā attanā rājānaṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā aṭṭhimattaṃ sesetvā sabbaṃ nhārucammamaṃsalohitaṃ khādi, avasesā yakkhā mahādvārato paṭṭhāya antonivesane kukkuṭakukkure ādiṃ katvā sabbe khāditvā aṭṭhimattasese akaṃsu.

Then, having bathed and anointed himself, he ate his evening meal and ascended the royal bed. That very demoness, having brought her own appropriate food, adorned and made ready, lay down on the royal bed with the king. When the king, filled with happiness by the pleasure of love, lay down, she turned over onto one side and wept. Then the king asked her, 'Why, dear, are you crying?' 'O king, I was brought here after you saw me on the road. In your household there are many women. Living among rivals, when a quarrel arises, they will say, "Who knows your mother or father, your clan or birth? You were merely brought here after being seen on the road." As if seized by the head and tormented, I will be humiliated. If you were to grant me authority and command over the entire kingdom, no one would be able to provoke my mind and speak thus.' 'Dear, I do not have direct authority over the inhabitants of the entire kingdom; I am not their master. I am master only of those who transgress the royal command and do what should not be done. For this reason, it is not possible to grant you authority and command over the entire kingdom or the city.' 'Then, O king, if you cannot grant me authority over the kingdom or the city, at least give me command over those who serve within the palace, so that they may be under my control.' Bound by divine touch, the king, unable to transgress her word, said, 'Very well, dear, I grant you authority over those who serve within the palace. You may make them subject to your will.' She accepted, saying, 'Very well.' Then, when the king had fallen asleep, she went to the city of the yakkhas, summoned the yakkhas, and having killed the king, leaving only his bones, she herself devoured all his sinews, skin, flesh, and blood. The remaining yakkhas, starting from the great gate, devoured all within the inner palace, including chickens and dogs, leaving only their bones.

Punadivase dvāraṃ yathāpihitameva disvā manussā pharasūhi kavāṭāni koṭṭetvā anto pavisitvā sabbaṃ nivesanaṃ aṭṭhikaparikiṇṇaṃ disvā “saccaṃ vata so puriso āha ‘nāyaṃ mayhaṃ pajāpati, yakkhinī esā’ti. Rājā pana kiñci ajānitvā taṃ gahetvā attano bhariyaṃ akāsi, sā yakkhe pakkositvā sabbaṃ janaṃ khāditvā gatā bhavissatī”ti āhaṃsu. Bodhisattopi taṃ divasaṃ tassāyeva sālāyaṃ parittavālukaṃ sīse katvā parittasuttañca parikkhipitvā khaggaṃ gahetvā ṭhitakova aruṇaṃ uṭṭhāpesi. Manussā sakalarājanivesanaṃ sodhetvā haritūpalittaṃ katvā upari gandhehi vilimpitvā pupphāni vikiritvā pupphadāmāni osāretvā dhūmaṃ datvā navamālā bandhitvā sammantayiṃsu “ambho, yo puriso dibbarūpaṃ māpetvā pacchato āgacchantiṃ yakkhiniṃ indriyāni bhinditvā olokanamattampi na akāsi, so ativiya uḷārasatto dhitimā ñāṇasampanno, tādise purise rajjaṃ anusāsante sabbaraṭṭhaṃ sukhitaṃ bhavissati, taṃ rājānaṃ karomā”ti. Atha sabbe amaccā ca nāgarā ca ekacchandā hutvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, tumhe imaṃ rajjaṃ kārethā”ti nagaraṃ pavesetvā ratanarāsimhi ṭhapetvā abhisiñcitvā takkasilarājānaṃ akaṃsu. So cattāri agatigamanāni vajjetvā dasa rājadhamme akopetvā dhammena rajjaṃ kārento dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

The next day, seeing the door still shut as it was, the people broke open the door panels with axes and, entering inside, saw the entire residence strewn with bones. They said, 'Truly, that man spoke the truth: "She is not my wife; she is a demoness." But the king, knowing nothing, took her and made her his wife. She must have summoned the yakkhas and devoured all the people before leaving.' On that very day, the Bodhisatta, in that same hall, placed sacred sand on his head, cast a protective circle with a thread, took up his sword, and stood thus until dawn. The people cleaned the entire royal residence, smeared it with fresh cow-dung, anointed it with perfumes, scattered flowers, hung flower garlands, offered incense, tied fresh garlands, and deliberated: 'Ah, that man who, when the demoness, having fashioned a divine form, came behind him, did not break control of his senses to even glance at her—he is indeed a being of great courage, steadfast and endowed with wisdom. With such a man ruling the kingdom, the whole kingdom will be happy. Let us make him king.' Then all the ministers and citizens, united in purpose, approached the Bodhisatta and said, 'Lord, may you rule this kingdom.' They led him into the city, placed him on a heap of jewels, and consecrated him as King of Takkasilā. Avoiding the four wrong paths, not violating the ten royal virtues, he ruled righteously, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having become fully enlightened, related this past story and spoke this verse:

96.

96.

“Samatittikaṃ [V 1.0382][P 1.0400][M 1.0424] anavasesakaṃ, telapattaṃ yathā parihareyya;

Evaṃ sacittamanurakkhe, patthayāno disaṃ agatapubba”nti.

Just as one would carry a bowl of oil filled to the brim, without spilling any, so should one guard one's own mind, aspiring to the direction not gone to before.

Tattha samatittikanti antomukhavaṭṭilekhaṃ pāpetvā samabharitaṃ. Anavasesakanti anavasiñcanakaṃ aparissāvanakaṃ katvā. Telapattanti pakkhittatilatelapattaṃ. Parihareyyāti hareyya, ādāya gaccheyya. Evaṃ sacittamanurakkheti taṃ telabharitaṃ pattaṃ viya attano cittaṃ kāyagatāsatiyā gocare ceva sampayuttasatiyā cāti ubhinnaṃ antare pakkhipitvā yathā muhuttampi bahiddhā gocare na vikkhipati, tathā paṇḍito yogāvacaro rakkheyya gopeyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Etassa hi –

Herein, 'filled to the brim' means filled evenly up to the line of the inner rim. 'Without spilling any' means making it so it does not overflow or drip. 'A bowl of oil' means a bowl into which sesame oil has been poured. 'One would carry' means one would bear it, one would take it and go. Thus, 'one should guard one's own mind' means that a wise practitioner of meditation should protect and watch over his own mind, like that bowl filled with oil, placing it between two things—the sphere of mindfulness directed to the body and its associated mindfulness—so that it is not distracted by external objects even for a moment. For what reason? Because of this:

“Dunniggahassa lahuno, yatthakāmanipātino;

Cittassa damatho sādhu, cittaṃ dantaṃ sukhāvaha”nti. (dha. pa. 35);

Hard to restrain, swift, alighting wherever it wishes—the taming of the mind is good; a tamed mind brings happiness.

Tasmā –

Therefore—

“Sududdasaṃ sunipuṇaṃ, yatthakāmanipātinaṃ;

Cittaṃ rakkhetha medhāvī, cittaṃ guttaṃ sukhāvahaṃ”. (dha. pa. 36);

Very difficult to see, exceedingly subtle, alighting wherever it wishes—the wise one should guard the mind. A guarded mind brings happiness.

Idañhi –

Moreover—

“Dūraṅgamaṃ ekacaraṃ, asarīraṃ guhāsayaṃ;

Ye cittaṃ saṃyamessanti, mokkhanti mārabandhanā”. (dha. pa. 37);

Far-ranging, solitary, bodiless, dwelling in the cave of the heart—those who will restrain this mind will be freed from Māra’s bonds.

Itarassa pana –

But as for the other—

“Anavaṭṭhitacittassa, saddhammaṃ avijānato;

Pariplavapasādassa, paññā na paripūrati”. (dha. pa. 38);

For one whose mind is unsteady, who does not know the True Dhamma, whose confidence is wavering, wisdom does not come to fulfillment.

Thirakammaṭṭhānasahāyassa pana –

Yet for one who has a firm meditation subject—

“Anavassutacittassa[V 1.0383], ananvāhatacetaso;

Puññapāpapahīnassa, natthi jāgarato bhayaṃ”. (dha. pa. 39);

For one whose mind is not drenched by defilements, whose mind is not struck by defilements, who has abandoned both merit and demerit, there is no fear for one who is vigilant.

Tasmā etaṃ –

Therefore—

“Phandanaṃ capalaṃ cittaṃ, dūrakkhaṃ dunnivārayaṃ;

Ujuṃ karoti medhāvī, usukārova tejanaṃ”. (dha. pa. 33);

The flickering, wavering mind, difficult to guard, difficult to restrain—the wise one makes it straight, as a fletcher an arrow.

Evaṃ [P 1.0401] ujuṃ karonto sacittamanurakkhe.

Thus, making it straight, one should protect one's own mind.

Patthayāno [M 1.0425] disaṃ agatapubbanti imasmiṃ kāyagatāsatikammaṭṭhāne kammaṃ ārabhitvā anamatagge saṃsāre agatapubbaṃ disaṃ patthento pihento vuttanayena sakaṃ cittaṃ rakkheyyāti attho. Kā panesā disā nāma? –

Desiring a direction not gone to before—having undertaken the practice in this meditation subject of mindfulness of the body, one should protect one’s own mind in the manner stated, longing for and desiring a direction not gone to before in the beginningless cycle of existence—this is the meaning. What, then, is this direction?

“Mātāpitā disā pubbā, ācariyā dakkhiṇā disā;

Puttadārā disā pacchā, mittāmaccā ca uttarā.

Parents are the eastern direction, teachers the southern direction, wife and children the western direction, friends and companions the northern direction.

“Dāsakammakarā heṭṭhā, uddhaṃ samaṇabrāhmaṇā;

Etā disā namasseyya, alamatto kule gihī”ti. (dī. ni. 3.273) –

Servants and employees are below, ascetics and brahmins above. These directions a competent householder should honor.

Ettha tāva puttadārādayo “disā”ti vuttā.

Here, indeed, children, wife, and so forth are called "directions."

“Disā catasso vidisā catasso, uddhaṃ adho dasa disā imāyo;

Katamaṃ disaṃ tiṭṭhati nāgarājā, yamaddasā supine chabbisāṇa”nti. (jā. 1.16.104) –

Four directions, four intermediate directions, above and below—these are the ten directions. In which direction does the six-tusked nāga-king dwell, whom I saw in a dream?

Ettha puratthimādibhedā disāva “disā”ti vuttā.

Here, the directions beginning with the east are called "directions."

“Agārino [V 1.0384] annadapānavatthadā, avhāyikā tampi disaṃ vadanti;

Esā disā paramā setaketu, yaṃ patvā dukkhī sukhino bhavantī”ti. (jā. 1.6.9) –

Householders who give food, drink, and clothing, who invite, they too speak of that direction. This is the supreme direction, the white banner; having reached which, the sorrowful become happy.

Ettha pana nibbānaṃ “disā”ti vuttaṃ. Idhāpi tadeva adhippetaṃ. Tañhi “khayaṃ virāga”ntiādīhi dissati apadissati, tasmā “disā”ti vuccati. Anamatagge pana saṃsāre kenaci bālaputhujjanena supinenapi agatapubbatāya agatapubbā disā nāmāti vuttaṃ. Taṃ patthayantena kāyagatāsatiyā yogo karaṇīyoti.

Here, however, Nibbāna is called 'a direction.' Here too, that very thing is intended. For it is seen and indicated by terms like 'destruction' and 'dispassion,' hence it is called 'a direction.' But in the beginningless cycle of existence, because it has never been gone to even in a dream by any foolish ordinary person, it is called 'a direction not gone to before.' One who aspires to it should undertake the practice of mindfulness of the body.

Evaṃ satthā nibbānena desanāya kūṭaṃ gahetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rājaparisā buddhaparisā ahosi, rajjappattakumāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, taking Nibbāna as the culmination of the teaching, connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the king's assembly was the Buddha's assembly, and the prince who attained the kingdom was none other than myself."

Telapattajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Telapatta Jātaka, the sixth.

[97] 7. Nāmasiddhijātakavaṇṇanā

[97] 7. The Commentary on the Nāmasiddhi Jātaka

Jīvakañca [M 1.0426] mataṃ disvāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ nāmasiddhikaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Eko kira kulaputto nāmena pāpako nāma. So sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajito bhikkhūhi [P 1.0402] “ehāvuso, pāpaka, tiṭṭhāvuso, pāpakā”ti vuccamāno cintesi “loke pāpakaṃ nāma lāmakaṃ kāḷakaṇṇibhūtaṃ vuccati, aññaṃ maṅgalapaṭisaṃyuttaṃ nāmaṃ āharāpessāmī”ti. So ācariyupajjhāye upasaṅkamitvā “bhante, mayhaṃ nāmaṃ avamaṅgalaṃ, aññaṃ me nāmaṃ karothā”ti āha. Atha naṃ te evamāhaṃsu – “āvuso, nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ, nāmena kāci atthasiddhi nāma natthi, attano nāmeneva santuṭṭho hohī”ti. So punappunaṃ yāciyeva. Tassāyaṃ nāmasiddhikabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo jāto. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ sannisinnā bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko kira bhikkhu nāmasiddhiko maṅgalaṃ nāmaṃ āharāpetī”ti. Atha satthā dhammasabhaṃ āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, so idāneva, pubbepi nāmasiddhikoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Seeing Jīvaka dead—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who desired success through his name. It seems that a certain clansman's name was Pāpaka (Evil One). Having dedicated himself to the Dispensation, he went forth as a monk. Being addressed by the monks, "Come, friend Pāpaka, stay, friend Pāpaka," he thought: "In the world, the name Pāpaka is said to be wretched and ill-omened. I shall get another name, one connected with auspiciousness." He approached his teachers and preceptors and said, "Venerable sirs, my name is inauspicious. Please give me another name." Then they said to him: "Friend, a name is merely a designation. No success is achieved by a name. Be content with your own name." Yet he kept requesting repeatedly. This desire of his for success through a name became well-known among the Sangha of monks. One day, the monks, sitting in the Dhamma hall, started a discussion: "Friends, it seems that such-and-such monk desires success through his name and wants to get an auspicious name." Then the Teacher arrived at the Dhamma hall and asked, "Monks, with what discussion are you assembled here now?" When they replied, "With this one," the Teacher said, "Monks, not only now, but even in the past he desired success through his name," and he related a past incident.

Atīte [V 1.0385] takkasilāyaṃ bodhisatto disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañca māṇavakasatāni mante vācesi. Tasseko māṇavo pāpako nāma nāmena. So “ehi, pāpaka, yāhi, pāpakā”ti vuccamāno cintesi “mayhaṃ nāmaṃ avamaṅgalaṃ, aññaṃ nāmaṃ āharāpessāmī”ti. So ācariyaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “ācariya, mayhaṃ nāmaṃ avamaṅgalaṃ, aññaṃ me nāmaṃ karothā”ti āha. Atha naṃ ācariyo avoca “gaccha, tāta, janapadacārikaṃ caritvā attano abhirucitaṃ ekaṃ maṅgalanāmaṃ gahetvā ehi, āgatassa te nāmaṃ parivattetvā aññaṃ nāmaṃ karissāmī”ti. So “sādhū”ti pātheyyaṃ gahetvā nikkhanto gāmena gāmaṃ caranto ekaṃ nagaraṃ pāpuṇi. Tattha ceko puriso kālakato jīvako nāma nāmena. So taṃ ñātijanena āḷāhanaṃ nīyamānaṃ disvā “kiṃ nāmako esa puriso”ti pucchi. “Jīvako nāmeso”ti. “Jīvakopi maratī”ti? “Jīvakopi marati, ajīvakopi marati, nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ, tvaṃ bālo maññe”ti. So taṃ kathaṃ sutvā nāme majjhatto hutvā antonagaraṃ pāvisi.

In the past, in Takkasilā, the Bodhisatta was a world-renowned teacher and taught five hundred young brahmins the Vedas. Among them was a young man named Pāpaka. Being called, 'Come, Pāpaka, go, Pāpaka,' he thought, 'My name is inauspicious. I must get another name.' He approached the teacher and said, 'Teacher, my name is inauspicious. Please give me another name.' Then the teacher told him, 'Go, dear one, travel through the countryside, find an auspicious name that pleases you, and return. When you come back, I will change your name and give you a new one.' Saying, 'Very well,' he took provisions and set out, wandering from village to village until he reached a certain city. There, a certain man named Jīvaka had died. Seeing him being carried to the charnel ground by his relatives, he asked, 'What was this man’s name?' 'His name was Jīvaka,' they replied. 'Does even a Jīvaka die?' he asked. 'A Jīvaka dies and a non-Jīvaka dies. A name is merely a designation. You seem to be a fool,' they said. Hearing this, he became indifferent to names and entered the city.

Athekaṃ [M 1.0427] dāsiṃ bhatiṃ adadamānaṃ sāmikā dvāre nisīdāpetvā rajjuyā paharanti, tassā ca “dhanapālī”ti nāmaṃ hoti. So antaravīthiyā [P 1.0403] gacchanto taṃ pothiyamānaṃ disvā “kasmā imaṃ pothethā”ti pucchi. “Bhatiṃ dātuṃ na sakkotī”ti. “Kiṃ panassā nāma”nti? “Dhanapālī nāmā”ti. Nāmena dhanapālī samānāpi bhatimattaṃ dātuṃ na sakkotīti dhanapāliyopi adhanapāliyopi duggatā honti, nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ, tvaṃ bālo maññeti. So nāme majjhattataro hutvā nagarā nikkhamma maggaṃ paṭipanno antarāmagge maggamūḷhapurisaṃ disvā “ambho kiṃ karonto vicarasī”ti pucchi. “Maggamūḷhomhi, sāmī”ti. “Kiṃ pana te nāma”nti? “Panthako nāmā”ti. “Panthakopi maggamūḷho hotī”ti? “Panthakopi apanthakopi maggamūḷho hoti, nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ tvaṃ pana bālo maññeti”. So nāme atimajjhatto hutvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ, tāta, nāmaṃ rocetvā āgatosī”ti vutte “ācariya, jīvakāpi nāma maranti ajīvakāpi, dhanapāliyopi duggatā honti adhanapāliyopi, panthakāpi maggamūḷhā honti apanthakāpi, nāmaṃ nāma paṇṇattimattaṃ, nāmena siddhi natthi, kammeneva siddhi. Alaṃ mayhaṃ aññena nāmena, tadeva me nāmaṃ hotū”ti āha. Bodhisatto tena diṭṭhañca katañca saṃsandetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then her masters made a certain slave woman, who was unable to pay her fee, sit at the door and beat her with a rope. Her name was Dhanapālī. As he was walking along the street, he saw her being beaten and asked, 'Why are you beating her?' 'She cannot pay her fee.' 'What is her name?' 'Her name is Dhanapālī.' 'Though named Dhanapālī, she cannot even pay a simple fee.' Thus, both those named Dhanapālī and those not named Dhanapālī can be destitute. A name is merely a convention, but you are a fool, methinks. Then, becoming more indifferent to names, he left the city and set out on the road. Along the way, he saw a man lost on the path and asked, 'Hey, what are you doing wandering about?' 'I am lost, sir.' 'What is your name?' 'My name is Panthaka.' 'Even Panthaka gets lost?' 'Whether one is named Panthaka or not, one can still be lost. A name is merely a convention, but you are a fool, methinks.' Now utterly indifferent to names, he went to the Bodhisatta and was asked, 'Dear one, have you come back pleased with some name?' He replied, 'Teacher, those named Jīvaka die just like those not named Jīvaka. Those named Dhanapālī are destitute, and so are those not named Dhanapālī. Those named Panthaka get lost, and so do those not named Panthaka. A name is merely a convention—there is no success through a name, only through action. Enough of other names for me—let my own name remain.' The Bodhisatta, reconciling what he had seen and done, spoke this verse:

97.

97.

“Jīvakañca [V 1.0386] mataṃ disvā, dhanapāliñca duggataṃ;

Panthakañca vane mūḷhaṃ, pāpako punarāgato”ti.

“Having seen Jīvaka dead, and Dhanapālī destitute, and Panthaka bewildered in the forest, Pāpaka has returned again.”

Tattha punarāgatoti imāni tīṇi kāraṇāni disvā puna āgato, ra-kāro sandhivasena vutto.

Herein, 'punarāgato' means having seen these three reasons, he came again; the letter 'ra' is inserted by way of euphonic conjunction.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa nāmasiddhikoyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā nāmasiddhiko idānipi nāmasiddhikoyeva, ācariyaparisā buddhaparisā, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said: 'Monks, not only now, but in the past too he was one who sought success through a name.' And he connected the Jātaka: 'The one who sought success through a name at that time is this very one now; the assembly of the teacher was the assembly of the Buddha, and the teacher was I myself.'

Nāmasiddhijātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Nāmasiddhi Jātaka, the Seventh.

[98] 8. Kūṭavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā

[98] 8. The Commentary on the Kūṭavāṇija Jātaka

Sādhu [P 1.0404][M 1.0428] kho paṇḍito nāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kūṭavāṇijaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi dve janā ekato vaṇijjaṃ karontā bhaṇḍaṃ sakaṭenādāya janapadaṃ gantvā laddhalābhā paccāgamiṃsu. Tesu kūṭavāṇijo cintesi “ayaṃ bahū divase dubbhojanena dukkhaseyyāya kilanto, idāni attano ghare nānaggarasehi yāvadatthaṃ subhojanaṃ bhuñjitvā ajīrakena marissati. Athāhaṃ imaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ tayo koṭṭhāse katvā ekaṃ tassa dārakānaṃ dassāmi, dve koṭṭhāse attanā gahessāmī”ti. So “ajja bhājessāma, sve bhājessāmā”ti bhaṇḍaṃ bhājetuṃ na icchi. Atha naṃ paṇḍitavāṇijo akāmakaṃ nippīḷetvā bhājāpetvā vihāraṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā katapaṭisanthāro “atipapañco te kato, idhāgantvāpi cirena buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ āgatosī”ti vutte taṃ pavattiṃ bhagavato ārocesi. Satthā “na kho so, upāsaka, idāneva kūṭavāṇijo, pubbepi kūṭavāṇijoyeva. Idāni pana taṃ vañcetukāmo jāto, pubbe paṇḍitepi vañcetuṃ ussahī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Indeed, a wise person is good.” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a deceitful merchant. For in Sāvatthī, two men, trading together, took goods by cart, went to the countryside, and having gained profit, returned. Among them, the deceitful merchant thought: 'This man has been exhausted for many days by bad food and an uncomfortable bed. Now, having eaten his fill of delicious food with various excellent flavors at his own home, he will die from indigestion. Then I will divide these goods into three portions: I will give one to his children, and I will take two portions myself.' So he was unwilling to divide the goods, saying, 'We will divide today, we will divide tomorrow.' Then the wise merchant, pressing him against his will, made him divide the goods. Afterwards, he went to the monastery, paid homage to the Teacher, and having exchanged friendly greetings, when it was said to him, 'You have been excessively delayed; even after coming here, you have come to attend upon the Buddha only after a long time,' he related that incident to the Blessed One. The Teacher said, 'Lay follower, that man is not only now a deceitful merchant; he was a deceitful merchant in the past as well. Now he desires to cheat you, but in the past, he even dared to cheat the wise.' Having said this, being requested by him, he related a past event.

Atīte [V 1.0387] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bārāṇasiyaṃ vāṇijakule nibbatti, nāmaggahaṇadivase cassa “paṇḍito”ti nāmaṃ akaṃsu. So vayappatto aññena vāṇijena saddhiṃ ekato hutvā vaṇijjaṃ karoti, tassa “atipaṇḍito”ti nāmaṃ ahosi. Te bārāṇasito pañcahi sakaṭasatehi bhaṇḍaṃ ādāya janapadaṃ gantvā vaṇijjaṃ katvā laddhalābhā puna bārāṇasiṃ āgamiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ bhaṇḍabhājanakāle atipaṇḍito āha “mayā dve koṭṭhāsā laddhabbā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Tvaṃ paṇḍito, ahaṃ atipaṇḍito. Paṇḍito ekaṃ laddhuṃ arahati, atipaṇḍito dve”ti. “Nanu amhākaṃ dvinnaṃ bhaṇḍamūlakampi goṇādayopi samasamāyeva, tvaṃ kasmā dve koṭṭhāse laddhuṃ arahasī”ti. “Atipaṇḍitabhāvenā”ti. Evaṃ te kathaṃ vaḍḍhetvā kalahaṃ akaṃsu.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a merchant family in Bārāṇasī. On his naming day, they gave him the name 'Paṇḍita.' When he came of age, he joined another merchant and engaged in trade together. That man's name was 'Atipaṇḍita.' Taking merchandise from Bārāṇasī in five hundred carts, they went to the countryside, traded, and returned to Bārāṇasī having made a profit. Then, when it was time to divide the goods, Atipaṇḍita said, 'I should receive two portions.' 'For what reason?' 'You are Paṇḍita, and I am Atipaṇḍita. Paṇḍita deserves to receive one, Atipaṇḍita two.' 'But were not the capital for our goods, our oxen, and so on, exactly equal for both of us? Why do you deserve to receive two portions?' 'Because of being Atipaṇḍita.' Thus, prolonging their discussion, they started a quarrel.

Tato atipaṇḍito “attheko upāyo”ti cintetvā attano pitaraṃ ekasmiṃ susirarukkhe [P 1.0405] pavesetvā “tvaṃ amhesu āgatesu [M 1.0429] ‘atipaṇḍito dve koṭṭhāse laddhuṃ arahatī’ti vadeyyāsī”ti vatvā bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “samma, mayhaṃ dvinnaṃ koṭṭhāsānaṃ yuttabhāvaṃ vā ayuttabhāvaṃ vā esā rukkhadevatā jānāti, ehi, taṃ pucchissāmā”ti taṃ tattha netvā “ayye rukkhadevate, amhākaṃ aṭṭaṃ pacchindā”ti āha. Athassa pitā saraṃ parivattetvā “tena hi kathethā”ti āha. “Ayye, ayaṃ paṇḍito, ahaṃ atipaṇḍito. Amhehi ekato vohāro kato, tattha kena kiṃ laddhabbanti. Paṇḍitena eko koṭṭhāso, atipaṇḍitena pana dve koṭṭhāsā laddhabbā”ti. Bodhisatto evaṃ vinicchitaṃ aṭṭaṃ sutvā “idāni devatābhāvaṃ vā adevatābhāvaṃ vā jānissāmī”ti palālaṃ āharitvā susiraṃ pūretvā aggiṃ adāsi, atipaṇḍitassa pitā jālāya phuṭṭhakāle aḍḍhajjhāmena sarīrena upari āruyha sākhaṃ gahetvā olambanto bhūmiyaṃ patitvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then Atipaṇḍita thought, “There is a way,” and having made his father enter a hollow tree, he instructed him, “When we come, you should say, ‘Atipaṇḍita deserves to receive two portions.’” Having said this, he approached the Bodhisatta and said, “Friend, this tree-deity knows whether it is fitting or unfitting for me to have two portions. Come, let us ask her.” He led him there and said, “Noble tree-deity, decide our case.” Then his father, changing his voice, said, “Very well, state your case.” “Noble one, this man is Paṇḍita, and I am Atipaṇḍita. We conducted business together; in this matter, what should each receive? Paṇḍita should receive one portion, but Atipaṇḍita should receive two portions.” Hearing the case thus decided, the Bodhisatta thought, “Now I will know whether this is a deity or not.” He brought straw, filled the hollow, and set it on fire. When the flames touched Atipaṇḍita’s father, with his body half-burnt, he climbed up, grabbed a branch, and while hanging there, fell to the ground and uttered this verse:

98.

98.

“Sādhu kho paṇḍito nāma, na tveva atipaṇḍito;

Atipaṇḍitena puttena, manamhi upakūḷito”ti.

“Indeed, one who is wise is good, but not one who is overly wise; by my overly wise son, I am slightly scorched.”

Tattha sādhu kho paṇḍito nāmāti imasmiṃ loke paṇḍiccena samannāgato kāraṇākāraṇaññū puggalo sādhu sobhano. Atipaṇḍitoti nāmamattena atipaṇḍito kūṭapuriso na tveva varaṃ. Manamhi upakūḷitoti thokenamhi jhāmo, aḍḍhajjhāmakova muttoti attho. Te ubhopi majjhe bhinditvā samaññeva koṭṭhāsaṃ gaṇhitvā yathākammaṃ gatā.

Herein, “Indeed, one who is wise is good” means that in this world, a person endowed with wisdom, who understands cause and what is not cause, is good and excellent. “Overly wise” refers to a deceitful person who is merely overly wise in name; he is not at all superior. “I am slightly scorched” means “I am slightly burnt, having escaped only half-burnt.” Both of them, having divided the profit in half, took equal portions and went their ways according to their kamma.

Satthā [V 1.0388] “pubbepi esa kūṭavāṇijoyevā”ti imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kūṭavāṇijo paccuppannepi kūṭavāṇijoyeva, paṇḍitavāṇijo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having related this past event, saying, “Even in the past, this man was a deceitful merchant,” connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the deceitful merchant was the same as the deceitful merchant of the present, and the wise merchant was none other than myself.”

Kūṭavāṇijajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Jātaka of the Deceitful Merchant, the Eighth.

[99] 9. Parosahassajātakavaṇṇanā

[99] 9. The Commentary on the Parosahassa Jātaka

Parosahassampi [M 1.0430] samāgatānanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto puthujjanapucchāpañcakaṃ ārabbha kathesi[P 1.0406]. Vatthu sarabhajātake (jā. 1.13.134 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Ekasmiṃ pana samaye bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitvā “āvuso, dasabalena saṃkhittena kathitaṃ dhammasenāpati sāriputto vitthārena byākāsī”ti therassa guṇaṃ kathayamānā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, sāriputto idāneva mayā saṃkhittena bhāsitaṃ vitthārena byākaroti, pubbepi byākāsiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Of more than a thousand gathered together”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the five questions put by ordinary people. The story will become clear in the Sarabha Jātaka. Now, at one time, the bhikkhus assembled in the Dhamma hall and sat discussing the virtues of the Elder, saying, “Friends, what the Ten-Powered One taught concisely, the General of the Dhamma, Sāriputta, explained in detail.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now assembled?” When they replied, “For this one,” he said, “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that Sāriputta explains in detail what I have spoken concisely; he did so in the past as well.” Having said this, he related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcābhiññā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattetvā himavante vihāsi. Parivāropissa pañca tāpasasatāni ahesuṃ. Athassa jeṭṭhantevāsiko vassārattasamaye upaḍḍhaṃ isigaṇaṃ ādāya loṇambilasevanatthāya manussapathaṃ agamāsi. Tadā bodhisattassa kālakiriyāsamayo jāto. Atha naṃ antevāsikā “ācariya, kataro vo guṇo laddho”ti adhigamaṃ pucchiṃsu. So “natthi kiñcī”ti vatvā ābhassarabrahmaloke nibbatti. Bodhisattā hi arūpasamāpattilābhino hutvāpi abhabbaṭṭhānattā āruppe na nibbattanti. Antevāsikā “ācariyassa adhigamo natthī”ti āḷāhane sakkāraṃ na kariṃsu.

In the past, while Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a northern brahmin family. After mastering all the arts at Takkasilā, he renounced sensual pleasures, went forth into the ascetic life, developed the five higher knowledges and the eight meditative attainments, and dwelled in the Himalayas. His retinue consisted of five hundred ascetics. Then his chief disciple, during the rainy season, took half the company of ascetics and went to the human world to obtain salt and sour condiments. At that time, the Bodhisatta’s time to pass away arrived. His disciples then asked about his spiritual attainment, saying, “Teacher, what special quality have you gained?” He replied, “There is nothing,” and was reborn in the Ābhassara Brahma world. For Bodhisattas, even though they may attain the formless meditative states, are not reborn in the formless realms because it is an unsuitable state for them. The disciples, thinking, “Our teacher has no attainment,” did not pay him respects at the cremation ground.

Jeṭṭhantevāsiko āgantvā “kahaṃ ācariyo”ti pucchitvā “kālakato”ti sutvā “api ācariyaṃ adhigamaṃ pucchitthā”ti āha. “Āma, pucchimhā”ti. “Kiṃ kathesī”ti? “Natthi kiñcīti tena vuttaṃ, athassa amhehi sakkāro na kato”ti āhaṃsu. Jeṭṭhantevāsiko “tumhe ācariyassa vacanatthaṃ na jānātha, ākiñcaññāyatanasamāpattilābhī ācariyo”ti [V 1.0389] āha. Te tasmiṃ punappunaṃ kathentepi na saddahiṃsu. Bodhisatto taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “andhabālā mama jeṭṭhantevāsikassa vacanaṃ na saddahanti. Imaṃ [M 1.0431] tesaṃ kāraṇaṃ pākaṭaṃ karissāmī”ti brahmalokā āgantvā assamapadamatthake mahantenānubhāvena ākāse ṭhatvā jeṭṭhantevāsikassa paññānubhāvaṃ vaṇṇento imaṃ gāthamāha –

The chief disciple returned and asked, “Where is the teacher?” Upon hearing, “He has passed away,” he said, “Did you ask the teacher about his attainment?” “Yes, we asked,” they replied. “What did he say?” “He said, ‘There is nothing,’ and so we paid him no respect,” they answered. The chief disciple said, “You do not understand the meaning of the teacher's words. The teacher was an attainer of the meditative state of the base of nothingness.” Even when he repeatedly explained this to them, they did not believe him. The Bodhisatta, knowing this matter, thought, “These blind fools do not believe the words of my chief disciple. I will make this matter clear to them.” Coming from the Brahma world, he stood in the sky with great power above the hermitage grounds and, praising the power of the chief disciple's wisdom, spoke this verse:

99.

99.

“Parosahassampi [P 1.0407] samāgatānaṃ, kandeyyuṃ te vassasataṃ apaññā;

Ekova seyyo puriso sapañño, yo bhāsitassa vijānāti attha”nti.

“Though more than a thousand without wisdom might gather, they would lament for a hundred years; better is the single wise person who understands the meaning of what is spoken.”

Tattha parosahassampīti atirekasahassampi. Samāgatānanti sannipatitānaṃ bhāsitassa atthaṃ jānituṃ asakkontānaṃ bālānaṃ. Kandeyyuṃ te vassasataṃ apaññāti te evaṃ samāgatā apaññā ime bālatāpasā viya vassasatampi vassasahassampi rodeyyuṃ parideveyyuṃ, rodamānāpi pana atthaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ vā neva jāneyyunti dīpeti. Ekova seyyo puriso sapaññoti evarūpānaṃ bālānaṃ parosahassatopi eko paṇḍitapurisova seyyo varataroti attho. Kīdiso sapaññoti? Yo bhāsitassa vijānāti atthaṃ ayaṃ jeṭṭhantevāsiko viyāti.

Here, 'more than a thousand' means over a thousand. 'Assembled' refers to fools who, though gathered, are unable to understand the meaning of what is spoken. 'They would weep for a hundred years, lacking wisdom' means that such assembled fools, lacking wisdom, like these foolish ascetics, might weep and lament for a hundred or even a thousand years; yet even while weeping, they would not understand the meaning or the reason—this is what is shown. 'Better is a single wise person' means that one wise person is superior and more excellent than even more than a thousand such fools. What kind of wise person? One who understands the meaning of what is spoken—like this senior resident pupil.

Evaṃ mahāsatto ākāse ṭhitova dhammaṃ desetvā tāpasagaṇaṃ bujjhāpetvā brahmalokameva gato. Tepi tāpasā jīvitapariyosāne brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesuṃ.

Thus, the Great Being, standing in the sky, taught the Dhamma and enlightened the assembly of ascetics, then departed to the Brahma world. Those ascetics too, at the end of their lives, had the Brahma world as their destination.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jeṭṭhantevāsiko sāriputto ahosi, mahābrahmā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having related this discourse, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the chief disciple was Sāriputta, and Mahābrahmā was indeed myself.'

Parosahassajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Parosahassa Jātaka, the Ninth.

[100] 10. Asātarūpajātakavaṇṇanā

[100] 10. Commentary on the Asātarūpa Jātaka

Asātaṃ sātarūpenāti idaṃ satthā kuṇḍiyanagaraṃ upanissāya kuṇḍadhānavane viharanto koliyarājadhītaraṃ suppavāsaṃ upāsikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā hi tasmiṃ samaye satta vassāni kucchinā gabbhaṃ pariharitvā sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhā ahosi, adhimattā vedanā pavattiṃsu. Sā [M 1.0432] evaṃ adhimattavedanābhibhūtāpi “sammāsambuddho vata so bhagavā, yo evarūpassa dukkhassa pahānāya dhammaṃ deseti. Suppaṭipanno vata tassa bhagavato sāvakasaṅgho, yo evarūpassa dukkhassa [V 1.0390] pahānāya paṭipanno. Susukhaṃ vata nibbānaṃ, yattheva rūpaṃ dukkhaṃ natthī”ti (udā. 18) imehi tīhi vitakkehi adhivāsesi. Sā sāmikaṃ pakkosetvā tañca attano pavattiṃ vandanasāsanañca ārocetuṃ satthu santikaṃ pesesi. Satthā vandanasāsanaṃ sutvāva “sukhinī [P 1.0408] hotu suppavāsā koliyadhītā, sukhinī arogā arogaṃ puttaṃ vijāyatū”ti āha. Saha vacaneneva pana bhagavato suppavāsā koliyadhītā sukhinī arogā arogaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. Athassā sāmiko gehaṃ gantvā taṃ vijātaṃ disvā “acchariyaṃ vata, bho”ti ativiya tathāgatassa ānubhāvena acchariyabbhutacittajāto ahosi.

The Teacher spoke this discourse beginning with, “The unpleasant in the guise of the pleasant,” while dwelling near the city of Kuṇḍiya, in the Kuṇḍadhāna Wood, concerning the lay follower Suppavāsā, the Koliyan princess. At that time, she had carried a child in her womb for seven years and for seven days suffered an obstructed labor; extreme pains arose in her. Though overwhelmed by such intense suffering, she endured it with these three thoughts: "Truly, the Blessed One is the Perfectly Enlightened One, who teaches the Dhamma for the abandoning of such suffering. Truly, the Blessed One’s Saṅgha of disciples is practicing well for the abandoning of such suffering. Truly, Nibbāna is supreme bliss, wherein such suffering does not exist." She summoned her husband and sent him to the Teacher to report her condition and convey her homage. Upon hearing the message of homage, the Teacher said, "May Suppavāsā, the Koliyan princess, be happy and well; may she, happy and healthy, give birth to a healthy child." Simultaneously with the Blessed One's words, Suppavāsā, the Koliyan princess, happy and healthy, gave birth to a healthy child. Her husband, returning home and seeing that she had given birth, exclaimed, "How wonderful, sir!" and his mind was filled with great astonishment and wonder at the Tathāgata’s power.

Suppavāsāpi puttaṃ vijāyitvā sattāhaṃ buddhappamukhassa saṅghassa dānaṃ dātukāmā puna nimantanatthāya taṃ pesesi. Tena kho pana samayena mahāmoggallānassa upaṭṭhākena buddhappamukho saṅgho nimantito hoti. Satthā suppavāsāya dānassa okāsadānatthāya theraṃ tassa santikaṃ pesetvā taṃ saññāpetvā sattāhaṃ tassā dānaṃ paṭiggahesi saddhiṃ bhikkhusaṅghena. Sattame pana divase suppavāsā puttaṃ sīvalikumāraṃ maṇḍetvā satthārañceva bhikkhusaṅghañca vandāpesi. Tasmiṃ paṭipāṭiyā sāriputtattherassa santikaṃ nīte thero tena saddhiṃ “kacci te, sīvali, khamanīya”nti paṭisanthāramakāsi. So “kuto me, bhante, sukhaṃ, svāhaṃ satta vassāni lohitakumbhiyaṃ vasi”nti therena saddhiṃ evarūpaṃ kathaṃ kathesi. Suppāvāsā tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sattāhajāto me putto anubuddhena dhammasenāpatinā saddhiṃ mantetī”ti somanassappattā ahosi. Satthā “api nu suppavāse aññepi evarūpe putte icchasī”ti āha. “Sace, bhante, evarūpe aññe satta putte labheyyaṃ, iccheyyamevāha”nti. Satthā udānaṃ udānetvā anumodanaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Sīvalikumāropi kho sattavassikakāleyeva sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajitvā paripuṇṇavasso upasampadaṃ labhitvā puññavā lābhaggappatto hutvā pathaviṃ unnādetvā arahattaṃ patvā puññavantānaṃ antare etadaggaṭṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi.

Suppavāsā, having given birth to her son, wished to offer alms to the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha for seven days, and sent her husband again to invite them. At that time, however, the Saṅgha headed by the Buddha had been invited by Mahāmoggallāna’s lay attendant. The Teacher, to grant Suppavāsā the opportunity for her offering, sent the Elder Moggallāna to his lay attendant to persuade him, and then accepted her alms for seven days along with the community of monks. On the seventh day, Suppavāsā adorned her son, the boy Sīvali, and had him pay homage to the Teacher and the Saṅgha of monks. When he was brought in due course before the Elder Sāriputta, the Elder greeted him, saying, “I hope you are well, Sīvali.” He replied, “How could I be well, venerable sir? I dwelt for seven years in a cauldron of blood,” and thus he conversed with the Elder. Hearing his words, Suppavāsā became joyful, thinking, “My seven-day-old son is conversing with the General of the Dhamma, an Anubuddha.” The Teacher asked, “Suppavāsā, would you wish for other such sons?” She replied, “Venerable sir, if I could obtain seven more such sons, I would indeed wish for them.” The Teacher uttered a solemn exclamation, gave a discourse of appreciation, and departed. The boy Sīvali, at the age of seven, dedicated himself to the Dispensation and went forth. Having completed his years, he received the higher ordination. Possessed of great merit and foremost in gains, he caused the earth to resound, attained Arahantship, and reached the foremost place among those possessed of merit.

Athekadivasaṃ [M 1.0433] bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitvā “āvuso, sīvalitthero nāma evarūpo mahāpuñño patthitapatthano pacchimabhavikasatto satta vassāni lohitakumbhiyaṃ vasitvā sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhabhāvaṃ āpajji, aho mātāputtā mahantaṃ dukkhaṃ anubhaviṃsu, kiṃ nu kho kammaṃ akaṃsū”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā tatthāgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “bhikkhave, sīvalino mahāpuññatova satta vassāni [P 1.0409] lohitakumbhiyaṃ nivāso ca sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhabhāvappatti ca attanā katakammamūlakāva, suppavāsāyapi satta vassāni kucchinā gabbhapariharaṇadukkhañca sattāhaṃ [V 1.0391] mūḷhagabbhadukkhañca attanā katakammamūlakamevā”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and raised a discussion: “Friends, the Elder Sīvali, a being of such great merit, one whose aspirations are fulfilled, in his final existence, dwelt for seven years in a cauldron of blood and for seven days experienced an obstructed labor. Alas, mother and son endured great suffering! What kamma, I wonder, did they perform?” The Teacher came there and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?” When it was said, “For this one,” he replied, “Monks, Sīvali's dwelling in a cauldron of blood for seven years and his experiencing an obstructed labor for seven days were rooted in a deed done by himself. For Suppavāsā, too, the suffering of carrying a child in her womb for seven years and the suffering of an obstructed labor for seven days were rooted in a deed done by herself.” Then, at their request, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa aggamahesiyā kucchismiṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā pitu accayena rajjaṃ patvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Tasmiṃ samaye kosalamahārājā mahantena balenāgantvā bārāṇasiṃ gahetvā rājānaṃ māretvā tasseva aggamahesiṃ attano aggamahesiṃ akāsi. Bārāṇasirañño pana putto pitu maraṇakāle niddhamanadvārena palāyitvā balaṃ saṃharitvā bārāṇasiṃ āgantvā avidūre nisīditvā tassa rañño paṇṇaṃ pesesi “rajjaṃ vā detu yuddhaṃ vā”ti. So “yuddhaṃ demī”ti paṭipaṇṇaṃ pesesi. Rājakumārassa pana mātā taṃ sāsanaṃ sutvā “yuddhena kammaṃ natthi, sabbadisāsu sañcāraṃ pacchinditvā bārāṇasinagaraṃ parivāretu, tato dārūdakabhattaparikkhayena kilantamanussaṃ nagaraṃ vināva yuddhena gaṇhissasī”ti paṇṇaṃ pesesi. So mātu sāsanaṃ sutvā satta divasāni sañcāraṃ pacchinditvā nagaraṃ rundhi, nāgarā sañcāraṃ alabhamānā sattame divase tassa rañño sīsaṃ gahetvā kumārassa adaṃsu. Kumāro pana nagaraṃ pavisitvā rajjaṃ gahetvā jīvitapariyosāne yathākammaṃ gato.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was conceived in the womb of his chief queen. Having come of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā. Upon his father's death, he ascended the throne and ruled righteously. At that time, the king of Kosala came with a great army, captured Benares, killed the king, and took that chief queen as his own chief queen. However, the son of the king of Benares, at the time of his father's death, escaped through a drainage conduit. Gathering his forces, he returned to Benares and stationed himself not far off. He sent a message to that king: "Either surrender the kingdom or fight." He sent a counter-message: "I will give war." Upon hearing this response, the prince's mother sent him advice: "There is no need for battle. Cut off all movement in all directions and surround the city of Benares. Then, when the people are exhausted from lack of firewood, water, and food, you will take the city without a fight." Following his mother's counsel, the prince cut off all movement for seven days and besieged the city. Unable to obtain passage, the citizens seized the head of that king on the seventh day and handed it to the prince. The prince then entered the city, took the throne, and at the end of his life, he passed on according to his deeds.

So etarahi satta divasāni sañcāraṃ pacchinditvā nagaraṃ rundhitvā gahitakammanissandena satta vassāni lohitakumbhiyaṃ vasitvā sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhabhāvaṃ āpajji. Yaṃ pana so padumuttarassa bhagavato pādamūle “lābhīnaṃ aggo bhaveyya”nti mahādānaṃ datvā patthanaṃ akāsi, yañca vipassibuddhakāle [M 1.0434] nāgarehi saddhiṃ sahassagghanakaṃ guḷadadhiṃ [P 1.0410] datvā patthanamakāsi, tassānubhāvena lābhīnaṃ aggo jāto. Suppavāsāpi “nagaraṃ rundhitvā gaṇha, tātā”ti pesitabhāvena satta vassāni kucchinā gabbhaṃ pariharitvā sattāhaṃ mūḷhagabbhā jātā.

Now, as a result of that deed of having cut off movement for seven days and besieged the city, he dwelt for seven years as if in a cauldron of blood and for seven days suffered an obstructed birth. But because at the feet of the Blessed Padumuttara he made the aspiration, "May I be the foremost among those who receive gains," having given a great gift, and because in the time of the Buddha Vipassī he gave molasses and curds worth a thousand together with the townspeople and made an aspiration—by the power of that, he became the foremost among those who receive gains. Suppavāsā, too, because she had sent the message, "Besiege the city and take it, my son," carried the child in her womb for seven years and for seven days suffered an obstructed labor.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having related this past event and having become fully enlightened, spoke this verse:

100.

100.

“Asātaṃ sātarūpena, piyarūpena appiyaṃ;

Dukkhaṃ sukhassa rūpena, pamattamativattatī”ti.

“The unpleasant in the guise of the pleasant, the unloved in the guise of the loved, and suffering in the guise of happiness, overwhelm the heedless.”

Tattha asātaṃ sātarūpenāti amadhurameva madhurapatirūpakena. Pamattamativattatīti asātaṃ appiyaṃ dukkhanti etaṃ tividhampi etena sātarūpādinā ākārena sativippavāsavasena pamattaṃ puggalaṃ [V 1.0392] ativattati abhibhavati ajjhottharatīti attho. Idaṃ bhagavatā yañca te mātāputtā iminā gabbhapariharaṇagabbhavāsasaṅkhātena asātādinā pubbe nagararundhanasātādipatirūpakena ajjhotthaṭā, yañca idāni sā upāsikā punapi sattakkhattuṃ evarūpaṃ asātaṃ appiyaṃ dukkhaṃ pemavatthubhūtena puttasaṅkhātena sātādipatirūpakena ajjhotthaṭā hutvā tathā avaca, taṃ sabbampi sandhāya vuttanti veditabbaṃ.

Therein, 'the unpleasant in the guise of the pleasant' means that which is not sweet having the counterfeit appearance of the sweet. 'Overwhelms the heedless' means that these three—the unpleasant, the disagreeable, and suffering—overwhelm, overpower, and engulf a heedless person through a lapse of mindfulness, by means of this appearance of the pleasant and so forth; this is the meaning. This was spoken by the Blessed One in reference to all of this: both how that mother and son were previously overwhelmed by the unpleasantness of carrying the child and dwelling in the womb, which resulted from the act of besieging the city that had the counterfeit appearance of pleasantness; and how now that female lay follower, having been overwhelmed again seven times by such unpleasant, disagreeable, and painful things which had the counterfeit appearance of pleasantness in the form of her son, an object of affection, spoke as she did. It should be understood that all this was said in reference to that.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā nagaraṃ rundhitvā rajjappattakumāro sīvali ahosi, mātā suppavāsā, pitā pana bārāṇasirājā ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher connected the birth story, saying: "At that time, the prince who besieged the city and attained the kingdom was Sīvali, the mother was Suppavāsā, and the father, the King of Benares, was I myself."

Asātarūpajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Asātarūpa Jātaka, the tenth.

Littavaggo dasamo.

The Litta Vagga, the Tenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its Summary:

Littatejaṃ mahāsāraṃ, vissāsa lomahaṃsanaṃ;

Sudassana telapattaṃ, nāmasiddhi kūṭavāṇijaṃ;

Parosahassa asātarūpanti.

Litta, Teja, Mahāsāra, Vissāsa, Lomahaṃsana, Sudassana, Telapatta, Nāmasiddhi, Kūṭavāṇija, Parosahassa, and Asātarūpa.

Majjhimapaṇṇāsako niṭṭhito.

The Middle Fifty is concluded.

11. Parosatavaggo

11. The Chapter on More Than a Hundred

[101] 1. Parosatajātakavaṇṇanā

[101] 1. The Commentary on the Parosata Jātaka

101.

101.

“Parosatañcepi [V 1.0393][M 1.0435] samāgatānaṃ, jhāyeyyuṃ te vassasataṃ apaññā;

Ekova seyyo puriso sapañño, yo bhāsitassa vijānāti attha”nti. –

“Even if more than a hundred unwise persons were gathered together, they might meditate for a hundred years; yet one wise person is better—he who understands the meaning of what is spoken.”

Idaṃ [P 1.0411] jātakaṃ vatthuto ca veyyākaraṇato ca samodhānato ca parosahassajātakasadisameva. Kevalañhettha “jhāyeyyu”nti padamattameva viseso. Tassattho – vassasatampi apaññā jhāyeyyuṃ olokeyyuṃ upadhāreyyuṃ, evaṃ olokentāpi pana atthaṃ vā kāraṇaṃ vā na passanti, tasmā yo bhāsitassa atthaṃ jānāti, so ekova sapañño seyyoti.

This Jātaka is similar to the Parosahassa Jātaka in terms of its story, its exposition, and its connection of characters. The only difference here is the single word "jhāyeyyuṃ." Its meaning is: Even if the unwise were to meditate, observe, or ponder for a hundred years, they would still not see the meaning or the cause. Therefore, the one who understands the meaning of what is spoken—he alone, being wise, is superior.

Parosatajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Parosata Jātaka, the first.

[102] 2. Paṇṇikajātakavaṇṇanā

[102] 2. The Commentary on the Paṇṇika Jātaka

Yo dukkhaphuṭṭhāya bhaveyya tāṇanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ paṇṇikaṃ upāsakaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthivāsī upāsako nānappakārāni mūlapaṇṇādīni ceva lābukumbhaṇḍādīni ca vikkiṇitvā jīvikaṃ kappeti. Tassekā dhītā abhirūpā pāsādikā ācārasīlasampannā hirottappasamannāgatā kevalaṃ niccappahasitamukhā. Tassā samānakulesu vāreyyatthāya āgatesu so cintesi “imissā vāreyyaṃ vattati, ayañca niccappahasitamukhā. Kumārikādhamme pana asati kumārikāya parakulaṃ gatāya mātāpitūnaṃ garahā hoti, ‘atthi nu kho imissā kumārikādhammo, natthī’ti vīmaṃsissāmi na”nti. So ekadivasaṃ dhītaraṃ pacchiṃ gāhāpetvā paṇṇatthāya araññaṃ gantvā vīmaṃsanavasena kilesasannissito viya hutvā rahassakathaṃ kathetvā taṃ hatthe gaṇhi. Sā gahitamattāva rodantī kandantī “ayuttametaṃ, tāta, udakato aggipātubhāvasadisaṃ, mā evarūpaṃ karothā”ti āha. “Amma, mayā vīmaṃsanatthāya [M 1.0436] tvaṃ hatthe gahitā, na ca kilesavasena. Vadehi, atthi dāni te kumārikādhammo”ti. “Āma, tāta, atthi[V 1.0394]. Mayā hi lobhavasena na koci puriso olokitapubbo”ti. So dhītaraṃ assāsetvā gharaṃ netvā maṅgalaṃ katvā parakulaṃ pesetvā “satthāraṃ vandissāmī”ti gandhamālādihattho jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā pūjetvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi, “cirassamāgatosī”ti ca vutte tamatthaṃ bhagavato ārocesi. Satthā “upāsaka, kumārikā ciraṃ paṭṭhāya ācārasīlasampannāva, tvaṃ pana na idāneva evaṃ vīmaṃsasi, pubbepi vīmaṃsiyevā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

'He who would be a refuge for one afflicted by suffering...' This discourse the Teacher delivered while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a certain lay devotee who was a greengrocer. It is said that this lay devotee, a resident of Savatthi, made his livelihood by selling various kinds of root vegetables, leafy greens, gourds, and the like. He had one daughter who was beautiful, graceful, endowed with good conduct and virtue, possessed of modesty and fear of wrongdoing, and always had a smiling face. When suitors from families of equal status came to ask for her hand, he thought: 'She is of marriageable age, yet she always has a smiling face. If a maiden lacks maidenly virtue, her parents are blamed when she goes to another family. I must investigate whether or not she possesses this maidenly virtue.' So one day, having his daughter take a basket, he went with her to the forest to gather greens. For the purpose of investigation, pretending to be overcome by defilements, he spoke to her in private and took her by the hand. As soon as he took her hand, she began to weep and cry out, saying: 'Father, this is improper! It is like fire emerging from water. Do not do such a thing!' 'My dear,' he said, 'I took your hand only to test you, not out of defilement. Now tell me, do you possess your maidenly virtue?' 'Yes, father, I do. I have never looked upon any man with desire.' Reassuring his daughter, he brought her home, arranged the wedding, and sent her to her husband’s family. Then, thinking, 'I will pay homage to the Teacher,' he went to Jetavana with perfumes and garlands in hand. After venerating and honoring the Teacher, he sat to one side. When the Teacher said, 'It has been long since you came,' he related the matter to the Blessed One. The Teacher said: 'Lay devotee, the maiden has long been endowed with good conduct and virtue. It is not only now that you have tested her; you have tested her in the past as well.' And being requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto [P 1.0412] araññe rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Atheko bārāṇasiyaṃ paṇṇikaupāsakoti atītavatthu paccuppannasadisameva. Tena pana sā vīmaṃsanatthāya hatthe gahitamattā paridevamānā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a forest. At that time, there was a lay devotee in Benares who was a greengrocer. The story of the past is the same as the present one. When her father took her by the hand for the purpose of testing her, she lamented and spoke this verse:

102.

102.

“Yo dukkhaphuṭṭhāya bhaveyya tāṇaṃ, so me pitā dubbhi vane karoti;

Sā kassa kandāmi vanassa majjhe, yo tāyitā so sahasaṃ karotī”ti.

“He who should be a refuge for one afflicted by suffering—that father of mine—acts wrongly in the forest. I, in the midst of the forest, to whom shall I cry? He who should be my protector now commits violence.”

Tattha yo dukkhaphuṭṭhāya bhaveyya tāṇanti kāyikacetasikehi dukkhehi phuṭṭhāya tāyitā paritāyitā patiṭṭhā bhaveyya. So me pitā dubbhi vane karotīti so mayhaṃ dukkhaparitāyako pitāva imasmiṃ vane evarūpaṃ mittadubbhi kammaṃ karoti, attano jātāya dhītari vītikkamaṃ kātuṃ maññatīti attho. Sā kassa kandāmīti kassa rodāmi, ko me patiṭṭhā bhavissatīti dīpeti. Yo tāyitā so sahasaṃ karotīti yo mayhaṃ tāyitā rakkhitā avassayo bhavituṃ arahati, so pitāyeva sāhasikakammaṃ karotīti attho.

Herein, He who should be a refuge for one afflicted by suffering means: he who should be a protector, a guardian, a support for one afflicted by bodily and mental suffering. That father of mine acts wrongly in the forest means: that very father, my protector from suffering, commits such an act of treachery against a friend in this forest, intending to transgress against his own daughter. I... to whom shall I cry? means: she indicates, 'To whom shall I weep? Who will be my support?' He who should be my protector now commits violence means: he who ought to be my protector, my guardian, my refuge—that very father—is committing a violent act.

Atha naṃ pitā assāsetvā “amma, rakkhitattāsī”ti pucchi. “Āma, tāta rakkhito me attā”ti. So taṃ gharaṃ netvā maṇḍetvā maṅgalaṃ katvā parakulaṃ pesesi.

Then her father consoled her and asked, “My dear, have you guarded yourself?” “Yes, father, I have guarded myself,” she replied. So he took her home, adorned her, performed the wedding ceremony, and sent her to her husband's family.

Satthā [M 1.0437] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne upāsako sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse and revealed the Truths, connected the birth story. At the conclusion of the discourse on the Truths, the lay devotee was established in the fruit of stream-entry.

Tadā [V 1.0395] pitā etarahi pitāva, dhītā ca etarahi dhītāva, taṃ kāraṇaṃ paccakkhato diṭṭharukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosinti.
