The father at that time was the present father, and the daughter was the present daughter. The tree deity who witnessed that event firsthand was none other than myself.

Paṇṇikajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Paṇṇika Jātaka, the Second.

[103] 3. Verijātakavaṇṇanā

[103] 3. The Commentary on the Veri Jātaka

Yattha verī nivisatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Anāthapiṇḍiko kira bhogagāmaṃ gantvā āgacchanto antarāmagge core disvā “antarāmagge vasituṃ na yuttaṃ, sāvatthimeva gamissāmī”ti vegena goṇe pājetvā sāvatthimeva [P 1.0413] āgantvā punadivase vihāraṃ gato satthu etamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “pubbepi gahapati paṇḍitā antarāmagge core disvā antarā avilambamānā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gamiṃsū”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“Where an enemy dwells...” This discourse the Teacher delivered while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning Anathapindika. It is said that Anathapindika, while returning from a journey to a revenue village, saw robbers on the road. Thinking, “It is not proper to stay on the road; I will go directly to Savatthi,” he quickly urged his oxen onward and returned to Savatthi. The next day, he went to the monastery and related this matter to the Teacher. The Teacher said: “Householder, in the past as well, wise men, upon seeing robbers on the road, did not linger on the way but went straight to their own dwelling place.” And being requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mahāvibhavo seṭṭhi hutvā ekaṃ gāmakaṃ nimantanaṃ bhuñjanatthāya gantvā paccāgacchanto antarāmagge core disvā antarāmagge avasitvāva vegena goṇe pājento attano gehameva āgantvā nānaggarasehi bhuñjitvā mahāsayane nisinno “corānaṃ hatthato muccitvā nibbhayaṭṭhānaṃ attano gehaṃ āgatomhī”ti udānavasena imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a merchant of great wealth. He had gone to a small village to partake of an invited meal. On his way back, seeing robbers on the road, he did not stop on the way but quickly drove his oxen and came straight to his own house. After enjoying a meal of various excellent flavors, while seated on his great couch, he uttered this verse as an exclamation of joy: “Having escaped from the hands of robbers, I have come to my own home, a place of safety!”

103.

103.

“Yattha verī nivisati, na vase tattha paṇḍito;

Ekarattaṃ dirattaṃ vā, dukkhaṃ vasati verisū”ti.

“Where an enemy dwells, a wise person should not stay. For a night or for two, one dwells in misery among enemies.”

Tattha verīti veracetanāsamaṅgipuggalo. Nivisatīti patiṭṭhāti. Na vase tattha paṇḍitoti so verīpuggalo yasmiṃ ṭhāne patiṭṭhito hutvā vasati, tattha paṇḍito paṇḍiccena samannāgato na vaseyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Ekarattaṃ dirattaṃ vā, dukkhaṃ vasati verisūti, verīnañhi antare vasanto ekāhampi dvīhampi dukkhameva vasatīti attho.

Herein, verī means a person endowed with hostile intent. Nivisati means establishes himself. A wise person should not stay there means: in whatever place that hostile person has established himself and dwells, a person endowed with wisdom should not stay. Why is that? For a night or for two, one dwells in misery among enemies means: for one dwelling among enemies, even for one day or for two, dwells only in misery.

Evaṃ [M 1.0438] mahāsatto udānaṃ udānetvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, the Great Being, having uttered this joyful exclamation and performed meritorious deeds such as giving, passed away according to his deeds.

Satthā [V 1.0396] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ahameva bārāṇasiseṭṭhi ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the Jātaka, saying, "At that time, I myself was the wealthy merchant of Varanasi."

Verijātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Verija Jātaka, the Third.

[104] 4. Mittavindakajātakavaṇṇanā

[104] 4. The Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka

Catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu heṭṭhā mittavindakajātake vuttanayena vitthāretabbaṃ. Idaṃ pana jātakaṃ kassapabuddhakālikaṃ. Tasmiñhi [P 1.0414] kāle uracakkaṃ ukkhipitvā niraye paccamāno eko nerayikasatto “bhante, kiṃ nu kho pāpakammaṃ akāsi”nti bodhisattaṃ pucchi. Bodhisatto “tayā idañcidañca pāpakammaṃ kata”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

“With four, he gained eight”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who was difficult to instruct. The story should be elaborated in the manner told in the Mittavindaka Jātaka below. This Jātaka, however, pertains to the time of Kassapa Buddha. At that time, a certain being in hell, who was being tormented while carrying a wheel on his chest, asked the Bodhisatta, “Venerable sir, what evil deed did I commit?” The Bodhisatta, intending to say, “You committed such and such evil deeds,” spoke this verse:

104.

104.

“Catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamā, aṭṭhāhipi ca soḷasa;

Soḷasāhi ca bāttiṃsa, atricchaṃ cakkamāsado;

Icchāhatassa posassa, cakkaṃ bhamati matthake”ti.

“From four you gained eight; and from eight, sixteen; and from sixteen, thirty-two. Being excessively greedy, you have come upon the wheel. Upon the head of a person struck by craving, the wheel spins.”

Tattha catubbhi aṭṭhajjhagamāti samuddantare catasso vimānapetiyo labhitvā tāhi asantuṭṭho atricchatāya parato gantvā aparā aṭṭha adhigatosīti attho. Sesapadadvayepi eseva nayo. Atricchaṃ cakkamāsadoti evaṃ sakalābhena asantuṭṭho atra atra icchanto parato parato lābhaṃ patthento idāni cakkamāsado idaṃ uracakkaṃ pattosi. Tassa te evaṃ icchāhatassa posassa taṇhāya hatassa upahatassa tava cakkaṃ bhamati matthake. Pāsāṇacakkaṃ, ayacakkanti imesu dvīsu khuradhāraṃ ayacakkaṃ tassa matthake punappunaṃ patanavasena bhamantaṃ disvā evamāha. Vatvā ca pana attano devalokameva gato. Sopi nerayikasatto attano pāpe khīṇe yathākammaṃ gato.

Here, “from four you gained eight” means that, having obtained four female spirits in celestial mansions amidst the ocean, and being dissatisfied with them, you went further out of excessive greed and obtained another eight. The same principle applies to the remaining two phrases. “Being excessively greedy, you have come upon the wheel” means that, being unsatisfied with all your gains, desiring this and that, and seeking more and more gain, you have now come upon the wheel, you have attained this chest-wheel. For you, a person thus struck by craving, harmed and afflicted by desire, the wheel spins upon your head. He spoke thus having seen the razor-edged iron wheel—as distinct from a stone wheel—spinning as it repeatedly fell upon his head. Having spoken, he went to his own celestial world. That hell-being, too, when his evil deeds were exhausted, went according to his karma.

Satthā [M 1.0439] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mittavindako dubbacabhikkhu ahosi, devaputto pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth story: “At that time, Mittavindaka was the stubborn monk, and the son of a deity was myself.”

Mittavindakajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Mittavindaka Jātaka, the Fourth.

[105] 5. Dubbalakaṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā

[105] 5. The Commentary on the Dubbalakaṭṭha Jātaka.

Bahumpetaṃ [V 1.0397] vane kaṭṭhanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ uttasitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthivāsī eko kulaputto satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā pabbajitvā maraṇabhīruko ahosi, rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānesu vātassa vā vījantassa sukkhadaṇḍakassa vā patantassa pakkhicatuppadānaṃ vā saddaṃ sutvā maraṇabhayatajjito mahāravaṃ ravanto palāyati. Tassa hi “maritabbaṃ mayā”ti satimattampi natthi. Sace hi so “ahaṃ marissāmī”ti jāneyya, na maraṇaṃ bhāyeyya. Maraṇassatikammaṭṭhānassa pana tassa abhāvitattāva bhāyati[P 1.0415]. Tassa so maraṇabhīrukabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo jāto.

“Much wood is broken in the forest”—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain frightened monk. It seems that he was a man of good family from Sāvatthī who, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, went forth, but became fearful of death. At night or by day, in places where he stayed, whenever he heard the sound of the wind blowing, or a dry twig falling, or the sound of birds and animals, he would be terrified by the fear of death, cry out loudly, and flee. For him, there was not even the slightest mindfulness, “I must die.” If he had known, “I will die,” he would not have feared death. But because he had not cultivated the meditation on mindfulness of death, he was afraid. His being fearful of death became well known among the Saṅgha of monks.

Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu maraṇabhīruko maraṇaṃ bhāyati, bhikkhunā nāma ‘avassaṃ mayā maritabba’nti maraṇassatikammaṭṭhānaṃ bhāvetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte taṃ bhikkhuṃ pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ maraṇabhīruko”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “bhikkhave, mā etassa bhikkhuno anattamanā hotha, nāyaṃ idāneva maraṇabhīruko, pubbepi maraṇabhīrukoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day, in the Dhamma hall, the monks started a discussion: “Friends, a certain monk is afraid of death, he fears death. A monk should develop the meditation on mindfulness of death, thinking, ‘I must surely die.’” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, what is the topic of discussion you are assembled here for now?” When they replied, “This one,” he had that monk summoned and asked, “Is it true that you are afraid of death?” When he said, “It is true, Venerable Sir,” the Teacher said, “Monks, do not be displeased with this monk. He is not only now afraid of death; he was afraid of death in the past as well.” And he brought forth a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto himavante rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tasmiṃ kāle bārāṇasirājā attano maṅgalahatthiṃ āneñjakāraṇaṃ sikkhāpetuṃ hatthācariyānaṃ adāsi. Taṃ āḷāne niccalaṃ bandhitvā tomarahatthā manussā parivāretvā āneñjakāraṇaṃ kārenti. So taṃ kāraṇaṃ kāriyamāno vedanaṃ adhivāsetuṃ asakkonto āḷānaṃ bhinditvā manusse palāpetvā himavantaṃ [M 1.0440] pāvisi. Manussā taṃ gahetuṃ asakkontā nivattiṃsu. So tattha maraṇabhīruko ahosi, vātasaddāni sutvā kampamāno maraṇabhayatajjito soṇḍaṃ vidhunitvā vegena palāyati, āḷāne bandhitvā āneñjakāraṇaṃ karaṇakālo viyassa hoti, kāyassādaṃ vā cittassādaṃ vā alabhanto kampamāno vicarati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in the Himalayas. At that time, the king of Benares gave his auspicious elephant to elephant trainers to train it in stillness. They tied it firmly to its post, surrounded it with men holding javelins, and began the training in stillness. Unable to endure the pain, the elephant broke its post, made the men flee, and fled into the Himalayas. The men, unable to catch it, turned back. There, it became fearful of death. Hearing the sounds of the wind, it would tremble, terrified by the fear of death, shake its trunk, and flee swiftly, as if it were being trained in stillness while tied to its post. It found no enjoyment of body or mind, and wandered about trembling.

Rukkhadevatā taṃ disvā khandhaviṭape ṭhatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing this, the tree deity, standing on a branch of the tree, spoke this verse:

105.

105.

“Bahumpetaṃ [V 1.0398] vane kaṭṭhaṃ, vāto bhañjati dubbalaṃ;

Tassa ce bhāyasi nāga, kiso nūna bhavissasī”ti.

“The wind breaks much weak wood in the forest; if you fear the sound of that, O elephant, you will surely become emaciated.”

Tatthāyaṃ piṇḍattho – yaṃ etaṃ dubbalaṃ kaṭṭhaṃ puratthimādibhedo vāto bhañjati, taṃ imasmiṃ vane bahuṃ sulabhaṃ, tattha tattha saṃvijjati. Sace tvaṃ tassa bhāyasi, evaṃ sante niccaṃ bhīto maṃsalohitakkhayaṃ patvā kiso nūna bhavissasi, imasmiṃ pana vane tava bhayaṃ nāma natthi, tasmā ito paṭṭhāya mā bhāyīti.

Here is the collected meaning: That weak wood which the wind from the east and other directions breaks is abundant and easily found in this forest; it exists here and there. If you fear that, then being constantly afraid, you will waste away in flesh and blood and surely become emaciated. But in this forest, there is no danger for you. Therefore, from now on, do not be afraid.

Evaṃ [P 1.0416] devatā tassa ovādaṃ adāsi, sopi tato paṭṭhāya nibbhayo ahosi.

Thus the deity gave him advice, and from that time on he was fearless.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā nāgo ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the truths, and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruition of stream-entry. “At that time, this monk was the elephant, and the tree deity was myself.”

Dubbalakaṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The explanation of the Dubbalakaṭṭha Jātaka, the fifth.

[106] 6. Udañcanījātakavaṇṇanā

The explanation of the Udañcanī Jātaka.

Sukhaṃ vata maṃ jīvantanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto thullakumārikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Vatthu terasakanipāte cūḷanāradakassapajātake (jā. 1.13.40 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Taṃ pana bhikkhuṃ satthā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhitosī”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhagavā”ti vutte “kattha te cittaṃ paṭibaddha”nti pucchi. So “ekissā thullakumārikāyā”ti āha. Atha [M 1.0441] naṃ satthā “ayaṃ te bhikkhu anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ etaṃ nissāya sīlabyasanaṃ patvā kampanto vicaramāno paṇḍite nissāya sukhaṃ labhī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Happily indeed I was living”—the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk enticed by a plump young maiden. The story will appear in the thirteenth book in the Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka. Then the Teacher asked that monk, “Is it true, bhikkhu, that you are discontented?” When he replied, “It is true, Blessed One,” the Teacher inquired, “To what is your mind attached?” He answered, “To a certain plump young maiden.” Then the Teacher said to him, “This woman, bhikkhu, is harmful to you. In the past, too, relying on her, you fell into moral ruin and wandered about trembling. It was by relying on the wise that you obtained happiness.” Having said this, he brought forth a past story.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārenteti atītavatthupi cūḷanāradakassapajātakeyeva āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana bodhisatto sāyaṃ phalāphale ādāya āgantvā paṇṇasālādvāraṃ vivaritvā pavisitvā puttaṃ cūḷatāpasaṃ etadavoca “tāta, tvaṃ aññesu divasesu dārūni āharasi, pānīyaṃ paribhojanīyaṃ āharasi, aggiṃ karosi, ajja pana ekampi akatvā kasmā [V 1.0399] dummukho pajjhāyanto nipannosī”ti? “Tāta, tumhesu phalāphalatthāya gatesu ekā itthī āgantvā maṃ palobhetvā ādāya gantuṃ ārabhi, ahaṃ pana ‘tumhehi vissajjito gamissāmī’ti na gacchiṃ, asukaṭṭhāne pana naṃ nisīdāpetvā āgatomhi, idāni gacchāmahaṃ tātā”ti. Bodhisatto “na sakkā etaṃ nivattetu”nti ñatvā “tena hi, tāta, gaccha, esā pana taṃ netvā yadā macchamaṃsādīni [P 1.0417] vā khāditukāmā bhavissati, sappiloṇataṇḍulādīhi vā panassā attho bhavissati, tadā ‘idañcidañcāharā’ti taṃ kilamessati. Tadā mayhaṃ guṇaṃ saritvā palāyitvā idheva āgaccheyyāsī”ti vissajjesi. So tāya saddhiṃ manussapathaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ sā attano vasaṃ gametvā “maṃsaṃ āhara, macchaṃ āharā”ti yena yena atthikā hoti, taṃ taṃ āharāpeti. Tadā so “ayaṃ maṃ attano dāsaṃ viya kammakāraṃ viya ca katvā pīḷetī”ti palāyitvā pitu santikaṃ āgantvā pitaraṃ vanditvā ṭhitakova imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares—this past story will also appear in the Cūḷanāradakassapa Jātaka. At that time, the Bodhisatta, having gathered fruits in the evening, returned, opened the door of the leaf-hut, entered, and said to his son, the young ascetic: “Dear son, on other days you bring firewood, fetch drinking water and water for use, and make the fire, but today, without doing even one thing, why are you lying down, dejected and brooding?” “Father, while you had gone to gather fruits, a certain woman came and, enticing me, tried to take me away. But I said, ‘I will go only when dismissed by you,’ and did not go. Instead, I made her sit in a certain place and have come back. Now, father, I will go.” The Bodhisatta, knowing that he could not be turned back, said, “Very well, dear son, go. But when she takes you away and desires to eat fish or meat, or when she needs ghee, salt, rice, and the like, she will weary you, saying, ‘Bring this and that.’ Then, remembering my virtue, escape and return here.” He then dismissed him. The young ascetic went with her along the path of humans. Then, having brought him under her control, she made him fetch whatever she desired, saying, “Bring meat, bring fish.” Then he thought, “She treats me like a slave or a laborer, tormenting me.” So he fled and returned to his father. Having paid respects to his father, he stood and spoke this verse:

106.

106.

“Sukhaṃ vata maṃ jīvantaṃ, pacamānā udañcanī;

Corī jāyappavādena, telaṃ loṇañca yācatī”ti.

“Happily indeed I was living, but this tormenting water-pot, this thief, under the pretext of being a wife, demands oil and salt.”

Tattha sukhaṃ vata maṃ jīvantanti tāta, tumhākaṃ santike maṃ sukhaṃ jīvantaṃ. Pacamānāti tāpayamānā pīḷayamānā, yaṃ yaṃ vā khāditukāmā hoti, taṃ taṃ pacamānā. Udakaṃ añcanti etāyāti udañcanī, cāṭito vā kūpato vā udakaussiñcanaghaṭikāyetaṃ nāmaṃ. Sā pana udañcanī viya, udakaṃ viya ghaṭikā, yena yenatthikā hoti, taṃ taṃ ākaḍḍhatiyevāti attho[M 1.0442]. Corī jāyappavādenāti “bhariyā”ti nāmena ekā corī maṃ madhuravacanena upalāpetvā tattha netvā telaṃ loṇañca yañca aññaṃ icchati, taṃ sabbaṃ yācati, dāsaṃ viya kammakāraṃ viya ca katvā āharāpetīti tassā aguṇaṃ kathesi.

Herein, Happily indeed I was living means: me, who was living happily in your presence, father. Pacamānā means tormenting, oppressing; or, whatever she wishes to eat, she makes him cook. Udañcanī is that by which water is drawn up; it is the name for a small pot for drawing water from a large jar or a well. She is like a water-pot; just as a pot draws water, so she draws out whatever she needs—this is the meaning. A thief under the pretext of being a wife means: a certain thief, using the name “wife,” enticed me with sweet words, took me there, and demands oil, salt, and whatever else she desires. She makes me fetch things like a slave or a hired laborer. Thus he spoke of her faults.

Atha naṃ bodhisatto assāsetvā “hotu, tāta, ehi tvaṃ mettaṃ bhāvehi, karuṇaṃ bhāvehī”ti cattāro brahmavihāre ācikkhi, ācikkhitvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ ācikkhi. So na cirasseva abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca uppādetvā brahmavihāre bhāvetvā saddhiṃ pitarā brahmaloke nibbatti.

Then the Bodhisatta comforted him, saying, “So be it, dear son. Come, cultivate loving-kindness, cultivate compassion.” He taught him the four divine abidings, and having taught these, he instructed him in the preliminary kasiṇa exercises. Not long after, the young ascetic developed the higher knowledges and meditative attainments, cultivated the divine abidings, and was reborn in the Brahma-world together with his father.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the truths, and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the truths, that bhikkhu was established in the fruition of stream-entry.

“Tadā [V 1.0400] thullakumārikāva etarahi thullakumārikā. Cūḷatāpaso ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu ahosi, pitā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

“The plump young maiden at that time was this plump young maiden now. The young ascetic was the discontented bhikkhu, and the father was myself.”

Udañcanījātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The explanation of the Udañcanī Jātaka, the sixth.

[107] 7. Sālittakajātakavaṇṇanā

The explanation of the Sālittaka Jātaka.

Sādhū [P 1.0418] kho sippakaṃ nāmāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ haṃsapaharanakaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kireko sāvatthivāsī kulaputto sālittakasippe nipphattiṃ patto. “Sālittakasippa”nti sakkharākhipanasippaṃ vuccati. So ekadivasaṃ dhammaṃ sutvā sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajitvā upasampadaṃ labhi, na pana sikkhākāmo, na paṭipattisādhako ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ ekaṃ daharabhikkhuṃ ādāya aciravatiṃ gantvā nhāyitvā nadītīre aṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ samaye dve setahaṃsā ākāsena gacchanti. So taṃ daharaṃ āha “imaṃ pacchimahaṃsaṃ sakkharāya akkhimhi paharitvā pādamūle pātemī”ti. Itaro “kathaṃ pātessasi, na sakkhissasi paharitu”nti āha. Itaro “tiṭṭhatu tāvassa orato akkhi, parato akkhimhi taṃ paharāmī”ti. Idāni pana tvaṃ asantaṃ kathesīti. “Tena hi upadhārehī”ti ekaṃ tikhiṇasakkharaṃ gahetvā aṅguliyā pariyante katvā tassa [M 1.0443] haṃsassa pacchato khipi. Sā “ru”nti saddaṃ akāsi, haṃso “parissayena bhavitabba”nti nivattitvā saddaṃ sotuṃ ārabhi. Itaro tasmiṃ khaṇe ekaṃ vaṭṭasakkharaṃ gahetvā tassa nivattitvā olokentassa parabhāge akkhiṃ pahari. Sakkharā itarampi akkhiṃ vinivijjhitvā gatā. Haṃso mahāravaṃ ravanto pādamūleyeva pati. Tato tato bhikkhū āgantvā garahitvā “ananucchavikaṃ te kata”nti satthu santikaṃ netvā “bhante, iminā idaṃ nāma kata”nti tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Satthā taṃ bhikkhuṃ garahitvā “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa etasmiṃ sippe kusalo, pubbepi kusaloyeva ahosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Indeed, skill is good.” The Teacher told this story while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a monk who struck geese with pellets. It is said that this monk, a clansman from Sāvatthī, had attained mastery in the 'sālittaka craft.' The 'sālittaka craft' is called the skill of throwing pellets. One day, after hearing the Dhamma, he dedicated himself to the Dispensation, went forth, and received the full ordination. But he had no desire for the training, nor was he diligent in the practice. One day, taking a certain young monk with him, he went to the Aciravatī River, bathed, and stood on the riverbank. At that time, two white geese were flying through the sky. He said to that young monk, “I will strike that rear goose in the eye with a pellet and make it fall at our feet.” The other replied, “How will you make it fall? You will not be able to strike it.” He said, “Let alone the eye on this side; I will strike it in the eye on the far side.” “Now you are speaking what is not true.” “Then observe!” Taking a sharp pellet and placing it on the tip of his finger, he threw it behind that goose. It made a “ru” sound. The goose, thinking, “There must be danger!” turned back and began to listen for the sound. At that moment, he took a round pellet and struck the eye on the far side as it turned back to look. The pellet pierced through that eye and the other eye as well. The goose, crying out loudly, fell right at their feet. Monks came from here and there, reproached him, saying, “What you have done is improper!” and led him to the Teacher. “Venerable sir, this monk has done such a thing,” they reported the matter. The Teacher rebuked that monk and said, “Monks, not only now is he skilled in this craft, but he was skilled in the past as well.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa amacco ahosi. Tasmiṃ kāle rañño purohito atimukharo hoti bahubhāṇī, tasmiṃ kathetuṃ āraddhe aññe okāsameva na labhanti. Rājā cintesi “kadā nu kho etassa vacanupacchedakaṃ kañci labhissāmī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya tathārūpaṃ ekaṃ upadhārento vicarati. Tasmiṃ kāle bārāṇasiyaṃ eko pīṭhasappī sakkharākhipanasippe nipphattiṃ patto hoti. Gāmadārakā taṃ rathakaṃ āropetvā [V 1.0401] ākaḍḍhamānā bārāṇasinagaradvāramūle [P 1.0419] eko viṭapasampanno mahānigrodho atthi, tattha ānetvā samparivāretvā kākaṇikādīni datvā “hatthirūpakaṃ kara, assarūpakaṃ karā”ti vadanti. So sakkharā khipitvā khipitvā nigrodhapaṇṇesu nānārūpāni dasseti, sabbāni paṇṇāni chiddāvachiddāneva ahesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was his minister. At that time, the king’s chaplain was extremely garrulous and talkative; when he began to speak, others received no opportunity at all. The king thought, “When, indeed, shall I find someone to cut off his speech?” From that day on, he went about looking for such a person. At that time, in Bārāṇasī, a certain cripple had attained mastery in the art of throwing pellets. The village boys would place him on a small cart, and pulling him along, they would bring him to a great banyan tree, endowed with many branches, that stood near the city gate of Bārāṇasī. There, they would surround him, give him small coins and the like, and say, “Make an elephant shape! Make a horse shape!” Throwing pellet after pellet, he would create various shapes on the banyan leaves, and all the leaves became riddled with holes, large and small.

Atha bārāṇasirājā uyyānaṃ gacchanto taṃ ṭhānaṃ pāpuṇi. Ussāraṇābhayena sabbe dārakā palāyiṃsu, pīṭhasappī tattheva nipajji. Rājā nigrodhamūlaṃ patvā rathe nisinno pattānaṃ chiddatāya chāyaṃ kabarakabaraṃ disvā olokento sabbesaṃ pattānaṃ chiddabhāvaṃ disvā “kenetāni evaṃ katānī”ti pucchi. “Pīṭhasappinā, devā”ti. Rājā “imaṃ nissāya brāhmaṇassa vacanupacchedaṃ kātuṃ sakkā bhavissatī”ti cintetvā “kahaṃ, bhaṇe, pīṭhasappī”ti pucchi. Vicinantā mūlantare nipannaṃ disvā “ayaṃ, devā”ti āhaṃsu. Rājā naṃ pakkosāpetvā parisaṃ ussāretvā pucchi “amhākaṃ santike eko mukharabrāhmaṇo atthi, sakkhissasi taṃ nissaddaṃ kātu”nti. Nāḷimattā ajalaṇḍikā labhanto sakkhissāmi, devāti. Rājā pīṭhasappiṃ gharaṃ netvā antosāṇiyaṃ nisīdāpetvā sāṇiyaṃ chiddaṃ kāretvā brāhmaṇassa chiddābhimukhaṃ [M 1.0444] āsanaṃ paññapetvā nāḷimattā sukkhā ajalaṇḍikā pīṭhasappissa santike ṭhapāpetvā brāhmaṇaṃ upaṭṭhānakāle āgataṃ tasmiṃ āsane nisīdāpetvā kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesi. Brāhmaṇo aññesaṃ okāsaṃ adatvā raññā saddhiṃ kathetuṃ ārabhi. Athassa so pīṭhasappī sāṇicchiddena ekekaṃ ajalaṇḍikaṃ pacchiyaṃ pavesento viya tālutalamhiyeva pāteti, brāhmaṇo āgatāgataṃ nāḷiyaṃ telaṃ pavesento viya gilati, sabbā parikkhayaṃ gamiṃsu. Tassetā nāḷimattā ajalaṇḍikā kucchiṃ paviṭṭhā aḍḍhāḷhakamattā ahesuṃ.

Then, the king of Bārāṇasī, while going to the park, arrived at that place. Fearing the clearing of the crowd, all the boys ran away, but the cripple lay right there. The king, having reached the foot of the banyan tree, while still seated in his chariot, saw the dappled shade caused by the perforated leaves. Looking up and seeing that all the leaves were perforated, he asked, “By whom was this done?” “By the cripple, Your Majesty.” The king thought, “Relying on this man, it should be possible to cut short the brahmin’s speech,” and he asked, “Tell me, where is the cripple?” Searching, they saw him lying among the roots and said, “Here he is, Your Majesty.” The king had him summoned, dismissed his retinue, and asked, “In our court there is a very talkative brahmin. Will you be able to silence him?” “If I can get a nāḷi-measure of dry goat droppings, I will be able, Your Majesty.” The king took the cripple to the palace, had him sit behind a curtain, made a hole in the curtain, and had a seat prepared for the brahmin facing the hole. He had a nāḷi-measure of dry goat droppings placed near the cripple. When the brahmin arrived at the time of attendance, the king had him sit on that seat and initiated a conversation. The brahmin, giving no opportunity to others, began to speak with the king. Then the cripple, through the hole in the curtain, dropped the goat droppings one by one right onto the brahmin’s palate, as if placing them in a basket. The brahmin swallowed each one as it came, as if pouring oil into a tube, until all were gone. That nāḷi-measure of goat droppings, having entered his belly, amounted to half an āḷhaka.

Rājā tāsaṃ parikkhīṇabhāvaṃ ñatvā āha – “ācariya, tumhe atimukharatāya nāḷimattā ajalaṇḍikā gilantā kiñci na jānittha, ito dāni uttari jīrāpetuṃ na sakkhissatha. Gacchatha, piyaṅgudakaṃ pivitvā chaḍḍetvā attānaṃ arogaṃ karothā”ti brāhmaṇo tato paṭṭhāya [P 1.0420] pihitamukho viya hutvā kathentenāpi saddhiṃ akathanasīlo ahosi. Rājā “iminā me kaṇṇasukhaṃ kata”nti pīṭhasappissa satasahassuṭṭhānake catūsu disāsu cattāro gāme adāsi. Bodhisatto rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “deva, sippaṃ nāma loke paṇḍitehi uggahitabbaṃ, pīṭhasappinā sālittakamattenāpi ayaṃ sampatti laddhā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The king, knowing that the droppings were finished, said: “Teacher, due to your excessive talkativeness, you swallowed a nāḷi-measure of dry goat droppings without realizing it. Now you will not be able to digest anything further. Go, drink an emetic of piyaṅgu-water, vomit, and make yourself well.” From that day on, the brahmin became as if his mouth were sealed, and he made it his habit not to speak, even when spoken to. The king, thinking, “This man has brought comfort to my ears,” gave the cripple four villages in the four directions, which yielded a revenue of one hundred thousand. The Bodhisatta approached the king and said, “Your Majesty, in this world a skill should be learned by the wise. This cripple has gained such prosperity with nothing more than the skill of throwing pellets.” Having said this, he spoke this verse:

107.

107.

“Sādhuṃ [V 1.0402] kho sippakaṃ nāma, api yādisa kīdisaṃ;

Passa khañjappahārena, laddhā gāmā catuddisā”ti.

“Indeed, skill is good, of whatever sort it may be; see how, through the cripple’s strike, villages in the four directions were obtained.”

Tattha passa khañjappahārenāti passa, mahārāja, iminā khañjapīṭhasappinā ajalaṇḍikāpahārena catuddisā cattāro gāmā laddhā, aññesaṃ sippānaṃ ko ānisaṃsaparicchedoti sippaguṇaṃ kathesi.

In this regard, ‘See, by the strike of a cripple’ means: ‘See, O great king, how by this cripple moving on a stool, through the striking with goat-dung pellets, four villages in the four directions were gained. What measurement of benefit could there be for other skills?’ Thus, he spoke of the virtue of skill.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā pīṭhasappī ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, rājā ānando, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, this bhikkhu was the cripple, the king was Ānanda, and the wise minister was I myself.”

Sālittakajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Sālittaka Jātaka, the Seventh.

[108] 8. Bāhiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[108] 8. The Commentary on the Bāhiya Jātaka.

Sikkheyya [M 1.0445] sikkhitabbānīti idaṃ satthā vesāliṃ upanissāya mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ viharanto ekaṃ licchaviṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira licchavirājā saddho pasanno buddhappamukhaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ nimantetvā attano nivesane mahādānaṃ pavattesi. Bhariyā panassa thūlaṅgapaccaṅgā uddhumātakanimittasadisā anākappasampannā ahosi. Satthā bhattakiccāvasāne anumodanaṃ katvā vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhūnaṃ ovādaṃ datvā gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, tassa nāma licchavirañño tāva abhirūpassa tādisā bhariyā thūlaṅgapaccaṅgā anākappasampannā, kathaṃ so tāya saddhiṃ abhiramatī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, esa idāneva, pubbepi thūlasarīrāya eva itthiyā saddhiṃ abhiramī”ti vatvā tehi yācito atītaṃ āhari.

“One should train in what should be trained.” The Teacher told this while dwelling in the Kūṭāgāra Hall in the Great Wood near Vesālī, concerning a certain Licchavi. It is said that this Licchavi king, faithful and devoted, invited the Saṅgha of bhikkhus headed by the Buddha and held a great almsgiving in his own residence. However, his wife had thick limbs and stout features, resembling a bloated corpse, and was lacking in grace. After the meal, the Teacher gave his blessing, returned to the monastery, gave advice to the bhikkhus, and entered his perfumed chamber. The bhikkhus in the Dhamma hall started a discussion: “Friends, how can such a handsome Licchavi king enjoy himself with such a wife—one with thick limbs, stout features, and lacking in grace?” The Teacher came and asked, “Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now gathered here?” When told, he said, “Bhikkhus, not only now, but even in the past, he enjoyed himself with a woman of such a large body.” Requested by them, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 1.0421] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tassa amacco ahosi. Athekā janapaditthī thūlasarīrā anākappasampannā bhatiṃ kurumānā rājaṅgaṇassa avidūrena gacchamānā sarīravaḷañjapīḷitā hutvā nivatthasāṭakena sarīraṃ paṭicchādetvā nisīditvā sarīravaḷañjaṃ muñcitvā khippameva uṭṭhāsi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bārāṇasirājā vātapānena rājaṅgaṇaṃ olokento taṃ disvā cintesi “ayaṃ evarūpe aṅgaṇaṭṭhāne sarīravaḷañjaṃ muñcamānā hirottappaṃ [V 1.0403] appahāya nivāsaneneva paṭicchannā hutvā sarīravaḷañjaṃ mocetvā khippaṃ uṭṭhitā, imāya nirogāya bhavitabbaṃ, etissā vatthu visadaṃ bhavissati, visade pana vatthusmiṃ eko putto labbhamāno visado puññavā bhavissati, imaṃ mayā aggamahesiṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti. So tassā apariggahitabhāvaṃ ñatvā āharāpetvā aggamahesiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. Sā tassa piyā ahosi manāpā, na cirasseva ekaṃ puttaṃ vijāyi. So panassā putto cakkavattī rājā ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was his minister. At that time, a certain woman from the countryside, with a large body and lacking elegance, was working for wages. As she walked not far from the royal courtyard, afflicted by a bodily need, she covered herself with her lower garment, sat down, relieved herself, and quickly stood up. At that moment, the king of Benares, looking out from a window onto the royal courtyard, saw her and thought: “This woman, relieving herself in such a public place, did not abandon shame and moral dread, but remained covered by her lower garment, relieved herself, and quickly stood up. She must be free from disease. Her womb must be pure, and if a son is conceived in such a pure womb, he will be pure and meritorious. It is fitting for me to make her my chief queen.” Knowing she was unattached, he had her brought to him and gave her the position of chief queen. She became dear and pleasing to him, and before long, she gave birth to a son. That son of hers became a wheel-turning monarch.

Bodhisatto tassā sampattiṃ disvā tathārūpaṃ vacanokāsaṃ labhitvā “deva, sikkhitabbayuttakaṃ nāma sippaṃ kasmā na sikkhitabbaṃ, yatra hi nāmāyaṃ mahāpuññā hirottappaṃ appahāya paṭicchannākārena sarīravaḷañjaṃ kurumānā tumhe [M 1.0446] ārādhetvā evarūpaṃ sampattiṃ pattā”ti vatvā sikkhitabbayuttakānaṃ sippānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ kathento imaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing her prosperity, the Bodhisatta, having obtained an opportunity to speak, said: “Your Majesty, why should one not learn a skill that is worth learning? For indeed, this woman of great merit, without abandoning shame and moral dread, by performing her bodily function in a covered manner, pleased you and has attained such prosperity.” Then, extolling the virtues of skills worth learning, he spoke this verse:

108.

108.

“Sikkheyya sikkhitabbāni, santi sacchandino janā;

Bāhiyā hi suhannena, rājānamabhirādhayī”ti.

“One should train in what is to be trained in, for there are people with their own inclinations; indeed, the woman from the outer district, by her discreet act, pleased the king.”

Tattha santi sacchandino janāti tesu tesu sippesu sacchandā janā atthiyeva. Bāhiyāti bahijanapade jātā saṃvaḍḍhā itthī. Suhannenāti hirottappaṃ appahāya paṭicchannenākārena hannaṃ suhannaṃ nāma, tena suhannena. Rājānamabhirādhayīti devaṃ abhirādhayitvā imaṃ sampattiṃ pattāti. Evaṃ mahāsatto sikkhitabbayuttakānaṃ sippānaṃ guṇaṃ kathesi.

Herein, ‘there are people with their own inclinations’ means there are indeed people who have an inclination for various crafts. ‘The woman from the outer district’ means a woman born and raised in an outer district. ‘By her discreet act’ means what is done in a covered manner without abandoning shame and moral dread is called a ‘discreet act’; by that discreet act. ‘Pleased the king’ means having pleased the king, she attained this prosperity. Thus, the Great Being described the virtue of the skills that are fitting to be learned.

Satthā [P 1.0422] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jayampatikā etarahipi jayampatikāva, paṇḍitāmacco pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: “The husband and wife at that time are the same husband and wife now, and the wise minister was indeed I myself.”

Bāhiyajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Bāhiya Jātaka, the Eighth.

[109] 9. Kuṇḍakapūvajātakavaṇṇanā

[109] 9. The Commentary on the Kuṇḍakapūva Jātaka.

Yathanno puriso hotīti idaṃ satthā sāvatthiyaṃ viharanto mahāduggataṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi kadāci ekameva kulaṃ buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa dānaṃ deti, kadāci tīṇi cattāri ekato hutvā, kadāci gaṇabandhanena, kadāci vīthisabhāgena, kadāci sakalanagaraṃ chandakaṃ [V 1.0404] saṃharitvā. Tadā pana vīthibhattaṃ nāma ahosi. Atha manussā buddhappamukhassa bhikkhusaṅghassa yāguṃ datvā “khajjakaṃ āharathā”ti āhaṃsu. Tadā paneko paresaṃ bhatikārako duggatamanusso tassaṃ vīthiyaṃ vasamāno cintesi “ahaṃ yāguṃ dātuṃ na sakkhissāmi, khajjakaṃ pana dassāmī”ti saṇhasaṇhaṃ kuṇḍakaṃ vaḍḍhāpetvā udakena temetvā akkapaṇṇena veṭhetvā kukkuḷe pacitvā “idaṃ buddhassa dassāmī”ti taṃ ādāya gantvā satthu santike ṭhito “khajjakaṃ āharathā”ti ekasmiṃ vacane vuttamatte sabbapaṭhamaṃ gantvā taṃ pūvaṃ satthu patte patiṭṭhāpesi, satthā aññehi dīyamānaṃ khajjakaṃ aggahetvā tameva pūvakhajjakaṃ paribhuñji.

This discourse, beginning with the words 'As is the food of a man,' the Teacher related while dwelling at Sāvatthī, concerning a very poor man. For in Sāvatthī, sometimes a single family would give alms to the community of monks headed by the Buddha; sometimes three or four families would join together; sometimes by forming a group; sometimes by street sections; and sometimes the entire city would collect contributions. At that time, there was what was known as a street-meal. Then, the people, having given gruel to the community of monks headed by the Buddha, said, 'Bring the hard food.' Now, at that time, a certain poor man, a hired laborer for others, living on that street, thought: 'I cannot afford to give gruel, but I will give some hard food.' He prepared a fine powder from broken rice, moistened it with water, wrapped it in an `akka` leaf, and baked it in hot ashes. Thinking, 'I will give this to the Buddha,' he took it and went to stand near the Teacher. At the very moment the words 'Bring the hard food' were spoken, he was the very first to go forward and place that cake in the Teacher’s bowl. The Teacher, not accepting the other hard food being offered, partook only of that very cake.

Tasmiṃyeva [M 1.0447] pana khaṇe “sammāsambuddhena kira mahāduggatassa kuṇḍakakhajjakaṃ ajigucchitvā amataṃ viya paribhutta”nti sakalanagaraṃ ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Rājarājamahāmattādayo antamaso dovārike upādāya sabbeva sannipatitvā satthāraṃ vanditvā mahāduggataṃ upasaṅkamitvā “handa bho, sataṃ gahetvā, dve satāni gahetvā, pañca satāni gahetvā amhākaṃ pattiṃ dehī”ti vadiṃsu. So “satthāraṃ paṭipucchitvā jānissāmī”ti satthu santikaṃ gantvā tamatthaṃ ārocesi. Satthā “dhanaṃ gahetvā vā aggahetvā vā sabbasattānaṃ pattiṃ dehī”ti āha. So dhanaṃ gahetuṃ ārabhi. Manussā diguṇacatugguṇaaṭṭhaguṇādivasena dadantā nava hiraññakoṭiyo adaṃsu. Satthā anumodanaṃ katvā vihāraṃ gantvā bhikkhūhi vatte dassite sugatovādaṃ datvā gandhakuṭiṃ pāvisi. Rājā sāyanhasamaye mahāduggataṃ pakkosāpetvā seṭṭhiṭṭhānena pūjesi.

At that very moment, the whole city was in an uproar: 'It is said that the Perfectly Enlightened One, without any disgust, partook of the broken-rice cake of the very poor man as if it were ambrosia!' The king, royal ministers, and others, down to the very gatekeepers, all gathered together. They paid homage to the Teacher and approached the very poor man, saying, 'Come, friend, take a hundred, take two hundred, take five hundred—give us a share of the merit!' He thought, 'I will ask the Teacher and find out,' and going to the Teacher, he reported the matter. The Teacher said, 'Whether you take the wealth or not, give a share of the merit to all beings.' He then began to accept the wealth. People, giving in double, quadruple, and other multiples, gave nine crores of gold. The Teacher, having given a discourse of appreciation, went to the monastery. After the monks had performed their duties for him, he gave the Sugata's advice and entered the Perfumed Chamber. In the evening, the king summoned the very poor man and honored him with the position of a treasurer.

Bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, satthā mahāduggatena dinnaṃ kuṇḍakapūvaṃ ajigucchanto amataṃ viya paribhuñji, mahāduggatopi bahudhanañca seṭṭhiṭṭhānañca [P 1.0423] labhitvā mahāsampattiṃ patto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva mayā ajigucchantena tassa kuṇḍakapūvo paribhutto, pubbepi rukkhadevatāya hutvā paribhuttoyeva, tadāpi cesa maṃ nissāya seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ alatthevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Truth: 'Friends, the Teacher, without disgust, partook of the broken-rice cake given by the very poor man as if it were ambrosia; and that very poor man, having gained great wealth and the position of a treasurer, attained great prosperity.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered together?' When it was said, 'Concerning this topic,' he replied, 'Monks, it is not only now that I partook of his broken-rice cake without disgust. In the past, too, when I was a tree-deity, I partook of it. And on that occasion also, on account of me, he attained the position of a treasurer.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ekasmiṃ ṭhāne eraṇḍarukkhe rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tadā tasmiṃ gāmake manussā devatāmaṅgalikā honti. Athekasmiṃ chaṇe sampatte manussā attano attano rukkhadevatānaṃ balikammaṃ akaṃsu. Atheko duggatamanusso te manusse rukkhadevatā paṭijaggante disvā ekaṃ eraṇḍarukkhaṃ paṭijaggi. Te manussā [V 1.0405] attano attano devatānaṃ nānappakārāni mālāgandhavilepanādīni ceva khajjabhojjāni ca ādāya gacchiṃsu. So pana kuṇḍakapūvañceva uḷuṅkena ca udakaṃ ādāya gantvā eraṇḍarukkhassa avidūre ṭhatvā cintesi “devatā nāma dibbakhajjakāni khādanti, mayhaṃ devatā imaṃ [M 1.0448] kuṇḍakapūvaṃ na khādissati, kiṃ imaṃ akāraṇena nāsemi, ahameva naṃ khādissāmī”ti tatova nivatti. Bodhisatto khandhaviṭape ṭhatvā “bho purisa, sace tvaṃ issaro bhaveyyāsi, mayhaṃ madhurakhajjakaṃ dadeyyāsi. Tvaṃ pana duggato, ahaṃ tava pūvaṃ na khāditvā aññaṃ kiṃ khādissāmi, mā me koṭṭhāsaṃ nāsehī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree-deity in a castor-oil tree in a certain place. At that time, the people in that village were devoted to deities and auspicious rites. When a certain festival arrived, the people made offerings to their respective tree-deities. Then a poor man, seeing those people attending to their tree-deities, also attended to a castor-oil tree. Those people brought various kinds of garlands, perfumes, ointments, and also hard and soft foods to their own deities. But that poor man, taking a broken-rice cake and water in a cup, went and stood not far from the castor-oil tree. He thought, 'Deities eat divine food; my deity will not eat this broken-rice cake. Why should I waste this for no reason? I myself will eat it,' and he turned back from there. The Bodhisatta, standing on a fork of the trunk, said, 'O man, if you were wealthy, you would give me sweet food. But you are poor. If I do not eat your cake, what else shall I eat? Do not destroy my portion!' And he spoke this verse:

109.

109.

“Yathanno puriso hoti, tathannā tassa devatā;

Āharetaṃ kuṇḍapūvaṃ, mā me bhāgaṃ vināsayā”ti.

“As is the food of the man, so is the food of his deity. Bring that broken-rice cake; do not destroy my share.”

Tattha yathannoti yathārūpabhojano hoti. Tathannāti tassa purisassa devatāpi tathārūpabhojanāva hoti. Āharetaṃ kuṇḍapūvanti etaṃ kuṇḍakena pakkapūvaṃ ānehi, mayhaṃ bhāgaṃ mā vināsehīti.

Therein, `yathanno` means: he has food of such a nature. `Tathannā` means: the deity of that man also has food of such a nature. `Āharetaṃ kuṇḍapūvaṃ` means: bring that cake baked with broken rice; do not destroy my share.

So nivattitvā bodhisattaṃ oloketvā balikammamakāsi. Bodhisatto tato ojaṃ paribhuñjitvā “purisa, tvaṃ kimatthaṃ maṃ paṭijaggasī”ti āha. “Duggatomhi, sāmi, taṃ nissāya duggatabhāvato muccitukāmatāya paṭijaggāmī”ti. “Bho purisa, mā [P 1.0424] cintayi, tayā kataññussa katavedino pūjā katā, imaṃ eraṇḍaṃ parikkhipitvā nidhikumbhiyo gīvāya gīvaṃ āhaccaṭhitā. Tvaṃ rañño ācikkhitvā sakaṭehi dhanaṃ āharāpetvā rājaṅgaṇe rāsiṃ kārehi, rājā te tussitvā seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ dassatī”ti vatvā bodhisatto antaradhāyi. So tathā akāsi. Rājāpi tassa seṭṭhiṭṭhānaṃ adāsi. Iti so bodhisattaṃ nissāya mahāsampattiṃ patvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Then, turning back, he looked at the Bodhisatta and made an offering. The Bodhisatta, having consumed the essence from it, asked, "Man, why do you attend upon me?" "I am destitute, lord, and wishing to be freed from destitution by relying on you, I attend upon you." "Good man, do not worry. You have made an offering to one who is grateful and acknowledges kindness. Around this castor oil plant, treasure jars are standing neck to neck. Inform the king, have the wealth brought by carts, and make a heap in the royal courtyard. The king, pleased, will give you the position of a seṭṭhi." Having said this, the Bodhisatta disappeared. The man did as instructed. The king also gave him the position of a seṭṭhi. Thus, relying on the Bodhisatta, he attained great prosperity and passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā duggato etarahi duggatova, eraṇḍarukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: "The destitute man of that time was the same destitute man of today, but the deity of the castor oil tree was none other than myself."

Kuṇḍakapūvajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The ninth, the commentary on the Kuṇḍakapūva Jātaka.

[110] 10. Sabbasaṃhārakapañhajātakavaṇṇanā

[110] 10. The Commentary on the Sabbasaṃhārakapañha Jātaka

Sabbasaṃhārako [V 1.0406] natthīti [M 1.0449] ayaṃ sabbasaṃhārakapañho sabbākārena umaṅgajātake āvi bhavissatīti.

This Sabbasaṃhārakapañha, which begins 'There is no Sabbasaṃhāraka,' will become fully manifest in all its aspects in the Umaṅga Jātaka.

Sabbasaṃhārakapañhajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The tenth, the commentary on the Sabbasaṃhārakapañha Jātaka.

Parosatavaggo ekādasamo.

The eleventh chapter, the Parosata Vagga.

Tassuddānaṃ –

Its summary:

Parosatampi paṇṇikaṃ, verī ca mittavindakaṃ;

Dubbalañca udañcanī, sālittampi ca bāhiyaṃ;

Kuṇḍakapūvasabbasaṃhārakanti.

Parosata, Paṇṇika, Verī, and Mittavindaka; Dubbala and Udañcanī; Sālittaka and Bāhiya; Kuṇḍakapūva and Sabbasaṃhāraka.

12. Haṃcivaggo

12. The Haṃci Chapter

[111] 1. Gadrabhapañhajātakavaṇṇanā

[111] 1. The Commentary on the Gadrabhapañha Jātaka

Haṃci [V 1.0407] tuvaṃ evamaññasīti ayampi gadrabhapañho mahāumaṅgajātakeyeva (jā. 2.22.590 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

This question concerning the ass, beginning with the words 'If you think thus,' will also become manifest in the Great Umaṅga Jātaka.

Gadrabhapañhajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The first, the commentary on the Gadrabhapañha Jātaka.

[112] 2. Amarādevīpañhajātakavaṇṇanā

[112] 2. The Commentary on the Amarādevīpañha Jātaka

Yena sattubilaṅgā cāti ayampi amarādevipañho nāma tattheva āvi bhavissati.

This question of Amarādevī, beginning with the words 'Yena sattubilaṅgā ca,' will also become manifest in that very same place.

Amarādevīpañhajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The second, the commentary on the Amarādevīpañha Jātaka.

[113] 3. Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā

[113] 3. The Commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka

Saddahāsi [M 1.0450] siṅgālassāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi samaye bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ [P 1.0425] sannipatitvā “āvuso, devadattena pañca bhikkhusatāni ādāya gayāsīsaṃ gantvā ‘yaṃ samaṇo gotamo karoti, na so dhammo. Yamahaṃ karomi, ayameva dhammo’ti te bhikkhū attano laddhiṃ gāhāpetvā ṭhānappattaṃ musāvādaṃ katvā saṅghaṃ bhinditvā ekasīmāya dve uposathā katā”ti devadattassa aguṇakathaṃ kathentā nisīdiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva musāvādī, pubbepi musāvādīyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘Saddahāsi siṅgālassa’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at the Bamboo Grove concerning Devadatta. At that time, the bhikkhus, having gathered in the Dhamma hall, were sitting discussing Devadatta’s faults, saying, ‘Venerable sirs, Devadatta, taking five hundred bhikkhus, went to Gayāsīsa and, declaring, “What the ascetic Gotama does is not the Dhamma. What I do is indeed the Dhamma,” made those bhikkhus accept his own view. Having uttered a deliberate falsehood and split the Saṅgha, he performed two Uposatha ceremonies within a single boundary.’ The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you assembled here now?’ When it was said, ‘For this one,’ he said, ‘Bhikkhus, Devadatta is not a liar only now; he was a liar in the past as well,’ and then he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0408] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto susānavane rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tadā bārāṇasiyaṃ nakkhattaṃ ghuṭṭhaṃ ahosi. Manussā “yakkhabalikammaṃ karomā”ti tesu tesu caccararacchādiṭṭhānesu macchamaṃsādīni vippakiritvā kapālakesu bahuṃ suraṃ ṭhapayiṃsu. Atheko siṅgālo aḍḍharattasamaye niddhamanena nagaraṃ pavisitvā macchamaṃsaṃ khāditvā suraṃ pivitvā punnāgagacchantaraṃ pavisitvā yāva aruṇuggamanā niddaṃ okkami. So pabujjhitvā ālokaṃ disvā “idāni nikkhamituṃ na sakkā”ti maggasamīpaṃ gantvā adissamāno nipajjitvā aññe manusse disvāpi kiñci avatvā ekaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ mukhadhovanatthāya gacchantaṃ disvā cintesi “brāhmaṇā nāma dhanalolā honti, imaṃ dhanena palobhetvā yathā maṃ upakacchakantare katvā uttarāsaṅgena paṭicchādetvā nagarā nīharati, tathā karissāmī”ti. So manussabhāsāya “brāhmaṇā”ti āha. So nivattitvā “ko maṃ pakkosatī”ti āha. “Ahaṃ, brāhmaṇā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti. “Brāhmaṇa, mayhaṃ dve kahāpaṇasatāni atthi. Sace maṃ upakacchakantare katvā uttarāsaṅgena paṭicchādetvā yathā na koci passati, tathā nagarā nikkhāmetuṃ sakkosi, tuyhaṃ te kahāpaṇe dassāmī”ti. Brāhmaṇo dhanalobhena “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā taṃ tathā katvā ādāya nagarā nikkhamitvā thokaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ siṅgālo pucchi “kataraṭṭhānaṃ, brāhmaṇā”ti? “Asukaṃ nāmā”ti. “Aññaṃ thokaṃ ṭhānaṃ gacchā”ti. Evaṃ punappunaṃ vadanto mahāsusānaṃ patvā “idha [P 1.0426] maṃ otārehī”ti [M 1.0451] āha. Tattha naṃ otāresi. Atha siṅgālo “tena hi, brāhmaṇa, uttarisāṭakaṃ pattharā”ti āha. So dhanalobhena “sādhū”ti patthari. Atha naṃ “imaṃ rukkhamūlaṃ khaṇāhī”ti pathavikhaṇane yojetvā brāhmaṇassa uttarisāṭakaṃ abhiruyha catūsu kaṇṇesu ca majjhe cāti pañcasu ṭhānesu sarīranissandaṃ pātetvā makkhetvā ceva temetvā ca susānavanaṃ pāvisi. Bodhisatto rukkhaviṭape ṭhatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a tree deity in a charnel-ground forest. At that time, a festival was proclaimed in Benares. People, thinking, ‘Let us make an offering to the yakkhas,’ scattered fish, meat, and other things in various places like crossroads and streets, and placed plenty of liquor in earthenware bowls. Then, a jackal, at midnight, entered the city through a drain, ate the fish and meat, drank the liquor, and entered a thicket of punnaga trees, where he slept until dawn. Upon waking and seeing the light, he thought, ‘Now I cannot leave.’ He went near the road and lay down, remaining unseen. Though he saw other people, he said nothing. But when he saw a brahmin going to wash his face, he thought, ‘Brahmins are greedy for wealth. I will tempt this one with money and have him conceal me under his arm, cover me with his upper robe, and get me out of the city.’ In human speech, he called out, ‘Brahmin!’ The brahmin turned back and asked, ‘Who is calling me?’ ‘It is I, brahmin.’ ‘For what reason?’ ‘Brahmin, I have two hundred coins. If you can conceal me under your arm, cover me with your upper robe so that no one sees me, and get me out of the city, I will give you those coins.’ Greedy for wealth, the brahmin agreed, saying, ‘Very well.’ He did as instructed, took the jackal, and left the city. After going a short distance, the jackal asked him, ‘Brahmin, what place is this?’ ‘It is such-and-such a place.’ ‘Go a little further.’ Repeating this several times, they reached the great charnel ground. The jackal said, ‘Lower me here.’ The brahmin set him down there. Then the jackal said, ‘Now, brahmin, spread out your upper garment.’ Greedy for wealth, the brahmin spread it out. The jackal then said, ‘Dig at the foot of this tree.’ While he set the brahmin to digging the earth, the jackal climbed onto the brahmin's upper garment and, in five places—the four corners and the middle—discharged his bodily waste, smearing and wetting it. Then he entered the charnel-ground forest. Standing on a tree branch, the Bodhisatta spoke this verse:

113.

113.

“Saddahāsi siṅgālassa, surāpītassa brāhmaṇa;

Sippikānaṃ sataṃ natthi, kuto kaṃsasatā duve”ti.

“Do you believe the jackal, O brahmin, who has drunk liquor? He has not a hundred shell-coins, so how could he have two hundred bronze coins?”

Tattha saddahāsīti saddahasi, ayameva vā pāṭho, pattiyāyasīti attho. Sippikānaṃ sataṃ natthīti etassa hi sippikāsatampi natthi. Kuto kaṃsasatā duveti dve kahāpaṇasatāni panassa kuto evāti.

In this regard, ‘saddahāsi’ means ‘do you believe,’ or this is the reading; the meaning is ‘do you have confidence.’ ‘There are not a hundred cowrie shells’ means that for him, there is not even a hundred cowrie shells. ‘Whence two hundred bronze coins?’ means whence indeed could he have two hundred kahāpaṇas?

Bodhisatto [V 1.0409] imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā “gaccha, brāhmaṇa, tava sāṭakaṃ dhovitvā nhāyitvā attano kammaṃ karohī”ti vatvā antaradhāyi. Brāhmaṇo tathā katvā “vañcito vatamhī”ti domanassappatto pakkāmi.

Having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta said, ‘Go, brahmin, wash your robe, bathe, and do your own work.’ Having said this, he vanished. The brahmin, having done so, departed afflicted with sorrow, thinking, ‘Alas, I have been deceived!’

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo devadatto ahosi, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the Jātaka: ‘At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, but the tree-deity was indeed myself.’

Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka, the Third.

[114] 4. Mitacintījātakavaṇṇanā

[114] 4. The Commentary on the Mitacintī Jātaka

Bahucintī appacintīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto dve mahallakatthere ārabbha kathesi. Te kira janapade ekasmiṃ araññāvāse vassaṃ vasitvā “satthu dassanatthāya gacchissāmā”ti pātheyyaṃ sajjetvā “ajja gacchāma, sve gacchāmā”ti māsaṃ atikkāmetvā puna pātheyyaṃ sajjetvā tatheva māsaṃ, puna māsanti evaṃ attano kusītabhāvena ceva nivāsaṭṭhāne ca apekkhāya tayo māse atikkāmetvā [M 1.0452] tato nikkhamma jetavanaṃ gantvā sabhāgaṭṭhāne pattacīvaraṃ paṭisāmetvā satthāraṃ passiṃsu. Atha ne bhikkhū pucchiṃsu “ciraṃ vo, āvuso, buddhupaṭṭhānaṃ akarontānaṃ, kasmā evaṃ cirāyitthā”ti? Te tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Atha nesaṃ so ālasiyakusītabhāvo [P 1.0427] bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo jāto. Dhammasabhāyampi tesaṃ bhikkhūnameva ālasiyabhāvaṃ nissāya kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte te pakkosāpetvā “saccaṃ kira tumhe, bhikkhave, alasā kusītā”ti pucchitvā “saccaṃ, bhante”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevete alasā, pubbepi alasā ceva nivāsaṭṭhāne ca sālayā sāpekkhā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘Bahucintī and Appacintī’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning two elderly theras. It is said that these theras, having spent the rains in a certain forest dwelling in the countryside, thought, ‘We will go to see the Teacher,’ and prepared their provisions. Then, saying, ‘We will go today, we will go tomorrow,’ they let a month pass by. Again they prepared their provisions and similarly let another month pass, and then another month. Thus, due to their own laziness and attachment to their dwelling place, they let three months pass by before setting out. Then they went to Jetavana, put away their bowls and robes in a suitable place, and saw the Teacher. Then the bhikkhus asked them, ‘Friends, it has been a long time since you attended upon the Buddha. Why have you delayed so long?’ They explained the reason. Then their laziness and indolence became known among the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Even in the Dhamma hall, a discussion arose among the bhikkhus based on their laziness. The Teacher arrived and asked, ‘Bhikkhus, with what discussion are you assembled here now?’ When they told him, he summoned those theras and asked, ‘Is it true, bhikkhus, that you are lazy and indolent?’ They replied, ‘It is true, Blessed One.’ The Teacher said, ‘Bhikkhus, it is not only now that these are lazy; in the past too, they were lazy and attached to their dwelling place.’ Then he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bārāṇasinadiyaṃ tayo macchā ahesuṃ, bahucintī, appacintī, mitacintīti tesaṃ nāmāni. Te araññato manussapathaṃ āgamiṃsu. Tattha mitacintī itare dve evamāha “ayaṃ manussapatho nāma sāsaṅko sappaṭibhayo, kevaṭṭā nānappakārāni jālakuminādīni khipitvā macche gaṇhanti, mayaṃ araññameva gacchāmā”ti. Itare dve janā alasatāya ceva āmisagiddhatāya ca “ajja gacchāma, sve gacchāmā”ti tayo [V 1.0410] māse atikkāmesuṃ. Atha kevaṭṭā nadiyaṃ jālaṃ khipiṃsu. Bahucintī ca appacintī ca gocaraṃ gaṇhantā purato gacchanti. Te attano andhabālatāya jālagandhaṃ asallakkhetvā jālakucchimeva pavisiṃsu. Mitacintī pacchato āgacchanto jālagandhaṃ sallakkhetvā tesañca jālakucchiṃ paviṭṭhabhāvaṃ ñatvā “imesaṃ kusītānaṃ andhabālānaṃ jīvitadānaṃ dassāmī”ti cintetvā bahipassena jālakucchiṭṭhānaṃ gantvā jālakucchiṃ phāletvā nikkhantasadiso hutvā udakaṃ āluḷento jālassa purato patitvā puna jālakucchiṃ pavisitvā pacchimabhāgena phāletvā nikkhantasadiso udakaṃ āluḷento pacchimabhāge pati. Kevaṭṭā “macchā jālaṃ phāletvā gatā”ti maññamānā jālakoṭiyaṃ gahetvā ukkhipiṃsu. Te dvepi macchā jālato muccitvā udake patiṃsu. Iti tehi mitacintiṃ nissāya jīvitaṃ laddhaṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there were three fish in the river of Benares; their names were Bahucintī, Appacintī, and Mitacintī. They came from the forest to the domain of humans. There, Mitacintī said to the other two, 'This domain of humans is perilous and fraught with fear. Fishermen cast various kinds of nets and traps to catch fish. Let us return to the forest.' But the other two, due to laziness and greed for food, kept saying, 'We will go today, we will go tomorrow,' and thus three months passed. Then the fishermen cast a net into the river. Bahucintī and Appacintī, seeking food, went ahead. Due to their own blind foolishness, they failed to notice the scent of the net and entered right into the belly of the net. Mitacintī, coming behind, noticed the scent of the net and realized that the other two had entered the belly of the net. Thinking, 'I will give the gift of life to these lazy and foolish ones,' he went to the outside of the net's belly and, acting as if he had broken through and exited, stirred the water and splashed down in front of the net. Then, entering the net's belly again and acting as if he had broken through the back part and exited, he stirred the water and splashed down in the back part. The fishermen, thinking, 'The fish have broken the net and escaped,' grabbed the net by its edges and lifted it. Both fish were freed from the net and fell into the water. Thus, they obtained their lives by relying on Mitacintī.

Satthā [M 1.0453] imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having related this story of the past, as the Fully Enlightened One, spoke this verse:

114.

114.

“Bahucintī [P 1.0428] appacintī, ubho jāle abajjhare;

Mitacintī pamocesi, ubho tattha samāgatā”ti.

Bahucintī and Appacintī, both were caught in the net; Mitacintī set them free, and both were reunited there.

Tattha bahucintīti bahucintanatāya vitakkabahulatāya evaṃladdhanāmo. Itaresupi dvīsu ayameva nayo. Ubho tattha samāgatāti mitacintiṃ nissāya laddhajīvitā tattha udake puna ubhopi janā mitacintinā saddhiṃ samāgatāti attho.

Therein, 'Bahucintī' is so named because of much thinking, because of an abundance of thoughts. The same principle applies to the other two. 'Both were reunited there' means that, having obtained their lives by relying on Mitacintī, both of them were reunited with Mitacintī there in the water; this is the meaning.

Evaṃ satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne mahallakā bhikkhū sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahiṃsu. Tadā bahucintī ca appacintī ca ime dve ahesuṃ, mitacintī pana ahameva ahosinti.

Thus the Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma and revealed the Truths, identified the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, the elderly bhikkhus were established in the fruit of stream-entry. At that time, Bahucintī and Appacintī were these two, but Mitacintī was myself.

Mitacintījātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Mitacintī Jātaka, the Fourth.

[115] 5. Anusāsikajātakavaṇṇanā

[115] 5. The Commentary on the Anusāsika Jātaka

Yāyaññe manusāsatīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ anusāsikaṃ bhikkhuniṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kira sāvatthivāsinī ekā kuladhītā pabbajitvā upasampannakālato paṭṭhāya samaṇadhamme ananuyuttā āmisagiddhā hutvā yattha aññā bhikkhuniyo na gacchanti, tādise [V 1.0411] nagarassa ekadese piṇḍāya carati. Athassā manussā paṇītapiṇḍapātaṃ denti. Sā rasataṇhāya bajjhitvā “sace imasmiṃ padese aññāpi bhikkhuniyo piṇḍāya carissanti, mayhaṃ lābho parihāyissati. Yathā etaṃ padesaṃ aññā nāgacchanti, evaṃ mayā kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti cintetvā bhikkhunūpassayaṃ gantvā “ayye, asukaṭṭhāne caṇḍo hatthī, caṇḍo asso, caṇḍo meṇḍo, caṇḍo kukkuro carati, saparissayaṭṭhānaṃ, mā tattha piṇḍāya caritthā”ti bhikkhuniyo anusāsati. Tassā vacanaṃ sutvā ekā bhikkhunīpi taṃ padesaṃ gīvaṃ parivattetvā na olokesi. Tassā ekasmiṃ divase tasmiṃ padese piṇḍāya carantiyā vegenekaṃ [M 1.0454] gehaṃ pavisantiyā caṇḍo meṇḍako paharitvā ūruṭṭhikaṃ bhindi. Manussā vegena upadhāvitvā dvidhā bhinnaṃ ūruṭṭhikaṃ ekato bandhitvā taṃ bhikkhuniṃ mañcenādāya bhikkhunūpassayaṃ nayiṃsu. Bhikkhuniyo “ayaṃ aññā bhikkhuniyo anusāsitvā sayaṃ tasmiṃ padese carantī ūruṭṭhikaṃ bhindāpetvā āgatā”ti parihāsaṃ akaṃsu. Tampi tāya katakāraṇaṃ na cirasseva bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭaṃ ahosi.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story concerning a certain admonishing bhikkhunī, beginning with 'Yāyaññe manusāsatī.' She was, it is said, a daughter of a good family from Sāvatthī who had gone forth. From the time of her higher ordination, she was not devoted to the duties of a recluse but was greedy for material gains, and she would go for alms in a certain part of the city where other bhikkhunīs did not go. There, people gave her choice almsfood. Bound by craving for flavors, she thought, 'If other bhikkhunīs also go for alms in this area, my gains will diminish. I must act in such a way that others do not come here.' Having thought this, she went to the bhikkhunīs’ residence and admonished them, saying, 'Sisters, in such-and-such a place, a fierce elephant, a fierce horse, a fierce ram, and a fierce dog roam about. It is a dangerous place—do not go there for alms.' Hearing her words, not a single bhikkhunī so much as turned her neck to look toward that area. One day, while that bhikkhunī was going for alms in that very place and hastily entering a house, a fierce ram struck her and broke her thighbone. People quickly rushed over, bound the two pieces of her broken thighbone together, and, carrying the bhikkhunī on a cot, brought her to the bhikkhunīs’ residence. The bhikkhunīs made fun of her, saying, 'After admonishing other bhikkhunīs, she herself went to that place and has now returned with a broken thighbone.' That deed of hers soon became known among the community of bhikkhus.

Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū [P 1.0429] “āvuso, asukā anusāsikā bhikkhunī aññaṃ anusāsitvā sayaṃ tasmiṃ padese caramānā caṇḍena meṇḍakena ūruṃ bhindāpesī”ti tassā aguṇakathaṃ kathesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesā aññe anusāsatiyeva, sayaṃ pana na vattati, niccakālaṃ dukkhameva anubhotī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day in the hall of Dhamma, the bhikkhus were discussing the demerits of that bhikkhunī, saying: 'Friends, that admonishing bhikkhunī, after instructing others, went walking in that very place herself and had her thigh broken by a fierce ram.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Bhikkhus, for what discussion are you now gathered together?' When they replied, 'For this one,' he said, 'Bhikkhus, not only now, but in the past as well, she would instruct others but did not practice accordingly herself; she always experienced suffering.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññe sakuṇayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā vayappatto sakuṇajeṭṭhako hutvā anekasakuṇasahassaparivāro himavantaṃ pāvisi. Tassa tattha vasanakāle ekā caṇḍasakuṇikā mahāvattanimaggaṃ gantvā gocaraṃ gaṇhāti. Sā tattha sakaṭehi patitāni vīhimuggabījādīni labhitvā “yathā idāni imaṃ padesaṃ aññe sakuṇā nāgacchanti, tathā karissāmī”ti cintetvā sakuṇasaṅghassa ovādaṃ deti “vattanimahāmaggo nāma sappaṭibhayo, hatthiassādayo ceva caṇḍagoṇayuttayānādīni ca sañcaranti, sahasā uppatitumpi na sakkā hoti, na tattha gantabba”nti. Sakuṇasaṅgho tassā “anusāsikā”teva nāmaṃ akāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a bird in the forest. When he reached maturity, he became the chief of the birds, and with a retinue of many thousands of birds, he entered the Himalayas. While he was living there, a certain fierce female bird would go to the great cart-track to gather food. There she would find grains of rice, mung beans, and other seeds that had fallen from the carts. She thought, 'I will act in such a way that other birds do not come to this place.' So she gave advice to the flock of birds, saying, 'The great cart-track is a place of danger. Elephants, horses, and the like, as well as vehicles yoked to fierce bulls, travel there. It is not possible to fly up suddenly, so you must not go there.' The flock of birds gave her the name 'The Admonisher.'

Sā ekadivasaṃ vattanimahāmagge carantī atimahāvegena āgacchantassa yānassa saddaṃ sutvā [V 1.0412] nivattitvā oloketvā “dūre tāvā”ti caratiyeva. Atha naṃ yānaṃ vātavegena sīghameva sampāpuṇi, sā uṭṭhātuṃ nāsakkhi, cakkena dvidhā chinditvā gatā. Sakuṇajeṭṭhako sakuṇe samānento taṃ adisvā “anusāsikā na dissati, upadhāretha na”nti āha. Sakuṇā upadhārentā taṃ mahāmagge dvidhā chinnaṃ disvā sakuṇajeṭṭhakassa ārocesuṃ. Sakuṇajeṭṭhako “sā aññā sakuṇikā vāretvā sayaṃ tattha caramānā dvidhā chinnā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

One day, while foraging on the great cart-track, she heard the sound of a vehicle approaching at great speed. Turning to look, she thought, 'It is still far off,' and continued foraging. Then the vehicle, with the speed of the wind, quickly reached her. She was unable to fly up and was cut in two by the wheel. The chief of the birds, while assembling the flock, did not see her and said, 'The Admonisher is not to be seen. Go and find out about her.' The birds investigated, and seeing her cut in two on the great cart-track, they reported it to their chief. The chief of the birds said, 'She, having forbidden the other female birds from going there, went foraging there herself and was cut in two,' and he spoke this verse:

115.

115.

“Yāyaññe [M 1.0455] manusāsati, sayaṃ loluppacārinī;

Sāyaṃ vipakkhikā seti, hatā cakkena sāsikā”ti.

“She who used to advise others, herself behaving greedily and recklessly, now lies with broken wings; the instructress slain by the wheel.”

Tattha [P 1.0430] yāyaññe manusāsatīti yakāro padasandhikaro, yā aññe anusāsatīti attho. Sayaṃ loluppacārinīti attanā loluppacārinī samānā. Sāyaṃ vipakkhikā setīti sā esā vihatapakkhā hutvā mahāmagge sayati. Hatā cakkena sāsikāti yānacakkena hatā sāsikā sakuṇikāti.

Herein, yāyaññe manusāsatī means yā aññe anusāsati, the 'ya' being for euphonic combination. Sayaṃ loluppacārinī means being herself greedy and reckless. Sāyaṃ vipakkhikā seti means this she, having her wings destroyed, lies on the great road. Hatā cakkena sāsikā means the admonishing bird killed by the wheel of a vehicle.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā anusāsikā sakuṇikā ayaṃ anusāsikā bhikkhunī ahosi, sakuṇajeṭṭhako pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection for the birth story: 'At that time, the admonishing female bird was this admonishing bhikkhunī, and the chief of the birds was I myself.'

Anusāsikajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Anusāsika Jātaka is the fifth.

[116] 6. Dubbacajātakavaṇṇanā

[116] 6. The Commentary on the Dubbaca Jātaka

Atikaramakarācariyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ dubbacabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa vatthu navakanipāte gijjhajātake (jā. 1.9.1 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantetvā “bhikkhu na tvaṃ idāneva dubbaco, pubbepi dubbacoyeva. Dubbacabhāveneva paṇḍitānaṃ ovādaṃ akaronto sattippahārena jīvitakkhayaṃ pattosī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story concerning a certain bhikkhu who was difficult to admonish, beginning with 'Atikaramakarācariyā.' The full story concerning him will become clear in the Gijjha Jātaka in the Ninth Nipāta. The Teacher addressed that bhikkhu, saying, 'Bhikkhu, it is not only now that you are difficult to admonish; you were so in the past as well. It was because you were difficult to admonish that you did not follow the advice of the wise and met your death from the blow of a spear.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto laṅghanaṭakayoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā vayappatto paññavā upāyakusalo ahosi. So ekassa laṅghanakassa santike sattilaṅghanasippaṃ sikkhitvā ācariyena saddhiṃ sippaṃ dassento vicarati. Ācariyo panassa catunnaṃyeva [V 1.0413] sattīnaṃ laṅghanasippaṃ jānāti, na pañcannaṃ. So ekadivasaṃ ekasmiṃ gāmake sippaṃ dassento surāmadamatto “pañca sattiyo laṅghissāmī”ti paṭipāṭiyā ṭhapesi. Atha naṃ bodhisatto āha “ācariya, tvaṃ pañcasattilaṅghanasippaṃ na jānāsi, ekaṃ sattiṃ hara. Sace laṅghissasi, pañcamāya sattiyā viddho marissasī”ti. So suṭṭhu mattatāya “tvañhi mayhaṃ pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī”ti tassa vacanaṃ anādiyitvā catasso laṅghitvā pañcamāya [M 1.0456] sattiyā daṇḍake madhukapupphaṃ viya āvuto paridevamāno nipajji. Atha naṃ bodhisatto “paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ akatvā imaṃ byasanaṃ pattosī”ti imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of acrobats. Having reached adulthood, he became wise and skilled in means. Having learned the art of vaulting over spears from a certain acrobat, he traveled about displaying his skill together with his teacher. His teacher, however, knew only the art of vaulting over four spears, not five. One day, while displaying his skill in a village, intoxicated with liquor, he arranged five spears in a row, intending, “I will vault over five spears.” Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “Teacher, you do not know the art of vaulting over five spears. Remove one spear. If you attempt to vault, you will be pierced by the fifth spear and die.” But the teacher, being greatly intoxicated, disregarded his words, saying, “You do not know my measure.” After vaulting over four, he was impaled on the fifth spear and lay there lamenting, threaded on it like a honey-flower on a stick. Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “By not following the words of the wise, you have met with this disaster,” and he spoke this verse:

116.

116.

“Atikaramakarācariya[P 1.0431], mayhampetaṃ na ruccati;

Catutthe laṅghayitvāna, pañcamāyasi āvuto”ti.

“Teacher, you have done too much, and this does not please me. Having leapt over the fourth, you are now impaled on the fifth.”

Tattha atikaramakarācariyāti ācariya ajja tvaṃ atikaraṃ akari, attano karaṇato atirekaṃ karaṇaṃ akarīti attho. Mayhampetaṃ na ruccatīti mayhaṃ antevāsikassapi samānassa etaṃ tava karaṇaṃ na ruccati, tena te ahaṃ paṭhamameva kathesinti dīpeti. Catutthe laṅghayitvānāti catutthe sattithale apatitvā attānaṃ laṅghayitvā. Pañcamāyasi āvutoti paṇḍitānaṃ vacanaṃ aggaṇhanto idāni pañcamāya sattiyā āvutosīti. Idaṃ vatvā ācariyaṃ sattito apanetvā kattabbayuttakaṃ akāsi.

Here, “Teacher, you have done too much” means: Teacher, today you have done an excessive thing; you have done an action beyond your capability. “And this does not please me” indicates: “This action of yours is not pleasing even to me, your pupil; for that reason I told you beforehand.” “Having leapt over the fourth” means: having vaulted over, without falling on the fourth spear-point. “You are now impaled on the fifth” means: “Not heeding the words of the wise, you are now impaled on the fifth spear.” Having said this, he removed his teacher from the spear and performed the necessary rites.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā ācariyo ayaṃ dubbaco ahosi, antevāsiko pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having related this story of the past, identified the birth: “At that time, the teacher was this monk who is difficult to admonish, and I myself was the pupil.”

Dubbacajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Dubbaca Jātaka is the sixth.

[117] 7. Tittirajātakavaṇṇanā

[117] 7. The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka

Accuggatātibalatāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kokālikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa vatthu terasakanipāte takkāriyajātake (jā. 1.13.104 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana “na, bhikkhave, kokāliko idāneva attano vācaṃ nissāya naṭṭho, pubbepi naṭṭhoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Excessively lofty and forceful…” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning Kokālika. The story about him will become clear in the Takkāriya Jātaka in the Thirteenth Nipāta. The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has been ruined on account of his own speech; he was ruined in the past as well,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0414][M 1.0457] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā kāme pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcābhiññā aṭṭha samāpattiyo nibbattesi. Himavantappadese sabbo isigaṇo sannipatitvā taṃ ovādācariyaṃ katvā parivāresi. So pañcannaṃ isisatānaṃ ovādācariyo hutvā jhānakīḷaṃ kīḷanto himavante vasati. Tadā eko cettha paṇḍurogī tāpaso kuṭhāriṃ gahetvā kaṭṭhaṃ phāleti. Atheko mukharatāpaso tassa santike nisīditvā “idha pahāraṃ dehi, idha pahāraṃ dehī”ti [P 1.0432] taṃ tāpasaṃ rosesi. So kujjhitvā “na dāni me tvaṃ dāruphālanasippaṃ sikkhāpanakācariyo”ti tiṇhaṃ kuṭhāriṃ ukkhipitvā naṃ ekappahāreneva jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Bodhisatto tassa sarīrakiccaṃ kāresi. Tadā assamato avidūre ekasmiṃ vammikapāde eko tittiro vasati. So sāyaṃ pātaṃ tasmiṃ vammikamatthake ṭhatvā mahāvassitaṃ vassati. Taṃ sutvā eko luddako “tittirena bhavitabba”nti cintetvā saddasaññāya tattha gantvā taṃ vadhitvā ādāya gato.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a northern brahmin family. Having come of age, he learned all the arts at Takkasilā, then renounced sensual pleasures and went forth into the ascetic life, attaining the five supernormal knowledges and the eight meditative attainments. In the Himalayan region, the entire community of ascetics gathered and, making him their instructional teacher, attended upon him. He became the instructional teacher for five hundred ascetics and dwelt in the Himalayas, delighting in meditative absorption. At that time, a certain ascetic among them who was afflicted with jaundice took an axe and was splitting firewood. Then a talkative ascetic, sitting near him, angered that ascetic by saying, “Strike here, strike here!” Becoming angry, he said, “You are not my teacher for instructing me in the art of splitting wood!” and raising his sharp axe, he brought about the end of his life with a single blow. The Bodhisatta had the funeral rites performed for him. At that time, not far from the hermitage, a partridge lived at the base of an anthill. Every morning and evening, it would stand atop that anthill and let out a loud cry. Hearing this, a hunter thought, “There must be a partridge,” and following the sign of the sound, he went there, killed it, and took it away.

Bodhisatto tassa saddaṃ asuṇanto “asukaṭṭhāne tittiro vasati, kiṃ nu kho tassa saddo na sūyatī”ti tāpase pucchi. Te tassa tamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. So ubhopi tāni kāraṇāni saṃsandetvā isigaṇamajjhe imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, not hearing its sound, asked the ascetics, “A partridge lives in such-and-such a place. Why is its sound no longer heard?” They informed him of the matter. He, connecting both these incidents, spoke this verse in the midst of the community of ascetics:

117.

117.

“Accuggatātibalatā, ativelaṃ pabhāsitā;

Vācā hanati dummedhaṃ, tittiraṃ vātivassita”nti.

“Speech, excessively lofty and forceful, spoken beyond measure, destroys the fool, just as its excessive calling destroys the partridge.”

Tattha accuggatāti atiuggatā. Atibalatāti punappunaṃ bhāsanena atibalasabhāvā. Ativelaṃ pabhāsitāti atikkantavelā pamāṇātikkamena bhāsitā. Tittiraṃ vātivassitanti yathā tittiraṃ ativassitaṃ hanati, tathā evarūpā vācā dummedhaṃ bālapuggalaṃ hanatīti.

Therein, “excessively lofty” means very lofty. “Forceful” means having a very forceful nature due to repeated speaking. “Spoken beyond measure” means spoken beyond the proper time, exceeding the limit. “Just as its excessive calling destroys the partridge” means: just as excessive calling kills a partridge, so does such speech kill a fool, an unwise person.

Evaṃ bodhisatto isigaṇassa ovādaṃ datvā cattāro brahmavihāre bhāvetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having given this instruction to the community of ascetics, cultivated the four divine abidings and was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā [M 1.0458] “na, bhikkhave, kokāliko idāneva attano vacanaṃ nissāya naṭṭho, pubbepi naṭṭhoyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā mukharatāpaso kokāliko ahosi, isigaṇo buddhaparisā, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher said, “Monks, it is not only now that Kokālika has been ruined on account of his own words; he was ruined in the past as well.” Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, he identified the birth: “At that time, the talkative ascetic was Kokālika, the community of ascetics was the Buddha’s assembly, and I myself was the teacher of the community.”

Tittirajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Tittira Jātaka is the seventh.

[118] 8. Vaṭṭajātakavaṇṇanā

[118] 8. The Commentary on the Vaṭṭa Jātaka
