Nācintayanto [V 1.0415] purisoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto uttaraseṭṭhiputtaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira uttaraseṭṭhi nāma ahosi mahāvibhavo. Tassa bhariyāya kucchiyaṃ eko puññavā satto brahmalokā cavitvā paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā vayappatto abhirūpo pāsādiko ahosi [P 1.0433] brahmavaṇṇī. Atha ekadivasaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ kattikachaṇe nakkhatte ghuṭṭhe sabbo loko nakkhattanissito ahosi. Tassa sahāyakā aññe seṭṭhiputtā sapajāpatikā ahesuṃ. Uttaraseṭṭhiputtassa pana dīgharattaṃ brahmaloke vasitattā kilesesu cittaṃ na allīyati. Athassa sahāyakā “uttaraseṭṭhiputtassapi ekaṃ itthiṃ ānetvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti sammantayitvā taṃ upasaṅkamitvā “samma, imasmiṃ nagare kattikachaṇo ghuṭṭho, tuyhampi ekaṃ itthiṃ ānetvā nakkhattaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti āhaṃsu. “Na me attho itthiyā”ti ca vuttepi punappunaṃ nibandhitvā sampaṭicchāpetvā ekaṃ vaṇṇadāsiṃ sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ katvā tassa gharaṃ netvā “tvaṃ seṭṭhiputtassa santikaṃ gacchā”ti sayanigharaṃ pesetvā nikkhamiṃsu. Taṃ sayanigharaṃ paviṭṭhampi seṭṭhiputto neva oloketi, nālapati. Sā cintesi “ayaṃ evaṃ rūpasobhaggappattaṃ uttamavilāsasampannaṃ maṃ neva oloketi, nālapati, idāni naṃ attano itthikuttalīlāya olokāpessāmī”ti itthilīlaṃ dassentī pahaṭṭhākārena aggadante vivaritvā hasitaṃ akāsi. Seṭṭhiputto oloketvā dantaṭṭhike nimittaṃ gaṇhi. Athassa aṭṭhikasaññā uppajji, sakalampi taṃ sarīraṃ aṭṭhikasaṅkhalikā viya paññāyi. So tassā paribbayaṃ datvā “gacchā”ti uyyojesi.

Beginning with 'Nācintayanto puriso,' the Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the son of Uttaraseṭṭhi. It seems that in Sāvatthī there was a wealthy man named Uttaraseṭṭhi, possessing great wealth. In his wife’s womb, a virtuous being, having passed away from the Brahma world, took rebirth and, having reached adulthood, was handsome, pleasing, and of Brahma-like complexion. One day, when the Kattika festival was announced in Sāvatthī, the whole populace was engaged in the festival. His friends, other merchants’ sons, were with their wives. But as for the son of Uttaraseṭṭhi, because he had lived for a long time in the Brahma world, his mind did not cling to defilements. Then his friends consulted, 'Let us bring a woman for the son of Uttaraseṭṭhi too, and we will enjoy the festival.' Approaching him, they said, 'Friend, in this city the Kattika festival has been announced; we will bring a woman for you too and enjoy the festival.' Though he said, 'I have no need for a woman,' they insisted repeatedly and persuaded him to agree. They adorned a courtesan with all ornaments, brought her to his house, and saying, 'You go to the merchant’s son,' sent her into the bedroom and then left. Even when she entered the bedroom, the merchant’s son neither looked at her nor spoke to her. She thought, 'This man neither looks at nor speaks to me, though I am endowed with such beauty and possessed of supreme charm. Now I will make him look at me by displaying my feminine wiles.' Displaying her feminine wiles, with a delighted air she parted her front teeth and laughed. The merchant’s son looked and took the sign in the bones of her teeth. Then the perception of bones arose in him, and her entire body appeared to him like a skeleton. He gave her payment and dismissed her, saying, 'Go.'

Taṃ tassa gharā otiṇṇaṃ eko issaro antaravīthiyaṃ disvā paribbayaṃ datvā attano gharaṃ nesi, sattāhe vītivatte nakkhattaṃ ositaṃ. Vaṇṇadāsiyā [M 1.0459] mātā dhītu āgamanaṃ adisvā seṭṭhiputtānaṃ santikaṃ gantvā “kahaṃ sā”ti pucchi. Te uttaraseṭṭhiputtassa gharaṃ gantvā “kahaṃ sā”ti pucchiṃsu. “Taṅkhaṇaññeva tassā paribbayaṃ datvā uyyojesi”nti. Athassā mātā rodantī “dhītaraṃ me na passāmi, dhītaraṃ me samānethā”ti uttaraseṭṭhiputtaṃ ādāya rañño santikaṃ agamāsi. Rājā aṭṭaṃ vinicchinanto “ime te seṭṭhiputtā vaṇṇadāsiṃ ānetvā tuyhaṃ adaṃsū”ti pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Idāni sā kaha”nti? “Na jānāmi, taṅkhaṇaññeva naṃ uyyojesi”nti. “Idāni taṃ samānetuṃ sakkosī”ti? “Na sakkomi, devā”ti. Rājā “sace samānetuṃ na sakkoti, rājāṇamassa karothā”ti āha. Atha naṃ pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā “rājāṇaṃ karissāmā”ti gahetvā pakkamiṃsu. “Seṭṭhiputtaṃ kira vaṇṇadāsiṃ [V 1.0416] samānetuṃ asakkontaṃ rājā rājāṇaṃ kāretī”ti sakalanagaraṃ ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Mahājano ure hatthe ṭhapetvā “kiṃ nāmetaṃ, sāmi, attano te ananucchavikaṃ laddha”nti paridevati. Seṭṭhipi puttassa pacchato pacchato paridevanto gacchati.

As she descended from his house, a certain influential man saw her in a side street, gave her payment, and took her to his own home. After seven days had passed, the festival was over. The courtesan’s mother, not seeing her daughter's return, went to the merchants' sons and asked, 'Where is she?' They went to the house of Uttaraseṭṭhi’s son and asked, 'Where is she?' He replied, 'I gave her payment and sent her away at that very moment.' Then her mother, weeping, took Uttaraseṭṭhi’s son and went to the king, saying, 'I do not see my daughter; bring my daughter to me!' The king, judging the case, asked, 'Did these merchants' sons bring the courtesan and give her to you?' 'Yes, Your Majesty.' 'Where is she now?' 'I do not know; I sent her away at that very moment.' 'Can you bring her now?' 'I cannot, Your Majesty.' The king said, 'If he cannot bring her, inflict the royal punishment on him!' Then they bound his hands behind his back and led him away, saying, 'We will inflict the royal punishment.' The whole city was in an uproar: 'It is said the king is having the royal punishment inflicted on the merchant's son because he is unable to bring back the courtesan!' The populace, placing their hands on their chests, lamented, 'What is this, master? You have received something unfitting for you!' The merchant, too, followed behind his son, lamenting.

Seṭṭhiputto cintesi “idaṃ mayhaṃ evarūpaṃ [P 1.0434] dukkhaṃ agāre vasanabhāvena uppannaṃ. Sace ito muccissāmi, mahāgotamasammāsambuddhassa santike pabbajissāmī”ti. Sāpi kho vaṇṇadāsī taṃ kolāhalasaddaṃ sutvā “kiṃsaddo nāmeso”ti pucchitvā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā vegena otaritvā “ussaratha, ussaratha, sāmī, maṃ rājapurisānaṃ daṭṭhuṃ dethā”ti attānaṃ dassesi. Rājapurisā taṃ disvā mātaraṃ paṭicchāpetvā seṭṭhiputtaṃ muñcitvā pakkamiṃsu. So sahāyakaparivutova nadiṃ gantvā sasīsaṃ nhāyitvā gehaṃ gantvā bhuttapātarāso mātāpitaro vanditvā pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā cīvarasāṭake ādāya mahantena parivārena satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajjañca upasampadañca labhitvā avissaṭṭhakammaṭṭhāno vipassanaṃ vaḍḍhetvā na cirasseva arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

The merchant's son thought, 'This kind of suffering has arisen for me because of living the household life. If I am freed from this, I will go forth in the presence of the Great Gotama, the Perfectly Enlightened One.' That courtesan, hearing the sound of the commotion, asked, 'What is this noise?' and upon hearing what had happened, quickly came down and showed herself, saying, 'Move aside, move aside, sirs! Let the king's men see me!' The king's men, seeing her, handed her over to her mother, released the merchant's son, and departed. He, surrounded by his friends, went to the river, bathed his head, returned home, and after eating his morning meal, paid respects to his parents and received their permission to go forth. Taking robes and cloth, and with a large retinue, he went to the Teacher. After paying homage, he requested to go forth, and received both the going forth and the higher ordination. With his meditation subject not abandoned, he developed insight and before long was established in Arahantship.

Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā bhikkhū “āvuso, uttaraseṭṭhiputto attano bhaye uppanne sāsanassa guṇaṃ jānitvā ‘imamhā dukkhā muccamāno pabbajissāmī’ti cintetvā tena sucintitena maraṇamutto ceva, pabbajito ca aggaphale patiṭṭhito”ti tassa guṇakathaṃ kathesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti [M 1.0460] pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, uttaraseṭṭhiputtova attano bhaye uppanne ‘iminā upāyena imamhā dukkhā muccissāmī’ti cintetvā maraṇabhayā mutto, atīte paṇḍitāpi attano bhaye uppanne ‘iminā upāyena imamhā dukkhā muccissāmā’ti cintetvā maraṇabhayato mucciṃsuyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Then one day, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall and spoke of his virtues: 'Friends, when danger arose for Uttara, the merchant's son, recognizing the quality of the Teaching, he thought, "Being freed from this suffering, I will go forth." Through that well-considered thought, he was freed from death and, having gone forth, was established in the highest fruit.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?' When they replied, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only Uttaraseṭṭhi’s son who, when danger arose for himself, thought, "By this means I shall be freed from this suffering," and was thus freed from the fear of death. In the past too, the wise, when danger arose for themselves, thought, "By this means we shall be freed from this suffering," and were indeed freed from the fear of death.' Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto cutipaṭisandhivasena parivattanto vaṭṭakayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Tadā eko vaṭṭakaluddako araññā bahū vaṭṭake āharitvā gehe ṭhapetvā gocaraṃ datvā mūlaṃ gahetvā āgatāgatānaṃ hatthe vaṭṭake vikkiṇanto jīvikaṃ kappeti. So ekadivasaṃ bahūhi vaṭṭakehi saddhiṃ bodhisattampi gahetvā ānesi. Bodhisatto cintesi “sacāhaṃ iminā dinnaṃ gocarañca pānīyañca paribhuñjissāmi, ayaṃ maṃ gahetvā āgatānaṃ manussānaṃ dassati. Sace pana na paribhuñjissāmi, ahaṃ milāyissāmi, atha maṃ milāyantaṃ disvā manussā na gaṇhissanti. Evaṃ me sotthi bhavissati, imaṃ upāyaṃ karissāmī”ti. So [V 1.0417] tathā karonto milāyitvā aṭṭhicammamatto ahosi. Manussā taṃ disvā na gaṇhiṃsu. Luddako bodhisattaṃ ṭhapetvā [P 1.0435] sesesu vaṭṭakesu parikkhīṇesu pacchiṃ nīharitvā dvāre ṭhapetvā bodhisattaṃ hatthatale katvā “kiṃ nu kho ayaṃ vaṭṭako”ti cintetvā oloketuṃ āraddho. Athassa pamattabhāvaṃ ñatvā bodhisatto pakkhe pasāretvā uppatitvā araññameva gato. Aññe vaṭṭakā taṃ disvā “kiṃ nu kho na paññāyasi, kahaṃ gatosī”ti pucchitvā “luddakena gahitomhī”ti vutte “kinti katvā muttosī”ti pucchiṃsu. Bodhisatto “ahaṃ tena dinnaṃ gocaraṃ aggahetvā pānīyaṃ apivitvā upāyacintāya mutto”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, passing from existence to existence, was reborn as a quail. At that time, a quail hunter would catch many quails in the forest, bring them home, provide them with food, and then sell the quails for a price to those who came, thus making his living. One day, he caught the Bodhisatta along with many other quails and brought him home. The Bodhisatta thought, 'If I consume the food and water given by this man, he will sell me to the people who come. But if I do not consume them, I will grow weak, and seeing me weak, people will not take me. Thus, I will be safe. I shall adopt this stratagem.' Acting accordingly, he withered away until he was just skin and bone. Seeing him, people did not take him. When the other quails were all gone, the hunter took the basket out, placed it by the door, took the Bodhisatta in his palm, and began to examine him, wondering, 'What could be the matter with this quail?' Realizing the hunter’s carelessness, the Bodhisatta spread his wings, flew up, and escaped into the forest. The other quails, seeing him, asked, 'Why were you not seen? Where have you gone?' When he told them, 'I was caught by the hunter,' they asked, 'How did you manage to escape?' The Bodhisatta replied, 'I did not take the food he gave, nor drink the water, and by devising a stratagem, I was freed.' Then he spoke this verse:

118.

118.

“Nācintayanto puriso, visesamadhigacchati;

Cintitassa phalaṃ passa, muttosmi vadhabandhanā”ti.

“A person who does not think does not attain a superior state; behold the fruit of my thinking: I am freed from death and bondage.”

Tatthāyaṃ piṇḍattho – puriso dukkhaṃ patvā “iminā nāma upāyena imamhā dukkhā muccissāmī”ti acintayanto attano dukkhā mokkhasaṅkhātaṃ visesaṃ nādhigacchati. Idāni pana mayā cintitakammassa phalaṃ passa. Teneva upāyena [M 1.0461] muttosmi vadhabandhanā, maraṇato ca bandhanato ca muttosmi ahanti. Evaṃ bodhisatto attanā katakāraṇaṃ ācikkhi.

Here is the concise meaning: A person who has met with suffering and does not think, 'By this means I shall be freed from this suffering,' does not attain the superior state known as liberation from his suffering. But now, behold the fruit of the action I have devised. By that very stratagem, I am freed from execution and bondage—I am freed from death and from bondage. Thus, the Bodhisatta explained the reason for his action.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā maraṇamutto vaṭṭako ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher connected the birth story: “At that time, the quail freed from death was I myself.”

Vaṭṭajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Quail Jātaka, the Eighth.

[119] 9. Akālarāvijātakavaṇṇanā

[119] 9. The Commentary on the Akālarāvi Jātaka

Amātāpitarasaṃvaddhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ akālarāviṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto sāsane pabbajitvā vattaṃ vā sikkhaṃ vā na uggaṇhi. So “imasmiṃ kāle mayā vattaṃ kātabbaṃ, imasmiṃ kāle upaṭṭhātabbaṃ, imasmiṃ kāle uggahetabbaṃ, imasmiṃ kāle sajjhāyitabba”nti na jānāti, paṭhamayāmepi majjhimayāmepi pacchimayāmepi pabuddhapabuddhakkhaṇeyeva mahāsaddaṃ karoti, bhikkhū niddaṃ na labhanti. Dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu evarūpe ratanasāsane pabbajitvā vattaṃ vā sikkhaṃ vā kālaṃ vā akālaṃ vā na jānātī”ti tassa aguṇakathaṃ kathesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha[V 1.0418], bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa akālarāvī, pubbepi akālarāvīyeva, kālākālaṃ ajānanabhāvena ca gīvāya vaṭṭitāya jīvitakkhayaṃ patto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher spoke this, beginning with “Brought up without mother or father,” while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain monk who made noise at the wrong time. It seems that a clansman residing in Sāvatthī, having gone forth in the Dispensation, did not learn the duties or the training. He did not know, 'At this time I should perform my duties, at this time I should attend, at this time I should study, at this time I should recite.' Whether in the first, middle, or last watch of the night, the moment he woke up he would make a great noise, and the monks could not get to sleep. In the Dhamma hall, the monks discussed his faults, saying, 'Friends, this monk named so-and-so, having gone forth in such a precious Dispensation, does not know his duties, the training, or what is timely and untimely.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?' When they told him, he said, 'Monks, this one is not an untimely noisemaker only now; he was so even in the past. And due to not knowing what was timely and untimely, his neck was twisted and he met his end.' Then he recounted a past incident.

Atīte [P 1.0436] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto sabbasippesu pāraṃ gantvā bārāṇasiyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañcasate māṇave sippaṃ vāceti. Tesaṃ māṇavānaṃ eko kālarāvī kukkuṭo atthi, te tassa vassitasaddena uṭṭhāya sippaṃ sikkhanti. So kālamakāsi. Te aññaṃ kukkuṭaṃ pariyesantā caranti. Atheko māṇavako susānavane dārūni uddharanto ekaṃ kukkuṭaṃ disvā ānetvā pañjare ṭhapetvā paṭijaggati. So susāne vaḍḍhitattā “asukavelāya nāma vassitabba”nti ajānanto kadāci atirattiṃ vassati, kadāci aruṇuggamane. Māṇavā [M 1.0462] tassa atirattiṃ vassitakāle sippaṃ sikkhantā yāva aruṇuggamanā sikkhituṃ na sakkonti, niddāyamānā gahitaṭṭhānampi na passanti. Atipabhāte vassitakāle sajjhāyassa okāsameva na labhanti. Māṇavā “ayaṃ atirattiṃ vā vassati atipabhāte vā, imaṃ nissāya amhākaṃ sippaṃ na niṭṭhāyissatī”ti taṃ gahetvā gīvaṃ vaṭṭetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā “akālarāvī kukkuṭo amhehi ghātito”ti ācariyassa kathesuṃ. Ācariyo “ovādaṃ aggahetvā saṃvaḍḍhitabhāvena maraṇaṃ patto”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into an Udicca Brahmin family. Having come of age and mastered all the arts, he became a world-renowned teacher in Benares, instructing five hundred young men in their craft. These young men had a rooster that crowed at the proper time; they would rise at its crowing and learn their craft. That rooster died. They went about searching for another rooster. Then one young man, while gathering firewood in a charnel ground, saw a rooster and brought it back, placing it in a cage to care for it. Having grown up in the charnel ground, it did not know when it should crow, so it sometimes crowed in the deep of night, and sometimes at dawn. When it crowed in the deep of night, the young men, practicing their craft, could not continue until dawn; growing drowsy, they could not even grasp what they had taken up. When it crowed late in the morning, they did not get a chance for recitation at all. The young men thought, 'This rooster crows either in the deep of night or too late in the morning. Relying on it, our studies will not be completed.' So they seized it, wrung its neck, and put it to death, then told their teacher, 'We have killed the rooster that crowed at the wrong time.' The teacher said, 'Having grown up without receiving instruction, it met its death,' and spoke this verse:

119.

119.

“Amātāpitara-saṃvaddho, anācerakule vasaṃ;

Nāyaṃ kālaṃ akālaṃ vā, abhijānāti kukkuṭo”ti.

“Reared without mother or father, dwelling in a family without a teacher, this rooster knows not the right time from the wrong time.”

Tattha amātāpitarasaṃvaddhoti mātāpitaro nissāya tesaṃ ovādaṃ aggahetvā saṃvaḍḍho. Anācerakule vasanti ācariyakulepi avasamāno, ācārasikkhāpakaṃ kañci nissāya avasitattāti attho. Nāyaṃ kālaṃ akālaṃ vāti “imasmiṃ kāle vassitabbaṃ, imasmiṃ na vassitabba”nti evaṃ vassitabbayuttakaṃ kālaṃ vā akālaṃ vā esa kukkuṭo na jānāti, ajānanabhāveneva jīvitakkhayaṃ pattoti. Idaṃ kāraṇaṃ dassetvā bodhisatto yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Herein, 'reared without mother or father' means one who was raised without relying on parents and without accepting their instruction. 'Dwelling in a family without a teacher' means not dwelling in a teacher's family; that is, not having lived relying on any instructor of proper conduct. 'This one knows not the time or the untimely season' means this rooster did not know the proper time to crow or the improper time, and it was through this ignorance that he reached the end of his life. Having pointed out this reason, the Bodhisatta, having remained for his full lifespan, passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā [V 1.0419] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā akālarāvī kukkuṭo ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, antevāsikā buddhaparisā, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection in the Jātaka: “At that time, the rooster who crowed at the wrong time was this bhikkhu; the pupils were the Buddha’s assembly; and the teacher was I myself.”

Akālarāvijātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The ninth, the commentary on the Akālarāvi Jātaka, is concluded.

[120] 10. Bandhanamokkhajātakavaṇṇanā

[120] 10. The Commentary on the Bandhanamokkha Jātaka.

Abaddhā [P 1.0437] tattha bajjhantīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ciñcamāṇavikaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassā vatthu dvādasakanipāte mahāpadumajātake (jā. 1.12.106 ādayo) āvi bhavissati. Tadā pana satthā “na, bhikkhave, ciñcamāṇavikā idāneva maṃ abhūtena abbhācikkhati, pubbepi abbhācikkhiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“Though unbound, they are bound there”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana with reference to Ciñcamāṇavikā. Her story will be made manifest in the Mahāpaduma Jātaka in the Book of Twelve (Jā 472). At that time, the Teacher said, “Bhikkhus, it is not only now that Ciñcamāṇavikā falsely accuses me; she has falsely accused me in the past as well,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte [M 1.0463] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto purohitassa gehe nibbattitvā vayappatto pitu accayena tasseva purohito ahosi. Tena aggamahesiyā varo dinno hoti “bhadde, yaṃ icchasi, taṃ vadeyyāsī”ti. Sā evamāha “na mayhaṃ añño varo nāma dullabho, ito pana te paṭṭhāya aññā itthī kilesavasena na oloketabbā”ti. So paṭikkhipitvā punappunaṃ nippīḷiyamāno tassā vacanaṃ atikkamituṃ asakkonto sampaṭicchitvā tato paṭṭhāya soḷasasu nāṭakitthisahassesu kilesavasena ekitthimpi na olokesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born in the house of the royal chaplain. Having come of age, upon his father’s passing, he became the chaplain of that very king. The king had granted a boon to his chief queen, saying: ‘Good lady, ask for whatever you desire.’ She replied, ‘For me, there is no other boon that is difficult to obtain. However, from this day forth, you must not look upon any other woman with lustful intent.’ The king refused, but being repeatedly pressured and unable to go against her word, he consented. From that time on, he did not look with lustful intent upon even one of the sixteen thousand dancing women.

Athassa paccanto kuppi, paccante ṭhitā yodhā corehi saddhiṃ dve tayo saṅgāme katvā “ito uttari mayaṃ na sakkomā”ti rañño paṇṇaṃ pesesuṃ. Rājā tattha gantukāmo balakāyaṃ saṃharitvā taṃ pakkosāpetvā “bhadde, ahaṃ paccantaṃ gacchāmi, tattha nānappakārāni yuddhāni honti, jayaparājayopi anibaddho, tādisesu ṭhānesu mātugāmo dupparihāro, tvaṃ idheva nivattāhī”ti āha. Sā “na sakkā, deva, mayā nivattitu”nti punappunaṃ raññā paṭikkhittā āha “tena hi ekekaṃ yojanaṃ gantvā mayhaṃ sukhadukkhajānanatthaṃ ekekaṃ manussaṃ peseyyāthā”ti. Rājā “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā bodhisattaṃ nagare ṭhapetvā mahantena balakāyena nikkhamitvā gacchanto yojane yojane ekekaṃ purisaṃ “amhākaṃ ārogyaṃ ārocetvā deviyā sukhadukkhaṃ jānitvā āgacchā”ti pesesi. Sā āgatāgataṃ purisaṃ “rājā kimatthaṃ taṃ pesetī”ti pucchitvā “tumhākaṃ sukhadukkhajānanatthāyā”ti vutte “tena hi ehī”ti tena saddhiṃ [V 1.0420] asaddhammaṃ paṭisevati. Rājā dvattiṃsayojanamaggaṃ gacchanto dvattiṃsa jane pesesi, sā [P 1.0438] sabbehipi tehi saddhiṃ tatheva akāsi.

Then his border region rose in rebellion. The soldiers stationed on the border, having fought two or three battles with the thieves, sent a letter to the king, saying, “We are unable to do more than this.” The king, wishing to go there, assembled his forces, had the queen summoned, and said, ‘Good lady, I am going to the border. There, battles of various kinds occur, and victory and defeat are not fixed. In such places, a woman is difficult to protect. You should remain here.’ She replied, ‘It is not possible for me to remain, Your Majesty.’ Though repeatedly refused by the king, she said, ‘In that case, after travelling each yojana, please send a man to learn of my well-being.’ The king agreed, saying, “Very well.” Leaving the Bodhisatta in the city, he set out with a great army. As he travelled, at every yojana he sent a man, instructing him, ‘Announce our good health, learn of the queen’s well-being, and return.’ Each man who arrived, she would ask, ‘For what purpose did the king send you?’ When he replied, ‘To learn of your well-being,’ she would say, ‘Then come,’ and would engage in immoral conduct with him. The king, travelling a path of thirty-two yojanas, sent thirty-two men, and she acted in the very same way with all of them.

Rājā paccantaṃ vūpasametvā janapadaṃ samassāsetvā puna āgacchantopi tatheva dvattiṃsa jane pesesi, sā tehipi saddhiṃ tatheva vippaṭipajjiyeva. Rājā āgantvā jayakkhandhāvāraṭṭhāne ṭhatvā “nagaraṃ paṭijaggāpetū”ti bodhisattassa paṇṇaṃ pesesi. Bodhisatto sakalanagaraṃ paṭijaggāpetvā rājanivesanaṃ paṭijaggāpento deviyā vasanaṭṭhānaṃ agamāsi. Sā bodhisattassa rūpasobhaggappattaṃ kāyaṃ disvā saṇṭhātuṃ asakkontī “ehi[M 1.0464], brāhmaṇa, sayanaṃ abhiruhā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “mā evaṃ avaca, rājāpi garu, akusalampi bhāyāmi, na sakkā mayā evaṃ kātu”nti āha. “Catusaṭṭhiyā pādamūlikānaṃ neva rājā garu, na akusalaṃ bhāyanti. Taveva rājā garu, tvaṃyeva ca akusalaṃ bhāyasī”ti. “Āma, devi, sace tesampi evaṃ bhaveyya, na evarūpaṃ kareyyuṃ”. “Ahaṃ pana jānamāno evarūpaṃ sāhasiyakammaṃ na karissāmī”ti. “Kiṃ bahuṃ vippalapasi, sace me vacanaṃ na karosi, sīsaṃ te chindāpessāmī”ti. “Tiṭṭhatu tāva ekasmiṃ attabhāve sīsaṃ, attabhāvasahassepi sīse chijjante na sakkā mayā evarūpaṃ kātu”nti. Sā “hotu, jānissāmī”ti bodhisattaṃ tajjetvā attano gabbhaṃ pavisitvā sarīre nakhavaḷañjaṃ dassetvā telena gattāni abbhañjitvā kiliṭṭhavatthaṃ nivāsetvā gilānālayaṃ katvā dāsiyo āṇāpesi ‘raññā kahaṃ devī’ti vutte ‘gilānā’ti katheyyāthā”ti.

The king, having pacified the border region and reassured the country, on his return journey again sent thirty-two men in the same way, and she misbehaved with them just as before. Having returned and established his victory camp, the king sent a message to the Bodhisatta, saying, ‘Have the city prepared.’ The Bodhisatta had the entire city prepared, and while preparing the royal palace, he went to the queen’s quarters. Seeing the Bodhisatta’s body, which was endowed with beauty and grace, she was unable to contain herself and said, ‘Come, brahmin, get into bed.’ The Bodhisatta replied, ‘Do not speak so. The king is venerable, and I fear what is unwholesome. It is not possible for me to do such a thing.’ She said, ‘For the sixty-four attendants at my feet, the king is not venerable, nor do they fear what is unwholesome. Is it only for you that the king is venerable, and only you who fears what is unwholesome?’ ‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ he replied. ‘If they knew as I do, they would not do such a thing. But I, knowing, will not commit such a reckless deed.’ ‘Why do you prattle so much? If you do not do as I say, I will have your head cut off.’ He replied, ‘Let alone my head in this single existence, even if my head were to be cut off in a thousand existences, it would not be possible for me to do such a thing.’ She said, ‘So be it. I will see to it,’ and after threatening the Bodhisatta, she entered her private chamber, made nail marks appear on her body, anointed her limbs with oil, put on a soiled garment, pretended to be ill, and commanded her female servants, ‘When the king asks, “Where is the queen?” you are to say she is ill.’

Bodhisattopi rañño paṭipathaṃ agamāsi. Rājā nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pāsādaṃ āruyha deviṃ apassanto “kahaṃ, devī”ti pucchi. “Gilānā, devā”ti. Sopi sirigabbhaṃ pavisitvā tassā piṭṭhiṃ parimajjanto “kiṃ te, bhadde, aphāsuka”nti pucchi. Sā tuṇhī ahosi. Tatiyavāre rājānaṃ oloketvā “tvampi, mahārāja, jīvasi nāma, mādisāpi itthiyo sassāmikāyeva nāmā”ti āha. “Kiṃ etaṃ, bhadde”ti? Tumhehi nagaraṃ rakkhanatthāya ṭhapito purohito “tumhākaṃ nivesanaṃ paṭijaggāmī”ti idhāgantvā attano vacanaṃ akarontiṃ [P 1.0439] maṃ paharitvā attano manaṃ pūretvā gatoti. Rājā aggimhi pakkhittaloṇasakkharā viya kodhena taṭataṭāyanto sirigabbhā nikkhamitvā dovārikapādamūlikādayo pakkosāpetvā “gacchatha, bhaṇe, purohitaṃ pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā vajjhabhāvappattaṃ katvā nagarā nīharitvā āghātanaṃ netvā sīsamassa chindathā”ti āha. Te vegena gantvā taṃ pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā vajjhabheriṃ carāpesuṃ.

The Bodhisatta also went to meet the king. The king, having circumambulated the city and ascended the palace, did not see the queen and asked, “Where is the queen?” “She is ill, your majesty.” He too entered the royal chamber and, stroking her back, asked, “What troubles you, my dear?” She remained silent. The third time, looking at the king, she said, “So, great king, you are alive? And women like me are still called wives with husbands?” “What is this, my dear?” “The chaplain, appointed by you to guard the city, came here saying, ‘I will look after your dwelling,’ and when I did not comply with his words, he struck me and, having fulfilled his desire, left.” The king, sputtering with anger like salt crystals thrown into a fire, left the royal chamber and summoned the doorkeepers and attendants, saying, “Go, men, bind the chaplain’s hands behind his back, declare him condemned to death, drag him out of the city, take him to the execution ground, and cut off his head.” They went quickly, bound his hands behind his back, and had the execution drum sounded.

Bodhisatto [V 1.0421] cintesi – “addhā tāya duṭṭhadeviyā rājā puretarameva paribhinno, ajja dānāhaṃ attano baleneva attānaṃ mocessāmī”ti. So te purise āha “bho, tumhe maṃ mārentā rañño dassetvāva mārethā”ti. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? “Ahaṃ rājakammiko, bahu me kammaṃ kataṃ, bahūni mahānidhiṭṭhānāni jānāmi, rājakuṭumbaṃ mayā vicāritaṃ. Sace maṃ rañño [M 1.0465] na dassessatha, bahudhanaṃ nassissati, mayā rañño sāpateyye ācikkhite pacchā kātabbaṃ karothā”ti. Te taṃ rañño dassayiṃsu. Rājā taṃ disvāva “kasmā bho, brāhmaṇa, mayi lajjaṃ na akāsi, kasmā te evarūpaṃ pāpakammaṃ kata”nti āha. “Mahārāja, ahaṃ sotthiyakule jāto, mayā kunthakipillikamattopi pāṇātipāto na katapubbo, tiṇasalākamattampi adinnaṃ nādinnapubbaṃ, lobhavasena paresaṃ itthī akkhīni ummīletvāpi na olokitapubbā, hassavasenāpi musā na bhāsitapubbā, kusaggenāpi majjaṃ na pītapubbaṃ, ahaṃ tumhesu niraparādho. Sā pana bālā lobhavasena maṃ hatthe gahetvā mayā paṭikkhittā maṃ tajjetvā attanā kataṃ pāpaṃ uttānaṃ katvā mama ācikkhitvā antogabbhaṃ paviṭṭhā. Ahaṃ niraparādho, paṇṇaṃ gahetvā pana āgatā catusaṭṭhi janā sāparādhā, te pakkosāpetvā “tāya vo vacanaṃ kataṃ, na kata”nti puccha, devāti. Rājā te catusaṭṭhi jane bandhāpetvā deviṃ pakkosāpetvā “tayā etehi saddhiṃ pāpaṃ kataṃ, na kata”nti pucchi. “Kataṃ, devā”ti vutte te pacchābāhaṃ bandhāpetvā “imesaṃ catusaṭṭhijanānaṃ sīsāni chindathā”ti āṇāpesi.

The Bodhisatta thought, “Assuredly, the king has already been turned against me by that wicked queen. Today, I will free myself by my own strength.” He said to those men, “Sirs, when you kill me, do so only after showing me to the king.” “For what reason?” “I am a servant of the king. I have performed much work and know the locations of many great treasures. I have managed the royal estate. If you do not show me to the king, much wealth will be lost. After I have informed the king of his property, you may then do what must be done.” They showed him to the king. Upon seeing him, the king said, “Why, Brahmin, did you feel no shame before me? Why have you done such an evil deed?” “Great king, I was born into a Brahmin family. I have never before killed a living being, not even an insect or an ant. I have never taken what was not given, not even a blade of grass. I have never, out of lust, looked upon another’s wife with open eyes. I have never spoken falsely, not even in jest. I have never drunk intoxicants, not even from the tip of a kusa grass. I am innocent in your regard. But that foolish woman, driven by lust, seized me by the hand. When I refused her, she threatened me and, making plain the evil she herself had done, accused me and retreated into her chamber. I am innocent. However, the sixty-four men who came bringing the message are the guilty ones. Summon them and ask them, ‘Did you act on her word, or not?’ your majesty.” The king had those sixty-four men bound and summoned the queen. He asked her, “Did you commit this evil act with them, or not?” When she replied, “I did, your majesty,” he ordered, “Bind their hands behind their backs and cut off the heads of these sixty-four men.”

Atha naṃ [P 1.0440] bodhisatto āha – “natthi, mahārāja, etesaṃ doso, devī attano ruciṃ kārāpesi. Niraparādhā ete, tasmā nesaṃ khamatha. Tassāpi doso natthi, itthiyo nāma methunadhammena atittā. Jātisabhāvo hi esa. Etāsaṃ khamitabbayuttameva hoti. Tasmā etissāpi khamathā”ti nānappakārena rājānaṃ saññāpetvā te catusaṭṭhipi jane tañca bālaṃ mocāpetvā sabbesaṃ yathāsakāni ṭhānāni dāpesi. Evaṃ te sabbe mocetvā sakaṭṭhāne patiṭṭhāpetvā bodhisatto rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā “mahārāja, andhabālānaṃ nāma avatthukena vacanena abandhitabbayuttakāpi paṇḍitā pacchābāhaṃ baddhā, paṇḍitānaṃ kāraṇayuttena vacanena pacchābāhaṃ baddhāpi muttā. Evaṃ bālā nāma abandhitabbayuttakepi bandhāpenti, paṇḍitā baddhepi mocentī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then the Bodhisatta said to him, “Great king, there is no fault in these men; the queen had them act according to her own desire. They are blameless; therefore, forgive them. There is no fault in her either, for women are by nature insatiable in matters of passion. Such is their innate disposition. It is only fitting to forgive them. Therefore, forgive her too.” Having thus persuaded the king in various ways, he secured the release of those sixty-four men and that foolish woman, and had them all restored to their respective positions. Having thus freed them all and established them in their proper places, the Bodhisatta approached the king and said, “Great king, by the baseless words of ignorant fools, even the wise who ought not to be bound are bound with their hands behind their backs; yet by the reasoned speech of the wise, even those who are bound are set free. Thus, fools cause those who should not be bound to be bound, while the wise bring about the release of even those who are bound.” And he spoke this verse:

120.

120.

“Abaddhā tattha bajjhanti, yattha bālā pabhāsare;

Baddhāpi tattha muccanti, yattha dhīrā pabhāsare”ti.

“Where fools speak, the innocent are bound; and where the wise speak, even the bound are freed.”

Tattha [V 1.0422][M 1.0466] abaddhāti abandhitabbayuttā. Pabhāsareti pabhāsanti vadanti kathenti.

Therein, ‘the innocent’ means those who ought not to be bound. ‘Speak’ means they speak forth, they talk, they declare.

Evaṃ mahāsatto imāya gāthāya rañño dhammaṃ desetvā “mayā imaṃ dukkhaṃ agāre vasanabhāvena laddhaṃ, idāni me agārena kiccaṃ natthi, pabbajjaṃ me anujāna, devā”ti pabbajjaṃ anujānāpetvā assumukhaṃ ñātijanaṃ mahantañca vibhavaṃ pahāya isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā himavante vasanto abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Thus the Great Being, having taught the king the Dhamma with this verse, said, “I have obtained this suffering because I was living the household life. Now I have no need for the household life. Grant me permission to go forth, your majesty.” Having obtained permission to go forth, he left behind his tearful relatives and great wealth. He went forth into the life of a sage and, dwelling in the Himalayas, he developed the spiritual powers and meditative attainments, and was destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā duṭṭhadevī ciñcamāṇavikā ahosi, rājā ānando, purohito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, identified the birth: “At that time, the wicked queen was Ciñcamāṇavikā, the king was Ānanda, and the chaplain was I myself.”

Bandhanamokkhajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The Commentary on the Bandhanamokkha Jātaka, the Tenth.

Haṃcivaggo dvādasamo.

The Haṃci Chapter, the Twelfth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Gadrabhapañhā amarā, siṅgālaṃ mitacinti ca;

Anusāsikadubbacaṃ, tittiraṃ vaṭṭakaṃ puna;

Akālarāvi bandhananti.

The Donkey's Question (Gadrabhapañha), the Immortal (Amarā), the Jackal (Siṅgāla), and the Thoughtful Friend (Mitacintī); the Advisor (Anusāsika), the Unruly (Dubbaca), the Partridge (Tittira), and also the Quail (Vaṭṭaka); the Untimely Crower (Akālarāvi), and Release from Bonds (Bandhana).

13. Kusanāḷivaggo

13. The Kusanāḷi Chapter

[121] 1. Kusanāḷijātakavaṇṇanā

[121] 1. The Commentary on the Kusanāḷi Jātaka

Kare [V 1.0423][P 1.0441] sarikkhoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto anāthapiṇḍikassa mittaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Anāthapiṇḍikassa hi mittasuhajjañātibandhavā ekato hutvā “mahāseṭṭhi ayaṃ tayā jātigottadhanadhaññādīhi neva sadiso, na uttaritaro, kasmā etena saddhiṃ santhavaṃ karosi, mā karohī”ti punappunaṃ nivāresuṃ. Anāthapiṇḍiko pana “mittasanthavo nāma hīnehipi samehipi atirekehipi kattabboyevā”ti tesaṃ [M 1.0467] vacanaṃ aggahetvā bhogagāmaṃ gacchanto taṃ kuṭumbarakkhakaṃ katvā agamāsīti sabbaṃ kāḷakaṇṇivatthusmiṃ vuttanayeneva veditabbaṃ. Idha pana anāthapiṇḍikena attano ghare pavattiyā ārocitāya satthā “gahapati, mitto nāma khuddako natthi, mittadhammaṃ rakkhituṃ samatthabhāvovettha pamāṇaṃ, mitto nāma attanā samopi hīnopi seṭṭhopi gahetabbo. Sabbepi hete attano pattabhāraṃ nittharantiyeva, idāni tāva tvaṃ attano nīcamittaṃ nissāya kuṭumbassa sāmiko jāto, porāṇā pana nīcamittaṃ nissāya vimānasāmikā jātā”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

This discourse, beginning with the words 'Kare sarikkho,' the Teacher, while residing at Jetavana, spoke concerning a friend of Anāthapiṇḍika. Anāthapiṇḍika's friends, companions, relatives, and kinsmen gathered together and repeatedly tried to dissuade him, saying, 'Great merchant, this man is not your equal in birth, lineage, wealth, or grain, nor is he superior. Why do you form a friendship with him? Do not do so.' But Anāthapiṇḍika, not heeding their words and thinking, 'Friendship should indeed be formed with those who are inferior, equal, or superior,' appointed him as the guardian of his household and went to a village of his revenues. This entire account should be understood in the manner told in the story of Kāḷakaṇṇi. Here, however, when Anāthapiṇḍika informed the Teacher about the events in his house, the Teacher said, 'Householder, there is no such thing as an insignificant friend. The measure in this is the ability to uphold the duties of friendship. A friend should be accepted whether they are equal to oneself, inferior, or superior. For all of them carry out the duty that falls to them. Now, by relying on your lowly friend, you have become the master of your wealth. But the ancients, by relying on a lowly friend, became masters of celestial mansions.' Having said this, and being requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto rañño uyyāne kusanāḷigacche devatā hutvā nibbatti. Tasmiṃyeva ca uyyāne maṅgalasilaṃ nissāya ujugatakkhandho parimaṇḍalasākhāviṭapasampanno rañño santikā laddhasammāno rucamaṅgalarukkho atthi, “mukhako”tipi vuccati. Tasmiṃ eko mahesakkho devarājā nibbatti. Bodhisattassa tena saddhiṃ mittasanthavo ahosi. Tadā rājā ekasmiṃ ekatthambhake pāsāde vasati, tassa so thambho cali. Athassa calitabhāvaṃ rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā vaḍḍhakī pakkosāpetvā “tātā, mama ekatthambhakassa maṅgalapāsādassa thambho calito, ekaṃ sāratthambhaṃ āharitvā taṃ niccalaṃ karothā”ti āha. Te “sādhu, devā”ti rañño vacanaṃ sampaṭicchitvā tadanucchavikaṃ [P 1.0442] rukkhaṃ pariyesamānā aññattha adisvā uyyānaṃ pavisitvā taṃ mukhakarukkhaṃ disvā rañño santikaṃ gantvā “kiṃ, tātā, diṭṭho vo tadanucchaviko rukkho”ti vutte “diṭṭho, deva, apica taṃ chindituṃ na visahāmā”ti āhaṃsu. “Kiṃkāraṇā”ti? Mayañhi aññattha rukkhaṃ apassantā uyyānaṃ [V 1.0424] pavisimha, tatrapi ṭhapetvā maṅgalarukkhaṃ aññaṃ na passāma. Iti naṃ maṅgalarukkhatāya chindituṃ na visahāmāti. Gacchatha, taṃ chinditvā pāsādaṃ thiraṃ karotha, mayaṃ aññaṃ maṅgalarukkhaṃ karissāmāti. Te “sādhū”ti balikammaṃ gahetvā uyyānaṃ gantvā “sve chindissāmā”ti rukkhassa balikammaṃ katvā nikkhamiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a deity in a clump of kusa grass in the king’s park. In that same park, near an auspicious stone slab, there was an auspicious Ruca tree, also called Mukhaka, with a straight trunk and perfectly rounded branches and boughs, which had received honor from the king. A powerful deva king was reborn in it. The Bodhisatta formed a friendship with him. At that time, the king lived in a single-pillared palace, and its pillar became unsteady. When they informed the king that it was unsteady, the king summoned the carpenters and said, 'Sirs, the pillar of my single-pillared auspicious palace is unsteady. Bring a pillar of heartwood and make it stable.' They replied, 'Very well, Your Majesty,' and accepting the king’s command, they searched for a suitable tree. Finding none elsewhere, they entered the park and saw that Mukhaka tree. They went to the king, and when he asked, 'Sirs, have you seen a suitable tree?' they said, 'We have seen one, Your Majesty, but we cannot bring ourselves to cut it down.' 'For what reason?' 'Because, seeing no other tree elsewhere, we entered the park. There too, apart from the auspicious tree, we see no other. Thus, because it is the auspicious tree, we cannot bring ourselves to cut it down.' The king said, 'Go, cut it down and make the palace firm. We shall make another tree the auspicious one.' They said, 'Very well,' and taking offerings, they went to the park. Saying, 'We will cut it tomorrow,' they made an offering to the tree and departed.

Rukkhadevatā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā “sve mayhaṃ vimānaṃ nāsessanti, dārake gahetvā kuhiṃ gamissāmī”ti gantabbaṭṭhānaṃ apassantī puttake gīvāya [M 1.0468] gahetvā parodi. Tassā sandiṭṭhasambhattā rukkhadevatā āgantvā “kiṃ eta”nti pucchitvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā sayampi vaḍḍhakīnaṃ paṭikkamanūpāyaṃ apassantiyo taṃ parissajitvā rodituṃ ārabhiṃsu. Tasmiṃ samaye bodhisatto “rukkhadevataṃ passissāmī”ti tattha gantvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ sutvā “hotu, mā cintayittha, ahaṃ rukkhaṃ chindituṃ na dassāmi, sve vaḍḍhakīnaṃ āgatakāle mama kāraṇaṃ passathā”ti tā devatā samassāsetvā punadivase vaḍḍhakīnaṃ āgatavelāya kakaṇṭakavesaṃ gahetvā vaḍḍhakīnaṃ purato gantvā maṅgalarukkhassa mūlantaraṃ pavisitvā taṃ rukkhaṃ susiraṃ viya katvā rukkhamajjhena abhiruhitvā khandhamatthakena nikkhamitvā sīsaṃ kampayamāno nipajji. Mahāvaḍḍhakī taṃ kakaṇṭakaṃ disvā rukkhaṃ hatthena paharitvā “susirarukkho eso nissāro, hiyyo anupadhāretvāva balikammaṃ karimhā”ti ekaghanaṃ mahārukkhaṃ garahitvā pakkāmi. Rukkhadevatā bodhisattaṃ nissāya vimānassa sāminī jātā.

The tree deity, understanding the reason, thought, 'Tomorrow they will destroy my celestial mansion. Taking my young children, where shall I go?' Seeing no place to go, she clasped her young children by the neck and wept. Her intimate and devoted friends, other tree deities, came and asked, 'What is this?' Hearing the reason, and themselves seeing no way to make the carpenters turn back, they embraced her and began to weep. At that moment, the Bodhisatta went there, thinking, 'I will see the tree deity.' Hearing the reason, he said, 'Let it be, do not worry. I will not let them cut the tree. Tomorrow, when the carpenters come, you shall see what I do.' Having thus comforted the deities, on the next day, at the time the carpenters arrived, he took the form of a chameleon. Going before the carpenters, he entered the space between the roots of the auspicious tree and, making the tree appear as if it were hollow, he ascended through the middle of the tree, emerged from the top of the trunk, and lay there, shaking his head. The chief carpenter, seeing the chameleon, struck the tree with his hand and said, 'This tree is hollow and without heartwood. Yesterday we made an offering without having investigated it.' Scolding the great, supposedly solid tree, he departed. The tree deity, by relying on the Bodhisatta, became the mistress of her celestial mansion.

Tassā paṭisanthāratthāya sandiṭṭhasambhattā [P 1.0443] bahū devatā sannipatiṃsu. Rukkhadevatā “vimānaṃ me laddha”nti tuṭṭhacittā tāsaṃ devatānaṃ majjhe bodhisattassa guṇaṃ kathayamānā “bho, devatā, mayaṃ mahesakkhā hutvāpi dandhapaññatāya imaṃ upāyaṃ na jānimha, kusanāḷidevatā pana attano ñāṇasampattiyā amhe vimānasāmike akāsi, mitto nāma sadisopi adhikopi hīnopi kattabbova. Sabbepi hi attano thāmena sahāyakānaṃ uppannaṃ dukkhaṃ nittharitvā sukhe patiṭṭhāpentiyevā”ti mittadhammaṃ vaṇṇetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

For the purpose of extending a friendly welcome to her, many intimate and devoted friend-deities assembled. The tree deity, with a delighted mind, thinking, 'My mansion has been secured,' spoke of the Bodhisatta's virtue in the midst of those deities: 'Venerable deities, although we are powerful, due to our slow wisdom we did not know this stratagem. The Kusa-grass deity, however, through his accomplishment in wisdom, has made us masters of our mansion. A friend—whether equal, superior, or inferior—should indeed be made. For all, by their own strength, deliver their companions from suffering that has arisen and establish them in happiness.' Praising the duty of friendship, she spoke this verse:

121.

121.

“Kare sarikkho atha vāpi seṭṭho, nihīnako vāpi kareyya eko;

Kareyyumete byasane uttamatthaṃ, yathā ahaṃ kusanāḷi rucāya”nti.

'One should make a friend who is similar, or superior, or even one who is inferior. In adversity, they accomplish the highest good, just as the Kusa-grass deity did for me, Rucā.'

Tattha [V 1.0425] kare sarikkhoti jātiādīhi sadisopi mittadhammaṃ kareyya. Atha vāpi seṭṭhoti jātiādīhi adhikopi kareyya. Nihīnako vāpi kareyya ekoti eko jātiādīhi hīnopi mittadhammaṃ kareyya. Tasmā sabbepi ete mittā kātabbāyevāti dīpeti. Kiṃkāraṇā? Kareyyumete [M 1.0469] byasane uttamatthanti sabbepete sahāyassa byasane uppanne attano attano pattabhāraṃ vahamānā uttamatthaṃ kareyyuṃ, kāyikacetasikadukkhato taṃ sahāyakaṃ moceyyumevāti attho. Tasmā hīnopi mitto kātabboyeva, pageva itare. Tatridaṃ opammaṃ – yathā ahaṃ kusanāḷi rucāyanti, yathā ahaṃ rucāyaṃ nibbattadevatā ayañca kusanāḷidevatā, appesakkhāpi mittasanthavaṃ karimha, tatrapāhaṃ mahesakkhāpi samānā attano uppannadukkhaṃ bālatāya anupāyakusalatāya harituṃ nāsakkhiṃ, imaṃ pana appesakkhampi samānaṃ paṇḍitadevataṃ nissāya dukkhato muttomhi. Tasmā aññehipi dukkhā muccitukāmehi samavisiṭṭhabhāvaṃ anoloketvā hīnopi paṇḍito mitto kātabboti.

Therein, 'one who is similar should act' means one who is similar in birth and other qualities should perform the duties of a friend. 'Or even one who is superior' means one who is superior in birth and other qualities should also act. 'Or even one who is inferior should act' means one who is inferior in birth and other qualities should also perform the duties of a friend. Thus, it is shown that all these should indeed be made friends. For what reason? 'These would accomplish the highest purpose in adversity' means that all these, when misfortune befalls a friend, bearing their respective burdens, would accomplish the highest purpose; that is, they would surely free that friend from physical and mental suffering. Therefore, even an inferior friend should be made, let alone the others. Herein is an illustration: 'As I, Rucā, and Kusanāḷī' means, just as I, the deity born in the Rucā tree, and this Kusanāḷī deity, though of little power, formed a friendship. And in that case, though I was of great power, due to foolishness and a lack of skill in means, I was unable to remove the suffering that had arisen for me. Relying, however, on this wise deity, though of little power, I was freed from suffering. Therefore, by others who wish to be freed from suffering, without regard for equal or superior status, even a wise friend who is of lower status should be made.

Rucādevatā imāya gāthāya devasaṅghassa dhammaṃ desetvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā saddhiṃ kusanāḷidevatāya yathākammaṃ gatā.

The Rucā deity, having taught the Dhamma to the assembly of deities with this verse, lived for the remainder of her lifespan and, together with the Kusanāḷī deity, passed away according to her kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā rucādevatā ānando ahosi, kusanāḷidevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the Rucā deity was Ānanda, and the Kusanāḷī deity was I myself.'

Kusanāḷijātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Kusanāḷi Jātaka, the First.

[122] 2. Dummedhajātakavaṇṇanā

[122] 2. The Commentary on the Dummedha Jātaka

Yasaṃ [P 1.0444] laddhāna dummedhoti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dhammasabhāyañhi bhikkhū “āvuso devadatto, tathāgatassa puṇṇacandasassirikamukhaṃ asītānubyañjanadvattiṃsamahāpurisalakkhaṇapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ byāmappabhāparikkhittaṃ āveḷāveḷābhūtā yamakayamakabhūtā ghanabuddharasmiyo vissajjentaṃ paramasobhaggappattaṃ attabhāvañca oloketvā cittaṃ pasādetuṃ na sakkoti, usūyameva karoti. ‘Buddhā nāma evarūpena sīlena samādhinā paññāya vimuttiyā vimuttiñāṇadassanena samannāgatā’ti vuccamāne vaṇṇaṃ sahituṃ na sakkoti, usūyameva karotī”ti devadattassa aguṇakathaṃ kathayiṃsu. Satthā āgantvā [M 1.0470] “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave[V 1.0426], idāneva devadatto mama vaṇṇe bhaññamāne usūyaṃ karoti, pubbepi akāsiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

'Having obtained fame, the foolish one...' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta. For in the Hall of Dhamma, the monks were discussing Devadatta's demerits, saying: 'Friends, Devadatta, even upon seeing the Tathāgata's face—glorious like the full moon, adorned with the thirty-two marks of a great man and the eighty minor characteristics, surrounded by a fathom-wide radiance, emitting dense Buddha-rays in swirling clusters and in pairs—and his person, which has attained supreme beauty, is unable to gladden his mind, and feels only envy. When it is said, "Buddhas are endowed with such virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation," he is unable to endure the praise and feels only envy.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered here?' When they replied, 'Concerning this matter,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta feels envy when my praise is spoken; he did so in the past as well.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte magadharaṭṭhe rājagahanagare ekasmiṃ magadharāje rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto hatthiyoniyaṃ nibbattitvā sabbaseto ahosi heṭṭhā vaṇṇitasadisāya rūpasampattiyā samannāgato. Atha naṃ “lakkhaṇasampanno aya”nti so rājā maṅgalahatthiṃ akāsi. Athekasmiṃ chaṇadivase sakalanagaraṃ devanagaraṃ viya alaṅkārāpetvā sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitaṃ maṅgalahatthiṃ abhiruhitvā mahantena rājānubhāvena nagaraṃ padakkhiṇaṃ akāsi. Mahājano tattha tattha ṭhatvā maṅgalahatthino rūpasobhaggappattaṃ sarīraṃ disvā “aho rūpaṃ, aho gati, aho līḷā, aho lakkhaṇasampatti, evarūpo nāma sabbasetavaravāraṇo cakkavattirañño anucchaviko”ti maṅgalahatthimeva vaṇṇesi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, in the city of Rājagaha, while a certain king of Magadha was ruling, the Bodhisatta was born as an elephant, and he was completely white, endowed with a beauty of form like that described below. Then, thinking, 'This one is endowed with auspicious marks,' the king made him the state elephant. On a certain festival day, having had the entire city decorated like a celestial city, the king mounted the state elephant, which was adorned with all ornaments, and circumambulated the city with great royal majesty. The populace, standing here and there and seeing the state elephant’s body, which had attained supreme beauty, praised only the state elephant, saying: 'Oh, what form! Oh, what a gait! Oh, what grace! Oh, what perfection of marks! Truly, such an all-white, excellent elephant is worthy of a universal monarch!'

Rājā maṅgalahatthissa vaṇṇaṃ sutvā sahituṃ asakkonto usūyaṃ uppādetvā “ajjeva taṃ pabbatapāde pātetvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpessāmī”ti hatthācariyaṃ pakkosāpetvā “kinti katvā tayā ayaṃ nāgo sikkhāpito”ti āha. “Susikkhāpito, devā”ti. “Na susikkhito, dusikkhito”ti. “Susikkhito, devā”ti. “Yadi susikkhito[P 1.0445], sakkhissasi naṃ vepullapabbatamatthakaṃ āropetu”nti. “Āma, devā”ti. “Tena hi ehī”ti sayaṃ otaritvā hatthācariyaṃ āropetvā pabbatapādaṃ gantvā hatthācariyena hatthipiṭṭhiyaṃ nisīditvāva hatthimhi vepullapabbatamatthakaṃ āropite sayampi amaccagaṇaparivuto pabbatamatthakaṃ abhiruhitvā hatthiṃ papātābhimukhaṃ kāretvā “tvaṃ ‘mayā esa susikkhāpito’ti vadesi, tīhiyeva tāva naṃ pādehi ṭhapehī”ti āha. Hatthācariyo piṭṭhiyaṃ nisīditvāva “bho tīhi pādehi tiṭṭhā”ti hatthissa paṇhikāya saññaṃ adāsi, mahāsatto tathā akāsi. Puna rājā “dvīhi purimapādehiyeva ṭhapehī”ti āha, mahāsatto dve pacchimapāde ukkhipitvā purimapādehi aṭṭhāsi. “Pacchimapādehiyevā”ti vuttepi dve purimapāde ukkhipitvā pacchimapādehi aṭṭhāsi, “ekenā”ti vuttepi tayo pāde ukkhipitvā ekeneva [M 1.0471] aṭṭhāsi. Athassa apatanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “sace pahosi, ākāse naṃ ṭhapehī”ti āha.

Hearing the praise of the state elephant, the king was unable to endure it. Becoming envious, he thought, 'This very day I will have him thrown from a mountain precipice and put to death.' He summoned the elephant trainer and asked, 'How have you trained this elephant?' 'He is well-trained, Your Majesty,' he replied. 'Not well-trained, but poorly trained,' said the king. 'He is well-trained, Your Majesty,' the trainer insisted. 'If he is well-trained, can you make him ascend to the summit of Mount Vepulla?' 'Yes, Your Majesty.' 'Then come,' said the king. He dismounted, had the trainer mount, and went to the foot of the mountain. With the trainer seated on its back, the elephant ascended to the summit of Mount Vepulla. The king, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, also climbed to the summit and had the elephant face the precipice. 'You claim that he is well-trained by you. First, make him stand on just three legs,' he said. The trainer, remaining on the elephant's back, gave a signal with his heel, and the Great Being did so. Then the king said, 'Make him stand on just his two front legs.' The Great Being lifted his two hind legs and stood on his front legs. When told, 'On just his hind legs,' he lifted his two front legs and stood on his hind legs. When commanded, 'On just one leg,' he lifted three legs and stood on one. Then, realizing that the elephant would not fall, the king said, 'If you are able, make him stand in the air.'

Ācariyo cintesi – “sakalajambudīpe iminā sadiso susikkhito hatthī nāma natthi, nissaṃsayaṃ panetaṃ esa papāte pātetvā māretukāmo bhavissatī”ti. So tassa kaṇṇamūle mantesi “tāta, ayaṃ rājā taṃ papāte pātetvā māretukāmo, na tvaṃ etassa anucchaviko. Sace te ākāsena gantuṃ balaṃ atthi, maṃ yathānisinnaṃyeva ādāya vehāsaṃ abbhuggantvā bārāṇasiṃ [V 1.0427] gacchā”ti. Puññiddhiyā samannāgato mahāsatto taṅkhaṇaññeva ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Hatthācariyo “mahārāja, ayaṃ hatthī puññiddhiyā samannāgato, na tādisassa mandapuññassa dubbuddhino anucchaviko, paṇḍitassa puññasampannassa rañño anucchaviko, tādisā nāma mandapuññā evarūpaṃ vāhanaṃ labhitvā tassa guṇaṃ ajānantā tañceva vāhanaṃ avasesañca yasasampattiṃ nāsentiyevā”ti vatvā hatthikkhandhe nisinnova imaṃ gāthamāha –

The trainer thought, "In all of Jambudīpa, there is no elephant so well-trained as this one. Without a doubt, this king intends to have him thrown from the precipice and killed." He conferred with him at his ear, saying, "My dear, this king wishes to have you thrown from the precipice and killed. You are not suited for him. If you have the power to travel through the air, take me just as I am seated, rise into the sky, and go to Bārāṇasī." The Great Being, endowed with the power of merit, immediately stood in the air. The elephant trainer, while still seated upon the elephant's back, said, "Great King, this elephant is endowed with the power of merit. He is not suited for one such as you, of little merit and poor wisdom. He is suited for a wise king who is endowed with merit. Indeed, those of little merit, upon gaining such a noble mount, not knowing its virtues, destroy both the mount itself and the remainder of their glory and fortune." Saying this, he spoke this verse:

122.

122.

“Yasaṃ laddhāna dummedho, anatthaṃ carati attano;

Attano ca paresañca, hiṃsāya paṭipajjatī”ti.

"Having gained glory, the fool works for his own ruin; he engages in what is harmful to himself and to others."

Tatrāyaṃ [P 1.0446] saṅkhepattho – mahārāja, tādiso dummedho nippañño puggalo parivārasampattiṃ labhitvā attano anatthaṃ carati. Kiṃkāraṇā? So hi yasamadamatto kattabbākattabbaṃ ajānanto attano ca paresañca hiṃsāya paṭipajjati. Hiṃsā vuccati kilamanaṃ dukkhuppādanaṃ, tadatthāya eva paṭipajjatīti.

Herein is the meaning in brief: Great King, such a foolish and unwise person, having gained a retinue and fortune, acts for his own ruin. For what reason? Because, intoxicated with the pride of glory, not knowing what ought and ought not to be done, he engages in what is harmful to himself and to others. Harm is said to be weariness and the production of suffering; it is for this very purpose that he acts.

Evaṃ imāya gāthāya rañño dhammaṃ desetvā “tiṭṭha dāni tva”nti vatvā ākāse uppatitvā bārāṇasinagaraṃ gantvā rājaṅgaṇe ākāse aṭṭhāsi. Sakalanagaraṃ saṅkhubhitvā “amhākaṃ rañño ākāsena setavaravāraṇo āgantvā rājaṅgaṇe ṭhito”ti ekakolāhalaṃ ahosi. Vegena raññopi ārocesuṃ. Rājā nikkhamitvā “sace mayhaṃ upabhogatthāya āgatosi, bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāhī”ti āha. Bodhisatto bhūmiyaṃ patiṭṭhāsi, ācariyo otaritvā rājānaṃ vanditvā “kuto āgatosi, tātā”ti vutte “rājagahato”ti vatvā sabbaṃ pavattiṃ ārocesi. Rājā “manāpaṃ te, tāta, kataṃ idhāgacchantenā”ti tuṭṭhahaṭṭho [M 1.0472] nagaraṃ sajjāpetvā vāraṇaṃ maṅgalahatthiṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā sakalarajjaṃ tayo koṭṭhāse katvā ekaṃ bodhisattassa adāsi, ekaṃ ācariyassa, ekaṃ attanā aggahesi. Bodhisattassa āgatakālato paṭṭhāyeva pana rañño sakalajambudīpe rajjaṃ hatthagatameva jātaṃ. So jambudīpe aggarājā hutvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ agamāsi.

Having thus taught the king the Dhamma with this verse, he said, "Now you remain here," rose into the sky, went to the city of Bārāṇasī, and stood in the air above the royal courtyard. The entire city was in an uproar, and a single clamor arose: "For our king, an excellent white elephant has come through the sky and is standing in the royal courtyard!" They quickly informed the king. The king came out and said, "If you have come for my use, please alight upon the ground." The Bodhisatta alighted upon the ground. The trainer dismounted, paid homage to the king, and when asked, "From where have you come, my dear?" he replied, "From Rājagaha," and recounted the entire affair. The king, delighted and joyful, said, "My dear, you have done a pleasing thing by coming here." He had the city decorated, placed the elephant in the stall of the state elephant, and divided the entire kingdom into three parts: one he gave to the Bodhisatta, one to the trainer, and one he took for himself. From the time of the Bodhisatta's arrival, the sovereignty over all of Jambudīpa came into that king's hands. Becoming the chief king in Jambudīpa, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving alms and passed on according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā magadharājā devadatto ahosi, bārāṇasirājā sāriputto, hatthācariyo ānando, hatthī pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher connected the birth story: "At that time, the king of Magadha was Devadatta, the king of Bārāṇasī was Sāriputta, the elephant trainer was Ānanda, and the elephant, indeed, was I myself."

Dummedhajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Dummedha Jātaka, the Second.

[123] 3. Naṅgalīsajātakavaṇṇanā

[123] 3. The Commentary on the Naṅgalīsa Jātaka

Asabbatthagāmiṃ [V 1.0428] vācanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto lāḷudāyittheraṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira dhammaṃ kathento “imasmiṃ ṭhāne idaṃ kathetabbaṃ, imasmiṃ ṭhāne idaṃ na kathetabba”nti yuttāyuttaṃ na jānāti, maṅgale avamaṅgalaṃ vadanto “tirokuṭṭesu tiṭṭhanti, sandhisiṅghāṭakesu cā”ti idaṃ avamaṅgalaṃ maṅgalaṃ katvā anumodanaṃ katheti. Avamaṅgalesu anumodanaṃ karonto “bahū devā manussā ca, maṅgalāni acintayu”nti vatvā “evarūpānaṃ maṅgalānaṃ satampi [P 1.0447] sahassampi kātuṃ samatthā hothā”ti vadati. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū “āvuso, lāḷudāyī yuttāyuttaṃ na jānāti, sabbattha abhāsitabbavācaṃ bhāsatī”ti kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, lāḷudāyī idāneva dandhaparisakkano yuttāyuttaṃ na jānāti, pubbepi evarūpo ahosi, niccaṃ lāḷakoyeva eso”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"Speech not fit for every place..."—this the Teacher told while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the Elder Lāḷudāyī. It is said that when teaching the Dhamma, he did not know what was appropriate and inappropriate, what should be said in one place and what should not be said in another. On an auspicious occasion, he would speak of inauspicious things, reciting "They stand outside the walls, and at the junctions and crossroads," making this inauspicious text into a blessing. And on inauspicious occasions, giving a blessing, he would recite "Many gods and men have pondered on blessings," and then say, "May you be able to perform a hundred, even a thousand, such blessings!" Then one day in the Dhamma hall, the monks started a discussion, saying, "Venerable sirs, Lāḷudāyī does not know what is appropriate and inappropriate; he speaks everywhere speech that ought not to be spoken." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" When they told him, "For this one," he said, "Monks, it is not only now that Lāḷudāyī is slow-witted and does not know what is appropriate and inappropriate; he was just so in the past. He has always been a simpleton." And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañca [M 1.0473] māṇavakasatāni sippaṃ vācesi. Tadā tesu māṇavesu eko dandhaparisakkano lāḷako māṇavo dhammantevāsiko hutvā sippaṃ uggaṇhāti, dandhabhāvena pana uggaṇhituṃ na sakkoti. Bodhisattassa pana upakāro hoti, dāso viya sabbakiccāni karoti. Athekadivasaṃ bodhisatto sāyamāsaṃ bhuñjitvā sayane nipanno taṃ māṇavaṃ hatthapādapiṭṭhiparikammāni katvā gacchantaṃ āha “tāta, mañcapāde upatthambhetvā yāhī”ti. Māṇavo ekaṃ pādaṃ upatthambhetvā ekassa upatthambhakaṃ alabhanto attano ūrumhi ṭhapetvā rattiṃ khepesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a great and wealthy brahmin family. Having come of age, he mastered all the sciences at Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher in Bārāṇasī, instructing five hundred young men in the arts. Among those young men was a slow-witted simpleton named Lāḷaka, who became a resident pupil to learn the arts. Due to his dullness, however, he was not able to master them. But he was of great service to the Bodhisatta, performing all duties like a servant. One day, after the Bodhisatta had eaten his evening meal and was lying on his couch, he said to the young man, who had just finished massaging his hands, feet, and back and was about to leave, "My dear, steady the legs of the couch before you go." The young man steadied one leg, but being unable to find a support for another, he placed that leg on his own thigh and so passed the night.

Bodhisatto paccūsasamaye uṭṭhāya taṃ disvā “kiṃ, tāta, nisinnosī”ti pucchi. “Ācariya, ekassa mañcapādassa upatthambhakaṃ alabhanto ūrumhi ṭhapetvā nisinnomhī”ti. Bodhisatto saṃviggamānaso hutvā “ayaṃ ati viya mayhaṃ upakāro, ettakānaṃ pana māṇavakānaṃ antare ayameva dandho sippaṃ sikkhituṃ na sakkoti, kathaṃ nu kho ahaṃ imaṃ paṇḍitaṃ kareyya”nti cintesi. Athassa etadahosi “attheko upāyo, ahaṃ imaṃ māṇavaṃ dāruatthāya paṇṇatthāya ca vanaṃ gantvā āgataṃ ‘ajja te kiṃ diṭṭhaṃ, kiṃ kata’nti pucchissāmi. Atha me ‘idaṃ nāma ajja mayā diṭṭhaṃ, idaṃ kata’nti ācikkhissati. Atha naṃ [V 1.0429] ‘tayā diṭṭhañca katañca kīdisa’nti pucchissāmi, so ‘evarūpaṃ nāmā’ti [P 1.0448] upamāya ca kāraṇena ca kathessati. Iti naṃ navaṃ navaṃ upamañca kāraṇañca kathāpetvā iminā upāyena paṇḍitaṃ karissāmī”ti. So taṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta māṇava, ito paṭṭhāya dāruatthāya vā paṇṇatthāya vā gataṭṭhāne yaṃ te tattha diṭṭhaṃ vā sutaṃ vā bhuttaṃ vā pītaṃ vā khāditaṃ vā hoti, taṃ āgantvā mayhaṃ āroceyyāsī”ti āha.

The Bodhisatta rose at dawn and, seeing him, asked, 'Why, dear one, are you sitting here?' 'Teacher, being unable to find a support for one leg of the bed, I placed it on my thigh and have been sitting.' The Bodhisatta, deeply moved, thought, 'This one is of great service to me, yet among so many young men, only this dull one cannot learn the craft. How then shall I make him wise?' Then it occurred to him: 'There is a way. I will ask this young man, upon his return from going to the forest for firewood and leaves, "What did you see today? What did you do?" Then he will tell me, "Today I saw such and such, and I did such and such." Then I will ask him, "What were the things you saw and did like?" He will then explain with similes and reasons. In this way, by having him relate new similes and reasons, I shall make him wise by this method.' He summoned him and said, 'Dear young man, from now on, when you go to a place for firewood or for leaves, whatever you see, hear, eat, drink, or chew there, you must come and report it to me.'

So “sādhū”ti paṭissuṇitvā ekadivasaṃ māṇavehi saddhiṃ dāruatthāya araññaṃ gato tattha sappaṃ disvā āgantvā “ācariya, sappo me diṭṭho”ti ārocesi. “Sappo nāma, tāta, kīdiso hotī”ti? “Seyyathāpi naṅgalīsā”ti. “Sādhu, tāta, manāpā te upamā āhaṭā, sappā nāma naṅgalīsasadisāva hontī”ti. Atha bodhisatto “māṇavakena manāpā upamā āhaṭā, sakkhissāmi naṃ paṇḍitaṃ kātu”nti cintesi. Māṇavo puna ekadivasaṃ araññe hatthiṃ disvā “hatthī me ācariya diṭṭho”ti āha. “Hatthī nāma, tāta, kīdiso”ti? “Seyyathāpi, naṅgalīsā”ti. Bodhisatto “hatthissa [M 1.0474] soṇḍā naṅgalīsasadisā honti, dantādayo evarūpā ca evarūpā ca. Ayaṃ pana bālatāya vibhajitvā kathetuṃ asakkonto soṇḍaṃ sandhāya kathesi maññe”ti tuṇhī ahosi. Athekadivasaṃ nimantane ucchuṃ labhitvā “ācariya, ajja mayaṃ ucchu khādimhā”ti āha. “Ucchu nāma kīdiso”ti vutte “seyyathāpi naṅgalīsā”ti āha. Ācariyo “thokaṃ patirūpaṃ kāraṇaṃ kathesī”ti tuṇhī jāto.

'Very well,' he agreed. One day, having gone to the forest with the young men for firewood, he saw a snake there. Upon returning, he reported, 'Teacher, I saw a snake.' 'What is a snake like, dear one?' 'It is like a plough-pole.' 'Good, dear one, you have brought a pleasing simile. Snakes are indeed like plough-poles.' Then the Bodhisatta thought, 'The young man has brought a pleasing simile; I shall be able to make him wise.' On another day, the young man saw an elephant in the forest and said, 'Teacher, I saw an elephant.' 'What is an elephant like, dear one?' 'It is like a plough-pole.' The Bodhisatta thought, 'An elephant’s trunk is like a plough-pole, but its tusks and other parts are of various other forms. This one, due to his dullness, is unable to explain with distinctions; I suppose he spoke with reference to the trunk,' and he remained silent. Then one day, having received sugarcane at an invitation, he said, 'Teacher, today we ate sugarcane.' When asked, 'What is sugarcane like?' he replied, 'It is like a plough-pole.' The teacher thought, 'He speaks a somewhat suitable reason,' and became silent.

Punekadivasaṃ nimantane ekacce māṇavā guḷaṃ dadhinā bhuñjiṃsu, ekacce khīrena. So āgantvā “ācariya, ajja mayaṃ dadhinā khīrena ca bhuñjimhā”ti vatvā “dadhikhīraṃ nāma kīdisaṃ hotī”ti vutte “seyyathāpi naṅgalīsā”ti āha. Ācariyo “ayaṃ māṇavo ‘sappo naṅgalīsasadiso’ti kathento tāva sukathitaṃ kathesi, ‘hatthī naṅgalīsasadiso’ti kathentenāpi soṇḍaṃ sandhāya lesena kathitaṃ. ‘Ucchu naṅgalīsasadisa’nti kathanepi leso atthi, ‘dadhikhīrāni pana niccaṃ paṇḍarāni pakkhittabhājanasaṇṭhānānī’ti idha [P 1.0449] sabbena sabbaṃ upamaṃ na kathesi, na sakkā imaṃ lāḷakaṃ sikkhāpetu”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Again one day at an invitation, some young men ate jaggery with curd, and some with milk. He returned and said, 'Teacher, today we ate with curd and milk.' When asked, 'What are curd and milk like?' he replied, 'They are like a plough-pole.' The teacher thought, 'This young man, in saying "a snake is like a plough-pole," spoke well. Even in saying "an elephant is like a plough-pole," he spoke with a subtle hint, referring to the trunk. In the statement "sugarcane is like a plough-pole," there is also a slight resemblance. But as for curd and milk, which are always white and take the shape of the vessel they are put into, in this case the simile is not fitting in any way at all. It is not possible to teach this Lāḷaka.' Thinking thus, he spoke this verse:

123.

123.

“Asabbatthagāmiṃ vācaṃ, bālo sabbattha bhāsati;

Nāyaṃ dadhiṃ vedi na naṅgalīsaṃ, dadhippayaṃ maññati naṅgalīsa”nti.

'A fool utters in every case speech that is not universally applicable. This one knows neither curd nor a plough-pole; he thinks curd and milk are like a plough-pole.'

Tatrāyaṃ [V 1.0430] saṅkhepattho – yā vācā opammavasena sabbattha na gacchati, taṃ asabbatthagāmiṃ vācaṃ bālo dandhapuggalo sabbattha bhāsati, “dadhi nāma kīdisa”nti puṭṭhopi “seyyathāpi, naṅgalīsā”ti vadateva. Evaṃ vadanto nāyaṃ dadhiṃ vedi na naṅgalīsaṃ. Kiṃkāraṇā? Dadhippayaṃ maññati naṅgalīsaṃ, yasmā ayaṃ dadhimpi naṅgalīsameva maññati. Atha vā dadhīti dadhimeva, payanti khīraṃ, dadhi ca payañca dadhippayaṃ. Yasmā dadhikhīrānipi ayaṃ naṅgalīsameva maññati, ediso cāyaṃ bālo, kiṃ imināti antevāsikānaṃ dhammakathaṃ kathetvā paribbayaṃ datvā taṃ uyyojesi.

Herein is the brief meaning: A foolish, slow-witted person utters in every case speech that, by way of simile, does not apply in all situations. Even when asked, 'What is curd like?' he just says, 'It is like a plough-pole.' Speaking thus, this one knows neither curd nor a plough-pole. For what reason? He thinks curd and milk are like a plough-pole, because he considers even curd to be a plough-pole. Alternatively, 'dadhi' is curd, 'paya' is milk, and 'dadhippayaṃ' is curd and milk. Since he considers even curd and milk to be a plough-pole, of what use is such a fool? After giving a Dhamma talk to his resident pupils and providing for his journey, he sent him away.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā lāḷakamāṇavo lāḷudāyī ahosi, disāpāmokkho ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: 'At that time, the young man Lāḷaka was Lāḷudāyī, and the world-renowned teacher was I myself.'

Naṅgalīsajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Naṅgalīsa Jātaka, the third.

[124] 4. Ambajātakavaṇṇanā

[124] 4. The Commentary on the Amba Jātaka.

Vāyametheva [M 1.0475] purisoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ vattasampannaṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira sāvatthivāsī kulaputto sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajito vattasampanno ahosi, ācariyupajjhāyavattāni pānīyaparibhojanīyauposathāgārajantāgharādivattāni ca sādhukaṃ karoti, cuddasasu mahāvattesu asītikhandhakavattesu ca paripūrakārīyeva hoti, vihāraṃ sammajjati, pariveṇaṃ vitakkamāḷakaṃ vihāramaggaṃ sammajjati, manussānaṃ pānīyaṃ deti. Manussā tassa vattasampattiyaṃ pasīditvā pañcasatamattāni dhuvabhattāni adaṃsu, mahālābhasakkāro uppajji. Taṃ nissāya bahūnaṃ phāsuvihāro jāto. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, asuko nāma bhikkhu attano vattasampattiyā mahantaṃ lābhasakkāraṃ nibbattesi, etaṃ ekaṃ nissāya bahūnaṃ phāsuvihāro jāto”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave[P 1.0450], etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepāyaṃ bhikkhu vattasampanno, pubbepetaṃ ekaṃ nissāya pañca isisatāni phalāphalatthāya araññaṃ agantvā eteneva ānītaphalāphalehi yāpesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

"A man should indeed strive"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a monk accomplished in his duties. It is said that a clansman from Sāvatthī, having dedicated himself wholeheartedly to the Dispensation, went forth and became accomplished in his duties. He performed well the duties towards his teachers and preceptors, as well as the duties concerning drinking water, water for use, the Uposatha hall, the steam bath, and so on. He was indeed a perfect fulfiller of the fourteen great duties and the eighty Khandhaka duties. He swept the monastery, the monastery grounds, the ambulatory, and the monastery paths. He provided drinking water for the people. Pleased with his accomplishment in his duties, the people offered him about five hundred regular meals, and great gain and honor arose. Relying on him, a comfortable living arose for many. Then one day, in the Hall of Dhamma, the monks raised a discussion: "Venerable sirs, a certain monk, through his accomplishment in his duties, has generated great gain and honor. Relying on this one monk, a comfortable living has arisen for many." The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" and when it was told, "For this one," he said, "Not only now, monks, was this monk accomplished in his duties; in the past, too, he was accomplished in his duties. In the past, relying on this one monk, five hundred seers did not go into the forest for the sake of fruits, but sustained themselves with the fruits he brought." So saying, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0431] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā pañcasataisiparivāro pabbatapāde vihāsi. Tadā himavante caṇḍo nidāgho ahosi, tattha tattha pānīyāni chijjiṃsu, tiracchānā pānīyaṃ alabhamānā kilamanti. Atha tesu tāpasesu eko tāpaso tesaṃ pipāsadukkhaṃ disvā ekaṃ rukkhaṃ chinditvā doṇiṃ katvā pānīyaṃ ussiñcitvā doṇiṃ pūretvā tesaṃ pānīyaṃ adāsi. Bahūsu sannipatitvā pānīyaṃ pivantesu tāpasassa phalāphalatthāya gamanokāso nāhosi. So nirāhāropi pānīyaṃ detiyeva. Migagaṇā cintesuṃ “ayaṃ amhākaṃ pānīyaṃ dento phalāphalatthāya gantuṃ okāsaṃ na labhati, nirāhāratāya ativiya kilamati, handamayaṃ katikaṃ karomā”ti. Te katikaṃ akaṃsu “ito paṭṭhāya pānīyaṃ pivanatthāya āgacchantena attano balānurūpena phalāphalaṃ gahetvāva āgantabba”nti. Te tato paṭṭhāya ekeko tiracchāno [M 1.0476] attano attano balānurūpena madhuramadhurāni ambajambupanasādīnigahetvāva āgacchati. Ekassa atthāya ābhataṃ phalāphalaṃ aḍḍhateyyasakaṭabhārappamāṇaṃ ahosi. Pañcasatatāpasā tadeva paribhuñjanti. Atirekaṃ chaḍḍiyittha.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a northern brahmin family. When he came of age, he went forth into the ascetic life and lived at the foot of a mountain with a retinue of five hundred seers. At that time in the Himalayas, there was a fierce summer, and water sources dried up here and there. The animals, unable to find water, were suffering. Then, one of the ascetics, seeing their suffering from thirst, cut down a tree, made a trough, drew water to fill the trough, and gave it to them to drink. As many animals gathered to drink, the ascetic had no opportunity to go for fruits. Even without food, he continued to give them water. The herds of animals thought, "While giving us water, this one has no opportunity to go for fruits. He suffers greatly from lack of food. Come, let us make an agreement." They made an agreement: "From now on, whoever comes to drink water must bring fruits according to their strength." From then on, each and every animal, according to its strength, would bring very sweet fruits such as mangoes, rose-apples, and jackfruits. The fruits brought for that one person amounted to two and a half cartloads. The five hundred ascetics consumed just that, and the excess was discarded.

Bodhisatto taṃ disvā “ekaṃ nāma vattasampannaṃ nissāya ettakānaṃ tāpasānaṃ phalāphalatthāya agantvā yāpanaṃ uppannaṃ, vīriyaṃ nāma kātabbamevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing this, the Bodhisatta thought, "Relying on one who is accomplished in his duties, sustenance has arisen for so many ascetics without their having to go for fruits. Indeed, effort must be made." So saying, he spoke this verse:

124.

124.

“Vāyametheva puriso, na nibbindeyya paṇḍito;

Vāyāmassa phalaṃ passa, bhuttā ambā anītiha”nti.

"A person should indeed strive; a wise one should not grow weary. Behold the fruit of striving: the mangoes were eaten, not from hearsay."

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – paṇḍito attano vattapūraṇādike kammasmiṃ vāyametheva, na ukkaṇṭheyya. Kiṃkāraṇā? Vāyāmassa nipphalatāya abhāvato. Iti mahāsatto [P 1.0451] “vāyāmo nāmesa saphalova hotī”ti isigaṇaṃ ālapanto “vāyāmassa phalaṃ passā”ti āha. Kīdisaṃ? Bhuttā ambā anītihaṃ. Tattha ambāti desanāmattaṃ, tehi pana nānappakārāni phalāphalāni ābhatāni. Tesu sampannatarānaṃ ussannatarānaṃ vā vasena “ambā”ti vuttaṃ. Ye imehi pañcahi isisatehi sayaṃ araññaṃ agantvā ekassa atthāya ānītā ambā bhuttā, idaṃ vāyāmassa phalaṃ. Tañca kho pana anītihaṃ, “iti āha iti āhā”ti evaṃ itihītihena gahetabbaṃ na hoti, paccakkhameva taṃ phalaṃ passāti. Evaṃ mahāsatto isigaṇassa ovādaṃ adāsi.

Here is the summary: a wise person should indeed strive in their work, such as fulfilling their duties, and should not be disheartened. Why? Because effort is never fruitless. Thus the Great Being, addressing the group of seers, said, "Effort is indeed fruitful," and declared, "Behold the fruit of effort." What kind of fruit? "The mangoes were eaten, not from hearsay." Here, 'mangoes' is just a manner of speaking; for they brought various kinds of fruits. It is in reference to the most excellent and abundant among them that 'mangoes' was said. Those mangoes eaten by these five hundred seers, brought for the sake of one without their having to go to the forest themselves—this is the fruit of effort. And this is not from hearsay; it is not to be taken on the basis of tradition, as in "so it was said, so it was said." Behold that fruit directly. In this way, the Great Being gave his instruction to the group of seers.

Satthā [V 1.0432] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā vattasampanno tāpaso ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, gaṇasatthā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma discourse, the Teacher connected the Jātaka: "The ascetic accomplished in his duties at that time was this monk, and the teacher of the group was I myself."

Ambajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Amba Jātaka, the Fourth.

[125] 5. Kaṭāhakajātakavaṇṇanā

[125] 5. The Commentary on the Kaṭāhaka Jātaka.

Bahumpi [M 1.0477] so vikattheyyāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ vikatthakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tassa vatthu heṭṭhā kathitasadisameva.

"Even if he should boast much"—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a boastful monk. His story is just the same as one told previously.

Atīte pana bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mahāvibhavo seṭṭhi ahosi. Tassa bhariyā puttaṃ vijāyi, dāsīpissa taṃ divasaññeva puttaṃ vijāyi. Te ekatova vaḍḍhiṃsu. Seṭṭhiputte lekhaṃ sikkhante dāsopissa phalakaṃ vahamāno gantvā teneva saddhiṃ lekhaṃ sikkhi, gaṇanaṃ sikkhi, dve tayo vohāre akāsi. So anukkamena vacanakusalo vohārakusalo yuvā abhirūpo ahosi, nāmena kaṭāheko nāma. So seṭṭhighare bhaṇḍāgārikakammaṃ karonto cintesi “na maṃ ime sabbakālaṃ bhaṇḍāgārikakammaṃ kāressanti, kiñcideva dosaṃ disvā tāḷetvā bandhitvā lakkhaṇena aṅketvā dāsaparibhogenapi paribhuñjissanti. Paccante kho pana seṭṭhissa sahāyako seṭṭhi atthi, yaṃnūnāhaṃ seṭṭhissa vacanena lekhaṃ ādāya tattha gantvā ‘ahaṃ seṭṭhiputto’ti vatvā taṃ seṭṭhiṃ vañcetvā tassa dhītaraṃ gahetvā sukhaṃ vaseyya”nti. So sayameva paṇṇaṃ gahetvā [P 1.0452] “ahaṃ asukaṃ nāma mama puttaṃ tava santikaṃ pahiṇiṃ, āvāhavivāhasambandho nāma mayhañca tayā, tuyhañca mayā saddhiṃ patirūpo, tasmā tvaṃ imassa dārakassa attano dhītaraṃ datvā etaṃ tattheva vasāpehi, ahampi okāsaṃ labhitvā āgamissāmī”ti likhitvā seṭṭhisseva muddikāya lañjetvā yathārucitaṃ paribbayañceva gandhavatthādīni ca gahetvā paccantaṃ gantvā seṭṭhiṃ disvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a wealthy merchant. His wife gave birth to a son, and on that very day, his slave woman also gave birth to a son. They grew up together. While the merchant’s son was learning to write, the slave’s son, carrying his writing board, would go along with him and also learn writing and arithmetic, and he engaged in two or three transactions.
