Gradually, he became skilled in speech and in business, a handsome young man named Kaṭāhaka. While working as a storekeeper in the merchant’s house, he thought, “They will not keep me as a storekeeper forever. If they find some fault, they will beat me, imprison me, brand me with a mark, and subject me to the treatment of a slave. However, in the borderlands, the merchant has a friend who is a merchant. What if I were to take a letter in the merchant’s name, go there, and deceiving that merchant by claiming to be his son, take his daughter and live happily?” So he himself took a leaf and wrote, “I have sent my son, so-and-so by name, to you. A marriage alliance between us is indeed fitting. Therefore, give your daughter to this boy and let him reside there. I too will come when I get the opportunity.” He stamped it with the merchant’s own seal, took suitable provisions, as well as perfumes, clothes, and so forth, and went to the borderlands. There, he saw the merchant, paid homage, and stood in attendance.

Atha naṃ seṭṭhi “kuto āgatosi, tātā”ti pucchi. “Bārāṇasito”ti. “Kassa puttosī”ti? “Bārāṇasiseṭṭhissā”ti. “Kenatthenāgatosī”ti? Tasmiṃ khaṇe kaṭāhako “idaṃ disvā jānissathā”ti paṇṇaṃ adāsi. Seṭṭhi paṇṇaṃ vācetvā “idānāhaṃ jīvāmi nāmā”ti tuṭṭhacitto dhītaraṃ datvā patiṭṭhāpesi. Tassa parivāro mahanto ahosi. So yāgukhajjakādīsu vā vatthagandhādīsu [V 1.0433] vā upanītesu “evampi nāma yāguṃ [M 1.0478] pacanti, evaṃ khajjakaṃ, evaṃ bhattaṃ, aho paccantavāsikā nāmā”ti yāguādīni garahati. “Ime paccantavāsibhāveneva ahatasāṭake vaḷañjituṃ na jānanti, gandhe pisituṃ, pupphāni ganthituṃ na jānantī”ti vatthakammantikādayo garahati.

Then the merchant asked him, “Where have you come from, my son?” “From Benares,” he replied. “Whose son are you?” “The son of the Benares merchant.” “For what reason have you come?” At that moment, Kaṭāhaka, handing him the letter, said, “Having seen this, you will know.” The merchant, having read the letter, overjoyed, said, “Now I truly live!” He gave his daughter to him and established him there. His retinue was large. When rice gruel, fried cakes, and so on, or cloth, perfumes, and so on, were brought to him, he would disparage them, saying, “Is this how they cook rice gruel? Is this how they make fried cakes? Is this how they cook rice? Oh, these borderlanders!” He would disparage the rice gruel and so on. “Because they live in the borderlands, they do not know how to use a new cloth, how to grind perfumes, or how to string flowers!” He disparaged the cloth-workers and others.

Bodhisattopi dāsaṃ apassanto “kaṭāhako na dissati, kahaṃ gato, pariyesatha na”nti samantā manusse payojesi. Tesu eko tattha gantvā taṃ disvā sañjānitvā attānaṃ ajānāpetvā āgantvā bodhisattassa ārocesi. Bodhisatto taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā “ayuttaṃ tena kataṃ, gantvā naṃ gahetvā āgacchissāmī”ti rājānaṃ āpucchitvā mahantena parivārena nikkhami. “Seṭṭhi kira paccantaṃ gacchatī”ti sabbattha pākaṭo jāto. Kaṭāhako “seṭṭhi kira āgacchatī”ti sutvā cintesi “na so aññena kāraṇena āgacchissati, maṃ nissāyevassa āgamanena bhavitabbaṃ. Sace panāhaṃ palāyissāmi, puna āgantuṃ na sakkā bhavissati. Atthi panesa upāyo. Mama sāmikassa paṭipathaṃ gantvā dāsakammaṃ katvā tameva ārādhessāmī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya parisamajjhe evaṃ bhāsati “aññe bālamanussā attano bālabhāvena mātāpitūnaṃ [P 1.0453] guṇaṃ ajānantā tesaṃ bhojanavelāya apacitikammaṃ akatvā tehi saddhiṃyeva bhuñjanti, mayaṃ pana mātāpitūnaṃ bhojanakāle paṭiggahaṃ upanema, kheḷamallakaṃ upanema, bhājanāni upanema, pānīyampi bījanimpi gahetvā upatiṭṭhāmā”ti yāva sarīravaḷañjanakāle udakakalasaṃ ādāya paṭicchannaṭṭhānagamanā sabbaṃ dāsehi sāmikānaṃ kattabbakiccaṃ pakāsesi.

The Bodhisatta, not seeing the slave, said, “Kaṭāhaka is not to be seen. Where has he gone? Search for him,” and sent people all around. Among them, one went there, saw him, and recognized him, but without revealing himself, he returned and reported to the Bodhisatta. Hearing this account, the Bodhisatta thought, “What he did was improper. I will go and fetch him,” and taking leave of the king, he set out with a large retinue. It became known everywhere that the merchant was going to the borderlands. Kaṭāhaka, hearing that the merchant was coming, reflected, “He is not coming for any other reason; his coming must be on my account. If I flee now, it will be impossible to return later. But there is a way. I will go to meet my master, perform the duties of a slave, and thus appease him.” From then on, he spoke thus in the midst of the assembly: “Other foolish people, unaware of their parents' virtues due to their own foolishness, eat with them without performing acts of respect at mealtime. We, however, when it is time for our parents to eat, bring a receiving bowl, a spittoon, and the dishes, and attend them with water and a fan.” He proclaimed all the duties that slaves should perform for their masters, up to carrying a water pot when they go to a private place for cleansing the body.

So evaṃ parisaṃ uggaṇhāpetvā bodhisattassa paccantasamīpaṃ āgatakāle sasuraṃ avoca “tāta, mama kira pitā tumhākaṃ dassanatthāya āgacchati, tumhe khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ paṭiyādāpetha, ahaṃ paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā paṭipathaṃ gamissāmī”ti. So “sādhu, tātā”ti sampaṭicchi. Kaṭāhako bahuṃ paṇṇākāramādāya mahantena parivārena gantvā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā paṇṇākāraṃ adāsi. Bodhisattopi paṇṇākāraṃ gahetvā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā pātarāsakāle khandhāvāraṃ nivāsetvā sarīravaḷañjanatthāya paṭicchannaṭṭhānaṃ pāvisi. Kaṭāhako attano parivāraṃ [M 1.0479] nivattetvā kalasaṃ ādāya bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā udakakiccapariyosāne pādesu patitvā “sāmi, ahaṃ tumhākaṃ yattakaṃ icchatha, tattakaṃ dhanaṃ dassāmi, mā me yasaṃ antaradhāpayitthā”ti āha. Bodhisatto tassa vattasampadāya pasīditvā “mā bhāyi, natthi te mama santikā antarāyo”ti samassāsetvā paccantanagaraṃ pāvisi. Mahanto [V 1.0434] sakkāro ahosi, kaṭāhakopissa nirantaraṃ dāsena kattabbakiccaṃ karoti. Atha naṃ ekāya velāya sukhanisinnaṃ paccantaseṭṭhi āha “mahāseṭṭhi, mayā tumhākaṃ paṇṇaṃ disvāva tumhākaṃ puttassa dārikā dinnā”ti bodhisatto kaṭāhakaṃ puttameva katvā tadanucchavikaṃ piyavacanaṃ vatvā seṭṭhiṃ tosesi. Tato paṭṭhāya kaṭāhakassa mukhaṃ ulloketuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi.

Having thus instructed the assembly, when the Bodhisatta approached the border region, Kaṭāhaka said to his father-in-law, “Father, it seems my father is coming to see you. Please prepare food and refreshments. I will take a gift and go to meet him on the way.” The father-in-law agreed, saying, “Very well, my son.” Kaṭāhaka took a large quantity of gifts and went with a great retinue. He paid homage to the Bodhisatta and offered him the gifts. The Bodhisatta accepted the gifts, exchanged pleasantries with him, and at the time of the morning meal, having set up camp, he entered a secluded place to attend to his person. Kaṭāhaka dismissed his retinue, took a water pot, and went to the Bodhisatta. After finishing his ablutions, he fell at his feet and said, “Lord, I will give you as much wealth as you desire, but do not cause my reputation to be destroyed.” Pleased with his excellent conduct, the Bodhisatta reassured him, saying, “Do not fear, there is no danger to you from me,” and then entered the border town. Great honor was shown to him, and Kaṭāhaka continuously performed the duties of a servant for him. One day, while the Bodhisatta was comfortably seated, the border merchant said to him, “Great merchant, as soon as I saw your letter, I gave my daughter to your son.” The Bodhisatta, treating Kaṭāhaka as his own son and speaking affectionate words suitable to the occasion, pleased the merchant. From then on, there was no one capable of looking Kaṭāhaka in the face.

Athekadivasaṃ mahāsatto seṭṭhidhītaraṃ pakkositvā “ehi, amma, sīse me ūkā vicināhī”ti vatvā taṃ āgantvā ūkā gahetvā ṭhitaṃ piyavacanaṃ vatvā “kathehi, amma, kacci te mama putto sukhadukkhesu appamatto[P 1.0454], ubho janā sammodamānā samaggavāsaṃ vasathā”ti pucchi. “Tāta, mahāseṭṭhi tumhākaṃ puttassa añño doso natthi, kevalaṃ āhāraṃ garahatī”ti. “Amma, niccakālamesa dukkhasīlova, apica te ahaṃ tassa mukhabandhanamantaṃ dassāmi, taṃ tvaṃ sādhukaṃ uggaṇhitvā mama puttassa bhojanakāle garahantassa uggahitaniyāmeneva purato ṭhatvā vadeyyāsī”ti gāthaṃ uggaṇhāpetvā katipāhaṃ vasitvā bārāṇasimeva agamāsi. Kaṭāhakopi bahuṃ khādanīyabhojanīyaṃ ādāya anumaggaṃ gantvā bahudhanaṃ datvā vanditvā nivatti. So bodhisattassa gatakālato paṭṭhāya atirekamānī ahosi. So ekadivasaṃ seṭṭhidhītāya nānaggarasabhojanaṃ upanetvā kaṭacchuṃ ādāya parivisantiyā bhattaṃ garahituṃ ārabhi. Seṭṭhidhītā bodhisattassa santike uggahitaniyāmeneva imaṃ gāthamāha –

One day, the Great Being called the merchant’s daughter and said, “Come, dear, pick the lice from my head.” When she came and stood picking lice, he spoke affectionate words to her and asked, “Tell me, dear, is my son attentive to your joys and sorrows? Do you both live together in harmony and concord?” “Father, great merchant, there is no other fault in your son, except that he finds fault with the food.” “Dear, he has always been of a difficult nature. But I will teach you a charm to silence him. Learn it well, and when my son complains about the food, stand before him and recite it in the very manner you have learned.” He taught her a verse and, after staying a few days, returned to Varanasi. Kaṭāhaka also took much food and drink and, after escorting him part of the way, giving him much wealth, and paying respects, he turned back. From the time the Bodhisatta left, he became exceedingly arrogant. One day, when the merchant’s daughter brought him a meal with various excellent flavors, as she was serving him with a ladle, he began to criticize the food. The merchant’s daughter, in the very manner she had learned from the Bodhisatta, recited this verse:

125.

125.

“Bahumpi so vikattheyya, aññaṃ janapadaṃ gato;

Anvāgantvāna dūseyya, bhuñja bhoge kaṭāhakā”ti.

“Though he may boast much, having gone to another country; having followed, he would bring ruin. Enjoy the riches, O Kaṭāhaka!”

Tattha bahumpi so vikattheyya, aññaṃ janapadaṃ gatoti yo attano jātibhūmito aññaṃ janapadaṃ gato hoti, yatthassa jātiṃ na jānanti, so [M 1.0480] bahumpi vikattheyya, vambhanavacanaṃ vañcanavacanaṃ vadeyya. Anvāgantvāna dūseyyāti imaṃ tāva vāraṃ sāmikassa paṭipathaṃ gantvā dāsakiccassa katattā kasāhi paharitvā piṭṭhicammuppāṭanato ca lakkhaṇāhananato ca muttosi. Sace anācāraṃ karosi, puna aññasmiṃ āgamanavāre tava sāmiko anvāgantvāna dūseyya, imaṃ gehaṃ anuāgantvā kasābhighātehi ceva lakkhaṇāhananena ca jātippakāsanena ca taṃ dūseyya upahaneyya. Tasmā imaṃ anācāraṃ pahāya bhuñja bhoge kaṭāhaka, mā pacchā attano dāsabhāvaṃ pākaṭaṃ kāretvā vippaṭisārī ahosīti ayamettha seṭṭhino adhippāyo.

In this regard, ‘Though he may boast much, having gone to another country’ means that when one has gone from his birthplace to another country where they do not know his origin, he might boast much, speaking words of contempt and words of deception. ‘Having followed, he would ruin’ means: for this time, you have been released from being beaten with whips, from having the skin stripped from your back, and from being branded with marks, because you went to meet your master and performed the duties of a slave. If you act improperly, on another occasion when he comes, your master would follow and ruin you; having followed you to this house, he would ruin and harm you by whipping, branding, and revealing your status. Therefore, abandoning this misconduct, enjoy the wealth, Kaṭāhaka. Do not later become regretful by making your slave status known. This is the merchant’s intention here.

Seṭṭhidhītā [V 1.0435] pana etamatthaṃ ajānantī uggahitaniyāmena byañjanameva payirudāhāsi. Kaṭāhako “addhā seṭṭhinā mama kulaṃ ācikkhitvā etissā sabbaṃ kathitaṃ bhavissatī”ti tato paṭṭhāya puna bhattaṃ garahituṃ na visahi, nihatamāno yathāladdhaṃ bhuñjitvā yathākammaṃ gato.

The merchant's daughter, however, not knowing this meaning, merely recited the words as she had learned them. Kaṭāhaka thought, 'Surely the merchant must have revealed my lineage to her and told her everything.' From then on, he did not dare to criticize the food again. With his pride humbled, he ate whatever he was given and went on his way according to his deeds.

Satthā [P 1.0455] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā kaṭāhako vikatthakabhikkhu ahosi, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, made the connection in the Jātaka: 'At that time, Kaṭāhaka was the boastful bhikkhu, and the Benares merchant was I myself.'

Kaṭāhakajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Kaṭāhaka Jātaka, the Fifth.

[126] 6. Asilakkhaṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[126] 6. The Commentary on the Asilakkhaṇa Jātaka

Tathevekassa kalyāṇanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kosalarañño asilakkhaṇapāṭhakaṃ brāhmaṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So kira kammārehi rañño asīnaṃ āhaṭakāle asiṃ upasiṅghitvā asilakkhaṇaṃ udāharati. So yesaṃ hatthato lābhaṃ labhati, tesaṃ asiṃ “lakkhaṇasampanno maṅgalasaṃyutto”ti vadati. Yesaṃ hatthato lābhaṃ na labhati, tesaṃ asiṃ “avalakkhaṇo”ti garahati. Atheko kammāro asiṃ katvā kosiyaṃ sukhumaṃ maricacuṇṇaṃ pakkhipitvā rañño asiṃ āhari. Rājā brāhmaṇaṃ pakkosāpetvā “asiṃ vīmaṃsā”ti āha. Brāhmaṇassa asiṃ ākaḍḍhitvā upasiṅghantassa maricacuṇṇāni nāsaṃ pavisitvā [M 1.0481] khipitukāmataṃ uppādesuṃ. Tassa khipantassa nāsikā asidhārāya paṭihatā dvidhā chijji. Tassevaṃ nāsikāya chinnabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo jāto. Athekadivasaṃ dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, rañño kira asilakkhaṇapāṭhako asiṃ upasiṅghanto nāsikaṃ chindāpesī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva so brāhmaṇo asiṃ upasiṅghanto nāsikāchedaṃ patto, pubbepi pattoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

‘Thus for one there’s good’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a brahmin who was a reader of sword-marks for the King of Kosala. It is said that when swords were brought to the king by the smiths, he would sniff the sword and declare its marks. To those from whose hands he received a gift, he would say of their sword, 'It is endowed with good marks and is auspicious.' To those from whose hands he received no gift, he would disparage their sword, saying, 'It is ill-marked.' Then one smith, having made a sword, placed finely ground pepper powder inside the scabbard and brought the sword to the king. The king summoned the brahmin and said, 'Examine the sword.' When the brahmin drew the sword and sniffed it, the pepper powder entered his nose, causing him to want to sneeze. As he sneezed, his nose was struck by the sword's edge and was cut in two. The fact that his nose was severed became well-known among the Saṅgha of bhikkhus. Then one day, the bhikkhus started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, it is said that the king's sword-mark reader, while sniffing a sword, had his nose cut off.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Bhikkhus, with what discussion are you assembled here now?' When they replied, 'With this,' he said, 'Bhikkhus, it is not only now that this brahmin, while sniffing a sword, suffered the cutting of his nose; he suffered it in the past as well,' and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente tassa asilakkhaṇapāṭhako brāhmaṇo ahosīti sabbaṃ paccuppannavatthusadisameva. Rājā pana tassa vejje datvā nāsikākoṭiṃ phāsukaṃ kārāpetvā lākhāya paṭināsikaṃ kāretvā puna taṃ upaṭṭhākameva akāsi. Bārāṇasirañño pana putto natthi, ekā dhītā ceva bhāgineyyo ca ahesuṃ. So ubhopi te attano santikeyeva vaḍḍhāpesi. Te ekato vaḍḍhantā aññamaññaṃ paṭibaddhacittā ahesuṃ. Rājāpi [V 1.0436] amacce pakkosāpetvā “mayhaṃ bhāgineyyopi imassa rajjassa sāmikova, dhītaraṃ etasseva datvā abhisekamassa karomī”ti vatvā puna cintesi [P 1.0456] “mayhaṃ bhāgineyyo sabbathāpi ñātakoyeva, etassa aññaṃ rājadhītaraṃ ānetvā abhisekaṃ katvā dhītaraṃ aññassa rañño dassāmi, evaṃ no ñātakā bahū bhavissanti, dvinnampi rajjānaṃ mayameva sāmikā bhavissāmā”ti. So amaccehi saddhiṃ sammantetvā “ubhopete visuṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti bhāgineyyaṃ aññasmiṃ nivesane, dhītaraṃ aññasmiṃ vāsesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, there was a brahmin who was a reader of sword-marks for him—all the circumstances are similar to the present story. The king, however, having provided him with physicians, had the tip of his nose healed and had a prosthetic nose made for him from lac, then appointed him again as his attendant. Now, the king of Benares had no son, but only a daughter and a nephew. He raised both of them in his own presence. Growing up together, they became deeply attached to each other. The king summoned his ministers and said, 'My nephew is indeed the rightful heir to this kingdom. I will give him my daughter and perform his consecration.' But then he reconsidered, thinking, 'My nephew is already my kinsman in every way. If I bring another king’s daughter for his consecration and give my daughter to another king, then our relatives will multiply, and we ourselves will become lords over two kingdoms.' After consulting with his ministers, he decided, 'It is proper to separate these two.' So he had his nephew reside in one house and his daughter in another.

Te soḷasavassuddesikabhāvaṃ pattā ativiya paṭibaddhacittā ahesuṃ. Rājakumāro “kena nu kho upāyena mātuladhītaraṃ rājagehā nīharāpetuṃ sakkā bhaveyyā”ti cintento “attheko upāyo”ti mahāikkhaṇikaṃ pakkosāpetvā tassā sahassabhaṇḍikaṃ datvā “kiṃ mayā kattabba”nti vutte “amma, tayi karontiyā anipphatti nāma natthi, kiñcideva kāraṇaṃ vatvā yathā mama mātulo rājā dhītaraṃ antogehā nīharāpeti, tathā karohī”ti āha. Sādhu, sāmi, ahaṃ rājānaṃ upasaṅkamitvā evaṃ vakkhāmi “deva, rājadhītāya upari kāḷakaṇṇī atthi, ettakaṃ kālaṃ nivattitvā olokentopi natthi, ahaṃ rājadhītaraṃ asukadivase [M 1.0482] nāma rathaṃ āropetvā bahuāvudhahatthe purise ādāya mahantena parivārena susānaṃ gantvā maṇḍalapīṭhikāya heṭṭhāmañce matamanussaṃ nipajjāpetvā uparimañce rājadhītaraṃ ṭhapetvā gandhodakaghaṭānaṃ aṭṭhuttarasatena nhāpetvā kāḷakaṇṇiṃ pavāhessāmī”ti evaṃ vatvā rājadhītaraṃ susānaṃ nessāmi, tvaṃ amhākaṃ tattha gamanadivase amhehi puretarameva thokaṃ maricacuṇṇaṃ ādāya āvudhahatthehi attano manussehi parivuto rathaṃ abhiruyha susānaṃ gantvā rathaṃ susānadvāre ekapadese ṭhapetvā āvudhahatthe manusse susānavanaṃ pesetvā sayaṃ susāne maṇḍalapīṭhikaṃ pasāretvā matako viya paṭikujjo hutvā nipajja. Ahaṃ tattha āgantvā tava upari mañcakaṃ attharitvā rājadhītaraṃ ukkhipitvā mañce sayāpessāmi, tvaṃ tasmiṃ khaṇe maricacuṇṇaṃ nāsikāya pakkhipitvā dve tayo vāre khipeyyāsi. Tayā khipitakāle [P 1.0457] mayaṃ rājadhītaraṃ pahāya palāyissāma. Atha tvaṃ rājadhītaraṃ sīsaṃ nhāpetvā sayampi sīsaṃ nhāyitvā taṃ ādāya attano nivesanaṃ gaccheyyāsīti. So “sādhu sundaro upāyo”ti sampaṭicchi.

When they reached the age of sixteen, they were deeply attached to each other. The prince thought, 'By what means might I be able to have my uncle’s daughter brought from the royal palace?' Realizing there was a way, he summoned a great soothsayer, gave her a thousand coins, and said, 'What is to be done? Mother, for you there is no such thing as failure. You must give some reason so that my uncle, the king, will have his daughter brought out from the inner palace.' She replied, 'Very well, my lord. I will approach the king and say this: “Your Majesty, a dark misfortune is upon the princess, and for some time it has not abated. On such-and-such a day, I will place the princess on a chariot, take many armed men, and go with a large retinue to the charnel ground. There, I will have a dead man laid on a bed beneath a circular platform and place the princess on a bed above it. Then, I will bathe her with one hundred and eight pots of scented water to wash away the misfortune.” Saying this, I will take the princess to the charnel ground. On the day we go, you must go there before us. Take a little pepper powder, and surrounded by your armed men, mount a chariot and go to the charnel ground. Park the chariot at one side of the charnel ground entrance, send your armed men into the charnel grove, and go yourself to the circular platform in the charnel ground. Lie there face down, as if you were a corpse. When I arrive, I will set up a bed above you, lift the princess, and lay her on the bed. At that moment, you must put the pepper powder in your nose and sneeze two or three times. When you sneeze, we will abandon the princess and flee. Then, you can bathe the princess’s head, and also bathe your own head, and take her to your own residence.' He agreed, saying, 'Good, an excellent plan.'

Sāpi gantvā rañño tamatthaṃ ārocesi, rājāpi sampaṭicchi. Rājadhītāyapi taṃ antaraṃ ācikkhi, sāpi sampaṭicchi. Sā nikkhamanadivase kumārassa saññaṃ datvā mahantena parivārena susānaṃ gacchantī ārakkhamanussānaṃ bhayajananatthaṃ āha – “mayā rājadhītāya mañce ṭhapitakāle heṭṭhāmañce matapuriso khipissati, khipitvā ca heṭṭhāmañcā nikkhamitvā yaṃ paṭhamaṃ passissati[V 1.0437], tameva gahessati, appamattā bhaveyyāthā”ti. Rājakumāro puretaraṃ gantvā vuttanayeneva tattha nipajji. Mahāikkhaṇikā rājadhītaraṃ ukkhipitvā maṇḍalapīṭhikāṭhānaṃ gacchantī “mā bhāyī”ti saññāpetvā mañce ṭhapesi. Tasmiṃ khaṇe kumāro maricacuṇṇaṃ nāsāya pakkhipitvā khipi. Tena khipitamatteyeva mahāikkhaṇikā rājadhītaraṃ pahāya mahāravaṃ ravamānā sabbapaṭhamaṃ palāyi, tassā palātakālato paṭṭhāya ekopi ṭhātuṃ samattho nāma nāhosi, gahitagahitāni āvudhāni chaḍḍetvā sabbe palāyiṃsu. Kumāro yathāsammantitaṃ sabbaṃ katvā rājadhītaraṃ ādāya attano nivesanaṃ agamāsi.

She also went and reported the matter to the king, and the king also agreed. The princess was also told of the arrangement, and she too agreed. On the day of departure, giving a signal to the prince, she went to the charnel ground with a large retinue. To frighten the guards, she said, 'When I place the princess on the bed, a dead man will sneeze from beneath the bed. After sneezing, he will come out from under the bed and seize the first person he sees. Be vigilant!' The prince went ahead and lay there as instructed. The great fortune-teller, lifting the princess, went to the circular platform, reassuring her, 'Do not fear,' and placed her on the bed. At that moment, the prince put pepper powder into his nose and sneezed. As soon as he sneezed, the great fortune-teller, abandoning the princess, let out a loud cry and was the first to flee. From the moment she fled, not a single one was able to stay; they all dropped the weapons they had seized and fled. The prince, having accomplished everything as planned, took the princess and went to his own dwelling.

Ikkhaṇikā [M 1.0483] gantvā taṃ kāraṇaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā “pakatiyāpi sā mayā tassevatthāya puṭṭhā, pāyāse chaḍḍitasappi viya jāta”nti sampaṭicchitvā aparabhāge bhāgineyyassa rajjaṃ datvā dhītaraṃ mahādeviṃ kāresi. So tāya saddhiṃ samaggavāsaṃ vasamāno dhammena rajjaṃ kāresi. Sopi asilakkhaṇapāṭhako tasseva upaṭṭhāko ahosi. Tassekadivasaṃ rājūpaṭṭhānaṃ āgantvā paṭisūriyaṃ ṭhatvā upaṭṭhahantassa lākhā vilīyi, paṭināsikā bhūmiyaṃ pati. So lajjāya adhomukho aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ rājā parihasanto “ācariya, mā cintayittha, khipitaṃ nāma ekassa kalyāṇaṃ hoti, ekassa pāpakaṃ. Tumhehi khipitena nāsikā [P 1.0458] chijjīyittha, mayaṃ pana khipantā mātuladhītaraṃ labhitvā rajjaṃ pāpuṇimhā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The fortune-teller went and reported the matter to the king. The king accepted, saying, 'By nature, she was raised by me for his sake. It has turned out like ghee discarded in rice-pudding.' Later, he gave the kingdom to his nephew and made his daughter the chief queen. He, living in concord with her, ruled righteously. That reader of sword marks also became his attendant. One day, while attending the king, standing facing the sun, the lac dissolved, and the artificial nose fell to the ground. Ashamed, he stood with his face downcast. Then the king, joking with him, said, 'Teacher, do not worry. Indeed, a sneeze brings fortune to one and misfortune to another. By your sneezing, your nose was severed; but we, by sneezing, obtained our uncle’s daughter and attained the kingdom.' And he spoke this verse:

126.

126.

“Tathevekassa kalyāṇaṃ, tathevekassa pāpakaṃ;

Tasmā sabbaṃ na kalyāṇaṃ, sabbaṃ vāpi na pāpaka”nti.

'Thus for one there’s good, thus for one there’s bad; Therefore not everything is good, nor indeed everything bad.'

Tattha tathevekassāti tadevekassa. Ayameva vā pāṭho. Dutiyapadepi eseva nayo.

Therein, `tathevekassa` means 'that very thing for one'. Or this is the reading. The same principle applies to the second line as well.

Iti so imāya gāthāya taṃ kāraṇaṃ āharitvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, having brought forth that matter with this verse, he performed meritorious deeds such as giving and went according to his kamma.

Satthā imāya desanāya lokasammatānaṃ kalyāṇapāpakānaṃ anekaṃsikabhāvaṃ pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā asilakkhaṇapāṭhakova etarahi asilakkhaṇapāṭhako, bhāgineyyarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having revealed through this discourse the non-absolute nature of what is held by the world to be good and evil, concluded the Jātaka by saying: “The reader of sword-marks at that time was the same as the reader of sword-marks of today, but the nephew king was I myself.”

Asilakkhaṇajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Asilakkhaṇa Jātaka is the sixth.

[127] 7. Kalaṇḍukajātakavaṇṇanā

[127] 7. Commentary on the Kalaṇḍuka Jātaka

Te [V 1.0438] desā tāni vatthūnīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ vikatthakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tattha dvepi vatthūni kaṭāhakajātakasadisāneva.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this concerning a boastful monk, beginning with the words: “Those lands, those things.” Here, both incidents are similar to the Kaṭāhaka Jātaka.

Idha [M 1.0484] panesa bārāṇasiseṭṭhino dāso kalaṇḍuko nāma ahosi. Tassa palāyitvā paccantavāsiseṭṭhino dhītaraṃ gahetvā mahantena parivārena vasanakāle bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pariyesāpetvāpi tassa gataṭṭhānaṃ ajānanto “gaccha, kalaṇḍukaṃ pariyesā”ti attanā puṭṭhaṃ sukapotakaṃ pesesi. Sukapotako ito cito ca vicaranto taṃ nagaraṃ pāpuṇi. Tasmiñca kāle kalaṇḍuko nadīkīḷaṃ kīḷitukāmo bahuṃ mālāgandhavilepanañceva khādanīyabhojanīyāni ca gāhāpetvā nadiṃ gantvā seṭṭhidhītāya saddhiṃ nāvaṃ āruyha udake kīḷati. Tasmiñca padese nadīkīḷaṃ kīḷantā issarajātikā tikhiṇabhesajjaparibhāvitaṃ khīraṃ pivanti, tena tesaṃ divasabhāgampi udake kīḷantānaṃ sītaṃ na [P 1.0459] bādhati. Ayaṃ pana kalaṇḍuko khīragaṇḍūsaṃ gahetvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā taṃ khīraṃ nuṭṭhubhati. Nuṭṭhubhantopi udake anuṭṭhubhitvā seṭṭhidhītāya sīse nuṭṭhubhati. Sukapotakopi nadītīraṃ gantvā ekissā udumbarasākhāya nisīditvā oloketvā kalaṇḍukaṃ sañjānitvā seṭṭhidhītāya sīse nuṭṭhubhantaṃ disvā “are, kalaṇḍuka dāsa, attano jātiñca vasanaṭṭhānañca anussara, khīragaṇḍūsaṃ gahetvā mukhaṃ vikkhāletvā jātisampannāya sukhasaṃvaḍḍhāya seṭṭhidhītāya sīse mā nuṭṭhubhi, attano pamāṇaṃ na jānāsī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In this case, there was a slave named Kalaṇḍuka belonging to a wealthy merchant of Bārāṇasī. Having fled, he took the daughter of a wealthy merchant dwelling in the border region and lived with a large retinue. The wealthy merchant of Bārāṇasī, though having him searched for, could not find his whereabouts. He then sent a young parrot, which he himself had raised, saying, “Go, search for Kalaṇḍuka.” The parrot, flying here and there, arrived at that city. At that time, Kalaṇḍuka, wishing to play in the river, had gathered many garlands, perfumes, and ointments, as well as food and drink, and went to the river. Boarding a boat with the merchant’s daughter, he played in the water. In that place, those of noble birth who played in the river drank milk infused with potent medicinal herbs; because of this, they could play in the water for a whole day without being troubled by the cold. But this Kalaṇḍuka, taking a mouthful of milk, rinsed his mouth and spat it out. Even while spitting, he did not spit into the water but spat on the head of the merchant’s daughter. The parrot, having gone to the riverbank, perched on a branch of a fig tree and watched. Recognizing Kalaṇḍuka, it saw him spitting on the merchant’s daughter’s head and said, “Hey, Kalaṇḍuka, slave, remember your birth and your dwelling place! Taking a mouthful of milk and rinsing your mouth, do not spit on the head of the high-born, well-nurtured merchant’s daughter! Do you not know your own measure?” Then it spoke this verse:

127.

127.

“Te desā tāni vatthūni, ahañca vanagocaro;

Anuvicca kho taṃ gaṇheyyuṃ, piva khīraṃ kalaṇḍukā”ti.

“Those lands, those things, and I, a forest-dweller; Having investigated, they would surely seize you. Drink the milk, Kalaṇḍuka.”

Tattha te desā tāni vatthūnīti mātukucchiṃ sandhāya vadati. Ayametthādhippāyo – yattha te vasitaṃ, na te khattiyadhītādīnaṃ kucchidesā. Yattha vāsi patiṭṭhito, na tāni khattiyadhītādīnaṃ kucchivatthūni. Atha kho dāsikucchiyaṃ tvaṃ vasi ceva patiṭṭhito cāti. Ahañca vanagocaroti tiracchānabhūtopi etamatthaṃ jānāmīti dīpeti. Anuvicca kho taṃ gaṇheyyunti evaṃ anācāraṃ caramānaṃ mayā gantvā ārocite anuvicca jānitvā tava sāmikā tāḷetvā ceva lakkhaṇāhatañca katvā taṃ gaṇheyyuṃ, gahetvā gamissanti, tasmā attano pamāṇaṃ ñatvā seṭṭhidhītāya sīse anuṭṭhubhitvā piva khīraṃ. Kalaṇḍukāti taṃ nāmenālapati.

Herein, when it is said, 'Those are your regions, those are your abodes,' it is spoken with reference to the mother's womb. This is the meaning here: where you dwelt were not the regions of the wombs of daughters of nobles and so forth. Where you were established were not the abodes of the wombs of daughters of nobles and so forth. Rather, you both dwelt and were established in the womb of a slave girl. 'And I, a forest-dweller' indicates: 'Even I, being an animal, know this matter.' 'Having investigated, they would seize you' means: 'If I were to go and report you who are behaving in such an improper manner, your masters, having investigated and known, would beat you and brand you with a mark, and they would seize you; having seized you, they will take you away. Therefore, knowing your own measure, spit on the head of the merchant's daughter and drink the milk.' 'Kalaṇḍuka' is how he addresses him by name.

Kalaṇḍukopi [V 1.0439][M 1.0485] suvapotakaṃ sañjānitvā “maṃ pākaṭaṃ kareyyā”ti bhayena “ehi, sāmi, kadā āgatosī”ti āha. Suko “na esa maṃ hitakāmatāya pakkosati, gīvaṃ pana me vaṭṭetvā māretukāmo”ti ñatvāva “na me tayā attho”ti tato uppatitvā bārāṇasiṃ gantvā yathādiṭṭhaṃ seṭṭhino vitthārena kathesi. Seṭṭhi “ayuttaṃ tena kata”nti vatvā gantvā tassa āṇaṃ kāretvā bārāṇasimeva naṃ ānetvā dāsaparibhogena paribhuñji.

Kalaṇḍuka, recognizing the young parrot and thinking, “He might expose me,” said out of fear, “Come, my lord, when did you arrive?” The parrot, knowing, “He does not summon me out of goodwill but intends to twist my neck and kill me,” replied, “I have no need of you.” Flying away from there to Bārāṇasī, he recounted in detail to the merchant what he had seen. The merchant, saying, “What he did was improper,” went and had his authority enforced over him. Bringing him back to Bārāṇasī, he made him serve as a slave.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kalaṇḍuko ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, bārāṇasiseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, Kalaṇḍuka was this monk, but the Bārāṇasī merchant was I myself.”

Kalaṇḍukajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Kalaṇḍuka Jātaka is the seventh.

[128] 8. Biḷāravatajātakavaṇṇanā

[128] 8. The Commentary on the Biḷāravata Jātaka

Yo [P 1.0460] ve dhammaṃ dhajaṃ katvāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā hi satthā tassa kuhakabhāve ārocite “na, bhikkhave, idāneva, pubbepesa kuhakoyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, told this story beginning with “He who makes the Dhamma his banner…” concerning a deceitful monk. At that time, when the monk's deceitful nature was reported, the Teacher said, “Not only now, monks, but in the past too he was deceitful,” and he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mūsikayoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā vuḍḍhimanvāya mahāsarīro sūkaracchāpakasadiso hutvā anekasatamūsikāhi parivuto araññe viharati. Atheko siṅgālo ito cito ca vicaranto taṃ mūsikayūthaṃ disvā “imā mūsikā vañcetvā khādissāmī”ti cintetvā mūsikānaṃ āsayassa avidūre sūriyābhimukho vātaṃ pivanto ekena pādena aṭṭhāsi. Bodhisatto gocarāya caramāno taṃ disvā “sīlavā eso bhavissatī”ti tassa santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, tvaṃ ko nāmo”ti pucchi. “Dhammiko nāmā”ti. “Cattāro pāde bhūmiyaṃ aṭhapetvā kasmā ekeneva ṭhitosī”ti. “Mayi cattāro pāde pathaviyaṃ ṭhapente pathavī vahituṃ na sakkoti, tasmā ekeneva tiṭṭhāmī”ti. “Mukhaṃ vivaritvā kasmā ṭhitosī”ti? “Mayaṃ aññaṃ na bhakkhayāma, vātameva bhakkhayāmā”ti. “Atha kasmā sūriyābhimukho [M 1.0486] tiṭṭhasī”ti? “Sūriyaṃ namassāmī”ti. Bodhisatto tassa vacanaṃ sutvā “sīlavā eso bhavissatī”ti tato paṭṭhāya mūsikagaṇena saddhiṃ sāyaṃ pātaṃ tassa upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a mouse. Having grown, he became large-bodied, like a young pig, and lived in the forest surrounded by many hundreds of mice. Then a jackal, wandering here and there, saw that group of mice and thought, “I will deceive and eat these mice.” So, standing on one leg not far from the mice’s dwelling, facing the sun, he pretended to drink the wind. The Bodhisatta, while out foraging, saw him and thought, “This one must be virtuous.” Approaching him, he asked, “Sir, what is your name?” “I am called Dhammika.” “Why do you stand on only one leg, instead of placing all four on the ground?” “If I place all four legs on the ground, the earth cannot bear it, so I stand on just one.” “Why do you stand with your mouth open?” “We do not eat anything else; we only consume the wind.” “Then why do you stand facing the sun?” “I pay homage to the sun.” Hearing his words, the Bodhisatta thought, “This one must indeed be virtuous,” and from then on, he and his group of mice went to attend upon him morning and evening.

Athassa [V 1.0440] upaṭṭhānaṃ katvā gamanakāle siṅgālo sabbapacchimaṃ mūsikaṃ gahetvā maṃsaṃ khāditvā ajjhoharitvā mukhaṃ puñchitvā tiṭṭhati. Anupubbena mūsikagaṇo tanuko jāto. Mūsikā “pubbe amhākaṃ ayaṃ āsayo nappahoti, nirantarā tiṭṭhāma. Idāni sithilā, evampi āsayo na pūrateva, kiṃ nu kho eta”nti bodhisattassa taṃ pavattiṃ ārocesuṃ. Bodhisatto “kena nu kho kāraṇena musikā tanuttaṃ gatā”ti cintento siṅgāle āsaṅkaṃ ṭhapetvā “vīmaṃsissāmi [P 1.0461] na”nti upaṭṭhānakāle sesamūsikā purato katvā sayaṃ pacchato ahosi. Siṅgālo tassa upari pakkhandi, bodhisatto attano gahaṇatthāya taṃ pakkhandantaṃ disvā nivattitvā “bho siṅgāla, idaṃ te vatasamādānaṃ na dhammasudhammatāya, paresaṃ pana vihiṃsanatthāya dhammaṃ dhajaṃ katvā carasī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then, at the time of their departure after having attended upon him, the jackal would seize the very last mouse, eat its flesh, swallow it down, wipe his mouth, and stand there. Gradually, the group of mice became diminished. The mice thought, “Before, this dwelling of ours was not large enough; we were packed together without any space. Now it is spacious, yet the dwelling does not fill up. What could be the reason for this?” They reported this matter to the Bodhisatta. The Bodhisatta, pondering, “For what reason have the mice become diminished?” placed his suspicion on the jackal and thought, “I will investigate him.” At the time of attendance, he placed the other mice in front and stayed behind himself. The jackal leaped upon him. The Bodhisatta, seeing him leaping to seize him, turned back and said, “O jackal, this undertaking of your vow is not for the sake of true righteousness; rather, you wander about having made the Dhamma a banner for the purpose of harming others.” Then he spoke this verse:

128.

128.

“Yo ve dhammaṃ dhajaṃ katvā, nigūḷho pāpamācare;

Vissāsayitvā bhūtāni, biḷāraṃ nāma taṃ vata”nti.

“He who makes the Dhamma his banner, while secretly committing evil, having gained the confidence of beings—that practice is called cat-like.”

Tattha yo veti khattiyādīsu yo kocideva. Dhammaṃ dhajaṃ katvāti dasakusalakammapathadhammaṃ dhajaṃ karitvā, kūṭaṃ karonto viya ussāpetvā dassentoti attho. Vissāsayitvāti “sīlavā aya”nti saññāya sañjātavissāsāni katvā. Biḷāraṃ nāma taṃ vatanti taṃ evaṃ dhammaṃ dhajaṃ katvā raho pāpāni karontassa vataṃ kerāṭikavataṃ nāma hotīti attho.

Therein, 'he who' means anyone whatsoever among nobles and others. 'Having made the Dhamma his banner' means having made the Dhamma of the ten wholesome courses of action his banner, raising it up and showing it as if erecting a flag—this is the meaning. 'Having gained the confidence of beings' means having inspired confidence in them through the perception, 'This one is virtuous.' 'That practice is called cat-like' means that the practice of one who, having thus made the Dhamma his banner, secretly commits evil deeds, is called a hypocritical practice.

Mūsikarājā kathentova uppatitvā tassa gīvāyaṃ patitvā hanukassa heṭṭhā antogalanāḷiyaṃ ḍaṃsitvā galanāḷiṃ phāletvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpesi. Mūsikagaṇo nivattitvā siṅgālaṃ “muru murū”ti khāditvā agamāsi. Paṭhamāgatāva kirassa maṃsaṃ labhiṃsu, pacchā āgatā na labhiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya mūsikagaṇo nibbhayo jāto.

The mouse king, even while speaking, leaped up and landed on the jackal's neck. He bit the windpipe inside, below the jaw, and tearing the windpipe, he brought about the end of its life. The throng of mice turned back and, making a 'muru muru' sound, devoured the jackal and departed. It is said that those who arrived first got its flesh, while those who came later did not. From then on, the throng of mice became fearless.

Satthā [M 1.0487] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo kuhakabhikkhu ahosi, mūsikarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time the jackal was the deceitful monk, but the king of the mice was I myself.”

Biḷāravatajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Biḷāravata Jātaka is the eighth.

[129] 9. Aggikabhāradvājajātakavaṇṇanā

[129] 9. The Commentary on the Aggikabhāradvāja Jātaka

Nāyaṃ [V 1.0441] sikhā puññahetūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kuhakaññeva bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi.

While dwelling at Jetavana, the Teacher told this story, which begins with the words, 'This crest is not for merit,' concerning a certain deceitful monk.

Atītasmiñhi bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mūsikarājā hutvā araññe vasati. Atheko siṅgālo davaḍāhe uṭṭhite palāyituṃ asakkonto ekasmiṃ rukkhe sīsaṃ [P 1.0462] āhacca aṭṭhāsi. Tassa sakalasarīre lomāni jhāyiṃsu, rukkhaṃ āhacca ṭhitaṭṭhāne pana matthake cūḷā viya thokāni lomāni aṭṭhaṃsu. So ekadivasaṃ soṇḍiyaṃ pānīyaṃ pivanto chāyaṃ olokento cūḷaṃ disvā “uppannaṃ dāni me bhaṇḍamūla”nti araññe vicaranto taṃ mūsikādariṃ disvā “imā mūsikā vañcetvā khādissāmī”ti heṭṭhā vuttanayeneva avidūre aṭṭhāsi. Atha naṃ bodhisatto gocarāya caranto disvā “sīlavā aya”nti saññāya upasaṅkamitvā “tvaṃ kinnāmosī”ti pucchi. “Ahaṃ aggikabhāradvājo nāmā”ti. “Atha kasmā āgatosī”ti? “Tumhākaṃ rakkhanatthāyā”ti. “Kinti katvā amhe rakkhissasī”ti? “Ahaṃ aṅguṭṭhagaṇanaṃ nāma jānāmi, tumhākaṃ pātova nikkhamitvā gocarāya gamanakāle ‘ettakā’ti gaṇetvā paccāgamanakālepi gaṇessāmi, evaṃ sāyaṃ pātaṃ gaṇento rakkhissāmī”ti. “Tena hi rakkha mātulā”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā nikkhamanakāle “eko dve tayo”ti gaṇetvā paccāgamanakālepi tatheva gaṇetvā sabbapacchimaṃ gahetvā khādati. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta, having been born as a king of mice, lived in the forest. Now, a certain jackal, unable to escape when a forest fire broke out, stood with his head pressed against a tree. The hair on his entire body was singed, but where his head was pressed against the tree, a small tuft of hair remained like a topknot on his head. One day, while drinking water from a pond and looking at his reflection, he saw the tuft and thought, 'Now I have a means of livelihood!' Roaming the forest, he saw that mouse-den and thought, 'I will deceive these mice and eat them.' So he stood not far off, in the manner described before. Then the Bodhisatta, while out foraging, saw him and, thinking, 'This one is virtuous,' approached him and asked, 'What is your name?' 'I am called Aggikabhāradvāja,' he replied. 'But why have you come?' 'For your protection.' 'How will you protect us?' 'I know the art of counting by the thumb. When you go out in the morning to forage, I will count you, and when you return, I will count you again. Thus, counting morning and evening, I will protect you.' 'Very well, uncle, protect us then,' said the Bodhisatta. The jackal agreed, saying, 'So be it,' and began counting them as they left: 'One, two, three.' He did the same when they returned, but he would always seize the very last one and eat it. The rest is just as before.

Idha pana mūsikarājā nivattitvā ṭhito “bho aggikabhāradvāja, nāyaṃ tava dhammasudhammatāya matthake cūḷā ṭhapitā, kucchikāraṇā pana ṭhapitā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Here, however, the king of mice turned back and stood still, saying, 'O Aggikabhāradvāja, this tuft on your head has not been placed there because of your righteous conduct, but rather it has been placed there for the sake of your belly.' Then he spoke this verse:

129.

129.

“Nāyaṃ [M 1.0488] sikhā puññahetu, ghāsahetu ayaṃ sikhā;

Nāguṭṭhigaṇanaṃ yāti, alaṃ te hotu aggikā”ti.

This tuft is not for merit; this tuft is for sustenance. The count by thumb is not met. Enough of you, O Aggika!

Tattha nāguṭṭhigaṇanaṃ yātīti “aṅguṭṭhigaṇanā”ti aṅguṭṭhagaṇanā vuccati, ayaṃ mūsikagaṇo aṅguṭṭhagaṇanaṃ na gacchati na upeti na pūreti, parikkhayaṃ gacchatīti attho. Alaṃ te hotu aggikāti siṅgālaṃ nāmena ālapanto āha. Ettāvatā te alaṃ hotu, na ito paraṃ mūsike khādissasi[V 1.0442]. Amhehi vā tayā saddhiṃ saṃvāso alaṃ hotu, na mayaṃ idāni tayā saddhiṃ vasissāmātipi attho. Sesaṃ purimasadisameva.

There, 'The count by thumb is not met' refers to 'counting by the thumb.' This population of mice does not reach, approach, or complete the thumb-count; the meaning is that it is dwindling. 'Enough of you, O Aggika!' he said, addressing the jackal by name. 'Let this be enough for you; you will not eat mice beyond this.' Or it means, 'Enough of our living together with you; we will no longer live with you.' The rest is just as before.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā siṅgālo ayaṃ bhikkhu ahosi, mūsikarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, identified the birth-story: 'At that time, the jackal was this monk, and the king of mice was I myself.'

Aggikabhāradvājajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The Commentary on the Aggikabhāradvāja Jātaka is the ninth.

[130] 10. Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā

[130] 10. The Commentary on the Kosiya Jātaka

Yathā [P 1.0463] vācā ca bhuñjassūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ sāvatthiyaṃ mātugāmaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sā kirekassa saddhāsampannassa upāsakabrāhmaṇassa brāhmaṇī dussīlā pāpadhammā rattiṃ aticaritvā divā kiñci kammaṃ akatvā gilānālayaṃ dassetvā nitthunamānā nipajjati. Atha naṃ brāhmaṇo “kiṃ te bhadde aphāsuka”nti pucchi. “Vātā me vijjhantī”ti. “Atha kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Siniddhamadhurāni paṇītapaṇītāni yāgubhattatelādīnī”ti. Brāhmaṇo yaṃ yaṃ sā icchati, taṃ taṃ āharitvā deti, dāso viya sabbakiccāni karoti. Sā pana brāhmaṇassa gehaṃ paviṭṭhakāle nipajjati, bahi nikkhantakāle jārehi saddhiṃ vītināmeti.

“Just as one speaks and eats”—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning a certain woman in Sāvatthī. She, it seems, was the wife of a devout brahmin lay follower, but was immoral and of wicked character. Engaging in misconduct at night, she would do no work during the day, feigning illness, groaning, and lying down. Then the brahmin asked her, 'What is wrong, my dear?' 'Winds are piercing me,' she said. 'Then what is proper to obtain?' 'Rich, sweet delicacies, the finest rice porridge, oil, and such things.' The brahmin brought and gave her whatever she desired, performing all tasks like a slave. But when the brahmin entered the house, she would lie down, and when he went out, she would spend time with her paramours.

Atha brāhmaṇo “imissā sarīre vijjhanavātānaṃ pariyanto na paññāyatī”ti ekadivasaṃ gandhamālādīni ādāya jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ pūjetvā vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīditvā “kiṃ, brāhmaṇa, na paññāyasī”ti vutte “bhante, brāhmaṇiyā kira me sarīre vātā vijjhanti, svāhaṃ tassā [M 1.0489] sappitelādīni ceva paṇītapaṇītabhojanāni ca pariyesāmi, sarīramassā ghanaṃ vippasannacchavivaṇṇaṃ jātaṃ, vātarogassa pana pariyanto na paññāyati. Ahaṃ taṃ paṭijaggantova idhāgamanassa okāsaṃ na labhāmī”ti āha. Satthā brāhmaṇiyā pāpabhāvaṃ ñatvā “brāhmaṇa, ‘evaṃ nipannassa mātugāmassa roge avūpasamante idañcidañca bhesajjaṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī’ti pubbepi te paṇḍitehi kathitaṃ, bhavasaṅkhepagatattā pana na sallakkhesī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Then the brahmin thought, 'There seems to be no end to the piercing winds in her body.' One day, taking perfumes and garlands, he went to Jetavana, honored the Teacher, paid homage, and sat to one side. When asked, 'Why have you not been seen, brahmin?' he replied, 'Venerable sir, winds are piercing my wife’s body, so I seek ghee, oil, and the finest foods for her. Her body has become firm and her complexion clear, yet there is no end to her wind ailment. While attending to her, I get no opportunity to come here.' Knowing the brahmin's wife’s wicked nature, the Teacher said, 'Brahmin, “When a woman lies thus and her illness does not subside, it is proper to prepare this and that remedy”—this was told to you by the wise in the past, but because it is obscured by rebirth, you do not recall it.' Then, at his request, the Teacher told a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto brāhmaṇamahāsālakule nibbattitvā vayappatto [V 1.0443] takkasilāyaṃ sabbasippāni uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo ahosi. Ekasatarājadhānīsu khattiyakumārā ca brāhmaṇakumārā ca yebhuyyena tasseva santike sippaṃ uggaṇhanti. Atheko janapadavāsī brāhmaṇamāṇavo bodhisattassa santike tayo vede aṭṭhārasa ca vijjāṭṭhānāni uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasiyaṃyeva kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā divase divase dvattikkhattuṃ bodhisattassa santikaṃ āgacchati[P 1.0464]. Tassa brāhmaṇī dussīlā ahosi pāpadhammāti sabbaṃ paccuppannavatthusadisameva.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into a wealthy brahmin family. Having come of age, he mastered all the arts at Takkasilā and became a world-renowned teacher in Benares. Princes and brahmin youths from one hundred and one royal cities mostly studied under him. Then, a certain young brahmin from the countryside, having learned the three Vedas and the eighteen branches of knowledge from the Bodhisatta, established his household in Benares and would visit the Bodhisatta two or three times daily. His wife was immoral and of evil character—all of this is just like the present story.

Bodhisatto pana “iminā kāraṇena ovādagahaṇāya okāsaṃ na labhāmī”ti vutte “sā māṇavikā imaṃ vañcetvā nipajjatī”ti ñatvā “tassā rogānucchavikaṃ bhesajjaṃ ācikkhissāmī”ti cintetvā āha “tāta, tvaṃ ito paṭṭhāya tassā sappikhīrarasādīni mā adāsi, gomutte pana pañcapaṇṇāni phalādīni ca pakkhipitvā koṭṭetvā navatambalohabhājane pakkhipitvā lohagandhaṃ gāhāpetvā rajjuṃ vā yottaṃ vā rukkhaṃ vā lataṃ vā gahetvā ‘idaṃ te rogassa anucchavikabhesajjaṃ, idaṃ vā piva, uṭṭhāya vā tayā bhuttabhattassa anucchavikaṃ kammaṃ karohī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthaṃ vadeyyāsi. “Sace bhesajjaṃ na pivati, atha naṃ rajjuyā vā yottena vā rukkhena vā latāya vā katici pahāre paharitvā kesesu gahetvā ākaḍḍhitvā kapparena potheyyāsi, sā taṅkhaṇaññeva uṭṭhāya kammaṃ karissatī”ti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā vuttaniyāmeneva bhesajjaṃ katvā “bhadde, imaṃ bhesajjaṃ pivā”ti āha. “Kena te idaṃ ācikkhita”nti? [M 1.0490] “Ācariyena, bhadde”ti. “Apanehi taṃ, na pivissāmī”ti. Māṇavo “na tvaṃ attano ruciyā pivissasī”ti rajjuṃ gahetvā “attano rogassa anucchavikaṃ bhesajjaṃ vā piva, yāgubhattānucchavikaṃ kammaṃ vā karohī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

But the Bodhisatta, upon being told, 'For this reason, I do not get the opportunity to come for instruction,' knew, 'This young woman is deceiving him and lying down.' He thought, 'I will tell him a medicine suitable for her illness,' and said: 'My dear man, from now on, do not give her ghee, milk, sweet drinks, and so on. Instead, put five kinds of leaves, fruits, and the like into cow's urine, pound them, place the mixture in a new copper vessel, and let it absorb the metallic smell. Then, taking a rope, a strap, a branch, or a vine, you should say, “This is a medicine suitable for your illness. Either drink this, or get up and do the work appropriate for the meal you have eaten.” If she does not drink the medicine, then strike her a few blows with the rope, strap, branch, or vine, seize her by the hair, pull her along, and strike her with your elbow. She will immediately get up and do her work.' The man agreed, saying, 'Very well.' Having prepared the medicine in the prescribed manner, he said, 'Good lady, drink this medicine.' 'Who told you this?' 'The teacher, good lady.' 'Take it away! I will not drink it.' The young brahmin, thinking, 'You will not drink this willingly,' took the rope and said, 'Either drink the medicine suitable for your illness, or do the work appropriate for the rice and porridge you have eaten.' Then he spoke this verse:

130.

130.

“Yathāvācā ca bhuñjassu, yathābhuttañca byāhara;

Ubhayaṃ te na sameti, vācā bhuttañca kosiye”ti.

“Eat in accordance with your words, and act in accordance with what you have eaten. For you, O Kosiya, these two do not align: your words and your food.”

Tattha yathāvācā ca bhuñjassūti yathā te vācā, tathā bhuñjassu, “vātā me vijjhantī”ti vācāya anucchavikameva katvā bhuñjassūti attho. “Yathāvācaṃ vā”tipi pāṭho yujjati, “yathāvācāyā”tipi paṭhanti, sabbattha ayameva attho. Yathābhuttañca byāharāti yaṃ yathā te bhuttaṃ, tassa anucchavikameva [P 1.0465] byāhara, “arogamhī”ti vatvā gehe kattabbaṃ karosīti attho. “Yathābhūtañcā”tipi pāṭho, atha vā arogamhīti yathābhūtameva vatvā kammaṃ karohīti [V 1.0444] attho. Ubhayaṃ te na sameti, vācābhuttañca kosiyeti yā ca te ayaṃ vācā “vātā maṃ vijjhantī”ti yañca te idaṃ paṇītabhojanaṃ bhuttaṃ, idaṃ ubhayampi tuyhaṃ na sameti, tasmā uṭṭhāya kammaṃ karohi. “Kosiye”ti taṃ gottenālapati.

Herein, 'Eat in accordance with your words' means: eat in a way that is consistent with your words. The meaning is: since you say, 'The winds pierce me,' eat only what is suitable for such words. The reading 'Yathāvācaṃ vā' is also fitting, and some read 'Yathāvācāyā'; in all cases, the meaning is the same. 'Act in accordance with what you have eaten' means: act in a way that is suitable for what you have eaten. The meaning is: having said, 'I am well,' do what ought to be done in the house. There is also the reading 'Yathābhūtañcā,' which means: having spoken the truth that 'I am well,' do your work. 'For you... these two do not align: your words and your food, O Kosiya' means: this statement of yours, 'The winds pierce me,' and this fine food that you have eaten—these two do not align for you. Therefore, get up and do your work. 'Kosiya' is how he addresses her, by her clan name.

Evaṃ vutte kosiyabrāhmaṇadhītā “ācariyena ussukkaṃ āpannakālato paṭṭhāya na sakkā mayā esa vañcetuṃ, uṭṭhāya kammaṃ karissāmī”ti uṭṭhāya kammaṃ akāsi. “Ācariyena me dussīlabhāvo ñāto, idāni na sakkā ito paṭṭhāya puna evarūpaṃ kātu”nti ācariye gāravena pāpakammatopi viramitvā sīlavatī ahosi. Sāpi brāhmaṇī “sammāsambuddhena kiramhi ñātā”ti sattharipi gāravena na puna anācāraṃ akāsi.

When this was said, the daughter of the Kosiya brahmin thought, 'From the time the teacher took an interest, it has not been possible for me to deceive this man. I will get up and do my work.' So she got up and did her work. She reflected, 'The teacher knows of my immoral nature. From now on, it will not be possible to do such a thing again.' Out of reverence for the teacher, she refrained from evil deeds and became virtuous. Likewise, the brahmin woman in the present story thought, 'It seems I am known by the Perfectly Enlightened One,' and out of reverence for the Teacher, she never again engaged in misconduct.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jayampatikā idāni jayampatikāva, ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, the Teacher connected the birth story: 'The husband and wife of that time are the husband and wife of today, and I myself was the teacher.'

Kosiyajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The commentary on the Kosiya Jātaka, the tenth.

Kusanāḷivaggo terasamo.

The Kusanāḷi Chapter, the thirteenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Kusanāḷi [M 1.0491] ca dummedhaṃ, naṅgalīsambakaṭāhaṃ;

Asilakkhaṇakalaṇḍukaṃ, biḷāraggikakosiyanti.

Kusanāḷi, Dummedha, Naṅgalīsa, Ambaka, Kaṭāha, Asilakkhaṇa, Kalaṇḍuka, Biḷāra, Aggika, and Kosiya.

14. Asampadānavaggo

14. The Chapter on Not Giving

[131] 1. Asampadānajātakavaṇṇanā

[131] 1. The Commentary on the Asampadāna Jātaka

Asampadānenitarītarassāti [V 1.0445] idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi kāle bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso devadatto, akataññū tathāgatassa guṇaṃ na jānātī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva devadatto akataññū, pubbepi akataññūyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“By not giving to others...” This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove with reference to Devadatta. For at that time, the monks had started a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma, saying, 'Venerable sirs, Devadatta is ungrateful; he does not recognize the qualities of the Tathāgata.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'For what discussion are you now gathered here, monks?' When they told him, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is ungrateful; he was ungrateful in the past as well.' And he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 1.0466] magadharaṭṭhe rājagahe ekasmiṃ magadharaññe rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto tasseva seṭṭhi ahosi asītikoṭivibhavo saṅkhaseṭṭhīti nāmena. Bārāṇasiyaṃ pīḷiyaseṭṭhi nāma asītikoṭivibhavova ahosi. Te aññamaññaṃ sahāyakā ahesuṃ. Tesu bārāṇasiyaṃ pīḷiyaseṭṭhissa kenacideva kāraṇena mahantaṃ bhayaṃ uppajji, sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ parihāyi. So daliddo appaṭisaraṇo hutvā bhariyaṃ ādāya saṅkhaseṭṭhiṃ paccayaṃ katvā bārāṇasito nikkhamitvā padasāva rājagahaṃ patvā saṅkhaseṭṭhissa nivesanaṃ agamāsi. So taṃ disvāva “sahāyo me āgato”ti parissajitvā sakkārasammānaṃ katvā katipāhaṃ vītināmetvā ekadivasaṃ “samma, kenaṭṭhena āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Bhayaṃ me, samma, uppannaṃ, sabbaṃ dhanaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ, upatthambho me hohī”ti. “Sādhu samma, mā bhāyī”ti bhaṇḍāgāraṃ vivarāpetvā cattālīsa hiraññakoṭiyo dāpetvā sesampi paricchadaparivāraṃ sabbaṃ attano santakaṃ saviññāṇakaṃ aviññāṇakaṃ majjhe bhinditvā upaḍḍhameva adāsi. So taṃ vibhavaṃ ādāya puna bārāṇasiṃ gantvā nivāsaṃ kappesi.

In the past, in the kingdom of Magadha, in the city of Rājagaha, while a certain king was ruling, the Bodhisatta was a treasurer named Saṅkhaseṭṭhi, possessing eighty crores in wealth. In Bārāṇasī, there was another treasurer named Pīḷiyaseṭṭhi, also possessing eighty crores. They were friends with each other. Now, in Bārāṇasī, Pīḷiyaseṭṭhi faced a great danger for some reason and lost all his wealth. Becoming destitute and without refuge, he took his wife and, placing his trust in Saṅkhaseṭṭhi, left Bārāṇasī and traveled on foot to Rājagaha. Upon arriving, he went to Saṅkhaseṭṭhi’s residence. Seeing him, Saṅkhaseṭṭhi, thinking, “My friend has come,” embraced him and showed him great honor. After a few days had passed, one day he asked, “Friend, for what reason have you come?” “Friend, a danger has befallen me, and all my wealth is gone. Please support me.” “Very well, friend, do not fear.” He had his treasury opened and gave him forty crores of wealth; he then divided all the remaining retinue and requisites, all his property, both animate and inanimate, in half and gave him one portion. Taking that wealth, Pīḷiyaseṭṭhi returned to Bārāṇasī and reestablished his residence.

Aparabhāge [M 1.0492] saṅkhaseṭṭhissapi tādisameva bhayaṃ uppajji. So attano paṭisaraṇaṃ upadhārento “sahāyassa me mahāupakāro kato, upaḍḍhavibhavo dinno. Na so maṃ disvā pariccajissati, tassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti cintetvā bhariyaṃ ādāya padasāva bārāṇasiṃ gantvā bhariyaṃ āha “bhadde, tava mayā saddhiṃ antaravīthiyā gamanaṃ nāma na yuttaṃ, mayā pesitayānamāruyha [V 1.0446] mahantena parivārena pacchā āgamissasi. Yāva yānaṃ pesemi, tāva idheva hohī”ti vatvā taṃ sālāya ṭhapetvā sayaṃ nagaraṃ pavisitvā seṭṭhissa gharaṃ gantvā “rājagahanagarato tumhākaṃ sahāyo saṅkhaseṭṭhi nāma āgato”ti ārocāpesi. So “āgacchatū”ti pakkosāpetvā taṃ disvā neva āsanā vuṭṭhāsi, na paṭisanthāraṃ akāsi, kevalaṃ “kimatthaṃ āgatosī”ti pucchi. “Tumhākaṃ dassanatthaṃ āgatomhī”ti. “Nivāso [P 1.0467] te kahaṃ gahito”ti? “Na tāva nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ atthi, seṭṭhigharaṇimpi sālāya ṭhapetvāva āgatomhī”ti. “Tumhākaṃ idha nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ natthi, nivāpaṃ gahetvā ekasmiṃ ṭhāne pacāpetvā bhuñjitvā gacchatha, puna amhākaṃ gharaṃ mā pavisathā”ti vatvā “mayhaṃ sahāyassa dussante bandhitvā ekaṃ bahalapalāpatumbaṃ dehī”ti dāsaṃ āṇāpesi. Taṃ divasaṃ kira so rattasālīnaṃ sakaṭasahassamattaṃ ophunāpetvā koṭṭhāgāraṃ pūrāpesi, cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ gahetvā āgato akataññū mahācoro sahāyakassa tumbamatte palāpe dāpesi. Dāso pacchiyaṃ ekaṃ palāpatumbaṃ pakkhipitvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ agamāsi.

Later, the same kind of danger befell the treasurer Saṅkha. Considering his own refuge, he thought, “I did a great favor for my friend; half of my wealth was given to him. Seeing me, he will not abandon me. I will go to him.” Taking his wife, he went on foot to Bārāṇasī and said to her, “My dear, it is not proper for you to walk with me through the streets. You shall mount the carriage I send and come later with a large retinue. Until I send the carriage, stay right here.” Having said this, he left her in a public hall and entered the city himself. He went to the treasurer’s house and had it announced, “Your friend, the treasurer Saṅkha, has come from the city of Rājagaha.” The treasurer said, “Let him come,” and had him summoned. But upon seeing him, he neither rose from his seat nor offered any hospitality. He simply asked, “For what purpose have you come?” “I have come to see you,” he replied. “Where have you taken up residence?” “I have not yet found a place to stay; I left my wife in a public hall and came here.” “There is no place for you to stay here. Take some provisions, cook them somewhere, eat, and then go. Do not enter our house again.” Having said this, he ordered a servant, “Tie up a tumba-measure of coarse chaff in the hem of his garment and give it to my friend.” It is said that on that very day, he had winnowed a thousand cartloads of red rice and filled his granary. This ungrateful great thief, who had received forty crores of wealth, had only a tumba-measure of chaff given to his friend. The servant put a tumba-measure of chaff in a basket and went to the Bodhisatta.

Bodhisatto cintesi – “ayaṃ asappuriso mama santikā cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ labhitvā idāni palāpatumbaṃ dāpesi, gaṇhāmi nu kho, na gaṇhāmī”ti? Athassa etadahosi “ayaṃ tāva akataññū mittadubbhī katavināsakabhāvena mayā saddhiṃ mittabhāvaṃ bhindi. Sacāhaṃ etena dinnaṃ palāpatumbaṃ lāmakattā na gaṇhissāmi, ahampi mittabhāvaṃ bhindissāmi. Andhabālā parittakaṃ laddhaṃ aggaṇhantā mittabhāvaṃ vināsenti, ahaṃ pana etena dinnaṃ palāpatumbaṃ gahetvā mama vasena mittabhāvaṃ patiṭṭhāpessāmī”ti. So palāpatumbaṃ dussante bandhitvā pāsādā oruyha sālaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ bhariyā “kiṃ te, ayya, laddha”nti pucchi. “Bhadde amhākaṃ sahāyo pīḷiyaseṭṭhi palāpatumbaṃ datvā amhe ajjeva [M 1.0493] vissajjesī”ti. Sā “ayya, kimatthaṃ aggahesi, kiṃ etaṃ cattālīsakoṭidhanassa anucchavika”nti rodituṃ ārabhi. Bodhisattopi “bhadde, mā rodi, ahaṃ tena saddhiṃ mittabhāvabhedanabhayena mama vasena mittabhāvaṃ patiṭṭhāpetuṃ gaṇhiṃ, tvaṃ kiṃkāraṇā rodasī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta thought, “This wicked man, having received forty crores of wealth from me, now has a tumba-measure of chaff given to me. Should I take it or not?” Then it occurred to him, “This ungrateful man, a betrayer of friends, has already broken our bond of friendship by his act of destroying the good that was done for him. If I, on account of its wretchedness, do not accept this measure of chaff given by him, I too will break the friendship. Blind fools destroy friendships by not accepting the little they receive. But I, by accepting this measure of chaff given by him, will preserve the friendship on my part.” So he tied the measure of chaff in the hem of his garment, descended from the mansion, and went to the public hall. His wife then asked, “My lord, what have you received?” “My dear, our friend, the treasurer Pīḷiya, gave us a measure of chaff and sent us away this very day.” She began to cry, saying, “My lord, why did you accept it? Is this a fitting return for forty crores of wealth?” The Bodhisatta said, “My dear, do not weep. I accepted it out of fear of breaking our friendship, in order to preserve the friendship on my part. For what reason do you weep?” And he spoke this verse:

131.

131.

“Asampadānenitarītarassa, bālassa mittāni kalībhavanti;

Tasmā [P 1.0468] harāmi bhusaṃ aḍḍhamānaṃ, mā me mitti jīyittha sassatāya”nti.

“Through non-acceptance, the friendships of a foolish and worthless person are destroyed. Therefore, I carry away this half-measure of chaff, that my friendship may not perish, but be eternal.”

Tattha [V 1.0447] asampadānenāti asampādānena. Akāralope sandhi, aggahaṇenāti attho. Itarītarassāti yassa kassaci lāmakālāmakassa. Bālassa mittāni kalībhavantīti dandhassa apaññassa mittāni kalīni kāḷakaṇṇisadisāni honti, bhijjantīti attho. Tasmā harāmi bhusaṃ aḍḍhamānanti tena kāraṇena ahaṃ sahāyena dinnaṃ ekapalāpatumbaṃ harāmi gaṇhāmīti dasseti. “Māna”nti hi aṭṭhannaṃ nāḷīnaṃ nāmaṃ, catunnaṃ aḍḍhamānaṃ, catasso ca nāḷiyo tumbo nāma. Tena vuttaṃ “palāpatumba”nti. Mā me mitti jīyittha sassatāyanti mama sahāyena saddhiṃ mitti mā bhijjittha, sassatāva ayaṃ hotūti attho.

Herein, ‘asampadānena’ is a form of ‘asampādānena’; the ‘a’ is elided by sandhi, and the meaning is ‘by not accepting.’ ‘Itarītarassa’ means of any base and worthless person. ‘Bālassa mittāni kalībhavanti’ means the friendships of a slow-witted and unwise person become full of strife, like a person of ill omen; they are broken, this is the meaning. ‘Tasmā harāmi bhusaṃ aḍḍhamānaṃ’ shows: for that reason, ‘I carry,’ meaning I accept, the single tumba-measure of chaff given by my friend. For ‘māna’ is the name for eight ‘nāḷi’; a half-māna is four; and four ‘nāḷi’ are called a ‘tumba.’ Hence it was said ‘palāpatumba’ (a tumba of chaff). ‘Mā me mitti jīyittha sassatāya’ means: may my friendship with my friend not be broken; may this friendship be eternal.

Evaṃ vuttepi seṭṭhibhariyā rodateva. Tasmiṃ khaṇe saṅkhaseṭṭhinā pīḷiyaseṭṭhissa dinno kammantadāso sālādvārena āgacchanto seṭṭhibhariyāya rodanasaddaṃ sutvā sālaṃ pavisitvā attano sāmike disvā pādesu nipatitvā roditvā kanditvā “kimatthaṃ idhāgatattha, sāmī”ti pucchi. Seṭṭhi sabbaṃ ārocesi. Kammantadāso “hotu, sāmi, mā cintayitthā”ti ubhopi assāsetvā attano gehaṃ netvā gandhodakena nhāpetvā bhojetvā “sāmikā, vo āgatā”ti sesadāse sannipātetvā dassetvā katipāhaṃ vītināmetvā sabbe dāse gahetvā rājaṅgaṇaṃ gantvā uparavaṃ akāsi. Rājā pakkosāpetvā “kiṃ eta”nti pucchi, te sabbaṃ taṃ pavattiṃ rañño ārocesuṃ.

Even when spoken to thus, the merchant’s wife only wept. At that moment, a work-slave, who had been given to the merchant Pīḷiya by the merchant Saṅkha, was approaching the hall's entrance. Hearing the sound of the merchant’s wife weeping, he entered the hall, saw his masters, fell at their feet, wept and cried out, asking, “Why have you come here, masters?” The merchant told him everything. The work-slave reassured them both, saying, “Let it be, master, do not worry.” He then took them to his own house, bathed them with scented water, and gave them food. Gathering the other slaves, he announced to them, “Your masters have come!” After a few days had passed, he took all the slaves to the royal courtyard and raised an uproar. The king had them summoned and asked, “What is this?” They reported the whole matter to the king.

Rājā [M 1.0494] tesaṃ vacanaṃ sutvā ubhopi seṭṭhī pakkosāpetvā saṅkhaseṭṭhiṃ pucchi “saccaṃ kira tayā mahāseṭṭhi pīḷiyaseṭṭhissa cattālīsakoṭidhanaṃ dinna”nti? “Āma, mahārāja, mama sahāyassa maṃ takketvā rājagahaṃ āgatassa na kevalaṃ dhanaṃ, sabbaṃ vibhavajātaṃ saviññāṇakaṃ aviññāṇakaṃ dve koṭṭhāse katvā samabhāge adāsinti. Rājā “saccameta”nti pīḷiyaseṭṭhiṃ pucchi. “Āma, devā”ti. “Tayā panassa taññeva takketvā āgatassa atthi koci sakkāro vā sammāno vā kato”ti. So tuṇhī ahosi. Api pana te etassa palāpatumbamattaṃ dussante pakkhipāpetvā dāpitaṃ [P 1.0469] atthīti. Tampi sutvā tuṇhīyeva ahosi. Rājā “kiṃ kātabba”nti amaccehi saddhiṃ mantetvā taṃ paribhāsitvā “gacchatha, pīḷiyaseṭṭhissa ghare sabbaṃ vibhavaṃ saṅkhaseṭṭhissa dethā”ti āha. Bodhisatto “mahārāja, mayhaṃ parasantakena attho natthi, mayā dinnamattameva pana dāpethā”ti āha. Rājā bodhisattassa santakaṃ dāpesi. Bodhisatto sabbaṃ attano dinnavibhavaṃ paṭilabhitvā dāsaparivuto rājagahameva gantvā kuṭumbaṃ saṇṭhapetvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

The king, having heard their words, summoned both merchants and questioned the merchant Saṅkha, “Great merchant, is it true that you gave the merchant Pīḷiya forty crores of wealth?” “Yes, great king. When my friend came to Rājagaha relying on me, I not only gave him wealth, but I divided all my possessions—animate and inanimate—into two and gave him an equal share.” The king asked the merchant Pīḷiya, “Is this true?” “Yes, Your Majesty,” he replied. “But when he came relying on you, did you show him any respect or honor?” He remained silent. “Did you even have so much as a measure of chaff placed in the hem of his garment and given to him?” Hearing this, he still remained silent. The king consulted with his ministers and, after rebuking Pīḷiya, declared, “Go, give all of the merchant Pīḷiya’s possessions to the merchant Saṅkha.” The Bodhisatta said, “Great king, I have no need for another’s possessions. Please have only what I gave returned to me.” The king had what belonged to the Bodhisatta given back. The Bodhisatta, having recovered all the wealth he had given, surrounded by his servants, returned to Rājagaha, reestablished his household, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and passed on according to his karma.

Satthā [V 1.0448] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā pīḷiyaseṭṭhi devadatto ahosi, saṅkhaseṭṭhi pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, the merchant Pīḷiya was Devadatta, but the merchant Saṅkha was indeed myself.”

Asampadānajātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Asampadāna Jātaka, the First.

[132] 2. Bhīrukajātakavaṇṇanā

[132] 2. The Commentary on the Bhīruka Jātaka

Kusalūpadese dhitiyā daḷhāya cāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ajapālanigrodhe māradhītānaṃ palobhanasuttantaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Bhagavatā hi ādito paṭṭhāya vuttaṃ –

“With firm fortitude in the instruction of what is wholesome…” The Teacher spoke this while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the discourse on the temptation by Māra’s daughters at the Ajapāla banyan tree. For, from the very beginning, it was said by the Blessed One:

“Daddallamānā āgañchuṃ, taṇhā ca aratī ragā;

Tā tattha panudī satthā, tūlaṃ bhaṭṭhaṃva māluto”ti. (saṃ. ni. 1.161);

“Shining brightly they came—Taṇhā, Arati, and Ragā. The Teacher dispelled them there, like the wind a fallen tuft of cotton.”

Evaṃ yāva pariyosānā tassa suttantassa kathitakāle dhammasabhāyaṃ sannipatitā bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, sammāsambuddho māradhītaro [M 1.0495] anekasatānipi dibbarūpāni māpetvā palobhanatthāya upasaṅkamantiyo akkhīnipi ummīletvā na olokesi, aho buddhabalaṃ nāma acchariya”nti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva mayhaṃ sabbāsave khepetvā sabbaññutaṃ sampattassa māradhītānaṃ anolokanaṃ nāma acchariyaṃ, ahañhi pubbe bodhiñāṇaṃ pariyesamāno sakilesakālepi abhisaṅkhataṃ dibbarūpaṃ indriyāni bhinditvā kilesavasena anoloketvāva gantvā mahārajjaṃ pāpuṇi”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

When that discourse had been spoken to its conclusion, the monks gathered in the Dhamma hall began a discussion: “Friends, the Perfectly Enlightened One, even when Māra’s daughters manifested many hundreds of divine forms to tempt him, did not look at them even with his eyes open. Ah, the power of a Buddha is truly marvelous!” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you gathered here now?” When they replied, “For this one,” he said: “Monks, it is no marvel that now, having destroyed all taints and attained omniscience, I do not look at Māra’s daughters. For in the past, while seeking the knowledge of enlightenment and still possessing defilements, I attained a great kingdom by proceeding without looking, through the power of those defilements, at a fabricated divine form, even as it assailed my senses.” Having said this, he recounted a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto bhātikasatassa kaniṭṭho ahosīti sabbaṃ heṭṭhā takkasilājātake [P 1.0470] vuttanayeneva vitthāretabbaṃ. Tadā pana takkasilānagaravāsīhi bahinagare sālāyaṃ bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā yācitvā rajjaṃ paṭicchāpetvā abhiseke kate takkasilānagaravāsino nagaraṃ devanagaraṃ viya, rājabhavanañca indabhavanaṃ viya alaṅkariṃsu. Tadā bodhisatto nagaraṃ pavisitvā rājabhavane pāsāde mahātale samussitasetacchattaṃ ratanavarapallaṅkaṃ abhiruyha devarājalīlāya nisīdi, amaccā ca brāhmaṇagahapatikādayo ca khattiyakumārā ca sabbālaṅkārapaṭimaṇḍitā parivāretvā aṭṭhaṃsu, devaccharāpaṭibhāgā soḷasasahassanāṭakitthiyo naccagītavāditakusalā uttamavilāsasampannā naccagītavāditāni [V 1.0449] payojesuṃ. Gītavāditasaddena rājabhavanaṃ meghatthanitapūritā mahāsamuddakucchi viya ekaninnādaṃ ahosi. Bodhisatto taṃ attano sirisobhaggaṃ olokayamānova cintesi “sacāhaṃ tāsaṃ yakkhinīnaṃ abhisaṅkhataṃ dibbarūpaṃ olokessaṃ, jīvitakkhayaṃ patto abhavissaṃ, imaṃ sirisobhaggaṃ na olokessaṃ. Paccekabuddhānaṃ pana ovāde ṭhitabhāvena idaṃ mayā sampatta”nti. Evañca pana cintetvā udānaṃ udānento imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was the youngest of one hundred brothers; all this should be elaborated in the manner told below in the Takkasilā Jātaka. At that time, the residents of the city of Takkasilā approached the Bodhisatta in a hall outside the city, and after requesting and having him accept the kingship, they performed the consecration. The residents of Takkasilā adorned the city like a city of the gods and the royal palace like the palace of Indra. Then the Bodhisatta entered the city, ascended the splendid jeweled throne under a raised white parasol on the great terrace of the palace, and sat with the grace of a divine king. Ministers, brahmins, householders, and noble princes, all adorned with every ornament, stood surrounding him. Sixteen thousand dancing women, who resembled celestial nymphs, were skilled in dance, song, and music, and were endowed with supreme grace, performed their dances, songs, and music. With the sound of song and music, the royal palace became a single roar, like the belly of the great ocean filled with the rumbling of thunder. As the Bodhisatta gazed upon his own glory and splendor, he reflected: “If I had gazed upon the fabricated divine forms of those ogresses, I would have met my death and would not be seeing this glory and splendor. It is because I stood firm in the advice of the Paccekabuddhas that I have attained this.” Having reflected thus, and wishing to utter an inspired utterance, he spoke this verse:

132.

132.

“Kusalūpadese dhitiyā daḷhāya ca, anivattitattā bhayabhīrutāya ca;

Na rakkhasīnaṃ vasamāgamimhase, sa sotthibhāvo mahatā bhayena me”ti.

“By firm resolve in the instruction of the skillful, and by not turning back due to an absence of fear and terror, we did not come under the power of the ogresses. That was my well-being, won from great danger.”

Tattha [M 1.0496] kusalūpadeseti kusalānaṃ upadese, paccekabuddhānaṃ ovādeti attho. Dhitiyā daḷhāya cāti daḷhāya dhitiyā ca, thirena abbocchinnanirantaravīriyena cāti attho. Anivattitattā bhayabhīrutāya cāti bhayabhīrutāya anivattitatāya ca. Tattha bhayanti cittutrāsamattaṃ parittabhayaṃ. Bhīrutāti sarīrakampanappattaṃ mahābhayaṃ. Idaṃ ubhayampi mahāsattassa “yakkhiniyo nāmetā manussakhādikā”ti bheravārammaṇaṃ disvāpi nāhosi. Tenāha “anivattitattā bhayabhīrutāya cā”ti. Bhayabhīrutāya abhāveneva bheravārammaṇaṃ disvāpi anivattanabhāvenāti attho. Na rakkhasīnaṃ vasamāgamimhaseti yakkhakantāre tāsaṃ rakkhasīnaṃ vasaṃ na agamimha. Yasmā amhākaṃ kusalūpadese dhiti ca daḷhā ahosi, bhayabhīrutābhāvena ca anivattanasabhāvā ahumhā, tasmā rakkhasīnaṃ vasaṃ [P 1.0471] na agamimhāti vuttaṃ hoti. Sa sotthibhāvo mahatā bhayena meti so mayhaṃ ayaṃ ajja mahatā bhayena rakkhasīnaṃ santikā pattabbena dukkhadomanassena sotthibhāvo khemabhāvo pītisomanassabhāvoyeva jātoti.

Here, 'in the instruction of the wholesome' refers to the instruction of the skillful, meaning the advice of the Paccekabuddhas. 'By firm resolve' means by firm resolve, and by stable, uninterrupted, and continuous energy. 'By not turning back from fear and terror' means by not turning back due to fear and terror. Here, 'fear' refers to mere mental alarm, a slight fear. 'Terror' means a great fear that has reached the point of bodily trembling. Both of these were absent in the great being, even when seeing the terrifying sight of the ogresses and thinking, 'These are man-eating ogresses.' Therefore, it is said, 'by not turning back from fear and terror.' The meaning is that due to the absence of fear and terror, there was no turning back even when seeing a terrifying sight. 'We did not come under the power of the ogresses' means in the demon-wilderness, we did not come under their power. Because our resolve in the instruction of the wholesome was firm, and because we were of a nature not to turn back due to the absence of fear and terror, therefore it is said that we did not come under the power of the ogresses. 'That well-being was mine from great danger' means that for me, this well-being, this security, this state of joy and gladness has arisen today from the great danger, from the suffering and distress that was to be obtained from the ogresses.

Evaṃ mahāsatto imāya gāthāya dhammaṃ desetvā dhammena rajjaṃ kāretvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Thus, the great being, having taught the Dhamma with this verse, ruled the kingdom righteously, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and passed away according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “ahaṃ tena samayena takkasilaṃ gantvā rajjappattakumāro ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story, saying: “At that time, I was the prince who went to Takkasilā and attained kingship.”

Bhīrukajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Bhīruka Jātaka, the Second.

[133] 3. Ghatāsanajātakavaṇṇanā

[133] 3. The Commentary on the Ghatāsana Jātaka

Khemaṃ [V 1.0450] yahinti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto aññataraṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi bhikkhu satthu santike kammaṭṭhānaṃ gahetvā paccantaṃ gantvā ekaṃ gāmakaṃ upanissāya araññasenāsane vassaṃ upagañchi. Tassa paṭhamamāseyeva piṇḍāya paviṭṭhassa paṇṇasālā jhāyittha. So vasanaṭṭhānābhāvena kilamanto upaṭṭhākānaṃ ācikkhi. Te “hotu, bhante, paṇṇasālaṃ karissāma, kasāma tāva, vapāma tāvā”tiādīni vadantā [M 1.0497] temāsaṃ vītināmesuṃ. So senāsanasappāyābhāvena kammaṭṭhānaṃ matthakaṃ pāpetuṃ nāsakkhi. So nimittamattampi anuppādetvā vutthavasso jetavanaṃ gantvā satthāraṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisīdi. Satthā tena saddhiṃ paṭisanthāraṃ katvā “kiṃ nu kho te, bhikkhu, kammaṭṭhānaṃ sappāyaṃ jāta”nti pucchi. So ādito paṭṭhāya asappāyabhāvaṃ kathesi. Satthā “pubbe kho, bhikkhu, tiracchānāpi attano sappāyāsappāyaṃ ñatvā sappāyakāle vasitvā asappāyakāle vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pahāya aññattha agamaṃsu, tvaṃ kasmā attano sappāyāsappāyaṃ na aññāsī”ti vatvā tena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this verse beginning with `Khemaṃ yahiṃ` concerning a certain monk. That monk, having received a meditation subject from the Teacher, went to the borderlands and spent the rainy season in a forest dwelling near a village. In the very first month, while he was on his alms-round, his leaf-hut burned down. Distressed by the lack of a dwelling, he informed his lay supporters. They said, 'Let it be, venerable sir, we will build a leaf-hut. But first let us plow, first let us sow,' and so on, and thus they let the three months pass. Due to the unsuitability of the dwelling, he was unable to bring his meditation subject to its culmination. Without having produced even a preliminary sign, when the rainy season was over, he went to Jetavana, paid homage to the Teacher, and sat to one side. The Teacher exchanged pleasantries with him and asked, 'Well, monk, did your meditation subject prove suitable?' He then explained from the beginning how it was unsuitable. The Teacher said, 'In the past, monk, even animals, knowing what was suitable and unsuitable for themselves, stayed during a suitable time and, during an unsuitable time, left their dwelling place and went elsewhere. Why did you not know what was suitable and unsuitable for yourself?' Being requested by him, the Teacher related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sakuṇayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā viññutaṃ patvā sobhaggappatto sakuṇarājā hutvā ekasmiṃ araññāyatane jātassaratīre sākhāviṭapasampannaṃ bahalapattapalāsaṃ mahārukkhaṃ upanissāya saparivāro vāsaṃ kappesi. Bahū sakuṇā tassa rukkhassa [P 1.0472] udakamatthake patthaṭasākhāsu vasantā sarīravaḷañjaṃ udake pātenti. Tasmiñca jātassare caṇḍo nāgarājā vasati. Tassa etadahosi “ime sakuṇā mayhaṃ nivāse jātassare sarīravaḷañjaṃ pātenti, yaṃnūnāhaṃ udakato aggiṃ uṭṭhāpetvā rukkhaṃ jhāpetvā ete palāpeyya”nti. So kuddhamānaso rattibhāge sabbesaṃ sakuṇānaṃ sannipatitvā rukkhasākhāsu nipannakāle paṭhamaṃ tāva uddhanāropitaṃ viya udakaṃ pakkudhāpetvā dutiyavāre dhūmaṃ uṭṭhāpetvā tatiyavāre tālakkhandhappamāṇaṃ jālaṃ uṭṭhāpesi. Bodhisatto udakato jālaṃ uṭṭhahamānaṃ disvā “bho, sakuṇā, agginā ādittaṃ nāma udakena nibbāpenti, idāni pana udakameva ādittaṃ. Na sakkā amhehi idha vasituṃ, aññattha gamissāmā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the bird realm. Having attained intelligence and beauty, he became a king of birds and lived with his retinue in a certain forest region, on the bank of a natural lake, relying on a great tree endowed with branches and boughs and with thick leaves and foliage. Many birds, dwelling on the branches of that tree spread over the water, dropped their bodily refuse into the water. In that natural lake lived a fierce nāga king.
