It occurred to him: 'These birds drop their bodily refuse into my dwelling, the natural lake. What if I were to raise fire from the water, burn the tree, and make them flee?' With an angry mind, during the night when all the birds had gathered and were resting on the tree branches, first he made the water boil as if placed on a stove, the second time he raised smoke, and the third time he raised a flame the size of a palm-tree trunk. The Bodhisatta, seeing the flame rising from the water, said, 'O birds, that which is ablaze with fire is extinguished with water, but now the water itself is ablaze. It is not possible for us to live here; we shall go elsewhere,' and he spoke this verse:

133.

133.

“Khemaṃ yahiṃ tattha arī udīrito, dakassa majjhe jalate ghatāsano;

Na ajja vāso mahiyā mahīruhe, disā bhajavho saraṇājja nobhaya”nti.

“Where there is safety, there an enemy has arisen; in the midst of the water, a fire blazes. Today there is no dwelling in this tree born of the earth; flee to the directions, for today fear comes to us from our refuge.”

Tattha [V 1.0451] khemaṃ yahiṃ tattha arī udīritoti yasmiṃ udakapiṭṭhe khemabhāvo nibbhayabhāvo, tasmiṃ attapaccatthiko sapatto uṭṭhito. Dakassāti udakassa. Ghatāsanoti aggi. So hi ghataṃ asnāti, tasmā “ghatāsano”ti [M 1.0498] vuccati. Na ajja vāsoti ajja no vāso natthi. Mahiyā mahīruheti mahiruho vuccati rukkho, tasmiṃ imissā mahiyā jāte rukkheti attho. Disā bhajavhoti disā bhajatha gacchatha. Saraṇājja no bhayanti ajja amhākaṃ saraṇato bhayaṃ jātaṃ, paṭisaraṇaṭṭhānato bhayaṃ uppannanti attho.

Here, ‘Where there is safety, there an enemy has arisen’ means that on the surface of the water, where there is a state of safety and fearlessness, a hostile adversary has arisen. ‘Dakassa’ means ‘of the water.’ ‘Ghatāsano’ is fire, for it consumes ghee, and therefore it is called ‘ghatāsano.’ ‘No dwelling today’ means today we have no dwelling. ‘Mahiyā mahīruhe’: a tree is called a `mahiruha`; the meaning is ‘in this tree born from this earth.’ ‘Flee to the directions’ means flee, go to the directions. ‘Today fear comes to us from our refuge’ means that today fear has arisen for us from our refuge; that is, danger has arisen from our place of sanctuary.

Evaṃ vatvā bodhisatto attano vacanakare sakuṇe ādāya uppatitvā aññattha gato. Bodhisattassa vacanaṃ aggahetvā ṭhitasakuṇā jīvitakkhayaṃ pattā.

Having spoken thus, the Bodhisatta, taking with him the birds who were obedient to his word, flew up and went elsewhere. The birds who did not heed the Bodhisatta's word and remained behind met the end of their lives.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi, saccapariyosāne so bhikkhu arahatte patiṭṭhāsi.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, revealed the Truths and connected the Jātaka. At the conclusion of the teaching on the Truths, that monk was established in Arahantship.

Tadā bodhisattassa vacanakarā sakuṇā buddhaparisā ahesuṃ, sakuṇarājā pana ahameva ahosinti.

At that time, the birds who were obedient to the Bodhisatta's word became the Buddha's assembly, and the king of the birds was I myself.

Ghatāsanajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The third, the Commentary on the Ghatāsana Jātaka.

[134] 4. Jhānasodhanajātakavaṇṇanā

[134] 4. The Commentary on the Jhānasodhana Jātaka

Ye [P 1.0473] saññinoti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto saṅkassanagaradvāre attanā saṃkhittena pucchitapañhassa dhammasenāpatino vitthārabyākaraṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tatridaṃ atītavatthu – atīte kira bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññāyatane kālaṃ karonto antevāsikehi pucchito “nevasaññīnāsaññī”ti āha…pe… tāpasā jeṭṭhantevāsikassa kathaṃ na gaṇhiṃsu. Bodhisatto ābhassarato āgantvā ākāse ṭhatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

‘Those who are percipient’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the detailed explanation given by the General of the Dhamma at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa, in response to a question briefly posed by himself. Herein is the story of the past: In the past, it is said, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, while passing away in a forest hermitage, was asked by his disciples and answered, “Neither-percipient-nor-non-percipient.” ... The ascetics did not accept the words of the senior disciple. The Bodhisatta, having come from the Ābhassara realm and standing in the sky, spoke this verse:

134.

134.

“Ye saññino tepi duggatā, yepi asaññino tepi duggatā;

Etaṃ ubhayaṃ vivajjaya, taṃ samāpattisukhaṃ anaṅgaṇa”nti.

“Those who are percipient are also in an unfortunate state, and those who are non-percipient are also in an unfortunate state. Avoid both of these; that bliss of attainment is flawless.”

Tattha [V 1.0452] ye saññinoti ṭhapetvā nevasaññānāsaññāyatanalābhino avasese sacittakasatte dasseti. Tepi duggatāti tassā samāpattiyā alābhato tepi duggatā nāma. Yepi asaññinoti asaññabhave [M 1.0499] nibbatte acittakasatte dasseti. Tepi duggatāti tepi imissāyeva samāpattiyā alābhato duggatāyeva nāma. Etaṃ ubhayaṃ vivajjayāti etaṃ ubhayampi saññibhavañca asaññibhavañca vivajjaya pajahāti antevāsikaṃ ovadati. Taṃ samāpattisukhaṃ anaṅgaṇanti taṃ nevasaññānāsaññāyatanasamāpattilābhino santaṭṭhena “sukha”nti saṅkhaṃ gataṃ jhānasukhaṃ anaṅgaṇaṃ niddosaṃ balavacittekaggatāsabhāvenapi taṃ anaṅgaṇaṃ nāma jātaṃ.

Herein, ‘those who are percipient’ indicates conscious beings, with the exception of those who have attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception. ‘They too are in an unfortunate state’ means that because they have not obtained that attainment, they are called ‘in an unfortunate state.’ ‘And those who are non-percipient’ indicates unconscious beings reborn in the non-percipient existence. ‘They too are in an unfortunate state’ means that because they too have not obtained this very attainment, they are indeed called ‘in an unfortunate state.’ ‘Avoid both of these’ means he advises the disciple, “One should avoid and abandon both: the state of being percipient and the state of being non-percipient.” ‘That bliss of attainment is flawless’ means that the jhāna-bliss—which is reckoned as ‘bliss’ on account of its peaceful nature by one who has attained the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—is flawless and faultless. Even by its nature of strong one-pointedness of mind, it is called flawless.

Evaṃ bodhisatto dhammaṃ desetvā antevāsikassa guṇaṃ kathetvā brahmalokameva agamāsi. Tadā sesatāpasā jeṭṭhantevāsikassa saddahiṃsu.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma and spoken of the virtues of the chief disciple, went to the Brahma world itself. Then the remaining ascetics placed their faith in the senior disciple.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jeṭṭhantevāsiko sāriputto, mahābrahmā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying: “At that time the senior disciple was Sāriputta, and the Great Brahmā was I myself.”

Jhānasodhanajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The fourth, the Commentary on the Jhānasodhana Jātaka.

[135] 5. Candābhajātakavaṇṇanā

[135] 5. The Commentary on the Candābha Jātaka

Candābhanti [P 1.0474] idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto saṅkassanagaradvāre therasseva pañhabyākaraṇaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Atīte kira bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto araññāyatane kālaṃ karonto antevāsikehi pucchito “candābhaṃ sūriyābha”nti vatvā ābhassare nibbatto. Tāpasā jeṭṭhantevāsikassa na saddahiṃsu. Bodhisatto ābhassarato āgantvā ākāse ṭhito imaṃ gāthamāha –

‘Moon-radiance’—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the Elder’s own explanation of the question at the gate of the city of Saṅkassa. In the past, it is said, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta, while passing away in a forest hermitage, was asked by his disciples and replied, “Moon-radiance, sun-radiance,” and was reborn in the Ābhassara realm. The ascetics did not believe the senior disciple. The Bodhisatta, having come from the Ābhassara realm and standing in the sky, spoke this verse:

135.

135.

“Candābhaṃ sūriyābhañca, yodha paññāya gādhati;

Avitakkena jhānena, hoti ābhassarūpago”ti.

“He who in this world fathoms with wisdom the moon’s radiance and the sun’s radiance, through meditation free from initial thought, becomes one who goes to the Ābhassara realm.”

Tattha candābhanti odātakasiṇaṃ dasseti. Sūriyābhanti pītakasiṇaṃ. Yodha paññāya gādhatīti yo puggalo idha sattaloke idaṃ kasiṇadvayaṃ paññāya gādhati, ārammaṇaṃ katvā anupavisati, tattheva patiṭṭhahati[M 1.0500]. Atha vā candābhaṃ sūriyābhañca, yodha paññāya gādhatīti yattakaṃ [V 1.0453] ṭhānaṃ candābhā ca sūriyābhā ca patthaṭā, tatthake ṭhāne paṭibhāgakasiṇaṃ vaḍḍhetvā taṃ ārammaṇaṃ katvā jhānaṃ nibbattento ubhayampetaṃ ābhaṃ paññāya gādhati nāma. Tasmā ayampettha atthoyeva. Avitakkena jhānena, hoti ābhassarūpagoti so puggalo tathā katvā paṭiladdhena dutiyena jhānena ābhassarabrahmalokūpago hotīti.

Herein, ‘moon-radiance’ indicates the white kasiṇa. ‘Sun-radiance’ indicates the yellow kasiṇa. ‘He who in this world fathoms with wisdom’ means a person who, here in this world of beings, fathoms this pair of kasiṇas with wisdom, making them his object, entering into them, and becoming established right there. Alternatively, ‘the moon’s radiance and the sun’s radiance, he who in this world fathoms with wisdom’ means that, having expanded the counterpart sign over as much space as the radiance of the moon and the sun are spread, and having made that the object while producing jhāna, one is said to fathom both these radiances with wisdom. Therefore, this too is the meaning here. ‘Through meditation free from initial thought, becomes one who goes to the Ābhassara realm’ means that person, having done so, through the second jhāna which he has attained, becomes one who goes to the Ābhassara Brahmā world.

Evaṃ bodhisatto tāpase bodhetvā jeṭṭhantevāsikassa guṇaṃ kathetvā brahmalokameva gato.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having caused the ascetics to understand and having spoken of the virtues of the chief disciple, went to the Brahma world itself.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jeṭṭhantevāsiko sāriputto, mahābrahmā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying: “At that time the senior disciple was Sāriputta, and the Great Brahmā was I myself.”

Candābhajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The fifth, the Commentary on the Candābha Jātaka.

[136] 6. Suvaṇṇahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā

[136] 6. The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇahaṃsa Jātaka

Yaṃ laddhaṃ tena tuṭṭhabbanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto thullanandaṃ bhikkhuniṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi aññataro upāsako bhikkhunisaṅghaṃ lasuṇena pavāretvā khettapālaṃ āṇāpesi “sace bhikkhuniyo āgacchanti, ekekāya bhikkhuniyā dve tayo bhaṇḍike dehī”ti. Tato paṭṭhāya bhikkhuniyo tassa gehampi [P 1.0475] khettampi lasuṇatthāya gacchanti. Athekasmiṃ ussavadivase tassa gehe lasuṇaṃ parikkhayaṃ agamāsi. Thullanandā bhikkhunī saparivārā gehaṃ gantvā “lasuṇenāvuso attho”ti vatvā “natthayye, yathābhataṃ lasuṇaṃ parikkhīṇaṃ, khettaṃ gacchathā”ti vuttā khettaṃ gantvā na mattaṃ jānitvā lasuṇaṃ āharāpesi. Khettapālo ujjhāyi “kathañhi nāma bhikkhuniyo na mattaṃ jānitvā lasuṇaṃ harāpessantī”ti? Tassa kathaṃ sutvā yā tā bhikkhuniyo appicchā, tāpi, tāsaṃ sutvā bhikkhūpi, ujjhāyiṃsu. Ujjhāyitvā ca pana bhagavato etamatthaṃ ārocesuṃ. Bhagavā thullanandaṃ bhikkhaniṃ garahitvā “bhikkhave, mahiccho puggalo nāma vijātamātuyāpi appiyo hoti amanāpo, appasanne pasādetuṃ, pasannānaṃ vā bhiyyosomattāya pasādaṃ janetuṃ, anuppannaṃ vā lābhaṃ uppādetuṃ, uppannaṃ vā [M 1.0501] pana lābhaṃ thiraṃ kātuṃ na sakkoti. Appiccho pana puggalo appasanne pasādetuṃ, pasannānaṃ vā bhiyyosomattāya pasādaṃ janetuṃ, anuppannaṃ vā lābhaṃ uppādetuṃ, uppannaṃ vā pana lābhaṃ thiraṃ kātuṃ sakkotī”tiādinā nayena bhikkhūnaṃ tadanucchavikaṃ [V 1.0454] dhammaṃ kathetvā “na, bhikkhave, thullanandā idāneva mahicchā, pubbepi mahicchāyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher related this, 'One should be content with what is obtained,' concerning the bhikkhunī Thullanandā, while dwelling at Jetavana. In Sāvatthī, a certain lay follower, having invited the community of bhikkhunīs for garlic, instructed the field-keeper: 'If the bhikkhunīs come, give two or three portions to each bhikkhunī.' From then on, the bhikkhunīs went to his house and field for garlic. Then, on a certain festival day, the garlic in his house was exhausted. The bhikkhunī Thullanandā, along with her retinue, went to the house and said, 'Friend, we need garlic.' Told, 'There is none, venerable lady, the garlic that was brought is exhausted; go to the field,' they went to the field and, not knowing the measure, had garlic brought. The field-keeper complained, 'How can the bhikkhunīs have garlic brought without knowing the measure?' Hearing his words, even those bhikkhunīs of few desires complained, and hearing them, the bhikkhus also complained. And having complained, they reported this matter to the Blessed One. The Blessed One rebuked the bhikkhunī Thullanandā and said, 'Bhikkhus, a person of great desires is disliked and unpleasant even to the mother who bore them. They are unable to inspire faith in the faithless, to increase the faith of the faithful, to generate unarisen gains, or to secure arisen gains. But a person of few desires is able to inspire faith in the faithless, to increase the faith of the faithful, to generate unarisen gains, or to secure arisen gains.' In this way, he delivered a Dhamma talk suitable to the occasion to the bhikkhus and said, 'Bhikkhus, Thullanandā is not greedy only now; she was greedy in the past as well.' So saying, he related a past event.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto aññatarasmiṃ brāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Tassa vayappattassa samānajātikā kulā pajāpatiṃ āhariṃsu. Tassā nandā nandāvatī sundarīnandāti tisso dhītaro ahesuṃ. Tāsu patikulaṃ agatāsuyeva bodhisatto kālaṃ katvā suvaṇṇahaṃsayoniyaṃ nibbatti, jātissarañāṇañcassa uppajji. So vayappatto suvaṇṇasañchannaṃ sobhaggappattaṃ mahantaṃ attabhāvaṃ disvā “kuto nu kho cavitvā ahaṃ idhūpapanno”ti āvajjento “manussalokato”ti ñatvā puna “kathaṃ nu kho me brāhmaṇī ca dhītaro ca jīvantī”ti upadhārento “paresaṃ bhatiṃ katvā kicchena jīvantī”ti ñatvā cintesi “mayhaṃ sarīre sovaṇṇamayāni pattāni koṭṭanaghaṭṭanakhamāni, ito tāsaṃ ekekaṃ pattaṃ dassāmi, tena me pajāpati ca dhītaro ca sukhaṃ jīvissantī”ti. So tattha gantvā piṭṭhivaṃsakoṭiyaṃ nilīyi, brāhmaṇī ca dhītaro ca bodhisattaṃ disvā “kuto [P 1.0476] āgatosi, sāmī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Ahaṃ tumhākaṃ pitā kālaṃ katvā suvaṇṇahaṃsayoniyaṃ nibbatto tumhe daṭṭhuṃ āgato. Ito paṭṭhāya tumhākaṃ paresaṃ bhatiṃ katvā dukkhajīvikāya jīvanakiccaṃ natthi, ahaṃ vo ekekaṃ pattaṃ dassāmi, taṃ vikkiṇitvā sukhena jīvathā”ti ekaṃ pattaṃ datvā agamāsi. So eteneva niyāmena antarantarā āgantvā ekekaṃ pattaṃ deti, brāhmaṇī ca dhītaro ca aḍḍhā sukhitā ahesuṃ.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born in a certain brahmin family. When he came of age, relatives brought him a wife from a family of equal status. They had three daughters named Nandā, Nandāvatī, and Sundarīnandā. While they had not yet gone to their husbands' families, the Bodhisatta passed away and was reborn as a golden swan, and the knowledge of his past existences arose in him. When he reached maturity, seeing his great body, covered in gold, endowed with beauty, he reflected, 'From where have I passed away and been reborn here?' Realizing, 'From the human world,' he further pondered, 'How are my brahmin wife and daughters living?' Realizing, 'They are struggling to survive by serving others,' he thought, 'My body has golden feathers that can endure striking and scraping. I will give them one feather at a time; with that, my wife and daughters will live comfortably.' He went there and perched on the ridge-pole. The brahmin woman and her daughters, seeing the Bodhisatta, asked, 'From where have you come, master?' He replied, 'I am your father, who passed away and was reborn as a golden swan. I have come to see you. From now on, you have no need to live a life of hardship by serving others. I will give you one feather at a time; sell it and live happily.' Giving them one feather, he departed. In this way, he returned from time to time, giving them one feather each time. The brahmin woman and her daughters became wealthy and happy.

Athekadivasaṃ sā brāhmaṇī dhītaro āmantesi “ammā, tiracchānānaṃ nāma cittaṃ dujjānaṃ. Kadāci vo pitā idha nāgaccheyya, idānissa āgatakāle sabbāni pattānipi luñcitvā gaṇhāmā”ti. Tā “evaṃ no pitā kilamissatī”ti na sampaṭicchiṃsu. Brāhmaṇī pana mahicchatāya puna ekadivasaṃ suvaṇṇahaṃsarājassa āgatakāle “ehi tāva, sāmī”ti vatvā taṃ attano santikaṃ upagataṃ ubhohi hatthehi gahetvā [M 1.0502] sabbapattāni luñci. Tāni pana bodhisattassa ruciṃ vinā balakkārena gahitattā sabbāni bakapattasadisāni ahesuṃ. Bodhisatto pakkhe pasāretvā gantuṃ nāsakkhi. Atha naṃ sā mahācāṭiyaṃ pakkhipitvā posesi. Tassa puna uṭṭhahantāni pattāni setāni sampajjiṃsu. So sañjātapatto uppatitvā attano vasanaṭṭhānameva gantvā na puna āgamāsi.

Then one day, the brahmin woman addressed her daughters: 'Dear ones, the minds of animals are hard to understand. Perhaps your father might not come here again; now, when he comes, let us pluck all his feathers and take them.' They replied, 'Thus our father would be distressed,' and did not agree. However, driven by great desire, the brahmin woman again one day, when the golden swan king arrived, said, 'Come here, master,' and as he approached her, she grabbed him with both hands and plucked all his feathers. But because they had been taken by force, without the Bodhisatta's consent, all of them became like heron's feathers. The Bodhisatta was unable to spread his wings and fly. Then she put him into a large pot and nourished him. When his feathers grew back again, they became white. Having regrown his feathers, he flew up and went to his own dwelling place, and did not come again.

Satthā imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, thullanandā idāneva mahicchā, pubbepi mahicchāyeva[V 1.0455], mahicchatāya ca pana suvaṇṇamhā parihīnā. Idāni pana attano mahicchatāya eva lasuṇamhāpi parihāyissati, tasmā ito paṭṭhāya lasuṇaṃ khādituṃ na labhissati. Yathā ca thullanandā, evaṃ taṃ nissāya sesabhikkhuniyopi. Tasmā bahuṃ labhitvāpi pamāṇameva jānitabbaṃ, appaṃ labhitvā pana yathāladdheneva santoso kātabbo, uttari na patthetabba”nti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having related this past event, said, 'Bhikkhus, Thullanandā is not greedy only now; she was greedy in the past as well. And due to her greed, she was deprived of gold. Now, because of her own greed, she will also lose garlic. Therefore, from now on, she will not be allowed to eat garlic. And just as Thullanandā, so too the other bhikkhunīs who rely on her. Therefore, even having gained much, the measure should be known; but having gained little, contentment should be practiced with what is obtained, and more should not be desired.' So saying, he spoke this verse:

136.

136.

“Yaṃ laddhaṃ tena tuṭṭhabbaṃ, atilobho hi pāpako;

Haṃsarājaṃ gahetvāna, suvaṇṇā parihāyathā”ti.

'One should be content with what has been obtained, for excessive greed is indeed evil; having seized the king of swans, you were deprived of gold.'

Tattha tuṭṭhabbanti tussitabbaṃ.

Here, 'tuṭṭhabbaṃ' means 'one should be satisfied.'

Idaṃ pana vatvā satthā anekapariyāyena garahitvā “yā pana bhikkhunī lasuṇaṃ khādeyya, pācittiya”nti (pāci. 794) sikkhāpadaṃ paññāpetvā jātakaṃ [P 1.0477] samodhānesi – “tadā brāhmaṇī ayaṃ thullanandā ahosi, tisso dhītaro idāni tissoyeva bhaginiyo, suvaṇṇahaṃsarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having said this, the Teacher, having rebuked her in various ways, then laid down the training rule: 'Whatever bhikkhunī should eat garlic, there is an offense of pācittiya.' He then identified the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the brahmin woman was this Thullanandā; the three daughters are now these same three sisters; and the golden goose-king was indeed myself.'

Suvaṇṇahaṃsajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Suvaṇṇahaṃsa Jātaka, the Sixth.

[137] 7. Babbujātakavaṇṇanā

[137] 7. The Commentary on the Babbu Jātaka

Yattheko labhate babbūti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kāṇamātusikkhāpadaṃ (pāci. 230 ādayo) ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyañhi kāṇamātā nāma [M 1.0503] dhītuvasena pākaṭanāmā upāsikā ahosi sotāpannā ariyasāvikā. Sā dhītaraṃ kāṇaṃ aññatarasmiṃ gāmake samānajātikassa purisassa adāsi. Kāṇā kenacideva karaṇīyena mātu gharaṃ agamāsi. Athassā sāmiko katipāhaccayena dūtaṃ pāhesi “āgacchatu kāṇā, icchāmi kāṇāya āgamana”nti. Kāṇā dūtassa vacanaṃ sutvā “amma, gamissāmī”ti mātaraṃ āpucchi. Kāṇamātā “ettakaṃ kālaṃ vasitvā kathaṃ tucchahatthāva gamissasī”ti pūvaṃ paci. Tasmiṃyeva khaṇe eko piṇḍacāriko bhikkhu tassā nivesanaṃ agamāsi, upāsikā taṃ nisīdāpetvā pattapūraṃ pūvaṃ dāpesi. So bhikkhu nikkhamitvā aññassa ācikkhi, tassapi tatheva dāpesi. Sopi nikkhamitvā aññassa ācikkhi, tassapi tathevāti evaṃ catunnaṃ janānaṃ dāpesi[V 1.0456]. Yathāpaṭiyattaṃ pūvaṃ parikkhayaṃ agamāsi, kāṇāya gamanaṃ na sampajji. Athassā sāmiko dutiyampi, tatiyampi dūtaṃ pāhesi. Tatiyaṃ pāhento ca “sace kāṇā nāgacchissati, ahaṃ aññaṃ pajāpatiṃ ānessāmī”ti pāhesi. Tayopi vāre teneva upāyena gamanaṃ na sampajji, kāṇāya sāmiko aññaṃ pajāpatiṃ ānesi. Kāṇā taṃ pavattiṃ sutvā rodamānā aṭṭhāsi.

'Where one obtains a babbu...' This the Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke concerning the training rule regarding Kāṇamātā. In Sāvatthī, there was a laywoman named Kāṇamātā, well-known by her daughter's name, a stream-enterer, a noble disciple. She gave her daughter, Kāṇā, to a man of equal birth in a certain small village. Kāṇā went to her mother's house for some reason. Then, after a few days, her husband sent a messenger, saying, 'Let Kāṇā come; I desire Kāṇā's coming.' Kāṇā, hearing the messenger's words, asked her mother, 'Mother, I will go.' Kāṇamātā replied, 'After staying so long, how can you go empty-handed?' and she fried some cakes. At that very moment, a bhikkhu on his alms round arrived at her house. The laywoman had him seated and had a bowlful of cakes given to him. That bhikkhu left and told another, and to him too she had them given in the same way. He too left and told another, and to him too in the same way. Thus she had them given to four people. The cakes that had been prepared were exhausted, and Kāṇā's departure did not take place. Then her husband sent a messenger a second time, and a third time. When sending the third messenger, he sent the message: 'If Kāṇā does not come, I will bring another wife.' On all three occasions, her departure did not take place by the same means, and Kāṇā's husband brought another wife. Kāṇā, hearing that news, stood weeping.

Satthā taṃ kāraṇaṃ ñatvā pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā pattacīvaramādāya kāṇamātāya nivesanaṃ gantvā paññattāsane nisīditvā kāṇamātaraṃ pucchi “kissāyaṃ kāṇā rodatī”ti? “Iminā nāma kāraṇenā”ti ca sutvā kāṇamātaraṃ samassāsetvā dhammiṃ kathaṃ kathetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ agamāsi. Atha tesaṃ catunnaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ tayo vāre yathāpaṭiyattapūvaṃ gahetvā kāṇāya gamanassa upacchinnabhāvo bhikkhusaṅghe pākaṭo jāto. Athekadivasaṃ bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, catūhi nāma bhikkhūhi tayo vāre kāṇamātāya pakkapūvaṃ khāditvā kāṇāya gamanantarāyaṃ katvā sāmikena pariccattaṃ dhītaraṃ nissāya mahāupāsikāya domanassaṃ uppādita”nti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya [P 1.0478] sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idāneva te cattāro bhikkhū kāṇamātāya santakaṃ khāditvā tassā domanassaṃ uppādesuṃ, pubbepi uppādesuṃyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, knowing the reason, having dressed in the morning, taking his bowl and robe, went to Kāṇamātā’s dwelling, sat on the prepared seat, and asked Kāṇamātā, “Why is this Kāṇā crying?” Hearing the reason, he consoled Kāṇamātā, gave a Dhamma talk, rose from his seat, and returned to the monastery. Then, the fact that those four monks had taken the prepared cakes three times, thereby cutting off Kāṇā’s journey, became known among the Saṅgha of monks. One day, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, four monks, having eaten the cooked cakes from Kāṇamātā three times, created an obstacle to Kāṇā’s journey and thereby caused distress to the great laywoman on account of her daughter, who was abandoned by her husband.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?” When they told him, he said, “Monks, it is not only now that these four monks have eaten what belonged to Kāṇamātā and caused her distress; they did so in the past as well.” Then he related a past incident.

Atīte [M 1.0504] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto pāsāṇakoṭṭakakule nibbattitvā vayappatto pariyodātasippo ahosi. Kāsiraṭṭhe ekasmiṃ nigame eko mahāvibhavo seṭṭhi ahosi, tassa nidhānagatāyeva cattālīsa hiraññakoṭiyo ahesuṃ. Athassa bhariyā kālaṃ katvā dhanasinehena gantvā dhanapiṭṭhiyaṃ mūsikā hutvā nibbatti. Evaṃ anukkamena sabbampi taṃ kulaṃ abbhatthaṃ agamāsi, vaṃso upacchijji. So gāmopi chaḍḍito apaṇṇattikabhāvaṃ agamāsi. Tadā bodhisatto tasmiṃ purāṇagāmaṭṭhāne pāsāṇe uppāṭetvā koṭṭeti. Atha sā mūsikā gocarāya caramānā bodhisattaṃ punappunaṃ passantī uppannasinehā hutvā cintesi “mayhaṃ dhanaṃ bahu nikkāraṇena nassissati, iminā saddhiṃ ekato hutvā idaṃ dhanaṃ datvā maṃsaṃ vikkiṇāpetvā khādissāmī”ti. Sā ekadivasaṃ ekaṃ kahāpaṇaṃ mukhena ḍaṃsitvā bodhisattassa santikaṃ agamāsi. So taṃ disvā piyavācāya samālapanto “kiṃ nu kho, amma, kahāpaṇaṃ gahetvā āgatāsī”ti āha. Tāta, imaṃ gahetvā attanāpi paribhuñja, mayhampi maṃsaṃ āharāti. So “sādhū”ti sampaṭicchitvā kahāpaṇaṃ ādāya gharaṃ gantvā ekena māsakena maṃsaṃ [V 1.0457] kiṇitvā āharitvā tassā adāsi. Sā taṃ gahetvā attano nivāsaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā yathāruciyā khādi. Tato paṭṭhāya imināva niyāmena divase divase bodhisattassa kahāpaṇaṃ deti, sopissā maṃsaṃ āharati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a family of stonecutters and, having come of age, became highly skilled in his craft. In a certain town in the Kāsī country, there was a very wealthy merchant who had forty crores of gold buried away. Then his wife passed away and, due to her attachment to wealth, was reborn as a mouse on top of the treasure. Thus, gradually, the entire family perished, and their lineage came to an end. That village too was abandoned and fell into obscurity. At that time, the Bodhisatta was quarrying and cutting stones in the old village site. Now, that mouse, while foraging for food, repeatedly saw the Bodhisatta and, feeling affection for him, thought: “My wealth is vast and will be lost for no reason. I will join with this man, give him this wealth, have him buy meat, and I shall eat.” One day, she took a kahāpaṇa coin in her mouth and went to the Bodhisatta. Seeing her, he spoke affectionately, saying, “Why, mother, have you come bringing a kahāpaṇa coin?” “Dear sir, take this and use it for yourself, and also bring me some meat,” she said. He replied, “Very well,” accepted the kahāpaṇa, went home, bought meat with one māsaka, and brought it to her. She took it, went to her dwelling place, and ate as she pleased. From then on, in this same way, day after day she gave the Bodhisatta a kahāpaṇa, and he in turn brought her meat.

Athekadivasaṃ taṃ mūsikaṃ biḷāro aggahesi. Atha naṃ sā evamāha “mā, samma, maṃ māresī”ti. Kiṃkāraṇā na māressāmi? Ahañhi chāto maṃsaṃ khāditukāmo, na sakkā mayā na māretunti. Kiṃ pana ekadivasameva maṃsaṃ khāditukāmosi, udāhu niccakālanti? “Labhamāno niccakālampi khāditukāmomhī”ti. “Yadi evaṃ ahaṃ te niccakālaṃ maṃsaṃ dassāmi, vissajjehi [P 1.0479] ma”nti. Atha naṃ biḷāro “tena hi appamattā hohī”ti vissajjesi. Tato paṭṭhāya sā attano ābhataṃ maṃsaṃ dve koṭṭhāse katvā ekaṃ biḷārassa deti, ekaṃ sayaṃ khādati. Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ aññopi biḷāro aggahesi, tampi tatheva saññāpetvā attānaṃ vissajjāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya tayo koṭṭhāse katvā khādanti. Puna añño aggahesi, tampi tatheva saññāpetvā [M 1.0505] attānaṃ mocāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya cattāro koṭṭhāse katvā khādanti. Puna añño aggahesi, tampi tatheva saññāpetvā attānaṃ mocāpesi. Tato paṭṭhāya pañca koṭṭhāse katvā khādanti. Sā pañcamaṃ koṭṭhāsaṃ khādamānā appāhāratāya kilantā kisā ahosi appamaṃsalohitā

One day, a cat caught that mouse. Then she said to him, “Friend, do not kill me.” “For what reason should I not kill you? I am hungry and wish to eat meat; I cannot refrain from killing you.” “But do you wish to eat meat just for one day, or always?” “If I can get it, I wish to eat always.” “If so, I will give you meat always; release me.” Then the cat said, “Very well, be heedful,” and let her go. From then on, she divided the meat she brought into two portions, giving one to the cat and eating one herself. Then one day another cat caught her, and she persuaded him in the same way and got herself released. From then on, they divided the meat into three portions and ate. Again, another cat caught her, and she persuaded him likewise and freed herself. From then on, they divided the meat into four portions and ate. Yet another cat caught her, and she persuaded him in the same way and freed herself. From then on, they divided the meat into five portions and ate. While eating the fifth portion, she grew weary from lack of nourishment, became thin, and had little flesh and blood.

Bodhisatto taṃ disvā “amma, kasmā milātāsī”ti vatvā “iminā nāma kāraṇenā”ti vutte “tvaṃ ettakaṃ kālaṃ kasmā mayhaṃ nācikkhi, ahamettha kātabbaṃ jānissāmī”ti taṃ samassāsetvā suddhaphalikapāsāṇena guhaṃ katvā āharitvā “amma, tvaṃ imaṃ guhaṃ pavisitvā nipajjitvā āgatāgatānaṃ pharusāhi vācāhi santajjeyyāsī”ti āha. Sā guhaṃ pavisitvā nipajji. Atheko biḷāro āgantvā “dehi, ajja me maṃsa”nti āha. Atha naṃ mūsikā “are, duṭṭhabiḷāra, kiṃ te ahaṃ maṃsahārikā, attano puttānaṃ maṃsaṃ khādā”ti tajjesi. Biḷāro phalikaguhāya nipannabhāvaṃ ajānanto kodhavasena mūsikaṃ gaṇhissāmī”ti sahasāva pakkhanditvā hadayena phalikaguhāyaṃ pahari. Tāvadevassa hadayaṃ bhijji, akkhīni nikkhamanākārappattāni jātāni. So tattheva jīvitakkhayaṃ patvā ekamantaṃ paṭicchannaṭṭhāne pati. Etenūpāyena aparopi aparopīti cattāropi janā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpuṇiṃsu. Tato paṭṭhāya mūsikā nibbhayā hutvā bodhisattassa devasikaṃ dve tayo kahāpaṇe deti. Evaṃ anukkamena sabbampi dhanaṃ bodhisattasseva adāsi. Te ubhopi yāvajīvaṃ mettiṃ abhinditvā yathākammaṃ gatā.

Seeing this, the Bodhisatta asked, “Mother, why are you wilting?” When she replied, “Because of this reason,” he said, “Why did you not tell me all this time? I would have known what to do.” After comforting her, he made a cave out of pure crystal rock and brought it to her, saying, “Mother, enter this cave, lie down, and threaten those who come with harsh words.” She entered the cave and lay down. Then a cat came and demanded, “Give me meat today!” The mouse scolded him, “Hey, wicked cat! Am I a meat-provider for you? Eat the flesh of your own offspring!” Unaware that she was lying in the crystal cave, the cat, driven by anger, thought, “I will catch the mouse!” and suddenly lunged, striking his chest against the crystal cave. Instantly, his heart shattered, and his eyes looked as if they would pop out. He died right there, falling in a hidden spot. By this method, one after another, all four cats met their end. From then on, the mouse lived without fear and gave the Bodhisatta two or three coins daily. Gradually, she gave all her wealth to the Bodhisatta. Both of them maintained their friendship unbroken for life and passed away according to their deeds.

Satthā [V 1.0458] imaṃ atītaṃ āharitvā abhisambuddho hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Teacher, having related this past incident, as one fully enlightened, spoke this verse:

137.

137.

“Yattheko [P 1.0480] labhate babbu, dutiyo tattha jāyati;

Tatiyo ca catuttho ca, idaṃ te babbukā bila”nti.

“Where one cat obtains, a second arises there; a third and a fourth. This is your hole, O cats!”

Tattha yatthāti yasmiṃ ṭhāne. Babbūti biḷāro. Dutiyo tattha jāyatīti yattha eko mūsikaṃ vā maṃsaṃ vā labhati, dutiyopi tattha biḷāro jāyati uppajjati, tathā tatiyo ca catuttho ca. Evaṃ te tadā cattāro biḷārā ahesuṃ. Hutvā ca pana divase divase maṃsaṃ khādantā te babbukā idaṃ phalikamayaṃ bilaṃ urena paharitvā sabbepi jīvitakkhayaṃ pattāti.

Therein, ‘where’ means in which place. ‘Cat’ means a wild cat. ‘A second arises there’ means where one finds a mouse or meat, a second cat also arises there, and similarly a third and a fourth. Thus, at that time, there were four cats. And then, eating meat day by day, those cats, striking this crystal cave with their chests, all met the end of their lives.

Evaṃ [M 1.0506] satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā cattāro biḷārā cattāro bhikkhū ahesuṃ, mūsikā kāṇamātā, pāsāṇakoṭṭakamaṇikāro pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Thus the Teacher, having delivered this discourse on the Dhamma, connected the Jātaka: “At that time, the four cats were the four monks, the mouse was Kāṇamātā, and the stone-carving jeweller was none other than myself.”

Babbujātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Babbu Jātaka is the seventh.

[138] 8. Godhājātakavaṇṇanā

[138] 8. The Commentary on the Godha Jātaka

Kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedhāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ kuhakabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu heṭṭhā kathitasadisameva.

“What use are your matted locks, O fool?” This the Teacher uttered while dwelling in Jetavana, concerning a deceitful monk. The present story is just like the one told before.

Atīte pana bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto godhāyoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. Tadā eko pañcābhiñño uggatapo tāpaso ekaṃ paccantagāmaṃ nissāya araññāyatane paṇṇasālāyaṃ vasati, gāmavāsino tāpasaṃ sakkaccaṃ upaṭṭhahanti. Bodhisatto tassa caṅkamanakoṭiyaṃ ekasmiṃ vammike vasati, vasanto ca pana divase divase dve tayo vāre tāpasaṃ upasaṅkamitvā dhammūpasaṃhitaṃ atthūpasaṃhitañca vacanaṃ sutvā tāpasaṃ vanditvā vasanaṭṭhānameva gacchati. Aparabhāge tāpaso gāmavāsino āpucchitvā pakkāmi. Pakkamante ca pana tasmiṃ sīlavatasampanne tāpase añño kūṭatāpaso āgantvā tasmiṃ assamapade vāsaṃ kappesi. Bodhisatto “ayampi sīlavā”ti sallakkhetvā purimanayeneva tassa santikaṃ agamāsi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a monitor lizard. At that time, a certain ascetic with the five higher knowledges and of intense austerity lived in a leaf hut in a forest hermitage, depending on a border village. The villagers respectfully attended to the ascetic. The Bodhisatta lived in an anthill at the end of his walking path. While living there, he would approach the ascetic two or three times a day, listen to words connected with the Dhamma and its meaning, pay homage to the ascetic, and then return to his dwelling place. Later, the ascetic took leave of the villagers and departed. After that virtuous and accomplished ascetic had left, another deceitful ascetic arrived and took up residence in that hermitage. The Bodhisatta, thinking, “This one too is virtuous,” approached him in the same manner as before.

Athekadivasaṃ [V 1.0459] nidāghasamaye akālameghe vuṭṭhe vammikehi makkhikā nikkhamiṃsu, tāsaṃ khādanatthaṃ godhā āhiṇḍiṃsu. Gāmavāsino nikkhamitvā makkhikākhādakā godhā [P 1.0481] gahetvā siniddhasambhārasaṃyuttaṃ ambilānambilaṃ godhāmaṃsaṃ sampādetvā tāpasassa adaṃsu. Tāpaso godhāmaṃsaṃ khāditvā rasataṇhāya baddho “idaṃ maṃsaṃ atimadhuraṃ, kissa maṃsaṃ nāmeta”nti pucchitvā “godhāmaṃsa”nti sutvā “mama santikaṃ mahāgodhā āgacchati, taṃ māretvā maṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti cintesi. Cintetvā ca pana bhājanañca sappiloṇādīni ca āharāpetvā ekamante ṭhapetvā muggaramādāya kāsāvena paṭicchādetvā paṇṇasālādvāre bodhisattassa āgamanaṃ olokayamāno upasantūpasanto viya hutvā nisīdi [M 1.0507] bodhisatto sāyanhasamaye “tāpasassa santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti nikkhamitvā upasaṅkamantova tassa indriyavippakāraṃ disvā cintesi “nāyaṃ tāpaso aññesu divasesu nisīdanākārena nisinno, ajjesa maṃ olokentopi duṭṭhindriyo hutvā oloketi, pariggaṇhissāmi na”nti. So tāpasassa heṭṭhāvāte ṭhatvā godhāmaṃsagandhaṃ ghāyitvā “iminā kūṭatāpasena ajja godhāmaṃsaṃ khāditaṃ bhavissati, tenesa rasataṇhāya baddho ajja maṃ attano santikaṃ upasaṅkamantaṃ muggarena paharitvā maṃsaṃ pacitvā khāditukāmo bhavissatī”ti tassa santikaṃ anupagantvāva paṭikkamitvā vicarati.

One day during the hot season, when an unseasonal rain fell, flies emerged from their anthills. Monitor lizards wandered about to eat them. The villagers came out, caught the fly-eating monitor lizards, and prepared a dish of sour and savory monitor lizard meat with rich ingredients, which they offered to the ascetic. Having eaten the monitor lizard meat, the ascetic became bound by craving for its taste. "This meat is extremely delicious—what kind of meat is it?" he asked. Upon hearing it was monitor lizard meat, he thought, "A large monitor lizard comes near me. I will kill it and eat its meat." After this thought, he had a pot, ghee, salt, and other things brought and set aside. Taking a club, he covered it with his ochre robe and sat at the door of his leaf hut, watching for the Bodhisatta’s arrival, appearing perfectly calm. In the evening, the Bodhisatta thought, "I will go to the ascetic," and set out. As he approached, he noticed the derangement of the ascetic's faculties and reflected, "This ascetic is not sitting in his usual manner today. Even as he watches me, his faculties are corrupted. I shall investigate him." Standing downwind, he caught the scent of monitor lizard meat and realized, "This deceitful ascetic must have eaten monitor lizard meat today. Bound by craving for its taste, he now intends to strike me with a club as I approach him, then cook my flesh and eat it." Without approaching him, he turned back and went on his way.

Tāpaso bodhisattassa anāgamanabhāvaṃ ñatvā “iminā ‘ayaṃ maṃ paharitukāmo’ti ñātaṃ bhavissati, tena kāraṇena nāgacchati, anāgacchantassāpissa kuto muttī”ti muggaraṃ nīharitvā khipi. So tassa agganaṅguṭṭhameva āsādesi. Bodhisatto vegena vammikaṃ pavisitvā aññena chiddena sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā “ambho kūṭajaṭila, ahaṃ tava santikaṃ upasaṅkamanto ‘sīlavā’ti saññāya upasaṅkamiṃ, idāni pana te mayā kūṭabhāvo ñāto, tādisassa mahācorassa kiṃ iminā pabbajjāliṅgenā”ti vatvā taṃ garahanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

The ascetic, knowing that the Bodhisatta was not coming, thought, "He must have realized that I intend to strike him. For that reason, he does not come. But even if he does not come, how can he escape?" He took out the club and threw it. It struck only the tip of the Bodhisatta's tail. The Bodhisatta quickly entered the anthill and, raising his head through another opening, said, "O deceitful matted-hair ascetic, when I approached you, I did so with the perception that you were virtuous. But now your deceitful nature is known to me. What use is this outward sign of renunciation to such a great thief?" Rebuking him, he spoke this verse:

138.

138.

“Kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedha, kiṃ te ajinasāṭiyā;

Abbhantaraṃ te gahanaṃ, bāhiraṃ parimajjasī”ti.

"What use are your matted locks to you, O fool? What use is your antelope-hide garment? Within, you are a tangled thicket, while you polish the exterior."

Tattha [P 1.0482] kiṃ te jaṭāhi dummedhāti ambho dummedha, nippañña etā pabbajitena dhāretabbā jaṭā, pabbajjāguṇarahitassa kiṃ te tāhi jaṭāhīti attho. Kiṃ te ajinasāṭiyāti ajinasāṭiyā anucchavikassa saṃvarassa abhāvakālato paṭṭhāya kiṃ te ajinasāṭiyā. Abbhantaraṃ te gahananti tava abbhantaraṃ hadayaṃ rāgadosamohagahanena gahanaṃ paṭicchannaṃ. Bāhiraṃ parimajjasīti so tvaṃ abbhantare gahane nhānādīhi ceva liṅgagahanena ca bāhiraṃ parimajjasi, taṃ [V 1.0460] parimajjanto kañjikapūritalābu viya visapūritacāṭi viya āsīvisapūritavammiko viya gūthapūritacittaghaṭo viya ca bahimaṭṭhova hosi, kiṃ tayā corena idha vasantena, sīghaṃ ito palāyāhi, no [M 1.0508] ce palāyasi, gāmavāsīnaṃ te ācikkhitvā niggahaṃ kārāpessāmīti.

Herein, “What use are your matted locks to you, O fool?” means: O fool, senseless one, these matted locks are to be worn by one who has gone forth. But for you, devoid of the qualities of renunciation, what use are those matted locks to you? “What use is your antelope-hide garment?” means: Since you lack the restraint appropriate to an antelope-hide garment, what use is that antelope-hide garment to you? “Within, you are a tangled thicket” means: Your inner heart is a thicket, overgrown and concealed by the thicket of lust, hatred, and delusion. “While you polish the exterior” means: While your interior is a thicket, you merely polish the outside with bathing and the signs of asceticism. By doing so, you are like a gourd filled with sour gruel, a vessel filled with poison, an anthill infested with vipers, or a painted pot filled with filth—outwardly polished. What is the use of you, a thief, living here? Flee quickly from this place! If you do not flee, I will inform the villagers and have you punished.

Evaṃ bodhisatto kūṭatāpasaṃ tajjetvā vammikameva pāvisi, kūṭatāpasopi tato pakkāmi.

Thus the Bodhisatta, having threatened the deceitful ascetic, entered the anthill, and the deceitful ascetic also departed from there.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kūṭatāpaso ayaṃ kuhako ahosi, purimo sīlavantatāpaso sāriputto, godhāpaṇḍito pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this discourse, the Teacher made the connection for the Jātaka: "At that time, the deceitful ascetic was this fraudulent monk, the virtuous ascetic of old was Sāriputta, and the wise monitor lizard was I myself."

Godhājātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Godha Jātaka, the Eighth.

[139] 9. Ubhatobhaṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā

[139] 9. The Commentary on the Ubhatobhaṭṭha Jātaka

Akkhī bhinnā paṭo naṭṭhoti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā kira dhammasabhāyaṃ bhikkhū kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, seyyathāpi nāma chavālātaṃ ubhatopadittaṃ majjhe gūthagataṃ nevāraññe kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati, na gāme kaṭṭhatthaṃ pharati, evameva devadatto evarūpe niyyānikasāsane pabbajitvā ubhato bhaṭṭho ubhato paribāhiro jāto, gihiparibhogā ca parihīno, sāmaññatthañca na paripūretī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva ubhato bhaṭṭho hoti, atītepi ubhato bhaṭṭho ahosiyevā”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“The eyes are broken, the cloth is lost”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove concerning Devadatta. At that time, it is said, the monks raised a discussion in the Dhamma hall: “Friends, just as a firebrand from a funeral pyre, ignited at both ends and smeared with dung in the middle, serves neither as firewood in the forest nor in the village, so too Devadatta, having gone forth in such a liberating dispensation, is ruined on both sides, excluded from both. He is deprived of a householder's enjoyments and does not fulfill the purpose of the ascetic life.” The Teacher arrived and asked, “Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?” When it was said, “For this one,” he replied, “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta is ruined on both sides; in the past, too, he was ruined on both sides.” And he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto rukkhadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Tadā ekasmiṃ gāmake bāḷisikā vasanti. Atheko bāḷisiko baḷisaṃ ādāya daharena puttena saddhiṃ yasmiṃ sobbhe pakatiyāpi bāḷisikā macche gaṇhanti, tattha gantvā baḷisaṃ khipi. Baḷiso udakapaṭicchanne [P 1.0483] ekasmiṃ khāṇuke laggi. Bāḷisiko taṃ ākaḍḍhituṃ asakkonto cintesi “ayaṃ baḷiso mahāmacche laggo bhavissati, puttakaṃ mātu santikaṃ pesetvā paṭivissakehi saddhiṃ kalahaṃ kārāpemi, evaṃ ito na koci koṭṭhāsaṃ paccāsīsissatī”ti. So puttaṃ āha “gaccha, tāta, amhehi mahāmacchassa laddhabhāvaṃ mātu ācikkhāhi, ‘paṭivissakehi [M 1.0509] kira saddhiṃ kalahaṃ karohī’ti vadehī”ti. So puttaṃ pesetvā baḷisaṃ [V 1.0461] ākaḍḍhituṃ asakkonto rajjucchedanabhayena uttarisāṭakaṃ thale ṭhapetvā udakaṃ otaritvā macchalobhena macchaṃ upadhārento khāṇukehi paharitvā dvepi akkhīni bhindi. Thale ṭhapitasāṭakaṃpissa coro hari. So vedanāppatto hutvā hatthena akkhīni uppīḷayamāno gahetvā udakā uttaritvā kampamāno sāṭakaṃ pariyesati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as a tree deity. At that time, fishermen lived in a certain small village. Then one fisherman, taking his fish-hook, went with his young son to a pond where fishermen usually caught fish, and there he cast his hook. The hook got caught on a submerged stump. Unable to pull it free, the fisherman thought, 'This hook must have caught a huge fish. I will send my son to his mother and have her start a quarrel with the neighbors; in this way, no one will expect a share.' He told his son, 'Go, dear, and tell your mother that we have caught a big fish, and say to her, "Please start a quarrel with the neighbors."' After sending his son away, still unable to retrieve the hook and fearing the line might break, he placed his upper garment on the bank, entered the water, and, while groping for the fish out of greed, he struck against the stump and pierced both his eyes. A thief also stole the garment he had placed on the bank. Overcome with pain, pressing his eyes with his hands, he got out of the water and, trembling, searched for his garment.

Sāpissa bhariyā “kalahaṃ katvā kassaci apaccāsīsanabhāvaṃ karissāmī”ti ekasmiṃyeva kaṇṇe tālapaṇṇaṃ piḷandhitvā ekaṃ akkhiṃ ukkhalimasiyā añjetvā kukkuraṃ aṅkenādāya paṭivissakagharaṃ agamāsi. Atha naṃ ekā sahāyikā evamāha “ekasmiṃyeva te kaṇṇe tālapaṇṇaṃ piḷandhitaṃ, ekaṃ akkhi añjitaṃ, piyaputtaṃ viya kukkuraṃ aṅkenādāya gharato gharaṃ gacchasi, kiṃ ummattikāsi jātā”ti. “Nāhaṃ ummattikā, tvaṃ pana maṃ akāraṇena akkosasi paribhāsasi, idāni taṃ gāmabhojakassa santikaṃ gantvā aṭṭha kahāpaṇe daṇḍāpessāmī”ti evaṃ kalahaṃ katvā ubhopi gāmabhojakassa santikaṃ agamaṃsu. Kalahe visodhiyamāne tassāyeva matthake daṇḍo pati. Atha naṃ bandhitvā “daṇḍaṃ dehī”ti pothetuṃ ārabhiṃsu.

His wife, thinking, 'I will start a quarrel to ensure no one expects a share,' wore a palm leaf on one ear, daubed one eye with pot-soot, took a small dog in her arms, and went to a neighbor's house. Then a female friend said to her, 'You are wearing a palm leaf on only one ear, you have daubed one eye, and you are carrying a small dog in your arms like a beloved child, going from house to house—have you gone mad?' 'I am not mad, but you scold and insult me without reason. Now I will go to the village headman and have you fined eight kahāpaṇas.' Having quarreled thus, both women went to the village headman. When the dispute was judged, the punishment fell upon her own head. Then they bound her and began to beat her, demanding, 'Pay the fine!'

Rukkhadevatā gāme tassā imaṃ pavattiṃ, araññe cassā patino taṃ byasanaṃ disvā khandhantare ṭhitā “bho purisa, tuyhaṃ udakepi kammanto paduṭṭho thalepi, ubhatobhaṭṭho jāto”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The tree deity, having seen this event concerning the wife in the village and the calamity of her husband in the forest, stood in the fork of the tree and said, 'O man, your enterprise has failed both in the water and on land; you have lost out on both sides.' Then she spoke this verse:

139.

139.

“Akkhī bhinnā paṭo naṭṭho, sakhigehe ca bhaṇḍanaṃ;

Ubhato paduṭṭhā kammantā, udakamhi thalamhi cā”ti.

“Your eyes are pierced, your garment is lost, and your wife is quarreling at a friend's house; your enterprises are ruined on both sides, in the water and on the land.”

Tattha [P 1.0484] sakhigehe ca bhaṇḍananti sakhī nāma sahāyikā, tassā ca gehe tava bhariyāya bhaṇḍanaṃ kataṃ, bhaṇḍanaṃ katvā bandhitvā pothetvā daṇḍaṃ dāpiyati. Ubhato paduṭṭhā kammantāti evaṃ tava dvīsupi ṭhānesu kammantā paduṭṭhāyeva bhinnāyeva. Kataresu dvīsu? Udakamhi thalamhi cāti, akkhibhedena paṭanāsena ca udake kammantā paduṭṭhā, sakhigehe bhaṇḍanena thale kammantā paduṭṭhāti.

Herein, 'and at a friend's house, a quarrel' means: a `sakhi` is a female friend, and in her house a quarrel was made by your wife. Having made a quarrel, she is bound, beaten, and made to pay a fine. 'Your enterprises are ruined on both sides' means that in both places your enterprises are indeed ruined, indeed destroyed. In which two? 'In the water and on the land.' By the piercing of your eyes and the loss of your garment, the enterprise in the water is ruined; by the quarrel at the friend's house, the enterprise on the land is ruined.

Satthā [V 1.0462][M 1.0510] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi “tadā bāḷisiko devadatto ahosi, rukkhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the fisherman was Devadatta, and the tree deity was none other than myself.'

Ubhatobhaṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The commentary on the Ubhatobhaṭṭha Jātaka, the ninth.

[140] 10. Kākajātakavaṇṇanā

[140] 10. The Commentary on the Crow Jātaka

Niccaṃ ubbiggahadayāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ñātatthacariyaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu dvādasakanipāte bhaddasālajātake (jā. 1.12.13 ādayo) āvi bhavissati.

'Always with an anxious heart'—this the Teacher related while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning conduct for the benefit of his relatives. The story of the present will become clear in the Bhaddasāla Jātaka in the Book of Twelve.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kākayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Athekadivasaṃ rañño purohito bahinagare nadiyaṃ nhāyitvā gandhe vilimpitvā mālaṃ piḷandhitvā varavatthanivattho nagaraṃ pāvisi. Nagaradvāratoraṇe dve kākā nisinnā honti. Tesu eko ekaṃ āha – “samma, ahaṃ imassa brāhmaṇassa matthake sarīravaḷañjaṃ pātessāmī”ti. Itaro “mā te etaṃ rucci, ayaṃ brāhmaṇo issaro, issarajanena ca saddhiṃ veraṃ nāma pāpakaṃ. Ayañhi kuddho sabbepi kāke vināseyyā”ti. “Na sakkā mayā na kātu”nti. “Tena hi paññāyissasī”ti vatvā itaro kāko palāyi. So toraṇassa heṭṭhābhāgaṃ sampatte brāhmaṇe olambakaṃ cālento viya tassa matthake vaccaṃ pātesi. Brāhmaṇo kujjhitvā kākesu veraṃ bandhi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born into the crow species. One day, the king's chaplain, having bathed in the river outside the city, anointed himself with perfumes, adorned himself with a garland, and, dressed in fine clothes, entered the city. At the archway of the city gate, two crows were perched. One of them said to the other, 'Friend, I am going to drop my excrement on this brahmin's head.' The other replied, 'Do not let this please you; this brahmin is a man of power, and enmity with the powerful is a wicked thing. If angered, he could destroy all the crows.' 'I cannot refrain from doing it.' 'In that case, you will find out what happens,' said the other crow, and flew away. As the brahmin reached the space beneath the archway, the crow, as if shaking loose something hanging down, dropped its excrement on his head. The brahmin, enraged, conceived a hatred for all crows.

Tasmiṃ kāle ekā bhatiyā vīhikoṭṭikadāsī vīhiṃ gehadvāre ātape pattharitvā rakkhantī nisinnāva niddaṃ okkami. Tassā pamādaṃ ñatvā eko dīghalomako eḷako āgantvā vīhiṃ khādi, sā pabujjhitvā taṃ disvā palāpesi. Eḷako dutiyampi, tatiyampi tassā tatheva niddāyanakāle āgantvā vīhiṃ khādi. Sāpi [P 1.0485] taṃ tikkhattuṃ palāpetvā cintesi “ayaṃ punappunaṃ khādanto upaḍḍhavīhiṃ khādissati, bahu me chedo bhavissati, idānissa puna anāgamanakāraṇaṃ karissāmī”ti. Sā alātaṃ gahetvā niddāyamānā viya nisīditvā vīhikhādanatthāya eḷake sampatte uṭṭhāya alātena [M 1.0511] eḷakaṃ pahari, lomāni aggiṃ gaṇhiṃsu. So sarīre jhāyante “aggiṃ nibbāpessāmī”ti vegena gantvā hatthisālāya samīpe ekissā tiṇakuṭiyā sarīraṃ ghaṃsi, sā pajjali. Tato uṭṭhitā jālā hatthisālaṃ gaṇhi. Hatthisālāsu jhāyantīsu hatthipiṭṭhāni jhāyiṃsu, bahū hatthī vaṇitasarīrā ahesuṃ. Vejjā hatthī aroge kātuṃ asakkontā [V 1.0463] rañño ārocesuṃ. Rājā purohitaṃ āha “ācariya, hatthivejjā hatthī tikicchituṃ na sakkonti, api kiñci bhesajjaṃ jānāsī”ti. “Jānāmi, mahārājā”ti. “Kiṃ laddhuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti? “Kākavasā, mahārājā”ti. Rājā “tena hi kāke māretvā vasaṃ āharathā”ti āha. Tato paṭṭhāya kāke māretvā vasaṃ alabhitvā tattha tattheva rāsiṃ karonti, kākānaṃ mahābhayaṃ uppajji.

At that time, a hired female rice-pounder, while guarding the paddy spread out in the sun at the house gate, fell asleep. Seeing her negligence, a long-haired goat came and ate the paddy. Waking up, she saw it and drove it away. The goat came a second and a third time, eating the paddy while she was asleep. After driving it away three times, she thought, 'This one keeps coming back to eat and will consume half the paddy, and I will suffer a great loss. Now I will do something to prevent it from coming again.' Taking a firebrand, she sat as if sleeping. When the goat approached to eat the paddy, she got up and struck it with the firebrand. The goat's fur caught fire. As its body was burning, it thought, 'I must put out this fire!' and quickly ran to a grass hut near the elephant stable, rubbing its body against it. The hut caught fire. The flames that rose from it spread to the elephant stable. As the stables burned, the elephants' backs were scorched, and many elephants suffered burns on their bodies. The veterinarians, unable to heal the elephants, informed the king. The king asked his chaplain, 'Teacher, the elephant doctors cannot treat the elephants. Do you know of any remedy?' 'I do, great king.' 'What is needed?' 'Crow fat, great king.' The king said, 'Then kill crows and bring the fat.' From then on, they killed crows, but obtaining no fat, they made piles of them here and there. Great terror arose among the crows.

Tadā bodhisatto asītikākasahassaparivāro mahāsusāne vasati. Atheko kāko gantvā kākānaṃ uppannabhayaṃ bodhisattassa ārocesi. So cintesi “ṭhapetvā maṃ añño mayhaṃ ñātakānaṃ uppannabhayaṃ harituṃ samattho nāma natthi, harissāmi na”nti dasa pāramiyo āvajjetvā mettāpāramiṃ purecārikaṃ katvā ekavegena pakkhanditvā vivaṭamahāvātapānena pavisitvā rañño āsanassa heṭṭhā pāvisi. Atha naṃ eko manusso gahitukāmo ahosi. Rājā “saraṇaṃ paviṭṭho, mā gaṇhī”ti vāresi. Mahāsatto thokaṃ vissamitvā mettāpāramiṃ āvajjetvā heṭṭhāsanā nikkhamitvā rājānaṃ āha – “mahārāja, raññā nāma chandādivasena agantvā rajjaṃ kāretuṃ vaṭṭati. Yaṃ yaṃ kammaṃ kattabbaṃ hoti, sabbaṃ nisamma upadhāretvā kātuṃ vaṭṭati. Yañca kayiramānaṃ nipphajjati, tadeva kātuṃ vaṭṭati, na itaraṃ. Sace hi rājāno yaṃ kayiramānaṃ na nipphajjati, taṃ karonti, mahājanassa maraṇabhayapariyosānaṃ mahābhayaṃ uppajjati[P 1.0486]. Purohito veravasiko hutvā musāvādaṃ abhāsi, kākānaṃ vasā nāma natthī”ti. Taṃ sutvā rājā pasannacitto bodhisattassa kañcanabhaddapīṭhaṃ dāpetvā tattha nisinnassa pakkhantarāni satapākasahassapākatelehi makkhāpetvā kañcanataṭṭake rājārahaṃ subhojanaṃ bhojāpetvā pānīyaṃ pāyetvā suhitaṃ vigatadarathaṃ mahāsattaṃ etadavoca “paṇḍita, tvaṃ ‘kākānaṃ vasā nāma natthī’ti vadesi, kena kāraṇena nesaṃ vasā na hotī”ti bodhisatto “iminā [M 1.0512] ca iminā ca kāraṇenā”ti sakalanivesanaṃ ekaravaṃ katvā dhammaṃ desento imaṃ gāthamāha –

At that time, the Bodhisatta lived in the great charnel ground, attended by a retinue of eighty thousand crows. Then one crow went and reported to the Bodhisatta the danger that had arisen for the crows. He reflected, 'Except for me, there is no one else capable of averting the danger that has befallen my kinsmen. I shall avert it.' Considering the ten perfections, he made the perfection of loving-kindness his forerunner and flew forth with a single burst of speed. Entering through a large open window, he went beneath the king’s seat. Then a certain man wished to seize him. The king restrained him, saying, 'He has come for refuge; do not seize him.' The Great Being rested for a moment, reflected on the perfection of loving-kindness, and emerged from beneath the seat. He said to the king: 'Great king, a king ought to rule without following the wrong courses of action, such as desire. Whatever deed is to be done, it should be done after careful investigation and consideration. Only that which can be successfully accomplished should be undertaken, and nothing else. For if kings undertake what cannot be successfully accomplished, a great danger, culminating in the fear of death, arises for the populace. The chaplain, acting out of hostility, spoke a falsehood. There is no such thing as fat in crows.' Hearing this, the king, with a pleased mind, had a golden ceremonial seat brought for the Bodhisatta. As he was seated there, he had the Bodhisatta's wings anointed with oil refined a hundred and a thousand times. In a golden dish, he had him served with fine food fit for a king and given drink. When the Great Being was satisfied and free from distress, the king said this to him: 'Wise one, you say, “There is no such thing as fat in crows.” For what reason do they have no fat?' Then the Bodhisatta, intending to teach the Dhamma, making the entire palace resound with his single voice, said, 'For this reason and for that reason,' and spoke this verse:

140.

140.

“Niccaṃ ubbiggahadayā, sabbalokavihesakā;

Tasmā nesaṃ vasā natthi, kākānamhāka ñātina”nti.

Always with anxious hearts, harassing all the world; Therefore, there is no fat in them, in these crows, our kinsmen.

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – mahārāja, kākā nāma niccaṃ ubbiggamānasā bhayappattāva viharanti, sabbalokassa ca vihesakā, khattiyādayo manussepi itthipurisepi kumārakumārikādayopi viheṭhentā kilamentāva vicaranti, tasmā imehi dvīhi kāraṇehi nesaṃ [V 1.0464] amhākaṃ ñātīnaṃ kākānaṃ vasā nāma natthi. Atītepi na bhūtapubbā, anāgatepi na bhavissatīti.

Herein is the meaning in brief: O great king, crows are ever of an anxious mind, dwelling as though stricken with fear. And they are harassers of the whole world; they go about vexing and tormenting everyone—nobles and others, men and women, boys and girls. Therefore, for these two reasons, there is no such thing as fat in them, in our kinsmen, the crows. It has never existed in the past, nor will it ever exist in the future.

Evaṃ mahāsatto imaṃ kāraṇaṃ uttānaṃ katvā “mahārāja, raññā nāma anisamma anupadhāretvā kammaṃ na kattabba”nti rājānaṃ bodhesi. Rājā tussitvā bodhisattaṃ rajjena pūjesi. Bodhisatto rajjaṃ raññoyeva paṭidatvā rājānaṃ pañcasu sīlesu patiṭṭhāpetvā sabbasattānaṃ abhayaṃ yāci. Rājā tassa dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sabbasattānaṃ abhayaṃ datvā kākānaṃ nibaddhadānaṃ paṭṭhapesi. Divase divase taṇḍulambaṇassa bhattaṃ pacitvā nānaggarasehi omadditvā kākānaṃ dīyati, mahāsattassa pana rājabhojanameva dīyittha.

Thus the Great Being, having made this reason plain, admonished the king, saying, 'O great king, a king should not act without proper investigation and consideration.' The king, being pleased, honored the Bodhisatta with the kingdom. The Bodhisatta, however, returned the kingdom to the king, established him in the five precepts, and requested amnesty for all beings. The king, having heard his Dhamma teaching, granted amnesty to all beings and established a regular provision of alms for the crows. Every day, cooked rice from an ambaṇa of rice grains was prepared, mixed with various excellent sauces, and given to the crows. As for the Great Being, he was given the king’s own food.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā bārāṇasirājā ānando ahosi, kākarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, made the connection for the Jātaka, saying: 'At that time, the king of Bārāṇasī was Ānanda, and the king of the crows was none other than myself.'

Kākajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The commentary on the Kāka Jātaka, the tenth.

Asampadānavaggo cuddasamo.

The Asampadāna Vagga, the fourteenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary verse thereof:

Asampadānabhīrukaṃ, ghatāsanajhānasodhaṃ;

Candābhaṃ suvaṇṇahaṃsaṃ, babbugodhubhatobhaṭṭhaṃ;

Kākarājāti te dasāti.

Asampadāna, Bhīruka, Ghatāsana, Jhānasodhana, Candābha, Suvaṇṇahaṃsa, Babbu, Godha, Ubhaṭa, and Kāka—these are the ten.

15. Kakaṇṭakavaggo

15. The Kakaṇṭaka Vagga

[141] 1. Godhājātakavaṇṇanā

[141] 1. The Commentary on the Godhā Jātaka

Na [V 1.0465][P 1.0487][M 1.0513] pāpajanasaṃsevīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ekaṃ vipakkhaseviṃ bhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu mahiḷāmukhajātake kathitasadisameva.

“One who does not associate with evil people”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning a monk who associated with a rival faction. The present story is similar to that told in the Mahiḷāmukha Jātaka.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto godhāyoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gaṇhi. So vayappatto nadītīre mahābile anekagodhāsataparivāro vāsaṃ kappesi. Tassa putto godhāpillako ekena kakaṇṭakena saddhiṃ santhavaṃ katvā tena saddhiṃ sammodamāno viharanto “kakaṇṭakaṃ parissajissāmī”ti avattharati. Tassa tena saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ godhārājassa ārocesuṃ. Godhārājā puttaṃ pakkosāpetvā “tāta, tvaṃ aṭṭhāne vissāsaṃ karosi, kakaṇṭakā nāma nīcajātikā, tehi saddhiṃ vissāso na kattabbo. Sace tvaṃ tena saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ karissasi, taṃ kakaṇṭakaṃ nissāya sabbampetaṃ godhākulaṃ vināsaṃ pāpuṇissati, ito paṭṭhāya etena saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ mā akāsī”ti āha. So karotiyeva. Bodhisatto punappunaṃ kathentopi tassa tena saddhiṃ vissāsaṃ vāretuṃ asakkonto “avassaṃ amhākaṃ etaṃ kakaṇṭakaṃ nissāya bhayaṃ uppajjissati, tasmiṃ uppanne palāyanamaggaṃ sampādetuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti ekena passena vātabilaṃ kārāpesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of a monitor lizard. Having reached maturity, he dwelt in a great burrow on the riverbank, surrounded by a retinue of many hundreds of monitor lizards. His son, a young monitor lizard, became friends with a certain kakaṇṭaka and, enjoying himself, lived happily with it. Thinking, “I will embrace the kakaṇṭaka,” he would lie upon it. They reported this familiarity to the monitor lizard king. The monitor lizard king summoned his son and said, “My dear, you are placing trust where it should not be placed. Kakaṇṭakas are of a low species; one should not become familiar with them. If you become familiar with this kakaṇṭaka, this entire clan of monitor lizards will be destroyed because of it. From now on, do not be familiar with it.” But he continued to do so. Though the Bodhisatta repeatedly advised him, he was unable to prevent this familiarity. He thought, “Surely, danger will arise for us because of this kakaṇṭaka. When it arises, it is proper to prepare an escape route.” So he had an escape hole dug on one side.

Puttopissa anukkamena mahāsarīro ahosi, kakaṇṭako pana purimappamāṇoyeva. Itaro “kakaṇṭakaṃ parissajissāmī”ti antarantarā avattharatiyeva, kakaṇṭakassa pabbatakūṭena avattharaṇakālo viya hoti. So kilamanto cintesi “sace ayaṃ aññāni katipayāni divasāni maṃ evaṃ parissajissati, jīvitaṃ me natthi, ekena luddakena saddhiṃ ekato hutvā imaṃ godhākulaṃ vināsessāmī”ti. Athekadivasaṃ nidāghasamaye meghe vuṭṭhe vammikamakkhikā uṭṭhahiṃsu, tato tato godhā [P 1.0488] nikkhamitvā makkhikāyo khādanti. Eko godhāluddako godhābilaṃ bhindanatthāya kuddālaṃ gahetvā sunakhehi saddhiṃ araññaṃ pāvisi. Kakaṇṭako taṃ disvā “ajja attano manorathaṃ pūressāmī”ti taṃ upasaṅkamitvā avidūre nipajjitvā “bho purisa[V 1.0466], kasmā araññe vicarasī”ti pucchi. So “godhānaṃ [M 1.0514] atthāyā”ti āha. “Ahaṃ anekasatānaṃ godhānaṃ āsayaṃ jānāmi, aggiñca palālañca ādāya ehī”ti taṃ tattha netvā “imasmiṃ ṭhāne palālaṃ pakkhipitvā aggiṃ datvā dhūmaṃ katvā samantā sunakhe ṭhapetvā sayaṃ mahāmuggaraṃ gahetvā nikkhantā nikkhantā godhā paharitvā māretvā rāsiṃ katvā yāhī”ti evañca pana vatvā “ajja paccāmittassa piṭṭhiṃ passissāmī”ti ekasmiṃ ṭhāne sīsaṃ ukkhipitvā nipajji. Luddakopi palāladhūmaṃ akāsi, dhūmo bilaṃ pāvisi, godhā dhūmandhā maraṇabhayatajjitā nikkhamitvā palāyituṃ āraddhā. Luddako nikkhantaṃ nikkhantaṃ paharitvā māresi, tassa hatthato muttā sunakhā gaṇhiṃsu. Godhānaṃ mahāvināso uppajji.

His son gradually grew to have a large body, but the kakaṇṭaka remained the same size as before. The other, thinking, “I will embrace the kakaṇṭaka,” would from time to time press down on him, making it seem to the kakaṇṭaka as if he were being crushed under a mountain peak. Becoming exhausted, he thought, “If this one keeps embracing me like this for a few more days, my life will be over. I must join forces with a hunter and destroy this entire clan of monitor lizards.” Then one day during the hot season, after a rain shower, winged termites emerged from an anthill. The monitor lizards came out from here and there to eat the termites. A monitor lizard hunter, intending to break open their burrow, took a spade and entered the forest with his dogs. Seeing him, the kakaṇṭaka thought, “Today I will fulfill my wish.” He approached the hunter, lay down nearby, and asked, “Sir, why are you wandering in the forest?” The hunter replied, “For monitor lizards.” The kakaṇṭaka said, “I know the dwelling place of many hundreds of monitor lizards. Bring fire and straw, and come.” He led the hunter there and instructed, “In this spot, place the straw, light a fire, and make smoke. Station the dogs all around, and taking a large club yourself, strike and kill the monitor lizards as they emerge, one by one. Make a pile of them and then you may go.” Having said this, he thought, “Today I will see the back of my enemy,” and lay down in a certain spot with his head raised. The hunter made smoke with the straw, and the smoke entered the burrow. The monitor lizards, blinded by the smoke and terrified by the fear of death, began to come out and flee. The hunter struck and killed them as they emerged, while the dogs caught those that escaped his hands. A great destruction befell the monitor lizards.

Bodhisatto “kakaṇṭakaṃ nissāya bhayaṃ uppanna”nti ñatvā “pāpapurisasaṃsaggo nāma na kattabbo, pāpe nissāya hitasukhaṃ nāma natthi, ekassa pāpakakaṇṭakassa vasena ettakānaṃ godhānaṃ vināso jāto”ti vātabilena palāyanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

The Bodhisatta, realizing that “danger has arisen because of the kakaṇṭaka,” thought, “One should not associate with a wicked person, for there is no welfare or happiness to be found by relying on the wicked. Because of one wicked kakaṇṭaka, the destruction of so many monitor lizards has occurred.” Fleeing through the escape hole, he spoke this verse:

141.

141.

“Na pāpajanasaṃsevī, accantasukhamedhati;

Godhākulaṃ kakaṇṭāva, kaliṃ pāpeti attāna”nti.

“One who associates with evil people does not attain ultimate happiness; just as the monitor lizard clan suffered ruin from the kakaṇṭaka, so he brings ruin upon himself.”

Tatrāyaṃ saṅkhepattho – pāpajanasaṃsevī puggalo accantasukhaṃ ekantasukhaṃ nirantarasukhaṃ nāma na edhati na vindati na paṭilabhati. Yathā kiṃ? Godhākulaṃ kakaṇṭāva. Yathā kakaṇṭakato godhākulaṃ sukhaṃ na labhati, evaṃ pāpajanasaṃsevī puggalo sukhaṃ na labhati. Pāpajanaṃ pana sevanto ekanteneva kaliṃ pāpeti attānaṃ, kali vuccati vināso, ekanteneva pāpasevī attānañca aññe ca attanā saddhiṃ vasante vināsaṃ pāpeti. Pāḷiyaṃ pana “phalaṃ pāpeyyā”ti likhanti. Taṃ byañjanaṃ aṭṭhakathāyaṃ natthi, atthopissa na yujjati. Tasmā yathāvuttameva gahetabbaṃ.

Here is the concise meaning: A person who associates with evil people does not increase, find, or obtain what is called ultimate happiness, absolute happiness, or continuous happiness. How so? Consider the monitor lizard clan and the kakaṇṭaka. Just as the monitor lizard clan does not obtain happiness from the kakaṇṭaka, so too a person who associates with evil people does not obtain happiness. Rather, by associating with an evil person, one inevitably brings ruin upon oneself. ‘Ruin’ here means destruction. Indeed, one who associates with evil people brings destruction upon oneself and upon others who live with them. In the Pāli text, however, some write ‘phalaṃ pāpeyyā.’ That expression is not in the commentary, nor does its meaning fit. Therefore, it should be taken only as stated above.

Satthā [P 1.0489] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kakaṇṭako devadatto ahosi, bodhisattassa putto anovādako godhāpillako vipakkhasevī bhikkhu, godhārājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

Having delivered this Dhamma teaching, the Teacher made the connection to the Jātaka, saying: “At that time, the kakaṇṭaka was Devadatta; the Bodhisatta’s disobedient son, the young monitor lizard, was the monk who associated with the rival faction; and the monitor lizard king was none other than myself.”

Godhājātakavaṇṇanā paṭhamā.

The First Exposition of the Godhā Jātaka.

[142] 2. Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā

[142] 2. The Exposition of the Siṅgāla Jātaka

Etañhi [V 1.0467][M 1.0515] te durājānanti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa vadhāya parisakkanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Dhammasabhāyañhi bhikkhūnaṃ kathaṃ sutvā satthā “na, bhikkhave, devadatto idāneva mayhaṃ vadhāya parisakkati, pubbepi parisakkiyeva, na ca maṃ māretuṃ asakkhi, sayameva pana kilanto”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“This, for you, is hard to know”—this the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning Devadatta’s attempt to murder him. Hearing the monks’ conversation in the Dhamma hall, the Teacher said: “Monks, it is not only now that Devadatta attempts to murder me; he attempted it in the past as well. But he was unable to kill me and only exhausted himself.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto siṅgālayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā siṅgālarājā hutvā siṅgālagaṇaparivuto susānavane vihāsi. Tena samayena rājagahe ussavo ahosi, yebhuyyena manussā suraṃ pivanti, surāchaṇoyeva kireso. Athettha sambahulā dhuttā bahuṃ surañca maṃsañca āharāpetvā maṇḍitapasādhitā gāyitvā gāyitvā surañca pivanti, maṃsañca khādanti. Tesaṃ paṭhamayāmāvasāne maṃsaṃ khīyi, surā pana bahukāva. Atheko dhutto “maṃsakhaṇḍaṃ dehī”ti āha. “Maṃsaṃ khīṇa”nti ca vutte “mayi ṭhite maṃsakkhayo nāma natthī”ti vatvā “āmakasusāne matamanussamaṃsaṃ khādanatthāya āgate siṅgāle māretvā maṃsaṃ āharissāmī”ti muggaraṃ gahetvā niddhamanamaggena nagarā nikkhamitvā susānaṃ gantvā muggaraṃ gahetvā matako viya uttāno nipajji. Tasmiṃ khaṇe bodhisatto siṅgālagaṇaparivuto tattha gato taṃ disvā “nāyaṃ matako”ti ñatvāpi “suṭṭhutaraṃ upaparikkhissāmī”ti tassa adhovātena gantvā sarīragandhaṃ ghāyitvā tathatovassa amatakabhāvaṃ ñatvā “lajjāpetvā naṃ uyyojessāmī”ti gantvā muggarakoṭiyaṃ ḍaṃsitvā ākaḍḍhi, dhutto muggaraṃ na vissaji, upasaṅkamantampi na [P 1.0490] olokento naṃ gāḷhataraṃ aggahesi. Bodhisatto paṭikkamitvā “bho purisa, sace tvaṃ matako bhaveyyāsi, na mayi muggaraṃ ākaḍḍhante gāḷhataraṃ gaṇheyyāsi, iminā kāraṇena tava matakabhāvo vā amatakabhāvo vā dujjāno”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a jackal and became the king of the jackals, dwelling in a charnel-ground forest surrounded by a pack of jackals. At that time, there was a festival in Rājagaha, and most people drank liquor; it was, they say, a liquor festival. Then, many rogues, having brought much liquor and meat, adorned and beautified themselves, and while singing, they drank liquor and ate meat. By the end of the first watch of the night, the meat was exhausted, but there was still plenty of liquor. Then one rogue said, 'Give me a piece of meat.' When told, 'The meat is finished,' he replied, 'While I am here, there is no such thing as running out of meat.' Saying, 'I will kill a jackal that has come to the charnel ground to eat the flesh of a dead person and bring back its meat,' he took a club, left the city by way of the sewer drain, went to the charnel ground, and, holding the club, lay down on his back as if dead. At that moment, the Bodhisatta, surrounded by his pack of jackals, went there. Seeing him, although he knew, 'This one is not dead,' he thought, 'I will examine him more carefully.' Going downwind of him, he smelled the scent of his body and thus knew for certain that he was not dead. Thinking, 'I will shame him and send him away,' he went and bit the end of the club and pulled. The rogue did not release the club; without looking at the one who had approached, he gripped it even more tightly. The Bodhisatta retreated and said, 'O man, if you were dead, you would not grip the club more tightly when I pull on it. For this reason, whether you are dead or not is difficult to know.' Then he spoke this verse:

142.

142.

“Etañhi te durājānaṃ, yaṃ sesi matasāyikaṃ;

Yassa te kaḍḍhamānassa, hatthā daṇḍo na muccatī”ti.

This of you is indeed difficult to know: that you lie as if dead, you from whose hand the club is not released when it is pulled.

Tattha [M 1.0516] etañhi te durājānanti etaṃ kāraṇaṃ tava duviññeyyaṃ. Yaṃ sesi matasāyikanti yena kāraṇena tvaṃ matasāyikaṃ sesi, matako viya hutvā sayasi. Yassa te kaḍḍhamānassāti yassa tava daṇḍakoṭiyaṃ gahetvā kaḍḍhiyamānassa hatthato daṇḍo na muccati, so tvaṃ tathato matako nāma na hosīti.

Herein, this of you is indeed difficult to know means this matter concerning you is difficult to discern. That you lie as if dead means for this reason you lie down, having become like one dead. You from whose hand... when it is pulled means: you from whose hand the club is not released when its end is grasped and pulled; therefore, you are not truly dead.

Evaṃ [V 1.0468] vutte so dhutto “ayaṃ mama amatakabhāvaṃ jānātī”ti uṭṭhāya daṇḍaṃ khipi, daṇḍo virajjhi. Dhutto “gaccha, viraddho dānisi mayā”ti āha. Bodhisatto nivattitvā “bho purisa, maṃ virajjhantopi tvaṃ aṭṭha mahāniraye soḷasa ca ussadaniraye aviraddhoyevā”ti vatvā pakkāmi. Dhutto kiñci alabhitvā susānā nikkhamitvā parikhāyaṃ nhāyitvā āgatamaggeneva nagaraṃ pāvisi.

When this was said, the rogue, thinking, 'This one knows I am not dead,' rose up and threw the club, but the club missed. The rogue said, 'Go, I have missed you now.' The Bodhisatta turned back and said, 'O man, though you have missed me, you have not missed the eight great hells and the sixteen subsidiary hells,' and then he departed. The rogue, having gained nothing, left the charnel ground, bathed in the moat, and entered the city by the same way he had come.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā dhutto devadatto ahosi, siṅgālarājā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story: 'At that time, the rogue was Devadatta, and the jackal king was I myself.'

Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā dutiyā.

The Commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka, the Second.

[143] 3. Virocajātakavaṇṇanā

[143] 3. The Commentary on the Viroca Jātaka

Lasī ca te nipphalitāti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto devadattassa gayāsīse sugatālayassa dassitabhāvaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Devadatto hi parihīnajjhāno lābhasakkāraparihīno “attheko upāyo”ti cintetvā satthāraṃ pañca vatthūni yācitvā alabhamāno dvinnaṃ aggasāvakānaṃ saddhivihārike adhunā pabbajite dhammavinayamhi akovide pañcasate bhikkhū gahetvā gayāsīsaṃ gantvā saṅghaṃ bhinditvā ekasīmāyaṃ āveṇikaṃ saṅghakammaṃ akāsi. Satthā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ ñāṇaparipākakālaṃ ñatvā dve aggasāvake pesesi. Te disvā devadatto [P 1.0491] tuṭṭhamānaso rattiṃ dhammaṃ desayamāno “buddhalīlaṃ karissāmī”ti sugatālayaṃ dassento “vigatathinamiddho kho, āvuso sāriputta, bhikkhusaṅgho, paṭibhātu taṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammīkathā, piṭṭhi me āgilāyati, tamahaṃ āyamissāmī”ti vatvā niddaṃ upagato[M 1.0517]. Dve aggasāvakā tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā maggaphalehi pabodhetvā sabbe ādāya veḷuvanameva paccāgamiṃsu.

'And your splendor is fruitless...' This the Teacher spoke while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, concerning the occasion of Devadatta displaying the manner of the Sugata at Gayāsīsa. For Devadatta, having declined in his meditative absorption and being deprived of gains and honor, thought, 'There is a way.' After requesting five articles from the Teacher and not receiving them, he took five hundred monks—pupils of the two chief disciples who were recently ordained and unskilled in the Dhamma and Vinaya—and went to Gayāsīsa. There he split the Sangha and performed a separate formal act of the Sangha within a single boundary. The Teacher, knowing the time was ripe for those monks' knowledge to mature, sent the two chief disciples. Seeing them, Devadatta was pleased in mind. While teaching the Dhamma at night, intending to perform the Buddha's graceful manner, he displayed the Sugata's style and said, 'Friend Sāriputta, the community of monks is free from sloth and torpor. Let a Dhamma talk for the monks occur to you. My back is weary; I shall stretch it.' Having said this, he fell asleep. The two chief disciples taught the Dhamma to those monks, awakened them with the paths and their fruits, and taking them all, returned to the Bamboo Grove itself.

Kokāliko vihāraṃ tucchaṃ disvā devadattassa santikaṃ gantvā “āvuso devadatta, parisaṃ te bhinditvā dve aggasāvakā vihāraṃ tucchaṃ katvā gatā, tvaṃ pana niddāyasiyevā”ti vatvā uttarāsaṅgamassa apanetvā bhittiyaṃ piṭṭhikaṇṭakaṃ phusanto viya paṇhiyā naṃ hadaye pahari. Tāvadevassa mukhato lohitaṃ uggañchi. So tato paṭṭhāya gilāno ahosi. Satthā theraṃ pucchi “sāriputta, tumhākaṃ gatakāle devadatto kiṃ akāsī”ti? Bhante, devadatto amhe disvā [V 1.0469] “buddhalīlaṃ karissāmī”ti sugatālayaṃ dassetvā mahāvināsaṃ pattoti. Satthā “na kho sāriputta, devadatto idāneva mama anukaronto vināsaṃ patto, pubbepi pattoyevā”ti vatvā therena yācito atītaṃ āhari.

Seeing the empty monastery, Kokālika went to Devadatta and said, 'Friend Devadatta, the two chief disciples have split your assembly and left the monastery empty, yet you just sleep!' Having said this, removing Devadatta's upper robe, he struck him on the chest with his heel as if to make his spine touch the wall. At that very moment, blood gushed from his mouth. From then on, he was ill. The Teacher asked the Elder, 'Sāriputta, when you went there, what did Devadatta do?' 'Venerable sir, upon seeing us, Devadatta, intending to perform the Buddha's graceful manner, displayed the Sugata's style and met with great destruction.' The Teacher said, 'Sāriputta, it is not only now that Devadatta has met with destruction by imitating me; he met with it in the past as well.' And being requested by the Elder, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto kesarasīho hutvā himavantappadese kañcanaguhāyaṃ vāsaṃ kappesi. So ekadivasaṃ kañcanaguhāya nikkhamitvā vijambhitvā catuddisaṃ oloketvā sīhanādaṃ naditvā gocarāya pakkanto mahāmahiṃsaṃ vadhitvā varamaṃsaṃ khāditvā ekaṃ saraṃ otaritvā maṇivaṇṇassa udakassa kucchiṃ pūretvā guhaṃ sandhāya pāyāsi. Atheko siṅgālo gocarappasuto sahasāva sīhaṃ disvā palāyituṃ asakkonto sīhassa purato pādesu patitvā nipajji. “Kiṃ, jambukā”ti ca vutte “ahaṃ te, sāmi, pāde upaṭṭhātukāmo”ti āha. Sīho “sādhu ehi, maṃ upaṭṭhaha, varamaṃsāni taṃ khādāpessāmī”ti vatvā siṅgālaṃ ādāya kañcanaguhaṃ agamāsi. Siṅgālo tato paṭṭhāya sīhavighāsaṃ khādati. So katipāhaccayeneva thūlasarīro ahosi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was born as a maned lion and lived in a golden cave in the Himalayan region. One day, he emerged from the golden cave, stretched, looked around in all four directions, roared a lion's roar, and set out for food. He killed a great buffalo, ate the choicest meat, went down to a lake, filled his belly with jewel-like water, and set out for his cave. At that time, a jackal, gone out in search of food, suddenly saw the lion and, unable to flee, fell at the lion's feet and lay down. When asked, "What is it, jackal?" he replied, "My lord, I wish to attend upon your feet." The lion said, "Very well, come, attend upon me, I will let you eat choice meats." With that, he took the jackal and went to the golden cave. From then on, the jackal ate the lion's leavings. In just a few days, he became plump.
