Atha naṃ ekadivasaṃ guhāya nipannakova sīho āha “gaccha jambuka, pabbatasikhare ṭhatvā pabbatapāde sañcarantesu hatthiassamahiṃsādīsu yassa [P 1.0492] maṃsaṃ khāditukāmosi, taṃ oloketvā āgantvā ‘asukamaṃsaṃ khāditukāmomhī’ti vatvā maṃ vanditvā ‘viroca, sāmī’ti vadāhi, ahaṃ taṃ vadhitvā madhuramaṃsaṃ khāditvā tuyhampi dassāmī”ti. Siṅgālo pabbatasikharaṃ abhiruhitvā nānappakāre mige oloketvā yasseva maṃsaṃ khāditukāmo hoti, kañcanaguhaṃ pavisitvā tameva sīhassa [M 1.0518] ārocetvā pādesu patitvā “viroca, sāmī”ti vadati. Sīho vegena pakkhanditvā sacepi mattavaravāraṇo hoti, tattheva naṃ jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā sayampi varamaṃsaṃ khādati, siṅgālassapi deti. Siṅgālo kucchipūraṃ maṃsaṃ khāditvā guhaṃ pavisitvā niddāyati. So gacchante gacchante kāle mānaṃ vaḍḍhesi “ahampi catuppadova, kiṃkāraṇā divase divase parehi posiyamāno viharāmi, ito paṭṭhāya ahampi hatthiādayo hanitvā maṃsaṃ khādissāmi, sīhopi migarājā ‘viroca, sāmī’ti vuttameva padaṃ nissāya varavāraṇe vadheti, ahampi sīhena ‘viroca, jambukā’ti maṃ vadāpetvā ekaṃ varavāraṇaṃ vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khādissāmī”ti.

Then one day, as the lion lay in the cave, he said to him: "Go, jackal, stand on the mountain peak and observe the elephants, horses, buffaloes, and other animals roaming at the foot of the mountain. Whichever animal's flesh you wish to eat, observe it, then come back and say, 'I wish to eat the flesh of such-and-such an animal,' bow to me, and say, 'Shine forth, my lord.' I will kill it, eat the sweet flesh, and give some to you too." The jackal climbed the mountain peak, observed various kinds of beasts, and whichever animal's flesh he wished to eat, he entered the golden cave, reported it to the lion, fell at his feet, and said, "Shine forth, my lord." The lion swiftly charged, and even if it was a mighty, rutting elephant, he would bring about its death right there, and would himself eat the best flesh and give some to the jackal too. The jackal, having eaten his fill of flesh, would enter the cave and sleep. As time went on, he grew proud, thinking: "I too am a four-legged creature. Why should I live day after day being fed by others? From now on, I too will kill elephants and other animals and eat their flesh. The lion, the king of beasts, kills mighty elephants just by relying on the words, 'Shine forth, my lord.' I too will have the lion say to me, 'Shine forth, jackal,' and then I will kill a mighty elephant and eat its flesh."

So sīhaṃ upasaṅkamitvā etadavoca “sāmi, mayā dīgharattaṃ tumhehi vadhitavaravāraṇānaṃ maṃsaṃ khāditaṃ, ahampi ekaṃ varavāraṇaṃ māretvā maṃsaṃ khāditukāmo, tasmā tumhehi nipannaṭṭhāne kañcanaguhāyaṃ [V 1.0470] nipajjissāmi, tumhe pabbatapāde vicarantaṃ varavāraṇaṃ oloketvā mama santikaṃ āgantvā ‘viroca, jambukā’ti vadetha, ettakamattasmiṃ maccheraṃ mā karitthā”ti. Atha naṃ sīho āha “na, tvaṃ jambuka, vāraṇe vadhituṃ samatthe sīhakule uppanno, vāraṇaṃ vadhitvā maṃsaṃ khādanasamattho siṅgālo nāma loke natthi, mā te etaṃ rucci, mayā vadhitavaravāraṇānaññeva maṃsaṃ khāditvā vasā”ti. So evaṃ vuttepi viramituṃ na icchi, punappunaṃ yāciyeva. Sīho taṃ vāretuṃ asakkonto sampaṭicchitvā “tena hi mama vasanaṭṭhānaṃ pavisitvā nipajjā”ti jambukaṃ kañcanaguhāyaṃ nipajjāpetvā sayaṃ pabbatapāde mattavaravāraṇaṃ oloketvā guhādvāraṃ gantvā “viroca, jambukā”ti āha. Siṅgālo kañcanaguhāya nikkhamitvā [P 1.0493] vijambhitvā catuddisaṃ oloketvā tikkhattuṃ vassitvā “mattavaravāraṇassa kumbhe patissāmī”ti pakkhanditvā virajjhitvā pādamūle pati. Vāraṇo dakkhiṇapādaṃ ukkhipitvā tassa sīsaṃ akkami, sīsaṭṭhīni cuṇṇavicuṇṇāni ahesuṃ. Athassa sarīraṃ vāraṇo pādena saṅgharitvā rāsiṃ katvā upari laṇḍaṃ pātetvā koñcanādaṃ nadanto araññaṃ pāvisi.

Approaching the lion, he said this: "Master, for a long time I have eaten the meat of excellent elephants killed by you. I too wish to kill an excellent elephant and eat its meat. Therefore, I will lie down in the golden cave where you rest. You should observe an excellent elephant roaming at the foot of the mountain, come to me, and say, 'Shine forth, jackal!' Do not be stingy in this small matter." Then the lion said to him: "No, jackal, you are not born of the lion lineage, which is capable of killing elephants. There is no jackal in the world capable of killing an elephant and eating its flesh. Do not let this please you. Live by eating the flesh of the excellent elephants I have killed." But even when told this, he did not wish to desist and begged again and again. Unable to dissuade him, the lion consented, saying, "Very well, enter my dwelling place and lie down." He made the jackal lie down in the golden cave, while he himself observed a rutting elephant at the foot of the mountain, went to the cave entrance, and said, "Shine forth, jackal!" The jackal emerged from the golden cave, stretched, looked around in all four directions, howled three times, and charged, thinking, "I will land on the frontal globe of this rutting elephant!" But he missed and fell at its feet. The elephant lifted its right foot and stepped on his head; the skull bones were crushed to powder. Then the elephant gathered his body with its foot into a heap, defecated on top of it, and making a cry like a curlew, entered the forest.

Bodhisatto imaṃ pavattiṃ disvā “idāni viroca, jambukā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Seeing this event, the Bodhisatta said, "Now shine forth, jackal," and spoke this verse:

143.

143.

“Lasī [M 1.0519] ca te nipphalitā, matthako ca padālito;

Sabbā te phāsukā bhaggā, ajja kho tvaṃ virocasī”ti.

"Your brain has burst forth, and your head is split open; all your ribs are broken—now indeed you shine forth!"

Tattha lasīti matthaluṅgaṃ. Nipphalitāti nikkhantā. Evaṃ bodhisatto imaṃ gāthaṃ vatvā yāvatāyukaṃ ṭhatvā yathākammaṃ gato.

Therein, 'lasī' means brain matter. 'Nipphalitā' means burst forth. Thus, having spoken this verse, the Bodhisatta remained for the extent of his lifespan and then passed on according to his karma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā siṅgālo devadatto ahosi, sīho pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the birth story: "At that time, the jackal was Devadatta, but the lion was I myself."

Virocajātakavaṇṇanā tatiyā.

The Commentary on the Viroca Jātaka, the Third.

[144] 4. Naṅguṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā

[144] 4. The Commentary on the Naṅguṭṭha Jātaka

Bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātavedāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ājīvakānaṃ micchātapaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tadā kira ājīvakā jetavanapiṭṭhiyaṃ nānappakāraṃ micchātapaṃ caranti. Sambahulā [V 1.0471] bhikkhū tesaṃ ukkuṭikappadhānavaggulivatakaṇṭakāpassayapañcātapatapanādibhedaṃ micchātapaṃ disvā bhagavantaṃ pucchiṃsu “atthi nu kho, bhante, imaṃ micchātapaṃ nissāya kusalaṃ vā vuḍḍhi vā”ti. Satthā “na, bhikkhave, evarūpaṃ micchātapaṃ nissāya kusalaṃ vā vuḍḍhi vā atthi, pubbe paṇḍitā ‘evarūpaṃ tapaṃ nissāya kusalaṃ vā vuḍḍhi vā bhavissatī’ti saññāya jātaggiṃ gahetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā aggijuhanādivasena kiñci vuḍḍhiṃ apassantā aggiṃ udakena nibbāpetvā kasiṇaparikammaṃ katvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇā ahesu”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher spoke this, beginning with 'Bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātaveda,' while dwelling at Jetavana, concerning the wrong ascetic practices of the Ājīvakas. At that time, it is said, the Ājīvakas were engaging in various kinds of wrong ascetic practices in the vicinity of Jetavana. Many monks, seeing their wrong ascetic practices—such as the practice of squatting, the bat-like practice, lying on a bed of thorns, the five-fire austerity, and so on—asked the Blessed One, “Venerable sir, is there any merit or increase based on these wrong ascetic practices?” The Teacher said, “No, monks, based on such wrong ascetic practices there is no merit or increase. In the past, wise men, thinking, ‘By relying on such ascetic practice there will be merit or increase,’ took up their birth-fire and entered the forest. Seeing no increase through fire sacrifice and so on, they extinguished the fire with water, performed the preliminary kasiṇa meditation, produced the higher knowledges and attainments, and were destined for the Brahma world.” Having said this, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [P 1.0494] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbatti. Tassa jātadivase mātāpitaro jātaggiṃ gahetvā ṭhapesuṃ. Atha naṃ soḷasavassakāle etadavocuṃ “mayaṃ te, putta, jātadivase aggiṃ gaṇhimha. Sacesi agāraṃ ajjhāvasitukāmo, tayo vede uggaṇha. Atha brahmalokaṃ gantukāmo, aggiṃ gahetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā aggiṃ paricaranto mahābrahmānaṃ ārādhetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo hohī”ti. So “na mayhaṃ agārena attho”ti aggiṃ gahetvā araññaṃ pavisitvā assamapadaṃ māpetvā aggiṃ paricaranto araññe vihāsi. So ekadivasaṃ paccantagāmake godakkhiṇaṃ labhitvā taṃ goṇaṃ [M 1.0520] assamapadaṃ netvā cintesi “aggibhagavantaṃ gomaṃsaṃ khādāpessāmī”ti. Athassa etadahosi “idha loṇaṃ natthi, aggibhagavā aloṇaṃ khādituṃ na sakkhissati, gāmato loṇaṃ āharitvā aggibhagavantaṃ saloṇakaṃ khādāpessāmī”ti. So taṃ tattheva bandhitvā loṇatthāya gāmakaṃ agamāsi. Tasmiṃ gate sambahulā luddakā taṃ ṭhānaṃ āgatā. Goṇaṃ disvā vadhitvā maṃsaṃ pacitvā khāditvā naṅguṭṭhañca jaṅghañca cammañca tattheva chaḍḍetvā avasesamaṃsaṃ ādāya agamaṃsu.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into an Udicca brahmin family. On the day of his birth, his parents took and established the birth-fire. When he reached sixteen years of age, they said to him: “Son, on the day of your birth, we took this fire for you. If you wish to live the household life, learn the three Vedas. But if you wish to go to the Brahma world, take the fire, enter the forest, and by serving the fire and propitiating the Great Brahma, you will be destined for the Brahma world.” He replied, “I have no need for the household life,” and taking the fire, he entered the forest, built a hermitage, and lived there serving the fire. One day, he received a gift of a bull from a border village. Taking that bull to his hermitage, he thought, “I will have the Lord Fire eat beef.” Then it occurred to him, “There is no salt here. The Lord Fire will not be able to eat unsalted meat. I will fetch salt from the village and have the Lord Fire eat it with salt.” So he tied the bull there and went to the village for salt. While he was gone, several hunters came to that place. Seeing the bull, they killed it, cooked the meat, and ate it. Leaving the tail, the shank-bones, and the hide there, they took the rest of the meat and departed.

Brāhmaṇo āgantvā naṅguṭṭhādimattameva disvā cintesi “ayaṃ aggibhagavā attano santakampi rakkhituṃ na sakkoti, maṃ pana kadā rakkhissati. Iminā aggiparicaraṇena niratthakena bhavitabbaṃ, natthi itonidānaṃ kusalaṃ vā vuḍḍhi vā”ti. So aggiparicariyāya vigatacchando “hambho aggibhagavā, tvaṃ attanopi santakaṃ rakkhituṃ asakkonto maṃ kadā rakkhissasi, maṃsaṃ natthi, ettakenapi tussāhī”ti naṅguṭṭhādīni aggimhi pakkhipanto imaṃ gāthamāha –

The brahmin arrived and, seeing only the tail and so forth, thought: “This Lord Fire cannot even protect his own property; when will he protect me? This service to the fire must be useless; there is no merit or increase to be gained from it.” So, having lost his desire for serving the fire, he said: “O Lord Fire, since you cannot even protect your own property, when will you protect me? There is no meat; be satisfied with just this.” As he threw the tail and so forth into the fire, he spoke this verse:

144.

144.

“Bahumpetaṃ asabbhi jātaveda, yaṃ taṃ vāladhinābhipūjayāma;

Maṃsārahassa [P 1.0495] natthajja maṃsaṃ, naṅguṭṭhampi bhavaṃ paṭiggahātū”ti.

“This is much indeed, O ignoble Jātaveda, that we worship you with a tail. For one worthy of meat, there is no meat today. May your reverence accept even the tail.”

Tattha [V 1.0472] bahumpetanti ettakampi bahuṃ. Asabbhīti asappurisa asādhujātika. Jātavedāti aggiṃ ālapati. Aggi hi jātamattova vediyati paññāyati pākaṭo hoti, tasmā “jātavedo”ti vuccati. Yaṃ taṃ vāladhinābhipūjayāmāti yaṃ ajja mayaṃ attanopi santakaṃ rakkhituṃ asamatthaṃ bhagavantaṃ vāladhinā abhipūjayāma, etampi tava bahumevāti dasseti. Maṃsārahassāti maṃsaṃ arahassa tuyhaṃ natthi ajja maṃsaṃ. Naṅguṭṭhampi bhavaṃ paṭiggahātūti attano santakaṃ rakkhituṃ asakkonto bhavaṃ imaṃ sajaṅghacammaṃ naṅguṭṭhampi paṭiggaṇhātūti.

Herein, 'bahumpetaṃ' means ‘even this is much.’ 'Asabbhi' means an ignoble person, one of ignoble birth. 'Jātaveda' is an address to the fire. For fire, as soon as it is born (jāta), is known (vediyati), becomes understood and manifest; therefore, it is called ‘Jātaveda.’ 'Yaṃ taṃ vāladhinābhipūjayāma' means: ‘That today we worship with a tail the Lord, who is unable to protect even his own property—this shows that even this is much for you.’ 'Maṃsārahassa' means: ‘For you, who are worthy of meat, there is no meat today.’ 'Naṅguṭṭhampi bhavaṃ paṭiggahātu' means: ‘May your reverence, being unable to protect your own property, accept even this tail along with the shank-bone and hide.’”

Evaṃ vatvā mahāsatto aggiṃ udakena nibbāpetvā isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā brahmalokaparāyaṇo ahosi.

Having said this, the Great Being extinguished the fire with water, went forth into the ascetic life of a sage, and having produced the higher knowledges and attainments, he became destined for the Brahma world.

Satthā [M 1.0521] imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “nibbutaggitāpaso ahameva tena samayenā”ti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: “The ascetic who extinguished the fire was I myself at that time.”

Naṅguṭṭhajātakavaṇṇanā catutthā.

The Commentary on the Naṅguṭṭha Jātaka, the Fourth.

[145] 5. Rādhajātakavaṇṇanā

[145] 5. The Commentary on the Rādha Jātaka.

Na tvaṃ rādha vijānāsīti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto purāṇadutiyikāpalobhanaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Paccuppannavatthu indriyajātake āvi bhavissati. Satthā pana taṃ bhikkhuṃ āmantetvā “bhikkhu mātugāmo nāma arakkhiyo, ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā rakkhantāpi rakkhituṃ na sakkonti. Tvampi pubbe etaṃ ārakkhaṃ ṭhapetvā rakkhantopi rakkhituṃ nāsakkhi, idāni kathaṃ rakkhissasī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

“You do not understand, Rādha” — this the Teacher spoke while dwelling at Jetavana concerning the enticement by a former wife. The story of the present will be made clear in the Indriya Jātaka. The Teacher then addressed that monk, saying: “Monk, a woman, by her nature, cannot be guarded. Even when one sets a guard over them, one cannot protect them. In the past, you too, though setting a guard, were unable to protect her. How will you protect her now?” So saying, he related a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto sukayoniyaṃ nibbatti. Kāsiraṭṭhe eko brāhmaṇo bodhisattañca kaniṭṭhabhātarañcassa puttaṭṭhāne ṭhapetvā posesi. Tesu bodhisattassa “poṭṭhapādo”ti nāmaṃ ahosi, itarassa “rādho”ti. Tassa pana brāhmaṇassa bhariyā anācārā hoti dussīlā. So vohāratthāya gacchanto ubhopi bhātaro āha – “tātā, sace vo mātā brāhmaṇī anācāraṃ ācarati, vāreyyātha na”nti. Bodhisatto āha “sādhu, tāta, vāretuṃ sakkontā vāreyyāma, asakkontā [P 1.0496] tuṇhī bhavissāmā”ti. Evaṃ brāhmaṇo brāhmaṇiṃ sukānaṃ niyyādetvā vohāratthāya gato.

In the past, when King Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a parrot. In the country of Kāsī, a certain brahmin, having placed the Bodhisatta and his younger brother in the position of sons, raised them. Of the two, the Bodhisatta's name was Poṭṭhapāda, and the other's was Rādha. Now, that brahmin’s wife was of improper conduct and immoral. When he was about to leave for business, he said to both brothers: 'My dears, if your mother, the brahmin woman, behaves improperly, you are to restrain her.' The Bodhisatta replied: 'Very well, father, if we are able to restrain her, we shall; if not, we shall remain silent.' Thus, the brahmin entrusted the brahmin woman to the parrots and left for business.

Tassa [V 1.0473] pana gatadivasato paṭṭhāya brāhmaṇī aticarituṃ āraddhā, pavisantānañca nikkhamantānañca anto natthi, tassā kiriyaṃ disvā rādho bodhisattaṃ āha – “bhātika, amhākaṃ pitā ‘sace vo mātā anācāraṃ ācarati, vāreyyāthā’ti vatvā gato, idāni cesā anācāraṃ ācarati, vārema na”nti. Bodhisatto “tāta, tvaṃ attano abyattatāya bālabhāvena evaṃ vadesi, mātugāmaṃ nāma ukkhipitvā carantāpi rakkhituṃ na sakkonti. Yaṃ kammaṃ kātuṃ na sakkā, na taṃ kātuṃ vaṭṭatī”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

From the day he left, the brahmin woman began to transgress. There was no end to those entering and leaving. Seeing her conduct, Rādha said to the Bodhisatta: 'Brother, our father said, "If your mother behaves improperly, you are to restrain her," and then he left. Now she is behaving improperly—shall we restrain her?' The Bodhisatta replied: 'My dear brother, you speak thus out of your own inexperience and foolishness. A woman, indeed, cannot be protected even by those who carry her about. That which cannot be done, one ought not to do.' So saying, he spoke this verse:

145.

145.

“Na [M 1.0522] tvaṃ rādha vijānāsi, aḍḍharatte anāgate;

Abyayataṃ vilapasi, virattā kosiyāyane”ti.

"You do not understand, Rādha, though midnight has not yet come; you lament in vain, for the Kosiyan woman is disaffected."

Tattha na tvaṃ rādha vijānāsi, aḍḍharatte anāgateti tāta rādha, tvaṃ na jānāsi, aḍḍharatte anāgate paṭhamayāmeyeva ettakā janā āgatā, idāni ko jānāti, kittakāpi āgamissanti. Abyayataṃ vilapasīti tvaṃ abyattavilāpaṃ vilapasi. Virattā kosiyāyaneti mātā no kosiyāyanī brāhmaṇī virattā amhākaṃ pitari nippemā jātā. Sacassā tasmiṃ sineho vā pemaṃ vā bhaveyya, na evarūpaṃ anācāraṃ kareyyāti imamatthaṃ etehi byañjanehi pakāsesi.

Therein, 'You do not understand, Rādha, though midnight has not yet come' means: 'Dear Rādha, you do not know. Even in the first watch, before midnight has arrived, so many people have come; who knows how many more will come now?' 'You lament in vain' means 'you utter a useless lament.' 'The Kosiyan woman is disaffected' means 'our mother, the Kosiyan brahmin woman, has become disaffected, devoid of love for our father. If she had any fondness or love for him, she would not commit such improper conduct.' He revealed this meaning with these phrases.

Evaṃ pakāsetvā ca pana brāhmaṇiyā saddhiṃ rādhassa vattuṃ na adāsi. Sāpi yāva brāhmaṇassa anāgamanā yathāruciyā vicari. Brāhmaṇo āgantvā poṭṭhapādaṃ pucchi – “tāta, kīdisī vo mātā”ti. Bodhisatto brāhmaṇassa sabbaṃ yathābhūtaṃ kathetvā “kiṃ te, tāta, evarūpāya dussīlāyā”ti vatvā “tāta, amhehi mātuyā dosassa kathitakālato paṭṭhāya na sakkā idha vasitu”nti brāhmaṇassa pāde vanditvā saddhiṃ rādhena uppatitvā araññaṃ agamāsi.

Having thus explained, he did not allow Rādha to speak with the brahmin woman. She, for her part, behaved as she pleased until the brahmin's return. When the brahmin returned, he asked Poṭṭhapāda: 'My dear, what is your mother like?' The Bodhisatta told the brahmin everything as it had truly happened, and saying, 'Father, what use is such an immoral woman to you?' and 'Father, from the time we spoke of our mother's fault, it has not been possible to live here,' he bowed at the brahmin’s feet and, together with Rādha, flew up and went into the forest.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā saccāni pakāsesi, saccapariyosāne ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhu sotāpattiphale patiṭṭhahi. “Tadā brāhmaṇo ca brāhmaṇī ca eteyeva dve janā ahesuṃ, rādho ānando, poṭṭhapādo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, revealed the Truths. At the conclusion of the exposition of the Truths, the discontented monk was established in the fruit of stream-entry. The Teacher then identified the births: 'At that time, the brahmin and the brahmin woman were that husband and wife; Rādha was Ānanda, and Poṭṭhapāda was I myself.'

Rādhajātakavaṇṇanā pañcamā.

The Commentary on the Rādha Jātaka, the Fifth.

[146] 6. Samuddakākajātakavaṇṇanā

[146] 6. The Commentary on the Sea-Crow Jātaka.

Api [V 1.0474][P 1.0497] nu hanukā santāti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto sambahule mahallake bhikkhū ārabbha kathesi. Te kira gihikāle sāvatthiyaṃ kuṭumbikā aḍḍhā mahaddhanā aññamaññasahāyakā ekato hutvā puññāni karontā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā “mayaṃ mahallakā, kiṃ no gharāvāsena, satthu santike ramaṇīye buddhasāsane pabbajitvā dukkhassantaṃ karissāmā”ti [M 1.0523] sabbaṃ sāpateyyaṃ puttadhītādīnaṃ datvā assumukhaṃ ñātisaṅghaṃ pahāya satthāraṃ pabbajjaṃ yācitvā pabbajiṃsu. Pabbajitvā pana pabbajjānurūpaṃ samaṇadhammaṃ na kariṃsu, mahallakabhāvena dhammampi na pariyāpuṇiṃsu, gihikāle viya pabbajitakālepi vihārapariyante paṇṇasālaṃ kāretvā ekatova vasiṃsu. Piṇḍāya carantāpi aññattha agantvā yebhuyyena attano puttadārasseva gehaṃ gantvā bhuñjiṃsu. Tesu ekassa purāṇadutiyikā sabbesampi mahallakattherānaṃ upakārā ahosi, tasmā sesāpi attanā laddhaṃ āhāraṃ gahetvā tassāyeva gehe nisīditvā bhuñjanti. Sāpi tesaṃ yathāsannihitaṃ sūpabyañjanaṃ deti. Sā aññatarena rogena phuṭṭhā kālamakāsi. Atha te mahallakattherā vihāraṃ gantvā aññamaññaṃ gīvāsu gahetvā “madhurahattharasā upāsikā kālakatā”ti vihārapaccante rodantā vicariṃsu. Tesaṃ saddaṃ sutvā ito cito ca bhikkhū sannipatitvā “āvuso, kasmā rodathā”ti pucchiṃsu. Te “amhākaṃ sahāyassa purāṇadutiyikā madhurahattharasā kālakatā amhākaṃ ativiya upakārā, ‘idāni kuto tathārūpiṃ labhissāmā’ti iminā kāraṇena rodimhā”ti āhaṃsu.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, related this concerning many elderly monks, with reference to the verse beginning, 'Are the jaws weary?' It is said that in their lay life, they were affluent, wealthy householders in Sāvatthī, friends to one another who performed meritorious deeds together. Having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma discourse, they thought, 'We are old—what use is the household life to us? In the Teacher's delightful dispensation, we shall go forth and make an end of suffering.' So, giving all their property to their sons and daughters, they left behind their tearful relatives, requested the going forth from the Teacher, and were ordained. After going forth, however, they did not practice the duties of an ascetic befitting the ordained life. Due to their old age, they did not master the Dhamma either. Just as in their lay life, so too in their ordained life, they had a leaf-hut built at the edge of the monastery and lived together. When going for alms, they did not go elsewhere but for the most part went to the homes of their own sons and wives to eat. Among them, the former wife of one monk was a benefactress to all the elderly theras. Therefore, the others also took the food they had received and would sit and eat in her house. She, in turn, would give them whatever curry and condiments were available. She was afflicted by a certain disease and passed away. Then those elderly theras went to the monastery, and embracing each other by the neck, they wandered about the monastery precincts, weeping, 'The laywoman with the delicious cooking has passed away!' Hearing their sound, monks gathered from all around and asked, 'Venerable sirs, why do you weep?' They replied, 'Our companion's former wife, whose cooking was so delicious, has passed away. She was of great service to us. Where shall we now find another like her? For this reason, we weep.'

Tesaṃ taṃ vippakāraṃ disvā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, iminā nāma kāraṇena mahallakattherā aññamaññaṃ gīvāsu gahetvā vihārapaccante rodantā vicarantī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevete tassā kālakiriyāya rodantā vicaranti, pubbepete imaṃ kākayoniyaṃ nibbattitvā samudde mataṃ nissāya ‘samuddaudakaṃ ussiñcitvā etaṃ nīharissāmā’ti vāyamantā paṇḍite nissāya jīvitaṃ labhiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Seeing their distress, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: 'Friends, for this reason, the elder monks, with their arms around each other's necks, are wandering and weeping in the precincts of the monastery.' The Teacher arrived and asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?' When they told him, 'For this one,' he said, 'Monks, it is not only now that they wander about weeping over her death. In the past, too, having been reborn in the crow existence, on account of her who had died in the ocean, they strove, thinking, "We will bail out the ocean water and retrieve her," and they received their lives by relying on a wise one.' So saying, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto samuddadevatā hutvā nibbatti. Atheko kāko attano bhariyaṃ kākiṃ ādāya gocaraṃ pariyesamāno samuddatīraṃ agamāsi[P 1.0498]. Tasmiṃ kāle manussā samuddatīre khīrapāyāsamacchamaṃsasurādīhi nāgabalikammaṃ katvā pakkamiṃsu. Atha so kāko balikammaṭṭhānaṃ gantvā khīrādīni disvā saddhiṃ kākiyā khīrapāyāsamacchamaṃsādīni [V 1.0475] bhuñjitvā bahuṃ suraṃ pivi. Te ubhopi surāmadamattā “samuddakīḷaṃ kīḷissāmā”ti velante nisīditvā nhāyituṃ ārabhiṃsu [M 1.0524] athekā ūmi āgantvā kākiṃ gahetvā samuddaṃ pavesesi. Tameko maccho maṃsaṃ khāditvā ajjhohari. Kāko “bhariyā me matā”ti rodi paridevi. Athassa paridevanasaddaṃ sutvā bahū kākā sannipatitvā “kiṃkāraṇā rodasī”ti pucchiṃsu. “Sahāyikā vo velante nhāyamānā ūmiyā haṭā”ti. Te sabbepi ekaravaṃ ravantā rodiṃsu. Atha nesaṃ etadahosi “idaṃ samuddaudakaṃ nāma amhākaṃ kiṃ pahosi, udakaṃ ussiñcitvā samuddaṃ tucchaṃ katvā sahāyikaṃ nīharissāmā”ti. Te mukhaṃ pūretvā pūretvā udakaṃ bahi chaḍḍenti, loṇūdakena ca gale sussamāne uṭṭhāyuṭṭhāya thalaṃ gantvā vissamanti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a sea deity. At that time, a certain crow, taking his wife, a female crow, went to the seashore in search of food. During that time, people had performed a nāga offering on the seashore with milk-rice, fish, meat, liquor, and other things, and then departed. Then that crow went to the offering site and, seeing the milk-rice and other items, ate them together with the female crow and drank much liquor. Both of them, intoxicated with the liquor, thought, 'Let us play in the ocean,' and sitting on the shore, they began to bathe. Then a wave came, seized the female crow, and carried her into the ocean. A certain fish devoured and swallowed her. The crow wept and lamented, 'My wife is dead!' Hearing his sound of lamentation, many crows gathered and asked, 'For what reason do you weep?' He replied, 'Your companion was carried off by a wave while bathing on the shore.' They all cried out with a single voice and wept. Then this occurred to them: 'What power does this ocean water have over us? Let us bail out the water, empty the ocean, and retrieve our companion.' They filled their beaks again and again and cast the water outside. And when their throats became parched from the salt water, they would rise up again and again, go to the land, and rest.

Te hanūsu kilantesu mukhesu sukkhantesu akkhīsu rattesu dīnā kilantā hutvā aññamaññaṃ āmantetvā “ambho, mayaṃ samuddaudakaṃ gahetvā bahi pātema, gahitagahitaṭṭhānaṃ puna udakena pūrati, samuddaṃ tucchaṃ kātuṃ na sakkhissāmā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāhaṃsu –

When their jaws were weary, their mouths dry, and their eyes red, they became wretched and exhausted. Addressing one another, they said, 'Friends, we take the ocean water and cast it outside, but the very spot from which it is taken fills up again with water; we will not be able to empty the ocean.' Having said this, they spoke this verse:

146.

146.

“Api nu hanukā santā, mukhañca parisussati;

Oramāma na pārema, pūrateva mahodadhī”ti.

"Our jaws are indeed weary, and our mouths are parched; we draw out the water but cannot reach the end, for the great ocean only fills up again."

Tattha api nu hanukā santāti api no hanukā santā, api amhākaṃ hanukā kilantā. Oramāma na pāremāti mayaṃ attano balena mahāsamuddaudakaṃ ākaḍḍhāma osārema, tucchaṃ pana naṃ kātuṃ na sakkoma. Ayañhi pūrateva mahodadhīti.

Therein, 'Our jaws are indeed weary' means: our jaws are weary, our jaws are exhausted. 'We draw out but cannot reach the end' means: by our own strength we draw out and diminish the water of the great ocean, but we are not able to make it empty. For this great ocean just keeps filling up.

Evañca pana vatvā sabbepi te kākā “tassā kākiyā evarūpaṃ nāma tuṇḍaṃ ahosi, evarūpāni vaṭṭakkhīni, evarūpaṃ chavisaṇṭhānaṃ, evarūpo madhurasaddo. Sā no imaṃ corasamuddaṃ nissāya naṭṭhā”ti bahuṃ vippalapiṃsu. Te evaṃ vippalapamāne [P 1.0499] samuddadevatā bheravarūpaṃ dassetvā palāpesi, evaṃ tesaṃ sotthi ahosi.

And having spoken thus, all those crows lamented greatly, saying, 'That female crow had such a beak, such round eyes, such a bodily form, and such a sweet voice. She, our companion, has perished on account of this thieving ocean.' While they were lamenting thus, the sea deity, showing a terrifying form, made them flee. In this way, they found safety.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā kākī ayaṃ purāṇadutiyikā ahosi, kāko mahallakatthero, sesakākā sesamahallakattherā, samuddadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka thus: 'At that time, the female crow was this former wife; the male crow was the elder monk; the remaining crows were the remaining elder monks; and the sea deity was none other than myself.'

Samuddakākajātakavaṇṇanā chaṭṭhā.

The Commentary on the Samuddakāka Jātaka, the sixth.

[147] 7. Puppharattajātakavaṇṇanā

[147] 7. The Commentary on the Puppharatta Jātaka

Nayidaṃ [V 1.0476][M 1.0525] dukkhaṃ aduṃ dukkhanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto ekaṃ ukkaṇṭhitabhikkhuṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi bhagavatā “saccaṃ kira tvaṃ bhikkhu ukkaṇṭhito”ti vutte “sacca”nti vatvā “kena ukkaṇṭhāpitosī”ti ca puṭṭho “purāṇadutiyikāyā”ti vatvā “madhurahattharasā, bhante, sā itthī, na sakkomi taṃ vinā vasitu”nti āha. Atha naṃ satthā “esā te bhikkhu anatthakārikā, pubbepi tvaṃ etaṃ nissāya sūle uttāsito etaññeva patthayamāno kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbatto, idāni naṃ kasmā puna patthesī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, while dwelling at Jetavana, spoke this concerning a discontented monk, with reference to the verse beginning, 'This is not suffering, that is not suffering.' For when the Blessed One asked him, 'Is it true, monk, that you are discontented?' he replied, 'It is true.' And when asked, 'By whom have you been made discontented?' he said, 'By my former wife,' adding, 'Venerable sir, that woman's touch is sweet; I cannot live without her.' Then the Teacher told him, 'This woman is a cause of harm to you, monk. In the past, too, on account of her, you were impaled on a stake, and dying while still longing for her, you were reborn in hell. Why do you long for her again now?' So saying, he related the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto ākāsaṭṭhadevatā ahosi. Atha bārāṇasiyaṃ kattikarattivārachaṇo sampatto hoti, nagaraṃ devanagaraṃ viya alaṅkariṃsu. Sabbo jano khaṇakīḷānissito ahosi. Ekassa pana duggatamanussassa ekameva ghanasāṭakayugaṃ ahosi. So taṃ sudhotaṃ dhovāpetvā obhañjāpetvā satavalikaṃ sahassavalikaṃ kāretvā ṭhapesi. Atha naṃ bhariyā evamāha “icchāmahaṃ, sāmi, ekaṃ kusumbharattaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā tava kaṇṭhe laggā kattikarattivāraṃ caritu”nti. “Bhadde, kuto amhākaṃ daliddānaṃ kusumbhaṃ, suddhavatthaṃ nivāsetvā kīḷāhī”ti? “Kusumbharattaṃ alabhamānā chaṇakīḷaṃ na kīḷissāmi, tvaṃ aññaṃ itthiṃ gahetvā kīḷassū”ti. “Bhadde, kiṃ maṃ pīḷesi, kuto amhākaṃ kusumbha”nti? “Sāmi, purisassa icchāya sati kiṃ nāma natthi, nanu rañño kusumbhavatthusmiṃ bahu kusumbha”nti. “Bhadde[P 1.0500], taṃ ṭhānaṃ rakkhasapariggahitapokkharaṇisadisaṃ, balavārakkhā, na sakkā upasaṅkamituṃ, mā te etaṃ rucci, yathāladdheneva tussassū”ti. “Sāmi, rattibhāge andhakāre sati purisassa agamanīyaṭṭhānaṃ nāma natthī”ti. Iti so tāya punappunaṃ kathentiyā kilesavasena tassā vacanaṃ gahetvā “hotu bhadde, mā cintayitthā”ti taṃ samassāsetvā rattibhāge jīvitaṃ pariccajitvā nagarā nikkhamitvā rañño kusumbhavatthuṃ gantvā vatiṃ madditvā antovatthuṃ pāvisi. Ārakkhamanussā vatisaddaṃ sutvā “coro coro”ti parivāretvā gahetvā paribhāsitvā koṭṭetvā bandhitvā pabhātāya rattiyā rañño dassesuṃ. Rājā [M 1.0526] “gacchatha, naṃ sūle uttāsethā”ti āha. Atha naṃ pacchābāhaṃ bandhitvā vajjhabheriyā vajjamānāya nagarā nikkhamāpetvā sūle uttāsesuṃ. Balavavedanā pavattanti, kākā sīse nilīyitvā kaṇayaggasadisehi tuṇhehi akkhīni vijjhanti.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Benares, the Bodhisatta was a deity dwelling in the sky. Then, the Kattika festival arrived in Benares, and the city was adorned as if it were a city of the devas. All the people were absorbed in festive amusements. However, there was one poor man who had only a single pair of thick cloths. He had them well washed, folded a hundredfold and a thousandfold, and then put them away. Then his wife said to him, 'Husband, I wish to wear one safflower-dyed garment and wrap myself in another, then cling to your neck and enjoy the Kattika festival.' 'My dear, where would we poor folk get safflower dye? Wear your clean clothes and enjoy the amusements.' 'If I do not get a safflower-dyed garment, I will not enjoy the amusements. You may take another woman and enjoy yourself with her.' 'My dear, why do you torment me? Where would we get safflower dye?' 'Husband, if a man has a desire, is there anything unattainable? Is there not much safflower in the king's safflower garden?' 'My dear, that place is like a lotus pond guarded by ogres—it is heavily protected, impossible to approach. Do not let this appeal to you. Be content with what you have.' 'Husband, at nighttime, in the darkness, there is no place a man cannot go.' Thus, as she kept speaking again and again, overcome by defilement, he took her words to heart. 'Very well, my dear, do not worry,' he reassured her. Then, risking his life in the dead of night, he left the city and went to the king’s safflower garden. Treading down the fence, he entered the inner enclosure. The guards heard the sound of the fence and surrounded him, shouting, 'Thief! Thief!' They seized him, abused him, beat him, bound him, and at dawn brought him before the king. The king said, 'Go, impale him on a stake.' So they bound his hands behind his back, led him out of the city to the sound of the execution drum, and impaled him on a stake. Severe pain arose. Crows perched on his head and pecked at his eyes with beaks like iron spikes.

So [V 1.0477] tathārūpampi dukkhaṃ amanasikaritvā tameva itthiṃ anussaritvā “tāya nāmamhi ghanapuppharattavatthanivatthāya kaṇṭhe āsattabāhuyugaḷāya saddhiṃ kattikarattivārato parihīno”ti cintetvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

He, however, paid no mind to such suffering, but kept recollecting that woman. Reflecting, 'I am deprived of the Kattika festival night with her, who would have been dressed in a garment dyed a deep floral red, her arms clinging to my neck,' he uttered this verse:

147.

147.

“Nayidaṃ dukkhaṃ aduṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ maṃ tudati vāyaso;

Yaṃ sāmā puppharattena, kattikaṃ nānubhossatī”ti.

This is not the suffering, that the crow pecks at me; that is the suffering: that my Sāmā will not enjoy the Kattika festival in a flower-dyed garment.

Tattha nayidaṃ dukkhaṃ aduṃ dukkhaṃ, yaṃ maṃ tudati vāyasoti yañca idaṃ sūle lagganapaccayaṃ kāyikacetasikadukkhaṃ, yañca lohamayehi viya tuṇḍehi vāyaso tudati, idaṃ sabbampi mayhaṃ na dukkhaṃ, aduṃ dukkhaṃ etaṃyeva pana me dukkhanti attho. Kataraṃ? Yaṃ sāmā puppharattena, kattikaṃ nānubhossatīti, yaṃ sā piyaṅgusāmā mama bhariyā ekaṃ kusumbharattaṃ nivāsetvā ekaṃ pārupitvā evaṃ ghanapuppharattena vatthayugena acchannā mama kaṇṭhe gahetvā kattikarattivāraṃ nānubhavissati, idaṃ mayhaṃ dukkhaṃ, etadeva hi maṃ bādhatīti? So evaṃ mātugāmaṃ ārabbha vippalapantoyeva kālaṃ katvā niraye nibbatti.

Herein, 'This is not the suffering... that is the suffering: that the crow pecks at me' means: 'Neither the physical and mental suffering from being impaled on a stake, nor that the crow pecks me with its iron-like beak—none of this is suffering for me. That alone is my suffering.' What is that? 'That my Sāmā will not enjoy the Kattika festival in a flower-dyed garment' means: 'That my wife, Sāmā of the golden complexion, will not get to experience the Kattika festival night, wearing one safflower-dyed garment and wrapped in another, thus covered with a pair of garments dyed a deep floral red, embracing my neck—this is my suffering. This alone torments me.' Thus, lamenting over the woman, he died and was reborn in hell.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā jayampatikāva idāni jayampatikā, taṃ kāraṇaṃ paccakkhaṃ katvā ṭhitā ākāsaṭṭhadevatā pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, connected the Jātaka: 'At that time, the husband and wife were the same as the husband and wife now; and the deity dwelling in the sky who stood witnessing that event was I myself.'

Puppharattajātakavaṇṇanā sattamā.

The Commentary on the Puppharatta Jātaka, the Seventh.

[148] 8. Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā

8. The Commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka.

Nāhaṃ [P 1.0501] punaṃ na ca punanti idaṃ satthā jetavane viharanto kilesaniggahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. Sāvatthiyaṃ kira pañcasatamattā sahāyakā mahāvibhavā seṭṭhiputtā satthu dhammadesanaṃ sutvā sāsane uraṃ datvā pabbajitvā jetavane antokoṭisanthāre vihariṃsu. Athekadivasaṃ tesaṃ aḍḍharattasamaye kilesanissito saṅkappo uppajji. Te ukkaṇṭhitvā [M 1.0527] attanā jahitakilese puna gaṇhituṃ cittaṃ uppādayiṃsu. Atha satthā aḍḍharattasamanantare sabbaññutaññāṇadaṇḍadīpakaṃ ukkhipitvā “katarāya nu kho ratiyā jetavane bhikkhū viharantī”ti bhikkhūnaṃ ajjhāsayaṃ olokento tesaṃ bhikkhūnaṃ abbhantare kāmarāgasaṅkappassa uppannabhāvaṃ aññāsi. Satthā ca nāma ekaputtikā itthī attano puttaṃ viya, ekacakkhuko puriso cakkhuṃ viya attano sāvake [V 1.0478] rakkhati. Pubbaṇhādīsu yasmiṃ yasmiṃ samaye tesaṃ kilesā uppajjanti, te tesaṃ kilese tato paraṃ vaḍḍhituṃ adatvā tasmiṃ tasmiṃyeva samaye niggaṇhāti. Tenassa etadahosi “ayaṃ cakkavattirañño antonagareyeva corānaṃ uppannakālo viya vattati, idāneva tesaṃ dhammadesanaṃ katvā te kilese niggaṇhitvā arahattaṃ dassāmī”ti. So surabhigandhakuṭito nikkhamitvā madhurassarena “ānandā”ti āyasmantaṃ dhammabhaṇḍāgārikaṃ ānandattheraṃ āmantesi. Thero “kiṃ, bhante”ti āgantvā vanditvā aṭṭhāsi. “Ānanda, yattakā bhikkhū antokoṭisanthāre viharanti, sabbeva gandhakuṭipariveṇe sannipātehī”ti. Evaṃ kirassa ahosi “sacāhaṃ teyeva pañcasate bhikkhū pakkosāpessāmi. ‘Satthārā no abbhantare kilesānaṃ uppannabhāvo ñāto’ti saṃviggamānasā dhammadesanaṃ sampaṭicchituṃ na sakkhissantī”ti. Tasmā “sabbe sannipātehī”ti āha. Thero “sādhu, bhante”ti avāpuraṇaṃ ādāya pariveṇena pariveṇaṃ āhiṇḍitvā sabbe bhikkhū gandhakuṭipariveṇe sannipātetvā buddhāsanaṃ paññapesi.

This story, beginning with the words, 'I will not again, and not again...', the Teacher, dwelling in Jetavana, told concerning the subduing of defilements. In Sāvatthī, it is said, about five hundred wealthy sons of merchants, who were friends, having heard the Teacher’s Dhamma teaching and dedicated themselves to the Dispensation, went forth and dwelt in the lodgings at the far end of Jetavana. Then one day, at midnight, a thought connected with defilement arose in them. Discontented, they aroused in their minds the intention to take up again the defilements they had abandoned. Then the Teacher, just after midnight, raising the lamp of omniscient knowledge, surveyed the inclinations of the monks, thinking, 'In what delight, I wonder, are the monks in Jetavana dwelling?', and knew that thoughts of sensual desire had arisen within those monks. Indeed, the Teacher protects his disciples as a mother protects her only child, and as a one-eyed man protects his eye. At whatever time—in the forenoon or otherwise—defilements arise in them, he restrains those defilements at that very moment, not allowing them to grow further. He thought, 'This is like the time when thieves arise in the inner city of a wheel-turning king. Right now I will teach them the Dhamma, restrain their defilements, and grant them arahantship.' Emerging from his fragrant chamber, he called in a sweet voice, 'Ānanda!'—addressing the Venerable Ānanda, the treasurer of the Dhamma. The elder approached, paid homage, and stood there, saying, 'What is it, Lord?' 'Ānanda, gather all the monks dwelling in the lodgings at the far end of the monastery in the courtyard of the fragrant chamber.' For it occurred to him, 'If I summon just those five hundred monks, they might think, "The Teacher knows that defilements have arisen within us," and, with their minds agitated, they will be unable to receive the Dhamma teaching.' Therefore, he said, 'Gather all.' The elder replied, 'Very well, Lord,' and taking a gong-stick, he went from precinct to precinct, gathered all the monks in the courtyard of the fragrant chamber, and prepared the Buddha’s seat.

Satthā pallaṅkaṃ ābhujitvā ujuṃ kāyaṃ paṇidhāya silāpathaviyaṃ patiṭṭhahamāno sineru viya paññatte buddhāsane nisīdi āveḷāveḷā yamakayamakā chabbaṇṇaghanabuddharasmiyo vissajjento. Tāpi rasmiyo pātimattā chattamattā kūṭāgārakucchimattā chijjitvā chijjitvā gaganatale vijjulatā viya sañcariṃsu, aṇṇavakucchiṃ khobhetvā bālasūriyuggamanakālo viya ahosi. Bhikkhusaṅghopi satthāraṃ vanditvā garucittaṃ paccupaṭṭhapetvā rattakambalasāṇiyā parikkhipanto viya parivāretvā nisīdi. Satthā brahmassaraṃ nicchārento bhikkhū āmantetvā [P 1.0502] “na, bhikkhave, bhikkhunā nāma kāmavitakkaṃ byāpādavitakkaṃ vihiṃsāvitakkanti ime [M 1.0528] tayo akusalavitakke vitakketuṃ vaṭṭati. Anto uppannakileso hi ‘parittako’ti avamaññituṃ na vaṭṭati, kileso nāma paccāmittasadiso. Paccāmitto ca khuddako nāma natthi, okāsaṃ labhitvā vināsameva pāpeti, evameva appamattakopi kileso uppajjitvā vaḍḍhituṃ labhanto mahāvināsaṃ pāpeti. Kileso nāmesa halāhalavisūpamo uppāṭitacchavigaṇḍasadiso āsīvisapaṭibhāgo asaniaggisadiso allīyituṃ na yutto āsaṅkitabbo. Uppannuppannakkhaṇeyeva paṭisaṅkhānabalena bhāvanābalena yathā muhuttampi hadaye aṭṭhatvā paduminipattā udakabindu viya vivaṭṭati, evaṃ pajahitabbo. Porāṇakapaṇḍi tāpi appamattakampi kilesaṃ garahitvā yathā puna abbhantare nuppajjati, evaṃ niggaṇhiṃsū”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

The Teacher, folding his legs crosswise and setting his body erect, sat on the prepared Buddha-seat, as firm as Mount Sineru established on its stone foundation, emitting dense six-colored Buddha-rays in pairs, one after another. Those rays, some the size of a bowl, some a parasol, some the interior of a peaked house, split apart repeatedly and wandered across the sky like flashes of lightning, agitating the ocean’s depths until it seemed like the time of the morning sun’s rising. The Sangha of monks, having paid homage to the Teacher and established reverence in their hearts, sat surrounding him as if enclosing him in a red woolen curtain. The Teacher, emitting a voice like Brahma’s, addressed the monks: 'Monks, it is not fitting for a monk to entertain these three unwholesome thoughts: sensual thought, ill will, or harmful thought. For a defilement that has arisen within should not be underestimated as 'insignificant.' A defilement is like an enemy. There is no such thing as a small enemy; given the opportunity, it brings destruction. In the same way, even a slight defilement, if it gets the chance to grow, leads to great destruction. A defilement is like deadly poison, like a boil with its skin torn off, resembling a venomous snake, like the fire of a thunderbolt—it should not be clung to, but regarded with apprehension. At the very moment of its arising, it should be abandoned through the power of reflection and the power of development, so that it does not remain in the heart even for a moment, but rolls off like a drop of water on a lotus leaf. The wise of old also despised even the slightest defilement, restraining it so that it would not arise again within.' Having said this, he brought forth a story of the past.

Atīte bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto siṅgālayoniyaṃ paṭisandhiṃ gahetvā araññe [V 1.0479] nadītīre nivāsaṃ kappesi. Atheko jarahatthī gaṅgātīre kālamakāsi. Siṅgālo gocarappasuto taṃ matahatthisarīraṃ disvā “mahā me gocaro uppanno”ti gantvā taṃ soṇḍe ḍaṃsi, naṅgalīsāya daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. So “natthettha khāditabbayuttaka”nti dantesu ḍaṃsi, thambhe daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Kaṇṇe ḍaṃsi, suppakoṭiyaṃ daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Udare ḍaṃsi, kusūle daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Pāde ḍaṃsi, udukkhale daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. Naṅguṭṭhe ḍaṃsi, musale daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. So “etthāpi natthi khāditabbayuttaka”nti sabbattha assādaṃ alabhanto vaccamagge ḍaṃsi, mudupūve daṭṭhakālo viya ahosi. So “laddhaṃ dāni me imasmiṃ sarīre mudu khāditabbayuttakaṭṭhāna”nti tato paṭṭhāya khādanto antokucchiṃ pavisitvā vakkahadayādīni khāditvā pipāsitakāle lohitaṃ pivitvā nipajjitukāmakāle udaraṃ pattharitvā nipajjati.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn as a jackal and made his dwelling in a forest by the riverbank. Then an old elephant died on the banks of the Ganges. The jackal, out seeking food, saw the dead elephant's body and thought, 'A great source of food has arisen for me!' He went and bit the trunk—it was like biting a plough-beam. 'There is nothing here suitable to eat,' he thought, and bit the tusks—it was like biting a post. He bit the ears—it was like biting the edge of a winnowing basket. He bit the belly—it was like biting a granary. He bit the feet—it was like biting a mortar. He bit the tail—it was like biting a pestle. 'There is nothing here suitable to eat either,' he thought, and finding no enjoyment anywhere, he bit the anus—it was like biting a soft cake. 'Now I have found a soft, edible place in this body!' he thought. And eating his way from there, he entered the inner belly. He devoured the kidneys, heart, and other organs, drank blood when thirsty, and when he wanted to lie down, he would spread out the stomach and lie down.

Athassa etadahosi – “idaṃ hatthisarīraṃ mayhaṃ nivāsasukhatāya gehasadisaṃ, khāditukāmatāya sati pahūtamaṃsaṃ, kiṃ dāni me aññattha kamma”nti [M 1.0529] so aññattha agantvā hatthikucchiyaṃyeva maṃsaṃ khāditvā vasati. Gacchante gacchante kāle nidāghe vātasamphassena ceva sūriyarasmisantāpena ca taṃ kuṇapaṃ sussitvā [P 1.0503] valiyo gaṇhi, siṅgālassa paviṭṭhadvāraṃ pihitaṃ, antokucchiyaṃ andhakāro ahosi. Siṅgālassa lokantarikanivāso viya jāto. Kuṇape sussante maṃsampi sussi, lohitampi pacchijji. So nikkhamanadvāraṃ alabhanto bhayappatto hutvā sandhāvanto ito cito ca paharitvā nikkhamanadvāraṃ pariyesamāno vicarati. Evaṃ tasmiṃ ukkhaliyaṃ piṭṭhapiṇḍi viya antokucchiyaṃ paccamāne katipāhaccayena mahāmegho pāvassi. Atha naṃ kuṇapaṃ temetvā uṭṭhāya pakatisaṇṭhānena aṭṭhāsi. Vaccamaggo vivaṭo hutvā tārakā viya paññāyi. Siṅgālo taṃ chiddaṃ disvā “idāni me jīvitaṃ laddha”nti yāva hatthisīsā paṭikkamitvā vegena pakkhanditvā vaccamaggaṃ sīsena paharitvā nikkhami. Tassa sañchannasarīrattā sabbalomāni vaccamagge allīyiṃsu. So tālakkhandhasadisena nillomena sarīrena ubbiggacitto muhuttaṃ dhāvitvā nivattitvā nisinno sarīraṃ oloketvā “idaṃ dukkhaṃ mayhaṃ na aññena kataṃ, lobhahetu pana lobhakāraṇā lobhaṃ nissāya mayā etaṃ kataṃ, ito dāni paṭṭhāya na lobhavasiko bhavissāmi, puna hatthisarīraṃ nāma na pavisissāmī”ti saṃviggahadayo hutvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Then this thought occurred to him: "This elephant's body is like a house, providing me comfort for dwelling, and when I desire to eat, there is abundant meat. What need have I now to go elsewhere?" So, without going elsewhere, he stayed right inside the elephant's belly, eating the flesh. As time passed, during the hot season, the carcass dried up from the wind's touch and the scorching heat of the sun's rays, and it became wrinkled. The jackal's entryway was blocked, and inside the belly, it became dark. The jackal's dwelling became like an inter-world hell. As the carcass dried, the flesh also dried, and the blood ceased. Unable to find an exit, the jackal became frightened and ran about, striking here and there, searching for an exit. Thus, while he was tumbling about inside the belly like a lump of dough in a pot, after a few days, a great cloud rained down. Then, moistened by the rain, the carcass swelled and returned to its original shape. The passage for excrement opened up, appearing like a star. Seeing that hole, the jackal thought, "Now I have regained my life!" He retreated as far as the elephant's head, then rushed forward swiftly, struck the passage with his head, and escaped. Because his body was covered with fur, all his hairs stuck to the passage. With a hairless body like a palm trunk, and with an agitated mind, he ran for a moment, then stopped and sat down. Looking at his body, he reflected: "This suffering was not caused by another—it was done by me because of greed, due to greed, relying on greed. From now on, I will not be under the power of greed. Never again will I enter an elephant's body!" With a heart shaken by urgency, he spoke this verse:

148.

148.

“Nāhaṃ punaṃ na ca punaṃ, na cāpi apunappunaṃ;

Hatthibondiṃ pavekkhāmi, tathā hi bhayatajjito”ti.

"I will not again, nor yet again, nor even repeatedly again, enter an elephant's body, for thus am I terrified by fear."

Tattha [V 1.0480] na cāpi apunappunanti a-kāro nipātamatto. Ayaṃ panetissā sakalāyapi gāthāya attho – ahañhi ito puna, tato ca punāti vuttavārato puna tatopi ca punappunaṃ vāraṇasarīrasaṅkhātaṃ hatthibondiṃ na pavekkhāmi. Kiṃkāraṇā? Tathā hi bhayatajjito, tathā hi ahaṃ imasmiññeva pavesane bhayatajjito maraṇabhayena santāsaṃ saṃvegaṃ āpāditoti.

Herein, in the phrase 'na cāpi apunappunaṃ,' the 'a' is merely a particle. This is the meaning of the entire verse: I will not again, nor yet again, nor even repeatedly again, enter the elephant's carcass. Why? Because I am terrified by fear; for indeed, in this very act of entering, I was terrified by the fear of death and brought to a state of dread and urgency.

Evañca [M 1.0530] pana vatvā tatova palāyitvā puna taṃ vā aññaṃ vā hatthisarīraṃ nivattitvāpi na olokesi. Tato paṭṭhāya na lobhavasiko ahosi.

Having said this, he fled from there and did not look back, either at that elephant's body or any other. From that time on, he was no longer under the sway of greed.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “bhikkhave, anto uppannakilesassa nāma vaḍḍhituṃ adatvā tattha tattheva naṃ niggaṇhituṃ vaṭṭatī”ti [P 1.0504] vatvā saccāni pakāsetvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi. Saccapariyosāne pañcasatāpi te bhikkhū arahatte patiṭṭhahiṃsu, avasesesu keci sotāpannā, keci sakadāgāmino, keci anāgāmino ahesuṃ. Tadā siṅgālo ahameva ahosinti.

The Teacher, having delivered this discourse, said, "Monks, it is fitting to restrain a defilement that has arisen within, not allowing it to grow, but to suppress it right there and then." Having declared the truths, he identified the birth story. At the conclusion of the truths, all five hundred of those monks were established in arahantship, while of the remaining monks, some became stream-enterers, some once-returners, and some non-returners. At that time, the jackal was I myself.

Siṅgālajātakavaṇṇanā aṭṭhamā.

The Commentary on the Siṅgāla Jātaka, the Eighth.

[149] 9. Ekapaṇṇajātakavaṇṇanā

[149] 9. The Commentary on the Ekapaṇṇa Jātaka

Ekapaṇṇo ayaṃ rukkhoti idaṃ satthā vesāliṃ upanissāya mahāvane kūṭāgārasālāyaṃ viharanto vesālikaṃ duṭṭhalicchavikumāraṃ ārabbha kathesi. Tasmiñhi kāle vesālinagaraṃ gāvutagāvutantare tīhi pākārehi parikkhittaṃ tīsu ṭhānesu gopuraṭṭālakayuttaṃ paramasobhaggappattaṃ. Tattha niccakālaṃ rajjaṃ kāretvā vasantānaññeva rājūnaṃ satta sahassāni satta satāni satta ca rājāno honti, tattakāyeva uparājāno, tattakā senāpatino, tattakā bhaṇḍāgārikā. Tesaṃ rājakumārānaṃ antare eko duṭṭhalicchavikumāro nāma ahosi kodhano caṇḍo pharuso sāhasiko, daṇḍena ghaṭṭitaāsīviso viya niccaṃ pajjalito kodhena. Tassa purato dve tīṇi vacanāni kathetuṃ samattho nāma natthi. Taṃ neva mātāpitaro, na ñātayo, na mittasuhajjā sikkhāpetuṃ sakkhiṃsu. Athassa mātāpitūnaṃ etadahosi “ayaṃ kumāro atipharuso sāhasiko, ṭhapetvā sammāsambuddhaṃ añño imaṃ vinetuṃ samattho nāma natthi, buddhaveneyyena bhavitabba”nti. Te taṃ ādāya satthu santikaṃ gantvā vanditvā āhaṃsu “bhante, ayaṃ kumāro caṇḍo pharuso kodhena pajjalati, imassa ovādaṃ dethā”ti.

"This tree is single-leaved," this story was told by the Teacher while dwelling near Vesālī, in the Great Forest, at the hall with the peaked roof, concerning a wicked Licchavi prince of Vesālī. At that time, the city of Vesālī, supremely splendid, was surrounded by three walls at intervals of a gāvuta, adorned with gates and watchtowers in three places. There were seven thousand, seven hundred, and seven kings, an equal number of viceroys, generals, and treasurers who ruled continuously. Among those royal princes was one named the Wicked Licchavi Prince—angry, violent, harsh, and reckless, always burning with anger like a venomous snake struck by a stick. No one was able to speak two or three words before him. Neither his parents, relatives, nor friends were able to discipline him. Then his parents thought, "This prince is excessively violent and reckless. No one but the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One is able to tame him. He must be one destined to be trained by the Buddha." Taking him, they went to the Teacher, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, this prince is fierce, harsh, and blazing with anger. Please give him advice."

Satthā [V 1.0481][M 1.0531] taṃ kumāraṃ ovadi – “kumāra, imesu nāma sattesu caṇḍena pharusena sāhasikena viheṭhakajātikena na bhavitabbaṃ, pharusavāco ca nāma vijātamātuyāpi pitunopi puttadārassapi bhātibhaginīnampi pajāpatiyāpi mittabandhavānampi appiyo hoti amanāpo, ḍaṃsituṃ āgacchanto sappo viya, aṭaviyaṃ uṭṭhitacoro viya, khādituṃ āgacchanto yakkho viya ca ubbejanīyo hutvā dutiyacittavāre nirayādīsu nibbattati. Diṭṭheyeva ca dhamme kodhano puggalo maṇḍitapasādhitopi dubbaṇṇova hoti, puṇṇacandasassirikampissa mukhaṃ jālābhihatapadumaṃ viya malaggahitakañcanādāsamaṇḍalaṃ viya ca virūpaṃ hoti duddasikaṃ. Kodhaṃ nissāya hi sattā satthaṃ ādāya attanāva attānaṃ paharanti, visaṃ khādanti, rajjuyā ubbandhanti, papātā papatanti. Evaṃ kodhavasena kālaṃ katvā nirayādīsu uppajjanti, viheṭhakajātikāpi diṭṭheva dhamme garahaṃ [P 1.0505] patvā kāyassa bhedā nirayādīsu uppajjanti, puna manussattaṃ labhitvā vijātakālato paṭṭhāya rogabahulāva honti. Cakkhurogo sotarogotiādīsu ca rogesu ekato uṭṭhāya ekasmiṃ patanti, rogena aparimuttāva hutvā niccaṃ dukkhitāva honti, tasmā sabbesu sattesu mettacittena hitacittena muducittena bhavitabbaṃ. Evarūpo hi puggalo nirayādibhayehi na parimuccatī”ti. So kumāro satthu ovādaṃ sutvā ekovādeneva nihatamāno danto nibbisevano mettacitto muducitto ahosi. Aññaṃ akkosantampi paharantampi nivattitvā na olokesi, uddhaṭadāṭho viya sappo, aḷacchinno viya kakkaṭako, chinnavisāṇo viya ca usabho ahosi.

The Teacher advised the prince: 'Prince, among these beings, one should not be fierce, harsh, reckless, or of a nature to harm. A person with harsh speech becomes displeasing and disagreeable even to their own mother, father, children, siblings, spouse, friends, and relatives—like a snake coming to bite, a bandit arisen in the forest, or a demon coming to devour. Such a person becomes alarming and, in the next existence, is reborn in hell and other miserable states. Even in this very life, an angry person, though adorned and well-dressed, appears ugly—their face, even if splendid like the full moon, becomes repulsive and unpleasant to behold, like a lotus struck by flame or a golden mirror covered in grime. Driven by anger, beings take up weapons and strike themselves, consume poison, hang themselves with ropes, or throw themselves from cliffs. Thus, dying in anger, they are reborn in hell and other woeful realms. Those of a nature to harm are censured in this very life and, after the dissolution of the body, are reborn in hell. Even if they regain human birth, they suffer from many diseases from birth onward. Afflictions like eye disease, ear disease, and others arise together and fall upon them at once. Not freed from sickness, they remain perpetually miserable. Therefore, one should cultivate a mind of loving-kindness, goodwill, and gentleness toward all beings. For such a person is not freed from the dangers of hell and other fears.' Hearing the Teacher’s advice, the prince was humbled by this single instruction. He became tamed, free from venom, filled with loving-kindness and gentleness. Even when others insulted or struck him, he did not turn to look back—he became like a snake with its fangs extracted, a crab with its claws cut off, or a bull with its horns broken.

Tassa taṃ pavattiṃ ñatvā bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, duṭṭhalicchavikumāraṃ sucirampi ovaditvā neva mātāpitaro, na ñātimittādayo dametuṃ sakkhiṃsu, sammāsambuddho pana taṃ ekovādeneva dametvā nibbisevanaṃ katvā mattavaravāraṇaṃ viya samuggahitāneñjakāraṇaṃ akāsi. Yāva subhāsitaṃ cidaṃ – ‘hatthidamakena, bhikkhave, hatthidammo sārito ekaṃyeva disaṃ dhāvati puratthimaṃ vā pacchimaṃ vā uttaraṃ vā dakkhiṇaṃ vā. Assadamakena…pe… godamakena…pe… dakkhiṇaṃ vā. Tathāgatena hi, bhikkhave, arahatā sammāsambuddhena purisadammo sārito aṭṭha disā vidhāvati, rūpī rūpāni passati. Ayamekā disā…pe… so [M 1.0532] vuccati ‘yoggācariyānaṃ anuttaro purisadammasārathī’ti (ma. ni. 3.312). Na hi, āvuso, sammāsambuddhena sadiso purisadammasārathī nāma atthī”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa mayā ekovādeneva damito, pubbepāhaṃ imaṃ ekovādeneva damesi”nti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

Knowing of this event, the monks started a discussion in the Dhamma hall: "Friends, though the wicked Licchavi prince was admonished for a long time, neither his parents, relatives, friends, nor others could tame him. Yet the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One tamed him with just one admonition, making him free from venom, like a noble elephant in rut that has been brought under control. How well it is said: 'Monks, an elephant tamed by an elephant trainer, when spurred on, runs in only one direction—east, west, north, or south. A horse tamed by a horse trainer... a bull tamed by a bull trainer... runs in only one direction. But a person tamed by the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One, when spurred on, runs in eight directions. One with form sees forms. This is one direction... He is called the unsurpassed trainer of persons to be tamed among teachers of the practice.' Indeed, friends, there is no trainer of persons to be tamed equal to the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One."

The Teacher arrived and asked, "Monks, for what discussion are you now gathered?" When they told him what it was, he said, "Monks, it is not only now that I have tamed him with a single admonition; in the past, too, I tamed him with a single admonition," and he recounted a past incident.

Atīte [V 1.0482] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto udiccabrāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilāyaṃ tayo vede sabbasippāni ca uggahetvā kiñci kālaṃ gharāvāsaṃ vasitvā mātāpitūnaṃ accayena isipabbajjaṃ pabbajitvā abhiññā ca samāpattiyo ca nibbattetvā himavante vāsaṃ kappesi. Tattha ciraṃ vasitvā loṇambilasevanatthāya janapadaṃ gantvā bārāṇasiṃ patvā rājuyyāne vasitvā punadivase sunivattho supāruto tāpasākappasampanno bhikkhāya nagaraṃ pavisitvā [P 1.0506] rājaṅgaṇaṃ pāpuṇi. Rājā sīhapañjarena olokento taṃ disvā iriyāpathe pasīditvā “ayaṃ tāpaso santindriyo santamānaso yugamattadaso, padavāre padavāre sahassatthavikaṃ ṭhapento viya sīhavijambhitena āgacchati. Sace santadhammo nāmeko atthi, imassa tenabbhantare bhavitabba”nti cintetvā ekaṃ amaccaṃ olokesi. So “kiṃ karomi, devā”ti āha. Etaṃ “tāpasaṃ ānehī”ti. So “sādhu, devā”ti bodhisattaṃ upasaṅkamitvā vanditvā hatthato bhikkhābhājanaṃ gahetvā “kiṃ, mahāpuññā”ti vutte “bhante, rājā taṃ pakkosatī”ti āha. Bodhisatto “na mayaṃ rājakulūpakā, hemavantikā nāmamhā”ti āha. Amacco gantvā tamatthaṃ rañño ārocesi. Rājā “añño amhākaṃ kulūpako natthi, ānehi na”nti āha. Amacco gantvā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā yācitvā rājanivesanaṃ pavesesi.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was ruling in Benares, the Bodhisatta was reborn in a northern Brahmin family. When he came of age, he mastered the three Vedas and all the crafts at Takkasilā. After living the household life for some time, upon the death of his parents, he went forth into the ascetic life. Having developed the supernormal powers and attainments, he took up residence in the Himalayas. Having lived there for a long time, he journeyed to the countryside to obtain salt and sour fare. Arriving in Benares, he stayed in the royal park. The next day, well-dressed and well-robed, possessing the perfect appearance of an ascetic, he entered the city for alms and reached the royal courtyard. The king, looking out from his lion-window, saw him and was pleased with his deportment. He thought, 'This ascetic has calm senses, a peaceful mind, and looks only a yoke's length ahead; with every footstep, he seems to place a purse of a thousand coins, and he comes with the majestic stride of a lion. If there is indeed such a thing as the peaceful Dhamma, it must be within him.' Reflecting thus, he glanced at a minister. The minister asked, 'What shall I do, Your Majesty?' The king replied, 'Bring that ascetic here.' The minister said, 'Very well, sire,' approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage, and took the alms bowl from his hands. When the Bodhisatta asked, 'What is it, O greatly meritorious one?' he replied, 'Venerable sir, the king summons you.' The Bodhisatta said, 'We are not teachers to the royal family; we are dwellers of the Himalayas.' The minister went and reported this to the king. The king said, 'We have no other teacher. Bring him.' The minister went back, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, implored him, and led him into the royal residence.

Rājā bodhisattaṃ vanditvā samussitasetacchatte kañcanapallaṅke nisīdāpetvā attano paṭiyattaṃ nānaggarasabhojanaṃ bhojetvā “kahaṃ, bhante, vasathā”ti pucchi. “Hemavantikā mayaṃ, mahārājā”ti. “Idāni kahaṃ gacchathā”ti? “Vassārattānurūpaṃ senāsanaṃ upadhārema, mahārājā”ti. “Tena hi, bhante, amhākaññeva uyyāne vasathā”ti paṭiññaṃ gahetvā sayampi [M 1.0533] bhuñjitvā bodhisattaṃ ādāya uyyānaṃ gantvā paṇṇasālaṃ māpetvā rattiṭṭhānadivāṭṭhānāpi kāretvā pabbajitaparikkhāre datvā uyyānapālaṃ paṭicchāpetvā nagaraṃ pāvisi. Tato paṭṭhāya bodhisatto uyyāne vasati. Rājāpissa divase divase dvattikkhattuṃ upaṭṭhānaṃ gacchati.

The king paid homage to the Bodhisatta, seated him on a golden couch under a raised white royal umbrella, and served him various delicious foods prepared for himself. Then he asked, "Venerable sir, where do you reside?" "We are dwellers of the Himalayas, great king," he replied. "And where are you going now?" "We are seeking a suitable lodging for the rainy season, great king." "Then, venerable sir, please stay in our very own park," the king, having obtained his consent, said. After eating himself, he took the Bodhisatta to the park, had a leaf-hut built, and also had places arranged for night and day residence. He provided the requisites for a renunciant, entrusted him to the park keeper, and returned to the city. From then on, the Bodhisatta lived in the park. The king too went to attend upon him two or three times a day.

Tassa pana rañño duṭṭhakumāro nāma putto ahosi caṇḍo pharuso, neva naṃ rājā dametuṃ asakkhi, na sesañātakā. Amaccāpi brāhmaṇagahapatikāpi ekato hutvā “sāmi, mā evaṃ kari, evaṃ kātuṃ na labbhā”ti kujjhitvā kathentāpi kathaṃ gāhāpetuṃ nāsakkhiṃsu. Rājā cintesi “ṭhapetvā mama ayyaṃ himavantatāpasaṃ añño imaṃ kumāraṃ dametuṃ samattho nāma natthi, soyeva naṃ damessatī”ti. So kumāraṃ ādāya bodhisattassa santikaṃ gantvā “bhante, ayaṃ kumāro caṇḍo pharuso[P 1.0507], mayaṃ imaṃ dametuṃ na sakkoma, tumhe naṃ ekena upāyena sikkhāpethā”ti [V 1.0483] kumāraṃ bodhisattassa niyyādetvā pakkāmi. Bodhisatto kumāraṃ gahetvā uyyāne vicaranto ekato ekena, ekato ekenāti dvīhiyeva pattehi ekaṃ nimbapotakaṃ disvā kumāraṃ āha – “kumāra, etassa tāva rukkhapotakassa paṇṇaṃ khāditvā rasaṃ jānāhī”ti? So tassa ekaṃ pattaṃ khāditvā rasaṃ ñatvā “dhī”ti saha kheḷena bhūmiyaṃ nuṭṭhābhi. “Kiṃ etaṃ, kumārā”ti vutte “bhante, idānevesa rukkho halāhalavisūpamo, vaḍḍhanto pana bahū manusse māressatī”ti taṃ nimbapotakaṃ uppāṭetvā hatthehi parimadditvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

Now, that king had a son named Duṭṭhakumāra, who was fierce and harsh. Neither the king nor his other relatives were able to tame him. Even when ministers, brahmins, and householders, having come together, spoke angrily, saying, "Lord, do not act thus; it is not proper to act thus," they were unable to make him accept their words. The king thought, "Apart from my noble Himalayan ascetic, there is no one else capable of taming this prince. He alone will tame him." So, taking the prince, he went to the Bodhisatta and said, "Venerable sir, this prince is fierce and harsh. We are unable to tame him. Please instruct him by some means." Having entrusted the prince to the Bodhisatta, he departed. The Bodhisatta, taking the prince and wandering in the park, saw a small neem sapling with just two leaves, one on one side and one on the other, and said to the prince, "Prince, first chew a leaf of this sapling and know its taste." He chewed one of its leaves, and knowing its taste, spat it out on the ground with saliva, saying, "Fie!" When asked, "What is this, prince?" he said, "Venerable sir, even now this tree is like a deadly poison. When it grows, it will kill many people." Then, uprooting that neem sapling and crushing it with his hands, he spoke this verse:

149.

149.

“Ekapaṇṇo ayaṃ rukkho, na bhūmyā caturaṅgulo;

Phalena visakappena, mahāyaṃ kiṃ bhavissatī”ti.

“This tree has but a single leaf, not yet four finger-breadths from the ground; with fruit that is like poison, what will it become when it is large?”

Tattha ekapaṇṇoti ubhosu passesu ekekapaṇṇo. Na bhūmyā caturaṅguloti bhūmito caturaṅgulamattampi na vaḍḍhito. Phalenāti phalarasena. Visakappenāti halāhalavisasadisena. Evaṃ khuddakopi samāno evarūpena tittakena paṇṇena samannāgatoti attho. Mahāyaṃ kiṃ bhavissatīti yadā panāyaṃ vuddhippatto mahā bhavissati, tadā kiṃ nāma bhavissati, addhā manussamārako bhavissatīti etaṃ uppāṭetvā madditvā chaḍḍesinti āha.

Here, 'of a single leaf' means one leaf on each of its two sides. ‘Not four finger-breadths from the ground’ means it has not grown even four finger-breadths from the ground. ‘With fruit’ means with the taste of its fruit. ‘Like poison’ means like the halāhala poison. The meaning is that even though it is small, it is endowed with such a bitter leaf. ‘What will it become when large?’ means when it grows and becomes large, what will it be then? Surely, it will become a killer of humans. Thinking this, he uprooted, crushed, and discarded it, and spoke the verse.

Atha [M 1.0534] naṃ bodhisatto etadavoca “kumāra, tvaṃ imaṃ nimbapotakaṃ ‘idāneva evaṃtittako, mahallakakāle kiṃ bhavissati, kuto imaṃ nissāya vuḍḍhī’ti uppāṭetvā madditvā chaḍḍesi? Yathā tvaṃ etasmiṃ paṭipajji, evameva tava raṭṭhavāsinopi ‘ayaṃ kumāro daharakāleyeva evaṃ caṇḍo pharuso, mahallakakāle rajjaṃ patvā kiṃ nāma karissati, kuto amhākaṃ etaṃ nissāya vuḍḍhī’ti tava kulasantakaṃ rajjaṃ adatvā nimbapotakaṃ viya taṃ uppāṭetvā raṭṭhā pabbājanīyakammaṃ karissanti, tasmā nimbarukkhapaṭibhāgataṃ hitvā ito paṭṭhāya khantimettānuddayasampanno hohī”ti. So tato paṭṭhāya nihatamāno nibbisevano khantimettānuddayasampanno hutvā bodhisattassa ovāde ṭhatvā pitu [P 1.0508] accayena rajjaṃ patvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ agamāsi.

Then the Bodhisatta said to him, "Prince, you uprooted, crushed, and discarded this young neem plant, thinking, 'Even now it is so bitter; what will it become in old age? From where can there be prosperity relying on this?' Just as you acted towards this, so too will the people of your kingdom think, 'This prince is so fierce and harsh even in his youth; when he is old and has attained the kingship, what will he do? From where can there be prosperity for us relying on him?' And they will not give you the kingship belonging to your family, but will uproot you like the neem sapling and perform the act of banishing you from the kingdom. Therefore, abandoning your nature which is like the neem tree, from this day forward be endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion." From that time onward, with his pride subdued and free from arrogance, he became endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion. Abiding by the Bodhisatta's advice, upon his father's passing, he attained the kingship, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and then went according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā “na, bhikkhave, idānevesa duṭṭhalicchavikumāro mayā damito, pubbepāhaṃ etaṃ damesiṃyevā”ti vatvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā duṭṭhakumāro ayaṃ licchavikumāro ahosi, rājā ānando, ovādadāyakatāpaso pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Master, having brought forth this Dhamma teaching, said: "Monks, it is not only now that this wicked Licchavi prince has been tamed by me; in the past, too, I tamed him." Having said this, he connected the Jātaka: "At that time, the wicked prince was this Licchavi prince, Ānanda was the king, and the ascetic who gave advice was I myself."

Ekapaṇṇajātakavaṇṇanā navamā.

The ninth, the commentary on the Ekapaṇṇa Jātaka.

[150] 10. Sañjīvajātakavaṇṇanā

[150] 10. The Commentary on the Sañjīva Jātaka

Asantaṃ [V 1.0484] yo paggaṇhātīti idaṃ satthā veḷuvane viharanto ajātasattussa rañño asantapaggahaṃ ārabbha kathesi. So hi buddhānaṃ paṭikaṇṭakabhūte dussīle pāpadhamme devadatte pasīditvā taṃ asantaṃ asappurisaṃ paggayha “tassa sakkāraṃ karissāmī”ti bahuṃ dhanaṃ pariccajitvā gayāsīse vihāraṃ kāretvā tasseva vacanaṃ gahetvā pitaraṃ dhammarājānaṃ sotāpannaṃ ariyasāvakaṃ ghātetvā attano sotāpattimaggassa upanissayaṃ bhinditvā mahāvināsaṃ patto. So hi “devadatto pathaviyaṃ paviṭṭho”ti sutvā “kacci nu kho mampi pathavī gileyyā”ti bhītatasito rajjasukhaṃ na labhati, sayane assādasukhaṃ na vindati, tibbakāraṇābhitunno hatthipoto viya kampamāno vicarati. So pathaviṃ phalamānaṃ [M 1.0535] viya, avīcijālaṃ nikkhamantiṃ viya, pathaviyā attānaṃ giliyamānaṃ viya, ādittāya lohapathaviyā uttānakaṃ nipajjāpetvā ayasūlehi koṭiyamānaṃ viya ca samanupassi. Tenassa pahaṭakukkuṭasseva muhuttampi kampamānassa avatthānaṃ nāma nāhosi. So sammāsambuddhaṃ passitukāmo khamāpetukāmo pañhaṃ pucchitukāmo ahosi, attano pana aparādhamahantatāya upasaṅkamituṃ na sakkoti.

The Teacher, while dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, related this concerning King Ajātasattu's support of the unworthy. For he, pleased with Devadatta—who was a thorn in the side of the Buddhas, immoral, and of evil character—supported that unworthy and unprincipled man. Thinking, "I will honor him," he gave up much wealth, had a monastery built for him at Gayāsīsa, and, following his words, had his father, the righteous king, a stream-enterer and noble disciple, killed. Thus, he destroyed the supporting condition for his own attainment of the stream-entry path and met with great ruin. For when he heard, "Devadatta has entered the earth," he became terrified and anxious, thinking, "Will the earth swallow me too?" He could not enjoy the pleasures of kingship, nor find comfort in his bed. Trembling like a young elephant struck by a sharp goad, he wandered about. He perceived the earth splitting open, the flames of Avīci emerging, the earth swallowing him, or himself lying face-up on a blazing iron ground, being pierced by iron spikes. Therefore, like a struck cock, he was constantly trembling and could not be still even for a moment. He wished to see the Fully Enlightened One, to ask for forgiveness, and to ask a question, but due to the enormity of his wrongdoing, he could not approach him.

Athassa rājagahanagare kattikarattivāre sampatte devanagaraṃ viya nagare alaṅkate mahātale amaccagaṇaparivutassa kañcanāsane nisinnassa jīvakaṃ komārabhaccaṃ avidūre nisinnaṃ disvā etadahosi “jīvakaṃ gahetvā sammāsambuddhassa santikaṃ gamissāmi, na kho pana sakkā mayā ujukameva vattuṃ ‘ahaṃ, samma jīvaka, sayaṃ gantuṃ na sakkomi, ehi maṃ satthu santikaṃ nehī’ti, pariyāyena pana rattisampadaṃ vaṇṇetvā ‘kaṃ nu khvajja mayaṃ [P 1.0509] samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā payirupāseyyāma, yaṃ no payirupāsataṃ cittaṃ pasīdeyyā’ti vakkhāmi, taṃ sutvā amaccā attano attano satthārānaṃ vaṇṇaṃ kathessanti, jīvakopi sammāsambuddhassa vaṇṇaṃ kathessati. Atha naṃ gahetvā satthu santikaṃ gamissāmī”ti. So pañcahi padehi rattiṃ vaṇṇesi “lakkhaññā vata bho dosinā ratti, abhirūpā vata bho dosinā ratti, dassanīyā vata bho dosinā ratti, pāsādikā vata bho dosinā ratti, ramaṇīyā vata bho dosinā ratti, kaṃ nu khvajja mayaṃ samaṇaṃ vā brāhmaṇaṃ vā payirupāseyyāma, yaṃ no payirupāsataṃ cittaṃ pasīdeyyā”ti (dī. ni. 1.150).

Then, in the city of Rājagaha, when the night of the Kattika festival arrived, the city was adorned like a celestial city. As the king sat on a golden throne in the great hall, surrounded by his retinue of ministers, he saw Jīvaka Komārabhacca sitting nearby, and this thought occurred to him: "I will take Jīvaka and go to the presence of the Fully Enlightened One. However, I cannot say directly, ‘Dear Jīvaka, I cannot go by myself—come, lead me to the Teacher’s presence.’ Instead, I will praise the splendor of the night in a roundabout way and say, ‘Which ascetic or brahmin should we visit today, that our minds might find peace in visiting him?’ Hearing this, the ministers will each praise their own teachers, and Jīvaka too will praise the Fully Enlightened One. Then, taking him, I will go to the Teacher’s presence." So he praised the night with five phrases: "Truly, sirs, the night is auspicious, the night is beautiful, the night is lovely to see, the night is pleasing, the night is delightful. Which ascetic or brahmin should we visit today, that our minds might find peace in visiting him?"

Atheko amacco pūraṇakassapassa vaṇṇaṃ kathesi, eko makkhaligosālassa, eko ajitakesakambalassa, eko pakudhakaccāyanassa, eko sañcayassa belaṭṭhaputtassa, eko nāṭaputtanigaṇṭhassāti[V 1.0485]. Rājā tesaṃ kathaṃ sutvā tuṇhī ahosi. So hi jīvakasseva mahāamaccassa kathaṃ paccāsīsati. Jīvakopi “raññā maṃ ārabbha kathiteyeva jānissāmī”ti avidūre tuṇhī nisīdi. Atha naṃ rājā āha “tvaṃ pana, samma jīvaka, kiṃ tuṇhī”ti? Tasmiṃ khaṇe jīvako uṭṭhāyāsanā yena bhagavā tenañjaliṃ paṇāmetvā “eso, deva, bhagavā [M 1.0536] arahaṃ sammāsambuddho amhākaṃ ambavane viharati saddhiṃ aḍḍhateḷasehi bhikkhusatehi. Taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ evaṃ kalyāṇo kittisaddo abbhuggato”ti nava arahādiguṇe vatvā jātito paṭṭhāya pubbanimittādibhedaṃ bhagavato ānubhāvaṃ pakāsetvā “taṃ bhagavantaṃ devo payirupāsatu, dhammaṃ suṇātu, pañhaṃ pucchatū”ti āha.

Then one minister spoke in praise of Pūraṇa Kassapa, one of Makkhali Gosāla, one of Ajita Kesakambala, one of Pakudha Kaccāyana, one of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta, and one of Nāṭaputta the Nigaṇṭha. The king, having heard their words, remained silent, for he was waiting for the words of the great minister Jīvaka. Jīvaka, too, sat silently nearby, thinking, "I will know only when the king speaks concerning me." Then the king said to him, "But you, dear Jīvaka, why are you silent?" At that moment, Jīvaka rose from his seat, extended his joined hands in reverence in the direction of the Blessed One, and said, "Your Majesty, the Blessed One, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is dwelling in our mango grove with twelve hundred and fifty bhikkhus. And of that Blessed One, this glorious repute has spread far and wide." He then proclaimed the nine qualities beginning with 'Arahant,' and revealed the majesty of the Blessed One by describing the various portents and other signs that occurred from his birth onwards. Finally, he said, "May Your Majesty visit the Blessed One, listen to the Dhamma, and ask him a question."

Rājā sampuṇṇamanoratho hutvā “tena hi, samma jīvaka, hatthiyānāni kappāpehī”ti yānāni kappāpetvā mahantena rājānubhāvena jīvakambavanaṃ gantvā tattha maṇḍalamāḷe bhikkhusaṅghaparivutaṃ tathāgataṃ disvā santavīcimajjhe mahānāvaṃ viya niccalaṃ bhikkhusaṅghaṃ ito cito ca anuviloketvā “evarūpā nāma me parisā na diṭṭhapubbā”ti iriyāpatheyeva pasīditvā saṅghassa añjaliṃ paggaṇhitvā thutiṃ katvā bhagavantaṃ vanditvā ekamantaṃ nisinno sāmaññaphalapañhaṃ pucchi. Athassa bhagavā dvīhi bhāṇavārehi paṭimaṇḍitaṃ sāmaññaphalasuttaṃ (dī. ni. 1.150 ādayo) kathesi. So suttapariyosāne attamano bhagavantaṃ khamāpetvā uṭṭhāyāsanā padakkhiṇaṃ katvā pakkāmi. Satthā acirapakkantassa rañño bhikkhū āmantetvā “khatāyaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā, upahatāyaṃ, bhikkhave, rājā. Sacāyaṃ[P 1.0510], bhikkhave, rājā issariyassa kāraṇā pitaraṃ dhammikaṃ dhammarājānaṃ jīvitā na voropessatha, imasmiṃyeva āsane virajaṃ vītamalaṃ dhammacakkhuṃ uppajjissatha. Devadattaṃ nissāya asantapaggahaṃ katvā sotāpattiphalā parihīno”ti āha.

The king, his heart's desire fulfilled, said, "Well then, dear Jīvaka, have the elephant vehicles prepared." Having had the vehicles prepared, he went with great royal splendor to Jīvaka's mango grove. There, in a circular hall, he saw the Tathāgata surrounded by the community of bhikkhus. Looking from one side to the other at the community of bhikkhus, motionless like a great ship in the midst of calm waves, he thought, "Never before have I seen such an assembly." Delighted by their very deportment, he raised his joined hands in reverence to the Sangha, offered praise, paid homage to the Blessed One, and, having sat down to one side, asked the question on the fruits of the contemplative life. Thereupon, the Blessed One expounded to him the Sāmaññaphala Sutta, adorned with two recitation sections. At the conclusion of the discourse, the king, delighted, asked forgiveness of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, circumambulated him to the right, and departed. Soon after the king had left, the Teacher addressed the bhikkhus: "Bhikkhus, this king is ruined; bhikkhus, this king is undone. If, bhikkhus, this king had not, for the sake of sovereignty, deprived his righteous father, the Dhamma King, of life, the dust-free, stainless eye of Dhamma would have arisen in him right on this very seat. By relying on Devadatta and supporting the unworthy, he has fallen away from the fruit of stream-entry."

Punadivase bhikkhū dhammasabhāyaṃ kathaṃ samuṭṭhāpesuṃ “āvuso, ajātasattu kira asantapaggahaṃ katvā dussīlaṃ pāpadhammaṃ devadattaṃ nissāya pitughātakakammassa katattā sotāpattiphalā parihīno, devadattena nāsito rājā”ti. Satthā āgantvā “kāya nuttha, bhikkhave, etarahi kathāya sannisinnā”ti pucchitvā “imāya nāmā”ti vutte “na, bhikkhave, ajātasattu idāneva asantapaggahaṃ katvā mahāvināsaṃ patto, pubbepesa asantapaggaheneva attānaṃ nāsesī”ti vatvā atītaṃ āhari.

On the following day, the monks raised a discussion in the Hall of Dhamma: 'Venerable sirs, it is said that King Ajātasattu, having supported an unworthy person and relying on the immoral and wicked Devadatta, is deprived of the fruit of stream-entry on account of having committed patricide. The king has been ruined by Devadatta.' The Teacher, having approached, asked, 'Monks, for what discussion are you now assembled?' When it was said, 'For this one,' he replied, 'Monks, it is not only now that Ajātasattu has met with great ruin by supporting an unworthy person; in the past, too, he destroyed himself by supporting an unworthy person.' So saying, he related a story of the past.

Atīte [V 1.0486] bārāṇasiyaṃ brahmadatte rajjaṃ kārente bodhisatto mahāvibhave brāhmaṇakule nibbattitvā vayappatto takkasilaṃ gantvā sabbasippāni [M 1.0537] uggaṇhitvā bārāṇasiyaṃ disāpāmokkho ācariyo hutvā pañca māṇavakasatāni sippaṃ vācesi. Tesu māṇavesu eko sañjīvo nāma māṇavo atthi, bodhisatto tassa matakuṭṭhāpanakamantaṃ adāsi.
