So uṭṭhāpanakamantameva gahetvā paṭibāhanamantaṃ pana aggahetvāva ekadivasaṃ māṇavehi saddhiṃ dāruatthāya araññaṃ gantvā ekaṃ matabyagghaṃ disvā māṇave āha “bho, imaṃ matabyagghaṃ uṭṭhāpessāmī”ti. Māṇavā “na sakkhissasī”ti āhaṃsu. “Passantānaññeva vo taṃ uṭṭhāpessāmī”ti. “Sace, māṇava, sakkosi, uṭṭhāpehī”ti. Evañca pana vatvā te māṇavā rukkhaṃ abhiruhiṃsu. Sañjīvo mantaṃ parivattetvā matabyagghaṃ sakkharāhi pahari, byaggho uṭṭhāya vegenāgantvā sañjīvaṃ galanāḷiyaṃ ḍaṃsitvā jīvitakkhayaṃ pāpetvā tattheva pati, sañjīvopi tattheva pati. Ubhopi ekaṭṭhāneyeva matā nipajjiṃsu.

In the past, when Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was born into a brahmin family of great wealth. Having come of age, he went to Takkasilā, learned all the arts, and became a world-renowned teacher in Bārāṇasī, instructing five hundred young men. Among those young men was one named Sañjīva. The Bodhisatta gave him the spell for reviving the dead. He learned only the spell for reviving, but not the counter-spell. One day, having gone to the forest with the young men for firewood, he saw a dead tiger and said to them, 'Sirs, I shall revive this dead tiger.' The young men said, 'You will not be able to.' 'I shall revive it while you are all watching,' he replied. 'If you are able, young man, then revive it,' they said. Having spoken thus, those young men climbed a tree. Sañjīva recited the spell and struck the dead tiger with gravel. The tiger, having risen, came swiftly, bit Sañjīva on the throat, and caused him to meet his end. It then fell right there. Sañjīva also fell right there. Both lay dead in the same place.

Māṇavā dārūni ādāya āgantvā taṃ pavattiṃ ācariyassa ārocesuṃ. Ācariyo māṇave āmantetvā “tātā, asantapaggahakārā nāma ayuttaṭṭhāne sakkārasammānaṃ karontā evarūpaṃ dukkhaṃ paṭilabhantiyevā”ti vatvā imaṃ gāthamāha –

The young men, having taken the firewood, returned and reported the incident to their teacher. The teacher addressed the young men, saying, 'My dears, those who support the unworthy, offering honor and respect in an unfitting place, indeed obtain suffering of this kind.' So saying, he spoke this verse:

150.

150.

“Asantaṃ [P 1.0511] yo paggaṇhāti, asantaṃ cūpasevati;

Tameva ghāsaṃ kurute, byaggho sañjīviko yathā”ti.

Whoever supports an unworthy person,

And associates with an unworthy person,

On that very one he feeds,

Just as the tiger did on Sañjīva.

Tattha asantanti tīhi duccaritehi samannāgataṃ dussīlaṃ pāpadhammaṃ. Yo paggaṇhātīti khattiyādīsu yo koci evarūpaṃ dussīlaṃ pabbajitaṃ vā cīvarādisampadānena, gahaṭṭhaṃ vā uparajjasenāpatiṭṭhānādisampadānena paggaṇhāti, sakkārasammānaṃ karotīti attho. Asantaṃ cūpasevatīti yo ca evarūpaṃ asantaṃ dussīlaṃ upasevati bhajati payirupāsati. Tameva ghāsaṃ kuruteti tameva asantapaggaṇhakaṃ so dussīlo pāpapuggalo ghasati saṃkhādati vināsaṃ pāpeti. Kathaṃ? Byaggho sañjīviko yathāti, yathā sañjīvena māṇavena mantaṃ parivattetvā matabyaggho sañjīviko jīvitasampadānena sampaggahito attano jīvitadāyakaṃ sañjīvameva jīvitā voropetvā tattheva pātesi, evaṃ aññopi yo asantapaggahaṃ karoti, so dussīlo taṃ attano sampaggāhakameva vināseti. Evaṃ asantasampaggāhakā vināsaṃ pāpuṇantīti.

Herein, unworthy means an immoral person of wicked nature, endowed with the three kinds of misconduct. Whoever supports means any person, such as a noble, who supports such an immoral one—be he a renunciate, by the gift of robes and so forth, or a householder, by the gift of a position such as viceroy or commander of the army; the meaning is that he shows him honor and respect. And associates with an unworthy person means one who frequents, serves, and attends upon such an unworthy, immoral person. On that very one he feeds means that immoral, wicked person consumes, devours, and brings to ruin that very supporter of the unworthy. How? Just as the tiger did on Sañjīva means: just as the dead tiger, revived and supported by the gift of life through the spell recited by the young man Sañjīva, having deprived its own life-giver, Sañjīva himself, of life, felled him on that very spot; so too, whoever else supports an unworthy person, that immoral person destroys his own supporter. Thus do supporters of the unworthy meet with ruin.

Bodhisatto [V 1.0487][M 1.0538] imāya gāthāya māṇavānaṃ dhammaṃ desetvā dānādīni puññāni katvā yathākammaṃ gato.

The Bodhisatta, having taught the Dhamma to the young men with this verse, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and went according to his kamma.

Satthā imaṃ dhammadesanaṃ āharitvā jātakaṃ samodhānesi – “tadā matabyagghuṭṭhāpanako māṇavo ajātasattu ahosi, disāpāmokkho ācariyo pana ahameva ahosi”nti.

The Teacher, having delivered this Dhamma discourse, identified the birth: 'At that time, the young man who revived the dead tiger was Ajātasattu, but the world-renowned teacher was I myself.'

Sañjīvajātakavaṇṇanā dasamā.

The tenth, the Commentary on the Sañjīva Jātaka.

Kakaṇṭakavaggo pannarasamo.

The Kakaṇṭaka Chapter, the fifteenth.

Tassuddānaṃ –

The summary thereof:

Godhasiṅgālavirocaṃ, naṅguṭṭharādhakākañca;

Puppharattañca siṅgālaṃ, ekapaṇṇañca sañjīvaṃ.

Godha, Siṅgāla, Virocana, Naṅguṭṭha, and Rādhakāka; Puppharatta, Siṅgāla, Ekapaṇṇa, and Sañjīva.

Atha vagguddānaṃ –

Now, the summary of the chapters:

Apaṇṇako sīlavaggo, kuruṅgo ca kulāvako;

Atthakāmo ca āsīso, itthīvaruṇapāyimhā.

Apaṇṇaka, Sīlavagga, Kuruṅga, and Kulāvaka; Atthakāma, Āsīsa, Itthī, Varuṇa, and Apāyimha.

Litto parosataṃ haṃci, kusanāḷā sampadāno;

Kakaṇṭako pannarasa, satapaṇṇāsa jātakāti.

Litta, Parosata, Haṃsi, Kusanāḷi, and Asampadāna; Kakaṇṭaka, the fifteenth, making one hundred and fifty Jātakas.

Ekakanipātavaṇṇanā niṭṭhitā.

Here ends the Commentary on the Book of Ones.

(Paṭhamo bhāgo niṭṭhito).

(The First Part is concluded.)
